challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners choose where and when to land near the lunar south pole. It shows, hour by hour, when the Sun is up for power and when Earth is in view for a direct radio link, over the real terrain horizon of each site.

- Sun and Earth positions come from NASA's SPICE ephemerides.
- The terrain comes from LRO's LOLA elevation model.
- Comparison: you can compare up to three sites.
- Any point: you can click any point on a 3D map and get results in under a second.

Our results match JPL Horizons to within 0.005° and NASA's PGDA illumination maps to within 1.5 percentage points on average.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, and Earth wobbles above and below it. A hill 10 km away can decide whether a lander has power or can talk to Earth, so flat-horizon estimates are not enough. Our tool builds the real 360° horizon of each site from NASA's LOLA terrain (including the Moon's curvature), tracks the Sun and Earth every hour from November 2026 to December 2028, and reports what a planner needs: how much of the Sun's disk is visible, whether Earth is in view, when the next sunset or Earthset comes, and how long the longest night lasts.

You can pick one of 10 candidate sites, search a crater name, type coordinates or click the 3D map. You can compare up to three sites for the next 30 days from any date. A month-by-month strip shows the share of hours with Sun, with Earth and with both for every month, so if a launch slips you see which month still works: at Malapert Massif, Sun and Earth together go from 37% of hours in April 2028 to 80% in October 2028. For students and the public, a four-step tour, "Why the south pole is hard", explains the physics with "Show me" buttons that set the app to the case that proves each point.

WHAT WE LEARNED

More sunlight does not always mean a better site. For a landing on 14 November 2026, Shackleton Rim is sunlit 87% of the time overall but has only 13 days with both Sun and Earth in the next 30 days. Malapert Massif has 22 days with both, because Earth stays in view much longer. The Shackleton crater floor, only about 10 km from the rim, gets 0% Sun and 0% Earth in two years: a permanently shadowed region where water ice may exist.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Terrain: the LRO LOLA polar elevation model (120 m per pixel) is used to cast 720 rays from each site, up to 150 km. The highest terrain angle in each direction is the horizon.

2. Sun and Earth: NASA/NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440) give their direction from the site every hour.

3. Visibility: we compare the Sun and Earth with the horizon (fraction of the Sun's disk above it; whether Earth's center is above it).

4. Browser: a static web app (Svelte, D3, three.js). For custom points it repeats the same calculation in the browser on a 240 m version of the terrain.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.005° (automated tests). The sunlit share matches NASA's PGDA average illumination maps within 1.5 percentage points on average across the 10 sites. The horizon code is tested on two cases with exact answers (a smooth sphere and a wall of known height). Limits are stated in the app: 120 m terrain resolution (240 m for custom points), no atmosphere or refraction, and Earth counts as visible when its center is above the horizon.

WHY IT MATTERS

Artemis missions plan to land near the south pole. A planner can use this tool to choose a landing date with the most days of both power and a direct link, see the exact hour when the Sun or Earth will disappear, and check any spot in seconds without installing software.

CODE

https://github.com/marcelin1555/lunar-landing-site-navigator

USE OF AI

We used an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) for research, discussing the architecture, generating and reviewing code, and helping translate this written submission from Portuguese to English. The author made all design decisions, checked the data and results against NASA references (JPL Horizons and PGDA maps), and reviewed the final work. No images, video or audio in this project were generated by AI: the demo is a screen recording of the real app.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: SEDNA - Explore the unseen
projectDetails.summary:
SEDNA is a public web tool: type a sky position or a name and watch NASA SPHEREx images of that patch change over time. Every visit is aligned on one north-up grid with a single brightness stretch. Blinking, differencing and summing them shows what moved or changed, across all six detectors from 0.75 to 5 µm. Gaia DR3 stars and IMCCE SkyBoT tell users whether a point is already catalogued.

Its signature is a distance focus. A distant world jumps out of the frame between visits, so a classic blink only shows a point that vanished. SEDNA shifts and stacks single exposures for each trial distance; at the right one, the body snaps into a sharp point. On real data it measured Haumea at 48.9 au (JPL Horizons: 49.4) and Pluto at 34.2 au (35.5), and it states its confidence honestly.

All five challenge targets were validated:
- Epsilon Indi B moved 6.25″ against 6.24″ predicted by Gaia DR3.
- WISE 0855 is tracked at 4.4–5 µm.
- RW Aurigae faded by up to 0.75 mag in a year.
- R Draconis's pulsation was recovered from its unsaturated wings.

SEDNA turns SPHEREx into something students and citizen scientists can explore hands-on.

projectDetails.name: Project Kbool4_on
projectDetails.summary:
The Kbool4_on Project 
Focuses on developing a Python-based platform for analyzing flame behavior in microgravity environments. The system combines image processing, computer vision, data analysis, and scientific visualization techniques to monitor and characterize combustion phenomena under reduced-gravity conditions. Using tools such as OpenCV, NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib, the platform automatically detects flame contours and extracts key parameters including diameter, area, brightness, and shape. The collected data are processed into graphs and statistical reports, providing a more accurate and efficient alternative to manual analysis methods. By improving the understanding of combustion dynamics in microgravity, the project contributes to spacecraft fire safety, future space exploration missions, and the advancement of combustion technologies. Its modular architecture also enables future integration of machine learning and predictive modeling techniques, creating a foundation for advanced research on fire behavior and safety in space environments.

Reference

NASA. NASA Studies Fire in Microgravity. NASA Scientific Visualization Studio. Available at: https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/31394. Accessed: November 14, 2026.

projectDetails.name: Project Superstars
projectDetails.summary:
Our team, Superstars, built Left Behind — Every machine has a story, a bilingual (English/Portuguese) interactive website about the machines humanity left on the Moon and Mars. It presents 21 machines with full stories across two worlds, from Apollo 11’s Eagle in 1969 to Perseverance and Ingenuity today. Visitors can spin 3D globes of the Moon and Mars to find each landing site, rover and instrument where it really is. They can also follow a timeline of milestones, hear audio narration of the stories, read “Did you know?” facts and take a ten-question quiz. Each story states how the machine’s mission ended, such as left by design, communication lost, or still operational. Every fact is traced to a source, and images are labeled as illustrations or computer-generated.

The project answers the challenge by treating discarded equipment as evidence of missions, engineering and discoveries, not as junk. It matters because it shows exploration as a chain: each machine, working or silent, made the next one possible.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Left Behind turns equipment that is usually seen as abandoned into stories people want to read. Each of the 21 machines is told in seven chapters, from meeting the explorer to its legacy. A “Deep science” switch adds technical depth for advanced readers. The Atlas has 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, with filters for equipment type, mission, period and status. The site also has a timeline, a gallery, “Did you know?” facts and a ten-question quiz. In Explorer Mission, a game, players walk to real sites, search for clues and investigate hardware to unlock science briefings. Their progress saves on their device.

Benefits and impact. We want students and curious visitors to see each object as a mission, an engineering achievement and a scientific discovery. The site is built to be trustworthy and accessible. Every fact links to a source, such as NASA mission archives. Every image is labeled as an illustration, a computer-generated view or a real photograph. Every status separates a completed mission from a failure. Narrated stories, keyboard controls, a skip-to-content link and two languages help more people take part, including Portuguese speakers. We hope visitors leave understanding that exploration builds on every machine before it.

Tools. The site is a single-page web app made with HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks. It uses canvas graphics for the globes and the game, separate data files for Moon and Mars machines, a translation script for English and Portuguese, and an audio-accessibility module. It is hosted on Netlify. We researched the stories using NASA’s public mission archives.

Creativity. Visitors can read, listen, explore or play, so one project suits different learning styles. We gave each machine its own ending, because “abandoned” is not one story.

What we considered. Our main concerns were scientific accuracy, honesty about what is real and what is generated, accessibility, and a language that fits our own community. Our team is six students aged 15–16 from Escola Integrada Educativa.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project EarthSound
projectDetails.summary: EarthSound is an accessible, bilingual web app inspired by NASA’s The Earth Information Jukebox challenge. It turns environmental observations into sound, allowing users to explore data visually and listen to patterns through interactive sonification. The MVP includes a 2021 global temperature-anomaly experience, an Antarctic ozone timeline spanning 1983–2018, and a library of nine NASA audiovisual resources. Using the Web Audio API, verified numerical data are mapped to sound features such as pitch and rhythm. When a source provides only visual categories, the sound is clearly labeled as a qualitative interpretation—not a measurement. The app supports Portuguese and English, keyboard navigation, spoken guidance, and text alternatives for browsers without voice recognition. EarthSound makes open Earth science more approachable, supports multimodal learning, and aims to broaden participation in understanding environmental change.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description

EarthSound turns environmental data into accessible audiovisual experiences. Inspired by the NASA Space Apps Challenge The Earth Information Jukebox, it lets people explore NASA visualizations and hear interpretations of the data. The MVP includes an exploration of 2021 global temperature anomalies, Antarctic ozone maps from 1983 to 2018, and a library of nine NASA audiovisual resources.

Where reliable numerical data are available, values are mapped to sound characteristics such as pitch and rhythm while the related visualization remains on screen. When a source provides only visual categories or states, the sound is identified as qualitative, not as a measurement. This helps prevent invented values or misinterpretations—for example, treating temperature anomalies as absolute temperatures. The experience also explains key references and limits: GISTEMP anomalies are relative to the 1951–1980 mean, and the ozone materials identify the 220 DU threshold.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Audio provides another way to perceive environmental patterns. It can make data exploration more accessible to people who are blind or have low vision, and support educators and audiences without a technical background. The project aims to bring people closer to open scientific data, encourage climate literacy, and show how environmental information can be understood through multiple senses. These are intended outcomes, not measured impact results.

Tools and Technologies

The MVP was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and CSS. It uses the Web Audio API to generate sound from data and the Web Speech API for spoken guidance and, where supported, voice commands. Sources include NASA Earth Information Center and Scientific Visualization Studio materials, NASA GISTEMP data, and resources from NASA Ozone Watch and NOAA. GitHub is used for version control.

No specialized hardware is required: the app runs in a browser on a computer or phone with audio. A microphone is optional; conventional controls and text alternatives allow people to use the app without voice commands.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Sonification is treated as a way to represent data—not as background music. The interface explains how data relate to sound and pairs audio with visual and textual information. The project also considers accessibility, keyboard navigation, screen readers, contrast, Portuguese and English support, and browser compatibility—including a text alternative when voice recognition is unavailable.

The team prioritized traceable sources, units, and scientific references, clear distinctions between measurements and qualitative interpretations, and preservation of NASA’s original visualizations.

Team: Anny Karoline, Isabella Marques, and Ana Luiza.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx

Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Space Health Sensor
projectDetails.summary:
O Space Health Sensor propõe o desenvolvimento de um sistema inteligente para monitorar continuamente a saúde dos astronautas durante missões espaciais. A tecnologia será composta por sensores corporais, pulseira inteligente e detector de radiação, responsáveis por coletar informações como batimentos cardíacos, respiração, temperatura, oxigenação, qualidade do sono, movimentação e exposição à radiação.

Os dados serão enviados para uma central de monitoramento, integrada a um painel digital interativo, desenvolvido para apresentar indicadores em tempo real, gráficos de evolução, histórico individual de cada astronauta e alertas automáticos diante de alterações preocupantes. O sistema também permitirá o cadastro e acompanhamento de diferentes integrantes da tripulação.

A proposta prevê o uso de inteligência artificial para analisar os dados e identificar possíveis riscos à saúde, auxiliando a equipe médica na tomada de decisões.

Objetivo: prevenir problemas de saúde, reduzir riscos durante as missões espaciais e garantir maior segurança e bem-estar aos astronautas.
projectDetails.details:
O space health sensor é um sistema inteligente de monitoramento contínuo da saúde dos astronautas durante missões espaciais. A proposta utiliza sensores corporais, pulseira inteligente e detector de radiação para acompanhar indicadores como batimentos cardíacos, respiração, temperatura, oxigenação, sono, movimentação e exposição à radiação.

Os dados serão enviados para uma central de monitoramento, que apresentará gráficos, históricos individuais e alertas automáticos diante de alterações preocupantes, com previsão de integração de inteligência artificial.

Foi desenvolvido um protótipo digital utilizando HTML, CSS e JavaScript, com cadastro de astronautas, indicadores de saúde, gráficos, histórico de medições e simulação de emergências.

O projeto busca prevenir problemas de saúde, facilitar o acompanhamento médico e aumentar a segurança dos astronautas, considerando desafios como microgravidade, isolamento e exposição à radiação.

projectDetails.name: Project Galactic Engineers
projectDetails.summary:
TerraSpace – Intelligent Discovery and Ranking of Terrestrial Planetary Analogs
TerraSpace is a geospatial analysis platform designed to discover and classify terrestrial environments that resemble the Moon and Mars. Using open scientific datasets from NASA and other space agencies, the project analyzes geological composition, topography, temperature, terrain morphology, and water availability to identify potential new planetary analog sites.
Its main innovation is a customizable similarity scoring system, ranging from 0 to 100, that ranks locations according to their resemblance to selected lunar and Martian environments. Through interactive maps and detailed characterization profiles, users can explore potential analog sites, compare environmental conditions, and understand the scientific factors behind each classification.
By going beyond existing analog catalogs, TerraSpace aims to identify previously overlooked locations and support the selection of environments for testing robotic systems, exploration technologies, and scientific equipment.
The project contributes to future space exploration by transforming open scientific data into practical insights, helping researchers improve mission preparation, reduce testing costs, and support safer and more efficient lunar and Martian missions.
projectDetails.details:
TerraSpace – Intelligent Discovery and Ranking of Terrestrial Planetary Analogs

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

TerraSpace is a geospatial analysis platform designed to discover, evaluate, and classify terrestrial environments that share characteristics with the Moon and Mars.

Unlike traditional planetary analog catalogs, which mainly present previously identified locations, TerraSpace aims to systematically discover new potential analog environments using open scientific datasets from NASA and other space agencies.

The platform combines data from different sources to analyze geological composition, topography, elevation, temperature, terrain morphology, climate conditions, mineral resources, and water availability.

Using a multi-criteria analysis model, the system compares terrestrial environments with selected lunar and Martian regions. Each candidate location receives a similarity score ranging from 0 to 100, indicating how closely its characteristics match the selected extraterrestrial environment.

The results are presented through an interactive map, allowing users to explore potential locations, apply customized filters, compare different environments, and access detailed characterization profiles explaining their similarities and differences.

2. What benefits does the project offer?

TerraSpace offers several benefits for scientific research, engineering development, and future space exploration missions.

·        Discovery of new analog environments: Identifies potential locations that may not yet be widely recognized or documented as planetary analogs.

·        Cost reduction: Supports testing robotic vehicles, scientific instruments, and exploration technologies on Earth before deployment in space.

·        Scientific decision support: Combines multiple scientific indicators into a structured evaluation system.

·        Customized analysis: Allows researchers to prioritize different environmental characteristics according to specific mission objectives.

·        Improved accessibility: Makes complex scientific and geographic information easier to understand through interactive maps and characterization profiles.

·        Environmental comparison: Helps researchers identify both similarities and differences between terrestrial and extraterrestrial environments.

·        Data integration: Brings together information from multiple scientific sources into a unified analytical platform.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact of TerraSpace is to improve how researchers identify and evaluate terrestrial environments for planetary exploration studies.

The project aims to move beyond conventional analog catalogs by introducing a systematic and reproducible approach to discovering and ranking potential locations based on multiple scientific criteria.

One of its main features is a customizable similarity index, ranging from 0 to 100, which evaluates how closely a terrestrial environment resembles selected regions of the Moon or Mars.

The platform also provides an interactive comparative map and detailed characterization profiles containing geological, topographic, and environmental information. These profiles explain which characteristics influenced each classification and identify important differences and data limitations.

By combining geographic visualization, multi-criteria analysis, and scientific data integration, TerraSpace aims to support better-informed decisions when selecting locations for field research, equipment testing, and planetary exploration simulations.

In the long term, the project seeks to contribute to safer and more efficient space missions, reduce technological development costs, encourage scientific collaboration, and expand the use of open data in planetary research.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used to develop the project?

TerraSpace proposes an integrated technological architecture combining geospatial processing, scientific data analysis, and interactive visualization.

The main technologies selected for the project include:

·        Python: For data collection, processing, statistical analysis, and development of the similarity classification algorithm.

·        QGIS: For geospatial analysis, terrain characterization, and geographic data processing.

·        NASA Earthdata: For accessing satellite observations and environmental datasets related to Earth.

·        NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): For obtaining scientific information about planetary exploration.

·        Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC): For lunar surface imagery and geological analysis.

·        Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA): For lunar elevation and terrain data.

·        High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE): For high-resolution images of the Martian surface.

·        Google Earth Engine: For processing satellite imagery and analyzing environmental characteristics.

·        Leaflet or Folium: For developing interactive geographic maps.

·        HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: For building the platform's interface and interactive features.

·        GeoJSON: For storing and representing geographic information.

·        Digital Elevation Models (DEMs): For analyzing elevation, slopes, terrain morphology, and surface formations.

The initial development can be performed using standard computers, without requiring specialized hardware.

5. What is the creative aspect of the project?

The main creative aspect of TerraSpace is its approach to planetary analog discovery.

Rather than simply displaying locations already known to resemble extraterrestrial environments, the platform proposes a systematic method for searching large geographic datasets to identify new potential analog sites.

Its main differentiators are:

1. Intelligent discovery and ranking

A multi-criteria scoring model evaluates terrestrial environments based on geological, topographic, and environmental characteristics. The relative importance of each criterion can be adjusted according to the objectives of a specific lunar or Martian mission.

2. Explainable scientific comparisons

Instead of providing only a numerical score, TerraSpace explains why a particular region received its classification. Users can examine which characteristics are similar, which are different, and which available datasets support the evaluation.

3. Discovery beyond known analog locations

The platform expands the search beyond established examples such as the Atacama Desert, Death Valley, and Antarctica, exploring other potentially valuable environments, including volcanic landscapes, polar regions, caves, arid terrains, and impact structures.

4. Scientific validation

The classification methodology can be evaluated using well-documented analog locations before being applied to less explored regions. This helps assess the reliability of the similarity model and improve its results.

These features transform TerraSpace from a conventional geographic catalog into an analytical decision-support tool for planetary science and exploration research.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The project considers several scientific, environmental, technological, and operational factors to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of potential analog environments.

Geological characteristics

·        Rock and soil composition.

·        Mineral distribution and geological formations.

·        Volcanic structures and impact craters.

·        Surface materials and geological processes.

Topographic characteristics

·        Elevation and slope.

·        Terrain roughness.

·        Crater distribution.

·        Surface morphology and geological structures.

Environmental conditions

·        Temperature variations and thermal extremes.

·        Climate conditions and atmospheric exposure.

·        Aridity and humidity.

·        Wind patterns and precipitation.

Water and natural resources

·        Presence of surface or underground water.

·        Ice deposits and potential water resources.

·        Minerals and other materials relevant to future exploration activities.

Environmental exposure

·        Solar radiation and sunlight exposure.

·        Extreme environmental conditions.

·        Potential for simulating extraterrestrial operational challenges.

Operational and accessibility factors

·        Geographic accessibility.

·        Terrain safety and logistical constraints.

·        Possibility of conducting scientific field research.

·        Suitability for testing robotic systems and exploration equipment.

Data quality and scientific reliability

·        Accuracy and resolution of available datasets.

·        Data availability and geographic coverage.

·        Reliability of scientific sources.

·        Uncertainty and limitations in the comparison process.

These factors are combined using a multi-criteria evaluation model. Their relative importance can be adjusted depending on whether the objective is to identify lunar analogs, Martian analogs, or environments suitable for specific technological tests.

7. AI Usage Disclosure

Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, including large language models, were used to support project research, planning, programming, data analysis strategies, and documentation. AI-assisted code, content, and data processing will be identified in their respective descriptions or metadata. Any AI-generated images or videos included in the project will contain visible AI watermarks, while AI-generated audio will be identified in its descriptions and metadata. Scientific data and results will be reviewed and validated by the team. No NASA logos, branding elements, or mission identifiers were generated or modified using AI.

Conclusion

TerraSpace proposes a new approach to identifying terrestrial environments that can support future lunar and Martian exploration.

By integrating open scientific datasets, geospatial technologies, and a customizable similarity classification model, the platform aims to discover potential analog environments that may not be included in existing catalogs.

Its greatest contribution is the transition from simply collecting known analog locations to systematically discovering, ranking, and scientifically explaining new possibilities.

Through interactive mapping, comparative analysis, and detailed environmental characterization, TerraSpace aims to become a practical decision-support tool connecting data science, engineering, geology, and planetary exploration.

Ultimately, the project seeks to help researchers better understand Earth's most extreme environments and use that knowledge to prepare for humanity's next steps beyond our planet.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Speculum
projectDetails.summary: Speculum is an interactive web tool for choosing where on Earth to test a rover, drill, habitat, or power system before it flies to the Moon or Mars. Its catalog has 89 locations: 23 backed by published analog literature and 66 candidates scored on climate alone, 61 of which came from a global climate scan of places outside the catalog. All sites are scored against lunar, Martian, and Europan targets. Users describe their project and get a ranked list that shows why each site scored as it did, how complete its data is, and where the analogy breaks down. All climate values come from 25 years of NASA POWER data, and the planetary reference values come from the NASA NSSDC Moon and Mars Fact Sheets.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Speculum has three tools, available at https://gpradines.github.io/speculum/.

Map: An interactive map of documented analog sites and climate-only candidates. Each site’s panel lists its climate values with confidence levels, its strengths and weaknesses, how testing there helps exploration, and access and permit warnings. It also has a “where the analogy breaks down” section, which compares the site with Moon and Mars reference values in plain language, for example how many times the site’s air pressure exceeds Mars’s.

Finder: The user picks a project type (wheeled rover, ice drilling, habitat and ISRU, power and communications, and others), a target environment (lunar south pole, lunar lava tubes, equatorial Mars, Mars mid-latitudes with ice, and others), logistics filters, and optional parameter weights. The tool returns the top 10 sites, split into Tier A (published analog evidence) and Tier B (climate similarity only). Each result has a per-parameter breakdown, and the list can be exported as CSV.

Methods: A page with the scoring method, a worked example, all 29 parameters, confidence rules, known limitations, and the full source list.

The problem

Teams preparing hardware for the Moon or Mars need field sites on Earth that stress their equipment realistically. Published analog studies are scattered across decades of papers, and no Earth location reproduces every condition of another world. Teams often fall back on a few famous sites without a systematic comparison.

How it works

Ranking is relative. No place on Earth reaches the absolute temperature, pressure, or dryness of Mars or the Moon. Each target defines a direction (equatorial Mars is colder, drier, and thinner-aired than most of Earth), and each site gets a percentile position among all other sites along those directions.

Each project type has its own parameter weights: a drilling project values ground ice and cold, a rover values terrain and dryness. Weights are scaled by data confidence, and users can adjust them.

Only parameters that have data are scored. Each result shows its coverage, such as “based on 7 of 12 parameters with data”, plus low-confidence warnings. Of the 29 parameters in the schema, only 12 currently have data. The rest (slope, rock abundance, soil bearing strength, radiation, and others) are listed as limitations and future work.

When a published paper and NASA POWER give different values for the same parameter, the paper wins. Where the coarse grid clearly misrepresents a mountain or island site, we removed the grid values instead of keeping misleading numbers.

To look beyond known analog sites, we scanned 64 regions not in the catalog, including the Gobi, Taklamakan, Pamir, Altiplano, Antarctic and Greenland ice domes, and Kamchatka. This produced candidates such as the Pamir Plateau and Altun Shan for equatorial Mars rovers, and Dome A and Axel Heiberg for the lunar south pole. They are labeled as hypotheses from climate data only, with no literature behind them.

The method re-ranks known analogs highly (Concordia for ice and cold, Atacama for astrobiology). We also built reference test cases with expected rankings and checked the site’s output against them, for example wheeled rover for equatorial Mars: Qaidam 74.0, MDRS 67.7, Death Valley 60.1, Atacama 54.2.

Where the analogy fails

Earth analogs never reproduce reduced gravity, lunar vacuum, the Martian atmosphere, or the radiation environment. Concordia ranks high for ice and cold, but it is an analog for isolation and extreme cold, and says little about terrain. Climate-only candidates have low confidence and need local verification before any real test campaign. Many coordinates are approximate.

Why it matters

Speculum puts scattered analog knowledge into one ranking tool and shows the uncertainty behind each result. The discovery scan points to less-studied regions that deserve a closer look.

Next steps

A continuous global grid scan instead of hand-picked regions, elevation-based slope and roughness from NASA and other agencies’ terrain data, ice and permafrost layers, local field-station verification, and more Europa and lunar-polar analogs.

Team

High school students from Recife, Brazil: Elias Cassemiro de Lucena Junior, Guilherme Pradines Falcão, Pedro Endry Garmes Veras, Victor Germano Peregrino, and Vinicius Soares Campelo.

Links

Website: https://gpradines.github.io/speculum/
Repository: https://github.com/gpradines/speculum

projectDetails.name: Project Star Promises
projectDetails.summary: Star Promises: Earth-to-Mars and Moon Analog Atlas is an interactive 3D Google Earth (KML) expedition connecting extreme terrestrial environments to Moon and Mars exploration sites. Starting from dual Ground Zeros at the Sorocaba Technology Park in Brazil and the Kennedy Space Center in the USA, our crew and five original characters guide users through 11 global and Brazilian planetary analogs. Powered by open NASA satellite datasets (Landsat, MODIS, ASTER, SRTM, ICESat-2, and LRO) and bilingual vertical video guides, the project combines remote sensing, pop-culture storytelling, and space education to support future Artemis and Mars missions.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:
Project Name
Mars Mission: Survival Map

High-Level Project Summary
Mars Mission: Survival Map is an interactive web atlas that helps future explorers judge where to land and move safely on Mars. It combines eight layers of NASA data for Ares Vallis into a simple green and red safety map. An astronaut guide explains the results.

Detailed Project Description
Mars Mission: Survival Map is an interactive web guide built around Ares Vallis, one of the largest outflow channels on Mars. It stretches about 1,600 to 2,000 km, from the highlands of Margaritifer Terra to the plains of Chryse Planitia.

The site has four screens:

  1. A landing page with a GO button.
  2. An introduction to Ares Vallis.
  3. A multilayer atlas on a Mars Odyssey (THEMIS) base image (about 100 m/pixel). It overlays eight data layers: topography, temperature, spectral data, optical imagery, geophysics, atmosphere, radiation and surface chemistry.
  4. A “safezone map” that turns the data into a safety overlay.

On the safezone map:

  • Green areas are flatter regions with fewer obstacles. They make landing and astronaut movement easier and lower the risk of accidents.
  • Red areas have craters, slopes and uneven terrain. They need caution.

A friendly astronaut guide explains the map in plain language, so students and the general public can understand it. Its conclusion is that green areas are only potential candidates for exploration. No region is completely safe without detailed studies.

We built it to turn complex planetary data into something anyone can read at a glance. It supports the idea that careful site selection is the first step of survival on another planet.

NASA Data

  • Mars Odyssey THEMIS (base imagery, thermal, optical)
  • Mars Global Surveyor MOLA (topography)
  • Mars Global Surveyor (geophysical layer)
  • Mars Climate Sounder, MCS (atmosphere)
  • MARIE (radiation)
  • CRISM (spectral and chemical)
  • Gamma Ray Spectrometer, GRS (chemistry)
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS)

projectDetails.name: Project GUMA
projectDetails.summary:
GUMA — Earth Intelligence is an independent platform designed to help users investigate environmental trends through Earth science data and statistical analysis.

Building on an existing project, we developed an interactive Trend Detective that retrieves the NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 global temperature record and allows users to upload their own environmental datasets. It applies the Mann–Kendall trend test with Hamed–Rao autocorrelation correction, Sen's slope estimation, and bootstrap confidence intervals. Users can also compare regional trends, explore spatial autocorrelation, and examine relationships between environmental variables.

GUMA addresses the challenge by helping users investigate what is changing, how much it is changing, and whether observed trends are statistically significant. Its broader research prototype explores additional Earth observation and agricultural data sources.

Our goal is to make scientific methods more accessible, encourage evidence-based environmental research, and support a deeper understanding of our changing planet.
projectDetails.details:
GUMA — Earth Intelligence

Project Description | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Challenge 02: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

GUMA is an independent Earth-intelligence platform designed to connect climate data, Earth observation, agricultural systems, and collaborative environmental research. Its goal is to make complex environmental information more accessible, understandable, and useful for exploring the relationships between climate, ecosystems, and human activities.

What does it do and how does it work?

GUMA brings together environmental datasets from multiple scientific and public sources in an interactive platform. Users can explore climate indicators, vegetation observations, geographic information, and agricultural variables, while examining historical patterns and comparing environmental conditions.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, GUMA's primary focus is its Earth System Trend Detective module. It uses NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 global temperature-anomaly data or annual datasets uploaded by users. The module allows users to select a time period, visualize a time series, and investigate long-term trends using statistical methods such as the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope estimator.

Beyond trend analysis, the broader platform includes:

  • Global climate indicators, including temperature anomalies and atmospheric greenhouse-gas measurements.
  • NASA POWER climate data and MODIS vegetation-index observations.
  • Global satellite-scene discovery through the Earth Search STAC API.
  • Active-fire observations from NASA FIRMS.
  • Agricultural climate screening and crop-cycle analysis.
  • FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration estimates and a simplified root-zone water-balance scenario.
  • Geographic exploration, data exports, and PDF reporting.
  • Community research features for sharing hypotheses and contributor-reported observations.

The platform is designed to make data provenance, methodological choices, and scientific limitations visible to users.

What benefits does it have?

Environmental information is often distributed across different institutions, datasets, and technical platforms. GUMA seeks to reduce this fragmentation by bringing complementary information into one accessible environment.

Its main benefits include:

  • Making scientific environmental data easier to explore without requiring advanced programming skills.
  • Helping users identify historical patterns and investigate possible environmental changes.
  • Connecting global climate indicators with agricultural and territorial contexts.
  • Supporting exploratory research, education, and evidence-informed discussions.
  • Encouraging transparency through source references, data-quality information, and explicit methodological limitations.
  • Providing tools for researchers, students, educators, agricultural professionals, and interested communities.

What is the intended impact?

GUMA aims to contribute to a more accessible and collaborative understanding of the Earth system.

Its long-term vision is to become a global platform where climate information, Earth-observation data, agricultural knowledge, and local research can be explored together. By connecting different scales of environmental information, GUMA hopes to help people ask better questions about climate change, land use, vegetation, water, and agricultural resilience.

The project is being developed in Brazil, but its architecture and vision are global. It is intended to support collaboration across countries and regions, rather than focus on a single territory.

GUMA does not claim to predict climate events, establish causal relationships, or replace scientific and professional assessment. Its purpose is to support exploration, transparency, and better-informed research.

What tools, programming languages, and software were used?

GUMA was developed primarily with:

  • Python: data processing, scientific calculations, environmental analysis, and application logic.
  • Streamlit: interactive web application and dashboard development.
  • Pandas and NumPy: data organization, numerical operations, and time-series processing.
  • Requests: communication with public data APIs.
  • Folium and Streamlit-Folium: interactive geographic visualization.
  • ReportLab: generation of PDF reports.
  • Supabase: authentication and optional user-project persistence.
  • Git and GitHub: source-code management, version control, and collaborative development.

The platform connects to public scientific and institutional data sources, including NASA GISS GISTEMP, NASA POWER, NASA FIRMS, MODIS, Earth Search, NOAA, IBGE, and Brazilian agricultural information resources. It also incorporates methodological references from FAO and Embrapa.

No specialized hardware or physical sensors were required for the current prototype. The project relies on public datasets, satellite-derived observations, computational methods, and web technologies.

How is the project creative and innovative?

GUMA's creativity lies in connecting areas that are often explored separately: global climate trends, satellite observations, agricultural systems, geographic context, and community research.

Instead of presenting environmental indicators as isolated numbers, it creates an exploratory environment where users can move between datasets, investigate patterns, compare evidence, and understand the limitations of each analysis.

Another distinctive aspect is its combination of global environmental intelligence with practical agricultural questions. It seeks to connect large-scale Earth-system observations with the territorial and agricultural contexts in which environmental changes are experienced.

The project also has an original visual identity inspired by the relationship between people, territory, the sea, and the horizon in Brazilian visual culture. Its name, GUMA, references the character from Jorge Amado's Mar Morto. This cultural foundation gives the platform a recognizable identity while keeping its scientific ambition international.

What factors did the team consider?

The development process considered several important factors:

  1. Scientific reliability: choosing recognized data sources and documented analytical methods.
  2. Transparency: identifying data sources, units, reference periods, assumptions, and limitations.
  3. Global applicability: designing the platform to work with environmental information beyond Brazil.
  4. Accessibility: making complex datasets easier to explore through an interactive interface.
  5. Agricultural relevance: connecting climate and vegetation information with agricultural systems and water-balance concepts.
  6. Data quality: considering missing observations, spatial resolution, temporal coverage, and differences between datasets.
  7. Responsible interpretation: avoiding unsupported causal claims, false precision, and unverified agricultural recommendations.
  8. Scalability and collaboration: creating a foundation that can evolve through partnerships, additional datasets, and community contributions.

GUMA is an evolving independent prototype. Its scientific methods and data integrations are subject to continued testing and validation. The project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

GUMA — Earth Intelligence
Territory • Climate • Future

projectDetails.name: Project Hi Five5 - Fire Guard
projectDetails.summary:
Summary

Our team was formed with the goal of developing a technological solution to contribute to the safety of future space missions. Based on research into fire behavior in microgravity environments and studies conducted by NASA, we created FIRE GUARD, a digital prototype designed to monitor and prevent fires in space habitats.

We aim to combine scientific knowledge, creativity, and innovation to address the challenges of space exploration, demonstrating that prevention is essential to making future missions safer.
projectDetails.details:
FIRE GUARD Prototype

The FIRE GUARD prototype is a digital dashboard that simulates fire monitoring and prevention in space habitats. It displays temperature and oxygen indicators, combustion charts, and alerts for potential environmental risks.

Objective: To demonstrate how technology can help identify risks and prevent fires in space environments.

Important Note: The prototype is a demonstration of the proposed solution and is not necessarily connected to real sensors aboard a spacecraft. It is important to distinguish between the features that have already been implemented and those that are still proposed for future development.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: BioOrbit — Astronaut Health OS
projectDetails.summary: BioOrbit is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support app for astronauts on long-duration missions. Astronauts log vital signs, sleep, mood and symptoms. They can also measure heart rate with a phone camera and take a 3-minute reaction test that screens for fatigue. BioOrbit turns these data into a colour-coded interactive body map, a readiness score and clear actions. It compares every value with the astronaut's personal baseline to catch problems early, and it combines signals into insights such as fatigue or possible infection. Escalation advice adapts to the communication delay of each environment, from the ISS to Mars. A compact report can be sent to the flight surgeon. Because crews on Mars cannot rely on real-time help from Earth, BioOrbit gives them the knowledge and autonomy to assess and act on their own health. The same tool serves remote communities on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

BioOrbit is a "health bridge" for each crew member:

  • Readiness score and duty status (Mission ready, Ready with caution, Limited duty, Medical attention), calculated from 14 indicators, symptoms and baseline changes.
  • Interactive body map: eight body systems (brain & behaviour, eyes/SANS, heart, lungs, metabolism, immune, muscles, skeleton). Each one is colour-coded, clickable and explains its function, what spaceflight does to it, the latest values and what to do now.
  • Guided logging: fields turn green, amber or red while you type, and explain why each indicator matters in space and how to measure it with onboard equipment.
  • Camera heart rate (photoplethysmography): a fingertip over the camera is enough, with no extra hardware. Tap-to-the-beat fallback.
  • Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT-B): the brief vigilance test validated for spaceflight, to detect fatigue before critical operations.
  • Personal-baseline drift detection: flags meaningful change even when values are still "normal".
  • Multi-signal insights: sleep debt + slower reactions → fatigue; fever + elevated heart rate/rash → possible infection; persistent low mood → behavioural health; vision change → possible SANS. Each comes with concrete onboard actions.
  • Mission environments: Space Station, Lunar Base, Mars Transit, Mars Surface and Earth Remote Care. Radiation dose rate (cumulative dose vs. the 600 mSv career limit), gravity, communication delay and escalation rules adapt to each one.
  • Delay-tolerant downlink: a structured TXT/JSON report with findings, actions and 7-day trends, showing the real arrival time at Earth.
  • Crew overview, mission routine with gamification (XP, levels, streaks, badges) and a knowledge library on the five NASA HRP hazards.

HOW IT WORKS

Values are classified against reference ranges. A personal-baseline model compares each person's last three days with their own previous 18 days (z-score plus a clinically meaningful minimum change), and rule-based patterns combine several signals. The camera pulse algorithm averages the red channel of the fingertip image, resamples it to 30 Hz, removes the slow trend and estimates heart rate by autocorrelation, with protection against octave errors (within ±3 bpm from 42 to 178 bpm on synthetic test signals). The PVT follows the PVT-B protocol (1–4 s intervals, lapses > 355 ms, false starts < 100 ms).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It helps astronauts who are not doctors understand and act on their own health far from Earth, detects early change instead of waiting for a critical value, works fully offline on any phone or laptop, and keeps data private on the device. On Earth, it fits remote care: isolated and riverside communities, Antarctic stations, ships and home monitoring. Next steps: wearable/Bluetooth sensors, ultrasound guidance, machine-learning baselines from analog-mission data and validation with health professionals.

TOOLS

HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript with no frameworks or external libraries (so it works offline); Canvas and SVG APIs for charts and the body map; MediaDevices/getUserMedia for the camera; localStorage for data; hosted on GitHub Pages.

projectDetails.name: Analog ATLAS
projectDetails.summary:
Analog Atlas is an interactive platform designed to identify, map, and catalog terrestrial environments that resemble the geological and environmental conditions of the Moon and Mars.

Our project features interactive maps with geographically located analog sites, organized into lunar and Martian categories. It also provides information about their geological characteristics, soil types, environmental conditions, and visual landscapes. These include volcanic terrains, regolith-like soils, arid deserts, and polar environments.

By addressing the challenge of identifying Earth locations analogous to the Moon and Mars, Analog Atlas creates an accessible resource for exploring potential research environments. These locations can support scientific studies, equipment testing, and the development of protocols for future space missions.

Our goal is to connect planetary exploration with terrestrial research, making relevant information easier to discover and understand.

With Analog Atlas, Earth becomes a starting point for exploring new worlds.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Analog Atlas is an interactive web platform designed to identify, map, and catalog terrestrial locations that share geological and environmental characteristics with the Moon and Mars.

The website uses Google Maps to display the geographical locations of terrestrial analogues, allowing users to explore different regions and discover information about their geological formations, soil characteristics, environmental conditions, and landscapes.

The platform organizes locations into lunar and Martian analogues, presenting categories such as basaltic terrains, regolith-like soils, high plateaus, arid deserts, and polar environments.

Additionally, users can submit data and register new locations, allowing the platform to expand through new contributions.

What benefits does it offer?

Analog Atlas centralizes geographical and scientific information in an accessible, interactive environment. It helps researchers, students, and space enthusiasts discover potential terrestrial analogues that may be useful for geological research, equipment testing, and the preparation of future space missions.

What is its intended impact?

Our goal is to support planetary exploration by connecting Earth-based research with future lunar and Martian missions. By making terrestrial analogue locations easier to identify and study, the platform aims to contribute to scientific research and the development of technologies and protocols for space exploration.

What tools and technologies were used?

The website was developed using Wix as its website-building platform, with Google Maps integrated to provide interactive geographical visualization and location mapping.

For scientific research and content development, we consulted NASA's scientific resources and information about planetary environments and terrestrial analogues. We also used visual resources and organized geographical information to present the locations and their characteristics.

What makes the project creative?

The main creative aspect of Analog Atlas is combining interactive geographical mapping, geological classification, scientific information, and collaborative data submission in one platform.

Rather than simply listing locations, the project connects each terrestrial environment to the planetary characteristics it resembles. Its contribution system also allows users to register new locations, making the platform expandable and open to further discoveries.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered geological similarities, soil composition, terrain characteristics, environmental conditions, geographical distribution, and scientific relevance when organizing the locations.

We also prioritized accessibility, intuitive navigation, clear scientific communication, visual organization, and the possibility of continuous expansion through user contributions.

projectDetails.name: Incredible stories of NASA space equipment on the Moon and Mars
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IS OUR PROJECT?

Incredible stories of NASA space equipment on the Moon and Mars is a digital storytelling project that shows the story of the multiple hardware that NASA left across the moon and mars. The main objective of our project is to provide in a accessible way, using interactive language, captivating characters and thrilling imagery, helping kids and adults understand how important each equipment was to science.

WHY IS IT RELEVANT?

The relevance of the project comes from the fact that, even if all of the information is public, most people are unable to understand it, either because the language is to complex, or simply due to lack of interest. Incredible stories of NASA space equipment on the Moon and Mars tries to solve both problems, using a simple language and combining it with amazing storytelling.

TARGET AUDIENCE AND STORY ORGANIZATION

The target audience is 5-12 years old children, and the stories are organized with that in mind. Each story has a didactic way of teaching, where we accompany the hardwares into their objectives. At the end of each story, there always is: a question, to instigate the reader to search for more; a curiosity, to fixate the new knowledge; and a link to a site made by NASA or another space focused organization, where we found the material for the story, in case the reader wants even more information about the specific hardware.

WHAT ARE THE STORIES ABOUT?

There are 8 stories on our demonstration, 4 of them being from hardware left on the Moon (RANGER 7, SURVEYOR 3, retroreflector apollo 11 and seismometer apollo 12), and 4 of them being from hardware left on Mars (Sojourner, Viking 1, Spirit and Opportunity).

WHAT TOOLS WHERE USED ON THE CREATION OF THE DEMO?

The entire project is made using Canva, the specific Canva tools that where used, aside from the basic slide creation tools, are:

  • Canva AI;
  • Background remover;
  • Hyperlinks between pages.
