projectDetails.name: RainShift
projectDetails.summary:
RainShift is a web tool that lets anyone check whether rainfall and air temperature have really changed on the northern coast of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, from the Macaé River headwaters to Campos dos Goytacazes. It takes two NASA records, GPM IMERG precipitation and MERRA-2 air temperature, and shows for the whole region and for every grid cell what changed, where, by how much, and how strong the statistical evidence is.

The problem it addresses is that a trend line is easy to draw and easy to over-read. RainShift reports every trend with its 95% confidence interval drawn against zero and gives one of three plain labels: increase, decrease, or insufficient evidence of a trend. With real data the two variables tell different stories. The region warmed by about 0.22 °C per decade (95% CI 0.12 to 0.32), close to 1 °C in 45 years. Rainfall shows an estimated decline of 76 mm per decade, but the interval runs from −218 to +76, so 26 years of data cannot tell a decline from no change, and the estimate nearly doubles if the record starts in 2001 instead of 1999.

This matters because students, teachers and people who manage water in the region need to know not only what the data suggest but how far the data can be trusted. Four guided cases, a period selector that recomputes the trend live, and a plain-language glossary turn a statistics lesson into a detective exercise on real NASA data.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

  • Shows a full-screen map of grid cells coloured by the estimated trend, and a time series with its trend line for the region average or any cell you click.
  • Covers two variables with four yearly metrics each. Precipitation: annual, wet-season and dry-season totals, and the wet-season share. Air temperature: annual, wet-season and dry-season means, and the wet-minus-dry contrast.
  • For every series, reports the trend per decade, the 95% confidence interval, the number of years, the period, the source and the unit, and one label: Increase, Decrease, or Insufficient evidence of a trend.
  • Lets you change the start and end year and recomputes the trend in the browser, so you can see how much an answer depends on the years chosen.
  • Offers four guided cases that set the controls and explain what to look at: "Getting warmer?", "Less rain?", "Does the start year matter?" and "Do the seasons differ?".
  • Includes a glossary, a one-sentence reading "in plain words" for every result, and CSV download of every series.

How does it work?

  • A Python pipeline downloads bounding-box subsets from NASA GES DISC through Harmony, checks units, coordinates, dates and missing values, and converts the monthly values (rain rate in mm/hr × hours in the month; temperature in K to °C).
  • The region average weights each cell by the geodesic area that lies inside the region.
  • The wet season is defined from the rainfall record itself (the run of months rainier than the average month: November to March). Years run from November to October so that a wet season is never split in two.
  • Trends use the Theil–Sen slope with Sen's 95% confidence interval and the Mann–Kendall test, with the Hamed–Rao correction when neighbouring years resemble each other. The map applies a Benjamini–Hochberg correction for testing many cells at once and is labelled exploratory.
  • The pipeline writes small JSON and GeoJSON files. The website is static: it needs no server and no NASA login, so it keeps working during judging.

What did we find?

  • Air temperature (MERRA-2, 1981–2025): +0.22 °C per decade, 95% CI +0.12 to +0.32. All 16 cells pass the many-tests correction. Both seasons warmed, but the data cannot tell whether one warms faster than the other: the wet-minus-dry contrast is −0.10 °C per decade, CI −0.25 to +0.04.
  • Precipitation (IMERG, 1999–2024): −76 mm per decade, 95% CI −218 to +76. None of the 204 cells passes the correction for the annual total. Starting the record in 2001 changes the estimate to −133 mm per decade, with the same label.
  • Two "significant" labels are not a comparison. To test whether seasons differ, RainShift fits the trend of the paired difference instead of comparing labels.

What benefits does it have?

  • It teaches how a trend is estimated and tested, with a real case where the answer is clear and a real case where it is not.
  • It keeps two things apart that are often mixed up: statistical uncertainty (how much the values jump from year to year) and the limits of the data products themselves.
  • Every series can be downloaded as CSV from the app, and the method page documents each step, so the numbers can be checked independently.

What do we hope to achieve?

A tool that classrooms and local water and climate groups can use to ask "has the climate here really changed?" and get an honest answer, and a pipeline that can be pointed at other regions and other NASA variables.

Limits

  • The region is a rectangular box aligned to the IMERG grid, not a watershed boundary.
  • IMERG is a merged satellite and rain-gauge estimate; MERRA-2 is a model reconstruction on cells of about 55 × 65 km that mix land, mountains and ocean.
  • The confidence interval covers year-to-year variability only. Trends are linear; the rainfall series looks more like a rise followed by a fall.
  • The period selector uses the same estimator in the browser without the Hamed–Rao correction and shows a caution note when it would matter.

Tools, languages and software

A Python pipeline for the data and the statistics, and a static website built with Next.js, React and CesiumJS. The project is licensed under Apache-2.0.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. An SI/AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Anthropic) was used throughout:

  • Planning: it helped turn the idea into a technical plan and checked the official rules and data catalogues.
  • Code: it wrote most of the Python pipeline, the tests and the web application, under the author's direction and review.

The project idea, the research question, the choice of region, data and methods, and all decisions were made by the author. No images, video or audio were generated with SI. No data values were generated: every number comes from the NASA products listed below. SI use is acknowledged in the application's "Method & credits" page, in the metadata file published with each dataset (`meta.json`, field `si_note`) and in the project's source files.

NASA Data

  • GPM IMERG Final Precipitation L3 1 month 0.1 degree x 0.1 degree V07 (GPM_3IMERGM), NASA GES DISC. DOI: 10.5067/GPM/IMERG/3B-MONTH/07. Variable `precipitation`, January 1998 to September 2025, 204 grid cells. Used for all rainfall series, maps and for defining the wet season.
  • MERRA-2 tavgM_2d_slv_Nx, monthly mean single-level diagnostics V5.12.4 (M2TMNXSLV), NASA GMAO / GES DISC. DOI: 10.5067/AP1B0BA5PD2K. Variable `T2M` (2-metre air temperature), January 1980 to September 2026, 16 grid cells. Used for all temperature series and maps.
  • NASA Earthdata Login, Harmony and the Common Metadata Repository (CMR): used to find the collections and to download bounding-box subsets.
  • NASA `earthaccess` and `harmony-py` Python libraries: used for authentication and downloads.

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

No Space Agency Partner data were used.

  • OpenStreetMap map tiles, © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL: base map, loaded at view time.
  • CesiumJS: map engine.
  • NASA earthaccess and harmony-py: data access.
  • Open-source software: Python scientific libraries (xarray, SciPy, pymannkendall, statsmodels) for the analysis; Next.js, React and Recharts for the website.

Methods

  • Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 63(324), 1379–1389.
  • Mann, H. B. (1945). Nonparametric tests against trend. *Econometrica*, 13(3), 245–259.
  • Hamed, K. H., & Rao, A. R. (1998). A modified Mann–Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data. *Journal of Hydrology*, 204(1–4), 182–196.
  • Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B*, 57(1), 289–300.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Location on Mars: The best guide for the astronauts
projectDetails.summary: Research conducted during the Perseverance rover expedition has revealed several similarities between Mars and Earth. However, certain obstacles to the existence of life on Mars have also been identified. For this reason, we have developed a project designed to assist astronauts in navigating their expeditions, helping them avoid any unforeseen issues that might arise.
projectDetails.details:
NASA’s Mars 2020 mission sent the Perseverance rover to Mars with the goal of exploring its surface, studying its environment, and investigating potential signs of past life.

The rover was launched on July 30, 2020, and landed in Jezero Crater—a region that, according to scientific studies, once held a large lake fed by rivers billions of years ago.

Throughout its exploration, Perseverance has traveled over 45 kilometers, collected various rock and soil samples, and analyzed geological formations that help us understand the planet’s history.

Among its discoveries are signs of an ancient lake and delta system, as well as rocks with chemical characteristics that could be linked to the existence of microbial life in the past.

The rover also recorded dust devils and electrical discharges in the Martian atmosphere, illustrating just how extreme the planet’s environment can be.

Another significant finding was the identification of potential organic compounds and chemical signatures that require further study to determine their origin.

Furthermore, the mission conducted experiments demonstrating that it is possible to produce oxygen from the carbon dioxide present in the Martian atmosphere.

All of this information is essential for understanding Mars’ past, identifying areas of scientific interest, and assisting NASA in planning future human missions—ultimately making the exploration of the planet safer and more efficient.

projectDetails.name: biosphere // mars
projectDetails.summary:
Imagine being stranded on Mars. 
How would you survive? 
What would happen if your habitat lost pressure, your food supply ran low, or you were exposed to dangerous levels of radiation?

These are some of the questions behind our project: an interactive 3D Mars survival simulator that helps young students discover what it takes to live on another planet.

Built with Three.js and Blender, the simulator lets players explore a Martian habitat, run experiments, and face challenges inspired by real NASA research. Instead of simply reading about atmospheric pressure, radiation, protective shielding, or food production, students can see how these factors affect survival and experiment with different solutions.

The simulator has two modes. 
In Experiments, players explore scientific concepts by changing conditions and observing what happens. In Missions, they put that knowledge to use, solving problems involving habitat safety, limited resources, and astronaut protection.

Our goal is to make space science something students can experience, not just study. By combining realistic scenarios, interactive experiments, and gameplay, we hope to spark curiosity, encourage problem-solving, and inspire more young people to explore science, engineering, and space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: MFIEC-AI: Effective Contribution Analysis for Complex Systems
projectDetails.summary:
MFIEC-AI is an experimental research framework designed to investigate adaptation, resilience, recovery, and structural reorganization in complex systems.

The project explores how variables contribute to system adaptation beyond traditional correlation-based analysis. Instead of focusing only on statistical relationships, MFIEC-AI analyzes dynamic state transitions, temporal continuity, and reorganization processes to identify potential effective contributors to change.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, the framework is applied to astronaut health monitoring, where adaptation, recovery, and stability are critical in long-duration space missions.

The project aims to provide a complementary analytical perspective for understanding how complex systems maintain functionality, recover from disturbances, and adapt under changing conditions.
projectDetails.details:
MFIEC-AI is an experimental framework designed to investigate adaptation, resilience, recovery, and structural reorganization in complex systems.

The project introduces the concept of Effective Contribution Analysis, which seeks to distinguish variables that may actively contribute to adaptation and recovery from variables that merely exhibit statistical correlation with observed outcomes.

The framework combines dynamic state representation, temporal monitoring, reorganization analysis, and Effective Contribution Assessment (ECM). Instead of analyzing isolated observations, MFIEC-AI evaluates how system states evolve over time and how specific factors participate in transitions associated with stability, recovery, and adaptation.

As a proof of concept, the project uses computational models, Python-based analytical pipelines, and publicly available scientific datasets. The initial application focuses on astronaut health monitoring and adaptation during long-duration space missions.

The expected impact is to provide a complementary analytical perspective for studying complex systems in aerospace, environmental science, and technology. The project emphasizes dynamic behavior, temporal continuity, and adaptive processes, offering a framework that may support future research on resilience and system stability under changing conditions.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AETHER-QKD
projectDetails.summary: AETHER-QKD is an interplanetary command and cryptography hub built by Team Aracus for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, combining futuristic Deep-Space Quantum Key Distribution (BB84) with historical Enigma code-breaking simulation suites. To address deep-space communication security, the platform simulates polarized photon transmission between deep-space probes and ground stations while integrating real-time atmospheric telemetry from the Meteomatics Weather API to dynamically model quantum channel noise and QBER safety thresholds. Furthermore, it features a dual-layer Enigma intercept and code-breaking lab to demonstrate robust encryption and signal decryption. This project is vital for advancing unhackable quantum communication architectures for future space missions.
projectDetails.details:
Aether-Net Interplanetary Command & Cryptography Hub (AETHER-QKD) is an advanced dual-layer security platform engineered for future interplanetary missions. It bridges futuristic Quantum Key Distribution (BB84) with historical Enigma-based code-breaking cipher suites, dynamically audited against real-time ground-station environmental data.

WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS:

- BB84 Quantum Protocol & Basis Sifting: Simulates Alice (deep-space probe) transmitting polarized photon streams across interplanetary distances to Bob (ground station), performing real-time basis sifting to generate secure cryptographic keys.

- Real-Time QBER Security Auditing: Integrates live meteorological data from the Meteomatics Weather API (/now/ endpoint) to dynamically evaluate the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) against real-world environmental noise factors (ground temperature, humidity, and wind speed) to ensure channel security remains below the critical 11% threshold.

- Enigma Intercept & Code-Breaking Lab: Provides a dual-mode rotor-based cipher interface for encrypting deep-space telemetry and decrypting intercepted operational intelligence.

- Interplanetary Telemetry Dashboard: A high-visibility, cinematic deep-space command interface featuring live atmospheric metrics, high-contrast typography, and atmospheric link status monitors.

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT:

As humanity reaches deeper into the cosmos, secure communication across interplanetary distances becomes paramount. Traditional encryption remains vulnerable to quantum computing advancements. AETHER-QKD ensures that deep-space probes and ground stations can establish unbreakable, error-audited quantum links while maintaining absolute operational readiness under varying atmospheric conditions.

TECHNOLOGY STACK:

- Frontend & UI: Python Streamlit (Community Cloud Deployed), Custom CSS High-Contrast Deep-Space UI Styling.

- Backend Logic: Python, Random, Pandas.

- API Integration: Meteomatics Weather API (/now/t_2m:C,relative_humidity_2m:p,wind_speed_10m:ms/) for real-time atmospheric auditing.

- Version Control & Deployment: Git, GitHub, Streamlit Cloud.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

challengeDetails.title: Dancing with the SARs

From wetland loss to forest wildfires, earthquakes, farming activities, glacier movement, and more, Earth is in a constant waltz of surface changes. Your challenge is to build an interactive application that uses radar remote sensing data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to track and visualize one or more types of surface change at locations around the world.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: OrbitCare: A Core Health monitoring, forecasting and prediction system.
projectDetails.summary:
Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to critical health risks like bone density loss and kidney stones, which are often diagnosed only after they become mission-threatening emergencies. Currently, tracking these interconnected issues requires time-consuming procedures that strain the crew's schedule.
Our solution is OrbitCare, an advanced predictive health monitoring software designed for maximum efficiency. OrbitCare transforms qualitative daily self-assessments—completed in under 60 seconds on a tablet—into quantitative, forecasted risk scores.

By analyzing the critical biological loops between bone loss, calcium excretion, spinal elongation, and reproductive health, our XGBoost machine learning engine calculates personalized risk profiles across three timelines: Current, Tomorrow, and Near Future. The software doesn’t just display data; its explainable AI identifies the root causes of elevated risks and instantly generates actionable countermeasures, such as automated hydration protocols or targeted resistive exercises.

Because real astronaut medical records are restricted, we validated our architecture using synthetic analog datasets built on robust clinical parameters. OrbitCare empowers astronauts to manage their health proactively and autonomously, mitigating serious medical events before they happen.
projectDetails.details:
How OrbitCare Works

OrbitCare operates as a highly efficient, closed-loop predictive health system. Astronauts interact with a minimalist UI to complete a daily 60-second digital assessment covering 38 critical biomarkers and subjective health indicators (e.g., hydration levels, pain scales, reproductive cycle data).

Behind the interface, an XGBoost Multi-Output Regressor processes these inputs. Instead of waiting for a threshold alert, the model maps the non-linear biological relationships and outputs a personalized Risk Percentage (0–100%) across three time horizons: Now, Tomorrow, and Near Future (3-months).
If a high risk is detected, our Explainable AI (Root Cause Analysis engine) extracts feature importances to tell the astronaut why the score is high (e.g., "85% Kidney Stone Risk due to high calcium excretion combined with low hydration"), and instantly triggers an actionable medical countermeasure.

Project Benefits

  • Extreme Time Efficiency: Replaces hours of cumbersome medical tracking with a sub-minute daily questionnaire.
  • Proactive vs. Reactive: Identifies the statistical trajectory of a kidney stone or spinal elongation pain days or weeks before it becomes physically debilitating.
  • Explainable AI Transparency: Doctors and astronauts require transparency. The system does not act as a "black box"; it justifies every high-risk score with concrete biological drivers.
  • Automated Countermeasures: Immediately translates predictive analytics into actionable steps, such as initiating targeted resistive exercises or adjusting fluid intake protocols.

Intended Impact

The primary impact of OrbitCare is enabling crew autonomy. As NASA looks toward Mars and deep-space Artemis missions, communication delays of up to 20 minutes make real-time telemedicine with Earth-bound flight surgeons impossible. OrbitCare empowers astronauts to independently monitor, forecast, and correct their own physiological degradation in microgravity, preventing mission-critical medical emergencies.
Tools, Languages, and Technologies

  • Machine Learning & Data Processing: Python, XGBoost, Scikit-learn (MultiOutputRegressor), Pandas, NumPy.
  • Development Environments: VS Code, Google Colab / Jupyter Notebooks, Python virtual environments.
  • Deployment & Backend: Flask/FastAPI (for the prediction endpoints) and Joblib for model serialization.
  • Frontend UI: HTML/CSS/JavaScript with responsive, space-friendly dark mode vectors and dynamic status charting.

Creativity and Innovation

Our core innovation is modeling the Calcium-Hormone Loop rather than treating health conditions in silos. Bone loss, kidney stones, and women's reproductive health are deeply intertwined in microgravity. Disruptions in menstrual cycles impact estrogen, which accelerates bone density loss, which dumps calcium into the urinary tract, which heavily spikes the risk of kidney stones.

By utilizing a Multi-Output Regression architecture, our AI maps these hidden, non-linear relationships across interconnected bodily systems simultaneously—something traditional linear monitoring software cannot do.

Key Factors Considered

  1. Astronaut Time Constraints: We heavily prioritized UI minimalism. Complex image-classification (CNN) workflows for daily scans were deemed too time-intensive for the crew. We pivoted to high-impact biomarker questionnaires that yield similar predictive value with zero setup time.
  2. Data Privacy Restrictions: Because real NASA Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) data is restricted by HIPAA, we engineered a robust Python-based synthetic data generator. This allowed us to train and validate our XGBoost architecture using mathematically sound, clinical analog data without violating privacy laws.
  3. The "Black Box" Problem: We recognized that medical professionals will not trust a blind percentage. We intentionally engineered the system to extract and display Feature Importance, ensuring the AI is always clinically explainable.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Orbital_minds
projectDetails.summary:
### Project Summary – AstroVia: One Implant. Complete Health Insight.

**AstroVia** is an innovative, non-invasive smart health-monitoring patch designed to continuously monitor astronauts' health during long-duration space missions. The project aims to address the challenges of limited medical facilities, delayed health diagnosis, and the difficulty of monitoring multiple health parameters in space.

We propose a lightweight, flexible, skin-friendly wearable patch equipped with advanced biosensors, wireless communication, and AI-based health analysis. The system is designed to monitor vital parameters such as heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, glucose levels, liver function, bone health, and immune responses. Collected data would be transmitted wirelessly for real-time monitoring, early detection of abnormalities, and timely medical intervention.

Unlike conventional monitoring systems, AstroVia aims to integrate multiple health-monitoring capabilities into a single compact device without requiring needles or invasive procedures.

**The importance of AstroVia** lies in its potential to improve astronaut safety, reduce medical risks, and support longer space missions. Beyond space exploration, the technology could also contribute to remote healthcare and continuous patient monitoring on Earth.

AstroVia represents a proposed next-generation solution for safer, smarter, and healthier space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – AstroVia

Our project, AstroVia, is a smart health-monitoring patch designed to help astronauts stay healthy and safe during space missions. Astronauts face many health challenges in space, especially during long missions, where getting immediate medical help can be difficult. Our idea is to develop a simple, lightweight, and comfortable patch that can continuously monitor their health without using needles.

The patch is designed to be attached directly to the astronaut's arm. It uses multiple sensors to monitor important health indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen levels, glucose levels, and other biomarkers related to liver, bone, and immune health. The collected information is sent wirelessly to a monitoring system, where AI can help analyze the data. If the system notices any unusual changes, it can alert the astronaut so that necessary action can be taken early.

The main benefit of AstroVia is that it aims to bring several health-monitoring functions together into one small device. Instead of depending on different medical instruments, astronauts could use a single patch to keep track of their health. This could save time, reduce discomfort, and make health monitoring easier during long space missions.

For the proposed development, we have considered technologies such as biosensors, microcontrollers, wireless communication, AI-based data analysis, and a digital health-monitoring dashboard. The exact hardware components, programming languages, and software tools will be finalized during prototype development.

What makes our project creative is the idea of combining multiple health-monitoring features into one non-invasive wearable patch specially designed for astronauts. While designing AstroVia, our team focused on important factors such as astronaut safety, comfort, accuracy, lightweight construction, low power consumption, and reliable performance in space.

Our goal is not only to support astronauts but also to explore how this technology could help people on Earth. In the future, a similar device could be useful for patients, elderly people, military personnel, and people living in remote areas where regular medical facilities are not easily available.

Currently, AstroVia is a proposed concept, and further research, prototype development, and testing are needed to confirm its performance.

Through AstroVia, our team hopes to make health monitoring simpler, smarter, and more accessible, helping astronauts stay healthier and making future space missions safer.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: "VITALIS"
projectDetails.summary: Long space missions expose astronauts to five hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and a hostile closed environment. These cause immune changes, bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular problems and behavioural health problems. Help is delayed, so astronauts must spot changes in themselves. The Space Apps challenge asks for a visual tool that gathers indicators and helps them judge and act on their own health.
projectDetails.details:
The idea in one line

An astronaut-first, offline-first self-check tool that compares each person to their own baseline, explains every result, and says what to do and when to call the ground. Guidance, never diagnosis.

What is measured

Hazard

Indicators moved

Radiation

Dose against a mission budget, body temperature

Isolation

Mood, sleep, workload

Distance

Escalation guidance, offline mode, shareable report

Gravity

Heart rate, blood pressure, exercise load, strength

Closed environment

Blood sugar, nutrition and hydration, temperature

The brief names six indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood). The plan added exercise load and radiation dose to carry the gravity and radiation hazards.

What I built

  1. ART style prompt to get the project outline: the plan i thought off revised through and rewritten using Act as / Request / Terms and then Prompted into Claude to build out the initial versions.
  2. v1 demo: clickable figure, Time Warp and scenarios (it felt like documentation).
  3. v2 app (current): green and white, human-centred flow: Home, a one-minute guided check-in, indicator detail with trend and actions, and a report for the flight surgeon.

Scenarios, data and plan

  • Scenarios: Skipped Gym, Isolation Slide, Radiation Event, Sugar Swing, Recovery Arc (stretch: EVA heat stress, cabin CO2).
  • Data: a browser simulator, shaped by public NASA bedrest and PhysioNet patterns, clearly labelled simulated.
  • Run plan: prep (10 to 13 Nov), then a 48-hour hackathon (14 to 15 Nov) with scope cut-lines and a feature freeze at hour 30. Never cut: the figure, the traffic lights, the Learn and Act panels, Time Warp, one working scenario.
  • Design: Streamlit for the front ends, FastAPI for the back ends, and SQLite through SQLModel. Both APIs read the same SQLite database.
  • Open questions: official deliverables, which indicators to go deepest on, clinician review, which datasets to cite, camera input.

I CANNOT call this A FINISHED project but its CREATIVE

There is still so much development to be done which isnt possible in a 48 Hours hackathon, a lot of refinement and error correction has to be done. Fitness tracker is fine and all. Why not something specific- something deeper catering to the need of the Astronauts in space, heck even those going to MARS its a worth while creative project in my opinion in terms of Space research.

Other Considerations

Originally i thought to make it like a game, then i realised you don't really need a game to keep such highly motivated astronauts engaged- So i made a health tracker. I thought also to add a mini doll like figure which monitors their activity but then it felt more underwhelming- It can be worked upon and refined later into the development cycle.

projectDetails.name: LUNA-VIEW (Lunar Landing Site Intelligence & Mission Planning System)
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA-VIEW is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform designed to simplify the evaluation and comparison of potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole. Lunar missions face challenges due to extreme variations in sunlight availability and limited direct communication with Earth. Even small changes in landing location or date can significantly affect mission operations.

LUNA-VIEW brings essential mission-planning information into one intuitive application. Users can explore lunar landing locations, select mission dates, and visualize Sun and Earth positions relative to the lunar horizon.

Key features include interactive 3D lunar exploration, solar illumination analysis, Earth visibility and communication window tracking, dynamic mission timelines, and side-by-side landing site comparisons. It also aims to provide mission suitability assessments and AI-powered insights to help users evaluate alternative scenarios.

By transforming complex astronomical and geographical data into clear visualizations, LUNA-VIEW helps users understand how changes in landing locations and dates affect power generation and communication opportunities. It aims to support informed mission planning while making lunar exploration more accessible to researchers, educators, students, and the public.
projectDetails.details:
LUNA-VIEW

Lunar Landing Site Intelligence & Mission Planning System

Live Project: https://luna-view-frontend.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/renuasmitha/Luna-View

Project Overview

LUNA-VIEW is an interactive web-based platform designed to simplify the evaluation and comparison of potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole. It addresses two major challenges in lunar mission planning: extreme and rapidly changing solar illumination conditions and limited direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

The platform brings essential astronomical information into one intuitive interface, allowing users to explore potential lunar landing locations, select mission dates, visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon, and compare environmental conditions across different mission scenarios.

What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

LUNA-VIEW combines astronomical calculations, interactive visualizations, and mission comparison capabilities to help users understand changing lunar surface conditions.

Its key capabilities include:

1. Interactive Lunar Explorer

Allows users to explore potential lunar landing locations, examine candidate sites, and work with geographical coordinates to investigate different lunar regions.

2. Sun Position Intelligence

Visualizes solar elevation and estimates sunlight availability at selected locations. Users can examine how illumination conditions change over time and identify potentially useful sunlight windows for mission planning.

3. Earth Communication Tracker

Tracks Earth's apparent position relative to the local lunar horizon and identifies periods of geometric Earth visibility. This helps users understand potential direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

4. Mission Timeline Simulator

Provides a time-based view of changing Sun and Earth positions. Users can explore how environmental conditions evolve throughout a selected mission period.

5. Mission Comparison Centre

Enables side-by-side comparison of different landing locations and mission dates, helping users understand trade-offs between solar illumination and Earth visibility.

6. Mission Rescheduling

Helps explore alternative landing dates and locations when mission schedules change due to delays or technical constraints.

The backend uses NASA/JPL Horizons for astronomical ephemeris calculations, with an analytical fallback model when the external data service is unavailable.

Benefits and Intended Impact

LUNA-VIEW aims to reduce the complexity of evaluating lunar landing scenarios by presenting important astronomical information through accessible visualizations and comparative analysis.

It can help users:

  • Understand solar illumination patterns at different landing locations.
  • Identify potential Earth visibility and communication windows.
  • Compare alternative landing sites and mission dates.
  • Explore the impact of mission schedule changes.
  • Understand the relationship between sunlight availability and communication opportunities.

Beyond mission planning, the platform can serve as an educational resource for students, educators, researchers, and the general public, making complex astronomical concepts easier to explore.

Tools and Technologies

The project uses:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI
  • Astronomical Data: NASA/JPL Horizons API
  • Scientific Computation: Python-based analytical calculations
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub

The architecture separates frontend visualization from backend calculations, allowing the platform to retrieve astronomical time-series data through API endpoints.

Creativity and Innovation

The innovation behind LUNA-VIEW lies in bringing lunar exploration, astronomical visualization, temporal analysis, and mission comparison together in a single accessible platform.

Instead of requiring users to navigate multiple complex scientific tools, LUNA-VIEW provides an integrated environment where changing a landing location or mission date reveals how important operational conditions change.

Its focus on both solar illumination and Earth visibility highlights the trade-offs involved in lunar mission planning. A location with favourable sunlight conditions may not necessarily offer equally favourable Earth visibility, making comparative analysis particularly valuable.

Factors Considered

The project considers several important factors affecting preliminary lunar mission planning:

  • Solar elevation and illumination availability.
  • Earth's apparent elevation and geometric visibility.
  • Potential communication opportunities.
  • Mission dates and timeline variations.
  • Differences between candidate landing locations.
  • Data availability and calculation accuracy.
  • Accessibility and clarity of scientific visualizations.

LUNA-VIEW also emphasizes scientific transparency. Geometric Earth visibility does not guarantee an actual communication link, and sunlight availability does not directly represent electrical power generation. Actual mission conditions would also depend on terrain, equipment, antenna orientation, and other operational constraints.

Our Ultimate Vision

Our ultimate vision is to make lunar mission planning more accessible, interactive, and understandable by transforming complex astronomical information into meaningful visual insights.

LUNA-VIEW aims to evolve into a comprehensive lunar mission decision-support platform by incorporating validated lunar terrain and illumination datasets, more detailed environmental analysis, and advanced mission-planning capabilities.

By connecting scientific data with intuitive technology, we hope to contribute to a future where exploring and understanding the Moon becomes easier for researchers, students, and everyone interested in space exploration.

LUNA-VIEW is an independent educational and decision-support project developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is not an official NASA product and is not endorsed or validated by NASA.

projectDetails.name: SAR-based flood detection project
projectDetails.summary:
Flooding can damage communities, agriculture, and infrastructure. Rapid identification of inundated areas is important for disaster response and planning. This project proposes a flood detection workflow using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery from the Sentinel-1 satellite. Unlike optical satellites, Sentinel-1 collects useful observations during day and night and is less affected by cloud cover, making it valuable during severe weather.

The project will compare Sentinel-1 images acquired before and after a flood event over a selected study area. The imagery will be preprocessed through radiometric calibration, speckle filtering, and terrain correction. Changes in radar backscatter will then be analysed to identify locations where water has likely inundated previously dry land. A threshold-based classification method will create a preliminary flood extent map. Where reference data are available, the results will be compared with reference maps or optical imagery to assess reliability.

Expected outputs include processed SAR images, a flood extent map, and an estimate of the affected area. The project demonstrates how Earth observation and remote sensing can support flood monitoring and disaster management. It also highlights limitations such as radar shadow, urban surfaces, vegetation, and confusion with permanent water bodies. It can also help authorities prioritize emergency response and relief.
projectDetails.details: This project focuses on detecting and mapping flood-affected areas using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite imagery from the Sentinel-1 satellite. It works by comparing satellite images captured before and after a flood event to identify changes in water coverage and detect flooded regions. SAR technology uses microwave signals, allowing it to collect useful data during cloudy weather and at night. The satellite images are processed using techniques such as speckle filtering, backscatter analysis, and threshold-based classification to distinguish flooded areas from non-flooded regions. The project uses Python as the programming language, Google Earth Engine and Google Colab for satellite data processing, and libraries such as NumPy, Matplotlib, Rasterio, and Geemap for analysis and visualization. QGIS can also be used to view and analyse the generated flood maps. The major benefits of this project include faster flood detection, monitoring of affected agricultural and residential areas, and the use of freely available satellite data. Its intended impact is to support disaster management authorities, emergency response teams, and local communities by providing useful information for rescue operations and relief planning. The creative aspect of this project is the application of AI and remote sensing techniques to identify flooded areas using radar imagery instead of relying only on optical satellite images. projectDetails.details:
Orbit Guard – AI-Powered Space Waste Detection, Tracking and Collision Risk Monitoring System

1. Abstract

Orbit Guard is an AI-powered space monitoring system designed to detect, classify, track, and monitor space debris orbiting Earth. Space debris, also known as space junk, includes inactive satellites, abandoned rocket parts, broken spacecraft components, and small fragments. These objects create serious risks for operational satellites, space stations, astronauts, and future space missions.

Orbit Guard uses Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and orbital tracking technologies to identify and monitor space debris. It collects satellite orbital information from available datasets, analyzes object characteristics, and classifies different types of orbital objects.

The system also provides orbit visualization and collision-risk monitoring features to identify potentially dangerous close approaches between objects. An interactive web dashboard displays satellite locations, debris information, orbital paths, and warning notifications.

The main objective of Orbit Guard is to improve space safety, support satellite monitoring, and contribute to reducing the risks associated with increasing space pollution.

2. Introduction

Space technology plays an important role in modern life. Satellites are used for communication, navigation, weather forecasting, television broadcasting, and scientific research. However, the increasing number of satellite launches has resulted in growing space pollution.

Space debris consists of artificial objects orbiting Earth that are no longer useful. These objects include inactive satellites, abandoned rocket stages, and broken spacecraft components.

Even small debris fragments can damage operational satellites because objects in orbit travel at extremely high speeds. Collisions can also generate additional debris, increasing the problem.

Orbit Guard aims to address this challenge by developing an intelligent monitoring platform that combines AI, orbital data analysis, and interactive visualization to identify space debris and monitor potential collision risks.

3. Problem Statement

The increasing amount of space debris is becoming a major challenge for space organizations and satellite operators. Monitoring thousands of orbital objects and predicting their movements requires continuous tracking and complex calculations.

Traditional monitoring systems depend on specialized infrastructure and expert analysis. Therefore, an accessible and intelligent system is needed to identify orbital objects, track their movements, and estimate potential collision risks.

Orbit Guard proposes an AI-powered platform that simplifies space debris monitoring through automated classification, orbital visualization, and collision-risk alerts.

4. Objectives

  • To detect and classify space debris using AI and Machine Learning.
  • To collect and analyze satellite orbital information.
  • To track the positions and movements of orbital objects.
  • To visualize satellites and debris using a 3D Earth model.
  • To estimate potential collision risks.
  • To generate alerts for potentially dangerous close approaches.
  • To provide a user-friendly monitoring dashboard.
  • To support space safety and environmental sustainability.

5. Proposed System

The proposed Orbit Guard system combines Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, orbital mechanics, and web technologies.

First, the system collects orbital data from available satellite tracking sources. The collected information is processed using Python and stored in a database.

Next, a machine-learning model analyzes available object characteristics and classifies orbital objects into categories such as active satellites, inactive satellites, rocket bodies, and debris.

The orbital tracking module estimates object positions and displays their movements around Earth. A collision-risk analysis module compares predicted positions to identify potentially dangerous close approaches.

Finally, the system generates notifications and displays the results through an interactive dashboard.

6. Technologies Used

Technology

Purpose

Python

Main programming language

Machine Learning

Object classification

Scikit-learn

ML model development

OpenCV

Image processing

NumPy and Pandas

Data processing

Skyfield and SGP4

Orbital calculations

Flask / FastAPI

Backend development

HTML, CSS, JavaScript

Frontend development

Three.js

3D Earth visualization

SQLite / MySQL

Database management

Streamlit

Interactive dashboard

7. Main Modules

Module 1: Data Collection

This module collects satellite and orbital information from available datasets and APIs. It stores object IDs, satellite names, orbital parameters, and other tracking details for further analysis.

Module 2: AI-Based Object Classification

This module uses Machine Learning to classify orbital objects into categories such as active satellites, inactive satellites, rocket bodies, and space debris. The model analyzes available object characteristics and historical datasets to identify different object types.

Module 3: Orbit Visualization

This module displays orbital objects using an interactive 3D Earth model. Users can view satellite positions, debris locations, orbital paths, and object information. Three.js can be used to create the visualization.

Module 4: Collision Risk Detection

This module analyzes the predicted positions of selected orbital objects to identify potentially dangerous close approaches. It estimates the separation distance and approach time and assigns Low, Medium, or High risk categories based on configured criteria.

A close approach does not automatically mean a collision. Reliable collision probability requires orbital uncertainty analysis.

Module 5: Alert and Notification

This module generates alerts when potentially dangerous close approaches are detected. Notifications include object IDs, estimated approach times, separation distances, and risk categories.

Module 6: Admin Dashboard

The dashboard displays total tracked objects, active satellites, identified debris, object classifications, orbital visualizations, and collision-risk alerts.

8. System Architecture

Orbital Data Sources

Satellite tracking datasets and APIs

Data Processing

Python, NumPy and Pandas

AI and Orbital Analysis

Classification, tracking and risk estimation

3D Orbit Map

Collision Alerts

Orbit Guard Web Dashboard

9. Working Process

  1. Collect orbital data from available satellite tracking sources.
  2. Process and store the collected information.
  3. Use AI to classify different orbital objects.
  4. Calculate estimated satellite and debris positions.
  5. Display orbital movements through a 3D Earth model.
  6. Compare predicted positions to identify close approaches.
  7. Generate collision-risk alerts.
  8. Display object details and monitoring results on the dashboard.

10. Advantages

  • Provides centralized space debris monitoring.
  • Supports AI-based object classification.
  • Displays orbital movements in 3D.
  • Identifies potentially dangerous close approaches.
  • Generates automated monitoring alerts.
  • Reduces manual data analysis efforts.
  • Supports space research and satellite safety.
  • Can be expanded with additional datasets and features.

11. Applications

  • Space research organizations.
  • Satellite operating companies.
  • Aerospace engineering institutions.
  • Space traffic management.
  • Educational institutions.
  • Space sustainability research.
  • Satellite monitoring programs.

12. Future Enhancements

  • Integration with additional real-time orbital datasets.
  • Improved AI classification accuracy.
  • Advanced collision probability estimation.
  • Mobile application development.
  • Historical space debris analysis.
  • Automated monitoring reports.
  • Integration with space debris removal mission-planning simulations.

13. Expected Outcome

The expected outcome is an intelligent web-based application that identifies and classifies orbital objects, tracks their movements, visualizes satellite orbits, and estimates potential collision risks.

Users can explore a 3D Earth model, view tracked objects, monitor their orbital paths, and receive alerts about potentially dangerous close approaches.

14. Conclusion

Orbit Guard is an innovative project that combines Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, orbital mechanics, and data visualization to address the growing problem of space debris. It provides an intelligent platform for detecting orbital objects, monitoring their movements, and estimating potential collision risks. Through its interactive dashboard and automated alert system, the project supports better space awareness and safer satellite operations.

Orbit Guard aims to contribute to a cleaner, safer, and more sustainable space environment for future generations.

15. Reference Websites

  • CelesTrak  – Satellite orbital datasets.
  • Space-Track  – Space object tracking information.
  • NASA  – Space research and orbital debris information.
  • European Space Agency  – Space debris research.

Recommended hackathon demonstration: Show an orbital object being detected, classified by AI, displayed on a 3D Earth, and monitored for a potential close approach. This will demonstrate the complete working concept of OrbitGuard.

projectDetails.name: Space Mission Design Game
projectDetails.summary:
Space Mission Design Game is an interactive, browser-based aerospace simulation prototype built using HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript. Players design multi-stage rockets, configure avionics and propulsion subsystems, manage mission budgets, and execute real-time orbital launches across targets like Low Earth Orbit, the Moon, and Mars.
​By integrating authentic astrodynamics—such as the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, planetary phase-angle launch windows, cold-gas RCS maneuvering, and cryogenic propellant boil-off—the game bridges complex orbital engineering with accessible visual simulation. This makes it an impactful educational and hackathon tool for demonstrating real-world spaceflight constraints, trade-off analysis, and mission planning interactively.

projectDetails.name: Mission X Spark
projectDetails.summary:
Mission X Spark is a free, mobile-first browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. Players run a Moon and Mars outpost for 10 days and manage three resources: power, oxygen and radiation safety. No download or account is needed.

It answers the challenge by turning real mission constraints into gameplay. Every decision has a cost. Boosting radiation shielding uses power that life support needs, and an extra experiment earns science points but strains oxygen. Solar storm events are based on real NASA space weather data (DONKI), so kids see how real solar activity affects survival. Events vary between playthroughs, and when a mission fails the game explains why, so kids learn from it.

It matters because most space content for kids shows the outcomes of missions, not the decisions behind them. Mission X Spark lets children experience the trade-offs that astronauts and mission planners handle, in plain language, with sources credited. They leave understanding that no choice in deep space is free.
projectDetails.details:
Mission X Spark is a mobile-first astronaut mission game for kids aged 7-12. Players act as junior astronauts running a Moon and Mars outpost over a 10-day mission. Each day they make decisions to balance three critical resources: power, oxygen, and radiation safety. We want to spark curiosity about space and science in young learners and show that space exploration depends on careful decisions as much as on rockets. By connecting gameplay to live NASA data, kids learn that space science is real, current, and something they could contribute to one day.

Tools and technologies

Deployment: Vercel (web hosting), with a custom domain at missionxspark.space https://mission-x-spark.vercel.app/

Front end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript [ e.g., React/Next.js, and any game or animation libraries]

Data: NASA space weather data ['DEMO_KEY', e.g., NASA DONKI, if that’s what you used]

Design: Mobile-first, responsive layout with a dark “space” theme [add design tools, e.g., Figma, Canva]

Hardware: Developed on [laptops/phones]; it runs on phones, tablets, and computers

It turns real, live NASA data into game events, so the game is never just a fixed script.

Balancing three competing resources creates real trade-offs: using more power may protect the crew, but it can drain oxygen.

Kids take on the role of mission commander rather than just answering quiz questions.

The Moon-to-Mars setting connects to NASA’s current exploration goals.

Age-appropriateness: Simple language, clear visuals, and a 10-day structure that is short enough to finish.

Accessibility: Mobile-first design, since many kids use phones or tablets, and no sign-up so there is no barrier to playing.

Scientific accuracy: Using real NASA data while simplifying concepts without making them wrong.

projectDetails.name: Project The Gang**INTERPLANETARY SURVIVAL GUIDE: MARTIAN MAP**  **Tagline:** Explore Mars. Understand the Risks. Survive Beyond Earth.
projectDetails.summary:
The Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map is an interactive, data-driven platform designed to support safer and smarter human exploration of Mars. It brings Martian geographical information, terrain visualization, environmental conditions, potential hazards, route-planning insights, mission information, and scientific discoveries together in one unified interface.

The platform transforms complex planetary information into accessible visual insights, helping users explore Martian regions, understand environmental challenges, and evaluate potential exploration routes. By utilizing NASA's free and open planetary datasets and relevant space agency partner data, the project aims to make Mars exploration information more understandable and useful for researchers, students, mission planners, and future explorers.

Our vision is to support informed decision-making and contribute to the future of sustainable human exploration beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
INTERPLANETARY SURVIVAL GUIDE: MARTIAN MAP

Problem Statement

Human exploration of Mars involves significant challenges, including unfamiliar terrain, extreme environmental conditions, potential hazards, and limited accessibility to complex planetary information. Understanding these challenges is essential for planning safer exploration missions.

Proposed Solution

We propose an interactive Martian exploration and survival guide that consolidates geographical, environmental, hazard, mission, and scientific information into one platform. It helps users explore Mars and understand important factors that could influence future exploration decisions.

Key Features

  • Interactive Martian geographical map
  • Multiple terrain and map visualization layers
  • Environmental information and analysis
  • Potential hazard visualization
  • Exploration route-planning functionality
  • Mars mission information
  • Scientific discoveries and research information
  • Survival-oriented decision-support insights

Technology Stack

Frontend: React.js, Vite, HTML, CSS, JavaScript

Backend: Python, FastAPI

Data Processing: Python-based data processing and JSON datasets

Visualization: Interactive map and geographical data visualization

Deployment: Vercel frontend and separately hosted FastAPI backend

NASA Open Data Contribution

NASA's free and open planetary datasets provide the scientific foundation for exploring Martian geography and environmental information. Relevant Space Agency Partner datasets can further enhance the platform's planetary exploration capabilities.

Target Users

  • Space researchers and scientists
  • Future Mars mission planners
  • Students and educators
  • Planetary exploration enthusiasts
  • Space technology developers

Expected Impact

The platform aims to improve access to Martian exploration information, simplify the understanding of planetary conditions, and support informed exploration planning.

Future Scope

  • Integration of additional NASA planetary datasets
  • Advanced AI-assisted hazard analysis
  • Improved terrain and elevation visualization
  • More advanced route optimization
  • Personalized astronaut survival recommendations
  • Expansion to other planetary exploration environments

Vision

To transform planetary data into actionable intelligence and help make humanity's journey beyond Earth safer, smarter, and more sustainable.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
