projectDetails.name: Project Ajnova
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA // Orbital EVA OS is a real-time health monitoring system and 3D digital twin for astronauts during spacewalks (EVA). We developed a Python backend and a Three.js dashboard that tracks heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO2), skin temperature, suit pressure and neutron radiation dose for each crew member, using simulated telemetry based on NASA's Risks of Human Spaceflight and radiation monitoring resources.

An AI co-pilot compares vitals against each astronaut's personal baseline, predicts drift toward danger 30 seconds ahead, and detects hypoxia, suit leaks, heat stress, radiation exposure and cumulative dose limits. It also separates real medical problems from sensor failures. When something goes wrong, ASTRA raises an alert, generates an incident report and recommends actions such as deploying shielding or boosting oxygen. A smart ring gives haptic warnings, and role-based access lets astronauts, doctors and admins see what they need.

This matters because on long missions with delayed communication with Earth, astronauts need early warning and autonomous decision support to stay safe.
projectDetails.details:
1) Startup

  1. You run demo2.py. It starts the server on 127.0.0.1:8050 and opens the browser automatically.
  2. It sets up a SQLite database with a table of astronauts (amira, lukas, yuki, each with a cumulative dose), an alerts table, and a users table. It also creates default accounts (user / doctor / admin) and prints them to the console.
  3. It starts a background worker thread and the AI.
  4. The server serves index.html, style.css and app.js from the static folder.

2) What the server does every second

The worker loops over every astronaut and runs step_simulation once per second:

  1. Reads the current scenario for that astronaut from the database. Each scenario has target values. For example, Suit Leak targets a heart rate of 154, SpO2 of 86% and suit pressure of 2.75 PSI.
  2. Applies fixes if they were pressed. Shielding returns neutron dose to 5.4, O2 Purge restores oxygen and pressure, and Cooling returns temperature to 36.5.
  3. Moves values gradually toward the target (ease_state), so a value drops or rises over about 30 seconds (radiation reacts about 5x faster). It then adds small random noise to look realistic.
  4. Generates a simulated PPG signal (260 samples, red and IR) containing a pulse at the current heart rate.
  5. Analyzes the signal (analyze_ppg): removes the baseline, smooths it, finds peaks, computes heart rate from the peak spacing, and computes SpO2 from the ratio between the two signals. If no pulse is found, it returns signal_ok = False.
  6. Updates the cumulative dose based on neutron rate and saves it to the database.
  7. Stores the result (HR, SpO2, temp, psi, neutron, cumulative dose) in LAST and sends it to the AI (AI.push).

3) What the AI does with each reading

  1. Checks for faults. Impossible values (e.g. heart rate 300) are classified as a sensor fault and ignored. If the PPG signal is lost 3 times in a row, heart rate and SpO2 are ignored.
  2. Smooths the latest readings.
  3. Applies clinical rules (assess). For example, SpO2 below 92 is a warning and below 88 is critical. Pressure below 3.5 is a warning and below 3.0 is critical.
  4. Predicts the future. After at least 10 samples, it computes the trend of each vital, predicts its value 30 seconds ahead, and converts the distance to the alert limit into a risk score from 0 to 1.
  5. Compares to a personal baseline. If a value moves far from that astronaut’s normal (4 standard deviations), it is logged as an anomaly. While everything is healthy, the baseline slowly updates.
  6. Determines the condition (Suit Leak, Heat Stress, Radiation, etc.) and picks the cause and recommended actions from the Playbook.
  7. Incidents. When a finding reaches warning level or higher, it opens an Incident Report, keeps updating it (worst values, timeline), closes it after 8 seconds of healthy data, and saves it to astra_incidents.jsonl.
  8. Watchdog. A second thread watches for silence. If no data arrives for 5 seconds, it declares “Telemetry Lost”.

4) What happens in the browser

  1. On load, app.js calls /api/me. If you are not logged in, the login screen appears.
  2. After login, permissions are applied to the interface: scenario buttons are locked for non-admins, fix buttons are locked for doctors, and astronauts see only themselves.
  3. Every second (setInterval) it calls /api/state/<astronaut> to get vitals, AI analysis and the PPG waveform. It also calls /api/ai/crew to color the crew dropdown with 🟢🟡🟠🔴 status icons and show the alert banner.
  4. It updates the HUD: values, panel colors (red on alert), the AI toast at the bottom (NORMAL / WARNING / CRITICAL / PREDICTIVE for early warnings), and the status dot at the top.
  5. ASTRA-Ring: during an alert the ring shakes and turns red or amber, and the ring and suit in the 3D scene change color too.
  6. The 3D scene (Three.js) runs in requestAnimationFrame (about 60 times per second), independent of the polling.

5) Full example: Suit Leak scenario

  1. The admin clicks Suit Leak, and the browser sends PUT /api/crew/amira/scenario.
  2. The server updates the scenario in the database.
  3. Over the next seconds, pressure falls from 4.30 toward 2.75, oxygen from 98.6 toward 86, and heart rate climbs.
  4. After about 10 seconds the AI notices the trend and shows a PREDICTIVE early warning, before any limit is crossed.
  5. Pressure crosses 3.5, so a warning fires, an Incident Report opens, and a red banner appears saying “HEALTH WARNING” with a View report button.
  6. The O2 Pressure Purge button lights up. When the astronaut or admin presses it, PUT .../overrides is sent.
  7. Values return gradually to normal. After 8 healthy seconds the incident closes, and the report stays available to copy or download.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: Project AL-AMN
projectDetails.summary: AXIOM is an AI-powered research assistant designed to improve how researchers assess fire-safety evidence from microgravity combustion experiments. It uses NASA combustion research resources to retrieve relevant findings, trace claims to their sources, and examine whether experimental conditions support a proposed mission scenario. Rather than treating every retrieved result as universally applicable, AXIOM highlights mismatches, identifies missing information, and can withhold unsupported conclusions. This addresses a key challenge in applying space-based combustion research to future mission safety: evidence must be interpreted within the conditions under which it was obtained. By making evidence, limitations, and uncertainty more transparent, AXIOM aims to help researchers make better-informed decisions and identify where further experiments are needed.
projectDetails.details:
AXIOM is an evidence-grounded research dashboard for exploring spacecraft fire safety in microgravity. It searches NASA combustion research and ties each surfaced claim to a source passage and page locator. Users can compare a hypothetical fire scenario with documented experiment conditions, see where evidence matches or is missing, and turn those gaps into clearly labeled experiment proposals that have not been conducted.

AXIOM helps users avoid applying results beyond the conditions they actually describe. Unknown or unreported values remain unknown; the dashboard does not present its comparisons as a fire-risk score, prediction, or safety certification. Its intended impact is to make research easier to trace and help identify questions for future study.

The project uses Python 3.12 and its standard library, a hand-written HTML/CSS/JavaScript dashboard, and pypdf for PDF text extraction. Optional hosted language models support research workflows; the core scenario comparison works locally without a key or network. Development and deployment tools include Docker and Docker Compose.

AXIOM’s creative approach is to make the limits of evidence visible: it works with located passages rather than unsupported summaries, compares conditions parameter by parameter, and converts documentation gaps into traceable proposals rather than invented results. Design factors include source provenance and reuse terms, scientific uncertainty, experimental context, and the need to distinguish research evidence from operational incidents and background material.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: ARES: The Mars Survival Map
projectDetails.summary: ARES is a browser game that teaches how to read a map of Mars in order to stay alive on it. You are an astronaut on foot in Jezero Crater with a limited oxygen tank. A stranded companion, ARES, needs three pieces of its ship. Every tile of the board is built from real NASA data: slope from the HiRISE 1 m terrain model, ground firmness from THEMIS night-time infrared, and the surface image from the HiRISE orthomosaic. An A* planner with a cost made from slope and ground softness draws the safest walk; the player can follow it or explore and pay for it in oxygen and risk. The game shows why this matters: at Perseverance's landing site the planned walk uses 15% less oxygen than the shortest one, crosses 8 dangerous tiles instead of 39, and cuts the chance of an accident from 68% to 18%. We checked the map against the real rover: Perseverance's own track stays on the ground our map calls safe. The game runs in 2D and 3D, in any browser, with nothing to install.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. ARES turns a 1.6 km × 1.52 km window of Jezero Crater, centred on Perseverance's landing site (18.4447° N, 77.4508° E), into a board of 40 × 40 tiles of 40 m each. The player walks tile by tile to recover three ship pieces and return before the oxygen runs out. Steep tiles and soft sand cost more oxygen; tiles steeper than 15° cannot be crossed; dangerous tiles carry a chance of an accident. Five map layers can be switched at any time: the game art, the real HiRISE photo, height, slope and night heat. A key switches between the 2D map and a 3D view of the same terrain, with third-person and first-person cameras. At the wreck, a ship computer holds every NASA image of the site, the four orbital maps and ground data measured live from the layers. The game has a main menu with settings and works on phones and tablets with touch controls.

How it works.

  • Data pipeline (Python, tools/): streams only the needed window of the HiRISE DTM by HTTP range requests, computes slope, reads THEMIS and HiRISE map tiles from NASA Mars Trek, and reads the Mars 2020 rover's waypoints, track and Navcam photos. Nothing is invented: every tile value comes from these products.
  • Route planner (game/astar.js): A* on the tile grid. Cost of a step = 40 m × (1 + 2.5 × (slope / 15°)² + 0.6 × softness), impassable above 15°. The tour over the three pieces is chosen by trying every order.
  • ARES, the companion (game/ares.js): not a language model. Directions are read off the real A* path; oxygen, slope and risk are computed from the data; other questions are answered by search over a written knowledge base about the NASA data and the mission, and each answer names its source. Unknown questions are refused instead of guessed.
  • Landing sites: besides Perseverance's site, the game offers three sites on ground no rover has reached (more than 200 m from the whole traverse), screened for slope, firmness and room like a real landing site.
  • Game (HTML, JavaScript, Canvas 2D, three.js for 3D). No build step, no server, no account.

Validation against the real rover. Perseverance drove across this same board (sols 14–386). On our map its tiles average 4.2° of slope against 6.1° for the whole board; 5.4% of its tiles are steeper than 10° against 10.1%; none of its 93 tiles is over our 15° limit; and our terrain heights match the rover's own recorded elevations to ±0.08 m at 85 stops. The real mission chose the same kind of ground our planner chooses.

Benefits and impact. Future crews will walk on Mars with a fixed amount of air. The shortest line on a map is often not the cheapest or the safest. ARES makes that visible and playable for children and students, from about age 10, and for the public: it teaches slope, thermal inertia and path planning through real mission data, and shows in numbers what a good route saves. The same method works for any place on Mars that has a terrain model.

What is not data (stated openly in the game and README). The story, the oxygen tank size, the accident probabilities, the 15° limit and the cost weights are our design choices. THEMIS is used as a relative measure inside this window, not as a calibrated temperature.

Tools and languages. JavaScript (ES modules), HTML/CSS, Canvas 2D, WebGL through three.js r160, Web Audio; Python with NumPy, SciPy and Pillow for the data tools; Git and GitHub Pages for hosting.

Links. Play: https://3zz2004.github.io/ARES-/ · Source code: https://github.com/3zz2004/ARES- · Project description (PDF): https://3zz2004.github.io/ARES-/demo/ARES_Project_Description.pdf

Use of AI (stated openly). AI tools were used to build what the team designed.

  • The team's own work: the idea and the design (a survival walk on real Mars data with a companion who reads the data for you; the rules, the levels, the oxygen, the landing sites); the decisions (e.g. a radiation layer was removed because no real data backed it; ARES may answer only from NASA data and must name his source; the route had to be checked against the real rover); direction, art direction and testing of every build.
  • Code: written with an AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) to the team's design, then tested and corrected by the team build by build. Stated in the README, in AI_DISCLOSURE.md, and in a comment and metadata tag in the game's HTML.
  • Images: the characters, ground textures, rocks and objects were generated with ChatGPT (OpenAI) image generation, to the team's art direction, then cut and placed by our own code. Every one is marked: a visible "AI-GENERATED ART" label on the game screen and in the opening cinematic, a banner on every source sheet in art_src/, and a text note in each PNG's metadata. No generated image contains NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
  • Not AI: all terrain, slope, thermal, rover-track and photo data is NASA/USGS data; no data was generated or changed by AI. No AI model runs inside the game: ARES answers with computation and search. The opening music is a human-made track from Pixabay; all other sound is synthesised by code.
  • Demo video: the pictures are rendered by code from the project's real map layers and routes and its AI-generated character art, and carry an "AI-generated visuals" label. The narration is an AI voice (ElevenLabs).

projectDetails.name: AlgoRythm
projectDetails.summary: AlgoRythm is an Earth Information Jukebox: it turns live NASA satellite data into sound you can explore with your ears and your keyboard. Choose one of seven datasets — Arctic sea ice, air temperature, sea surface temperature, rain and snow, severe storms, wildfires or volcanoes — then move a listening point across the real NASA frame. Pitch follows latitude, stereo follows longitude, brightness opens the filter, colour changes timbre and sharp edges become soft accents, while dark or missing data falls quiet. Nothing is a loop: every parameter is computed from the pixels under your listening point. An eight-second Time Machine morphs between two dated sea-ice frames and speaks the measured change: 7.1 to 4.2 million square kilometres between 31 August 1984 and 31 August 2026. Everything is keyboard-operable, captioned and transcribed, with a blindfold mode and a screen-reader mode. It matters because Earth science is published as colour imagery, which quietly excludes blind and low-vision learners from the data itself.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. AlgoRythm lets a person "listen to" a NASA Earth-data image instead of

reading its colour scale. The app requests a real frame from NASA GIBS, analyses it in the

browser, and maps what it finds to a continuous sound field. Moving the listening point —

by mouse, touch or arrow keys — changes pitch, stereo position, filter cutoff, timbre and

accents in real time, so a coastline, a storm eye or a shrinking ice edge becomes an audible

boundary rather than a colour you have to recognise.

How it works. Frames come through one small server-side caching proxy that serves NASA

GIBS imagery and EONET event metadata, so the browser never hits CORS problems and

the demo needs no API keys. Each frame is drawn to an OffscreenCanvas inside a Web

Worker; pixel colour is inverted through NASA's own published colormaps back into

physical values (degrees Celsius, mm per hour, ice fraction), and the analyser builds a 128-

column feature grid of hue, lightness, saturation, edge strength and decoded value. Those

features drive persistent Tone.js voices with smoothed ramps: vertical position sets pitch

quantised to the dataset's musical scale, horizontal position sets stereo and HRTF

placement, intensity sets a lowpass cutoff of 180 x 18^L Hz plus gain, the hue spectrum

crossfades four timbres, Sobel edge strength adds soft percussive accents, and wholeframe statistics shape an ambient bed. Sea-ice extent is computed with area weighting and

a 15 percent concentration threshold. Reverb uses real acoustic impulse responses, a

limiter protects the mix, and narration ducks the music by 12 decibels.

Time Machine. On sea ice and air temperature, one key plays an earlier frame and morphs

to a later one over eight seconds while the listening point sweeps the map. Pitch, cutoff,

gain and timbre are interpolated cell by cell between the two real analyses, so the sound

changes exactly as much as the data does, and the measured result is both displayed and

spoken: 7.1 to 4.2 million square kilometres of Arctic sea-ice extent between 31 August 1984

and 2026 (minus 41 percent), and 16.1 to 17.0 degrees Celsius of mean August air

temperature between 1980 and 2026.

Benefits and intended impact. Blind and low-vision learners, teachers and anyone who

cannot stare at a screen get a genuine way into NASA Earth data rather than a summary of

it. Keyboard-only operation, live captions, a full transcript, an aria-live region, a blindfoldand-reveal mode and a screen-reader mode are built in, not bolted on. The intended

impact is classroom and public use: a teacher can hand one dataset and one listening task

to a mixed-ability class, and a low-vision user can explore the same data independently.

Tools and stack. React and TypeScript with Vite on the front end; Tone.js and the Web

Audio API for synthesis, spatialisation and dynamics; Web Workers with OffscreenCanvas

for pixel analysis; a Node.js proxy with a disk cache; Python for the analysis and narrationbaking pipeline; deployed on Vercel. All imagery, event data and colormaps come from

NASA GIBS, EONET, Worldview and the Scientific Visualization Studio.

What made it creative. The design treats sonification as an instrument rather than an

alarm: a continuous, playable field you can move through, with a jukebox framing that

invites choosing a "track" of the planet. The Time Machine interpolates two real analyses

cell by cell instead of cross-fading two recordings, and blindfold mode asks listeners to

build a mental map before checking it against the picture.

What we considered. Scientific honesty first: the two sea-ice frames come from different

sensors and products, the 1984 polar gap is counted as ice, and the app says plainly that

this is a comparison of two frames, not a trend analysis, with NASA's long-term records as

the authority. We also weighed accessibility (contrast, focus order, reduced motion, no

mouse-only path), demo reliability (cached proxy, no key management), and licensing,

crediting every NASA source and the royalty-free impulse responses in the app and in the

video.

projectDetails.name: Project Mission Ares
projectDetails.summary:
Mission ARES is a browser game for kids aged 7–12 in which they run a small Mars outpost for two sols. Every choice trades three shared resources, Power, Water and Air: water the greenhouse or save it for the shield, heat the rover or risk the cold, wait for advice from Earth or go now.

Real NASA data drives the rules, not just the facts on screen. A live solar storm from NASA DONKI (with the WSA-Enlil model) sets the storm forecast, and the forecast can be wrong, so building a thicker water shield is a real gamble. Today's Earth–Mars message delay, worked out from NASA/JPL planet positions, decides how long players wait for help. Real Curiosity radiation readings from NASA RadLab and a space-plant study from NASA OSDR show what happened on Mars.

Kids learn that in space, and on Earth, nothing is free: every resource you use is one you can't use for something else. The game ends by linking each lesson to life on Earth, from water recycling to desert farming in Egypt.
projectDetails.details:
## What it does

Mission ARES is a story-driven resource-management game for kids aged 7–12 (ages 9–12 can play alone; younger players with a parent or teacher). The player is a boy who joins a crew landing at Jezero Crater on Mars. Over two Martian days the crew must keep three shared resources, Power, Water and Air, alive while doing their mission work:

- Greenhouse: choose how much water and light to give a real space crop (radish, lettuce, chile pepper...). More water means more food, but less water for later.

- Garage and rover: pick a heater for today's real Mars temperature, wait for advice from Earth or leave now, and drive to collect the rock scientists asked for.

- Night: solve an oxygen puzzle as the base runs on batteries until sunrise.

- Solar storm: a real solar eruption heads for Mars. Mission Control sends a forecast, and the player picks a thin, medium or thick water shield. Thicker is safer but costs more Power and locks up Water.

At the end, players get a score, see every choice they made and its effect, and read "Back on Earth" cards that connect each lesson to real life.

## How NASA data drives the game

- NASA DONKI (CME, with WSA-Enlil runs): the game fetches a real coronal mass ejection from the last 30 days that NASA's model sends toward Mars. Its speed and proton events set the storm forecast and the arrival date. If NASA can't be reached, one of three saved real events is used. The DONKI event ID is shown on screen.

- NASA/JPL planet positions: today's Earth–Mars radio delay is calculated live. It sets how long the rover waits for Earth's reply, and explains why a big flare's particles arrive before any forecast can.

- NASA RadLab (OSDR): real hourly radiation readings from Curiosity's RAD in May 2024 are drawn as a chart, flat at about 4 µGy/h, then 304 µGy/h when a storm hit Mars (about 74× higher).

- NASA OSDR (OSD-268): a real study of plants grown in space is shown in the greenhouse.

- Perseverance MEDA weather, NASA/JPL Photojournal images of Jezero's delta and of a solar eruption, and NASA Earth Observatory images of Egypt's farmland support the scenes.

Every fact on screen shows its source, and a "NASA data" screen lists them all, including a separate list of numbers we made up for game balance.

## Why it matters (impact)

The challenge asks kids to understand trade-offs: in a closed habitat, every resource you use is one you can't use for something else. That is also true on Earth. In Egypt, only about 4% of the land can grow crops and almost all water comes from the Nile. Water recycling, growing food with little water, and preparing for space weather that can hit satellites and power grids are real Earth problems. The game ends by linking each Mars decision to one of them, so kids carry the lesson home.

## What makes it creative

- Live data is part of the rules, not just shown: the real forecast can be wrong, so kids learn to plan for uncertainty, the way real mission planners do.

- The real Earth–Mars message delay turns "waiting for help" into a decision.

- Kids see real Mars data (a radiation chart, a real eruption photo, a real delta photo), not just numbers in text.

- All the art, animation and sound are made in code: no image or sound files besides two real NASA photos.

## Design choices we considered

- Three resources only (Power, Water, Air) plus crew mood, as the challenge suggests, so kids can track everything on one tablet screen.

- No choice is free and no choice is always right. We wrote a balance checker that played every possible choice combination (540 situations, 1.86 million games) to make sure of this, and set the badge scores from the results.

- Short sentences and a pause button for young readers, plus story speed controls.

- Works offline or when NASA's servers are slow: every live call has a saved real fallback.

- Judge Mode and a "For judges" panel make the demo repeatable and jump straight to the key moments.

- Honesty: a "Made up for the game" list separates game rules from real NASA data.

## Tools and technologies

React, TypeScript and Vite; SVG for all graphics; the Web Audio API for sound; NASA Open APIs (DONKI); NASA OSDR RadLab data API; Node's built-in test runner (automated tests) and oxlint. Runs in any modern browser, on a laptop or a tablet.

## Team

Fares Mostafa, Merna Hossam, Eman Ahmed, Amr Obaia, Ahmed Zahran (Team Alienated, NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026).

## Use of AI

We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write and review code and text. No AI-generated images, video or audio are in the game. All facts are checked against the NASA sources listed in the game.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Outpost 0: The Mission Of A Lifetime
projectDetails.summary:
Skibidi toilet gets more attention from kids than the Moon does. Outpost 0 is our way of fighting back. 
Outpost 0 is an educational game that teaches children aged 7 to 12 about space through play. Players manage a space outpost and make decisions that have real consequences. Every choice, from rationing oxygen to repairing equipment, changes the base’s resources and safety, so players learn what it takes to survive and work in space.
Our game addresses the Junior Astronaut challenge by turning NASA data into events and scenarios that players face. Instead of reading facts, kids see how real space data shapes decisions, which makes the science easier to remember.
Many children find space and science hard to connect with. Outpost 0 gives them a safe, fun way to build curiosity, problem-solving skills and an understanding of life beyond Earth. We tested the game with our team member, 11 years old, in our target age group, and her feedback shaped its design.
projectDetails.details:
Outpost 0 is a 3D browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player is sent from Earth to save the crew of Outpost 0, a base on the Moon or Mars that was damaged by a solar storm. They start in Mission Control, pick the Moon or Mars, pack their rocket and fly there. On the base they keep three resources alive: Power, Shield and Air & Water. Problems come in over the radio, and each one is a short mini-game, like aiming solar panels, blocking radiation, cleaning water or drilling for ice. After each mission they get a real space fact, and at the end they fly the crew home. There’s also a short training mode with 3 levels.

The game runs on real NASA data. We use DONKI (https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/tools/DONKI/) for real solar flares, CMEs and geomagnetic storms: a bigger flare sends more radiation at the base, a faster CME gives less time to protect the solar panels, and a stronger storm adds more radio noise. We use NASA APIs (https://api.nasa.gov) for the Photo of the Day, Earth photos and asteroids passing Earth today. We use NASA EONET (https://eonet.gsfc.nasa.gov) to show real fires, storms and volcanoes on a map. Because the data is live, every game is a bit different.

What makes it different is that the NASA data isn’t just text on a screen, it changes the game itself. There are no multiple-choice tasks, so kids learn by doing. It also has a full story, from launch to rescue to coming home. Kids get a small alien buddy called Zee who shows them where to go, they can design their own astronaut and rocket, and they unlock new gear by learning.

Most space information is only available in English, so we built a full Arabic version with a talking commander, so kids in Egypt and the Arab world can learn in their own language. We kept everything simple for young kids, with short sentences, big buttons, and voice with subtitles. Every fact comes from a NASA or published source.

We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using Three.js (https://threejs.org) for the 3D. It runs in any browser with no install and is hosted on GitHub Pages. Moon radiation facts come from the Chang’e 4 study (Science Advances, 2020).

This is a working prototype. In the future we want to add more missions, more NASA data, and more languages so kids everywhere can learn about space.

We used Claude and Manus AI to help debug the game's code (HTML, CSS and JavaScript). Claude also translated the game into Arabic for the translation option. The idea, story, game design and testing with our 11-year-old team member are our own work. All AI-assisted code and text were reviewed by our team. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used in the game.

projectDetails.name: A Little Hero
projectDetails.summary: Welcome to A Little Hero! Meet NEILO, an Egyptian child from the land of the Nile, who helps children around the world become the heroes of a mission to sustain life on Mars. We developed an interactive, personalized learning experience for children aged 7–12. Each child leads the mission, and the journey is designed to adapt to their choices. Guided by NEILO and characters inspired by our team’s backgrounds in agricultural engineering, petroleum engineering, medicine, and AI, children face challenges involving water, energy, food, crew health, communication with Earth, and protecting the crew from radiation. NASA data helps reveal the risks behind these challenges and brings them into the experience. More than a game, A Little Hero makes space exploration a hands-on learning experience that builds curiosity, problem-solving skills, and awareness of how to care for people and resources. Today’s children are tomorrow’s engineers and doctors, so helping them become informed and make responsible decisions is important for life on Earth and beyond.
projectDetails.details:
NEILO’s Project Solution

NEILO: First Signal is an educational adventure game designed for children approximately 7–12 years old. The game places the player inside an abandoned research base on Mars after a guidance problem separates the player’s capsule from the main crew.

With the help of NEILO, a small companion robot, the player must restore the base and make important decisions about energy, water, agriculture, and radiation. The game turns Mars science into interactive missions instead of presenting it as a simple slideshow.

The player begins by exploring the Arrival Bay, following the glowing objective, and finding NEILO. After that, the player completes four main missions that are connected to one another:

Agriculture: Choose and grow food for the crew.

Power Generation and Engine Activation: Repair the water-pump circuit.

Radiation Discovery: Study Curiosity/RAD measurements and repair the relay.

Water Preparation: Prepare enough water for the waiting crew.

How Does Our Solution Work?

In the game, the player progresses through a sequence of missions. Each mission has a clear objective, a limited number of actions, and a visible result. The missions demonstrate that a Mars base depends on several connected systems.

Agriculture — Plan the First Fresh Food

The player enters the Garden Workshop and chooses between two crops that growing in suitable space conditions : lettuce and soybean. The selected seed packet must be dragged into the growing tray.

After planting, the player must:

Turn on the grow light.

Give the crop water.

Advance the growth simulation.

Wait for the crop to reach the correct growth stage.

Harvest the crop.

This mission teaches that agriculture on Mars requires planning. The player must consider crop type, growth time, water, light, harvesting, and the needs of the crew

Power Generation and Engine Activation — Give the Water Pump a Heartbeat

In this mission, the player repairs the water-pump circuit. The player must turn on the breaker and connect the two cables correctly:

Connect the amber output cable to the amber socket on the water pump.

Connect the blue return cable to the blue socket.

Close the circuit so power can reach the pump motor.

The game explains that power moves the motor, and the motor turns the pump. This gives the player a simple introduction to electrical circuits, motors, machines, and energy management.

The task teaches that energy is limited and that the player must decide which system should operate first.

Radiation Discovery — Study Mars Field Evidence

The player opens the Field Notes mission and studies evidence collected from Mars. The mission shows a Murray Buttes diagram and a graph connected to the Curiosity rover and the RAD instrument.

The player can see:

The Curiosity/RAD measurement graph.

The Mars surface location.

The date of the observation.

The absorbed dose-rate reading in µGy/hour.

The task called “Repair the relay”, which allows the crew to receive the field notes.

This mission teaches children how scientific data should be read. Every measurement needs a place, instrument, date, and unit. The game presents the radiation readings as scientific evidence, not as a human safety limit.

Water Preparation — Prepare Water for the Waiting Crew

The player must prepare water before informing the crew that the base is ready. The water unit is connected to the power system and used to prepare water packs.

One water cycle:

Uses 2 battery units.

Prepares 2 water packs.

Helps the player reach the goal of 5 prepared water packs.

The water mission teaches that life-support resources must be prepared before communication or exploration. The crew cannot depend on the base until essential water supplies are ready.

What Benefits Does It Have?

NEILO helps children understand how a Mars habitat works through direct interaction and problem solving.

The game provides several benefits:

It teaches systems thinking by connecting power, water, food, communication, and safety.

It develops planning skills through crop selection and growth timing.

It teaches children how to read scientific measurements and understand their limits.

It encourages decision-making because the player has limited energy and must complete tasks in the correct order.

It makes science more accessible through NEILO’s explanations and guidance.

What Do We Hope to Achieve?

We hope to make Mars exploration understandable, educational, and enjoyable. Players should learn that living on Mars would require much more than landing a spacecraft.

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas and Web Audio

projectDetails.name: Almatafi
projectDetails.summary: We developed Almatafi, a web platform that merges 25 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections from MODIS and VIIRS into one consistent record, so any month anywhere on Earth can be judged against its own history. The two sensors cannot simply be joined: in one week of real FIRMS data, VIIRS reported 300,095 hotspots where MODIS reported 58,127, so a plain join shows a false surge in 2012. Almatafi converts MODIS to VIIRS-equivalent counts per region, season and overpass time, fitted on the years both sensors flew and tested on years the fit never saw. Users draw any area and get its burning calendar since 2001: the normal range for each month, how unusual this month is, the long-term trend, each hotspot on the map, and downloads for GIS tools. A learning game, a guide character and a voice-controlled accessibility mode open it to non-experts. This matters because fire managers need to tell a routine season from an unprecedented one, as in Río Negro in July 2026 or the Nile Delta's rice-straw season, and that answer should not depend on which satellite was watching. At submission, the method and the app are complete and tested; the 25-year record on the live site still runs on a simulated FIRMS-format data set, which the site labels, while the globe, the map imagery, the cloud cover and the live hotspots are real NASA data.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Almatafi answers one question for any place on Earth: is this fire season normal? You choose an area (draw a polygon or a box, search a place, pick a province, or type a latitude and longitude) and the site shows:

1.    The answer in one sentence, for example "October 2026: 589 hotspots. Unusually high: 2.4 times a typical October, and the most for October in 26 years."

2.    A burning calendar: every month since 2001 as a grid of years and months, on one consistent record.

3.    Statistics for the chosen month: typical value, usual range, rank, percentile, z-score, and the long-term trend.

4.    A map of the individual hotspots with their details (time, satellite, fire power, confidence), each detection's pixel footprint, the satellite image of that day and a smoke layer.

5.    Downloads: hotspots as CSV, GeoJSON or KML, the calendar as CSV, and the 0.1° grid as a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF. A share link reopens the same view.

The explorer on the live site: the answer for the chosen month, its statistics, the burning calendar since 2001 and the hotspots on the map. Nile Delta, October 2026 (simulated record; see Limitations).

The challenge's own case, Río Negro in July 2026, against every July since 2001.

How to try it

Two minutes, no login.

1.    Home page, "Open Río Negro, July 2026": read the answer, then click any other month in the calendar.

2.    Open the Nile Delta and switch between "MODIS only", "VIIRS only" and "Harmonized". The same fires give different counts. The slider under the map moves from the raw join to our record and the step at 2012 disappears.

3.    Press "Play" and try one chapter of "Normal or not?".

"Try it in two minutes" on the home page.

The problem

MODIS (since 2000, 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m pixels) detect the same fires differently. VIIRS sees smaller and cooler fires, so it reports several times more hotspots. In the real FIRMS week of 27 October to 3 November 2026, VIIRS on NOAA-20 reported 300,095 detections and MODIS on Terra and Aqua 58,127 (5.2 times more); over the Nile Delta it was 88 against 7. Joined as they are, the two records show fire seeming to explode in 2012, and no month before 2012 can be compared with one after it.


The raw dataset combines MODIS observations with VIIRS observations starting in 2012, creating an apparent jump in fire activity.

The harmonized dataset adjusts for differences between the two sensors, removing the artificial jump and providing a more consistent historical record.

How it works

1.    Clean. Each FIRMS row is parsed strictly. Low-confidence detections are dropped (MODIS confidence under 30, VIIRS "low"). Only vegetation fires are kept; cells that the archive flags again and again as static sources (gas flares, industry, volcanoes) are masked.

2.    Common grid. Both sensors are counted on the same global 0.1° grid (about 10 km), per month, satellite and day or night pass, as detections and as fire days. This removes the pixel-size difference.

3.    Sensitivity. VIIRS detections are split at the fire power MODIS needs to see a fire (its detection floor, which grows with pixel area; Sofiev and Kouznetsov 2026). Fires above the floor are converted from MODIS by a ratio learned per 10° tile and calendar month. Fires below the floor, which MODIS cannot see, come from each cell's own VIIRS record, scaled by how active that year was.

4.    Overpass time. Aqua and VIIRS pass at about 13:30, Terra at 10:30. Aqua is calibrated against VIIRS on 2012 to 2022, Terra against Aqua on 2003 to 2011, day and night separately. NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 fill gaps in Suomi NPP after their own calibration, and carry the record since Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026.

5.    Model choice. Four conversion models (ratio, log-linear, quantile mapping, and the split model above) are scored by leave-one-year-out: fit without a year, predict it, compare. The best one is used.

6.    Analysis. For an area, the monthly count is the sum of the cells whose centre is inside it. The baseline is the same month in the other years. Percentile, z-score, Sen's slope for the trend. The current month is compared with the same days of past years.

7.    Clouds (optional view). A fire under cloud is not detected. Each cell's count can be divided by its clear-sky share, using NASA's daily MODIS cloud fraction averaged per month, capped at five times. Months that were more than half under cloud are marked.

The Method page: the three differences between the sensors and the fix for each.

Evidence

The pipeline was developed on a simulated data set in the exact FIRMS file format: six regions, 26 years, with known true fires that each simulated sensor sees with its own pixel size, sensitivity and overpass time. Because the truth is known, the method can be checked against it. Results on that data set:

1.    Leave-one-year-out, predicting VIIRS from MODIS for years left out of the fit: R² 0.976 on 1,341 tile-month totals (0.968 on small 1° areas).

2.    Break at 2012 (hotspots after 2012 divided by before): raw join 4.61 times, our record 1.03 times.

3.    Pettitt change-point test: raw join p = 0.0003 (a break), our record p = 0.85 (none).

4.    Placebo break years inside one sensor's era (2005, 2007, 2017, 2020): 0.85 to 1.08 times, so 1.03 at 2012 is ordinary.

5.    Against the known true fires, per region: raw join 3.2 to 15.0 times, our record 0.95 to 1.08 times.

On real NASA data so far: real FIRMS country files (MODIS 2010 for Egypt, Argentina and Chile, 71,180 rows; VIIRS 2019 for Egypt, 67,424 rows) pass through the cleaning step with no row rejected, and the format matches. The code has 559 automated tests (228 pipeline, 229 backend, 102 frontend) that run on every change.

The Method page: validation results, published in the app.

Working now

1.    The whole web app at the link above: explorer, calendar, statistics, map, downloads, share links, the Method page with the validation.

2.    The full pipeline: clean, grid, harmonize, validate, and a tool that downloads the FIRMS archive and near-real-time data.

3.    Real NASA data on the live site: the globe's week of fires (FIRMS public 7-day files), all map and globe imagery (GIBS), the cloud cover behind the cloud-corrected view (MODIS cloud fraction, 2000 to 2026), and live hotspots from the FIRMS API for the last days in any area.

4.    "Normal or not?", a five-chapter game with 14 questions that teaches what a hotspot is, why the two satellites disagree, and how to read a fire season.

5.    Wel3a, a flame guide on every page: written tips, and a chat that answers questions from a fixed fact sheet and the numbers on screen.

6.    An accessibility mode with eight tools, listed under "Accessibility tools" below.

7.    A guided tour of the explorer, a narrated story on the home page with captions, and an offline copy of the two demo regions if the server cannot be reached.

"Normal or not?", the learning game.


Wel3a, the guide; its answer notes that the numbers are simulated.

How the site explains its three NASA FIRMS sources to visitors.

Accessibility tools

One round button on every page (bottom right, or Alt + A on the keyboard) opens the accessibility panel. With the mode off, the site is unchanged. With it on, these tools are available, and the choices are remembered on the device:

1.    Text size: Normal, Large, Larger or Largest, with A− and A+ buttons. All text grows, including the calendar's numbers; the map keeps its size.

2.    High contrast: pure black and white, thick outlines, underlined links, and no scenery behind the numbers.

3.    Reduce motion: still images instead of the 3D globe, the films and the page transitions.

4.    Keyboard mode: a focus ring that is always visible, skip links at the top of every page (to the content, the answer, the calendar, the map and the downloads), arrow keys to move between months in the calendar, and the Alt shortcuts below.

5.    Voice reading: the site says aloud what you land on (its name, what kind of control it is and its state), reads the answer when the month changes and announces each new page. "Read this page" reads the whole page from the top; Escape stops the voice.

6.    Voice commands ("Say a command", or Alt + M): "open the explorer", "method", "play the game", "home", "read the page", "stop", "bigger text", "smaller text", "high contrast", "contrast off", "reduce motion", "Nile Delta", "Río Negro", "next month", "previous month", "show MODIS", "show VIIRS", "show harmonized", "click" followed by a button's name, and "help". "Keep listening" leaves the microphone on for one command after another.

7.    Keyboard shortcuts: Alt + A opens the panel, Alt + K lists the shortcuts, Alt + R reads the page, Alt + V turns voice reading on or off, Alt + M listens for a command, Alt + plus and Alt + minus change the text size, and Alt + 1, 2, 3 and 4 go to the story, the explorer, the Method page and the game.

8.    A six-step guide opens the first time the mode is turned on, with the real controls inside each step, and can be reopened from the panel ("Open the guide"). "Shortcuts and commands" shows the full list at any time.

Voice reading and voice commands use the browser's own speech features (Chrome, Edge and Safari).

The accessibility panel with the mode on: every tool in one place.


"Shortcuts and commands": the keyboard shortcuts and the voice commands.

The explorer in high contrast with Larger text.

Step 5 of the six-step guide: voice reading and voice commands, with the real controls inside the step.

Limitations

1.    The 25-year record on the live site is built from the simulated data set, not yet from the real FIRMS archive. The calendar numbers for the Nile Delta and Río Negro, and the validation numbers above, are therefore simulated. The site says so on the home page, the Method page and in the guide's answers.

2.    A hotspot is not a fire, and no hotspot is not proof of no fire: clouds, smoke, small fires and timing hide fires. The calendar counts detections, not burned area.

3.    The record sits on a 0.1° grid, so areas smaller than four cells are coarse and get a warning.

4.    January 2001 to June 2002 has Terra only; single months there are less reliable where fires burn in the afternoon.

5.    The cloud-corrected view leans high (thin cloud and haze count as cloud); read it as an upper bound.

6.    "Alert me" shows a preview of the alert email; no email is sent yet.

7.    Voice commands depend on the browser's speech recognition (Chrome, Edge, Safari).

The limits, as shown on the Method page.

Future plans

1.    Build the record from the real FIRMS archive, first for Egypt, Argentina and Chile, then globally, and publish the validation on real data.

2.    Use FIRMS's own list of days without data for coverage, and add land-cover classes to the conversion.

3.    Compare with burned-area products as an independent check that no 2012 step remains.

4.    Send real "unusual month" alerts by email.

Benefits and aim

Fire managers can tell a routine season from a surge on one record that does not change meaning when the satellites do. Scientists get one sensor-independent monthly series from 2001 with its validation published. Land managers and farmers can see the critical months before they arrive. Students and the public can learn how fire is seen from space through the game and the guide. Our aim is a public tool that gives the same answer for the Nile Delta's rice-straw season and for a winter outbreak in Patagonia, whichever satellite was overhead.

Tools

Pipeline: Python 3.12, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, DuckDB, Parquet and GeoParquet. Backend: FastAPI, DuckDB, Shapely, pyproj, rasterio (Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF), httpx; Docker image run with Podman. Web app: Next.js, React and TypeScript; MapLibre GL with Terra Draw for the map; three.js for the globe; GSAP and Lenis for scrolling; TanStack Query and Zustand. Hosting: Cloudflare Workers (site and the guide's AI function), a small server behind Cloudflare Tunnel (API), GitHub Actions for tests and deployment. Video: Remotion and FFmpeg.

projectDetails.name: Refaey on the Moon
projectDetails.summary: Refaey on the Moon is a web app for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. At the Moon's south pole, the Sun and Earth stay within a few degrees of the horizon, so a single ridge can cut a lander's solar power and its direct radio link to Earth. Our app lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates quickly: a guide character, Refaey, walks you through choosing a site, standing on it in 3D, seeing the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, comparing sites, and picking a launch date. Then it tells you what went wrong and what would have been better. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons, and the terrain horizon from NASA's LRO laser altimeter (LOLA). We checked the results against JPL Horizons and published NASA values. It turns a complicated expert task into a few clear choices, so anyone can understand why site and timing matter for power and communication at the lunar poles.
projectDetails.details:
Refaey on the Moon is a lunar landing-site navigator for the Moon's south pole. There, the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon, and a single ridge can decide whether a lander gets power or can see Earth. You pick a site and a landing date, and the app shows, through each lunar day, when the Sun clears the real terrain (power) and when Earth is in view (communications). It also shows how long until sunset and Earthset, and the best landing windows across several months.

How it works. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons. The horizon is the real skyline, traced in 720 directions from NASA LOLA elevation maps (PGDA products 81 and 90). The Sun counts as "up" when any part of its disk clears that skyline. We checked our engine carefully: its Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.01°, it matches the Sun angles at four Apollo landings within 0.1°, and over a full year at the IM-2 site it agrees with NASA's long-term illumination maps within 3 percentage points. Every number on screen carries a label saying where it came from.

The story. Refaey, our guide, is a fictional astronaut whose launch slipped. You become his mission planner. First he walks you through six real landings: Apollo 11, Apollo 15, Lunokhod 1, Chang'e 4, Chandrayaan-3 and Athena. Each one is placed on its site's real terrain at the minute of touchdown, with the Sun and Earth computed from JPL Horizons for that minute, and teaches one lesson about power, communications or timing. Then you plan his landing step by step. The conversations use choice buttons rather than AI chat, and any fact Refaey states comes with a "How do you know?" link to its source.

Impact. It gives mission planners a quick first look at a site, and gives teachers and students an honest feel for why south-pole landings are so hard.

Tools. React, TypeScript and Vite; Three.js (React Three Fiber) and GSAP for the 3D Moon and terrain; Node.js scripts for terrain processing and Python for the sprite pipeline; Vercel, with a serverless proxy for Horizons; Vitest and Playwright for tests.

Limits and next steps. Trip time from launch to landing is assumed (7.72 days, like IM-1). Dust, light scattered by terrain and ground stations on Earth are not modelled. At the Shackleton Rim point our Earth visibility still differs from NASA's long-term map, and we are checking the terrain data there. Next: let users choose the trip type, add more sites and a north-pole set.

What we considered. Scientific honesty: we label the limits of our data, such as the terrain resolution near each site. Accessibility: keyboard use, a reduced-motion setting and readable contrast. Performance on weak laptops and projectors. A source for every claim.

## 1. Challenge Overview

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge focuses on finding and evaluating suitable landing locations on the Moon. Choosing the right landing site is an important step in planning successful lunar missions. Scientists and mission planners need to understand the Moon's surface conditions before deciding where a spacecraft should land.

However, the lunar surface is not uniform. Different areas have different elevations, slopes, sunlight conditions, shadows, and communication possibilities. These factors make choosing a safe and suitable landing location a challenging process.

Our goal is to make this process easier by using scientific data and interactive technology.

Finding a suitable landing site requires analyzing several scientific factors at the same time.

Some areas have steep slopes or uneven terrain, which may make landing difficult. Other locations experience long periods of darkness, limiting sunlight availability. Communication with Earth can also be challenging depending on the selected location.

Therefore, users need a simple way to explore different lunar locations, understand their conditions, and compare them before making a decision.

1. Project Overview

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive 3D web platform designed to help users explore the Moon and evaluate potential landing locations using scientific data.

The main idea is to transform complex lunar information into an accessible visual experience. Instead of requiring users to examine separate scientific datasets, our platform brings important information together in one place.

The website combines 3D visualization, NASA scientific data, interactive maps, and landing-site evaluation to help users understand the conditions of different lunar locations.

Our platform is designed for scientists, researchers, students, space enthusiasts, and anyone interested in lunar exploration.

2. Project Concept and Design

The website starts with an immersive interface featuring a realistic 3D visualization of the Moon.

Users can explore the Moon through an interactive environment rather than simply viewing a static image. The design aims to create an engaging experience while keeping scientific information clear and easy to understand.

An astronaut guide character is also included to introduce users to the platform and help explain its main features.

projectDetails.name: AnalogAtlas
projectDetails.summary:
AnalogAtlas is an interactive, data-driven platform designed to identify Earth locations that resemble potential permanent Moon base sites and Mars locations. We developed MERIDIAN, a multi-evidence ranking engine that analyzes terrain, geological characteristics, and environmental processes to identify meaningful similarities beyond visual appearance.

Our platform uses open Earth-observation and planetary datasets to compare 135 locations across Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Instead of presenting information in only one format, AnalogAtlas provides several ways to explore the results. Users can view ranked lists of the closest Earth analogs, compare multiple locations side by side, explore locations through interactive maps, examine detailed similarity scores, and understand which geological or environmental features contribute to each match. The platform also provides data provenance, uncertainty estimates, and explanations to make the results more transparent and reliable. It further distinguishes between physical similarity and practical site suitability, helping users evaluate locations from different perspectives.

AnalogAtlas addresses the NASA challenge by turning complex planetary data into accessible and scientifically grounded insights. It is important because Earth can serve as a natural testing environment for studying conditions similar to those on the Moon and Mars, helping researchers explore potential challenges and support future space exploration .
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – AnalogAtlas

How it works:

AnalogAtlas is an interactive scientific platform that identifies Earth locations that resemble potential permanent Moon base sites and Mars locations. Its core engine, MERIDIAN (Multi-Evidence Ranking with Domain-Integrated Agreement Navigation), processes planetary datasets and compares locations using geological, topographical, and environmental features.

The platform is built around five evidence channels that evaluate different aspects of similarity. It does not simply compare images or surface appearance; it analyzes terrain characteristics, geological patterns, and environmental processes. The engine then produces ranked Earth analogs, similarity scores, uncertainty estimates, and explanations for the results.

Multiple ways to explore the results:

We designed AnalogAtlas to make complex scientific information accessible through different interactive tools:

  • Ranking: Displays the closest Earth analog locations for a selected Moon or Mars site.
  • Side-by-Side Comparison: Allows users to compare locations and understand their similarities and differences.
  • Interactive Maps: Shows the geographical distribution of analog locations.
  • Similarity Analysis: Breaks down the evidence behind each match and explains which features contribute to the result.
  • Portfolio Selection: Helps users select a complementary group of analog sites instead of relying only on the highest-ranked location.
  • Data Provenance: Provides information about the datasets and sources behind the results.
  • CSV Export: Allows users to download results for further analysis.

The platform also separates physical similarity from practical suitability, allowing users to consider factors such as terrain hazards, slope, roughness, thermal conditions, and ice context without confusing them with the similarity score.

Tools and technologies:

The scientific processing and ranking engine was developed using Python 3.11, with NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, and Scikit-learn. Pytest was used for mathematical contract testing. We worked with open scientific datasets from NASA, ESA/Copernicus, JAXA, and USGS, including elevation models, satellite observations, geological information, and crater databases. Microsoft Planetary Computer and its STAC API support additional Earth-location screening.

Creativity and innovation:

One of our main creative contributions is MERIDIAN's integration of five earlier algorithmic approaches — PRISM, CALIPER, CAPER, ORCA, and SAGE — into one unified ranking system. Instead of depending on a single similarity method, it combines multiple evidence channels and uses agreement between different ranking approaches to provide more informative results. It also communicates uncertainty and preserves data provenance, making the analysis more transparent and scientifically traceable.

Factors considered and intended impact:

During development, we considered differences in planetary data resolution, geological and terrain characteristics, environmental processes, data availability, measurement uncertainty, and the distinction between similarity and mission suitability. We also aimed to discover less familiar Earth analog environments rather than focusing only on well-known deserts and polar regions.

Our intended impact is to make planetary comparison more systematic and accessible, help researchers identify promising Earth environments for studying Moon and Mars conditions, and support future space exploration research and technology testing.

projectDetails.name: Skyblink
projectDetails.summary:
We built SkyBlink: a high-performance, zero-install, open-source web application and astronomical data pipeline engineered for
NASA's upcoming SPHEREx space observatory. SkyBlink ingests calibrated multi-epoch near-infrared FITS datacubes (0.75–5.0 µm),
performs automated World Coordinate System (WCS) tangent-plane reprojection, computes instant difference images (∆I), executes
robust σ-clipping statistical transient candidate detection, locks real-source centroids with an interactive 5× magnification loupe, and
renders instantaneous 102-band pixel spectra for citizen and professional discovery.
projectDetails.details: SPHEREx surveys the entire sky every six months across 102 spectroscopic bands, yielding multi-extension FITS images where wavelength varies across the detector plane. Standard desktop tools (like DS9 or TOPCAT) require complex installations, command-line syntax, and manual coordinate reprojection. This steep technical barrier shuts out citizen scientists, classrooms, and amateur astronomers, leaving vast amounts of temporal infrared data uninspected. As a consequence, faint moving Solar System bodies, cold sub-stellar brown dwarfs, and rapid variable stars risk remaining hidden inside massive raw archives.

projectDetails.name: Margin
projectDetails.summary:
Margin is a 2D pixel-art platformer, made in Godot, that teaches children aged 7 to 12 how astronauts survive. The player is Max, a young astronaut who lands on Mars. A solar radiation storm forces him into a lava tube cave with no breathable air.

To get through, players share a small suit battery between Air, Shield and Light. Every cell given to one system is taken from another, so each choice has a cost. Power stations add new cells and forecast the area ahead, so kids plan the way real mission planners balance power, oxygen and radiation protection.

The danger comes from real NASA data. At startup, the game checks NASA's DONKI database for recent solar particle storms. If none happened, it uses a real stored storm and says so. Hidden scrolls unlock short, kid-friendly science chapters with their NASA sources, such as Curiosity's radiation readings and astronaut oxygen needs.

This matters because space science often feels distant to children. Margin turns it into decisions they make with their own hands, where failing is gentle and trying a new plan is part of the fun.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Margin is a 2D pixel-art platformer about surviving on Mars. The player is Max, a young astronaut who has just landed. A solar radiation storm hits, and Max must shelter in a lava tube cave with no breathable air, full of lava pits, crumbling platforms, a radiation skylight and dark tunnels.

The core mechanic is a suit power budget. The suit starts with 3 battery cells, shared between three systems:

- Air: more cells make oxygen last longer.

- Shield: more cells make radiation build up more slowly.

- Light: more cells give a bigger headlamp, so you can see dangers and find secret paths.

Every cell given to one system is taken from another. Each Power Station adds one new cell, shows a forecast of the next area, and lets the player re-plan, the way real mission planners balance limited power.

Real NASA data drives the danger. When the game starts, it asks NASA's DONKI database for solar particle storms from the last 30 days. A strong real storm makes radiation build faster. If the Sun was quiet or the device is offline, the game uses one of 16 real storms measured by GOES satellites, and it always says which case applies. Three hidden scrolls unlock chapters in an in-game Book of Books, with kid-friendly science and NASA sources.

Benefits

- Children learn by doing: they feel the trade-off between air, radiation and light instead of reading about it.

- Every run uses a real storm, so the same plan can work one time and fail the next. That teaches kids to check conditions before acting.

- Failure is gentle. Max respawns nearby with air left, so experimenting is encouraged.

- Every fact in the game shows its source, and a NASA Data screen separates real science from game invention.

Intended impact

We want children to come away understanding that astronaut survival is about planning and trade-offs, and to become curious about real space science and NASA data. The game can be played alone, or used in a classroom where students compare the power plans they chose and how those plans turned out.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Game engine: Godot 4.7, programmed in GDScript.

- Art and sound: our own Python 3 scripts (using Pillow and NumPy) that generate the pixel art, tilesets, characters, portraits, logo and sound effects.

- Data: NASA DONKI API (api.nasa.gov) and NASA CCMC.

- Fonts: Silkscreen and Pixelify Sans (Open Font License).

- Version control: Git and GitHub.

- AI assistance: Claude Code, as described in our AI disclosure.

- Builds: exported for Windows, Linux and the web browser. Developed on desktop PCs; played with a keyboard.

How it is creative

Margin mixes a tight, fast platformer, inspired by games like Celeste, with a strategy layer about resource planning. Live space weather from NASA changes each run, so real events on the Sun change the game. The story adds humour through OG, a rude old wizard who laughs at Max. The main menu shows the MARGIN title over an animated Martian dust storm. Collectible scrolls reward exploration with real science instead of points.

Factors our team considered

- Age 7 to 12: short dialogue, big readable pixel text, and only three resources named in plain words.

- Honesty: stored data is never shown as live, every fact cites its source, and game fiction (like hot lava in a cold Martian lava tube) is labelled as fiction.

- Reliability: the game still works offline or when NASA's shared API key hits its request limit, by using real stored storms.

- Fun first: values are tuned for play, but every effect works in the same direction as real life.

- Replayability: different storms, secrets to find, and different power plans to try.

- No NASA logos or mission insignia in the artwork.

projectDetails.name: Project apollo12
projectDetails.summary:
We built Solar Explorer Academy: 3D Planetary Odyssey, an interactive 3D space flight and discovery game that lets kids and beginners explore our solar system firsthand. Players pilot a virtual spacecraft through a living 3D solar system, warp directly to any planet, inspect real planetary photography, read curated astronomy facts, look up terms in a kid-friendly scientific glossary, and take interactive quizzes.
Traditional astronomy lessons often rely on flat diagrams and dense vocabulary, making space feel abstract and difficult for young learners to grasp. When science feels too passive or technical, kids can quickly lose interest.
Solar Explorer Academy solves this by turning space science into an active, self-paced adventure. Intuitive flight controls make exploring effortless, real imagery connects players to authentic space discoveries, and plain-language facts, glossary definitions, and quizzes reinforce learning naturally.
Sparking curiosity early matters because it inspires the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers. By making planetary science visual, accurate, and genuinely fun, Solar Explorer Academy lowers the barrier to STEM and helps young minds connect with the universe around them.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does and How It Works

Solar Explorer Academy: 3D Planetary Odyssey is an interactive, browser-based 3D space flight and planetary discovery game built for kids and beginners. Players step into the cockpit of a virtual spacecraft and navigate a living 3D model of our solar system.

Explorers can fly freely through space to experience the layout of our cosmic neighborhood or use an instant planetary warp system to travel directly to any planet. Upon arriving at a world, players can inspect real planetary photography up close, read curated astronomy facts, look up unfamiliar terms in a built-in scientific glossary, and complete interactive quizzes to test what they have learned.

Key Benefits

  • Active, Hands-On Learning: Replaces static textbook diagrams with interactive 3D exploration, helping learners understand spatial relationships and planetary environments intuitively.
  • Built-In Vocabulary Support: Whenever players encounter complex astronomy terms—such as orbits, atmospheres, or surface geology—the integrated glossary translates them into plain, kid-friendly language on the spot.
  • Immediate Knowledge Reinforcement: Interactive quizzes at each destination turn passive reading into active recall, helping concepts stick without feeling like a traditional test.
  • Zero-Barrier Access: Because it runs directly in a web browser, students, parents, and teachers can launch the academy instantly without downloading large files or buying specialized equipment.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to spark early curiosity in astronomy and lower the barrier to STEM education for young learners. By combining the excitement of piloting a spacecraft with authentic space imagery and accessible science, Solar Explorer Academy transforms space from an abstract school subject into a living universe kids want to explore. Ultimately, we aim to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers by connecting them directly with real-world planetary discoveries.

Tools, Coding Languages, Software, and Hardware Used

  • Coding Languages & Frameworks: Built with React, TypeScript/JavaScript, HTML5, and Tailwind CSS to create a responsive, dark-mode spacecraft interface.
  • 3D Rendering & Design: Powered by real-time 3D web graphics (WebGL) for smooth planetary flight and camera warping, paired with clean, readable typography (Outfit, Plus Jakarta Sans, and JetBrains Mono).
  • Software & Data Sources: Developed and deployed using Google AI Studio, integrating authentic, publicly available NASA planetary photography and verified astronomical facts.
  • Hardware: Developed on standard team laptops and optimized to run smoothly across everyday consumer hardware—including desktops, laptops, and tablets—through standard web browsers.

How Our Project Is Creative

Instead of separating entertainment from education, Solar Explorer Academy merges three experiences—a 3D space flight simulator, a digital gallery of real NASA photography, and a gamified learning academy—into one seamless adventure. Our dual-navigation design lets players choose between free-roaming flight for open discovery and instant planetary warping for focused study, ensuring they experience the wonder of space travel without getting lost or frustrated in empty space.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Age-Appropriate Cognitive Load: We carefully structured the interface, flight controls, and glossary definitions so young learners can navigate independently and grasp real space science without feeling overwhelmed by technical jargon.
  • Playability vs. Astronomical Scale: Real planetary distances are vast and mostly empty; we balanced scientific authenticity with responsive flight speeds and warp mechanics to keep gameplay engaging.
  • Scientific Accuracy: We prioritized real planetary photography and verified astronomical data over purely fictional visuals so players build genuine scientific understanding.
  • Device Accessibility & Performance: Knowing many students access educational tools on school laptops or home tablets, we designed the application to be lightweight, fast-loading, and compatible with standard web browsers.

projectDetails.name: Project Apollo 26
projectDetails.summary:
We have developed LunaNav, a visual, interactive web application designed to support the planning and comparison of candidate landing sites near the lunar South Pole.
How it addresses the challenge:
South Pole missions face severe lighting and communication constraints due to low solar angles and long shadows cast by crater rims and ridges. Moving away from complex, specialized interfaces and fragmented datasets, LunaNav integrates lunar terrain elevation models with solar and Earth ephemeris calculations into a single, intuitive platform. Users can identify candidate sites, browse timelines to visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the true local horizon, and compare multiple locations and dates side-by-side.
Why it matters:
LunaNav accelerates early-stage decision-making for mission planners and engineers by providing immediate assessments of potential sunlight exposure and direct-to-Earth visibility windows. It also lowers technical barriers, enabling educators, students, and the general public to interactively explore and understand the trade-offs involved in lunar exploration.
projectDetails.details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

LunaNav   is an interactive, browser-based visual decision-support platform designed to evaluate and compare candidate landing sites near the Moon’s south pole.

• Site & Time Selection: Users select a candidate landing site (such as Shackleton Crater Rim or Malapert Massif) and choose a specific date or mission timeframe using an interactive timeline scrubber.

• Terrain-Aware Horizon Simulation: The application computes a 360-degree local terrain horizon profile from lunar elevation datasets and overlays the real-time azimuth and elevation paths of both the Sun and Earth.

• Visibility & Comparison Engine: By comparing celestial elevation angles against the local terrain horizon, LunaNav distinguishes between ideal geometric visibility and actual unobstructed line-of-sight. Users can compare multiple landing sites or dates side-by-side to evaluate potential sunlight duration and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows.

2. Benefits

• Unified Situational Awareness: Eliminates the need to mentally combine fragmented astronomical tables and topographic maps by merging illumination, Earth visibility, and terrain obstruction into one visual workspace.

• Rapid Trade-Off Analysis: Allows mission planners and engineers to screen and compare multiple candidate sites under consistent assumptions in seconds rather than hours.

• Dual-Mode Accessibility: Features a simplified educational view with intuitive indicators for students and the public, alongside an engineering view exposing precise azimuth/elevation telemetry and data exports.

 3. Expected Impact

• Accelerating Early Mission Planning: Provides aerospace researchers, rover teams, and mission designers with a fast, transparent preliminary screening tool for polar lunar operations.

• Democratizing Space Science (STEM): Empowers educators, students, and the general public to actively explore the real engineering challenges behind NASA’s Artemis program and lunar exploration without needing specialized command-line software.

 4. Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware & Software Used

 • Data Sources & Ephemeris: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO LOLA) Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for lunar topography, paired with NAIF SPICE kernels and JPL Horizons data for planetary positions.

• Backend & Scientific Computation: Python (utilizing SpiceyPy, Astropy, and NumPy) to transform coordinate frames, calculate local azimuth/elevation angles, and pre-compute 360-degree horizon profiles into lightweight JSON datasets.

• Frontend & Visualization: JavaScript / TypeScript, React, and Three.js / WebGL (alongside HTML5/CSS3) to render interactive 3D/2D horizon plots, dynamic timelines, and side-by-side comparison dashboards.

• Hardware & Collaboration Software: Standard developer laptops, cloud hosting (Vercel / GitHub Pages) for instant web deployment, Git/GitHub for version control, and Figma for UI/UX wireframing.

   5. Creative Aspects

• Visualizing "Hidden" Obstructions: Rather than displaying abstract numerical coordinates, LunaNav places the user directly on the lunar surface with a 360-degree panoramic horizon view, making low-angle polar shadows and Earth-blocking crater rims immediately intuitive.

• Transparent Uncertainty Communication: Instead of giving an opaque "best site" score, LunaNav creatively separates "above ideal horizon" from "clear of local terrain" using clear visual states and timelines, teaching users why a site works or fails.

 6. Team Considerations & Design Factors

• Scientific Integrity vs. False Precision: Our team prioritized responsible communication by clearly labeling outputs as potential sunlight and potential direct-to-Earth line of sight, explicitly noting terrain resolution limits and unmodeled factors (such as antenna link-budgets or solar panel efficiency).

• Performance & Accessibility: To ensure smooth performance on standard school laptops and tablets without heavy GPU loads, we pre-computed horizon elevation profiles and used color-blind-friendly visual palettes.
