projectDetails.name: Project Apollo V
projectDetails.summary:
**APOLLO V** is an interactive space mission design game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Space Mission Design Game challenge. It puts players in the role of mission planners, allowing them to experience key decisions involved in designing and managing a lunar mission. Players explore rocket configuration, resource management, launch procedures, space navigation, and lunar exploration through an engaging game experience.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming complex space mission concepts into interactive gameplay, helping players understand how engineering choices and resource trade-offs can affect a mission. APOLLO V aims to make space exploration more accessible and engaging, especially for students and beginners interested in science, technology, and aerospace engineering. Its goal is to encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and interest in real-world space missions.
projectDetails.details:
APOLLO V – Project Details

APOLLO V is an interactive web-based space mission design game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Space Mission Design Game challenge. It gives players the opportunity to experience the role of a space mission planner and explore the challenges of designing and managing a mission to the Moon.

How It Works

The game takes players through the main stages of a lunar mission. Players begin by learning the game mechanics and exploring the mission objectives. They then experience rocket design, mission preparation, launch, spaceflight, and lunar exploration through interactive gameplay.

The rocket design experience introduces important components such as payload, rocket structure, propulsion systems, boosters, and power systems. Players explore how different design choices and resource limitations can affect mission performance.

The game also introduces the challenges of spacecraft navigation and lunar landing, helping players understand that a successful space mission requires careful planning and decision-making.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our main goal is to make space exploration and aerospace engineering concepts easier to understand and more engaging, especially for students and beginners.

APOLLO V aims to:

  • Introduce players to the basic principles of rocket design and space mission planning.
  • Demonstrate the importance of managing resources and making engineering decisions.
  • Encourage critical thinking, problem-solving, and experimentation.
  • Make learning about space exploration more interactive and enjoyable.
  • Inspire young people to explore science, technology, and aerospace engineering.

Tools and Technologies

We developed the project as a web-based game using modern development technologies:

  • Visual Studio Code: Code editor.
  • Node.js and npm: Development environment and package management.
  • Vite: Development server and build tool.
  • TypeScript: Programming language.
  • React: User interface development.
  • Tailwind CSS: Interface styling.
  • Zustand: Game state management.
  • Framer Motion: Animations and transitions.
  • Canvas 2D: 2D graphics rendering.
  • Git and GitHub: Version control and collaboration.

The project is software-based and does not require additional physical hardware.

NASA Resources

We used NASA images as visual resources to support the game's space exploration environment and connect the experience with real-world space exploration.

One of our reference sources is the official NASA Images and Video Library:
https://images.nasa.gov/

These images help create an engaging visual experience and strengthen the connection between the game and actual space exploration.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative idea behind APOLLO V is to turn the complex process of planning a lunar mission into an interactive experience. Instead of presenting players with technical information alone, the game allows them to explore mission decisions through gameplay.

We combine educational concepts, game mechanics, visual storytelling, and interactive design to make space mission planning more accessible to a wider audience.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors when designing the experience:

  • Accessibility: Making the game understandable for beginners.
  • Educational Value: Connecting gameplay with real space mission concepts.
  • Resource Management: Showing how engineering choices involve limitations and trade-offs.
  • User Experience: Keeping the interface clear and the gameplay engaging.
  • Visual Quality: Using space-related imagery and animations to create an immersive environment.
  • Technical Feasibility: Building a web-based experience that can be accessed without specialized hardware.

Conclusion

APOLLO V aims to bring space mission planning closer to players by combining technology, education, and interactive gameplay. projectDetails.name: AQUA SAR Eye
projectDetails.summary: AQUA SAR Eye is a working web prototype that shows how Lake Burullus, on Egypt's Nile Delta coast, changed between 2019 and 2026 using radar satellites. Radar works day and night and through clouds, so it can map water every year. Our featured layer is the new NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar (June to October 2026, provisional data). We classify it with its own machine-learning model and check it against Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical images. In the lake's 226 km2 permanent-water core, NISAR and Sentinel-1 agree within 1.4 km2 on open water. Sentinel-1 gives the 2019 to 2026 history: water and fish ponds fell from 288.5 to 270.5 km2 (-6.2%), mostly by 2023. The site has a map, a year slider, charts, tables and an AI chat assistant that only explains numbers computed by our analysis function. Radar shows what changed, not why, so we make no claims about causes. The tool gives researchers and decision-makers clear evidence to plan restoration and protect the fishing communities around the lake.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

AQUA SAR Eye gives decision-makers and researchers a ready analysis of Lake Burullus. The home page has a 3D Earth; the lake page has a map, a year slider (2019-2026), charts, tables and a chat assistant. The slider has two zones: Sentinel-1 archive years (blue) and the NISAR 2026 layer (gold).

HOW IT WORKS

1. NISAR (featured layer): five L-band GCOV scenes (path 129, frame 17; 23 Jun, 17 Jul, 22 Aug, 15 Sep, 21 Oct 2026, HH/HV, provisional) are combined into one composite. A separate Random Forest labels water, vegetation and land. Because HH brightness is sensitive to stems standing in water, we also measure bright non-water surface in the lake core (HH >= -14 dB) and validate it against Sentinel-2.

2. Sentinel-1 comparison and archive layer (2019-2026): one method, same season every year, fixed 496.6 km2 study area, processed in Google Earth Engine.

3. Labels and checks: Sentinel-2 gives training labels and a greenness reference; the JRC Global Surface Water map defines the 226.3 km2 permanent-water core and gives an independent check.

4. Backend (FastAPI on Vercel) serves map tiles and numbers. The chat assistant (an AI language model) only explains what our analysis function returns; a number guard blocks any number not in the analysis result.

MAIN RESULTS

- NISAR 2026 (provisional): 213.0 km2 of open water in the core (94.1%), within 1.4 km2 of Sentinel-1 (214.4 km2).

- NISAR sees 11.6 km2 of bright non-water surface in the core; 73% of it is green vegetation in Sentinel-2.

- Sentinel-1: water plus fish ponds fell from 288.5 km2 (2019) to 270.5 km2 (2026), -6.2%; most of the loss happened by 2023, then about flat.

- Accuracy: Sentinel-1 water vs non-water F1 about 0.98; four classes about 80%; NISAR model OA 0.82, water F1 0.95. About 99% of our water is also water in JRC.

- Trend is shown as a range (-0.85 to -4.22 km2 per year if the 2019-2026 trend continues), not a prediction; our backtest was off by about 10.5 km2.

HONEST LIMITS

NISAR data are provisional and cover one season. NISAR and Sentinel-1 are different sensors, so we never calculate a change between them. Validation uses Sentinel-2 and JRC, not field data. Radar shows what changed, not why, so we make no claim about causes. Not yet tested with real decision-makers.

IMPACT

Burullus gives about 19% of Egypt's fish production (published research). Clear evidence on what changed, where and by how much supports decisions to restore the lake and protect the fishing communities around it.

TOOLS

Google Earth Engine, Python, FastAPI, Vercel, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Three.js, MapLibre GL JS, Chart.js, ASF Data Search (NISAR). Code: https://github.com/yussef862/AQUA-SAR

projectDetails.name: Project Arcturus
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive 3D web experience that brings the story of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars to life. Users can explore 3D planetary environments, discover spacecraft and scientific equipment, and learn about their missions, historical significance, and landing locations through images, descriptions, and 3D models.

The project features 10 lunar artifacts and 9 Martian spacecraft, including Apollo 11's Lunar Module, Lunokhod 1, Curiosity, Perseverance, and Ingenuity. We used NASA mission records, scientific resources, images, and available 3D models, alongside selected external resources, to build an informative and engaging exploration experience.

Our solution addresses the challenge of making discarded space equipment easier to discover, understand, and appreciate. By transforming mission records and scattered historical information into an interactive journey, we aim to preserve the story of humanity's exploration beyond Earth and help students, educators, and space enthusiasts connect with the history of space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Our project is an interactive 3D web experience that transforms the history of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars into an engaging space exploration journey.

Users can explore 3D representations of the Solar System, select the Moon or Mars, and navigate their planetary environments to discover spacecraft and equipment left behind by past and recent missions. The project features 10 lunar artifacts and 9 Martian spacecraft, including Apollo 11's Lunar Module, Apollo 15's Lunar Roving Vehicle, Lunokhod 1, Curiosity, Opportunity, Perseverance, and Ingenuity. Each featured object is presented through its mission story, historical background, images, available 3D models, and landing location.

To develop the experience, we used NASA mission records, scientific resources, images, and available 3D models, alongside selected resources from other space agencies and external providers. These resources help connect each object to its real mission and historical context.

The frontend was developed using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, with Three.js and WebGL for interactive 3D visualization. We used GLB/GLTF assets for planetary environments and spacecraft models, and Python's HTTP server for local development and testing.

The creative aspect of our project is the combination of space history, 3D exploration, and storytelling in one experience. Instead of presenting discarded equipment as a static list or collection of facts, we allow users to discover these objects in the context of the worlds where they were left behind.

During development, we considered historical accuracy, the reliability of information, the availability and quality of 3D assets, the clarity of the user experience, and the distinction between confirmed mission facts and visual representations.

Our intended impact is to make space exploration history more accessible and engaging for students, educators, and space enthusiasts. By revealing the stories behind equipment that remains on other worlds, we aim to encourage curiosity, support space education, and highlight the lasting human footprint beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: Project AsrtTales
projectDetails.summary:
The problem

NASA has left dozens of spacecraft, rovers and landers on the Moon, Mars and deep space. They are abandoned and silent, and most people, especially kids, never hear about them. Space facts are usually taught in dry, text-heavy ways that children quickly lose interest in.

The idea

What if the abandoned machines could speak for themselves? In AstroTales, each device is a friendly character. Opportunity, Ingenuity, Pathfinder and the Eagle lander each tell their own story in their own voice, as postcards sent from space. Instead of being forgotten, they become heroes with personalities.

How we solved it

Story: Kids meet each device, follow its journey and learn why it was left behind.
Play: Short mini-games, such as landing on the Moon or hunting planets, make learning fun. Quizzes reward collectible postcards.
Explore: A level map takes kids from the Moon to Mars to deep space. They can also dress their own astronaut and view the devices in AR.
Trust: Every fact is sourced from NASA. Nothing is invented.
Safe for kids: There are no ads, streaks, accounts or personal data.

The result is a free website kids can open on any phone, where history turns into an adventure.
projectDetails.details:
AstroTales turns the equipment NASA left on the Moon, Mars and in deep space into talking characters that tell kids aged 8-12 their own story.

WHAT IT DOES

The child becomes an astronaut. They pick a character, launch from Earth, and fly through a 3D solar system to three worlds: the Moon, Mars and deep space. At real landing sites they meet 14 NASA machines (Eagle, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Kepler, Dawn, Pioneer 10 and more). Each machine tells its own story in first person, with voice and typed subtitles, as four short Story cards. Then the child plays a mini-game based on the real mission: land the lunar module, wipe dust off Opportunity's solar panels, or hunt for planets like Kepler. Each machine has a profile with real facts, NASA photos and source links, and 11 of them can be placed in the child's room in augmented reality on a phone. A treasure chest opens only after the child answers "Fact or Cap?" cards correctly. Completing a world earns coins and unlocks the next one, and coins also unlock secret places.

WHY STORIES

Gen Alpha kids are trained for short, swipeable content, so we don't fight the scroll, we give it a destination. Each card is under about 10 seconds and 20 words, and each machine takes about two minutes. First-person voice is the same approach NASA's own social team found more engaging. Phones get a full-screen Stories view and laptops get a game-scene view, both fed by the same content.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Brings NASA's archive (NSSDCA and science.nasa.gov) to an audience that would never open it: every profile links back to the official source.

- Teaches media literacy: "Fact or Cap?" trains kids to ask "is this real?", using the viral "my battery is low" Opportunity line as an example. That line was a poetic translation of data, not its literal words.

- Turns retired hardware into lasting ambassadors that inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers.

- Works for classrooms, museums and outreach events: one link, no sign-up, no install.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a quiz or a fact sheet, the machines are characters with personalities. The learning is wrapped in play: a real 3D solar-system flight, physics mini-games, AR, and collectible cards.

DESIGN FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: every fact carries a NASA or NSSDCA source link; the story is the machine's voice, the profile is the official science. Facts without a source do not ship.

- Child safety and ethics: no ads, no streaks, no random loot boxes, no personal data, no accounts and no backend. Rewards are earned and the mission has a natural end.

- Accessibility: large touch targets, readable contrast, real buttons, reduced-motion support, and a typeface built for young readers.

- Scalability: each machine is a single content file (4 story cards, quiz cards, facts, sources), so new missions can be added without code, and text is stored so more languages can be added.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, GSAP (animation), three.js (3D solar system), Google model-viewer (AR and 3D, with Draco-compressed NASA models), Howler.js and Web Audio (sound), Zustand (progress saved in the browser), Vercel (hosting). Voices generated with ElevenLabs. Data and media from NASA, NSSDCA and NASA/JPL-Caltech; planet textures from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0). Open source under Apache 2.0. No NASA endorsement is implied.

projectDetails.summary:
Astera Watch is a web-based platform that uses satellite data and AI-powered models to detect potential fire-affected areas, analyze changes caused by fires, and explore their environmental impacts. Users can view affected locations, access information about fire events, and understand how surrounding ecosystems may be impacted.
The platform addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by bringing satellite-based observations and analysis into one accessible environment. It also includes a dedicated research space where scientists can organize studies around affected areas and connect their work with relevant datasets.
Astera Watch is important because wildfire damage does not end when the fire is extinguished. Understanding its lasting effects is essential for environmental research and better-informed decisions. Our future vision is to expand the platform with a mobile app, citizen and researcher alerts, community data contributions, geographic annotations, expert-reviewed research, and continuously improving AI models.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Astera Watch

Astera Watch is a satellite-based wildfire monitoring and environmental impact analysis platform. It uses satellite observations and AI-powered models to identify potential fire-affected areas, analyze changes in the surrounding landscape, and provide information about the environmental impacts of fire events.

How It Works

The platform brings fire-related information and satellite-based analysis into one web application. Users can explore potential fire locations on an interactive map, examine detected surface changes, and access information about affected areas and their possible environmental consequences.

Astera Watch also includes a dedicated Research Center where scientists can organize research projects, explore datasets, and study specific fire-affected locations. This connects satellite analysis with scientific investigation.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Wildfires can leave long-lasting damage even after the flames disappear. Astera Watch aims to make this damage easier to explore and understand, support environmental research, and provide a shared space for studying fire events and their consequences.

Our long-term vision is to develop a growing reference platform for wildfire events and environmental damage. Future plans include a mobile application for alerts to citizens and researchers, researcher-contributed datasets, geographic annotations, published studies, and expert-reviewed scientific contributions. These contributions could also help improve the training and validation of future AI models.

Tools and Technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, and Vite.
  • Backend foundation: Python and FastAPI.
  • Spatial database technology: PostgreSQL and PostGIS.
  • Data sources and research: NASA NISAR, NASA FIRMS, MODIS MCD64A1, Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2, and Natural Earth geographic data.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Astera Watch goes beyond displaying fire locations. Its creative approach connects three important stages: detecting potential fire-affected areas, understanding their environmental impacts, and enabling scientists to investigate those areas further.

Our team considered scientific reliability, satellite-data limitations, accessibility, usability, and the different needs of ordinary users and researchers. We also considered the importance of distinguishing actual observations from demo data and potential detections from confirmed fire events.

The current web prototype provides the interface and browser-based research workflows. Live data integrations, fully validated end-to-end analysis, mobile alerts, community data contributions, and expert review are planned future developments.

FLAMEVERSE is an innovative AI-powered platform designed to explore and understand how flames and combustion behave in microgravity environments, particularly aboard spacecraft.

By utilizing NASA scientific experiment data, FLAMEVERSE transforms complex scientific information into interactive visualizations and accessible explanations. The platform allows users to explore flame behavior in space, analyze experimental results, understand combustion phenomena, and discover how microgravity changes the way fire behaves compared to Earth.

Our solution combines artificial intelligence, scientific data analysis, interactive 3D visualization, and educational tools to make advanced space research easier to understand and explore.

Our mission is to bridge the gap between complex NASA research and accessible scientific knowledge, helping students, researchers, and space enthusiasts better understand the science of combustion in space.
projectDetails.details:
FLAMEVERSE – Project Details

FLAMEVERSE is an innovative AI-powered educational and scientific platform designed to explore flame behavior and combustion in microgravity environments.

The Problem

Fire behaves very differently in space compared to Earth due to the absence of normal gravitational convection. Understanding these differences is essential for astronaut safety, spacecraft fire prevention, and future space missions. However, scientific data about combustion in microgravity can be difficult for students and the general public to understand and explore.

Our Solution

FLAMEVERSE transforms complex scientific research into an accessible and interactive experience. By combining artificial intelligence, NASA scientific datasets, data analysis, and interactive visualizations, our platform helps users understand how flames behave in microgravity.

Key Features

  • AI-powered assistant for answering questions about combustion in space.
  • Interactive visualizations explaining flame behavior in microgravity.
  • NASA scientific data exploration and analysis.
  • Educational explanations of combustion concepts.
  • Scientific insights that help users compare flame behavior on Earth and in space.

Impact

FLAMEVERSE aims to make space science more accessible, support STEM education, and raise awareness about the challenges of fire safety in spacecraft. It also demonstrates how artificial intelligence can help transform complex scientific information into meaningful knowledge.

Our Vision

We believe that understanding fire in space is an important step toward safer human space exploration. Through FLAMEVERSE, we aim to make scientific discovery more interactive, accessible, and inspiring for everyone.

projectDetails.name: astra_health
projectDetails.summary: Astronauts on long missions face space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, distance from Earth, and hostile closed environments, while medical support from Earth becomes harder to receive. ASTRA HEALTH is an AI-powered health monitoring and decision-support platform that tracks health indicators against each user’s personal baseline, flags unusual changes, and explains readings through an AI assistant grounded in the user’s own data and a registry of medical reference standards. Preventive recommendations, exercise guidance, and a mission planner turn insight into action. It supports, and does not replace, professional medical judgment.
projectDetails.details:
### Project Description

ASTRA HEALTH is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to support astronauts' health and well-being throughout space missions.

The platform brings together several interconnected features. Its health monitoring dashboard organizes physiological data into clear visualizations, helping users track important health indicators and understand changes over time. An AI-powered analysis system interprets available health data, identifies potentially unusual patterns, and provides personalized health insights based on relevant medical reference standards.

The platform also includes an interactive AI Assistant that allows astronauts to ask questions about their health information and receive contextual explanations. In addition, ASTRA HEALTH provides exercise-related guidance, explains the benefits of recommended exercises and the potential consequences of consistently skipping them, and offers tools for managing missions and tracking daily activities.

### Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA HEALTH aims to make astronaut health monitoring more proactive, personalized, and accessible. By connecting health information with AI analysis and scientifically supported medical knowledge, it helps users better understand their health status and recognize potential changes that may require attention.

Its intended impact includes improving health awareness, supporting preventive care, encouraging healthier routines, and providing accessible health information to support informed decisions during space missions. It is designed to complement medical professionals, not replace clinical diagnosis or medical judgment.

### Tools and Technologies

The project is developed as a web-based software platform, combining frontend development, backend services, database management, and AI integration.

The confirmed technical components include:

- **Backend:** TypeScript-based backend services and APIs.

- **AI Integration:** Google Gemini for AI-powered health conversations and contextual responses.

- **Medical Knowledge:** A structured, cited medical standards registry containing health reference values and supporting scientific sources.

- **Data Management:** Database-backed user accounts, personalized health information, and health-related records.

- **Frontend:** An interactive web interface with dashboards, visualizations, and user-facing health management features.

The current platform is software-based and does not depend on a custom-built hardware device. Any wearable or sensor integration should be described according to the actual implemented capabilities.

### Creativity and Innovation

The main creative aspect of ASTRA HEALTH is the integration of multiple health-support capabilities into one astronaut-focused platform rather than treating health monitoring as simple data collection.

Instead of only displaying physiological readings, the platform connects health information with AI-powered interpretation, personalized insights, and relevant medical standards. Its conversational AI Assistant makes health information easier to understand, while its exercise and activity management features extend the experience beyond monitoring into preventive health support.

### Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors:

- **Spaceflight-specific health risks:** Microgravity, radiation, isolation, confinement, and disrupted sleep.

- **Medical reliability:** Using credible scientific references and distinguishing general human reference ranges from astronaut-specific considerations.

- **Personalization:** Ensuring health information and insights are associated with the correct user.

- **Data privacy and security:** Protecting personal health information and maintaining separation between users.

- **Usability:** Presenting complex health information through an accessible and understandable interface.

- **Scalability:** Designing an integrated platform that can support additional health metrics and capabilities in the future.

- **Responsible AI:** Avoiding unsupported medical conclusions and presenting AI as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for professional medical care.

Through this integrated approach, ASTRA HEALTH aims to contribute to a more informed, personalized, and preventive approach to astronaut health management.

projectDetails.name: Project Astro Space
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive platform designed to support safer and more informed lunar landing site selection, particularly in the Moon’s south polar region.

The platform combines NASA lunar elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with solar and Earth position data from NASA JPL Horizons to analyze real terrain horizons, sunlight availability, and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities. Users can explore candidate landing sites, visualize terrain, examine environmental conditions over selected date ranges, and compare up to three locations side by side.

By evaluating how surrounding terrain affects solar exposure and Earth visibility, the platform helps identify potential operational challenges that could impact power generation and communication during lunar missions.

Our goal is to transform complex lunar datasets into clear, interactive, and mission-relevant insights, supporting better-informed decisions for future robotic and human exploration of the Moon.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive platform designed to help mission planners identify and compare potential lunar landing locations, particularly in the Moon’s south polar region.

The Problem

The Moon’s south pole presents unique challenges for future missions. The Sun remains close to the horizon, while surrounding mountains and craters can obstruct sunlight and direct communication with Earth. These conditions can cause power interruptions and communication blackouts, making landing site selection and mission scheduling difficult.

NASA Data Sources

Our project uses multiple NASA data sources:

  • NASA/JPL Horizons API: Provides the Sun’s and Earth’s positions as observed from selected lunar locations, including azimuth and elevation.
  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA: Provides lunar elevation data used to analyze real surface topography and calculate terrain horizons.
  • NASA PGDA: Provides access to the LOLA elevation datasets.
  • Artemis III Candidate Landing Regions: Used as candidate locations for analysis and comparison.
  • Apollo Landing Site Data (NSSDC): Provides historical landing locations for additional comparisons.

How It Works

The platform combines celestial positioning with real lunar terrain analysis.

First, NASA JPL Horizons provides the positions of the Sun and Earth over a selected date range. Second, NASA LOLA elevation maps are processed to calculate the surrounding terrain horizon in 360 directions, up to 250 km, while accounting for lunar curvature.

The system then compares the Sun’s and Earth’s elevations with the terrain horizon at each time step. Earth visibility also includes a 2-degree antenna elevation margin.

This allows the application to calculate sunlight availability, Earth communication windows, simultaneous visibility, and the longest periods of darkness.

Technology Stack

Backend and Scientific Computing: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, and Requests.

Frontend and Visualization: React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei.

Development and Collaboration: Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub.

Benefits and Innovation

Users can explore candidate landing sites, select mission date ranges, compare up to three locations, and visualize results through interactive timelines, terrain horizon panoramas, and 3D sky views.

Our key innovation is evaluating solar and Earth visibility against the actual surrounding lunar terrain rather than relying on a simplified flat-horizon model.

The platform aims to make complex lunar environmental data easier to understand and use, helping mission planners assess operational risks, compare landing opportunities, and make better-informed decisions for future lunar exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project ASTRA TECH
projectDetails.summary: Astra Tech is an advanced spacesuit safety monitoring system designed for the NASA Space Competition to protect astronauts by fusing four critical life-support signals into a single, intuitive interface. The project addresses the silent and invisible danger of carbon dioxide buildup, undetected scrubber degradation, unmonitored purge valves, and stress-induced voice changes inside the helmet.   Unlike traditional setups where telemetry data is scattered across separate devices, Astra Tech integrates carbon dioxide levels, scrubber temperature differentials, valve states, and voice integrity into a unified risk score with a clear color-coded display. Operating locally inside the helmet, it provides real-time, multi-severity warnings within fractions of a second—bypassing communication delays inherent in deep space or Mars missions. This solution is crucial because it gives astronauts and flight crews immediate, life-saving clarity, preventing cognitive impairment and physiological risks before they escalate.
projectDetails.details:
• What it does / How it works: Astra Tech is a spacesuit safety monitoring system that continuously reads four critical helmet signals—carbon dioxide concentration, scrubber efficiency (via temperature differential), purge valve state, and voice integrity (stutter detection)—and fuses them into a single, intuitive risk score with real-time, multi-severity alerts. It operates locally inside the helmet to provide instant warnings within fractions of a second.
  • Benefits & Intended Impact: The project prevents silent physiological risks and cognitive impairment caused by invisible hazards like $CO_2$ buildup. Its intended impact is to enhance astronaut safety during deep space missions, spacewalks, or Mars operations by eliminating telemetry data overload and bypassing communication delays with ground control.
  • Tools, Languages & Software Used: The interactive prototype was developed using Flutter and Web technologies (under the name AstroPulse).
  • Creativity & Factors Considered: The project is creative because it shifts from scattered, multi-screen telemetry to a unified, human-centric interface that combines physiological and environmental indicators (including voice stress analysis). The team carefully considered critical constraints such as avoiding false alarms, preventing astronaut distraction, and ensuring local processing for deep space environments where Earth communication is delayed.

projectDetails.name: TrendLens
projectDetails.summary: TrendLens helps agricultural planners and water-management researchers explore whether unusually hot and dry days are becoming more frequent around Minya, Egypt. Using NASA GLDAS-2.1 Noah data accessed through Giovanni, we developed an interactive dashboard covering 2001–2023 for one rectangular study area. It identifies compound hot-and-dry days, displays annual frequency and conditional proportions, and compares nine event definitions alongside trend estimates and uncertainty. The primary definition identifies 126 compound days among 8,400 valid days. Results remain exploratory and do not establish a reliable increase. TrendLens makes uncertainty and sensitivity visible, allowing users to understand how conclusions depend on analytical choices. Users can inspect the study footprint, compare definitions, and download evidence reports to support research and planning.
projectDetails.details:
TrendLens addresses the Earth System Trend Detective challenge by investigating historical changes in concurrent high temperature and low root-zone soil moisture. It is designed for agricultural planners, water-management researchers, and students who need to understand environmental patterns together with the strength and limitations of the evidence.

Our analysis uses NASA GLDAS-2.1 Noah data accessed through Giovanni for a rectangular study area around Minya, Upper Egypt: 30–31° east and 27–28.95° north. Each daily record represents the region as a whole. Temperature is the highest available value among eight three-hourly regional readings per day. Soil moisture is the daily mean of the native GLDAS RootMoist variable, expressed in kg/m² and understood as a model estimate.

We use 2001–2023 as both the study period and the fixed reference period. Thresholds are calculated separately for each calendar month. A compound day occurs when temperature is at or above its heat threshold and RootMoist is at or below its moisture threshold on the same valid day.

The dashboard distinguishes two indicators: the percentage of all valid days that were both hot and dry, and the historical percentage of valid hot days that were also dry. It displays annual counts, coverage, Theil–Sen trend slopes, trend-test results, adjusted statistical values, and uncertainty intervals.

Our sensitivity explorer compares nine definitions, combining heat percentiles of 90, 92.5, and 95 with moisture percentiles of 10, 15, and 20. Full-year and June–August results are available separately. The primary full-year definition identifies 126 compound days among 8,400 valid days, with 845 hot days.

The findings remain exploratory. Some methods and definitions disagree, and the evidence does not establish a reliable environmental increase. Insufficient evidence does not prove that no change occurred. Approximate uncertainty intervals also depend on assumptions that have not been independently verified.

We developed the analysis in Python using NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pymannkendall, and openpyxl. The current frontend uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet. It includes satellite/street maps, synchronized filters, separate analysis pages, light/dark modes, and downloadable evidence.

Our contribution is making the reliability of environmental evidence understandable: users can see how changing a reasonable definition affects the results. Satellite imagery provides geographic context only. The project does not claim farm-level measurements, district rankings, forecasts, causal explanations, or irrigation recommendations.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: BAYMAX
projectDetails.summary:
Baymax is an onboard AI health companion developed by the ASTRA VITAL team for NASA Space Apps 2026. It aims to protect astronauts' physical and mental health during long-duration space missions, especially when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

The system provides continuous health and environmental monitoring, rule-based emergency detection, AI-powered first-aid guidance grounded in medical reference documents, radiation hazard mapping, and isolation detection. It also supports astronauts' mental well-being through family messages, photos, videos, and voice-pattern monitoring.

Baymax uses an offline-first architecture that stores events and reports locally and synchronizes them with Mission Control when connectivity returns. Flight surgeons can remotely update medical protocols and safety thresholds through Update Packs.

Its AI layer analyses health data, detects abnormal patterns, and generates automated reports to support informed decisions. The system combines AI assistance with auditable safety rules to ensure that emergency decisions never depend on an AI language model.

Baymax aims to make space missions safer, more autonomous, and more supportive for astronauts, with potential applications in other remote and isolated environments on Earth.

projectDetails.name: Project Astravitalis
projectDetails.summary: Project Astravitalis is Nabd, a crew health-monitoring and decision-support web app for long-duration space missions. On a Mars mission, a message to a flight surgeon can take up to 22 minutes each way, so astronauts must assess their own health. Nabd gathers a 2-minute daily check-in (camera-based pulse, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood, nutrition, training and a reaction-time test) and maps every result to NASA's five spaceflight hazards on an interactive body map. A rules engine compares each astronaut with their own baseline, gives a green, amber or red status with plain-language reasons, and recommends specific actions. Mission modes (space station, Mars transit, lunar base) change hazards, gravity, radiation and communication delay, with offline-first behavior and structured reports for the flight surgeon. Scenarios such as a solar storm show how risks develop over time. Nabd is decision support, not diagnosis, and all mission data in the demo is simulated.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Nabd helps astronauts evaluate and act on their own health when Earth cannot help in real time. A 2-minute daily check-in collects pulse (including a camera-based reading processed in the browser), blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, hydration, nutrition, exercise and a short reaction-time test. An interactive body map shows the status of each system (heart, brain, bones, muscles, metabolism, immune system, mind). Selecting a zone explains its function, why spaceflight affects it, which NASA hazard is responsible, and what to do next.

HOW IT WORKS

A transparent rules engine compares every value with the individual's own baseline and approximate reference ranges, then returns green (continue), amber (self-care actions) or red (contact the flight surgeon) with a plain-language reason. Trend detection highlights slow drift before a threshold is crossed. Mission modes (space station, Mars transit, lunar base) change radiation rates, gravity and communication delay. In Mars mode, reports to the flight surgeon show delivery states while an "autonomous decision window" lists safe actions to take while waiting. Scenarios such as a solar storm, CO2 rise and isolation drift show how hazards affect indicators over time.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Long missions will place crews far from hospitals. Nabd lets them notice problems early, understand them, and escalate with a structured report. The same approach applies on Earth to Antarctic stations, submarines and remote clinics, where help is delayed and bandwidth is limited.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Personal-baseline early warning instead of fixed thresholds; every status explained and linked to a NASA hazard; mission modes with communication delay; a beginner-friendly design that explains how and why each measurement is taken.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, Framer Motion, Supabase (database, storage, realtime), browser-based camera pulse estimation (vitallens.js), jsPDF for reports. [EDIT: list only what your app actually uses.]

NASA AND PARTNER RESOURCES

Hazard-to-indicator mapping and educational text are based on NASA Human Research Program pages on hazards, risks and ongoing research. The radiation indicator is informed by Canadian Space Agency material. Reference ranges and radiation rates are approximate public figures and are labelled as such in the app.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE

We used SI tools as follows: Lovable (AI app builder) generated much of the application code; built-in AI provides in-app explanations, daily plans and photo-scan observations; image generation produced crew avatars, backgrounds and icons, each carrying a visible "AI-generated" watermark; Claude (Anthropic) assisted with planning, prompts, slide text and documentation. Our team defined the concept and requirements, chose the science sources, tested the app and reviewed all content.

LIMITATIONS

Nabd is decision support, not a medical device, and gives no diagnoses, drug names or doses. Camera pulse accuracy depends on lighting and motion. All mission data in the demo is simulated; no real astronaut data was used.

projectDetails.name: Project Flare Nova
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary

ASTRAVITALL is an autonomous, Earth-independent astronaut health monitoring and clinical decision support platform designed for deep-space exploration missions. Built with FastAPI and a React cyber-metallic interface, it integrates real-time telemetry across vital signs, sleep cycles, radiation dosimetry (GCR/SPE), exercise countermeasures, cognitive readiness, and mental health check-ins.

The system addresses the challenge of deep-space communication latency—where real-time consultation with Earth-based flight surgeons is impossible. ASTRAVITALL bridges this critical gap through onboard automated anomaly detection against NASA-STD-3001 clinical standards, an interactive 3D holographic neurological scanner, a multi-organ anatomical status model, encrypted mission diary logging, and automated generation of tamper-evident clinical PDF health dossiers with cryptographic SHA-256 verification.

Autonomous health oversight is paramount for human survival on long-duration journeys like Artemis and crewed Mars missions. By transforming disparate biomedical telemetry into actionable clinical intelligence directly aboard the spacecraft, ASTRAVITALL empowers astronauts to detect microgravity-induced physiological degradation early, safeguard crew operational performance, and preserve human life without relying on continuous ground control intervention.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

ASTRAVITALL is an Earth-independent medical operations (EIMO) platform designed to monitor, analyze, and protect the health of astronaut crews during long-duration deep-space missions.

  • Multi-Stream Telemetry Ingestion: Aggregates physiological metrics (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, body temperature, respiratory rate), environmental radiation dosimetry (Galactic Cosmic Rays and Solar Particle Events), sleep architecture, physical countermeasure compliance (ARED resistive/T2 aerobic training), and cognitive vigilance scores.
  • Autonomous Anomaly Detection Engine: Continuously benchmarks live telemetry against established spaceflight medical thresholds (NASA-STD-3001) using algorithmic screening to identify physiological deterioration before it escalates into a medical emergency.
  • Interactive Diagnostic Interfaces: Features an interactive 3D anatomy viewer and a holographic 3D rotating neuro-scanner rendering dynamic cross-sectional cranial slices and biomarker metrics.
  • Clinical Health Dossiers & Mission Logging: Generates certified medical evaluation reports (Physical Health, Pre-EVA clearance, Neurological, Dosimetry) downloadable as tamper-evident PDFs with cryptographic SHA-256 validation, accompanied by an encrypted mission diary for crew reflections and operational logging.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Latency Clinical Autonomy: Fully functional locally onboard the spacecraft, resolving the up to 22-minute light-speed communication delay between Earth and Mars.
  • Holistic Health Triad: Unifies physical vitals, psychological well-being (mood and stress journaling), and cognitive readiness into a single cohesive interface.
  • Early Preventative Intervention: Displays normal baseline reference ranges beneath every physiological attribute, enabling instant deviation recognition.
  • Crew Compliance Tracking: Directly tracks daily microgravity countermeasure protocols (resistive and aerobic exercise) to combat bone density loss, cardiovascular deconditioning, and muscle atrophy.
  • Verifiable Medical Provenance: Cryptographically seals clinical reports with SHA-256 digital signatures, ensuring data integrity across flight surgeon reviews and post-mission epidemiology.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to enable sustainable human life beyond low Earth orbit. On missions to the Moon, Mars, and deep space, astronauts cannot abort to Earth or await real-time advice during acute medical scenarios. ASTRAVITALL bridges the gap between mission control and the autonomous spacecraft, reducing mission-critical health risks, preventing preventable medical aborts, and providing astronauts with the medical self-sufficiency required to explore the solar system safely.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend:
    • Languages & Core: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3
    • Framework & Build: React 18, Vite
    • Styling & Design: Tailwind CSS (cyber-metallic glassmorphism aesthetic)
    • Data Visualization & Graphics: HTML5 Canvas (3D rotating wireframe/particle scanner), Recharts, Lucide React icons
    • Language: Python 3.11+
    • Web Framework: FastAPI (high-throughput asynchronous REST APIs)
    • Database & ORM: SQLite, SQLAlchemy
    • Data & Machine Learning: NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn
    • Document Generation: ReportLab (vectorized clinical PDF generation engine)
    • Git, GitHub, Uvicorn ASGI server
    • Cloudflare Edge Tunneling (TLS/HTTPS end-to-end encryption)
    • JWT (JSON Web Token) authentication architecture

5. How is your project creative?

  • Cyber-Metallic "Liquid Spacecraft" Aesthetic: Replaces intimidating hospital charts with a sleek, mission-grade dark UI featuring brushed metallic tones, frosted glassmorphism cards, and liquid neon status accents engineered for low eye-strain in dimly lit spacecraft modules.
  • Holographic 3D Neuro Scanner: Features an interactive 3D spatial brain model that crews can rotate and inspect alongside synchronized CT cross-sectional scans, laser sweep diagnostics, and reaction-time metrics.
  • Interactive Anatomy Mapping: Astronauts can visually inspect localized organ and musculoskeletal statuses on an intuitive interactive body diagram rather than deciphering raw numerical tables.
  • Dual Mission Diary: Combines clinical telemedicine logging with an encrypted personal astronaut journal—acknowledging that psychological decompression is just as vital as physical maintenance.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Communication Latency & Offline-First Reliability: Deep-space missions cannot rely on cloud servers or ground-based APIs. The entire platform was designed with a local-first architecture capable of running 100% offline aboard spacecraft computing hardware.
  • NASA Medical Standards Compliance: Data thresholds, countermeasure targets, and vital ranges were modeled around NASA-STD-3001 (Space Flight Human-System Standard) and the NASA Human Research Program (HRP) Evidence Books.
  • Cognitive Load & Alarm Fatigue: Spaceflight environments are high-stress. The UI organizes alerts into clean severity hierarchies (Normal, Attention, Critical) with explicit normal range indicators so crews can assess status at a single glance without information overload.
  • Data Integrity & Confidentiality: Implemented multi-tier privacy levels for crew logs and SHA-256 hashing on exported medical dossiers to maintain clinical chain-of-custody.

projectDetails.name: ASTRIX
projectDetails.summary:
FireSync is an interactive web platform that brings NASA FIRMS active-fire observations into one place, making it easier to explore fire activity and understand how different satellite sensors observe it. Users can explore a global fire map, investigate specific regions, view detection statistics, compare observations from MODIS and VIIRS, and inspect individual detection records alongside the methodology and limitations behind the data.

The project addresses the challenge of making satellite fire observations easier to explore and interpret. Different sensors have different spatial resolutions and observation times, so their records do not always tell exactly the same story. FireSync helps users examine these differences through interactive maps and comparisons, while keeping the underlying observations and their limitations visible.

Understanding these observations matters because informed interpretation of satellite data can support awareness, research, and better understanding of fire activity on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
FireSync is an interactive web platform designed to make NASA FIRMS active-fire satellite observations easier to explore, compare, and understand.

The platform brings fire-detection records from different satellite sensors into one interface. Users can explore a global map of detected fire activity, select an area of interest, view regional statistics, compare observations from MODIS and VIIRS, and inspect individual detection records. It also provides information about the methodology and limitations of the data, helping users understand what satellite observations can—and cannot—tell them.

FireSync offers several benefits: it makes large collections of satellite observations more accessible, helps users investigate regional fire activity, and makes differences between satellite sensors easier to examine. For example, MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and observation times. Comparing their observations can reveal differences in coverage and detection patterns, rather than assuming that every sensor observes the same events in exactly the same way.

Our project’s creative approach is to bring exploration, regional analysis, sensor comparison, and individual-record inspection together in a single interactive experience. Instead of presenting hotspot counts alone, FireSync encourages users to investigate the evidence behind the numbers.

During development, our team considered data accessibility, map usability, sensor differences, observation timing, spatial resolution, and scientific limitations. We also considered the importance of avoiding misleading conclusions: a satellite detection does not necessarily represent a unique fire, and the absence of a detection does not prove that no fire exists.

We used NASA FIRMS data, Python for backend development and data processing, web technologies for the interactive frontend, and Git/GitHub for version control and project collaboration. AI-assisted tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Manus, supported parts of our planning, development workflow, and project preparation.

Our intended impact is to help people explore satellite-based fire observations more clearly and critically, supporting greater awareness and understanding of fire activity on Earth.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroBase
projectDetails.summary:
AstroBase is a bilingual (Arabic and English) educational web game where players build and run a human base on the Moon. Players control an astronaut who collects supplies and crystals, constructs and upgrades seven essential buildings (such as habitat, life support, power, communications, and protection), and keeps resources above zero while surviving solar storms and meteor showers. Underground tunnels, cables, and pipes connect the buildings, showing how each system depends on the others.

The project makes real lunar science easy to understand. Interactive comparisons of the Moon, Earth, and Mars cover gravity, temperature, air pressure, day length, size, and communication delay. A weight calculator, a quiz, a memory game, and an AI companion named Robo, who answers space questions, keep learners engaged. All figures are drawn from NASA and Canadian Space Agency data.

It matters because it turns the abstract idea of living on the Moon into hands-on learning that inspires young people, especially Arabic speakers, to explore space science.
projectDetails.details: AstroBase is a bilingual (Arabic and English) educational web game in which players build and manage a human base on the Moon. The player moves an astronaut, collects materials and crystals, constructs and upgrades seven buildings (Habitat, Life Support, Power Station, Communications, Farm, Storage and Radiation Shield), and keeps five resources (Energy, Oxygen, Water, Food and Shield) above zero while surviving solar storms and meteor showers. Tunnels, cables and pipes appear as the base grows, showing that no system on the Moon can function alone. The game also includes a quiz, a memory game, a before-and-after slider, a weight calculator, and comparisons of the Moon, Earth and Mars (air pressure, temperature, day length, size and message delay). The project helps students understand what living on the Moon requires and how power, air, water, food and communication depend on one another. It also brings space-agency science to Arabic-speaking learners, who have few interactive resources in their own language, and it runs in any browser without installation. Published NASA and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) science shaped the game design: NASA DONKI data on solar flares and storms inspired the solar storm event, NASA RadLab data on radiation doses aboard the International Space Station inspired the Shield bar, NASA OSDR studies on astronaut health informed the "Did you know?" facts, and the CSA food-production toolkit inspired the Greenhouse mission. The comparison figures for the Moon, Earth and Mars are drawn from published NASA data. In this prototype, these figures are stored within the game and are not yet retrieved live from NASA; NASA Mars Trek is planned for a future Mars level. The game was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single self-contained file, with the HTML canvas used for the game world, and it is hosted on Cloudflare Workers. The game illustrations and characters were created using AI image-generation tools and are labelled "AI-generated image" in our demonstration. An AI assistant was also used to support the development of parts of the code and text. The robot guide "Robo" provides built-in responses on four topics; open-ended AI responses are available only on platforms that support the Claude AI feature, and therefore, on the public website, Robo may rely solely on its built-in responses. No NASA logos or branding elements were used or modified in this project. The project is creative in that, instead of a textbook, learners operate a living base featuring an astronaut, the friendly robot guide Robo, hazard events, and a base that visibly grows with tunnels and lights, so that interdependence between systems is learned through play in a fully bilingual experience. Our team considered accessibility (browser-based, Arabic and English, simple on-screen controls), age-appropriate language for young learners, scientific accuracy, and transparency about what has been built and what is planned. The first level of the prototype is currently playable. Planned future work, not yet built, includes live NASA data feeds, a Mars level, and school activities using CSA resources.

projectDetails.name: AstroCare
projectDetails.summary: We are the AstroByteX team, and we chose the "Create Health Monitoring Software" challenge. We built AstroCare, a health monitoring platform that helps astronauts keep track of their health during space missions. Living in space comes with unique challenges, including isolation, exposure to space radiation, and limited access to immediate medical support. Astronauts need to monitor different health measurements, but it can be difficult to understand what these numbers mean, notice changes over time, and know when something may need attention. AstroCare lets users record their health measurements and complete daily check-ins about how they feel. It then analyzes this information to show health graphs, highlight unusual readings, and provide alerts and recommendations. This helps astronauts better understand their health, recognize changes that may need attention, and make more informed decisions during their missions.
projectDetails.details:
What it does?

Overview: Shows heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, body temperature, and blood glucose, with a color-coded overall Health Status.

Daily Check-in: Records sleep, mood, and factors affecting the day, with daily reminders.

Analytics: Interactive graphs over 7 days or a month, with unusual readings highlighted.

Reports: Detailed health assessment with averages, ranges, changes, and practical recommendations.

Alerts: Warnings at two levels (Watch and Outside Range), plus a prominent on-screen alert for serious concerns that explains the issue and the next step.

Extras: Individual accounts, mission day tracking, and support for English, Arabic, and German.

How it works?

The astronaut enters measurements and daily check-ins.

Data is saved to their personal account, building a continuous health record.

AstroCare compares readings with expected ranges and past readings to find unusual values and patterns.

It produces an overall Health Status, or says more data is needed instead of assuming everything is fine.

Results appear in Overview, Analytics, and Reports, with alerts and recommendations explaining what was detected, why it matters, and what to do.

projectDetails.name: Analog Fingerprint
projectDetails.summary:
Analog Fingerprint is a web tool, in English and Arabic, that finds the best place on Earth to practice for a specific Moon or Mars mission.

Before astronauts and rovers leave Earth, they rehearse in deserts, polar valleys and lava fields. But looking like Mars is not the same as preparing for Mars. A site can match the ground but not the cold, or hold Moon-like rock hidden under plants.

Our tool lets you pick a mission (test a rover, train astronauts in geology, make water and fuel from local ice, or run a Moon base) and a target on the Moon or Mars, including de Gerlache Rim 2, a NASA Artemis candidate landing region. It then ranks Earth sites using open NASA data, such as LRO LOLA and Diviner, MODIS and Mars mission data. For each site, it shows what can be tested there, what cannot, and what no place on Earth can copy.

Tested on well-known analog sites, 3 of 5 ranked for the work they are really used for. Missing data is never guessed.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES
Analog Fingerprint helps mission teams, scientists and students find the best place on Earth to practice for a Moon or Mars mission. It compares Earth sites with Moon and Mars targets, one property at a time, and shows what each site can and cannot test.

HOW IT WORKS
The website is a short journey of four steps:
1. Which one is Mars? Two photos, one from Chile's Atacama Desert and one from Mars. It is hard to tell, which shows that looks can fool us.
2. Are they really alike? The user compares the two places layer by layer: slopes, rocks, water, temperature, and air and gravity.
3. What do you want to test? The user picks one of four missions and one of five targets: Gale crater, Jezero crater and Arcadia Planitia on Mars, and Shackleton crater rim and de Gerlache Rim 2 (a NASA Artemis candidate landing region) on the Moon.
4. Where on Earth should we test it? The tool ranks 16 Earth sites. Each site has a card with one verdict per property (similar, partly similar, different or no data), a list of what can be tested there, a list of what cannot, and a fixed row for what Earth cannot copy: gravity, air and radiation.

EXAMPLE
Input: "Test a rover" at Jezero crater. The tool compares slopes, bare ground, rocks, temperature and dryness. Sites without similar slopes and bare ground are not ranked, because a rover on Mars never drives through plants.
Output: Holuhraun (Iceland) ranks first, then Yungay (Atacama) and Haughton crater (Canada).

RESULTS
- 3 of 5 well-known analog sites ranked for the work they are really used for. For example, Holuhraun ranked first for rover testing, and NASA really tested rovers there.
- Earth cannot copy the Moon's south pole cold. Earth's coldest ground is about −98 °C, while Shackleton's rim reaches about −210 °C, so Earth covers only 39% of its temperature range.
- All 11 Earth sites we checked with Moon-like rock (anorthosite) look covered by plants or ice in our satellite data.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
Mission teams can choose a test site in minutes and see its blind spots before money and months go into fieldwork.
Scientists get a comparison they can check: every value links to its source, and every rule is written down.
Students and the public get a simple, honest way to understand space exploration.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
It ranks places by mission, not by looks. It is honest about Earth's limits on every result. It tests itself against known analog sites and publishes its misses. And it can say "no site fits yet" instead of forcing a winner.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERD:
Fair comparison: the same 240 m grid and slope method on all three worlds, and ground temperature compared with ground temperature.
Scientific honesty: missing data is shown as missing, never guessed, and every result states what Earth cannot copy.
Transparency: every value links to its source, and every rule is written down on the "How we know" page.
Accessibility: plain words, English and Arabic, and no login needed.
Simplicity: we designed every screen so a first-time visitor can understand it in about five seconds.
Storytelling: the four steps lead the user from a question to an answer, so they discover the problem before they see the solution.
Scale: our satellite data sees about 250 m, so small rock outcrops can be missed, and we say so.

TOOLS
Google Earth Engine (JavaScript), Node.js, Next.js, React, TypeScript, MapLibre, Vitest and Playwright (143 automated tests), hosted on Vercel.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS
This is a working prototype with 16 Earth sites. A search of all land on Earth is built and tested on small areas but not finished. Next, we will finish that search, add a sharper 20 m bare-ground test, add more Artemis landing regions, and add Canadian Space Agency radar data.

AI USE
The code, data scripts and documentation were developed with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) under our team's direction and review. ChatGPT helped us shape the story and weigh our ideas. The demo voice-over was generated with ElevenLabs. Our team chose the challenge, the direction and every final decision.

LINKS
Code: https://github.com/Gharbawy1/Nasa-2026
Live Demo: https://nasa-demo-nine.vercel.app/en
Every source, rule and limit: the "How we know" page on the website.

projectDetails.name: Flamo
projectDetails.summary:
Flamo is an SI-powered, voice-first fire-safety copilot designed to support astronauts, researchers, and learners throughout space missions. It combines an interactive 3D animation of different space environments, including an ISS-like spacecraft, a lunar base, and a spacesuit, with an intelligent SI companion that adapts its assistance to the user's surroundings.

Through voice or text interaction, Flamo serves two main purposes: providing crews with emergency fire-response guidance and mission assistance, while giving students, researchers, and engineers access to relevant scientific information, experimental results, and research findings.

Its intelligence is powered by a unified database integrating NASA's PSI combustion data and Combustion Science research. We connected scattered experimental records, NASA technical documents, and research papers into one queryable scientific knowledge base, making decades of microgravity combustion research accessible and interconnected.

Flamo uses this knowledge to retrieve relevant experiments, compare scientific findings with the user's environment, and present results through an interactive dashboard featuring visualizations, experimental data, and traceable NASA references. It also identifies research gaps rather than presenting unsupported conclusions.
projectDetails.details:
Github : https://github.com/AhmedAbdELMoneim1/flamo-astroentropy-web-app


MOTIVATION & OBJECTIVE


Motivation

Fire is one of the few emergencies a crew must handle alone, and the Moon base will make it harder. Apollo 1 was lost to fire in an oxygen-rich cabin, and both Apollo 13 and Mir survived oxygen-system failures. On Artemis II a smoke alarm went off about 80,000 miles from home. The atmospheres planned next raise the stakes: a Moon base or pressurized rover at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, and spacesuits at 100% oxygen and 4.3 psi.

NASA has decades of flight data on how flames behave without gravity, but it is spread across 24 PSI investigations, thousands of test rows in different formats, scanned data sheets, reports and papers. A researcher who asks "what burns near 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi?" must today open several tables and documents and reconcile units by hand. A student cannot easily learn why a microgravity flame is a sphere, or why that changes how fabric burns.


Objective

an SI-powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets the PSI combustion investigations for fire safety, in one conversation. Concretely, Flamo should:

  1. Find the investigations and tests that matter for a given habitat, atmosphere or question, and rank them by relevance.
  2. Extract comparable data (oxygen, pressure, flow, fuel, sample, outcome, spread rate, extinction) that supports predictive modeling.
  3. Interpret results in plain language, always with the source, and say clearly what the data does not cover yet (spacesuit atmosphere, partial gravity, Mars).
  4. Serve two audiences: a crew that needs a short, action-first answer, and students, researchers and engineers who need the evidence.

HOW IT WORKS

Solution Diagram

You ask Flamo by voice or chat. A router sends the question to NASA test data for numbers, or to NASA reports and papers for explanations. A checker makes sure every number is in the source. Flamo then speaks a short answer while the dashboard shows the evidence.

HOME

The user starts in the cabin hub and chooses one of 4 pillars: Prevention, Flammability & Fire Behavior, Detection, Suppression. Each pillar has sub-categories the user can click, or the user can just ask Flamo.

  • Prevention: Ignition, Materials
  • Flammability & Fire Behavior: Flame Spread
  • Detection: Smoke
  • Suppression: Suppression

Flamo Status

Flamo's face shows its state: Connecting, Idle, Listening, Thinking, Speaking, Disconnected. 

Dashboard

Ask by voice. Flamo answers and the dashboard updates 

KPIs and a chart, not just text

Every answer is cited

Ask by voice or text. Flamo speaks sentences, and the dashboard shows the full answer: KPIs, a chart, the nearest real tests, the most relevant investigations, gaps in the data, and numbered NASA sources that open at the cited page.

Scenarios

The same question, answered for the atmosphere you are in:

  • ISS (21% O₂, 14.7 psi): 221 tests in 8 investigations, High coverage.
  • Moon Base (≥30% O₂, ≤10.2 psi): 51 tests in 2 investigations, Medium coverage.
  • Space Suit (100% O₂, 4.3 psi): no test in the PSI data we integrated ran this atmosphere, so Flamo shows it as a gap instead of guessing. 
  • Custom: move the oxygen and pressure sliders, or just say “34% at 8.2 psi”. Flamo finds the nearest tests (29 here) and computes the oxygen partial pressure.


TECHNICAL ASPECTS

Data Pipeline Extraction

Two pipelines build Flamo’s knowledge.

Numbers

22 NASA experiment tables are merged into one test database. Gaps are filled from NASA documents only with an exact quote and page. Papers become 322 verified findings.

Explanations

Papers and reports are parsed by Docling. Text is chunked as is, tables are kept as tables, and figures by their captions. Everything is embedded (Cohere) into pgvector, tagged with its investigation and page.

Voice SI

Flamo is a LiveKit voice agent running Gemini Live. It doesn’t answer from memory: for every question it calls our server’s answer tool, which returns what to say and what to show. Emergencies take a fast path to a fixed checklist with no search.

Backend

A Python FastAPI server holds the answer engine. It reads the test database (SQLite), searches NASA reports and papers (Postgres + pgvector), reranks the results (Cohere), and serves NASA PDFs to the in-app viewer. Voice and chat use the same engine, so both give the same answer. 


How a Query Happens in the DB

The router reads the question and picks a path: data tools for numbers, or a search limited to the relevant investigations for explanations. The composer writes the answer, and a checker drops any sentence whose number isn’t in the source. Flamo then speaks and the dashboard opens.

TOOLS USED

Data Acquisition & Storage: NASA PSI, Python, SQLite, PostgreSQL, pgvector
Data Processing & AI: Docling, OCR, Gemini Flash-Lite, Groq, Cohere (Embed v4.0, Rerank) 

Voice AI: LiveKit, Gemini Live

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn 

Frontend & Visualization: React, Vite, TypeScript, WebGL, SVG 

Development & Deployment: Docker, Git, GitHub, Claude Code

IMPACT, LIMITS & FUTURE WORK

Impact

  • Crews: a fast, cited, action-first answer when time matters.
  • Researchers and engineers: comparable test data for predictive modeling, in one conversation instead of several tables and papers.
  • Students and professors: a way to learn why microgravity flames behave differently, with sources.
  • Mission planners and NASA: a clear view of where data is missing (spacesuit atmosphere, partial gravity, Mars), which helps decide what to test next.
  • Earth: the same insights support fire-safety technology on Earth. Fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for the ISS, smoke detection and firefighter gear all grew from this kind of research

Limits

Flamo is an educational and research tool. It is not flight-certified and supports, but does not replace, approved crew procedures. Its emergency checklist is a fixed, no-search path and would need review by fire-safety specialists before

any real-world use. There is no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI yet, and the challenge scope leaves out rockets and propellants. Where data is missing, Flamo says so instead of guessing.

Future work

  • Add partial-gravity results when LUCI and FM2 data appear in PSI. New investigations go through the same pipeline and appear in the same views.
  • Rank which missing test conditions matter most for crew safety.
  • Add data export so researchers can use the matched test data in their own flammability models.
  • Review the emergency checklist with fire-safety experts.
