projectDetails.name: Project ASTRO X
projectDetails.summary:
Rovers, landers and science stations have sat on the Moon and Mars for decades. Each is a real record of a mission, and for a child an open mystery. Today that mystery stays closed: museum labels give one photo and one caption, teachers rebuild every story from scratch, and children aged 6–13 never get to ask what the equipment did or what it found.
RAMIM — Discover the Story. Explore the Science. — is a web experience that turns one space artifact into one interactive story a child can explore.
A child scans a QR code, picks an age band, and reads a short comic built around equipment left on the Moon or Mars. Tapping a glowing hotspot opens a verified NASA fact, a real NASA mission photo or video, or a rotatable 3D model. An AI guide then answers the child's questions in plain language from the same NASA sources, and marks fictional story details as fiction.
Children gain curiosity grounded in real science. Teachers gain a ready-made lesson where every fact carries a NASA source. Museums and outreach teams carry many artifacts on one screen, in more than one language.
In 48 hours we built a working prototype: comic reader, NASA-based hotspots, embedded NASA videos, a 3D model viewer and an AI question guide.
projectDetails.details:
What RAMIM does

RAMIM turns a single piece of space equipment into a single interactive story that a child can explore. A child scans a QR code printed on a museum card, a classroom worksheet or a poster, chooses an age band (8-12, 12–15 or 15–18), and lands in a short digital comic built around one artifact: a science station left on the Moon, a rover on Mars, an instrument that is still sitting there today. The story is the entry point; the science is the payload.

How it works

The comic reader renders the story and overlays hotspots on the equipment in each panel. Every hotspot is bound to a content record that holds a verified NASA fact, a NASA mission photo or video, or a 3D model. Tapping a hotspot opens a card with the fact, the NASA source it comes from, and the media itself; the 3D viewer lets the child rotate the model and see how the parts fit together. At any point the child can ask the AI question guide a question in plain language. The guide receives the question together with the NASA context of the active artifact, answers at the reading level the child selected, stays inside that NASA content, and says explicitly when a detail belongs to the fictional story rather than to science. Characters and story events are fictional and labelled as fiction; equipment, missions, discoveries and media are real and linked to their source.

Benefits and intended impact

Children aged 6–13 currently meet space equipment as one photograph and one caption. RAMIM replaces that with a story they control: they read, tap, explore and ask, so curiosity turns into a question they can actually answer. Teachers get a ready-made lesson in which every fact already carries a NASA source, instead of rebuilding the story themselves. Museums and outreach programmes can put many artifacts on one screen, in more than one language, and add new content without new hardware. The intended impact is a shift in how children encounter space heritage: from looking at an object to understanding what it did, what it found, and why it still matters, and a model in which every artifact already on the Moon and Mars becomes a doorway into real NASA science.

Tools and technologies

We built RAMIM as a browser-based web application so that it runs on the devices children, classrooms and museums already have, with no installation and no special hardware. The prototype was built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, a comic reader and hotspot system we wrote ourselves, an embedded 3D model viewer for rotating the equipment, and a generative AI API for the question guide. NASA facts, photos and videos are linked directly from NASA Science and the NASA Image and Video Library. We used AI-assisted coding and design tools to build the prototype inside the hackathon window, and checked every scientific statement against its NASA source before it shipped.

How it is creative

Most space education content is organised around a mission and reads like a timeline. RAMIM is organised around the object: the artifact is the main character, and its parts are the chapters. A hotspot turns a static image into a question, a QR code turns a physical card or poster into an entrance, and the AI guide turns a child's curiosity into an answer at their own reading level. The creative decision we are proudest of is keeping fiction and science visibly separate: the story can be imaginative precisely because the facts beside it are real and sourced. And because a new artifact is new content rather than new code, the idea scales from one story to a whole museum.

Factors we considered

We designed around the constraints of the people we are serving. For children: short sentences, large tap targets, strong contrast, reading levels instead of a single version, and no accounts, logins or personal data collected. For teachers: facts that are traceable, so a lesson can be defended to a parent or a principal. For museums: deployment on a shared screen or a visitor's own phone, multiple languages, and the ability to add artifacts without rebuilding the product. For trust: a visible source on every hotspot, and an AI that is allowed to explain but not to invent. For reach: a lightweight web app that works on low-bandwidth connections, so the experience is not limited to well-funded institutions.

Honest status

What works today in our prototype: the web app and comic reader, hotspots with NASA-based facts, embedded NASA videos, the 3D model viewer, and the AI question guide. Planned next, and not yet built: more artifact stories, teacher tools, testing with children in classrooms and museums, and printed comics connected through QR codes.

projectDetails.name: Galactic Museum
projectDetails.summary:
Problem:
Dozens of robotic explorers, landers, rovers, and scientific stations from past lunar and Martian missions now sit silent beyond Earth—from Viking 1 and Pathfinder to Apollo hardware and Opportunity. To students and the general public, these machines often feel distant, fragmented across technical archives, or reduced to "space junk," obscuring the engineering breakthroughs and human stories they represent.

Solution:
Galactic Museum transforms NASA's resting off-world spacecraft into an interactive, bilingual (English & Arabic RTL) digital heritage museum and educational arcade. Visitors can explore:

A Walkable 3D Odyssey Museum: Glass showcase wings for the Moon, Mars, Orbital Telescopes, and Deep Space with glowing holographic reconstructions and Connor, a voiced spatial tour guide.
Interactive 3D Hardware Inspector: 23 cataloged space vehicles and 27 historical artifacts with NASA-grounded 3D models, annotated engineering hotspots, mission timelines, and verified landing coordinates.
STEM Learning Lab & Playable Mission Arcade: Interactive physics quizzes, collectible Cosmic Passport badges, and playable missions—including AFTERLIGHT, Lunar Lander, Mars Rally, Moonfall, and Every Woman's Earth—playable on both desktop keyboards and mobile touchscreens.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Galactic Museum is an interactive, browser-based 3D space heritage museum and educational platform built for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge. Instead of leaving lunar and Martian exploration hardware buried in technical PDFs, visitors walk through a virtual museum and inspect real NASA spacecraft up close:

  • 3D Odyssey Museum: A multi-wing Three.js museum featuring the Central Hall, East Wing (Moon), West Wing (Mars), Observation Deck (Earth/ISS/Hubble/JWST), Research Library, and Education Zone. Clicking any glass showcase activates a live holographic reconstruction above the central podium and lets visitors zoom into the vitrine or summon Connor, our spatial audio tour guide.
  • Interactive 3D Worlds & Engineering Inspector: Visitors explore 23 space vehicles across the Moon, Mars, Outer Giants, and Observatories, and 27 detailed artifacts with interactive 3D models (GLB), annotated component hotspots (RTGs, cameras, drills, solar arrays), mission timelines, and exact landing coordinates.
  • Playable Mission Arcade & STEM Learning Lab: Visitors can test their knowledge with physics challenges, earn Cosmic Passport badges, and play 5 in-app space games (AFTERLIGHT, Lunar Lander, Mars Rally, Moonfall, and Every Woman’s Earth) plus NASA Space Place simulations—all playable on desktop or mobile touchscreens.

What benefits does it have?

  • Turns static archives into hands-on exploration: Replaces dense tables with interactive 3D inspection, spatial audio storytelling, and mission gameplay.
  • Accessible across devices and languages: Runs directly in any modern browser without downloads, supports full English and Arabic localization, and includes responsive mobile touch controls and landscape guidance so phone users can explore and play seamlessly.
  • Scientifically grounded clarity: Every artifact uses transparent mission status classifications (Operational, Inactive, Lost Contact, Partially Retrieved, Impact) backed by official NASA sources.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Designed for students (ages 10–16), educators, and space enthusiasts worldwide—especially Arabic- and English-speaking learners who rarely see interactive 3D STEM archives in both languages—Galactic Museum aims to:

  1. Reframe dormant spacecraft on the Moon and Mars from "space junk" into historic monuments of human curiosity and engineering.
  2. Spark STEM interest by connecting historical missions (Apollo, Viking 1, Surveyor 3, Opportunity, InSight, Perseverance) to playable physics simulations.
  3. Provide an extensible archive ready to add upcoming Artemis and future planetary surface sites.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages & Core Web Stack: TypeScript, HTML5/CSS3, React 18, Vite 6, Tailwind CSS 3, React Router 6, Zustand 5.
  • 3D Graphics & Animation: Three.js, @google/model-viewer, PlayCanvas (playcanvas, @playcanvas/react), GSAP + ScrollTrigger.
  • Audio & Voice: Web Audio API, spatial positional audio (THREE.PositionalAudio), ElevenLabs speech synthesis (for Connor’s bilingual tour narration), and CC BY 3.0 ambient soundtrack ("Aurora" by Stellardrone).
  • Datasets & References: NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), NASA 3D Resources, NASA Image and Video Library, Apollo Lunar Surface Journal (ALSJ), and NASA JPL Mission Archives.
  • Development Hardware & Tooling: Standard Windows development PCs, Git/GitHub, Node.js, and Chromium DevTools for desktop/mobile WebGL testing.

How is your project creative?

  • Museum + Holo-Deck + Arcade in One Experience: Rather than building a standard info website or a single standalone game, we combined an architectural 3D museum (Odyssey), an interactive 3D engineering teardown inspector, a cinematic planetary chronicle, and a playable mission arcade into one cohesive story.
  • Unified Curatorial Voice: Connor, our holographic guide, connects architectural wings, historical breakthroughs, and playable kiosks through synchronized spatial audio and subtitles.
  • Reframing Debris as Heritage: Even status badges and glass vitrine placards mirror real-world museum curation—honoring machines like Viking 1, Surveyor 3, and Opportunity as enduring monuments.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Historical & Scientific Accuracy: We audited 3D models, coordinates, power sources, and mission timelines against NASA PDS and JPL records (for example, ensuring Viking 1 displays its authentic lander mesh, Chryse Planitia coordinates, dual SNAP-19 RTG specs, and 2,245-sol lifespan).
  • Performance & Mobile Usability: Large 3D scenes use pooled dynamic lighting (8 fixed Three.js PointLight slots), Draco compression, lazy-loaded routes, and custom on-screen multi-touch controls so mobile phones remain smooth and playable.
  • Bilingual & Cultural Inclusion: Full RTL layout mirroring, Arabic typography (IBM Plex Sans Arabic), and bilingual telemetry/subtitles make the museum native in both English and Arabic.
  • User Experience & Polish: Careful UI spacing, unobtrusive background music controls, and guided camera transitions prevent visual clutter while keeping navigation intuitive for younger learners.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. projectDetails.name: NOVA
projectDetails.summary:
NOVA is an interactive, gamified simulation developed to bridge the gap between space exploration and the general public. Designed for space enthusiasts and everyday users with little to no technical background, the project demystifies complex aerospace and planetary mission concepts through engaging, hands-on gameplay.

In NOVA, players encounter realistic space mission scenarios where they must make critical decisions, manage resources, and troubleshoot failures. By intentionally introducing challenges and safe-to-fail learning loops, the game allows users to learn from their mistakes in real-time.

This project is important because it transforms passive observers into active participants, fostering science literacy, critical thinking, and a genuine curiosity about space science. By making aerospace education accessible and entertaining, NOVA empowers the next generation of space explorers and innovators from all walks of life.
projectDetails.details:
NOVA is an interactive, gamified simulation designed to demystify space exploration. The game places players into realistic aerospace and planetary mission scenarios where they must make critical decisions, manage resources, and troubleshoot system failures. It operates through intuitive hands-on gameplay that allows users to experience real-world space engineering challenges firsthand.

The project bridges the gap between complex space science and the general public. It serves as an accessible educational tool that transforms passive observers into active participants, fostering science literacy, critical thinking, and a genuine curiosity about aerospace domains without requiring a heavy technical background.

The primary impact is to make space education engaging, approachable, and fun for everyday users and aspiring space enthusiasts. By introducing safe-to-fail learning loops, users learn from their mistakes in real-time, empowering a broader, more diverse audience to take an interest in STEM fields and future space innovations.

The project was developed using modern web technologies and frameworks, primarily utilizing React and Vite for building a fast, component-based user interface and interactive simulation environment, styled with CSS/Tailwind, and managed via standard JavaScript/Node ecosystem development tools.

NOVA creatively translates complex, highly technical space mission architectures into an engaging gaming experience. Instead of dry theoretical learning, it uses interactive trial-and-error mechanics and gamified problem-solving to make learning about space intuitive and entertaining.

The team focused heavily on user experience (UX) and accessibility, ensuring that players with little to no prior technical knowledge could easily understand the mechanics. We prioritized real-world authenticity while keeping the learning curve friendly, ensuring a balance between educational value and entertaining gameplay.

projectDetails.name: Mars (x)
projectDetails.summary: Martian Map is a platform we developed to help plan rover routes and explore the Martian surface. One of the main difficulties in Mars exploration is finding routes that are safe to travel while still reaching locations worth investigating. To address this, we use Martian geospatial data, such as elevation, slope, and terrain characteristics, to analyze the surface and calculate least-cost routes based on selected parameters and safety limits. We also developed a Science Mode that considers the distribution of resources, including water (H₂O), iron (Fe), and silicon (Si), to help identify areas of scientific interest. Through the platform, users can select destinations, view proposed routes, and examine details such as elevation profiles, slope variations, route length, estimated travel time, and resource distribution. What makes Martian Map useful is that it considers both the conditions a rover must cross and the scientific value of the places it may reach. Instead of selecting a route based only on distance or terrain, users can evaluate different paths while keeping exploration objectives in mind. This can help make rover route planning more practical and better aligned with the goals of a mission.
projectDetails.details:
Martian Map was developed to investigate how geospatial analysis can improve rover route planning by accounting for both terrain conditions and scientific objectives. The platform processes multiple Martian geospatial datasets, including elevation, slope, temperature, wind, and radiation, to evaluate the characteristics of the surface along potential routes.

The routing system is based on a least-cost path approach. Using Python, we process the input datasets as raster layers, normalize their values, and combine selected parameters through adjustable weights to generate a cost surface. Safety constraints are incorporated to identify terrain that may be unsuitable for rover movement. The pathfinding algorithm then searches this surface for a route with the lowest accumulated cost between the selected coordinates. This approach allows route selection to reflect terrain conditions rather than relying solely on geographical distance.

A separate Science Mode incorporates spatial resource data, including water (H₂O), iron (Fe), and silicon (Si), into the exploration process. This allows users to examine the distribution of these resources and consider their scientific relevance when evaluating potential destinations and routes.

The backend was implemented using Python and Django, with NumPy, Rasterio, Pandas, SciPy, and scikit-image supporting numerical computation, raster processing, and pathfinding. The frontend uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript to provide interactive maps, destination selection, route visualization, and analytical profiles. Users can examine elevation changes, slope conditions, route length, estimated travel time, and resource distribution. Vehicle-related parameters are also considered in route planning.

Several factors guided our design, including terrain accessibility, rover safety, the influence of individual environmental variables, computational efficiency, and the scientific relevance of exploration sites. A central aspect of the project is the integration of terrain-based navigation with resource analysis, allowing route evaluation to account for both operational feasibility and potential scientific value.

projectDetails.name: Astromoon Lunar South pole Landing Planner
projectDetails.summary: We developed Astromoon, an interactive web application and landing planner specifically designed to address the complexities of lunar exploration at the Moon's South Pole. Astromoon serves as a comprehensive tool to help mission planners and researchers analyze terrain challenges, evaluate lighting conditions, and optimize landing sites in permanently shadowed regions or high-relief areas. By providing an intuitive interface for visualizing critical lunar data, our solution directly tackles the logistical and environmental hurdles of safe spacecraft descent and resource scouting. This project is vital because unlocking the potential of the lunar South Pole—home to crucial water ice reserves—requires precise, accessible planning tools to ensure the safety and success of future crewed and robotic missions.

projectDetails.name: Analog Finder
projectDetails.summary: Analog Finder measures how closely places on Earth match specific Moon and Mars sites, so mission teams can pick analog test sites by data instead of habit. We measured 9 real targets from orbital data (LRO LOLA, Diviner and Lunar Prospector in LROC QuickMap; MGS MOLA in Google Colab), then measured 10 factors for 59 Earth sites and whole-world scans in Google Earth Engine. NASA EMIT minerals, ESA permafrost maps and Sentinel-2 images check the best candidates, and an interactive map lets anyone pick a target and see every Earth site re-rank, with the source of every number. Results: the closest matches to Jezero Crater are two plateaus never proposed for Jezero, Aksai Chin (Karakoram-Kunlun) and the limestone plateau east of Kharga, Egypt, tied at 75% and above Haughton Crater (68%); EMIT shows Kharga's carbonate is uniform, making it the practical first field site. For a permanent Moon base, Harrat Khaybar, Saudi Arabia, is the best lava-tube shelter analog (76%) and the eastern Karakoram the best south-pole terrain outside Antarctica. The method ranks 13 of 15 known analog pairs in the top quarter.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Analog sites for Moon and Mars missions are usually chosen because they are known and reachable, not because anyone measured how well they match a specific target. Analog Finder measures it. For 9 real targets (lunar south pole, Mare Imbrium, the Mare Tranquillitatis pit, Descartes highlands; Jezero, Gale, Arcadia Planitia, the Arsia Mons pits and Meridiani Planum) we measured each target's conditions from orbital data: slope, iron, hydrogen, temperature and rock cover on the Moon in LROC QuickMap, and slope on Mars from MOLA in Google Colab.

HOW IT WORKS

We measured 10 factors for 59 Earth sites in Google Earth Engine: cold, dryness, temperature swing, thin air (altitude), relief, rock type, vegetation, ground ice, and site features such as caves and impact craters. A weighted similarity gives each site a match score per target. World scans at 5 km and 250 m close-ups search the whole planet for new areas; NASA EMIT minerals, ESA permafrost maps and Sentinel-2 images check the best ones. The interactive map lets anyone pick a target, re-rank every site, adjust the weights, and see a radar chart and the source of every number, plus travel time and protected status.

RESULTS

- Jezero Crater: two plateaus never proposed for Jezero, Aksai Chin (Karakoram-Kunlun, a disputed border area) and the limestone plateau east of Kharga Oasis, Egypt, tied at 75%, both above the classic Haughton Crater (68%). EMIT shows Kharga's carbonate is uniform (99-100% of detections at 6 spots) while Aksai Chin's is patchy, and Kharga is 4 hours from a city: the practical first field site. Egypt's Western Desert was compared to Mars in NASA-funded studies by Farouk El-Baz (1979-82), but its carbonate plateaus were never proposed for Jezero.

- Permanent Moon base: Harrat Khaybar, Saudi Arabia, is #1 of 59 sites for a lava-tube shelter (76%), ahead of NASA's cave analogs Lava Beds and El Malpais; the eastern Karakoram is the best match to the lunar south pole outside Antarctica.

- Mars base ice (Arcadia): the Tibetan Plateau (74%) is the best match outside Antarctica.

- Gale and Meridiani: Chile's Atacama coast range is a new #1.

DOES IT WORK?

13 of 15 well-known analog pairs rank in the top quarter, and 2,000 random re-weightings test how stable each result is. Scores are relative, so sites within about one point are treated as ties.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission planners and field scientists can find and justify analog sites for a specific landing site or base, compare options on the same scale, and see what each site lets a team practise (ice drilling, carbonate sampling, lava-tube operations).

TOOLS

Google Earth Engine (JavaScript), Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pandas, matplotlib), LROC QuickMap, NASA AppEEARS, Google Colab, D3.js and TopoJSON for the map, GitHub Pages for hosting.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

Scans run at 1-5 km, so caves come from catalogs; EMIT covers only latitudes below 54 degrees; crew factors (isolation, dust, regolith) are not scored yet; no field visit yet. Next: visit the Kharga plateau, add crew factors, global mineral and cave catalogs, and the Artemis III and Mars human landing sites.

Use of AI: code and text were written with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic); all measurements were run and checked by the team.

projectDetails.name: BEYONDX
projectDetails.summary:
BeyondX is an interactive space museum that brings the stories of humanity's forgotten space explorers back to life. We developed an immersive website where users can explore three environments: the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space, discovering the spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific equipment left behind.
Each artifact has its interactive experience, providing visitors with information about its identity, purpose, mission, and scientific contributions, supported by engaging voice-over narration.
To make space exploration accessible to different audiences, BeyondX features two experiences: Kids Mode, which presents information through simple, fun, and engaging storytelling, and Adult Mode, which offers a more detailed educational experience.
Our project directly addresses NASA's challenge, *"Abandoned but not Forgotten,"* by transforming historical mission information into an interactive storytelling experience rather than simply presenting technical facts. It helps users understand not only what equipment was left behind, but also why it was sent, what it accomplished, and how it contributed to our understanding of the universe.
BeyondX is important because these forgotten machines represent decades of human curiosity, innovation, and scientific achievement. By preserving their stories in an accessible and engaging digital museum, we aim to inspire the next generation, encourage curiosity about space, and remind everyone that even when a mission ends, its legacy lives on.
projectDetails.details:
BEYONDX

Some missions end. Their stories remain.

What exactly does it do?

BEYONDX is an interactive 3D web experience that turns the equipment humanity left behind in space into stories anyone can explore. Instead of reading a list of missions, the user travels to a world, lands on its surface, and discovers each object for themselves.

The experience has three collections and 29 independent stories:

Moon (16 stories): the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the three Lunar Roving Vehicles, the five ALSEP science stations, and the seven Surveyor landers, including the two that crashed.

Mars (8 stories): Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, and the Ingenuity helicopter, plus a timeline showing how each generation asked a new question about Mars.

Deep Space (5 stories): Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, and the Kepler Space Telescope.

Every story answers the same six questions: What was it? Why was it sent? What did it do? What did it discover? What happened to it? Why does it still matter?

How does it work?

The user chooses a world from the Space Hub and watches a cinematic descent to its surface.

Glowing markers show where equipment is waiting. There is no fixed order; the user picks any marker.

The camera flies to the object, which first appears only as a dark silhouette.

The user is asked “What do you think this is?” with three choices (or can skip).

The object is revealed as a 3D model, and its story unfolds step by step while the relevant part of the model lights up.

The story ends with the object’s final fate: a timeline, key facts, its real coordinates, and NASA sources.

A single switch turns on Kids Mode. The facts stay exactly the same, but the whole experience changes: simpler language, a friendly astronaut guide named Cosmo who reacts to the child’s answers, star-based progress, confetti for correct guesses, and a quiz with a certificate. Each story also has recorded narration in both a Kids and an Adults version.

What benefits does it have?

Makes space history accessible. Complex missions become short, clear stories that need no prior knowledge.

Serves two audiences with one product. Adults get a documentary-style experience with dates, instruments and sources; children get an adventure built on the same facts.

Learning by discovery. Guessing before the reveal makes users curious and helps them remember what they learn.

Scientific honesty. We separate launch, landing, last contact and official mission end; we never present life on Mars as proven; and we clearly label our 3D terrain and models as illustrative reconstructions while showing the real coordinates as text.

Easy to extend. Stories are stored as data, separate from the interface, so new missions can be added without rebuilding the site.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want people to see these objects not as abandoned machines but as part of humanity’s history. Our goals are to preserve the stories behind the hardware, to give teachers and families a tool that works for both adults and children, and to inspire the next generation of explorers. In the future we hope to add more missions, real NASA imagery and terrain data, and more languages.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS, GLSL (procedural noise for terrain and textures)

Framework and build: React, Vite

3D graphics: Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei. All spacecraft models and both planetary surfaces are generated procedurally in code.

Animation: GSAP (cinematic camera movement), Motion (interface transitions)

State management: Zustand

Styling: Tailwind CSS

Audio: recorded narration for every story group in Kids and Adults versions, plus Web Audio for small interface sounds

Data and references: NASA, NASA Science, NASA JPL, and the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)

Hardware: none required. It runs in any modern web browser on desktop or mobile.

projectDetails.name: LunaQuest
projectDetails.summary:
LunaQuest is an educational game created by our team, AstroNexa_2, to help children aged 7–12 explore what life on the Moon might actually be like.
We wanted to make learning about space more exciting by giving children the chance to become junior astronauts and experience the challenges of running a lunar base. Throughout the game, players face different situations where they need to make decisions about oxygen, energy, radiation protection and how to use their limited resources wisely.
What makes LunaQuest special is that every choice matters. Players can see how their decisions affect their mission, learn from mistakes, and try different ways to solve problems.
Using scientific information and resources from NASA as a foundation, we aim to make the challenges of lunar exploration easier to understand through fun missions and interactive gameplay.
With LunaQuest, we hope to inspire children's curiosity about space while helping them develop problem-solving skills and understand how real astronauts make important decisions.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Luna-Quest: The Living Moon Colony is a single-player educational game for children aged 7–12. The player is the mission commander of a Moon colony inspired by the lunar south pole. Children walk into every functional building (habitat, mission control, greenhouse, workshop), meet eight human crewmates with their own routines and stories, and solve problems by measuring, repairing, planning and deciding. There are no quizzes, no combat and no permanent game over. Mistakes are explained and can be fixed.

Main use

Luna-Quest answers NASA’s Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Its main use is to teach children how a Moon outpost really works by making trade-offs between power, air, water, food, radiation and communications.

How it works

Each activity follows one loop: explore, discover, understand, choose, act, see the result, reflect. The colony systems are linked. Dust on solar panels lowers power, low power dims the greenhouse lights, and the child must decide what to protect first. Crewmates speak, gesture and react, so children read less. A knowledge journal records each concept the child met. Hints adapt to how the child plays. An optional Lunar Day mode lasts 30 Earth days, about one Moon day.

How NASA data supports it

DONKI: space-weather events drive radiation alerts and shelter decisions.

LRO CRaTER: radiation measured in lunar orbit.

LRO LOLA and Moon Trek: terrain and slopes for rover routes and building sites.

NASA SVS illumination maps: sunlight and shadow for solar-power planning.

LRO Diviner: surface temperature.

JPL Horizons: Sun and Earth positions.

OSDR: plant studies for the greenhouse.

Each value keeps its source, unit and evidence type: direct Moon measurement, orbital data, spaceflight or Earth analogue, or future concept.

Benefits and goals

Children learn three lessons: the Moon has no breathable air, power depends on sunlight, and space radiation is a real hazard. They also practise teamwork, systems thinking and careful decision-making. We hope to make space engineering something children can experience through play.

Tools and technology

A shared C# simulation core (.NET Standard 2.1) holds all the rules (power, water, air, heat, dust, food, radiation, incidents) and runs without a game engine.

Unity 6.3 LTS is the target for the browser version.

Godot 4.7.2 .NET is a possible desktop version using the same core.

3D assets are made in Blender and the data is stored as JSON.

Delivered now vs future plans

Delivered: the full game design document, the technical architecture, the crew and player data for all characters, the research and evidence-labelling system, and this demo presentation.

MVP scope in progress: one connected Moon zone, four enterable buildings (habitat, mission control, greenhouse, workshop), six optional activities and the knowledge journal.

Future plans: Arabic and English play, a teacher and family guide, more buildings and crew stories, and player-built colony expansion.

Limitations

All in-game numbers are simplified game values, not NASA measurements.

A solar flare or proton flux is not a radiation dose, and the game does not convert one into the other.

Apollo-inspired stories say where the real event happened. Apollo 12 and 13 problems occurred in flight, not on the Moon.

Future technology such as a surface fission reactor is shown only as a research concept.

The game is educational and does not replace real engineering or medical guidance.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroNexx
projectDetails.summary: AstroNex is an integrated software platform designed to monitor and support astronauts' physical health and psychological well-being during space missions. projectDetails.name: AstroPulse — Autonomous Spaceflight Crew Health Monitor
projectDetails.summary:
AstroPulse is an autonomous astronaut health monitoring platform developed by Team AstroNode for deep-space missions such as Artemis IV. Because communication delays of up to 22 minutes and solar conjunction blackouts prevent real-time Earth medical support, crews need onboard clinical autonomy during acute emergencies.

AstroPulse provides a real-time medical HUD that tracks crew physiological vitals (heart rate, SpO2, core temperature, and stress) alongside cabin conditions (CO2, pressure, and radiation). Instead of acting as a passive dashboard, it pairs anomaly detection with closed-loop countermeasures—guiding crew members through immediate corrective actions and verifying physiological recovery. It features dual views for the Flight Surgeon and individual astronauts, isolates communication dropouts from false clinical alerts, and integrates AURA, a Gemini-powered AI assistant with an offline fallback engine. Built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, this prototype simulates telemetry calibrated to NASA HRP and ECLSS standards.
projectDetails.details:
When our team (Team AstroNode) started looking into deep-space missions like Artemis IV, one question kept coming back to us: what happens when an astronaut gets into medical trouble millions of kilometers away from Earth, and the radio takes 22 minutes just to say "help"?

In Low Earth Orbit, flight surgeons on the ground are practically in the room with the crew. Beyond the Moon and on the way to Mars, that safety net disappears. That realization became the heart of AstroPulse—an onboard medical companion and health monitoring HUD built to give crews real medical autonomy when Earth is out of reach.

How AstroPulse Works Instead of building another passive screen full of blinking numbers, we wanted a system that thinks alongside the crew under pressure. AstroPulse tracks core physiological vitals (heart rate, SpO2, core temperature, and stress) right next to spacecraft cabin conditions (CO2 levels, pressure, and radiation), calibrated to NASA HRP and ECLSS baselines. When an emergency hits—like a CO2 scrubber failure or a sudden solar flare—AstroPulse doesn't just sound an alarm. It connects the alert to closed-loop countermeasures, guiding the crew through the exact corrective action and watching their vitals recover in real time.

What We Cared About Most (Human Factors & Design) Every design choice came from putting ourselves in the crew's boots during a high-stress emergency:

  • No False Panic During Blackouts: Deep-space links drop all the time. We made sure a lost radio signal never triggers a fake medical emergency on a healthy astronaut.
  • Respecting Privacy & Roles: A Flight Surgeon needs to triage the whole crew at a glance, while an individual astronaut just wants a calm, private space to check their own health and talk through stress. We built tailored views for both.
  • AURA—Always There, Even Offline: We integrated Google's Gemini AI into our assistant, AURA, so crew members can ask natural questions about their health. Because space missions lose connectivity, we also engineered a deterministic offline brain so AURA never goes silent when the internet or ground link drops.
  • Calm Under Pressure: We designed a clean 3-column HUD with low-glare space themes (Deep Space, Nebula, and NASA Tactical) and alert filtering so the crew never suffers from alarm fatigue.

How We Built It We built AstroPulse from the ground up using React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand, backed by a custom physiological-environmental simulation engine, automated tests with Vitest, and Google Gemini API. Our open-source repository is available on GitHub :[https://github.com/Ganat1337/nasa-health-monitoring-final](https://github.com/Ganat1337/nasa-health-monitoring-final)

and deployed live on Vercel ([https://nasa-health-monitoring-final.vercel.app](https://nasa-health-monitoring-final.vercel.app)).

Intended Impact Our hope with AstroPulse is simple: as humanity pushes farther into deep space, technology shouldn't just collect data—it should stand beside the crew as a calm, reliable medical partner when they are truly on their own.

projectDetails.name: Project Astronuts
projectDetails.summary: Lunar Outpost: Survival Equation is a browser-based isometric survival game that teaches kids aged 7-12 the real science of lunar exploration. Players command a damaged moon base and balance power, water, and oxygen while facing solar storms, extreme heat, and the 14-day lunar night. Every decision is a two-option trade-off, built on one principle: no choice is free. Wrong choices cause realistic damage, and the game explains the cause and the best solution. Across three levels, players repair sensors, forecast solar events with a telescope, and expand the base. The game uses NASA’s DONKI, OSDR, and Artemis lunar surface data, and it runs instantly on any device with no installation.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details (English, for the NASA portal field)

What it does and how it works
Lunar Outpost: Survival Equation is a browser-based isometric survival simulator that teaches children aged 7-12 the real science behind living on the Moon. The player commands a damaged lunar base and keeps power, water, and oxygen balanced while facing solar radiation storms, extreme daytime heat, and the 14-day lunar night. Every crisis is a quick two-option decision built on one engineering principle: no choice is free.

The game has three levels:

  • Level 1, Emergency & Survival: Repair the environmental sensor array and stabilize core resources. The solar telescope is locked, so radiation storms arrive unpredictably.
  • Level 2, Forecasting & Adaptation: The battery-powered telescope unlocks. Players observe sunspots and incoming meteors to anticipate radiation events and respond in time.
  • Level 3, Base Expansion & Mission Completion: Players upgrade base modules, earn a Hint Key, and return safely to Earth for a final performance evaluation.

Solving tasks earns Wrench & Bolts currency for repairs and upgrades. Unresolved malfunctions reduce efficiency: one causes a minor loss, two trigger a critical alert, and three drop the base to 50%. Wrong choices cause realistic damage, and the game explains the cause, the effect, and the best solution. Difficult terms have built-in kid-friendly definitions.

How NASA data supports it

  • DONKI: Shapes solar flare timing, sunspot activity, and coronal mass ejection events.
  • OSDR: Calibrates radiation exposure effects on the crew and shielding requirements.
  • Artemis & lunar surface data: Governs the 14-day day/night cycle, temperature extremes, and landing-site terrain.

The data is stored as structured JSON profiles that drive events, resource drain, and consequences.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Makes lunar engineering understandable and fun for children without heavy reading.
  • Teaches cause and effect, resource management, and decision-making under constraints.
  • Runs instantly on any device with a browser and needs no installation, so it is easy to use in schools and at home.
  • Intended impact: inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers by showing that real space missions are built on trade-offs.

Tools, languages, and software

  • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript for the web application
  • JSON for structured scientific data profiles
  • Deployed as a live web app, playable on any modern browser [add hosting platform]
  • Manus AI as a development assistant for code generation, kid-friendly glossary text, isometric sprites, and audio cues. All generated content is disclosed in the project metadata and description.
  • Hardware: no special hardware required.

How the project is creative

  • It turns real NASA datasets into game mechanics, so each gameplay moment (a storm, a heat wave, the long night) comes from actual space science.
  • The "no choice is free" rule makes trade-offs the core of the game, instead of simple right-or-wrong quizzes.
  • Wrong choices become learning moments, because the game explains exactly what went wrong and why.
  • The fair-play Hint system (one use, minus 3 points, confirmation warning) keeps the educational assessment honest.

Factors the team considered

  • Age range: The game had to work for both 7-year-olds and 12-year-olds, so we used high-contrast icons, color-coded gauges, guided onboarding, and minimal text.
  • Scientific accuracy vs. simplicity: We kept the NASA-based events and trade-offs authentic but simplified the values for children.
  • Accessibility: A zero-installation web app works across devices, including low-cost ones.
  • Responsible use of SI: The team conceived the idea, structure, and data mapping. Manus AI supported implementation only, all generated content is disclosed, and no NASA branding was used or modified.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Astro play
projectDetails.summary:
Adam is 9 years old and dreams of becoming an astronaut. He reads books and watches videos about space, but he never gets to experience it. He can learn about space, but he can't experience it. Many young learners face the same problem: space content is either too abstract to show the trade-offs behind a real mission, or too technical for their age, and quality Arabic content is rare.

Astro Play is our answer: a bilingual (Arabic and English) 3D game for ages 8–17 with an age-adaptive AI assistant. For this challenge, we built Outpost Command, where players run a lunar or Martian outpost sol by sol. They split limited power between life support, radiation shielding, communications and science, and every choice has a cost. Radiation risk follows live solar activity from NASA's DONKI feed, and fact cards use OSDR studies, with every source labeled and archived data never shown as live.

The impact: players learn by deciding, build critical thinking and problem-solving skills, and spark scientific curiosity. Adam no longer just reads about space. He lives its trade-offs, grounded in real NASA science, in his own language.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRO PLAY – Project Description

1. What It Does and How It Works

Astro Play is a 3D educational game available in both Arabic and English, designed for players aged 8–17.

Players begin by customizing their astronaut, reading a mission briefing, and then exploring the Moon or Mars from a first-person perspective.

During exploration, players use four essential tools:

- Scan: Examine the surrounding environment and objects.

- Collect: Gather scientific samples.

- Analyze: Study collected samples and discover scientific information.

- Repair: Fix equipment and machinery.

Players must also monitor their oxygen levels throughout the mission. By completing five objectives per mission, they earn experience points (XP) and unlock short scientific fact cards.

At any time, players can press Q to open the AI Space Assistant.

For this challenge, we developed Outpost Command.

In this mode, players manage a lunar or Martian outpost over a series of sols (space mission days).

Each sol, players must distribute limited power across four essential systems:

- Life Support.

- Radiation Shielding.

- Communications.

- Science.

At the same time, they must monitor their oxygen and food supplies.

Every decision comes with a cost. For example, strengthening radiation shielding before a solar event may consume the power needed for the night, while using oxygen reserves to conduct additional research introduces another risk.

After each mission, players receive a debrief explaining the reasons behind every outcome and the consequences of their decisions. Failure is treated as a learning opportunity rather than a punishment.

2. Live NASA Data

The likelihood and severity of radiation events within the game are influenced by current solar activity through NASA's DONKI space-weather feed.

A dedicated data panel displays:

- The date and time when the data was retrieved.

- The date of the latest recorded NASA event.

- A clear explanation that the in-game risk level is a game-based mapping of recent event counts, not an official NASA radiation measurement.

If the live data feed becomes unavailable, the game switches to a labeled archived dataset, clearly identifying it as archived rather than presenting it as live data.

Short scientific fact cards are also sourced from the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).

The game clearly distinguishes NASA's original titles and descriptions from our own simplified educational explanations, while providing links to the original scientific study pages.

3. AI Space Assistant

The AI Space Assistant uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to provide answers based on NASA sources.

It can:

- Explain scientific terms such as "Radiation Dose" and "Sol" in simple, age-appropriate language.

- Adapt its responses to the player's age and selected language.

- Encourage critical thinking and exploration instead of simply providing ready-made answers.

- Politely decline questions that fall outside its available sources and guide players back to their educational mission.

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

Players learn why space mission planners cannot have everything they need at once by making decisions and experiencing their consequences.

We expect Astro Play to contribute to:

- Improving scientific understanding.

- Developing critical thinking.

- Strengthening problem-solving skills.

- Encouraging curiosity and scientific exploration.

The game also provides schools, STEM centers, and parents with an Arabic-language educational tool featuring transparent scientific sources and an AI assistant designed to avoid generating unsupported information.

The difficulty level gradually increases according to the player's age, ranging from guided missions for 8-year-olds to more demanding scenarios for 17-year-olds.

5. Tools and Technologies

- Python 3.12 and Ursina Engine (Panda3D): For 3D gameplay development and the dashboard.

- NASA Open APIs (DONKI) and OSDR datasets: For accessing scientific and space-related data.

- ChromaDB: For vector-based retrieval, with keyword search as a fallback.

- Google Gemini (google-genai): For powering the RAG-based AI assistant.

- SQLite: For storing player profiles, progress, and achievements.

- arabic-reshaper and python-bidi: For proper Arabic text rendering and right-to-left layout.

- pytest: For software testing.

- GitHub: For collaboration and code management.

- Hardware Requirements: Standard laptops.

- Fonts: Cairo, Orbitron, and Rajdhani, all licensed under the SIL Open Font License (OFL).

6. Creativity and Innovation

- Turning Real-World Decisions into Gameplay: Transforming the actual challenges faced by space mission planners into an interactive experience where no safe choice comes without a cost.

- Connecting Gameplay to Real Space Weather: Using real solar activity data to influence in-game risks, connecting radiation-shielding decisions to actual solar events.

- Scientific Transparency: Clearly distinguishing between live and archived data, as well as NASA's original information and our simplified educational explanations.

- Multiple Space Environments: Using one game engine to power different environments, including the Moon, Mars, an orbital laboratory, and Europa, each with its own missions, objectives, and difficulty levels.

- Arabic-First Design: Providing an Arabic educational space experience in a field where high-quality Arabic space education games remain limited.

7. Factors We Considered

- Scientific Accuracy: Our AI lead reviews the scientific content, and the AI assistant is restricted to NASA sources.

- Age Range: Players are divided into three age groups: 8–11, 12–14, and 15–17, with different difficulty levels and language complexity.

- Safe Failure: Events vary between playthroughs, allowing players to learn from failure instead of being punished.

- Reliability: An archived dataset is available as a fallback whenever the live data feed becomes unavailable.

- Usability: A clear dashboard and proper right-to-left Arabic layout, tested through playtests with players aged 8–17 in both Arabic and English.

- Attribution: Every scientific data source is clearly identified within the game.

projectDetails.summary:
# MOON BASE ADVENTURE
### The Journey to Build, Protect, and Explore

Moon Base Adventure is an educational STEM game that takes players on an exciting journey to build and protect a future human habitat on the Moon.

As the Mission Commander, players work alongside Nova, an intelligent mission guide, and Pip, a curious robot companion, solving scientific challenges and making important decisions.

Across **5 levels and 26 missions**, players learn to establish life-support systems, manage water resources, generate and store energy, build a lunar greenhouse, and protect the crew from space hazards.

Each level introduces new scientific concepts and interactive challenges, gradually transforming the Moon Base into a functional and protected habitat.

In the final level, players embark on a virtual educational journey to Mars, exploring its reddish surface, Olympus Mons, water ice, and robotic explorers before returning to the Moon Base.

Through science, teamwork, and exploration, players become true **Moon Base Guardians and Ultimate Moon Explorers**.

**Build the Base. Protect the Crew. Explore Beyond.**
projectDetails.details:
MOON BASE ADVENTURE

Project Description & Technical Overview

STEM Educational Game | Ages 7–12

1. Project Overview

Moon Base Adventure is an interactive educational STEM game designed to introduce children to space science, engineering, resource management, and planetary exploration through an engaging mission-based experience.

The player takes the role of a Mission Commander, working alongside two main characters, Nova, an intelligent mission guide, and Pip, a curious robotic companion.

The main objective is to establish, maintain, and protect a future human habitat on the Moon by solving scientific challenges, managing essential resources, and making decisions that affect the success of the mission.

The adventure consists of five progressive levels and 26 missions, gradually introducing more advanced scientific concepts and practical problem-solving activities. The journey concludes with a virtual educational exploration mission to Mars.

2. The Story & Mission Journey

The story begins when the player arrives at a newly established lunar habitat. Although the Moon Base is ready for development, it lacks the essential systems required to support human life.

With guidance from Nova and assistance from Pip, the player must complete a sequence of missions to transform the habitat into a functional and protected Moon Base.

Level 1 – Breathe to Survive

Focus: Life Support & Oxygen Systems

The player discovers that the Moon has no breathable atmosphere like Earth. The first challenge is to establish a suitable habitat environment by learning about oxygen generation through electrolysis, carbon dioxide removal, ventilation, and environmental monitoring.

Level 2 – Every Drop Counts

Focus: Water Management & Recycling

After stabilizing the air system, the crew discovers that water supplies are limited. Players learn about water recovery, filtration concepts, water-quality monitoring, and resource conservation while ensuring essential crew needs remain protected.

Level 3 – Power the Moon

Focus: Energy Generation & Management

The Moon Base experiences power fluctuations. Players learn how solar panels generate electricity, how batteries store energy, and how to distribute available power while prioritizing essential habitat systems and maintaining energy reserves.

Level 4 – Grow Your Future

Focus: Space Agriculture & Food Production

With the essential systems becoming more stable, the crew begins experimenting with food production. Players design a controlled greenhouse, discover plant-growth requirements, explore hydroponics, balance water and energy resources, and complete their first harvest.

Level 5 – Protect the Crew

Focus: Space Radiation, Crew Safety & Mars Exploration

The final level introduces the challenges of the space environment. Players investigate radiation sources, compare Earth's natural protection with the Moon's environment, explore shielding concepts, and respond to fictional space-weather alerts.

The level concludes with Mission 6: Journey to Mars – The Red Planet, where players explore four major discovery topics:

  • Mars and its reddish surface.
  • Olympus Mons, a giant Martian volcano.
  • Water ice on Mars.
  • Robotic explorers and Mars rovers.

Players complete the virtual exploration, review what they discovered, and return to the Moon Base.

3. Gameplay & Interactive Learning

The game combines storytelling, scientific explanations, and interactive challenges instead of relying entirely on traditional educational questions.

Each mission follows a structured gameplay cycle:

  1. Mission Briefing: The player discovers a new problem through character dialogue and story events.
  2. Learn & Discover: Scientific concepts are introduced through accessible explanations and visual demonstrations.
  3. Interactive Challenge: The player solves the problem through activities such as matching, sorting, connecting, arranging, resource allocation, or exploration.
  4. Feedback & Retry: The game provides helpful explanations and hints when an incorrect choice is made.
  5. Mission Completion: Successful completion unlocks the next mission and awards an achievement badge.

This approach encourages players to understand scientific concepts and apply them rather than simply memorize information.

4. Educational Objectives

Moon Base Adventure aims to develop several important learning skills:

Scientific Knowledge

  • Understanding basic space science and environmental systems.
  • Exploring planetary environments and space exploration technologies.
  • Learning fundamental concepts related to oxygen, water, energy, agriculture, and radiation.

Critical Thinking & Problem-Solving

  • Analyzing situations and identifying appropriate solutions.
  • Understanding the relationship between different habitat systems.
  • Making decisions based on available resources and mission requirements.

Resource Management

  • Understanding why essential resources are limited.
  • Balancing energy and water usage.
  • Prioritizing critical systems during simulated shortages.

Environmental & Space Awareness

  • Understanding the challenges of living beyond Earth.
  • Discovering how science and engineering support future exploration.
  • Recognizing the importance of sustainability and efficient resource utilization.

5. Assessment & Achievement System

The game contains 26 individual missions across five levels.

Each mission has a defined learning objective, an interactive completion condition, and a unique achievement badge.

At the end of every level, players complete a separate knowledge assessment:

  • Levels 1–4: Five questions per level.
  • Level 5: Six questions after completing the Mars exploration mission and returning to the Moon Base.

Players receive supportive feedback and opportunities to review concepts.

The final achievement is:

THE ULTIMATE MOON EXPLORER

6. Main Characters

Nova – The Mission Guide

Nova serves as the player's scientific mentor, explaining complex ideas in simple language, introducing missions, and guiding players through important discoveries.

Pip – The Robotic Companion

Pip is a curious and friendly robot who adds humor and personality to the adventure. Through questions and discoveries, Pip helps make scientific concepts more approachable for younger players.

The Mission Commander – The Player

The player is at the center of the experience, making decisions, solving problems, completing objectives, and taking responsibility for the Moon Base.

7. Technology & Development Approach

The project is designed as a Unity-based educational game with a modular mission structure.

Key technical design principles include:

  • Interactive 3D environments and cinematic storytelling.
  • Dedicated mission and progression systems.
  • Character dialogue, voice-over, and subtitles.
  • Interactive scientific activities and resource-management challenges.
  • Achievement badges and level progression.
  • Local save and load functionality.
  • Child-friendly UI/UX and accessible gameplay interactions.
  • Support for keyboard, mouse, and touch input where the platform allows.

Basic gameplay and player progression are designed to work offline, with progress stored locally on the player's device rather than requiring an external server or online database.

8. Innovation & Project Significance

What distinguishes Moon Base Adventure is its combination of educational storytelling, interactive scientific challenges, and progressive mission management within one connected experience.

Rather than presenting STEM subjects as separate lessons, the game connects them through a single evolving environment.

For example, the player first learns how to maintain breathable air, then discovers the importance of water recovery, understands the energy required to operate habitat systems, and finally applies resource-management knowledge to food production and crew safety.

This interconnected structure helps players understand how scientific and engineering systems depend on one another.

The Mars exploration mission extends the experience beyond the Moon Base, introducing planetary science and the achievements of robotic exploration.

9. Expected Impact

Moon Base Adventure aims to make STEM education more engaging, accessible, and memorable for children aged 7–12.

By combining scientific knowledge with interactive challenges, the project encourages curiosity, independent thinking, experimentation, and problem-solving.

Ultimately, the game seeks to inspire young learners to explore science, understand engineering challenges, and develop an interest in the technologies that may shape humanity's future in space.

PROJECT VISION

BUILD THE BASE. PROTECT THE CREW. EXPLORE BEYOND.

Moon Base Adventure transforms learning about space into an interactive journey where every challenge is an opportunity to discover, experiment, and think like a scientist.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroResponse
projectDetails.summary:
AstroResponse

AI-Assisted Eye-Health Screening and Decision Support for Astronauts

AstroResponse is a prototype web application designed to support astronaut eye-health monitoring during long-duration space missions, with a focus on Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).

In microgravity, fluid shifts toward the head can contribute to changes in the eyes and optic nerve. These changes may affect astronauts' vision and create challenges for medical monitoring, especially during missions far from Earth.

AstroResponse allows users to upload retinal fundus images for AI-assisted screening using a Roboflow model, which classifies images into Normal, Papilledema, or Pseudopapilledema categories and provides a confidence score for human review. The platform also includes symptom check-ins, side-by-side image comparison, a scan-log interface, and an editable daily planning draft with customizable reminders.

Additionally, AstroResponse integrates timestamped public NOAA GOES proton data to provide space-weather context alongside eye-health information.

By bringing these features together in one platform, AstroResponse helps astronauts and flight surgeons review potential eye-health concerns, organize monitoring information, and support medical decision-making during long-duration space missions, including situations where communication with Earth may be delayed.

AstroResponse is a screening and decision-support prototype, not a diagnostic medical system.
projectDetails.details: AstroResponse AI-Assisted Eye-Health Screening and Decision Support for Astronauts 1. Project Overview AstroResponse is a prototype web application designed to support astronaut eye-health monitoring during long-duration space missions. It focuses on Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), a condition associated with changes in the eyes and optic nerves during spaceflight. In microgravity, body fluids shift toward the head, which can contribute to optic disc swelling, retinal folds, and changes in the shape of the back of the eye. These changes may affect astronauts' vision and create challenges for medical monitoring, especially during missions far from Earth. AstroResponse brings several eye-health monitoring and decision-support features together in one platform, helping astronauts and flight surgeons review relevant information and organize follow-up. 2. How the Solution Works The prototype follows a simple workflow: 1. Retinal Image Upload Users upload a retinal fundus image (a photograph of the back of the eye) in JPG or PNG format, with a maximum size of 10 MB. The image is previewed locally before analysis. 2. AI-Assisted Image Screening After the user gives consent and selects "Analyze Image," the image is sent to a hosted Roboflow retinal classification model. The model returns one of three categories: - Normal - Papilledema - Pseudopapilledema The result also includes a confidence score. Papilledema refers to optic disc swelling, while pseudopapilledema can have a similar appearance without representing true swelling. The confidence score is provided for human review and should not be interpreted as diagnostic certainty. 3. Image Comparison and Symptom Check-ins Users can view a new retinal image beside an earlier reference image to support visual review. The platform also includes symptom inputs and a scan-log interface to help organize monitoring information during a session. 4. Space-Environment Context AstroResponse displays timestamped public NOAA GOES proton data alongside clearly labelled simulated readings. This provides environmental context about space-weather conditions, but does not represent an astronaut's personal radiation dose or actual spacecraft telemetry. 5. Daily Planning and Reminders The platform generates an editable daily planning draft with NASA-linked guidance and customizable reminders. These features are intended to help organize rest and mission-approved visual checks. 6. Human Review The information is presented for review by the crew member and flight surgeon. AstroResponse is a screening and decision-support tool, not a diagnostic system, and does not replace medical professionals or mission procedures. 3. NASA Data and Its Role NASA research resources provided the scientific foundation for AstroResponse. We used NASA's research on Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome to understand the effects of fluid shifts during spaceflight and identify relevant ocular findings, particularly optic disc swelling. NASA resources on eye-health research aboard the International Space Station also informed our decision to include retinal fundus-image screening. In addition, NASA-reported findings and prevalence figures were used in our project documentation to explain the importance of the problem and illustrate the frequency of SANS-related ocular changes. Alongside NASA research, the platform displays public NOAA GOES proton data as space-weather context. NOAA data is not a NASA dataset and is not used to calculate individual radiation exposure. 4. Tools, Technologies, and Software - Manus: An AI agent used to help build the prototype application and its interface. It also hosts the published web application. - Roboflow: Hosts the AI model used to classify uploaded retinal fundus images. - NOAA GOES public data: Provides timestamped space-weather context. - HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: Standard web technologies used to build the application, with parts of the code generated through Manus. - Web-based platform: The application is accessible through a browser on computers and mobile devices. - English and Arabic interface: Supports users in both languages. The current prototype does not require dedicated eye-imaging hardware; users upload existing fundus images. 5. What Currently Works The delivered prototype includes: - Fundus-image upload with local preview and a consent step before cloud analysis. - Roboflow-based image classification with three output categories and a confidence score. - Side-by-side comparison between a new image and an earlier reference image during the session. - Symptom inputs and a scan-log interface. - A context panel displaying labelled simulated readings and timestamped NOAA GOES proton data. - An editable daily planning draft and customizable reminders. - English and Arabic user interfaces. These features are demonstrated through screenshots of the working prototype in our project documentation. 6. Current Limitations AstroResponse is an early-stage prototype, and several limitations remain: - Scan history is not permanently stored, and authenticated medical-history management is not yet implemented. - The platform is not connected to medical eye-testing devices. - Image comparison is currently a visual, side-by-side review; it does not automatically calculate disease progression. - Simulated readings are not actual spacecraft telemetry. - NOAA proton data does not represent an astronaut's personal radiation dose. - The AI model's confidence score is not a medical diagnosis, and its accuracy has not been established in our project documentation. - The prototype has not been tested or clinically validated in spaceflight conditions. 7. Future Development Our future plans focus on expanding AstroResponse into a more comprehensive astronaut eye-health monitoring and decision-support platform. Planned improvements include: - Saved Medical History: Adding secure scan-history storage and authenticated medical records to support comparisons across multiple sessions. - Advanced Eye-Monitoring Integration: Connecting compatible visual-testing devices and additional ocular-health measurements. - Improved Environmental Monitoring: Integrating spacecraft environmental information, including cabin conditions such as CO2, and relevant dosimeter data when available. - Enhanced Medical Review: Developing a structured workflow for flight-surgeon review and mission-approved medical protocols. - Clinical Validation: Evaluating the retinal classification model using appropriate clinical fundus-image datasets and establishing its performance before any medical use. - Expanded Decision Support: Exploring how environmental and health information could be organized to support more informed, mission-specific medical review. Any future radiation-exposure analysis or personalized risk assessment would require validated dosimeter measurements, mission-specific data, and appropriate scientific models. 8. Expected Impact AstroResponse aims to contribute to safer long-duration human spaceflight by: - Making eye-health information easier for astronauts and flight surgeons to review. - Supporting the organization of retinal images, symptoms, and monitoring information. - Helping users identify image-classification results that may need further human review. - Providing relevant space-weather context alongside eye-health information. - Supporting more organized medical follow-up, particularly when communication with Earth is delayed. In the long term, we hope to develop AstroResponse into a more comprehensive health-monitoring and decision-support platform that can support astronauts during missions beyond low Earth orbit. AstroResponse is currently a screening and decision-support prototype. Its purpose is to support human review, not to diagnose medical conditions or independently make medical decisions.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroSpark
projectDetails.summary:
FlameLens is a free web dashboard that tells a spacecraft or habitat engineer whether a cabin atmosphere has been tested in NASA's microgravity fire experiments.
Future Moon bases and pressurized rovers are expected to use 30 % oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less, which makes materials burn more easily. NASA has studied fire on the International Space Station for years, and the results are public in its Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, but they are spread over many tables and reports that are hard to compare.
We merged 2,003 runs from 18 PSI flight investigations into one table. The user enters oxygen, pressure, airflow, material and gravity. FlameLens marks each condition as supported, weak or not tested, scores how strong the evidence is, shows the closest real NASA runs and exactly how they differ, and proposes the next experiment that would close the gap. A plain-language explanation and an "Ask the NASA reports" panel use AI, but every AI claim must cite a NASA run or quote a NASA page, or it is removed.
This answers the "Flame in Freefall" challenge: it summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA combustion data for fire-safety decisions. It is useful because an engineer gets an answer they can check and defend in minutes, and the gaps are visible. Where there is no evidence, FlameLens says so instead of guessing. It never gives a safety verdict.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

FlameLens is a web dashboard that tells a habitat engineer whether a cabin atmosphere has been backed by NASA's microgravity fire experiments. You enter the cabin's air (oxygen %, pressure, airflow, material, gravity) or pick a preset: ISS cabin, spacesuit, pressurized rover, Moon base, Mars habitat. FlameLens compares it with 2,003 real runs from 18 NASA PSI flight investigations and returns:

- an evidence case: each condition marked Supported, Weak or No evidence, with the IDs of the matching runs (only runs with the same material count);

- an evidence strength score from 0 to 100, with its four parts visible (it is not a safety rating);

- the closest NASA evidence when nothing matches, and exactly what differs;

- the next experiment to run, and a campaign planner (if NASA can fly 3 more tests, which ones cover the most designs);

- tested options with less oxygen, seven science lenses, a mission journey, and a printable design review brief.

Every number links to its PSI run, data table and DOI. "Ask the NASA reports" answers questions from 1,899 passages of 20 NASA PSI documents, and a claim is kept only if its quote is word for word on the cited page.

BENEFITS

- Engineers get a defensible answer in minutes instead of days of searching scattered tables and reports, with the gaps in plain view.

- Researchers and students get one comparable table of 2,003 runs, 43 measured flame-spread rates and links to 27 NASA papers, all downloadable.

- Mission planners get a short list of the experiments that would close the most gaps.

INTENDED IMPACT

In 1967 the Apollo 1 crew died in a ground test that no one had identified as hazardous, in a pure-oxygen cabin full of flammable materials. Today, Moon bases and pressurized rovers are planned with 30 % oxygen or more at about 10.2 psi, which makes materials burn more easily. FlameLens makes sure that before anyone breathes that air, the team knows what NASA has already tested and what it has not. On Earth, the same research supports smoke detectors that tell smoke from dust, firefighter clothing and breathing equipment.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: Python and JavaScript, with HTML and CSS.

- Backend: FastAPI and Pydantic; data scripts in Python; 95 automated tests (pytest) and a 137-check script against the live site.

- Frontend: plain JavaScript with our own SVG charts; light and dark themes; works at phone width.

- Hosting: Vercel. Code on GitHub.

- AI: Google Gemini 2.5 Flash for "Ask the NASA reports", both behind our own citation verifier. AI coding assistants (Claude, Gemini) helped write code and docs.

- Data: NASA PSI experiment tables (CC0), NASA Technical Reports Server, NASA Spinoff.

- Video: our own Python scripts with ffmpeg, Whisper for subtitle timing; the voice is our team member's.

- Hardware: none beyond our laptops.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It gives a decision, not a list of search results: what is backed, how strongly, and what to test next.

- It is honest about gaps. "No evidence" is a valid answer, and the rover result shows it: its oxygen and pressure were only tested with gas flames and fuel droplets, never with a solid material ("Other fuels only").

- When there is no match, it shows the closest real runs and cited NASA tests outside PSI (Saffire spacecraft fires, lunar-gravity drop tests) without counting them.

- It treats a mission as a journey (ISS, spacesuit, rover, Moon base) that is only as strong as its weakest stage.

- The AI cannot invent facts: a verifier removes any claim whose run, number or quote is not in the NASA source.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Trust: no invented values, no safety verdicts; every value shows whether it was measured, read from text or assumed.

- Decisions use no AI, and the app still works with the AI off.

- Limits of the data: every PSI run is in microgravity, so we say so and do not stretch it to Moon or Mars gravity.

- Users: a simple 1-2-3 flow (enter the air, compare, check the source), readable on a phone.

- Open science: public links, CC0 data cited by DOI, AI use disclosed.
