projectDetails.name: ASTROS
projectDetails.summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer (Mars Base: Mission Control)
Developed by team ASTROS SPACE for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge (Cairo), the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based 3D educational game where players aged 7–15 act as rookie Mission Controllers managing a fictional Mars outpost. Built using React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js, the platform challenges users to balance six vital life-support systems (Oxygen, Water, Food, Energy, Radiation Protection, and Temperature Control) across four progressive missions while handling realistic crises like dust storms and air leaks. The game emphasizes systems thinking through immediate visual feedback, a privacy-first local design requiring no accounts, and a Mission Brief system that links every decision to real NASA and Canadian Space Agency science.
projectDetails.details:
• What it does or how does it work: The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive 3D educational management game where a young player acts as a rookie Mission Controller for a Martian science outpost. Across four progressive missions (13 total events), players walk an astronaut avatar around a 3D base using keyboard or touch controls, investigating highlighted systems and choosing responses to events like dust storms, air leaks, or radiation alerts. Every choice updates a six-resource engine (Oxygen, Water, Food, Energy, Radiation Protection, and Temperature Control) and is summarized in a Mission Brief with deltas, timelines, and NASA science cards.
  • What benefits does it have: It teaches children aged 7–15 complex systems thinking ("one decision affects many systems") through short, friendly decisions with no time pressure, no violence, and no punitive "game over" screens. If resources run out, a supportive "Stabilization Protocol" lets players retry. It also features AstroBot, a pre-mission assistant that answers space questions from a curated encyclopedia with source links, jargon definitions, and collectible badges.
  • What is the intended impact of the project: The project aims to make space STEM education accessible, engaging, and grounded in real engineering trade-offs. By connecting game decisions to actual NASA and Canadian Space Agency science, it inspires curiosity about space exploration and helps children understand the interconnected nature of life-support systems used in missions like Artemis.
  • What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project: The project frontend is built using React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 8, with global state managed via Zustand. The 3D world is rendered using Three.js through @react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei, built entirely from primitive geometry. Development tools included Git/GitHub, ESLint, and VS Code, with static production deployment hosted on Vercel. AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Google Antigravity, OpenAI Codex) were used to help draft code, documentation summaries, and knowledge bases, which were thoroughly reviewed by the human team.
  • How is your project creative: It creatively combines a fully walkable, browser-based 3D Mars base (built without external 3D assets) with a personal astronaut identity system, including an in-browser webcam/upload helmet portrait studio. Instead of traditional win/lose mechanics, it uses a constructive Mission Brief and a curiosity-driven AstroBot assistant that rewards players with space badges.
  • What factors did your team consider: The team prioritized child-friendly design features (large touch targets, short sentences, icons, and clear color/word resource states rather than color alone). They also emphasized strict privacy (no accounts, databases, or API keys required; local storage only)and scientific honesty—ensuring all game numbers are explicitly labeled as normalised educational indicators rather than physical measurements, while accurately paraphrasing real space agency facts.

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA – Astronaut Smart Health & Risk Assessment
ASTRA is an intelligent health monitoring platform designed to support astronaut health awareness during space missions. Spaceflight conditions can affect human physiology, making continuous and personalized health monitoring essential.
Unlike traditional monitoring systems that rely on fixed health thresholds, ASTRA focuses on understanding each astronaut's individual health patterns. It establishes a Personal Health Baseline, analyzes incoming health indicators, and detects unusual changes that may require attention.
The platform provides a Mission Health Dashboard to visualize vital indicators and health trends, an Anomaly Detection system to identify abnormal patterns, and Explainable Alerts that highlight what changed and which data supports the alert. ASTRA also aims to support offline-first operation, allowing local health-data analysis when internet connectivity is unavailable.
By combining personalized monitoring, anomaly detection, and explainable insights, ASTRA aims to help astronauts and ground-support teams make more informed decisions and improve health awareness during space missions.
Our Vision: Moving beyond monitoring health numbers toward understanding individual health patterns and identifying unusual changes.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA – Astronaut Smart Health & Risk Assessment is an intelligent health-monitoring platform designed to support astronaut health awareness during space missions.
Spaceflight conditions can affect the human body in different ways. Traditional monitoring systems often rely on fixed thresholds, but individual astronauts may have different normal health patterns. ASTRA addresses this challenge by focusing on personalized health monitoring.
The platform establishes a Personal Health Baseline for each astronaut and analyzes available health indicators to identify unusual changes or patterns. It presents these insights through a Mission Health Dashboard and provides Explainable Alerts that highlight what changed and which data supports the alert.
ASTRA is designed to support offline-first operation, allowing health data to be analyzed locally when internet connectivity is unavailable.
The project's main benefits include improved health awareness, easier monitoring of individual health trends, and better-informed decisions for astronauts and ground-support teams. Its creative approach is the shift from monitoring isolated health readings to understanding each astronaut's personal health patterns.
The project draws on relevant space-health research and data resources, including NASA's Open Science Data Repository, while distinguishing available research data from demonstration or synthetic data.
Our vision is to make astronaut health monitoring more personalized, understandable, and supportive of safer space missions.

projectDetails.details:
SOLBOUND – Project Details

Project Overview

SOLBOUND is an interactive, NASA data-driven educational platform that transforms the challenges of surviving on the Moon or Mars into an engaging learning experience for children aged 7-12.

Our solution combines three interconnected components: a 10-day space survival simulation game, an interactive educational comic book, and Nova, a bilingual AI learning companion. Together, these components help children understand space science through storytelling, experimentation, and engineering-based decision-making rather than passive memorization.

How Does SOLBOUND Work?

1. Interactive Space Survival Simulation

Players become mission commanders responsible for establishing and maintaining a human outpost on either the Moon or Mars.

Throughout a 10-day mission, they manage three interconnected survival systems:

  • Life Support: Maintaining the resources necessary for astronaut survival.
  • Power: Managing energy generation, consumption, and storage.
  • Protection: Defending the crew and habitat against environmental hazards, including radiation and dust storms.

Each mission day introduces decisions, environmental challenges, and engineering trade-offs. Players must analyze their available resources, choose how to distribute power, configure equipment, and respond to unexpected events.

Unlike traditional games, SOLBOUND does not offer cost-free solutions. Every choice has consequences that can affect future mission days. The simulation also incorporates realistic communication delays between Earth and the Moon or Mars, encouraging players to make independent decisions when immediate assistance is unavailable.

2. Interactive Educational Comic Book

SOLBOUND integrates an interactive comic book that introduces children to the scientific and engineering challenges of building an extraterrestrial settlement.

Through a seven-day learning journey alongside an astronaut, players explore essential concepts such as life-support systems, energy management, radiation protection, and environmental survival.

The comic book connects storytelling with practical challenges, helping children understand scientific concepts before applying them within the simulation.

3. Nova – Bilingual AI Learning Companion

Nova is an AI-powered educational assistant that supports players throughout their mission.

Available in English and Arabic, Nova explains scientific concepts, clarifies mission challenges, and helps children understand the consequences of their decisions.

Instead of providing direct answers or automatically solving problems, Nova encourages independent thinking through age-appropriate explanations and guided questions. Its responses are designed to remain connected to the current mission state and available resources.

A local rule-based fallback also supports guidance when internet connectivity is unavailable.

NASA Data Integration

SOLBOUND incorporates authentic NASA scientific resources to connect its educational experience with real space exploration research.

The project draws on:

  • NASA Open APIs: Access to publicly available NASA datasets and scientific information.
  • DONKI (Space Weather Database): Solar activity and space weather information used to inform radiation hazards and mission events.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): Space biology and astronaut health research supporting the educational representation of human survival challenges.
  • RadLab: Radiation dosimetry research supporting radiation exposure and protection concepts.
  • Mars Trek: Martian terrain and surface information supporting planetary exploration and environmental understanding.

SOLBOUND distinguishes between live and archived information, making scientific data provenance transparent rather than presenting simulated values as real measurements.

Tools and Technologies

SOLBOUND's development approach uses web technologies and scientific data integration to create an accessible educational experience.

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: Building the browser-based interface, game mechanics, and interactive components.
  • Figma: Designing the user interface, visual experience, and child-friendly interactions.
  • NASA Open APIs and DONKI: Accessing authentic scientific and space weather information.
  • Local JSON datasets: Providing archived NASA information and supporting offline functionality.
  • Rule-based simulation engine: Modeling resource consumption, environmental hazards, and consequences across mission days.
  • AI-assisted educational guidance: Supporting Nova's bilingual explanations and mission-based learning.

The platform is designed to run through a web browser without requiring an account, with a local offline execution option.

Creativity and Innovation

SOLBOUND's innovation comes from combining scientific authenticity with interactive storytelling and consequence-driven gameplay.

Rather than simply presenting facts about space, the project allows children to experience the complexity of extraterrestrial survival through decisions that directly affect their mission.

Its distinctive features include persistent consequences across mission days, realistic communication delays, NASA-informed environmental challenges, an integrated educational comic book, and a bilingual AI companion that encourages learning without removing the challenge.

This creates a connected learning journey in which children discover scientific concepts, apply them in simulations, learn from mistakes, and improve their strategies.

Benefits and Intended Impact

SOLBOUND aims to make space science and engineering accessible, engaging, and meaningful for younger learners.

For children, the experience develops critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, scientific reasoning, and systems thinking.

For educators, it provides an interactive STEM learning resource that can encourage classroom discussions, experimentation, and collaborative problem-solving.

By supporting Arabic and English, accessible interface settings, and offline use, SOLBOUND also aims to reduce barriers to participation.

Our long-term vision is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers by allowing them to experience how engineering decisions shape the success or failure of real-world space missions.

Design Considerations

Throughout development, our team prioritized scientific accuracy, educational accessibility, and meaningful player engagement.

We focused on simplifying complex engineering concepts without removing their underlying scientific relationships. Limiting the main simulation to three interconnected survival systems reduces cognitive overload while preserving challenging

projectDetails.details:
Behind the Spacesuit: A Lunar Mission Design Game

Overview

Behind the Spacesuit is an interactive lunar survival and mission design game for ages 4+. The player guides an astronaut who lost his memory after his spacecraft crashed on the Moon. To bring him home, the player must design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission, making engineering decisions and managing limited resources along the way.

The Challenge

Designing a space mission means balancing competing demands: mission objectives, spacecraft design, power, mass, communications, and budget. Students rarely get to experience a whole mission from concept to operation, so these trade-offs stay abstract. Our game makes them hands-on.

How the Game Works

The game has 5 levels, from easy to difficult. A mission dashboard stays on screen throughout and tracks four limited resources:

Budget

Mass

Power

Life-support supplies (food, water, oxygen)

Every decision the player makes spends or saves these resources. At the end of each level, a mission score (1 to 3 stars) explains how the player’s choices affected the mission’s success.

The 5 Levels

Level 1: Survive the Crash

The player learns how astronauts get water, food, exercise, and sleep. With limited supplies, the player must decide how to ration them.

Trade-off: ration evenly (lasts longer, less energy) or use more now (more energy, runs out sooner).

Level 2: Power the Base

The player explores the Moon’s surface and its very low gravity, and designs solar cells to power the base.

Trade-off: large panels (more power, more mass) or small panels (less power, less mass).

Level 3: Recover the Mission

The player helps the astronaut regain his memory by solving clues and collecting objects, which reveal the mission objectives.

Trade-off: rush the clues (saves time, less information) or explore first (more information, costs time).

Level 4: Call Home

The player reconnects with the space station and Earth after the collision damaged the systems.

Trade-off: strong antenna (fast signal, high power use) or weak antenna (slow signal, saves power).

Level 5: Return to Earth

The player selects the fuel cell, thruster valve, and navigation chip within the remaining budget and mass, then contacts mission control to return home and meet his family.

Trade-off: extra fuel (safer, more mass) or saving fuel (lighter, riskier).

Learning Outcomes

Players learn that:

Every engineering choice has a cost and a benefit.

Resources in space are limited and must be planned carefully.

Power, mass, communications, and budget all affect each other.

Astronauts face real daily challenges in space, such as food, water, sleep, exercise, and low gravity.

Why It Matters

The game turns complex mission design into a heartfelt story that anyone can follow. It builds engineering thinking, builds empathy for astronauts, and sparks curiosity about space exploration. Because the story and visuals are simple, children as young as 4 can enjoy it, while the decisions and score feedback give older players a real sense of how missions are planned.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroVitaCS
projectDetails.summary:
We developed AstroVitaCS, a web prototype that helps flight surgeons and astronauts monitor crew health on long missions. Each astronaut has a dashboard with vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature), sleep, mood, hydration, exercise, nutrition and supplement targets, four brain games, box-breathing sessions, and cabin readings (temperature, lighting, noise, radiation). The flight surgeon has a view with a crew overview, alerts, trend charts, and AI analysis for each astronaut, plus a chat to communicate with the crew. All data is simulated.

It addresses the challenge by turning health indicators into readable trends and early alerts, and by supporting prevention in areas NASA identifies as spaceflight risks. NASA Human Research Program pages, JSC-67378, and NASA-STD-3001 guided our indicators and reference ranges. Our additions, such as AI explanations and a fasting-plan idea, are proposals that need medical review, not approved NASA protocols.

It matters because when help from Earth is delayed, noticing health changes early supports crew safety. The AI supports awareness only; flight surgeons remain essential.
projectDetails.details:
​WHAT EXACTLY DOES IT DO?

AstroVitaCS is a web prototype for monitoring crew health on long space missions. It has two views.

Astronaut view: a personal dashboard with vitals (heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, HRV), sleep, mood check-ins, water and exercise logging, meals with calorie, protein, carbohydrate and healthy-fat targets, daily supplement tracking, four brain games, box-breathing sessions, cabin readings (temperature, lighting, noise, CO2, radiation), and a demo fasting plan.

Flight-surgeon view: a crew overview with health status, critical alarms, an analysis page for each astronaut, trend charts with normal ranges, and a chat with the crew.

All data in the prototype is simulated.

​HOW DOES IT WORK?

The backend is written in JavaScript (Node.js) with Express. Data is stored in JSON files, and the frontend is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Readings and logs are compared with reference ranges (for example SpO2 95-100% and heart rate 60-100 BPM) and labelled Normal, In range, or Critical. Out-of-range readings create alerts for the medical team. The "AI Analysis" page uses rule-based logic (if/else rules) over recent history to describe patterns and give a risk level. It does not use an AI model. Astronauts and doctors communicate through a built-in chat. Passwords are hashed with scrypt and sessions use signed tokens. Judges can enter without a password using the "Doctor demo" or "Astronaut demo" buttons. Thresholds are demo thresholds inspired by ACLS/ATLS guidelines and need professional validation.

​AI ANALYSIS MODULE

AstroVitaCS was built with the assistance of Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic. The AI Analysis page is a rule-based decision-support tool, not a machine-learning model.

​HOW DOES IT WORK?

Each vital sign is compared with a reference range and rated normal, warning or critical. Abnormal readings are grouped into a pattern for each astronaut, such as short sleep with high stress. Current values are compared with the astronaut's own 14-day average. The most severe finding sets the risk level: low, moderate or high. "Run AI Analysis" re-evaluates the latest data and logs the run. The same rules drive doctor alerts, the critical alarm and fasting exemptions.

​WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

It puts crew health data in one place, helps astronauts and flight surgeons notice changes early, and supports prevention (sleep, nutrition, hydration, exercise, mental health, cabin environment). This matters when help from Earth is delayed. The analysis supports awareness only. It does not diagnose, and flight surgeons remain essential.

​WHAT DO YOU HOPE TO ACHIEVE?

We hope to grow the prototype with real NASA datasets, wearable sensors, and validation by clinicians, and to add more languages. Longer term, the same approach could support remote or isolated communities on Earth. Our additions, including the fasting-plan idea, are proposals, not approved NASA protocols.

​LIMITATIONS

All thresholds are fictional demo values. They need medical approval before any real use. Results are advisory only. They are not diagnoses, and the system does not prescribe treatment. All data is fictional.

​TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, SOFTWARE

​Backend: JavaScript (Node.js 22+), Express 5, cors; JSON file storage (no database); Node built-in crypto module (scrypt for password hashing, HMAC-SHA256 for signed tokens).

​Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript.

​Hosting: GitHub Pages (frontend).

​Presentation: Gamma.

​AI assistance used: Claude and ChatGPT helped write code; Claude helped write each frontend file; AI-generated images in the slides are labelled.

​Hardware: none (software only, simulated data).

​References: NASA Human Research Program risk pages, NASA JSC-67378, NASA Human Adaptation to Spaceflight, NASA-STD-3001, NIH Office of Dietary Supplements.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroVitaL2026
projectDetails.summary:
**AstroVital – Project Summary**

AstroVital is an AI-powered health-monitoring platform designed to support astronaut well-being during space missions.

It addresses spaceflight-related health challenges, including cardiovascular changes, immune alterations, sleep disturbances, and fatigue.

The platform integrates three types of health data:

1. **Physiological:** Heart rate, SpO₂, blood pressure, and other available measurements.
2. **Biochemical:** Periodic laboratory measurements, including CBC and selected immune biomarkers.
3. **Behavioral:** Sleep quality, physical activity, and fatigue indicators.

Using personalized health baselines, trend analysis, and AI-driven anomaly detection, AstroVital identifies unusual patterns, explains changes, and provides understandable alerts and follow-up guidance.

The platform draws on NASA research resources, including the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), and uses simulated telemetry where applicable.

Its web-based dashboard visualizes health trends and supports astronaut self-assessment and informed medical review.

**Our vision: Transform isolated health measurements into personalized health intelligence for safer, long-duration space missions.**
projectDetails.details:
Background & Literature Review NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) identifies five major hazards associated with human spaceflight and conducts ongoing research to understand their effects on astronaut health. These hazards provide the scientific foundation for selecting relevant health indicators and developing monitoring strategies. NASA research addresses physiological and behavioral risks involving cardiovascular adaptation, hypoxia, immune-system changes, nutrition, sleep, and behavioral health. The Canadian Space Agency (CSA) also contributes to astronaut health protection through radiation monitoring and exposure assessment programs. Scientific research further supports individualized and longitudinal health monitoring. Studies involving astronauts have demonstrated the importance of tracking biological and physiological changes over time rather than relying exclusively on population-wide reference values. AstroVital builds upon these research directions by combining personalized health baselines, repeated measurements, transparent classification rules, and accessible guidance. Unlike complex clinical research platforms, AstroVital focuses on providing a practical, crew-facing interface that supports health awareness and preventive decision-making. The system is designed as a decision-support prototype and does not replace professional medical evaluation. Methodology A. Step-by-Step Process Step 1 — Scientific Research and Indicator Selection. Studied NASA HRP's five hazards and ongoing research, together with CSA radiation-monitoring resources, to identify relevant health indicators: • Sleep quality and duration • Fatigue • Resting pulse • Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2 ) • Blood pressure • Mood • Nutrition • Physical exercise • Body temperature Step 2 — Personalized Health Baselines. Established an individual health baseline for each crew member using their own first week of recorded measurements. This allows the system to identify deviations from an astronaut's normal physiological patterns rather than relying exclusively on general population thresholds. Step 3 — Deterministic Rules Engine. Each new health check-in is processed through a deterministic rules engine that classifies the result into four categories: • Green: Measurements are within the expected range. • Yellow: A potential deviation requires attention or monitoring. • Red: An explicit critical symptom or configured emergency limit has been detected. • Grey: Data are missing or outdated. Step 4 — Personalized Guidance Cards. Each finding is converted into a plain-language, symbol-first card containing: what changed; why it matters; what action to take; when to recheck; and when to contact medical support.

Step 5 — Closed-Loop Action Tracking. The astronaut can start and complete recommended actions, with each action recorded in the health timeline. When a Red event occurs, the system generates a structured onboard report. The report remains queued until a simulated communication uplink and acknowledgement are completed. Step 6 — Testing and Verification. The system's behavior was verified through 11 engine tests and a UI smoke test covering all scenarios. B. Algorithms and Technologies Technology stack: Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, Plotly. The application runs locally and fully offline without requiring an external API key. Personal Baseline Algorithm: The system uses the median and Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) to establish robust individual health reference ranges. Persistence Detection: A signal must remain outside its expected range in at least 3 of the last 4 entries before being considered persistent. For SpO2 , the requirement is 2 of the last 4 entries. Multi-Signal Detection: Recovery drift requires at least two abnormal indicators among sleep, fatigue, and resting pulse. The system identifies co-occurring changes without claiming that one indicator directly causes another. Outlier Detection: A single outlier is flagged for retesting at 3 robust standard deviations rather than automatically being interpreted as a persistent health issue. Emergency Classification: Red classification is triggered only by explicitly configured emergency criteria or critical symptoms. Missing Data Management: Grey classification is used when measurements are missing or stale. Guidance System: A local, source-linked guidance library provides relevant information and recommendations. No AI model makes medical decisions. C. Fit With the Challenge AstroVital supports astronaut self-assessment through an intuitive visual interface combining color, shape, and written status indicators. The platform provides: • Interactive body mapping • Personalized health trend charts • Preventive health guidance • Flight-surgeon escalation pathways • Offline functionality during communication delays • Gamification to encourage consistent monitoring • An evidence library connected to NASA and CSA resources Solution AstroVital is a web-based astronaut health dashboard that transforms physiological measurements and behavioral observations into understandable, personalized health information. The solution consists of several integrated components: • 1. Health Monitoring Dashboard — a centralized overview of the astronaut's health indicators and current status. • 2. Personalized Baseline Engine — establishes individual reference values and identifies unusual changes over time. • 3. Health Classification Engine — assigns Green, Yellow, Red, or Grey classifications using transparent rules.

• 4. Interactive Guidance System — personalized action cards explaining detected changes and recommended next steps. • 5. Health Timeline — records check-ins, alerts, completed actions, and health events. • 6. Onboard Medical Reporting — generates structured reports for critical events and keeps them queued until simulated communication becomes available. • 7. Evidence Library — scientific context and source-linked guidance based on NASA, CSA, and relevant research. Implementation Process • Collecting health check-ins and simulated wearable telemetry • Establishing personal baselines • Processing measurements through the rules engine • Displaying classifications and health trends • Providing appropriate guidance • Recording actions and health events • Testing the complete workflow, including emergency reporting and communication delays The current prototype uses simulated wearable telemetry to demonstrate continuous monitoring. Value Proposition AstroVital provides value by transforming complex health measurements into understandable and actionable information. For astronauts, the platform offers a simple way to monitor personal health trends, recognize unusual changes, and understand recommended actions. For mission medical teams, it provides structured health records, documented events, and organized reports that can be reviewed when communication becomes available. Its main advantages include: • Personalization: Each astronaut is monitored against their own baseline. • Transparency: Classifications are based on understandable deterministic rules. • Offline Capability: Operates without continuous internet connectivity. • Preventive Monitoring: Persistent deviations can be identified before they meet emergency criteria. • Action Tracking: Recommended actions and their completion are documented. • Scientific Foundation: Guidance is connected to NASA and CSA resources. • Communication Resilience: Critical reports can remain queued during communication delays. Unlike conventional dashboards that primarily display raw measurements, AstroVital connects monitoring with interpretation, guidance, and action tracking. It is designed to complement existing medical monitoring systems and professional medical judgment, not replace them. Role of Team Members • Remon Asaad — Research & Database. Scientific research, identifying relevant NASA and CSA resources, studying astronaut health indicators, organizing scientific references, and managing the project's database and evidence-linked guidance library. • Mahmoud Ahmed Hussein — Storytelling. Project storytelling, communicating the problem and proposed solution, developing the presentation narrative, and ensuring health information and recommendations are communicated clearly and effectively. • Abdulrahman Mahmoud — Technical Development. Technical implementation, application development, integrating the health-monitoring engine, data processing, the Streamlit interface, visualizations, and software testing.

projectDetails.name: Beyond Signal
projectDetails.summary:
Beyond Signal is an educational platform and interactive simulation game designed in the style of NASA to teach space mission engineering and planning. Combining scientific space knowledge with practical engineering decisions ("Knowledge is the tool, decisions are the game"), the platform features 4 main modes:

Agency: Explores NASA’s history, centers, directorates, and key scientific questions.

Academy: A 5-level knowledge quiz testing mission understanding, complete with hints and a Leaderboard.

Mission Lab: The core gameplay where you turn a scientific goal into a spacecraft by balancing mass, power, communications, budget, time, and risk, then launch, simulate the journey, and manage unexpected events for a performance evaluation.

Studio: A tool to design, customize, and share your own space mission scenarios, constraints, and events.

Additional Features:

Historical Missions Study: Engineering analysis of iconic missions including Apollo 11, James Webb, Perseverance, and Artemis II.

Challenge Scenarios: Ranging from beginner (Cadet: CubeSat Pathfinder) to Flight Director (Deep Field Observatory).

Multiplayer (Crew Operations): Play solo or with up to 4 teammates via a shared room code, assigning roles (Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Communications & Resources Officer) to make launch decisions together.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview & How It Works

Beyond Signal is an interactive educational platform and space mission engineering simulator modeled after NASA’s operational philosophy: "Knowledge is the tool, decisions are the game." Rather than passively reading about space exploration, users actively step into the shoes of NASA engineers, scientists, and flight directors.

The experience is structured into four interconnected modes:

  1. Agency (Exploration & Foundation): Users explore NASA’s history, research centers, mission directorates, and the core scientific questions driving deep-space exploration.
  2. Academy (Knowledge Verification): A 5-level interactive assessment system that tests users' understanding of orbital mechanics, spacecraft subsystems, and mission logic. It includes smart hints to guide learning and a global Leaderboard to encourage healthy competition.
  3. Mission Lab (Core Engineering Simulation): The heart of the platform. Players select a scientific objective and must design a viable spacecraft from scratch. They face real-world engineering trade-offs—balancing mass, power generation, communications bandwidth, budget, development timeline, and mission risk. Once built, players launch the spacecraft, simulate its trajectory, and respond to dynamic, unexpected in-flight anomalies. At the end of the mission, a comprehensive post-flight debrief evaluates their scientific return, resource efficiency, and risk management.
  4. Studio (User-Generated Scenarios): A sandbox creation tool that empowers educators, students, and enthusiasts to build custom space missions—defining unique scientific goals, engineering constraints, and mid-flight events—and share them with the community.

Key Features & Creative Approach

  • Historical Missions Case Studies: Users can analyze the real-world engineering constraints and breakthroughs behind iconic missions, including Apollo 11, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the Perseverance Rover, and Artemis II.
  • Progressive Challenge Scenarios: Designed for all skill levels, starting from beginner missions (Cadet: CubeSat Pathfinder) up to complex, high-stakes deep-space operations (Flight Director: Deep Field Observatory).
  • Crew Operations (Collaborative Multiplayer): Space exploration is a team effort. Beyond Signal supports up to 4 players in real-time via a shared room code. Each team member is assigned a specialized role—Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, or Communications & Resources Officer—requiring active communication and collaborative decision-making to achieve mission success.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Bridging Theory and Practice: Transforms abstract STEM concepts (physics, systems engineering, budget management) into tangible, cause-and-effect decisions.
  • Cultivating Systems Thinking: Teaches students that in aerospace engineering, optimizing one subsystem (e.g., adding larger scientific instruments) directly impacts others (increasing mass, power draw, and launch costs).
  • Accessible STEM Outreach: Provides a free, browser-based, high-engagement tool for classrooms, science clubs, and aspiring aerospace engineers worldwide to experience the realities of mission control.

Development Factors & Tools

  • Design Philosophy: Our team prioritized authentic NASA-inspired UI/UX telemetry aesthetics, clear visual feedback for engineering trade-offs, and low-latency multiplayer synchronization so teams can collaborate seamlessly.
  • Technical Stack: Built as a responsive web application utilizing modern frontend frameworks (HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript/TypeScript), interactive state-management engines for real-time physics/resource calculations, and cloud-hosted room synchronization for multiplayer Crew Operations

projectDetails.name: Atheer
projectDetails.summary:
Jennifer had always dreamed of going to space. So when her best friend Sara finally went, she was just as excited as her.

But things went wrong when Sara’s oxygen level dropped. Getting medical help in space wasn't as simple as on Earth. Every minute mattered, and Sara’s mission ended earlier than planned.

Sara was fine, but Jennifer became afraid. If it happened to Sara, it could happen to her.

Weeks later, Jennifer discovered something called **Atheer**. It was a smart suit connected to an app that continuously monitors oxygen, heart rate, and blood pressure.

When something goes wrong, an alarm sounds and a voice guides the astronaut through the necessary steps. For example: "Alert. Low oxygen. Stop moving. Breathe slowly. Backup oxygen activated. Medical team notified."

Meanwhile, the suit responds automatically, and the medical team receives an alert.

Jennifer also discovered that every incident is recorded on a dashboard, showing what happened, when it happened, and how it was handled. This helps Atheer learn from previous events and improve future responses.

Jennifer thought about Sara. Space would always have risks, but with Atheer, astronauts wouldn't have to wait hours to know what to do. They could receive guidance within seconds.

She closed her laptop and looked up at the night sky. For the first time in months, it didn't scare her anymore.
projectDetails.details:
Atheer is a smart space suit designed to protect astronauts from sudden health problems, and its central idea is simple: reach the problem before it reaches the astronaut.

In space, medical help is far away, and a health issue can take a long time to resolve. The body’s vital signs can also change quickly, sometimes without the astronaut noticing at all. Low oxygen, a heart rate that is too high or too low, and blood pressure that rises or falls are among the most serious cases, and every minute of delay makes them more dangerous.

Atheer addresses this with sensors built into the suit that monitor oxygen level, heart rate, and blood pressure continuously. The moment a reading moves outside the safe range, the suit sounds an alert and a voice tells the astronaut exactly what to do. If oxygen drops, for example, the voice says: “Alert. Low oxygen. Stop moving. Breathe slowly. Backup oxygen is starting. Medical team notified.” If the heart rate is high, the astronaut is told to stop, rest, and drink water. If it is low, the voice asks them to stop any activity, sit down, and breathe slowly. High blood pressure calls for ten minutes of rest, and low blood pressure for sitting or lying down. The astronaut never has to wait for instructions or think clearly under pressure, because the guidance arrives at the same moment as the alert.

The system works on two levels. A warning signals a mild change and brings gentle guidance and a re-check, while an alert signals a serious problem and sets off the alarm, urgent steps, and an immediate notification to the medical team. If the readings do not improve, the case escalates to the medical team and the flight surgeon.

Every event is also recorded on a dashboard, which shows what happened, when it happened, and how it was resolved. Over time, this record helps the team review cases and make each response faster than the last.

Atheer does not claim to remove every risk, because space is a demanding environment by nature. What it does is make sure the astronaut never faces danger alone, and that the response begins within seconds instead of hours. The medical limits and recommended steps would, of course, need to be reviewed and approved by medical specialists before any real use.

Atheer: the solution arrives with the problem.

If you would like, I can also write a shorter version of about one minute for speaking in front of the judges.

projectDetails.name: Atheera
projectDetails.summary:
Atheera is a research-prototype software system that watches over astronauts using the Wi-Fi already on board a station. As Wi-Fi signals cross a module, a person’s breathing and movement create tiny ripples in them. Atheera reads those ripples and reports each crew member’s breathing rate, activity, falls, unusual movement and rest during sleep. It shows them on a dashboard with clear alerts that include their evidence and what to do next. It needs no cameras, wearables or new sensors.

It addresses the NASA challenge of creating health monitoring software for astronauts. It gathers the indicators that need nothing worn and nothing to remember, and flags when a result needs attention. Where the signal is unclear, it says “lost” instead of guessing.

This matters because on long missions the crew is small and help is far away, and one missed moment, such as a fall or struggling breathing in sleep, can be serious. On public recordings, Atheera reads breathing within 0.40 breaths/min of a chest belt, recognises activity with 96% accuracy on unseen recordings, and caught all 16 held-out falls. It supports crews and flight surgeons and is not a medical device.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Atheera is software that watches over astronauts using the Wi-Fi already on a station. Every Wi-Fi packet carries channel state information (CSI), which records how the signal changed on its way from sender to receiver. A chest rising and falling, or a body moving, alters that path. Atheera processes this in five steps:

  1. It takes in CSI from 52 usable subcarriers.
  2. It cleans the signal with filtering, resampling and phase correction.
  3. Four readers estimate breathing, activity and falls, unusual movement, and rest.
  4. A fusion engine applies context-aware limits (sleep, rest, active, exercise) and raises alerts only when a problem persists.
  5. A dashboard shows each alert with its evidence and what to do next.

Breathing comes from signal processing with Viterbi tracking and a confidence score. Activity and falls come from an ensemble of four ResNet-18 networks. Simple, inspectable rules, not a model, decide when an alert is raised.

Benefits

  • Someone is always watching, including during sleep, and the crew has to do nothing.
  • It adds no mass, power or cabling, because it uses hardware the spacecraft already has.
  • Every alert shows its evidence and how sure the system is, and the system says "lost" instead of guessing.
  • On held-out public recordings, breathing error was 0.40 breaths/min against a chest belt, activity accuracy was 96.0%, and all 16 falls were caught with 1 false alarm in 96 recordings.

Intended impact

Atheera is meant to support crews and flight surgeons on long missions, where sleep loss, injury risk and isolation are named NASA concerns. It runs beside the medical kit and does not replace it. The same idea could fit any closed habitat with Wi-Fi, such as a base or a rover. It covers three of NASA's five hazards (isolation and confinement, closed environment, gravity fields).

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Models and signal processing: Python 3.12, PyTorch, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn.
  • Backend: FastAPI with WebSockets and a REST API, driven by a YAML scenario replay engine.
  • Dashboard: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Radix, TanStack Query, Three.js (React Three Fiber) and Recharts.
  • Packaging: Docker Compose, with an optional Caddy HTTPS setup.
  • Hardware: none for the demo. A live system needs a CSI-capable radio such as an Intel 5300 card or an ESP32.
  • AI assistance: Claude helped write and review code, run experiments and draft documents. Results were checked against the result files.

What is creative about it

  • It turns Wi-Fi into a health sensor, so there are no cameras and nothing to wear or remember.
  • It brings wrist actigraphy (the method NASA's ARCHeR research uses) to Wi-Fi to estimate rest time.
  • It is honest about uncertainty: low-confidence readings are shown as "lost", and unclear time is never counted as rest.
  • The dashboard has a 3D station view where a module turns red at a fall, plus a guided tour and a replayable night shift.

Factors the team considered

  • Scope: the indicators were chosen from NASA's hazard and risk pages. Heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature and mood were left out because Wi-Fi cannot measure them reliably.
  • Privacy and comfort: cameras are unwelcome in crew quarters, and wearables are uncomfortable and need charging.
  • Rigour: every split holds out whole recordings. The standard benchmark's 98.3% is inflated, since 499 of its 500 test windows share recordings with training. On the stricter split the same recipe scores 91.9% and Atheera scores 96.0%.
  • False alarms: a fix for receiver gain steps cut false movements from 17.3 to 2.8 per hour.
  • Safety: Atheera does not prescribe treatment, and it is not a medical device.
  • Limits: all data comes from recordings made on Earth, and no microgravity CSI exists yet. The slow-breathing demo event is real data stretched in time. Next steps are a live stream, a metal-walled mock-up, more people and rooms, and review by flight surgeons.

projectDetails.name: StellarIS
projectDetails.summary: StellarIS is a browser-based Space Mission Design Game that lets players plan and fly a complete mission to the Moon or Mars. Players choose an objective, design a spacecraft (instruments, engine, propellant, power system, antenna, shielding), pick a real launch vehicle, then watch the mission unfold with live telemetry and launch and landing scenes. Along the way they face random anomalies such as solar flares, power shortfalls and trajectory errors, and must choose between solutions that each cost mass, power, money or science. The simulation uses the rocket equation, orbital mechanics and published specifications of real launch vehicles and power systems. A final report explains why the mission succeeded or failed, so players learn that engineering is about trade-offs. This addresses the challenge by teaching complete mission design in a fun, replayable way. It matters because it turns hard aerospace concepts into decisions anyone can practice. Built with AI-assisted tools, then reviewed and tested by Team Atlantis 505.
projectDetails.details:
StellarIS is a browser-based Space Mission Design Game. Players pick one of four missions (Moon orbit, Moon landing, Mars orbit, Mars landing), design the spacecraft, and then fly it. They choose a launch vehicle (Electron, Falcon 9, Atlas V 551, Falcon Heavy), an engine (hydrazine, hypergolic, methane/oxygen or xenon ion), a power system (solar arrays or an MMRTG), science instruments, an antenna and radiation shielding. Live meters show launch mass, delta-v, power and budget. During flight the game simulates the rocket equation, Kepler orbits, sunlight falling with distance, radiation dose and radio delay, and pauses for random anomalies where the player must pick between solutions that each cost mass, power, money or science. A final report explains why the mission succeeded or failed and links the result to a real mission such as NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. The benefit is learning that engineering is a set of trade-offs. It is a single HTML, CSS and JavaScript file with canvas graphics, Web Audio and reduced-motion support. Part values are based on published specifications or approximated for game balance.

Use of SI: We used SI tools for ideation, research, coding and debugging, and writing. Manus generated the game code from our design specification, and Claude (Anthropic) helped us plan the design, write texts and review the work. The team directed the design, tested the game and checked the data.

projectDetails.name: AstroVitals
projectDetails.summary:
We developed AstroVitals, a prototype web application that helps astronauts understand and track their physical and psychological well-being throughout a space mission. It combines an interactive 3D body with clickable organ-system status, vital readings, daily wellness assessments, and a medical-officer dashboard showing crew health trends over time.

Our recovery-readiness model was trained using PMData’s sleep and activity data. Daily check-ins complement those readings by capturing symptoms, mood, stress, and isolation, with wellness summaries and optional AI-assisted guidance. A built-in Mission Guide explains the interface to first-time users.

AstroVitals addresses the challenge by bringing health indicators, self-assessment, and understandable visual feedback into one experience. NASA’s Human Research Program hazard framework informed our physical and mental health focus. This matters because long-duration missions place greater responsibility on astronauts to recognize changes in their health and seek support.

The current demo uses simulated telemetry. Real wearable integration, privacy enforcement, and spaceflight validation are planned next steps. AstroVitals supports awareness and medical review—not diagnosis.
projectDetails.details:
We developed AstroVitals, a prototype web application for the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge. It brings physiological readings, recovery estimates, and physical and psychological check-ins into one experience for astronauts and medical officers.

Astronauts can explore an interactive 3D human body and select an organ system to view its status and supporting readings. The home dashboard and organ view share simulated monitoring data, including heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, and respiratory rate. A built-in Mission Guide introduces first-time users to the application’s main features.

In AI Analysis, users enter sleep and activity information. Our tree-based readiness model, trained using PMData’s sleep and activity data, processes these inputs to estimate recovery and classify readiness as Recover, Normal, or Hard. These categories support awareness; they are not medical clearance for exercise. PMData is an Earth-based dataset, not NASA astronaut data.

Daily assessments capture information that readings alone cannot provide, including symptoms, energy, sleep quality, mood, stress, isolation, and motivation. Local rules produce a wellness score and review flags. When configured, the Manus API uses a predefined prompt to provide general wellness guidance and follow-up conversation. Medical officers can review overall crew status and each astronaut’s composite health trend over the last 14 days.

Our intended impact is to help astronauts understand changes in their well-being and support informed medical review throughout a long mission. Combining readings with self-reported experiences creates a broader picture than either source alone. Our creative approach makes the person—not a spreadsheet—the starting point: an interactive body for exploration, a guide for understanding, and crew-level trends for supervision.

We used React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the interface; Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for the interactive body; and Recharts for visualizations. Python and NumPy support readiness-model inference, while server-side TypeScript endpoints connect the optional Manus API guidance service. Browser state and local storage connect the demo workflows. No physical wearable hardware is integrated yet; current telemetry is simulated.

NASA’s Human Research Program hazard framework informed our physical and psychological health focus. We considered usability, individual baseline differences, sensitive health information, and the limitations of applying terrestrial training data to spaceflight. Current authentication and privacy controls are demo-level. Real wearable integration, stronger authorization and data minimization, mission-connectivity testing, and spaceflight validation are next steps. AstroVitals supports awareness and medical review—not diagnosis or replacement of the flight surgeon.

projectDetails.name: Project Auroraa
projectDetails.summary: Auroraa is an offline-first astronaut health and spacewalk-readiness system that runs onboard the spacecraft, with a working dashboard prototype showing how a crew member would use it. As crews travel farther from Earth, the radio delay stretches from seconds at the Moon to about 20 minutes at Mars, so flight surgeons can no longer monitor astronauts in real time — and the earliest warning signs of trouble (fatigue, dehydration, a lapse in attention, shaky hands) are the easiest to miss. Auroraa turns those scattered signals into one clear go / no-go decision: a guided pre-spacewalk checklist and physical, neurological and environmental clearance; quick daily gamified check-ins for reaction time, working memory, fine-motor stability and mood; and onboard sensor data on heart rhythm, temperature, circadian rhythm, hydration and exercise load. Everything is processed at the edge, so it keeps working through communication blackouts and syncs only summaries to mission control. That gives crews the autonomy to decide safely alone, and Earth a trustworthy low-bandwidth picture of crew health — a design that also transfers to diving, aviation, remote industry and rural clinics.
projectDetails.details:
Auroraa is an offline-first astronaut health and spacewalk (EVA) readiness system. Its main use is the moment before a spacewalk: a crew member works through a guided readiness protocol at a console and receives a single, explained go / no-go decision, produced onboard from their own recent health data instead of waiting for a reply from Earth. It addresses the loss of real-time medical supervision as crews travel farther out. Communication delay grows from seconds in low Earth orbit to roughly 20 minutes at Mars, and the earliest warning signs of trouble — fatigue, dehydration, a lapse in attention, a small loss of hand stability — are exactly what is easy to miss over a delayed, low-bandwidth link.

The delivered project is a working, interactive web prototype of the crew dashboard. It includes a mission shell with navigation, status chips and crew profile; a telemetry grid with live panels for ECG, thermal and circadian trends, hydration, cognition and exercise load; a body-status stage that marks the flagged system with biomarker hotspots; and a mission-critical row consolidating alerts, readiness status and recommended actions. Alerts escalate from nominal to caution to critical with the reason in plain language rather than raw numbers. The layout is responsive down to a 390 px phone width and exposes keyboard focus states, and all artwork is served locally so the interface renders with no network connection. The readiness protocol itself is also specified and demonstrated: automated equipment checklist, physical check, neurological screening (reaction time, working memory, fine-motor stability), environmental clearance and a daily well-being self-report.

The design is a three-layer edge system. Wearable and suit sensors plus short crew tests produce timestamped measurements — heart rhythm, temperature, circadian phase, hydration, exercise load, reaction time, memory accuracy, tap stability and mood. Onboard compute compares each against the crew member's own rolling baseline rather than a population average, because individual baselines are far more informative for a small crew. A readiness score is computed from weighted cardiovascular, thermal, hydration, cognitive, motor and psychological domains, and any domain crossing its threshold produces a plain-language reason and an action. Only a compact summary, never the raw stream, is queued for mission control when a link exists. In practice, a crew member who slept poorly, is mildly dehydrated and shows slower reaction time and less stable tapping than their own baseline receives a caution naming those reasons plus an action such as rehydration, rest or repeating the motor test; if every domain is inside baseline, the result is a clear go.

The benefit is autonomy under delay: the crew can decide safely during a communication blackout, when a 20-minute round trip is unacceptable, while flight surgeons still receive a decision-ready picture. Personalised trend baselines catch drift a single reading would miss, and one explained decision replaces a wall of telemetry for a tired crew member. The same architecture transfers to diving, aviation, remote industrial sites and rural clinics.

The front end is React and TypeScript with a custom design system (dark obsidian base, aurora-green accent, Space Grotesk and Inter), charts and the body stage drawn as scalable vectors, locally bundled assets and no external CDN dependency at runtime. Data is simulated in the prototype but shaped to match real sensor fields. Domain framing follows NASA Human Research Program hazard and risk categories and Canadian Space Agency life-science material. The prototype runs in a browser; the intended target is radiation-tolerant onboard compute with wearable and suit sensor feeds, and no flight hardware was built.

Limitations are stated plainly. Thresholds and weights are engineering heuristics informed by published risk domains, not clinically validated cutoffs, so Auroraa is decision support rather than a medical device and does not replace a flight surgeon. The prototype runs on simulated telemetry with no real astronaut or suit data and no sensor integration; the cognitive and motor tasks are faithful in spirit but not formally calibrated; and there is no radiation qualification, flight certification or security hardening, with offline sync and multi-crew support designed but not implemented. Future work covers sensor integration and a hardware bench prototype, per-crew baseline learning with drift detection, mission-control and clinician views, encrypted store-and-forward sync, and an Earth pilot in a high-risk operations or rural care setting

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: FLAMEPRINT
projectDetails.summary:
Understanding combustion in reduced gravity is essential to spacecraft fire-safety research, yet experimental findings are dispersed across publications, repository records, and incompatible test conditions. FLAMEPRINT, an AURYNTIS LABS project for NASA Space Apps 2026's Flame in Freefall challenge, brings this evidence into a structured scientific exploration workflow.

Its documented foundation combines a React-based research interface with a curated NASA-source evidence package: published Lunar Combustion Investigation (LUCI) flame-spread results and references to six Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations.

The analytical design supports source-linked visualizations, transparent comparisons, and research-relevance ranking, with an evidence-grounded AI assistant included in the integration architecture. Published values are kept distinct from points calculated using reported regression fits, and incomplete or incompatible evidence is flagged rather than disguised as certainty.

FLAMEPRINT aims to make reduced-gravity combustion research more accessible and traceable while supporting careful interpretation of findings relevant to future human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
A. The Scientific Problem

Combustion behaves differently when gravity is reduced. On Earth, buoyancy-driven convection influences flame shape, heat transfer, and the transport of combustion products. In microgravity, these effects are greatly diminished; partial-gravity environments introduce different flow conditions and physical behavior.

Understanding these differences is important for fundamental combustion science, spacecraft material selection, and research into fire safety during long-duration human exploration.

NASA has conducted extensive combustion investigations across orbital, suborbital, and ground-based experimental environments. However, scientific findings are distributed among publications, investigation repositories, experimental metadata, mathematical models, and graphical results.

Researchers must often reconstruct the context of a result before interpreting it. Differences in fuel materials, gravity levels, oxygen conditions, experimental geometry, and measurement methods can make seemingly similar findings scientifically incompatible.

The central problem FLAMEPRINT addresses is therefore not simply a lack of data. It is the difficulty of transforming existing scientific evidence into an accessible, comparable, and traceable research workflow.

B. Our Solution — FLAMEPRINT

FLAMEPRINT is an evidence-centered scientific research exploration platform developed by AURYNTIS LABS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Flame in Freefall challenge.

Its purpose is to organize documented combustion research into a structured environment where users can discover investigations, examine reported measurements, explore scientific visualizations, compare appropriate experimental results, and trace conclusions to their original sources.

The project follows three principles aligned with the challenge: summarize research evidence, rank findings by documented relevance, and interpret results within their scientific limitations.

The supplied implementation material establishes a React-based scientific frontend and a curated NASA-source evidence package. An integrated backend, database, and evidence-grounded AI research assistant are specified in the completion architecture; their final operational status requires verification against the delivered software.

FLAMEPRINT is a research-support platform, not an operational fire detection system or a certified spacecraft hazard predictor.

C. Core Features and Functionality

FLAMEPRINT's scientific workspace is organized around complementary research activities.

Research Overview: Presents investigation coverage, available experimental records, and evidence categories, helping users distinguish source availability from actual numerical coverage.

Investigation Explorer: Provides a structured interface for searching, filtering, and reviewing combustion investigations, with supporting identifiers, experimental context, and provenance information.

Investigation Details: Connects individual studies with their documented conditions, relevant scientific variables, reported measurements, and original NASA references.

Scientific Lab: Is designed to visualize supported time-dependent scientific quantities through interactive charts, variable selection, time-window inspection, and clear measurement units. Curves evaluated from published regression equations are identified as derived mathematical results rather than raw observations.

Scientific Comparison: Organizes compatible published measurements into side-by-side analytical views. Its intended compatibility rules consider units, physical quantities, experimental conditions, and evidence limitations.

Research Rankings: The analytical design prioritizes investigations according to explainable research relevance. Ranking is conceptually separate from estimating fire hazard, scientific quality, or operational safety.

Sources and Exports: Source references, document identifiers, and numerical provenance support review and reproducibility. The full integration design includes exporting selected research records and visualizations.

AI Research Assistant: A retrieval-based assistant is specified to support source-grounded summaries, questions, and research interpretation. Live inference remains unverified until a configured provider and functioning application are demonstrated.

The original frontend contains the project's principal research areas. Their complete backend integration, runtime behavior, and production readiness have not yet been independently established.

D. NASA Data Integration

FLAMEPRINT's documented scientific foundation uses NASA-published combustion evidence, with particular emphasis on the Lunar Combustion Investigation (LUCI).

The primary numerical reference is the 2025 NASA Technical Reports Server publication Lunar Combustion Investigation: Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket (NTRS 20250010653).

This investigation reports material flammability observations under simulated lunar gravity, generated through centrifugal acceleration aboard a rotating sounding rocket, alongside reference comparisons at Earth's gravity.

The supplied research package also contains metadata references for six NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigations: FLEX, BASS-II, Saffire-I, SPICE, SAME, and SAME-R.

These PSI entries provide scientific discovery and contextual references. They do not constitute six imported numerical experimental datasets.

The curated input package contains seven catalog records, four experimental contexts, twelve published numerical summary metrics, three cross-gravity comparison records, and eight fitted series represented by eighty calculated plotting points.

Importantly, those eighty points are mathematical evaluations derived from published fits. The supplied package does not include original raw sensor measurements or raw time-series telemetry.

This distinction is fundamental to FLAMEPRINT's scientific approach.

E. Scientific Analysis Methodology

The project's methodology emphasizes traceability, reproducibility, and scientifically defensible comparisons.

The curated dataset separates source-reported numerical results from evaluated mathematical models. Published regression equations can be used to calculate representative points within documented time windows, allowing experimental trends to be visualized without misrepresenting the calculated points as newly measured observations.

For example, a published linear position fit can be evaluated using:

x(t) = mt + b

Here, the slope and intercept originate from the published research, while individual plotted coordinates are produced through deterministic mathematical evaluation.

The analysis design preserves scientific variables, units, experimental identifiers, source references, and applicable limitations.

Comparisons require compatible physical quantities and meaningful experimental context. Missing conditions must remain explicitly unknown rather than being interpreted as zero.

Because fitted sample points are not independent sensor measurements, statistical quantities calculated from them cannot be used to invent experimental confidence intervals, measurement uncertainty, or statistical significance.

Source attribution and evidence classification remain integral to the intended analytical workflow.

F. Concrete Scientific Example — LUCI SIBAL

One important example comes from NASA's LUCI research involving SIBAL, a cotton-fiberglass composite fabric.

The NASA presentation reports flame-tip spread rates derived from linear fits for two gravity conditions:

Experimental condition

Reported flame-tip spread rate

Simulated lunar gravity

1.1 mm/s

Earth gravity reference (1 g)

2.8 mm/s

Published partial-gravity / 1-g ratio

0.39

Source: Ferkul et al., 2025, NASA NTRS 20250010653, PDF page 33.

For this documented comparison, the flame-tip spread rate under simulated lunar gravity is approximately 39% of the reported 1-g reference value.

The result illustrates why gravity-dependent combustion research matters. It also demonstrates the importance of retaining experimental conditions and source attribution when comparing findings.

This observation does not establish that all materials burn more slowly under lunar gravity, nor does it quantify the overall fire risk of a lunar habitat.

FLAMEPRINT's intended comparison workflow makes such study-specific evidence accessible while preserving these important boundaries.

G. Software Architecture

The established frontend uses React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 8, supported by modern routing, state management, typed data validation, and interactive visualization technologies.

Apache ECharts provides the scientific charting foundation, while TanStack libraries support structured data handling and asynchronous application workflows.

The planned integrated architecture follows a modular frontend-backend pattern.

A Python/FastAPI service is specified to manage scientific records, API access, evidence retrieval, and controlled analytical operations. PostgreSQL is the proposed relational evidence store, with schema validation and provenance-preserving ingestion processes.

Scientific calculations are intended to be deterministic and implemented independently of the language model.

For AI interactions, the architecture separates evidence retrieval, numerical computation, comparison policy, and natural-language generation.

These backend technologies and workflows are defined in the technical implementation requirements, but their successful deployment and integration have not been confirmed by post-implementation evidence.

H. AI-Assisted Scientific Research

The AI component is designed to support scientific interpretation rather than replace experimental investigation.

Its architecture combines structured scientific tools, research-document retrieval, and a configurable large language model.

A research question is intended to trigger retrieval of relevant investigation records, published metrics, and supporting source material. The scientific services determine appropriate numerical results and comparison boundaries, while the language model synthesizes evidence into accessible explanations.

The design includes source citations, explicit handling of missing information, and responses that acknowledge insufficient evidence.

The assistant is not intended to create unverified combustion measurements, train a new predictive physics model, or provide certified spacecraft fire-risk assessments.

Its operational availability depends on actual backend integration, indexed source coverage, and live model-provider configuration, none of which has been independently verified in the supplied handover.

I. Innovation and Creativity

FLAMEPRINT's distinctive contribution is its evidence-centered research workflow.

Instead of treating combustion studies as interchangeable numerical records, the project emphasizes scientific provenance and experimental compatibility throughout the analytical process.

It combines research discovery, source-linked visualization, contextual comparison, explainable relevance ranking, and a constrained AI interpretation architecture within a unified interface.

Another important design choice is the explicit separation of published findings from mathematical values calculated from those findings.

This helps address a common problem in scientific visualization: displaying a convincing graph without adequately communicating what the underlying points represent.

The project's originality lies in connecting accessible research exploration with transparent scientific evidence, not in claiming to discover new combustion laws or replace NASA's experimental methods.

J. Benefits and Intended Impact

FLAMEPRINT is intended to benefit combustion researchers, aerospace engineers, students, and scientific educators.

Its proposed workflow can help users locate relevant investigations, understand experimental variables, compare compatible results, and investigate the sources supporting particular findings.

Clear visualizations and contextual explanations may also make complex combustion research easier to understand for non-specialist audiences.

Over time, a wider verified evidence collection could support preliminary scientific literature reviews and identify gaps deserving further investigation.

The project has not established a measured improvement in researcher productivity, predictive accuracy, or spacecraft fire-safety outcomes. These remain potential benefits requiring systematic evaluation.

K. Scientific and Engineering Considerations

Several considerations guide FLAMEPRINT's design.

Data integrity: Published findings and derived mathematical values must remain distinguishable.

Scientific validity: Experimental comparisons require compatible quantities, units, and relevant conditions.

Provenance: Numerical results should retain traceable references to their original publications.

Reproducibility: Mathematical transformations and plotting methods should be documented and repeatable.

Transparency: Missing measurements, uncertain interpretations, and limited dataset coverage must be visible.

Responsible AI: Generated explanations must not be presented as original experimental evidence or NASA-endorsed scientific conclusions.

Together, these principles establish the project's intended standard for reliable research communication.

L. Limitations and Future Development

The current documented dataset is intentionally limited.

Its numerical evidence is concentrated in published LUCI results, while the six included PSI investigations are represented by metadata rather than imported experimental measurements.

The calculated time-series points are evaluations of published mathematical fits, not raw telemetry. The available source information does not justify new uncertainty estimates or generalized predictions.

The backend, complete AI integration, production deployment, and comprehensive application testing also require verification before being described as delivered.

Future work could extend FLAMEPRINT through broader ingestion of verified NASA experimental datasets, additional source-document indexing, stronger compatibility validation, and systematic evaluation of AI-generated scientific explanations.

FLAMEPRINT's long-term objective is to make reduced-gravity combustion evidence easier to discover, explore, and interpret—while preserving the scientific precision necessary for research relevant to future human space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.details:
Project Title: AYO-X: Alexandria Precipitation Trend Analysis (2010–2025)

Project Summary:

AYO-X addresses the challenge of extracting meaningful insights from complex Earth observation data by analyzing 15 years of monthly precipitation trends along Egypt's northern coast (Alexandria). By transforming raw satellite datasets (NASA GPM IMERG) into a clean, reproducible Python workflow, the project uncovers seasonal variability and extreme precipitation patterns.

Value & Impact:

This work provides scientists, researchers, and urban planners with a ready-to-use analytical foundation, saving significant time and effort in local climate research.

Future Roadmap:

The next phase focuses on scaling this pipeline into an interactive web-based analytics tool capable of evaluating multiple regions, identifying clear climate trends, and conducting advanced scientific research to correlate these precipitation shifts with drought and flood events.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
