projectDetails.summary:
Fire sync is an end-to-end geospatial wildfire intelligence and crisis response platform powered by NASA Earth observations. Wildfires across the Amazon, North America, and Mediterranean ecosystems are intensifying, yet operational teams and civilians struggle with fragmented satellite streams, inconsistent sensor resolutions, and delayed evacuation pathways. 

Fire sync solves this by harmonizing multi-sensor satellite fire observations from NASA’s MODIS (Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP/NOAA-20/21), unifying 2,819 verified fire detections into a real-time risk intelligence dashboard. The platform features automated wildfire detection, 24-72h AI-driven risk modeling, weather-wind propagation analysis, smoke/aerosol dispersion monitoring, and an interactive Evacuation Command Center with automated convoy dispatch. Crucially, Fire sync provides a dual-interface experience: a tactical GIS command hub for first responders and an intuitive, panic-free safety portal for affected civilians.
projectDetails.details:
# Fire sync — NASA Earth Wildfire Intelligence & Evacuation System

**Fire sync** is an AI-driven geospatial intelligence and crisis response platform powered by NASA Earth observations. It transforms raw satellite telemetry into real-time, life-saving operational intelligence for wildfire containment, infrastructure safeguarding, and civilian evacuation.

Key Capabilities:

- **Multi-Sensor Harmonization:** Unifies high-resolution NASA VIIRS (375m) and MODIS (1km) feeds into a single, high-fidelity active fire tracking engine.

- **Predictive AI Risk Modeling:** Forecasts fire outbreak trajectories and smoke plume dispersion across 24h, 48h, and 72h horizons using atmospheric vector analysis (NASA MERRA-2 & GOES-16).

- **Critical Infrastructure Defense:** Computes dynamic geodesic buffers around vital civil assets (hospitals, power grids, and transit networks).

- **Evacuation Command Center:** Dynamically maps open escape corridors, calculates safest evacuation routes, and directs emergency medical convoys away from active flame fronts.

- **Dual-Role Architecture:** Features a tactical GIS command hub for firefighters alongside a simplified, panic-free safety portal for local civilians.

Validated across 2,819 verified satellite detections spanning three diverse global biomes: the Amazon Basin (Brazil), Boreal Forests (Canada), and Agricultural Corridors (Egypt).


## 1. Unified Multi-Sensor Fire Intelligence

**Fire sync** bridges the critical gap between space observations and ground crisis management. Our platform unifies fragmented Earth data from NASA’s primary satellite sensors:

- **MODIS (Terra & Aqua - 1km):** Deep historical tracking and broad thermal anomaly mapping.

- **VIIRS (Suomi-NPP & NOAA-20/21 - 375m):** High-resolution active fire detection for early spot fires day and night.

By harmonizing millions of satellite fire records across Brazil, Canada, and Egypt, Fire sync delivers an automated, single source of truth for global wildfire intelligence.
## 2. Real-Time Tactical Dashboard & Satellite Overpass

The central command dashboard translates complex satellite feeds into immediate situational awareness:

- **Satellite Overpass Ticker:** Live countdown timers predicting exactly when Suomi-NPP, Aqua, and Sentinel satellites will pass over the fire zone for fresh observations.

- **Interactive Multi-Layer GIS:** Displays real-time thermal perimeters with Fire Radiative Power (FRP) heat signatures and weather overlays (wind direction, humidity, KBDI drought index).

- **Anomaly Detection & Critical Metrics:** Tracks fire anomalies (+312% surge detection), affected populations (3.9M), burnt area (284,000 ha), and active danger clusters in real time.

## 3. Citizen Safety Portal: Dual-Role Experience

To ensure space observations directly protect vulnerable populations, **Fire sync** provides a dedicated, panic-free **Civilian Safety Portal**:

- **Localized Threat Awareness:** Delivers real-time fire risk percentages (e.g., 75% High Risk), local air quality index (AQI), and immediate evacuation status ("No Immediate Evacuation - Area Safe").

- **Proximity Alerts & Safety Guidance:** Tracks nearby active fires within a 100 km radius and provides vetted, emergency video tutorials and actionable safety steps.

- **Human-Centric GIS:** Strips away overwhelming military/technical jargon, allowing citizens to search their city or GPS coordinates to monitor local smoke plumes, fire fronts, and safe shelters.

## 4. Atmospheric Dynamics & Meteorological Radar

Wildfire behavior is fundamentally dictated by local meteorology. The **Weather Operations Engine** correlates NASA atmospheric models (MERRA-2) and GOES-16 feeds to forecast fire propagation:

- **Wind Vector & Gust Streamlines:** Live particle animations mapping wind speed (38 km/h with 57 km/h gusts) and thermal advection direction (NW 310°) pushing the fire front.

- **Critical Fuel Dryness Metrics:** Tracks Relative Humidity (28% critical fuel dryness) and Keetch-Byram Drought Index (KBDI 580 High) to identify extreme ignition vulnerabilities.

- **Diurnal Peak Burning Window:** Analyzes the daily solar peak and sub-20% humidity window (12:00–18:00 Local) to forecast rapid wildfire flare-ups and firestorm formation.
## 5. Active Fire Detection & Satellite Telemetry

The core **Fire Detection Hub** harmonizes multi-resolution satellite observations into real-time active fire perimeters:

- **Dual-Sensor Harmonization:** Ingests high-resolution VIIRS (375m I-band) and MODIS (1km thermal) data to detect both intense wildfire fronts and nascent spot fires.

- **Precision Threat Scoring:** Calculates Fire Radiative Power (FRP) exceeding 1,490+ MW and confidence scores (>80%), distinguishing real active flames from thermal industrial anomalies.

- **Dynamic Orbital Telemetry:** Streams live orbital feeds, solar irradiance levels (1,020 W/m²), and FLIR dual EO/IR thermal imaging (412°C hotspots) directly linked to our FastAPI backend.## 6. Historical Climatological Analytics & Anomaly Tracking

Understanding future fire behavior requires historical context. The **Historical Analytics Engine** mines multi-year NASA satellite archives (2018–2024) to establish baseline climatological patterns:

- **Comprehensive Fire Archive:** Analyzes 2,819 verified detections and 321,000 hectares of burned area across 5-year longitudinal satellite records.

- **Surge & Anomaly Quantification:** Detects critical climatological deviations (+98% fire surge in 2024 compared to historical averages).

- **Seasonal Waveform Modeling:** Maps multi-year monthly averages (2021–2024 curves) identifying the peak fire window (July–August) to enable proactive resource allocation and pre-season fireproofing.## 7. Predictive AI Modeling & Wildfire Risk Forecasting

Transitioning from reactive firefighting to proactive crisis prevention, the **Predictive Fire Risk Engine** forecasts wildfire outbreaks across multiple temporal horizons (12h, 24h, 72h, and 7 days):

- **Multi-Factor Risk Inputs:** Synthesizes real-time surface temperatures (34.2°C avg), extreme drought indices (KBDI 680/800), and wind vector forecasts into a continuous risk probability surface.

- **Micro-Targeted Hazard Zones:** Categorizes 911 territorial zones into distinct severity tiers (24 Critical, 112 High, 245 Moderate), pinpointing extreme ignition sectors (such as Peace River Boreal at 98% Critical Risk).

- **7-Day Trend Forecaster:** Projects upcoming fire intensity curves across the week, enabling fire response authorities to pre-position resources days before a catastrophe strikes.## 8. Smoke Dispersion & Atmospheric Air Quality Monitoring

Wildfire smoke is often more lethal to distant populations than direct flames. Leveraging **Sentinel-5P (TROPOMI)** satellite telemetry and aerosol indexing, the **Smoke & Air Quality Engine** tracks particulate hazards in real time:

- **Macro-Plume Dispersion Modeling:** Maps a massive 385,000 km² smoke plume trajectory with dynamic atmospheric vectors showing downwind transport across population centers.

- **Urban AQI Impact Scoring:** Continuously calculates local EPA Air Quality Indices for downstream cities (e.g., Fort McMurray at 178 Unhealthy, PM2.5: 89.4 µg/m³).

- **Multi-Hour Plume Progression:** Provides progressive satellite forecasts across 16h, 20h, 45h, and 72h timelines, issuing automated respiratory health advisories for vulnerable civilians.
## 9. Ground Truth & Citizen Scientist Verification

Satellite observations often suffer from false positives (such as heated sand, agricultural flares, or industrial emissions). The **Ground Truth Verification Module** bridges space data with ground validation:

- **Field & Drone Incident Reporting:** Enables rangers, drone pilots, and local spotters to submit geolocated photo evidence directly correlated with NASA satellite clusters.

- **Bi-Directional Verification:** Validates intense fire clusters (e.g., Canada Cluster #2197 at 1,496.9 MW FRP, 479.8 K brightness temperature) with 100% confidence while filtering out false alarms.

- **Incident Audit Trail:** Maintains an active verification queue (Confirmed, Pending, False Detection) to prioritize firefighter dispatch to confirmed catastrophic fronts.## 10. Automated Early Warning & Multi-Channel Dispatch

Seconds count during rapid wildfire outbreaks. The **Emergency Alert & Dispatch System** automates space-to-ground warning triggers:

- **Radiometric Anomaly Triggers:** Continuously scans orbital telemetry, instantly firing critical alerts when thermal spikes exceed severe thresholds (e.g., 1,496.9 MW heat signatures at 479.9 K).

- **Rule-Based Custom Automation:** Allows command centers to configure custom logic rules based on trigger type (New Fire Detection), risk tier, and target biome.

- **Multi-Channel Distribution:** Automatically dispatches emergency notifications via Email Dispatch, SMS/Cell Broadcast, and in-app HUD popups to mobilize first responders before fires breach containment lines.## 11. Post-Fire Ecological Recovery & Burn Scar Rehabilitation

Disaster management extends beyond fire containment to ecological restoration. The **Ecological Recovery Hub** utilizes Sentinel-2 multi-spectral imagery to monitor post-fire forest regeneration:

- **Interactive Split-Screen Satellite Slider:** Compares pre-fire canopy (Before 2023) against burn scars (After 2024), mapping 273,341 hectares of impacted boreal forest.

- **NDVI & dNBR Time-Series Regrowth:** Computes Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI: +0.44) and Differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR) to quantify a +37% vegetation recovery trajectory.

- **Ecological Stage Classifier:** Tracks rehabilitation through 4 biological milestones (Severe Impact, Early Recovery, Vegetation Return, and Near Normal), estimating a full 3–5 year ecosystem restoration timeline.## 12. Critical Infrastructure Exposure & Proximity Buffering

Wildfires become catastrophic disasters when they intersect civil infrastructure. The **Infrastructure Exposure Intelligence Engine** calculates geodesic proximity buffers around vital lifelines:

- **Real-Time Geodesic Buffers:** Computes dynamic circular danger zones (immediate impact, warning, and surveillance perimeters) around critical population centers.

- **Critical Asset Prioritization:** Continuously tracks distance to the closest flame front (4.8 km) and rates vulnerability across 5 vital sectors: Urban Centers (HIGH), Hospitals (5.9 km HIGH), High-Voltage Power Grids (240 kV / 1,200 MW HIGH), and Air Tanker Bases (12.1 km HIGH).

- **Evacuation Artery Safeguarding:** Monitors key escape corridors (Highway 63 at 15.9 km MODERATE), preventing first-responder and civilian entrapment.
## 13. Evacuation Command Center & Safe Corridor Routing

The ultimate objective of space intelligence is humanitarian action. The **Evacuation Command Center** transforms satellite thermal perimeters into dynamic, life-saving transit corridors:

- **AI-Assisted Corridor Calculation:** Dynamically evaluates multiple evacuation paths (Route A: 26.5 km Low Risk, Route B: 34.2 km Moderate, Route C: 52.8 km High) to divert convoys away from active thermal fronts.

- **Real-Time Obstacle & Debris Detection:** Automatically flags blocked road segments compromised by dense smoke and fallen debris, tracking safe corridors (2 of 3 open) and 3 active medical escort convoys.

- **Turn-by-Turn Humanitarian Navigation:** Generates step-by-step waypoint directions safely guiding 1,520 staged evacuees to verified emergency hubs (such as Lac La Biche Hub) with zero fire front exposure.

MISSIONCRAFT – Interactive Space Mission Design Game

MISSIONCRAFT is an interactive educational game that allows players to experience the challenges of designing and planning real-world space missions. The game puts players in the role of space mission designers, assigning them scientific objectives that require them to build and configure suitable spacecraft.

Players select spacecraft components, scientific instruments, and essential systems while managing limited resources such as budget, mass, and power. Each mission introduces different objectives, environmental conditions, and unexpected challenges, requiring players to make strategic decisions and adapt their designs to achieve mission success.

Once the spacecraft is ready, players launch their missions and experience their progress through interactive scenes, unexpected events, and decision-making scenarios that directly influence the mission's outcome.

The main goal of MISSIONCRAFT is to make space science and mission engineering more accessible and engaging, especially for students and young learners. It helps players develop problem-solving, critical thinking, strategic planning, and resource-management skills while introducing them to the complexity of space exploration.

What makes MISSIONCRAFT creative is its combination of educational content and interactive gameplay. Instead of simply presenting scientific information, it allows players to learn through experimentation, decision-making, and experiencing the consequences of their choices.

The project aims to inspire curiosity about space exploration and encourage the next generation to explore careers in science, engineering, and space technology.

projectDetails.summary:
# keepsake
## Comprehensive Project Summary

### 1. Introduction

keepsake is an AI-powered cinematic storytelling project that explores the forgotten traces of human exploration on Mars. It focuses on the spacecraft components, landing systems, and engineering equipment that were essential to successful Mars missions but remained scattered across the Martian surface after completing their intended functions.

When people think about space exploration, they usually remember the astronauts, rovers, spacecraft, and scientific discoveries. However, behind every successful mission, there are numerous engineering components that make the journey possible. Some of these components are released, separated, or left behind during different stages of the mission, becoming permanent reminders of humanity's attempt to explore another world.

keepsake brings attention to these overlooked objects and transforms them from ordinary pieces of engineering hardware into the central subjects of compelling visual stories.

The project particularly focuses on NASA's Mars 2020 Perseverance mission, examining the different components involved in transporting the rover through the Martian atmosphere and delivering it safely to the surface.

projectDetails.name: Still Out There: Stories Beyond Earth
projectDetails.summary:
Still Out There is an interactive space exploration experience that brings the stories of spacecraft, rovers, and scientific equipment left across our Solar System to life.

Through an illustrated interactive journey, users travel from the Solar System to real planetary missions, discovering the locations, journeys, scientific discoveries, and final communications of robotic explorers.

Our first featured story follows NASA’s Opportunity rover (Oppy), which explored Mars for nearly 15 years, far beyond its planned 90-day mission. After a massive Martian dust storm disrupted its power, Opportunity stopped communicating with Earth, leaving behind an extraordinary scientific legacy.

By combining NASA's real mission data, authentic imagery, educational storytelling, and an engaging visual interface, Still Out There makes space science more accessible and emotionally meaningful, especially for younger audiences.

Our goal is to help people discover that even when a mission ends, its story remains.
projectDetails.details:
Oppy’s Tiny Clues is a digital illustrated storybook and companion web experience that turns NASA’s Opportunity rover mission into a child-led investigation. The reader follows an imagined young explorer across Mars, tracks Opportunity’s wheel marks to Eagle Crater, and investigates the Berry Bowl. NASA’s Pancam observations and rover-instrument information become clues the child can examine before learning what hematite-rich spherules tell scientists about ancient water.

The experience uses short comic scenes, prediction questions, and simple evidence reveals to make the science approachable. A print-friendly version lets children follow the same story without needing an interactive device. The project introduces school-age readers to a real piece of NASA hardware and the science it made possible, while showing the difference between an observation, an interpretation, and proof. It clearly states that Opportunity found evidence related to ancient water, not evidence of life.

The project responds to “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” by making the rover’s hardware and scientific legacy memorable for young readers. The current web prototype is hosted on Manus. ChatGPT assisted with story development and early text drafts; the team reviewed the scientific claims against NASA sources. projectDetails.name: Forgotten Footprints
projectDetails.summary:
Forgotten Footprints is a bilingual space museum and scientific archive documenting physical traces of human exploration beyond Earth, focusing on the Moon and Mars. It highlights spacecraft, instruments, and equipment left behind, recovered, or deployed.

The archive contains 22 sourced records (17 lunar and 5 Martian) and 35 timeline events. Each record presents an object's identity, mission, purpose, status, condition, location confidence.

Visitors can explore planetary galleries, search and filter artifacts, compare records, follow mission families, and inspect conceptual 3D models. Features include a timeline, discovery journal, glossary, quiz, myth-versus-fact cards, and a guided presentation route.

The platform supports English and Arabic, including right-to-left layouts, and adapts to mobile screens. Built with HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and custom WebGL, it runs from index.html without a server, installation, build step, external libraries, APIs, or internet connection.

Scientific accuracy is central. The archive distinguishes recovered hardware from objects still on another world and labels coordinates as verified, approximate, mission markers, or unplotted. 3D models and planetary scenes are illustrative, not engineering reconstructions or maps. The project is independent and does not claim NASA endorsement.

Forgotten Footprints makes overlooked space hardware accessible, preserving the historical value of exploration beyond Earth for curious learners too.
projectDetails.details:
Forgotten Footprints is a bilingual, interactive space museum and scientific archive documenting the physical traces of human exploration on the Moon and Mars. Visitors can explore 22 individually sourced artifact records, follow a timeline of mission events, and examine interactive 3D exhibits. The archive also includes search and filtering, artifact comparisons, and short learning activities.

The project looks at landers, rovers, instruments, and other mission hardware as part of the history of exploration. By making these objects easier to discover and understand, it aims to support public learning and encourage more thoughtful preservation of humanity’s presence beyond Earth.

We built the website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using browser-native WebGL for the 3D scenes. Planet surfaces and artifact models are generated in the browser, and original SVG illustrations provide additional visuals. The core experience works offline and requires no installation. The site supports both English and Arabic, including right-to-left layouts.

The creative idea is to tell the story of exploration through what missions leave behind. Visitors can inspect an artifact’s parts and read about its purpose, present condition, and significance. To keep the archive reliable, we considered source quality, object identity, location uncertainty, and the limits of each model. The 3D exhibits are clearly presented as conceptual models, and records link to their sources.

projectDetails.details:
# Mars: Last 30 Days – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Mars: Last 30 Days is an interactive educational survival simulation game designed for children aged 7–12, inspired by the challenges of human exploration and establishing a sustainable presence on Mars.

The player takes on the role of a Mars mission commander, responsible for managing a Martian outpost and ensuring the survival and safety of its crew throughout a 30-day mission.

Throughout the game, players receive mission briefings, encounter unexpected events, and face different challenges that require critical thinking and strategic decision-making. These challenges include solar radiation storms, equipment failures, and limited resources.

Players must choose between different actions, evaluate their consequences, and carefully manage essential resources, including oxygen, water, food, and energy, while maintaining crew health and radiation protection.

Every decision affects the outpost's condition and the crew's ability to survive. Poor decisions can put the mission at risk, while effective resource management and problem-solving increase the chances of success.

Our goal is to transform complex concepts of space exploration into an engaging and accessible learning experience, helping young learners understand the challenges of living on Mars while developing scientific thinking, problem-solving skills, and awareness of sustainable resource management.

Through gameplay, children experience the responsibility and excitement of being part of a real space exploration mission.

projectDetails.name: Earthify
projectDetails.summary:
Earthify is an interactive, bilingual (English/Arabic) planetary analog platform developed by Team Creovate to bridge Earth-based field research with lunar and Martian exploration. Built on verified orbital datasets from NASA (ASTER, SRTM, MODIS, MGS MOLA, LRO Diviner) and CSA (RADARSAT), Earthify profiles four extreme terrestrial analog sites—Devon Island, Kverkfjöll, the Danakil Depression, and Svalbard—and benchmarks them against Mars’s Jezero Crater and the Moon’s Shackleton Crater.

Through a 3D orbital atlas, an animated Comparison Engine, real field photography, and an interactive 3D Surface Simulation with custom environment-matched rovers, users can analyze surface temperatures, elevation relief, and mineralogy while transparently reviewing physical limitations where terrestrial analogs break down. Paired with Cero AI, our research assistant, Earthify helps mission engineers, scientists, and students select accurate Earth testbeds and rehearse planetary exploration before hardware ever leaves our planet.
projectDetails.details:
### Introduction & Problem Statement

Testing planetary rovers, drills, and astronaut habitats directly on Mars or the Moon costs billions of dollars and carries high mission risk. Before hardware leaves Earth, engineers and planetary scientists rely on terrestrial analog sites—extreme environments on Earth that replicate specific geological, thermal, or chemical conditions of off-world destinations. However, orbital datasets across space agencies are fragmented, raw, and difficult to cross-compare, and many teams overlook critical physical limitations where terrestrial analogs fall short.

### Our Solution: How Does Earthify Work?

Developed by Team Creovate, Earthify is a unified, bilingual (English & Arabic) planetary analog exploration and simulation web platform designed for mission planners, researchers, and students. Earthify ingests calibrated orbital telemetry across four scientifically validated Earth analog sites—Haughton Impact Crater (Devon Island, Canada), Kverkfjöll Subglacial Volcano (Iceland), the Danakil Depression / Dallol (Ethiopia), and Bockfjord Volcanic Complex (Svalbard, Norway)—and benchmarks them directly against Mars (Jezero Crater) and the Moon (Shackleton Crater / Lunar South Pole).

### Key Platform Capabilities

- 3D Orbital Atlas (Home): Interactive WebGL planetary globe enabling instant switching between Earth analog markers, Mars Jezero topography, and Lunar South Pole thermal maps, paired with a live orbital telemetry ticker.

- Explore Sites & Field Gallery: Comprehensive scientific dossiers and real field photography for all four sites, detailing elevation relief, surface kinetic temperature, thermal emissivity, VNIR reflectance, and expedition heritage (Haughton-Mars Project, AMASE).

- Animated Comparison Engine: Side-by-side benchmarking of Earth sites against Mars and the Moon across four transparent pillars (Geochemistry & Mineralogy, Geomorphology & Terrain, Thermal Regime, and Mission Testbed Utility), integrated with real field photo comparisons and an explicit "Where the Analogy Breaks Down" panel highlighting gravity, atmospheric pressure, and radiation differences.

- Interactive 3D Surface Simulation: Full-stage 3D procedural terrain environments driven by NASA elevation telemetry where users drive custom environment-matched rovers (NASA K10 Arctic, NASA DuAxel, Dallol-Hex, AMASE Drill Rover, Perseverance + Ingenuity, and NASA VIPER) and run mineral spectrometer scans.

- Cero AI & Open Data Pipeline: A domain-grounded bilingual AI research assistant and a transparent showcase of our multi-agency data calibration pipeline.

### Tools & Technologies Used

React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js / WebGL (3D Globe & Procedural Terrain/Rover Simulation), Framer Motion, Full-Stack LLM API (Cero AI), Python (NASA HDF4/PDS/GeoTIFF telemetry extraction), Manus Cloud Hosting, and ElevenLabs.

projectDetails.name: Project CrewSentiq
projectDetails.summary:
CrewSentiq is an offline-first crew health monitoring platform for long-duration space missions. We built a working web app that compares every crew member only against their own baseline, using a sustained 15% change rule and a robust z-score, built on NASA’s Human Research Program hazard and risk data. It maps results onto 11 NASA-linked conditions and shows the computed severity stage on an interactive human digital twin, with the possible outcomes and NASA reference text.

It addresses the challenge by giving a crew early, explainable health awareness without internet or a ground link. It also protects privacy: administrators see all crew, while each crew member sees only their own data.

This matters because on missions far from Earth, radiation, isolation and altered gravity change each person’s body slowly, and help may be minutes away. The platform runs from one command, uses simulated data (clearly labelled), and has 24 passing automated tests.

This is about 150 words, inside the 50-200 range. If the challenge page uses specific wording, tell me and I’ll mirror it.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

CrewSentiq monitors crew health on long missions and checks each person only against their own history. It stores nine metrics per crew member: heart rate, sleep, activity, hydration, body temperature, radiation dose, cabin CO2, mood and workload. It sets each person’s baseline from their earlier readings.

  • Alerts: it raises a review alert when a metric stays at least 15% off baseline for 3 consecutive readings. It raises a watch alert when the robust z-score, Z = (X - median) / (1.4826 x MAD), reaches |Z| of 3 or more.
  • Condition Atlas: it maps results onto 11 conditions linked to NASA risk modules. Each has five severity stages, a spectrum of states, possible outcomes and NASA reference text.
  • Digital twin: the affected organs light up on an interactive human body.
  • Access: an administrator sees all crew, and a crew account sees only its own data. The server enforces this.

Benefits

  • It works with no internet, cloud or database server, and starts with one command.
  • It judges each person against themselves, which avoids false alarms from population averages.
  • Every alert shows its evidence, formula and NASA source, so it is explainable.
  • It protects each crew member’s data from the others.
  • It includes a filter engine, CSV export and a NASA reference library.

Intended impact

We want crews and mission operators to notice slow, individual health changes early, even when the link to Earth is delayed. Our longer-term aim is a transparent, open tool that analog habitats, research programmes and commercial missions could adopt, and that isolated-work settings on Earth could use too. Real impact would need real sensor data and clinical validation, which we have not done yet.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG
  • Backend: FastAPI and uvicorn
  • Database: local JSON files
  • Frontend: vanilla JavaScript with hand-built SVG charts, no build tools
  • Testing: pytest (24 tests, all passing)
  • Hardware: an ordinary laptop or desktop; no special sensors for the demo
  • Software: Python 3.9 or newer and a web browser
  • Data: NASA Human Research Program hazard, risk and metric datasets

How it is creative

  • Within-person approach: it asks “is this normal for THEM?” instead of using population ranges.
  • Digital twin: it turns slow numerical drift into a visible picture of the affected organs and stage, which a non-specialist can follow.
  • Spectrum view: it shows the whole range from baseline to a possible medical event, not just a single alert.
  • Single-folder design: one process serves the whole app and plain JSON files act as the database, which makes it unusually simple to install and inspect.

Factors our team considered

  • Offline use: deep-space links are slow or absent.
  • Privacy: access control is enforced on the server, not just hidden in the interface.
  • Data honesty: all measurements are simulated and labelled as such, since NASA files describe what to measure and contain no real crew records.
  • Safety: thresholds are screening aids, not clinical cut-offs, and the app says it does not diagnose.
  • Explainability: every alert traces back to its readings and rule.
  • Reviewer experience: judges can install, run and test it in minutes without a team present.
  • Honest scope: three conditions are reference-only because no sensor feed exists, and the next steps are real sensor adapters, a SQL database, TLS and clinical validation.

projectDetails.name: Project CrewSync
projectDetails.summary:
SYMBIOSIS X lets an astronaut check their own health during a mission. We built it inside a small
playable mission so we could test it under pressure instead of on an empty form.
The astronaut enters a reading, for example resting heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature,
sleep, mood or symptoms. We compare it with two things and keep them separate: the astronaut's own
normal values, and a published range for people on Earth. The result says why it was flagged. If we
don't know how a reading was taken, we say "unknown" rather than "normal".
Readings taken the same way build a trend. When a reading falls outside the astronaut's own range, the
next step becomes "measure again and talk to the crew medical officer". Chest-pain and collapse drills
are handled by the crew on board, without waiting for Earth. NASA's Human Research Program names
distance from Earth as one of the five main hazards of spaceflight, and that is the problem we designed
around. Flight surgeons on Earth get a short case status after a simulated 300-second delay. The
readings and private notes stay with the crew.
projectDetails.details:
There are two parts that share one mission clock. The health tool is where an astronaut measures and reviews their health. Flight is the game: four fictional astronauts launch on the ship Horizon, dock with the ISS and come back to Earth. Along the way the CO2 scrubber fails, a wristband gives a bad reading, two crew go on a spacewalk and Mara runs a chest-pain drill. Working features Seven health readings, each with its unit (bpm, mmHg, mg/dL, °C, minutes, mood from 1 to 5, a list of symptoms) and a short note on how to measure it and which device to use. Two checks on every reading: one against the astronaut's personal baseline, one against an Earth range from MedlinePlus, the American Heart Association or the American Diabetes Association. The Earth range is only used when the measuring method matches, so lab glucose limits are not applied to a finger-stick meter. Each result names the rule and source it used. Trends from comparable readings only. Three resting heart rates at least 20 bpm above baseline open a review, and the review lists the readings that caused it. A reminder schedule for each reading. An out-of-range result moves the reminder to "repeat and review with the crew medical officer". Chest-pain and collapse drills that work during a communication blackout. The case names who responds on board and lists short training steps. An open emergency comes before routine reminders. A Ground view that arrives 300 mission seconds late and shows only a case ID, priority and status, plus when it was observed, when it arrived and how old it is. Heart rate, wearable data, check-in notes and medical history are never sent. A ship twin: cabin CO2 goes up when the scrubber fails and down after the repair, and the astronaut who was exposed gets flagged. A body figure for each astronaut with anatomy, skeleton, muscle, heart and lung, sensor and suit layers. Clicking it shows which sensor took which reading and how old the sample is. A check on wearable data. A wristband sample spoiled by movement is held back, a crewmate takes the reading again, and the new one is accepted.

How it works A Python and FastAPI service runs the mission clock and the health rules, and stores everything in SQLite. Each run can be read in two ways. The crew view has the full private record. The Ground view is built from a fixed list of fields that are allowed to leave the ship. The React app and the Flight game both read from these views. Runs use a fixed seed (4242), so a mission plays out the same way each time. How we tested it We generated a 30-day made-up mission with 960 scheduled readings and hid problems in it: abnormal values, slow drifts, sensor errors, late and duplicate packets, missed readings and emergencies. The tool caught all 78 of the hidden events. On 20 clean crew-days it raised no false review, and it never showed a missing reading as normal. Our automated tests also pass from a clean checkout: 120 backend unit tests, 74 integration tests, 56 browser tests, and one privacy test that checks nothing private reaches Ground. Who it helps The astronaut gets a quick check with a reason they can read. The crew member who responds to an emergency gets a case they can act on without waiting for Earth. Flight surgeons get data that tells them how old it is, without private details they don't need. Limitations All astronauts and readings are fictional. We did not use any real health records. The personal ranges, the review rule, the 3,200 ppm CO2 limit and the 300-second delay are our demo choices. They are not clinical limits or NASA limits. The emergency steps are training placeholders based on American Red Cross first-aid pages. They are not approved medical procedures. The tool says when to measure again and when to bring in the crew medical officer or Ground. It does not suggest treatment. The 30-second demo and parts of the Flight game are scripted playback. The health tool itself runs live through the API. Future plans Connect real devices: a wrist sensor, a blood pressure cuff and a glucose meter. Add NASA's general countermeasure advice from the HRP risk pages, such as exercise, sleep timing and lighting. Ask flight surgeons to review our review rules and emergency steps. Tools and languages Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite and pytest. Frontend: JavaScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS and HTML canvas. Browser tests: Playwright. We did not use hardware; the sensors are simulated.

projectDetails.summary:
Earth Listens is an accessible interactive platform that transforms real-world Earth science data into music, allowing people to experience and understand our planet through sound.

By converting environmental measurements such as temperature, atmospheric CO₂ levels, Arctic sea ice changes, and wildfire activity into musical patterns, the project makes complex scientific information easier to explore and understand.

The platform is designed with accessibility in mind, particularly for blind and visually impaired users.
projectDetails.details:
Problem

Scientific information about Earth's environmental changes is often presented through complex charts, maps, and visualizations. This creates accessibility barriers, especially for people who are blind or have low vision.

Solution

Earth Listens transforms environmental data into sound and music, creating an alternative way to experience Earth's changing conditions.

How It Works

1. Collect environmental datasets from scientific sources.

2. Process and normalize the measurements.

3. Convert data patterns into musical elements using sonification.

4. Allow users to explore environmental information through an interactive globe.

5. Provide audio descriptions, captions, and accessible interactions.

Expected Impact

- Make Earth science more accessible.

- Help users understand environmental changes through sound.

- Support inclusive scientific education.

- Introduce an innovative way to communicate climate and environmental data.

projectDetails.name: Project CTRL + SPACE
projectDetails.summary: CTRL+SPACE is a mobile-first research platform that makes NASA research on fire and combustion in microgravity easier to explore and understand. It addresses the challenge of improving fire safety in spacecraft by organizing scientific reports, experiment data, and verified research findings in one accessible place. Users can search NASA reports, explore experiments, compare documented results, and use an AI-assisted research feature that provides answers grounded in scientific sources with citations when an AI provider is available. The platform currently organizes 10 research reports, 87 verified passages, and 10 experiments. By making complex research easier to access and trace back to its original sources, CTRL+SPACE helps students and researchers better understand the science needed for safer future space missions.
projectDetails.details:
CTRL+SPACE is a mobile-first research platform designed to help students and researchers explore NASA studies about fire and combustion in microgravity. It addresses the challenge of understanding how fire behaves in spacecraft and how scientific research can contribute to safer space missions.

The platform brings together NASA research reports, verified scientific passages, and structured experiment information in one place. Users can search for research, explore report details, read evidence linked to its original source, and compare documented experiments. The project covers three important areas of spacecraft fire safety: fire prevention, smoke detection, and flame suppression.

One of its main features is an evidence-grounded AI research assistant. It uses BM25 search to retrieve relevant passages from verified NASA reports. When an AI provider is configured, it can generate answers based on the retrieved evidence and provide citations. The system is designed to avoid unsupported answers and identify information that is missing or not reported. Without an AI provider, users can still search and explore the scientific evidence in retrieval-only mode.

Other features include an experiment explorer, side-by-side experiment comparison, a research library, saved collections, personal notes, learning lessons, quizzes, and community discussions. The interface supports English and Arabic, including right-to-left layout, and provides offline access to previously downloaded research.

The platform was developed using Python 3 and Flask for the backend, SQLite for database management, and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES Modules for the frontend. It uses BM25 for research retrieval, a configurable integration with AI providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama, and Playwright for browser testing. The mobile experience is implemented as a dedicated Progressive Web App (PWA), with Capacitor packaging prepared for Android and iOS. No specialized physical hardware is required.

Our creative approach is combining scientific research discovery, evidence verification, experiment comparison, and AI-assisted explanations in one accessible mobile experience. We considered scientific accuracy, source traceability, missing data, usability on different screen sizes, bilingual accessibility, and offline availability throughout development.

The intended impact is to make complex microgravity combustion research easier to access and understand, helping students and researchers explore the science behind spacecraft fire safety. Future development will focus on expanding the verified research collection, extracting more information from scientific figures and tables, improving AI-assisted search, and completing further native mobile deployment and testing.

CTRL+SPACE is an independent student-developed project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

FlameLens is a scientific data exploration and visualization platform designed to make NASA's spacecraft fire research more accessible, understandable, and interactive. The project focuses on organizing and analyzing microgravity combustion experiment data, helping researchers, students, and engineers explore experimental conditions, materials, sensor measurements, and visual observations through a unified dashboard.

Built using Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, and Plotly, FlameLens provides tools for exploring experiments, visualizing telemetry, comparing samples, and identifying data quality issues. A key feature of the platform is scientific traceability: every measurement and visualization should remain connected to its original source, with clear units and documented limitations.

By transforming scattered scientific information into an organized and interactive research environment, FlameLens aims to support a better understanding of fire behavior in microgravity and contribute to safer future human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
# FlameLens — Phase 1 Project Audit

**Audit date:** 14 November 2026  

**Inspected scope:** `/mnt/data` (the only directory containing supplied project materials). The execution shell's initial current directory was `/`; no separate FlameLens repository or science-data directory was supplied.  

**Audit rule:** no local experiment identity, measurement, unit, image observation, or record count is inferred from the research brief.

## Executive result

The supplied workspace contains **2 top-level files**: one Markdown master prompt and one 28-page Word research brief/master prompt. The Word document contains **7 tables**, **722 non-empty paragraphs**, and **3 embedded PNG conceptual diagrams**. Its Office Open XML package contains **22 members**. No CSV, TSV, Excel workbook, scientific binary, source image sequence, video, raw telemetry file, or research-data archive was supplied.

**Phase 1 status: complete for the supplied attachments; project data audit blocked by missing science files.** The documents establish project intent and background context, not the user's local dataset. In accordance with the uploaded master prompt, full dashboard implementation is not started because the experiment identity and available data structure cannot yet be resolved.

## 1. Project root inspected

- Working directory at inspection: `/` (container shell).

- Supplied project-material directory audited: `/mnt/data`.

- At inspection start, `/mnt/data` contained only `FlameLens_Master_Prompt.md` and `FlameLens_Research_and_Master_Prompt.docx`.

- No existing `FlameLens/` source tree (`app.py`, `pages/`, `src/`, etc.) was present in the supplied material directory.

## 2. Complete file inventory summary

| Type | Count |

|---|---:|

| Markdown specifications | 1 |

| Word research/specification documents | 1 |

| Actual local CSV/TSV/Excel datasets | 0 |

| Actual telemetry / scientific binary datasets | 0 |

| Standalone experiment image/video files | 0 |

| User-supplied research ZIP/TAR archives | 0 |

| Embedded DOCX PNG diagrams | 3 |

The full inventory contains 24 rows: two supplied files plus all 22 DOCX package members. Each row includes the relevant path, size, SHA-256 and inspection status. See `file_inventory.csv`.

## 3. Discovered investigations and identity confidence

| Identifier | What the supplied material supports | Local dataset confidence |

|---|---|---|

| NASA PSI-98 / SAFFIRE-I | The project brief states this is the NASA PSI accession for SAFFIRE-I (DOI `10.60555/0t15-1z43`). NASA's current PSI page search result also labels PSI-98 as Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I and reports Version 4, updated 3 June 2025. | **Not established locally.** Mentioned in project documentation; no matching local science files. |

| NASA PSI-117 | The brief warns this is not SAFFIRE-I. NASA's 2 March 2026 article associates PSI-117 with a cool-flame research project leveraging historic FLEX data and says the research data would be available in PSI-117. | **Not established locally.** No PSI-117 data file or accession metadata package supplied. |

| FLEX | Appears as historical source context for the cool-flame research mentioned with PSI-117. | **Not established locally.** |

**No experiment can be claimed as discovered in the supplied local data.** Do not assign the project to SAFFIRE-I solely because the project brief is about Saffire, and do not interpret a folder/accession string as content evidence.

## 4. Usable datasets

**None supplied.** There are no measurement files, worksheet names, telemetry record counts, variable columns, calibration files, sensor maps, raw image frames, or video assets to load. The 7 tables in the Word document are research/specification tables, not measurement tables. `dataset_dictionary.csv` is intentionally header-only rather than inventing variables or units.

## 5. Verified variables and units

No local measurement variables or units can be verified because no data files were supplied.

The research brief describes expected/documented Saffire-I measurement categories — cameras/flame images, thermocouples, radiometers, pressure, O₂, CO₂, and anemometers/airflow — and the PSI-98 NASA record describes these categories. These are **literature/metadata context only**, not evidence of local channels or their exact column names, calibration, units, sample rate, timestamps, or sensor locations.

Literature/context values mentioned in the supplied brief (such as sample dimensions around 0.94 m × 0.40 m, airflow 20 cm/s, and oxygen around 21.7%) must remain labelled as source-reported context rather than local observations. The brief also flags literature discrepancies (for example 165 W vs 182 W ignition power, and about 400 s vs 420 s burn interval); both claims should be preserved with source-level citations if later displayed.

## 6. Images and video

- **3 embedded PNGs** were found inside the Word document (each 1710 px wide) and visually inspected.

- They depict (1) a conceptual Saffire-I apparatus layout, (2) a conceptual FlameLens evidence-first pipeline, and (3) a conceptual dashboard information architecture. The document explicitly marks these as illustrative, not NASA engineering drawings or original experiment imagery.

- The Word package also contains a `docProps/thumbnail.jpeg` preview; it is not an experiment observation.

- **0 standalone experimental images** and **0 videos** were supplied. No image timestamp, camera assignment, flame spread sequence, pixel measurement or frame-to-telemetry relation can be established.

## 7. Research and documentation inspected

The source register records the materials supplied in the brief and the additional online references checked for this audit. Major sources and roles:

- NASA PSI-98: accession identity, Saffire-I sample, flow and documented instrument categories; current search result shows PSI-98 Version 4 and an update dated 3 June 2025.

- NASA PSI-117 / NASA Science (2 March 2026): identity separation; NASA describes the cool-flame/FLEX research as PSI-117, not Saffire-I.

- NASA Glenn (23 June 2016): Saffire-I mission story; its 40,989 images/data files and >25 Gbit figure is a mission-wide downlink total, not a count of local files.

- NASA Glenn (14 February 2024): Saffire-VI was the final mission of the six-investigation Saffire series and concluded on 9 January 2024.

- NASA NTRS reports 20170000230, 20170001636, 20170008805 and 20180005168: development, design, conditions and selected test results; planned values must remain separate from as-flown values.

- Peer-reviewed papers by Urban et al., Li et al. and Jomaas et al.: scientific interpretation and flame-spread/model context.

- W3C PROV-DM and RO-Crate 1.3: useful standards for traceable processing and portable, machine-readable research metadata.

- TREC 2025 RAG work and 2026 CiteGuard-RAG: support hybrid retrieval, query decomposition, sentence-level citations, verification and abstention as potential future AI-assistant design patterns; these are not validated specifically on Saffire data.

## 8. Data-quality issues, limitations and contradictions

1. **Missing source data:** no telemetry, tables, raw images, calibration or source-data archives. Consequently, missingness rates, duplicates, time gaps, record counts, unit conflicts and numeric ranges are not measurable.

2. **Experiment assignment unresolved:** PSI-98 and PSI-117 are both discussed in the documents, but no local files prove which investigation the eventual dataset belongs to.

3. **Source-metadata anomaly to preserve:** NASA PSI-98's current search-result content shows a project title and dates (2001–2008) that do not straightforwardly match the 2016 Saffire-I flight narrative. The version history also shows a PSI-98 record referencing a ZIP named with PSI-166 and Saffire-I. These are metadata/provenance discrepancies to expose, not silently reconcile.

4. **Published-value disagreements:** the brief reports differences in ignition power (165 W / 182 W) and duration (~400 s / 420 s). The relevant source tables/pages must be inspected before choosing or comparing a claim.

5. **DOCX core metadata is not trustworthy as creation provenance:** its core XML lists 2013-12-23 as created and modified despite the document containing a stated 14 November 2026 research baseline. Filesystem modification time is recorded separately and is not treated as experiment time.

6. **Archive checks:** the DOCX package has 22 members; duplicate member names: 0; path traversal flags: 0; nested archives: 0; highest member compression ratio: 32.16. It is a standard Office package, not a source dataset archive.

7. **No app source exists in the supplied directory:** there is no existing codebase to extend or test.

## 9. Feature feasibility

### Can be prepared now (requirements and reference layer only)

- Project identity and research source registry.

- A clear PSI-98 vs PSI-117 identity warning and accession-aware ingestion rules.

- Visual design direction and navigation blueprint described in the supplied brief.

- Audit manifest format, source-citation conventions and provenance model.

- A proposed competitive feature blueprint (see `competitive_feature_blueprint.md`).

### Partially feasible after the actual project folder is provided

- Experiment Explorer, configuration tables and dataset availability map, once file-level identity evidence is available.

- Data Quality reports and variable dictionary, after raw files and documentation/calibration are inspected.

- Source and reference panel, using the verified research register.

### Blocked by missing local data

- Telemetry time series, native time alignment, event annotations and sensor metadata.

- Experimental image/video browser, camera/frame time sync, calibrated image analysis.

- Sample/run comparison and statistical/correlation analysis.

- Real data-quality metrics and row-level provenance.

- AI/RAG grounded in local source documents and experimental tables.

### AI/RAG implementation gate

The uploaded master prompt explicitly schedules the AI assistant after the core data inventory, validation, telemetry charts and image browsing are stable, and says not to add paid model/API dependencies without explicit approval. I have therefore **not** implemented an LLM, embeddings, vector store or generated “AI insights” in this Phase 1 audit. The future design should default to local/on-device inference or an adapter interface, hybrid search, sentence-level citations, validation and refusal when evidence is missing.

## 10. Proposed next stage (non-destructive)

1. Supply the actual FlameLens project folder or the scientific source directory (including original files, archives, READMEs, calibration and sensor documentation).

2. Re-run inventory recursively against that exact root. Inspect archive members before any extraction.

3. Resolve PSI-98 / PSI-117 identity using actual file contents, DOI/accession metadata and scientific descriptions. Keep separate investigations separate.

4. Build the experiment registry and variable dictionary from verified evidence.

5. Only after the audit is scientifically complete, proceed to architecture and the working dashboard.

**No source files were edited, renamed, moved, overwritten, or deleted.** All outputs in this folder are generated audit artifacts.

projectDetails.name: VitalOrbit
projectDetails.summary: VitalOrbit is onboard health-monitoring software for astronauts on a Mars mission. Up to 20 light-minutes from Earth, a question to Mission Control and its answer can take up to 40 minutes, so the crew must be its own first responder. VitalOrbit learns each astronaut's personal normal from real wearable heart rate, activity and sleep data, using one machine-learning model per person. It raises an alert only when a problem persists, escalates it and asks the astronaut how they feel. An offline assistant then guides first aid step by step, checking every medicine against the onboard pharmacy and its radiation-shortened expiry. The app also projects NASA's long-mission risks (radiation, bone and muscle loss, eye problems, mental health and cabin CO2) to mission end. Case reports reach the flight surgeon with the real light-time delay applied. In testing it caught 12 of 12 simulated emergencies, with a median of 45 minutes to the first alert and no false critical alarms. Early detection matters because far from Earth, small problems must be caught before they become emergencies.
projectDetails.details: VitalOrbit is onboard health-monitoring software for astronauts on a Mars mission. It addresses the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". On the International Space Station, doctors at Mission Control are seconds away. On Mars, Earth can be up to about 20 light-minutes away (19.1 minutes in our modelled mission), so a question and its answer take about 38 minutes, and during solar conjunction the link is lost for about two weeks. The crew has to be its own first responder. VitalOrbit does four jobs that normally sit with doctors on the ground: It watches. A personal machine-learning model for each astronaut learns that person's own normal heart rate, activity and sleep from real wearable data. It flags readings that are abnormal for that person, not for an average person. It escalates and asks. An alert opens only when a problem persists (30 min, 90 min, 3 h), and the app asks the astronaut how they feel. "I was exercising" closes the alert, and "I don't feel well" opens help. It guides. An offline assistant gives step-by-step first-aid protocols with timers. It checks every suggested medicine against the onboard pharmacy and its radiation-shortened expiry, and it keeps working with no internet and no AI model. It remembers. It projects slow long-mission risks to mission end: radiation dose, bone and muscle loss, eye problems (SANS), mental health and cabin CO2, following NASA's five RIDGE hazards. It sends structured case reports to the flight surgeon with the real light-time delay applied. This matters because on a deep-space mission the window in which a problem is still cheap to fix is short. In our evaluation the system detected 12 of 12 injected emergencies, with a median of 45 minutes to the first alert, no false critical alerts and 0.08 false warnings per crew-day. The same idea applies on Earth wherever the doctor is far away: Antarctic stations, submarines and remote clinics.

projectDetails.name: Cycle
projectDetails.summary: Cycle is a working web platform that connects two things the plastic problem keeps apart: the plastic on the ground and the satellite evidence about the place it sits in. People photograph, classify and post recyclable plastic; verified recyclers and plants publish the material they need; the platform matches the two, records the hand-off and turns every collection into an environmental figure. Alongside it, an Earth Intelligence Engine reads open NASA MODIS data for seven Egyptian zones and any coordinate on Earth, and reports vegetation, surface-temperature and land-cover trends with quality flags, sample counts and 95% confidence intervals, stating openly when a record is too short to support a conclusion. Each zone ends in a plain-language change story and a recommended local action. For the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective" challenge this matters because a trend is only useful if someone can act on it: Cycle turns a defensible satellite signal into a decision about material that is physically there. The platform is live and fully functional; the listings and impact figures currently on it are demonstration data.
projectDetails.details: What Cycle does. Cycle is a working web platform with two connected layers. The community layer turns recyclable plastic into a published, searchable listing and matches it with industrial demand. The Earth layer is an Earth Intelligence Engine that reads open NASA satellite products for an area, separates a real trend from year-to-year noise, states how confident it is, and translates the result into a local action. The two layers meet on the same zone page, which is the core idea: a satellite trend gets a physical counterpart, and a material flow gets environmental context. How it works, main task A — try this one. Open https://cycle-studio.ai.studio, go to Plastic Reports and filter by polymer and status to see posted material. Then open Organization Needs: each open requirement shows how many published reports match it and the best match score. Open the requirement, compare the matching listing, and the hand-off is recorded as collected. Every completed hand-off is converted on impactMetrics into weight diverted, CO₂e avoided, landfill volume avoided and energy conserved. A person reporting plastic goes through Report Plastic Waste: photo, polymer, estimated weight, location. How it works, main task B. Open Earth Intelligence and choose one of seven Egyptian case-study zones, or type any latitude and longitude. The engine retrieves the matching MODIS products for that area and shows four indicator cards: vegetation index, day and night land-surface temperature, land-cover class, and local Cycle supply. The map tab compares NASA GIBS imagery for a chosen date with Cycle pins on top. Vegetation Trends gives the NDVI and EVI slope per year, its 95% confidence interval, the baseline anomaly and how many composites passed the quality filter, with a standard and a strict filter. Thermal and Land Cover shows day and night temperature curves and land-cover composition. The Change Story tab explains the result in plain language and recommends an action; the export panel produces a GeoTIFF or NetCDF4 request through AppEEARS. Benefits. Households and small businesses get a direct route for sorted plastic. Recyclers get a ranked demand board instead of phone calls. Municipalities, journalists and students get a defensible reading of vegetation, heat and land-cover change for a district, with the caveats printed next to the numbers. Researchers get quality-filtered data they can export and repeat. Goals. Near term, prove a repeatable loop in one district: material collected, matched and counted, alongside a satellite record that shows the context. Medium term, onboard verified organizations with an audit trail and let municipalities use the zone page in planning. Long term, a decision layer where a visible environmental trend and the material flow that feeds it are read together, in any city, on open data. Tools, languages and hardware. HTML, CSS and JavaScript single-page application with client-side routing and a full Arabic/English right-to-left interface; Leaflet with NASA GIBS WMTS tiles and OpenStreetMap base data; charting for the vegetation and temperature time series; NASA AppEEARS for product subsetting; MODIS MOD13Q1, MOD11A2 and MCD12Q1 (Collection 6.1) as the measurements; Git and GitHub for version control; Google AI Studio for deployment and hosting; FFmpeg for assembling the demo video. Hardware: ordinary laptops. No sensors, no field equipment and no paid data subscriptions. What works now. Reporting, listing, search and filtering; organization demand publishing; matching with match score; collection status; impact accounting; individual and organization accounts; the bilingual interface; and the whole Earth Intelligence layer — seven zones, global coordinate query, four indicator cards, GIBS map explorer with date and opacity controls, vegetation trends with quality filters, thermal and land-cover analysis, change stories, export panel and a provenance and limits panel. What is not finished. The community layer runs on demonstration data: every listing, organization, need and figure currently displayed is seeded sample data, not a field result. The Egyptian zones carry less than five years of MODIS record, so long-term trends are labelled exploratory and no decadal projection is offered. MCD12Q1 is annual at 500 m, so narrow urban strips can be misclassified as barren; the interface says so next to the percentages. GIBS imagery is a visual aid only and is never used for a quantitative claim. There is no pickup scheduling engine yet, and organization verification is manual, without an automated audit trail. What we plan to add. A verified onboarding flow with an audit trail; pickup scheduling and confirmation inside the application; alerts when a zone slope or anomaly crosses a threshold; one-click PDF and CSV impact statements for municipal partners and sponsors; saved areas beyond the pre-loaded Egyptian zones; and evaluation of further NASA products, such as rainfall or soil moisture, under the same quality-first discipline.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
