projectDetails.name: Project Data Wizards
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Rhythm AI is an interactive web observatory that turns complex NASA–ISRO NISAR radar data into understandable stories about Earth’s changing surface. We developed a scientific processing pipeline and a web application using ten satellite acquisitions over Egypt’s Fayoum Oasis. Animated maps, before-and-after comparisons, time-series charts, six guided story chapters, and an AI guide help users explore seasonal crop growth, harvest patterns, and changes in water and land surfaces. The platform also includes exploratory shoreline-inundation scenarios and explainable next-pass forecasts.

Our project addresses the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge by showing how different radar polarizations reveal vegetation structure and surface conditions, while making these insights accessible to non-specialists. Every layer retains its source and metadata, and the interface clearly separates observations, detected changes, and interpretations.

Earth Rhythm AI matters because understanding agricultural and water-system changes can support better resource management in water-scarce regions. It connects satellite science with local concerns while making uncertainty and limitations visible.
projectDetails.details:
PROJECT DETAILS — EARTH RHYTHM

Listening to the Nile's 120-Day Pulse with NASA-ISRO L-Band Radar

Earth Rhythm is an interactive radar-science observatory and guided story experience built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 ("Dancing with the SARs"). Over 10 consecutive 12-day satellite passes (June 23 – October 21, 2026), it turns raw NASA-ISRO SAR (NISAR) microwave echoes over Egypt's Fayoum Oasis into a living story—helping anyone see how crops grow, how farmers irrigate dry soil, how wind ripples desert lakes, and how shorelines shift before the next flood arrives.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Earth Rhythm Observatory — Chapter 1 Physical Scattering Map and Story Mode" ]

Earth Rhythm Observatory — Chapter 1 Physical Scattering Map and Story Mode

How Does Our Solution Work?

Every 12 days, NISAR flies over Fayoum Oasis (Track 129 / Frame 016, 4,912 km²) and beams 24 cm L-band radio waves down through clouds, dust, and upper leaves. Unlike normal optical satellites that only photograph green leaf color, 24 cm waves penetrate deep into plant stems and wet soil—listening back in two "orientations" (polarizations) at once:

  • HV (Cross-Polarization — The Plant Volume Detector): Horizontally transmitted waves bounce around inside 3D tangles of stems and leaves, twisting back vertically. More canopy volume = brighter HV.
  • HH (Co-Polarization — The Soil Moisture, Plowing & Water Detector): Horizontally transmitted waves bounce straight back off wet soil, plowed furrows, city walls, and wind-rippled water.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Mermaid diagram" ]

Instead of drowning visitors in raw radar noise, Earth Rhythm guides you through Fayoum's 120-day rhythm in six interactive chapters, assisted by Echo (our built-in AI science companion):

  • Chapter 1 — The Desert & The Oasis in Four True Radar Colors: Right outside the 1,934 km² green agricultural oasis lies the hyper-arid Western Desert. Independent NASA POWER weather records show just 0.15 mm of total rain across 133 days (0.00 mm on all 10 satellite passes), proving every drop powering this oasis arrives via the Bahr Youssef Nile canal. Our decoupled color map separates Lush Green (HV crop canopies), Vivid Red (HH urban buildings), Deep Blue to Cyan (calm water to wind ripples), and Warm Sand (bare soil and limestone desert).
  • Chapter 2 — The Summer Growth Wave (June 23 → August 10): Using our Split-Screen Swipe Slider, you watch 763.88 km² (39.5%) of farmland ignite in HV brightness as summer maize, sorghum, and cotton thicken. At our eastern oasis checkpoint (Sennuris / Tamia), HV climbs +10.77 dB, tracking independent Sentinel-2 optical greenness (NDVI) with a strong correlation of r=0.93r = 0.93r=0.93.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Split-Screen Swipe Comparison and Linear-Power Calibration Tables" ]

Split-Screen Swipe Comparison and Linear-Power Calibration Tables

  • Chapter 3 — Harvest Meets Autumn Emergence (August 10 → October 21): Basin-wide averages barely budge (2.05 dB), hiding an intense seasonal handoff: 594.83 km² of summer crops are harvested (-HV) right next to 174.17 km² of newly planted autumn fields (+HV) rising steadily across eight straight passes (+11.54 dB). Even better, when tiny winter seedlings sprout in late October, optical NDVI rebounds to 0.661 while 24 cm radar HV stays quiet (-19.89 dB)—because thin blades are smaller than the wavelength (Rayleigh-transparent) until woody stems develop.
  • Chapter 4 — The Plot Twist: When HH and HV Disagree: Across 440.7 km² of farmland, HH and HV tell completely different stories. At our southeastern farmland spot, HV drops -2.60 dB after harvest while HH jumps +8.24 dB from deep chisel plowing and immediate flood irrigation. A single-channel radar would mistake that wet bare dirt for sudden crop growth; dual-polarization catches both events in our 7-Class Regime Map. Meanwhile, southern drainage basins swing 12.35 dB in HH as smooth mirror-like standing water drains into rough wet mudflats.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"What Changed Map, 10-Date Time Series Chart, Sentinel-2 Cross-Check, and Rain-Free Weather Strip" ]

What Changed Map, 10-Date Time Series Chart, Sentinel-2 Cross-Check, and Rain-Free Weather Strip

  • Chapter 5 — Wind Ripples on Lake Qarun & Rescuing El-Qarn Island: Over Lake Qarun, HV stays pinned near the sensor noise floor (~ -24.9 dB), while HH swings by 11.17 dB whenever 2–5 m/s winds stir tiny capillary Bragg waves across the water. By combining 10 backscatter passes with 9 interferometric coherence pairs (γ\gammaγ) and wind-variability checks, Earth Rhythm maps 310.18 km² of pure open water (IoU = 0.9243, 99.19% precision against NASA's optical OPERA DSWx-HLS water benchmark) without erasing +43 m-tall El-Qarn Island (99.2% preserved).

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Overview Basin Dashboard Showing Seasonal Growth vs. Harvest Balance" ]

Overview Basin Dashboard Showing Seasonal Growth vs. Harvest Balance

  • Chapter 6 — Honest Noise Rulers & The 12-Day Forecast (November 2, 2026): Before trusting any pixel change, we measure 218,705 unchanging limestone desert pixels (349.93 km²) as a natural calibration ruler and filter speckles strictly in physical power before converting to decibels. We also inspect exploratory 12-day interferograms (L2_GUNW)—and honestly refuse to claim ground sinking because natural atmospheric water-vapor ramps (8.80–18.78 mm) outweigh 12-day ground compaction (< 0.5 mm). Finally, our Explainable Forecaster projects next-pass (November 2) flood risk, crop regimes, and drainage surge impacts across Lake Qarun's closed basin.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Explainable Flood Risk Forecast Map and Drainage Surge Simulator" ]

Explainable Flood Risk Forecast Map and Drainage Surge Simulator

The Math Behind the Scenes (Light & Honest)

  • Energy-Conserving Speckle Smoothing: Radar echoes contain salt-and-pepper speckle. Converting pixels to decibels before averaging computes a geometric mean instead of an arithmetic mean (log⁡10P‾<log⁡10Pˉ\overline{\log_{10} P} < \log_{10} \bar{P}log10​P​<log10​Pˉ, Jensen's inequality), creating a fake -0.5 to -2.5 dB dark bias. We aggregate 10 m pixels 4×4 to 40 m and apply a 3×3 Adaptive Lee filter strictly in linear power (γ0\gamma^0γ0, m2/m2\text{m}^2/\text{m}^2m2/m2)—boosting the Equivalent Number of Looks (ENL=μ2/σ2\text{ENL} = \mu^2 / \sigma^2ENL=μ2/σ2) from 4.9 to 153–481 while preserving true mean power within 0.08%—before converting to decibels: γdB0=10log⁡10(γ0),ΔdB=10log⁡10 ⁣(PafterPbefore)\gamma^0_{\text{dB}} = 10 \log_{10}(\gamma^0), \qquad \Delta\text{dB} = 10 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_{\text{after}}}{P_{\text{before}}}\right)γdB0​=10log10​(γ0),ΔdB=10log10​(Pbefore​Pafter​​)
  • Desert-Locked Change Thresholds: Over 1.97 million stable desert pixel-pairs, we set each channel's change cutoff τ\tauτ as the conservative maximum of theoretical speckle noise (3σspeckle3\sigma_{\text{speckle}}3σspeckle​), robust desert spread (3σMAD3\sigma_{\text{MAD}}3σMAD​), and the empirical 99th percentile (P99P_{99}P99​): τHH=2.73 dB,τHV=2.03 dB\tau_{\text{HH}} = 2.73\text{ dB}, \qquad \tau_{\text{HV}} = 2.03\text{ dB}τHH​=2.73 dB,τHV​=2.03 dB Any smaller shift is treated as background noise rather than surface change.
  • Exploratory Interferometry Guard: Unwrapped radar phase (Δϕ\Delta\phiΔϕ) converts to apparent line-of-sight range via ΔdLOS=−λ4πΔϕ\Delta d_{\text{LOS}} = -\frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\Delta\phiΔdLOS​=−4πλ​Δϕ (λ≈24 cm\lambda \approx 24\text{ cm}λ≈24 cm), strictly masking out unstable targets with coherence γ<0.50\gamma < 0.50γ<0.50.
  • Explainable Flood & Next-Pass Forecasting: Four transparent physical signals—HH dielectric water index (38%), 12-day phase instability 1−γ1-\gamma1−γ (24%), 3-pass wetting velocity (22%), and NISAR_DEM shoreline proximity (16%)—combine with a damped trend backscatter model. Hid Pass 10 (Oct 21) and predicted it strictly from Passes 1–9: ROC-AUC = 0.9998 (full basin) / 0.9976 (1.5 km shoreline), shoreline IoU = 0.8871, HH RMSE = 1.03 dB, and HV RMSE = 0.95 dB, feeding a hydraulically connected Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) surge simulator (15,434 ha baseline to 24,815 ha at +1.0 m).

What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Unmasks Hidden Agricultural Signals: Separates true crop biomass growth from bare-soil flood irrigation (440.7 km² of divergence) where optical cameras or single-channel radar mislead.
  • Works in Any Weather & Lighting: 24 cm radar penetrates clouds, dust, and upper leaves on a guaranteed 12-day cadence.
  • Speaks Human & Scientist Fluently: Plain-language summaries, interactive dashboards, a 3-minute reading guide, and Echo AI help students and policymakers understand every map—while GIS experts can inspect exact dB ribbons, 11 provenance fields, and download calibrated Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs.
  • Lightweight on Bandwidth & Hardware: Selective cloud range-streaming trims 657+ GB of satellite scenes down to 455 MB locally (99.93% reduction) with zero loss of native calibration.
  • Honest by Design: Every finding separates what was Observed, what Changed above noise, and what is an Interpretation (hypothesis)—never disguising weather noise or assumptions as certainty.

What Is the Intended Impact?

Because Bahr Youssef Nile canal water drives 100% of Fayoum's irrigation (0.15 mm total summer rainfall), Earth Rhythm turns NISAR's 12-day cadence into a practical blueprint for arid river basins worldwide:

  1. Canal-Scale Irrigation Auditing: Spotting bare-soil wetting and flood ponding across irrigation districts so water ministries can catch tail-end canal shortages early.
  2. All-Weather Crop & Phenology Monitoring: Pairing L-band stem structure (HV) with optical leaf greenness (NDVI) to track staggered planting and harvesting across millions of smallholder plots.
  3. Closed-Basin Lake & Shoreline Early Warning: Tracking Lake Qarun and Wadi El Rayan margins (165.85 km² dynamic zone) and quantifying cropland (313–659 ha) and road corridors exposed during drainage surges.
  4. Preventing Radar Misinterpretation: Teaching communities and analysts why single-pair InSAR phase ramps are mostly atmospheric moisture rather than sinking land until 20–30+ passes accumulate.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Coding Languages: Python (scientific radar processing, statistical analysis, and data serving) and TypeScript / HTML / CSS (interactive browser observatory).
  • Scientific & Mapping Software: NASA Earthdata / ASF discovery tools, HDF5 multidimensional cube tools, GDAL / PROJ geospatial raster & Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF tooling, NumPy & SciPy vectorized math, React & MapLibre GL JS dual-canvas interactive web mapping, and hand-crafted SVG charts.
  • Datasets & AI Companions: NASA-ISRO NISAR (L2_GCOV & L2_GUNW), NASA OPERA DSWx-HLS, NISAR_WATERMASK & NISAR_DEM, NASA POWER daily weather, ESA Sentinel-2 L2A optical NDVI, and multi-provider Echo AI support (Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Mistral, and local Ollama).
  • Deployment & QA: Docker containerization, Hugging Face Spaces serverless static hosting, automated scientific invariant verification (11 physical & metadata checks), and manual end-to-end UI verification.
  • Hardware: Engineered deliberately to run on a standard consumer workstation / laptop (verified on a 64-bit Windows 11, 12-core Intel CPU machine with no GPU or compute cluster required), made possible by selective cloud range-streaming.

How Is Our Project Creative?

  • Streaming the Needle, Not the Haystack: Reading internal satellite chunk maps over HTTPS shrinks 657+ GB down to 455 MB so everyday laptops can work directly with NASA's flagship L-band data.
  • Turning the Sahara into a Calibration Lab: Instead of guessing a change cutoff, we let 350 km² of lifeless desert define our exact statistical noise bar (2.73 dB HH, 2.03 dB HV).
  • Breaking the "Purple Radar" Curse: Traditional HH / HV / HH-HV composites paint both windy lakes and dry dirt purple; our Decoupled Physical Composite gives plants, concrete cities, calm/windy water, and bare soil distinct, intuitive colors.
  • Saving a Forgotten Island with Pure Radar Physics: Standard hole-filling flooded +43 m-tall El-Qarn Island inside Lake Qarun (100% false water); stacking 9 interferometric coherence maps and wave-roughness checks cut false island water down to 0.80% using radar alone.
  • A Storyteller That Refuses to Hallucinate: Pairing a 6-chapter guided tour and Echo AI with hard scientific truth labels (Observation vs. Change vs. Hypothesis), plus a compressed client-side cube so live pixel clicks work even without a backend server.

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

  • Strict Scientific Honesty: Keeping linear-power math separate from decibels, masking low-signal desert dunes near the -24.5 dB sensor noise floor, treating wind waves as a confounder rather than land change, and refusing to overclaim subsidence from 12-day atmospheric phase noise.
  • Version & Geometry Consistency: Never mixing early BETA granules with calibrated PROVISIONAL (CRID P05023) passes, and locking every comparison to identical Track 129, Frame 016, and Ascending orbit geometry so viewing angles never masquerade as physical change.
  • No Fabricated Data & Independent Cross-Checks: Zero simulated pixels in the product, strict separation between primary NISAR measurements and external optical/weather context, explicit Pass 10 temporal holdout backtesting (seed = 42), and strict error reporting if an Echo AI key is missing.
  • Human-Centered Accessibility & Bandwidth: Progressive disclosure (5 clean tabs, plain-English readouts, minimizable legends, and downloadable COGs) paired with 30× cloud payload compression (255.6 MB → 9.46 MB) so anyone—on any connection—can explore the story in under 3 minutes.

projectDetails.name: Twin Sands: Finding the Moon and Mars on Earth
projectDetails.summary:
Twin Sands will take you, with all your senses, on a journey to Mars, the Moon, and the places on Earth that secretly look just like them, with a little hanging rover as your guide the whole way. You'll walk through red dust, hear the real winds recorded by NASA's Perseverance rover, smell the rust and the burnt powder of the Moon, and feel what the ground is like under your boots.

On the way, you discover that pieces of Mars and the Moon are already hiding on Earth: deserts, craters and icy lands that are their twins.

Watch Earth's land squeeze into a ball the size of Mars. Follow trails of air, soil and water across all three worlds. Walk real 3D terrain of Gale Crater, Jezero and Olympus Mons with a talking rover, or the Moon's south pole and highlands with an astronaut by your side.

Then meet each twin. We compared every Moon and Mars site with Earth locations around the world using real data from NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA: terrain, temperature, ground heat and minerals. Each pair gets a Twin Score that shows how alike they are, which helps choose where to train astronauts and test rovers.

And we went out ourselves, to find Mars right here in Egypt's deserts and shared our trips!
projectDetails.details:
From a squeezing Earth to a dust storm on Mars to a footprint on the Moon, Twin Sands is a five-stop journey, with a little hanging rover as your guide!

It is a journey in five stops:

  • Meet Mars: watch all of Earth's land squeeze into a ball almost exactly the size of Mars, then meet its two tiny moons circling around it.
  • Twin Trails: Rust, Soil, Water, Dust and the Moon's South Pole. For each one, you first SEE a story about Mars and the Moon, told in our own voices. Then you HEAR real sounds (Perseverance's microphone on Mars, silence on the airless Moon), SMELL what each world would smell like, and FEEL how hot, cold or dry it is. Each trail ends with Earth, Mars and the Moon side by side on matching maps with one colour scale, so anyone can compare them at a glance.
  • Explore: walk real 3D terrain built from elevation data, at Gale Crater, Jezero Crater (inside a khamaseen dust storm) and Olympus Mons (with a then-and-now eruption slider) on Mars, and at Shackleton, Malapert and the lunar highlands on the Moon. A talking rover on Mars, or an astronaut leaving bootprints on the Moon, walks with you and explains what you're seeing.
  • Twin Score: pick a Moon or Mars site and meet its closest Earth twin, with real photos, height maps, a side-view profile, and every number behind the match.
  • Boots on the Ground: our own trips to the deserts of Egypt and Saudi Arabia, where Mars is right here on Earth.

HOW IT WORKS

Twin Trails: real maps, real sounds

Each trail is built from real data, shown on the same colour scale for all three worlds so they can be compared directly:

  • Rust: iron-rich ground on Mars and the Moon (NASA Mars Trek and Moon Trek, Clementine iron map) next to Earth's red deserts.
  • Soil: how much the ground heats and cools between day and night. Earth uses JAXA GCOM-C land temperature (day and night), Mars uses TES thermal inertia (NASA PDS), the Moon uses LRO Diviner.
  • Water: where water hides. Mars Odyssey's water map (NASA PDS), Lunar Prospector hydrogen on the Moon, and ESA CCI permafrost on Earth, plus a CSA RADARSAT-1 radar image of Haughton Crater taken in the dark of polar night.
  • Dust: Earth's dust from NASA MERRA-2 (via GIBS) next to the Mars dust cover map.
  • South Pole: LRO maps of the Moon's south pole, where sunlight and shadow decide where a base can go.

The sounds are real recordings: Perseverance's microphone on Mars, and field recordings on Earth. The Moon stays silent on purpose, because there is no air to carry sound.

Explore: walking on real ground

The three Mars walks (Gale, Jezero, Olympus Mons) and the three Moon walks (Shackleton, Malapert, the highlands) are built from real elevation models: MRO CTX and MOLA/HRSC on Mars, LRO LOLA on the Moon. The ground under your feet is the real shape of the place, and a 120 km backdrop of real terrain fills the horizon. The rover is NASA's Perseverance 3D model and speaks with the browser's voice. Each walk has its own weather and ground: layered rocks at Gale, a khamaseen dust storm at Jezero (the rover wears storm gear), and lava fields with a then-and-now eruption slider at Olympus Mons. On the Moon, the astronaut leaves bootprints and talks over radio "beeps", like Apollo.

Twin Score: finding the twins

For each site we read a 12 km window of real measurements: height and roughness (Copernicus DEM on Earth, CTX on Mars, LOLA on the Moon), slope, surface temperature and its day-to-night swing, thermal inertia (how fast the ground heats and cools), brightness and minerals. Each feature becomes a percentile so three different worlds can be compared fairly, and the Twin Score is the average closeness across seven features. It is a transparent ranking, not a black box: the site shows which features match and which don't, and never pretends a match where data is missing. We checked our ranking against real NASA analog test sites such as Haughton Crater, the Atacama Desert and Mauna Kea.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Astronauts and rovers are trained and tested on Earth before they fly, and choosing the right analog site saves money, time and risk. Twin Sands makes that choice open, repeatable and easy to understand.

It is also for everyone. Anyone, with no science background, can learn what Mars and the Moon are really like and how much they have in common with our own planet: the same red dust, the same cold deserts, the same frozen ground. Seeing a piece of Mars in a desert you can drive to truly opens people's minds. Space stops feeling far away, and becomes something you can understand, feel and even visit. That matters most in places like Egypt and Saudi Arabia, where Mars-like land is right next door, and where we hope the next generation of space explorers will start their journey.

TOOLS

  • Website: React, TypeScript, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber (3D terrain and models), Framer Motion (animation), Web Audio API (live sound design), Web Speech API (rover voice).
  • Data pipeline: Python with rasterio, NumPy and Pillow, reading data from NASA, ESA, CSA, JAXA and USGS.

WHY IT'S CREATIVE

Most data sites ask you to read charts. Twin Sands asks you to travel. We used very little text and a lot of visuals, sound and movement, so the data is something you experience, not just read. Every planet has its own voice, sounds, ground and weather, and every comparison is backed by real measurements.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Honesty: a twin that matches in temperature but not in height is labelled that way; the site does not pick safe landing or habitat sites.
  • Fair comparison: the same 12 km window and the same scales for all three worlds.
  • Accessibility: simple words, big visuals, and it works in any modern browser with no install.
  • Using as many challenge resources as possible: 10 of the 11 listed, including NASA PDS, LRO, Earthdata, GIBS, CSA RADARSAT-1, ESA Copernicus and Open Science Catalog, and JAXA G-Portal.

DATA SOURCES

Real data from four space agencies powers every part of Twin Sands.

NASA → the heart of the project. Through NASA's Planetary Data System, we used LRO Diviner temperatures for every Moon site, TES thermal inertia for Mars, and Mars Odyssey's water map, which shows where water hides under the Martian ground. LRO's LOLA heights and LROC photos let us rebuild the Moon's south pole and highlands as real 3D ground you can walk on, and MRO's CTX elevation models did the same for Gale, Jezero and Olympus Mons. NASA Earthdata Search gave us EMIT minerals, ECOSTRESS temperatures and MODIS brightness for every Earth location we compared, and NASA Worldview (GIBS) gave us Earth maps of dust, snow and land temperature for the Twin Trails. Real sounds from Perseverance's microphone, NASA photos, and NASA's Perseverance 3D model bring it all to life.

ESA → Copernicus DEM gave us the height of every Earth location in the Twin Score, and Sentinel-2 images show what each Earth twin looks like from above. Through ESA's Open Science Catalog, we found the CCI permafrost map, which shows Earth's frozen ground next to Mars' in the Water trail.

CSA → a RADARSAT-1 radar image of Haughton Crater in Canada, taken in the dark of polar night in January 2001, read and displayed by following CSA's SAR Python tutorial. It shows how radar sees through darkness, just like it would at the Moon's shadowed south pole.

JAXA → GCOM-C land temperature data, from JAXA G-Portal, gave us Earth's day-to-night temperature swing, compared in the Soil trail with how fast the ground heats and cools on Mars and the Moon.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: CrewSense
projectDetails.summary:
CrewSense, developed by Digital Minds, is a browser-based prototype designed to help astronauts answer three questions: What changed? What does it mean? What should I do next?

It simulates ISS, lunar and Mars missions with 22 health indicators covering vital signs, sleep, mood, body mass, bone health and radiation exposure. Users explore an interactive body schematic, review clearly identified trends, and enter measurements and symptoms. Explainable rules highlight the most urgent finding and provide illustrative guidance on monitoring, action and flight-surgeon escalation. English and Arabic interfaces make the information accessible.
NASA Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency resources inform the indicator coverage and explanations. The measurements and scenario settings are synthetic; the prototype is not clinically validated and does not transmit medical messages. CrewSense addresses the challenge through self-assessment, understandable visualization and mission-aware guidance, aiming to make onboard health information clearer when ground support is delayed.
projectDetails.details:
CrewSense, by Digital Minds, turns astronaut health readings into a clear next decision when ground support is delayed. Our working browser prototype simulates an ISS expedition, a lunar base and a Mars mission, tracking 22 synthetic indicators across eight systems, including vital signs, sleep, mood, body mass, bone health and radiation exposure.

Users select a mission, inspect trends, enter eight measurements and choose symptoms. Transparent, fixed-band rules return a plain-language status and illustrative next steps, including when to involve a flight surgeon. The dashboard prioritizes the worst flag, offers a flagged-only view and links a clickable 2D body to indicator explanations. Codes, units, line patterns and status glyphs distinguish signals without relying on color alone. English and Arabic interfaces support accessibility.

Built with React, TypeScript and Vite, CrewSense uses NASA HRP hazards, risks and research plus CSA resources to inform coverage and explanations. Communication-delay context supports onboard autonomy. Traces, mission settings and decision bands are prototype assumptions, not NASA patient data. No real sensor feed, messaging or clinical validation is implemented. The intended impact is clearer onboard understanding; next steps are clinician review, usability testing and secure data integration.

projectDetails.name: Planetary Twin Finder
projectDetails.summary: Planetary Twin Finder finds the places on Earth whose ground best matches the sites NASA has proposed for landing humans on Mars and the Moon. Astronauts and rovers rehearse at a handful of Earth analogs, chosen mostly by field experience. We compared the whole dry planet instead. Every patch of ground on Earth, Mars and the Moon is described with the same four numbers (slope, roughness, relief and brightness) at the same 463 m pixel size as NASA's Mars elevation map. Earth ground with plants, water or ice is removed, and each NASA site gets a ranked, explained list of its closest Earth twins. In a blind test, without being told where NASA trains, 92.5% of our Mars matches landed in the Atacama Desert and Death Valley, NASA's best-known analogs. The method also found new ones: Jezero crater's closest twin, #1 of 148,925 dry places in Africa and the Americas, is in Egypt's Eastern Desert. Mission planners, field-test teams and students can use the website to find nearer, cheaper and more varied places to rehearse for the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

The website has two parts. A scroll story explains the problem, the method and the results. The Twin Finder lets anyone pick one of NASA's 47 proposed landing sites (the 38 candidate human Exploration Zones on Mars and the nine Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar south pole) and see its 25 closest twins on Earth on a satellite map. Each twin card shows its score, its rank among all dry places on Earth and within its continent, how close each of the four features is, a side-by-side shaded relief of the target and the twin, what Earth cannot copy (for the Moon, Diviner temperatures and ice-stability shares), and links to Google Maps, NASA Worldview and the Copernicus Browser. An "Ask the analyst" panel answers questions about the result on screen, using only our data.

HOW TO TRY IT

Open https://duplicaa.vercel.app, click "Launch the Twin Finder", keep Mars and Jezero selected, and open twin #1 (Egypt). Then switch to the Moon and pick any Artemis region.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Every world is cut into tiles about 9.26 km across (20 x 20 pixels of 463 m, the resolution of NASA's MOLA map of Mars). Earth and Moon elevation are averaged down to the same pixel size, so all three worlds are measured the same way.

2. Each tile gets four numbers: mean slope, slope spread (roughness), relief (highest minus lowest point) and albedo (brightness).

3. On Earth, a tile is kept only if it could look like Mars: median NDVI below 0.15 (no plants), under 5% permanent water, and under 50% permanent snow and ice. That leaves 148,925 dry tiles in Africa and the Americas south of 50 N (130,060 in Africa).

4. Features are standardized together, and each Earth tile's distance to a NASA site is its mean distance to the site's 10 nearest tiles. The score is 100 x exp(-distance / 0.4), so 100 is a perfect match. Twins in a list are at least 25 km apart.

5. The Moon is matched on terrain only, with its own scaler. Its scores (best 5 to 33) are much lower than Mars scores (best 63 to 98), because the lunar south pole is rougher than almost any dry land, so the site shows ranks rather than scores for the Moon.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

We tested the method blind. Without telling it where NASA trains, 92.5% of its Mars matches fell in the Atacama Desert and Death Valley; a wet farmland control box (the Nile Delta) got 7.5%, and those were desert tiles east of Cairo, not farmland. We kept the failures too: adding heat as a feature dropped the result to 84.3%, and ranking by percentiles within each world let the farmland control rise to 28.3%. Known answers check the terrain code: Shackleton crater comes out 4.06 km deep (published 4.2 km).

BENEFITS

Mission teams can shortlist new analog sites from data, then visit only the best ones. Countries without a famous analog can find their own: Egypt's Eastern Desert is the closest twin of Jezero crater, where Perseverance landed. Every result is explained feature by feature, and every limit is stated.

WHAT WORKS NOW AND LIMITS

Working now: the full website, all 47 NASA sites, 25 twins each, the Egypt tab and the analyst. Limits: matching uses terrain shape and brightness at about 460 m (no rock chemistry, no temperature, no boulders); the Earth grid covers Africa and the Americas south of 50 N so far; the Moon has no brightness feature yet. Results are a ranked shortlist, not a substitute for visiting a site.

NEXT

Cover the rest of the world, add Moon brightness (LOLA albedo), add an image-based engine, and a reverse mode that finds the nearest good twin to any city.

TOOLS

Python 3.11 (rasterio, GDAL, GeoPandas, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, pytest), Google Earth Engine, JavaScript with Vite, three.js, MapLibre GL JS, GSAP and Lenis, Google Gemini for the analyst, hosted on Vercel.

Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Dust & Decades
projectDetails.summary:
We created a storytelling project called “Forgotten Explorers,” which tells the stories of NASA’s two twin rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, which were operating on Mars. These rovers were designed for 90 days of operations, but Opportunity continued to work for approximately 14 years. We have an interactive bilingual (English/Arabic) website with a 10 page storybook you can read to them, a rover-parts explorer to explore, real NASA pictures, a dust-storm game, and a quiz. We also developed a printable storybook, a 10 slide presentation, a 25 second video and coloring book.

The project is designed to work out the challenge and put the dense mission data like water evidence, the first marathon on another planet and the 2018 dust storm as a simple, emotional story for school age children. This does not only represent active missions, but also the silent rovers!

It's significant because it demonstrates how history inspires the next generation on space exploration. The lesson the twins learn is that there is no time like the present to be determined, and that you can have big dreams.
projectDetails.details:
Clear, concise, and informative description of what it does and how it works.

This book, “Forgotten Explorers,” narrates the stories of NASA’s two Mars rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, in different forms for kids. The main part is a bilingual (English/Arabic) website. It features a 10 page storybook which children can flip through, tap to make come to life, and have read to them. It also includes a “Did you know?” fact per page, an explorer of the rover parts that you can click on, a gallery of real images taken by NASA, a dust-covered solar panel power-drop game, a 5 question quiz, and a time line. We created a printable story book, a ten slide presentation, a 25 second video and a coloring book around the site.

Benefits

Children learn complex science in simple terms, their own terms, with pictures, sound and play. These formats are suited to different contexts – classroom, screen, print.

Intended impact

We want children to recognise that there is some history in the old, silent, space machines and we want them to feel curious about Mars and space exploration. The twins' message is that determination never ends and that “big dreams” can come true!

Tools and technologies

All the website was developed in HTML, CSS and JavaScript without using any frameworks. For the read aloud button, it utilises the speech feature built into the browser.

NASA, JPL Mars Exploration Rover pages provided facts and images.

To write and structure the website in code, we utilized the AI assistant Claude, as well as to summarise our research.

Include the tools you employed in the presentation, video and coloring book.

Creativity

We did not treat the rovers as a data sheet, but as characters with a story to tell. The dust game had them feel the problem that the mission ended with, and the storybook, video, coloring book had them engage in different ways.

Factors we considered

Target audience: school-aged children, using simple language, short pages, large illustrations.

Language: Arabic and English - to allow more families to read.

Accuracy: checked with NASA dates and numbers, corrected inconsistencies in own text.

Accessibility: keyboard controls, image text and minimised movement for those sensitive to it.

projectDetails.name: TerraPulse
projectDetails.summary:
TerraPulse is a web app that turns NASA Earth observation data into explanations of environmental change. Users select a place and explore vegetation greenness (MODIS NDVI), daytime land surface temperature (MODIS), rainfall (GPM IMERG), or nitrogen dioxide air pollution (OMI). An interactive map shows how results differ across locations.
TerraPulse builds and checks time series, then uses the seasonal Mann-Kendall test to identify significant trends and Sen's slope to measure their rate of change with a 95% range. It accounts for seasonal patterns, guards against false findings when testing many cells, and reports when evidence is insufficient. To avoid a false cooling trend caused by Terra's earlier overpass time since 2020, the daytime temperature analysis ends in December 2021. The method found 28 of 28 planted trends in simulated data and agreed with an Alexandria ground weather station on warming. Results include New Delta greening of about +0.039 NDVI per decade since 2001 and Nile Delta land surface warming of about 0.4 °C per decade from 2001 to 2021.
TerraPulse makes Earth science understandable without programming or statistics skills. Kemet, its English- and Arabic-speaking AI guide, uses only TerraPulse's computed numbers and documented facts to explain results without inventing causes.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

TerraPulse is a web app that investigates environmental change using NASA Earth observation data. Users select a variable and location; TerraPulse builds a time series (measurements over time), measures the rate of change and tests whether a trend is statistically significant.

It covers vegetation greenness (MODIS Terra NDVI, monthly, 1 km), daytime land surface temperature (MODIS Terra, 1 km), rainfall (GPM IMERG monthly) and nitrogen dioxide air pollution (Aura OMI). A NOAA weather station in Alexandria provides a ground check. Users can select preset regions, click a single map cell of about 5 km, or draw a box for live analysis.

MODIS data comes through NASA AppEEARS, GPM IMERG and OMI area averages through NASA Giovanni, and weather records from NOAA. TerraPulse removes fill values, applies scale factors and quality flags, drops impossible values and spikes, and calculates monthly averages. Missing data is never invented. The 1 km grids are averaged into about 5 km cells (2,520 cells over the Nile Delta).

NASA's Terra satellite stopped correcting its orbit in 2020, causing daytime temperatures to read cooler each year. To avoid a false cooling trend, temperature analysis ends at December 2021. The seasonal Mann-Kendall test compares the same months across years, while Sen's slope measures the rate of change with a 95% range. Benjamini-Hochberg q-values correct for false discoveries across hundreds of cells.

Results receive clear verdicts: confirmed trend, possible trend, real but too small to matter, no significant trend, or not enough data (records shorter than 10 years). Interactive maps, charts and an Evidence tab display results and explain p-values, q-values and the 95% range. Kemet, the AI guide, answers questions in English or Arabic.

Testing on simulated data with planted trends found 28 of 28 planted trend cells, with 1 false alarm in 89 no-trend cells. The Alexandria weather station warmed about 0.60 °C per decade (2000–2023), compared with MODIS land surface warming there of about 0.51 °C per decade (2001–2021). Other findings include New Delta greening of about +0.039 NDVI per decade since 2001 (p < 0.001), Alexandria browning (about -0.038 NDVI per decade), Nile Delta land surface warming of about 0.40 °C per decade from 2001 to 2021, and rising nitrogen dioxide over Greater Cairo since 2004. Rainfall shows no significant trend in the Nile Delta, on the Mediterranean coast, or in the Central Amazon (1998–2025).

Benefits:

Students, teachers and the public can explore NASA data without programming or statistics skills. TerraPulse saves hours of data preparation and analysis. Simple variable definitions, a guided tour and a narrated walkthrough video help beginners. English and Arabic support accessibility, while clear uncertainty reporting prevents unsupported conclusions.

Intended impact:

TerraPulse helps people understand environmental changes through evidence, particularly vegetation, surface heat and air quality in Egypt. It highlights changes such as new farmland in the New Delta, browning around Alexandria and rising air pollution over Cairo. It also treats the absence of a significant trend as a meaningful finding.

Future plans, not yet built, include worldwide region and time-period selection through NASA's AppEEARS and Giovanni services, additional variables such as soil moisture and evaporation, and a cautious forecast with its uncertainty shown, as planned in our proposal.

Tools and technologies:

- Data: NASA AppEEARS, Giovanni (Earthdata Login) and NOAA Climate Data Online.

- Analysis: Python, pandas, xarray, NumPy, SciPy, netCDF4 and pymannkendall.

- Web: FastAPI, JavaScript, Leaflet, Leaflet. draw, Plotly.js and Esri World Imagery.

- AI: free NVIDIA Nemotron language models through OpenRouter.

- Hosting and code: Vercel and GitHub.

No special hardware is needed; everything runs in a web browser.

What makes it creative:

Kemet takes its name from the ancient name of Egypt, meaning "the Black Land", referring to the Nile's fertile soil. It uses only TerraPulse's computed numbers and documented facts about each place, never inventing causes. Every answer names the model that wrote it. Everyday verdicts distinguish statistical significance from practical importance. Users can draw a box for a full trend test in seconds. The "Oasis" colour palette reflects the Nile's land, water and palm trees, while ground weather observations provide an independent satellite check.

Factors we considered:

We considered data quality, sensor orbit drift, seasonal cycles and false discoveries. Without correction, about 5% of cells could appear significant by chance. Records shorter than 10 years are labelled "not enough data", while changes smaller than the instrument's uncertainty are labelled "real but tiny". TerraPulse and Kemet avoid unsupported explanations of causes. We prioritised simple language and two languages for the challenge's high school and college students and the public. Everything uses free NASA data, free and open-source software, and free AI models, so the tool costs nothing to run.

Website: https://terrapulse-website.vercel.app

Code: https://github.com/ramaabdelgadir/terrapulse-web

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

node.title: Early Echo
node.excerpt: Detecting fire using sound!

projectDetails.name: Early Echo
projectDetails.summary: Early Echo answers Flame in Freefall in two parts. A website that puts 1,939 records from 18 NASA microgravity fire experiments in one searchable table, ranks 35 groups of similar tests by how often the flame went out, maps every flame by oxygen and pressure, and uses small machine learning models, scored on test days they never saw, to predict which flames go out. It shows why early detection is really important: in NASA’s gas flame tests, 0 of 41 flames kept burning below 25% oxygen, but 18 of 21 small flames kept burning in 33 to 40% oxygen, a range that includes the 34% NASA recommends for Moon and Mars homes. The second part is a fire alarm made of sound. In orbit smoke doesn’t rise, but sound still crosses the room, and it travels faster through warm air. Our Android app turns two phones into a heat alarm by timing a sound sent between them both ways. A real candle made the sound arrive 2 to 4 microseconds early at a laptop’s microphone.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

Fire behaves differently in orbit. Nothing rises, so heat and smoke stay around a flame or drift wherever the fans push them, instead of rising to a detector on the ceiling. NASA's recommended air for Moon and Mars homes is 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi, so crews can go outside more often with less preparation. The space station keeps 21% oxygen at full pressure. More oxygen helps a fire. NASA has run nearly 2,000 fire tests in orbit, but the results sit in separate records, tables and papers, so it is hard to ask "would this flame keep burning in our air?"

Part 1:

We downloaded the records of all 24 fire experiments in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics archive and the 22 tables that list each test. After cleaning, 1,939 records from 18 experiments remain, and 613 of them say how the flame ended.

- Summarize: one searchable table of every test, each row linked to NASA's own record.

- Rank: 35 groups of similar tests (same experiment, fuel, pressure range and oxygen range), ranked by how often the flame went out on its own.

- Interpret: a map of every test by oxygen and pressure, with station air, the air used before a spacewalk and the planned habitat air marked. Click any point and it reads the nearest tests, or says "Too few to call".

- Predict: small machine-learning models, each scored on whole test days it never saw: gas flames 110 of 133 right (a simple nearest-tests rule got 116), droplets 186 of 206, inverse flames 118 of 139.

- Watch: a program read 130 of NASA's flame videos. In oxygen-rich air, flicker in a flame's last seconds told a dying flame from a steady one for 75 of 80 flames, looking back from the end of each test.

- 3D view: NASA's 3D model of the station's US Lab, with a fire the size of NASA's Saffire-I test placed in it. The spread of its heat there is our estimate.

What we found: below 25% oxygen, 0 of 41 gas flames kept burning. In 33 to 40% oxygen, 18 of 21 small flames did. So in NASA's tests, small gas flames kept burning in the air planned for the Moon and Mars, while they went out in station-like air. Finding a fire early matters more there.

Part 2:

Sound travels at about 343 m/s in room air, and about 0.6 m/s faster for each degree warmer. If the air along a 1 m line warms by 1 °C, a sound sent there and back returns about 10 microseconds sooner (a microsecond is a millionth of a second). A smoke detector waits for smoke to reach it, and a thermometer measures one spot. A sound line feels the whole path between two devices. Phones, laptops and speakers are already on board, so it needs no new hardware.

How the app works:

1. Install it on two Android phones on the same Wi-Fi or hotspot. They find each other by themselves.

2. Each phone plays a short, very high chirp (13 ms, 17 to 21 kHz) 23 times a second and records both phones' chirps. One chirp rises in pitch and the other falls, so they are never confused.

3. Each phone times the chirps far more finely than one audio sample (21 microseconds); in our simulation, to a fraction of a microsecond. The phones share their gaps over Wi-Fi and add them up. Clock offsets and wind cancel out; heat speeds the sound both ways, so it stays.

4. For the first 12 seconds the app learns the room's normal wobble. The alarm level is 6 times that, and never less than 1 microsecond.

5. If the sound arrives early by more than that for 1 second, both screens turn orange. A hand or a person in the line makes the sound late instead, and the app says "Something's in the way".

A debug screen shows every reading, and each test can be saved. A "Not a flame" button marks people, hands and fans, so a later model can learn to tell them apart from fire.

How we tested it

- A real candle: one laptop played a chirp through a soundbar about 0.9 m away and recorded it with its own two microphones, with a candle under the middle of the line. Each of the 3 times we lit it, the sound arrived early: 2 to 4 microseconds at one microphone and 1 to 2 at the other. One cut sorted 115 of 117 seconds right as lit or out at the first microphone, but we set that cut on the same recording, so it is not a blind test. This was one laptop timing one way, and on Earth the heat rises into the line.

- Nine simulated tests: two simulated phones 1 m apart with drifting clocks, echoes, noise and Wi-Fi delay. A small heat change sets off both phones; a gust of wind, slow warming, a hand and a standing person do not. All nine pass.

- A 3D estimate: in NASA's US Lab model, with six sound lines between four laptops and the station's air flow, a Saffire-I-sized fire trips the first line after about 10 seconds and 4 of 6 lines within 2 minutes. This comes from a model, not a measurement.

Limits

The phone app has not been tested on a real flame, and nothing has been tested in orbit. A fire's heat has to cross a sound line to be seen. A smouldering fire with little heat may not show, and a warm person near the line can shift it almost as much as a candle, so an alarm means "go and look". NASA has few tests near habitat air, and the site marks where a model is guessing.

Our future plans

1. A blind flame test with the phones in a safe lab: one person lights the flame or doesn't, another reads the screen.

2. More than two phones, so sound lines cross the whole room.

3. A model that tells a flame from a person or a fan, trained on saved tests.

4. The same app on the laptops and speakers already aboard the station, as an early second opinion next to the smoke detectors.

Tools

Python with numpy and scikit-learn (data and models), ffmpeg (video reading), React, TypeScript, Vite and three.js (website), Kotlin and the Android SDK (phone app). No special hardware: two Android phones, or a laptop and a speaker.

projectDetails.name: Earth Guardians Ai
projectDetails.summary: Earth Guardian AI answers the challenge “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots”. NASA’s MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m pixels) detect the same wildfires at different times, sizes and confidence scales, so one fire can appear twice and results are different most of the time. Our web app merges both sensors’ live NASA FIRMS detections, matches those within about 1.2 km, and gives every hotspot one harmonized confidence score from 0 to 100. The hotspots appear on an interactive 3D NASA globe with a sensor-agreement panel, grouped fire events and a wind-direction arrow from NASA POWER. The app also gives a wildfire risk score for any place, a what-if simulator and an AI assistant with voice in 20 languages, including Egyptian Arabic, so people can understand fire danger in their own language.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Earth Guardian AI is a browser-based 3D globe for live wildfire monitoring. It harmonizes NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into one deduplicated list with a single 0 to 100 confidence score, shows where the sensors agree, estimates local wildfire risk from NASA weather data, and explains results in plain language in 20 languages.

How it works.

  1. The server downloads near-real-time detections from NASA FIRMS (VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS) for the area on screen.
  2. Each VIIRS detection is matched to the nearest MODIS detection within about 0.012 degrees (about 1.2 km). A matched pair becomes one fire. Unmatched detections stay as single-sensor fires.
  3. Confidence is normalized to 0..1 (VIIRS l/n/h = 0.2/0.6/1.0, MODIS 0..100 divided by 100).
  4. Harmonized score (max 100) = agreement (45 if both sensors, 10 if one) + sensor confidence (up to 25) + fire radiative power (up to 15) + closeness of the two detections (up to 15). Label: HIGH = both sensors, MEDIUM = one confident sensor, LOW otherwise.
  5. Extra products: fire events (nearby detections grouped), a persistent-hotspot flag (same cell on 2 or more days, for example industrial heat sources), age of each detection, and agreement statistics for the view.
  6. A wildfire risk score (0 to 100) uses NASA POWER temperature, humidity, rainfall, soil moisture and wind, plus nearby harmonized fires. It is a simplified index inspired by the Canadian Fire Weather Index (Van Wagner, 1987), not the full operational system.
  7. NASA GIBS thermal-anomaly layers are shown under the dots as a visual cross-check.

Benefits. One trusted fire layer instead of two confusing ones; transparent scoring (every point is explained); faster understanding of which fires are real and strong; access in the user's own language, including Egyptian Arabic, by text or voice.

What we hope to achieve. Make satellite fire information easier to trust and to understand for the public and for early responders, and show how MODIS and VIIRS together are better than either alone (VIIRS finds many small fires MODIS misses; MODIS adds a longer-heritage confirmation).

Limitations (stated openly). Satellites pass only a few times a day, so detections can be hours old and small or short fires can be missed. NASA POWER weather lags real time by a few days. The risk index is simplified. The 1.2 km matching distance follows the MODIS pixel size and has not been validated against ground-truth fire perimeters. In the 10-year chart the past bars are a modelled reconstruction (not measured history) and the future bars are scenarios, not predictions. Translations other than English and Arabic are AI-generated. Not for emergency decisions.

Tools, languages and software. TypeScript, Next.js 16 (React), Tailwind CSS, CesiumJS with Resium (3D globe), Node.js server routes, Groq API for language models (assistant, explanations, translation), Web Speech API (voice), SVG charts. Data scripts in Node/TypeScript. Open-source packages from npm.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. We used SI in two ways, and we are clearly identifying both.

  1. During development: an AI coding assistant helped us write and debug much of the code (TypeScript/React/Next.js, API routes, the harmonization and risk functions, the data-preparation scripts) and parts of the text and documentation. Our team chose the challenge and the design, directed the work, tested the application and reported and decided every change, and we take responsibility for the result. AI-assisted parts are code, descriptive text and documentation; no images, audio or video in the project were generated by AI, and the project contains no NASA logos or mission identifiers that we modified.
  2. Inside the product at run time: the app calls Groq-hosted large language models for the AI assistant (chat and voice), the plain-language "why this risk / why this confidence" explanations, and on-demand translation into 20 languages. These outputs are generated text from the model and are not NASA content. The numeric scores themselves come from deterministic code in lib/fireHarmonize.ts and lib/riskEngine.ts, not from the language model.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Earth Second Moon Earth Trend Detective website
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Earth System Trend Detective website, is an interactive, automated, and regularly updated global environmental monitoring platform designed to detect, analyze, and visualize significant changes across interconnected Earth systems.

We developed six interactive, automated, and continuously updated dashboards in 1)global agriculture monitoring , 2)global water bodies monitoring , 3)global water cycle monitoring , 4)global carbon sequestration monitoring ,5)global day and night LST monitoring , 6)global air pollution monitoring, enabling users to explore environmental variables, investigate regional changes, visualize historical trends, and assess their statistical significance. The platform is supported by 24 real-world environmental case studies, covering phenomena such as European drought, East African locust invasion, Lake Mead depletion, UAE flash flooding, Amazon productivity, and the Pacific Northwest heat dome.

Our integrated workflow combines satellite data acquisition, regional analysis, time-series visualization, and statistical significance testing using multiple statistical methods to distinguish meaningful environmental trends from random fluctuations like P-value significance 

By transforming complex Earth science data into accessible, interactive insights, our solution empowers students, researchers, and decision-makers to understand environmental changes, identify emerging risks, and support evidence-based decisions for a more sustainable future.
projectDetails.details:
Earth System Trend Detective Website is an integrated, interactive, automated, and continuously updated global environmental monitoring platform that transforms satellite-derived Earth observation data into meaningful information about changes and trends across interconnected Earth systems.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

We developed six interactive, automated, and continuously updated global monitoring dashboards, each dedicated to a major Earth system component:

  1. Global Agriculture Monitoring: Detecting changes in vegetation conditions, agricultural productivity, and vegetation trends.
  2. Global Water Bodies Monitoring: Monitoring changes in the extent and distribution of lakes, reservoirs, and other surface water bodies.
  3. Global Water Cycle Monitoring: Investigating changes in water-cycle variables and their interconnected environmental patterns.
  4. Global Carbon Sequestration Monitoring: Tracking changes in carbon-related indicators and ecosystem productivity.
  5. Global Day and Night Land Surface Temperature (LST) Monitoring: Analyzing global temperature patterns and long-term thermal changes during daytime and nighttime.
  6. Global Air Pollution Monitoring: Investigating changes in atmospheric pollution indicators and their spatial and temporal trends.

Each dashboard follows an integrated workflow:

Variable Selection → Satellite Data Acquisition → Regional Analysis → Time-Series Visualization → Statistical Significance Testing.

Users can investigate environmental variables, explore historical trends, compare different geographical regions, and determine whether observed changes are statistically significant.

2. Global Environmental Case Studies

To demonstrate the platform's practical capabilities, we incorporated 24 real-world environmental case studies (four per dashboard). These include European drought, East African locust invasion, Lake Mead water depletion, UAE flash flooding, Amazon ecosystem productivity, and the Pacific Northwest heat dome.

The platform also demonstrates statistical evidence through p-value analysis, t-tests, Wilcoxon tests, Mann–Whitney tests, permutation tests, and autocorrelation-adjusted statistical testing.

Examples of investigated findings include:

  • 70% decline in East African Leaf Area Index (LAI).
  • Significant contraction of Lake Urmia's water area.
  • A temperature increase of +12.5°C during the Pacific Northwest heat dome.
  • Significant rising Net Primary Productivity (NPP) trends in Australia and Europe.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

The project makes complex Earth science information accessible through interactive visualizations and scientific evidence. Its intended impact includes:

  • Helping researchers identify and investigate significant environmental trends.
  • Supporting decision-makers with evidence-based environmental information.
  • Raising public awareness of global environmental changes.
  • Enabling students to explore real-world Earth system phenomena.
  • Improving understanding of the interconnected nature of Earth's environmental systems.

Ultimately, the platform aims to transform environmental monitoring from simply observing changes into understanding their direction, magnitude, geographical distribution, and statistical significance.

4. Tools and Technologies

The solution is based on cloud computing of google cloud satellite-derived Earth observation data of NASA and its partners , automated data acquisition and processing, interactive dashboard development, time-series analysis, and statistical testing.

The specific programming languages are JavaScript , HTML , CSS .

5. Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation is bringing six major Earth system monitoring components together within one integrated global trend-detection concept.

Rather than presenting satellite maps as isolated observations, our platform connects spatial analysis, historical time series, regional case studies, and statistical significance testing. This allows users to investigate not only whether an environmental variable is increasing or decreasing, but also whether the observed trend is statistically meaningful.

We also considered global accessibility, automated updates, scientific reliability, ease of interpretation, and the needs of different audiences, including students, researchers, and decision-makers.

Our vision is to make everyone an Earth System Trend Detective website, capable of discovering, investigating, and understanding the changes shaping our planet.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Change Courtroom: Punjab fields
projectDetails.summary: EchoTrace built Change Courtroom: Punjab fields, an interactive investigation space on real NASA NISAR L2 GCOV radar data. It follows 24 radar passes over a 16x16 km mixed agricultural and urban area in Punjab, India (21 Nov 2025 - 11 Oct 2026), tracking HH and HV backscatter per pixel. Visitors act as data detectives: pick one of 12 candidate change areas, browse deviation maps for every date, read per-area time series, and weigh competing explanations against the documented crop calendar from Punjab Agricultural University. The app states what the data shows and what stays a hypothesis, and shows its selection rule so visitors can judge it. Every number is computed from the 24 NASA granules listed inside, accessed via ASF DAAC. Built to make radar change readable to non-specialists.
projectDetails.details: Change Courtroom: Punjab fields is an interactive web app that turns 324 days of NASA NISAR radar observations into an investigation space. Visitors choose one of 12 candidate change areas, browse deviation maps for 24 acquisition dates, read HH/HV time series, and weigh competing explanations against the measured data and documented regional crop-calendar context. How it works: 24 NISAR L2 GCOV granules from 21 November 2025 to 11 October 2026 were accessed via NASA's ASF DAAC. They cover a 16x16 km mixed agricultural and urban area in Punjab, India, on a 10 m grid. Gamma0 power is converted to dB and compared with each pixel's temporal median. The exploratory selection rule flags changes greater than 3 dB on at least 4 dates in each channel, not necessarily the same dates. The 12 displayed areas are selected examples, not proven anomalies. All 24 granule identifiers are listed inside the app. Tools: Python, h5py and NumPy for data extraction; React and TypeScript for the app. Punjab Agricultural University and ICAR publications provide regional agricultural context, not field-level validation. The intended benefit is to help non-specialists ask what changed and when, with evidence and uncertainty visible together. Plain-language definitions, guided entry questions and worked examples support this data-detective approach. Limits: the analysis uses no land-cover mask or independent field validation. Radar changes can reflect moisture, vegetation, roughness and other factors, so we do not claim crop classification or proven causes. The data has PROVISIONAL maturity. Four expected acquisition cycles have no matching catalog scene, including one within the documented instrument gap. Original cluster-grouping parameters were not archived, so the exact cluster selection is not fully reproducible. The app and current source archive do not constitute a fully reproducible open-source release.

projectDetails.details:
Earth Trend Detective

https://understanding-channel-279685.framer.app/#experience

Project Description

Earth Trend Detective is an interactive scientific platform designed to explore long-term changes and patterns in Earth's systems using NASA Earth observation data and statistical analysis.

The project aims to make complex scientific datasets more accessible and understandable by transforming raw observations into meaningful analytical insights through data processing, statistical methods, and interactive visualizations.

The Problem

Earth science datasets contain valuable information about our planet, but extracting meaningful long-term patterns from these datasets can be challenging. Users may struggle to process large amounts of scientific data, identify trends, evaluate their statistical significance, and interpret the results.

Earth Trend Detective addresses this challenge by providing a structured and interactive approach to scientific data exploration and trend analysis.

Our Solution

We are developing a web-based platform that allows users to explore defined geographical study areas and investigate historical scientific observations.

The platform processes scientific datasets, applies statistical analysis techniques, detects long-term trends, and presents the findings through interactive charts, geographical visualizations, and statistical summaries.

Our approach focuses on making the analytical process transparent, understandable, and scientifically reliable.

Data Sources

Our project uses NASA Earth science resources, including:

  • NASA Giovanni
  • NASA Earth Science Data resources

projectDetails.name: Project EcoNova (EcoFilter Intelligence)
projectDetails.summary: EcoFilter Intelligence is a research-based engineering concept that explores a modular approach to reducing selected industrial air pollutants while allowing production to continue. The project connects environmental data with a proposed multi-stage filtration tower. The concept includes a pre-filter for particles, catalytic oxidation research for carbon monoxide, an adsorption stage proposed for nitrogen dioxide, limestone-based flue-gas desulfurization for sulfur dioxide, and electrostatic precipitation for particulate matter. A final monitoring chamber uses sensors and an ESP32-based dashboard concept to display parameters such as airflow, pressure, and pollutant readings, helping indicate system conditions and maintenance needs. NASA resources, such as satellite air-quality observations and atmospheric data, support the trend investigation. The website presents the engineering design, research evidence, and simulated dashboard values. EcoFilter has not been built or experimentally validated; therefore, no removal efficiency or measured performance is claimed. It is a proposed concept for study and testing under real industrial conditions.
projectDetails.details:
EcoFilter Intelligence – Project Description EcoFilter Intelligence is a research-based engineering concept designed to explore smarter ways of reducing industrial air pollution without requiring permanent interruption of industrial production. The project proposes a modular, multi-stage filtration tower that targets different pollutants through specialized treatment stages. It includes a pre-filter for large particles, a catalytic oxidation stage proposed for carbon monoxide (CO), an adsorption stage investigated for nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), limestone-based flue-gas desulfurization for sulfur dioxide (SO₂), and an electrostatic precipitator for particulate matter such as PM2.5 and PM10. The system also proposes an intelligent monitoring chamber using an ESP32-based architecture and environmental sensors to monitor parameters such as airflow, pressure, and pollutant concentrations. A digital dashboard concept presents this information and helps identify possible maintenance needs. The project combines NASA Earth observation resources, including OMI and MODIS data, with engineering research to investigate air pollution trends and connect environmental evidence with a potential engineering solution. Its main benefit is presenting a modular and potentially adaptable approach to industrial emission control, supporting environmental awareness, cleaner industrial processes, and more informed maintenance decisions. The creative aspect is the integration of satellite-based environmental research, multi-stage filtration technologies, and smart monitoring within one proposed engineering concept. The website was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with interactive visualizations and simulated dashboard data. Research also involved NASA datasets, scientific publications, and engineering references. Important development factors included pollutant-specific treatment methods, industrial continuity, modular design, monitoring requirements, maintenance, and scientific reliability. EcoFilter Intelligence is currently a proposed concept. It has not been physically built or experimentally validated, and its removal efficiency and operational performance remain to be tested.

Research-Based Filtration Performance The proposed EcoFilter system is based on established air pollution control technologies. Published research reports removal efficiencies of 90–100% for carbon monoxide in specific catalytic oxidation tube tests. Industrial wet flue-gas desulfurization systems can achieve up to 99% SO₂ removal, while electrostatic precipitators can achieve approximately 99.5% particulate matter removal in certain industrial applications. These figures represent reported performance of individual technologies under specific operating conditions, not the performance of EcoFilter Intelligence. The nitrogen dioxide adsorption stage remains under research, and its efficiency requires further experimental validation. The overall system efficiency has not yet been determined and will depend on gas composition, temperature, airflow, contact time, filter materials, and system design.

projectDetails.name: Astronaut health AI  (ecu nova)
projectDetails.summary:
Astronaut Health AI is an offline-first health companion for astronauts, built as a hackathon prototype. It tracks six vitals: heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep and mood. Each reading is compared with the astronaut's own baseline, and the app explains every change it detects. Alerts come only from fixed, reviewable rules, never from AI. The app works fully offline: reports queue during loss of signal and sync when the link returns.

An AI voice companion, powered by Claude or Gemini through a secure server, understands natural English and Egyptian Arabic, follows the conversation, and supports hands-free voice. Red-flag symptoms trigger an immediate fixed safety response, and the app never diagnoses or prescribes.

NASA Research Mode adds 1,336 real measurements from the SpaceX Inspiration4 crew (OSDR datasets OSD-575 and OSD-569). Every value is kept as published, with its source, and verified against NASA's original files. Metrics NASA doesn't publish are shown as "not available", never invented.

The app is bilingual (Arabic RTL and English), with light and dark themes. It is tested with 121 automated tests and is live on Vercel.

NASA Research Mode adds 1,336 real measurements from the SpaceX Inspiration4 crew (OSDR datasets OSD-575 and OSD-569). Every value is kept as published, with its source, and verified against NASA's original files. Metrics NASA doesn't publish are shown as "not available", never invented.

The app is bilingual (Arabic RTL and English), with light and dark themes. It is tested with 121 automated tests and is live on Vercel.
