projectDetails.name: Radiation-Coupled Physiological Twin (RCPT)
projectDetails.summary: RCPT (Radiation-Coupled Physiological Twin) is an offline health-monitoring app for astronauts on Moon and Mars missions. Messages between Mars and Earth can take up to about 20 minutes each way, so a crew cannot always wait for doctors on the ground. Space radiation, lost sleep and heart-rate strain also make each other worse, and this is hard to judge by eye. RCPT combines these three signals into one live risk score from 0 to 100 with three levels: nominal, elevated and emergency. It then suggests an action, such as a rest or shelter protocol. Every number can be opened and explained, and every value is labelled as simulated, derived or not modeled. It also shows a body view by organ system, gives rule-based cues from eye and skin photos, and includes an offline assistant called Nova in English, Arabic and Spanish. It matters because crews far from Earth need clear, trustworthy health information that works without a connection. This is a research prototype that uses simulated data. It is not a medical device.
projectDetails.details:
Our project pairs three lightweight wearable sensor nodes with an offline software “physiological twin” that runs entirely inside the spacecraft. It turns raw body signals, radiation exposure and sleep debt into one clear risk score, explains how that score was reached, and shows which part of the body is under the most strain. No Earth link is needed to detect, understand or react to a developing medical problem.

The Problem

On a Mars mission, Earth is too far to be a first responder. A signal takes up to 22 minutes to arrive, so a call for help and a reply can take 44 minutes or more. For a cardiac event, a radiation-driven crisis or a sudden neurological problem, that gap can decide the outcome.

Moreover, astronauts are expected to run a mission and also act as their own doctors. In a cramped habitat, with altered gravity, fatigue and a heavy workload, they cannot reliably or regularly assess their own condition, even when diagnostic equipment is on board.

So the real need is not more medical equipment. It is continuous, automatic, local health awareness that asks nothing of the crew.

Our Solution

We built a two-part system:

•     Hardware: a tri-node wearable network (head, chest, wrist) that measures continuously and is always ready on the body.

•     Software (RCPT): an offline web application that fuses those signals with radiation and sleep data, scores crew risk in real time, and explains every number.

Everything runs locally on the ship. Nothing depends on the signal to Earth.

How the System Works

Step 1. Sense. Head and chest nodes capture microvolt-level brain (EEG) and heart (ECG) signals and clean them locally.

Step 2. Aggregate. They send compact data packets over Bluetooth Low Energy to the wrist hub, which adds blood pressure, oxygen saturation and in-suit environment readings.

Step 3. Transmit. The wrist hub sends one synchronized telemetry packet through the suit by RF link to the habitat’s local server.

Step 4. Understand. RCPT software combines the telemetry with radiation dose and sleep debt and computes a live risk index from 0 to 100.

Step 5. Act. The crew sees the score, the affected organ systems and a plain-language explanation, by screen or by voice, and gets the right alert tier: nominal, elevated or emergency.

Hardware: The Tri-Node Wearable System

Instead of one bulky device, we spread the sensing across three small nodes. Each sits where its signal is strongest, so no single piece is heavy, restrictive or awkward during work or sleep.

Why this design works

•     Edge processing first. Head and chest nodes filter and digitize their own signals, so only clean, compact data travels. That saves power and bandwidth.

•     One hub, one link. Only the wrist hub talks to the habitat, which keeps the wireless footprint small and the data synchronized.

•     Always ready. The nodes are worn continuously, so the system already has a baseline when an emergency begins.

Built for the Martian environment

•     Radiation hardening: silicon-on-insulator microcontrollers and error-correcting memory protect against bit-flips from cosmic rays.

•     Thermal control: electronics are encapsulated in thermally conductive, electrically insulating epoxy that passes

heat into the suit’s liquid cooling garment.

•     Dust protection: sealed housings (IP69K-equivalent) with PTFE membranes keep out abrasive, electrostatically charged regolith.

•     Low-gravity securement: elastomeric tensioners and micro-boa dials hold electrodes against the skin. Capacitive sensors track skin contact and warn the wearer if a node loses it.

Software: RCPT

•     Live risk index (0–100). Merges radiation dose, HRV and sleep debt into a single number.

•     Interaction model. These stressors compound instead of simply adding up, so a tired crew is hit harder by the same radiation.

•     Offline edge engine. All calculations stay on the device, so the app works with no connection at all.

•     Scenario buttons. Jump between calm orbit, a sleep-deprived crew and an acute solar storm. One click shows how the whole system reacts.

•     40-hour telemetry simulation. Shows risk climbing over time and tiers shifting from nominal to elevated to emergency.

•     Crew avatar. Breaks the overall score into organ systems so the most strained part of the body is visible.

•     Crew Quarters. Shows a sleeping astronaut and their organs in one scene, making sleep and recovery part of the picture.

•     Image assessment. Reads a photo of the eye or skin and returns color and pupil cues. It is rule-based and states clearly that it is not a diagnosis.

Validity

•     “How it is computed” panels. Every number can be opened and explained. Nothing is a black box.

•     Honest labelling. Each value is tagged simulated, derived or not modeled, so a simulation is never mistaken for a measurement.

•     Data and Validation area. The validation tab compares our radiation model with published Curiosity rover results and admits where it falls short. The sensitivity tab shows which assumptions move the result most. The sources tab lists every reference.

AI Assistant

•     NOVA AI is a chatbot available to answer questions through text or voice.

Simulated guided tutorials

•     Mars atlas and terrain tools. Place dose and conditions at real locations so mission planners can compare sites.

•     Guided tour and three languages. Anyone can open it, learn it and test the claims for themselves.

What Is Real and What Is Simulated

•     In our demo, we don’t have actual hardware, so sensor inputs are simulated from three parameters: sleep debt, radiation exposure and mission time.

•     In a flight version, the same inputs would come live from the tri-node hardware and crew dosimetry.

•     Outputs are decision support, not diagnosis. RCPT flags risk and explains it. It does not replace medical judgment.

Conclusion

The difference our solution makes is that health awareness moves from Earth to the crew itself. Instead of waiting 44 minutes for an answer, astronauts get a continuous, explainable picture of their own condition, built from light-weight wearable sensors and software that never needs a signal home. It is simple enough to use under stress, and stand by to act in emergencies.

projectDetails.name: Project Egypt Lotus
projectDetails.summary:
AstroHealth — 2026 NASA Space Apps ChallengeAstroHealth tackles the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" through a dual-level solution: a custom, bare-metal operating system and a concept hardware platform, ASTRO-BOOK.   1. AstroHealth OS (Software)
Built from scratch in freestanding C and x86 assembly (~3,800 lines across 23 files), AstroHealth OS eliminates external dependencies to ensure maximum reliability on flight hardware. Booting via GRUB Multiboot2 into 32-bit protected mode (1024×768×32 framebuffer), the kernel integrates custom interrupt handling, PS/2 keyboard support, a 8×16 bitmap font, and a custom UI kit. Its core telemetry engine (telemetry.c) processes physiological readings into color-coded green, yellow, and red status indicators for instant crew assessment. The build compiles into a bootable ISO (astrohealth.iso) verifiable in QEMU, backed by a 9-milestone roadmap mapping OS features directly to mission requirements.   2. ASTRO-BOOK (Concept Hardware)
Complementing the OS is ASTRO-BOOK, a solar-powered medical laptop concept powered by an 8-core RISC-V SoC (32 TOPS NPU) and a radiation-hardened 2TB NVMe SSD storing an offline medical atlas. Equipped with non-invasive, zero-radiation sensors—including QUS bone ultrasound, ECG palm pads, and BIA—alongside lockstep safety cores and SEL protection, the system enables autonomous, real-time crew diagnostics without relying on delayed Earth communications.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — AstroHealth OS + ASTRO-BOOK
What exactly does it do?
AstroHealth OS is an operating system built from scratch whose native, built-in application is an autonomous astronaut crew health monitor (for the 2026 Space Apps challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions"). When it boots, it presents a full mission console that tracks, for a crew of 4:

Vitals per crew member: heart rate, SpO₂, core temperature, blood pressure, respiration rate, HRV, and a Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) reaction-time test for fatigue.
Environment: radiation dose rate + lifetime dose, CO₂ / CO₂ partial pressure, cabin pressure, and ICP/ONSD estimates (intracranial pressure — the Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome risk).
At-a-glance color coding: every indicator is classified OK / CAUTION / WARN with green–yellow–red status, an alert feed with acknowledgements, trend history charts (160 samples per metric), a live animated ECG/PPG waveform, a clickable human body map where each body system shows its metric, finding, and recommended action, and an anomaly/scenario engine (you can inject a medical event and watch the system detect, alert, and guide).
Clinical decision support: when a reading goes red, the system displays concrete guidance on what to do — not just the number.
Alongside the OS, we designed ASTRO-BOOK — the concept hardware it would run on: a 2.77 kg solar-powered space medical laptop integrating an octa-core radiation-hardened RISC-V SoC with a 32-TOPS NPU, a 2 TB rad-hard NVMe SSD, medical sensors (6-lead ECG + BIA palm pads, QUS bone-density probe with zero radiation, CMUT ultrasound, LOC blood-analysis lab, 60 GHz contactless radar), a cold-plasma sterilization waste unit, and an integrated triple-junction solar array — documented with a full electrical schematic and an interactive 3D model.

How does it work?
The OS is real, working software, not a mockup. It is a freestanding 32-bit C kernel with no libc: GRUB boots it via a Multiboot2 header, the kernel parses the Multiboot2 framebuffer tag to get a 1024×768×32 display, sets up its own IDT/interrupt system, runs a PIT-driven 100 Hz scheduler loop (~25 fps render loop), and drives polled PS/2 keyboard + mouse input. On top of that we wrote our own mini GUI framework (windows, buttons, widgets, 8×16 bitmap font, rounded rects, gradients) and the telemetry/clinical engine in pure C.
Build pipeline: NASM (boot/ISR asm) + i686 GCC (freestanding C) → ld with a custom linker script → grub-mkrescue → bootable ISO (tested in QEMU; the repo ships astrohealth.iso and astrohealth.bin).
The concept hardware is specified with a complete electrical architecture: a 28 V mil-spec power tree through a GaN multi-stage PMIC (96.8% efficiency) feeding regulated rails (+12 V pumps, +5 V sonar/touch, +3.3 V SSD, 0.8–1.0 V CPU core), a 4 kV galvanic isolation barrier for the medical analog front-end, and a system bus matrix (MIPI-DSI, LVDS/SPI, I²C/UART, SpaceWire/MIL-STD-1553, PWM actuator lines) — all drawn in the schematic SVG, with the physical layout as a Wavefront OBJ model and a Three.js viewer with exploded view, part inspection, and lid/explode animation.
What benefits does it have?
Zero ground dependence: all diagnosis, alerting, and guidance run locally on the spacecraft — no downlink latency, no connectivity required.
One glance, whole crew: color-coded status bands mean a crewmember without medical training can spot a problem in seconds; the body map turns an abnormal number into "what it affects → what to do."
Radiation-free diagnostics where it matters: bone density via ultrasound (QUS) instead of X-ray DEXA; contactless radar and optical/impedance sensors instead of invasive hardware; cold-plasma sterilization instead of consumable biocides.
Built to survive space: the hardware spec addresses the actual failure modes of computing in space — latch-up immunity, TMR registers, pSLC flash with STT-MRAM cache for 20-year data retention, AES-256 hardware encryption for private medical records.
Lightweight and verifiable: the OS boots in seconds on any x86 machine from a single 55 KB kernel — no cloud, no container, no dependencies.
What do you hope to achieve?
Complete the OS roadmap: chart engine polish, a timed-measurement scheduler (mission routine reminders), gamification (points/streaks to keep crews engaged with daily health tasks), and environment profiles (ship / station / rover / lunar base).
Demonstrate that a purpose-built OS — where the health app is the kernel's first-class citizen, not an afterthought app on Linux — is a credible architecture for autonomous crew health autonomy on Artemis-era missions.
Have the interactive 3D hardware concept serve as a concrete, reviewable vision of the flight computer this software targets.
Tools, languages, and software used
Languages: C (freestanding, GNU C11, no libc) and x86 assembly (NASM) for the OS; HTML/CSS/JavaScript (Three.js r128, canvas-generated textures) for the interactive 3D viewer; Mermaid for architecture diagrams; Wavefront OBJ for the hardware model.
Toolchain: GCC (-m32 -ffreestanding -fno-pie -mno-sse), NASM, GNU ld with custom linker.ld, grub-file/grub-mkrescue/xorriso, GNU Make.
Testing/debugging: QEMU (qemu-system-i386, with GTK display and GDB remote-debug target), serial-port logging, VGA text fallback for early boot errors.
Design/diagramming: hand-built SVG electrical schematic (power tree, compute/storage core, isolated medical AFE, dual-touch display controller), Mermaid flowcharts (boot flow, build pipeline, dashboard layout).
Platform: Ubuntu Linux development machine; everything builds with make and runs with make run.

projectDetails.summary:
TerraTwin is an interactive, data-driven planetary atlas developed to identify and compare potential Earth analog environments for future Moon and Mars exploration missions.

Addressing the challenge of finding reliable terrestrial analog sites, TerraTwin goes beyond visual similarities to evaluate measurable terrain characteristics. Using NASA and USGS datasets, the platform analyzes parameters such as slope distribution, local relief, and terrain ruggedness to compare planetary reference locations with candidate environments on Earth.

At its core, TerraTwin features the Terrain Analog Similarity Index (TASI), a transparent multi-criteria scoring model that helps users assess and rank potential analog sites. It highlights locations such as Egypt's Western Desert and Gilf Kebir, turning complex geospatial data into accessible interactive maps and comparisons.

By supporting more informed site selection and realistic pre-mission testing, TerraTwin aims to reduce engineering uncertainty and help prepare safer, more reliable planetary exploration missions.
projectDetails.details:
TerraTwin – Detailed Project Description

1. Project Overview

TerraTwin is an interactive planetary atlas designed to help researchers and mission planners identify and evaluate potential terrestrial analog environments for future Moon and Mars exploration missions.

The project addresses a major challenge in planetary exploration: an Earth location may visually resemble the surface of Mars or the Moon without sharing the physical terrain characteristics required for realistic rover testing and mission preparation. TerraTwin replaces subjective visual comparisons with a structured, data-driven approach to terrain analysis.

2. How the Platform Works

TerraTwin combines planetary and terrestrial geospatial datasets to compare selected reference locations with potential Earth analog sites.

Its main workflow consists of four stages:

A. Scientific Data Integration

The platform uses NASA and USGS geospatial resources, including Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) elevation products, NASA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) elevation data, and relevant thermal datasets where available.

B. Terrain Analysis

Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) are processed to extract measurable terrain characteristics, including:

  • Slope Distribution: Evaluates the steepness and distribution of terrain gradients.
  • Local Relief: Measures elevation variation within a defined neighborhood.
  • Terrain Ruggedness: Characterizes surface elevation variability and roughness.

C. Terrain Analog Similarity Index (TASI)

TerraTwin introduces an experimental, transparent multi-criteria scoring model called the Terrain Analog Similarity Index (TASI).

The model combines normalized terrain metrics using the following proposed weighting scheme:

  • Slope Distribution: 40%
  • Local Relief: 35%
  • Terrain Ruggedness: 25%

The resulting score provides a comparative indication of terrain similarity between a planetary reference site and an Earth candidate location. It is intended as a decision-support metric rather than a definitive scientific validation of an analog site.

D. Interactive Geospatial Visualization

Users can explore candidate locations, inspect terrain information, compare locations, and view analytical results through an interactive mapping interface.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

TerraTwin aims to make planetary analog research more accessible, transparent, and reproducible.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Supporting the identification of promising terrestrial environments for rover mobility experiments and equipment testing.
  • Reducing reliance on subjective visual similarity when selecting analog sites.
  • Helping researchers identify terrain mismatches before conducting field experiments.
  • Highlighting scientifically interesting terrestrial environments, including Egypt's Western Desert.
  • Making complex planetary and geospatial information easier to explore through an interactive interface.

Ultimately, TerraTwin aims to support better-informed mission preparation and reduce engineering uncertainty before future planetary exploration missions.

4. Creativity and Innovation

The central innovation of TerraTwin is its shift from appearance-based analog selection to quantitative terrain comparison.

Rather than simply displaying images of deserts and planetary surfaces, the platform combines geospatial data processing, measurable terrain characteristics, and a transparent scoring methodology in one interactive environment.

The TASI framework also makes the comparison process easier to understand by showing how different terrain characteristics contribute to the overall similarity score.

The project further emphasizes Egypt's potential contribution to planetary analog research by bringing attention to its desert environments as candidates for future scientific investigation.

5. Factors Considered

The team considered several factors when designing the comparison methodology:

  • Terrain slope and elevation variability.
  • Local topographic relief.
  • Surface ruggedness and terrain complexity.
  • Spatial resolution and compatibility between datasets.
  • Data quality, missing values, and measurement limitations.
  • The importance of transparent calculations and reproducible comparisons.

We recognize that terrain similarity alone cannot establish complete environmental equivalence. Soil composition, mineralogy, atmospheric conditions, thermal behavior, and mechanical properties require additional datasets and dedicated analysis.

6. Technology and Development Tools

The project uses a combination of web development technologies and scientific computing tools.

Frontend:

  • React and TypeScript
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Leaflet / React-Leaflet for interactive maps
  • Recharts for analytical visualizations

Backend and Scientific Processing:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • NumPy and Pandas
  • Rasterio
  • SciPy

Geospatial Data:

  • NASA MOLA elevation products
  • NASA SRTM elevation data
  • Relevant NASA thermal datasets
  • USGS geological and terrestrial reference resources

The platform is designed as a browser-based application to make its maps, comparisons, and analytical results accessible without specialized desktop GIS software.

7. Current Implementation and Future Development

The current project focuses on its delivered Mars-to-Earth terrain comparison capabilities, including interactive mapping, terrain metric analysis, and the TASI scoring framework, to the extent implemented in the submitted version.

Future development plans include integrating NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data for lunar polar terrain analysis, expanding mineralogical and multispectral comparisons, and incorporating additional environmental and mechanical parameters.

These improvements would extend TerraTwin from a terrain-focused comparison platform into a more comprehensive planetary analog research tool.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: El Gatto
projectDetails.summary:
Ask a kid what happens to a rover when its mission ends, and you’ll probably hear a movie plot. The real story is better. Machines from decades of missions are still sitting on the Moon and Mars, silent, right where they stopped, and each one changed what we know about the universe. Ghosts of Space brings them back to tell their stories.

Our 3D interactive website lets kids and teens explore the vehicles humanity left behind. They can spin, zoom, and inspect real 3D models, then dive into each vehicle’s story through real mission footage and see what it actually discovered. Every vehicle they learn about earns XP, so curiosity becomes progress.

The adventure doesn’t stop at the screen. Our custom-built console, shaped like our cat mascot El Gatto (yes, that’s our team name too), connects to the website and runs a mini-game. Players drive a rover across the Moon, collecting samples and dodging hazards.

Space isn’t magic. It’s engineering, patience, and discovery, and that’s exactly what makes it exciting.
projectDetails.details:
Brief description

Our project is a whole system that complements itself. It's divided, roughly, into three main parts: the 3D interactive website that has the rovers still left on the Moon and Mars, where the user can explore, inspect, and learn about each piece of equipment (except those that are NOT standing on any of the two surfaces), the video integrated with NASA's media (e.g., videos and sounds recorded of astronauts on these missions), with the voice narration performed by the team members telling the story of the rover, and a custom-made console with a playable game that was programmed using a 16-Megabytes ESP on a (128*160 pixels) screen.

The website includes quizzes about each rover after viewers watch the video and learn about it. When the player gets the quiz right, they receive a power-up in the console game. The score that the player gets is recorded on a leaderboard on the website for the database of all players. The player's XP on the website increases each time they learn about a rover.

(Technical details: Ghosts of Space is a React and TypeScript web app built with Vite. Its 3D worlds run on three.js and React Three Fiber, with custom shaders that render the Moon and Mars realistically from real NASA elevation data. A Node.js and Express backend stores progress in SQLite and talks to our ESP32 handheld console over WebSockets, while all mission content lives in validated JSON files.)

Descriptions about the rovers, alongside videos and sounds of astronauts, were retrieved from NASA's website. A demonstrated example of the usage of the website and one of the small videos for a rover is in the following video:

The console is programmed just one time using the Arduino IDE (C++ programming language). Then, it's put into its designed case (the cat mascot, El Gatto), which was 3D printed. It weighs 111 grams and was printed in about 3.5 hours. The console has a joystick and a button as the cat's eyes.

(Technical details: The cat mascot model was designed in Fusion 360 software)

Expected Impact

Ghosts of Space turns forgotten hardware into a reason to stay curious. By pairing real 3D models and mission footage with play, we expect kids and teens to leave with a more accurate picture of space research: slow, collaborative, built on engineering, and still producing knowledge long after a mission ends. The XP system and the El Gatto console give them a reason to come back, and every return means another vehicle learned. Because the website runs in any browser with no installation, science teachers can use it in class as a ready-made resource. To show real learning gains rather than assume them, we will measure understanding with a short quiz before and after the experience.

Further Recommendations

To reach a larger audience, the next step is expanding beyond the Moon and Mars to hardware across the solar system, such as Voyager in deep space and the Huygens probe on Titan. The stories should also be translated into Arabic and other languages. Partnerships with schools and science museums would bring the experience to students who would never find it alone, supported by a teacher dashboard with lesson plans and class leaderboards. Commercially, the website can stay free while revenue comes from selling the El Gatto console as an educational kit, licensing to schools and museums, and new mission packs.

projectDetails.name: Project Elly
projectDetails.summary: The Last Known Signal is a Unity game that teaches how real space missions are designed. A relay satellite has gone silent and the player, working from a NASA-style mission base, must design and fly a rescue. In Design Mode and the Planner, the player balances ship mass, redundancy, power and mission days against the limits of a real launch vehicle (NASA's Space Launch System). Then they fly through missions where real NASA data creates the challenges: solar flares and coronal mass ejections, close approaches of near-Earth asteroids, radio signal delay, falling sunlight at distance, and a rocky exoplanet (TRAPPIST-1 e). Every debrief shows the NASA source behind what just happened. It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by letting players experience the trade-offs mission designers face, which makes space-mission engineering understandable to students and the public.
projectDetails.details:
Main use. A player-facing way to learn mission design trade-offs: a heavier ship is safer but harder to launch, and every extra system costs power and mass. The result is a "planned success" figure that changes with the player's choices and with events during the mission.

What it does (built, from the project log)

A story campaign of missions (M1 and M2 ground tests and launch preparation, M3 deep-space flight, M4 landing on a rocky exoplanet, a final call-home scene) with a risk gauge, a father's-log story, and a mascot guide named Pip.

A reusable Planner where the player trades part grade and redundancy against a mass budget, with a live resource box (power, mission days, launch vehicle) and a 5-step skippable tutorial.

Design Mode with destinations, a build screen, a launch-vehicle picker (SLS Block 1, 1B, Block 2) and a lift check that blocks launch with a stated reason if the ship is too heavy.

M3 free 3D flight with floating origin and no soft-locks, and four challenge sites. Each site opens a NASA DATA card (dataset, source link, why NASA cares, real values), offers three choices with costs, and changes the player's supplies, hull, power and planned success. A seeded random picks the site order, so runs differ.

Flight visuals: Earth, Moon and Sun, solar-flare bursts, asteroid close-pass warnings, a comms beam with visible light delay, eclipse dimming.

A skippable opening scene of about 38 seconds, and subtitled narration with 43 voice clips.

A DATA & SOURCES screen, a NASA DATA block on every debrief, and an end card listing the datasets that shaped the run.

Verification so far: 87 automated EditMode tests (86 pass, 1 explicit skip) and a Windows player build that succeeded with a smoke run that logged no errors.

How it works. Game data is loaded from CSV files in the project. Each file has a source link and retrieval date, and every dataset is registered in data_sources.csv. The risk model combines the player's plan with event outcomes into a success probability. Choices carry costs; each scenario has a free fallback option so the game never soft-locks.

Tools. Unity 6000.6.9f1 with the Universal Render Pipeline, C#, HLSL shaders, Blender and Node.js scripts for models, Piper text-to-speech for narration, Git. Language of the game and all content: English.

Limitations

NASA data is a snapshot retrieved on 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14, not live.

Reliabilities, subsystem masses, mass budgets, supply days, mission days and event costs are game-balance values, not NASA data, and are tagged on screen.

In M3 the Mars and Moon rows from Horizons are story stand-ins for the ship and the relay; the Mars-to-Moon distance is derived and labelled so. Solar flux is derived from the inverse-square law and labelled so.

Event scenarios use real values but the situations themselves are fictional.

Narration is synthetic placeholder-quality voice.

A full human play-through, a frame-rate check, and a human re-check of each NASA source link were still pending when this was written. ⟦update once done⟧

Windows only.

Future plans

Live data feeds instead of snapshots.

More missions and destinations, human-voiced narration, other platforms.

projectDetails.name: AgriLens
projectDetails.summary:
AgriLens is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that helps farmers make smarter crop rotation decisions using NASA Earth observation data.

Farmers face increasing challenges from changing temperatures, unpredictable rainfall, water scarcity, and declining soil health. AgriLens addresses these problems by combining NASA's historical climate data with local soil conditions, crop requirements, and farmers' priorities to evaluate different crop rotation strategies.

Through an interactive interface, farmers can explore alternative planting sequences, compare their expected effects on water consumption, soil health, and climate suitability, and understand the reasoning behind each recommendation. Instead of presenting complex scientific datasets, AgriLens translates them into clear, practical insights that support better agricultural decisions.

By connecting space-based observations with everyday farming needs, AgriLens aims to make scientific data accessible, help farmers use resources more efficiently, protect long-term soil productivity, and build resilience against changing environmental conditions.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem

Farmers must make decisions that affect their land for years, often without easy access to reliable environmental information. Choosing the wrong crop rotation can increase water consumption, expose crops to unfavorable temperatures, and reduce long-term soil productivity.

Although NASA provides decades of valuable Earth observation data, translating that information into practical farming decisions remains difficult for people without scientific or technical backgrounds.

Our Solution: AgriLens

AgriLens is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that uses NASA climate data to help farmers evaluate and improve their crop rotation strategies.

Rather than simply displaying weather statistics, AgriLens connects historical environmental conditions with agricultural knowledge to answer a practical question: Which crop rotation is better suited to my farm, and why?

How It Works

  1. Farm Setup: The farmer selects a region, provides basic farm information, and defines their existing crop rotation.
  2. NASA Data Analysis: AgriLens processes historical temperature and precipitation data from NASA POWER to understand local climate patterns and environmental risks.
  3. Crop Evaluation: The system considers crop growing seasons, water requirements, temperature sensitivity, and agricultural compatibility.
  4. Rotation Comparison: A decision engine evaluates the farmer's original rotation alongside two alternative strategies, comparing water requirements, historical heat exposure, and soil-related considerations.
  5. Climate Scenarios: Farmers can explore how different rotations perform under average, unusually hot, or unusually dry historical conditions.
  6. Actionable Results: The platform presents understandable comparisons, trade-offs, and explanations so farmers can make informed decisions based on their priorities.

What Makes AgriLens Different?

AgriLens focuses on turning scientific data into decisions rather than simply visualizing it.

Its main innovation is comparing complete crop rotation strategies instead of recommending individual crops in isolation. A crop that performs well in one season may not be the best choice when considering the entire rotation, water requirements, and future soil productivity.

The platform also makes the reasoning behind its evaluations understandable. Farmers can see why one rotation may be preferable for water conservation while another may offer better suitability under historical temperature conditions.

By comparing multiple climate scenarios, AgriLens helps users understand trade-offs instead of presenting one supposedly perfect solution.

Technical Approach

AgriLens uses a web interface connected to a modular backend organized around three main components:

  • NASA Climate Service: Retrieves, validates, and processes historical climate records from NASA POWER.
  • Crop and Agriculture Service: Organizes agricultural reference data, including growing seasons, crop water requirements, and rotation considerations.
  • Comparison and Decision Engine: Combines climate and crop information to evaluate rotation alternatives and generate explainable comparisons.

The system uses NASA POWER's historical daily temperature and precipitation records, agricultural reference information, data-processing logic, and web APIs. Its modular architecture separates environmental data retrieval, agricultural knowledge, and decision-making.

Expected Impact

AgriLens aims to make satellite-derived climate information useful to farmers who would otherwise struggle to interpret it.

By helping farmers compare agricultural strategies before implementing them, the platform can support more efficient water use, better climate adaptation, and more sustainable crop rotation planning.

Ultimately, our goal is to bridge the gap between space-based scientific observations and everyday agricultural decisions, making data-driven farming more accessible, understandable, and practical.

projectDetails.name: Project ElMazra3a EL sa3ida
projectDetails.summary:
welcome to ElMazra3a El Sa3ida  . it's an interactive agricultural decision-support tool and simulation platform tailored for smallholder farmers in Egypt & America  . It integrates an interactive field grid with satellite-derived Earth observations to track local soil health, root depth, and nutrient levels across farm plots.

How It Addresses the Challenge?   The platform directly addresses the challenge by combining  NASA climate datasets including long-term temperature trends and soil moisture observations with localized agricultural parameters and farmer priorities. Farmers can run real-time stress tests to simulate severe heatwaves and irrigation water reductions, allowing them to evaluate multi-season crop rotation strategies and project financial risks across historical weather patterns using probabilistic yield models.
Why It Is Important ? Faced with unpredictable climate fluctuations, water scarcity, and degrading soil quality, growers need data-driven rotation strategies to build farm resilience . By guiding strategic crop sequencing such as introducing nitrogen-fixing legumes after cereal crops the system restores soil fertility, reduces synthetic fertilizer reliance, conserves irrigation water, breaks recurring pest cycles, and safeguards farmer livelihoods even during adverse climate years
projectDetails.details:
ElMazra3a EL sa3ida — Crop Rotation Advisor is a bilingual (Arabic/English) web app that recommends a 3-season crop rotation for a specific field, based on NASA Earth observation data and a climate risk simulation.

1. Choose your land and previous crop

  • The farmer picks Egypt or the USA.
    • Egypt presets: Nile Delta – Gharbia, Minya, New Valley (priced in EGP/feddan).
    • USA presets: California Central Valley, Iowa Corn Belt, Kansas Wheat Belt (priced in USD/acre).
    • Any point on the map can also be clicked to update the coordinates.
  • The previous crop (Wheat, Potato, Tomato or Maize) sets the plant family. For example, wheat is Poaceae, and the app uses that to catch rotation clashes.
  • A toggle overlays the NASA MODIS NDVI vegetation-health layer on the satellite map.
  • The header shows live NASA indicators: the 10-year temperature anomaly (+0.74°C), SMAP soil moisture (46%) and the projected savings (11.1 urea sacks and 22% water).

2. Climate stress testing

  • One-click presets (Mild Season, Moderate Heat, Extreme Drought) and two sliders: extra heat wave (+0 to +4.5°C) and irrigation water deficit (0 to -45%).
  • Four data tabs: Soil Moisture (SMAP root-zone), Crop Health, 10-Yr Climate and SAR Radar. The soil moisture tab shows the root-zone value and a plain-language irrigation tip.

3. Compare three pathways

  • Smart Balanced Rotation (recommended): Soybean → Sugar Beet → Alfalfa/Berseem. Legumes fix nitrogen and cut urea use.
  • Cash-First Intensive (high risk): Maize → Potato → Wheat. It needs about 7.2 extra urea sacks and shows a botanical clash warning (-18%) because maize after wheat repeats the Poaceae family.
  • Climate & Water Resilient: Fava Bean → Sunflower → Sugar Beet. Deep-rooted, heat-tolerant crops that save 37% water.
  • Each card shows expected median income, worst-year income, urea sacks saved or needed and water saved.

4. Risk and tradeoff analysis for the selected pathway

  • A radar chart compares it against the cash baseline on five axes (the recommended rotation scores Cash Return 90, Water Saving 64, Soil Fertility 92, Heat Tolerance 61, Pest Break 87).
  • 10-year profit and risk bands show worst year (P10), median (P50) and best year (P90), with the cash baseline marked.
  • A 10-year historical replay (2015–2024) marks heatwave years in amber.
  • A "Why does this rotation protect your income and soil?" panel summarizes the logic.

5. AI Agronomy Copilot and field grid

  • The Gemini-powered copilot gives a plain-language recommendation based on the field's NDVI and root moisture.
  • The interactive field grid models 1 feddan (or acre) as 9 plots across three seasons. Each plot shows its crop, family and soil health (74–82%), plus season nitrogen (+50 kg), water use (1,900 m³) and root depth (115 cm).

6. Regional Data Blog

  • For six Egyptian governorates (Gharbia, Dakahlia, Beheira, Minya, Fayoum, New Valley) and the three US belts.
  • It includes region cards, monthly NASA POWER temperature charts, monthly GWETROOT root-wetness charts, an interactive correlation explorer and a 7×7 Pearson correlation matrix.
  • A crop suitability heatmap (11 crops × regions, scored 0–100) responds to the heat and water-weight sliders.
  • Key EDA findings and a "data quality caveats and how our engine solved them" section.

7. Farm Rescue (game)

  • A pixel-art teaching game built in Godot 4 and embedded in the site. It has a start screen, "How to play", saved best scores and a reset option.
  • Three scenarios on the same nine plots:

  • Players sow Wheat, Corn, Barley or Sunflower, each with its own water cost, growth time and maximum yield. They use the Water, Harvest and Plough-in tools while weather changes weekly (clear skies, overcast, heatwave, rain).
  • Each plot tracks moisture, salinity, nutrients and growth. Rotating to a different plant family restores nutrients, and heavy irrigation adds salt from the well.
  • The final score is out of 1,000: Crop Yield 30%, Water Efficiency 25%, Soil Health 25% and Sustainability 20%. A "Season in review" panel explains what went right or wrong.

Benefits

  • Lower costs: less urea (11.1 sacks saved in the Gharbia example) and 22% less irrigation water.
  • Income protection: the worst-year view compares downside risk across pathways, not only averages.
  • Soil health: legume rotation restores nitrogen and breaks pest cycles.
  • Accessibility: Arabic/English, light/dark mode, local currency and area units, and a game for beginners.
  • Transparency: a "Raw NASA JSON" view and a "Judge Pitch" mode.

Intended impact

  • Give farmers satellite-based guidance on rotation choices, so decisions are based on measured soil moisture and heat trends.
  • Make farms more resilient to heat and drought and lower the water and fertilizer footprint of farming.
  • Use Farm Rescue to teach the same concepts to young people and beginner farmers.
  • Support regional planning: the heatmap shows which crops suit which governorate, for example New Valley's much lower suitability for maize and soybean.

Tools and technologies

  • NASA data: SMAP (soil moisture), MODIS Terra NDVI via GIBS, NASA POWER (2015–2024), MERRA-2 GWETROOT and Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter.
  • Mapping: Leaflet with Esri World Imagery.
  • AI: Google Gemini for the Agronomy Copilot.
  • Game engine: Godot 4, served from the site's assets.
  • [Your stack]: front-end framework, languages, charting library, backend and hosting, and any AI-assisted tools you used.
  • Hardware: none beyond a browser, so it works on ordinary phones and laptops.

How it's creative

  • It turns NASA data into a decision and a money figure, not a dashboard.
  • It shows risk as P10/P50/P90 bands from a 10-year replay, so farmers see the worst case.
  • The stress sliders let users test their own farm against heat and drought before the season.
  • It flags botanical-family clashes automatically.
  • The AI copilot explains each recommendation in plain language.
  • Farm Rescue turns rotation, salinity and water budgeting into three playable challenges.
  • One engine works in two very different regions (Egypt and the US).

Factors the team considered

  • Coarse data: MERRA-2 cells are 0.5° × 0.625°, so Gharbia and Dakahlia share one cell. The engine separates them with local soil type and 250 m MODIS NDVI.
  • Climate risk needs more than one year: it uses the full 2015–2024 series to build the bands.
  • Irrigation isn't captured by the model: GWETROOT doesn't see canal pumping and NDVI is a single-date snapshot, so the app adds water-deficit sliders and SAR backscatter.
  • Regional differences: New Valley has the highest aridity stress (21% root moisture, NDVI 0.37), and Fayoum loses root moisture in summer, so recommendations vary by region.
  • Audience: language, units, currency and a beginner-friendly game. The game is labeled as simplified teaching data for a school activity.

projectDetails.name: Cosmic Tracker
projectDetails.summary:
Cosmic Tracker is an interactive web platform built for the NASA SPHEREx Challenge to bridge the gap between complex astrophysical data and human curiosity by visualizing the user journey across the cosmos. NASA’s SPHEREx mission surveys the entire sky in near-infrared light to uncover the origins of the universe, galaxies, and life-sustaining water in planetary systems. However, raw spectroscopic and astronomical datasets from archives like IRSA, Gaia, and NEOSSat are often difficult for students, educators, and space enthusiasts to interpret.

Cosmic Tracker transforms these multi-dimensional datasets into an intuitive, story-driven visual journey. Instead of navigating static tables, users embark on a guided cosmic exploration—tracking how infrared light travels from distant galaxies and interstellar ices to space telescopes, and interacting with real celestial coordinates, spectral signatures, and 3D spatial maps. 

By integrating open-source datasets from NASA’s SPHEREx and NEOWISE archives alongside Canadian Space Agency (NEOSSat) and ESA (Gaia) resources, our platform democratizes space science. Cosmic Tracker makes deep-space spectroscopy accessible, educational, and engaging, inspiring the next generation of explorers to understand our cosmic origins through interactive data visualization.
projectDetails.details: What it does & How it works: Cosmic Tracker is an interactive web platform designed specifically for the NASA SPHEREx challenge. It ingests and parses raw spectroscopic and astronomical data from missions like SPHEREx, Gaia, and NEOSSat, transforming complex numbers into an engaging, story-driven "user journey." Users can navigate an interactive 2D/3D interface that simulates traveling through the near-infrared universe, allowing them to trace how light and celestial bodies are mapped across the sky, examine spectral signatures, and explore cosmic coordinates dynamically. Benefits & Intended Impact: The project democratizes astrophysics. It bridges the gap between complex scientific archives and public curiosity. By turning dense astronomical data into an accessible and visual exploration, Cosmic Tracker empowers students, educators, and space enthusiasts to learn about the origins of the universe, galaxies, and water without needing a PhD in astrophysics. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, & Software Used: - Frontend: React.js, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (for 3D space and journey visualizations). - Backend & Data Processing: Python, Flask, Pandas, and Astropy. - Data Sources & Archives: NASA SPHEREx Mission Archive, ESA Gaia Archive, and Canadian Space Agency (NEOSSat) datasets. - AI/Super Intelligence (SI) Tools: Utilized Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist with code optimization, debugging, and structuring educational descriptive metadata (fully acknowledged per challenge guidelines). Creativity & Design Considerations: We focused on "gamifying" and humanizing data exploration. Instead of presenting users with static tables or boring charts, Cosmic Tracker turns data analysis into an immersive adventure. We carefully considered UI/UX design to ensure smooth performance in browser-based 3D environments, making space science visually stunning, intuitive, and interactive for all age groups.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.

projectDetails.name: DELTA 2100 — THE LAST LINE OF DEFENSE
projectDetails.summary:
DELTA 2100 — The Last Line of Defense is an interactive environmental risk intelligence platform built for NASA’s Earth System Trend Detective challenge. Coastal regions and river deltas face growing threats from sea-level rise, land subsidence, erosion, and flooding, but the information about them is scattered across many sources. DELTA 2100 brings it together in three connected experiences:

The Past – Disaster Archive: Explore real locations hit by severe environmental disasters, land loss, or displacement, and learn what happened, why, and how communities were affected.
The Present & Future – Risk Intelligence: Investigate five vulnerable regions: the Nile Delta, Ganges–Brahmaputra Delta, Mississippi Delta, Venice, and the Maldives. Use satellite imagery, environmental indicators, and regional risk data to see how these areas are changing and to visualize possible scenarios toward 2100.
The Future – Survival Simulation: Play an interactive game, make decisions, and test protective strategies to see how today’s actions shape tomorrow’s outcomes.

By linking historical evidence, environmental trends, and future scenarios in one accessible platform, DELTA 2100 helps people understand these risks and the importance of acting before it is too late.
projectDetails.details:
DELTA 2100 — Project Details

1. What Does DELTA 2100 Do?

DELTA 2100 is an interactive climate-risk intelligence and environmental awareness platform designed to explore how climate change is reshaping vulnerable coastal regions and river deltas around the world.

The platform focuses on three interconnected experiences that transform environmental information into meaningful, accessible insights.

1. Disaster Archive — When Nature Changes Everything

This section documents real-world environmental disasters and disappearing or severely affected locations. Users can explore historical events, discover the environmental factors behind them, and compare before-and-after imagery to understand how landscapes and communities have changed over time.

Rather than presenting climate change as abstract statistics, this archive connects scientific and environmental changes to real places, real events, and their human consequences.

2. Risk Intelligence — Explore the Threat

This section allows users to explore five vulnerable geographical regions and understand the environmental threats they face.

It focuses on key factors such as sea-level rise, coastal erosion, land subsidence, extreme rainfall, and flooding. Through geographical visualization and environmental indicators, users can explore why these locations are vulnerable and how climate-related pressures may affect their future.

3. LAST 100 YEARS — A Survival Simulation

This interactive experience places users in the role of decision-makers responsible for protecting vulnerable communities.

Users explore possible future scenarios, make strategic decisions, and allocate limited resources between different adaptation and protection strategies. The simulation demonstrates how decisions made today can influence the resilience of communities over time.

The experience is designed to make long-term environmental challenges understandable through interaction, exploration, and decision-making.

2. Benefits and Intended Impact

DELTA 2100 aims to:

  • Raise awareness of the environmental threats facing coastal communities and river deltas.
  • Make historical environmental disasters easier to understand through visual storytelling.
  • Help users explore geographical vulnerability and climate-related risks.
  • Demonstrate the importance of early preparation and climate adaptation.
  • Encourage informed decision-making through interactive future scenarios.
  • Make Earth observation and environmental information more accessible to students, researchers, educators, and the public.

Our ultimate goal is to bridge the gap between environmental data and public understanding, transforming complex scientific information into an experience that encourages awareness, preparedness, and action.

3. Technology and Development

The platform is developed as a web-based interactive experience.

The development work includes:

  • Frontend: Web technologies for building the user interface and interactive experiences.
  • Backend: Node.js and Express.js for server-side logic and API development.
  • Database: MongoDB for managing and organizing application data.
  • Data Visualization: Interactive geographical and environmental visualizations.
  • Deployment: Web-based deployment to make the platform accessible online.

The architecture is designed to support the integration of Earth observation datasets, geographical information, historical records, and future scenario simulations.

4. Creativity and Innovation

DELTA 2100 combines three approaches that are often presented separately: historical environmental storytelling, geographical risk exploration, and interactive future decision-making.

Its creative strength lies in connecting the past, present, and possible future within one experience.

Users do not simply read about climate change. They explore places that have already experienced environmental disasters, investigate locations facing growing risks, and experience the consequences of strategic decisions through simulation.

By combining scientific context, visual storytelling, geographical exploration, and interactive decision-making, DELTA 2100 turns a complex global challenge into an engaging and understandable experience.

5. Factors Considered

The project considers:

  • Environmental vulnerability and geographical differences between regions.
  • The relationship between sea-level rise, erosion, subsidence, and flooding.
  • The human, ecological, agricultural, and infrastructural consequences of environmental change.
  • The importance of reliable scientific sources and transparent data attribution.
  • The accessibility of environmental information to non-specialist audiences.
  • The uncertainty of long-term climate scenarios and the need to communicate possible futures rather than guaranteed predictions.

DELTA 2100 is built around one central idea:

The future of vulnerable communities should not be discovered only after it is too late.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project Energy is good
projectDetails.summary:
Farm Profile & Goals: Configured for District A with Loam soil and Low water availability during the Kharif season. It targets a 50% max risk tolerance and a minimum profit floor of ₹10,000.  
​Weather & Forecast: The 7-day forecast predicts a cumulative 65.0 mm of rainfall with peaks on Oct 19, 24, and 25. It warns of potential surface runoff, waterlogging, and high fungal pathogen risk due to 94% humidity.  
​NASA POWER Integration: Satellite parameters (temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, solar irradiance, soil wetness, and wind speed) supplement ground telemetry to refine evapotranspiration models, crop maturity calculations, and yield forecasts.  
​Action Plan: Farmers should balance drainage with moisture retention, use mulch to manage high thermal stress, apply preventative fungicides, and input their exact acreage and capital budget into the Smart Crop Advisor to select resilient Kharif crops.
projectDetails.details: ​1. Farm Configuration & Economic Filters (Smart Crop Advisor) ​Location & Soil: The farm is set in District A on Loam soil, which offers balanced drainage, nutrient retention, and broad crop compatibility. ​Resource Constraints: Operates under a "Low" water availability classification (restricting water-intensive crops) during the Kharif growing season. ​Financial & Risk Parameters: Configured with a maximum risk tolerance of 50% to filter out high yield/price volatility, and enforces a minimum net profit expectation floor of ₹10,000. ​Pending Inputs: The user still needs to input their exact farm size in hectares and their total investment budget into the sidebar. ​2. Local Meteorology & 7-Day Forecast (District A) ​Reference Observation (Oct 19, 2025): Recorded ambient temperatures ranged from 22^{\circ}C to 31^{\circ}C (9^{\circ}C diurnal spread) alongside 94% relative humidity, overcast skies, and 18.2 mm of daily rainfall. ​7-Day Precipitation & Temperature Trend: ​The week accumulates 65.0 mm of rainfall, featuring distinct wet bursts on Oct 19 (18.2 mm), Oct 24 (14.4 mm), and Oct 25 (17.1 mm). ​Mid-week days (Oct 20–22) transition to clear/sunny conditions with daytime highs peaking up to 35^{\circ}C. ​Operational Weather Advisories: ​Heavy Rainfall Warning: Surface runoff and waterlogging are likely on loam soils during peak events, requiring verified field drainage channels. ​Fungal Pathogen Risk: Prolonged canopy wetness combined with warm daytime highs (29^{\circ}C-35^{\circ}C) creates high vulnerability for foliar fungal outbreaks. ​3. NASA POWER Satellite Agroclimatology Integration ​The report integrates 0.5^{\circ} \times 0.5^{\circ} satellite and reanalysis data from NASA POWER (GMAO MERRA-2 and GPM IMERG) to bridge gaps in ground station telemetry: ​T2M_MAX / T2M_MIN: Validates thermal ranges (18^{\circ}C-35^{\circ}C) and computes Growing Degree Days (GDD) for Kharif crop maturity. ​PRECTOTCORR: Supplies bias-corrected total precipitation to evaluate whether low water availability requires supplemental irrigation. ​RH2M: Benchmarks the 94% humidity spike against seasonal norms to calibrate disease alerts. ​ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN: Quantifies photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) during sunny vs. cloudy intervals to refine yield forecasts. ​GWETTOP / GWETROOT: Tracks 0–5 cm and 0–100 cm soil wetness in loam soil between rainfall pulses. ​WS2M: Measures 2-meter wind speed to feed into FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET_0) calculations. ​4. Integrated Agronomic Synthesis & Action Matrix ​Moisture vs. Drainage: Construct perimeter bunds or farm ponds to capture surplus runoff from the 65.0 mm weekly rainfall while preventing acute waterlogging. ​Thermal Stress & ET_0 Management: High mid-week temperatures (34^{\circ}C-35^{\circ}C) under clear skies increase evapotranspiration; retaining crop residue mulch helps preserve surface soil moisture. ​Proactive Disease Control: Preventative biological or low-cost fungicide applications should be prioritized within the budget to protect the ₹10,000 minimum net profit threshold against high humidity risks. ​Model Execution Readiness: Entering precise farm acreage and capital budget into the application triggers machine-learning rankings for drought-resilient Kharif crops (like millets, pulses, or oilseeds) suited for loam soils.

projectDetails.name: PyroAtlas
projectDetails.summary:
PyroAtlas is a global geospatial platform designed to improve how people explore, interpret, and investigate satellite-based fire observations.
Using NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire datasets as its primary sources, PyroAtlas brings observations from different satellite systems into a harmonized analytical environment. Rather than simply displaying individual hotspots, the platform organizes geographically and temporally related observations into dynamic fire clusters
projectDetails.details: PyroAtlas is our response to the NASA Space Apps challenge on harmonized MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data. We built it on NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active-fire detections) and turned those detections into an evidence trail instead of a map of dots. A user selects a region, by drawing on the map or entering coordinates, and a date range. The app shows a burning-activity calendar of monthly detection counts from the early 2000s to the present, using accessible color ramps, an anomaly view against the same month in other years, and a rank against history. The monthly counts can be downloaded as CSV. A daily engine also groups detections into clusters, follows them across days, measures them with deterministic indicators, and selects up to ten for investigation. Each selection stores its parameters, input file hashes and seed, so anyone can reproduce it. We hope this helps early-warning teams, scientists and land managers see fire history and unusual activity quickly, without mistaking a detection for a fire or a count for severity. We built the data pipeline in Python (standard library only), and the web app in JavaScript, HTML and CSS with Leaflet and OpenStreetMap, hosted on GitHub and Vercel. We developed it on my computer, and tested it with Python unittest, Node and Playwright. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and test the code, but no AI is used in the analysis: every result is a deterministic calculation from NASA data, and the data source is acknowledged in the app. The creative part is how the project keeps NASA's data honest. Clusters are ranked by percentile ranks of several indicators, with no invented weights, then chosen by a seeded draw that anyone can reproduce. Labeled reference regions fill the slots when too few clusters qualify, so the app never implies findings that aren't there. If NASA revises its data, the original selection is kept and a revision is added. We respect the differences between the sensors (MODIS 1 km, VIIRS 375 m, different record start dates) and never add them together, we flag near-real-time data as provisional, and we account for the end of Suomi-NPP delivery on 2 Nov 2026. We also considered accessibility (colorblind-safe colors, values in every cell, keyboard use) and storage, keeping only small derived files instead of a copy of NASA's archive. Our thresholds are explicit defaults that still need sensitivity testing with NASA's historical data.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots

projectDetails.name: Project Engigrammers
projectDetails.summary:
We developed FLOWTRACE, an interactive web platform that turns NASA’s BASS/BASS-II combustion data into an accessible investigation of flame survival in microgravity. It combines a functional backend with experiment search, filtering, interactive airflow charts, side-by-side comparisons, and links to NASA evidence.
FLOWTRACE addresses the “Flame in Free Fall” challenge by helping users explore how initial and final airflow, oxygen concentration, and material properties relate to recorded outcomes such as sustained burning, low-flow quenching, and blowoff. Its central investigation uses 31 SIBAL fabric experiments with paired airflow measurements. The platform clearly separates confirmed outcomes from unspecified results, avoiding unsupported predictions.
This project matters because understanding combustion under changing ventilation conditions can inform spacecraft fire-safety research and astronaut protection. Our submission demonstrates how existing NASA data can become a practical, transparent learning and research tool, making complex space-combustion evidence easier for students, researchers, and the public to understand.
projectDetails.details:
Project: Flame in Freefall

What it does and how it works
Flame in Freefall studies how a flame behaves when gravity’s effects are removed. On Earth, a flame is teardrop-shaped because hot gases are lighter and rise, and this buoyancy-driven flow pulls fresh air in from below. In freefall there is no buoyancy, so the flame becomes a small, dim, blue sphere. Oxygen reaches it only by slow diffusion instead of convection. We built a compact drop rig that releases a small combustion chamber with a candle-type flame into freefall. A camera and sensors record the flame as it falls. We then compare its shape, size, color, and burn rate against a ground-based control run under identical conditions. An automated pipeline collects the data and produces the comparison for each run.

Benefits

  • It makes microgravity combustion visible and measurable with low-cost equipment, without a drop tower or spaceflight.
  • It shows clearly that flame behavior depends on gravity-driven airflow, which is often mistaken for a property of fire itself.
  • Automating data collection and comparison makes each experiment repeatable and fast to analyze.

Intended impact
The project aims to make an advanced area of combustion science accessible to students and educators. Fire safety on spacecraft depends on understanding how flames spread in microgravity, where they behave very differently from Earth flames. Our short-term goal is a reproducible, affordable teaching tool. Our longer-term goal is to show that meaningful combustion experiments can be done outside large research facilities.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Hardware: a sealed combustion chamber, a small flame source, a high-frame-rate camera, a light sensor, an accelerometer to confirm the freefall window, and a microcontroller for timing and release
  • Languages: Python for data analysis and image processing; C/C++ for the microcontroller
  • Software: OpenCV for flame shape and size measurement, n8n to automate data transfer and trigger analysis through webhooks, and plotting libraries for the comparison charts
  • Networking: the rig sends results over the local network to the machine running n8n

How it’s creative
Combustion research in microgravity normally needs drop towers, parabolic flights, or the International Space Station. We reproduce the key phenomenon in a small, affordable setup. The n8n automation layer is also unusual for an experiment like this. It turns a one-off demonstration into a repeatable data pipeline that runs without manual handling.

Factors considered

  • Safety: we used a very small flame in a sealed, fire-safe chamber with a controlled fuel amount and a safe landing system.
  • Freefall duration: the window is short, so camera frame rate and sensor timing were critical.
  • Fair comparison: the ground-based control uses the same chamber, fuel, and camera settings.
  • Reliability: accelerometer data confirms each run was true freefall before it’s included in the analysis.
  • Cost and accessibility: we chose inexpensive, widely available components so others can rebuild it.
  • Data integrity: we added webhook authentication and checks so only valid runs enter the pipeline.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: Project Engineers Might Fly
projectDetails.summary: Sol Health is an offline health app for an astronaut alone on a deep-space mission, where the flight surgeon is minutes away. It compares each reading with the astronaut's own normal, says whether something is wrong and why, tells them what to do, and sends what matters to Earth. It covers the indicators the challenge names (heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood) plus cabin air, radiation and an eye check.
projectDetails.details:
Sol Health takes three kinds of input: hourly readings from a wearable (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, sleep), a short daily check-in the astronaut fills in (mood, stress, blood sugar, urine and stool results, an eye photo), and cabin sensors for CO2 and radiation.
An engine on board compares each reading with the astronaut's own normal range, learned from their earlier days. Fixed medical limits handle clear emergencies, and small statistical models watch for slow or unusual changes. It runs without an internet connection, and every alert says in one sentence what changed and by how much.



The app then shows a status of clear, watch or act now, with a short checklist. Act-now alerts reach the flight surgeon on Earth right away, and watch alerts go in a daily report. When the radiation level jumps to more than twice its weekly normal, for example, the app tells the astronaut to go to the storm shelter and alerts Earth at the same time.
We tested the engine on real data. Across five months of records from 16 people, it gave about one false alarm per person per month. It also caught the real solar storm of 20 May 2024, recorded by NASA's Curiosity rover, within its first hour.

From rovers and instruments that completed their science missions to probes still traveling away from Earth this hardware varies widely in both its purpose and current level of functionality. Your challenge is to tell the story of some or all of this equipment that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the hardware and the science it made possible.

challengeDetails.title: Space Mission Design Game
challengeDetails.excerpt: Designing a space mission requires careful consideration of competing demands, including mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communications, and orbital constraints. For students who  rarely get to experiment with an entire mission from concept to operation, these trade-offs often remain abstract. Your challenge is to create an interactive game that allows participants to design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission while making engineering decisions, managing limited resources, and evaluating how each choice shapes the success of their mission.
