projectDetails.name: AI-Powered Flame in Freefall Dashboard
projectDetails.summary:
AI-Powered Flame in Freefall Dashboard is an AI-powered microgravity combustion and spacecraft fire-safety intelligence platform that transforms complex NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) experimental datasets into actionable, role-tailored insights. In microgravity, the absence of buoyancy fundamentally alters flame spread, smoke aerosol behavior, and material flammability, making Earth-based (1g) fire testing dangerously misleading for spacecraft design.

Our platform ingests official NASA microgravity fire investigations—including SAFFIRE-I, SAFFIRE-II, BASS, FLARE, SAME, DAFT, and NASA Spinoff fire-detection archives—into a ChromaDB semantic vector database. Through a FastAPI backend powered by Google Gemini and strict Pydantic schemas, users query the system across four specialized personas: Undergraduate Student, Postgraduate Researcher, University Professor, and Spacecraft Design Engineer. To eliminate AI hallucinations in safety-critical domains, a deterministic URL-filtering engine restricts every citation strictly to verified NASA source links. Flame in Freefall bridges the gap between raw spaceflight archives and real-world engineering, education, and safer crewed space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
1. WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

The AI-Powered Flame in Freefall Dashboard is an end-to-end Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) knowledge platform that transforms NASA's microgravity combustion and spacecraft fire-safety archives into structured, citation-verified briefings. In microgravity, the absence of buoyancy eliminates natural convection and fundamentally alters flame spread, smoke aerosol behavior, and material flammability—meaning normal-gravity (1g) fire tests on Earth can be dangerously misleading for spacecraft engineering.

Our system operates across three integrated stages:

- Automated Data Ingestion and Semantic Indexing: Automated Playwright scripts extract structured scientific summaries, experimental setups, diagnostics, and canonical source URLs from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), NASA Glenn Research Center's Combustion Science program, and NASA Spinoff archives. These records are cleaned and embedded into a local persistent ChromaDB semantic vector database.

- Multi-Persona AI Synthesis Engine: When a user submits a query through the React and Vite web dashboard or the FastAPI REST endpoint (/api/explain), ChromaDB performs semantic similarity search to retrieve the most relevant NASA investigation records. Google Gemini (via the google-genai SDK) then synthesizes the retrieved evidence into strict JSON structures enforced by Pydantic schemas.

- Four Specialized User Roles:

* Undergraduate Student: Delivers intuitive physics explanations comparing 1g (Earth) vs. 0g (microgravity) buoyancy and flame behavior, spacecraft analogies, and self-assessment quiz questions.

* Postgraduate Researcher: Provides deep experimental methodology breakdowns (such as two-color DSLR tomography, Unsteady Flamelet Generated Manifold modeling, and P-Trak aerosol sizing), parameter sensitivities, and open research gaps.

* University Professor: Generates structured lecture talking points, comparative 1g vs. low-g classroom examples, and student discussion prompts.

* Spacecraft Design Engineer: Translates experimental findings into actionable hardware design rules, material selection trade-offs (highlighting 1g vs. 0g discrepancies across SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric, thick PMMA slabs, and silicone), smoke-detector false-alarm mitigation, and engineering caveats.

2. BENEFITS OF THE PLATFORM

- Prevents Dangerous 1g-to-0g Engineering Assumptions: Surfaces counterintuitive microgravity fire behaviors before spacecraft materials or detection systems are selected.

- Eliminates AI Citation Hallucinations: Guarantees 100% traceable references pointing strictly to verified NASA investigation URLs.

- Cuts Research Synthesis Time from Hours to Seconds: Consolidates scattered multi-mission data from International Space Station (ISS) racks and uncrewed Cygnus flight experiments into immediate, structured takeaways.

- Adapts Depth to User Expertise: Replaces generic one-size-fits-all chatbot replies with tailored cognitive formats matched to students, educators, researchers, and flight engineers.

3. INTENDED IMPACT

- Safer Crewed Spacecraft and Habitats: Equips aerospace engineers designing orbital stations, lunar landers, and deep-space habitats with rapid access to flight-validated fire-safety lessons.

- Democratizing NASA Open Science: Lowers the technical barrier to NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics repository, turning dense archival pages into ready-to-use STEM learning and teaching modules worldwide.

- Blueprint for Trustworthy Scientific AI: Demonstrates a reproducible, low-latency RAG + Pydantic + deterministic link-filtering architecture applicable to other safety-critical NASA research domains.

4. TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE USED

- Coding Languages: Python (web scraping, vector indexing, AI orchestration, REST API, schema validation) and TypeScript / JavaScript with HTML/CSS (frontend user interface).

- AI and Vector Search Software: Google Gemini API (google-genai Python SDK) for structured reasoning; ChromaDB for local persistent semantic vector storage and embeddings.

- Backend and Data Extraction Software: FastAPI (RESTful /api/explain backend with CORS and OpenAPI documentation), Uvicorn (ASGI web server), Pydantic (strict per-persona JSON schema enforcement), Playwright (automated NASA PSI web scraping), and python-dotenv (environment configuration).

- Frontend Software: React and Vite interactive web dashboard.

- Hardware and Compute Environment: Developed and tested on a local engineering workstation (Intel Core i5 / NVIDIA RTX 4050 laptop environment running local persistent ChromaDB storage and Uvicorn server) without requiring expensive cloud GPU infrastructure for retrieval.

- NASA Datasets and Archives: NASA PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I), NASA PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II), NASA PSI-62 (BASS), NASA Glenn Physical Sciences Combustion Science (FLARE, SAME, DAFT), and NASA Spinoff (Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector).

5. HOW THE PROJECT IS CREATIVE

- Deterministic Anti-Hallucination URL Firewall: Instead of relying solely on prompt instructions to prevent fake citations, we engineered a deterministic Python verification filter that cross-checks every generated link against the exact ChromaDB retrieval manifest for that query, stripping any unverified URL before delivery.

- Cognitive Role Adaptation: Rather than returning a single generic summary, the platform reshapes the exact same NASA empirical evidence into four distinct pedagogical and engineering structures (quiz-backed intuition, diagnostic/modeling critique, lecture outlines, and hardware caveats).

- Cross-Mission Knowledge Synthesis: Connects small-scale ISS Combustion Integrated Rack studies (BASS, FLARE, SAME, DAFT) with large-scale uncrewed Cygnus fire experiments (SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-II) and Shuttle-derived smoke sensor spinoffs in one unified query workflow.

6. KEY FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Life-Safety Reliability and Hallucination Control: Because spacecraft fire-safety errors carry severe mission and crew risks, we prioritized strict source grounding, Pydantic schema validation, and explicit engineering caveat fields over open-ended text generation.

- Terrestrial (1g) vs. Microgravity (0g) Physical Discrepancies: We specifically designed our retrieval context to highlight cases where 1g screening diverges from microgravity flight results (such as silicone flammability differences in SAFFIRE-II and recondensed polymer droplets vs. soot aerosols in SAME/DAFT).

- Transparent AI Disclosure and Primary-Source Access: Every AI-generated response is explicitly labeled as AI-synthesized from NASA records and paired with direct clickable NASA links so users can inspect the raw investigation pages.

- Current Scope and Future Roadmap: Our current working system indexes curated experimental summaries and investigation metadata on a local ChromaDB instance rather than multi-gigabyte raw high-speed flame video or time-series sensor CSV logs; our next engineering phase integrates direct CSV telemetry plotting (temperature, O2/CO2 levels, and radiometer curves) and cloud multi-user deployment.

projectDetails.name: Sunchaser
projectDetails.summary:
Sunchaser is a free web app that tells mission planners where and when to land at the Moon's south pole so a lander keeps both its power and its link to Earth. There, the Sun skims the horizon: a ridge kilometres away can cut a lander's power for days, and the same terrain can hide Earth. In 2025, IM-2 Athena touched down in a crater near the pole and never recharged.

For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, Sunchaser traces the real skyline from NASA LRO LOLA terrain and places the Sun and Earth on it with NASA/JPL SPICE. For any site and hour it shows sunlight, contact through the Deep Space Network, and the best landing windows. It compares 25 sites, checks 466,825 landing hours to 2028, replans a launch slip in one click, routes rovers through moving shadows and works at any point on the Moon, with 3D shadows drawn from the same data as the numbers.

Every result is checked against NASA: Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to 0.0000015°, and sunlight matches NASA Goddard's published study within 0.2 points. Expert analysis becomes answers anyone can get in seconds.
projectDetails.details:
Live app: https://sunchaserapp.vercel.app (start with the 90-second guided tour on the home screen)
Source code: https://github.com/Fares098XI/sunchaser-nasa

What it does

Sunchaser helps mission planners choose where and when to land at the Moon's south pole by the two things a lander cannot live without: sunlight for power and line of sight to Earth for communication.

  • Explore: fly over real south-pole terrain in 3D. Drag the Sun and the computed shadows move. Click any point for its sunlight, Earth contact, a mission clock ("sunset in…", "Earthset in…") and landing slope, with links to NASA QuickMap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons.
  • Compare: 25 sites side by side (10 south-pole sites chosen by a written rule from NASA sources, plus 15 historic landings: Apollo, Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, CLPS) for any date, stay and panel height.
  • Landing windows: set the mission's needs and every landing hour from Nov 2026 to Dec 2028 is checked. When none passes, it shows the smallest change that would open a window.
  • Replan a slip: what a launch delay does to the site, the next good date and the nearest Plan B.
  • Light Path: rover routes through moving shadows that keep the battery above its reserve (VIPER-class values).
  • Astronaut: stand on the surface and see the Sun and Earth on the real horizon.
  • Any point on the Moon: tap or type coordinates; the horizon is computed in your browser from NASA's global maps.
  • Learn, Stories and Ask Sunchaser: 15 plain-language chapters, real landings (Apollo, IM-2), and an AI copilot (English and Arabic) whose every number comes from the engine.

How it works

  • Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA elevation maps of the south pole (5–240 m per pixel); LOLA and SLDEM2015 global maps elsewhere.
  • Horizons: an exact ray walk in up to 1,440 directions finds the true skyline, including mountains hundreds of kilometres away and the Moon's curvature.
  • Sun and Earth: NASA/JPL SPICE (DE440) positions every 10 minutes, in the same lunar frame as the terrain.
  • Power: the visible fraction of the Sun's disc drives a solar-panel and battery model you can set.
  • Communication: Earth above the skyline, and the Moon at least 6° above a Deep Space Network 70 m antenna (DSN Handbook 810-005).
  • Same data everywhere: a TypeScript engine reproduces the Python pipeline (golden files agree to about 10⁻¹²), so everything runs live in the browser and the 3D shadows come from the same horizons as the numbers.

How we know it is right

19 checks against NASA references. Each pass rule was written before its check ran, and failures stay on view in the app's Validation page.

  • Sun and Earth directions vs JPL Horizons: max error 0.0000017°
  • Sunlight at Connecting Ridge: 91.26 % vs 91.11 % in NASA Goddard's study (Barker et al. 2021)
  • Whole-ridge sunlight vs NASA Goddard's 60 m map: correlation 0.965
  • Rover routes: 133/133 confirmed by an independent checker; copilot: 151/151 numbers traced to the engine

Benefits and impact

Artemis astronauts and CLPS landers are heading to the south pole, where light and Earth contact change hour by hour and metre by metre. Today this analysis lives in research papers and specialist tools. Sunchaser puts it in one free app that runs on a laptop or a phone:

  • Mission planners screen sites and dates in minutes and see why a window fails.
  • Teachers and students see why a crater rim is a good landing site.
  • Anyone can stand on the surface and watch Earth rise and set.

What makes it creative

  • The real terrain horizon, computed exactly, not a flat one.
  • Sun and Earth with equal weight, down to the Deep Space Network dishes on Earth.
  • The 3D view is the analysis itself, not an illustration.
  • Every number is traceable and checked, and the failures are shown.

Factors we considered

Accuracy before features; honest limits shown in every view (terrain resolves about 20 m, communication is geometric, the solar panel is ideal); speed on an ordinary laptop with integrated graphics; phones; accessibility; plain language for non-experts.

Tools

TypeScript, Python, GLSL · React 19, Vite, Three.js / React Three Fiber, Web Workers · SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE), NumPy, Numba, SciPy, rasterio · Vitest, pytest · Vercel · Google Gemini and Groq for the copilot (it also works offline).

Next steps

Deep Space Network scheduling and more landing sites.

projectDetails.details:
المخاطر الخمسة للسفر البشري في الفضاء (ناسا)

حددت ناسا خمسة مخاطر رئيسية يواجهها رواد الفضاء في الرحلات الطويلة، خاصة إلى المريخ:

* الإشعاع الفضائي (Space Radiation): إشعاع غير مرئي من جسيمات يمكن أن يضر الخلايا ويزيد المخاطر الصحية على المدى الطويل.

* العزلة والحبس في مكان مغلق (Isolation and Confinement): العيش في مساحة صغيرة ومعزولة مع نفس الطاقم لفترة طويلة، وهو ما يؤثر على السلوك والمشاعر والصحة النفسية.

* البُعد عن الأرض (Distance from Earth): صعوبة التواصل والإمدادات والتعليمات والرعاية الطبية، مع تأخر الاتصالات وصعوبة العودة السريعة أو تلقي مساعدة فورية.

* مجالات الجاذبية (Gravity Fields): تكيف الجسم مع مستويات جاذبية مختلفة (الفضاء، القمر، المريخ، الأرض) وتأثير ذلك على التوازن وكثافة العظام وقوة العضلات والأذن الداخلية والأعضاء.

* البيئات المغلقة أو المعادية (Hostile and Closed Environments): تحدي الحفاظ على بيئة آمنة وصحية داخل المركبة عبر التحكم في الهواء والماء والحرارة والضغط والإضاءة والضوضاء والميكروبات واستجابات المناعة.

* لوحة متابعة صحة الطاقم (ORBIT — Crew Health System): واجهة مراقبة طبية تعرض مؤشرات حيوية مثل معدل ضربات القلب (78 bpm)، وأكسجين الدم (98.2%)، ومعدل الأيض (312 kcal/h)، وحرارة الجسم الأساسية (37.1 °C)، مع رسم بياني للإنفاق الأيضي وقائمة مراجعة إكلينيكية وحالة المستشعرات.

* ملخص المخاطر الخمسة (NASA Space Apps — Risk Explorer): يستعرض المخاطر الخمسة (RAD/01 إلى ENV/05) وإجراءات المواجهة لكل خطر (الحماية والمراقبة، الدعم النفسي والعمل الجماعي، دعم القرار على متن المركبة، التمارين والتأهيل، وأنظمة دعم الحياة) ومسار الرحلة من الأرض إلى القمر ثم المريخ.

3. ملخص السكرين ريكورد (منصة ASTRA Health Monitoring)

* نظرة عامة على المهمة (Mission Overview): إجمالي 516 قراءة (509 قراءة تاريخية من ناسا لمهمة Inspiration4 ودراسة OSD-575، و7 قراءات محاكاة).

* ربط المخاطر الخمسة بالمنصة:

* Space Radiation: مراقبة غير مباشرة عبر لوحات الأيض والمناعة.

* Isolation and Confinement: غير متتبع حاليًا.

* Distance from Earth: تنبيهات على متن المركبة عبر باك إند ولوحة تحكم محلية.

* Gravity Fields: توسع مخطط له.

* Hostile and Closed Environments: مراقبة صحية جزئية عبر لوحة القلب والأوعية.

* أساس البيانات والمحاكاة: يعتمد على NASA OSD-575 لتحميل بيانات مهمة Inspiration4، ويوفر إدخال قراءات محاكاة (Simulated Sensor Input) لاختبار استجابة مركز التنبيهات، مع رسم يوضح مصادر القراءات (Observation Sources).

* لوحة صحة الرواد (Health Dashboard): تعرض أحدث قراءة لـ albumin بقيمة 5.1 (بتغير +4.1% أي +0.2 عن القراءة السابقة، ضمن 7 قراءات مختارة) مع منحنى اتجاه القياس عبر الزمن (Measurement Trend).

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: RoverQuest
projectDetails.summary:
**RoverQuest: Beyond the Silent Machines** is an educational 3D space exploration game that takes players on an immersive storytelling adventure across Mars and the Moon, uncovering the stories of historic NASA robotic missions.

Players take the role of an astronaut stranded on Mars or the Moon after their spacecraft crash-lands. To find their way home, they must explore abandoned mission sites, discover historic NASA machines, and uncover the stories behind their missions, technologies, challenges, and scientific discoveries.

Each encounter combines engaging storytelling with interactive learning experiences, allowing players to explore scientific concepts through interactive 3D holograms, physics-based mini-games, and evidence analysis. Rather than simply reading about space exploration, players become part of the story, actively experiencing how these missions contributed to our understanding of the Solar System.

The experience adapts its educational content to different age groups and features TARS, a robotic companion that guides players throughout their journey.

By combining storytelling, immersive exploration, and hands-on learning, RoverQuest transforms the legacy of NASA's space missions into an engaging adventure that inspires curiosity, scientific thinking, and a passion for STEM.

https://github.com/Jo-Shaheen/roverquest_github.io


### What it does

RoverQuest is a story-driven educational game about the spacecraft that space agencies have retired, lost contact with or left behind.

1. **Crash-land.** The player enters their name and age. TARS, a robot partner, adapts its wording to the player's age (10–18) and uses their name throughout.

2. **Explore in 3D.** Two complete 3D worlds can be explored with keyboard, mouse or touch, using a radar and a place picker.

   

- **Mars (9 places, restore any 5).** Sojourner, Spirit & Opportunity, Viking 1 & 2, Phoenix & InSight and Ingenuity stand on the plain as 3D models. Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 & 11 and Kepler never went to Mars, so they appear as clearly labelled holo-beacon stations that say where the real spacecraft is today.

- **The Moon (4 sites, restore any 3).** The Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor 3 and the Apollo laser retroreflectors, on a grey plain with Earth in the black sky.

3. **Play.** Every place has a hands-on mini-game, 14 in total. In each one the player uses how the real machine worked:

   - Signal-Delay Driver (Sojourner), Dead-Wheel Dig and Blueberry Hunt (Spirit & Opportunity), Scoop & Bake (Viking)

   - Marsquake Catcher (Phoenix & InSight), First Flight (Ingenuity), Orbit Hopper (Dawn)

   - Soft Touch on Eros (NEAR Shoemaker), Slingshot (Pioneer), Transit Hunter (Kepler)

   - Lighten & Lift (Eagle), Walk-back Rule (Lunar Rover), Pinpoint Landing (Surveyor 3), Hit the Mirror (retroreflectors)

4. **Discover.** Winning unlocks the real NASA finding, a NASA photo or a labelled illustration, and links to the mission's NASA page and NSSDCA record. Each discovery separates documented observations, scientific interpretations and teaching simplifications.

5. **Launch home.** Restoring enough places brings the ship's systems online. A final launch check is built from the player's own places, and a personalized ending lets the player present what they learned.

### How it works

- It is a static web app (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) with no server-side code, no accounts and no tracking. Progress is saved only in the browser's local storage.

- The 3D worlds use Three.js r128, bundled locally. Terrain, machines, holograms, the astronaut and TARS are built procedurally in code. One shared engine re-skins itself for Mars or the Moon from a per-world configuration.

- 32 NASA/JPL photographs are bundled locally with credits, so the whole game works offline after it is downloaded once. The only exception is an optional NASA video, which loads only when the player clicks it. That makes it useful in classrooms with weak internet.

- The mini-games are self-contained canvas and DOM simulations. Physics are simplified and labelled as such.

- The game is responsive: on phones it shows on-screen movement and interact buttons, larger touch targets and a layout that fits.

- Quality: `node tools/check.mjs` runs 27 automated groups covering code syntax, local links, the image manifest and credits, the science rules of each investigation, the world and place setup, offline assets, save-data validation and the companion's visibility. All 27 pass. The project also includes a Playwright end-to-end and accessibility (axe-core) test suite, and a science fact-check document that maps each claim to a NASA source.

### Benefits

- Learners explore 13 real missions by doing, not just reading.

- It builds scientific thinking: observation vs. interpretation, and real photos vs. models.

- Choice (any 5 of 9, any 3 of 4) gives agency and replay value.

- It is free, runs offline on almost any device and needs no installation or sign-up.

### Goals and intended impact

We want students to see retired spacecraft as a living source of science rather than space junk, and to remember why each machine mattered. Next, we plan to add Arabic and other languages, a teacher mode with class progress, more silent machines, and pilot sessions with students in Egyptian schools.

projectDetails.name: Project EYE FROM ABOVE
projectDetails.summary: Eye from Above is an AI-powered disaster response web platform and interactive decision-support dashboard built using NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) L-Band observations for the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge. During catastrophic monsoon floods, thick storm clouds blind optical satellites for days while raw SAR backscatter data is too complex for field responders to interpret. Our platform converts multi-temporal NISAR L-band imagery into plain-English, life-saving intelligence: (1) cloud-penetrating flood maps separating shallow water from deep boat-only channels, (2) population-ranked trapped village priorities, (3) AI-scored rescue base selection and verified dry truck corridors, (4) predictive flood-surge simulations (+0m to +300m) with automatic boat drop-off relocation, (5) 72-hour Sphere humanitarian supply calculations, and (6) zero-internet offline responder kits.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS:

Eye from Above transforms all-weather NASA NISAR L-Band (~24 cm wavelength) radar backscatter data into an operational flood rescue command system, validated on the August 2026 monsoon flood in the Koshi River Basin (Saptari District, Nepal).

1. All-Weather SAR Physics & Flood Segmentation (analyze_disaster.py): Unlike optical cameras blocked by storm clouds, NISAR's active L-band radar penetrates monsoon clouds and crop canopies. Smooth standing floodwater causes specular mirror reflection (backscatter < -17.5 dB, appearing jet-black), while rough dry terrain scatters energy back (bright gray). Comparing pre-flood baseline scans (Aug 19, 2026) with peak flood scans (Aug 31, 2026) isolates 35.86 km² of active inundation and separates shallow floodwater from deep boat-only channels (< -19.5 dB) in metric UTM Zone 45N (EPSG:32645).

2. Priority Village Exposure Ranking (fix_zones.py): Fuses NISAR flood polygons with OpenStreetMap building footprints within a 500 m buffer to deduplicate and rank the top 5 trapped villages by exposed population (led by Gobargadha Island with ~3,992 people and Tilathi Koiladi with ~4,768 people).

3. MCDA AI Rescue Base Scoring & Safe Dry Routing (app.py): Prunes 24 submerged road segments from the road graph and evaluates 5 rescue bases out of 100 using weighted Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (45% dry road speed via Dijkstra routing, 35% medical/boat capacity, 20% route flood safety). It routes trucks from the top-ranked base (Central Koshi High-Ground Medical Post, Score: 86.8/100) along a 7.73 km (~13 min) verified dry road to the exact Boat Drop-Off point (26.3515° N, 86.6565° E).

4. Predictive Flood Surge Simulator (+0m to +300m): Simulates radial water expansion. When water rises >= +100m (expanding flooding to 326.88 km² and blocking 100 road sections at +250m), the system detects that the boat launch point is submerged and automatically relocates it to higher dry ground (26.3645° N, 86.6490° E; 6.24 km / ~10 min drive).

5. 72-Hour Sphere Supply Calculator & Offline Field Kit: Computes 3-day water (3 L/person/day), ready meals, tents, boats, and trucks per Sphere standards, and exports standalone offline .html maps, .geojson GPS tracks, and .md mission sheets.

TOOLS & CODING LANGUAGES USED:

Python 3.10+, Streamlit, GeoPandas, Rasterio, OSMnx, NetworkX, Folium, Shapely, NumPy, PyProj, Matplotlib, HTML5, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript (ES6+), and Leaflet.js.

Source Code Repository: https://github.com/ahmedsaberasa/eye-from-above

SAMPLE TASK FOR JUDGES TO TRY:

Open our Live Streamlit App (https://eye-from-above-cky3vjkcrdmbcbzdlws3uh.streamlit.app/), select any of the 5 trapped villages in the sidebar, drag the Flood Expansion Simulator slider from +0m to +250m to watch the Boat Drop-Off point relocate automatically, inspect Before/After radar scans, and download the offline field files. You can also explore our 7-slide interactive demo at https://ahmedsaberasa.github.io/eye-from-above/.

WHAT WORKS NOW, CURRENT LIMITATIONS & FUTURE PLANS:

- What Works Now: Full interactive Streamlit dashboard, 7-slide live satellite presentation, MCDA base ranking, Dijkstra dry road routing, +0m to +300m surge simulation, Sphere supply math, and offline .html/.geojson/.md exports.

- Current Limitations: Raw multi-temporal SAR GeoTIFFs exceed GitHub's 25 MB web upload limit, so our public repo stores pre-extracted vector flood polygons (GeoJSON) and pruned road graphs (GraphML); the surge simulator uses planar metric buffering in EPSG:32645 rather than a 3D hydrodynamic solver; population counts rely on static OSM building footprints.

- Future Plans: Direct NASA Earthdata / ASF Vertex cloud API streaming for real-time global NISAR scenes, integration of NASA SRTM 30m DEM elevation contours, and two-way SMS / LoRa mesh updates from field rescue boats.

projectDetails.name: Jezero Safe Walk
projectDetails.summary:
Jezero Safe Walk is an interactive Mars terrain analysis and route-planning application focused on the Jezero Crater region. It helps users explore the Martian surface, understand terrain conditions, and compare potential rover routes based on distance and slope-related difficulty.

The platform combines elevation data from the USGS with Mars 2020 Rover observations from NASA's Planetary Data System (PDS). It uses terrain analysis and an A* pathfinding algorithm to generate and compare shortest and safer route options across different mission scenarios and mobility profiles.

Through an interactive map, terrain layers, route visualizations, and analytical charts, Jezero Safe Walk makes complex terrain information easier to explore and interpret. The project demonstrates how open planetary data can support transparent, data-driven mobility analysis for Mars exploration. It is a research and educational prototype, not a certified astronaut safety or operational mission-planning system.
projectDetails.details:
# Jezero Safe Walk

## Project Overview

Jezero Safe Walk is an interactive terrain analysis and route-planning application designed to explore mobility challenges in the Jezero Crater region of Mars. The project demonstrates how planetary elevation data and rover observations can be combined to analyze terrain conditions and compare potential walking routes.

## The Problem

Planning a route based only on distance can lead to paths crossing steep or difficult terrain. For future Mars exploration, understanding terrain characteristics is essential when evaluating possible routes and mobility constraints.

## Our Solution

Jezero Safe Walk provides an interactive map that allows users to explore Martian terrain, select predefined mission scenarios, choose different mobility profiles, and compare two route-planning strategies:

- Shortest Route: prioritizes minimizing travel distance.

- Safest Route: uses a terrain-based cost surface to penalize steeper areas and avoid cells classified as forbidden under the selected profile.

The application also provides route summaries, terrain visualization, analytical charts, and validation information.

## Data Sources

The project uses two primary datasets:

1. USGS Digital Elevation Model (DEM): provides elevation information used to derive terrain slope, construct the cost surface, and support route planning. The project uses a 20-meter terrain grid.

2. NASA Mars 2020 Rover PLACES dataset from the Planetary Data System (PDS): provides Perseverance rover observations, including position, pitch, roll, and elevation. These observations are used to evaluate the terrain model and replay rover movement.

## Technical Methodology

The terrain-processing workflow consists of:

1. Loading and processing the USGS elevation grid.

2. Calculating terrain slope using the Horn 3×3 method.

3. Building a slope-based terrain cost surface.

4. Applying the A* pathfinding algorithm with 8-neighbor grid movement.

5. Generating route alternatives and presenting their characteristics through the interactive application.

Three configurable terrain mobility profiles are provided: Conservative, Standard, and Extended. Their slope thresholds are project modeling assumptions and are not certified human astronaut safety limits.

## Scientific Validation and Results

The terrain model was evaluated against 32,003 Perseverance rover observations.

In the rover replay analysis, the safest planned route reduced peak slope from 16.13° to 9.86°, a reduction of 38.9%, while increasing planned route distance from 1,421.1 meters to 1,514.8 meters. This represents an additional 93.7 meters, or 6.6%.

The application also presents validation metrics for pitch, roll, tilt, and elevation to help users understand the relationship between rover observations and the terrain model.

## Main Features

- Interactive Leaflet map of Jezero Crater.

- Shortest and safest route comparison.

- Three configurable mobility profiles.

- Four predefined route scenarios.

- Terrain layers and slope visualization.

- Route statistics and analytical charts.

- Mission brief and rover replay validation information.

- Scientific data and methodology transparency.

## Technologies

The project combines geospatial data processing, terrain analysis, pathfinding algorithms, and web-based visualization. Its main technologies include Leaflet for interactive mapping, A* for route planning, and Python-based data processing and scientific analysis.

## Impact and Future Potential

Jezero Safe Walk demonstrates how open planetary datasets can support transparent, data-driven terrain analysis for Mars exploration. It provides an interactive way to understand the trade-off between route distance and terrain difficulty.

Future improvements could include finer-resolution terrain data, additional rover observations, more detailed hazard layers, and further research into mobility thresholds.

## Limitations

The 20-meter DEM cannot represent every small rock or local terrain feature. Rover pitch and roll observations validate aspects of the terrain model against vehicle movement, not human walking. Vertical datum equivalence is not claimed as proven.

Jezero Safe Walk is a research and educational prototype. It is not certified for astronaut safety or operational mission planning, and its mobility thresholds must not be interpreted as validated human safety limits.

projectDetails.name: AstroHeritage: The Museum of Forgotten Space Artifacts
projectDetails.summary:
Our team developed an interactive, bilingual (English/Arabic) web application titled 'AstroHeritage: The Museum of Forgotten Space Artifacts'. We addressed the challenge by shifting the narrative around NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars from 'space debris' to valuable 'space heritage'. The platform features an immersive 3D virtual environment with an orbital particle network and an artifact map, bringing the history of off-world artifacts to life using NASA NSSDC archive imagery and data.

To deeply engage diverse audiences, we integrated age-tiered Space Archaeology Labs tailored for different age groups (Little Explorers, Junior Astronauts, and Heritage Protectors). These labs offer interactive, hands-on STEAM activities designed to teach sustainability and preserve humanity's legacy in space.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between traditional archaeology and space science. It educates the next generation about sustainable space exploration and inspires the public to appreciate and protect our historical legacy across the solar system.
projectDetails.details:
"AstroHeritage: The Museum of Forgotten Space Artifacts" is a fully interactive, bilingual (English/Arabic) web platform designed to preserve and educate about off-world artifacts. The project functions as a unified learning environment divided into two main modules:

  1. Space Museum (Gallery & Map): Users navigate an interactive artifact map featuring distinct Moon and Mars galleries. Each artifact (e.g., Apollo 11 Descent Stage, Perseverance Parachute) opens in an immersive 3D-styled display case ("Artifact Registry") with an Environmental HUD showing surface temperature, hazards, and a Structural Integrity Meter.
    • Little Explorers (5-8 yrs): Rover assembly puzzles and space coloring activities.
    • Junior Astronauts (9-13 yrs): Martian dust-sweeping simulations and historical timeline reconstruction.
    • Heritage Leaders (14-18 yrs): Advanced modules like "Space Hieroglyphics" (binary code decoding), power management simulators (balancing heat, comms, and sensors), radar coordinate scanning, and heritage classification law debates.

Benefits & Intended Impact The primary benefit is transforming the concept of "space debris" into "space heritage" through gamified, cross-generational learning. By grouping activities by age and cognitive level, the platform benefits diverse audiences—from young children discovering space to teens engaging in complex physics and ethical debates. The intended impact is to foster a sense of global responsibility for off-world preservation, ensuring future generations value the historical significance of our early steps into the cosmos.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

  • Core Architecture: Developed as a unified web application using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (Vanilla JS).
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS for responsive layouts, combined with custom CSS glassmorphism, animations (pulse, spin, holographic scans), and orbital particle networks rendered via HTML5 Canvas.
  • Interactive Elements: JavaScript for state management, interactive modal logic, and dynamic DOM manipulation (e.g., the interactive dust sweeper, binary decoder, and power sliders).
  • Data Visualization: Chart.js integrated for "Lifespan Analysis" (Expected vs. Actual lifespan of artifacts).
  • Assets & Fonts: Google Fonts (Cairo for Arabic, Inter/Orbitron for English/Tech aesthetics), Phosphor Icons, and FontAwesome. NASA NSSDC imagery was utilized for artifact visualization.

Creativity & Team Considerations The creativity of AstroHeritage lies in its dual-identity: it is both a historical archive and a futuristic simulator. We designed the UI to mimic a "Space Archaeologist Dashboard," complete with glowing neon accents, holographic loading screens, and scanning radars, which deeply immerses the user in the role.

Our team, "Family Space," prioritized accessibility and inclusivity. We engineered a seamless bilingual toggle (English/Arabic) with full Right-to-Left (RTL) support to serve the MENA region. Furthermore, the single-page application (SPA) architecture with iframe-based module isolation ensures the platform is lightweight, fast, and easily scalable for future NASA hackathons or educational deployments.

projectDetails.name: Ag Root
projectDetails.summary:
Ag Root is an intelligent astronaut health assessment platform that transforms health data and interactive tests into actionable medical insights, helping protect astronaut well-being and maintain mission readiness throughout space exploration.
That is the central idea everything in the project should communicate: 
We don't just monitor astronauts. We assess their health, understand how it changes, and help predict when something needs attention.
projectDetails.details:
### Ag Root – Project description

Ag Root is a software-based astronaut health assessment and monitoring platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It aims to address the physical, cognitive, and psychological challenges astronauts face during space missions, including cardiovascular deconditioning, muscle and bone loss, cognitive changes, psychological stress, and sleep disruption.

The platform combines interactive health assessments, gamified testing, AI-assisted analysis, and a centralized medical dashboard to provide a comprehensive picture of astronaut health.

Ag Root evaluates five main health domains:

* Cardiovascular Health: Evaluating heart performance and cardiovascular responses.

* Musculoskeletal Health: Assessing muscle strength, endurance, and physical performance.

* Cognitive Health: Testing reaction time, memory, attention, and concentration.

* Psychological Health: Evaluating stress, mood, and psychological well-being.

* Sleep Health: Tracking sleep quality, duration, and fatigue.

The system works through a continuous cycle of data collection, interactive assessment, AI-assisted analysis, health visualization, and medical decision support. It compares assessment results over time to identify unusual changes, potential health deterioration, and areas requiring further evaluation.

### What Makes Ag Root Different?

Instead of relying solely on passive health monitoring and traditional questionnaires, Ag Root introduces gamified, performance-based assessments that make health evaluation more interactive and engaging while generating measurable results.

### Expected Impact

* Earlier Risk Detection: Identifying potential health deterioration through continuous assessment and individual health comparisons.

* Improved Mission Readiness: Helping medical teams make better-informed decisions about astronaut health, performance, and mission safety.

### Future Vision

Ag Root aims to expand through wearable device integration, personalized health baselines, predictive health analytics, advanced assessment simulations, and improved remote medical collaboration.

The Core Vision:

Ag Root goes beyond monitoring astronaut health. It assesses physical and cognitive performance, tracks changes over time, identifies potential risks, and transforms health data into actionable medical insights to help protect astronauts and support safer, more successful space missions.

projectDetails.name: Fasa egypt
projectDetails.summary:
Field Shift is a prototype agricultural decision-support website that helps users explore which crops may suit a location and compare possible crop-rotation strategies. Users select a place on a map and review environmental indicators—including weather, water availability, soil moisture, and terrain—in one view. The prototype flags missing data and presents potential crop matches and rotation options for further consideration.
The project addresses the challenge of fragmented environmental information, which can make agricultural planning harder as heat, rainfall, and water conditions change. By making relevant indicators easier to inspect and compare, Field Shift aims to help farmers and planners make more informed, location-aware decisions. It is an exploratory tool, not a substitute for local agronomic advice; its data connections and recommendations still require further validation.
projectDetails.details:
Field Shift is a bilingual, map-first web prototype for agricultural decision support. A user selects a location on an interactive map and reviews available environmental information—such as climate, rainfall, soil moisture, terrain and satellite-derived vegetation indicators—in a dashboard. The prototype includes source and data-quality cues, including flags for missing information, alongside two separate decision-support components: a crop-suitability classifier and a crop-rotation planner that can consider crop history and farming constraints.

The goal is to make scattered environmental indicators easier to explore together, helping farmers, researchers and planners ask better-informed questions before making decisions. The interface is designed for both Arabic and English users. Its creative approach is to pair a map-based workflow with transparent data limitations, while keeping crop matching distinct from rotation planning. The team considered local differences in soil and climate, changing water availability, data gaps and source coverage, prior crops and other farm constraints. The tool is intended to support—not replace—local agronomic expertise.

The project materials describe a Random Forest crop classifier evaluated on Crop_recommendation.csv, with a reported 99.32% test accuracy on that dataset. This is not evidence of global field accuracy or validation with NASA satellite data. The demo visibly shows NASA POWER metrics and a GIBS layer selector; other listed data connections and recommendations should not be assumed to be independently verified or live.

node.title: FASA DESTINATION TEAM
node.excerpt: FASA Destination Team is tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge with SUHAIL, a tool that helps mission planners and students compare lunar south-pole landing sites by date, using Sun and Earth positions to judge power and communicatio...

projectDetails.name: FASA DESTINATION TEAM
projectDetails.summary:
SUHAIL is an interactive landing-site navigator for the Moon's south pole. It answers two questions: where to land and when.

In Expert mode, a planner enters the mission: its duration, dates, power system, and limits for sunlight, darkness, Earth communication, slope and distance to science targets. SUHAIL tests 74 candidate points across NASA's seven Artemis III regions on every possible start date. It uses real NASA LOLA elevation data and computes the Sun and Earth positions hour by hour. For each site it simulates solar power, battery charge and surface temperature. A council of five specialists debates the best five sites, and a flight director gives a go/no-go with the best dates.

In Student mode, the Lunar Landing Academy teaches the same five aspects through the real stories of Odysseus and Athena, short lessons, and a 2D game.

This matters because reaching the Moon is not enough. Both landers touched down near the pole and tipped over, which cut short their power, communication and science. SUHAIL makes those risks visible, explains its reasoning with real numbers, and is honest about its limits.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

SUHAIL is a landing-site navigator for the Moon's south pole. It tells a mission team where and when to land, and it explains why.

Expert mode (Mission planner): the planner enters the mission type, duration, Earth launch and Moon lift-off dates, the power system (solar array, battery, depth of discharge, loads) and Off/Low/Medium/High limits for five aspects: solar radiation, thermal environment and day cycle, Earth communication, terrain slope, and distance to a scientific target. SUHAIL tests 74 candidate points across NASA's seven Artemis III candidate regions on every possible start date in a 180-day window. For each point it simulates, hour by hour, solar irradiance with terrain shadowing, array power, battery state of charge and surface temperature, and rates the site as highly suitable, suitable with constraints, high energy risk, or not feasible. The best five sites go to a council of five specialists who debate them using the computed numbers. The user votes, and the flight director gives a go/no-go with the best start dates and a downloadable report. Example: a science rover for 8 days gets Faustini Rim A, GO, 91/100, starting 13 Sept 2027, with 94.8% of hours in sunlight and a 4° slope.

Student mode (Lunar Landing Academy): Watch the real stories of Odysseus (2024) and Athena (2025). Learn the five aspects, each with a quick check. Play "Save the Mission", a 2D game where students overrule a silly crew across five decisions.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Reaching the Moon does not guarantee a working mission: Odysseus and Athena both reached the south-polar region and ended up on their side. SUHAIL makes these risks visible. Planners can compare sites with clear numbers and dates, and students and the public learn why one place is better than another. Learning and decision-making share one framework.

TOOLS AND DATA

- NASA LOLA south-pole elevation model, 80 m/pixel (PGDA product 90): terrain, slopes, horizon profiles, maps and 3D terrain

- NASA LOLA permanently shadowed regions (LPSR): distance to cold traps

- NASA Artemis III candidate regions, outlines from LROC QuickMap

- NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (visualization 5013): region flyovers

- Python (numpy, rasterio, astropy) for the data pipeline and the hourly Sun and Earth positions

- JavaScript, React, Vite and three.js for the web app; deployed on Vercel and also available as one offline HTML file

- 38 automated tests; no special hardware

CREATIVITY

Two experiences share one scientific engine. The project is named after Suhail (Canopus), the star Arab navigators steered by. Instead of a dashboard, the science is delivered as a conversation: specialists react to each other, and every number they say comes from the data. Student mode uses the team's own comic crew. The Expert-mode specialists are original characters inspired by the fields of real Arab scientists and astronauts.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Importance levels and default limits are team assumptions, not NASA standards, and they are editable.

- The 80 m grid cannot show boulders or small craters, so slope screening is regional, not touchdown safety.

- Sun and Earth positions come from a model close to, but not exactly, NASA SPICE/JPL Horizons.

- Missing data is marked "Unverified" and is never treated as a pass.

- Distance to a shadowed crater is only a proxy for possible ice.

- SUHAIL supports a decision; it does not replace engineering review.

FUTURE PLANS

An AI agent for each specialist that debates the planner live, validation against JPL Horizons, a finer 20 m terrain grid, and an Arabic version.

projectDetails.name: Project Fieldorex
projectDetails.summary: We a decision-support tool for Egyptian farmers, delivered as a localhost REST API with PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Redis and Celery. A farmer registers a field polygon, a one-time soil input, priority weights and the crops already grown. The system then combines NASA Earth observations (SMAP, GAEZ, NASA POWER), a soil dataset fallback for blank fields, a seasonal forecast, and market prices. It scores every crop transition with a feasibility gate and five component scores, searches multi-season paths with beam search, and simulates weather, price and parameter risk. Each run returns at least three ranked strategies, including the existing rotation, with a comparison matrix, a High/Medium/Low confidence label, and a traceable explanation.  The challenge is that rotation choices depend on local climate, water, soil and prices, which most farmers cannot weigh across several seasons. The tool makes those trade-offs explicit and traceable, while leaving the final decision to the farmer and local experts. It is important because it supports soil health, water use and income in a water-scarce, intensively farmed region.  Current status: the engine runs end to end and is tested offline (145 tests). Live data connectors and crop values are limited to Egypt.
projectDetails.details:
What we built

Fieldorex is a planning tool that helps a farmer decide which crops to plant over the next three to six seasons. The farmer enters the field's boundary, what they know about the soil, the crops grown there so far, and what matters most to them, such as profit, soil health or water use. Fieldorex then returns several ranked plans. Each plan lists the crop for every season and shows how it scores on each part of the decision. The farmer's current rotation is always included, so every option can be compared with what they already do.

The tool is delivered as a backend service with a REST API. It stores field records and soil data, runs the planning calculations, and returns results that can be used by any app or dashboard built on top of it.

The problem it addresses

Choosing a crop rotation is hard. What grows well in one season affects what can grow in the next, and the right choice depends on weather, water availability, soil condition, pests and disease history, and market prices. Most farmers make these decisions from experience alone, and it is difficult to weigh several seasons of trade-offs in your head. Mistakes are costly: a poor rotation can deplete soil, raise disease risk, waste water, or lead to a weaker harvest and income.

How it helps

Fieldorex makes those trade-offs visible. Each option comes with a plain-language explanation of why it was suggested, what evidence supports it, what benefits to expect, what information is missing, and which risks a local expert should review. Every result also carries a confidence level (High, Medium or Low), so the farmer knows how much weight to give it. Where a soil measurement is missing, the tool fills the gap with an estimate and flags it, so estimates are never mistaken for measurements.

The tool supports the farmer and local agricultural expertise. It does not replace them. The final decision stays with the farmer, informed by advisers who know the land.

Why it matters

Better rotation planning can protect soil fertility, reduce disease and pest pressure, use water more efficiently, and improve the reliability of a farmer's income. For Egypt, where farmland is limited and water is a constant concern, these gains matter for both household livelihoods and national food production. Making this kind of planning accessible, traceable and easy to compare gives farmers and advisers a shared, evidence-based starting point.

Scope

Fieldorex is built for the Egyptian locale. It covers the Egyptian region and a set of 25 crops commonly grown in Egypt.

projectDetails.name: Project FieldWise
projectDetails.summary:
FieldWise is a location-based Agricultural Decision Support System helping farmers make smarter crop rotation decisions in a changing climate. it selects suitable crops using local environmental conditions rather than generalized recommendations.

FieldWise integrates NASA environmental data—like temperature and precipitation—with agricultural knowledge on crop requirements and pest risks. Its decision-support engine evaluates multiple rotation strategies, featuring direct price comparisons between crops to highlight their environmental suitability, economic benefits, and potential risks.

Initially focused on Egypt, FieldWise uses a scalable, modular architecture. This enables future expansion to new crops and global regions, alongside the integration of advanced soil data and analytical capabilities.

By transforming complex environmental, agricultural, and market data into actionable insights, FieldWise empowers farmers to make informed decisions and build resilient, profitable agricultural systems.
projectDetails.details:
What FieldWise Does and How It Works

FieldWise is a smart agricultural system powered by NASA data. It helps farmers choose the best crops to plant over multiple years to keep the soil healthy and increase profits.

How It Works: Step 1. Farm Location: Farmers select their exact field on a map. The system checks if the location and soil type match perfectly. Step 2. Live Climate Data: FieldWise pulls 20 years of real time weather data from NASA for that specific location, including temperature, rain, and sunlight. Step 3. Smart Recommendations: The system evaluates different crop choices based on clear rules. It looks at climate fit, water needs, soil type, natural fertilizers, pest control, expected profits, farming seasons, and long term sustainability. Step 4. Easy Reports: It creates a simple bilingual report in Arabic and English. This report gives farmers clear schedules and watering guides.

Key Benefits of FieldWise

Water Conservation: Shows farmers how switching from traditional crops to better alternatives saves huge amounts of water, especially when using modern irrigation. Less Chemical Fertilizer: Uses specific plants to naturally add nutrients to the soil, reducing the need to buy chemical fertilizers. Natural Disease Control: Replaces expensive chemicals with natural crop rotation methods that stop soil diseases. Real Profit Calculator: Calculates expected costs and profits using official local crop prices to help farmers manage their money. Fully Bilingual: Works perfectly in both Arabic and English.

Intended Impact

FieldWise aims to solve water scarcity, soil problems, and food security in Egypt and other dry regions. By giving farmers free and smart planting schedules, it aims to: Reduce the need for chemical fertilizers. Lower water usage in dry areas. Stop major crop losses caused by planting the same crop every year. Significantly increase the yearly income of small farmers.

Tools, Software and Data Used

Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, HTML, and CSS. Frameworks: Next.js and Tailwind CSS for building the website. Mapping: Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for interactive maps. Data Sources: NASA POWER for climate data, NASA SMAP and Landsat for satellite imaging, FAO databases for farming rules, and official Egyptian portals for crop prices. Quality Testing: Custom automated tests to ensure all data and rules work perfectly

How FieldWise is Creative

Clear Science: Every recommendation is based on clear math and agricultural rules, not a hidden artificial intelligence box. Smart Error Detection: If a user enters a location that does not match the selected soil type, the system automatically detects the mistake and alerts them. Making Space Data Local: It translates complex NASA satellite data into simple local farming units and local currency

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

Real Local Climate: We adjusted the broad satellite data to match the actual climate of specific local farms to calculate precise water needs. Accurate Plant Nutrition: We carefully calculated exactly how much natural fertilizer a plant leaves in the soil for the next crop. Real Disease Risks: We focused on the actual plant diseases that affect local farmers and warned them about soil salt levels before planting sensitive crops.

node.title: Fireium : The Element of Fire
node.excerpt: We are a group of STEM October students

projectDetails.name: Fireium
projectDetails.summary: Fireium is a web-based platform that articulates NASA's combustion research in ways including data charts, SI chatbots, PDF reports, and prediction models, in addition to mapping research gaps. Fireium allows researchers and engineers to predict the behavior of fire in different habitats (space station, moon base, etc.) by matching it to a specific NASA experiment after ranking them based on match accuracy. In the case of untested conditions (conditions that don’t match any of the NASA investigations), the platform maps them as a research gap. Beyond that, the platform is equipped with an SI chatbot, providing personalized resource navigation while maintaining factual consistency, as every claim is cited to its source (the sources consist only of the 3530 passages from NASA documents). Furthermore, the platform provides 4 different levels of data navigation ranging from beginner to expert, serving a broad audience with variable expertise.
projectDetails.details:
1. What our project does

FIreium is a web platform that collects, analyzes and organizes NASA’s combustion data in order to give useful fire-safety insights, and improve the understanding of fire behavior under different conditions (space stations, spacecraft, pressurized rovers, and bases on the Moon and Mars)

NASA has studied fire without gravity for decades. The results are spread across many sources:

  • 24 combustion investigations in the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository
  • 2,005 rows of measured test data in 22 run tables
  • 3530 scientific passages
  • fact sheets, NASA videos, history pages and Spinoff articles

The project aims to provide insights to the behavior of fire in microgravity in variable levels of expertise, encompassing undergraduate students, graduate students, aerospace engineers and researchers.

Our platform does exactly that. It does three things, and every feature is built around them:

  1. Starts from the habitat. Choosing a crew environment re-orders the whole site around that atmosphere: the ranking, predictions, research gaps and Mission Report.
  2. Never invents. Every statement on the site, including every AI answer, leads back to a NASA source with its page number. Code checks this; the model is not trusted to do it alone.
  3. Says how sure it is. Predictions carry a confidence score. Missing data is shown as a research gap instead of being hidden or guessed.

 

2. How it works, feature by feature

2.1 Start page:

What it does

  • Four guided paths follow, each marked with its level. Based on the expertise of the user, the website creates customized highly detailed plan for the user to offer optimal learning efficiency:

 

2.2 Research Explorer: all 24 NASA investigations

What it does

  • First, the user chooses a habitat then the page generates a short summary which includes 3 main parts: the safety requirements for the environment, the main findings from NASA’S research about the environment, and the research gaps which are the weakly researched aspects of the environment.
  • Along with the environment summary the page lists all the investigations in the selected environment. These experiments can be filtered by fuel state, material, safety area (prevention, detection, suppression), gravity, facility, topic, and the oxygen, pressure and airflow ranges tested. ==

How it is built

  • Data pipeline:
    • fetch_psi.py downloads every PSI combustion record, run table and image.
    • build_db.py normalises them into a SQLite database (flame.db): investigations, tables, runs, text passages.
  • Search: the text search matches word stems, so "smoke detection" also finds records that say "detector".
  • Range filters: a range filter keeps an experiment only if its tested range overlaps the requested one. An experiment that never reported a value is never matched as if it had.

Investigation profiles. Each investigation has its own page with:

  • a plain-language summary written by our team, clearly labelled as ours
  • NASA's own record text, copied unchanged
  • test conditions, run data, publications and related experiments
  • links to the NASA PSI record and the dataset DOI
  • what the official NASA resources say about that experiment

2.3 AI Research Assistant

Our AI Assistant uses only relevant NASA documents as a primary source of information and cites these documents in the generated answers so that the user can verify the accuracy of the claims and to prevent made-up answers. An example of the citation feature would be like:

    • 7 of 8 statements cite NASA.
    • 2 of 2 numbers were found in the cited passage.
    • 4 passages are cited, with page numbers.
    • 0 citations had to be removed.

If no relevant NASA data is found to answer the question, the assistant assigns a “research gap” tag to the answer so that the user knows that there is little or no research on the topic. Additionally, to increase accessibility, the AI assistant can adjust the wording level from student to expert, and the user can limit the searchable experiments to only a few experiments.

How it is built (research.py, retrieval.py)

  1. Library. NASA reports, science documents and analysed-data sheets are read page by page with pypdf (build_docs.py). The 10 official challenge resources are read too: web pages, PDFs and the video captions (build_resources.py). Together with the PSI records this gives 3,530 searchable passages, each tagged with its kind (NASA report, PSI record, run table, NASA resource and so on).
    • keyword search (TF-IDF, scikit-learn) catches exact names such as "PMMA" or "BASS-II"
    • meaning search (the BAAI bge-small-en-v1.5 model, run on our own server with FastEmbed and ONNX, with no paid API) catches passages that answer the question in other words

The two rankings are merged with reciprocal rank fusion.

  1. Ask. The best passages go to Claude (Haiku, low effort) as numbered sources. The instructions say: answer only from these sources and cite them.
    • every citation must point to a passage the model was actually given, or it is removed
    • the answer is split into statements, each labelled with the kind of evidence behind it
    • every number with a unit is looked up in the cited passage
    • sentences where the model talks about its own sources instead of NASA's findings are removed
  2. Stream. The answer streams in and is written out word by word, without the page jumping.

Without an AI key the same search runs and the passages are quoted directly, so the site still works and nothing is generated.

2.4 Fire Safety Insights: prevention, detection, suppression

What it does

This page explains the three main themes of the challenge using NASA's own evidence. Prevention covers material flammability, oxygen limits and airflow. Detection covers smoke and particle sensing. Suppression covers CO₂, helium and other gases that put flames out. The page uses NASA photos, small charts and word-for-word quotes, and it ends with a 10-question quiz so the user can test what they learned.

How it is built

Every point on the page carries a quote from a PSI record, the challenge text or an official NASA resource. When the server starts, verify() looks for each quote in its source. If one cannot be found, the server refuses to start, so the page can never drift away from the data.

2.5 Lessons & Applications: history, physics and Earth

What it does

This page is divided into four sections and includes a second quiz:

  1. Lessons from accidents: Apollo 1 (1967), Apollo 13 (1970) and the Mir fire (1997), taken from NASA's own history pages.
  2. Earth vs. microgravity: explains why a candle flame becomes a sphere in microgravity, and shows the Saffire-II table of the same materials burned in orbit and on Earth.
  3. Next-generation equipment: what NASA's records point to for future detectors, suppression systems and material tests.
  4. Uses on Earth: three NASA Spinoff technologies (firefighters' air tanks, fire detectors and fire-resistant clothing), plus ground testing in drop towers.

Drop towers are used to test fire on Earth. A falling package is weightless for a few seconds, which is enough time to light a flame and watch it. The page links two facilities:

  • NASA Glenn: 5.18 s of free fall, a combustion rig, and a centrifuge for partial gravity.
  • ZARM Bremen: 4.7 s of free fall, or 9.3 s with the catapult. Its GraviTower can reproduce Moon and Mars gravity.

This points directly at the biggest gap we found, which is that none of the 24 investigations were run in partial gravity.

2.6 Charts: NASA's measured data, interactive

What it does

The Charts page lets the user explore NASA's measured data directly:

  • Build your own chart from 18 NASA run tables. The chart can be a scatter, line, bar, histogram or box plot, coloured by any column.
  • Upload your own CSV file and chart it the same way.
  • Choose from 8 ready-made charts that show key results.
  • Download the plotted data as a CSV file, or open the original NASA file.

The "Where has NASA tested?" chart plots 1,009 NASA tests by oxygen and pressure against the cabin atmospheres of the five habitats. The Moon Base box shows at a glance which tests are relevant to it, and that no solid-material test falls inside it.

How it is built

  • Charts are drawn in the browser with Plotly, using run-table rows served by the API.
  • Each ready-made chart names real column names, and verify() checks them at startup, so a chart can never show a measurement that NASA's table does not contain.
  • Notes warn the user where a column means something different, for example oxygen measured in the burner gas rather than in the chamber.

2.7 Experiment Ranking: which NASA results matter for your habitat

What it does

Every investigation gets a relevance score from 0 to 100 for the chosen habitat. For Moon Base, FLEX ranks first (77.4), followed by ACME BRE (72.6) and FLEX-2 (70.5). Each card also says where its points came from, for example "oxygen match (+25), fire-safety directness (+18.8)".

How it is built (environments.py)

  • Seven factors are scored from 0 to 1 using the database: fire-safety directness, gravity relevance, oxygen match, pressure match, cabin-material relevance, ventilation data, and whether run data is available.
  • The habitat atmospheres are taken from the NASA challenge text. For example, the Moon is described as "30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less".
  • The user can drag the weight sliders or choose a safety focus (prevention, detection or suppression), and the ranking updates live.
  • The AI can also rank the experiments by a criterion that the user writes in their own words, and it cites the reasons.
  • The page states clearly that this is the project's own method and not a NASA score, and it shows the formula and the breakdown of every result.

2.8 Compare: two to four experiments side by side

What it does

The page starts with three summary boxes: what the selected experiments have in common, where they differ, and what information is missing. A full table follows, row by row. Suggested pairs (BASS-II vs BASS, SAME vs SAME-R, FLEX vs FLEX-2) make it quick to get started, and the AI can interpret the comparison on request.

How it is built

The rows come straight from the database. A missing value is shown as "Not reported" and is never filled in by guessing.

2.9 Predictions: what would a fire do in this atmosphere?

What it does

The Predictions page answers three questions: how fast a fuel droplet burns, whether the flame will go out, and how hot a gas flame gets. The user can either choose a habitat or set the oxygen, CO₂, helium and pressure levels manually. The page then gives a prediction with a likely range, a confidence score, and how the result changes compared with normal cabin air. In the example above, methanol burns at about 0.66 mm²/s at Moon Base air, with 87% confidence. The user can also upload a CSV file of conditions, and every row will be predicted.

How it is built (models.py, predict.py, scikit-learn)

The models follow strict rules so that the predictions can be trusted:

  • Tested on unseen data: the tests use 5-fold cross-validation grouped by test day, so tests run on the same day are never split between training and testing.
  • Must beat a guess: a model is offered only if it cuts the error of the no-model guess by at least 20%. Two candidate models failed this test (CFI-G ignition and burn time), so they are not shown, and the code says why.
  • Confidence falls with distance: the score drops and the likely range widens as the request moves away from real NASA tests. Outside a tested range the result is labelled as an extrapolation.
  • Impossible inputs are refused: an atmosphere whose gases add up to more than 100% gets no number.
  • Labelled as a prediction: every output says "model prediction, not a NASA measurement".

2.10 Research Gaps: what NASA has not tested

What it does

The gap map crosses what was burned with the oxygen level tested, or with other pairs that the user picks. It shows how many investigations fill each cell, and red dashed circles mark the empty combinations. With all 24 investigations there are 11 empty combinations. For example, no solid material has been tested above 22.5% oxygen, yet a Moon base will have 30% or more. The page also lists the main gaps and suggests research questions.

How it is built (gaps.py)

Everything is counted from the database for the investigations that pass the user's filters. A gap means "not in this NASA collection", and never a claim that no such research exists anywhere. The page says this clearly.

2.11 Mission Report: one click, one PDF

What it does

For any habitat, the page builds a fire-safety report with a reference list. The report is previewed on the page and can be downloaded as a PDF. It has six sections:

  1. The environment
  2. An AI-written briefing from NASA sources
  3. The most relevant experiments
  4. Fire-safety insights
  5. Research gaps
  6. The model estimate

The report can also be focused on prevention, detection or suppression.

How it is built (mission.py, fpdf2)

The report does not compute anything new. Each part comes from the module that owns it (ranking, insights, gaps and predictions), so the report always agrees with the rest of the site. Every statement carries a reference.

2.12 NASA Resources: full transparency on the data

What it does

This page lists the 10 official NASA resources for the challenge. All 10 are used, which adds up to 19 documents, 231 passages and 36,644 words, and every quote is checked. For each resource, the page shows:

  • what share of its text was read and used
  • which parts of the site use it (AI assistant, data pages, experiment pages, Insights, Lessons and Research Gaps)

Any file that could not be read is listed together with the reason, instead of being hidden.

3. Benefits

  • For mission planners and engineers: a ranked and cited answer to "which NASA results apply to my habitat?" in minutes instead of weeks of reading, plus a PDF report that is ready to share.
  • For researchers: fast search across 3,530 NASA passages with page-level citations, side-by-side comparison, interactive charts of the raw run data, and a map of untested conditions to guide new experiments.
  • For students and teachers: four levels of explanation, two quizzes, NASA photos and real data to learn from and teach with.
  • For everyone: trust, because every number can be traced to NASA and every prediction says how sure it is.

4. Intended impact

Fire is one of the most dangerous emergencies in space. There is nowhere to escape, and help is days or months away. As NASA prepares for long stays on the Moon and missions to Mars, crews will live in oxygen-rich, low-pressure atmospheres where fire has barely been studied.

Our goal is to make sure that this knowledge is used:

  • Show what is already known: bring NASA's decades of combustion results to the people designing future habitats, in a form that they can act on.
  • Show what is still unknown: gaps such as partial gravity and solid materials above 22.5% oxygen become a clear agenda for the next experiments, including affordable ground tests in drop towers.
  • Teach the next generation: students learn fire safety in space from real NASA data, at their own level.

5. Tools, languages and software

 

 

Data

  • NASA PSI combustion repository: 24 investigations, 22 run tables, PSI images and documents.
    • NASA Combustion Science
    • the Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science
    • the NASA ScienceCast video and its captions
    • Apollo 1 and Apollo 13 (NASA Safety Center)
    • the Mir fire (NASA History)
    • three NASA Spinoff articles, read in full from NASA's Technical Reports Server
  • NASA Glenn's drop-tower facility page and ZARM Bremen, for ground testing.

6. How the project is creative

  • Habitat first, not database first: instead of another list of experiments, the site asks where the crew will live, and re-orders all of NASA's evidence around that atmosphere.
  • An AI that is checked by code: most AI tools only ask the model to be accurate. Ours removes citations that point to nothing, looks up every number in its source, and shows the reader a ledger of how well each answer is backed.
  • Predictions that admit their limits: models are offered only if they beat a simple guess on unseen test days. Confidence falls away from real tests, and models that failed the test are openly left out.
  • Missing data becomes a result: the Research Gaps map and the habitat chart show where NASA has not tested, and link to the facilities that could close those gaps.
  • One source of truth: the Mission Report, the AI and every page draw on the same checked data, so they can never disagree.

7. Factors our team considered

  • Accuracy over impressiveness:
    • Every quote is verified at startup.
    • Every model prediction is labelled as a prediction, never as a NASA measurement.
    • Our own methods (the relevance score and the plain-language summaries) are labelled as ours, not NASA's.
  • Honest limits: each model lists what it does not cover, for example droplets are not cabin fabrics. A research gap means "not in this collection", not "never studied".
    • We chose a small, fast model (Claude Haiku, low effort), which costs about $0.002 and takes 4–11 seconds per answer.
    • Meaning search runs on our own server at no cost per question.
    • The whole site fits on a small cloud server with 512 MB of memory.
  • Accessibility and design: light and dark modes, phone and desktop layouts, motion that respects "reduce motion" settings, and keyboard shortcuts.

  • Testing: a 100-check test suite runs locally. An end-to-end test of the live site checks every page and feature, including real AI answers and PDF downloads.
