projectDetails.name: Project FireOrbit
projectDetails.summary:
FireOrbit is a spacecraft fire-safety dashboard and AI assistant built on NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) combustion data. A preprocessing pipeline turns PSI investigation metadata, experiment records and PDF reports into a normalized knowledge base. A FastAPI backend and web dashboard let researchers rank investigations, explore and compare experiments, and find coverage gaps, such as Moon-cabin oxygen levels and reduced pressure. Its “Ask FireOrbit” assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): hybrid keyword and semantic retrieval, with query routing for oxygen level, fuel and outcome, feeds Gemini. Answers come with cited sources, and a what-if tool estimates burn likelihood from the nearest observed experiments, not a made-up model.

Fire is one of the most dangerous risks on crewed missions, yet decades of microgravity combustion evidence sit scattered across reports and tables. FireOrbit makes that evidence searchable, comparable and traceable, so mission planners can see what is known, what is uncertain, and what still needs testing.
projectDetails.details:
FireOrbit: project details

What it does and how it works

FireOrbit turns NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) combustion data into a decision tool for spacecraft fire safety. It has three layers.

1. Data pipeline. Scripts extract text and tables from PSI PDF reports, parse the ISA-Tab investigation files, and normalize the experiment CSVs. The output is a knowledge base of investigations plus normalized experiment records (fuel, O₂ %, pressure, flow, outcome). Each investigation is scored for relevance and for Moon-base applicability, grouped by safety pillar (Prevention, Detection, Suppression, Fundamental). Values the pipeline had to assume are flagged. The text is split into 4,518 chunks: 2,777 report pages, 1,589 experiment records and 152 investigation summaries.

2. Backend (FastAPI). It serves the dashboard data, ranking, comparison and coverage-gap analytics, and the AI endpoints.

  • Retrieval. Hybrid retrieval combines BM25 keyword search with dense vector search, merged by reciprocal-rank fusion. A rule-based query router turns phrases like "85% oxygen", "methanol", "self-extinguished" or "SAMER" into metadata filters. This lets the system answer counting questions ("how many tests…") from structured metadata instead of guessing.
  • Fallbacks. FireOrbit keeps working when parts of the stack are unavailable. If the vector index or embedding libraries can’t load (for example on a small free server), the backend switches from hybrid to keyword search over the same report and experiment chunks, and its /health endpoint reports which mode is active. If no Gemini key is configured, the API returns the retrieved passages without a generated answer. If the backend can’t be reached at all, the dashboard loads an offline data snapshot and the Ask tab searches it locally by keyword, with a status line showing which mode the user is in.
  • Answers. A Gemini model writes the answer only from the retrieved passages, with numbered citations. A no-answer gate means greetings and unsupported questions don't produce invented answers.
  • What-if engine. It estimates burn likelihood from the nearest observed experiments. It reports confidence and warns about extrapolation, missing pressure data and the lack of partial-gravity data.

3. Dashboard. A static web app has tabs for Overview, Rank, Explore data, Compare, Ask FireOrbit, and Gaps & Earth. It is deployed on Vercel and has a keyword-search fallback if the backend is unreachable.

Benefits

  • Evidence scattered across reports and tables becomes searchable and comparable in one place.
  • Every AI answer points back to its source document and page, so it can be checked.
  • The tool states its limits openly: assumed data, extrapolation, single-source results.
  • Gap analysis shows which conditions, such as Moon-cabin oxygen or reduced pressure, have little or no data.

Intended impact

The goal is to help mission planners, safety engineers and researchers see what combustion evidence exists for exploration environments, how reliable it is, and where new experiments are needed. It supports safer cabin-atmosphere decisions and better prioritization of future fire-safety testing. It is a research aid, not a certification tool, and the dashboard says so.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS
  • Backend: FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn
  • Data processing: pandas, PyMuPDF
  • Retrieval: rank-bm25, ChromaDB, sentence-transformers (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 for local use), NumPy, and a lightweight retriever for serverless (BM25 plus precomputed Gemini embeddings)
  • LLM: Google Gemini via the google-genai SDK
  • Deployment and tooling: Vercel (static frontend plus Python serverless API), Git/GitHub, pytest
  • Hardware: no specialized hardware. It runs on a laptop, and the live site runs on Vercel's serverless platform.

What makes it creative

  • It combines semantic search, keyword search and structured metadata routing, so the system can reason over whole sets of experiments, not just a few text snippets.
  • The what-if tool uses nearest-neighbour evidence from real experiments instead of a black-box model, and it tells the user how far to trust the result.
  • The "Gaps" view reverses the usual question. It shows what the data cannot answer about the Moon, as well as what it can.
  • The retrieval stack was redesigned to fit serverless limits: large ML libraries stay local, while the deployed version uses small dependencies and precomputed vectors.

Factors considered

  • Trust and traceability: citations, an answer gate, and the model barred from using outside knowledge.
  • Data quality: flagged assumed and invalid values, and warnings when evidence is thin.
  • Domain relevance: Moon-base scoring and coverage of exploration-relevant oxygen and pressure ranges.
  • Evaluation: an evaluation question set (eval_set.json) with answerable and unanswerable questions, used to calibrate retrieval.
  • Deployment constraints: serverless size limits, optional API keys, and graceful fallback to keyword search.

projectDetails.name: Fire Link
projectDetails.summary:
Wildfire responders receive two separate NASA hotspot feeds — VIIRS and MODIS — with no
quick way to tell which detections are the same fire seen twice and which are real. FireLink
reconciles both feeds into a single interactive map. Every hotspot is classified as
Confirmed (both satellites agree), Likely (one satellite plus a nearby detection from the
other), Single or Weak, and drawn with size, a white ring and a halo so the classes stay
readable without relying on colour. Users draw a box or type coordinates and immediately
get detection counts, an activity calendar that flags anomalous days and multi-day critical
periods, a multi-year monthly history compared with the long-term average, a burned-area
estimate in km² exportable as CSV or PDF, filters by satellite, fire radiative power and
brightness, NASA GIBS true-colour imagery, wind-driven spread direction, nearby protected
areas, shareable URLs that store coordinates and date, and automatic email alerts when a
region crosses a threshold. It also separates forest fires from agricultural burning. The
whole app runs from one Python file with no framework and no database.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
FireLink turns NASA FIRMS fire detections into a decision tool for people who have to act
on them. The user draws a box on the map or types west/east/south/north coordinates, picks
a date, and the app queries NASA FIRMS for both VIIRS (S-NPP) and MODIS. Instead of showing
two overlapping layers, it runs a reconciliation pass: detections from the two instruments
that fall inside the same pixel footprint and time window are merged into one fire event
with a confidence class — Confirmed, Likely, Single or Weak. The map colours detections by
fire radiative power using a colour-blind-safe palette and adds size, a white ring and a
halo, so severity is readable without colour alone.

Around the map, three tabs summarise the region: a burned-day calendar that marks days with
unusual activity and groups consecutive critical days, a history view with the monthly fire
count compared with the multi-year average and the anomaly, and a headline panel with the
number of fires, confirmed detections, peak intensity and a burned-area estimate in km².
Reports export to CSV and PDF. Optional layers add NASA GIBS true-colour imagery, wind
direction from OpenWeather so an alert can say which way a fire is spreading, and protected
or agricultural land so an alert states whether a fire is inside a reserve or on farmland.
Shareable URLs encode the box and date, and a built-in email notifier sends an alert when a
region crosses the configured threshold.

Why it matters
Two feeds, two answers, and no shared confidence is exactly the confusion that delays a
response. Merging them cuts duplicate reports, surfaces single-satellite fires that a
layer overlay hides, and gives an explicit confidence level for every alert. The burned-area
estimate and the CSV/PDF export plug straight into a situation report, and the calendar and
history views answer the question a land manager actually asks: is this normal for this
month or not? The app also distinguishes forest fires from agricultural burning, because
the response is different: a field being prepared is not an evacuation.

Tools, languages and technology
Python 3 standard library for the backend (http.server, no web framework), plain JavaScript
with Leaflet 1.9.4 and Leaflet.draw for the interface, canvas for the charts, and requests
for the NASA FIRMS HTTP API. No database and no build step: the app is one server file plus
one HTML page, so it runs anywhere Python runs, including a container.

Hardware and software used
A standard laptop for development, plus free hosting for the public demo. Only free and
open tools were used: Python, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap and CartoDB basemaps, NASA FIRMS and
NASA GIBS.

Creativity
The core idea is using satellite agreement as a confidence signal rather than drawing two
layers and leaving the interpretation to the user. That single decision drives the whole
interface: confidence classes, the alert levels, and the wording of the email alert. The
burned-area estimate is computed from the real pixel footprint of each instrument (VIIRS
0.1406 km², MODIS 1 km²) instead of a guess. The app also handles NASA's publication lag,
so a day that is still being published is labelled as partial instead of looking like a
quiet day.

Factors considered
Accuracy: every detection is traceable to its satellite, instrument, confidence and
brightness value. Accessibility: a colour-blind-safe palette, redundant shape and size
encoding, and readable contrast. Usability: the coordinate inputs and the GeoJSON upload
are visible, not buried in text. Performance: the interface stays responsive with thousands
of points by drawing on canvas. Cost: the entire stack is free and open source, so any
fire brigade can run it without a licence.

projectDetails.name: Earth Jukebox
projectDetails.summary: Earth Jukebox is an accessible web application that transforms NASA Earth data into dynamic, real-time soundscapes (sonification). By mapping critical climate variables—such as global temperature, Arctic sea ice, wildfires, and CO₂ levels—to musical parameters like pitch, volume, and rhythm, the app makes complex scientific trends accessible to blind and low-vision users. It bridges the gap between data and the senses, proving that science can be heard, not just seen.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem: At least 2.2 billion people worldwide have vision impairment. NASA’s Earth Information Center publishes stunning visualizations daily, but they are exclusively visual. Even sighted users often skim past charts without truly feeling the urgency of climate change.

The Solution: Earth Jukebox translates sight into sound. Users can select specific Earth data tracks (Temperature, Sea Ice, Wildfires, CO₂) and immediately hear a generated soundscape. For example, rising temperatures produce ascending notes, while melting ice produces fading tones.

How it works: Each data value is mapped to a note on a pentatonic musical scale. Data intensity is mapped to volume, and the data type dictates the waveform (e.g., a low drone for CO₂). The audio is synthesized in real-time using the Web Audio API, ensuring no audio files are required.

Accessibility First: The interface features screen-reader optimized descriptions, full keyboard operability, aria-live announcements, and high-contrast UI with reduced-motion support.

projectDetails.name: Burnwise: Harmonizing NASA MODIS and VIIRS Fire Hotspots for Early Warning
projectDetails.summary:
Burnwise is an interactive fire-monitoring platform that transforms NASA satellite fire detections into a consistent historical record to help identify unusual fire activity and support early warning.

The project addresses a major challenge: MODIS and VIIRS satellites detect fires at different spatial resolutions, creating artificial jumps when their data are combined. Burnwise harmonizes both datasets using a Random Forest model and a statistical ratio baseline, producing a monthly fire record from 2003 to 2026.

Users can explore fire activity through an interactive map, a monthly burning calendar, historical comparisons, anomaly alerts, and high-risk fire clusters. The platform also supports CSV exports for further analysis.

Focusing on Egypt and the Nile Delta, Burnwise aims to support environmental monitoring, emergency planning, and understanding seasonal agricultural burning and its impact on air quality.
projectDetails.details:
How Burnwise Works

Burnwise is an end-to-end satellite fire-monitoring and analytics platform designed to provide a reliable historical view of vegetation fire activity.

1. Data Collection and Processing

We collected historical active-fire detections from NASA FIRMS, using MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP 375m datasets. The data were cleaned by removing duplicates, filtering non-vegetation detections, applying confidence thresholds, and aggregating fire counts into a 0.25° spatial grid with monthly resolution.

2. Cross-Sensor Harmonization

Since MODIS and VIIRS have different detection resolutions and sensitivities, combining their raw observations can produce misleading trends. We developed two harmonization approaches:

  • A statistical baseline using a constant VIIRS/MODIS ratio.
  • A Random Forest model trained on the 2013–2022 overlapping period.

The Random Forest achieved a 9.1% leave-one-year-out yearly error, compared with 17.6% for the ratio baseline.

3. Interactive Monitoring and Analytics

The web application allows users to:

  • Select geographic areas and date ranges through an interactive map.
  • Explore a 283-month historical burning calendar covering January 2003 to July 2026.
  • Compare current fire activity against historical monthly medians.
  • Receive anomaly alerts using robust statistical scoring.
  • Identify and visualize high-risk fire clusters using HDBSCAN.
  • Export selected monthly fire data as CSV files.

Impact and Innovation

Burnwise makes satellite fire data easier to understand and use without requiring advanced GIS expertise. It can support environmental researchers, emergency managers, and land managers in identifying unusual burning patterns, understanding seasonal agricultural fires, and improving resource planning.

The project focuses on the Nile Delta, where agricultural residue burning contributes to seasonal air pollution and the autumn black cloud phenomenon.

Technologies Used

Python, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Random Forest, SHAP, HDBSCAN, Google Colab, FastAPI, JavaScript, Leaflet, Leaflet Draw, and Chart.js.

Creative Approach

Our main innovation is combining cross-sensor data harmonization, transparent model validation, historical anomaly detection, and spatial clustering in one accessible platform. We also openly report model limitations and compare our results against simpler baselines rather than presenting machine learning performance without context.

projectDetails.name: BlinkSphere
projectDetails.summary: NASA’s SPHEREx telescope generates thousands of sky images every six months across 102 infrared wavebands, yet utilizing this massive data remains challenging due to sluggish web platforms and a lack of user guidance. BlinkSphere was developed to solve this by integrating dynamic tile-based loading to eliminate lag, seamless navigation across spectral bands and timeframes, an AI agent for automated celestial object detection, and advanced RGB-driven water mapping tools. This platform is vital because it empowers passionate students with an accessible, hands-on space exploration experience while easing the heavy processing workload for scientists through smart, efficient analytical tools.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

BlinkSphere (powered by our SPHEREx Spectral Lab engine) is an interactive, web-based astronomical platform built to simplify the exploration and analysis of massive hyperspectral telescope datasets, specifically targeting NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Instead of forcing users to download heavy raw files, BlinkSphere processes 3D spectral data cubes (128×128 spatial pixels across 102 infrared wavebands) and streams them smoothly to the browser using dynamic tile-based lazy loading. Users can seamlessly scrub through all 102 infrared bands and historical timeframes, generate custom RGB composite maps to detect water and ice signatures (H_2O and CO_2 absorption lines), and inspect individual celestial spectra in 2D and 3D. Additionally, an integrated AI anomaly-detection agent (using Isolation Forest) automatically flags unusual objects and classifies light sources against scientific reference templates (Pickles, EAZY, and Prism libraries).  

Key Benefits & Intended Impact

Traditional astronomical tools are sluggish, steep in learning curve, and resource-heavy. BlinkSphere eliminates platform lag and lowers the technical barrier to entry. Our intended impact is dual-fold:  

1. Democratizing Space Science for Students & Enthusiasts: Giving learners a hands-on, intuitive sandbox to explore deep-space data without needing supercomputers or advanced coding skills.  

2. Accelerating Research for Scientists: Lifting the heavy data-wrangling burden so researchers can rapidly isolate spectral anomalies, compare temporal shifts, and map water/ice distributions.  

Creativity & Accessibility Factors Considered

To make cosmic data truly inclusive and engaging, our team incorporated several creative features and human-centric design factors:

 Spectrum Sonification (Web Audio API): Converts light spectra into audio frequencies, allowing visually impaired users and researchers to "hear" cosmic anomalies and absorption dips.  

 Bilingual & Inclusive UI: Designed with a space-inspired dark theme, full mobile responsiveness, and native Right-to-Left (RTL) Arabic support alongside English to bridge the language gap in space education.  

 Citizen Science Micro-Tasks: Includes a lightweight voting system (⁠localStorage⁠ / ⁠SQLite⁠) where volunteers can help validate AI-flagged candidates.  

 Transparency & Rapid Prototyping: Because full-scale SPHEREx public archives are rolling out, we engineered a synthetic spectral cube generator (⁠prepare_data.py⁠)—clearly labeled as Synthetic / Demo Data in the UI—to validate our pipeline ahead of direct integration with the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive via ⁠astroquery⁠.  

Tools, Coding Languages & Architecture

 Programming Languages: Python 3.14.3, TypeScript 5.6, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, and PowerShell.  

 Backend & Scientific Computing: FastAPI and Uvicorn (RESTful API & ASGI server), Pydantic (data validation), NumPy 2.5.4 & SciPy 1.18 (102×128×128 spectral cube math), Astropy 7.0+ (FITS handling & astronomical calculations), Astroquery 0.4.9 (NASA/IPAC IRSA archive integration), scikit-learn 1.5+ (Isolation Forest anomaly detection), and SQLite.  

 Frontend & Visualization: React 18.3, Vite 5.4, Tailwind CSS 3.4, Plotly.js 2.35 (3D cubes, heatmaps, and spectral plots), HTML5 Canvas API (real-time RGB/band rendering), Web Audio API (spectrum sonification), and Lucide-React.  

 Data Formats & Deployment: Compressed Binary Float32 (⁠.bin⁠) cubes, JSON metadata, Docker/Docker-Compose, Vercel (Frontend), and Render/Railway (Backend).

projectDetails.name: FIREMIND
projectDetails.summary:
FIREMIND is a geospatial intelligence platform that addresses the challenge of comparing active-fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite systems.

Using H3 spatial indexing, weekly temporal aggregation, and machine learning, FIREMIND estimates VIIRS-equivalent fire counts from MODIS-only observations, creating a more consistent framework for analyzing fire activity across different satellite systems.

Through an interactive dashboard, users can explore historical fire patterns, visualize geographic hotspots, identify unusual activity, and examine model estimates alongside uncertainty intervals.

By transforming fragmented satellite observations into more comparable and accessible information, FIREMIND aims to help researchers, environmental organizations, and fire managers better understand how fire activity evolves across locations and over time.

FIREMIND — See the signal. Understand the gaps.
projectDetails.details:
FIREMIND — Intelligent Fire Activity Harmonization

Project Description

FIREMIND is a geospatial intelligence platform designed to make historical and ongoing fire activity easier to understand by addressing a major challenge in satellite-based fire monitoring: the differences between MODIS and VIIRS observations.

Although both satellite systems detect active fires, they differ in spatial resolution, observation characteristics, and detection counts. These differences make their records difficult to compare directly, creating inconsistencies in long-term fire activity analysis.

FIREMIND addresses this challenge through a data-driven harmonization approach. Using H3 spatial indexing and weekly temporal aggregation, our system organizes fire observations into consistent geographic and temporal units. It uses MODIS-only features to estimate VIIRS-equivalent fire counts, with NOAA-20 VIIRS observations serving as a comparison reference.

The platform transforms these processed observations into an interactive dashboard where users can explore historical fire activity, examine geographic patterns, navigate weekly fire activity timelines, identify unusual activity, and inspect individual geographic cells alongside calibrated uncertainty intervals.

Benefits and Intended Impact

FIREMIND aims to make satellite fire observations more consistent, accessible, and useful for understanding fire activity over time.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Improved data comparability: Provides a consistent analytical framework for examining observations from different satellite systems.
  • Historical analysis: Helps researchers explore long-term fire activity patterns and identify recurring periods of increased burning.
  • Unusual activity detection: Highlights deviations from expected fire activity to support further investigation.
  • Geographic insights: Allows users to examine fire activity at different locations and across different time periods.
  • Transparent uncertainty: Communicates uncertainty alongside model estimates rather than presenting estimates as exact observations.

Our intended impact is to support researchers, environmental organizations, land managers, and fire-monitoring professionals in making better-informed decisions through more consistent satellite-derived fire activity information.

Tools and Technologies

FIREMIND was developed using a combination of web technologies, programming, geospatial processing, and machine learning.

  • Python: Data processing, analytical workflows, and model development.
  • JavaScript: Interactive dashboard functionality and data visualization.
  • HTML and CSS: Dashboard structure and interface design.
  • H3 Geospatial Indexing: Organizing geographic observations into consistent spatial cells.
  • MODIS and VIIRS satellite datasets: The primary Earth observation data sources.
  • NOAA-20 VIIRS observations: Used as a comparison reference for model development and evaluation.

Creativity and Innovation

FIREMIND goes beyond simply displaying satellite fire hotspots on a map.

Its central innovation is addressing differences between satellite observation systems through a model that estimates VIIRS-equivalent fire counts using MODIS-only features.

Rather than treating satellite observations as directly interchangeable, FIREMIND uses spatial and temporal harmonization to establish a more consistent analytical framework.

The platform also combines historical exploration, unusual activity detection, model estimates, and uncertainty visualization in one interactive environment.

We further evaluate our approach against a seasonal-ratio baseline using held-out testing, allowing us to measure whether our approach improves count estimation rather than relying on visual results alone.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors:

  1. Scientific reliability: Ensuring that satellite observations and model estimates are represented accurately.
  2. Different satellite characteristics: Accounting for differences in spatial resolution, observation patterns, and detection behavior.
  3. Spatial and temporal consistency: Establishing comparable geographic and weekly units for analysis.
  4. Model uncertainty: Making limitations and uncertainty visible to users.
  5. Accessibility: Designing an interactive interface that makes complex geospatial information understandable without requiring advanced technical knowledge.
  6. Practical feasibility: Developing a solution that can process satellite datasets and present meaningful results through an accessible web application.

Ultimately, FIREMIND aims to turn fragmented satellite observations into a more coherent understanding of fire activity, helping users see not only where fires are detected, but also how burning patterns evolve over time.

FIREMIND — See the signal. Understand the gaps.

projectDetails.name: EmberEye
projectDetails.summary: EmberEye is a web platform for exploring a consistent record of active-fire detections from NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS products. It normalizes sensor and satellite metadata, removes duplicate detections, and uses the 2012–2022 overlap to calibrate pre-2012 MODIS activity into explicitly labeled VIIRS-equivalent estimates. These are model-dependent estimates, not observations from VIIRS. Users can choose a region and date range, browse daily and monthly fire-activity calendars and a map, compare time series and climatology, inspect fire episodes, and export filtered results. The current offline demo contains real NASA FIRMS detections for the Nile Delta and clearly labeled deterministic synthetic demo data for the other five preset regions. EmberEye exposes provenance and uncertainty and is intended for research and exploration, not operational fire alerts or forecasts.
projectDetails.details:
EmberEye addresses the challenge’s need for a comparable burning-activity record and a web app for selecting an area and time range, exploring patterns, and downloading results. It ingests NASA FIRMS active-fire products: MODIS Collection 6.1 from Terra and Aqua, and 375 m VIIRS from Suomi-NPP (historical), NOAA-20, and NOAA-21. The pipeline maps records to a common schema, keeps sensor/product provenance and provisional NRT status, and applies sensor-specific duplicate suppression. An optional NASA GIBS MODIS Terra thermal-anomaly layer and public basemaps provide map context.

For the harmonized series, VIIRS is the reference. During the 2012–2022 overlap, EmberEye fits month-of-year transfer factors on daytime, non-static detections and evaluates them with leave-one-year-out validation. It uses those factors to estimate pre-2012 MODIS activity in VIIRS-equivalent units, with uncertainty intervals; the estimate is explicitly not presented as a historical VIIRS observation. Native VIIRS is used in the VIIRS era, and overlapping satellites are not simply summed. The app also provides daily/monthly calendars, an interactive map and date scrubber, time-series and climatology views, fire-episode summaries, area-of-interest selection, and CSV/GeoJSON exports.

The v1.0.8 offline snapshot contains 171,855 real FIRMS detections for the Nile Delta; its other five preset regions contain deterministic synthetic demo records. On that Nile Delta snapshot, annual pooled leave-one-year-out MAPE was 7.03%, mean bias was −2.01%, and the empirical 95% prediction interval was [−18.15%, +12.21%]. Those are snapshot- and annual-aggregation-specific diagnostics, not a global accuracy guarantee; monthly and weekly MAPE were 33.77% and 83.52%. NRT observations are provisional. The app is a research and exploration prototype, not a fire forecast, operational alert system, or substitute for official incident information.

The implementation uses Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL/SQLite, React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, Apache ECharts, and Docker Compose.

projectDetails.name: Galactic Glitch
projectDetails.summary:
Galactic Glitch is an AI-powered Earth analog discovery platform built to support NASA's challenge of identifying candidate landing sites and habitat zones on the Moon and Mars.

Using a Dynamic Multi-Metric Weighted KNN model (GalacticGlitch-ML-v2.1, 95.4% accuracy), the platform analyzes real NASA and USGS scientific datasets — including MOLA/HiRISE elevation, Horn-method derived slope, and 5×5 RMS surface roughness — to match Martian and lunar terrain features against known Earth analogs. This helps scientists and mission planners rapidly identify regions on other worlds that behave geologically and environmentally like places we already understand on Earth.

The platform features an interactive 3D globe explorer rendering photographic NASA texture maps of Earth, Moon, and Mars, with toggleable scientific data layers, landmark pins, and telemetry readouts. Users can submit coordinates, receive analog match predictions with confidence scores, and explore historical search records.

By translating complex multi-dimensional terrain data into intuitive visual comparisons, Galactic Glitch makes planetary surface analysis accessible to both researchers and the public — accelerating the path toward safe, informed human exploration beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Galactic Glitch is an AI platform that finds matching Earth locations for terrain on the Moon and Mars. Users click coordinates on an interactive 3D globe, and the system returns a confidence-scored Earth analog match using real terrain features — elevation, slope, surface roughness, and temperature.

How it works: A custom Dynamic Multi-Metric Weighted KNN model (95.4% accuracy) processes the terrain features and matches them against Earth reference data. Scientific layers (slope, roughness, elevation) can be toggled as colored overlays directly on the 3D globe. All results and search history are saved.

Benefits & Impact: Helps mission planners identify safe landing zones by comparing alien terrain to well-studied Earth locations. Supports NASA Artemis and Mars exploration by making complex planetary data visually accessible to both researchers and the public.

Tools & Data:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js (WebGL 3D globe)
  • ML & Backend: Python, Weighted KNN, Flask/FastAPI REST API
  • Data: Sourced from Kaggle via kagglehub — originating from NASA instruments (MODIS, SRTM, MOLA, HiRISE, LRO LOLA)
  • Deployment: Vercel

Creativity & Considerations: Real NASA photographic planet textures on a live rotating globe, with scientific overlays painted directly on the surface. The team prioritized scientific accuracy with calibrated real data ranges, honest labeling of data limitations, and a cinematic space UI that makes planetary science feel approachable

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. projectDetails.name: LunaSlip
projectDetails.summary: LunaSlip is an interactive 3D lunar landing navigator that visually evaluates how mission delays impact landing windows at the Moon's south pole. By combining verified NASA terrain data with JPL ephemerides, it allows users to simulate launch slips and instantly identify viable alternative dates based on precise Sun and Earth visibility constraints.
projectDetails.details: LunaSlip turns a delayed lunar landing into an explainable search problem by combining a horizon-first visual model with synchronized date and site alternatives. Built using React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, and a Cloudflare Worker proxy, the application is driven by a framework-independent calculation engine that strictly classifies data provenance as live, cached, precomputed, or analytical to ensure scientific validity and offline reliability. The platform integrates a mission dashboard with synchronized 3D lunar context covering three verified 2-meter LROC stereo sites (Shackleton rim, Connecting Ridge, and Malapert Massif) alongside an 80-meter LOLA south-pole overview. A 360° interactive D3 horizon simulator calculates extended-disk Sun and Earth visibility against the exact local skyline, while an interactive OpenLayers GIS map utilizes NASA Moon Trek WMTS layers for spatial exploration. To handle delays, a Web Worker-powered launch-slip simulator executes configurable searches across 8,763 precomputed 2027 JPL Horizons observations, allowing mission planners to search nearby dates and regions against explicit constraints to see exactly why each candidate passes or fails. While the application functions fully offline using the bundled 2027 dataset and generated 3D meshes, querying live ephemeris data outside of this window requires an active connection to the proxy service.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.

projectDetails.name: Geo Depth
projectDetails.summary: GeoDepth is an interactive website that helps people understand earthquakes and their effects on Earth and society. It brings together earthquake data, satellite images, maps, and educational content in one place. Using SAR and InSAR technologies, especially data from NASA–ISRO’s NISAR mission, the project explores how earthquakes change and deform Earth’s surface. Users can explore earthquake locations, understand how satellites detect ground changes, and learn about their impact on people and infrastructure. GeoDepth also provides a safety guide to help people prepare for earthquakes and stay safe. Our goal is to make earthquake science easier to understand and show how satellite technology helps us study our changing planet.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem

Earthquake-related satellite data and scientific information can be difficult to access, understand, and interpret, especially for people without a scientific background.

Researchers and students may struggle to explore different sources of Earth observation data, while ordinary users often lack simple tools to understand how earthquakes change Earth's surface and affect human communities.

Our Solution – Geo Depth

Geo Depth is an interactive platform that connects earthquake information with satellite-based Earth observation to make scientific data easier to explore and understand.

The platform provides:

- Earth Impact: Explore earthquake events and their effects on Earth's surface.

- Earth Explorer: Discover Earth through interactive maps and satellite observations.

- Human Impact: Understand how earthquakes affect people and communities.

- Satellite Explorer: Learn how satellites observe and monitor changes on Earth.

- Safety Guide: Access practical earthquake preparedness and safety instructions.

Target Audience

Geo Depth serves three main groups:

1. Researchers: Explore Earth observation information and discover useful scientific data for further investigation.

2. Students: Learn about earthquakes, satellite technology, and Earth science through interactive visualizations.

3. General Public: Understand earthquake events, their potential impacts, and how to stay safe.

Our Goal

Our goal is to make Earth observation science more accessible, understandable, and engaging by turning complex scientific information into an interactive learning and exploration experience.

projectDetails.name: Project GHEIT NASA
projectDetails.summary: FieldShift helps farmers explore crop rotations using NASA Earth observations, agricultural crop references, and their own priorities. Our prototype focuses on a study point in Kafr El Sheikh, Egypt, combining five years of NASA POWER weather data with quality-screened MODIS vegetation observations and a 15-crop catalog. It compares two-season crop sequences, explains their suitability, and flags water constraints instead of forcing unsuitable recommendations. The result is a transparent starting point for climate-aware planning—not a promise of higher yield or a replacement for local agricultural expertise.
projectDetails.details:
## FieldShift — Earth Data for Smarter Crop Rotations

### The problem we address

Choosing what to plant next involves balancing water availability, seasonal heat, crop diversity, and the farmer’s priorities. A rotation that appears attractive may require more water than is available, while repeating familiar crops can limit opportunities to introduce legumes or diversify the sequence.

FieldShift addresses the challenge of using NASA Earth observations and agricultural knowledge to make these trade-offs easier to understand. Our prototype focuses on a study point in Kafr El Sheikh, Egypt, rather than claiming to represent every farm in the governorate.

### What we built and its main use

We built a working, explainable crop-rotation decision-support engine. A user provides the previous crop and its season, water access, and priorities such as water conservation, soil-health considerations, and heat resilience.

The engine generates two-season crop sequences, checks their compatibility with declared water constraints, and returns up to three ranked alternatives with explanations, reference sources, and limitations. It can also display a supported current rotation as a comparison-only baseline.

A main use is helping a farmer or agricultural adviser explore alternatives before deciding what to plant next. If no option passes the water screen, the engine returns no recommendation and explains why, instead of forcing three unsuitable choices.

The delivered AI-only prototype runs directly in Python using a JSON input file and produces structured JSON results. An optional local FastAPI interface is also included. This demonstration does not depend on a completed mobile application.

### How the data supports the solution

Our Kafr El Sheikh study point is located at **31.11°N, 30.94°E**. Its historical dataset contains **1,826 daily NASA POWER records covering 2021–2025**, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, and solar radiation. These records provide historical climate context for comparing crop sequences and screening water and heat constraints. The evaporative-demand proxy used in scoring is not a measured irrigation requirement.

The dataset also contains **115 NASA MODIS vegetation composites**. Only observations passing the strict-good quality screen are used as vegetation context, and accepted observations remain on their actual composite dates. We do not manufacture daily satellite measurements or interpret NDVI as measured soil moisture.

A separate **15-crop agricultural reference catalog** supplies crop characteristics and water-reference ranges. These crop references are not NASA measurements. Egyptian Berseem clover is retained with a documented, treatment-specific water reference from Sakha research rather than being confused with alfalfa.

### How the engine works

TerraShift uses explicit rules and weighted suitability calculations, not a black-box prediction model. Users can change their priorities and understand why rankings change.

Water screening can exclude unsuitable options before ranking. Soil-health indicators reflect crop roles and a stated legume heuristic; they do not represent measured improvements in the farmer’s soil. Income scoring remains neutral because reliable local prices, costs, and yield outcomes are unavailable.

### Working features, evidence, and limitations

Working features include historical-data loading, crop-sequence generation, configurable priorities, water screening, ranked explanations, source metadata, and safe empty results.

Automated software tests and reference-based safety checks have been completed. Source checks also compared the weather records and a sample of vegetation observations with NASA responses. These checks support software reliability and source consistency—not a claim of agricultural accuracy.

The engine has not been trained on expert-ranked rotations or verified farm outcomes. A single study point is not a governorate average or a confirmed farm field. Recommendations still require local review, particularly for soil conditions, crop calendars, irrigation management, pests, and market factors.

### Tools, languages, hardware, and software

The tested AI engine uses **Python, NumPy, Pandas, Pydantic, and FastAPI**, with **Pytest and Ruff** supporting software checks. CSV and Excel store datasets and references; JSON carries inputs, configuration, and results. It runs on a standard computer without specialized sensors or a dedicated GPU.

Wider application development included **Flutter/Dart mobile work and .NET/C# backend work**. Integration of the corrected Python engine into that application is separate from the independently tested AI-only demonstration.

AI-assisted tools included ChatGPT Go for data discovery, Gemini for API/backend and chatbot work, Codex for AI implementation, Google Antigravity for Flutter development, and Manus for data corrections, checks, and documentation.

### Benefits and future plans

FieldShift aims to make climate-informed rotation comparisons more accessible and support clearer conversations between farmers and agricultural specialists. Its current benefit is transparent comparison, not a proven increase in yield or profit.

Next, we hope to collect expert-ranked cases and field outcomes, incorporate measured local soil information and crop calendars, and calibrate water and economic assumptions. We would then evaluate recommendations on held-out cases before claiming real-world agricultural performance.

projectDetails.name: Project Ghurba
projectDetails.summary:
bandoned but Not Forgotten

We developed Abandoned but Not Forgotten, an interactive, AI-powered educational web application designed for students aged 10–16. The platform allows users to discover and converse with the NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars—specifically Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage.

To address the challenge of making space exploration engaging and accessible, we built a localized RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline using LangChain, ChromaDB, and Ollama. Instead of a static textbook, students chat with an AI that speaks in the first-person voice of the hardware, grounded entirely in factual NASA mission data.

To ensure the experience is safe and accurate for a younger audience, we eliminated free-text input. Users interact exclusively through pre-written "question chips," making prompt injection structurally impossible. The app also features multi-media galleries, short stories, and an "Adopt an Artifact" feature to generate personalized certificates.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between historical space exploration and modern generative AI, preserving the legacy of these abandoned machines by giving them a voice to inspire the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, web-based educational platform that gives a voice to the NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars. Users (students aged 10–16) select a specific artifact—Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, or the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage—and engage in a first-person chat with it.

Under the hood, the React frontend sends a specific question_id to a Flask backend. Flask resolves this ID to a secure, pre-written question and passes it to a LangChain pipeline. The pipeline queries a ChromaDB vector database, which is strictly filtered by artifact_id so a question about Spirit never pulls data from Opportunity. Finally, Ollama's qwen3:8b model generates a grounded, in-character response. The Flask backend also maintains the last 6 messages of conversation per session, giving the artifact contextual memory.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
The primary benefit is safe, accessible AI for kids. By restricting the chat to pre-written "question chips" and blocking free-text input, we structurally prevent prompt injection and hallucinations. The browser never sends raw text to the AI; it only sends an ID. This guarantees the AI stays within the factual boundaries of NASA's data. The intended impact is to transform passive, textbook-style learning into an active, conversational relationship with space history. The "Adopt an Artifact" feature further personalizes the experience, allowing students to generate a certificate and take ownership of the mission's legacy.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router
  • Backend: Python, Flask, flask-cors
  • AI / RAG Stack: LangChain, ChromaDB, Ollama (qwen3:8b for chat, nomic-embed-text for embeddings)
  • Storage: ChromaDB (persistent vector index), Flask in-memory dictionary (session memory), localStorage (certificates)

Creativity and Design Considerations:
Our creative approach was designing a "terminal" aesthetic for the chat widget, complete with a glowing uplink header and animated "Receiving Data" bouncing dots to keep the UI engaging during CPU inference times.

Crucially, our team considered the security and accessibility of generative AI for minors. We chose a localized, chip-based approach over a standard chatbot to ensure total factual accuracy. Furthermore, we engineered the system to run entirely locally. By using Ollama and not relying on external APIs, we eliminate API costs and keep the app fully functional even without internet access—making it a viable tool for classrooms with limited connectivity.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational website designed to introduce people to astronaut training and space exploration. It is not just a Mars simulation game; it is a complete learning experience that takes users from understanding the basics of space science to exploring the challenges of real space missions.

The website combines educational modules, interactive activities, quizzes, mini-games, progress tracking, and mission simulations in one platform. It is designed for beginners and anyone interested in learning about space, without requiring previous knowledge of astronautics.

1. Astronaut Learning Academy

The website provides educational content that introduces users to important topics related to astronaut training and space missions, including:

  • Space Science: Understanding the space environment, planets, space weather, and the conditions astronauts face beyond Earth.
  • Space Radiation: Learning about radiation in space, its sources, and its possible effects on astronauts.
  • Astronaut Health: Exploring how spaceflight affects the human body through real space research.
  • Spacecraft Systems: Learning about essential spacecraft systems such as oxygen, water, power, and food supplies.
  • Mission Preparation: Understanding the challenges astronauts must prepare for before and during a mission.

The lessons are supported by interactive explanations, quizzes, and activities to help users understand and remember the information.

2. Interactive Learning and Mini-Games

Instead of relying only on reading, users can interact with what they learn through quizzes, challenges, and mini-games. These activities help them test their knowledge, make decisions, and understand scientific concepts through practical examples.

The platform is designed to make learning more engaging while encouraging curiosity, critical thinking, and problem-solving.

3. Learning Progress and Assessment

The learning experience includes a structured progression system that helps users follow their journey through the different learning topics.

Users can track their progress, complete activities, test their understanding, and work toward completing different learning stages. The goal is to make astronaut learning feel like a continuous journey rather than a collection of unrelated lessons.

4. Mars Mission Simulation

One of the main interactive experiences on the website is the Mars Mission Simulation.

Users go through a mission journey, starting with spacecraft preparation and continuing through different stages of exploring Mars.

The simulation includes:

  • Selecting a suitable Mars landing site.
  • Understanding radiation risks and protection methods.
  • Building a Mars habitat and considering essential resources such as solar power and life-support systems.
  • Responding to possible mission emergencies.
  • Managing communication with Earth and understanding communication delays.

Users explore different situations, make decisions, and learn why each stage matters for the success and safety of a Mars mission.

5. NASA Data and Scientific Resources

An important part of the website is connecting educational content with real space science.

We used NASA resources such as Mars exploration information, radiation measurements, and astronaut research to support the learning material and mission scenarios.

Resources such as NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), Mars radiation research, DONKI, and NASA's Mars exploration resources help provide scientific context for different learning topics.

6. Tools and Development

The project uses structured JSON to organize educational content, mission stages, scenarios, and simulation information.

AI tools supported different parts of the development process:

  • ChatGPT: Assisted with development, content organization, simulation structures, and documentation.
  • Claude: Assisted with reviewing technical structures and improving development content.
  • Google NotebookLM: Helped research and organize information from scientific sources, including NASA materials.

The team reviewed and adapted AI-assisted outputs and used scientific sources to support the educational information.

7. Creativity and Intended Impact

What makes Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer different is that it combines learning and practical mission experiences in one website.

Users do not simply read about becoming an astronaut. They learn the science behind space exploration, test their knowledge, follow their progress, and eventually apply what they have learned through interactive mission scenarios.

Our goal is to make astronaut training concepts more accessible to a wider audience, encourage interest in science and engineering, and help people better understand the scientific, technical, and human challenges involved in exploring other planets.

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, accessibility for beginners, educational value, ease of navigation, and the importance of connecting every interactive experience to real space exploration challenges.

projectDetails.name: Project HALO: Health & Autonomic Longevity in Orbit
projectDetails.summary:
HALO (Health Autonomic Longevity in Orbit) is a web application designed to monitor crew health on long-duration, deep-space missions where communication with Earth is delayed.

We developed a dual-view platform featuring an astronaut interface with an interactive 3D body hologram and an Earth Command Center for flight surgeons. HALO addresses the challenge by centralizing fragmented data—including wearable ring metrics, spacecraft sensors (radiation and cabin CO2), and daily check-ins—into a single database. Built-in analytical and diagnostic engines evaluate these metrics against medical thresholds to safely flag spaceflight hazards and provide actionable, NASA-protocol-based guidance.

This project is important because deep-space exploration exposes astronauts to severe physiological risks. By enabling early anomaly detection, supporting crew autonomy, and bridging the information gap between spacefarers and ground control, HALO keeps astronauts safe, healthy, and performing at their peak far beyond Earth's reach.
projectDetails.details:
• What does it do or how does it work? HALO (Health Autonomic Longevity in Orbit) is a health-monitoring web application designed for astronauts on long deep-space missions and for flight surgeons on Earth. It centralizes data from wearable rings, spacecraft sensors (such as radiation and cabin $\text{CO}_2$), and astronaut daily check-ins into a single shared database. A built-in health and diagnosis engine checks these readings against medical thresholds and cross-references them with symptoms to flag potential spaceflight conditions (like sleep strain, radiation exposure, or possible decompression sickness) without making definitive unconfirmed diagnoses. It features two synchronized views: an astronaut view featuring an interactive 3D body hologram that highlights troubled areas in yellow or red with actionable NASA-protocol steps, and an Earth Command Center where flight surgeons can view fleet-wide status, open read-only mirrors of astronaut screens, and send directives.
    • Spots small health shifts early (e.g., compounding sleep debt or rising resting heart rate) before they become critical emergencies.
    • Reduces mission reliance on constant, delayed communication links with Earth.
    • Ensures serious health issues stand out immediately instead of getting lost in averages or hidden by otherwise normal metrics (enforced by health score caps when body zones turn red).
    • Establishes perfect situational awareness alignment, as astronauts and ground doctors see the exact same body hologram and underlying evidence.
    • Maintains clinical honesty by clearly separating confirmed data from conditions that require further medical imaging (labeled as "needs confirmation").
  • What is the intended impact of the project? To provide a reliable, autonomous baseline for crew health management on deep-space missions to the Moon and Mars. By keeping astronauts safe, informed, and performing at their peak, HALO aims to safeguard long-duration spacefarers against the physiological hazards identified by NASA's Human Research Program.
    • Backend: Node.js, Express, and SQLite.
    • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js (for rendering the 3D body model).
    • AI Guidance (Optional): Gemini AI SDK, used to generate supplemental briefings in the diagnostics panel.
    • Hardware: None. Wearable rings, radiation sensors, cabin $\text{CO}_2$ sensors, and blood-test analyzers are simulated.
    • Sources/References: NASA Human Research Program hazard/risk pages and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) radiation monitoring articles.
    • It merges acute spaceflight medical protocols with a modern longevity framework (inspired by Bryan Johnson’s Blueprint approach, scoring sleep, heart health, recovery, radiation, and mood on a 0–100 scale).
    • It uses a unique health-score capping mechanic where an astronaut's overall score cannot look healthy if vital body zones are flagged red (capping at 75 for 1–2 red zones and 65 for 3+), preventing a high score from masking severe localized issues.
    • It combines automated diagnostic logic with an interactive 3D human body atlas, turning dry numerical logs into an intuitive spatial diagnostic tool.
    • Autonomy vs. Control: Balancing astronaut self-sufficiency in deep space with oversight capabilities for ground-based flight surgeons.
    • Medical Integrity and Transparency: Ensuring the app never oversteps its bounds—explicitly labeling rules that are pending verification and marking unconfirmable conditions (like microgravity-related blood clots or vision changes) as "possible" or "missing evidence" rather than claiming a false positive diagnosis.
    • Unified Data Pathways: Designing the system architecture so that simulated demo data and incoming real-world wearable data (such as an actual Oura Ring) flow through the exact same ingestion pipeline.

projectDetails.name: Harmonix
projectDetails.summary:
HARMONIX is a web-based platform combining active-fire hotspot observations from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites.

It harmonizes observations while preserving original sensor information. Users select an Area of Interest and time period, filter records by satellite and data quality, and explore hotspots on an interactive map. They can review records, regional summaries, and downloadable CSV files.

A demonstration dataset covers the Southern Amazon in September 2024, enabling comparison of MODIS and VIIRS observations. Machine-learning models, including Random Forest, help analyze historical fire-activity patterns.

HARMONIX improves access to harmonized satellite data and supports researchers, environmental organizations, land managers, and emergency responders in understanding wildfire activity and making informed decisions through accessible interactive data visualization tools.

The prototype provides data exploration and reporting. Future improvements include broader coverage, stronger model validation, environmental datasets, and advanced anomaly detection.

Technologies include Python, React, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Node.js, FastAPI, Google Colab, CSV, and machine learning.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — HARMONIX

Project Overview

HARMONIX is an AI-powered wildfire intelligence platform designed to analyze historical fire activity across North America (USA and Canada) using NASA satellite observations. The project addresses an important challenge in wildfire monitoring: MODIS and VIIRS satellites detect active fires differently because of their differences in spatial resolution, observation characteristics, and detection capabilities. Comparing their hotspot records directly can lead to misleading conclusions about changes in fire activity over time.

HARMONIX addresses this problem by harmonizing NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS data into a more consistent dataset. It then uses the harmonized information to explore historical fire patterns, identify unusual activity, and estimate future geographical fire activity through machine-learning models.

The main goal is to help emergency responders, researchers, firefighters, and land managers better understand wildfire activity and make more informed preparedness and monitoring decisions.

How the Solution Works

HARMONIX follows an integrated data-processing, harmonization, analysis, and prediction workflow:

1. Satellite Data Collection and Preprocessing

The platform uses active-fire observations from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), including MODIS and VIIRS datasets. The collected records cover the period from 2021 to 2026 and focus on the USA and Canada.

The data is cleaned, processed, and standardized to handle differences in data formats, missing values, and sensor-specific attributes. Original observations and relevant sensor information are retained to support traceability.

2. Spatial and Temporal Harmonization

Since MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection characteristics, their observations need to be aligned before meaningful comparisons can be made.

HARMONIX uses spatial matching and geographic aggregation with the H3 grid system, together with temporal matching, to identify observations that can be compared.

It also analyzes Fire Radiative Power (FRP), hotspot distributions, and differences between the satellite sensors.

3. Machine-Learning-Based Calibration

To investigate and model the differences between MODIS and VIIRS, HARMONIX evaluates multiple algorithms:

- XGBoost

- Random Forest

- HistGradientBoostingRegressor

- HistGradientBoostingClassifier

- Logistic Regression

- Linear Regression

These models support the calibration and analysis of sensor observations. Their performance is evaluated using statistical measures such as MAE, RMSE, and R², alongside comparisons of sensor behavior.

The purpose is to create a more consistent historical representation of fire activity while accounting for differences between satellite instruments.

4. Historical Fire Activity Analysis

After harmonization, the processed data supports an interactive historical Burning Activity Calendar.

Users can explore fire activity by geographical region, month, and year. The application provides:

- Interactive geographical visualization of active-fire hotspots.

- Monthly and yearly fire activity heatmaps.

- Historical fire activity trends.

- Comparisons with historical median activity.

- Activity anomaly analysis to highlight unusual patterns.

- Filtering by region and date range.

- CSV export for additional analysis.

These features help users investigate seasonal patterns, compare different years, and identify periods of unusually high or low fire activity.

5. Wildfire Activity Prediction

HARMONIX also includes an integrated machine-learning prediction component that estimates future geographical fire activity.

The prediction stage evaluates several algorithms:

- Random Forest

- CatBoost

- Support Vector Machine (SVM)

- XGBoost

- Decision Tree

Random Forest achieved the best performance among the evaluated prediction models and was selected as the preferred model.

The model uses historical fire information to estimate future activity and support geographical risk assessment. Its outputs are intended to help users understand potential areas of increased fire activity and improve preparedness.

Main Benefits and Expected Impact

HARMONIX provides several benefits:

- More consistent historical analysis:** Reduces the risk of misleading comparisons caused by differences between MODIS and VIIRS observations.

- Better understanding of fire patterns:** Helps users examine seasonal changes and long-term wildfire activity.

- Early identification of unusual activity:** Historical median comparisons and anomaly analysis help highlight unusual fire patterns.

- Data-driven preparedness: Machine-learning-based geographical activity estimates can support planning and resource allocation.

- Accessible scientific information:** Presents satellite observations through interactive maps, charts, and downloadable datasets.

- Support for different users: Provides useful information for emergency responders, researchers, firefighters, and land managers.

Our goal is to transform raw satellite observations into meaningful and accessible fire intelligence that supports better understanding, monitoring, and preparedness.

Technologies, Tools, and Resources

Data Sources

- NASA FIRMS active-fire datasets.

- MODIS satellite observations.

- VIIRS satellite observations.

Programming Languages

- Python

- JavaScript

- HTML

- CSS

Data Processing and Machine Learning

- Google Colab

- Pandas

- NumPy

- Scikit-learn

- XGBoost

- CatBoost

- H3 geospatial indexing

Application Development

- React

- Node.js

- FastAPI

Data Storage

- CSV files.

Hardware

- Standard computer hardware and cloud-based computational resources through Google Colab. No specialized hardware is required.

Current Implementation and Future Development

Implemented in the current HARMONIX prototype:

- NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS data collection.

- Data cleaning, standardization, and preprocessing.

- Spatial and temporal matching.

- H3-based geographic aggregation.

- FRP comparison and sensor harmonization experiments.

- Machine-learning-based calibration and model evaluation.

- Historical Burning Activity Calendar.

- Interactive hotspot visualization and activity heatmaps.

- Historical median and anomaly analysis.

- CSV export.

- Integrated wildfire activity prediction using the selected Random Forest model.

Potential future development:

- Integrating additional environmental datasets, such as weather, precipitation, humidity, and vegetation indicators.

- Expanding geographical coverage beyond North America.

- Incorporating additional historical and real-time satellite observations.

- Further improving model validation, uncertainty estimation, and geographical generalization.

Limitations

HARMONIX is designed to support wildfire monitoring and preparedness, not to replace professional emergency systems.

Its analysis depends on satellite-detected active-fire observations, which may be affected by satellite coverage, observation timing, cloud conditions, spatial resolution, and sensor detection limitations.

The current prediction model relies on historical FIRMS fire data and does not yet integrate additional weather or environmental datasets. Consequently, its estimates should be interpreted as indicators of potential future fire activity rather than precise forecasts.

The platform does not predict exact ignition locations, determine fire spread, or guarantee that a wildfire will occur in a particular area. Its outputs should be considered alongside other environmental information and professional assessments.

HARMONIX — Turning satellite observations into a clearer understanding of wildfire activity, helping people recognize patterns, investigate unusual changes, and prepare for what comes next.

projectDetails.name: Track Your Health
projectDetails.summary:
Track Your Health (TYH) is our response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge to develop health monitoring software for astronauts on long-duration missions. As humanity prepares for deep-space exploration, astronauts face the RIDGE risks: Radiation, Isolation, Distance from Earth, Gravity fields, and hostile Environments.

TYH is a visually immersive, client-side React application designed to help astronauts independently monitor their physical and mental health. Its features include an interactive "Living Body Twin" that visualizes health status, daily vital tracking, mental well-being check-ins, and dynamic health charts.

To address psychological challenges and communication delays, TYH offers a "Calm Zone" featuring guided breathing, simulated delayed messages from home, and NOVA, a rule-based AI coach. It also includes a "Mission Simulator" where astronauts practice responding to emergencies such as solar storms and medical crises, alongside an educational nutrition guide based on NASA and CSA data.

We chose this challenge because future space exploration requires astronauts to take a more active role in managing their own health. By combining health monitoring, psychological support, and interactive emergency training in one offline-capable platform, TYH aims to improve astronaut safety, preparedness, and performance during long-duration space missions.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Track Your Health (TYH) is an immersive, self-contained health monitoring and training web application for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It functions as a digital health companion. The app features a "Living Body Twin"—an interactive, animated SVG human body where astronauts can click on organs (like the heart, lungs, or brain) to see their current health status, related indicators, and spaceflight risks. Users input their daily vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, mood) into a Daily Check-in form. The app evaluates this data against NASA-informed thresholds, providing real-time Green/Yellow/Red assessments and actionable guidance. It also includes a time-pressured Mission Simulator to train for emergencies, a Calm Zone for mental health support, and a rule-based AI coach named NOVA that provides personalized tips.

What benefits does it have?
TYH bridges the critical gap in autonomous deep-space healthcare. By shifting health management from Earth-based flight surgeons to the crew, it directly addresses the communication delays of missions to Mars. It provides a unified platform that tracks physical health, mitigates psychological isolation, and trains astronauts to make life-saving decisions under pressure. Furthermore, it is fully client-side, ensuring zero-latency performance and privacy without requiring continuous internet connectivity.

What is the intended impact of the project?
The intended impact is to ensure the safety, performance, and mental well-being of astronauts embarking on humanity's most ambitious journeys to the Moon and Mars. By gamifying health tracking and emergency training, TYH builds a culture of proactive health management. Beyond space, the app's educational content on nutrition, radiation, and isolation serves as a powerful tool to inspire students and the public about the realities of human spaceflight.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS.
  • Frontend: React, TanStack Router (for seamless SPA navigation), Tailwind CSS (for a responsive, space-themed UI), Recharts (for dynamic radar/trend charts), and Lucide (for iconography).
  • Deployment: GitHub for version control and Vercel for static hosting.

How is your project creative?
Our creativity lies in transforming dry medical data into an engaging, interactive experience. The "Living Body Twin" uses SVG animations to make the human body feel "alive"—the heart pulses at the astronaut's real-time heart rate, and lungs breathe. The Mission Simulator is a unique addition; it creates a cinematic, high-pressure environment with screen shakes and countdown timers to train astronauts for sudden solar storms or medical crises. Furthermore, the Calm Zone creatively tackles isolation by simulating delayed "Home Link" messages from Earth, giving astronauts a psychological lifeline.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Accuracy: We relied strictly on NASA’s "RIDGE" hazard framework and CSA research (e.g., lunar dust impacts, radiation limits) to ensure educational content is factual.
  • User Experience (UX): We designed the UI to be high-contrast, dark-mode, and large enough for tap targets, considering the stress and physical constraints astronauts face.
  • Technical Constraints: We prioritized a lightweight, fully client-side architecture to ensure the app functions flawlessly in deep space where internet connectivity is non-existent.
  • Accessibility: The app includes a help section for beginners, ensuring that users (even those without a medical background) can understand their health data.

projectDetails.summary: RainSight is an AI-powered web application designed to help people understand and predict rainfall in different locations. It uses Machine Learning to analyze weather conditions such as temperature, humidity, wind speed, and cloud cover. Users can search for a city or select a location on an interactive map to see rain predictions and a 5-day weather forecast. projectDetails.details:
RainSight is an AI-powered web application designed to predict the possibility of rainfall based on weather conditions. Users can enter a city or select a location on an interactive map to receive a rain prediction.

The system collects weather data, including temperature, humidity, wind speed, and cloud coverage, through the OpenWeatherMap API. It then uses a Machine Learning model based on Random Forest to analyze these features and predict whether rain is likely or not.

The project provides an easy-to-understand result, helping users make better decisions about outdoor activities, agriculture, and daily planning.

The main benefits include early awareness of possible rainfall, better agricultural planning, water resource management, and reducing the impact of unexpected weather conditions.

The project was developed using Python, Flask, Scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy, Joblib, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet.js. It also uses OpenWeatherMap for weather information and OpenStreetMap for map visualization.

What makes RainSight creative is the integration of Machine Learning, real-time weather information, and interactive maps into one simple application. Our team focused on usability, accessibility, prediction accuracy, and the potential environmental and agricultural impact of the solution.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: off world
projectDetails.summary:
OFF-WORLD is an interactive narrative exploration experience where an alien expedition discovers humanity through the machines we left behind in space.

In 2231, humanity broadcasts an emergency signal into the universe. Years later, the Kalamithians receive it, decode its meaning, and begin a sixteen-year journey to the source. When they arrive, nobody answers.

Players take the role of the expedition’s explorer and investigate humanity through real NASA missions, spacecraft, rovers, scientific instruments, and mission data. They encounter Voyager 1 and its Golden Record, investigate robotic exploration on Mars, and explore human equipment left on the Moon. Instead of simply reading facts, players identify unfamiliar objects, decode information, reconstruct their purposes, solve scientific challenges, and interpret evidence.

The experience combines real space exploration history with a fictional first-contact mystery, making NASA science part of an emotional investigation. By the time the expedition reaches Earth, players have discovered humanity through its curiosity, exploration, and attempts to communicate—making its final silence meaningful.
projectDetails.details:
Off-World is an interactive science-fiction experience that explores one haunting question: What if humanity sent a distress signal into space, but help arrived only after humanity had disappeared?

Set in the year 2231, the story begins with Earth's civilization collapsing as power grids, industries, supply chains, and public knowledge fail. Two political blocs must cooperate to send a distress message to the Kalamith, an alien civilization on Proxima Centauri b. Players participate in this process through meaningful decisions and interactive challenges, including repairing systems, negotiating over an encryption key, assembling a transmission, and helping decode the message.

The experience then follows the signal across interstellar space. The Kalamith receive and decode it, launch an expedition, and eventually arrive at a silent Earth. Through orbital scans and archived conversations with ARCHIVE-9, the last surviving artificial intelligence, players uncover humanity's fate. The journey continues through an interactive Voyager 1 object-recovery experience, where users explore the spacecraft and its Golden Record, before moving to a Mars survey featuring an ice prospect at Arcadia Planitia.

Off-World combines interactive storytelling, scientific exploration, and immersive 3D environments. Rather than presenting information through ordinary articles, it turns the narrative into an experience where users interact with spacecraft, inspect objects, solve challenges, make decisions, and gradually uncover the story.

The project was developed using React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, GSAP, Zustand, and CSS, with the Web Audio API for sound and interaction feedback. Its visual experience combines 3D planetary environments, animated spacecraft, camera transitions, starfields, and a retro-inspired computer interface.

Its creativity lies in connecting a fictional future with recognizable space exploration concepts and real scientific locations. The project aims to encourage curiosity about space, planetary science, spacecraft, and humanity's responsibility to preserve knowledge. We considered narrative clarity, scientific context, interaction design, accessibility, visual immersion, and performance while developing the experience.
