projectDetails.name: Next Best Test
projectDetails.summary:
Next Best Test is a browser-based prototype that helps astronauts decide what to check when support from Earth is delayed. It displays simulated heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, and fatigue on an interactive 3D body map. When readings change, a Bayesian model weighs possible explanations, including a faulty sensor. It ranks follow-up checks by how much they could improve the crew’s decision per minute and stops recommending checks when the expected benefit is small.

During limited contact windows, Next Best Message gives critical alerts priority and selects the most useful evidence that fits the available bandwidth. NASA’s Inspiration4 blood panels illustrate how to compare measurements with personal preflight baselines. JPL Horizons provides the one-way Earth–Mars signal delay used in the demo.

Across 1,000 simulated cases, the adaptive approach averaged 2.8 minutes of crew time and matched the model’s reference action in 88% of cases. The fixed checklist averaged 17 minutes and matched it in 89%.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

On a long-duration mission, a crew may have to investigate a health reading before Earth can respond. Next Best Test helps the crew decide which reading to verify first, when to stop testing, and what to send during the next contact window.

How it works

The browser-based monitor displays simulated vital signs alongside personal preflight baselines. An interactive 3D body map lets the crew select a measurement and see its trend, source, and relevant checks. A Bayesian model updates the likelihood of explanations such as fatigue, low blood oxygen, or a faulty sensor as new evidence arrives.

The engine estimates how much each follow-up check could improve the choice of action and ranks checks by the expected benefit per crew-minute. In our demo, a high wearable temperature prompts a two-minute check with an independent thermometer. When that result confirms the elevated reading, the model stops recommending further checks and queues an alert for Earth.

Communication with Earth

Next Best Message applies the same principle to a limited communications link. Critical alerts go first. The remaining space goes to the evidence most likely to improve Earth’s assessment per byte. The prototype also demonstrates configurable sharing levels and integrity checks for received messages.

NASA data and development tools

The project uses NASA’s Inspiration4 blood count and metabolic panel datasets, OSD-569 and OSD-575, to show how preflight baselines help interpret postflight lab results. NASA JPL Horizons supplies the one-way Earth–Mars signal delay used in the scenario. We built the prototype with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, used Three.js to render HuBMAP reference anatomy, and used Python to prepare the NASA datasets.

Results and intended impact

Across 1,000 simulated cases, adaptive testing averaged 2.8 crew-minutes compared with 17 minutes for a fixed checklist. The recommended action matched the model’s reference action in 88% and 89% of cases, respectively. Selective messages averaged 190 bytes of payload compared with 10,269 bytes for sending all available evidence. These results show how the approach could save crew time and bandwidth under the simulation’s assumptions.

projectDetails.name: Exploring the Earth
projectDetails.summary: Exploring the Earth is an interactive, audio-first web application prototype designed to help blind and visually impaired users independently explore Earth observation and NASA climate data.  Most platforms that share environmental and satellite data rely almost entirely on visual maps, charts, and images, creating a major barrier for people with vision loss. Our solution bridges this accessibility gap by turning raw NASA climate data—such as temperature shifts, wind patterns, and terrain features—into an engaging auditory experience.  Using full screen-reader support and AI voice navigation, users can explore environmental changes across two contrasting regions, East Africa and Northern Europe, along an interactive timeline from 2000 to 2026. When a user selects a specific location, a calm AI narrator tells the story of that environment like a documentary, supported by dynamic 3D spatial soundscapes—such as coastal breezes or directional wind audio that shifts between left and right headphones based on real data. This matters because it makes Earth science inclusive, allowing blind and low-vision learners to genuinely experience and understand how our planet is changing.
projectDetails.details:
1. What it does :

Exploring the Earth is an interactive, audio-first web application prototype designed to bridge the accessibility gap for blind and visually impaired users. It transforms raw NASA Earth observation and climate data—such as surface temperature anomalies, wind vectors, and regional topography—into an engaging, cinema-grade auditory experience. Focusing on two pilot regions, East Africa and Northern Europe, the platform allows users to explore multi-decade environmental changes across a chronological timeline from 2000 to 2026 (in 5-year intervals up to 2025, plus 2026).

​2. How it works :

​AI Voice Navigation & Authentication: Users log in securely via screen-reader compatibility and interact with a voice assistant that confirms spoken commands and guides them seamlessly to their regional hub.

​Auditory Timeline & Topography Discovery: Users navigate the 2000–2026 timeline through dynamic screen-reader voice prompts, select a target year, and browse an accessible list of regional terrains—culminating in an option for a Full Location Audio Tour.

​Cinematic Storytelling & Spatial Audio Engine: Upon selecting a specific terrain, a soothing AI narrative describes NASA climate metrics like a documentary. Behind the story, the Web Audio API (StereoPannerNode) renders dynamic spatial soundscapes where environmental sounds (such as wind or coastal breezes) shift their stereo pan between left and right headphones based on real directional data vectors.

​3. Benfits & What we Hope to Achieve :

​Inclusivity & Empowerment: Democratizes scientific discovery, ensuring that the over 2.2 billion people globally with vision impairment are not excluded from exploring planetary science.

​Cognitive Immersion: Replaces dry, fragmented numerical metadata with emotionally resonant storytelling and spatial immersion, transforming passive accessibility compliance into an intuitive educational tool.

​4. Toools, Technologies & Hardware / software used :

​Frontend Architecture: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript / React (WCAG AAA and WAI-ARIA compliant design for screen readers and keyboard navigation).

​Audio Engineering: Web Audio API (AudioContext, StereoPannerNode) for 3D spatial sound panning and dynamic ambient soundscape generation.

​Voice & AI Pipeline: Web Speech API (SpeechRecognition & SpeechSynthesis) combined with LLM-driven narrative storytelling templates.

​Data Sources: NASA Earth Observing System Data and Information System (EOSDIS) / Giovanni surface temperature and wind datasets (2000–2026), and NASA POWER API.

​5. Main use case, Date support & Limitations :

​Main Use Case: Enabling a blind student or curious learner to independently "hear" and experience how climate change has shaped East Africa or Northern Europe over the last 26 years.

​Data Support: Longitudinal NASA meteorological and topographical datasets directly drive the narrative tone, temperature shifts, and stereo wind panning.

​Current Limitations (Prototype Scope): Currently limited to two pilot regions (East Africa and Northern Europe) and pre-curated checkpoint years rather than real-time live streaming of all global satellite feeds.

​Future Scalability: Expanding global regional coverage, converting the web prototype into a fully native mobile application, and integrating live NASA telemetry APIs.

projectDetails.name: Hot Source
projectDetails.summary:
Trend Detective is an interactive Earth observation analytics platform designed to solve a central problem in climate data science: distinguishing real, multi-decadal planetary trends from cyclical seasonal noise and short-term weather shocks. Built for the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, the platform connects NASA GLDAS-2.1 and Giovanni satellite observations directly to an intuitive 4-Pillar Detective Framework.     
Users simply drop a pin on a global map and select an Earth system variable—such as soil moisture, precipitation, temperature, or evapotranspiration. Under the hood, the system removes recurring seasonal cycles, tests for serial autocorrelation to prevent false positives, computes robust Theil-Sen slopes and true hyperbolic confidence intervals, and pairs physical drivers (like rainfall vs. soil moisture) to reveal the root cause of environmental shifts.                                         
By translating complex remote sensing archives into transparent, statistically verified verdicts, Trend Detective democratizes climate intelligence for students, educators, farmers, and policymakers worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

Trend Detective turns complex Earth observation data into an interactive, four-step investigative experience:

- Step 1 (What): The user selects a plain-language Earth system variable (Temperature, Rainfall, Soil Moisture, Evapotranspiration, Surface Runoff, or Chlorophyll-a).

- Step 2 (Where): The user clicks any location on an interactive Leaflet map or selects benchmark testbeds, with support for dual-region comparative divergence.

- Step 3 (By how much): The system decomposes decades of satellite records into non-seasonal monthly anomalies and calculates non-parametric Theil-Sen slopes and OLS linear trajectories with exact 95% hyperbolic confidence bands.

- Step 4 (Is it significant?): The platform tests for serial autocorrelation. If red-noise autocorrelation (r1 > 0.20) is detected, it automatically executes the Hamed-Rao Modified Mann-Kendall test to correct variance and prevent false alarms. It also isolates episodic shocks using Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) and pairs background physical drivers (e.g., rainfall rate vs. soil drying) to attribute root causes.

2. What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?

- Zero-Jargon Accessibility: Eliminates scientific gatekeeping by letting students and non-specialists explore multi-decadal satellite trends without writing code or parsing raw HDF/NetCDF files.

- Scientific Rigor: Prevents researchers from mistaking cyclical summer peaks or episodic floods for true 20-year climate trends.

- Actionable Attribution: Helps agricultural planners and environmental journalists understand whether regional drying is driven by precipitation deficit or land-surface feedback.

3. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

- Frontend: Next.js 14 (React, TypeScript), Tailwind CSS, Leaflet Maps (CARTO dark basemaps), React-Plotly.js, Lucide Icons.

- Backend & Statistics: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy (Welch’s epoch t-test), PyMannKendall (Hamed-Rao variance correction & Sen’s slope), HTTPX async client.

- Data & Caching: NASA GLDAS-2.1 Data Rods, NOAA Climate at a Glance, NASA Giovanni, Supabase PostgreSQL (JSONB caching for sub-100ms response times).

4. How is your project creative?

- The 4-Pillar Detective Framework: Translates abstract climate science into four intuitive questions: What, Where, By how much, and Is it significant?

- Silent Physical Driver Pairing: Instead of presenting isolated numbers, the engine concurrently pulls coupled physical drivers in the background to explain why an anomaly is occurring.

- Dual-Region Divergence Mode: Allows users to place two pins simultaneously (e.g., Kansas vs. Nile Delta) to contrast opposing ecological trajectories under global forcing.

5. What factors did your team consider?

- Serial Autocorrelation: Climate data often violates standard regression assumptions due to red noise; we explicitly implemented the Hamed-Rao variance correction factor.

- Incomplete Boundary Years: Incomplete current-year satellite dumps can artificially skew slopes, so we enforced minimum threshold filters (≥ 10 valid months for annual aggregates).

- Spatial Boundaries: Implemented guardrails to gracefully handle ocean clicks on land-only reanalysis models and redirect to marine Giovanni data.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project Hotspot Hunters
projectDetails.summary:
Hotspot Hunters is a satellite fire intelligence platform designed to harmonize and compare active fire detections from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments.

The project addresses a key challenge in satellite-based fire monitoring: MODIS and VIIRS observations differ in spatial resolution, acquisition timing, sensitivity, and data characteristics, making direct comparison and combined analysis difficult.

Hotspot Hunters brings these datasets into one unified platform. It collects and standardizes fire detection data, applies spatial and temporal matching techniques, and distinguishes between detections identified by both sensors and those reported by only one. This enables users to explore the similarities and differences between satellite observations through interactive maps, timelines, comparison tools, and analytical visualizations.

The platform is designed to support fire management agencies, GIS and remote-sensing specialists, environmental researchers, and policymakers by making satellite fire data easier to interpret, compare, and analyze.

Our vision: Turn fragmented satellite fire observations into clearer, more comparable, and more actionable intelligence.
projectDetails.details:
Hotspot Hunters is a satellite fire intelligence platform developed to address the challenge of harmonizing active fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments.

How it works:

The platform brings MODIS and VIIRS active fire data together in one unified environment. It aims to standardize the datasets and compare observations based on their geographic locations and acquisition times. Through spatial and temporal matching, the platform helps identify detections reported by both sensors, as well as those detected by MODIS or VIIRS individually. Users can explore the observations through interactive maps, timelines, comparison views, and analytical visualizations.

Benefits and intended impact:

By making satellite observations easier to compare and interpret, Hotspot Hunters can help fire management agencies, GIS specialists, environmental researchers, and policymakers gain a clearer understanding of active fire data. It supports more informed analysis, helps users recognize differences between satellite observations, and makes valuable NASA data more accessible for research and decision-making. Our intended impact is to contribute to better-informed environmental monitoring and fire assessment.

Tools and technologies:

The project is built around NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) and its MODIS and VIIRS active fire datasets. It uses a web-based platform approach, combining data processing, spatial and temporal comparison, interactive mapping, and data visualization. No dedicated hardware is required; the solution focuses on satellite data and software-based analysis.

Creativity and innovation:

The creative aspect of Hotspot Hunters is not simply displaying fire hotspots on a map. It focuses on bringing two different satellite observation systems into a comparable analytical environment. Instead of treating MODIS and VIIRS as separate data sources, the platform helps users understand where their observations agree, where they differ, and how those differences affect interpretation. This transforms fragmented observations into a more coherent view of satellite fire intelligence.

Factors considered during development:

Our team considered differences in spatial resolution, observation time, sensor characteristics, detection confidence, data consistency, and usability. We also considered the importance of presenting scientific information clearly, making the platform accessible to users with different technical backgrounds, and avoiding misleading conclusions when comparing detections from different instruments.

Our vision:

Every satellite detection carries information. Hotspot Hunters aims to connect those signals and make their story easier to understand.

Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project _IGNIS_
projectDetails.summary:
IGNIS — Space Fire Intelligence** is an AI-powered research platform developed to make NASA’s microgravity combustion data easier to explore, analyze, and understand.

Fire behaves differently in space, creating unique safety challenges for astronauts and future space missions. Although NASA has conducted valuable combustion experiments, the resulting data can be complex and difficult to interpret.

To address the *Flame in Freefall* challenge, we developed IGNIS, integrating **403 real NASA experimental records** from FLEX and BASS-II into an interactive platform featuring intelligent experiment exploration, data analytics, side-by-side comparisons, and evidence-based scientific insights.

Our **AI-powered Predictive Lab** uses machine learning to estimate droplet burning rates under different experimental conditions, helping researchers explore combustion behavior through interactive visualizations.

By transforming complex experimental data into accessible scientific insights, IGNIS aims to support future fire-safety research for spacecraft, space stations, and lunar and Martian habitats.

IGNIS — Turning space fire research into intelligence that could save lives.
projectDetails.details:
IGNIS — Space Fire Intelligence

Project Details

1. The Problem — Fire in Microgravity

Fire behaves differently in microgravity, creating unique challenges for astronaut safety and future space exploration. NASA's valuable combustion research contains complex experimental data that can be difficult to explore, compare, and interpret.

2. Our Solution — IGNIS

IGNIS is an AI-powered research platform that transforms NASA's microgravity combustion data into accessible scientific insights. It combines experiment exploration, interactive analytics, machine-learning predictions, and scientific visualizations in one unified dashboard.

3. Mission Control — Research Dashboard

Our Mission Control dashboard introduces users to microgravity combustion research through key statistics, scientific highlights, and cinematic space-inspired visuals. It provides an intuitive starting point for exploring NASA's combustion experiments.

4. Experiment Explorer — Discover NASA Research

IGNIS integrates 403 real NASA experimental records from FLEX and BASS-II into a searchable research interface. Users can explore experimental conditions, filter records, and examine detailed information about individual experiments.

5. Data Analytics — Visualize Combustion Patterns

Interactive charts transform experimental measurements into meaningful visual insights. Researchers can explore data distributions, relationships between combustion parameters, and patterns across NASA's recorded experiments.

6. Compare Experiments — Understand the Differences

Our comparison tool allows researchers to examine experiments side by side, highlighting differences in experimental conditions and recorded outcomes. This makes it easier to identify meaningful variations across NASA's combustion research.

7. Predictive Lab — AI-Powered Combustion Prediction

Our Predictive Lab uses machine-learning regression models trained on historical NASA FLEX measurements to estimate the droplet burning rate constant (K). Users can adjust fuel type, oxygen concentration, pressure, and droplet diameter to explore how different conditions influence predicted combustion behavior.

8. AI Insights — From Data to Knowledge

The AI Insights section highlights evidence-linked observations and relationships found within the experimental records. It helps researchers interpret combustion patterns and connect scientific findings to their underlying data.

9. Submit New Experiment — Future Vision

Our future vision includes a researcher submission feature for contributing new combustion experiment information. This feature is currently a prototype concept and is not connected to NASA's official research systems.

10. Scientific Visualization — Bringing Space Fire to Life

IGNIS features cinematic 3D visuals and animated microgravity-inspired flames to create an engaging scientific exploration experience. These visualizations illustrate combustion concepts but are not physically validated simulations of flame geometry.

11. Technology & Development

We developed IGNIS using React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, and Tailwind CSS for the frontend, alongside Python, FastAPI, and Scikit-learn for data processing, APIs, and machine-learning predictions. Git was used for collaborative development, and Vercel hosts the frontend demonstration.

12. Scientific Integrity & Limitations

Our platform uses real NASA experimental records rather than fabricated research data. Predictive results are model estimates, and warnings identify experimental inputs that fall outside the training range; the publicly hosted frontend demonstration does not necessarily provide live backend functionality.

13. Impact — Advancing Space Fire Safety

IGNIS bridges the gap between complex microgravity combustion research and accessible scientific understanding. By helping researchers discover, compare, analyze, and interpret experiments more efficiently, we aim to support future fire-safety research for spacecraft, space stations, and lunar and Martian habitats.

IGNIS — Turning Space Fire Research into Intelligence That Could Save Lives.

projectDetails.name: Flame Scope
projectDetails.summary:
Team Ignis 9th developed Flame Scope, an interactive website for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It brings together NASA’s microgravity combustion studies so students, educators, and engineers can find relevant evidence without searching through individual reports and test tables.

Users can compare experiments side by side, rank studies by a research question, and trace AI-generated answers back to their sources. The Evidence Map shows which conditions, such as material and airflow, were tested together and where evidence is missing. Kids Lab introduces younger learners to the same science through an interactive gravity slider and games.

Fire can behave differently in microgravity, so understanding the conditions behind each finding matters for spacecraft fire-safety research. Flame Scope makes those findings easier to verify and gives learners a hands-on way to explore why fire behaves differently in space.
projectDetails.details:
We built Flame Scope, an interactive research and learning website for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It brings NASA’s microgravity combustion investigations into one place so researchers, engineers, educators, and students can find relevant experiments and check what the evidence supports.

Users can search studies, compare experiments side by side, and rank investigations by a research question, test conditions, or crew environment. The Evidence Map shows whether conditions such as material and airflow were reported together in a single test, appeared in separate tests, or had no matching record. Users can open the original source to check the match. Ask AI provides cited explanations from retrieved NASA records and flags questions where the available evidence is insufficient.

We built the interface with TypeScript, React, and Three.js and the backend with Python and FastAPI. Our data pipeline reads NASA reports and experiment tables, organizes reported conditions, and indexes source passages in PostgreSQL with pgvector on Supabase. The search combines keyword and semantic matching, and Google Geminidrafts explanations from the retrieved evidence.

We used the same research to build two ways to explore the science. The research dashboard helps users inspect the details behind a finding. Kids Lab lets younger learners move a gravity slider to see how an illustrated flame changes. Quizzes and the Fire Safety Officer missions help learners explore fire prevention, detection, and suppression through play.

We considered source traceability, differences in audience expertise, and gaps in experimental coverage. For example, a study can be relevant to lunar fire safety even when its tests provide no direct evidence at lunar gravity. By making those distinctions visible, Flame Scope helps researchers spend less time locating records and gives educators and students a practical way to connect spacecraft fire science to real experiments.

projectDetails.name: Surveyor 3
projectDetails.summary:
Humanity has sent many spacecraft to the Moon, Mars and deep space. Several made major discoveries, yet most people know them only as a name in a textbook or a small photo. Official mission pages are accurate but technical, so students and casual space fans rarely learn why these machines mattered, and the ones that went silent are easily forgotten.

Our solution is "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," an interactive website where each machine tells its own story. We built 13 animated 3D characters (3 on the Moon, 6 on Mars and 4 in deep space), each modeled on its real hardware so visitors see its true shape instead of a flat photo. Surveyor 3 is the host and introduces the others. When a visitor selects a machine, it speaks in the first person, in its own voice, like a friend: who it is, why it was built, when it launched, what it discovered and what condition it is in today. A side panel adds the science, pictures, a timeline and extra facts.

The impact is that space history becomes something visitors experience, not just read. Young learners and casual enthusiasts understand each mission faster, remember it longer and see how these machines helped us learn about other worlds. Every machine's legacy and current status stays visible, so none is forgotten.

The project meets the challenge by explaining what each artifact is, why it was sent, what it discovered and its current status, through a story-driven experience for school-age and casual audiences.
projectDetails.details:
"Abandoned, Not Forgotten" is an interactive 3D web experience that brings the machines humanity left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space back to life. Instead of reading a technical fact sheet, visitors explore a real-looking globe, meet each machine as an animated 3D character, and hear it tell its own story in the first person, like a friend. It is built for school-age learners and casual space fans.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Visitors choose a world (Moon, Mars or Deep Space) and explore it on an interactive globe with a timeline of missions. Selecting a landing site or machine opens an information panel and a character card. The machine introduces itself and tells its story in a fixed order: who it is, why it was built, when it launched, what it achieved, what we learned from it, and what condition it is in today. The narration is spoken aloud, and the text highlights in sync. The host character, Surveyor 3, welcomes visitors and comments on other machines along the way.

Each panel has five tabs: Story, Purpose and Science, Pictures, Facts and Timeline, and More. Every machine has its own 3D model built from its real hardware, so visitors see its true shape rather than a flat photo.

HOW TO USE IT

1. Open the website and choose "Turn on audio" or "Stay silent." Click Surveyor 3 to hear the introduction.

2. Choose a world from the top-left buttons: Moon, Mars or Deep Space.

3. Use the timeline buttons and arrows to move through the missions in order (for example, Moon: 1966-68, 1969, 1969-71, 1971-72, Now). On Mars, press Resume to play the tour automatically.

4. Click a site on the globe, or open Index to jump straight to any machine. Free Orbit lets you rotate and explore the surface freely.

5. Press Play Story to hear the machine speak. Use Pause and Replay as needed, and press Continue on the character card to move on.

6. Switch tabs for the science, pictures, key dates and extra facts. The NASA Data button shows the sources behind the content.

7. Press ESC or the close button to leave a panel. The speaker icon at the top right mutes everything.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Space history becomes something visitors experience, not just read. Learners understand each mission faster, remember it longer and see how these machines helped us learn about other worlds. Every machine's current status is shown, so silent spacecraft stay visible instead of being forgotten.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

React 19 and TypeScript for the app, three.js with @react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei for the 3D globe and characters, Tailwind CSS 4 and motion for design and animation, and the Web Audio API with edge-tts for narration. Development used GitHub, and the site is hosted on Cloudflare Workers.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Each machine narrates its own story in its own voice. Every character looks different and is based on its real hardware. A host character connects the stories, and the globe, timeline and narration turn history into a guided journey.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: all mission data was checked against NASA and NSSDC sources, and the site is honest about each machine's role (for example, Columbia explains that it was the command module, not the lander). Age-appropriate, plain language. Accessibility: sound is optional, and every story is also readable as text. Smooth performance on phones and computers.

DATA AND CREDITS

Mission data and images come from NASA sources and are credited to NASA.

projectDetails.name: Infinite galaxia
projectDetails.summary:
SpaceCare – Multimodal AI-Powered Astronaut Wellbeing Monitoring System

SpaceCare is an AI-powered web application that integrates three different data sources to assess astronauts' mental wellbeing during space missions:

1. Mental Health Survey: Uses the Global Mental Health & Lifestyle Survey dataset to train an AI model. Astronauts complete an interactive survey, and the model analyzes their answers to predict their mood and psychological state.

2. Smartwatch Monitoring: Uses a smartwatch dataset to analyze health indicators such as heart rate, sleep quality, and activity levels. The system compares incoming readings with learned patterns to identify possible signs of stress, fatigue, or abnormal conditions.

3. Facial Expression Analysis: Uses a facial emotion recognition dataset as a reference to train a computer vision model. The astronaut can upload an image or use a live camera stream to analyze facial expressions and estimate emotions.

Final Integration: The three AI models work together in one integrated system. Their individual predictions are combined to generate a final mood and wellbeing assessment, identify potential concerns, and provide personalized recommendations.

The entire solution is connected to a web application where astronauts can submit their data, view AI-generated results, track their wellbeing, and receive recommendations through a single dashboard.
projectDetails.details:
5. Project Details

AI-Powered Astronaut Mental Health Monitoring and Support Platform

1. Project Description and Main Purpose

Our project is a web-based platform designed to monitor and support astronauts' mental well-being during long-duration space missions.

Astronauts face several challenges during space exploration, including prolonged isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, changes in gravity, and living in restricted environments. These conditions may affect their psychological and physical well-being, while communication delays can make immediate access to psychological support more difficult.

To address these challenges, we developed a website that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) to analyze different types of information about astronauts, estimate their psychological state, and recommend personalized interactive games to support their well-being.

The website is the main product. Astronauts can access the platform, provide their information, interact with its AI features, receive an assessment, and access recommended games without needing a separate application.

2. How Does the System Work?

The proposed system consists of three main stages:

A. Data Collection

The website collects information through three different sources:

1. Personal Information

The astronaut enters basic personal and health-related information, including age, gender, blood pressure, and communication frequency.

2. Physiological Data (Smartwatch)

The platform allows astronauts to enter measurements obtained from a smartwatch or wearable monitoring device, such as heart rate, sleep duration, and blood oxygen level (SpO2).

In the current prototype, these measurements are entered manually. Direct integration with wearable devices is a potential future improvement.

3. Facial Detection and Analysis

The website provides two ways to capture facial information: uploading an existing photograph or taking a live photograph using the device's camera.

The facial analysis component examines facial features and expression patterns to provide additional information for the AI assessment.

B. AI-Powered Psychological Assessment

After collecting the available information, the integrated AI system uses machine learning techniques and facial analysis to estimate the astronaut's psychological state.

The intended assessment produces six psychological indicators:

1. Sadness: Estimates signs associated with sadness and low mood.

2. Anxiety: Estimates signs associated with anxiety and psychological tension.

3. Irritability: Identifies potential signs of increased irritability.

4. Fatigue: Estimates fatigue-related conditions using physiological and behavioral information.

5. Loneliness: Estimates potential indicators associated with social isolation.

6. Emotional Stability: Evaluates indicators related to emotional well-being and stability.

These indicators are the outputs of the psychological assessment, not the information initially entered by the astronaut.

The system is designed to identify the indicator that requires the most attention and use this result to determine the most suitable supportive activity.

C. Personalized Game Recommendation

The final stage connects the AI assessment to the website's game library.

Based on the psychological indicator requiring the most attention, the platform is designed to recommend a suitable interactive game.

Examples include:

- Anxiety: Relaxation-based games.

- Sadness: Engaging games that encourage positive interaction.

- Irritability: Activities focused on emotional regulation.

- Fatigue: Suitable low-effort activities.

- Loneliness: Interactive games that encourage engagement.

- Emotional Stability: Activities focused on relaxation and emotional regulation.

The astronaut will be able to access the recommended game directly through the website.

The purpose of these games is to provide accessible and engaging supportive activities, not to replace professional psychological assessment or treatment.

3. Datasets and Data Usage

To develop and test the machine learning components, we selected two publicly available datasets from Kaggle:

1. Fitbit Fitness Tracker Dataset

https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/arashnic/fitbit?resource=download

This dataset contains activity and fitness-related information, including sleep and activity measurements. It is used as a development resource for analyzing physiological and behavioral patterns.

2. Global Mental Health and Lifestyle Survey Dataset

https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dhrubangtalukdar/global-mental-health-and-lifestyle-survey-dataset

This dataset contains mental health and lifestyle-related information. It supports the development of machine learning models that estimate psychological indicators.

Both datasets are used in the model development and evaluation process through training and testing.

Importantly, these datasets do not represent actual astronauts. They are publicly available development resources selected to help build the initial prototype.

4. NASA Hazards Alignment

Our project is based on four hazards identified by NASA's Human Research Program:

Isolation and Confinement

Prolonged isolation and limited social interaction may contribute to loneliness, sadness, and emotional difficulties. Our platform aims to identify potential psychological changes and recommend suitable interactive activities.

Distance from Earth

Communication delays and limited access to immediate assistance make autonomous support systems important. Our website aims to provide AI-based assessment and supportive activities without depending entirely on real-time communication with Earth.

Gravity Fields

Different gravity environments require astronauts to adapt physically. The platform considers physiological information, such as heart rate and sleep patterns, which may help monitor changes associated with physical adaptation and fatigue.

Hostile/Closed Environments

Living in restricted spacecraft environments exposes astronauts to environmental conditions such as limited space, artificial lighting, and noise. Our system aims to monitor relevant physiological and behavioral information that may reflect changes in their overall well-being.

These four NASA hazards provide the scientific context and design foundation for our solution.

5. Benefits and Expected Impact

The project aims to provide several benefits:

- Continuous Monitoring: Helping astronauts keep track of changes in their psychological well-being.

- Early Awareness: Identifying potential warning signs through the analysis of different information sources.

- Personalized Support: Recommending activities according to the astronaut's estimated psychological needs.

- Accessibility: Providing assessment and supportive activities through one integrated website.

- Autonomous Operation: Reducing complete dependence on immediate communication with Earth for basic psychological support.

Our ultimate goal is to contribute to astronauts' psychological well-being and help them cope with the challenges of isolation, confinement, and long-duration space exploration.

6. Technologies and Tools Used

The project combines web development, machine learning, and image analysis.

The main technologies and tools include:

- HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for frontend development.

- A web-based application as the main platform.

- Machine learning techniques for psychological assessment.

- Facial detection and expression analysis tools.

- Kaggle datasets for model development and evaluation.

- A camera-enabled device for capturing facial images.

- A smartwatch as a source of physiological measurements.

The camera allows users to upload or capture facial images, while smartwatch measurements are currently entered manually through the website.

7. Current Implementation and Future Development

To clearly distinguish the current prototype from the intended final system, the project has the following development status:

Implemented in the Current Prototype:

- A web-based platform serving as the main user interface.

- Personal information input forms.

- Manual entry of physiological measurements.

- Facial image uploading.

- Live camera functionality for facial detection.

- Machine learning model development using the selected Kaggle datasets.

- Training and testing of the developed model.

Planned / Still Under Development:

- Completing the unified psychological assessment that generates all six indicators.

- Integrating the different analysis outputs into one assessment.

- Connecting the psychological assessment results to the game recommendation system.

- Automatically selecting and displaying the most appropriate game.

- Direct smartwatch integration for automatic physiological data collection.

- Further model validation using more relevant astronaut-related data.

The six-indicator assessment and automatic game recommendation are the intended final workflow and should not be considered fully implemented in the current prototype.

8. Limitations and Considerations

The current prototype uses publicly available datasets that may not fully represent the unique conditions experienced by astronauts during space missions.

Additionally, facial expressions and physiological measurements alone cannot reliably determine complex psychological conditions. For example, loneliness requires additional behavioral or self-reported information.

The AI system is intended to estimate psychological indicators and provide supportive recommendations, not to make clinical diagnoses.

Further testing, validation, and adaptation using astronaut-specific data would be necessary before deploying the platform in actual space missions.

9. Final Goal

Our project aims to create an integrated and accessible web platform that combines multiple data sources, AI-powered psychological assessment, and personalized game-based support.

By providing astronauts with a way to monitor their well-being and access suitable supportive activities within one platform, we hope to contribute to healthier and more sustainable long-duration human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project InnoBotix
projectDetails.summary:
HALO is a web-based wellbeing companion for astronauts on long missions. It combines wearable data sleep, heart rate, activity with a daily check in under two minutes covering mood, stress, loneliness, depression-scale and crew questions. Over about 14 days it learns each astronaut's personal normal, then shows a green, yellow or red status with the reasons behind it. When a trend worsens, it offers support such as breathing exercises; in an emergency it alerts base and the crew doctor. A private memory collection keeps photos and messages from loved ones close. HALO works offline, keeps data on the device, never diagnoses and never suggests medication.

This addresses the challenge directly: on a Mars mission, messages take 20–22 minutes one way, so astronauts must notice health changes themselves before Earth can help. NASA lists behavioral health monitoring as an open research gap, and existing tools each cover only one piece Astroskin the body, CIMON emotion from speech, ESA's VR relaxation sessions. None joins body, mind and crew into one daily picture.

It matters because health is connected: when physical, psychological or social health falls, the others follow. HALO monitors them together, compares each person only with themselves, and gives support without waiting for Earth.
projectDetails.details: Background and evidence NASA's behavioral risk page says isolation and confinement can raise the risk of anxiety and depression and can affect sleep, morale and decision making. It lists journaling, windows and privacy as countermeasures but gives no efficacy data. Crews respond very differently: in the Mars-520 simulation, three of six crew accumulated stress and three did not, so one threshold for everyone misses people. Astronauts sleep about 6 hours in space (seven studies) against 7.9 hours on Earth in a Shuttle crew survey, and about three-quarters of Shuttle and ISS astronauts used sleep medication, which sped falling asleep but did not lengthen sleep (NASA sleep Evidence Report). Basner et al. (2013) tracked a crew of six with wrist sensors for 520 days: sedentariness rose, sleep time increased by 8.4% and light exposure fell. Existing tools each cover one dimension. Astroskin (Hexoskin with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency) measures activity, heart, breathing, skin temperature, blood pressure and blood oxygen, but covers the body only. CIMON uses IBM Watson Tone Analyzer to detect emotion from the tone of conversation and mainly assists with tasks. ESA's VR headset experiment (HTC Vive Focus 3, EveryWear app) pairs VR video with questionnaires for isolation and stress. Our sources do not describe daily tracking or early warnings for the last two. The gap is integration, a personal baseline and early warning. How we built HALO 1. Problem analysis: We analyzed the problem and its impact using NASA sources, covering sleep quality, isolation and behavior. 2. Research and gap analysis: We read NASA documents and analog studies to choose indicators, and found that existing tools (CIMON, Astroskin, ESA VR Mental Care) each solve only part of the problem. 3. Questions and data: From our sources, we chose the daily check-in questions and the data HALO needs. 4. Indicators: Sleep duration and quality, heart rate, activity, mood, stress, loneliness and fatigue. Daily depression-scale questions, and crew questions on team missions. 5. Personal baseline: Learn each astronaut's normal over about 14 days, then compare every signal only with that person's own normal. 6. Status logic: One bad day does nothing. Yellow means a trend has formed across days in at least two signals. Red means a sustained change in several signals. Self-report counts for no more than the passive signals. *[confirm weights]* 7. Support logic: Breathing exercises, contact with a crewmate, routine adjustments and the memory collection. Red always offers "talk to a professional or the crew doctor". 8. Visual identity: We chose the color palette and created the HALO visual identity. 9. Prototype: We used AI to help make a first design of the website in Figma, then built the 3D astronaut avatar. 10. Working website: We turned the Figma prototype into a working website with the check-in, scoring and offline storage. 11. Technical details: Html css java script What HALO does and how it works • What HALO does with it: HALO turns scattered signals into one personal picture. It syncs wearable data (design: Bluetooth link to a device such as Astroskin), scores the daily check-in, compares every signal with the person's own baseline, and computes the green/yellow/red status with the reasons behind it. ]* • What comes out: A daily status with reasons, early support actions, emergency alerts to base and the crew doctor, and personal settings such as medication reminders for chronic conditions. They see there health on the screen The daily check-in Stress: 0-4 (PSS-4) -How often today have you felt that you were unable to control the important things in your life? -How often today have you felt confident about your ability to handle your personal problems? -How often today have you felt that things were going your way? -How often today have you felt difficulties were piling up so high that you could not overcome them? Depression:0-4 (PHQ-9) -Little interest or pleasure in doing things. -Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless. -Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much. -Feeling tired or having little energy. -Poor appetite or overeating. -Feeling bad about yourself or that you are a failure or have let yourself or family down. -Thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself in some way. How lonely do you feel today? 0-10 How is your mood today? 0-10 Implementation steps in the build 1. Sync wearable data (design: Bluetooth link to a device such as Astroskin). 2. Build the daily check-in and score. 3. Add the green/yellow/red status with reasons. 4. Add support actions, the memory collection and emergency alerts. 5. Add personal settings, such as medication reminders for chronic conditions. 6. Test with simulated data. Testing We tested with simulated crew data modelled on the Mars-520 pattern, where half the crew drift and half stay stable. All simulated data is labelled as simulated. Tools, coding languages, hardware and software • Design: Figma, Canva, Adobe Illustrator • 3D: Blender, used for the 3D astronaut avatar • Website: Visual Studio Code; built with help from Copilot, an AI tool. https://sketchfab.com/feed • AI tools: see section 5. Benefits and goals HALO's goal is to protect astronauts' mental and physical health when help from Earth is far away. It aims to give early support before a small change becomes a serious problem. Its method monitors physical and psychological signals together, works offline, and does not depend on Earth. Against alternatives: Astroskin tracks the body only, CIMON works in conversation, and ESA's VR experiment gives sessions; HALO joins all of this and adds a daily, personal baseline with early warning. Working features, limits and future plans • Working features: it measures and blends all the body and mind indecators • Limits and unfinished parts: The wearable link is a design, not a working integration. The status weights are not confirmed. All testing used simulated data. Only the prototype is done • Future plans: make it easier to access and add a calling feature 3. NASA data and resources At least one NASA resource is required to qualify for a Global Award, so fill all links. Resource 1: NASA CBS Problem Statement and behavioral risk material • What we used from it: The problem statement on isolation, confinement and communication delay, and the open research gap on validated behavioral health monitoring (BMed2). • How it helped our solution: It defined the problem and told us validated monitoring measures are an open gap, which HALO targets. Resource 2: NASA sleep Evidence Report • What we used from it: In-space sleep duration (about 6 hours, seven studies), the 7.9 hours Earth baseline, and the finding that about three-quarters of Shuttle and ISS astronauts used sleep medication without lengthening sleep. • How it helped our solution: It justified making sleep a core passive indicator and comparing each astronaut only with their own baseline. https://www.nasa.gov/reference/risk-of-behavioral-changes-and-psychiatric-disorders/ https://www.nasa.gov/reference/risk-of-inadequate-teamwork/ https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/hazards/ 4. Other resources and source credits Resource 1: Basner et al. (2013), Mars-520 mission study • Link: *[ ]* • What we used from it: The 520-day wrist-sensor findings (sedentariness rose, sleep time increased 8.4%, light exposure fell) and the finding that three of six crew accumulated stress while three did not. • How it helped our solution: It showed one threshold misses people, grounding the personal baseline and two-signal trend logic, and it is the pattern for our simulated test data. Resource 2: Astroskin (Hexoskin with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency) • What we used from it: Its measured signals, as the model for the wearable data HALO syncs. • How it helped our solution: It defined the physical layer of the input. Resource 3: CIMON and ESA's VR headset experiment (HTC Vive Focus 3, EveryWear app) • What we used from it: Their capabilities, as the psychological layer we integrate. • How it helped our solution: It showed existing tools cover one dimension each, defining the gap. 5. AI and SI use We used AI tools to support our work. AI did not create our idea for solving the challenge. The idea, the research and the visual identity were made by our team. • Website development: We used Git hub copilt to help us build the website. • First website design: We used figma to help create a first design of the website, based on the color palette we chose. • Visual identity: Our team created the HALO visual identity from our research. We used illustrator only to help improve it and show it clearly in Figma. • Simulated test data: the codes were in ai 6. Project links • NASA Project page: https://youtu.be/cRqMRDZqQmE?si=h4DDtoGWhVpEWw2B • Demo: https://youtu.be/aNZV9PgNrN0?si=4iyOz5ygxwbS3DsI • Working website: https://www.figma.com/design/WlMhRQoRyoUod2nFR8qurb/Untitled?node-id=0-1&t=4GIafIVpSqssR318-1 The PDF must be exported as PDF, checked page by page, and uploaded to a host with a viewing link that needs no login, then tested in an incognito window. 7. Team and workflow Team and roles • Lina Ahmed Elsayed, Leader and Visual Designer: Coordinated tasks, researched sources, designed the UX and HALO's visual identity. • Zainab Abdulwahab, Co-Leader and Clinical Psychology Researcher: Coordinated tasks, researched sources, and developed the daily health questions and required data. • Omar Emad Hegazy, AI and Software Developer: Organized AI prompts around our research and turned it into the website design. • Andrew Emad, Designer and 3D Artist: Organized research data visually and created the 3D models for the presentation. Collaboration and milestones We met on site when needed to assign tasks, held Discord meetings while working to help each other and see what was missing, and used WhatsApp to share sources and tasks. Day 1 (Nov 12): research across all sources (7 hours), then 1 hour to compile the website ideas. Day 2 (Nov 13): built the prototype, the 3D avatar and the presentation.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: Insider Lens
projectDetails.summary: When a day looks quiet on a fire map, what did the satellites actually see? Insider Lens brings NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one calendar and keeps the source of each observation visible. In our southern Canada study area, VIIRS recorded detections on 27 days in June 2023. Adding MODIS brought the total to 28. On June 1, Terra MODIS recorded two detections that a VIIRS-only calendar leaves out. Fire analysts and land managers can use the map to trace a day back to its source before drawing conclusions about local fire history.
projectDetails.details:
On June 1, 2023, a fire analyst looking at our southern Canada study area would see a blank day with VIIRS selected. Switching on MODIS reveals two Terra detections, both recorded at 18:41 UTC. Insider Lens lets the analyst trace those observations back to their source and see why the calendar changed.

We built an interactive map and fire activity calendar using NASA FIRMS observations from Terra and Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS. We group records by 10 km equal-area grid cell and UTC date while preserving the original sensor and record count. Users can select a region and month, compare either sensor family or both, inspect a day on the map, and export the same selection as a CSV.

In the June 2023 study area, combining both sources preserved detections on 28 days, compared with 27 for VIIRS alone. Across 568 cell-days with detections, 34 appeared only in MODIS, 199 appeared in both, and 335 appeared only in VIIRS. This helps analysts and land managers check whether a gap reflects their choice of sensor. Different satellite overpass times and coverage limit what a blank day can tell us about fires on the ground.

We built the interface with React, TypeScript, Vite, and MapLibre GL JS. Python, SQLite, and pyproj handle the data. A separate verification program checked exact counts across 12 test cases, and Playwright tested the browser workflows.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: ARES
projectDetails.summary: ARES is an interactive Mars exploration platform designed to support future human missions by transforming NASA planetary data into accessible scientific insights. The platform features a 3D interactive Mars globe, terrain visualization using MOLA elevation data, and the locations of 14 historical Mars landing missions. It also integrates SWIM research data to explore potential subsurface water ice deposits and highlights NASA's MOXIE experiment, demonstrating oxygen production from the Martian atmosphere. Additionally, ARES provides mission imagery, planetary information, and an oxygen requirement calculator to help users understand essential survival considerations for future explorers. By bringing planetary mapping, scientific research, and mission-related resources together in one platform, ARES aims to improve understanding of the Martian environment and support more informed exploration planning.
projectDetails.details:
ARES

Advanced Reconnaissance & Exploration System

Interactive Mars Exploration and Survival Platform

1. Project Overview

ARES is an interactive planetary exploration and survival platform designed to make real scientific data about Mars accessible, understandable, and useful for future human exploration missions.

The project brings together planetary mapping, topographical information, historical mission locations, subsurface water ice research, atmospheric resources, and survival-related calculations into a unified digital environment.

Rather than presenting Mars as simply a distant planet to explore, ARES approaches it as an environment that future explorers must understand, evaluate, and prepare for.

Its primary objective is to bridge the gap between complex planetary science datasets and practical exploration knowledge by providing an accessible interface for visualizing scientific information and understanding the challenges of operating on Mars.

2. The Problem

Future human exploration of Mars presents significant scientific and operational challenges.

Mars has an extremely thin atmosphere, harsh temperatures, limited accessible liquid water, and environmental conditions that make long-term human presence difficult.

Future exploration missions must consider several important questions:

  • Where have previous spacecraft successfully landed?
  • How does the Martian surface vary in elevation and terrain?
  • Where might accessible subsurface water ice exist?
  • Can local Martian resources contribute to human survival?
  • How could oxygen be produced using resources available on Mars?
  • What scientific information should be considered when planning future exploration missions?

Although NASA and other scientific organizations have collected extensive planetary data, this information is distributed across multiple datasets, research publications, visualization platforms, and mission archives.

ARES addresses this accessibility challenge by bringing several relevant scientific resources together in one interactive platform.

3. Project Objectives

ARES aims to:

  1. Make authentic Mars planetary data easier to explore and understand.
  2. Provide an interactive visualization of the Martian surface.
  3. Present historical Mars landing missions and their locations.
  4. Explain the importance of subsurface water ice for future exploration.
  5. Demonstrate the potential of utilizing local Martian resources.
  6. Help users understand oxygen requirements for future exploration crews.
  7. Connect scientific discoveries with practical mission-planning considerations.

4. Core Features and Functionalities

A. Interactive 3D Mars Globe

ARES provides an interactive three-dimensional representation of Mars using planetary imagery and elevation tiles from NASA Mars Trek.

Users can:

  • Rotate and explore the Martian globe.
  • Zoom in and out of the planetary surface.
  • Examine different geographical regions.
  • View selected landing locations.
  • Access location information, including latitude, longitude, and elevation where available.
  • Explore different planetary map layers.

The globe provides an intuitive way to understand the geographical distribution of important Martian locations.

B. Historical Mars Landing Missions

The platform presents 14 historical Mars landing locations, including 10 successful landings and four missions that were lost or crashed.

Each location can be explored through the interactive map, allowing users to understand the geographical history of robotic Mars exploration.

This feature connects historical exploration achievements with the planning of future missions.

C. Martian Terrain and Topographical Analysis

ARES integrates Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) elevation information to visualize the planet's topography.

The platform presents elevation variations across the Martian surface, including:

  • Lowest elevation: approximately 8.2 km below the reference level.
  • Highest elevation: approximately 21.2 km above the reference level.

Color gradients and terrain shading help users understand differences in elevation and geographical structure.

This information provides important scientific context for understanding potential exploration environments.

D. Subsurface Water Ice Exploration — NASA SWIM

Water is one of the most important resources for future human exploration of Mars.

ARES incorporates scientific information from NASA/JPL's Subsurface Water Ice Mapping (SWIM) project.

The SWIM research combines multiple orbital datasets, including observations from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Odyssey, and Mars Global Surveyor, to identify regions where subsurface water ice is more likely to exist.

The platform explains why buried ice is important:

  • It could provide water for future explorers.
  • Water can support essential life-support requirements.
  • Water can potentially be processed into resources needed for rocket propellant.
  • Identifying accessible ice deposits could influence future exploration strategies.

ARES helps users understand the relationship between geographical location and the availability of potentially important resources.

E. Oxygen Production — NASA MOXIE

Another essential aspect of future Mars exploration is oxygen availability.

Mars' atmosphere consists predominantly of carbon dioxide, making direct human respiration impossible.

ARES highlights NASA's Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE), which demonstrated the ability to extract oxygen from the Martian atmosphere.

The MOXIE experiment aboard the Perseverance rover demonstrated oxygen production through an electrochemical process.

Its reported achievements include:

  • First successful oxygen production on Mars on April 20, 2021.
  • 5.4 grams of oxygen during its first operation.
  • 122 grams of total oxygen across 16 operations.
  • A maximum production rate of approximately 12 grams per hour.
  • Oxygen purity of at least 98%.

ARES presents this achievement to demonstrate how locally available Martian resources could contribute to future human missions.

F. Crew Oxygen Requirement Calculator

ARES includes an interactive calculator that estimates oxygen requirements based on:

  • Number of explorers.
  • Duration of the mission in days.

The calculator estimates the total oxygen required for breathing and compares that requirement with the maximum reported production rate of MOXIE.

It also estimates how many equivalent MOXIE-sized units would be required to operate continuously to cover the calculated oxygen demand.

The calculation uses an approximate consumption assumption of 0.685 kg per person per day.

This feature helps users understand the scale of life-support requirements and the importance of resource production during extended missions.

The calculator provides educational estimates rather than a complete engineering model of a human life-support system.

G. Martian Environmental Information

The platform includes environmental information to help users understand the conditions future explorers may encounter.

It presents a modeled Martian weather interface with information such as:

  • Temperature.
  • Wind speed.
  • Atmospheric pressure.

The displayed weather information is model-based rather than a live surface sensor reading.

ARES also explains important environmental measurements and their implications for exploration.

H. NASA Mission Image Gallery

ARES integrates NASA's Image and Video Library to present authentic imagery from planetary exploration missions.

Images are retrieved through NASA's public image API, allowing users to explore real mission photographs and scientific visuals.

This provides visual context for the information presented throughout the platform.

5. Scientific Data Sources and Technologies

ARES is built around publicly available scientific information and planetary datasets.

Its main data sources include:

NASA Mars Trek

  • Planetary imagery.
  • Viking MDIM 2.1 imagery.
  • MOLA elevation data.
  • Additional terrain visualization layers.

NASA/JPL SWIM

  • Subsurface water ice research.
  • Regional ice probability information.
  • Scientific observations from multiple Mars orbital missions.

NASA MOXIE Research

  • Oxygen production experiments.
  • Oxygen production rates.
  • Experimental results and scientific publications.

NASA Image and Video Library

  • Authentic mission photographs.
  • Publicly available planetary exploration imagery.
  • Mission-related visual resources.

Mars Mission Landing Records

  • Landing coordinates.
  • Mission dates.
  • Mission outcomes.
  • Historical exploration information.

The platform combines these resources into an accessible interface rather than attempting to replace the original scientific datasets.

6. Technical Approach and Platform Architecture

ARES operates as a web-based interactive platform.

Its approach combines:

  1. Scientific data integration: Gathering relevant planetary information from publicly available scientific sources.
  2. Data visualization: Transforming geographical and numerical information into understandable visual representations.
  3. Interactive exploration: Allowing users to navigate the Martian globe and examine selected locations.
  4. Scientific interpretation: Explaining the relevance of terrain, water ice, oxygen production, and environmental conditions.
  5. Estimation tools: Providing simplified calculations to demonstrate resource requirements for future exploration.

The platform is designed to make planetary science more approachable through interactive digital experiences.

7. Innovation and Unique Value

The primary value of ARES lies in integrating multiple aspects of Mars exploration into one accessible environment.

Instead of focusing exclusively on maps, historical missions, or scientific discoveries, ARES connects these subjects through a common exploration and survival perspective.

Its distinguishing aspects include:

  • Combining planetary visualization with resource-related scientific information.
  • Connecting historical landing missions with geographical exploration.
  • Presenting subsurface water ice research alongside oxygen production technologies.
  • Translating scientific oxygen-production data into understandable crew requirement estimates.
  • Providing a unified interface for exploring different aspects of future Martian missions.

ARES emphasizes the connection between understanding a planet and preparing to operate within its environment.

8. Potential Applications and Expected Impact

ARES can serve as:

An Educational Platform
Helping students and science enthusiasts understand Mars through real planetary data.

A Scientific Exploration Interface
Providing an accessible way to explore topographical information, historical landing sites, and published resource research.

A Mission Planning Learning Tool
Demonstrating how geographical conditions and resource availability may influence future exploration decisions.

A Space Science Visualization Platform
Connecting complex scientific datasets with interactive geographical representations.

Its long-term vision is to support better scientific understanding of the challenges associated with human exploration of Mars.

9. Current Limitations and Future Development

ARES is an evolving project. Its current version focuses on visualization, scientific information integration, and educational resource estimation.

Several advanced capabilities remain future development goals.

These include:

  • Calculating terrain slope and surface roughness directly from elevation datasets.
  • Integrating more detailed SHARAD-derived subsurface ice information.
  • Developing evidence-based landing-site evaluation methods.
  • Improving geographical resource visualization.
  • Expanding environmental datasets and mission-related analysis.
  • Developing more advanced decision-support capabilities.

Importantly, the current version does not claim to calculate scientifically validated landing safety scores or exact subsurface ice percentages.

These capabilities require additional data processing, validation, and scientific development.

10. Vision

The future of Mars exploration will depend not only on the ability to reach the planet, but also on our ability to understand its environment and use available resources responsibly.

ARES aims to make that understanding more accessible by connecting planetary science, interactive technology, and exploration-focused information.

By transforming complex scientific data into an understandable exploration experience, ARES takes a step toward a more informed approach to humanity's future beyond Earth.

ARES — Explore with Evidence. Decide with Confidence.

projectDetails.name: Project Interstellar Overdrive
projectDetails.summary:
AURA AstroVitals is an offline-first health-monitoring prototype for astronauts, built by Team Interstellar Overdrive for the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.”
On long missions, such as a trip to Mars, messages to Earth can take up to about 44 minutes for a round trip and can be blocked for weeks. A crew cannot always wait for help from the ground, so AURA helps astronauts understand their own health on board.
AURA brings together body signals, daily check-ins, and cabin conditions such as CO₂, temperature and noise. It compares each astronaut with their own normal, not with Earth averages. Its main safety rule is: “The models advise. The rules decide.” Only clear, readable rules reviewed by medical staff can raise an official alert. Small AI models run quietly in the background and can only post labelled advisory notices, such as a slow drift in heart rate and sleep, or a short trend forecast with its uncertainty.
Future crews will be far from Earth, and a tool that works without a connection and keeps rules in charge of alerts can help them notice problems early.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
AURA AstroVitals is a health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long missions, when help from Earth is delayed or cut off. It gathers body signals (heart rate, heart-rate variability, sleep, activity, skin temperature), a short daily check-in (mood, fatigue, pain, hydration, symptoms) and cabin readings (CO₂, temperature, humidity, noise, light, radiation level). It shows each astronaut’s status, any alerts or notices, and the reason behind them, all on local equipment without needing the cloud.
How it works
Every reading is checked first. A missing, frozen or impossible value gives a “sensor problem” message, not a false health alert.
Each astronaut is compared with their own recent normal, not with Earth averages, because spaceflight changes the body.
Rules lane: clear, readable rules, written and reviewed by medical teammates, can raise official alerts. Each alert shows which rule fired and a suggested checklist.
Advisory lane: four small machine-learning models run quietly on the local computer. One looks for unusual combined changes in the body, one for unusual cabin conditions, one gives a low/moderate/elevated risk band for heart and fitness decline, and one forecasts resting heart rate, heart-rate variability and sleep for the next 7–14 days with an uncertainty band. They can only post labelled advisory notices (“not a diagnosis”, no alarm sound), and only after a pattern persists across several checks.
If a model fails, only that model is switched off and the rules keep running.
The guiding principle is: “The models advise. The rules decide.”
Benefits and intended impact
Crews get a clear picture of their own health when Earth is far away.
People stay in control: the AI never raises official alerts, and every alert has a readable reason.
Fewer false alarms, because each person is compared with their own normal and bad sensors are flagged.
We hope AURA shows a safe, explainable design pattern that medical and engineering experts can review, test and improve. It is a prototype and a starting point, not a finished medical system.
What makes it creative
Splitting decisions into a rules lane and an advisory AI lane, with a firm limit on what the AI may do.
Designing for real space limits: no cloud, small models on local equipment, and queued messages for Earth.
Training and testing the AI on a simulator of virtual astronauts with known ground truth, so we can measure whether the models catch problems we injected. We label this clearly as simulated.
Honest labelling in the interface: advisory notices, official alerts, bad-sensor messages and “model unavailable” each look different.
Factors the team considered
Communication delay and blackouts (up to about 44 minutes round trip, and weeks without contact).
Limited power, memory and computing on board.
Safety: AI must not diagnose or trigger alarms alone.
Evidence: we based our choices on NASA reports and published studies, and we state what is not proven.
Privacy and consent for sensitive mood and behavioural data.
Sensor quality, because a bad reading should not look like a health problem.
Tools used
[Website languages and frameworks] · [Python libraries for the simulator and models; model types such as Isolation Forest or One-Class SVM, and LSTM/GRU or a trend baseline] · [Hosting, repository] · [Hardware, or “runs in a standard web browser”] · SI tools are listed in the AI/SI section.
Working features, limits and future plans
Working now: [list exactly what judges can open and use] and the simulator with four AI models trained and tested on it.
Limits: The AI was trained and tested only on simulated astronauts, so results show behaviour on simulated scenarios only. AURA is not a medical device, is not clinically validated and does not diagnose. Rule thresholds are starting examples that need review by medical experts. Sensor data are simulated, and real hardware is not connected.

Future plans (not built): context detection, signal-quality and sensor cross-checks, circadian monitoring, offline voice check-in, camera-assisted exercise and fatigue checks, a shared-cause crew check, and a radiation event screen.
