projectDetails.name: Project INVICTA | 2026
projectDetails.summary:
Before They Went Silent is a 2.5-minute cinematic educational video that tells the stories of historic space exploration equipment, including Surveyor 3, ALSEP, NASA’s Opportunity rover, and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming the histories of these machines into an engaging visual narrative. Through AI-generated cinematic scenes, English voice-over narration, and sound effects, it explains what each piece of equipment was designed to do, what it achieved, and why its contribution to space exploration still matters.

The video is important because the end of a mission does not mean the end of its story. By making scientific and engineering achievements accessible to younger audiences and casual space enthusiasts, the project aims to preserve the legacy of these machines and inspire greater curiosity about space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Before They Went Silent is a 2.5-minute cinematic educational video that brings the stories of four historic space exploration systems to life: Surveyor 3, the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), NASA’s Opportunity rover, and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

What does it do?

The video introduces each piece of equipment, explaining its original purpose, key achievements, and mission outcome. It transforms scientific and historical information into an engaging visual experience for school-age audiences and casual space enthusiasts.

How does it work?

The project combines verified mission research with AI-generated cinematic scenes and English voice-over narration. It follows a structured sequence, presenting each machine through visuals that illustrate its environment and role in space exploration. Sound effects and on-screen text support the narration and help communicate the information clearly.

The production process involved:

- Researching the selected missions and checking historical details against NASA documentation and scientific references.
- Writing the narration and planning the visual scenes.
- Generating cinematic video scenes using AI.
- Producing the English voice-over.
- Editing and assembling the scenes, narration, sound effects, and text into the final video.

Benefits and Expected Impact

The project makes space exploration history more accessible to younger and non-specialist audiences. It highlights the scientific and engineering contributions of equipment that is no longer operating, while showing that the end of a mission does not mean the end of its legacy. We hope to encourage curiosity about space science, engineering, and future exploration.

Tools and Technologies Used

- Google Flow: AI-assisted generation of cinematic video scenes and visual reconstructions.
- ChatGPT: Developing and refining precise, detailed prompts for AI-generated scenes.
- TTSMaker: Generating the English text-to-speech voice-over.
- CapCut: Editing the video, arranging scenes, synchronizing narration, adding sound effects and on-screen text, and exporting the final film.
- NASA mission documentation and scientific publications: Research and fact-checking.

The project was completed independently. No programming languages or hardware development were required. AI-generated visuals are used as illustrative reconstructions, not presented as authentic NASA archival footage.

projectDetails.name: Never Forgotten
projectDetails.summary:
Good morning, everyone!

Welcome to a journey through the forgotten history of space exploration!

For the NASA challenge, inspired by the theme **"Abandoned but Not Forgotten,"** we didn't just collect information; we brought forgotten space missions back to life.

Throughout history, humanity has sent remarkable spacecraft to explore the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Yet, many of these missions have gradually disappeared from public attention, despite their incredible achievements and contributions to science.

From **ALSEP**, which allowed scientists to continue studying the Moon, to **Viking, Phoenix, and InSight**, which helped us explore Mars, and from **NEAR Shoemaker** to **Pioneer 10 and 11 and Dawn**, every mission has a story worth telling.

But how can we make these stories reach people again?

We created an educational website that brings these missions together, presenting their journeys, discoveries, and achievements. We also developed an interactive game for children, transforming space exploration into an enjoyable learning experience.

Our mission is simple: to reconnect people with humanity's forgotten achievements, inspire curiosity in younger generations, and prove that a spacecraft may stop operating, but its legacy never truly disappears.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

​Our project is an interactive platform dedicated to exploring "forgotten" or lesser-known NASA space missions, spacecraft, and artifacts. It works through a user-friendly website that features detailed historical timelines (launch and landing dates), precise specifications like dimensions and sizes, and immersive 3D models. Additionally, it includes an educational mini-game designed specifically for children to make learning about space history fun and engaging.

​What benefits does it have?

​It rescues important pieces of space history from being forgotten, turning them into accessible digital knowledge. For children and students, the interactive 3D models and educational game simplify complex aerospace concepts, fostering curiosity in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields.

​What is the intended impact of the project?

​The intended impact is to spark a lifelong interest in space exploration and science among the younger generation. By highlighting historical missions that laid the groundwork for modern space exploration, we aim to educate the public and preserve aerospace heritage in an entertaining, digital-first format.

​What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

​We utilized web development languages (such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) to build the website. For the 3D models and interactive elements, we used specialized graphics tools and libraries (like Three.js or Blender), alongside game development tools to create the kids' educational game.

​How is your project creative?

​Our project stands out by combining historical archiving with modern interactive technology. Instead of a traditional text-based database, we brought forgotten space missions back to life using 3D visualization and gamification, turning passive reading into an active, playful learning adventure.

​What factors did your team consider?

​Our team carefully considered user experience (UX) and age-appropriate design, ensuring the platform is intuitive and engaging for children. We also prioritized historical accuracy by verifying launch/landing dates and vehicle specifications, alongside optimizing website performance for smooth 3D rendering.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Trendoscope
projectDetails.summary:
Trendoscope is an interactive website that lets anyone investigate whether a climate variable in a region is truly changing, and understand the answer, in under three minutes. It is built around the Earth System Trend Detective challenge and uses NASA Earth data.

Users pick a region, time range, and variable (water, land, weather, or vegetation). A Python backend runs the trend analysis and returns a time-series graph, key statistics, and a plain-language verdict. A “Chance Machine” shuffles the data to show visually whether a trend is real or just random noise. Users can also compare two regions, play a detective-style game that links events such as floods to their possible causes, follow a kids’ story mode, and ask an LLM questions limited to the data. Demo cases focus on Egypt and the MENA region.

It addresses the challenge by turning raw satellite data into guided, trustworthy analysis that needs no statistics background. This matters because science only creates impact when it reaches the public. Trendoscope helps students and communities see climate change in their own region, and judge it with evidence rather than guesswork.
projectDetails.details:
Trendoscope turns NASA Earth observation data into a guided investigation. The user chooses a region (by dropdown or map), a time range, a resolution, and a variable (water, land, weather, or vegetation). A Python backend processes the data and runs a trend test. The site returns an interactive time-series graph, key statistics, and a plain-language “verdict” on whether the change is real. The “Chance Machine” shuffles the data many times to show visually whether the observed trend could happen by luck. Users can also compare two regions, play a detective game that links events such as floods to their possible causes, follow a kids’ story mode with a two-date slider and quiz, and ask an LLM questions restricted to the data.

Benefits and intended impact

A student with no statistics background can investigate a climate variable and understand the answer in under three minutes. We want climate evidence to reach the public, not just scientists, so people can judge changes in their own region (with demo cases for Egypt and MENA) from data rather than headlines.

Tools and technologies

  • Python, Jupyter, and pandas for data processing and trend analysis
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with Plotly.js for the interactive front end
  • GitHub for the repository, with GitHub Pages for hosting
  • An LLM, limited to the project’s data, for explanations and Q&A
  • Ubuntu laptops for development
  • AI tools to help build the website, demo video, and slides, as disclosed in our AI-use statement

How it is creative

  • A detective case-file theme with a verdict stamp
  • The Chance Machine, which makes statistical significance visible
  • A kids’ story mode and a detective game that make the data approachable
  • Avatar-style mascot powers for water, land, weather, and vegetation

Factors we considered

  • Validity: the verdict relies on a statistical test, and the LLM answers only from the data, to limit made-up claims
  • Accessibility: no statistics background required
  • Feasibility: a 24-hour hackathon with a four-person team and limited front-end experience, so we built a static website and added features in phases (core analysis, then comparison, then the LLM explainer)
  • Honesty about limits: we are transparent about what the data can and cannot show

projectDetails.name: Jericho
projectDetails.summary: Climate shifts and water scarcity are threatening traditional farming calendars, leading to widespread crop failures. To address this, we developed Vinland, a satellite-powered web application that translates complex Earth observations into immediate, actionable agricultural intelligence. Vinland connects directly to the NASA POWER Agroclimatology (AG) API, fetching 14-day rolling telemetry including temperature extrema, root-zone soil wetness, and precipitation. By running these variables through an agronomic threshold engine across 21 global crops, Vinland delivers instant binary crop suitability diagnostics ("Suitable" vs. "High Risk"). If a field faces environmental stress such as unseasonal frost or drought, the system dynamically recommends viable substitute crops and outlines 12-to-24-month regenerative rotation pathways. By transforming raw satellite telemetry into an intuitive, pre-planting decision dashboard, Vinland empowers farmers worldwide to mitigate climate risk, conserve water, and protect yields.

projectDetails.name: LunaLens
projectDetails.summary:
LunaLens is a web tool that helps mission planners choose where and when to land on the Moon. Landing is a problem of light and line of sight: sunlight must reach the solar arrays, and Earth must be in view for direct communication. Both change sharply with small shifts in site or date.

We built LunaLens to answer these questions in seconds. For any curated site (Apollo landing sites, CLPS targets, and other missions) or custom coordinates, it shows the Sun and Earth relative to the true local horizon, using NASA LOLA topography and JPL Horizons ephemerides. A Site Ranking Engine scores each site from 0 to 100 with a green, yellow or red status. A Sky Visibility Radar and Mission Timeline report sunlight duration and Earth visibility windows. An Astronaut Eye View shows, in first-person 3D, where terrain blocks the Sun or Earth.

LunaLens addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by making site and date comparison fast and intuitive. It reports geometric visibility, not guaranteed power or radio performance.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

LunaLens lets a user pick a landing site, either from a curated list (Apollo landing sites, NASA CLPS targets, other commercial and national missions) or by entering custom coordinates, and choose a date or mission window. For that site and time, it computes where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the true local horizon. Terrain from NASA LOLA elevation data is used to test whether ridges block either body, and Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons ephemerides.

A Python backend precomputes hourly results for each site and serves them through FastAPI, so every part of the interface reads the same data. Four connected features turn this geometry into decisions:

  • Site and Date Comparison: sites are compared side by side, so alternatives can be evaluated quickly when a launch is delayed.
  • Site Ranking Engine: each site receives a weighted 0-100 suitability score, led by sunlight and Earth visibility, with a per-criterion breakdown and a green, yellow or red status against mission requirements. Slope and roughness are included as terrain-safety criteria.
  • Sky Visibility Radar and Mission Timeline: these show solar elevation, sunlight duration, Earth visibility windows, and time remaining before sunset or Earthset. A slider and animation move through a lunar day or the whole mission.
  • Astronaut Eye View: an interactive first-person 3D scene at the chosen site and time, with the Sun and Earth placed in the sky and blocked by terrain where appropriate.

(If completed: an AI assistant explains sites, dates and scores, answering only from LunaLens's own computed results.)

Benefits and intended impact

The required data already exists, but it is spread across specialist tools such as Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, which are hard to combine and interpret. LunaLens brings it into one guided tool, so planners can see which site ranks best, why, and when conditions are favorable. The traffic-light status gives an instant answer, and the 3D view builds an intuition that tables and maps cannot, such as how a ridge blocks Earth at a given hour. We aim to make early-stage site and date comparison faster and more accessible for mission planners, educators, and students, while keeping results transparent and reproducible through open NASA data.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA LOLA digital elevation models (LRO mission); JPL Horizons ephemeris system
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy / SciPy
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS
  • 3D: Three.js and React Three Fiber
  • Collaboration: GitHub (feature branches and reviewed pull requests) and Discord
  • Optional: an LLM API for the assistant

Creativity

LunaLens combines three things that are usually separate: real local-horizon geometry, side-by-side site and date comparison, and a first-person view of the same data. Most illumination studies are static and site-specific, and most portals are built for experts. Treating the Sun and Earth relative to the terrain horizon, rather than a flat horizon or the Sun's centre alone, makes the results more realistic and easier to understand.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy and limits: the Moon has no atmosphere, so the horizon is set by terrain and the edge of the lunar sphere. LunaLens reports geometric visibility only, not guaranteed power generation or radio link performance, and we state this clearly.
  • Validation: results are compared with published data for known landing sites, and edge cases are tested.
  • Usability: the design targets non-specialists, with clear status colors, adjustable weights for different mission priorities, and answers within seconds.
  • Process: a phased plan in which each feature works standalone before integration, with the assistant started only after the integrated prototype exists.

Before submitting, adjust this to match what you actually built. For example, if you used a simplified terrain model or fewer sites than planned, say so, and remove the assistant line if it isn't working. I can also trim this to a specific word limit if the form has one.

projectDetails.name: Kemetis Apricity
projectDetails.summary: Kemetis is a web-based health-monitoring platform designed to support astronaut health awareness during long-duration space missions. Spaceflight conditions such as microgravity, radiation, isolation, and confinement can affect several aspects of human health, making continuous awareness of physiological and behavioral changes important. Kemetis brings health indicators together in a central interface, helping users review information and observe potential changes through visual data presentation. The project is informed by NASA human-spaceflight research on risks to astronaut health. Our goal is to develop a clearer, more accessible way to organize and interpret health information, supporting informed monitoring when immediate medical assistance may be limited.
projectDetails.details:
Kemetis is a web-based health-monitoring platform developed to address the physiological and behavioral health challenges astronauts may experience during long-duration space missions.

The platform is designed around the need to gather, organize, visualize, and interpret health indicators in a clear and accessible interface. Its dashboard-based approach allows users to observe health information, examine changes through dynamic charts, and receive alerts that draw attention to potential concerns.

The project focuses on supporting astronaut awareness of their health status and helping them recognize changes that may require further assessment. This is particularly relevant to deep-space missions, where communication delays and limited access to medical assistance increase the importance of onboard health awareness.

Development involved JavaScript, TypeScript, and Node.js. Google AI Studio was used to assist with code structure, Antigravity supported implementation and interface development, and Claude assisted with UI/UX development.

Kemetis is a software prototype intended to demonstrate how digital health-monitoring tools could support future human space exploration. It is not a clinically validated diagnostic system, and its outputs should not replace professional medical assessment.

Future development could include integration with validated physiological datasets, wearable health sensors, personalized baseline comparisons, more advanced anomaly detection, and additional behavioral-health monitoring capabilities.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Voyage Beyond
projectDetails.summary: Welcome to Voyage Beyond! For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I did not just build a game, I built a junior astronaut mission trainer powered by real space data. Kids aged 7–12 take command of their own outpost on the Moon or Mars, where survival depends on every decision. Oxygen runs low, power has to be shared, and when a real solar storm erupts from the Sun, the crew needs shelter before the radiation arrives. But this is not just a story, it is you in action. As the player, you choose your landing site on real Martian terrain, manage your base's resources, and face space weather events pulled live from NASA's own databases. By surviving them, you learn how astronauts plan for life beyond Earth, how NASA monitors the dangers of space, and why every choice on a mission matters.
projectDetails.details:
Kochab's Project Solution 

Voyage Beyond is a pixel-art educational game that teaches children what it really takes to survive beyond Earth, turning real NASA data into an interactive survival mission. Players run a lunar or Martian outpost, balance limited resources, and respond to real space weather events, making space science both fun and accessible.

How Does the Solution Work

  • Players join a crew of astronauts and run an outpost on the Moon (3 sols), then choose a real landing site and survive on Mars (3 sols). 
  • Each sol they get 3 actions to balance oxygen, power, food and radiation shielding. They can’t fix everything, so every choice is a trade-off. 
  • There are 10 mini-games, five for the Moon and five different ones for Mars. In each, the game’s rules and facts come from real NASA data: 
  • Storm Watch / Siren Watch use DONKI coronal mass ejection reports. Players work out arrival times (distance ÷ speed), then shelter the crew. 
  • Tend Garden / Water Loop draw on OSDR space-biology studies and ISS water recycling. 
  • Shield Lab / Regolith Wall draw on RadLab-style radiation research and measured dose rates: about 1.37 mSv/day on the Moon and 0.67 on Mars. Hydrogen-rich materials beat metal. 
  • Landing Site uses Mars Trek map imagery and the real coordinates and elevations of Jezero, Gale, Hellas, Phoenix Plains and Olympus Mons, each with trade-offs between water, safety, shielding and sunlight. 
  • MOXIE Reactor, Refinery, Solar and Rover games are built on Perseverance MOXIE and Mars rover dust records. 
  • The cast is the Warped Portraits characters, and the game includes Canadian Space Agency facts (Canadarm, Radi-N2). Music is an original, generated cinematic space score, so there are no licences to clear. 
  • It runs as a static site that deploys to Vercel. If a live NASA call fails, it falls back to built-in data and says so on screen.

Impact

Voyage Beyond makes NASA data playable by allowing children to interact with real datasets through meaningful decisions and mission outcomes. Through gameplay, players develop transferable STEM understanding, including concepts such as distance, speed, time, resource management, radiation protection, and the trade-offs involved in selecting different planetary destinations. The solution is designed to be accessible and low-cost, requiring only a web browser and working on both desktop and mobile devices without sign-ups, advertisements, or software installation, making it freely available to schools and families. However, some game values are simplified for educational purposes, and I have not yet conducted classroom studies to measure learning outcomes. Looking ahead, I plan to further develop the platform to ensure it is inclusive for all children, including children with disabilities, by incorporating accessibility features and adaptive learning experiences that enable every child to participate in and enjoy space exploration education.

How it meets the challenge

Voyage Beyond is built on real NASA data sources, including DONKI, OSDR, RadLab-based research, and Mars Trek, while clearly labeling any fallback or simulated data to maintain transparency. The experience combines education with engagement through a narrative-driven adventure featuring characters, mini-games, and a scoring system that rewards scientific understanding, such as accurately predicting solar storm arrival times. Designed specifically for children aged 7-12, the game uses simple language, intuitive touch-friendly controls, and short gameplay sessions of approximately 10-15 minutes to suit young learners' attention spans. The solution has been tested end-to-end across all ten mini-games and the complete Moon-to-Mars journey, demonstrating that it functions reliably as a lightweight web application that can be easily accessed through any modern browser. As development continues, I plan to expand both educational content and accessibility features to ensure that children of all abilities, including those with disabilities, can fully participate in and benefit from the experience.

The game benefits 

Children, Parents, Teachers, and the wider community by: 

  • Teaching kids how astronauts survive in space through experience rather than memorization. 
  • Introducing real NASA science, including space weather, planetary maps, and radiation measurements, in a way young players can understand. 
  • Building critical thinking and problem-solving skills through decisions with real consequences. 
  • Bridging the gap between NASA's open datasets and young learners in a fun, engaging way.

My goal 

To make space science more accessible, inspire curiosity, and encourage children to think critically and solve problems, because the next generation of space explorers should not just dream about going beyond Earth, they should start preparing for it. Despite my attempt to reflect real conditions, the game simplifies the science for young learners: time is scaled (one sol is about two weeks), radiation numbers are adjusted for gameplay rather than mission planning, and the offline snapshot uses approximate values. The game also focuses on the Moon and Mars and does not yet cover other destinations or hazards such as micrometeoroids or dust storms.

Tools and Technologies Used 

Coding Languages: 

  • JavaScript (Phaser), HTML, and CSS
  • Browser localStorage → for caching NASA data for 6 hours. 

Design and Media: 

  • Piskel and Warped Portraits by Luis Zuno → for sprites and pixel-style art. 
  • Vercel → for hosting and deploying the game. 
  • Kokoro (open-source text-to-speech) → for the demo video narration. 

GitHub Link : LayaliLucia/Voyage-Beyond

projectDetails.name: orbital eye
projectDetails.summary:
ORBITAL EYE is an interactive astronomical data exploration platform that transforms SPHEREx space telescope observations into a visual journey across the infrared universe. It allows users to explore selected regions of the sky, retrieve available observations across different epochs and detectors, and visualize how celestial objects and their surroundings change over time.

By processing, aligning, and comparing multi-epoch infrared images, ORBITAL EYE helps users investigate potential motion and brightness variations in astronomical targets. The platform aims to make complex space telescope data more accessible through an intuitive interface, interactive visualizations, and scientific analysis tools.

Built around NASA’s SPHEREx mission data, ORBITAL EYE bridges the gap between raw astronomical observations and meaningful exploration, encouraging discovery, learning, and a deeper understanding of our dynamic universe.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – ORBITAL EYE

What Does It Do?

ORBITAL EYE is an interactive astronomical exploration platform designed to make infrared space observations easier to access, visualize, and understand. Using data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission, the platform allows users to explore different regions of the sky and investigate how celestial objects appear across multiple observations taken at different times.

Our project focuses on five astronomical targets: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. Users can explore available observations, compare images across different epochs and detectors, and investigate potential changes in an object's position or brightness.

How Does It Work?

The platform combines astronomical data retrieval, image processing, and interactive visualization into one workflow:

  1. Data Retrieval: Finds available SPHEREx observations for selected astronomical targets.
  2. Image Processing: Loads FITS astronomical images, handles image quality information, and prepares observations for comparison.
  3. Image Alignment: Uses World Coordinate System (WCS) information to align observations onto a common sky reference.
  4. Multi-Epoch Comparison: Enables users to examine observations from different dates and investigate possible changes over time.
  5. Scientific Exploration: Provides tools for image comparison, difference analysis, spectral exploration, and catalog-based investigation.

The goal is to turn complex astronomical datasets into a more understandable and interactive experience.

What Are Its Benefits and Intended Impact?

ORBITAL EYE makes publicly available astronomical data more approachable for students, researchers, and space enthusiasts. Instead of requiring users to manually download and process large scientific datasets, the platform brings important exploration and visualization capabilities into a unified interface.

Its intended impact includes:

  • Encouraging hands-on exploration of real NASA space telescope observations.
  • Supporting the investigation of celestial motion and brightness variability.
  • Making infrared astronomy more accessible to people without extensive experience in scientific data processing.
  • Demonstrating how open space data can support education, research, and scientific curiosity.

What Makes the Project Creative?

The creative aspect of ORBITAL EYE lies in combining astronomical image processing with an interactive, time-based exploration experience. Rather than treating each observation as an isolated image, the platform encourages users to compare observations across time and explore how the infrared sky changes.

It brings together data retrieval, image alignment, multi-epoch visualization, spectral tools, and catalog information in a single platform, creating a more engaging way to explore the universe.

Technologies and Tools Used

Backend:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Astropy
  • Astroquery
  • NumPy
  • Photutils
  • Reproject

Frontend:

  • Next.js
  • React
  • TypeScript

Scientific Data and Processing:

  • NASA SPHEREx FITS observations
  • World Coordinate System (WCS)
  • Infrared image processing and analysis
  • Astronomical catalog resources

Factors Considered by Our Team

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, data quality, image alignment, missing or corrupted observations, and differences between observation dates and detectors. We also considered usability, performance, and the importance of presenting scientific results responsibly.

We recognize that preliminary image comparisons are not equivalent to confirmed astronomical discoveries. Therefore, the platform is designed to support further investigation while clearly acknowledging current data limitations and the need for additional validation.

projectDetails.name: Ladies In Black : Don't Trust The Signal
projectDetails.summary:
Project Description

What if designing a space mission became part of a story worth experiencing?

Our project reimagines space exploration as a cinematic, story-driven interactive game that unfolds much like an interactive film. Through illustrated scenes, dialogue, and character interactions, players follow the story of six characters connected by a shared past and an unexpected discovery that brings them together again.

As they embark on a journey beyond Earth, players witness their evolving relationships and the challenges they face. The narrative remains the heart of the experience, with players following the characters rather than controlling a single protagonist.

Throughout the story, interactive missions invite players to step beyond watching and actively participate in the expedition. They engage with real-world space mission design concepts, including spacecraft configuration, scientific instrument selection, resource management, and engineering trade-offs.

Our goal is to make the unfolding story the driving force behind engagement, keeping players intrigued, emotionally invested, and eager to discover what happens next. Each mission becomes a step toward unlocking the next chapter, blending scientific learning with the excitement of a cinematic adventure.

Ultimately, we aim to turn space exploration into an experience where storytelling sparks curiosity and interactive challenges bring the journey to life.

node.title: Landing Went South

projectDetails.name: TrueSouth
projectDetails.summary:
TrueSouth is a web app that answers one question: where and when can a mission land on the Moon?

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays within about two degrees of the horizon, Earth hangs low, and mountains block both. So whether a lander has power and a radio link depends on the exact site and date, and a launch slip changes the answer.

We built a pipeline that turns NASA's LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons positions into a skyline and an hourly record of the Sun and Earth over six years, for 25 sites and for any coordinates you type. Mission Control scores a landing date against a mission's rules and gives GO, CAUTION or NO-GO with the rule that decided it. Planners can slip the date, compare sites and explore 3D views. The Academy teaches the same physics in guided lessons.

Our Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.0061°.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works TrueSouth tells a mission planner whether a lunar landing date works at a chosen site. A Python pipeline takes NASA's LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons positions and computes, for 25 sites, a skyline out to 300 km and an hourly record of the Sun and Earth for six years (2026 to 2031). The browser then scores any landing date against a mission's rules and gives GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, with the rule that decided it. Users can also type their own coordinates, which a server computes on demand.

It has two modes on the same data. Mission Control is for planners: a 3D view of the Moon, Earth and Sun, a polar map, a view from the lander's position, a timeline, a "Slip Planner" that shows every landing date for six years, and a Compare table. The Academy teaches the same physics in four guided lessons.

Benefits and intended impact Near the Moon's south pole the Sun stays within about two degrees of the horizon and mountains block it, so a short launch slip can turn a workable landing into a failed one. Existing tools show maps and positions; TrueSouth turns them into a decision in seconds, and shows why. We want planners to compare sites and dates quickly, and students and the public to understand why the south pole is hard.

Tools Python (NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, Pydantic, FastAPI) for the science and the server. TypeScript, React, Vite and three.js for the web app. pytest and vitest for tests, Docker for deployment. AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity) wrote and reviewed the code under the team's direction.

How it is creative It treats landing as a question of time, not only place. Slip the date and every site is re-scored at once; "Next GO" jumps to the next date that works; and the Slip Planner shows six years of landing dates for each site on one strip. The view from 2 m above the ground shows exactly which ridge hides the Sun, and Compare sets two sites at two dates side by side. Every mission number is marked as sourced or assumed, so a planner knows what to trust.

The same engine also teaches. In the Academy, a moon mascot called Luna guides learners through four short lessons to land a small lander: they drag the Sun through a month, sketch a skyline and see the real one laid over it, and find the bug in a calculation, all checked against the same real numbers a planner sees.

What we considered Honesty first. Every mission number is tagged as sourced or assumed. Our Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.0061°, and we publish the comparisons where we disagree with NASA's maps. Drawn shadows are decoration, never a result. We also considered speed on ordinary laptops and clear wording for non-specialists. TrueSouth is a planning aid, not flight certification.

projectDetails.name: Moon And Mars
projectDetails.summary: LEFT BEHIND is an interactive, bilingual (English/Arabic) website about the spacecraft and hardware humans have left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It turns 15 hardware records from 14 missions, based on NASA’s official mission pages and NSSDC records, into 3D models that visitors can rotate, take apart with Explode View, and watch in short event simulations. A voice narrator explains each record, a Telemetry Matrix compares them in one table, and the Mission Academy quiz (eight questions with points and a leaderboard) lets visitors test what they learned. Every record has a clear status label and a link to its official source. The page is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js (WebGL), GLSL shaders and SVG, with Manus and Claude used as AI assistants. It is an independent educational project, not affiliated with NASA, and its 3D models are illustrations generated in code.
projectDetails.details:
Summary
LEFT BEHIND is an interactive, bilingual (English/Arabic) web experience about spacecraft and hardware that were left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It turns 15 hardware records from 14 missions into 3D models that visitors can explore, instead of a list of facts to read.

What It Does

  • Shows each record as a procedural 3D model that can be rotated in Inspect mode and taken apart with Explode View.
  • Plays a short event simulation for each record and a “Then vs. Now” timeline.
  • Offers a voice narrator for each record.
  • Includes the Mission Academy, a quiz of eight questions drawn from the records, with points and a leaderboard.
  • Provides a Telemetry Matrix that compares all records in one table, and a source directory linking to the official NASA pages.
  • Works fully in Arabic (right-to-left) and English.

How We Handled the Information
Each record separates the mission, the spacecraft and the surviving component. It uses five status labels, shows both values when official sources disagree, and labels artist concepts as illustrations and archival photographs as photographs. The narrator never claims to be an astronaut, engineer or witness.

Development Tools
HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6, no framework), Three.js r128 (WebGL), GLSL shaders, SVG, and the Web Speech, Web Audio and browser storage APIs. Manus and Claude were used as AI assistants during development, supporting planning, content writing and building the page.

Important Note
LEFT BEHIND is an independent educational project. It is not endorsed by, affiliated with, or operated by NASA. The 3D models are procedural illustrations generated in code, not NASA imagery, and they are not to scale.

Project Summary
​Project Name: Legacy Pioneer
Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars
​What we developed:
Legacy Pioneer is an interactive educational ecosystem combining physical collectible cards and a simplified gaming experience. It brings NASA's historical space missions—such as deep space probes, Martian rovers, and lunar modules—back to life for space enthusiasts and children.
​How it addresses the challenge:
The project transforms complex archival data from NASA (NSSDCA) into engaging, easy-to-understand stories categorized into four unique themes: The Pioneers, The Survivors, The Discoverers, and The Silent Legends. Each card features key mission details, simplified scientific discoveries, final resting statuses, and interactive QR codes linked to rich digital content.
​Why it is important:
By turning discarded space equipment into engaging storytelling cards, Legacy Pioneer preserves space heritage, sparks children's curiosity, and makes aerospace science accessible, educational, and fun for the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details: SPACE LEGACY is an interactive 3D educational space exploration experience that takes users on a journey through the history of space exploration. The project combines a spaceship journey with immersive 3D environments where users can explore historical space missions and the technologies behind them. Users begin their journey from Earth and travel to the Moon and Mars. By selecting a destination, they can enter an interactive exploration environment, discover historical spacecraft, landers, rovers, and scientific instruments, and interact with 3D representations of these technologies. Selecting a piece of hardware reveals its mission history, purpose, discoveries, current status, and contribution to space exploration. The project also includes a Deep Space section featuring important missions that explored asteroids, distant planets, and the wider universe. Benefits and Intended Impact: SPACE LEGACY aims to make space science more accessible, engaging, and understandable, especially for students and young learners. Instead of presenting space missions through static text and images, it allows users to explore space technology through interactive 3D experiences. The project helps users understand how different spacecraft and scientific instruments work, why they were developed, and how they contributed to our understanding of the Moon, Mars, and the universe. Its intended impact is to encourage scientific curiosity, support informal STEM education, and inspire the next generation to explore science, engineering, and space technology. Technologies and Tools: The project was developed using React 19, JavaScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, React Three Drei, and CSS. These technologies enable interactive 3D environments, animated planetary scenes, spacecraft movement, camera transitions, and interactive hardware exploration. NASA mission information and publicly available space exploration resources are used to build the educational content and connect users with the history of real missions. Creativity and Innovation: The creative aspect of SPACE LEGACY is its combination of two experiences: a cinematic journey through space and an interactive hardware museum. Users do not simply read about historical missions; they travel to destinations and explore the technologies associated with them in immersive 3D environments. The experience connects the history of space exploration with the actual hardware used to achieve scientific discoveries. Design Considerations: The team considered educational accuracy, accessibility, usability, responsive design, realistic visual representation, and smooth navigation. Particular attention was given to making complex scientific information easy to understand while preserving the historical and scientific significance of each mission. The project is designed to provide an engaging educational experience across different screen sizes and devices.

projectDetails.name: VITALIS
projectDetails.summary:
VITALIS is an astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to support crew members during long-duration space missions. It brings health records, laboratory results, radiation records, exercise data, and wellbeing information into one unified workspace.

VITALIS uses a structured ten-stage workflow to validate incoming data, analyze personal health trends, generate preliminary assessments, cross-check evidence, and route reports to the assigned medical officer for human review.

The platform also provides role-based dashboards for astronauts, medical officers, and mission supervisors, alongside health alerts, wellness tools, cognitive games, and supported offline data synchronization.

Its key innovation is combining health information with data-quality checks, transparent evidence, and human medical oversight, helping users distinguish reliable information from incomplete or suspicious records.

VITALIS is a research and demonstration prototype, not a certified medical device or diagnostic system. Simulated health records are clearly identified, while NASA OSDR research metadata supports a separate educational research feature.
projectDetails.details:
VITALIS is a web-based astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform developed to address the challenges of maintaining crew health during long-duration space missions.

The platform provides three main user roles:

  1. Astronaut: Accesses personal health dashboards, medical records, health trends, alerts, exercise tracking, and wellbeing features.
  2. Medical Officer: Reviews assigned astronauts' health records, preliminary assessments, alerts, medical reports, and follow-up decisions.
  3. Mission Supervisor: Oversees system operations, demonstration scenarios, synchronization status, and audit records.

CORE TECHNOLOGY AND WORKFLOW

VITALIS uses a ten-stage health analysis workflow:

  • Collects available health, laboratory, radiation, exercise, and wellbeing records.
  • Checks data quality and identifies missing or suspicious measurements.
  • Analyzes historical trends and individual baselines.
  • Generates a preliminary interpretation using the configured analysis engine.
  • Cross-checks the assessment against available medical reference information.
  • Independently verifies evidence, consistency, and data provenance.
  • Produces a structured assessment with uncertainty and supporting evidence.
  • Routes the report to the assigned medical officer.
  • Requires a qualified human medical professional to review and make decisions.
  • Records audit information and supported synchronization evidence.

INNOVATION AND IMPACT

The key innovation is integrating health monitoring with data-quality validation, evidence verification, and human-supervised decision support. Rather than treating every incoming measurement as reliable, VITALIS highlights incomplete or suspicious records and preserves uncertainty.

The platform also includes VITALIS LIFE, which provides wellbeing tools, exercise features, family communication, and six cognitive and engagement games. The Demo Center offers ten repeatable scenarios to demonstrate different health and data-quality situations.

TECHNOLOGIES USED

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS.
Backend: Node.js and Express.js.
Database: SQLite.
Other technologies include REST APIs, role-based access control, authentication, data visualization, Progressive Web App functionality, and SHA-256 integrity verification.

NASA DATA AND LIMITATIONS

VITALIS connects to NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), specifically the OSD-575 Inspiration4 study metadata, for research questions in the Games Arena. This is not a live astronaut vital-sign feed.

Health measurements displayed in the prototype are simulated and clearly identified as demonstration data. Physical medical sensors and operational NASA telemetry are not connected.

VITALIS is a research and demonstration prototype. It does not diagnose diseases, prescribe treatments, or replace qualified medical professionals.

projectDetails.name: Project LOOP
projectDetails.summary:
Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to radiation, microgravity, isolation and
stress, while the distance from Earth makes real-time medical support impossible.
AstroPulse is a modular health and environmental monitoring software suite that
addresses this gap. It simulates astronaut telemetry (heart rate, blood oxygen, radiation,
bone density, stress, sleep), processes it in a backend core, keeps data safe through a
Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) layer during communication blackouts, and
presents everything on a real-time Heads-Up Display (HUD) for mission control.
An AI-assisted triage engine continuously assesses each crew member, flags risks such
as cardiovascular strain, space radiation exposure, hypoxia and neuro-ocular risk, and
issues recommendations with a confidence level. We chose this challenge because
astronaut health is the limiting factor for deep-space exploration, and because it
combines data engineering, networking, machine learning and UX in one end-to-end
system. AstroPulse meets the challenge requirements by delivering a working pipeline
from data generation to decision support that remains reliable under delayed and
disrupted links, and can be launched with a single click on any Windows machine.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

AstroPulse is a modular health and environmental monitoring suite for astronauts on deep-space missions. A telemetry simulator generates real-time vital signs (heart rate, blood oxygen, radiation exposure, bone density, stress, sleep) for each crew member. A FastAPI backend ingests, stores and serves this data. An offline Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) layer queues the data during communication blackouts and delivers it in order when the link returns. An AI triage engine classifies each astronaut as Nominal, Warning or Critical, names the likely risk (such as cardiovascular strain, space radiation exposure, hypoxia or neuro-ocular risk) and recommends an action with a confidence level. Everything appears on a real-time Heads-Up Display (HUD) with crew status cards, live charts and a medical alert feed.

Benefits

  • Early warning of health problems without waiting for Earth.
  • No data loss during delays or blackouts.
  • Raw numbers become clear, prioritized decisions.
  • Mission control sees every crew member and the link delay on one screen.
  • The whole system launches or stops with a single click.

Intended impact

AstroPulse supports safer long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where real-time medical support from the ground is not possible. It gives crews and flight surgeons a foundation for autonomous health monitoring that can later be connected to real sensors and flight data.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript (ES modules), JSX, CSS, HTML, PowerShell, SQL.
  • Backend and ML: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, SQLite.
  • Frontend: React, React DOM, Recharts, Vite, Tailwind CSS, PostCSS, Autoprefixer.
  • Data: hybrid real datasets and CSV files loaded with download_data.py, plus simulated telemetry, informed by NASA resources such as the Space Apps challenge page and the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).
  • Hardware: standard Windows laptops.

How it is creative

It combines telemetry, DTN, AI triage and a live HUD in one modular system designed for deep-space conditions. Most health dashboards assume a stable connection, while AstroPulse assumes delays and outages from the start. It also interprets the data instead of just displaying it, and its modular design lets teams swap the simulator for real sensors without changing the rest.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delay (up to about 20 minutes one-way) and blackouts.
  • Reliable, ordered data delivery.
  • Clarity of the interface for quick decisions under pressure.
  • Modularity, so each component can be developed, tested and replaced independently.
  • Easy deployment through automation scripts.
  • The limits of simulated and public data, since real astronaut data is restricted. Validating with real flight data is the next step.

Project Documentation: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1VQ9E7pTMexo0PNkSRzIvdJQVnhyBYuBD/view?usp=sharing

projectDetails.name: Project Lost in Space🚀🌌
projectDetails.summary:
LOST IN SPACE is an immersive, web-based 3D storytelling experience developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It brings attention to the often-overlooked stories of NASA's exploration equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

Our project transforms the histories of three remarkable missions into an interactive journey: the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), the twin Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity, and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter. Through immersive 3D environments, animations, synchronized narration, and accessible scientific information, visitors can explore the purpose, achievements, discoveries, and eventual fate of these machines.

By turning NASA's mission histories into engaging visual stories, LOST IN SPACE directly addresses the challenge of making the legacy of abandoned space equipment more accessible and meaningful. It is important because these machines were not simply left behind; they played essential roles in expanding our understanding of other worlds. Our goal is to inspire younger generations to explore science, engineering, and space while ensuring that the stories of these machines are not forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – LOST IN SPACE

LOST IN SPACE is an immersive, web-based 3D storytelling experience that brings the overlooked stories of NASA's exploration equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars to life.

The project works through a guided scrolling journey divided into three chapters, featuring the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), NASA's twin Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity, and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter. Each chapter combines 3D visuals, animations, synchronized narration, and scientific information to tell the story of each machine, explaining its purpose, achievements, discoveries, and eventual fate.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project makes space exploration history more accessible and engaging, especially for younger audiences. It encourages curiosity about science, engineering, robotics, and planetary exploration while highlighting the contributions of machines that helped humanity understand other worlds.

Tools and Development:

The project was developed as an HTML-based website. Our team used Claude and ChatGPT as AI-assisted tools for brainstorming, developing and refining narratives, generating and reviewing code, debugging, and improving the overall experience. All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and adapted by the team.

Creativity and Innovation:

Our main creative approach is transforming historical NASA mission information into an immersive visual storytelling journey. Instead of simply reading facts, visitors experience the stories through interactive 3D environments, animations, and narration.

Design Considerations:

Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, historical authenticity, ease of understanding, visual engagement, storytelling quality, website performance, readability, and accessibility across desktop and mobile devices.

projectDetails.name: AstroCare
projectDetails.summary:
AstroCare is a web-based prototype designed to help astronauts monitor their health during space missions, where access to medical support from Earth can be limited or delayed.

Our application brings health readings, trends, and alerts into one accessible interface. Users can record measurements, review changes over time, and explore an interactive 3D body visualization to make health information easier to understand. AstroCare also includes reminders and a mental well-being support section, recognizing that astronaut health involves both physical and psychological needs.

By organizing health information and highlighting readings that may need attention, AstroCare aims to support crew awareness and more informed communication with ground teams. It is a monitoring and information tool, not a replacement for medical professionals. Our goal is to make everyday health tracking clearer and more accessible, helping astronauts focus on their mission.
projectDetails.details:
AstroCare – Onboard Health Monitoring for Deep-Space Crews
Team Lunaries · NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 · Challenge: Health Monitoring Software

THE PROBLEM
On a Mars mission, a message to Earth and back can take up to 24 minutes, and there is no doctor on board. Astronauts are not physicians, yet they must notice early warning signs themselves. Generic “normal ranges” also miss what matters most: a heart rate of 74 bpm is normal on Earth, but not for an astronaut whose personal baseline is 63.

OUR SOLUTION
AstroCare is an offline, on-device health companion for astronauts. It compares every reading with the astronaut’s own baseline, not only with population ranges, catches small changes early, shows which part of the body is affected on an interactive 3D model, and tells the crew exactly what to do now, without waiting for Earth. Every alert explains the rule that fired, the threshold, the recommended action and the scientific source behind it.

HOW IT WORKS

  • Mission console: mission day and time (MET), live Earth communication delay, crew of four, open alerts and a one-tap Emergency button.
  • Mission environments: ISS, Moon, Mars transit and Mars surface. Switching changes the Earth delay, daily radiation dose and bone-loss rate across the whole app.
  • Interactive 3D body (Three.js): real anatomy where each organ system (heart, mind and sleep, bones, metabolism, radiation) is colored by its health status. Tap a part to focus on it and see its readings and alerts.
  • Three ways to record vitals: manual entry with validation, a simulated smart watch (built on the same interface a real wearable will use), and photo capture with on-device OCR.
  • Guided measurement: for each vital, why it matters in space, how to measure it step by step, how microgravity affects it and which signs are dangerous.
  • Daily check-in: sleep, mood, stress, exercise, water, meals and 18 symptoms. Five red-flag symptoms open Emergency mode immediately.
  • Personal baseline and trends: each chart shows the general normal range and the astronaut’s own 7-day baseline band, so drift is visible early.
  • Combined insights: the app links signals, e.g. “heart rate is rising while sleep is falling” or “headache while cabin CO2 is above the NASA limit: likely CO2-related”.
  • Emergency mode: step-by-step protocols, including a microgravity CPR metronome (Evetts-Russomano method). “Act now. Do not wait for Earth.”
  • Mind support: when mood is low or stress is high, it suggests NASA’s behavioral-health countermeasures.
  • Reminders and Earth report: daily routines, and a crew status summary for ground medical teams.

DEMO STORY (Omar Farid, flight engineer, 10 days)
Day 1 builds his baseline. Day 6: heart rate 74 bpm, still “normal”, but above his 63.4 baseline three days in a row, so AstroCare raises an early warning. Day 9: poor sleep, a headache and cabin CO2 at 3.2 mmHg (NASA limit 3) are linked into combined insights. Day 10: low water intake. A built-in day-by-day player replays the story.

NASA DATA AND SCIENCE
Health domains follow NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight (RIDGE): Radiation, Isolation and confinement, Distance from Earth, Gravity, and Hostile/closed environments. Rules and thresholds come from NASA Human Research Program risk pages (bone, cardiovascular, fitness, sleep, SANS, immune), NASA OCHMO technical briefs (radiation, CO2, life support), NASA space radiation data, and Canadian Space Agency radiation and space-medicine resources.
In numbers: 28 data-driven rules · 34 cited sources (17 NASA, 4 CSA, 6 peer-reviewed, 6 medical guidelines) · 6 vitals · 18 symptoms · 2 emergency protocols · 6 reminders · 4 mission environments.

TECHNOLOGY
React + Vite, Three.js / React Three Fiber for the 3D body (BodyParts3D anatomy, CC BY-SA), Zustand for state, and Zod-validated JSON for all data, rules and sources. No backend: it runs fully offline and saves readings in the browser (LocalStorage). The analysis logic is separate from the UI, so real sensors and wearables can plug in later. GitHub for version control, deployed on Vercel.

IMPACT
In space: earlier detection, clearer self-care and better-informed conversations with ground teams on long missions to the Moon and Mars.
On Earth: the same baseline-first approach fits people far from a doctor: Antarctic stations, offshore rigs, remote villages and elderly people living alone.

DESIGN APPROACH
A calm, dark mission console where color is used only for meaning: green for normal, amber for watch, red for action. The astronaut gets a quick view; the crew medical officer can drill into trends, rules and sources.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS
AstroCare supports awareness and does not diagnose or replace medical care. Some thresholds are estimates and are labeled as such. Next: clinical validation of the rules, usability testing with analog-mission crews, real wearable integration, and evaluation under realistic mission conditions.

projectDetails.name: Planetary Analog Finder
projectDetails.summary:
Planetary Analog Finder is a data-driven project developed to identify and compare Earth locations that may serve as analogs for future lunar and Martian exploration. The project focuses on Shackleton Crater on the Moon and Jezero Crater on Mars, comparing their terrain characteristics with three potential Earth analog sites: Lake Salda in Turkey, the North Gobi region in China, and Paleolake Tushka in Egypt.

We processed and analyzed planetary and Earth observation datasets to generate elevation models, slope and surface roughness measurements, satellite imagery, maps, and comparative datasets. These outputs help evaluate similarities in topography and surface features, while geological and mineralogical context provides additional insight into the potential scientific relevance of each location.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming open space-agency data into an organized, visual comparison framework. It is important because identifying suitable terrestrial analogs can support scientific research, technology testing, and preparation for future human and robotic missions to the Moon and Mars. The proposed analog matches are preliminary and require further geological validation.

Planetary Analog Finder is a geospatial analysis project designed to identify and evaluate Earth locations that may serve as scientific analogs for important lunar and Martian exploration sites. The project focuses on Shackleton Crater near the Moon’s south pole and Jezero Crater on Mars, comparing their surface characteristics with three potential Earth analog locations: Lake Salda in Turkey, the North Gobi region in China, and Paleolake Tushka in Egypt.

### How the Project Works

The project follows a multi-stage workflow:

1. **Data Collection:** We gathered publicly available planetary and Earth observation datasets from NASA, USGS, and other scientific data repositories.

2. **Terrain Analysis:** We processed elevation data to derive digital elevation models (DEMs), slope maps, surface roughness measurements, and local relief information.

3. **Satellite Imagery:** We collected and processed Sentinel-2 imagery to visualize the three Earth candidate sites.

4. **Planetary Comparison:** We organized the resulting measurements and spatial datasets into comparative tables, maps, and visual outputs.

5. **Candidate Evaluation:** We compared topographic characteristics and considered geological and mineralogical context to identify potential analog candidates.

### Tools and Technologies

The scientific analysis was developed using Python in Google Colab, with GDAL and QGIS for geospatial processing and visualization.

The website frontend was developed using **HTML, CSS, and JavaScript**. We used **CesiumJS** to integrate the map with the website.

### Benefits and Intended Impact

The project provides an organized way to compare planetary environments with potential Earth analog locations. It can support planetary research, geological investigations, and preparation for future lunar and Martian exploration missions.

### Creativity and Key Considerations

The project combines lunar, Martian, and terrestrial geospatial datasets in one comparative workflow and presents the results through a website with an integrated interactive map. We considered spatial resolution, dataset quality, coordinate systems, data availability, and the limitations of comparing different planetary environments. The proposed Earth sites are potential analogs and require further geological validation.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: SELENE: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary: SELENE is a working web tool that helps mission planners choose where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. There, the Sun and Earth sit low on the horizon, so nearby hills can hide them for days. Without the Sun a lander loses power; without Earth it loses its direct link home. A planner picks one of 12 ready-made sites, a landing time in UTC and a mission length. SELENE shows when the lander will see the Sun and reach Earth, gives a plain-English Good/Marginal/Poor verdict, and shows what changes if launch slips by hours or days. It also ranks the best landing dates and sites and compares plans side by side. It is built on NASA data: JPL Horizons positions of the Sun and Earth seen from the lunar surface, LRO LOLA terrain for each site's skyline, and NASA Deep Space Network dish geometry. This turns days of manual analysis into a quick, explainable check before a site or date is chosen.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

SELENE answers one practical question for a lunar south-pole mission: "If we land here, at this time, will we have sunlight for power and a line to Earth for communication, and what changes if we are late?"

- Plan: choose one of 12 ready-made south-pole and comparison sites, a landing time (UTC) and a mission length (3, 7, 14 or 30 days). SELENE reports the share of time in sunlight, the longest stretch of darkness, the Sun's height above the local hills, the share of time with a two-way Earth link, the longest silence, ground slope, and a plain-English Good / Marginal / Poor verdict.

- What if launch is late: one click shifts the landing by +6 h, +24 h, +7 days or a custom delay and shows the planned and late plans side by side. Example from the live site: at Mons Mouton Plateau, a 14-day mission landing 17 Dec 2026 00:00 UTC is Good; a 7-day slip turns it Poor, with 158 hours (6.6 days) of darkness.

- See why: a 3D view of the real terrain around the site with Sun and Earth directions, a lander's-eye view, and an hour-by-hour timeline of Sun, Earth in view, Earth link and an illustrative battery level.

- Best dates: a verdict for every landing day from 1 Dec 2026 to 1 Feb 2028.

- Best sites: all sites ranked for the chosen date.

- Compare: plans side by side, with the best value marked in each row.

- How it works: an in-app page explaining the method, the data and the limits.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Ephemeris: a Python pipeline asks the NASA JPL Horizons API (DE441) for the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth as seen from each site on the lunar surface.

2. Terrain: it builds each site's skyline from layered NASA LRO LOLA elevation models (5-20 m near the pole, coarser farther out), every 0.05 degrees of azimuth.

3. Visibility: the Sun or Earth counts as visible when its disc clears that skyline. This gives the Sun and Earth time windows.

4. Earth link: a two-way link exists when at least one NASA Deep Space Network 70 m dish (Goldstone DSS-14, Canberra DSS-43, Madrid DSS-63) is above the lander's skyline and the lander is above that dish's minimum elevation. Station data follows the NASA DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook (810-005).

5. Results are pre-computed into compact per-site files. The web app clips these windows to any landing time and mission length, intersects them, and turns them into verdicts, rankings and comparisons in the browser, with no server needed.

BENEFITS

At the lunar south pole, sunlight and Earth contact change hour by hour and depend on local hills. SELENE lets a planner compare sites and dates in seconds instead of days of manual analysis, see the cost of a launch delay before it happens, and understand every result in plain words backed by the underlying numbers.

INTENDED IMPACT

Help mission planners, students and outreach teams make safer, explainable landing choices for Artemis-era south-pole missions, where power and communication margins decide whether a lander survives. Next steps: custom coordinates, re-validation against NASA PGDA illumination maps, and a headline "hours with both sunlight and Earth in view in the first 72 hours" result for every delay.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (NumPy) for the data pipeline; TypeScript, React 18 and Vite for the web app; Three.js for the 3D terrain view; Vitest for tests; GitHub Pages for hosting. Optional in-app assistant "Luna" uses the Google Gemini API through a small Node server. No hardware.

Live site: https://abowarda0.github.io/selene-lunar-navigator/

Source code: https://github.com/yossefhady/selene-lunar-navigator

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It turns complex orbital and terrain geometry into a one-line verdict anyone can read, while keeping every number one click away.

- The "what if launch is late" comparison shows a delay's real cost, not just one snapshot.

- The lander's-eye 3D view lets users see why the Sun or Earth disappears behind real lunar hills.

- The AI assistant can only reword numbers SELENE has already computed: the site rejects any answer containing a number not shown on the page, so it cannot invent results.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: real NASA ephemeris and terrain data, with the whole Sun and Earth discs checked against the skyline, not just their centres.

- Communication realism: a direct-to-Earth link needs a real DSN dish in view, not only Earth above the horizon.

- Honesty: Good / Marginal / Poor are our team's planning rule of thumb, not a NASA standard; the Earth link is geometry only, not a booked antenna; battery presets are illustrative; site samples are labelled as samples, not official landing sites; the current fine-terrain engine has not yet been re-checked against NASA PGDA maps (an earlier version was).

- Usability: no install, works in the browser, plain language, and every time shown in UTC.

- Scope: 12 pre-computed sites in this prototype; custom coordinates are planned.

projectDetails.name: Project LUNAVISTA
projectDetails.summary:
Lunavista is an interactive lunar mission-planning prototype designed to make selecting and comparing Moon landing locations more accessible and understandable.

The platform combines a NASA-derived 3D Moon model, historical lunar landing sites, candidate landing regions, and configurable mission requirements. Users can explore how different mission architectures, spacecraft, crew sizes, power demands, communication needs, and science-versus-engineering priorities influence landing-site evaluation.

A distinctive feature is our Lunar DNA concept, which represents mission requirements and environmental conditions as comparable patterns. Lunavista also introduces crew-aware planning scenarios and a See Why explanation that helps users understand the factors behind a selection.

The current prototype demonstrates interactive exploration, mission configuration, and educational decision support. Future development will integrate validated time-dependent illumination, terrain, and communication calculations using NASA data.

Our goal is to make lunar landing decisions easier to explore, compare, explain, and communicate between scientists, engineers, students, and the public.
projectDetails.details:
LUNAVISTA — Lunar Mission Decision System

Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
Event: 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge — Cairo

The Problem

Selecting a lunar landing site is not simply about finding a flat surface. Mission planners must consider sunlight for solar power, Earth visibility for communications, terrain conditions, scientific opportunities, spacecraft limitations, and—in crewed missions—human operational requirements.

These factors can conflict. A location that offers significant scientific value may also present challenges for energy availability, communication, or astronaut activities. Changes in mission dates or spacecraft requirements can further complicate the decision.

Our Solution

Lunavista is an interactive web-based lunar mission decision-support prototype that allows users to explore landing locations, configure a mission, examine operational trade-offs, and understand the factors that influence site selection.

The prototype combines five main elements:

1. Interactive Lunar Atlas

Users explore a 3D Moon visualization based on NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter resources. The atlas includes historical crewed and robotic mission locations alongside candidate landing regions. Users can navigate the globe, inspect coordinates, and select locations for further investigation.

2. Mission Configuration

The interface allows users to select robotic, crewed, or combined crewed–robotic missions; choose from relevant launch-vehicle configurations; specify mission dates, duration, crew size, and operational requirements; and explore how these selections change the mission scenario.

3. Lunar DNA and Crew-Aware Planning

Our Lunar DNA concept represents mission requirements as a structured operating profile, including energy, communication, workload, and crew-related constraints.

For crewed missions, users can select historical lunar travelers and experiment with explicitly fictional health and performance scenarios. These include metabolic heat generation, cooling capacity, EVA duration, and thermal sensitivity. This demonstrates why different operational requirements may favor different lunar environments.

The medical parameters are educational assumptions, not actual medical records or assessments of named astronauts.

4. Science vs. Engineering Trade-off

An interactive slider demonstrates the competing priorities of scientific exploration and engineering reliability. Users can adjust these priorities to understand how mission preferences influence decisions.

Mandatory safety and feasibility requirements should not be overridden by preference weights.

5. Explainable Decision Support — “See Why This Site?”

Instead of presenting an unexplained recommendation, Lunavista provides a numbered explanation addressing mission architecture, spacecraft, terrain, sunlight, communication, crew considerations, operational workload, scientific priorities, and missing evidence.

It also compares fictional environmental scenarios to illustrate how changing requirements can affect suitability.

Implementation

The prototype uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for browser-based 3D interaction. It incorporates NASA lunar visualization resources, historical mission information, interactive forms, custom filtering, and scenario-based decision explanations.

The application is intended to run directly in a modern web browser without specialist software.

Current Capabilities

The implemented prototype includes interactive mission setup, a lunar location catalog, a NASA 3D model loading interface, configurable crew scenarios, a science–engineering priority slider, and an explanation panel. The crew and environmental comparisons use educational simulation values.

Current Limitations

Lunavista is not a flight-certified mission-planning tool. It does not yet perform fully validated, terrain-aware Sun and Earth visibility calculations for every selected site and date. The site comparisons do not prove actual landing safety, and historical location markers may use approximate coordinates.

The high-resolution NASA 3D model may require a separate download or manual loading in some browsers.

Future Development

We aim to integrate JPL Horizons ephemerides, high-resolution LOLA/LROC terrain data, local horizon calculations, solar-power estimation, direct-to-Earth communication-window prediction, improved uncertainty analysis, and validated mission-constraint checking.

We also envision extending Lunar DNA into a time-dependent environment-matching engine and developing an “Ask the Moon” system that identifies which missing observations would most improve a landing decision.

Impact

Lunavista aims to bridge the gap between complex lunar datasets and understandable mission decisions. It can support early-stage mission concept exploration, communication between science and engineering teams, and education about the challenges of lunar exploration.

Our central principle is simple: selecting a landing site should involve not just identifying a location, but understanding why it may—or may not—fit the mission.
