projectDetails.name: Project LUNEX TEAM
projectDetails.summary: Lunar Mission Control is an interactive, decision-support web platform engineered for lunar south pole exploration, aligning with NASA’s Artemis objectives. Developed for the LUNEX Team during the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, our solution solves the critical operational triad of lunar landing site selection by integrating real-time solar illumination metrics, Earth line-of-sight communications visibility, and synthetic terrain-hazard modeling into a unified dashboard. Using Skyfield and the NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris, the platform evaluates candidate regions (such as Shackleton and de Gerlache rims), features an interactive rover battery survival simulator, renders 3D crater topography, and provides a multi-parameter candidate leaderboard to guide future sustainable lunar surface operations.
projectDetails.details:
> What it does & How it works:

> Lunar Mission Control acts as a comprehensive mission-planning dashboard that enables users and mission planners to screen and compare candidate lunar south pole landing regions. The application evaluates candidate sites using a weighted scoring model: 40% direct-to-Earth communications visibility, 30% solar illumination for power availability, and 30% terrain safety based on slope and rock hazards. It features a dynamic site selector, interactive telemetry charts (Sun/Earth elevation and horizon profiles), a 100% to shadowed-depletion rover battery survival model, and a coordinate-dependent 3D crater topography visualizer.

> Tech Stack & Tools Used:

> * Programming & Core Logic: Python 3.12, NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Plotly.

> * Astronomy & Ephemeris Engine: Skyfield library powered by the NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris (de421.bsp, pck00008.tpc, and lunar orientation data).

> * Web Interface & Deployment: Streamlit for the interactive dashboard UI, hosted and deployed live via Streamlit Cloud and GitHub.

>

>

> Intended Impact & Creativity:

> The project bridges complex orbital mechanics and practical mission design into an accessible tool. By consolidating power, communication, and terrain constraints into an intuitive interface, it empowers researchers and engineers to make rapid, data-driven decisions for future crewed and robotic Artemis missions to the lunar south pole.

AI/SI Disclosure: Super Intelligence tools were used to assist with code optimization, documentation drafting, and audio/visual demo generation.

projectDetails.name: M1SSIONX
projectDetails.summary: We developed an interactive educational browser game designed for kids and teens, following a young astronaut Engineer and a Doctor traveling to Mars to face realistic, high-stakes NASA-inspired challenges that require scientific problem-solving and critical thinking. The game guides players through four critical mission modules covering invisible space radiation and energy shielding, blurry vision microgravity effects (SANS), fitness equipment maintenance, and space agriculture combined with NASA's ECLSS water recycling technology. Featuring a three-heart health system, energy meters, and interactive mini-games like wire-connecting, wrong choices deduct lives and require corrective action while correct choices trigger scientific pop-up explanations and award persistent achievement badges saved via browser storage. Built using pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with supplemental visual assistance from design tools, all core concepts, storylines, and logic were entirely created and verified by the team.
projectDetails.details:
Project DetailsWhat it does and how it works (Step-by-Step):Navigation & HUD: Players navigate through three clean pages (Home, Game, and Logbook) linked via a top navigation bar. A persistent Heads-Up Display (HUD) tracks remaining hearts (3 lives), spacecraft energy levels, and unlocked badges. Interplanetary Missions: The player guides the crew through 4 critical scenarios:Mission 1 (Solar Storm & Radiation Defense): Dealing with invisible space radiation and coronal mass ejections, activating radiation shields, managing energy, and solving a wire-connecting mini-game. Mission 2 (Blurry Vision & Microgravity / SANS): Handling microgravity fluid shifts affecting the optic nerve, choosing the correct medical reporting path over risky actions. Mission 3 (Fitness & Equipment): Balancing crew exercise needs and equipment maintenance against energy conservation. Mission 4 (Space Agriculture & Water Recycling): Exploring how astronauts grow food in space and managing dwindling water supplies by implementing NASA’s ECLSS technology to recycle cabin humidity, sweat, and wastewater. Feedback Loop & Pop-ups: After every choice (whether correct or incorrect), an instant pop-up message appears. Correct choices reward the player with an achievement badge and unlock the next phase, while wrong choices deduct a heart (turning grey and lost), explain the scientific consequence, and require corrective mini-game action before re-trying. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Used:Frontend Core: Pure HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (No heavy frameworks or complex build steps, ensuring lightweight and fast execution). Styling & Animation: Custom CSS animations, inline SVG elements, responsive design, and Google Fonts ("Baloo 2"). Data Persistence: Browser localStorage to save collected badges in the Logbook. Benefits and Goals:

Promotes active engagement, scientific accuracy, quick decision-making under pressure, and independent learning through trial, error, and clear explanations. Working Features vs. Future Plans:Working Features: Fully functional multi-page browser game structure, dynamic HUD (hearts & energy meter), 4 complete mission modules with branching choices and pop-up explanations, interactive wire-connecting mini-game, and persistent badge Logbook. Future Plans: Expanding the game with additional deep-space missions, introducing multiplayer collaborative modes, and integrating rich sound effects and voiceovers.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: EarthTrend Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
EarthTrend Explorer is a scientifically grounded climate intelligence platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge: "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" Leveraging 43 years (1981–2023) of authentic NASA POWER (MERRA-2) atmospheric reanalysis records across Egyptian climate regimes—Greater Cairo, Alexandria, and Aswan—the platform functions as a statistical laboratory detecting multi-decadal warming, abrupt hydrologic breaks, and future climate anomalies.

Directly addressing the challenge, EarthTrend Explorer rigorously investigates: what is changing, where, by how much, and with what statistical confidence? It couples robust non-parametric trend estimators (Theil-Sen slope, Mann-Kendall, Hamed-Rao serial autocorrelation corrections, and Pettitt regime-shift detection) with a multi-scalar drought engine (SPI) and a forward-looking predictive engine (Holt-Winters ETS, SARIMAX) verified via expanding-window backtesting and newly released 2024 observations.

This tool is critical because climate adaptation in water-stressed regions demands transparent, physically guarded evidence rather than unverified black-box claims. By uncovering steady warming (+0.26 to +0.43 °C/decade), an abrupt 2015 rainfall shift (+181% to +266%), and a tripling of compound hot-dry months, EarthTrend Explorer transforms authentic NASA Earth observations into actionable, uncertainty-quantified insight for regional resilience.
projectDetails.details:
EarthTrend Explorer

1. What does the project do?

EarthTrend Explorer is an interactive platform for analyzing climate changes in Egypt using real NASA data.

It studies 43 years of climate data (1981–2023) across three different regions in Egypt:

  • Greater Cairo: Urban climate.
  • Alexandria: Mediterranean coastal climate.
  • Aswan: Hot and dry desert climate.

The platform works through four main steps:

  1. Data Collection: Collects monthly temperature and rainfall data from NASA and prepares it for analysis.
  2. Climate Trend Analysis: Uses statistical methods to identify whether temperatures and rainfall are increasing or decreasing over time.
  3. Climate Anomaly Detection: Detects unusual weather patterns, sudden changes in rainfall, and drought conditions.
  4. Climate Forecasting: Uses different time-series models to predict climate conditions for the next 12 months.

2. What are its main benefits?

  • Provides reliable, long-term climate analysis based on real NASA observations.
  • Shows whether climate trends are statistically significant.
  • Helps identify unusual climate events and potential drought conditions.
  • Provides future climate predictions with uncertainty ranges.
  • Handles the special challenges of dry regions, especially Aswan, where rainfall is extremely rare.
  • Includes 71 automated tests, all passing, to check the reliability of the system.

3. What is the expected impact?

The project aims to make climate data easier to understand and use.

It provides insights into how climate conditions have changed across different Egyptian regions and how they might change in the future.

These insights could support research, agricultural planning, and water-resource management, especially in areas affected by water scarcity.

4. What technologies did we use?

  • Programming Language: Python 3.10+
  • Data Processing: Pandas and NumPy
  • Scientific Calculations: SciPy
  • Statistical Analysis: Statsmodels and PyMannKendall
  • Climate Data: NASA POWER API and MERRA-2
  • Data Visualization: Plotly
  • User Interface: Streamlit
  • Testing: Pytest and Streamlit AppTest

5. What makes the project creative?

  • Forecasting Model Competition: Instead of choosing one forecasting model, we compare three different models using historical data and select the one that performs best.
  • 2024 Reality Check: We compare our predictions with actual NASA observations from 2024 to evaluate how accurate the forecasts were.
  • Regional Climate Comparison: We investigate whether temperature trends are different between Upper Egypt and northern coastal regions.
  • Advanced Statistical Analysis: We use several statistical methods to detect long-term trends, sudden climate changes, and drought conditions.

6. What challenges did our team consider?

  • Understanding NASA Data: We carefully checked what each NASA climate variable represents to avoid incorrect calculations or interpretations.
  • Limited Rainfall in Aswan: Since Aswan has very little rainfall, standard drought measurements may not always work reliably. We added special checks to handle this problem.
  • Data Accuracy: We checked the data for missing values and ensured that monthly observations were complete.
  • Forecast Reliability: We tested different models using historical data instead of assuming that one model would always perform best.
  • Scientific Transparency: We made sure to distinguish between statistical relationships and actual physical causes. We also avoided generating or inventing scientific data using AI.

projectDetails.name: MissionForge
projectDetails.summary:
MissionForge is a browser-based 3D game where players become a mission team and design a real robotic space mission from start to finish. You walk through a mission facility, choose instruments, power, communications, propulsion and a launch vehicle, carry the parts by hand, install them on the spacecraft, fuel it, pass a Go/No-Go review and launch. The flight then plays out with real orbit physics and random emergencies based on problems NASA actually faced. The debrief traces success or failure back to the player's own decisions and compares the design with the real mission.

Four missions unlock in order: a Lunar Orbiter (inspired by LRO), a Mars Orbiter (MRO), a Mars Lander (InSight) and a Europa Flyby Explorer (Europa Clipper), using real instrument mass, power and cost figures from NASA and JPL sources. One to four players share four engineering roles, on one screen or online.

MissionForge answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning the real trade-offs of mission design (mass, power, data, budget and risk) into hands-on decisions, so students learn why every component choice matters. It runs in any browser, with no installation or login.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

MissionForge puts the player inside a 3D mission facility: a central Assembly Hall with the spacecraft and ten themed rooms around it (four instrument labs, power, communications, protection and entry, propulsion and fueling, the launch vehicle hall, and mission control). The player builds a spacecraft step by step, by carrying parts, installing them, pumping propellant and running four pre-launch checks, while watching mass, power, data, propellant and budget against real NASA safety margins.

HOW IT WORKS

- Four missions: Lunar Orbiter (LRO), Mars Orbiter (MRO), Mars Lander (InSight) and Europa Flyby Explorer (Europa Clipper). Three modes: Campaign, Sandbox, and Replay a Real Mission (start from the real NASA design).

- Four roles (Systems Engineer, Science Lead, Launch and Orbit Lead, Budget and Risk Manager). Every stage needs all four to approve before it locks, like a real concurrent engineering team. Solo players get an advisor. Online multiplayer for 1 to 4 players uses a 4-letter room code.

- A Go/No-Go review board in Mission Control: each reviewer gives GO or NO-GO with a reason.

- An educational 3D flight: liftoff, staging, cruise, gravity assists, the asteroid belt, orbit insertion or landing, then the data sent home by radio. The flight panel works through real equations with the player's own design: the rocket equation, Hohmann transfer, Kepler's third law and vis-viva, using NASA planetary constants.

- Random flight emergencies based on real cases (safe mode, comet Siding Spring's dust, collision warnings, the asteroid belt, Juno's propellant valve). The correct answer is what NASA actually did.

- A debrief with the score explained, a cause trace from failure back to the exact decisions that caused it, and a comparison with the real mission.

- Change requests that cost more the later they are made, as in real projects.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students and the public learn systems engineering by doing: why mass drives propellant, why power falls with distance from the Sun, why margins and reviews exist, and why late changes are expensive. Every number shown as real comes from a cited NASA or JPL source, and game assumptions are clearly labelled "approximate". It runs on laptops, tablets and phones with no installation, so classrooms can use it directly.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

JavaScript, React 18, Three.js, Vite, Vitest (tests for the simulation engine), MQTT.js for online multiplayer, the Web Audio API for sound, and GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions for deployment. The simulation engine is plain JavaScript, separate from the 3D layer, and new missions or instruments are added as JSON data with no new code.

CREATIVITY

Instead of menus and sliders, players physically build the spacecraft in 3D, and the game explains which of their own decisions made the mission succeed or fail. Real NASA history becomes playable emergencies, and real missions become a benchmark to beat.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Scientific accuracy and source citation, accessibility (touch controls, a low-graphics mode, an interactive tour, optional hints, a glossary), teamwork, and NASA brand rules: no NASA logos are used and no endorsement is implied. All 3D models, textures and sounds are generated in code, so no third-party assets are used.

projectDetails.name: AuraMed
projectDetails.summary:
Project Auramed is an AI-powered health monitoring and assistance system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. We developed an intelligent assistant that combines a chatbot and voice-based interaction, allowing astronauts to communicate naturally with the system, receive health-related guidance, and better understand potential risks to their well-being.
The system uses Machine Learning models to analyze health data, identify unusual patterns, and help detect potential health risks associated with the challenges of spaceflight. It also integrates an AI assistant that provides accessible explanations and recommendations based on relevant health information. The project brings together a web platform, a mobile application, and AI services to make health monitoring and interaction more accessible.

Auramed addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by focusing on the difficulty of monitoring astronauts' health and providing timely support when direct communication with medical professionals on Earth may be delayed. By combining data analysis, AI-powered assistance, and interactive interfaces, the system aims to help astronauts recognize potential health concerns earlier and make more informed decisions.
This project is important because astronauts face unique health risks in space, including the effects of microgravity, radiation, sleep disruption, and isolation. Auramed explores how AI can help bridge the gap between continuous health monitoring.
projectDetails.details:
AuraMed – AI-Powered Astronaut Health Assistant

AuraMed is an AI-powered system designed to help astronauts monitor their health and understand potential risks during space missions.

What does it do and how does it work?

AuraMed combines Machine Learning models with an interactive AI assistant that supports both text and voice conversations. It analyzes available health data to identify unusual patterns and potential health risks, then provides astronauts with understandable information and guidance. Users can interact with the system through a web platform and a mobile application.

Benefits and expected impact:

AuraMed aims to support early awareness of health concerns, make health information easier to access, and help astronauts make more informed decisions when communication with medical professionals on Earth is limited or delayed. It focuses on the health challenges of spaceflight, helping improve astronaut safety during long-duration missions.

Tools and technologies used:

- AI/ML: Python and Machine Learning models.

- AI Backend: FastAPI for AI services and model integration.

- Backend: Laravel for application logic and API management.

- Web Frontend: React.

- Mobile Application: Flutter.

- AI Interaction: Chatbot and voice-based assistant.

Our goal is to create a unified, accessible health-support system that demonstrates how AI can contribute to safer and more sustainable human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project MAJIX
projectDetails.summary: Team MAJIX built Lunar Sentinel to address the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by connecting three questions: where to land, when to land, and how to stay connected at the Moon’s south pole. We researched terrain, shadow, power, and communication risks, then used NASA LOLA elevation maps, LRO imagery, and JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions to calculate slopes, terrain horizons, sunlight, and Earth visibility. Our website lets users explore map layers, select locations, inspect five-meter terrain detail at four study sites, and identify useful landing windows. We also developed a proposed relay-satellite simulation to explore reducing communication gaps and a LIDAR demonstration showing how laser sensing could support touchdown decisions. Our creative contribution is linking terrain, timing, and communication to the same selected location in one interactive workflow. We built an offline-capable HTML, CSS, and JavaScript website with a Python data pipeline, implemented 25 automated tests, checked results against NASA products and Apollo 17 conditions, and clearly separated measured data, calculations, and proposals while documenting limitations. The result is a transparent planning and learning prototype—not a flight-certified system—that makes lunar mission trade-offs easier to understand.
projectDetails.details: We’re Team MAJIX, and we built Lunar Sentinel to help people explore three big questions about landing at the Moon’s south pole: where to land, when to land, and how to stay connected to Earth. We used NASA terrain maps, lunar images, and Sun and Earth positions to create a website where users can choose a location, inspect slopes and shadows, and find landing windows with useful sunlight and Earth visibility. We also explored a proposed relay satellite that could reduce communication gaps and created a LIDAR demonstration to explain how laser sensing could help during touchdown. What makes our project creative is that everything stays connected to the same selected location, turning separate datasets into one clear, interactive experience. We developed it with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas, used Python to process the data, and checked our work with 25 automated tests and comparisons against NASA products and Apollo 17 conditions. Throughout development, we considered terrain hazards, power needs, communication outages, data quality, and ease of use. Our goal is to make lunar planning more understandable for students, educators, and people exploring mission ideas, so we made the website work offline and clearly labeled what comes from NASA, what we calculated, and what we proposed. It’s a planning and learning prototype—not a flight-ready system—and we’re honest about its limits, including remaining relay gaps and hazards too small for the maps to show.

projectDetails.name: Project MarsGO (Mango's Mars map)
projectDetails.summary: Our Project is a Clear Map representing Mars's clear path for the Jezero Crater Mission for the first astronauts on Mars. It does not just display Mars data, it turns layered NASA data into a route an astronaut can actually walk, then tells the crew whether that walk is survivable. And we faced alot of challenges while developing this web app, like learning how to use "USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping" To build images for the unsafe places and hazard detection using Mars geologic data and implementing the JPL Mars Trek library using Leaflet.js and organising all of the work while we all faced the "MidTerm" exams. Our project implements real Mars data from NASA, telling future astronauts that it will be safe to go there, and we are making sure everything is ready for them and calculated.
projectDetails.details:
What this is

MarsGo is a Python web app prototype for planning a hypothetical astronaut walk—an EVA—around Jezero Crater on Mars. Instead of just displaying Mars imagery, it combines terrain, geology, rover history, suit-consumable estimates, weather and radiation assumptions to suggest a route and give a GO / NO-GO planning verdict.

Its intended impact is to make exploration data more useful for human mission planning: help a crew consider where to walk, what science to do at stops, and what hazards or resource limits matter

Github Repo: https://github.com/asaadzx/marsgo

Stack

  • Language(s): Python 3.12; Dockerfile for packaging.
  • Framework: Streamlit web app, with Folium/Leaflet maps.
  • Notable libraries: NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Pillow, and streamlit-folium.
  • Data and services: Cached NASA/JPL Mars Trek, Perseverance imagery and traverse data, USGS Jezero geology, Esri Astro CTX/HiRISE imagery, and an MSL/REMS weather snapshot. The app reads these cached files at runtime, so the demo can work offline.

How it fits together: The data scripts fetch NASA, USGS and imagery products and prepare local map layers. At runtime, app.py reads those files, lets the user choose a science objective, stations and suit limits, then calls routing.py to find a terrain-costed traverse and suit.py to assess the plan. The map and results show route distance and terrain, consumables, safety checks, station context and a verdict.

Benefits and creative choices: The central idea is to turn a map into a planning conversation: MarsGo combines a rover’s previously travelled corridor with a separate human walking route, science stops and suit constraints. The team also made trade-offs visible: for example, the terrain elevation source is coarse, so the app uses CTX image texture as a roughness proxy; it labels this limitation rather than presenting it as fine-resolution terrain truth. The weather data comes from Gale Crater, not Jezero, and is identified as an analogue. Suit and radiation values are explicitly planning assumptions, not mission rules.

Factors considered include terrain and hazards, walk-back reserve, oxygen, water, battery, EVA duration, radiation, dust, science objectives, rover-visited waypoints, offline operation and the tablet/glove-use context. The app’s main benefit is that it brings these considerations together and can explain why a proposed plan fails a modelled constraint—not merely draw a line on a map.

We used SI while gathering Data and working on the project plan and organising it only.

projectDetails.name: Mission Ripple
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Ripple — Every Choice Creates a Ripple

How can children learn to think like scientists instead of simply memorizing facts?

Mission Ripple is an interactive, story-driven Mars adventure developed by Team MARO for NASA Space Apps' Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.

Designed for children aged 7–12, our playable web game puts young explorers in charge of a simulated Mars research base. Guided by Nuri, a friendly robot companion, players explore six interconnected missions inspired by real NASA data, including Curiosity rover radiation measurements, solar activity records, and plant research.

Players must make meaningful decisions, manage limited power, investigate scientific evidence, and respond to unexpected challenges.

Our Ripple Effect system makes every choice matter. Decisions create immediate and delayed consequences, affecting the base, future challenges, and three possible endings. Players can also recover from mistakes and learn from their results.

Real NASA science provides the educational foundation, while simplified simulations make complex space challenges accessible.

Our goal is to turn scientific curiosity into critical thinking, problem-solving, and learning through experience.
projectDetails.details:
Mission Ripple is an interactive educational Mars adventure developed by Team MARO for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.

Designed for children aged 7 to 12, our browser-based game allows players to become commanders of a simulated Mars research base. Guided by Nuri, a friendly robot companion, children explore scientific challenges, manage limited resources, make decisions, and discover how their choices affect the mission.

The game features six interconnected missions inspired by authentic NASA scientific data, including Curiosity rover radiation measurements, DONKI solar activity records, NASA plant research from the Open Science Data Repository, and Mars Trek geographical information.

Our main innovation is the Ripple Effect system. Every important decision can create immediate or delayed consequences. For example, using limited energy for scientific monitoring may affect greenhouse lighting and plant growth. Players must consider trade-offs, respond to unexpected problems, and learn how to recover from mistakes.

The game includes three animated endings based on player decisions and the simulated base's condition. A final recap explains how previous choices influenced the outcome, encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific reasoning.

Mission Ripple was developed using Phaser, TypeScript, Vite, custom pixel-art assets, and ElevenLabs for Nuri's English voice dialogue. AI-assisted development tools supported implementation and testing. The playable prototype includes interactive exploration, scientific missions, resource management, recovery mechanics, achievements, and cinematic sequences.

NASA data provides the scientific foundation, while resource values, plant growth, and mission consequences are simplified educational simulations rather than accurate predictions of real Mars operations.

Our future plans include expanding scientific missions, adding language support, and conducting educational testing with children to evaluate learning outcomes.

Mission Ripple aims to make space science more accessible and engaging, helping children move beyond memorizing facts to understanding evidence, making decisions, and learning from experience.

Every choice creates a ripple.

projectDetails.name: MARS INVADERS
projectDetails.summary: We built an autonomous 3D safe pathfinding and geological exploration system to help astronauts and rovers navigate hazardous Martian terrain. Inside Jezero Crater, steep slopes (>10°), sand ripples, and boulder fields pose severe risks of rollover, energy loss, and communication blackouts. Our prototype transforms authentic NASA Mars Trek datasets into an interactive 3D survival map powered by an A* algorithm that computes the safest, most energy-efficient extravehicular activity (EVA) route. By ensuring traversal safety while guiding exploration toward astrobiological targets like the Delta Front, this tool protects surface crews and maximizes the discovery of ancient biosignatures.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Invaders's Project Solution

Mars Invaders is an autonomous 3D safe pathfinding and geological exploration system designed to help astronauts and robotic rovers navigate hazardous Martian terrain by transforming real NASA planetary data into an interactive 3D survival map. The system bridges complex geospatial datasets with mission-critical operational safety, making surface exploration both secure and scientifically impactful.

How Does Our Solution Work

In Mars Invaders, the system processes raw orbital data to compute safe exploration corridors across Jezero Crater. The operational workflow is structured into key technical phases:

Geospatial Data Processing (QGIS):

We ingest authentic NASA Mars Trek Digital Elevation Models (DEM) and Orthomosaic imagery into QGIS under the planetary coordinate system ESRI:103885. This allows the system to analyze surface topography, extract exact elevation profiles, and generate raw Float32 slope matrices.

Constraint-Based Pathfinding (Python & A*):

Using Python (NumPy and Rasterio), our pathfinding engine converts slope rasters into navigable cost grids, strictly enforcing a hard safety threshold of <10° slope to prevent rover rollovers, excessive astronaut fatigue, and wheel slippage.

Interactive 3D Simulation & Telemetry (CesiumJS):

The computed ~2 km extravehicular activity (EVA) traverse from the Octavia E. Butler landing site to the Delta Front is rendered inside an interactive 3D Cesium web environment. Users can toggle hazard layers, verify direct Line-of-Sight (LoS) communication, and explore geological science waypoints along the route:

Stop 1 (Basaltic Regolith): Crater floor early volcanic history and regolith characteristics.

Stop 2 (Olivine-rich rocks): Mineralogical composition points along the traverse.

Stop 3 (Clay minerals / Smectite at the Delta Front): High-priority astrobiological targets for ancient biosignatures.

The project benefits

The system benefits mission planners, astronauts, and the wider scientific community by:

Educating users on Martian topographical hazards and surface survival constraints.

Demonstrating practical, data-driven strategies for safe extravehicular activity (EVA) routing.

Bridging the gap between multi-gigabyte NASA datasets and real-world planetary exploration planning in an interactive way.

Our goal

To make NASA’s open planetary data accessible and actionable, helping future missions prepare for severe agricultural and environmental challenges on other worlds while fostering global awareness of space exploration dynamics. Despite our detailed global modeling, the prototype focuses on regional Jezero Crater hazards and does not account for micro-scale obstacles like unmapped meter-scale boulders.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages & Libraries:

Python (with NumPy and Rasterio) → for geospatial array processing and A* pathfinding execution.

JavaScript / HTML / CSS (with CesiumJS) → for 3D web application development and telemetry rendering.

Data Sources:

NASA Mars Trek real-time datasets → for environmental and topographical data. Through NASA’s open access, we utilized HiRISE/CTX DEM mosaics to extract precise slope and elevation profiles, alongside CTX Orthomosaic imagery for high-resolution surface texturing.

Software & Tools:

QGIS 3.44 LTR → for spatial alignment, coordinate referencing (ESRI:103885), and slope matrix extraction.

Cesium ion → for 3D terrain tiling, streaming, and visualization.

GitHub Link

https://github.com/janaabdeen/mars-invaders-jezero-3d?tab=readme-ov-file

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI tools as a supportive engineering resource throughout the project. Specifically:

Design: When brainstorming creative user interface layouts and architectural approaches, we used AI to explore possible design patterns.

Implementation Guidance: When uncertain about how to implement specific geospatial raster processing steps or Cesium integrations, we prompted AI for coding suggestions and best practices.

Debugging Assistance: During development, AI was used to help identify, explain, and resolve scripting and data-alignment errors efficiently

projectDetails.name: Project Mars Pathfinders
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Pathfinders is an integrated web-based platform designed to make Mars exploration more accessible, intelligent, and data-driven. It brings together scientific data from trusted sources, including NASA/JPL and USGS, into one interactive environment for exploring, analyzing, and planning surface missions on the Red Planet.

The platform provides five advanced observation modes: Optical, Thermal, Spectral, Topographic, and Geophysical. These modes allow users to investigate Martian surface imagery, temperature patterns, mineral composition, elevation, terrain structure, and geological features.

It also features interactive Mars maps, geological analysis tools, and a smart route planner that helps users explore potential paths based on terrain conditions and slope analysis. In addition, its hazard advisory system highlights potential environmental and geological risks, supporting better-informed exploration decisions.
projectDetails.details:
MARS PATHFINDERS

An Integrated Mars Exploration Platform

Mars Pathfinders is an interactive web-based platform designed to improve the way users explore, analyze, and plan scientific missions on Mars. It integrates planetary datasets from NASA/JPL and the USGS into one unified environment, transforming complex scientific information into accessible visual tools for exploration and decision-making.

1. What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

The platform provides five advanced observation modes:

- Optical Mode: Displays Mars surface imagery and rover photographs.

- Thermal Mode: Explores daytime and nighttime temperature patterns and thermal inertia.

- Spectral Mode: Visualizes mineralogical information, including pyroxene, plagioclase, and dust distribution.

- Topographic Mode: Displays elevation, slope gradients, and terrain features using MOLA data.

- Geophysical Mode: Provides information about surface roughness, geological structures, and mapped geological units.

Users can interact with Mars maps, switch between scientific data layers, explore geological regions, inspect surface locations, and use the Smart Route Planner to create hypothetical exploration routes based on terrain conditions and slope analysis.

The platform also includes an Astronaut Hazard Advisory System that highlights potential risks such as extreme temperatures, radiation exposure, volcanic terrain, dust storms, and geological instability.

2. What Are the Benefits of the Project?

- Combines multiple planetary science datasets in one platform.

- Makes complex scientific information easier to understand through interactive visualization.

- Supports terrain analysis and hypothetical route planning.

- Helps identify potential geological and environmental hazards.

- Provides an organized environment for studying Mars surface features.

- Encourages scientific learning, research, and exploration.

3. What Is the Intended Impact?

Our goal is to support future planetary exploration by making Mars-related scientific data more accessible, understandable, and useful.

Mars Pathfinders aims to contribute to scientific education, planetary research, and mission-planning concepts by connecting geological information, terrain analysis, and hazard awareness in one integrated platform.

It can also help students, researchers, and space enthusiasts better understand the challenges of exploring the Red Planet.

4. What Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware, and Software Were Used?

The project is designed as a web-based application that integrates planetary data and interactive mapping technologies.

Scientific Data Sources:

- NASA/JPL Mars Trek.

- USGS SIM 3292 Global Geologic Map.

- MOLA (Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter) elevation and slope data.

- THEMIS (Thermal Emission Imaging System) datasets.

- Mars orbital imagery and scientific observations.

Development Technologies:

The specific programming languages, frameworks, mapping libraries, and development tools used should be listed according to the actual project implementation.

Hardware: A computer for development, testing, and accessing the web platform. No specialized space hardware is required.

5. How Is the Project Creative and Innovative?

The main innovation of Mars Pathfinders is bringing several scientific exploration capabilities together in one interactive platform instead of requiring users to navigate multiple separate scientific resources.

Its creative features include:

- Five specialized scientific observation modes.

- Interactive 2D and 3D Mars exploration views.

- Integration of geological and topographic information.

- Terrain-aware hypothetical route planning.

- Visual hazard advisories for exploration awareness.

- A futuristic, mission-control-inspired interface that makes scientific exploration more engaging.

6. What Factors Did the Team Consider?

During development, the team considered:

- Scientific Accuracy: Using recognized NASA/JPL and USGS datasets.

- Data Integration: Bringing different scientific information sources together.

- User Experience: Making the interface intuitive and easy to navigate.

- Terrain Safety: Considering elevation, slopes, and mapped hazard regions during route planning.

- Accessibility: Presenting complex scientific data in a clear visual format.

- Technical Limitations: Distinguishing available mapped information from unavailable live weather, seismic, and radiation telemetry.

- Future Scalability: Designing the platform to support additional datasets and exploration capabilities.

Conclusion

Mars Pathfinders transforms planetary scientific data into an interactive exploration experience. By combining multiple observation modes, geological intelligence, smart route planning, and hazard awareness, the project provides a unified approach to understanding Mars and supporting the concepts behind safer, smarter future exploration.

MARS PATHFINDERS — Explore Beyond the Surface.

node.excerpt: We are Martian Phoenix, a multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration, science, and emerging technologies. Our interests span planetary science, AI, Machine Learning, software development, 3D visualization, and immersive technologies.

projectDetails.name: Project Martian Phoenix
projectDetails.summary:
Terra Twin is a free, no-login web tool that helps teams find places on Earth resembling Mars’s Jezero Crater for training and equipment testing. Built for NASA Space Apps, it focuses on the deserts and dry riverbeds of the Middle East and North Africa, a region that has seen little screening for Mars analogs.

Using NASA climate, elevation and imagery data alongside global elevation tiles, Terra Twin scores each 1° × 1° cell for terrain similarity, dryness and suitability for rover driving. Users can adjust the weights, explore the map, compare a 60 km stretch of terrain side by side with Jezero in 3D, and drive a virtual rover across it. A WebXR mode is available but still awaits headset testing.

Mission teams, researchers and educators can use Terra Twin to shortlist sites and see why each one scores well. In a six-site check, terrain similarity alone did not clearly distinguish known analogs from other sites, so the tool shows all three scores separately. Its roughly 500 m resolution supports regional screening, while assessing rover-scale terrain requires finer data.
projectDetails.details:
Terra Twin is a free, no-login web tool that screens 1,650 land cells across the Middle East and North Africa for potential Mars practice sites. We compare each cell’s slope, roughness and elevation relief with Jezero Crater, then score dryness and rover slope suitability separately. Users can adjust the weights to see which locations rise or fall and why.

The same terrain can be explored at three scales. Users can select a cell on a regional map, compare a 60 km section side by side with Jezero in 3D, and drive a virtual rover across it in an arcade game. Our goal is to help researchers shortlist locations for fieldwork and give educators a hands-on way to teach planetary terrain.

We kept the scores separate because a flat, dry site may be worth investigating for rover trials even if it looks little like Jezero. In our six-site test, terrain similarity alone failed to distinguish four known analogs from two controls. We published that result. The coarse elevation data, lack of mineral data and provisional rover slope limit restrict the tool to regional screening.

We built Terra Twin on team laptops using Python for analysis and JavaScript with React, Leaflet and three.js for the website. We used NASA POWER climate data, MOLA elevation data, Mars Trek and GIBS imagery, and AWS Terrain Tiles. Docker and Nginx serve the site.

projectDetails.name: Project Mashy El7al
projectDetails.summary: Pyroscope is a wildfire-monitoring tool that combines fire detections from two NASA satellite instruments, MODIS and VIIRS, into one consistent picture. The two instruments see the same fires at different resolutions and with different detection rules. That produces overlapping, inconsistent records that are hard to compare across years and countries. Pyroscope merges them into a single harmonized dataset, shows it on an interactive map, and adds a Python forecast model that predicts fire activity country by country instead of as one regional number. It addresses Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. It matters because responders, researchers and planners need a trustworthy view of where fire is happening and where it is likely to occur next. Pyroscope uses only open NASA data, so anyone can reproduce it.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Pyroscope takes NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (about 1 km resolution) and VIIRS (375 m) and harmonizes them into one fire record. It displays the result on a web map and forecasts fire activity per country.

How it works.

  1. It ingests FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS detections. Our test dataset covers Egypt, 2015 to 2025.
  2. It aligns the fields of the two sources and merges overlapping detections.
  3. It shows the harmonized data on an interactive map.
  4. A Python model trained on real FIRMS data produces a forecast, displayed as a country-by-country map at the bottom of the page.

Working features and evidence.

  • The harmonization tool exists in two versions: a single-file JavaScript/HTML app and a second version in a project package.
  • Egypt 2015 to 2025 FIRMS data is loaded and harmonized.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project MEGA
projectDetails.summary: On a mission to the Moon or Mars, a doctor on Earth is minutes away by radio, so astronauts must notice and act on health problems themselves. For the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions", we built MEGA Health, an interactive health bridge for each crew member. The astronaut clicks a 3D body: every body zone is coloured green (normal), yellow (moderate) or red (critical) from its readings, and the head, heart, lungs, arms and legs open a 3D view of the organ or muscles inside. Each zone explains, in plain language, which measurements can be taken in space, why they matter, how NASA's spaceflight hazards affect them, who should act (the astronaut, the crew, or the flight surgeon on Earth) and what to do now. A hazard simulator shows how a solar flare, a spacewalk or skipped exercise would hit the body; daily countermeasure quests raise a mission-readiness score; and Ask MEGA, a voice assistant running on a local AI with no link to Earth, answers health questions from the astronaut's own record. This matters because on long missions the crew is the first line of medical care: MEGA Health turns many numbers into one glance, one tap and one clear next step.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

MEGA Health is a web application ("the bridge") that lets each astronaut assess their own health and decide what to do. Main use: an astronaut opens their profile, sees at a glance which body zones are yellow or red, taps one to understand the problem and follows the recommended countermeasure — or escalates to the flight surgeon when the reading is red.

WORKING FEATURES (all in the live project)

- 3D astronaut with 12 clickable body zones (head, eyes, heart, lungs, abdomen, back & spine, upper arms, forearms, hands, thighs, calves, feet), each coloured green / yellow / red from its readings.

- Inside view: clicking the head, heart, lungs, an arm or a leg flies the camera into the body; the skin fades and the brain, heart, lungs or the limb's muscles appear in place.

- Zone panel: every reading with its value, normal range and status; a trend chart over mission days; "Why this exam matters"; "How to measure" with the onboard device; the zone's hazards; countermeasures; and an "Earth medical spinoff" note.

- Triage that says who acts: green = self-care, yellow = crew countermeasure, red = ground flight-surgeon consult. Red zones can queue a telemetry packet to the flight surgeon, showing the 4 min 44 s one-way radio delay (simulated).

- Mission readiness score (0–100) from the database formula, raised by starting countermeasures and completing daily quests, lowered by hazards.

- Space hazard simulator: solar particle event, 6-hour spacewalk, 60 days without exercise — shows which zones degrade and the real change in readiness.

- Daily countermeasure quests with streaks and XP (gamification).

- Crew overview: 5 astronauts, sleep chart, vital-sign trends (heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, blood sugar, mood), cabin environment (pressure, O2, CO2, temperature, noise), space weather and the CSA CANS neutron-dose reading.

- Ask MEGA voice assistant (local only): speak a question, hear the answer. It runs on Bionic, a local AI app, with the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B model, and is briefed with the astronaut's readings, normal ranges and statuses so its answers come from the record.

HOW IT WORKS AND HOW THE DATA SUPPORTS IT

The team built a SQLite astronaut health database (11 tables) with 5 crew profiles, 12 body zones and 53 health metrics. Each metric has units, green/amber thresholds, trend history, "why it matters" and "how to measure" text, written from the NASA Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency resources. A Python script exports it to JSON for the website. Zone colours come from the thresholds; readiness follows the database formula (100 − 5 per amber metric − 20 per red metric, kept between 0 and 100), and the live readiness logic is checked by an automated test of every astronaut × hazard × quest combination (about 40,000 checks). The 3D body was split into the 12 zones in Blender.

BENEFITS

Fast self-assessment (colour → tap → action), clear escalation rules that save scarce radio time, plain-language education so astronauts don't need to be doctors, and an assistant that works with no Earth link. The same approach fits remote clinics, polar stations and ships on Earth.

LIMITATIONS

- All readings are simulated mission data; no live sensors are connected and there is no manual data-entry screen yet.

- It is decision support, not a medical device; red results always point to the flight surgeon.

- Ask MEGA needs the Bionic local AI on the same computer and Chrome or Edge for voice, so it is not available in the online version; answers take about 8–20 seconds.

- The telemetry packet to the flight surgeon is simulated.

- Designed for desktop/laptop screens.

FUTURE PLANS

Connect wearables and onboard devices and add manual entry with measurement reminders; a flight-surgeon dashboard that syncs over the delayed link; personal baselines and early-warning trend detection; an offline installable version for ship hardware with a smaller, faster on-board model; clinical validation and more languages.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

JavaScript (React 19, Vite), CSS, three.js with React Three Fiber, drei and three-mesh-bvh, Draco 3D compression, Python and SQLite (database), Blender 5.2 (3D processing), FFmpeg (video), Bionic local AI app with NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, Web Speech API, Git and GitHub (code), Cloudflare Pages (hosting).

projectDetails.name: FireScope - MENORBIT
projectDetails.summary:
FireScope is a satellite-based wildfire monitoring and analysis platform that transforms real fire observations from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) into accessible and meaningful insights.

Using MODIS and VIIRS satellite data, FireScope processes and harmonizes active fire hotspot observations, allowing users to explore wildfire activity across different regions and time periods. The platform provides interactive maps to visualize hotspot locations, historical analysis to identify trends, and analytical tools to detect unusual changes in fire activity. It also presents findings through charts and reports to make complex satellite data easier to understand.

FireScope addresses the challenge of making large volumes of satellite fire data more accessible, organized, and useful. By connecting raw observations with interactive visualization and analysis, it helps users better understand wildfire patterns and monitor changes in fire activity.

This matters because timely access to reliable fire observations can support environmental awareness, research, and more informed decision-making for wildfire monitoring and management.
projectDetails.details:
FireScope – Project Details

1. What does it do and how does it work?

FireScope is an interactive wildfire monitoring and analysis platform built around real satellite observations from NASA FIRMS. It retrieves fire hotspot data from MODIS and VIIRS through the NASA FIRMS API or imports historical NASA FIRMS CSV files. The system processes the observations, organizes them in a SQL Server database, and presents them through an interactive global map and analytical dashboard.

Users can explore fire hotspots by country or geographic coordinates, filter observations by year, month, satellite sensor, confidence level, and day or night detection. They can inspect individual hotspots and their characteristics, including acquisition time, brightness, confidence, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

FireScope also provides:

  • Interactive Fire Map: Visualizes hotspot locations and allows users to inspect individual observations.
  • Burning Activity Calendar: Displays monthly fire activity across multiple years.
  • Historical Trends: Compares yearly and seasonal fire activity using charts.
  • Anomaly Analysis: Highlights unusual changes compared with historical monthly activity.
  • Data Export: Allows users to export processed observations as CSV files.
  • Executive Briefs: Summarizes key indicators for selected regions and time periods.

2. Benefits and intended impact

FireScope makes satellite fire observations easier to access, explore, and understand. Instead of working directly with large and complex datasets, users can interact with visual maps, historical comparisons, and analytical summaries.

Our intended impact is to support environmental researchers, students, and decision-makers in understanding wildfire patterns, identifying periods of unusual activity, and making more informed decisions about environmental monitoring and fire management.

3. Technologies and tools

Backend: C#, ASP.NET Core, Entity Framework Core, SQL Server, and CsvHelper.

Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Tailwind CSS.

Mapping and visualization: Leaflet, D3.js, TopoJSON, Chart.js, and Esri World Street Map.

Data source: NASA FIRMS, using MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations.

4. What makes FireScope creative?

Our approach combines satellite observations from different sensors in one exploration environment. Rather than simply displaying fire locations, FireScope connects geographic visualization with historical trends, seasonal comparisons, hotspot telemetry, and experimental anomaly indicators.

The platform is designed to help users move from individual satellite detections to a broader understanding of how fire activity changes across locations and time.

5. Factors considered

We considered data reliability, geographic coverage, historical context, sensor differences, observation confidence, usability, and responsible interpretation. Fire detections are treated as satellite-observed hotspots or thermal anomalies, not automatically as confirmed fires. Cross-sensor harmonization and anomaly indicators are experimental and require further scientific calibration and validation.

projectDetails.details:
• Hassouna Green is an interactive 3D farm prototype in Arabic and English built by Team Mentalist for the Field Shift challenge to help users plan crop rotations across several seasons
  • Users pick Cairo or the Nile Delta and choose a priority and a starting rotation and then plant and water and add soil cover and harvest during a 12-day demo season

  • Daily temperature and rainfall drive simple game rules for moisture and crop growth while a SoilGrids example for the Nile Delta is included only as background
  • The rotation scores come from open rules we wrote ourselves based on crop water needs and diversity and legumes and do not use NASA or SoilGrids values
  • Working now are the bilingual 3D demo and the rotation comparison and the season report and progress saved in the browser and public code that judges can open without logging in
  • It is not yet a validated recommendation system and does not predict yield or income or irrigation needs and it has no farmer feedback backend or field trials
  • Future plans are local soil and field data and agronomist-calibrated models and a farmer feedback loop and more NASA datasets and field trials with farmers
  • Built with HTML and CSS and JavaScript and Three JS and Node JS and VS Code with the public demo hosted on Manus and no special hardware needed beyond a browser that supports WebGL.

projectDetails.name: Mesh Men El Ard (GeoPulse)
projectDetails.summary:
Geo Pulse is an interactive environmental platform that transforms Earth science data into accessible insights.

The Problem: Understanding environmental changes is difficult because scientific datasets are complex, and trends vary across time and regions. Yet, these changes affect agriculture, water resources, public health, and urban planning.

Our Solution: Geo Pulse simplifies environmental analysis through interactive maps, visualizations, and statistical tools, using data accessed through NASA's Giovanni platform.

The platform offers two main systems:

• Global Earth Dashboard: A 3D interactive globe and geographic map for exploring temperature, precipitation, and vegetation trends, with regional comparison tools.

• Cairo Climate Analytics: A detailed climate study covering 2000–2025, featuring 9,406 daily records, 51 environmental indicators, and eight specialized analytical pages.

Our Goal:Make Earth science accessible to everyone, especially school and university students, allowing users to explore locations, analyze environmental trends, and understand climate changes without advanced technical knowledge.
projectDetails.details:
Geo Pulse is an interactive, web-based environmental intelligence and educational platform. It turns

Earth observation data and model-derived datasets into visual, explorable and scientifically

interpretable insight, so that anyone curious about our planet can see how environmental conditions

change over time and place.The problem

Earth’s land, atmosphere and vegetation are constantly changing, but the evidence sits inside very large and

technical datasets. Long-term environmental trends are slow, regional, and easily confused with seasonal cycles

and natural variability. Understanding them matters because they inform water planning, agriculture, urban

design, public health and education. Yet scientific files, units, aggregation choices and statistical tests are out of

reach for most people.

What Geo Pulse does

Geo Pulse bridges the gap between raw scientific data and practical environmental understanding. It connects

satellite-based observations and atmospheric model products, accessed through NASA’s Giovanni platform, with

interactive visualization and transparent statistical analysis. The platform offers two integrated experiences:

• Global Earth Dashboard – an interactive 3D Earth, a Leaflet map for choosing regions, time series for Land

Surface Temperature (LST), precipitation and NDVI, trend statistics, and a two-region comparison tool.

• Cairo Climate Analytics – a deep case study of Greater Cairo’s climate built on 9,406 daily records and 51

indicators from January 1, 2000 to October 1, 2025, with eight specialized scientific analysis pages.

Users do not need programming, statistics or Earth-science expertise. They choose a place, pick a variable, adjust

a date range, and read charts that are paired with plain-language interpretation.

Who it is for

Ordinary people and curious citizens, school students, university students and educators, and early-stage analysts

who want to inspect trends, regional contrasts and data-quality checks before committing to deeper analysis.Why the solution is valuable

• Accessible: complex Earth science data becomes interactive and visual.

• Multi-scale: global exploration and a deep city-level case study work together.

• Scientifically careful: trend direction, magnitude and statistical significance are kept distinct;

correlation is never presented as causation.

• Educational: every specialized Cairo page follows a six-step explanatory structure that moves from

chart to takeaway.

• Impactful: it contributes to environmental awareness, scientific literacy and data-driven

decision-making.This guide is written for a judge who has never seen Geo Pulse. It walks through the two experiences

in the order a first-time visitor would naturally explore them, and ends with a short suggested demo

flow.

A. Global Earth Dashboard

A1. Interactive 3D Earth

• A Three.js-powered 3D Earth that users can rotate and explore.

• It introduces the idea of global environmental monitoring: every dataset in the platform describes some part of

this planet.

A2. Interactive Environmental Intelligence Dashboard

• A Leaflet-based interactive map where users select geographical regions.

• Selectable environmental variables include Land Surface Temperature (LST), Precipitation and the

Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), a measure of how green and photosynthetically active

vegetation is.

• Each selection produces a time-series visualization and statistical trend analysis, presenting trend direction,

estimated rate of change and statistical-significance indicators where supported by the selected dataset and

analysis method.

A3. Regional Comparison Tool

• Compare two regions for the same variable side by side.

• It shows that one variable can behave differently in different places, building intuition for regional variation in

Earth’s interconnected environmental systems.

A4. About Data

• Explains where the Earth observation data comes from and introduces the scientific methodology.

• Clarifies the difference between correlation and causation, so users interpret results responsibly.

B. Cairo Climate Analytics Platform

A dedicated, detailed case study of Greater Cairo’s climate, designed to show how environmental trends can be

examined in depth once a place and a long record are chosen.

B1. Overview Dashboard

• Interactive date filtering: the eight Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and charts recalculate for the selected

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:
MARS FRONTIER NAVIGATOR

Complete Project Architecture & Backend Technical Documentation

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

==================================================

  1. PROJECT OVERVIEW
    ==================================================

Project Name: Mars Frontier Navigator

Project Description:

Mars Frontier Navigator is an intelligent navigation platform designed to help astronauts explore the Martian surface safely and efficiently.

The system analyzes geographical data, terrain elevation, slope angles, radiation levels, and potential hazards to calculate the safest and shortest walking routes between two locations on Mars.

The platform also estimates astronaut resource consumption, including oxygen, battery power, and estimated walking time.

Main Objectives:

  • Calculate the safest and shortest walking routes on Mars.
  • Avoid dangerous slopes and hazardous geographical areas.
  • Analyze radiation levels and terrain conditions.
  • Estimate oxygen consumption and battery usage.
  • Provide estimated mission duration.
  • Display geographical information through an interactive map.
  • Provide geographical layers and scientific points of interest.

Technology Stack:

Backend:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Uvicorn
  • Pydantic
  • NumPy
  • Shapely

Database:

  • PostgreSQL
  • PostGIS
  • PostGIS Raster
  • GIST Spatial Indexes

Frontend:

  • React
  • Leaflet
  • TailwindCSS

API Documentation:

  • Swagger UI
  • OpenAPI

│

Database Technology:

  • PostgreSQL: Main relational database.
  • PostGIS: Spatial data storage and geographical queries.
  • PostGIS Raster: Raster-based geographical data support.
  • GIST Indexes: Accelerate spatial queries.

SQL Files:

  1. 01_extensions.sql

Purpose:
Enable the required PostgreSQL extensions.

Required extensions:

  • PostGIS
  • PostGIS Raster
  1. 02_tables_schema.sql

Purpose:
Create the main database tables.

Main data structures:

TERRAIN_GRID:

  • Geographical coordinates.
  • Elevation values.
  • Slope angles.

HAZARD_ZONES:

  • Radiation zones.
  • Rock hazard polygons.
  • Geographical hazard information.

Other logical entities:

  • TILES
  • WAYPOINTS
  • MISSIONS
  1. 03_spatial_indexes.sql

Purpose:
Create GIST spatial indexes to improve the performance of geographical queries.

  1. 04_seed_nasa_data.sql

Purpose:
Insert sample geographical data.

Required reference areas and datasets:

  • Mount Sharp.
  • MOLA data.

Database Responsibilities:

  • Store geographical and terrain information.
  • Store radiation and hazard zones.
  • Support spatial queries.
  • Retrieve geographical information efficiently.
  • Provide data required by the pathfinding engine.

The backend consists of four main layers:

  1. Database Layer
  2. Algorithms and Engine Layer
  3. Models Layer
  4. API Layer

A. DATABASE LAYER

Location:
app/database/

FILE: connection.py

Responsibilities:

  • Establish PostgreSQL connections.
  • Manage database connection pooling.
  • Handle database connection configuration.
  • Provide database access to backend services.

FILE: spatial_queries.py

Responsibilities:

  • Retrieve terrain information using PostGIS.
  • Retrieve geographical elevation data.
  • Detect obstacles and hazardous areas.
  • Calculate geographical distances.
  • Retrieve spatial information required by the pathfinding engine.

B. ALGORITHMS AND ENGINE LAYER

Location:
app/engine/

FILE: grid_builder.py

Purpose:
Convert geographical data retrieved from PostgreSQL/PostGIS into a 2D Grid that can be processed by the pathfinding algorithm.

Responsibilities:

  • Retrieve geographical coordinates.
  • Retrieve elevation and slope information.
  • Convert geographical data into grid cells.
  • Prepare the grid for pathfinding.

FILE: cost_function.py

Purpose:
Calculate the movement cost of each grid cell.

The cost function considers:

  • Distance.
  • Slope angle.
  • Radiation level.

Required cost formula:

Total_Cell_Cost = Distance + (Slope_Angle × 2.5) + (Radiation_mSv × 5.0)

Important Rule:

Any slope greater than 25 degrees must be considered completely dangerous.

Its cost must be set to Infinity so the pathfinding algorithm excludes that cell.

FILE: astar_pathfinder.py

Purpose:
Implement the A* pathfinding algorithm to calculate the safest and shortest route.

Responsibilities:

  • Find an optimal path between starting and ending points.
  • Avoid dangerous slopes.
  • Avoid geographical obstacles.
  • Avoid areas with high radiation.
  • Use the cost function to evaluate possible paths.
  • Return the selected route.

FILE: telemetry_calc.py

Purpose:
Calculate astronaut resource consumption based on the selected route.

Required calculations:

  • Oxygen consumption.
  • Battery consumption.
  • Estimated walking time.

Calculations must consider:

  • Total route distance.
  • Terrain conditions.
  • Slope and route difficulty.

C. MODELS LAYER

Location:
app/models/

FILE: request_models.py

Purpose:
Define the structure of incoming JSON requests.

Required information:

  • Starting point coordinates.
  • Ending point coordinates.
  • Mission type.

FILE: response_models.py

Purpose:
Define the structure of outgoing JSON responses.

Required information:

  • Route coordinates.
  • Elevation information.
  • Total distance.
  • Estimated walking time.
  • Oxygen consumption.
  • Battery consumption.
  • Safety index.
  • Warnings.

D. API LAYER

Location:
app/api/v1/

FILE: router.py

Purpose:
Register and combine all API endpoints.

FILE: path_endpoints.py

Purpose:
Handle path calculation requests.

Main endpoint:

POST /api/v1/pathfinding/calculate

Responsibilities:

  • Receive starting and ending coordinates.
  • Validate the request.
  • Retrieve geographical information.

projectDetails.name: Project METL
projectDetails.summary:
We have created an interactive neuroscience-based game called the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. This uses real NASA data and space exploration to create an educational 3d game. It contains interconnected missions which allow young people to experience what it would be like to become an astronaut. The missions include exploring mars, creating habitats, investigating storms and managing resources. 
 
We have used Series Game Mechanics (SGM) and Neuroscience-Informed SGM (NI-SGM). We have used increasing challenges, interactive simulations, mini games and data dashboards to create an active way to learn, think critically and make decisions. 
 
This project solves the problem by making space science more accessible, engaging and practical for younger generations. The young people can explore real mission situations, analyse data from NASA, interpret scientific evidence and make decisions. 
 
This project is important as it helps to connect real life STEM education with space exploration. This inspires the next generation of scientists, engineers and astrnauts.
projectDetails.details:
The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an educational mission based game which introduces children to space exploration.

This project simplifies complex space science topics and turns them into a mission driven game. Children will become junior astronauts who will go through various scenarios such as exploring Mars, investigating storms, creating habitats and managing resources. Alongside this, they will discover scientific data, analyse images and environmental data, solve problems and make decisions based on the information available.

We have used Series Game Mechanics (SGM) and Neuroscience-Informed Series Game Mechanics (NI-SGM). SGM helps to structure the missions into a learning journey. NI-SGM uses learning theories such as engagement, concentration, feedback and retention.

This project will help to improve scientific knowledge, critical thinking, problem solving, decision making and increase interest in STEM. This will make space science more accessible to children and encourage them to pursue a career in science.

Our project is creative as it uses real NASA resources to create an educational game. We encourage children to engage with the information and use it to solve problems within the missions.

When designing our project we considered the age and level of education of the children. We also considered how easy it would be to access, how scientific it was, how engaging it would be, how challenging the missions would be and how it links to real NASA data.

This project uses NASA resources, scientific data, images and mission information. This can be created using programming and interactive tools to create an engaging

learning environment.

projectDetails.name: Project Midnight Nova
projectDetails.summary:
ChronoGuard is a lunar crew health companion, built as a working web prototype. It helps identify potential fatigue risks in astronauts during long-duration space missions.

On long missions, sleep loss, circadian disruption, and heavy workloads build up gradually and are easy to miss, especially when a fatigued crew member is preparing for a safety-critical task such as a spacewalk. Our project addresses this through the Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions challenge.

ChronoGuard combines sleep records, physiological measurements, and self-reported check-ins. It uses statistical methods to detect deviations from personal baselines and a published fatigue model to estimate sleepiness. When concerning indicators appear, it shows an explainable “Review Suggested” status and lists the contributing factors in plain language. It also offers a mission-aware schedule with light guidance, guided breathing, and an Earth-view grounding page. It does not diagnose; it supports human review and decision-making.

NASA research resources informed the design. In a simulated test, three consecutive short nights before a planned spacewalk triggered a review suggestion.

ChronoGuard is an early prototype tested on example crew records. Its fatigue estimates are not individually calibrated or clinically validated, and its communication feature is a placeholder. Still, it shows how explainable health monitoring could support crew safety on the Moon and beyond.
projectDetails.details:
ChronoGuard lets a crew member log sleep, heart rate, HRV, blood pressure, temperature, mood, sleepiness (KSS) and stress. It compares each night with that person's own baseline using robust z-scores (flagged only if a deviation appears on 2+ consecutive nights) and estimates alertness with the published Three-Process Model (Ingre et al., 2014). When the signs add up, it shows a calm "Review suggested" status with plain-language reasons and a clear "Not a diagnosis" note, pointing to human review such as a flight surgeon. Support tools: a mission schedule with circadian light guidance, countermeasure suggestions, guided breathing and an Earth-view grounding page.

Benefits and impact: it catches fatigue before a safety-critical task like a spacewalk, explains every flag so people can question it, compares each person with their own pattern, and keeps humans in charge. It follows NASA HRR gap BMed-102 (early, pre-clinical indicators of risk).

Tools: Python, FastAPI, SQLModel, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pytest; TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts. No special hardware, just a computer and a web browser.

Creativity: an "Observation Deck" interface with NASA imagery, a Mars-sol mission clock, and "Simple navigation" and "Reduce effects" modes.

Factors considered: explainability, calm wording, personal baselines, and honest limits. It is an early prototype tested on example crew records; the model is not personally calibrated and the status rule is provisional.

projectDetails.name: Mira Quest
projectDetails.summary:
MIRA Quest is an interactive educational web game that brings the stories of NASA’s forgotten machines to life. Designed for children but enjoyable for all ages, it takes players on a journey to Mars and the Moon to meet Opportunity, the Mars rover, and Eagle, the Apollo 11 lunar module.

Through personalized conversations, scientific investigations, interactive challenges, and a collectible photo archive, players explore real NASA discoveries and learn how these missions expanded our understanding of space.

By combining authentic NASA data and imagery with immersive storytelling, MIRA Quest makes space history more accessible, engaging, and memorable, inspiring curiosity about the science and people behind these achievements.
projectDetails.details:
What MIRA Quest does

MIRA Quest is a browser-based storytelling game developed for NASA's Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge. It brings two historic NASA machines to life through interactive exploration, dialogue, scientific discoveries, and player decisions, turning mission history into an engaging adventure.

How a player experiences it

1. Follow a signal. Players enter their names, answer a mysterious transmission, and choose between two signals leading to Mars and the Moon. Each journey includes space travel, an environmental scan, and an interactive search for the machine.

2. Meet Opportunity on Mars. Through personalized dialogue and interactive challenges, players discover how a planned 90-sol mission lasted 5,111 sols. They investigate Martian “blueberries” as evidence of ancient water, examine the rover's scientific instruments, solve a navigation challenge, and explore real NASA photographs documenting its journey. The chapter concludes with the 2018 dust storm and Opportunity's final communications.

3. Meet Eagle on the Moon. Players explore Apollo 11's lunar module, investigate its ascent and descent stages, and discover why part of Eagle remained on the Moon. A simplified landing exercise, historical photographs, and lunar science experiments reveal the engineering behind the first crewed Moon landing.

4. Keep the discoveries. NASA photographs unlock in a collectible archive, where players can enlarge images, read explanations, and revisit discoveries. Completing both missions unlocks a closing tribute to the people behind these achievements.

Educational value and impact

Designed primarily for school-age space enthusiasts but enjoyable for anyone, MIRA Quest introduces scientific facts naturally through storytelling and gameplay. Authentic NASA data supports the educational content, while fictional conversations create an emotional connection to the machines. The goal is to make space exploration more accessible, memorable, and inspiring.

Technology and design

Built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, MIRA Quest features responsive layouts, cinematic visuals, interactive panoramas, image magnification, dialogue choices, mini-games, and locally saved progress. Accessibility features include keyboard navigation, audio controls, and reduced-motion settings. Ambient sound effects enhance the experience without a musical soundtrack.

Scope: The game currently features Opportunity and Eagle. Engineering exercises are simplified for educational purposes, character dialogue is fictional, and AI-generated reconstructions are distinguished from authentic NASA imagery.

challengeDetails.title: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware across the solar system–on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space.
