projectDetails.name: MISSION EL GHEET
projectDetails.summary:
MISSION EL GHEET ("el gheet" is Egyptian Arabic for "the field") is a working web app for the Field Shift challenge. A farmer near Sakha, in Egypt's Nile Delta, plans four seasons on one field by voice or by tapping pictures, in Egyptian Arabic or English.

The farmer starts with what can't change. Say, the last berseem (clover) cut on 20 May, because the cattle need it. Our Promise Test, a fixed set of rules, checks all four seasons against that promise and explains every clash in plain words. If the farmer lets something move, the app looks for options inside those limits and shows at most two.

For each candidate sowing date it compares the same 14 days in every year from 2001 to 2025, using NASA POWER daily weather at that spot. In our example, 28 May and 1 June differ by about 0.3 °C. That's less than the normal swing between years, and the app says so.

A plan is "feasible" only when approved local evidence backs every rule. No local agronomist has signed off our 27 crop rules yet, so the example plan is rejected and both new dates need review. The app doesn't guess.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

MISSION EL GHEET ("el gheet" is Egyptian Arabic for "the field") is a working prototype web app for one field near Sakha, Kafr El-Sheikh, in the Nile Delta. A farmer plans the next four growing seasons by voice or by tapping pictures, in Egyptian Arabic (right to left) or English. The farmer also says what must not change, for example the last berseem (clover) cut on 20 May, because the cattle need it.

The app then runs the Promise Test, a fixed set of rules that checks whether the plan breaks that promise or another hard rule, and says why in plain words. If the farmer allows some things to move, the app searches only inside those permissions, offers at most two alternatives, and shows what the weather was like near each candidate sowing date over 25 past years of NASA POWER data.

Every plan gets one of three results. "rejected" means a rule is clearly broken. "needs_review" means evidence is missing. "feasible" means every required rule is backed by approved evidence. The app never guesses its way to "feasible".

A main use: a protected fodder cut

This is the example we built and tested end to end, with a fictional farmer we call Uncle Hussein (scenario UH-001). His plan: berseem for fodder in winter 2026/27 with the last cut protected on 20 May 2027, then grain maize sown 15 May 2027, then wheat on 20 November, then grain sorghum on 1 June 2028. He lets the maize date move to 28 May or 1 June.

What the running app returns:

- The original plan is rejected (sowing_before_protected_cut). The maize would go in while the field is still kept for the berseem cut.

- Maize on 28 May: needs_review. Maize on 1 June: needs_review. No rule is broken, but the new maize harvest and field-release dates are unknown, and no local crop rule has been approved yet. The app does not make those dates up.

- Feasible alternatives: zero. The protected 20 May cut stays in every option.

Zero is the right answer today. There is no approved local evidence that would prove a full repair, so the app says "no sure alternative", keeps the original plan, and lists what an extension worker would need to check next. Under each result, a "What research says" section shows sourced notes from the reviewed knowledge base for each crop, and marks whether the farmer's date falls before, inside or after the sourced window. These notes are for reading. They never change a plan's status.

How it works

The planner core is a Python package, meg_core, written with the standard library only. Same input, same output. It holds the Promise Test, a bounded search for alternatives (up to 256 combinations by default, and it reports when the search was cut short), and a 12-crop catalogue graded by evidence level.

The agricultural knowledge base has 27 sourced rules for wheat, berseem, grain maize and grain sorghum (release sakha-agricultural-review-2026-11-14.1). Each rule records its source, location, scientific status and approval state. A rule can enforce a result only after local agronomic sign-off. Today 0 of 27 are signed off, which is why results come out rejected or needs_review and never feasible. Where two sources disagree, for example on the wheat sowing window, both are kept and the rule stays blocked.

The app offers the four crops that have reviewed-knowledge-base evidence. The other crops in the catalogue (rice, faba bean, sugar beet, Egyptian cotton, plus watermelon, strawberry, cantaloupe and harankash for information only) are shown greyed out and can't be picked yet.

The backend is a FastAPI REST API with SQLite storage. It turns the farmer's answers into a planner input, runs the Promise Test, saves an evidence card as a review draft, and renders every message from bilingual templates, each with a written form and a spoken form (numbers spelled out in Egyptian Arabic words). The frontend is a React app built for phone screens: picture tiles, push-to-talk speech input through the browser, and a spoken read-back of every fact before checking, including the unknown ones ("Berseem sowing date: unknown").

Data, and how it supports the use

We use NASA POWER daily data (Daily API v2.10.3, community AG) at 31.10°N, 30.95°E near Sakha, for 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2025: daily maximum and minimum temperature, dew point, humidity, wind, solar radiation, surface pressure and corrected precipitation. The raw files are stored with SHA-256 checksums, fill values (-999) are rejected, and all 9,131 daily rows were checked for gaps and duplicates. The app verifies checksums before use and never downloads data at run time.

From that record we compute FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0) and a seasonal climatology (2001-2018, 10th/50th/90th percentile per calendar day).

Season Replay uses this for the main example. For each candidate sowing date it takes the same 14-day window in every year from 2001 to 2025 and compares them. For the 28 May and 1 June windows, mean daily maximum temperature was 36.59 °C and 36.90 °C. The 0.30 °C gap is smaller than the year-to-year spread (standard deviation 1.33 and 1.51 °C), and the later window was hotter in 14 of 25 years, close to a coin toss. 14-day ET0 was 119.0 mm against 119.6 mm. So the weather gives no strong reason to prefer either date, and the screen says that. It also says "Historical 14-day planting-window comparison, not a full crop-season analysis".

ET0 is how much water the air would pull from a standard grass surface. It is not the crop's water use and not an irrigation amount, and the app labels it "Not irrigation". Weather results never change a plan's status.

We also tested machine-learning forecasts. A simple seasonal climatology beat both a Ridge regression (2019-2021 validation, daily max temperature MAE 2.53 °C for climatology against 2.58 °C for Ridge) and the Chronos-2 foundation model with LoRA fine-tuning (July-October 2026 holdout, 1.66 °C against 1.99 °C). So the app uses climatology for "typical conditions". Forecasting is an experimental side channel, and no forecast can decide whether a plan is feasible.

What works today, and how we checked it

Working in the delivered code: four-season plan entry in Arabic and English, by voice or taps; the Promise Test with protected commitments and reasons; bounded alternatives within the farmer's permissions; "What research says" notes; Season Replay with climatology; the bilingual evidence card saved as a review draft. The app also runs without a backend, using a labelled development adapter that replays real planner output for the UH-001 example only.

Checks we ran on 14 November 2026: planner 118 tests OK (3 skipped); backend 81 passed, 1 skipped; frontend typecheck, 30 unit tests and production build pass. The Season Replay numbers for UH-001 match an independent recomputation from the NASA POWER file to within 1e-14. The full UH-001 journey was clicked through in a browser against the running backend at 12 screen widths (360-1440 px), in both languages.

For a public demo the backend has per-client rate limits, request-size caps and a daily ceiling on voice calls. The app is public at https://mission-el-gheet.vercel.app/ (frontend on Vercel, backend on Render). It also runs on any laptop, CPU only, with no internet needed at run time; the commands are in AGENTS.md.

Next

Field tests with farmers near Sakha. Formal review and sign-off of the 27 rules by Sakha experts. Asking for harvest and field-release dates in the app. Adding more crops only once they have approved local calendars. Native Arabic review, real recorded voice and real crop pictures. Adding NASA GPM rainfall and MODIS field history. Later, other areas of the Delta.

Tools, languages, hardware

Python 3.12 (planner, climate code, backend). FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn and SQLite for the API. TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8 and Tailwind CSS 4 for the frontend, with the browser Web Speech API for speech input. Optional services: Google Gemini API (reading a spoken answer; its output is checked by fixed rules and confirmed by the farmer) and ElevenLabs (75 Arabic voice clips, generated offline). Data science: Python scripts for the NASA POWER download, FAO-56 ET0 and climatology, plus Ridge and Chronos-2 experiments for research only. Testing: pytest, unittest, Vitest, Playwright for screenshots. Dependencies are exact-pinned with hashed lock files and a 14-day minimum package age. Git and GitHub. Ordinary Windows and Linux laptops, CPU only.

projectDetails.name: Project MISSION ODYSSEY
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Odyssey is a browser game that trains children aged 7-12 to think like a real space crew. The child commands Gale Station, a small base for four crew in Gale Crater on Mars, the crater where NASA's Curiosity rover works.

In Mission 01, "The Missing Cargo" (about 8-12 minutes), the child inspects the base's oxygen, water, power and weather, reacts to a real solar radiation alert, drives a rover through a boulder field to a supply lander, and must choose one crate out of five, because the rover can carry only one. The game then runs the base forward one Mars day (sol) at a time and shows what that choice meant: for example, "food runs out on sol 23; resupply arrives on sol 26."

This answers the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge by letting children practise what a crew does on a mission: observe, decide under limits, and live with the consequences. The consequences are calculated from NASA numbers: crew oxygen, water and food use from NASA's life-support reference (BVAD), radiation measured by Curiosity, and nine real solar events from NASA's DONKI database, including whether the real forecast came in time. Every number in the game is labelled as NASA measured, NASA forecast, NASA model, NASA reference, Calculated, or Game rule, so children also learn the difference between a measurement and a game rule.

Mission Odyssey teaches children through real decision-making and visible consequences. It supports Arabic and English, two age modes.
projectDetails.details:
Mission Odyssey is a 3D browser game for children aged 7-12. Before playing, the child picks English or Arabic and an age mode: Cadet (7-9, simple words) or Commander (10-12, adds science units). Noor, a friendly robot base assistant, guides the child throughout with voiced lines and subtitles that are always on.

Mission 01, "The Missing Cargo", has 8 phases:

1. Read the briefing.

2. Inspect the base: oxygen, water, power, weather. The greenhouse and antenna are optional stops.

3. Survive a solar particle (radiation) alert.

4. Prepare the rover.

5. Drive about 90 m through a boulder field.

6. Choose ONE of five crates. The rover carries only one.

7. Return to base.

8. Install the crate and send a report, then see the debrief.

Each run hides one of three faults (leaking water recycler, failing battery cells, or broken greenhouse lights) and replays one of nine real NASA solar-event days, giving 27 combinations. The mission can fail if oxygen runs out or CO2 reaches 2.00 kPa, the emergency level quoted in NASA's BVAD, and the game explains why.

MAIN USE: THE CARGO DECISION (input, process, output)

- Input: what the child observed during inspection (for example "Grow lights: LED driver failed"), the resource status, and optionally Mission Control's advice if the child fixed the antenna.

- Process: the child picks one crate. The game runs the same outpost simulation forward, sol by sol, using NASA BVAD crew rates (for example 0.895 kg of oxygen per crew member per day) with every system as the child left it.

- Output: a debrief with a 26-sol outlook (for example "food runs out on sol 23; resupply arrives on sol 26"), the real problem at the base, every decision made, the radiation dose, a score, and "What you learned" cards with NASA sources.

HOW THE DATA SUPPORTS IT

The trade-offs run on NASA's own numbers, so a wrong choice fails for the same reason it would on a real mission.

- Radiation decision: everyone to the shelter (lowest dose, but about 2 hours lost while a dust storm approaches), crew to the shelter while the child works outside (higher personal dose), or everyone keeps working (no time lost, higher dose for all). In our test runs the simulated crew dose was about 64 microgray with the shelter versus about 141 microgray when working. Normal outdoor radiation (6.40 microgray per hour) comes from Curiosity's RAD detector.

- Real forecast timing: with the antenna fixed, the warning time equals the real lead time of that archived DONKI event (first REleASE forecast versus first SOHO detection): +25, -19, +93, -4, -14, +152 and -12 minutes, with no forecast on two days. If the real forecast was late or missing, the child gets no warning, and the game explains why.

- Other trade-offs: charging the rover uses 8 kWh of base power; folding the solar panels protects them from dust but makes less power; switching off grow lights saves power but hurts crops; fixing the antenna brings Mission Control's advice after a 12-minute delay. Causes chain together: dusty panels mean less power, the CO2 scrubber shuts down, and CO2 reaches the danger level within about 6 sols in the outlook.

WORKING FEATURES (verified in play-testing on 14 November)

- Two age modes: Cadet and Commander.

- Kid-friendly status bar: each resource shows a word and a shape (OK / Low / Danger), not colour alone; time left as "N sols left"; units behind a "Units" button; one-time explainer cards for sol, EVA and dose; a kid question above each objective ("Do we have enough air?").

- English and Arabic, with a full right-to-left layout.

- Noor: 77 voice lines, subtitles always on, hints after 45 seconds without progress, 11 verified science facts, mute and volume controls. Audio is built in, with no text-to-speech or internet at run time.

- Cinematic scenes: intro, radiation alert, cargo choice, mission success or failure.

- Data honesty: every number carries a badge (NASA measured / NASA forecast / NASA model / NASA reference / Calculated / Game rule), and a "NASA Science & Data" page lists each dataset, its limits, its validation status and all game assumptions.

- Debrief cards with NASA research: fresh food in space (OSDR OSD-745), crew health (Inspiration4; the card says the game calculates no health effects), and Mars versus ISS radiation (Mars about 0.15-0.31 mGy/day from Curiosity RAD, ISS about 0.20-0.36 mGy/day from OSDR EDA, both labelled detector dose).

- Offline version: one file of about 5 MB with all voice files and images, making no external requests. In an offline test, all 5 bundled datasets validated at start-up.

EVIDENCE

- 75/75 unit tests pass; TypeScript typecheck passes; lint shows 0 errors.

- Scripted browser play-through (end-to-end test) passes 45/45.

- No console errors during manual play.

- Playtest with children.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React 19, three.js with @react-three/fiber and drei (3D world), Zustand (game state and saving), Tailwind CSS 4, Vite 8 with vite-plugin-singlefile (offline build), Vitest and oxlint (testing). Python with requests, pypdf, netCDF4 and numpy for the NASA data pipeline and verification scripts. No special hardware: a desktop or laptop with a modern browser.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

- Children learn by deciding, not only by reading.

- They see why life-support numbers matter: one choice changes how many sols the crew can last.

- They learn to tell a measurement from a model, a forecast and a game rule.

- Arabic-speaking children can play the whole game in their own language, and schools with weak internet can use the offline file.

KNOWN LIMITS (this is a prototype)

- Only Mission 01 is playable.

- Designed for desktop or laptop with keyboard and mouse.

- Outdoor temperatures come from the NASA Ames Mars climate model, not measurements at Gale Crater.

- Radiation values are detector dose, not body dose. The game calculates no health effects.

- DONKI solar events were measured near Earth, not at Mars; the game uses them as real examples of solar events and forecast timing.

- Noor's English voice is a placeholder made with Windows speech synthesis.

FUTURE PLANS

- Replace modelled temperatures with measured temperatures from Curiosity's REMS weather station.

- Mission 2, "The Long Storm".

- A silent robot exploration companion as a Mission 2 reward (it will not carry a second crate, because the one-crate limit is the core lesson).

- A lunar south-pole mission using Moon Trek illumination and Earth-visibility layers.

- A teacher guide.

- Touch play on tablets and phones.

projectDetails.name: HotOrNot
projectDetails.summary: Hot or Not is a web app that answers one question for any area in four fire-prone regions: is this place burning more than usual? It turns NASA FIRMS fire detections into one consistent monthly record from 2000 to today. The challenge is that two NASA sensors count fires differently. VIIRS, with its sharper 375 m pixels, detects 3 to 10 times as many fires as the older MODIS, so simply joining their records makes fires seem to explode in 2012. We studied 908,862 VIIRS fires that MODIS also looked at within 15 minutes, learned how likely MODIS was to see each one, and weight every VIIRS detection by that chance and a regional factor. Tested on years the model never saw (2012-2019), yearly totals land within 2.9 to 11.3% of MODIS. That is 5.6% on average, against 11.4% for a simple ratio. With MODIS retiring and S-NPP's fire data ending on 2 November 2026, the record continues on NOAA-20, within 3% of S-NPP. Draw any area and get a burning calendar and a verdict: HOT, NORMAL or NOT.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
Hot or Not shows how much an area burns, month by month, from 2000 to today, on one consistent scale. Pick one of four demo regions (Nile Delta, California and Nevada, south-east Australia, northern Argentina and the Paraguayan Chaco), draw your own area on the map, or type coordinates. You then see:

  • a verdict for the latest month, HOT, NORMAL or NOT, ranked against the same days in every year since 2003
  • a calendar of every month since 2000, as fire counts or compared with normal
  • every fire detection behind the numbers as a dot on the map, with its satellite, time and fire power, and how much it counts
  • a chart of every year, where a click shows all of that year's fires

The data can be downloaded as CSV. A guided "Tell me the story" tour and a "How it works" page with interactive diagrams explain the method to non-experts, and give scientists the full test results.

How it works

  1. Download: about 13.1 million fire detections from NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 on Terra and Aqua; VIIRS 375 m on S-NPP and NOAA-20), plus NASA CMR overpass records, so we know when each satellite was looking.
  2. Clean: remove duplicates and non-vegetation heat sources such as gas flares, using NASA's labels. For recent unlabelled data, also remove detections near known flares or seen at the same spot on 20 or more days in 90.
  3. Match: from 2012 to 2019, find the 908,862 S-NPP VIIRS fires that Aqua MODIS looked at within 15 minutes, and note whether MODIS saw each one.
  4. Learn: a logistic regression on VIIRS-side features (fire radiative power, pixel size, day or night, land cover, cluster size) predicts how likely MODIS is to see a fire. A coverage factor per region and month adds the looks MODIS had that VIIRS lacks, such as Terra's morning pass.
  5. Weigh and add up: each VIIRS fire counts as its weight, and fires add up per month on a 0.05 degree (about 5 km) grid.
  6. Test: hide two years at a time, predict them, and compare with real MODIS counts. The model ships only if it beats a simple ratio method. It did, in 4 of 4 regions.
  7. Publish: a small database and compressed map tiles that the web app reads.

Benefits and intended impact
Anyone can ask whether a fire season is unusual without remote-sensing expertise: journalists, farm cooperatives, environment and air-quality agencies, researchers, students. The 26-year record stays comparable across sensor changes, which matters now that MODIS is retiring and S-NPP stopped sending fire data. It can show the effect of policies. For example, autumn rice-straw burning in the Nile Delta, the source of Cairo's "black cloud", fell from about 500 detections a year (2003-2016) to about 215 (2017-2025). Every number can be traced to the dots behind it, and the method and its tests are public.

Tools

  • Pipeline: Python 3.12 (standard library only) and SQLite.
  • Web app: Node.js 24 built-ins and plain JavaScript (no framework, no build step), MapLibre GL, Apache ECharts, Terra Draw, the OpenFreeMap basemap, and IBM Plex Sans.
  • Hosting: a Linux VPS with systemd and Caddy.
  • Automated tests check the pipeline and the app.
  • Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding assistant) helped write and test the code and documentation, under the team's direction.
  • No hardware.

What is creative about it

  • Instead of one fixed ratio, every VIIRS fire gets its own weight, so small fires count less and big ones more, and the correction adapts to place and season.
  • A one-word verdict (HOT, NORMAL, NOT) and a calendar heatmap make 26 years readable at a glance.
  • "How it works" lets readers follow one real day (13 September 2017, Nile Delta) through every step, and watch a gas flare get caught.
  • The dots on the map are the same data as the calendar, so the numbers can be checked.

Factors we considered

  • Honest testing: the model is checked on years it never saw. We report where it is weaker: on 2020-2025, the simple ratio does better, partly because MODIS orbits have drifted.
  • Sensor handovers: S-NPP's fire data ended on 2 November 2026. NOAA-20 carries on, calibrated to agree within 3%.
  • Gas flares versus real fires.
  • Gaps shown as "no data", never as zero, for example the Bolivian and Brazilian parts of the Chaco region.
  • Recent months marked as provisional.
  • Plain language, keyboard access, colour-blind-safe colours, and phone layouts.
  • Current limits: four demo regions. Covering any place on Earth is the next step.

projectDetails.name: TerraMatch
projectDetails.summary:
TerraMatch is an interactive planetary exploration platform designed to support the identification and evaluation of potential landing sites on the Moon and Mars. It connects extraterrestrial landscapes with similar environments on Earth, helping users better understand planetary geology and surface conditions.

The platform features an interactive 3D planetary globe, allowing users to explore candidate landing locations and examine their environmental characteristics. Its Terrestrial Twin system identifies Earth locations with comparable geological and environmental features, while comparison metrics highlight similarities in terrain, mineralogy, climate, and other relevant factors.

TerraMatch also presents key mission-planning indicators, including solar illumination, landing feasibility, surface conditions, and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) potential. An AI-powered Mission Analyst provides interactive scientific briefings and helps users explore mission-related questions.

By combining interactive visualization, planetary data resources, Earth-based analogues, and AI-assisted analysis, TerraMatch aims to make planetary exploration concepts more accessible and support preliminary research into future lunar and Martian missions.
projectDetails.details: TerraMatch – Interactive Planetary Landing Site Analysis 1. Project Overview TerraMatch is an interactive planetary exploration platform designed to support the preliminary analysis of potential landing sites on the Moon and Mars. It provides a unified environment where users can explore planetary surfaces, compare geological characteristics, and understand factors that may influence future exploration missions. 2. The Problem Selecting suitable landing locations for future lunar and Martian missions requires understanding several complex factors, including surface topography, slope, roughness, solar illumination, environmental conditions, and available resources. Scientific information is often distributed across different tools and datasets, making it difficult for users to explore and compare these factors in one accessible environment. 3. Our Solution TerraMatch brings these exploration concepts together through an interactive platform that combines 3D planetary visualization, Earth-based analog comparisons, and mission-planning indicators. 4. Main Features - Interactive 3D Planetary Globe: Explore the Moon and Mars, switch between planetary environments, and select candidate landing locations. - Terrestrial Twin Matching: Compare extraterrestrial locations with similar environments on Earth, such as Shackleton Crater, Jezero Crater, Taurus-Littrow Valley, Mauna Kea, and the Pilbara region. - Environmental Comparison Metrics: Present comparisons involving geology, mineralogy, climate, sediments, and terrain characteristics. - Solar Illumination Analysis: Explore lighting conditions and their potential implications for solar-powered missions. - Landing Feasibility Assessment: Present indicators related to slope, surface roughness, and potential landing hazards. - ISRU Potential: Explore the potential availability of locally useful resources, including water-related materials, carbon dioxide, and lunar resources. - Official Mission Resources: Provide access to NASA's Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap, JPL Horizons, and the Canadian Space Agency's lunar exploration resources. - AI Mission Analyst: Generate interactive mission briefings and explore questions related to landing risks, energy systems, and planetary exploration. 5. Expected Impact TerraMatch aims to make planetary exploration more accessible by bringing important exploration concepts into one interactive interface. It can serve as an educational and preliminary research tool for students, space enthusiasts, and researchers interested in future lunar and Martian exploration. 6. Development Approach The platform was developed as an interactive web application, combining 3D visualization, user-interface design, planetary exploration concepts, external scientific resources, and AI-assisted development.

projectDetails.name: MOONSDAY - Dr Moon
projectDetails.summary:
DR. MOON is a spaceflight wellness project designed to explain astronaut health and mission challenges. It brings research, crew self-reports, learning, and motivation into a mission-control interface, while making the limits of its data clear.
The website includes a mission dashboard, interactive astronaut body map, telemetry charts, NASA and CSA educational resources, spaceflight hazards, analytics, settings, training checklists, and a rewards store. The prototype hardware is not working, so vital and habitat readings are fixed fictional examples, labeled as simulated—not real astronaut or NASA data. NASA sources guide context, but do not provide the fictional sample readings. Users can report mood, stress, sleep, symptoms, and activity. Each check-in generates a non-diagnostic summary from the user’s answers; reports remain separate from telemetry.
Users can log workouts, mission tasks, and learning activities to earn points and spend them on humorous digital badges. The integrated local Ollama AI works online or offline and answers educational questions about human health in spaceflight.
Future work includes repairing and connecting the MAX30102 and DHT22, validating real sensor readings, and replacing fictional examples only when trustworthy data is available. DR. MOON is educational, not a medical device or diagnostic system.
projectDetails.details:
DR. MOON is a spaceflight wellness and education platform that helps people explore astronaut health, mission routines, and the challenges of living in space. Its mission-control-style interface brings together educational research, crew self-reports, an AI assistant, training activities, and rewards.

What it does and how it works

The dashboard and interactive astronaut body map present health-related information, while the telemetry pages demonstrate how sensor readings could be displayed. Since our prototype hardware is not currently working, these readings are fixed fictional examples, clearly labeled as simulated—not real astronaut measurements or NASA data. NASA and Canadian Space Agency materials inform the educational context, not the sample values.

Users can voluntarily report their mood, stress, sleep, symptoms, and activity. After submission, the site displays a non-diagnostic summary based only on the user’s own answers. Check-in responses remain separate from the simulated telemetry. Users can also complete learning checklists or log workouts and mission tasks to earn local points, then spend those points on humorous digital badges. The integrated Ollama AI assistant answers educational questions about human health in spaceflight and is designed to work with the project’s online or offline setup.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes spaceflight health topics more approachable and interactive. It demonstrates how educational content, self-reported wellbeing, AI, and gamification can support engagement while making data limitations visible. Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about astronaut health and responsible technology—not to diagnose, treat, or replace professional medical support.

Tools and technology

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules for the website, with a Node.js backend for the application’s local services and Ollama for the AI assistant. The planned hardware includes a MAX30102 optical pulse/oxygen-saturation sensor and a DHT22 ambient temperature/humidity sensor. These sensors are not currently providing working data; repairing and validating the hardware integration is future work.

Creativity and design considerations

The project combines a cinematic space-console interface with an interactive astronaut illustration, NASA- and CSA-informed learning, conversational AI, self-check-ins, and playful rewards. We considered privacy, offline use, clear source labels, the difference between user reports and sensor readings, and the risk of presenting simulated data as real. For that reason, demo values are explicitly labeled, check-ins are described as self-reported, and the wellness summary is not presented as a medical diagnosis.

projectDetails.name: TerraLunaMars
projectDetails.summary:
**ENGLISH (about 200 words)**

TerraLunaMars is a screening model that studies candidate Moon and Mars sites by comparing them with well-documented analogue sites on Earth, using open NASA, ESA and USGS data.

The problem: choosing where to land or build on the Moon or Mars requires knowing slope, surface texture, rock type and thermal extremes. Field study is impossible before a mission, and orbital data is hard to interpret without a familiar reference.

Our solution: we compare each target with a geologically similar site on Earth, so terrain can be examined on the ground, not only from orbit. We built two pairs: Flaugergues Crater on Mars with the Lut Desert in Iran, and the Gruithuisen Domes on the Moon with Sugarloaf Dome in Arizona.

Method: we used MOLA, LOLA and Copernicus DEM GLO-30 data, resampled each pair to one grid and window, and computed relief, slope, roughness and elevation scatter in Python.

Results: Mars and Lut reached 86.3% topographic similarity, and Moon and Sugarloaf 74.1%. Lut is best framed as a hyper-arid wind-erosion analogue, not a thermal one.

Limitations: 68.4% of the Mars window is interpolated, and gravity, atmosphere and temperature differ. This is a screening tool, not proof of equivalence.

Code, report and results: github.com/nil258199-coder/TerraLunaMars
projectDetails.details: What does the project do? TerraLunaMars is a screening model for Moon and Mars sites. It compares each target with a geologically similar site on Earth, using open terrain data, so planners can understand slope, roughness, relief and rock context from a familiar reference. We built two pairs: Flaugergues Crater (Mars) with the Lut Desert (Iran), and the Gruithuisen Domes (Moon) with Sugarloaf Dome (Arizona). How does it work? We select comparable sites, assemble open NASA MOLA, LRO LOLA and ESA Copernicus GLO-30 elevation data, and resample each pair to one grid and analysis window. Python then computes relief, slope, local roughness (after removing the regional trend) and elevation scatter. Similarity per metric is S = 100 x (1 - |a - b| / max(|a|, |b|)). We also scored 19 indicators across geology, topography, temperature and mineralogy, and combined them into an equal-weight index. What are its benefits? It gives a consistent first screening step before mission resources are committed. Anyone can recompute, audit and challenge the metrics. It also bridges terrestrial field geology with planetary data, and it shows clearly which aspects match (topography, wind erosion) and which do not (temperature). What is the intended impact? To help narrow where to look and which hypotheses to test for future Moon and Mars landing or base sites, such as the Gruithuisen Domes, the planned Lunar-VISE target in 2027. It does not replace mission data. Its impact is making questions about other worlds measurable and open to verification. Tools, languages, devices and software used Python (NumPy, including numpy.gradient for slope) for the terrain metrics, Google Colab for running the analysis, and GIS for the initial comparison. Data: NASA PDS (MOLA MEGDR, LRO LOLA), ESA Copernicus DEM GLO-30, USGS Astrogeology, NASA Earth Observatory. Gemini NotebookLM helped organise sources and slides, Claude supported coding and drafting, and Manus accelerated the interface and code build. GitHub hosts the report, atlas and results. How is the project creative, and what factors did the team consider? The idea links three bodies (Terra, Luna, Mars) through Earth analogues, turning hard-to-read orbital numbers into something familiar. We considered scientific honesty throughout: a strict same-grid rule so results measure the ground, not the grid; clear labels separating computed values from literature estimates; open reporting of limits (68.4% of the Mars window is interpolated, window size affects results, gravity, atmosphere and temperature differ); and bilingual English-Arabic material so the work is accessible. We also chose the analogue’s process, not the planet, as the basis for comparison.

projectDetails.name: NABD: Daily Health Check-ins for Astronauts Far From Earth
projectDetails.summary: NABD ("pulse" in Arabic) is a daily health check-in for astronauts on missions too far from Earth to call a doctor, built for the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". In 4 minutes, a phone reads the astronaut's face, voice and reaction time, compares them with her own normal, and gives four readiness scores with one concrete step for today. It adds a body map grounded in NASA's human spaceflight risks, an AI doctor that works with the ship's medical kit and flags emergencies even offline, private women's health tracking, and family contact. Mission Control and the flight surgeon each see only what their role needs. It matters because small changes in sleep, mood and health build up quietly, and astronauts often don't report them; NABD catches them early. It is also useful anywhere help is far away.

TRY IT: https://nabd-nasa-space-apps.vercel.app (best on a phone; on a laptop use Chrome → Inspect → device mode for the crew app. Mission Control and the flight surgeon are designed for laptops.)

Crew: tap Sara Haddad, PIN 1404 (also Adam 2201, Mei 3302, Lucas 4403). Mission Control: any email and password. Flight surgeon: after Mission Control, go to /surgeon. Family: /send. Code: https://github.com/malakanwarr/Nabd-NASA-Space-Apps

NABD (نبض, "pulse" in Arabic) is a daily health check-in for astronauts who are too far from Earth to call a doctor. Team MoonWalkerz · NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 · Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.

THE PROBLEM

On a Mars mission a message to Earth takes up to 20 minutes each way. The flight surgeon cannot see the crew every day, and NASA notes that astronauts can be reluctant to report when they are struggling. Small changes in sleep, mood, bone and heart build up quietly until they become a problem.

WHAT EXACTLY DOES IT DO?

NABD is one web app (installable on a phone, works offline) with four views, each built for one person's job:

- Crew member: a 4-minute morning check-in that reads her face (blink rate, eyelid openness, smiles), her voice (loudness, pitch range, pauses, pace) and her reactions (the Pollen catch game, based on NASA's vigilance test), plus six sleep questions. NABD compares every number with her own normal and returns four separate scores, never one diagnosis: cognitive readiness, physical readiness, sleep recovery and emotional wellbeing. Each is shown as Stable, Watch or Act, with the reason, a 7-day trend and one next step.

- Body map: a clickable astronaut with eight body systems (bones and muscles, mind and sleep, kidneys, heart, eyes, immune system, radiation, cycle). Each shows what it does, why space affects it and its NASA hazard, her own numbers and trend, what to do today, and when to get help.

- Act on it: "Adjust my workout" builds a plan from her muscle strength, energy and cycle, and a muscle "twin" does every move with her. Guided measurements (for example blood sugar) explain how to measure in space and what the result means.

- AI doctor that works without Earth: answers with her own data and the ship's medical kit, cites NASA research, never diagnoses, and shows an emergency banner with "Call the crew medical officer" for danger signs, checked before the AI is even called. She decides which answers go to her flight surgeon.

- No male default: private cycle tracking or period suppression that adjusts what counts as normal for each phase. Only she sees it.

- Habitat garden: sleep, water, exercise, vitamin D and mood become plants that grow or droop.

- Family: relatives hold one button to send a hug that makes her phone buzz, and see only her heartbeat and a simple mood. She has a "window home" with her family's avatars and messages.

- Mission Control (laptop): every crew member's status, readiness, last check-in and alerts, with filters and "add crew member". It never sees cycle data, face or voice details, or AI doctor chats.

- Flight surgeon (laptop): vitals, allergies and the AI doctor's notes with their send and arrival times, the cycle summary only with consent, and replies that show "reaches the ship in about 18 minutes".

HOW DOES IT WORK?

- On the phone, offline: Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker runs in the browser and turns about 10 frames a second into three numbers; the voice check (Meyda and pitchy) keeps four numbers from the first word to the last. Video and audio never leave the phone.

- Her own baseline: each score drops by how far each signal moves in the "tired" direction, weighted, with missing signals dropped and the rest reweighted. It reproduces all six days of our sample astronaut's history exactly (84, 82, 83, 74, 70, 66).

- AI doctor: Google Gemini with a summary of her data and a knowledge base built from NASA Human Research Program material; red flags are checked on the server first; safe fallback if the AI is unavailable.

- One React app and one Node/Express server with MongoDB, deployed on Vercel. The signed-in role (crew, Mission Control, flight surgeon, family) decides every page and every API answer.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- The astronaut notices slow changes she might not report, and gets a concrete step for today.

- Mission Control sees who needs attention at a glance; the flight surgeon gets useful notes despite the delay.

- Privacy by design: each role sees only what it should.

- Beyond Mars: anyone far from a doctor (polar stations, ships, remote communities) needs only a phone.

HOW WE TESTED IT

- Energy score matches all six sample days of our fictional astronaut.

- Fatigue experiment: we tested NABD on one team member, on Friday afternoon (her baseline) and again on Saturday morning after a 13-hour hackathon day and about 6 hours of sleep. Against her own normal, NABD labelled the second check-in "tired" (72 vs. 84): 6 of 8 signals moved in the tired direction, led by smiling (-80%) and voice pitch range (-62%).

- AI doctor safety tests: 10 scripted questions, each run twice; 10 of 10 passed both runs. Chest pain and low oxygen always gave the emergency answer first; it refused amoxicillin (penicillin allergy) and doses above the label; it linked symptoms to her own data and cited NASA correctly. The emergency word check, which works without the AI, was 20 of 20 correct with no false alarms. Offline mode gave 3 of 3 safe answers in 0.2 seconds.

- Face, voice and game check-in tested on iPhone over HTTPS.

Limits: a prototype, not a medical device; thresholds need clinical testing. Sara's history is fictional sample data, with vitals and sleep standing in for the wearables crews already wear; the check-in, game, AI doctor and hugs are live. Sign-in is simulated. The fatigue test is one person, one night and a different time of day: a first signal, not proof.

WHAT DO WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE?

Test with analog crews (HERA, Antarctic stations), run the AI doctor on the spacecraft with a local model, connect real wearables, and review every threshold with flight surgeons.

INTENDED IMPACT

Catch health changes days before they become a problem, when no doctor is in reach, and give the crew, Mission Control and the flight surgeon the right picture without overloading or exposing anyone. The same phone-only check-in can serve polar stations, ships and remote communities on Earth.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?

- No wearables or lab needed: a 4-minute check-in on any phone reads fatigue from face, voice and a reaction game.

- Compared with HER normal, not a population average, and never one diagnosis: four scores, each with a reason and one step.

- An AI doctor designed for 20-minute delays: it uses only the ship's kit, cites NASA, and catches emergencies with a keyword check before the AI and even offline.

- No male default: the cycle adjusts what counts as normal, privately.

- Human touches that matter on long missions: a garden that grows with healthy habits, and family hugs that make her phone buzz.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Privacy: video and audio never leave the phone, and each role sees only what it should (Mission Control never sees cycle, face/voice details or AI chats; the surgeon sees the cycle only with consent).

- Safety: no diagnosis, label doses only, allergy checks, emergency escalation to the crew medical officer, and a tested offline fallback.

- Communication delay and no internet: works offline; surgeon replies show their arrival time.

- Under-reporting: a short, friendly daily routine instead of asking astronauts to report problems.

- Women's health and the fact that crews differ: personal baselines and cycle-aware norms.

- Honesty: we label sample data, simulated sign-in and the limits of our small tests.

TOOLS

React, Vite, React Router, vite-plugin-pwa, Recharts · Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker, Web Audio API, Meyda, pitchy · Node.js, Express, MongoDB Atlas, Mongoose, Vercel · Google Gemini API · JavaScript, HTML, CSS · Hardware: any phone with a camera and microphone, and a laptop. AI assistance: Claude and Claude Code (planning, design, code), Gemini (AI doctor), Manus (documents); all ideas and decisions are the team's.

projectDetails.name: Sonata
projectDetails.summary:
SONATA (Earth Information Jukebox) is a web app that turns NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model data into music, so people can hear the ocean instead of only looking at it. Each ocean metric is mapped to its own instrument, and users can toggle instruments on and off to hear how different measurements change across place and time.

It addresses the challenge by making complex Earth data approachable through sound. A scientific mode keeps the audio faithful to the data. A separate fun mode allows freer tuning and instruments, and lets users bring in their own musical taste. Users can choose a location and share what they hear as a short clip.

It matters because most ocean data is locked behind charts and maps. SONATA treats visually impaired users as a primary audience, with keyboard and screen reader access, a live data readout, audio cues, panning, and text equivalents, and it passes accessibility checks with zero violations. Sound makes ocean change easier to understand for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

SONATA turns NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model data into sound. Each ocean metric [confirm which, e.g. temperature, salinity, currents, sea surface height] is mapped to its own instrument, and users can toggle instruments on and off to hear how different measurements change across place and time. A scientific mode keeps the audio faithful to the data. A separate fun mode allows freer tuning and instrument choices, and lets users select or import music they like to shape the output. Users can pick a location, hear its ocean data, and share the result as a clip, card, or animation.

Benefits

  • Makes dense ocean data easier to grasp by ear, without needing to read charts or maps.
  • Works for curious people with no science background and for visually impaired users.
  • Lets people connect to ocean change in a personal way, through a place they know or music they like.
  • Gives everyone a shareable output, so the data spreads beyond the app.

Intended impact

We want more people to engage with NASA ocean data and understand what it says about a changing planet. Treating visually impaired users as a primary audience widens who can access this data at all. A clip someone can send to a friend turns a single visit into a conversation about the ocean and climate.

Tools and technology

  • Data: NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model
  • Development: mostly AI-assisted (vibe-coded), starting once the UI/UX design was ready
  • Hosting: sonata.manus.space
  • Accessibility testing: axe-core, with 0 violations on the latest checkpoint
  • [Add framework, language, and audio engine, e.g. Web Audio API, if that is what you used]
  • [Add the design and video tools used by the UI/UX and motion graphics members]

Creativity

  • Sonification of a global ocean model, with one instrument per metric that users can mix like a band.
  • Two modes, so scientific accuracy and playful exploration each get what they need.
  • “Local” works at two levels: local to a place and local to a person’s own musical taste.
  • Accessibility is built into the core experience through keyboard and screen reader access, a live readout, audio cues, panning, and text equivalents.

Factors the team considered

  • Audience: a core experience for curious people first, with visually impaired users as a second priority but a primary group.
  • Scientific integrity: culture and personal taste must never distort the data-driven audio, which is why they live only in fun mode. We dropped the maqam idea for this reason and because judges may not be invested in Arabic music.
  • Team skills: we have no musician, so the design had to work without deep musical expertise.
  • Scope and time: we restarted the core engine from scratch to get a presentable demo on a clear dataset within the hackathon window.

projectDetails.name: SPACE TALES
projectDetails.summary:
Space Tales: Chronicles of the Cosmos

Space Tales is an interactive educational web application that brings the forgotten history of space exploration back to life. It explores 13 historic space missions and their equipment, including Apollo 11, Surveyor 1, Viking, and Voyager.

Through engaging first-person storytelling, audio narration, and educational visuals, users discover the journeys, achievements, and historical significance of spacecraft and scientific equipment left behind after their missions.

The platform combines four interactive experiences: Story Mode, an educational Mars Rover Game, a Space Quiz, and an Exploration Gallery featuring historical facts and AI-generated image prompts.

By combining storytelling, gamification, and authentic NASA mission information, Space Tales makes space history accessible and engaging, encourages scientific curiosity, and inspires young learners to explore space.

The project was developed using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, with Web Audio API and LocalStorage. Generative AI tools supported brainstorming, storytelling, visual concepts, and development. All AI-assisted content was reviewed by Team MYAHY using authoritative NASA resources.
projectDetails.details:
Project Name

Space Tales: Chronicles of the Cosmos

Project Summary

Space Tales is an interactive, gamified educational web application designed to bring the forgotten history of space exploration back to life.

Throughout decades of space exploration, numerous robotic spacecraft, scientific instruments, and exploration vehicles have completed their missions and remained on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Although these machines played important roles in advancing our understanding of space, their stories are often overlooked.

Space Tales transforms this forgotten space history into an engaging educational experience by combining storytelling, authentic NASA mission information, interactive games, quizzes, audio-visual content, and creative exploration.

Our mission is to make space history more accessible, exciting, and memorable, especially for young learners and future space explorers.

Detailed Description

1. What It Does

Space Tales takes users on an interactive journey through 13 historic space missions and their equipment, including missions such as Apollo 11, Surveyor 1, Viking, and Voyager.

Each featured mission introduces users to the spacecraft's journey, purpose, achievements, and historical significance through engaging first-person storytelling, educational information, and visual content inspired by real space exploration history.

Rather than presenting facts as ordinary textbook material, Space Tales turns each mission into a story waiting to be discovered.

2. How It Works

The platform combines four main interactive experiences:

A. Interactive Story Mode

Users can explore 13 historic space missions through engaging, child-friendly narratives written from the perspective of the spacecraft itself. Audio narration and visual elements help bring each mission's journey and scientific importance to life.

B. Interactive Rover Game

An educational mini-game where players guide a Mars rover across a grid, collect scientific samples, avoid obstacles, and manage battery power. The game includes score tracking and visual feedback, introducing basic concepts of planetary exploration through play.

C. Space Quiz

An interactive quiz that tests users' knowledge of space missions and equipment. Players answer questions based on the stories and educational content, earn stars, and track their scores while learning.

D. Exploration Gallery & AI Image Prompts

A visual gallery featuring mission cards, historical facts, and creative AI image prompts that help users imagine and visualize important moments in space exploration.

3. Benefits and Impact

Space Tales aims to transform overlooked space exploration history into an exciting educational opportunity.

By combining storytelling, interactive learning, and gamification, the platform:

- Makes complex space history easier for young learners to understand.

- Encourages curiosity about science, technology, and space exploration.

- Introduces users to real NASA missions and the equipment behind them.

- Promotes active learning through games, quizzes, and exploration.

- Helps preserve the stories and historical significance of space equipment left behind after missions.

Our goal is to remind people that even when a space mission ends, the discoveries, achievements, and stories behind it deserve to be remembered.

4. Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using:

- HTML5 – Web application structure.

- CSS3 – Styling, animations, and responsive space-themed design.

- JavaScript (ES6+) – Interactive features, games, and application functionality.

- Web Audio API – Audio-related functionality.

- LocalStorage – Saving user progress and scores.

The educational content is based on research from authoritative NASA resources, including NASA's National Space Science Data Center (NSSDC), NASA History Office, and NASA Image and Video Library (images.nasa.gov).

5. Artificial Intelligence (AI) Disclosure

Generative AI tools were used as supporting technologies throughout the development of Space Tales.

AI assisted our team in creative brainstorming, refining educational storytelling, developing visual concepts and image prompts, and supporting parts of the development process.

All AI-assisted content was reviewed and adapted by the team to maintain educational clarity and consistency with verified historical information from NASA sources.

AI served as a supporting tool in our creative and development workflow, while the project concept, decisions, integration, and final implementation were guided and reviewed by Team MYAHY.

projectDetails.name: Health_E
projectDetails.summary:
HEALTH_E is a browser-based educational prototype developed by Team METH for the Astronauts Health challenge. It brings together three experiences: a seven-stage interactive space-health narrative, a dashboard for manually entering selected health indicators, and a CSV analyzer that plots heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature, and cabin CO₂, with rule-based anomaly flags.
The project responds to the challenge by showing how mission-relevant health information could be presented in a visual interface for crew review. This matters because long-duration missions expose astronauts to health hazards, while distance from Earth can make clear communication especially important. HEALTH_E demonstrates a possible way to explore health topics and sample indicators together; it is not a validated medical tool. Its sample data and hard-coded rules should not be used to make care decisions.
projectDetails.details:
HEALTH_E is a browser-based educational prototype with three complementary modules. Its seven-stage narrative includes Explorer and Science modes and an interactive 3D scene to introduce spaceflight-health topics. The monitoring page lets users enter 11 selected indicators—such as heart rate, blood pressure, body-mass change, sleep and reaction time—and displays summary cards, charts and rule-triggered messages. Its built-in scenarios are synthetic examples. The analysis page accepts a user-selected CSV containing a time field and heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature and cabin CO₂; it plots the values and flags observations using programmed limits and a rolling statistical check. These pages do not share a medical record or connect to live sensors.

The prototype aims to make selected health topics and sample indicators easier to explore and review. Its creative approach is to pair an interactive educational narrative with separate, practical-looking monitoring and telemetry demonstrations. This may support awareness and discussion, but no usability study or health benefit has been measured.

The supplied project uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js and GLTFLoader for 3D content and browser-side charts and CSV handling. No dedicated medical hardware or live sensor integration is documented. Design considerations included spaceflight hazards, clarity of information, and distinguishing synthetic examples and software flags from clinical findings. Thresholds and messages are not clinically validated, so they should not guide treatment or operational decisions.

projectDetails.name: Still Listening: Signals from the Dust
projectDetails.summary:
STILL LISTENING
3D Sci-Fi Action & Adventure Game | 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge

We developed STILL LISTENING, a 3D sci-fi action-adventure game inspired by NASA’s 2026 Space Apps Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.

Players battle alien creatures across extraterrestrial worlds to free abandoned NASA spacecraft and bring them back to life. Meticulously modeled after real NASA hardware, each liberated machine shares its history, original purpose, and scientific achievements—directly addressing the challenge by giving forgotten equipment a voice, identity, and emotional bond with players.

Immersive sound effects and dynamic voiceovers accompany every action. Players personalize their journey by naming and customizing both their avatar and spacecraft, while progressive difficulty levels welcome all ages and skill levels. Each stage features a distinct 3D celestial environment where gravity, climate, and terrain directly shape movement, mechanics, and mission challenges.

An integrated AI Agent powered by NASA’s database lets players explore verified space history, alongside in-game trivia unlocking bonus points and rewards. This matters because it turns passive history into hands-on learning—teaching real planetary physics, inspiring curiosity for space exploration, and ensuring these silent pioneers are never forgotten.

STILL LISTENING — Every machine has a story worth hearing.
projectDetails.details:
N1 Solution

STILL LISTENING is an interactive 3D browser game built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Its purpose is to make space history engaging and accessible by turning retired NASA hardware on the Moon and Mars—specifically Apollo 11 Eagle, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Ingenuity, and Opportunity—into the central focus of a playable rescue mission rather than passive archival entries.

How does it Work:

Players start by setting up a profile (name, age, avatar, rover choice, and difficulty mode). They then drive across two distinct 3D environments—the Moon and Mars—to defend stranded NASA landers and rovers from enemy scavengers and reconnect them into a communication relay chain. Each environment alters gameplay mechanics: the Moon features low-gravity jumps and ground-based enemies, while Mars introduces dust storms, seismic shockwaves, and slope-tilt hazards. Rescuing each spacecraft unlocks a visual hologram card with verified NASA mission facts, synthesized audio/voice narration, a quick trivia check, and an interactive in-game Q&A archive (AURA) where players can explore each machine's history.

Benefits of the Game

  • Bite-Sized STEM Education: Presents real NASA landing coordinates, mission timelines, and discoveries through clean visual stat cards and trivia instead of dense text.
  • Story-Driven Engagement: Connects players emotionally to the real history of NASA's retired missions—culminating in Opportunity reactivating to restore the final signal.
  • Easy Access & Playability: Runs directly in a standard web browser with no installation required, offering three difficulty levels (Cadet, Ranger, Commander) and assisted laser targeting so players of different ages can play smoothly.

Our Goal

Our goal is to preserve the legacy of NASA’s abandoned lunar and Martian explorers through interactive storytelling—sparking curiosity about planetary science and inspiring players to learn more about the real missions that paved the way for future space exploration.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Coding Languages & Web Technologies:
    • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+): Core game logic, UI overlays, state management, and interactive Q&A archive.
    • Three.js (WebGL): Real-time 3D terrain generation, lighting, particle dust effects, rover movement, and spacecraft models.
    • Web Audio API & Web Speech API: Browser-native synthesized sound effects (lasers, explosions, radio chimes) and voice narration.
    • NASA Science Mission Archives (science.nasa.gov): Verified mission timelines, landing coordinates, hardware specifications, and historical discoveries for Apollo 11, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Ingenuity, and Opportunity.
    • Design: Used to brainstorm mission pacing, structure clear UI/UX layouts for the hologram data cards, and generate visual/audio clips for our 30-second demo video.
    • Implementation Guidance: Used to structure the Three.js scene setup, implement gravity and slope-tilt variables, and organize verified NASA facts into interactive in-game Q&A prompts.
    • Debugging Assistance: Used to resolve Three.js CDN loading fallbacks, refine laser-to-target collision detection, and fix browser audio/speech compatibility issues.

projectDetails.name: NABA'
projectDetails.summary:
Naba (نبأ, Arabic for “news”) is a newsroom for the Earth. It turns measurements from NISAR, the new NASA–ISRO L-band radar satellite, into short news stories on an interactive 3D globe. Each story gives a headline, a place, one measured number, a chart over time, possible causes, why it matters, and what to check next.
Radar sees through cloud and smoke, day and night, but its images are hard for non-specialists to read. Our Python pipeline streams only the small part of each NISAR product that covers a site, measures the change, and writes it as a plain-language story. Today Naba shows seven measured stories: a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in Panama, two wildfire burn scars in the USA, and wetland water changes at Lake Manzala (Egypt), the Okavango Delta (Botswana) and the Everglades (USA).
For the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, Naba makes SAR data understandable to the public, journalists, teachers and local decision makers, starting with Egypt’s own Nile Delta.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Naba turns NISAR radar measurements into news. Open the site and you see a dark 3D globe with coloured pins. Each pin is a story about a real place where NISAR measured a change. Click a pin and the globe flies there. A panel shows the headline, the measured number, a chart with one point per radar pass, what is happening, possible causes (as possibilities, never as proof), why it matters, and what to check next. A slider steps through the radar passes or months, and “Compare dates” puts radar images from two dates side by side.

Try it (main task)

1.    Open the website. Watch the 24-second narrated intro, or skip it.

2.    Take the guided tour. It shows an earthquake (Panama), a flood pulse (Okavango) and a wildfire (Big Sur) in under a minute.

3.    Click the red pin in California (“Radar maps a burn scar of about 31 km² in Big Sur”).

4.    Drag the slider from 16 August to 15 October and watch the burn scar appear pass by pass.

5.    Press “Compare dates” to see the radar false-colour image before and after the fire.

Direct link to one story: add /?story=plaskett-burn-scar to the site URL. Add /?demo=1 to autoplay the main path.

How it works

1.    Search. The Python pipeline (naba-data) queries NASA’s Common Metadata Repository for NISAR products over a site and period. Only metadata moves.

2.    Select. It keeps dual-polarisation (HH + HV) passes from one track, direction and frame, so every date is seen from the same angle and brightness can be compared.

3.    Stream. Each NISAR product is 4–6 GB. Naba uses HTTPS range requests to read only the HDF5 chunks over the site. For the two fires it read about 252 MB out of about 61 GB of products (0.4%). Every subset is cached as a GeoTIFF, so a re-run downloads nothing.

4.    Measure. Wetlands: each pixel is classed as open water (dark in HH and HV), flooded vegetation (bright HH, large HH−HV gap) or other, then composited per month. Fires: the HV signal of every pass is compared with the last pass before the fire; a drop of more than 3 dB is “likely burned” and 2–3 dB is “possibly burned”. Earthquakes: the unwrapped interferogram phase is converted to centimetres of ground motion along the satellite’s line of sight, keeping only pixels with coherence of 0.3 or more.

5.    Map. Class masks are turned into polygons with areas measured on the WGS84 ellipsoid, plus image frames for “Compare dates”.

6.    Tell. Each measurement is written as a story from fixed templates filled with the measured numbers. No language model writes the stories. Every number is traceable in provenance.json, which lists every granule, threshold, date and megabyte used.

The seven measured stories

Result

Tools and languages

•     Web app: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS 5 (globe projection), Zustand, lucide-react icons.

•     Data pipeline: Python with earthaccess, h5py, fsspec/aiohttp, xarray, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, pyproj, Shapely and Pillow. 51 automated tests (pytest) cover thresholds, burn tiers, polygon areas, story format and dataset merging; all pass.

•     Mixed reality (extra): Unity 6 with the Meta XR SDK, OpenXR and URP, for Meta Quest 3S. The same stories float on a globe in your room; tapping one unrolls it into a flat map with the radar layer.

Benefits and goals

•     Makes SAR readable by anyone: one headline, one number and a plain explanation, instead of a raw radar image.

•     Works when optical satellites cannot: through cloud, smoke and darkness.

•     Honest by design: every story lists causes as possibilities and says what to check next. Radar burn areas are shown next to the officially reported fire size.

•     Cheap to run: no backend, no API keys, and only the needed part of each product is read.

What works now, limits and next steps

Works now: the website with globe, story panel, charts, slider, Compare dates, narrated intro and guided tour, all seven stories measured from real NISAR data, the reproducible pipeline and the Quest version (built from the repo in Unity).

Limits: NISAR data is still PROVISIONAL. The wetland and burn classes are exploratory dB thresholds, not validated flood or burn-severity maps; wind on water, wet soil and look angle can move the numbers, so no story claims high confidence. Earthquake motion is along the line of sight only, from one pair. The globe shows simplified outlines, not full 20 m detail. The Quest version needs a headset and Unity to build.

Next: more sites through the same pipeline (more Egyptian sites first); validation against water gauges, official fire perimeters and GPS; a FastAPI + PostGIS service serving the same data (the frontend already supports it through one setting); and tiled rasters so the globe can zoom to full resolution.

projectDetails.name: Sols of Survival
projectDetails.summary: Welcome to Sols of Survival! For this NASA Space Apps challenge, we wanted more than a building game, so we made a survival adventure where every storm is real. Meet Nova, Cosmo, Rocket and Luna, four Space Kittens sent to run a tiny base on Mars. Their mission sounds simple: keep the crew alive for five Sols (a Sol is one day on Mars). But the Sun has other plans. Along the way, the crew faces events that really happened, like the giant sunspot of 2014, the 2017 solar storm that doubled radiation on Mars, the 2018 dust storm that silenced NASA's Opportunity rover, and the record-breaking storm of May 2024 measured by Curiosity. And this isn't just a story, it's you in charge. As the player, you pack the rocket, build the base and jump into hands-on missions like cleaning solar panels, melting ice for water and stacking bricks against radiation. Every choice helps one thing and costs another, just like it does for real mission planners. This is NASA space weather data like kids have never seen it before: not in charts or reports, but as a base they have to protect.
projectDetails.details:
Nah, We'd Win’s Project Solution

Sols of Survival is an educational survival game that teaches kids aged 7 to 12 what it really takes to keep a crew alive on Mars or the Moon, by turning real NASA space weather data into a story-driven base-building game. Players team up with a Space Kitten, build their own outpost, and use hands-on mini games to protect their crew from real solar storms, making space science both fun and easy to understand.

How Does Our Solution Work

In the game, four Space Kittens, Nova, Cosmo, Rocket and Luna, are sent to run a small base on Mars. The player picks one as their partner, packs a rocket with only 7 crates out of 11, and builds a base with Power Stations, Greenhouses, Water Stations, Radiation Shields and a Research Lab. Then they have to keep three bars above zero: Power, Life Support and Crew Health. Every Sol (one day on Mars), the base faces a space weather event that really happened, and the player spends 2 actions on hands-on missions before deciding how to face it.

  • A Calm Day (Mars, Sol 1):
    The crew lands on a quiet day, and the kitten shows the player around the base. But even calm days aren’t safe on Mars. NASA’s Curiosity rover measured about 0.67 millisieverts of radiation per day on the surface, so the crew’s health slowly drops every Sol. The player uses this day to build up their base before the storms arrive.
  • The Giant Sunspot (October 2014):
    Sunspot AR 2192, the biggest of its solar cycle, fires an X3.1 flare on 24 October 2014. It looks scary, but no cloud of particles comes toward the planet. Players who hide in the shelter lose a whole day of work for nothing, while players who did the Watch the Sun mission in the Research Lab already know the storm won’t follow. Through this, players learn that forecasting the Sun is hard and that good data changes everything.
  • The Storm That Reached the Ground (September 2017):
    On 10 September 2017, an X8.2 flare sends a particle storm across the solar system, and Curiosity measures radiation on the Martian surface at more than double anything it had seen before. In the gameplay, players protect the crew by choosing:
    Choice 1: Hide in the Radiation Shield bunker, which blocks most of the radiation but stops all work.
    Choice 2: Use a saved action to reinforce the walls.
    Choice 3: Keep working and take the risk.
    Players can also press Ask Earth, but Mars was on the far side of the Sun that day, so the reply takes 40 minutes and arrives after the storm hits. Through this, players learn why real crews on Mars have to make their own decisions.
  • The Dust Storm That Ended Opportunity (June 2018):
    A dust storm grows until it covers the whole planet, and sunlight drops so low that solar panels barely work. This is the same storm that silenced NASA’s Opportunity rover, which sent its last message on 10 June 2018. In the gameplay, players save their base by:
    Task 1: Rubbing the dust off the solar panels in the Dust Off the Panels mini game.
    Task 2: Connecting the right wires to charge the battery before the storm.
    Task 3: Deciding whether to power down the greenhouse or keep everything running.
    Through this, players discover that energy on Mars depends on the environment.
  • The Strongest Storm Ever Measured on Mars (May 2024):
    The final test. On 20 May 2024, a flare estimated at X12 sends the biggest burst of radiation Curiosity has ever recorded, 8,100 micrograys, which is about the same as 30 chest X-rays for an astronaut standing next to the rover. Everything the player built is tested at once: shields, shelter and stored power.
  • The Moon Base (Lunar Night and August 1972):
    Players can also choose the Moon’s south pole instead. There they face the lunar night, about 14 Earth days without sunlight, and the August 1972 solar storm that hit between the Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 missions. On the Moon, Earth answers in about a second, which shows kids how much distance changes everything.
  • Today’s Space Weather (Live NASA Data):
    In this mode, the game asks NASA’s DONKI database about the last 7 days of real solar activity and turns it into 3 Sols. If NASA can’t be reached, the game clearly switches to stored events and marks them OFFLINE, so stored data is never shown as live.

Every station also has 2 hands-on missions, and each one comes with a real science fact, from planting and harvesting crops (ISS astronauts first ate space-grown lettuce in 2015) to melting ice (Phoenix found ice on Mars in 2008), recycling water (the ISS recycles about 98% of its water) and stacking regolith bricks against radiation.

When the crew makes it through all five Sols, the kitten celebrates with a Certificate of Survival and a chart of everything that happened. If the crew doesn’t make it, there’s no “Game Over”. The kitten explains what went wrong and what to try next!

The game benefits

kids, students, teachers and families by:

  • Teaching how space weather, radiation and energy affect life on Mars and the Moon.
  • Showing that every engineering choice has a cost, using real events from NASA’s records.
  • Turning NASA’s open data into something kids can see, play and remember, instead of charts and reports.
  • Giving teachers a Family/Class mode with discussion questions and a printable debrief.

Our goal

To make NASA’s space weather data accessible and exciting for young kids, and to help them understand what real crews will face when they live on Mars and the Moon. Our game is a prototype, so bar sizes and station outputs are simplified to keep it playable, and the game says so on its “Real vs. Simplified” screen. We focused on solar storms, radiation and dust storms, and our game doesn’t yet cover other challenges like the long-term effects of space on the human body, which we’d like to add next using NASA’s space biology data.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS → for the whole game, which runs in any browser with no account.
  • Web Audio API → for all the music and sound effects, made in code.

Data Sources:

  • NASA DONKI → for the real dates and strengths of our solar flares and particle storms, and for live space weather from the last 7 days.
  • NASA Open APIs → for the live DONKI connection, the Astronomy Picture of the Day on the title screen, and real Curiosity photos.
  • Curiosity RAD measurements and NASA mission news → for the real radiation numbers and the story behind each event.

Github Link:

https://github.com/2009abdr30-eng/Sols-Of-Survival

Use of AI:

Manus AI
How it was used: Used to structure the core game logic, state flow, and turn-by-turn resource trade-off mechanics. All scientific rules and numbers were verified by our team.
Claude (Anthropic)
How it was used: Used for writing and refactoring front-end HTML/CSS/JavaScript code and fixing gameplay bugs.
Google Flow (Google Labs)
How it was used: Used to generate initial 2D illustration drafts for our Space Kitten characters, isometric habitat buildings, station interiors, and event cards, which were then cropped, cleaned, and color-matched by the team.

projectDetails.name: X-Monitor
projectDetails.summary: AstroVitals OS (incorporating the Oslo Pulse Protocol v1.0) is an autonomous, 100% local-first hardware and software medical telemetry platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. During deep-space missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays of up to 22 minutes one-way and periodic satellite blackouts prevent real-time reliance on Earth Flight Surgeons. AstroVitals OS empowers non-physician crews to monitor, interpret, and act on their vital signs autonomously.   Built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, and Zustand, the platform merges live Wi-Fi telemetry from a wearable ESP32 biometric node (MAX30102 optical Heart Rate, $\text{SpO}_2$, and Skin Temperature) with guided crew inputs for Blood Pressure, Blood Glucose, and Cabin $\text{CO}_2$. A Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) layer encapsulates sensor streams into space-grade CCSDS frames and utilizes a Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) store-and-forward buffer so zero medical packets are lost during orbital blackouts.   Mapped directly to NASA’s 5 RIDGE Hazards, our adaptive risk engine dynamically recalibrates Green, Yellow, and Red thresholds across Spacecraft, Orbital Station, Rover, and Planetary Base modes—featuring an interactive 2D spacesuit scanner, microgravity measurement guides, a 10-second hypoxia cognitive reflex game, radiation dosimetry, and gamified XP countermeasure quests
