projectDetails.name: Qamar Square
projectDetails.summary:
Qamar Square is an educational space game built for NASA Space Apps’ “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. Players act as a Junior Astronaut running a lunar base through real life-support emergencies during the 14-day lunar night: power loss, extreme cold, a failing oxygen generator, and a clogged water recycler. Every choice maps to a real NASA engineering option, explained simply as what it does, why it helps, and what can go wrong, so playing means learning how astronauts and engineers actually make these trade-offs.

The team researched each subsystem against 56 NASA Technical Reports Server publications, peer-reviewed papers, and agency program pages, then ran a scientific-verification pass to correct early drafts and label every technology by its true maturity: flight-proven, ground-tested, or lab research only. Four AI tools supported the work: Claude Code and Codex built the game, ChatGPT checked research against submission guidelines, and Gemini AI Plus supported the demo, which the team recorded manually from real gameplay. The result turns dense engineering trade-offs into an interactive mission trainer that is scientifically accurate and genuinely fun to play.
projectDetails.details:
Qamar Square is a 2D browser-based educational lunar survival game designed for children aged 7–12, inspired by NASA’s Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players take on the role of junior mission commanders, responsible for managing a lunar base and keeping its crew safe until sunrise.

The game consists of four connected challenges: Power & Food, Heat & Shelter, Oxygen, and Water & Waste. Players make decisions while managing limited resources, and each decision can affect the availability of resources in subsequent challenges. Through this experience, players learn how essential lunar-base systems work and how they depend on one another. The game also includes simplified scientific explanations and real examples from space exploration to connect gameplay with real science.

Benefits and Intended Impact: The project makes complex space-related concepts easier and more engaging for children. It encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, and responsible decision-making. Its main impact is to introduce young learners to the challenges of lunar exploration and demonstrate the importance of sustainability and interconnected life-support systems in future space missions.

Tools and Technologies: The project was developed using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SVG. We used Vite as the development and build tool, Node.js for the development environment, GitHub for version control and collaboration, and Vercel for deployment. The game runs in a web browser and does not require specialized hardware.

Creativity and Innovation: Qamar Square combines educational gaming with a realistic lunar-survival scenario. Rather than teaching each system independently, it connects power, temperature, oxygen, water, and waste management through decisions that have consequences throughout the mission. It transforms scientific concepts into interactive challenges while maintaining an age-appropriate experience.

Factors Considered: Our team considered the target age group, scientific accuracy, accessibility, interface simplicity, limited resources, and the consequences of player decisions. We also considered how to simplify complex scientific information without losing its essential meaning, and how to make the game accessible on different devices while keeping its educational purpose central to the experience.

 * Interactive Inspection: Clicking on any planet, moon, or celestial body in 3D space—or selecting it via the navigation bar—opens an information panel displaying its classification (such as Terrestrial Planet), a brief description, and key planetary details.

projectDetails.details:
3D solar system Explorer is an interactive, browser-based 3D visualization web application built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js.

* Core Functionality: Users can explore a dynamic 3D model of the solar system by dragging to orbit, scrolling to zoom, and adjusting the orbital simulation speed (e.g., 1.0x).

* Interactive Inspection: Clicking on any planet, moon, or celestial body in 3D space—or selecting it via the navigation bar—opens an information panel displaying its classification (such as Terrestrial Planet), a brief description, and key planetary details.

* Architecture: Developed as a lightweight, single-file web app (index.html) designed for smooth, real-time 3D rendering directly in the browser without external backend dependencies.

[11:31 AM, 11/14/2026] Mazin Zabady: The 3D Solar System Explorer is an interactive, browser-based 3D visualization web application that simulates our solar system in real time. Users can freely navigate 3D space by dragging to orbit around celestial bodies, scrolling to zoom in and out, and dynamically adjusting the orbital simulation speed (e.g., 1.0x). Clicking on any planet, moon, or celestial body—or selecting it through the quick navigation bar—smoothly focuses the camera on that object and opens an educational side panel displaying its classification (such as Terrestrial Planet), core description, and planetary metrics.

Traditional 2D diagrams and textbooks often make it difficult for students and enthusiasts to grasp orbital mechanics, relative planetary positions, and spatial relationships in space. This project transforms astronomy education into an intuitive, hands-on experience. By making space exploration accessible directly through any standard web browser without requiring heavy installations or specialized hardware, it aims to inspire curiosity, enhance spatial understanding, and support STEM learning for students, educators, and space enthusiasts worldwide.

To develop this project, our team used HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+), powered by the Three.js (WebGL) library for real-time 3D rendering, lighting, camera controls, and orbital animations, along with Google Fonts for clean UI typography. The entire application is built as a lightweight, self-contained single-file web app (index.html) hosted on OneApp for instant, zero-setup access across both desktop and mobile browsers without external backend dependencies.

What makes our project creative is the combination of scientific clarity with an engaging, game-like user interface. Key design factors our team considered include:

* Performance and Accessibility: Optimizing the codebase into a single lightweight file to ensure smooth frame rates and fast loading times on standard consumer devices.

* Intuitive User Experience (UX): Offering dual navigation so users can either explore freely in 3D space or jump directly between the 9 featured celestial bodies using a clean bottom navigation bar and live speed controller.

* Educational Clarity: Structuring the side information panel so complex astronomical details are presented in bite-sized, easy-to-read cards without cluttering the visual space.

projectDetails.name: TRUSTLINE
projectDetails.summary:
Space missions come with challenges that go far beyond reaching new destinations. Astronauts live in an environment where even small changes in their health can matter, and getting medical help from Earth is not always possible. That's why we developed TRUSTLINE.
TRUSTLINE is an AI-powered platform designed to help monitor astronaut health and make sense of the data collected during missions. It brings together health sensors, machine learning, medical documents, and specialized AI agents to analyze health signals, detect unusual patterns, and provide useful insights.
The platform also features a 3D human digital twin to visualize health data, an interactive dashboard, and a hybrid AI system that can continue supporting operations when communication with Earth is limited.
Our goal is simple: give astronauts and medical teams a clearer picture of what's happening, help them make better-informed decisions, and make health monitoring more reliable in one of the most challenging environments humans can explore.
projectDetails.details:
TRUSTLINE — Intelligent Astronaut Health Monitoring & Decision Support

TRUSTLINE is a research prototype designed to make astronaut health monitoring smarter, more connected, and more reliable during space missions. Our idea is to bring physiological data, medical knowledge, and AI-powered analysis together in one platform, helping astronauts and medical teams better understand changes in health conditions, especially when communication with Earth is limited.

How does it work?

TRUSTLINE collects and processes physiological signals such as heart rate, ECG, blood oxygen, skin temperature, respiration, EDA, and movement data. Its processing pipeline checks sensor quality before the data is used for further analysis.

The platform uses three specialized AI agents:

  • Sensor Quality Agent: Evaluates incoming signals and identifies missing, noisy, or potentially unreliable measurements.
  • Personal Health Agent: Analyzes health data in relation to an astronaut's personal baseline.
  • Risk Assessment Agent: Combines available evidence to identify potential concerns and support informed decisions.

A LangGraph Supervisor coordinates these agents. The system also includes machine learning for anomaly detection, medical document processing, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), allowing relevant information to be retrieved from medical documents and presented with supporting evidence.

Benefits and intended impact

Our goal is to help astronauts and medical teams move beyond simply viewing sensor readings. TRUSTLINE aims to turn complex health data into clearer, evidence-supported insights. Its hybrid AI architecture is designed to support local processing and fallback capabilities when cloud services or communication with Earth become unavailable.

The platform also incorporates a 3D human digital twin concept to make physiological information easier to understand and connect different measurements to their corresponding body locations.

Technology and tools

We developed the AI and data-processing components primarily using Python, alongside FastAPI for backend services. Our technology stack includes:

  • AI and orchestration: LangGraph, LangChain, and specialized AI agents.
  • AI models and providers: Groq API, Hugging Face Inference API, and Ollama for local model execution.
  • Machine Learning: Scikit-learn and the WESAD dataset for physiological signal analysis and experimentation.
  • Medical intelligence: Groq Vision for document OCR and medical RAG pipelines.
  • Data and persistence: Structured data processing, SQLite-based storage, and evidence tracking.
  • Testing: Automated tests, regression testing, and simulated sensor scenarios.

Development and testing were carried out using an Apple Silicon Mac, with simulated physiological sensor data used to experiment with different conditions and system responses.

What makes TRUSTLINE creative?

What makes TRUSTLINE different is the way it combines multiple technologies into one health-monitoring workflow rather than relying on a single AI model. It connects signal-quality validation, personal health baselines, risk assessment, medical knowledge retrieval, and hybrid AI execution.

We also considered several important factors: limited communication with Earth, unreliable sensor readings, individual differences between astronauts, data privacy, uncertainty in AI-generated insights, and the importance of keeping simulated data separate from operational health information.

Ultimately, TRUSTLINE is built around one important idea: when astronauts are millions of kilometers away from Earth, understanding their health should never depend on a single data source, a single model, or a constant internet connection.

TRUSTLINE is a research prototype and is not clinically validated or approved for medical use.

projectDetails.name: Field Wise
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Field Shift, a bilingual Arabic/English agricultural decision-support website that helps farmers and agricultural advisors compare crop rotations in Egypt’s northern Nile Delta.
The prototype combines NASA rainfall, temperature, soil-moisture, terrain and Landsat observations with Sentinel-2 vegetation information and FAO/IIASA crop-suitability data. For a selected agricultural study cell, users can compare 13 crop-rotation options and adjust the importance of land suitability, modeled irrigation requirements and local agricultural practice. The dashboard presents ranked alternatives, component scores and historical environmental context, making the comparison transparent rather than providing an unexplained recommendation.
Field Shift addresses the challenge by turning Earth observation data into an accessible tool for water-aware agricultural planning. It helps users explore how different priorities affect their choices and discuss alternatives with local experts. The current pilot covers Sidi Salem and Qallin using historical, processed data. It supports informed decisions without claiming live measurements, guaranteed yields or proven water savings.
projectDetails.details:
What we developed and how it works

Field Shift is a bilingual Arabic/English agricultural decision-support website that helps farmers and agricultural advisors compare crop rotations in Egypt’s northern Nile Delta. Our prototype covers Sidi Salem and Qallin in Kafr El-Sheikh, using a grid of 560 approximately one-kilometre study cells, including 556 eligible agricultural cells.

Users select a study cell on the interactive map or enter a farm’s coordinates to match it to an eligible cell. The dashboard displays historical environmental indicators and compares 13 crop-rotation options involving wheat, sugar beet, potato, maize, rice, cotton, soybean and year-round alfalfa.

Each option receives three component scores: land suitability, modeled irrigation requirement and local agricultural practice. Users can adjust the importance of these criteria, and the system recalculates the ranking using a transparent weighted average. This lets users explore alternatives instead of accepting one unexplained recommendation.

Data and tools

We combined NASA POWER temperature data, GPM rainfall estimates, SMAP soil-moisture information, SRTM terrain data and NASA/USGS Landsat observations with ESA Sentinel-2 vegetation information and FAO/IIASA GAEZ agricultural data. NASA resources provide environmental context, while GAEZ supplies crop-specific suitability, modeled irrigation requirements and local-practice inputs.

The frontend uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet for interactive mapping. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, pandas and Pydantic for data handling, validation and scoring. We used pytest and HTTPX for automated testing, GitHub for version control and Vercel for hosting. The prototype is software-based and requires no specialised hardware or field sensors.

AI tools supported planning, coding and debugging after our team independently developed the original project idea.

Benefits, creativity and intended impact

Field Shift makes complex environmental and agricultural information easier to explore through maps, historical indicators and explainable comparisons. Its creative approach connects Earth observation data with an interactive, farmer-facing workflow where users control their decision priorities.

Arabic support makes the interface more accessible to local users. Farm checklists and JSON report export help users organise their planning and share comparisons with agricultural advisors.

Our intended impact is to support better-informed, water-aware agricultural decisions—not replace farmers’ experience or local agricultural expertise.

Factors considered and current limitations

We considered water requirements, land suitability, established agricultural practice, usability, language accessibility and data quality. We also accounted for differences in dataset resolution and the uncertainty of historical and modeled information.

The current version is limited to the pilot area. Study cells are not surveyed farm parcels, irrigation estimates are not measured consumption, and saved farms and tasks remain in the user’s browser. We do not claim guaranteed yields, higher profits or proven water savings. Future development would focus on broader coverage, updated data, additional agronomic and economic factors, and field validation with farmers and specialists.

projectDetails.name: Flame in freefall
projectDetails.summary:
Flame in Freefall – Project Summary

Flame in Freefall is a scientific and educational project that explores how flames behave under different gravitational conditions, especially in microgravity environments in space.

On Earth, flames usually move upward due to gravity-driven buoyancy and convection. However, in microgravity, these effects become weaker, causing flames to behave differently and sometimes form nearly spherical shapes.

Our project aims to develop an interactive web platform that helps users understand and compare combustion behavior on Earth and in space.

Main Features

- Scientific Simulation: Visualizes flame behavior under normal gravity and microgravity.
- AI Analysis: Uses artificial intelligence to analyze combustion data and identify patterns.
- Interactive Dashboard: Displays scientific data, graphs, and comparisons.
- NASA Open Data: Uses publicly available NASA research and experimental data.

Technologies Used

- Artificial Intelligence (AI)
- Data Analysis
- NASA Open Data
- Web Development
- Scientific Simulation

Project Impact

Flame in Freefall makes complex space science easier to understand through interactive simulations and data visualization. It also highlights the importance of studying combustion in space to improve scientific knowledge and support astronaut safety in future space missions.

Our Vision: To transform NASA's scientific research into an interactive learning experience that inspires curiosity and innovation.

projectDetails.name: AeroHealth OS - ( Nexora by Hindawy )
projectDetails.summary:
AeroHealth OS is an autonomous, client-side health monitoring and Clinical Decision Support (CDS) system engineered for astronauts on deep-space exploration missions, such as Mars Transit and Lunar Gateway. During deep-space transit, round-trip communication latencies with Earth range from 3 to 22 minutes, rendering real-time telemedicine and remote mission control interventions impossible during acute medical emergencies. 

To address this challenge, AeroHealth OS empowers non-physician crew members to autonomously detect, evaluate, and mitigate critical spaceflight hazards. The platform integrates an interactive anatomical body map, real-time procedural ECG waveform streaming with arrhythmia detection, diagnostic Frisén staging for Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), millisecond-accurate NASA PVT-B cognitive reaction testing, and behavioral gamification protocols to ensure physical countermeasure compliance. 

Grounded entirely in empirical datasets from the NASA Twins Study (OSDR-379) and MSL Curiosity cruise radiation telemetry, AeroHealth OS provides deterministic, color-coded triage protocols and clear step-by-step clinical countermeasures without requiring ground assistance.
projectDetails.details:
How it Works:

AeroHealth OS operates entirely client-side with zero external software dependencies, providing resilient offline performance in deep space. It ingests simulated physiological and environmental telemetry, running them through an autonomous triage state-machine:

1. Interactive Anatomical HUD: Astronauts click on key organs (Brain, Eyes, Heart, Lungs, Spine, Muscles) to inspect empirical biomarkers, etiology, and targeted mitigations.

2. Real-Time Cardiovascular Stream: Continuously plots procedural P-Q-R-S-T ECG waveforms on an HTML5 Canvas at 100ms intervals, with simulated arrhythmia anomaly injection.

3. SANS Staging: Diagnostic optical evaluation using clinical Frisén scale (Grades 0-4) mapped to retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness and Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) protocols.

4. Cognitive Readiness: A functional Psychomotor Vigilance Test (NASA PVT-B) measuring reaction latency to detect micro-sleep lapses (>380ms).

5. Behavioral Gamification: Daily mission quest hub awarding XP, ranks, and streak tracking for completing mandatory 2.5-hour resistance exercises.

Tools & Technology Stack:

- Frontend: Pure Vanilla HTML5, modern CSS3 Glassmorphism, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).

- Rendering: HTML5 Canvas 2D API running at 60 FPS.

- Data Science Engine: Python 3.10, Matplotlib, and Pandas in Jupyter Notebook for empirical baseline validation.

- Interoperability: HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) telemetry export standard.

Benefits & Impact:

Provides autonomous self-reliance during critical communications blackouts, protects crew vision from microgravity cephalad fluid shifts, tracks cumulative cosmic radiation exposure against NASA career career limits (REID model), and standardizes medical telemetry for Earth-return synchronization.

projectDetails.name: Delta Sentry — 30 m Early Warning for the Nile Delta
projectDetails.summary:
Delta Sentry is an early-warning system for crop health in Egypt's Nile Delta. Egypt farms a thin strip of irrigated land, and district averages hide field-level failure: by the time a problem is visible from the road, it is already a loss.

We built a working web application that fuses 30-metre NASA HLS imagery with a fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model to forecast next month's vegetation, compares that forecast against what the satellite actually observed, and converts the disagreement into a ranked list of contiguous field patches. An inspector opens the site, sees 59 flagged blocks and the 12 worth visiting first, and prints a field order with coordinates and an observation checklist.

We audited 44 flagged patches against high-resolution imagery and published the result: 18 confirmed decline, 26 classified as harvest, cloud artefact or unclear. We report our error budget openly, including the baselines we do not beat.
projectDetails.details:
Delta Sentry turns a satellite forecast error into a work order.

THE PROBLEM

Egypt grows its food on a thin strip of irrigated land along the Nile. When a block of fields begins to fail, district-level averages do not move: a governorate mean stays flat while a hundred hectares go under, and by the time the loss is visible from the road it is already a compensation claim. Satellite monitoring of Egyptian agriculture is not new. What is missing is the step between a map and a decision. An agronomist cannot act on a raster of NDVI values, but they can act on a short list with a place, an area and a reason.

HOW IT WORKS

The pipeline runs in five steps.

1. We extract 30 m Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel imagery and 25 years of MODIS NDVI through NASA AppEEARS.

2. Every scene is cloud-masked with Fmask and reduced to monthly median composites.

3. A fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M model, with a frozen backbone and a custom U-Net decoder, predicts next month's NDVI from the previous four months of imagery.

4. The forecast is subtracted from what the satellite actually observed. Negative gaps are clustered into contiguous field patches.

5. Patches are ranked by area and exported as a printable field order with coordinates and an observation checklist.

An inspector opens one page and sees 59 flagged patches covering 175 feddan, and the 12 worth driving to first.

EVIDENCE, INCLUDING WHAT FAILS

We trained on 500 spatial-temporal samples spanning 2013 to 2023 and evaluated on held-out 2025 data. Seasonal climatology scores an RMSE of 0.1767, persistence 0.1858, and our model 0.1823. We beat persistence by 1.9 percent and we do not beat climatology. A 12-year same-month climatology is a genuinely strong baseline for a seasonal signal, and we say so on the site rather than in a footnote.

What we claim is narrower and testable: the model produces a spatial ranking that a climatology cannot, because a climatology is smooth across space by construction. A district average and a climatology are both blind to which field is failing. That is the gap this project fills.

We also audited 44 flagged patches one by one against high-resolution imagery. Eighteen, or 40.9 percent, showed a visible vegetation decline. Twelve were normal harvest or crop rotation, nine were cloud or sensor artefact, and five were unclear. We publish the 26 failures because a false-alarm rate is the number a ministry needs before it trusts a list.

Separately, a pixel-wise Seasonal Mann-Kendall test with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction on 25 years of MODIS found 78.6 percent of the area significantly greening, 21.4 percent with no significant trend, and 0.04 percent declining. The Delta is greening in aggregate, which is exactly why district averages hide the blocks that matter.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The direct benefit is time. An inspector with a vehicle and a finite week gets a ranked shortlist instead of a district to drive around. The second benefit is early warning: the alert fires when reality departs from a model's expectation, which can happen before the decline is visible to the eye. The intended impact is a working interface between satellite data and a field visit, at a cost a governorate can carry, because the whole application is a static site and the model runs on a free hosting tier.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python, PyTorch, TerraTorch, Xarray, Rasterio, NumPy and pymannkendall for the science. FastAPI on a Hugging Face Docker Space for live inference. A zero-dependency HTML, CSS and JavaScript front end with canvas rendering, no framework and no build step, so the entire application runs from a static host and loads without a server.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The first creative decision was to build the product around the forecast error rather than the forecast. Most vegetation models are judged on how close they get to reality. We treat the distance from reality as the signal: a model that is confidently wrong is not a failure here, it is an alert. The second decision was to end the pipeline at a printable field order rather than a map, because the unit of action for an inspector is a visit, not a pixel. The third was to make the model runnable from the browser, so a judge or a ministry officer can press one button and watch inference happen rather than take our word for it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Cloud cover over the Delta, which is why every scene is masked before compositing. The difference between seasonal senescence and genuine stress, which is why a flagged block is labelled bare soil when that is what the data shows instead of being called a stressed crop. The cost of a false alarm to a ministry with limited vehicles, which is why we audited our own alerts and published the failures. And the risk of presenting a prototype as a finished service, which is why every claim in the application is paired with its limit.

LIMITS

This is one pilot tile of about 12 square kilometres in Kafr El-Sheikh, not the Delta. An alert is an indicator for investigation, not a diagnosis of crop failure. Patch coordinates are mapped from the grid and are approximate, not surveyed GPS. In the December pilot month the district-wide NDVI drop is partly harvest and bare soil rather than stress. Re-basing the anomaly on same-month multi-year climatology, masking cells below NDVI 0.05, and adding Sentinel-1 SAR to separate harvest from failure are the next steps.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project AfterTrace
projectDetails.summary:
NEXUS CHRONICLES is an interactive web platform developed around NASA’s InSight Mars lander for the Forgotten Equipment challenge.

We built an immersive Mars exploration experience that allows users to navigate mission locations, discover InSight’s story, and explore its scientific instruments and engineering systems.

The platform includes an interactive Investigation section where users examine real mission evidence and scientific visuals, a Go Deeper mode that presents InSight’s scientific findings and data in an accessible way, and an Interactive Engineering Game where users build and develop a space station through progressive levels, applying engineering concepts through hands-on challenges.

Using authentic NASA mission resources and scientific data, NEXUS CHRONICLES turns an abandoned spacecraft into an opportunity to explore real engineering decisions, understand mission challenges, and apply problem-solving skills to future space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
NEXUS CHRONICLES is an interactive web-based educational experience developed around NASA’s InSight Mars lander for the Forgotten Equipment challenge.

The platform begins with an interactive Mars map, allowing users to explore the Red Planet and discover space missions. Users can then explore InSight’s mission story, scientific instruments, and engineering systems through an immersive digital experience.

Our main features include:

- Interactive Mars Exploration: An interactive map that introduces users to Mars and its mission locations.

- Investigation: A scientific exploration experience designed to help users examine mission evidence and understand InSight’s discoveries.

- Go Deeper: A functional scientific exploration mode presenting deeper mission information, scientific findings, and data in an accessible format.

- Interactive Engineering Game: A progressive space-station building experience where users explore engineering concepts through challenges and hands-on interaction. This feature is partially implemented.

We developed the platform using JavaScript and React, with Three.js for 3D experiences, Tailwind CSS v4 for styling, and Vite 8 as our development tool. We also used the Web Audio API and canvas-confetti for interactive effects, Playwright for testing, and Vercel for hosting.

Our creative approach combines cinematic storytelling, interactive exploration, authentic NASA resources, and engineering-based learning. Rather than presenting forgotten equipment as obsolete hardware, we use its scientific and engineering legacy to encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and problem-solving.

The project prioritizes scientific accuracy, accessibility, engaging interaction, and connecting real mission challenges to future engineering possibilities.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project NileSpark
projectDetails.summary: BurnCal turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one comparable burning calendar. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fires very differently. VIIRS's finer pixels detect 2.4 to 8 times more fires, so raw counts jump when the sensors change and long-term trends become misleading. We count each fire once per ~1 km equal-area grid cell per day. We then convert MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent units with a factor fitted on 2012–2017, when both sensors were flying and before the MODIS orbits drifted. Days when a satellite failed are detected automatically and filled by the next-best sensor, or shown as "no data" instead of fake zeros. Tested on years it never saw, the method predicts within 2.7% for Brazil, 4.9% for Australia and 16.5% for Egypt, and every MODIS-era value carries a 95% uncertainty band. Users select any area on a map and get a monthly calendar from 2000 to 2025, each month compared with its historical median, plus a CSV of the underlying detections. Agriculture and environment agencies and researchers can see whether burning in a place like Egypt's Nile Delta is really rising or falling, instead of mistaking a sensor change for a trend.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. BurnCal answers a simple question: is burning in this area unusual compared with its own history? Pick an area on the map and choose a date range. You get a monthly calendar of fire activity from 2000 to 2025 on one consistent scale. Each month is compared with the median of the same month in other years and shown with an uncertainty band. You can also download the raw detections as a CSV.

How it works.

  1. Load. We read NASA FIRMS active-fire records from MODIS (Terra and Aqua), VIIRS S-NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20: 79 million detections, covering over 200 countries for 2025 and the full history for Egypt, Brazil and Australia. We keep only vegetation fires (gas flares and industrial heat are about 70% of Egypt's VIIRS hotspots) and drop low-confidence detections.
  2. Count the same way. Each fire counts once per ~1 km equal-area grid cell per day. This removes VIIRS's advantage of having several small pixels on the same fire.
  3. Convert. S-NPP VIIRS is the reference. MODIS is converted with a factor fitted on 2012–2017, when both satellites overlapped and before the MODIS orbits drifted. Egypt's yearly factor varies between 7 and 11 from 2012 to 2017, peaks at 14 in 2018, then falls to 4.4 by 2025. Fitting on recent years would cut Egypt's history in half.
  4. Uncertainty. Each factor has a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Small areas lean on their country's factor, so a few fires can't give a wild result.
  5. Satellite outages. The pipeline finds days when a satellite failed, such as Terra's 18-day shutdown in June 2001, and uses the next-best sensor. Where no other sensor exists, the month is shown as "no data".
  6. Serve. A FastAPI service answers calendar, map and CSV requests in about 0.15 seconds for any area.

Benefits and impact. Agencies tracking crop-residue burning, haze and wildfire risk can trust long-term trends instead of being fooled by a sensor change. Researchers get a documented, reproducible method with its uncertainty stated. Every number links back to the raw NASA detections.

Tools. Python, DuckDB, FastAPI, Pydantic, SlowAPI and pytest (70 automated tests); React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and MapLibre GL JS with OpenFreeMap tiles; Git and GitHub. The full pipeline runs in about 2 minutes on a laptop with under 2 GB of RAM.

What's creative. We put both sensors on a common unit (fire cell-days on an equal-area grid). We chose the calibration window to avoid orbit drift. The changing yearly factor itself works as a diagnostic: drift matters for Egypt's small farm fires but barely affects Brazil's or Australia's large fires. And we show "no data" honestly instead of zero.

Factors we considered. Gas flares and other non-fire heat sources; differences in pixel size; satellite orbit drift; satellite outages; noisy factors for small areas; areas that cross borders where countries have records of different lengths; and running on ordinary laptops.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: PROJECT OSIRIS
projectDetails.summary:
What if the machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars were not forgotten — but became the beginning of a new generation's journey into space?

PROJECT OSIRIS (Team NileStro) answers the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge by turning real space heritage into one story told through three formats: an interactive 2D pixel-art game (ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN), a visual 3D comic book, and The Silent Archive — a research PDF for educators and adult learners.

Players follow Tariq and Zain, two Egyptian brothers separated across the Moon and Mars with their AI companion Suhail. Through exploration and science challenges inspired by real hardware — the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the PSEP seismometer, the LRRR reflector, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, InSight and Opportunity — they discover why each machine was sent, how it works, and what it discovered. A built-in NASA Mission Manual links every machine to its official NASA source. The game is bilingual (English/Arabic, full RTL), runs in any browser with zero dependencies, and is fully playable on desktop and mobile.

At the heart of OSIRIS is a simple idea: a mission's end does not mean the end of its legacy. By making NASA's discarded equipment the hero of an adventure, we help students, young enthusiasts and non-specialists connect with space history — sparking curiosity, critical thinking, and inspiration for the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
What PROJECT OSIRIS Does and How It Works

PROJECT OSIRIS is a connected storytelling and educational experience that transforms the history of NASA's space technologies and historic missions into an engaging journey of exploration, discovery, and learning. It combines documented scientific and historical information with an original fictional story set in the future, imagining a collaboration between NASA and the Egyptian Space Agency (EgSA).

The project follows a structured process, from researching real space technologies to transforming that research into one shared narrative presented through three complementary formats: an interactive game, a visual comic, and a research-based educational PDF.

Step 1: Researching Historic Space Equipment

We begin by researching NASA's historical missions and the scientific equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Using reliable NASA sources and mission documentation, we investigate the original purposes, scientific functions, and contributions of these technologies to space exploration.

The selected equipment includes Apollo-era technologies on the Moon, such as the Passive Seismic Experiment Package (PSEP), the Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR), and the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), as well as Mars exploration missions and equipment such as Sojourner, InSight, and Opportunity.

We select equipment based on two main considerations: its scientific and historical significance, and its relevance to the central idea of the project—that the end of a space mission does not mean the end of its legacy.

Step 2: Creating a Fictional Story Based on Real Science

After selecting the equipment, we develop an original fictional story set in the future, imagining a collaboration between NASA and the Egyptian Space Agency. The story follows two Egyptian brothers, Tariq and Zain, who become separated during a space mission. Tariq finds himself stranded on the Moon, while Zain continues his journey to Mars. Both encounter historic space technologies that become important elements in their journey to overcome challenges and reunite.

Their AI companion, Suhail, helps them identify the equipment and understand its scientific background.

The characters, mission, and events are fictional, while the historical equipment and its documented scientific purposes are based on real space exploration missions. The real capabilities of the technologies inspire the fictional challenges and interactions within the story, allowing scientific knowledge to become part of the narrative.

Step 3: Turning Scientific Knowledge into Interactive Gameplay

The interactive game, ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN, brings the story to life through exploration, interaction, and problem-solving. Players control both Tariq and Zain as they explore the Moon and Mars, encounter historic NASA equipment, and interact with objects to progress through the story.

On the Moon, Tariq encounters Apollo-era equipment, including:

- Passive Seismic Experiment Package (PSEP): The Apollo 11 experiment used seismometers to detect moonquakes and meteorite impacts and provide information about the Moon's internal structure. Its radioisotope heaters helped protect its electronics from the extreme cold of the lunar night.

- Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR): An array of optical reflectors deployed on the Moon to reflect laser pulses sent from Earth back toward their source, allowing scientists to measure the Earth–Moon distance with high precision.

- Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV): The Apollo lunar rover that allowed astronauts to travel farther across the lunar surface. The rover also supported communications equipment, including an antenna system used to transmit information and television signals toward Earth.

On Mars, Zain encounters:


- Sojourner: The rover delivered by the Mars Pathfinder mission in 1997, which demonstrated the use of a wheeled robotic vehicle on the Martian surface.

- InSight: A stationary lander that studied the interior of Mars using a highly sensitive seismometer and other scientific instruments. It detected more than 1,300 marsquakes during its mission.

- Opportunity: A Mars rover that operated for almost 15 years, traveled more than 45 kilometers, and provided important evidence about the planet's ancient environmental conditions.

These encounters introduce players to the original purposes and scientific contributions of each technology. The game then uses their real capabilities as inspiration for fictional problem-solving challenges. These imagined interactions are part of the game's narrative and are not presented as the equipment's actual historical uses.

Throughout the journey, Suhail helps players learn about the technologies they encounter. Players use the left and right arrow keys to move and the E key to interact with objects and equipment. In this way, scientific discovery becomes part of the gameplay rather than information presented separately from the experience.

Step 4: Presenting the Same Story Through a Visual Comic

The visual comic adapts the same story into an illustrated narrative. It follows the same characters, events, and historic equipment featured in the game, allowing readers to experience Tariq and Zain's journey through visual storytelling.

Through its scenes and illustrations, the comic presents the environments of the Moon and Mars, the equipment the brothers encounter, and the challenges they face. It offers another way to understand the story and become familiar with the historic technologies without needing to play the game.

The comic is not a separate storyline. It is another presentation of the same narrative, designed for audiences who prefer reading and visual storytelling.

Step 5: Exploring the Science Through The Silent Archive

The Silent Archive is a research-based PDF designed in an investigative style. While the game and comic bring the story to life, this resource allows readers to look more closely at the real scientific and historical background behind the equipment.

It brings together relevant images, scientific information, data, and historical documents about the selected space technologies. It also includes educational guidance for teachers and educators, helping them use the material to encourage students and learners to investigate the equipment, ask questions, examine evidence, and develop critical-thinking skills.

By presenting information in an investigative format, The Silent Archive encourages readers to look beyond the fictional events and explore what the technologies actually were, what they were designed to do, and what their missions contributed to space exploration.

It also helps distinguish documented historical facts from the fictional events created for the story, connecting the imaginative experience to reliable scientific knowledge.

Step 6: Connecting the Three Formats into One Learning Experience

The game, comic, and The Silent Archive are not three independent projects or unrelated stories. They are three connected ways of experiencing the same narrative and exploring the same historic space technologies.

Each format serves a different purpose and learning preference:

- The game encourages active exploration, interaction, and problem-solving.

- The comic communicates the story and its scientific ideas through visual storytelling.

- The Silent Archive provides a deeper research-based experience that encourages investigation, questioning, and critical thinking.

Together, these formats make PROJECT OSIRIS accessible to school students, young children, young space enthusiasts, non-specialist audiences, teachers, and adult learners. Audiences can choose the format that best suits their age, interests, and preferred way of learning while remaining connected to the same story and scientific foundation.

Ultimately, PROJECT OSIRIS communicates one central message: a mission's end does not mean the end of its legacy. Historic space technologies remain valuable engineering achievements that carry knowledge, inspiration, and possibilities for future exploration. By connecting real space heritage with an imaginative future story across interactive gameplay, visual storytelling, and educational investigation, PROJECT OSIRIS aims to inspire the next generation of explorers and innovators.

projectDetails.name: Mission Zero
projectDetails.summary:
MISSION ZERO: The Lunar Expedition is an educational 3D game developed in Unity 6 that transforms spacecraft engineering and lunar exploration into an interactive experience. Players take on the role of mission designers, configuring spacecraft systems, managing limited resources, and making engineering decisions that influence their mission. They explore essential spacecraft components, consider different routes to the Moon, face simulated mission risks, and experience the stages of a lunar expedition.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex space science and engineering concepts more accessible and engaging, especially for students and beginners. Instead of only reading about spacecraft, players learn by interacting with systems and seeing how their decisions affect the mission. MISSION ZERO encourages curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and an understanding of how multiple engineering systems work together to make space exploration possible.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – MISSION ZERO: THE LUNAR EXPEDITION

MISSION ZERO is an educational 3D space exploration game developed in Unity 6. It allows players to experience the decision-making involved in planning a lunar mission by taking the role of spacecraft designers and mission planners.

How It Works

Players begin by configuring a spacecraft through an interactive workshop. They can explore and manage eight major subsystems: propulsion, propellant tanks, solar panels, batteries, communications, navigation sensors, landing gear, and scientific payload. They must consider resource limits and engineering trade-offs when selecting components.

After configuring their spacecraft, players progress through a simulated lunar expedition. They encounter mission-planning decisions, compare different routes to the Moon, consider potential risks such as solar particle events, and experience key stages of the journey, including launch, spaceflight, lunar approach, and a landing scenario.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project makes space science and engineering more approachable through interactive learning. Rather than simply reading about spacecraft systems, players can explore components, make decisions, and understand how different systems depend on one another. It aims to encourage curiosity about space exploration while developing critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, and systems-thinking skills.

Tools and Technologies

  • Unity 6: Main game engine and development environment.
  • C#: Programming language used for gameplay systems and interactions.
  • Universal Render Pipeline (URP): 3D rendering.
  • glTFast: Importing NASA-provided 3D models in GLB format.
  • NASA 3D resources: Earth and Moon models used to represent the planetary environments.

The project was developed as a desktop 3D game using software-based tools and assets; no specialized external hardware is required to play it.

Creativity and Design Considerations

MISSION ZERO combines spacecraft configuration, resource management, mission planning, and lunar exploration into one connected educational experience. Its visual direction draws inspiration from modern aerospace interfaces and spacecraft control systems, using a premium glass-inspired interface to make the experience feel immersive.

During development, the team considered accessibility for beginners, clarity of information, visual quality, resource constraints, the relationship between spacecraft subsystems, and the consequences of engineering decisions. The project uses simplified simulations to communicate engineering concepts in an engaging way rather than claiming to reproduce the accuracy of a real spacecraft or flight simulator.

projectDetails.name: TerraMatch: Measuring Which Places on Earth Really Behave Like the Moon and Mars
projectDetails.summary: TerraMatch is an open web tool that finds and scores Earth analog sites for Moon and Mars landing sites using measurements instead of visual resemblance. We measure the same ten physical and chemical properties (terrain and slopes, surface texture, brightness, temperature, thermal inertia, minerals, dryness, water and ice, dust and wind, radar roughness, plus an AI landform-shape score) on Earth, the Moon and Mars from open NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA data, and rank every pair by how well it fits a mission goal (landing, search for life, permanent base, dust). It addresses the challenge by screening all 70,718 land cells on Earth instead of a handful of famous sites, and by reporting exactly which properties match and where an analog breaks (gravity, atmosphere, radiation, biology). This matters because better-chosen analogs make hardware tests and astronaut training for Artemis and future Mars missions cheaper and more reliable.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraMatch answers: which places on Earth behave like Moon-base and Mars landing sites, and in what ways? Instead of picking analogs by how they look, it measures the same properties on all three worlds and scores each Earth-target pair. Every result shows its data source and the reasons behind the score, including where the match fails.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Ten properties are computed the same way for Earth, the Moon and Mars: terrain and slopes (common 200 m grid), surface texture, brightness, temperature (each body's relative hot/cold position plus day-night swing), thermal inertia, minerals (as mineral families), dryness, water and ice, dust and wind, radar roughness, and a landform-shape score from an AI vision model (DINOv2 on hillshades, 72 views).

2. Per-property similarity = exp(-difference / scale).

3. Mission profiles (landing, search for life, permanent base, dust) weight the properties. A pair is ranked only when at least 50% of the mission's weight has data on both sides, so missing data never helps a site.

4. A global screen with NASA MERRA-2 scores every one of 70,718 land cells (~50 km) against targets such as Jezero Crater; the best regions are then analysed in full detail.

5. Results are shown in a web app with Dashboard, Explore, Analysis, Ranking and Report views.

KEY FINDINGS

- The method was never told which sites are famous analogs, yet Atacama ranks in the top 0.2% of Earth's land for Jezero, and the Antarctic plateau (Dome A) in the top 0.1% for a lunar polar base (Haworth).

- It surfaced regions not commonly used as analogs: Kumtag Desert/Lop Nur (China) 66% for Arcadia Planitia, northern Ellesmere Island (Canada) 65% for Haworth (Moon), Nubian Desert (Sudan) 64% for Arcadia Planitia.

- Egypt's Western Desert ranks first for all three Mars rover sites: White Desert for Jezero (EMIT detects calcite, minerals match 100%), Gilf Kebir for Oxia Planum (kaolinite clays on very flat plains, terrain 91%), Gebel Kamil for Gale (same clay family, AI landform similarity 92%). It breaks on brightness, dust and temperature (Egyptian nights are ~100 K warmer than Gale's).

- L-band radar (JAXA ALOS PALSAR) reveals a buried drainage network near Gebel Kamil that is invisible in Sentinel-2 optical imagery. This makes the area a process-analog test field for Mars subsurface radars (SHARAD, MARSIS).

- Lunar polar matches are weaker, as expected: nothing on Earth is ~20 K cold and airless.

BENEFITS

Mission planners and researchers get a reproducible, data-based way to choose where to test rovers, radars and habitat technology, and an honest list of what each analog cannot reproduce (gravity, atmosphere, radiation, biology).

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A searchable, open reference of Earth analog sites for the Moon and Mars that can grow as new data and mission targets are added.

TOOLS

Live app: https://terramatch-five.vercel.app/ (hosted on Vercel). Code: https://github.com/KarimAshraf04/TerraMatch

Stack: [list: e.g. Python / geospatial libraries / JavaScript framework for the web app]. AI model: DINOv2 for landform features. Validation: 22 automated tests covering the maths, data checks against known facts, and the AI model.

projectDetails.summary:
ELSEWHERE - Exploring other worlds starts with understanding our own.

We developed ELSEWHERE, a web app that finds places on Earth whose terrain resembles any place on the
Moon or Mars, addressing the challenge "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base
Locations and Mars."

Before astronauts and rovers explore the Moon or Mars, they train on Earth, and training on the wrong
kind of ground can hide problems that appear only on the real surface. In ELSEWHERE, a user picks any
spot on a 3D Moon or Mars globe. The app measures that 20 x 20 km area from NASA elevation data
(slopes, relief and roughness) and searches over a million areas of Earth's land for the closest match
in under a second.

For each match it shows real satellite images of both places, a 3D view of both terrains, and what is
similar and what is different, including NASA climate data and the conditions Earth cannot copy, such
as lower gravity.

This helps mission teams find realistic, lesser-known training grounds quickly and understand each
one's limits.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- One method for three worlds: Earth, Mars and the Moon are measured with exactly the same 20 km,

1000 m terrain fingerprint, so any site on the Moon or Mars can be compared with any place on Earth.

- Pin anywhere, not a fixed list: users can explore any crater, valley or plain, not only famous sites,

and most results fall outside the well-known analog areas.

- "What is similar, how similar, what is different" in one view: instead of a single score, each result

shows where the analog holds (terrain, sometimes dryness) and where it breaks (climate, gravity,

atmosphere, radiation).

- Explainable without machine learning: no labelled analog pairs exist, so instead of a black box we

use a fixed distance whose every part can be read and adjusted by the user.

- Storytelling for everyone: a cartoon astronaut jumps to the chosen world, a "what experiment will you

run?" question frames the search, and both terrains appear as 3D blocks built from the real elevation -

making planetary science approachable without hiding the numbers.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: the index is a heuristic, not a probability; we never claim a "first discovery";

measured values, computed scores, context data and AI text are kept clearly separate.

- Fair comparison: identical grid, window size and metrics on all three bodies, each projected on its

own figure; the same vertical exaggeration for both 3D terrains.

- Data quality: we compared 1 km and 30 m Earth data and disclose the ~20% roughness bias; we reject

windows with missing data or likely water; we flag climate values that are unreliable in mountains.

- Earth's limits: gravity, vacuum or thin CO2 air, and radiation cannot be reproduced, and the app says so.

- Reproducibility: open NASA data, SHA-256 records for every file, automated tests, and a deterministic

decision record.

- Accessibility and performance: keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, sound off by default,

works on phones; the global search runs in under half a second.

- Responsible AI: the optional AI chat only explains server-computed evidence and never produces

scores; AI-assisted work is disclosed.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project No Planet B
projectDetails.summary: ONE MORE SOL is an interactive, science-based Mars survival game where players take command of Ares-7, a fictional research outpost, and lead a five-person crew through 10 Martian days (Sols) after an unexpected supply delay, making critical decisions, managing essential resources and habitat systems, completing interactive challenges, and facing interconnected emergencies whose consequences shape the mission's outcome, while learning about real space science through data and educational resources from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency, with three possible endings determined by the player's choices and survival strategy.
projectDetails.details:
ONE MORE SOL is a browser-based, interactive Mars survival game that puts players in command of Ares-7, a fictional research outpost on Mars, where they must lead a five-person crew through 10 Martian days (Sols) after an unexpected supply spacecraft delay. Each Sol introduces a new emergency, combining crew dialogue, interactive mini-games, and strategic decisions that affect essential resources, habitat systems, and crew health. Players must manage oxygen, water, food, energy, medical supplies, and six habitat systems while considering the delayed consequences of their decisions, with three possible mission endings based on their performance.

The project aims to make space science more accessible and engaging, particularly for younger audiences, by transforming the challenges of living on Mars into an educational gaming experience. It introduces players to real challenges such as radiation exposure, resource recycling, food production, solar energy, and life-support systems, helping develop problem-solving, critical thinking, and resource-management skills.

The game incorporates scientific information and resources from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency, including NASA DONKI, RadLab, the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), and Mars Trek. These resources provide real scientific context and educational facts, while simulated gameplay values are clearly distinguished from actual measurements.

The application was developed using React and Vite for the frontend, JavaScript, Node.js, and Express for the backend, and MongoDB for persistent game data. NASA data sources and APIs support the scientific content and environmental context. The backend game engine handles resource calculations, system conditions, delayed consequences, decision validation, and mission outcomes.

What makes ONE MORE SOL creative is its combination of interactive mini-games, strategic survival mechanics, specialist-based crew decisions, and interconnected storytelling. Rather than simply presenting scientific facts, it allows players to experience the consequences of decisions in a simulated Mars mission. Our team considered scientific accuracy, age-appropriate language, accessibility, replayability, responsive design, and gameplay balance to create an engaging experience that combines learning with entertainment.

Our intended impact is to inspire curiosity about space exploration and help players understand the complexity of sustaining human life beyond Earth, showing that surviving on Mars requires more than technology: it requires teamwork, scientific knowledge, planning, and responsible decision-making.

projectDetails.name: SpaceX
projectDetails.summary:
SpaceX is a browser-based space mission design game built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. A player picks one of three missions — POLAR WATCH at Earth, LUNAR ICE at the Moon, MARS DUST at Mars — reads the science brief, assembles a spacecraft on a live 3D bench, flies the mission, and gets a scored report explaining exactly why it worked or failed. Five stages, no reloads: mission select, brief, design, flight, report.

It addresses the challenge by making real mission trade-offs playable instead of abstract. Every part choice feeds a deterministic model of mass, power, downlink, radiation and cost against the mission's budget and launch capacity, and Fly only unlocks when the design can actually do the job. The 3D spacecraft, the resource meters and the flight scene all read one shared assembly model, so what you build is what you fly. NASA Earth and planetary imagery is shipped with the site and credited in-app.

It matters because it turns NASA data and engineering constraints into something a student, a classroom or a team can experience in minutes — and multiplayer party mode lets a whole room design and fly the same mission together.
projectDetails.details:
**SpaceX** is a browser-based space mission design game. A player chooses one of three missions — POLAR WATCH (Earth), LUNAR ICE (Moon), MARS DUST (Mars) — reads the science brief, builds a spacecraft on a live 3D bench, flies the mission, and receives a scored report explaining why it worked or failed. Five stages run without reloads: mission select, brief, design, flight, report.

It works as a single deterministic model. The bench asks five questions — spacecraft, power, payload, orbit and lifetime, flight configuration — and every choice feeds the same evaluator, checking mass, power margin, downlink, radiation and cost against the mission's budget and launch capacity. **Fly** unlocks only when the design can genuinely do the job. The 3D hull, the resource meters and the flight scene all read one shared assembly model, so the craft you build is the craft you fly. Flight plays as one continuous shot: launch, ascent, orbit insertion, operations, then a 0–100 report.

The benefit is that mission engineering becomes something a student or a classroom can attempt in minutes: the constraints are real, the feedback is immediate, and failure is explanatory rather than a wall. Multiplayer party mode extends this — one room code and a team designs, flies and reads the same report together.

Built with Preact 11, strict TypeScript, Vite 6, three.js with hand-written GLSL, three isolated 3D renderers, Vitest, and Cloudflare Workers with Durable Objects. Creativity came from making the design bench, the brief and the flight one spacecraft instead of three illustrations, and from the shared-session party mode. We prioritised offline reliability, honest educational data, accessibility, and never showing a blank frame between stages.

projectDetails.name: planetary intelligence Norla
projectDetails.summary:
We've been working on Planetary Intelligence, a scientific project developed by Team NORLA for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
Our goal is to build a scientific workbench that helps users investigate changes on Earth and explore lunar conditions through actual data, statistical analysis, and numerical methods.
The platform brings together three main engines:
Earth Intelligence: NASA POWER data, trend analysis, seasonal analysis, regional comparisons, and data quality diagnostics.
SAR Change Intelligence: Raster inspection and radar-based surface change analysis using GeoTIFF and HDF5 files.
Lunar Intelligence: Meeus-based calculations for lunar illumination, Earth visibility, and optional terrain horizon analysis.
We built the project using React, TypeScript, Python, FastAPI, NumPy, and Rasterio, without relying on AI or machine learning for scientific results.
Some limitations remain. SAR demo scenes are synthetic, and real-data processing depends on the input products and backend configuration. Not all documented data sources are connected yet.
We're sharing what we've built so far, including its capabilities and limitations, and there's still more to come.
Explore the project:
https://planetary-intelligence.vercel.app/
Team NORLA | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
projectDetails.details:
Planetary Intelligence – Project Details

Planetary Intelligence is a scientific analysis platform developed by Team NORLA to help users investigate environmental changes on Earth and explore scientific conditions relevant to lunar missions.

The platform goes beyond simply displaying scientific data. Its Earth Intelligence engine allows users to examine environmental variables, analyze historical observations, identify trends, and evaluate their statistical significance. It uses NASA POWER data and applies statistical methods to help distinguish meaningful changes from ordinary variation.

The platform also includes additional analytical capabilities for Earth surface-change investigations and lunar mission analysis. Its lunar engine uses astronomical calculations to examine solar geometry, illumination conditions, and potential communication opportunities at lunar locations.

One of the project's main benefits is making scientific analysis more accessible, transparent, and reproducible. Users can examine the underlying data, understand the methods used, and recognize the assumptions and limitations behind analytical results.

Our approach is based on deterministic scientific calculations rather than AI-generated scientific conclusions. Statistical methods and scientific validation are central to the platform's design.

The project was developed as a modular software platform using web technologies and scientific computing tools. Its design emphasizes accuracy, traceability, usability, and the responsible interpretation of scientific data.

Our goal is to provide researchers, students, and scientifically interested users with a practical environment for exploring planetary and environmental data and turning observations into evidence-based investigations.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.summary: Our project aims to develop an intelligent wildfire monitoring and detection system using Earth observation satellite data, particularly MODIS and VIIRS. The system analyzes satellite observations to identify active fire hotspots, harmonize data from different satellite sources, and monitor fire activity over time. By combining multiple datasets and applying data analysis and machine learning techniques, the platform seeks to improve fire detection accuracy, reduce false alarms, and provide timely insights to support wildfire management, environmental protection, and faster emergency response.
projectDetails.details: Intelligent Wildfire Detection and Monitoring System Our project is an AI-powered wildfire detection and monitoring system that leverages Earth Observation (EO) satellite data to identify, analyze, and track fire events across different geographical regions. The system integrates data from multiple satellite sources, particularly NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments, through a data harmonization process that ensures consistency and comparability between observations. By combining satellite-based thermal anomaly data with machine learning and geospatial analysis techniques, the platform aims to improve fire detection reliability, reduce false positives, and provide a more comprehensive understanding of fire behavior and spread. The proposed solution will provide an interactive monitoring platform featuring fire hotspot visualization, temporal analysis, geographical insights, and early alerts for potential fire events. It is designed to support environmental agencies, researchers, and decision-makers in responding more effectively to wildfires, monitoring agricultural burning, and protecting ecosystems. Ultimately, our goal is to transform complex satellite observations into actionable intelligence that enables faster, smarter, and more informed environmental decision-making.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

Nova – Software of Healthcare Monitor
projectDetails.details:
1. Executive Summary

Software of Healthcare Monitor is a web-based health monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. It centralizes 18 types of medical examinations into one simple interface that a non-physician Crew Medical Officer can use without real-time help from Earth.

The system features Nove, an AI voice assistant that guides the astronaut, AI Suggestions that analyze trends, and a Yesterday – Daily Checks panel for the 4 most critical daily tests: Blood Pressure (BP), ECG, Oxygen Saturation (SpO2), and Temperature & Breathing (Temp).

Our solution is based entirely on NASA HRP data, NASA Glenn, and CSA radiation research. It solves the core problem: when communication delay reaches up to 44 minutes round-trip to Mars, astronauts must diagnose, monitor, and act independently.

2. The Problem

 At every moment, an astronaut faces the challenges of space—including radiation, isolation, gravity, and a confined environment—which can impact the immune system and lead to cardiovascular issues. Astronauts must be empowered to monitor their own health and medical data, allowing them to assess their condition independently rather than waiting 44 minutes for a response from doctors back on Earth

3. NASA Data Used

All sources are official NASA and partner agency pages:

  • NASA HRP Hazards – 5 hazards RIDGE. Used to define the 18 exams.
  • NASA HRP Risks – Detailed risks: immune, heart, bone, SANS, sleep, DVT.
  • NASA HRP Ongoing Research – CIPHER, B-Complex, Immune Biomarkers, Standard Measures, Tempus Pro, Omics Archive.
  • CSA Radiation / CANS – Neutron radiation is ~30% of radiation in spacecraft. Justified Radiation Dose exam.
  • CSA Why Science in Space – Dual benefit: space health + Earth health (aging, osteoporosis).
  • NASA Glenn MIM Devices – Tempus Pro / Ambulance in a Box. One device for ECG, NIBP, ultrasound, vitals.

AI Disclosure

We used manus and claude code  in programming the frontend ( UI ) .

Meta AI for research and translation of NASA sources,. All medical facts were checked against NASA sources. 

4. Our Solution

Dashboard: right: Nova with you ( Ai chatbot ) + Nova AI  Analysis and Suggestions.

 Center: 18 Test Types. Right: Yesterday – Daily Checks.

Left : model hologram (full body scane ).

4. Our Solution – 18 Exams

  • 1. Blood Test   2. Urine Test   3. Saliva Test
  • 4. Sweat Test   5. Immune Test   6. DNA / Microbe Test
  • 7. Ultrasound   8. X-Ray   9. Eye / Retina Scan
  • 10. Vision Test   11. Blood Pressure   12. ECG
  • 13. Oxygen Saturation   14. Temperature & Breathing
  • 15. Sleep Test   16. Radiation Dose
  • 17. Skin / Wound Test   18. IV Fluid Test

5. How It Works

  • Step 1: Astronaut opens dashboard, sees Yesterday Checks + AI Suggestions.
  • Step 2: Says to Nove: Start Blood Pressure check. Nove guides him by messages.
  • Step 3: Device measures, result appears on monitor.
  • Step 4: AI compares result to personal baseline and NASA thresholds.
  • Step 5: AI Suggestions updates: Green = normal, Yellow = watch, Red = act now.
  • Step 6: a system with ai model ready to trained on earth health data 

6. Technology Used 

Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript  

Backend: Python, fastABI

7. Impact & Future Work

Impact on Space

Early detection of bone loss, heart issues, immune changes, radiation exposure, and SANS before they become emergencies. Reduces dependence on Earth.

Impact on Earth

  • Same dashboard can help remote clinics, bedridden patients, elderly care, and isolated areas where no doctor is nearby.
  • Can be used in hospitals with simple modification to the interface.

Future Work

  • Connect it to sensors: Bio-Monitor, sweat patch, Tempus Pro.
  • Add personal baseline AI using AVATAR organ-on-a-chip concept.
  • Add Mini X-Ray and IVGEN Mini when they fly within 1 year.
  • Add Arabic + English toggle, and 3D body visualization.

  • asc-csa.gc.ca – Radiation / CANS 2026
  • asc-csa.gc.ca – Why Science in Space
  • nasa.gov/glenn – Multifunctional Integrated Medical Devices
