projectDetails.name: Project NovaCore-Team
projectDetails.summary: Mars Survival Academy is an educational game for kids aged 7–12 that turns real mission trade-offs into play. Players run a Mars outpost for 30 Sols with a limited daily power budget, so every building (life support, farming, radiation shielding, research) competes for the same energy and no choice is free. Space-weather alerts are grounded in real NASA data: a NASA DONKI solar energetic particle event and Curiosity MSL-RAD radiation measurements from NASA OSDR RadLab, shown in the game on a Data Sources screen. It answers the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge by letting young players feel why astronauts must balance power, oxygen and radiation protection, instead of only reading facts about them.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Mars Survival Academy is a 2D top-down colony-management game for kids aged 7–12. The player is a trainee astronaut who must keep a Mars outpost alive for 30 Sols (Martian days). Three core meters are always visible: Energy, Oxygen and Shield (radiation protection). Food, water, ore and science are secondary resources.

How it works

Each Sol the outpost has a limited power budget. The player chooses from 7 structures, such as a solar panel, oxygen generator, water extractor, greenhouse, shield generator and research lab. Every structure has a construction cost and a power use, so helping one system (for example, powering the research lab) takes power from another (for example, shielding or oxygen). No choice is free. Space-weather alerts appear with a severity class and test the plan the player has built. At the end, a Mission Complete screen summarizes energy efficiency, atmospheric stability, radiation defense and colony status.

NASA data used

- NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database): a real solar energetic particle (SEP) event dated 2017-09-06 drives the in-game space-weather alert.

- NASA OSDR RadLab, MSL-RAD instrument on the Curiosity rover: daily mean absorbed dose rates measured on the Martian surface (7.68 µGy/h on 2017-09-06 and 17.87 µGy/h on 2017-09-11).

- Five short educational facts with source citations.

All of this data is archived, not live. It is labeled as archived NASA data in the game, and an in-game Data Sources screen lists every source. Power costs, production rates and shield effects are our own game design, built to teach the trade-off. They are not NASA figures.

Benefits

Kids experience the decisions behind a mission, not just its facts. The game uses plain language and short, repeatable play sessions, and can be used at home or in a classroom.

What we hope to achieve

We want young players to leave understanding one real constraint of deep-space survival: power, oxygen and radiation protection compete, and every choice has a cost.

Tools

Godot Engine and GDScript for the game, GitHub for version control and teamwork, and pixel-art UI and assets. We used AI tools (Claude and Manus) to help write and debug code and to draft text. The team reviewed and tested the results.

projectDetails.details:
Project identity and summary

Project Name: Nova Knights

Selected Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Nova Knights Adventure is a free browser game that trains children aged 7 to 12 to think like Mars mission crew. The child runs a Mars base. Each Mars day an alarm goes off in one room: a solar storm, a hot battery, a clogged water recycler. The child has a few seconds to pick one of two choices, plays a short skill mini game to do it, then gives each of the four astronauts a job before night falls.

It addresses the challenge by teaching real mission trade-offs through play instead of reading. Every choice shows what it costs, what it gives and what may happen later, and no choice is free. Oxygen, water, food, power and the radiation shield all run down, so the child must balance mission against keeping the crew safe.

The problems come from real NASA data. The storms are real records from NASA's DONKI space-weather database, and each of the 24 problems carries a NASA fact with a source the player can open.

It matters because most space content for children is either posters of facts or simulators that are too hard. This game lets a 9-year-old feel why mission decisions are difficult. It needs no download, login or personal data, and it works on a cheap phone or a classroom projector.

What it does?

The player commands a four-person Mars outpost. There are two modes:

Casual: 7 Mars days. Send 20 science stars to Earth and keep the crew's radiation badge out of the red.

Survival: no last day. Alarms get faster each day, down to 4 seconds, and the run ends when food, water or oxygen runs out or radiation gets too high. Scores go on a high-score board.

Each day follows the same loop:

1) Alarm: A problem appears in one room of the base, with a countdown.

2) Choose a tool: Two tools are offered. Each lists its costs and what it gives, then what may happen later.

3) Mini game: A short skill game applies the tool. There are 26 different ones, such as cranking, tracing, wiring and sorting.
4) Crew jobs: Each astronaut gets one job: lab science, refill oxygen, dig ice for water, garden, repair or rest.

5) Night: Supplies are used up; results arrive and the base changes visibly.

o   A guide character, Nova, teaches the first day with a spoken tutorial. Nothing is scary: if the mission fails, "Mission Control brings the crew home safely". Every ending shows what happened, which choice caused it and a true NASA story about a similar situation.

o   Rewards keep children coming back: 19 badges that pay stars during play, five ranks and a shop with 32 base decorations. A Training room lets them practice each mini-game and see "why this tool matters" cards with real NASA photographs.

 

How does it work?

A rules engine holds all the game logic. It is deterministic: the same seed always gives the same game, so every rule can be tested. All game content (60 events, of which 24 are in the kid game) is generated from one written specification, where each science fact carries a numbered source.

An automatic content check fails the build if any action card has no cost. This is how "no free lunch" is enforced.

A simulator plays thousands of games with five strategies to check balance. In 1,000 simulated games a crew that only does science never win, and balanced play wins about three games in four.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Benefits

o   Children learn systems thinking: every gain has a cost, and upkeep matters as much as discovery.

o   They meet real space science in context: radiation, life support, power budgets and communication delay.

o   Teachers can use it in one lesson. A teacher guide is included, and a game takes about 10 minutes.

o   It is safe and accessible: no accounts, tracking or adverts. It has large tap targets, readable text and keyboard control, and it never relies on color alone.

What we hope to achieve

We want children to finish a game able to explain one real trade-off a Mars crew faces, and curious enough to open the NASA source behind it. Next steps are playtests with children in the target age range, an Arabic version, and a "today's Sun" mode that reads live DONKI data.

Tools and technology

Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS, with Python for one build script.

Frameworks and build: Preact, Vite, Vitest (145 automated tests).

Graphics and sound: all art is SVG drawn in code. Sound effects and ambience are synthesised in the browser with the Web Audio API.

Voice: Nova's tutorial voice is computer speech from Piper, an open-source text-to-speech engine, using a voice trained on public-domain recordings.

Data: NASA DONKI API, NASA OSDR, NASA mission pages and NASA image library.

Assets: Twemoji icons (CC-BY 4.0), Atkinson Hyperlegible font (OFL).

Hosting: Vercel. Play at https://nova-knights-hazel.vercel.app/

AI use: the code and game text were written with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude Code), directed and reviewed by the team. No AI-generated images, video or music are in the game.

How is your project creative?

The creativity of Nova Knights Adventure lies not just in being an educational game, but in how it integrates real NASA scientific data into an engaging, simplified experience tailored for children (ages 7 to 12), through the following innovations:

  • Play-Based Real-World Trade-offs (No "Free Lunch" Rule): Unlike traditional games that give players free rewards, every choice in the game has an immediate or future cost and consequence (such as balancing oxygen, water, and power), teaching children strategic thinking and real resource management.
  • Direct Integration of Real NASA Science (DONKI & Real Data): Solar storms and technical glitches are not random; they are pulled from real NASA logs (such as the May 2024 solar storms and solar-weather data from the DONKI database). With every problem a child faces, an authentic scientific fact and a verifiable source are available to open.
  • Interactive Storytelling with a Friendly Guide (Nova): A welcoming digital guide named Nova uses a calm, computer-generated voice (powered by Piper text-to-speech) to make children feel safe. Even if a mission fails, they are met with a reassuring message from "Mission Control bringing the crew home safely."
  • Zero-Friction, Lightweight Web Architecture: The game runs smoothly directly in any browser with no login, downloads, or user tracking required, making it instantly accessible on cheap smartphones or classroom projectors.

What factors did your team consider?

During the design and development of the project, the team carefully factored in several critical pedagogical, technical, and accessibility standards:

  • Pedagogical Alignment & Target Age Group: The interface was designed specifically for children (7-12 years old) using highly readable typography (Atkinson Hyperlegible), large tap targets, and non-frightening mechanics. Each game takes about 10 minutes, making it ideal for a single classroom lesson.
  • Scientific Accuracy & Complete Transparency: While game mechanics are streamlined for pacing (e.g., speeding up processes by 15x), the team maintained strict honesty. A dedicated data screen clearly distinguishes between fun "game rules" and authentic "NASA facts."
  • Rigorous Balance Simulation & Automated Testing: To ensure the game is neither impossible nor trivial, the team built a simulator that ran over 1,000 automated test games across five strategies, proving that balanced play wins roughly three out of four games. They also wrote 145 automated code tests to ensure total system reliability.
  • Accessibility & Lightweight Tech Stack: Built using clean, modern web technologies (TypeScript, Preact, Vite), SVG graphics coded directly, and local browser audio synthesis (Web Audio API), the game ensures full keyboard and touch accessibility without relying on color alone to convey critical information.

projectDetails.name: NOVALITH_SUT
projectDetails.summary:
Team NOVALITH developed Mars Explorer, an interactive web prototype for planning a simulated science traverse across the western delta of Jezero Crater. It addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by combining NASA orbital imagery, HiRISE elevation data, USGS regional geology, and Perseverance observations in one layered map.

Users can explore science sites, choose a start and destination, and compare routes by distance and slope. When a route crosses a simulated dust storm, the app can calculate a detour and show how the change affects travel time and estimated oxygen and battery reserves. A shared Mission Control view lets teammates follow the simulated traverse and discuss route decisions.

The shortest route can cross steep terrain or a hazard, while a detour can use more time and resources. Mars Explorer makes those trade-offs visible and gives students and teams a practical way to explore how real planetary data can inform a simulated mission.
projectDetails.details:
How it works

Team NOVALITH built Mars Explorer for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It is a web prototype for planning and simulating science traverses in a roughly 2 × 2 km area of Jezero Crater’s western delta. The map combines NASA/JPL orbital imagery, HiRISE stereo elevation data, USGS regional geology, and observations from the Perseverance rover.

Users can switch map layers, inspect a point’s elevation and slope, and explore science sites such as Skinner Ridge. In Route Planner, they select a start and destination, add optional waypoints, and compare the shortest route with an alternative that accounts for slope. The app displays distance, maximum sampled grade, an elevation profile, and nearby science sites.

What makes it creative

The map turns a route into a decision users can test. They can add a simulated dust storm, see whether it intersects the planned route, and calculate a detour. The app shows how route choices affect estimated travel time, oxygen, and battery reserves. During a simulated traverse, teammates can use a mission code to follow progress in Mission Control. They can also report a route obstacle and review or replay the traverse afterward.

In one test of the hosted app, the weather detour avoided the simulated storm and added about 71 meters, while reducing the maximum sampled grade from 22.3° to 16.3°. That example shows why we made both distance and terrain effort visible.

Tools, design choices, and intended impact

We built the interface with JavaScript, React, HTML, and CSS, using OpenLayers for mapping and Three.js for 3D views. Python and FastAPI handle terrain sampling and route calculations. Vercel hosts the app, and Neon PostgreSQL stores shared missions and incident reports. The prototype runs in a standard web browser.

We considered map alignment, terrain resolution, access to science targets, uncertainty in resource estimates, and availability of live NASA feeds. The core route planner uses bundled terrain data. The approximately 20 m analysis grid cannot resolve small obstacles or soil strength, and the simulated hazards and suit estimates cannot establish astronaut safety. Our goal is to help students and teams understand how planetary data informs route decisions and explain why a plan changes when conditions change.

challengeDetails.title: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map
challengeDetails.excerpt: NASA has explored Mars robotically for decades, studying its extreme environment, mapping its surface, and collecting many types of data. Far from home, the first astronauts to set foot on Mars will want the best map possible, with information on the details of their routes and destinations, updates on current conditions, and the data needed to complete their mission quickly and safely. Your challenge is to create a layered, integrated view of a location or route on the Martian surface that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions and could help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk while conducting new and exciting science along the way.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroGuard
projectDetails.summary:
AstroGuard is an integrated astronaut health-monitoring software prototype developed by Team NovaPharma for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It brings seven health domains into one platform, using individual baselines to track changes, visualize health trends, and identify potential concerns. The platform features a Mission Control dashboard, an interactive Digital Twin, an Alerts Center, an Action Center for structured follow-up, scenario comparisons, and AURA, a rule-based digital companion.

AstroGuard addresses the challenge by connecting health indicators into a clearer, more explainable monitoring workflow: Monitor, Analyze, Visualize, and Respond. This is important because long-duration space missions expose astronauts to multiple interacting health risks, making continuous awareness and timely follow-up essential. The current prototype uses simulated data and is designed to support not replacemedical teams.
projectDetails.details:
AstroGuard is a browser-based astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support crew health awareness during long-duration space missions.

It monitors seven health domains using simulated crew data and individual baselines to identify changes over time. Its features include a Mission Control dashboard, health analytics, an interactive Digital Twin, an Alerts Center, an Action Center for structured follow-up, scenario comparisons, and AURA, a rule-based digital companion.

The platform follows a Monitor, Analyze, Visualize, and Respond workflow. It helps users explore health trends, understand potential concerns, and organize follow-up actions. Its intended impact is to support earlier awareness of changing health patterns and improve communication between astronauts and medical teams.

AstroGuard was developed using JavaScript, React, and ES modules, with esbuild for bundling into a self-contained HTML application. Its Digital Twin uses a custom WebGL2 renderer. Node.js and Playwright were used for testing, while GitHub and Vercel supported source control and deployment. No dedicated hardware is required for the current prototype.

The project's creativity lies in combining personalized baselines, multi-domain monitoring, explainable alerts, interactive visualization, and structured follow-up in one platform. The team considered spaceflight health risks, data reliability, usability, scientific accuracy, and the limitations of simulated data.

AI Declaration: AI tools, including ChatGPT and Claude, were used to assist with research organization, brainstorming, coding, debugging, documentation, and content refinement. The team reviewed and refined AI-assisted outputs and remains responsible for the final project and its submitted materials.

projectDetails.name: NovaQuest
projectDetails.summary:
We developed TerraTwin, a web app that helps users find places on Earth that resemble landscapes on Mars or the Moon. Users upload a photo, and the app compares its visual features with 720 satellite images from 177 countries and areas. The closest matches appear as coloured flags on a 3D globe. Clicking a flag shows the Earth location beside the original photo and explains their similarities.
TerraTwin addresses the difficulty of finding Earth analogue sites—environments that can help researchers study planetary landscapes and plan equipment tests before space missions. We also developed a terrain dataset and machine-learning models to support terrain analysis.
The project makes planetary science more accessible to students, educators and researchers through real images and clear comparisons. Its results suggest candidate visual analogues, not exact locations or confirmed mission sites, providing a useful starting point for further investigation.
projectDetails.details: TerraTwin is a web app that helps people find places on Earth that look like landscapes on Mars or the Moon. Users upload a photo, and the app compares its colour, brightness, contrast and texture with 720 satellite images from 177 countries and areas. The closest matches appear as coloured flags on a 3D globe; clicking a flag shows the real place beside the uploaded photo and explains the similarities. We also built a terrain dataset and two machine-learning models to classify Earth landscapes and calculate terrain scores. We used TypeScript, React and Python, with tools such as Three.js and scikit-learn, while Manus helped with development and documentation. Its creative feature is combining real images, an interactive globe and clear explanations to make planetary science easier to explore. It can help students, teachers and researchers discover possible Earth analogue sites for study and equipment testing. Our team considered privacy, ease of use, data quality and differences between satellite and rover photos, so the app shows visual similarity—not an exact location or proof that a site is suitable for a mission.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. projectDetails.name: Project Nova Rover Systems
projectDetails.summary:
**Planet X and SPHEREx** is an interactive web platform designed to make NASA’s massive infrared space archives accessible, visual, and engaging for everyone.

### What We Built

We created a dual-interface web application consisting of an immersive 3D cinematic storytelling landing page and an advanced **Sky Explorer dashboard**. The platform features instant coordinate lookup, pre-tested celestial target presets, an automated guided tour, and real-time infrared spectral band visualization.

### The Problem It Addresses

NASA space telescopes—such as SPHEREx, WISE, and Euclid—generate vast, petabyte-scale data about the infrared universe. However, this raw data is traditionally locked behind complex technical barriers, making it slow and difficult for students, educators, and citizen scientists to explore, query, or analyze without heavy network latency.

### How It Helps and Why It Matters

Our platform solves this by using optimized spatial indexing ("Sky Zoning") and a **Difference Mode** that subtracts background starlight across multiple time epochs. This allows users to instantly "time-travel" across the infrared sky, strip away static background stars, and effortlessly spot moving or flaring cosmic anomalies (like variable stars, comets, or outer-system bodies) in milliseconds.

By turning complex astrophysical telemetry into an intuitive, browser-based exploration tool, our project democratizes space data, empowers classrooms, and inspires the next generation .
projectDetails.details:
Project Technical Explanation & Submission Dossier

Project Name: Planet X and SPHEREx

Team Name: Nova Rover Systems

Event: NASA Space Apps Challenge (Cairo 2026)

1. Executive Summary & Core Mission

Planet X and SPHEREx is an advanced, dual-interface astronomical exploration platform engineered to democratize access to NASA’s petabyte-scale infrared archives. By bridging the gap between raw, complex astronomical telemetry and intuitive interactive exploration, our application empowers citizen scientists, educators, and researchers to time-travel across the infrared cosmos, track transient cosmic objects, and analyze stellar spectra with unprecedented ease and precision.

Main Use Case (Cairo Submission Focus)

The primary operational use case of our platform is the rapid isolation and multi-epoch spectral analysis of astronomical transients and moving targets (such as high-proper-motion brown dwarfs, distant comets, variable stars, and hypothetical outer-solar-system bodies like Planet X). Using pre-tested celestial patches (e.g., Andromeda, the Galactic Center, Orion Nebula, and WISE 0855), users can instantly query coordinate zones, compare baseline epochs, and detect shifting or flaring anomalies without suffering the massive latency typically associated with querying raw all-sky astronomical databases.

2. Technical Architecture & How It Works

Our architecture is built around three core pillars designed to handle massive data volumes efficiently:

  • Spatial Partitioning & Sky Zoning: To eliminate network and rendering latency, the celestial sphere is partitioned into indexed Sky Zones. Instead of streaming massive all-sky maps simultaneously, the application focuses client-side rendering on optimized, pre-tested high-interest target patches where astronomical targets are pre-validated.
    • Single Mode: Renders direct observational flux frames at specific epochs, allowing users to study baseline static sky brightness and morphology.
    • Difference Mode: Executes differential image processing by subtracting the multi-epoch mean background. This instantly strips away static background stars and highlights moving or transient sources.
  • Spectral Band Analysis: The platform maps out 102 infrared spectral bands across detectors D1 through D6 (modeled after the SPHEREx instrument framework), enabling users to inspect flux-versus-wavelength curves and identify ice absorption features, galactic structures, and stellar classifications.

3. How NASA Data Supports the Solution

Our platform is directly anchored in NASA’s premier astrophysics missions:

  • SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer): Provides the foundational framework for our 102-band near-infrared spectral processing and cosmological ice-mapping storytelling.
  • WISE, NEOWISE, and Euclid Archives: Utilized for multi-epoch temporal comparison baselines, supplying the historical sky coverage required for differential time-series analysis.

This data is integrated into our spatial indexing pipeline, transforming raw fits and catalog data into smooth, client-side interactive visual frames and flux graphs.

4. Tools, Languages, Software, and Hardware

  • Frontend & User Interface: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), Tailwind CSS for responsive, high-performance styling.
  • 3D Graphics & Animation: Three.js (for immersive space rendering and starfield visualization), GSAP (GreenSock Animation Platform) with ScrollTrigger, and Lenis for cinematic smooth scrolling.
  • Backend & Data Processing Utilities: Python (leveraging pandas and openpyxl for background data pipelining, astronomical catalog formatting, and roster management).
  • Deployment & Hosting: Git/GitHub for version control; Firebase Hosting for global, low-latency production deployment.
  • Development Environment: Windows development workstations running Visual Studio Code.

5. Benefits, Impact, and Long-Term Goals

  • Democratization of Science: Lowers the barrier to entry for space data, turning complex infrared spectroscopy into an accessible, engaging web experience.
  • Educational Empowerment: Serves as an interactive virtual observatory for classrooms and universities to teach observational astronomy and data science.
  • Citizen Science Acceleration: Provides tools that can scale to assist amateur astronomers in flagging real sky anomalies.

6. Current Working Features vs. Future Roadmap

To assist judges inspecting the delivered static and hosted project without a live walkthrough, features are strictly categorized below:

🟢 Fully Working & Verified Features (Delivered in Current Prototype)

  • Cinematic 3D Landing Page (index.html): Fully interactive Three.js space narrative comparing legacy missions with SPHEREx.
  • Advanced Sky Explorer Dashboard (explorer.html): Fully operational query interface supporting coordinate input (RA/Dec) and pre-tested celestial presets.
  • Automated Guided Tour: An interactive, step-by-step onboarding walkthrough that triggers automatically upon entering the explorer.
  • Mode Switching & Temporal Scrubbing: Functional UI toggles for Single vs. Difference mode and frame playback controls.
  • Spectral Plotting Simulation: Dynamic visualization of infrared spectral bands across detectors D1–D6.

🔵 Future Roadmap (Post-Hackathon Expansion)

  • Live NASA API Integration: Transitioning from optimized pre-tested local data patches to live, streaming queries against NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive REST endpoints.
  • Advanced Machine Learning Classification: Integrating automated anomaly detection models to flag genuine transient candidates in real-time.

7. System Limitations

  • Client-Side Processing Bounds: To maintain high frame rates and zero-latency interaction in a browser environment, the current prototype relies on pre-tested, high-density target patches rather than querying raw petabyte-scale all-sky FITS files directly on the client.
  • Simulated Telemetry vs. Live Stream: While scientific math, spectral band distributions, and differential processing logic strictly reflect authentic mission parameters, live real-time telemetry streaming from active orbital observatories is reserved for the production roadmap phase.

projectDetails.name: Orbit Forge
projectDetails.summary: Orbit Forge is a browser-based, pixel-art educational game that teaches space mission design through hands-on systems engineering. Space missions require balancing competing demands—budget, mass, power, data, communications, and time—where upgrading one subsystem impacts every other. Designed for students, teens, and aspiring engineers, Orbit Forge lets players assemble spacecraft, validate launch vehicle and orbit compatibility in real time, navigate branching in-flight anomalies, and analyze detailed post-mission reports explaining why their mission succeeded or failed
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works: Orbit Forge turns abstract space mission trade-offs into an interactive, progressive game loop:

  1. Scenarios & Mission Briefing: Players choose from multiple mission scenarios (such as Earth Observation, Moon, and Mars), each featuring 5 progressively challenging missions with strict resource budgets and objectives.
  2. Spacecraft & Orbit Assembly: Players select a launch vehicle, spacecraft platform, scientific instruments, power systems, communications, and target orbit. A live validation engine checks mass-to-orbit limits, power balance, budget, and downlink capacity, providing plain-language explanations for any design conflict.
  3. In-Flight Branching Decisions & Tasks: During flight, players respond to incoming transmissions (e.g., solar storms, power dips, communication blackouts) via two-choice branching trees that dynamically alter resources and mission outcomes, followed by destination-specific task execution.
  4. Post-Mission Analysis: Every run ends with a comprehensive debrief showing resource usage, star rating, and plain-language root-cause explanations ("WHY?" learning cards) for any failure.

Tech Stack & Current Status: Built with Next.js (static export), JavaScript, Tailwind CSS (custom pixel-art design system), Motion, and GSAP for flight choreography, powered by static JSON datasets and localStorage for instant, account-free browser play.

  • Currently Working: Full gameplay loop across scenarios, real-time 6-resource HUD, live launch vehicle/orbit compatibility validator, interactive tutorials library, and local progress saving.
  • Limitations & Future Plans: Currently single-player with static datasets; planned additions include 4-player role-based team mode, sandbox mode, cloud saves, and Arabic localization.

projectDetails.name: Project Nova sync
projectDetails.summary:
SAR Detective is an interactive web app that makes radar satellite imagery understandable to anyone, not just remote-sensing experts. Radar can see Earth's surface through clouds and darkness, but SAR images are grainy, grayscale and hard to read without training, so most people never use this data.

The app uses radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission (GCOV products from NASA Earthdata), with NASA Worldview/GIBS imagery for context. Users explore an interactive map and compare optical and radar views side by side. They can highlight surface types such as water, vegetation and urban areas. A lightweight machine-learning model classifies radar patterns, and an AI assistant explains in plain language what the user is seeing, for example why a river looks dark or why cities look bright.

This matters because radar watches our planet constantly, through floods, storms and nights. By turning complex SAR observations into something people can explore, SAR Detective can help students, journalists and local communities understand how Earth is changing.
projectDetails.details: SAR Detective is a website that shows where the ground changed after a flood, using NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which sees through storm clouds that block ordinary satellite photos. We tested it on the October 2026 San Juan River flood in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, comparing two NISAR GCOV scenes taken 12 days apart on the same track (Oct 14 and Oct 26). In a reproducible Colab notebook, we applied the product's quality masks, filtered radar speckle, corrected a −0.57 dB processing offset, and flagged pixels whose radar echo changed by 3 dB or more. Flagged change was about 8× more common within 200 m of the river than 1 km or more away (2.85% vs 0.35%), and the USGS river gauge independently confirms the flood timing. The live site has a before/after slider, a change map with the river overlay, example spots, a printable report, an open API, and a question box that answers only from our verified results. It's meant to help residents, responders and planners see where to look after a flood without needing radar expertise, while being honest about limits, such as not being able to confirm whether a specific street flooded. What makes it creative is its built-in near-river vs. far-from-river control, a deliberately shown false-alarm spot, and the grounded question box, instead of just a raw radar image. We based our choices on using a real, verifiable event, the timing of the passes, data quality and processing differences, the change threshold, a non-expert audience, and reproducibility. We built it with Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Google Colab, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, pandas, Matplotlib, earthaccess, FastAPI, Leaflet, Vercel and GitHub, with Claude (Anthropic) used for coding assistance and grounded answers.

projectDetails.name: the red planet
projectDetails.summary: Mars Survival Map by team Null Orbit helps astronauts plan a safe Marswalk in Jezero Crater on Mars.We used NASA data to build an interactive map that shows terrain, slope, hazards, science points, and water ice. Users can turn layers on and off, draw a route, and get a survival score for that route based on safety and science value.For example, a flat route near water ice and science points gets a high score, while a steep route near hazards gets a low score.Our goal is to turn complex NASA data into a simple tool that helps future astronauts walk on Mars safely, avoid danger, and do great science
projectDetails.details:
What does it do?

Mars Survival Map is an interactive web map for Jezero Crater. The astronaut can explore the map, turn layers on and off, draw a route, and instantly see if the route is safe.How does it work?

We used NASA Mars data for terrain, elevation, and slope. We added layers for hazards like steep slopes and rough terrain, science points like interesting rocks and minerals, and water ice locations. When the user draws a route, our system calculates a survival score from 0 to 100 based on slope, distance, hazards, science value, and access to water ice.What tools did we use?

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with Leaflet for the map, and NASA open data for Jezero Crater. We designed the interface to be simple and clear, even for non-experts.What is the impact?

It helps astronauts avoid danger, save energy, and choose routes that give the most science. It also helps students and the public understand Mars exploration.What is innovative?

Instead of showing just a static map, we turn the map into a decision tool. The user does not just look at Mars, they plan a real Marswalk and get a score that explains why one route is safer than another.What did we consider?

We considered safety first, then science, then simplicity. We made the colors clear, the buttons big, and the score easy to understand for anyone.

projectDetails.name: SPHEREx sky time machine
projectDetails.summary: SPHEREx Sky Time Machine is a free website that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared survey into short videos of the sky. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, but its data comes as hundreds of separate image files per spot, which NASA’s archive shows one at a time. Our pipeline finds every SPHEREx photo of a position, removes bad pixels and the glow of solar-system dust, lines the photos up on one grid, and stacks each six-month sky pass into a video frame. The website plays these frames like a flip-book, with a “what changed” view that makes moving or brightening objects stand out. Clicking a target shows its spectrum across all colours and how its brightness changed. Known stars from Gaia and WISE are drawn on top to check what is new. Tested on real data, it recovered all 14 sightings of two known fast-moving stars and confirmed a pulsating star’s change. A faint, slowly moving Planet X or a cold brown dwarf would look just like this. Our tool lets students, citizen scientists and researchers look for them, no code needed.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. SPHEREx Sky Time Machine plays NASA SPHEREx infrared photos of one spot in the sky as a short video, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out. For any position, our Python pipeline asks NASA’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx photo that covers it and downloads only the patch it needs. It removes bad pixels and the glow of solar-system dust, lines every photo up on one north-up grid, and averages each six-month sky pass into one video frame. The website offers a flip-book, a “what changed” view, a deep stack, single-colour views, and a spectrum and light curve for each target. Known stars from Gaia and WISE are drawn on top, moved to each photo’s date.

Benefits and impact. SPHEREx data comes as hundreds of separate files per spot, which today takes code and astronomy skills to use. Our tool lets students, teachers and citizen scientists simply look. Volunteers already found brown dwarfs by flipping through older WISE photos; we bring that method to NASA’s newest survey. A faint, slow-moving Planet X would look exactly like the movers we show.

Results (real data only). The pictures line up with Gaia stars to within 0.03″. The mover finder recovered all 14 sightings of two known fast-moving stars. WISE 0855’s brightness agrees with NASA WISE. The pulsating star R Draconis changes about 1.6×, while control stars stay steady. We claim no new objects.

Tools. Python (Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy), JavaScript with React and Vite, an optional Flask API, and GitHub Pages for hosting. We worked on our own laptops with no special hardware, and used Claude (AI) with full disclosure.

Creativity. One tool shows both motion over time and make-up across 102 colours, using the same photos.

What we considered. We considered honesty first. Every light curve gives a verdict: “steady”, “changes” or “inconclusive”. Unreliable data is flagged, not hidden, and we report our limits openly. We also wanted the tool free, with no login, shareable links and plain-language explanations.

projectDetails.name: AstroCare
projectDetails.summary: AstroCare is an educational astronaut-health monitoring Android prototype with a tested backend. The interface presents vital readings, measurement entry, guidance and safety information. The backend accepts heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature and sleep records, preserves history, supports duplicate-safe synchronisation, and returns seven-day trends with rule-linked evidence. NASA Human Research Program hazard material provides space-health context for the guidance. The demonstration uses synthetic data, not real astronaut measurements. AstroCare aims to help a crew member notice and understand a change in routine health indicators; it does not diagnose, prescribe treatment or replace a flight surgeon.
projectDetails.details:
AstroCare addresses the challenge of gathering health indicators and making self-assessment understandable during a space mission. The intended workflow is to record a measurement or symptom, synchronise the record when a connection is available, and review the latest values, recent trends and evidence behind an indicator flag.

The team's actual Android screenshots show an English interface with Overview, Data, Trends and Settings navigation. Overview displays five vital indicators with units, timestamps and Demo labels. Data Entry lets a user choose a metric, enter a reading and optional note, then select Save & evaluate. Measurement guides explain the steps and label alert boundaries as illustrative. Safety information explicitly states that the app is decision support, not a medical diagnosis. Settings show sync and Wi-Fi-only controls. Screenshots demonstrate these UI states, not full end-to-end network or physical-sensor validation.

The reviewed implementation is a Node.js 22+/Express/MongoDB backend using Mongoose, Zod and JSON Schema validation, with shared contract version 1.0.0. It supports five measurement categories: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), temperature and sleep. A batch can also contain symptom check-ins and alert evidence. The API validates record structure and timestamps, enforces cross-field rules such as systolic pressure exceeding diastolic pressure, and returns item-level created, duplicate or rejected results.

Stable record identifiers and database unique indexes make ordinary retries duplicate-safe. History endpoints restore records using metric and time filters. An implemented proposed overview extension recomputes current status from the latest relevant evidence and returns derived alerts without saving them to uploaded alert history. Seven-day trend reports include daily points, baseline summaries, direction labels and insights. The production algorithm is deterministic Node code; it does not call a remote LLM or invoke Python in production. Versioned rules and measurement guides are available as immutable assets.

A reproducible local demonstration loaded 126 synthetic measurements and one symptom check-in. Repeating the seed inserted zero new records and skipped 127 existing fixtures. With the clock fixed to 13 November 2026 at 19:00 UTC, trends returned five metrics and one insight for 7–13 November, while overview returned a warning with two evidence-linked derived rules. The backend test suite was rerun successfully: 64 tests passed, zero failed and zero skipped; contract verification passed as well. This establishes tested software behavior, not clinical or flight suitability.

Current limits include a single demo astronaut, API-key-only access rather than production user authentication, synthetic fixtures, illustrative rules, and backend tests that do not establish Android-device/end-to-end integration. Sync batches are not all-or-nothing transactions. Future work includes secure individual accounts, tested client/sensor integration, clearer visualisation and expert review of health interpretation. Real human research data would require a specifically identified dataset and documented access, licence and processing before reuse.

projectDetails.name: Project Earth Print
projectDetails.summary: NUN is a scientific intelligence platform that combines satellite imagery, Earth observation data, and AI to monitor and analyze environmental changes in ancient Egyptian lake landscapes. By connecting modern scientific data with Ancient Egyptian heritage, NUN transforms complex environmental information into meaningful insights, interactive visualizations, and immersive storytelling.
projectDetails.details:
NUN: From Ancient Wisdom to Earth Observation Intelligence

1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

NUN is an Earth Observation Intelligence Platform that transforms satellite data into meaningful environmental insights through geospatial analysis, scientific indicators, and interactive storytelling.

Our first case study focuses on the Lake Chad Basin, one of the world's most environmentally significant and vulnerable freshwater systems.

NUN investigates three fundamental questions:
- Where is surface water changing?
- How rapidly are these changes occurring?
- Are the observed trends statistically significant?

The platform follows a scientific workflow that integrates satellite observations, processes environmental indicators, analyzes changes over time, and translates complex geospatial information into accessible visual insights.

Our proposed analytical pipeline includes:
1. Collecting Earth observation data from NASA and other relevant scientific sources.
2. Processing satellite reflectance data and applying water indices such as NDWI and MNDWI.
3. Identifying surface-water patterns and estimating water extent in square kilometers.
4. Aggregating observations across monthly and historical time periods.
5. Applying statistical methods, including the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope, to investigate long-term trends.
6. Presenting the findings through interactive visualizations and an engaging digital storytelling experience.

2. What benefits does your project have?

NUN provides several important benefits:

- Environmental Awareness: Makes long-term changes in water resources easier to understand.
- Data Accessibility: Converts complex satellite observations into understandable visual information.
- Scientific Decision Support: Provides a framework for identifying environmental trends and supporting further investigation.
- Historical Perspective: Connects present-day environmental observations with historical changes.
- Educational Value: Makes Earth observation and environmental science more engaging and accessible.
- Scalability: Establishes a methodology that can potentially be extended to other lakes, wetlands, and vulnerable ecosystems.

Instead of simply displaying satellite images, NUN aims to explain what those images reveal about environmental change.

3. What is the intended impact of your project?

Our intended impact is to make environmental change measurable, understandable, and actionable.

By investigating Lake Chad, NUN aims to support awareness of freshwater vulnerability, encourage evidence-based environmental research, and demonstrate how Earth observation technologies can contribute to understanding complex environmental challenges.

In the longer term, we envision NUN evolving into a scalable environmental intelligence platform that connects satellite data, scientific analysis, and human understanding.

Our ambition is to bridge the gap between scientific data and the people who need to understand it, including researchers, educators, environmental organizations, and decision-makers.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Our technical approach is built around Earth observation, geospatial analysis, statistical methods, and interactive web technologies.

Scientific Data Sources and Platforms:
- NASA Earthdata: Access to Earth observation datasets.
- NASA Giovanni: Environmental data exploration and visualization.
- NASA AppEEARS: Satellite data access and processing workflows.
- MODIS MOD09A1 Version 6.1: Surface reflectance data used as a primary source for the proposed water-index analysis.
- NASA IMERG and GLDAS: Supporting precipitation and land-surface context.
- NASA SWOT LakeSP: Potential complementary lake-observation data.

Scientific and Analytical Methods:
- NDWI and MNDWI water indices.
- Geospatial analysis and surface-water area estimation.
- Monthly and historical temporal aggregation.
- Mann–Kendall trend analysis.
- Sen's slope estimation.


Proposed Development Technologies:
- Python for data processing and scientific analysis.
- FastAPI for backend services.
- React for the interactive frontend.
- Geospatial visualization tools for presenting environmental information.

The project does not depend on specialized physical hardware; its core architecture is designed around satellite data and software-based analysis.

5. How is your project creative?

NUN introduces a distinctive approach by combining modern Earth observation science with the cultural and visual heritage of Ancient Egypt.

The name NUN is inspired by the primordial waters of Ancient Egyptian cosmology, creating a meaningful connection between the ancient understanding of water as the origin of life and modern scientific efforts to monitor freshwater systems.

Our creativity is reflected in three dimensions:

Scientific Innovation: Transforming satellite observations into measurable environmental indicators and long-term trend analysis.

Cultural Storytelling: Using Ancient Egyptian visual language and the symbolism of water to communicate environmental change through a meaningful narrative.

Digital Experience: Combining scientific intelligence, interactive data visualization, and immersive visual storytelling rather than presenting disconnected satellite images or static charts.

NUN is designed to make environmental science not only informative but also understandable, memorable, and engaging.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several essential factors throughout the project:

- Scientific Accuracy: Selecting credible datasets and appropriate analytical methods.
- Data Quality: Considering cloud contamination, missing observations, spatial resolution, and temporal consistency.
- Environmental Complexity: Recognizing the influence of rainfall, evaporation, seasonal variation, and other environmental factors.
- Statistical Reliability: Distinguishing genuine long-term trends from short-term fluctuations.
- User Experience: Making complex scientific information accessible through clear visualizations and storytelling.
- Cultural Relevance: Building a visual identity inspired by Ancient Egyptian heritage without compromising scientific credibility.
- Scalability: Designing a methodology that can eventually be adapted to other freshwater ecosystems.
- Transparency: Distinguishing measured observations from interpretations and avoiding unsupported conclusions.
Our Vision
NUN represents a bridge between the wisdom of the past and the intelligence of modern Earth observation.

We believe that satellite data should do more than show us how our planet looks. It should help us understand how our planet changes, why those changes matter, and how knowledge can support a more sustainable future.

NUN — Reading Earth's Waters. Revealing the Stories Behind Change.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AstroScout AI
projectDetails.summary:
AstroScout AI is a hybrid artificial intelligence system developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 9. It aims to find the most accurate geological environments on Earth that simulate Martian and Lunar terrains.
​The core idea goes beyond mere visual similarity by building a cloud-based engine that relies on three technical pillars:
​Data Engineering: Sanitizing and standardizing NASA maps into true-color, noise-free, nadir (satellite) views.
​Hybrid AI: Integrating three advanced computer vision models (ResNet-50, VGG-16, MobileNetV2) to deeply analyze terrain roughness and spatial patterns.
​Geochemical Reranking: Applying a mathematical algorithm that balances AI topographical similarity with chemical color signatures, ensuring the actual geological makeup (like iron or basalt) matches.
​The ultimate goal is to provide NASA with highly reliable data to pinpoint exact, safe simulation sites. These locations are crucial for training astronauts and testing rovers before space missions launch, significantly minimizing risks and ensuring mission success.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem:
Testing rovers and training astronauts for extraterrestrial missions requires highly accurate simulation sites on Earth. Relying on basic visual similarities often leads to selecting terrains with the wrong geochemical makeup or structural hazards.

Our Solution (AstroScout AI / GEO-MATCH):
We built a robust, cloud-deployed AI engine that doesn't just look at shapes, but analyzes the deep geological footprint of space terrains. Our solution is divided into three main pillars:
1. Data-Centric AI (Sanitization & Standardization): We prioritized clean data over complex generic models. We calibrated Mars/Moon inputs to true-color, nadir (satellite) views, and stripped text noise.
2. Hybrid Ensemble Architecture: We deployed a decentralized Cloud API on Hugging Face using three specific models: ResNet-50 (60% weight for topographical roughness), VGG-16 (20% for spatial patterns), and MobileNetV2 (20% for rapid feature extraction). We also integrated Gemini for intelligent data interpretation.
3. Mathematical Geochemical Reranking: To prevent "Texture Dominance", we developed a dual-evaluation algorithm. We extract the deep AI feature vector (Cosine Similarity) and penalize it using a mathematical color signature (Euclidean Distance of RGB mean/std) representing chemical makeup (e.g., Iron=Red, Basalt=Dark Gray).

Result:
A highly accurate matched Earth analog (like Jezero Crater to Atacama Desert), stored and retrieved instantly via a Supabase backend.

projectDetails.name: Mars Lifeline
projectDetails.summary: Mars Life Line is a browser game that puts young players in charge of a Martian outpost. Players choose a landing site, restore power and life support, grow food, and respond to a radiation warning. Each choice has a benefit and a cost: backup power helps immediately but leaves the solar panels dusty, while Emergency Mode saves power by pausing crop growth. The game makes the engineering trade-offs of living on Mars interactive and easier to understand.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Life Line is a browser-based junior astronaut mission trainer set at a fictional future outpost on Mars. Players explore the habitat in first person, choose a landing site, restore life-support systems, and manage power, air, water, and food. They can also view the station from above to see how its systems connect.

The game presents choices with visible trade-offs and explains their consequences. In the demonstration, both comparison runs begin at the same checkpoint: backup power raises the battery from 40% to 75% immediately, while cleaning the solar panels restores generation. After three simulated minutes, the clean-panel run reaches 79% charge and the backup-power run falls to 57%. During a radiation warning, Emergency Mode reduces power use but pauses crop growth; keeping the greenhouse lights on grows the tray but uses more power. These are game simulation results, not NASA measurements.

PEBBLE, the outpost’s robot companion, provides contextual guidance through the game’s onboard responder. The prototype was built with TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Rapier, and Zustand. We authored 3D assets with Kiln and exported them as glTF/GLB.

Super Intelligence disclosure: Codex assisted with code, documentation, gameplay capture, trailer editing, and procedural music scripting. ImageGen was used for visual references and selected game art. The trailer’s instrumental score uses an AI-assisted procedural arrangement, and the trailer includes a visible AI-generated-art watermark and audio disclosure metadata. The trailer has no voice-over.

projectDetails.name: Project Odyssey Cartography
projectDetails.summary: Odyssey is a browser-based survival map that turns real NASA data into a safe walking route across Gale Crater. Future crews will explore Mars on foot, but the elevation, imagery, mineral and geology data they need is scattered across separate tools. Odyssey merges the MSL Gale DEM, CTX orbital imagery, 21 CRISM mineral indices, USGS geology and Curiosity photos into one interactive 3D map. An A* route planner traces the safest walk between any two points under a strict 20-degree slope limit, reporting distance, walk time, climb and slope. A first-person EVA helmet visor previews the route, and a printable mission card summarizes it. The app runs fully offline in the browser - no login, no backend - so it works where Mars work happens.
projectDetails.details: Odyssey is a Vite + React + TypeScript web app that renders Gale Crater as an interactive 3D terrain (vendored Three.js r128) from a local 20 m DEM (238x238 cells, ~4.7 km patch in northwest Gale near 4.80S, 137.40E). Pick a start and destination; an A* search over the slope grid traces the safest walk under a 20-degree limit, with four planner modes (Balanced, Distance, Gentler, Safest) and full route stats: distance, walk time, max/mean slope, climb, descent, warnings. Safety screening estimates walk time, suit-hours with a 25% reserve and EVA radiation dose. A first-person helmet visor walks the route with a live HUD; a printable mission card summarizes the traverse. Benefits: one map instead of five scattered datasets, fully offline with no login or backend. Working now: all of the above; demo route 3.31 km, about 2 h 46 min, 13.9-degree max slope. Limits: 20 m screening DEM, synthetic demo waypoints (not rover telemetry), safety values are unverified demo assumptions. Planned: larger coverage, live orbital data, rover-scale obstacle detection, thermal modeling.

projectDetails.name: Astra
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA is an autonomous, offline-first clinical decision support system designed to safeguard astronaut health during deep-space missions (such as Artemis and Mars transit) where up to 22 minutes of signal latency prevents real-time consultation with Earth-based flight surgeons. Built for non-medical crew members, the application transforms a 60-second daily check-in of wearable vitals, point-of-care blood biomarkers, and guided self-assessments into clear diagnostic predictions and countermeasure protocols.

To eliminate AI medical hallucinations in safety-critical environments, Astralis uses a two-tier hybrid architecture: a deterministic System 1 risk classifier (Laya AI, fine-tuned on 6,000 NASA-parameterized mission logs across 10 physiological attributes) calculates calibrated probabilities for 10 spaceflight conditions—including Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), Space Anemia, Decompression Sickness, and Renal Stone Risk—while a System 2 generative advisor translates active alerts into plain-English explanations and step-by-step NASA countermeasure checklists. Featuring an interactive anatomical dashboard, guided measurement tooltips, and one-click mission presets in a responsive Flutter interface, Astralis empowers astronauts to self-triage silent microgravity hazards before they escalate into mission-threatening emergencies.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

1. Guided 60-Second Assessment & Education Layer:

  • Astronauts input 10 essential physiological, environmental, and psychological attributes organized across three rapid stages:
    • Stage 1 — Essential Vitals (Cardiovascular & Thermal): Resting Heart Rate (heart_rate in bpm), Systolic Blood Pressure (systolic_bp in mmHg), Diastolic Blood Pressure (diastolic_bp in mmHg), Blood Oxygen Saturation (spo2 in %), and Core Body Temperature (body_temp in °C).
    • Stage 2 — Blood & Habitat (Biomarkers & Exposure): Fasting Blood Glucose (blood_glucose(fasting) in mg/dL), Daily Radiation Dose (radiation_dose_daily in mSv/day), and Cabin $CO_2$ Partial Pressure (cabin_co2 in mmHg).
    • Stage 3 — Mental & Sleep (Neuro-Vestibular, Sleep & Readiness): Total Sleep Duration (sleep_hours in hours over the last 24h) and Mood & Cognitive Stress Score (mood_stress_score on a 1–10 scale).
  • Because astronauts are not all medical specialists, every metric features built-in "How & Why" measurement guides explaining proper collection technique in microgravity and why orbital baselines differ from Earth norms.

2. Tier 1 — Deterministic Diagnostic Engine (Random Forest Classifier):

  • Raw numerical inputs are serialized into a 10-feature state vectorand evaluated locally in milliseconds by a custom-trained Random Forest Classifier (scikit-learn).
  • Rather than guessing with generative text, Tier 1 uses ensemble decision-tree bagging to output calibrated probability scores (predict_proba) across 10 physiological states: Healthy, Cardiovascular Deconditioning, Immune/Viral Reactivation, Fatigue/Circadian Disorder, Hypoxia/$CO_2$ Anomaly, Space Anemia, Acute Radiation Stress, Renal Stone Risk, Decompression Sickness, and SANS (Neuro-Ocular Syndrome).

3. Tier 2 — Grounded Countermeasure Advisor & Gamified Bio-Sync:

  • Only conditions crossing the calibrated probability threshold ($P \ge 0.50$) are passed to the Tier 2 advisor (FastAPI backend with AI/local LLM integration).
  • The advisor translates the structured medical flags into plain-English physiological explanations and a 3-step operational protocol (immediate hydration/nutrition intervention, exercise/habitat countermeasure adjustment, and follow-up verification timing), clearly distinguishing between Level 1 Crew Self-Care and Level 2 Flight Surgeon Escalation, while rewarding crew adherence through a gamified Bio-Sync streak and task system.

2. Benefits & Expected Impact

  • Deep-Space Autonomy: Operates completely offline during communication blackouts or high-latency lunar and Martian missions.
  • Zero Medical Hallucinations & Explainable Triage: Strictly separates deterministic tree-based risk classification (System 1 Random Forest) from natural-language guidance (System 2), ensuring clinical reliability and transparent feature importance.
  • Cognitive Offloading & Gamified Engagement: Replaces spreadsheet telemetry and alarm fatigue with color-coded visual triage ribbons, interactive diagnostic wizards, and daily health streaks, allowing fatigued astronauts to grasp their health status in seconds.
  • Terrestrial Spin-Off Value: Directly adaptable to isolated, resource-constrained environments on Earth, including polar research stations, submarines, offshore rigs, and rural telemedicine clinics.

3. Space Agency Data & Resources Used

Because real astronaut medical telemetry is protected under medical privacy regulations, we grounded our diagnostic architecture, feature thresholds, and synthetic dataset generation in official space agency literature and hardware frameworks:

  • NASA Human Research Program (HRP) Evidence Books & Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC): Used to define our 10 target conditions, establish physiological perturbation rules across the "RIDGE" hazards (Radiation, Isolation, Distance, Gravity, Environment), and calibrate two-tier clinical alert thresholds.
  • NASA Crew Health and Performance Integrated Data Architecture (CHP-IDA): Inspired our unified aggregation of disparate habit logs, habitat environmental sensors (cabin_co2, radiation_dose_daily), wearable vitals, and metabolic markersinto a single clinical decision support interface.
  • ISS Point-of-Care & Environmental Monitoring Standards: Selected point-of-care metabolic (blood_glucose(fasting)) and spacecraft life-support/dosimetry indicators (cabin_co2, radiation_dose_daily)that match operational monitoring hardware flown aboard the International Space Station.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Frontend: Flutter & Dart (responsive dark-mode web/desktop terminal featuring custom starfield canvas painter, 3-stage assessment wizard, mission presets, gamified streak/task tracker, and interactive diagnostic dashboard).
  • Machine Learning (System 1): Python and scikit-learn (Random Forest Classifier trained and validated on our 10-attribute physiological & habitat dataset, serialized via joblib/pickle for ultra-fast local CPU inference).
  • Backend & System 2 Advisor: FastAPI (Python), REST API integration with Gemini API and local offline LLM fallback (Ollama / Gemma / Llama).
  • Data Engineering: Python (numpy, pandas) synthetic physiological dataset generator producing 6,000 training logs (60 simulated crew profiles) and 2,000 unseen test logs (20 separate crew profiles) across the 10 core telemetry featureswith zero subject leakage.
  • Design & Presentation: Stitch AI, Figma, and Manus / Gamma AI.

5. Honest Limitations & Next Steps

  • Current Limitation: The Random Forest classification model is trained and validated on parameterized synthetic telemetry rather than de-identified clinical flight records.
  • Next Step 1 (Hardware & Sensor Ingestion): Integrate Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) APIs for automated wearable syncing, spacecraft ECLSS telemetry streaming (for cabin_co2 and radiation_dose_daily), and webcam-based remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) for contactless heart_rate estimation.
  • Next Step 2 (Analog Validation): Validate the software workflow, gamified task adherence, and calibration accuracy in terrestrial space-analog missions (such as NASA HERA or the Mars Desert Research Station).

projectDetails.name: On Fire
projectDetails.summary:
On Fire is a web application that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for the Middle East & North Africa and North America. NASA's MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) sensors count fire very differently, so their records cannot be compared directly. We harmonize them: instead of raw hotspots we count "burning units" (a ~10 km square with fire on one day) and convert MODIS to the VIIRS scale with a model fitted per country and season. On years held out from fitting, this cut the disagreement between the two sensors from 144.1% to 30.3%.

Users pick any country, draw any area or type latitude/longitude, choose any date range, and see which months and years burn most, how this month compares with the historical median, and download the calendar (CSV, PNG) and every hotspot detected (CSV). For fires burning now, On Fire shows where they are heading, which towns they could reach and when, how big they are compared with past fires at the same place, and exports a CAP alert file for authorities. An AI fire-risk model, tested against what really burned, adds early warning.

It helps fire services, civil protection, scientists and land managers see what is normal for a place and act early when a season is not.
projectDetails.details: WHAT IT DOES 1. A harmonized burning-activity calendar for every country and both regions: 25 years month by month (amount or "compared to normal"), the fire season (the fewest months holding 75% of a year's fire), the worst month, the trend since 2001, the busiest years and months, and this month against the median of the same month. Hovering a month shows its burning units, its % of normal and the raw hotspots each sensor detected. 2. Any area of interest: draw a box on the map or type its latitude/longitude corners. The area gets its own 25-year calendar, extended to the latest satellite day, and "this month so far vs the same dates in 2012-2025" (median, middle half, rank). A box outside the covered countries is refused with a clear message instead of a false "no fire". 3. Any date range (Nov 2000 to yesterday): total burning, % of normal, busiest month, hotspots detected, a monthly chart, and downloads: monthly summary (CSV), every hotspot in the range (CSV, MODIS + VIIRS), calendar (CSV, PNG). 4. Live fires from five satellites (refreshed every 20 minutes, gas flares removed) on one map for both regions. 5. One fire: projected spread for +3/+6/+12/+24 h from the wind forecast, the first town it could reach and when, smoke, air quality, people nearby, emissions, its size compared with every fire within 50 km since 2012, and a CAP 1.2 alert file for authorities. Alerts are decision support labelled as estimates; the app never issues evacuation orders. 6. AI fire risk per ~50 km cell with the reasons behind each cell, and Truth vs Prediction, which replays past fires (Dixie, Kabylie, Manavgat 2021 and three chosen by rule) against the frozen model's earlier risk map, including its misses. HOW IT WORKS 1. Collect NASA FIRMS detections: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Nov 2000 - Dec 2025) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m (Jan 2012 - Dec 2025) yearly country archives; 2026 and live data from the FIRMS API. 2. Clean both sensors the same way: vegetation fires only, a common confidence filter, static heat sources (gas flares, industry) removed. 3. Count the same thing: fire cell-days = distinct (0.1 degree cell, day) pairs with fire. This removes most of the pixel-size difference. 4. Calibrate MODIS to VIIRS on the 2012-2025 overlap per country and season (power law + small-fire background), chosen on inner validation years and scored only on held-out years 2014, 2017, 2020, 2023. 5. One record: VIIRS from 2012, calibrated MODIS before, with an uncertainty band; then calendar statistics (mean, median, anomalies, fire season). EVIDENCE - Disagreement between MODIS-derived and VIIRS monthly country totals on held-out years: 144.1% before, 30.3% after. At the 2012 sensor switch the harmonized series is off by a factor of 1.25 against MODIS alone; a naive switch is off by 6.5. - Gas flares: in Qatar 93.7% of VIIRS detections are static industrial sources; our detector agrees with NASA's static-source flag with 96.2% precision and 97.0% recall. - Risk model (LightGBM, trained to 2018, tuned 2019-2020, frozen, scored 2021-2025): 59.2% of 8,728 large fires began inside the model's top 10% of risk vs 47.8% for the fire map alone (assumes a perfect 7-day weather forecast). TRY IT (main task) On Windows, install Node.js and Python 3.11+, download the GitHub repository and double-click setup.bat. Click "Area", type North 37.2, South 35.5, West 3, East 9 (northern Algeria): you get "fires peak in August", the 25-year calendar, this month vs the median, and CSV downloads. TOOLS JavaScript, Python, HTML/CSS. React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts, Node.js/Express, FastAPI/Uvicorn, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, Shapely, PyArrow. A standard Windows PC. WORKING NOW / LIMITS / FUTURE Working: everything above runs locally with setup.bat. Limits: prototype on the user's PC (no public hosting yet); values before 2012 are estimates (typically 0.58x-1.51x for a country-month); satellites miss fires under cloud; spread is a rule-of-thumb estimate; the risk model ranks places and cannot say where a fire starts; coverage is two regions. Future: extend to every region, add NOAA-20/21 VIIRS to the long record, public hosting for agencies.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project OnFire🔥
projectDetails.summary:
OnFire brings two different satellite perspectives together to make active fire data easier to explore and understand. Using NASA's MODIS and VIIRS observations, the platform allows users to examine hotspot distribution and changes in fire activity across Punjab, India, during October–November 2025.

By presenting both datasets in one interactive environment, OnFire helps users explore where observations overlap, where they differ, and how satellite resolution and observation characteristics affect the picture of fire activity.

Instead of treating each satellite dataset separately, OnFire offers a clearer, more accessible way to investigate their complementary observations. The goal is to support better understanding of satellite-based fire monitoring data and make it easier to explore patterns that may otherwise be difficult to see.
projectDetails.details:
OnFire is a web-based platform that brings NASA MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot observations into one interactive environment. It helps users explore fire activity, compare observations from two satellite instruments with different spatial resolutions, and understand their differences.

The project focuses on Punjab, India, using NASA FIRMS data collected between October 20 and November 30, 2025. Our workflow includes data acquisition, cleaning, geographic filtering, validation, database storage, and interactive visualization through a web interface.

Users can explore hotspot locations, examine observations over time, and compare MODIS and VIIRS data through the platform's available visualization features.

OnFire aims to make satellite fire data more accessible and understandable, supporting researchers, environmental analysts, and other users interested in monitoring agricultural burning and fire activity.

The backend was developed using C# and ASP.NET Core, with a database and data importer pipeline. The frontend uses web technologies for interactive visualization. The project also uses Python for data processing and analysis. The exact frameworks and libraries are documented in the project source code.

Our approach focuses on combining different satellite perspectives in one platform while considering data quality, spatial resolution differences, observation timing, and the limitations of hotspot detection.

projectDetails.name: MISSION OBBY
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Oppy is a pixel-art story game developed by Team Oppy (Marwan Magdy and Anas Hassany) for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing "Abandoned but not Forgotten." Players travel to Mars to retrace the mission of NASA's Opportunity rover and find her where she fell silent during the 2018 planet-wide dust storm. Designed for 90 sols, Opportunity operated for more than 14 years.

Players complete three interactive tasks inspired by real discoveries: identifying hematite at Eagle Crater, reconstructing rock layers at Endurance Crater, and restoring rover photographs at Victoria Crater. A final drive leads them to Oppy.

The game integrates NASA data directly into gameplay, using authentic Photojournal images, mission facts, and key locations from Opportunity's exploration. Each task reveals real NASA imagery with its title, date, and image ID, while the in-game Resources page links to the original sources.

By turning a real mission into an accessible interactive experience, Mission Oppy makes planetary science engaging for younger audiences and celebrates the rover and the people behind her.
