projectDetails.name: digital ibis
projectDetails.summary:
Digital Ibis is a smart agriculture project designed to help farmers make better, data-driven decisions about crop selection and crop rotation. It combines NASA Earth observation data with local soil and environmental measurements collected through a proposed integrated sensor station. The station is designed to monitor key parameters such as soil moisture, temperature, electrical conductivity (EC), and pH, alongside weather conditions.

By combining satellite data, ground measurements, and crop requirements, the project aims to support an AI-powered decision-support system that evaluates field conditions and provides practical agricultural recommendations. An application MVP demonstrates how farmers can interact with the system and access these insights.

Digital Ibis is designed to be adaptable to agricultural land in different regions worldwide, rather than being limited to one country. Its goal is to bridge the gap between satellite observations and real field conditions, supporting more informed and sustainable farming decisions.
projectDetails.details:
Digital Ibis – Smart Agriculture Powered by NASA Data and Ground Sensors

**What does the project do and how does it work?**

Digital Ibis is a smart agriculture project designed to help farmers make better decisions about soil conditions, crop suitability, and sustainable crop rotation. It combines NASA Earth observation data, environmental information, crop requirements, and ground-level measurements from a proposed integrated agricultural sensor station.

The station is designed to measure soil moisture, soil temperature, electrical conductivity (EC), and pH, along with weather conditions such as air temperature, humidity, wind speed, wind direction, and rainfall. These measurements complement satellite observations by providing information about actual conditions at the field location.

The collected information is intended to be processed and analyzed through an AI-powered decision-support system. The system aims to evaluate field conditions, assess crop suitability, and generate understandable agricultural recommendations. An application MVP demonstrates how farmers can interact with the proposed solution and access its insights.

**What are its benefits and expected impacts?**

Digital Ibis aims to bridge the gap between large-scale satellite observations and real field conditions. It could help farmers make more informed crop-selection and crop-rotation decisions, improve awareness of soil and environmental conditions, and support more efficient use of agricultural resources. Its location-based design is intended to make it adaptable to agricultural land in different regions worldwide.

**What tools, software, programming languages, and hardware were used?**

The project development includes NASA Earth observation and environmental data sources, agricultural datasets, an application MVP, and a conceptual 3D design of the sensor station. The proposed hardware architecture includes an ESP32 microcontroller, a TEROS 12 soil sensor, a separate pH probe, an SHT31 temperature and humidity sensor, wind sensors, a tipping-bucket rain gauge, data storage, 4G connectivity, and a solar power system.

AI-assisted tools were used to support research, organize technical information, and develop project documentation and visual design concepts. The exact programming languages and software frameworks depend on the tools used by the application and development teams.

**What new skills did the team learn?**

Through this project, the team developed skills in researching NASA Earth observation resources, understanding agricultural and environmental datasets, designing sensor-based monitoring systems, exploring AI-assisted decision support, developing application prototypes, and communicating technical ideas through 3D visualization and documentation.

**What challenges did the team face?**

One of the main challenges was integrating multiple data sources that differ in spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and measurement formats. Another challenge was designing a system that can adapt to different geographical locations rather than depending on data from a single country. The team also considered the technical challenges of sensor compatibility, calibration, data quality, and combining ground measurements with satellite observations. Developing a meaningful AI-based recommendation approach while ensuring that its outputs are scientifically supported is another important challenge.

Digital Ibis brings these elements together in a unified concept that connects Earth observation, ground sensing, AI-assisted analysis, and a farmer-facing application to support more informed and sustainable agricultural decisions.

projectDetails.name: Project Pirates of the Caribbean
projectDetails.summary:
**ASTRA – Intelligent Astronaut Health Monitoring Ecosystem**

ASTRA is an intelligent astronaut health-monitoring ecosystem designed to support crew health and mission awareness during spaceflight. It brings together three connected interfaces: an Astronaut Health Profile, a Ground Control Dashboard, and a VR-based Digital Twin with a Helmet HUD.

ASTRA organizes vital health telemetry, including heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, respiration, temperature, sleep, and radiation exposure. Its analytical approach compares readings with each astronaut’s personal baseline, assesses signal quality, and uses AI-assisted analysis to identify unusual health trends.

The system also explores gravity-adaptive health baselines for different environments, including Earth, the Moon, Mars, and deep space, alongside delay-tolerant telemetry to address communication challenges between astronauts and Earth.

ASTRA addresses the challenge of monitoring human health in extreme space environments by connecting individual health data, intelligent analysis, mission control, and immersive visualization in one ecosystem.

Its importance lies in supporting earlier awareness of potential health changes, improving access to meaningful health information, and helping advance safer, more informed human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — ASTRA

How it works

ASTRA is an integrated astronaut health-monitoring ecosystem that connects three main interfaces: an individual Astronaut Health Dashboard, a Ground Control Dashboard, and a 3D VR Digital Twin with a Helmet HUD.

The system organizes astronaut health telemetry, including heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen (SpO₂), respiration, core temperature, sleep, HRV, and radiation exposure. It compares health readings with individual baseline values, evaluates signal quality to identify potentially unreliable measurements caused by motion artifacts, and supports AI-assisted analysis of unusual health trends.

The Ground Control interface provides a shared view of crew health information, while the VR Helmet HUD presents relevant telemetry in an immersive 3D mission environment.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA aims to improve astronaut health awareness by bringing important health information into one connected ecosystem. It helps make changes in health trends easier to identify, supports communication between onboard systems and ground control, and provides a more intuitive way to understand complex telemetry during missions.

Its intended impact is to contribute to safer, better-informed long-duration space missions, where continuous health awareness and communication challenges are critical.

Tools and Technologies

We developed the web-based system using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Vite as the development environment and Three.js/WebGL for 3D visualization and the VR-style Helmet HUD. The project was developed and tested using laptop-based software tools, without requiring dedicated VR hardware. AI-assisted development tools supported parts of the development workflow.

Creativity and Engineering Considerations

ASTRA goes beyond displaying isolated vital signs by combining individual baseline monitoring, a proposed Gravity-Adaptive Baseline Calibration (G-ABC) approach, synchronized 3D visualization, and delay-tolerant telemetry concepts.

Our team considered the physiological challenges of different gravity environments, communication delays, motion-related signal errors, data reliability, interface usability, and the distinction between verified research data and simulated demonstration scenarios. These considerations shaped ASTRA as a connected, space-focused health-monitoring concept rather than a conventional health dashboard.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: AFTERLIGHT
projectDetails.summary:
AFTERLIGHT is an interactive 3D storytelling experience created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten".

We built AFTERLIGHT to make learning about the objects left behind on the Moon and Mars more fun and engaging. Instead of reading long, text-heavy articles, users can listen to narrated stories, explore interactive 3D models of real space equipment, and learn about the missions behind them.

Our goal is to highlight the forgotten tools and machines that helped explore space. Even though these objects were left behind, they remain part of space exploration history. We believe their stories deserve to be told, and the missions behind them should never be forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
AFTERLIGHT is a chapter-based interactive storytelling website that helps people discover the objects left behind by space exploration missions on the Moon and Mars. Users start at a hero section and navigate through different chapters, with each chapter focusing on a specific object and the mission behind it.

Each chapter explains what the object was used for, its role in the mission, and why it was left behind. Instead of relying on long articles and static images, users can explore interactive 3D models, rotate them, zoom in, and listen to narrated stories. They can also pause and replay the narration at any time.

The main benefit of AFTERLIGHT is that it makes learning about space exploration more interesting and accessible. It helps users understand the history and purpose of these objects while creating a stronger connection with them through interaction and storytelling. The project is intended for students, teachers, space enthusiasts, and anyone curious about space. Our goal is to bring attention to these forgotten objects and make sure the missions and achievements behind them are not forgotten.

We developed AFTERLIGHT using Next.js and Tailwind CSS, with Three.js for displaying and handling the interactive 3D models and GSAP for animations and smooth transitions throughout the website. We downloaded existing models from NASA's 3D resources and used information from NASA and the National Space Science Data Center (NSSDC) for our content. ElevenLabs was used to create the voice narration.

What makes AFTERLIGHT creative is the way it combines storytelling, voice narration, animations, and interactive 3D models to turn traditional educational content into an experience people can actively take part in. Rather than simply reading about an object, users can explore it while hearing its story.

Throughout development, our team focused on keeping scientific information easy to understand, making the experience visually engaging, using accurate information and models, and creating a website that is accessible and easy to navigate.

challengeDetails.title: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware across the solar system–on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. From rovers and instruments that completed their science missions to probes still traveling away from Earth this hardware varies widely in both its purpose and current level of functionality. Your challenge is to tell the story of some or all of this equipment that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the hardware and the science it made possible.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Mission Forge
projectDetails.summary:
MISSION FORGE: Design. Decide. Simulate. Discover.

MISSION FORGE is an interactive, educational space mission design and simulation game that transforms complex aerospace engineering concepts into an engaging, hands-on experience.

Players take on the role of space mission directors, designing and managing scientific missions from initial objectives to final operations. They make real-world-inspired decisions about spacecraft architecture, propulsion, scientific instruments, orbital trajectories, power systems, communications, budgets, and mission risks.

Unlike traditional space games focused on arcade challenges, MISSION FORGE emphasizes strategic thinking, scientific reasoning, and engineering trade-offs. Players experience realistic mission scenarios, respond to unexpected operational challenges, analyze simulated scientific data, and evaluate mission performance.

By incorporating NASA mission design principles, relevant NASA resources, and interactive visualizations, the platform makes space exploration and systems engineering more accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts. Its progressive learning modes support beginners while offering increasingly challenging experiences for advanced users.

MISSION FORGE aims to turn learning about space missions into an immersive experience where every decision matters and every mission becomes an opportunity to discover.
projectDetails.details:
MISSION FORGE – STARBOUND EDITION is an interactive space mission design game that helps players understand how real space missions are planned and the engineering decisions behind them.

Designing a space mission involves balancing several challenges, including spacecraft mass, scientific instruments, power, propulsion, communication, launch vehicle capacity, and mission cost. Our project turns these complex decisions into an interactive learning experience.

Players choose a scientific mission, build and configure their spacecraft, select instruments and technical systems, and check whether their design meets the mission requirements. They then launch their spacecraft and face simulated mission events where their decisions can affect mission performance, reliability, and scientific results.

The game provides feedback, performance scores, and a final mission report to help players understand the consequences of their choices and learn from both successful and unsuccessful designs.

Our goal is to make space mission engineering more accessible and engaging, allowing students and space enthusiasts to explore the challenges of spacecraft design through hands-on experimentation.

projectDetails.name: SpaceSoil
projectDetails.summary:
SpaceSoil is a smart web platform that bridges the gap between NASA’s satellite data and everyday farmers, helping them protect their crops before extreme weather and climate shifts cause real damage. Simply put, farmers usually don’t notice hidden soil moisture loss or crop stress until yields are already suffering, and raw space data is way too complex to interpret on their own.
We solved this by creating an easy-to-use tool where a farmer just enters their land location and crop type, and the system pulls, cleans, and merges data from four NASA sources (MODIS, SMAP, POWER, and GPM) into a clear, map-based dashboard showing soil moisture, rainfall, and crop greenness. Beyond just monitoring current conditions, SpaceSoil compares them against historical patterns to spot unusual anomalies early and send alerts, empowering farmers to make smarter irrigation and field-care decisions before stress turns into loss.
projectDetails.details:
SpaceSoil is a web-based agricultural monitoring and decision-support platform designed to bridge the gap between space-based Earth observation data and everyday farming. It transforms complex satellite datasets into clear, actionable insights to help farmers detect environmental stress early and adapt to unpredictable weather conditions.

The platform operates through a structured, data-driven pipeline:

  1. User Input: Farmers or agricultural specialists enter basic contextual information about their land, including geographic location and selected crop type.
  2. NASA Earth Observation Integration: SpaceSoil retrieves multi-year satellite data (covering December 2019 – December 2025) primarily from NASA MODIS (MOD13Q1.061) for vegetation health (NDVI and EVI), complemented by NASA SMAP (soil moisture) and NASA POWER (agro-climatology).
  3. Data Quality Filtering & Preprocessing: Raw satellite observations are cleaned by inspecting pixel reliability, filtering out cloud-contaminated or unreliable measurements, and handling missing values.
  4. Temporal & Feature Analysis: Using engineered features—such as NDVI Change Rate, EVI Trend, Seasonal Vegetation Patterns, and Vegetation Anomalies—the system tracks multi-year, seasonal, and monthly shifts to flag abnormal crop behavior before visible damage becomes severe.
  5. Accessible Decision Support: Complex metrics are translated into intuitive visualizations and clear risk alerts on a user-friendly web interface without requiring technical expertise.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Early Stress Detection: Identifies subtle vegetation deterioration early, helping farmers respond proactively to droughts, excessive rainfall, or shifting climate patterns.
  • Cost-Effective Wide-Area Monitoring: Replaces expensive, labor-intensive manual field scouting across large agricultural areas with consistent 16-day satellite monitoring.
  • Democratizing Space Data: Makes publicly available NASA datasets understandable and practical for non-technical users, empowering data-driven farming decisions and strengthening local food security.
  • Target Beneficiaries: Designed to support smallholder and commercial farmers, agricultural extension specialists, and environmental researchers.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • NASA Datasets & Portals: NASA MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices (MOD13Q1.061), NASA SMAP, NASA POWER, NASA Earthdata, AppEEARS, and LP DAAC.
  • Programming & Data Science: Python, Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Jupyter Notebook / Google Colab.
  • Application & Development: Modern Web Technologies (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) for building the interactive, public-facing web interface, alongside AI-assisted tools for code refinement and documentation support.

Creativity & Innovation

Rather than presenting raw, intimidating geospatial rasters or scientific jargon, SpaceSoil acts as a "translation layer" between orbit and field. By combining quality-filtered historical baselines with custom temporal anomaly features (comparing current vegetation behavior against expected seasonal norms), the platform turns passive satellite archives into a practical early-warning companion tailored to a farmer's specific crop context.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Data Reliability & Cloud Interference: Satellite optical data is prone to cloud cover and atmospheric noise; therefore, strict filtering using MODIS Pixel Reliability and VI Quality flags was prioritized before generating any insights.
  • Scientific Transparency & Limitations: Our team explicitly accounted for spatial resolution constraints (250m pixels represent regional trends rather than individual plants) and the 16-day revisit cycle, positioning SpaceSoil as an ethical decision-support tool that complements—rather than replaces—agronomic expertise and laboratory soil testing.
  • Accessibility & Zero-Friction UX: Designed the web platform to be publicly accessible without login barriers or complex setup so farmers can explore environmental indicators effortlessly.

projectDetails.name: Mars Mission Commander
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Mission Commander is a playable browser-based learning game developed by plus c for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players become the commander of a Mars outpost and complete a six-turn mission, balancing oxygen, power, water, food, research, and crew protection. Guided conversations, resource forecasts, and feedback help players understand how each decision affects survival and scientific progress.

The prototype connects gameplay to NASA resources, including MOXIE’s oxygen-production demonstration, archived ISS radiation observations from RadLab, space-plant research from OSD-314, and Perseverance imagery. Scientific evidence is clearly distinguished from fictional game rules.

Our project addresses the challenge by turning space-survival concepts into decisions young explorers can practise. It aims to make the connections between engineering, science, and resource management easier to understand through exploration and experimentation. Its educational impact remains a goal for future learner testing.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Mission Commander is a browser-based educational game in which players become the commander of a Mars outpost. Developed by plus c for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, the prototype turns space-survival concepts into decisions players can explore, compare, and learn from.

Players begin with an illustrative Earth-to-Mars arrival and meet Dr. Maya, Alex, and NOVA, a scripted guide. They explore the outpost and inspect facilities such as the power station, life-support unit, greenhouse, science laboratory, and radiation shelter. Across six turns, players allocate electricity, manage oxygen, water, and food, and choose a crew task. Tasks include research, rover sampling, sheltering, improving shielding, requesting delayed Earth advice, or conserving power.

Before committing a turn, players can compare predicted resource changes and revise their plan. Resources are spent only when they select Advance turn. The game then explains the outcome, making trade-offs visible: producing oxygen costs electricity, growing food requires power and water, and sheltering protects the crew while using an opportunity for research. A final debrief connects decisions to crew safety, scientific progress, and remaining supplies.

NASA resources give these choices scientific context. MOXIE informs the oxygen-production explanation; archived ISS radiation observations support the radiation chart; OSD-314 research informs the plant-lighting lesson; and Perseverance imagery provides geological context. The game clearly separates this evidence from its fictional resource rates, exposure points, event schedule, and growth times.

The intended benefit is to help young explorers understand that space missions involve connected systems and competing priorities. Rather than memorising isolated facts, players practise planning, interpreting forecasts, and explaining consequences. Potential settings include classrooms, science clubs, and family learning. These are intended benefits; educational effectiveness still needs testing with learners.

Our development tools included:

  • React, TypeScript, and Vite for the application and interface.
  • Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for the interactive 3D environment.
  • Blender and Python for procedural models and asset preparation.
  • Zod and browser local storage for validating and saving mission progress.
  • Vitest, Playwright, and ESLint for automated checks and code quality.
  • GitHub and Vercel for source management and publishing.
  • Miro for brainstorming, mapping the player journey, and connecting ideas about crew, facilities, resources, and consequences.
  • OpenAI Codex for AI-assisted development and documentation; ElevenLabs, Whisper, and FFmpeg for demo narration, caption alignment, and video production.

The project’s creativity comes from combining an explorable outpost, character-guided storytelling, and a decision-based resource model. Scientific explanations appear alongside relevant actions, allowing players to connect evidence with the choices they make.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, clear language, manageable complexity, accessibility, performance, and honest representation of progress. The prototype includes keyboard and touch controls, reduced-motion support, lower rendering quality, an alternative 2D mission map, and replayable guidance. Further work includes supervised learner testing, broader device and browser checks, and manual accessibility evaluation.

projectDetails.name: Project Pluto's Revenge
projectDetails.summary:
AstroVita is a browser-based astronaut health exploration prototype developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It brings spaceflight health context to life through an interactive 3D anatomy view, where users can explore the heart, lungs, brain, skeleton, and immune system. The dashboard also demonstrates crew profiles, simulated mission scenarios, optional self-reported check-ins, 14-day history views, and CSV export.

Because the official challenge resources provide research context rather than a connected astronaut telemetry dataset, AstroVita clearly separates NASA-linked information from synthetic demonstrations and user-entered values. It does not present mock readings as NASA data or offer diagnoses and unvalidated medical thresholds.

This matters because crews on long-duration missions need clear ways to understand and review health information, especially when far from Earth. AstroVita demonstrates how thoughtful visualization and transparent data boundaries can make a health-monitoring workflow engaging without overstating what the available evidence supports.
projectDetails.details:
AstroVita is a browser-based prototype developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps users explore astronaut health through an interactive 3D anatomy dashboard focused on the heart, lungs, brain, skeleton, and immune system. Users can select a body-system marker to view relevant NASA Human Research Program context, switch between three fictional crew profiles and four scripted scenarios, enter optional health check-ins, review a 14-day history, and export their entries as a CSV file.

The project’s key benefit is making a complex topic easier to explore while clearly distinguishing source-based context, simulated demonstration values, and user-entered information. The official challenge resources reviewed provide research context, but no astronaut telemetry dataset or live sensor feed. AstroVita therefore does not present demo values as NASA data, diagnose conditions, or set medical thresholds. Check-ins stay in the user’s browser and are not sent to a server.

The intended impact is educational: to demonstrate how a clear, interactive health-information workflow could support exploration during space missions, while showing what would need real data and qualified medical review before any clinical use. The project was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, Tailwind CSS, Wouter, Recharts, React Hook Form, and Zod. It requires no special hardware, only a modern web browser.

Creatively, the human body itself becomes the main navigation interface. The team considered the constraints of long-duration missions, usability, data provenance, privacy, accurate health interpretation, model licensing, and fallback behavior if 3D rendering is unavailable. All anatomy visuals are educational assets, not astronaut scans or NASA data.

projectDetails.name: Project-99: Flame in freefall
projectDetails.summary:
Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered scientific discovery platform designed to help researchers understand and investigate combustion behavior in microgravity environments.

The project integrates NASA combustion experiment data with machine learning, time-series forecasting, physics-informed analysis, and a scientific AI agent. It processes experimental measurements, identifies combustion patterns, explores relationships between physical variables, and forecasts future measurements. Its intelligent agent helps users investigate scientific questions, interpret results, compare experimental evidence, and explore what-if scenarios while reporting uncertainty and data limitations.

Flame in Freefall addresses the challenge of understanding how flames behave differently in microgravity, where the absence of normal buoyancy-driven convection changes combustion processes. By combining experimental evidence, physical principles, and AI-driven analysis, the platform makes complex combustion research more accessible and supports scientific exploration.

This project is important because understanding microgravity combustion can contribute to safer spacecraft environments, better fire-risk research, and future space missions. Ultimately, Flame in Freefall aims to transform NASA experimental data into an accessible, intelligent tool for scientific discovery.
..
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered scientific discovery platform designed to help researchers investigate and understand combustion behavior in microgravity environments.

In microgravity, flames behave differently because buoyancy-driven convection is greatly reduced. This changes how heat, fuel, and oxygen move around a flame, creating combustion behaviors that are not commonly observed on Earth.

Our platform uses NASA experimental data to explore these behaviors through several connected components:

NASA Data Integration: Organizes experimental measurements and preserves information about their scientific sources and limitations.

Machine Learning: Analyzes experimental measurements to identify patterns and relationships between combustion variables.

Time-Series Analysis: Studies how combustion measurements change over time and explores forecasting future measurements.

Physics-Informed Analysis: Uses relevant physical relationships, such as the D²-law for liquid-droplet combustion, to support scientific interpretation.

Scientific AI Agent: Helps users investigate research questions, retrieve relevant scientific information, interpret model outputs, and explore hypothetical scenarios.

Uncertainty and Explainability: Communicates the evidence, assumptions, and limitations behind analytical results instead of presenting every prediction as a scientific fact.

The system is designed to distinguish between experimental observations, model predictions, physics-based calculations, and research-supported explanations.

2. What benefits does it have?

Flame in Freefall makes complex combustion research more accessible by bringing experimental data, machine learning, physical principles, and scientific information together in one platform.

Its benefits include:

Helping researchers explore NASA combustion experiments more efficiently.

Identifying patterns that may deserve further scientific investigation.

Supporting the analysis of how combustion measurements evolve over time.

Making scientific information easier to investigate through an AI-powered interface.

Allowing users to explore hypothetical scenarios and understand the limitations of available evidence.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our long-term goal is to support a better understanding of fire behavior in microgravity. This research is important for future space missions, where understanding combustion, flame development, and fire-related phenomena is essential.

By making NASA experimental data easier to analyze and explore, Flame in Freefall aims to support scientific discovery, encourage further research, and contribute to the broader study of spacecraft fire risks.

The platform is a research-support prototype, not a certified spacecraft fire-safety or emergency-response system.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software did you use?

The project was developed primarily as a software-based scientific platform.

Programming language: Python.

Data processing: Pandas and NumPy.

Machine learning: Scikit-learn and neural-network-based modeling.

Time-series modeling: A Transformer-based architecture for experimental sequence analysis.

Scientific analysis: Physics-based calculations and experimental data validation.

Data storage and retrieval: Structured datasets, SQLite, and a hybrid scientific retrieval approach.

AI integration: A scientific AI agent supported by retrieval and analytical tools.

Development environment: Visual Studio Code.

We did not require specialized combustion hardware to develop the software prototype. The project uses existing NASA experimental data as its scientific foundation.

5. How is the project creative?

The creative aspect is not simply applying an AI model to combustion data. It is combining several approaches into a unified scientific investigation platform
Instead of treating an AI chatbot as the entire solution, Flame in Freefall connects an intelligent agent to specialized analytical components. The agent can help formulate investigations and interpret results, while numerical models and physical calculations perform the actual analysis.

Another important aspect is our focus on scientific reliability. The platform considers data provenance, experimental limitations, uncertainty, and the difference between measured and predicted values. This helps prevent AI-generated explanations from being mistaken for experimental evidence.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered:

Scientific reliability: Results must be grounded in actual experimental evidence and relevant physical principles.

Data quality: Different NASA experiments may have different conditions, measurement methods, and variables, so they should not be combined without scientific justification.

Model limitations: A model trained on a limited number of experiments cannot automatically be assumed to generalize to other combustion conditions.

Transparency: Predictions should include their limitations and uncertainty wherever possible.

Usability: Scientific analysis should be accessible to users without requiring them to understand every underlying algorithm.

Future development: The architecture should allow additional NASA datasets, scientific models, and research capabilities to be integrated as they become available.

Ultimately, Flame in Freefall aims to transform NASA's experimental combustion data into an intelligent and accessible environment for scientific exploration.

projectDetails.name: Zar3a AI – Smart Crop Rotation for Sustainable Agriculture
projectDetails.summary: Zar3a AI is a smart agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make better crop rotation decisions. The project analyzes climate and soil-related information to recommend crop rotation strategies that consider water use, soil health, and climate suitability. It provides alternative rotation scenarios to help users compare possible choices and understand their potential benefits and risks. By combining NASA Earth observation data with agricultural datasets and optimization techniques, Zar3a AI aims to support more sustainable farming, improve resource management, and help farmers adapt to changing environmental conditions.
projectDetails.details:
Zar3a is a voice-first agricultural decision-support prototype developed for Egyptian farmers. Its main feature is an Arabic voice assistant that communicates in Egyptian dialect, asks farmers about their governorate, current crop, previous crops, and farming priorities, and generates three crop-rotation strategies for comparison.

The rotation engine evaluates three-season crop sequences using preliminary crop parameters and indicators related to water requirements, soil effects, and climate suitability. It uses NASA POWER monthly climate data, including temperature, precipitation, and solar radiation. The recommendations are generated through transparent agricultural rules and weighted scoring, rather than machine learning.

Zar3a also includes a Crop Health tool based on an EfficientNet-B3 deep-learning classifier, with Grad-CAM visual explanations, to identify possible plant diseases from leaf images and provide general treatment and prevention guidance.

The platform was developed using React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Python, FastAPI, PyTorch, and related libraries.

Its main innovation is combining voice-first interaction in Egyptian Arabic with explainable crop-rotation comparisons and plant-disease image analysis in one platform. The system is a working prototype, and its recommendations are preliminary decision-support estimates that require agricultural expert validation.

projectDetails.name: Precrop Payoff Atlas
projectDetails.summary: Egyptian Nile Delta farmers decide every year what winter crop (wheat, berseem clover, sugar beet, faba beans) to plant before summer rice, maize, or cotton under canal rotation scarcity, soil salinity, and MWRI Decree 26/2025 rice limits. Generic advice claims clover improves next-season rice, yet local block-level proof is scarce. Precrop Payoff Atlas turns 10 years (2016-2025) of NASA satellite observations into an interactive 90 m decision advisor across Sidi Ghazi (Kafr El-Sheikh, 34,682 blocks), Zankalon (Sharqia), and out-of-region Mallawi (Minya, 14,497 blocks). Using within-block switcher fixed effects on 17,371 Sharqia blocks, our worked example measures that rice after clover consumes +11.9 mm (+2.4%, ~50 m3/feddan; 95% CI 10.8-13.1 mm) more summer NASA ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration (~0.6M m3/year across the Sharqia study area) while showing no net late-season rice greenness gain once May-June clover carryover is separated.
projectDetails.details:
What We Built (Three-Lane Modular Architecture):

1. Lane 1 - Multi-Year Satellite Measurement Engine (pipeline/): Builds 28-day NASA HLS composites (2016-2025) on aligned 90 m UTM blocks (EPSG:32636), trains LightGBM and NASA/IBM Prithvi-EO-2.0 against FAO WaPOR crop maps (held-out LightGBM OA 0.819 on SGZ S2023; rice area within ~10% of FAO ground reference), ingests NASA ECOSTRESS daily ET, NASADEM elevation, NASA POWER agroclimatology, and OpenStreetMap waterways, matches ~10 analog blocks via 1024-d Prithvi embeddings, and estimates 10-year two-way within-block fixed effects with lead-placebo falsification.

2. Lane 2 - Causal Inference, Hydrology & Constraint Engine (science/): Runs cross-fitted Double/Debiased ML and R-Learner Causal Forests with 900 m super-block CR3 cluster CIs; executes 6 robustness checks (temporal placebo, 200-draw stratified permutation, [0.05, 0.95] overlap trimming, Cinelli-Hazlett sensitivity, 200-draw confusion-matrix misclassification propagation, agronomic direction check); computes FAO-56 Dual-Kc Eq. 62 water budgets; and enforces Maas-Hoffman salinity thresholds plus Egypt MWRI Decree 26/2025 rice legality. Standalone science/ passes 14/14 pytest tests (95% coverage), ruff, and strict mypy.

3. Lane 3 - Bilingual Farmer & Planner UI (app.py, ui_data.py): Live at https://precrop-payoff-atlas.streamlit.app/ in English & Egyptian Arabic (RTL) with a 3-step quick guide, 90 m block explorer across SGZ (34,682 blocks) and Mallawi (14,497 blocks, Decree 26 rice auto-blocked), optional user-entered EGP crop prices, M2 10-year charts, verification/confusion tables, and tool-grounded Q&A.

Honest Limits & Roadmap:

Estimates describe 90 m blocks (~1.9 feddan), not sub-pixel individual farms; we do not claim satellite soil-health measurements, ton/feddan yield, or causal separation of late May-June clover ET from early rice ET. Single-year SGZ v1 snapshots enforce Honest-Null Gate G3 (deferring full causal selection to Tab 2's 10-year panel). Out-of-region summer LightGBM drops on unseen Upper Egypt (MLL OA 0.36-0.38); next step is fine-tuning across more governorates.

projectDetails.name: RIMLIGHT — Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary: At the lunar South Pole, the Sun never rises above ~1.54° and there is no atmosphere, so landing meters off-target inside a crater rim means total darkness and lost Earth radio contact. RIMLIGHT is an interactive, physics-backed Lunar Landing Site Navigator that lets mission planners, engineers, and students inspect any coordinate south of 80°S on a 60 FPS 3D Moon Globe and 2D Polar Stereographic Map. Powered by NASA LOLA 80 m/pixel topography and NAIF SPICE DE440 ephemerides, RIMLIGHT computes exact sunlit hours, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows, longest continuous night, minimum battery sizing, a 30-day animated 360° horizon panorama, solar mast trade-offs (2–50 m), 1 m boulder shadows, and NASA Artemis III 4-rule eligibility—validated against Gläser et al. (2014) and Mazarico et al. (2011).
projectDetails.details:
What RIMLIGHT Does

RIMLIGHT transforms complex lunar South Pole topography and orbital mechanics into instant, actionable landing decisions. Users can click any curated NASA/ESA site (such as Connecting Ridge, Shackleton Rim, Shackleton Floor, or Mons Mouton) or any custom coordinate south of 80°S to evaluate power survival, Earth communications, and terrain slope.

How It Works (3-Stage Physics Pipeline)

1. Stage 1 — Ephemeris (SPICE): Computes high-precision Sun and Earth topocentric vectors across 315,576 time steps using NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (naif0012.tls, de440.bsp, moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc, moon_de440_250416.tf, pck00011.tpc).

2. Stage 2 — Terrain Horizon Raycasting: Samples NASA PGDA Product 90 LOLA South Pole DEM (LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ.TIF, 80 m/pixel) across 360 azimuths to build each site's exact terrain horizon mask and 100 m ground slope.

3. Stage 3 — Mission & Artemis III Engine: Calculates sunlit hours, Earth DTE contact (accounting for ±7° lunar libration), longest dark period, battery capacity for configurable 100–200 W loads, mast height trade-offs (2 m, 5 m, 10 m, 20 m, 50 m), 1 m boulder shadow lengths, nearby better-spot search (150–1500 m), and NASA Artemis III 4-rule eligibility (Earth ≥ 25%, Sun ≥ 5%, Slope < 10°, Lat ≤ −84°).

Tech Stack & Validation

- Frontend: React, Vite, Three.js (4K albedo/normal maps + LOLA relief cap + live Earth DTE beacon), Leaflet (L.CRS.Simple), proj4js — hosted on Vercel.

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SpiceyPy, Rasterio, PyProj — hosted on Railway with 53 passing pytest unit tests.

- Validation: Cross-checked against Gläser et al. (2014) on Connecting Ridge (-89.4667°, -136.6667°; 92.27% sunlit at 2 m mast, 95.65% at 10 m) and Mazarico et al. (2011) for Shackleton Floor (0% PSR).

- Source Code (MIT License): https://github.com/lydiasalib/NASA-Space-Apps-2026

projectDetails.name: Project Promise
projectDetails.summary:
Aura-bio, developed by Team Promise, addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health during space missions, when medical support from Earth may be delayed. It brings sensor telemetry, personal baselines, cross-system alerts and daily check-ins into one crew-oriented console.

Instead of treating each reading separately, Aura-bio connects changes in sleep, reaction performance, cardiovascular signals, immune indicators and the spacecraft environment. Alerts explain what changed, show the supporting values and sources, and suggest responses for astronauts and medical teams. Six interactive games support cognitive-performance tracking, while crew-wide notices and lightweight briefings help share important information.

Public NASA and research datasets calibrate the simulator and inform cited limits; all demonstrated crew data is simulated. The prototype also supports local operation without public internet while its server remains available.

Aura-bio matters because crews need understandable, actionable information—not just more measurements. It aims to support onboard awareness and autonomy, while remaining a research prototype rather than a diagnostic medical device.
projectDetails.details:
What Aura-bio does and how it works

Aura-bio, developed by Team Promise, is an astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed for missions where medical support from Earth may be delayed. It helps answer three questions: How am I doing? What changed? What should I do next?**

The system receives sensor and simulated laboratory readings through an MQTT telemetry pipeline. Its backend validates each message, stores it and compares available signals with the astronaut’s personal baseline and configured limits.

Aura-bio connects changes across body systems rather than displaying only isolated measurements. For example, reduced sleep, increased reaction-test lapses and a change in mood can produce one explainable pattern alert. Each alert identifies the contributing values, its urgency, supporting sources and suggested responses for the crew and medical team.

The console includes a clickable body-system map, trends, daily check-ins, crew-wide notices and delayed ground reports. An optional contribution chart explains which signals contribute to the research drift score. Six interactive games—Lunar Alien Reaction, Coloring Shapes, Memory Test, Reaction Test, Speed Click and Number Hunt—provide cognitive-performance activities and session history.

Benefits and intended impact

Aura-bio aims to make health information easier to interpret under demanding mission conditions. Personal baselines provide context for individual differences, while cross-system alerts bring related changes into one explanation.

Crew-wide notices help members stay aware of important developments without replacing their own selected health view. Lightweight briefing files support concise information sharing, and mission presets account for communication delays between the spacecraft and Earth.

The intended impact is stronger onboard awareness and autonomy: helping astronauts and crew medical officers recognize changes, review the evidence and decide when further assessment is needed. These are intended benefits, not demonstrated clinical outcomes.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

We developed the backend in Python, using **]FastAPI** for APIs and WebSocket updates, SQLite for storage, and Mosquitto MQTT with Paho MQTT for telemetry transport.

The web console uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Chart.js for visualization. The games use Python, Pygame and Pygbag/WebAssembly to run in the browser. The research scoring service combines a PyTorch two-day autoencoder for sudden changes with an EWMA drift score for sustained changes.

The hardware pathway uses ESP32 firmware, C/C++, PlatformIO and Wokwi, including simulated sensor and analyzer components. A Serial-to-MQTT bridge connects firmware output to the backend. We used Docker, GitHub, pytest and browser checks for integration and verification.

Data and scientific grounding

Public NASA OSDR Environmental Data Application measurements help calibrate CO₂ variation, while RadLab data informs radiation-dose simulation. Inspiration4 laboratory datasets anchor selected immune-signal ranges and scenario changes. PhysioNet BIDSleep informs normal heart-rate and sleep variation.

Published research and NASA technical references support selected limits and response wording. These sources calibrate the simulation; they do not establish clinical accuracy. All demonstrated crew data is simulated, and optional retimed NASA measurements are explicitly labeled as replayed.

What makes the project creative

Aura-bio’s central idea is to connect signals across systems and present an understandable reason for an alert—not simply a collection of colored numbers. It combines environmental telemetry, physiology, check-ins and interactive games with a shared crew workflow.

Explainability is built into the experience: users can inspect the evidence, distinguish published limits from proposed thresholds, and request deeper model detail without overwhelming the main screen.

Factors our team considered

We considered delayed communication, limited connectivity, individual variation, missing sensors, privacy, readability and alert fatigue. The interface uses urgency words alongside colors, supports dark and light modes, and keeps important status information visible while placing supporting detail behind disclosure controls.

Local game operation does not require public internet once the server and dependencies are available; Wokwi itself remains an online service. Missing measurements are not shown as healthy.

We also prioritized honest limitations. Aura-bio is not a medical device. Physical-device calibration, independent clinical validation and real OS/mobile push verification remain future work. Metabolic measurements are not yet implemented, and the radiation/immune pattern requires a configured dose threshold before it can trigger.

Our project, Space Mission Design Game, is an interactive educational game developed using Godot to make the complex process of space mission planning easier to understand and more engaging. Players take on the role of mission designers, making decisions about science objectives, spacecraft, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, and orbits while balancing important constraints such as mass, power, budget, communications, and mission lifetime.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming traditional mission design concepts into a hands-on experience where players can explore the consequences of their decisions, experiment with different configurations, and learn through trial and error. We aim to make space mission planning more accessible, engaging, and collaborative, helping students and space enthusiasts understand the engineering and scientific trade-offs behind real NASA missions.

Ultimately, our goal is to inspire curiosity about space exploration and encourage the next generation to think like mission designers.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Space Mission Design Game

Our project, Space Mission Design Game, is an interactive educational game designed to introduce players to the challenges of planning and designing space missions. Developed using Godot, the game allows players to experience the role of a space mission designer by making decisions that influence the success of a mission.

How It Works

Players begin by selecting a scientific objective for their mission. They then make important design decisions, including choosing a spacecraft, scientific instruments, launch vehicle, and orbit. Throughout the process, they must consider and balance different mission constraints, such as mass, power consumption, budget, communication capabilities, and mission lifetime. The game aims to evaluate mission configurations and demonstrate how each decision can affect the final outcome.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project makes complex aerospace engineering concepts easier to understand through practical interaction rather than theory alone. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and teamwork. Our intended impact is to make space exploration and mission engineering more accessible to students and space enthusiasts, while inspiring interest in STEM fields.

Tools and Technologies

The main development platform is Godot, with C# used for game programming. We also aim to incorporate relevant NASA open data, mission information, and educational resources to make the game scenarios more realistic and informative.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of our project is turning the complex process of space mission design into an interactive game. Instead of simply reading about spacecraft and mission requirements, players can experiment with different configurations, discover trade-offs, and learn from the results of their decisions.

Factors Considered

Our team considered scientific objectives, engineering limitations, resource management, mission feasibility, educational value, and user experience. We also considered how to make the experience understandable for beginners while still presenting meaningful challenges. Our goal is to combine learning, creativity, and the excitement of space exploration in one engaging experience.

projectDetails.name: Aegis Health: The first astronaut health monitoring website
projectDetails.summary: Aegis Health is an offline-first astronaut health companion for missions with limited connectivity. The crew app enables routine check-ins, guided measurements, personal-baseline comparisons, reminders, action recommendations, and an Emergency Quick Action flow. It focuses on sleep, heart signals, hydration, mood, activity, radiation exposure, symptoms, and mission-relevant indicators, while clearly showing uncertainty, data quality, and provenance. The future mission-control web console lets medical and mission personnel review trends, evidence, escalations, acknowledgments, and synchronization history. The system uses encrypted local storage, scheduled notifications, explicit sync states, versioned records, and human-review safeguards. NASA and Canadian Space Agency sources provide contextual evidence rather than invented diagnostic thresholds. A phased roadmap begins with shared data contracts and an offline app shell, then adds measurements, routines, mission modes, evidence, console capabilities, hardware integrations, and validation. The initial demonstration follows an astronaut on Mars transit managing gradual recovery drift and an urgent simulated symptom event offline.
projectDetails.details:
Purpose

We are developing Aegis Health as an astronaut health and mission-monitoring prototype. Our purpose is to bring physiological and environmental readings onto a local touchscreen and a website, with a private mission record for each astronaut account.

What does this do?

Our proposed system receives measurements from connected sensors, presents available readings on an ESP32-driven 3.5-inch touchscreen, and sends data over USB to a Windows computer. The website can collect these readings into an active mission, preserve their timestamps, and produce observational reports.

Radiation monitoring

The Geiger module detects ionizing-radiation events. Our firmware counts these events over a rolling 60-second window and displays the result in counts per minute (CPM). This provides a record of detected radiation counts alongside other mission readings. Converting counts to a personal dose or dose rate requires detector calibration and information about the radiation field.

Heart rate and atmospheric CO2

Our optical sensor supplies a pulse signal for an experimental heart-rate estimate. The CO2 sensor measures atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration in parts per million (ppm). The local display and Windows console present these readings, while the website can save them as mission data.

Additional connected devices

The website also accepts oxygen saturation, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body temperature, respiration rate, and ECG, optical-pulse or respiratory waveform samples when compatible acquisition hardware supplies them through the supported data format. Each measurement needs its appropriate sensor or instrument. The included optical, CO2 and Geiger modules provide the measurements described above.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Aegis Health helps astronauts manage their health independently while reducing reliance on continuous communication with Earth. It supports early recognition of concerning changes, encourages healthy routines, reduces alert fatigue, and preserves a reliable record of health events during offline periods. The intended impact is to improve crew safety, support faster and better-informed medical review, and make health monitoring practical during long-duration missions to the Moon or Mars.

The system is designed as decision support rather than a diagnostic tool. It uses personal baselines, repeated measurements, data-quality indicators, uncertainty labels, and human oversight instead of presenting unexplained risk scores or unsupported medical conclusions.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software

The existing demonstration surface is a React-based web application intended to serve as a mission-control dashboard and browser demonstration. The planned crew application uses React Native and Expo, with TypeScript shared across the mobile app and web console. Local SQLite or an equivalent encrypted database stores measurements, check-ins, routines, emergency events, evidence summaries, and pending synchronization records. Local notifications support scheduled check-ins and mission routines.

The first implementation can use manual data entry and simulated telemetry. Future versions may connect validated wearable devices, medical sensors, or other approved data sources through common adapter interfaces. A synchronization service and server-side database will support authorized mission-control review, role-based access, audit history, and conflict resolution.

Creativity and Design Considerations

The project is creative because it combines astronaut self-care, offline-first software, explainable decision support, mission-environment awareness, and NASA evidence in one coordinated experience. Rather than treating health as a single score, it connects measurements to understandable actions and personal trends. Its interactive body and system map can help non-medical users explore how different spaceflight hazards relate to body systems.

The team considered five major spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile or closed environments. Additional considerations included communication delays, accessibility, privacy, data security, notification fatigue, uncertain or incomplete measurements, role-based permissions, emergency escalation, and the differences between operational telemetry, self-reported information, clinical measurements, and research evidence.

NASA and Canadian Space Agency sources provide scientific context, but the project avoids inventing diagnostic thresholds or turning research findings into individual medical advice. The design also ensures that astronauts can continue using essential features offline and that every recommendation remains explainable, traceable, and subject to qualified human review.

projectDetails.summary:
PyroNova - Flame in Freefall
 is a space-fire safety and research platform that helps users understand fire behavior in microgravity and respond to fire emergencies in space.

Using real NASA experimental data, PyroNova transforms complex research into accessible insights through two connected platforms: a mobile application and a website.

The mobile application simulates fire emergencies, alerts  members in the same spacecraft module, and provides emergency guidelines and AI-powered assistance. The website offers an interactive dashboard to explore NASA fire experiments under different conditions, along with an AI research assistant that helps users search, understand, and explore scientific data.

PyroNova bridges the gap between complex NASA research and practical understanding, making space-fire knowledge more accessible to astronauts, students, professors, and researchers.
projectDetails.details:
PyroNova – Flame in Freefall

About the Project

Have you ever imagined being an astronaut and suddenly facing a fire emergency inside your spacecraft? How would you react? What would you do?

We have talked about this scenario before. Now, *PyroNova* helps you understand how to respond to fire emergencies and explore how fire behaves under different conditions in space.

Our project transforms complex and distributed NASA data into meaningful, accessible insights for students, professors, researchers, and astronauts. Instead of spending a long time collecting and navigating raw datasets, users can explore fire behavior through interactive visualizations and communicate with an AI chatbot powered by NASA research data.

PyroNova also provides an AI-powered research assistant that helps users search, understand, and explore NASA fire research data.

Project Components

PyroNova consists of two connected systems: a *Mobile Application* and a *Website*, supported by a shared backend.

1. PyroNova Mobile Application

The mobile application is primarily designed for astronauts.

In a real spacecraft, fire sensors would normally detect emergencies. However, since this project is a simulation, we use simulated fire scenarios instead.

When a user triggers a fire simulation:

- An emergency notification is sent to all users assigned to the same spacecraft module.

- The notification guides astronauts to the initial emergency guidelines.

- Astronauts can access the AI chatbot for further assistance.

The mobile application is also connected to the website, allowing users to access their previous AI chatbot conversations across both platforms.

2. PyroNova Website

The website is primarily designed for students, professors, and researchers.

Instead of spending a long time collecting and navigating datasets, users can:

- Explore an interactive dashboard visualizing real NASA experimental data and fire behavior under different conditions.

- Ask questions and explore the data through an AI chatbot powered by NASA research data.

- Use voice interaction to communicate with the AI chatbot.

Technology Stack

Backend

- Laravel

- MySQL Database

- Clever Cloud (Online Database Hosting)

- Laravel Sanctum & Breeze for Authentication

- REST API Development

- Push Notifications

Mobile Application – Android

*Language & UI*

- Kotlin 2.1

- Custom Canvas animations (splash mini-game, SAFFIRE-III smoke chart)

- Navigation Compose

*Architecture*

- MVVM: ViewModel, Kotlin Coroutines, and StateFlow

- Repository Pattern with real API and fake offline demo implementations

*Networking & Data*

- Retrofit + OkHttp: REST client for the Laravel backend (authentication, OTP, chats, AI `/ask`, guidelines, and simulation)

- kotlinx.serialization (JSON)

- DataStore + Android Keystore (AES-GCM): encrypted session token

- Bundled NASA PSI data (JSON assets) for the Home research-archive card, with offline support

*Emergency & Notifications*

- Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM): fire alerts sent to every crew member in the same module

- Full-screen alert notification (incoming-call style) with an alarm-channel siren (MediaPlayer) and SOS vibration

*Voice*

- Android SpeechRecognizer: ask the AI by voice

- Android TextToSpeech: read AI answers and emergency steps aloud

*Build & Tools*

- Android Studio

- Gradle (Kotlin DSL)

- Android SDK (minimum API 26, target API 35)

Frontend

- HTML

- JavaScript

- Next.js

- Vercel

*UI/UX Design Tools*

- Canva

Data Engineering

- NASA data integration and processing

- Data pipeline development

AI Service – PyroNova Research Assistant & Fire-Risk API

*Technologies & Frameworks*

- FastAPI + Uvicorn: REST API (`/ask`, `/risk/current`, `/experiments`), called by the Laravel backend

*Data Sources & Storage*

...

- FAISS

- BM25 hybrid search

- Cross-Encoder reranker

- Built with Jupyter Notebooks

*Large Language Models (LLMs)*

- NVIDIA Nemotron (fallback)

- Generates answers based on retrieved NASA evidence, with sources.

*Machine Learning*

- Trained on 175 real ISS tests

projectDetails.name: Project Qamar 14
projectDetails.summary:
Qamar 14 is a free 3D browser game that trains kids aged 7–12 as junior astronauts on a full round trip to Mars. It works on computers and phones, in Arabic and English.

The mission has seven stages: launch, Moon slingshot, crew health, building a Mars base, a solar storm, ascent and docking, and the return home. In each stage the child controls a different crew member. They make the decisions themselves through quick, simple challenges: choosing a safe weather window, steering a gravity assist, diagnosing fluid shift, growing lettuce under LED light, sheltering from radiation, and setting Orion’s parachutes in order.

Everything is built on real NASA science and data. The Mars terrain comes from HiRISE imagery of Victoria Crater, the solar storm is the real May 2024 X5.8 flare from DONKI, and the Moon, Sun and Earth come from LRO, SDO and Blue Marble. The game also teaches lessons from missions such as Phoenix, MOXIE, Veggie and Artemis. Mission Control on Earth sends messages that arrive late, about 1.3 seconds from the Moon and minutes from Mars, so children feel why astronauts must think for themselves.

The game turns real space science into play. It builds problem-solving, teamwork and curiosity, and lets kids see themselves as the future explorers of the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Qamar 14 is a 3D browser game that turns a child aged 7–12 into the Captain of a crewed round trip to Mars. A short cinematic opening, narrated in English with Arabic and English subtitles, previews the journey. The player then completes seven stages seen from above, like a strategy game:

Launch from Kennedy Pad 39B

Moon gravity-assist slingshot

Crew health during the 7-month cruise

Building a Mars base

A real solar storm

Ascent and docking

Return and splashdown

In each stage the child controls a different crew member:

PICO, the robot assistant

Kiro, the engineer

Jana, the medical officer

Hekal, the resources scientist

the Captain

Each stage is a chain of short challenges. The child:

chooses a launch window under NASA’s lightning rule

steers a 2D gravity assist around the Moon

diagnoses fluid shift (SANS)

packs astronaut food

puts out a lab fire with sound waves (clearly labeled a research idea)

drills for ice and routes water into a radiation shield

splits water for oxygen

grows lettuce under red and blue LEDs

shares limited solar power between systems

shelters from the storm and repairs a comms dish using data

times the ascent and docks at 0.1 m/s

picks a safe entry angle

sequences Orion’s 11 parachutes

Mission Control on Earth (Adam and Nour) sends messages that visibly arrive late: about 1.3 seconds from the Moon and about 12.5 minutes from Mars, shown as a time-lapse. This teaches why crews must make their own decisions. Every challenge ends with a real NASA fact card and its source.

Real NASA data used

Mars terrain built from a HiRISE heightmap of Victoria Crater

The real May 2024 X5.8 flare and CME from DONKI

The Moon from LRO (LROC and LOLA)

The Sun from SDO/AIA

Earth from Blue Marble and Black Marble

Stars from NASA SVS

Mission facts from Phoenix, MOXIE, Veggie, FLEX, Artemis and Orion

A small backend fetches live NASA data and keeps the API key on the server, never in the browser. The game reads saved snapshots of that data, so it never hits NASA’s rate limits while children play.

Benefits and impact

Children learn real space science by doing it, not by reading it.

It builds decision-making, teamwork, problem-solving and data literacy.

Wrong answers explain why and let the child try again, so failure is safe.

It is free and runs on a phone or PC with no install.

It is fully bilingual: English, Arabic, or Arabic with English subtitles.

Our goal is to inspire Arabic- and English-speaking kids to see themselves as future Moon and Mars explorers.

Tools and technologies

Code: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, built with Vite.

3D: three.js with custom shaders (animated Sun, CME, plasma, planets), plus GSAP for animation.

Backend: Node.js, TypeScript, Express and Zod, with automated tests in Vitest.

3D models: Blender, and Meshy AI for props.

Audio: Web Audio API sound effects, and Web Speech narration.

Music: an original celebration track composed in code with Python and NumPy, so there are no copyright issues.

Testing: Playwright automated playthroughs on desktop and mobile layouts.

Development: AI coding assistance (Claude).

Hosting: GitHub and Vercel.

Creativity

One story with seven playable crew roles, each with its own personality and humor.

Cinematic transitions between stages built from real NASA imagery.

The light-speed communication delay becomes a playable, visible moment, including a dance celebration at Mission Control when a signal arrives.

Kid-friendly humor makes real science memorable: the jerrycan that’s too heavy, the sofa in zero gravity, the disco lights for lettuce.

Factors we considered

Age fit: short, simple challenges for ages 7–12.

Scientific accuracy: on-screen notes say when sizes and distances are not to scale, when numbers are simplified learning models, and when an idea is still research.

Accessibility: mobile touch joystick, two languages, subtitles.

Performance on low-end phones.

Security: the NASA API key stays on the server.

Copyright and licensing: NASA public imagery, our own models, and original music.

Responsible data use: snapshots instead of live API calls during play.

projectDetails.summary:
Quantum Frontier
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Project Summary

Quantum Frontier is an interactive educational platform that brings the forgotten stories of space exploration back to life.

Over the years, numerous scientific machines and pieces of equipment have been left behind on the Moon and Mars after completing their missions. Despite their scientific importance, many people are unaware of their existence, and students passionate about space exploration often struggle to find reliable, accessible, and engaging information about them.

Our solution is a digital space archive that allows users to explore abandoned space equipment, discover its original mission, understand its scientific purpose, and learn why it was left behind.

Through an engaging and accessible experience, Quantum Frontier transforms forgotten space technology into meaningful scientific stories, inspiring curiosity and helping a new generation connect with humanity's journey beyond Earth.

Our mission: Every machine has a story. No discovery should be forgotten
projectDetails.details:
# Project Details: Quantum Frontier

## 1. What does our project do and how does it work?

*Quantum Frontier* is an interactive 3D web application that transforms space history into an immersive educational exploration experience. It allows users to explore the surfaces of the Moon and Mars, discover abandoned spacecraft and scientific equipment, and learn the stories behind humanity's missions beyond Earth.

*Starting in Orbit:*

Users begin their journey in Low Earth Orbit, experiencing a first-person astronaut perspective with visible spacesuit gloves and an orbital information display. Through the "Pick Your World" interface, they can choose to explore either the Moon or Mars.

*Exploring Planetary Heritage Sites:*

After landing, users enter an interactive 3D planetary environment featuring an informational HUD that displays planetary and mission-related data, including surface gravity, atmospheric composition, temperature, day length, and other environmental and suit indicators.

*Interactive Navigation and Mission Logs:*

Users navigate the terrain using familiar PC gaming controls (WASD to move, mouse drag to look around, Space to hop, and Shift to bound). Glowing orange navigation beacons guide them toward real historical spacecraft and scientific equipment left behind on both worlds.

The experience features three heritage sites on the Moon and five on Mars. Upon reaching each site, users can unlock an interactive mission log containing historical information, mission objectives, and scientific discoveries associated with that equipment.

## 2. What benefits does it have?

*Experiential Space Learning:*

Instead of relying on static text and traditional 2D images, Quantum Frontier allows users to explore planetary environments through an immersive first-person experience, making complex space science more engaging and memorable.

*Preserving Forgotten Space History:*

The platform brings attention to the spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments that remain on the Moon and Mars, highlighting their contributions to scientific discovery and space exploration.

*Accessible Educational Experience:*

Quantum Frontier runs directly in a standard web browser, without requiring a VR headset or specialized hardware, making interactive space exploration accessible to students and space enthusiasts.

*Learning Through Discovery:*

By combining exploration, navigation, and interactive mission logs, users actively discover scientific information rather than simply reading it.

## 3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to bridge the gap between scattered space mission information and accessible, engaging educational experiences.

Many students interested in space exploration struggle to find a simple and engaging way to discover reliable information about the spacecraft and scientific equipment left behind on other worlds.

Quantum Frontier addresses this challenge by transforming space archives into an interactive exploration experience.

We aim to:

- Inspire curiosity about planetary science, astronomy, and aerospace engineering.

- Make NASA mission history more accessible and engaging for students.

- Raise awareness of humanity's scientific and cultural heritage beyond Earth.

- Encourage the next generation of explorers, researchers, and innovators.

Our vision is simple: *Every piece of abandoned technology has a story worth discovering.*

## 4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

To develop Quantum Frontier, our team combined AI-assisted development, research, and scientific data analysis.

*Lovable – Frontend Development and 3D Integration:*

We used Lovable to build the web application's frontend, interactive interface, component structure, and 3D experience. It helped us integrate WebGL/Three.js scene rendering, astronaut visual elements, planetary selection, and HUD interfaces.

*Manus – Research and Workflow Assistance:*

We used Manus to assist with research, organize mission documentation, structure information about historical spacecraft, and support the development workflow.

*Gemini – Scientific Research and Data Analysis:*

We used Gemini to assist with analyzing planetary science information, organizing scientific data, and reviewing content to support the educational accuracy of the experience.

*Languages and Development Environment:*

- HTML5

- CSS3

- JavaScript

- WebGL

- Three.js

- Lovable, Manus, and Gemini

- Visual Studio Code on Windows

## 5. How is our project creative?

*First-Person Astronaut Immersion:*

Rather than creating another educational information website, we designed an astronaut-inspired interface that places users inside the exploration experience. Visual elements such as the compass heading, distance-to-beacon indicators, spacesuit gloves, and environmental HUD make the experience feel like an actual planetary expedition.

*Gamified Space Archaeology:*

We transformed the discovery of historical space equipment into an interactive exploration mission. Users follow navigation beacons, travel across planetary terrain, and unlock mission logs as they discover different heritage sites.

*Planet-Specific Exploration:*

The Moon and Mars offer different environmental conditions and exploration experiences, making the journey more than simply switching between two backgrounds.

*Combining Science with Storytelling:*

Each discovered spacecraft represents a chapter in humanity's exploration history, allowing users to connect scientific achievements with the stories behind them.

## 6. What factors did our team consider?

*Scientific Accuracy:*

We considered the importance of presenting reliable planetary and mission information. Our team used scientific research and AI-assisted analysis to organize the educational content and planetary data.

*Browser Performance:*

We aimed to create an immersive 3D environment while keeping the experience accessible through standard web browsers without requiring specialized equipment.

*Intuitive User Experience:*

We selected familiar PC gaming controls and high-visibility orange navigation beacons to make exploration straightforward, even for first-time users.

*Educational Clarity:*

We organized the experience into individual heritage sites, each with its own mission log. Progress indicators (LOG 0/3 on the Moon and LOG 0/5 on Mars) help users track their discoveries and encourage them to explore every site.

*Balancing Immersion and Information:*

We wanted the experience to be visually engaging without overwhelming users with technical information. Each interaction is designed to connect exploration with concise, meaningful scientific storytelling.

---

*Quantum Frontier transforms abandoned space technology into an interactive journey through humanity's scientific legacy. We don't just show users what was left behind; we invite them to discover why it matters.*

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
