projectDetails.name: Project Ra7al
projectDetails.summary:
Discovery Atlas: Meet the Machines We Left Behind

Discovery Atlas is a mobile app that lets kids aged 6–12 discover NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. Players create their own astronaut, choose a robot guide, and travel a solar-system map. Each lost machine appears as a character pinned on its planet. Our first story is Spirit and Opportunity, the Mars rovers built for a three-month mission that kept working for years. It is told as a comic, or as an animated video, in the voice of a storyteller.

After each story, kids play four challenge levels tied to what they just read. A green progress bar fills as they answer, and they earn a badge for completing the story. Every fact comes from NASA mission pages, and our invented dialogue is clearly separate from the verified facts.

The app turns forgotten hardware into characters children care about. It explains how the rovers worked: solar power, cameras, rock-grinding tools, and the search for ancient water. It also shows why every machine we leave behind still teaches us something. We are also planning a facts mode for older readers and parents.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Discovery Atlas is a mobile-first app for kids aged 6–12 that tells the stories of NASA machines left behind on the Moon and Mars. A child creates an astronaut (five suits and a name), picks a robot guide, and explores a solar-system map where Mars and the Moon are open. Each planet has pins, and each pin is a lost machine, such as Sojourner, Ingenuity, Apollo hardware and Surveyor. Our first complete story is Spirit & Opportunity, told as a vertical comic. After reading, the child plays four challenges tied to the story: ordering the rover’s parts, matching discoveries to rovers, driving a rover through a crater, and clearing a dust storm off its solar panels. Stars are earned per level, finishing all four marks the machine as found and its pin turns green, and a certificate unlocks. Progress is saved on the device.

What benefits does it have?
Children learn how real missions worked (solar power, cameras, rock-grinding tools, the search for ancient water) by reading and playing. The app is fully bilingual (English and Arabic with right-to-left layout), has large touch targets and nothing frightening.

What is the intended impact?
We want kids to see forgotten hardware as characters with stories, so they remember why we explore. The app is built to grow: 15 more machines are already placed on the maps and waiting for their stories.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?
Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Radix UI, Framer Motion, Zustand, Cairo and Baloo Bhaijaan 2 fonts, and Playwright for automated testing. We used Claude Code Pro, Manus, ChatGPT and v0.dev to build and iterate. We used Gemini to generate comic backgrounds, and Figma for design.

How is it creative?
The lost machines are the characters, and the child is the astronaut with their own robot guide. A glowing “signal line” runs through the comic story. The challenges are rebuilt from the story, so every game teaches one real mission fact.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Age-appropriate language and short, forgiving levels for 6–12.
  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA mission pages, and invented dialogue is kept separate from verified facts.
  • Accessibility: two languages, big buttons, and difficulty softened after testing.
  • Scope: one complete story with a structure ready for more.
  • Team: five members, covering backend, graphic design, content creation, Flutter development, video editing, and project and business management.

projectDetails.name: RED PLANET LAB
projectDetails.summary:
Red Planet Lab is an intelligent Mars exploration decision-support platform that fuses multi-mission orbital and in-situ planetary datasets into an interactive 3D environment for autonomous rover traverse planning.

Addressing the challenge of navigating hazardous extraterrestrial terrain, we developed a system that harmonizes NASA MOLA topographic elevation models, Viking orbital imagery, USGS geologic stratigraphic maps, and real in-situ atmospheric telemetry from Perseverance (MEDA) and Curiosity (REMS). Users can explore any sector on a 3D Martian globe, reconstruct 3D surface meshes, and run a physics-constrained A∗ routing engine that evaluates three strategies: Fastest, Safest (which actively detects and bypasses dynamic dust storms and slope hazards), and Scientific Exploration (maximizing scientific ROI across geologic outcrops).

Crucially, traverses are benchmarked against historical NASA rover paths and verified with in-situ surface photography. Red Planet Lab bridges the gap between raw planetary data and explainable mission operations, reducing rover risk, safeguarding payloads, and accelerating scientific discovery on Mars.

projectDetails.name: Remontada Health care
projectDetails.summary:
Remontada Health System is an intelligent health monitoring platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It addresses the physical and mental health risks caused by space radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and the challenges of living in space.

The system combines health monitoring, an interactive virtual clinic, mental health support, and computer vision to help astronauts track their health, identify potential health concerns, and receive preliminary guidance. It also uses gamification elements to encourage astronauts to complete health-related tasks and maintain healthy habits.

Our goal is to empower astronauts to take a more active role in managing their health, especially when immediate medical assistance from Earth is limited.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Remontada Health System is a web-based health monitoring platform designed to help astronauts monitor and manage their physical and mental well-being during long-duration space missions.

The platform addresses the challenges of healthcare in space, where astronauts face limited access to immediate medical assistance and must take greater responsibility for monitoring their own health.

_____________________

Main Features

1. Dynamic Health Dashboard

The dashboard presents important health indicators, including blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, and body temperature. It is designed to display sensor data through interactive dynamic charts, allowing astronauts to track changes in their health indicators over time.

2. Virtual Clinic

The Virtual Clinic provides an interactive human body model. Astronauts can select the body part where they experience pain or discomfort. The system then asks relevant questions about their symptoms and analyzes their answers to provide a preliminary health assessment and appropriate guidance.

3. Mental Health Support

This module focuses on astronauts' psychological well-being and includes:

Sleep monitoring based on daily sleep hours.

Interactive sleep-related chat.

Daily journal cards for recording thoughts and feelings.

Motivational cards to encourage positive habits.

Mental games to support cognitive engagement.

4. Computer Vision

This feature usescamera-based eye detection and analysis to identify potential visual signs of fatigue, eye strain, and drowsiness, supporting the monitoring of astronauts' well-being.

________________________

How It Helps

By combining physical and mental health monitoring in one platform, Remontada helps astronauts become more aware of their health status. It encourages early attention to potential health concerns and provides accessible guidance to support better health decisions.

Gamification is included as a motivational element to encourage astronauts to complete health-related tasks and maintain consistent self-care habits.

______________________

Expected Impact

We aim to improve astronauts' ability to monitor their health independently, recognize potential health changes, and maintain healthier routines throughout long-duration space missions.

The project may also inspire similar healthcare solutions for people living in remote areas with limited access to medical services.

________________________

Technologies and Tools

The Remontada Health System website was developed and deployed using the following technologies and tools:

HTML: Used to structure the website and organize its content.

CSS: Used to design the user interface and style the website.

JavaScript: Used to implement interactive features and dynamic functionality.

Google Gemini:Used to support AI-powered interactions and intelligent assistance.

Netlify: Used to deploy and host the website, making it accessible online.

projectDetails.name: Project RE:SOURCE
projectDetails.summary: We selected the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge and built [RE:SOURCE], an interactive, browser-based 7-day survival simulation game designed for youth (ages 7–12). Players act as planetary base commanders managing vital life-support resources—including water, oxygen, food, power, base integrity, and crew energy. The project addresses the gap in space education by transforming abstract aerospace engineering concepts into engaging, hands-on gameplay. It matters because it teaches young learners critical problem-solving and resource-management trade-offs inspired by real NASA mission architectures like the ISS ECLSS, empowering the next generation of space explorers.
projectDetails.details:
# RE — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

RE is an interactive educational game that introduces players to the challenges of maintaining a sustainable human presence on the Moon. It transforms the complex systems involved in lunar habitation into an engaging, hands-on survival experience, allowing players to understand how astronauts depend on interconnected life-support systems and how decisions about limited resources can affect an entire mission.

The experience begins with a visual-novel storyline that introduces the player to the idea of lunar exploration. The player then wakes up aboard a spacecraft and enters a guided Day 0 tutorial, where they meet Commander Nova, the Engineer, and the Scientist. Through conversations and interactive machine inspections, players learn about the habitat's essential systems before beginning the lunar survival mission.

Following the landing, the player must manage a lunar outpost for seven simulated days while maintaining six critical indicators: water, oxygen, food, electrical power, habitat integrity, and crew stamina. Each resource is interconnected. For example, water recycling requires electrical power, oxygen generation consumes water and power, habitat repairs require energy and crew effort, and greenhouse cultivation requires water, power, seeds, and nutrients before food can be harvested.

Players plan and queue actions, monitor resource availability, inspect equipment, and respond to changing mission conditions. At the end of each simulated day, the game processes crew consumption, machine operations, crop growth, environmental events, and survival conditions. The resulting daily report helps players understand the consequences of their decisions and adjust their strategy. Resource depletion or critical habitat damage can lead to mission failure, while maintaining the necessary systems through the final day results in mission completion.

The scientific foundation of RE is informed by trusted institutional and research references concerning human-spaceflight life-support systems, environmental control, water recovery, oxygen generation, space biology, radiation, and bioregenerative food production. These include NASA's Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) documentation, NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), NASA RadLab, and peer-reviewed research on closed ecological life-support systems for lunar missions. These references inform the scientific concepts represented in the game, while its numerical resource settings and gameplay parameters are simplified, evidence-informed values designed for an educational simulation rather than official NASA engineering specifications.

Technically, RE is developed as a browser-based application using Next.js, React, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3. The core game is implemented in a self-contained HTML environment, incorporating pixel-art graphics, animated scenes, interactive dialogue, resource-management interfaces, game-state persistence, and simulation logic. The project also includes a React-based prototype and a standalone Windows desktop version.

The main objective of RE is to make lunar sustainability understandable through experience rather than explanation alone. By allowing players to experiment with resource-management decisions and observe their consequences, the project connects scientific concepts with interactive learning. It demonstrates why water recovery, oxygen production, food generation, energy management, and habitat maintenance must work together to support long-duration human exploration beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: REVO
projectDetails.summary: REVO is a browser game that turns the 2026 challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” into a 20-minute classroom mission. A student commands a Martian outpost at Jezero Crater for 30 sols: five build missions, five crises, a rover expedition and three endings. Every action spends one of five meters — power, water, oxygen, radiation and readiness — so a cheap fix on Sol 3 can cause a blackout on Sol 11. Five NASA sources set the ranges, and a companion robot narrates 131 clips, reads aloud and keeps the tone kind for 8-12 year olds. It runs on any browser, installs offline, needs no login, and ends with a report card and stickers the teacher can read. It matters because it makes a real mission trade-off physical in one tap instead of abstract on a page.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES: REVO is a single-page web game set at Jezero Crater. The run has four beats: build the base in five missions (solar array, water recycler, oxygen garden, radiation shelter, lab), survive five crises between Sol 11 and Sol 26 (dust storm, nitrogen leak, solar particle event, water loss, hull breach), explore with a battery-limited rover on Sols 27-30, then graduate with a report card, a sticker album and one of three endings. Five meters drive everything and are shown as bars a child can read at a glance; below two bars the companion robot N.E.I.L. speaks a warning. Junior Mode shortens text, enlarges targets and reads aloud, and a Safe-Mode capsule replaces hard failure so a young player can recover and keep learning.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT: a 20-minute STEM session with no prep, no accounts and no install; screen time that ends in a conversation; a visible record of learning (stickers + science passport) that a parent or teacher can read.

HOW NASA DATA MADE IT POSSIBLE: Mars Trek shaped the Jezero surface tiles and base sites; MEDA supplied dust, pressure and wind behaviour that set the storm calendar and solar output; DONKI classified the flare timing behind the Sol 21 particle event; MSL RAD sized the radiation meter drain; the MER Opportunity archive supplied the June 2018 dust-storm timeline behind the Sol 11 crisis and the emergency ending. CSA Canadian Nutrient File set the ration costs.

TOOLS: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Canvas 2D for the dust storm, Web Audio API for mixing, a Service Worker for offline play, Python + NumPy + FFmpeg for the asset pipelines, Vitest for tests, GitHub and Vercel for source and hosting. No backend, no database, no hardware.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED: the storm on screen is driven by the same state as the meters, so the world visibly reacts to the choice; stickers act as learning receipts; the companion is the difficulty dial. We balanced reading level (short lines, one idea per screen), safety (no gore, no punishment loop), honesty (documented simplifications) and accessibility (read-aloud, large targets, colour plus labels).

TRY IT IN 60 SECONDS: open the site, NEW GAME, skip the intro, play the solar array mission, CONTINUE to Sol 11, choose “Robot panel sweep”, swipe three panels. Power recovers, a sticker unlocks.

WHAT WORKS / WHAT DOES NOT: the full 30-sol loop, all five crises, the rover, three endings, stickers, logbook, Junior Mode and offline install are live and were played through in a browser on 14 November 2026; 57 automated tests pass and the type-check is clean. Not finished: small-phone layout for the surface grid, cloud saves, adaptive difficulty, and the teacher dashboard and worksheet pack.

NEXT: pilot in three Cairo schools, Arabic voice pack, teacher dashboard, a mission editor so a class can design its own sol.

projectDetails.name: RedSight
projectDetails.summary:
RedSight is a walk planner for astronauts exploring Mars on foot, built for one real place: the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where NASA’s Curiosity rover is driving today.

Mars maps are made for whole regions, but a crew of two leaving their habitat needs a plan for the next kilometre or two, and for the oxygen in their suits. A message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, so the crew has to decide on the spot.

RedSight puts NASA orbital and rover data on one walk-scale map. The crew picks a science stop at a real Curiosity site and compares two modeled routes, the fastest and the one over the easiest ground, with walking time and oxygen for each astronaut. An oxygen slider shows where they would have to turn back, and a no-return line marks how far they can go and still get home. Mission Replay plays the walk with an oxygen gauge and drills such as a suit leak.

Every figure is a modeled estimate built from NASA sources, and each one is labelled Observed, Derived or Scenario.

projectDetails.name: RootRise
projectDetails.summary:
RootRise is an AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make smarter and more sustainable farming decisions. It addresses critical challenges such as water scarcity, soil degradation, climate change, and inefficient crop rotation, with an initial focus on Egypt and other climate-vulnerable regions.

The proposed platform combines NASA satellite observations, climate data, soil characteristics, and agricultural information to generate intelligent crop rotation recommendations tailored to individual farms. By integrating Earth observation technologies with an explainable AI decision-support system, RootRise aims to help farmers compare agricultural strategies based on water consumption, soil health, productivity, and climate resilience.

The project is important because agriculture faces increasing environmental pressures, while many farmers lack access to advanced data-analysis tools. RootRise aims to transform complex scientific data into practical recommendations, supporting sustainable farming, efficient resource management, and long-term food security.
projectDetails.details:
RootRise – AI-Powered Agricultural Decision-Support Platform

RootRise is an innovative AI-powered agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make smarter, more sustainable, and data-driven farming decisions. The project focuses on addressing major agricultural challenges, including soil degradation, water scarcity, climate change, declining soil fertility, and inefficient crop rotation practices, particularly in arid and climate-vulnerable regions such as Egypt and the Nile Delta.

The platform aims to combine satellite observations, environmental and climate data, soil characteristics, and agricultural information to generate intelligent crop rotation recommendations tailored to individual farms.

How It Works:

RootRise is designed to collect and analyze several types of data, including:

  • Satellite observations and vegetation indices such as NDVI and EVI.
  • Climate information, including temperature, rainfall, and drought indicators.
  • Soil characteristics such as pH, salinity, organic matter, and nutrient levels.
  • Crop characteristics, including water requirements, growing seasons, and nitrogen fixation capabilities.
  • Historical agricultural records and farmers' priorities.

Using this information, the proposed AI decision-support engine will evaluate different crop rotation strategies and compare them based on water conservation, soil health, agricultural productivity, climate resilience, and economic feasibility. It will provide farmers with understandable recommendations, explain the advantages and disadvantages of each strategy, and highlight potential agricultural risks.

Technology and Tools:

The planned technology stack includes Python, TypeScript, Next.js, React, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, PostGIS, GeoPandas, Rasterio, NumPy, and Pandas. The project also proposes integrating publicly available Earth observation and environmental datasets from NASA Earthdata, Landsat, MODIS, SMAP, and NASA POWER API.

The initial AI architecture is designed around an explainable hybrid decision-support system combining agricultural rule-based filtering and multi-criteria weighted scoring. This approach prioritizes transparency and scientifically explainable recommendations rather than relying entirely on black-box predictions.

Benefits and Expected Impact:

RootRise aims to:

  1. Reduce unnecessary agricultural water consumption through better crop selection and rotation planning.
  2. Improve soil fertility and support sustainable agricultural practices.
  3. Help farmers adapt to changing climate conditions and environmental risks.
  4. Reduce unnecessary fertilizer and agricultural input costs.
  5. Make satellite and scientific environmental data more accessible to small and medium-sized farmers.
  6. Support food security and long-term agricultural sustainability.

Innovation and Creativity:

The main innovation of RootRise is its integration of satellite-based Earth observation, climate intelligence, soil science, and AI-powered decision support into one accessible platform. Instead of simply displaying environmental data, the platform is designed to transform complex scientific information into practical, understandable agricultural strategies.

Development Status:

RootRise is currently in its conceptual and architectural planning phase. Its software architecture, proposed technologies, data sources, and development roadmap have been defined. The implementation of the application and its AI decision-support engine is planned as the next development stage.

Our long-term vision is to contribute to more sustainable and climate-resilient agriculture by connecting space-based environmental intelligence with real-world farming decisions.

projectDetails.name: AstroHealth
projectDetails.summary:
AstroHealth is a web-based health monitoring and decision-support application designed to help astronauts monitor their health during long-duration space missions, where access to immediate medical assistance may be limited.

The platform combines wearable-style vital-sign monitoring, daily manual health check-ins, and photo-based skin and wound assessments in a unified dashboard. It uses transparent, predefined health thresholds to classify readings, alongside trend forecasting and an LSTM-based anomaly detection model to identify unusual heart-rate patterns. When urgent situations arise, astronauts can access 11 predefined emergency medical protocols that operate fully offline.

Additionally, AstroHealth features an AI-powered medical assistant that retrieves information from NASA medical and human-spaceflight resources, providing answers with traceable source references.

By transforming health data into understandable status indicators, early warnings, and actionable guidance, AstroHealth aims to support astronaut self-monitoring and medical decision-making during missions where communication delays and limited medical resources create additional challenges.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Overview

AstroHealth is a web-based health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions.

Space missions expose astronauts to multiple health risks, while distance from Earth, communication delays, and limited access to medical professionals make continuous health monitoring and timely assistance essential.

AstroHealth brings health monitoring, data analysis, anomaly detection, emergency guidance, and AI-powered medical information retrieval together in one platform. It aims to help astronauts understand their health status, identify unusual patterns, and access structured guidance when needed.

The system is designed as an integrated prototype that combines traditional rule-based monitoring with machine learning and AI-powered assistance.

2. Problem & Motivation

Astronauts face unique health challenges during long-duration space missions. NASA identifies five major hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and the hostile or closed environment.

These conditions can affect astronauts' physical and psychological health. At the same time, communication delays and limited access to medical professionals make immediate medical support more challenging.

Traditional health monitoring alone may not be sufficient to provide a unified view of an astronaut's health, identify unusual patterns over time, and offer accessible guidance during emergencies.

AstroHealth addresses this challenge by bringing health monitoring, data analysis, anomaly detection, emergency protocols, and medical information retrieval into one integrated platform.

3. How AstroHealth Works

AstroHealth follows an integrated workflow that transforms health information into understandable monitoring results and decision-support guidance.

The system brings together three main sources of information:

  • Wearable-Style Readings: Simulated time-series health readings representing data that could be collected from wearable devices.
  • Manual Health Check-ins: Daily health information and observations entered by the astronaut.
  • Photo-Based Assessments: Images submitted for experimental skin and wound-related analysis.

The collected information is processed by the platform's monitoring and analysis services, then presented through a unified dashboard.

Based on the available information, users can view health status indicators, follow trends, identify unusual heart-rate patterns, access emergency protocols, and retrieve relevant medical information through the AI-powered assistant.

The system combines rule-based logic, statistical analysis, and machine learning rather than depending on a single AI model for every function.

4. Health Monitoring & Interactive Dashboard

The AstroHealth dashboard provides a centralized view of astronaut health information, making it easier to monitor multiple indicators in one place.

It combines wearable-style readings and manual health check-ins to present health information in an organized and accessible format.

The platform uses predefined threshold-based rules to classify health readings into three status levels:

  • Green: The reading is within the configured normal range.
  • Yellow: The reading requires attention or monitoring.
  • Red: The reading has reached a configured alert threshold.

These classifications are generated through transparent rule-based logic, not by an AI model.

The dashboard also presents health trends and monitoring results to help users understand changes over time and identify readings that may require further attention.


5. AI, Trend Forecasting & Anomaly Detection

AstroHealth integrates machine learning and statistical analysis to provide additional insights into health data.

Heart-Rate Anomaly Detection

An LSTM Autoencoder model analyzes heart-rate time-series data to learn recurring patterns and identify observations that differ from the learned patterns.

Instead of relying only on fixed thresholds, this approach focuses on unusual patterns in the heart-rate data that may deserve further attention.

Health Trend Forecasting

The platform uses Linear Regression as its default forecasting method to estimate short-term trends in health indicators. It also includes an optional Chronos-based forecasting integration, which is disabled by default.

Statistical Monitoring

For health indicators other than heart rate, the platform applies statistical checks to highlight unusual readings.

Together, these components complement the rule-based monitoring system by providing trend information and additional signals for identifying potentially unusual health patterns.

These outputs are intended for screening and decision support, not medical diagnosis.

6. Emergency Assistance & Offline Protocols

During a space mission, access to immediate medical assistance may be limited. AstroHealth addresses this challenge through a collection of 11 predefined emergency decision-tree protocols.

These protocols provide structured, step-by-step guidance for different emergency scenarios.

Users can follow the decision paths to access relevant instructions based on the situation. The protocols are designed to operate fully offline, allowing astronauts to access predefined guidance even when an internet connection is unavailable.

This feature aims to make emergency instructions accessible and organized when timely support is essential.

The protocols provide informational guidance and do not replace professional medical care or mission-specific medical procedures.

7. AI-Powered Medical Assistant (RAG)

AstroHealth includes an AI-powered medical assistant built using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach.

The assistant retrieves relevant information from a collection of NASA human-spaceflight and medical resources before generating a response to the user's question.

The retrieval system combines:

  • Semantic Search: Uses the BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 embedding model to retrieve passages based on their meaning.
  • BM25 Keyword Retrieval: Helps identify relevant passages using keyword matching.
  • Context-Based Generation: Uses the retrieved passages as context for generating an answer.

The assistant displays source references alongside its responses, allowing users to trace the information back to the retrieved material.

This approach helps connect AI-generated responses to relevant reference material instead of relying only on the language model's internal knowledge.

The assistant is designed to provide informational support and does not replace professional medical judgment.


8. Photo-Based Skin & Wound Assessment

AstroHealth includes an experimental photo-based assessment feature that allows users to submit images for skin and wound-related analysis.

The feature combines a vision-language model with an offline MobileNetV2 image classifier to analyze submitted images.

This adds a visual assessment component to the platform alongside its numerical health-monitoring capabilities.

The feature is intended as an experimental prototype for informational support. Its results are not medical diagnoses, and the component has not been validated as a medical-grade diagnostic system.

9. Technologies & System Architecture

AstroHealth is developed using a modular web architecture that combines frontend, backend, data processing, and AI components.

Backend Development

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Pydantic
  • SQLAlchemy
  • SQLite

Frontend Development

  • React
  • Vite
  • Recharts
  • Three.js

Machine Learning & AI

  • PyTorch
  • LSTM Autoencoder
  • Linear Regression
  • Optional Chronos integration
  • ONNX Runtime
  • MobileNetV2
  • OpenAI-compatible language and vision model endpoint

Retrieval-Augmented Generation

  • ChromaDB
  • Sentence Transformers
  • BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5
  • BM25

Development & Deployment

  • Docker
  • GitHub

The modular architecture allows the platform's monitoring, forecasting, anomaly detection, emergency assistance, and retrieval components to work together while maintaining separate responsibilities.

10. Expected Impact & Limitations

AstroHealth aims to support astronaut health monitoring and decision-making during long-duration space missions by bringing multiple capabilities into one accessible platform.

Its main contributions include:

  • Centralized Health Monitoring: Bringing different health indicators and daily check-ins into one dashboard.
  • Early Awareness: Highlighting unusual heart-rate patterns and health trends that may require attention.
  • Accessible Emergency Guidance: Providing 11 predefined emergency protocols that remain accessible offline.
  • NASA-Based Information Retrieval: Helping users access relevant information from NASA human-spaceflight resources through a source-referenced AI assistant.
  • Integrated Visual Assessment: Exploring photo-based analysis as an additional source of health information.

Prototype Limitations

AstroHealth is a working prototype and is not a certified medical device or diagnostic system.

Wearable-style readings used in the prototype are simulated rather than collected from astronauts in actual space missions. AI-based outputs and photo assessments are experimental and require further validation before any real-world medical use.

The platform is intended to demonstrate how monitoring, data analysis, machine learning, and information retrieval can be combined to support astronaut health awareness and decision-making.

projectDetails.name: Planetary Analog Finder
projectDetails.summary:
Planetary Analog Finder is an interactive search engine that finds places on Earth resembling a chosen location on the Moon or Mars.

NASA rehearses lunar and Martian missions at analog sites on Earth, but those sites are few, well known, and mostly chosen by appearance. We built a system that turns the Moon, Mars and Earth into one shared global grid described by the same measurable features: terrain relief, slope, roughness, surface temperature, and day-night temperature range. The user clicks any point on a 3D globe of Mars or the Moon, and the system scans Earth and returns the five closest matches. Each result shows a per-dimension similarity score, the measured differences, and a clear “where the analogy breaks” section covering gravity, atmosphere and radiation. A Hidden Gems filter hides famous sites so users can discover new candidates.

It is built on NASA open data: [MODIS, LRO LOLA and Diviner, MGS MOLA; list only what you actually used].

It matters because it makes analog-site selection a repeatable, data-driven search that can reveal overlooked regions, and it makes planetary comparison easy to explore for mission planners, researchers and students.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars

Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: SAKAN SPACE
projectDetails.summary:
SAKAN SPACE is an offline-capable web application that organizes NASA microgravity-combustion research into a structured, source-cited knowledge base to support spacecraft fire-safety research.

The platform features three core modules: Mission Design Validator, Earth Spinoff & Research Hub, and Crisis Evidence Co-Pilot. It also includes a Search page and Ask SAKAN AI, with online AI integration through OpenRouter and an offline local AI fallback.

SAKAN promotes scientific transparency by labeling evidence as VERIFIED, NOT VERIFIED, NOT REPORTED, or NOT AVAILABLE, while assessing source reliability and maintaining traceability.

It is a research and decision-support tool, not a certified safety system or an emergency-procedure source. It never declares any condition safe.
projectDetails.details:
SAKAN SPACE is an offline-capable research platform that organizes NASA microgravity-combustion research into a structured, traceable knowledge base containing 27 investigations and 88 scientific findings, each linked to source IDs and an evidence reliability score.

Evidence reliability is calculated using the OEC model: OEC = 0.30·SC + 0.20·DQ + 0.35·ES + 0.15·RR, with 19 High, 57 Moderate, 9 Low, and 3 Very Low findings.

The platform consists of three main modules:

01 — Mission Design Validator uses a 20-rule engine to assess mission-design conditions, calculate oxygen partial pressure (PO₂ = XO₂ × Ptotal), and generate evidence-backed assessments ranging from INSUFFICIENT DATA to HIGH RISK.

02 — Earth Spinoff & Research Hub provides an Arabic-English glossary of 84 scientific terms, interactive charts, research evolution, and Earth-based applications.

03 — Crisis Evidence Co-Pilot uses a weighted bilingual matching system to retrieve relevant published evidence for described scenarios, supported by voice input, text-to-speech, timers, and checklists. It identifies missing evidence without inventing emergency procedures.

SAKAN features two AI systems. SAKAN Local AI operates entirely in the browser without an internet connection, combining a bilingual BM25 retriever, trained intent classifier, rule engine, and numerical flame-behaviour models trained on ACME data. It is a specialized research system, not a generative LLM.

Online SAKAN AI, powered by OpenRouter language models through a FastAPI backend hosted on Replit, provides real-time AI assistance. In automatic mode, it explains scientific assessments and crisis evidence in the user's language, referencing verified findings and their evidence status. If the online backend becomes unavailable, the application automatically falls back to SAKAN Local AI.

Model evaluation using grouped, held-out 70/30 splits achieved 0.633 PSI router top-1 accuracy and 0.984 top-3 accuracy, 0.851 intent-classifier accuracy (template split), and 0.83 balanced accuracy for the self-extinguishing model. The burn-time model achieved an R² of 0.20, indicating limited predictive performance. Hot-ignition and cool-flame targets were excluded because the available data were unsuitable.

SAKAN prioritizes scientific transparency and safety. It distinguishes VERIFIED, NOT VERIFIED, NOT REPORTED, and NOT AVAILABLE evidence, and never declares any condition safe. Its reliability scores reflect source quality, not physical safety.

The platform is not a certified safety system or an emergency-procedure source. Its findings are limited to publicly available research, online AI availability depends on free-tier services, and speech recognition depends on browser support.

Future development includes expanding the knowledge base as NASA publishes new investigations, improving numerical models as more consistent experimental data become available, and obtaining expert review of the validation rules.

Technology Stack: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), Node.js, Python FastAPI, Vercel, Replit, and OpenRouter API.

projectDetails.name: SARlock: Interactive L-Band SAR Investigation Platform
projectDetails.summary:
SARlock is an open-source, interactive 3D WebGL investigation platform that makes NASA’s NISAR L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data accessible through guided scientific storytelling. While radar satellites see through clouds, ash, and darkness to capture major disasters, raw backscatter data remains difficult for students, journalists, and decision makers to interpret.

Guided by Sar—a narrator speaking as NISAR itself—users explore real 2026 events on a 3D Earth across five progressive stages: Encounter, Discovery, Challenge, Explanation, and Impact. The platform features a before/after swipe slider, live HH/HV polarization toggling, RGB change composites, and quantitative Region-of-Interest (ROI) radiometry derived from cloud-streamed NISAR Level-2 GCOV granules.

By demonstrating flood inundation in Chókwè, Mozambique, and mid-eruption volcanic changes at Krasheninnikov, Russia (+8.19 dB rough lava vs. -7.03 dB fine tephra), SARlock bridges the gap between raw orbital physics and public understanding while openly disclosing product calibration limits.
projectDetails.details:
SARlock: Interactive L-Band SAR Investigation Platform

SARlock is an interactive 3D Earth investigation experience designed to teach users how to read surface changes in NASA’s NISAR L-band radar data, turning complex orbital physics into a story-driven detective mystery. Guided by Sar—a narrator speaking as the NISAR satellite itself—users travel across a 3D globe, inspect real floods and volcanic eruptions using before/after radar swipe tools and polarization toggles, and solve geophysical challenges, making radar science both intuitive and accessible.

What It Does & How It Works

SARlock is a zero-backend, open-source 3D WebGL web application that transforms NASA’s L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data into interactive scientific investigations. Guided by "Sar"—a narrator speaking as the NISAR satellite itself—users select real 2026 disaster events on a 3D Earth and progress through five structured stages:

1. Encounter: Sets the geographic context and dates with a mystery hook question (strictly free of event spoilers).

2. Discovery: Provides a before/after swipe slider, a live HH/HV polarization toggle, an RGB change composite (Cyan = brightening/roughening, Red = darkening/smoothing), and three spatial hotspots.

3. Challenge: Asks users to diagnose the physical cause among four plausible geophysical options with progressive hints.

4. Explanation: Reveals quantitative Region-of-Interest (ROI) radiometry in unstretched decibels (dB), dual-polarization scattering physics, and calibration caveats.

5. Impact: Places users in an operational decision-maker role with educational feedback on every choice.

Scientific Cases & Proven Results

- Case 01 (Chókwè Flood, Mozambique — NISAR L2 GCOV BETA_V1): Demonstrates sharp HH and HV backscatter drops along the Limpopo River corridor caused by specular reflection off smooth floodwaters, while openly disclosing pre-calibration background limits.

- Case 02 (Krasheninnikov Volcano, Kamchatka — NISAR L2 GCOV PROVISIONAL_V1): Tracks mid-eruption surface evolution, showing +8.19 dB HV brightening over rough new lava flows, -7.03 dB HV darkening over fine tephra deposits, and +0.18 dB stability on a pre-existing control flow.

Benefits & Intended Impact

SARlock bridges the gap between complex orbital radar archives and non-specialist audiences—including students, educators, journalists, and emergency planners. Rather than showing static maps without explanation or requiring PhD-level remote sensing software, it teaches users how to read backscatter physics and distinguish observation from inference. Its modular JSON contract ("5-experiences-v1") allows educators and researchers to add new global disaster cases without modifying application code.

Tools, Languages & Cloud Architecture

- Data & Scientific Pipeline: Python (asf_search, earthaccess, fsspec, h5py, NumPy, Pillow, pyproj) to stream windowed UTM subsets of NISAR Level-2 GCOV granules (HHHH and HVHV) directly from NASA Earthdata Cloud without multi-gigabyte local downloads.

- Frontend & Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, and WebGL for fast, client-side 3D rendering hosted on GitHub Pages.

- Version Control & QA: Git, GitHub, and automated pre-commit Python validation scripts.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered

- First-Person Satellite Storytelling: Framing NISAR as an investigative guide ("Sar") turns abstract decibel shifts into an engaging detective mystery.

- Strict Scientific Honesty & Rigor: Our pipeline averages linear gamma-0 power before converting to dB to avoid logarithmic bias, enforces a "No Source, No Number" validation rule, isolates display stretches from raw ROI radiometry, and transparently discloses product maturity levels (BETA_V1 vs. PROVISIONAL_V1).

projectDetails.name: Project SARrealists
projectDetails.summary:
SARrealists is an interactive web experience that makes NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data understandable to non-experts. A Mapbox globe takes visitors through three regions: California (wildfire scars and Central Valley subsidence), the Himalayas (glacier change and GLOF risk) and the Nile Delta (soil moisture and coastal subsidence). Regional analysis pages show NISAR-derived layers. Captain DIO, a bilingual (English/Arabic) pixel-art game, teaches players which SAR measurements answer which questions. LUMEN, an AI assistant, explains the data for four audiences (scientist, decision maker, student, enthusiast), with answers grounded in curated NASA/NISAR sources. 

NISAR sees through cloud, smoke and darkness and detects centimetre-scale ground motion, but its products are large and technical. By turning them into a story, a game and a conversation, SARrealists shows why radar matters, including for food security and subsidence in Egypt’s Nile Delta.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

SARrealists turns NISAR radar data into an experience people can scroll through, play and question. It has four parts that reinforce each other.

1. A data pipeline. A Python pipeline searches ASF DAAC with asf_search and streams only the area of interest from each NISAR granule (about 7 GB each) instead of downloading it whole. It computes calibrated layers from the GCOV, GUNW and SME2 products and exports Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs, plots, GeoJSON and a catalog. The website reads these exports directly.

2. A scrollytelling globe. A full-screen Mapbox globe walks visitors through California (wildfire scars and Central Valley subsidence), the Himalayas (glacier change and GLOF risk) and the Nile Delta (soil moisture and coastal subsidence). Each region has a human character and a scientist guide. A Mission Control Dashboard then lets visitors explore freely, jumping between regions, toggling NISAR layers and switching HH/HV polarization. Three regional analysis pages go deeper into the physics and the data.

3. The Captain DIO game. Captain DIO is an astronaut who lands on an Earth-like planet and uses a SAR satellite to protect his crew. The player goes through four missions. In each one they read a briefing and choose two SAR “lenses” (for example, which polarization or product to analyse) to answer the mission’s question. The engine scores the quality of that choice. A good choice keeps the crew safe, while a poor one leaves crew members injured and out of action, so every pick has a visible cost. Crew state carries across missions and ends in a final mission report, and the player’s best report is saved. A lens codex explains each radar measurement in plain language, so the game doubles as a reference. At the end the player learns the planet was Earth all along and is invited to explore the real data. Before that reveal the story deliberately avoids real place names and coordinates, so the twist works. The game has 22 original pixel-art mission images, plus pixel-art charts, sprites and crew portraits. It is fully bilingual (English and Arabic, with right-to-left layout), supports keyboard play and reduced motion, and has optional looping theme music.

4. LUMEN, an AI assistant. It is available on every page and has four personas: Scientist, Decision Maker, Student and Enthusiast. The question, persona, language and optional map-click context go to a server-side route, which applies a small rate limit. LUMEN retrieves matching chunks from a curated NASA/NISAR source set, builds a grounded prompt, and gets an answer from a Gemini or OpenAI-compatible model. The answer comes back with sources and confidence notes. With no model key configured, a local grounded fallback answers from the bundled references and labels itself as such.

Benefits and intended impact

NISAR will produce an enormous amount of freely available data, but most of its potential value is lost if only specialists can read it. SARrealists lowers that barrier in three ways.

  • Understanding: students and the public learn what radar can see that cameras cannot, such as burn scars under smoke, millimetre-scale ground motion, and soil moisture from space. They learn it by doing, not by reading a definition.
  • Relevance: the Nile Delta story ties NISAR to food security and coastal subsidence in our own region. The Arabic interface means the content reaches people who rarely get Earth-observation material in their language.
  • Decision-making: a decision maker can ask LUMEN what a layer means for their question, in plain terms and with sources, without becoming a radar expert first.
  • Support for the mission: missions like NISAR depend on public understanding and support. People who have “used” the data are more likely to see why it was worth building.

We also see the project as reusable. The pipeline and site structure can take new regions, and the game’s content is data-driven, so educators could adapt missions to other sites.

Tools

  • Web: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Mapbox GL, Recharts, Framer Motion, Zod
  • Data: Python, asf_search, COG/Zarr export, Google Colab for heavy processing
  • AI: a Gemini or OpenAI-compatible model for LUMEN, behind a server-side route
  • Quality: Vitest, pytest, a content-validation script
  • Hosting: Vercel, with GitHub and jsDelivr serving the data export

Creativity

Instead of building another viewer, we built a narrative. Real-feeling people guide each region, the game makes the choice of SAR lens a decision with consequences, and the final reveal makes players realise that the story was about their own planet. LUMEN adapts its explanation to who is asking.

Factors we considered

  • Data size and bandwidth: streaming only the area of interest, with heavy processing moved to Colab.
  • Accessibility: Arabic with RTL support, keyboard-accessible controls and reduced-motion support.
  • Trust: grounded, cited AI answers, and automated tests for the game, content and LUMEN. A validation script also stops the game’s pre-reveal content from leaking place names.
  • Honesty about limits: the regional pages use static exports, some game visuals are illustrative placeholders, and nothing here is an operational hazard or alert service.

projectDetails.name: RIDGE Crew Health Monitoring System
projectDetails.summary:
The RIDGE Crew Health Monitor is a web based prototyping tool that allows astronauts to collect data about their health. This includes logging observations, tracking trends in vital signs, sleep and mood and exploring different body systems using an interactive body map. It shows the differences against the user's individual baselines, whilst also showing any changes to cabin conditions and radiation.

The tool was designed based on NASA's 5 hazards of human spaceflight. This provides astronauts with a greater understanding of how their health is changing as it provides both health and environmental data. It also demonstrates how a summary of health can be sent to the ground medical team to be reviewed at a later date.

This project aims to give crew members a greater understanding of how their health is changing and provides a greater amount of information to the ground medical team. This tool is a prototype and is not a diagnostic tool. More testing is required to determine how reliable, easy to use and safe it is clinically.
projectDetails.details:
The RIDGE Crew Health Monitor is a browser based prototype which aims to allow astronauts and medical officers to easily view health data in a space environment. This allows for the user to view health indicators, self-reported information and mission details.

The prototype was split into the 5 major hazards of human spaceflight (Radiation, Isolation and Confinement, Distance from Earth, Gravity Fields, Hostile/Closed Environments) as part of the RIDGE framework. This combines physiological data like blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, sleep and mood to create a picture of their health trends and mission details. It provides a more accurate insight of how their health is changing over time relative to their baseline values rather than standard medical advice.

The data entry section includes sections to input measurements, self-reported information, tools used, annotations and visibility to the user. Specific data types are separated such as bodily fluids and scan imaging, these are recorded as events. There is an interactive 3D model of the body which allows users to view different parts of the body and different layers (muscles, organs, nervous system etc.) to visualise bodily systems.

The Context & Exposure section includes information regarding the environment of the habitat. This includes data about the cabin such as CO2 levels, pressure, temperature, noise, light, microbial levels, radiation exposure and communication latency times. The amount of radiation is separated from any damage this may cause to the user. This project has a list of tools which include what data they collect, units, what hazard they relate to and references to research.

During the development of the project, we used a browser based prototype with charts to view health data, forms to input data and a 3D model of the body. The science behind the project uses the NASA Human Research Program. This includes the 5 hazards, current research (CIPHER) and information from the Canadian Space Agency on neutron radiation monitoring. This helps to structure information but does not provide specific medical advice.

RIDGE combines information. Users can view health trends, explore the relevant anatomy and environmental factors. The prototype also includes regular checklists and reminders to ensure regular logging. It does not make any claims about how effective it will be medically.

As a team we considered factors such as communication latency, availability of the tool on the spacecraft, confidentiality, using personal baselines, ensuring data is complete and ensuring information is clearly communicated. The prototype allows for a summary of health which can be reviewed later by the ground team. However, only a simulation of sending data to the ground has been carried out. A main aim was to have a tool that can be used mainly on the spacecraft however we need to test how reliable it is when offline and how it stores the records.

The aim is to improve clarity when reviewing health data and improve information sharing between the crew and medical. As this is still a concept and prototype it will not act as a diagnostic tool or medically approved. The readings are just examples and usability and safety for medical purposes needs to be tested.

projectDetails.name: Astroberry
projectDetails.summary:
Astroberry is an interactive, browser-based educational game for children aged 7–12. Players act as mission commanders of a human outpost on Mars, managing oxygen, water, food, and power for a crew of astronauts.

The problem: Most learning materials present space facts, while most space games focus on entertainment without reflecting real engineering constraints. Children rarely experience the decisions that determine whether a mission succeeds or fails.

Our solution: Across six progressive missions, players face real engineering trade-offs: reducing heating saves electricity but affects the crew. After every decision, the game explains what happened, why it happened, and which scientific concept it represents. Failure becomes a lesson: the game explains the cause and lets children try a new strategy.

Real NASA data: DONKI space-weather events drive solar-threat scenarios, Perseverance MEDA measurements shape temperature and dust conditions, and OSDR research informs health-related explanations. Real data and simulated gameplay values are clearly separated and labeled as live or archived.

Why this challenge: It combines NASA science, open data, and STEM education to inspire young learners. The game is built with React and JavaScript and hosted on Vercel, allowing children to play instantly in any browser with no installation required.
projectDetails.details:
Astroberry is an interactive, browser-based educational game where children aged 7–12 become commanders of a Mars outpost. Players manage oxygen, water, food, and power across six progressive missions. Each decision creates a trade-off: for example, reducing heating saves power but can affect the crew. The game simulates these consequences through a daily turn-based system, then provides immediate feedback explaining what happened and the scientific concept behind it.

The main benefit is learning by doing. Instead of only reading about space, children make decisions, experience their consequences, learn from failure, and try new strategies. This develops scientific understanding, critical thinking, resource management, and problem-solving while keeping the experience engaging. Parents and teachers also get an accessible, no-installation STEM learning tool.

Our intended impact is to help young learners understand that space exploration is not only about discovering planets, but also about solving complex engineering problems and keeping people alive in extreme environments.

The project was developed using React.js, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Framer.js, GitHub, and Vercel, with OpenCode and Manus used as AI-powered development and research assistants. NASA open data from DONKI, MEDA, and OSDR was integrated to make scenarios scientifically grounded.

Astroberry is creative because it combines real NASA data, simplified engineering trade-offs, and game-based learning in a child-friendly experience. We considered the target age, accessibility, scientific accuracy, gameplay balance, clarity of feedback, resource limitations, and the need to clearly distinguish real NASA data from simulated gameplay values.

projectDetails.name: SESHAT
projectDetails.summary:
On Mars, every minute of exploration is a decision: Where should we go? What should we discover? And when should we turn back?

SESHAT is an interactive, science-driven Mars navigation and mission-planning platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map."

Using real NASA and USGS terrain and scientific datasets from Jezero Crater, SESHAT transforms traditional mapping into intelligent exploration planning. It helps astronauts evaluate reachable destinations, calculate terrain-aware routes, and balance scientific opportunities against limited mission time.

Explorers can select destinations, approve routes, simulate traverses, and record scientific observations. When new discoveries emerge or mission conditions change, SESHAT reevaluates available options and recommends where to explore next.

Unlike conventional maps, SESHAT connects navigation with adaptive scientific decision-making through a transparent, data-driven prototype.

Our mission is simple: Make every step on Mars meaningful, and every minute count.
projectDetails.details:
SESHAT — Navigate Mars. Discover More.

1. The Challenge: Every Minute Matters on Mars

Imagine being an astronaut exploring Mars. You have limited time, unfamiliar terrain, multiple scientific targets, and a critical decision to make: Which destination is worth exploring, and can you safely complete the journey within your available time?

A traditional map can show where destinations are, but it cannot fully explain which scientific opportunities remain achievable when time is running out or when new discoveries change mission priorities.

This is the problem SESHAT addresses.

2. Our Solution: Beyond Navigation

SESHAT is an interactive, science-driven Martian navigation and mission-planning platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map."

Inspired by the accessibility of modern navigation applications, SESHAT brings a new dimension to planetary exploration: connecting real Martian terrain, scientific objectives, route feasibility, and adaptive decision-making.

Instead of simply answering "How do I get there?", SESHAT helps explorers answer a more important question:

"Given my remaining time and scientific priorities, where should I go next, and why?"

3. How SESHAT Works

SESHAT provides an interactive exploration workflow built around real data from Jezero Crater, the landing region of NASA's Perseverance rover.

Step 1 — Explore and Select

Users explore an interactive Martian map and select scientifically interesting destinations. The application combines terrain information with geological and scientific context to support exploration planning.

Step 2 — Calculate and Approve

SESHAT evaluates potential routes using terrain elevation, travel costs, distance, and available mission time. Users review the proposed exploration plan before approving their traverse.

Step 3 — Navigate and Observe

After approval, users begin a simulated traverse and follow the active route. Upon reaching a destination, they can record scientific observations and document findings.

Step 4 — Adapt to New Discoveries

Exploration is unpredictable. When a new scientific discovery or mission constraint is introduced, SESHAT reevaluates the remaining exploration opportunities and supports alternative destination recommendations.

Step 5 — Make Every Minute Count

The system estimates reachable destinations within the remaining exploration time, helping users understand the trade-offs between scientific value, travel requirements, and mission constraints.

4. Powered by Real Martian Data

SESHAT uses authentic NASA and USGS planetary resources rather than fictional Martian terrain.

Our scientific foundation includes:

  • NASA/JPL Mars Trek terrain imagery and elevation products.
  • NASA Mars 2020 scientific resources and Perseverance mission observations.
  • USGS geological mapping of Jezero Crater.
  • Martian thermal-inertia data for surface-property context.
  • NASA Mars 2020 environmental observations.

Geospatial datasets are processed into a locally centered Mars Azimuthal Equidistant coordinate system, allowing the application to perform terrain-aware route calculations.

The scientific planning engine uses deterministic graph-based algorithms, including Dijkstra/A*, and precomputed terrain-cost data to evaluate traversal options.

This makes the project's computational decisions reproducible and explainable rather than dependent on unpredictable AI-generated answers.

5. Technology and Development

SESHAT is a browser-based interactive application built using modern web and scientific computing technologies.

Frontend:
Next.js, React, TypeScript, Leaflet, Tailwind CSS, StyleX, and Astryx UI components.

Scientific Processing:
Python, Rasterio, PyProj, NumPy, SciPy, and Pillow.

Routing and Visualization:
Terrain-based graph algorithms, precomputed geospatial data, interactive 2D mapping, and an HTML5 Canvas-based 3D terrain visualization.

Testing:
Automated scientific verification, unit tests, and Playwright end-to-end browser tests.

The final application runs its exploration-planning calculations deterministically without requiring a cloud AI service for runtime decisions.

6. What Makes SESHAT Innovative?

SESHAT's innovation is not simply placing a navigation interface on Mars.

It is connecting navigation with scientific reasoning and changing mission conditions.

Three ideas distinguish our approach:

Science-Aware Navigation:
Destinations are evaluated as scientific opportunities, not merely geographic coordinates.

Adaptive Mission Planning:
When exploration conditions or scientific priorities change, the system can reconsider the existing plan instead of following a fixed route.

Explainable, Time-Aware Decisions:
SESHAT combines terrain-based routing, mission-time constraints, and scientific priorities to make exploration alternatives easier to evaluate.

Together, these capabilities transform a Martian map into an interactive scientific decision-support experience.

7. Benefits and Potential Impact

SESHAT demonstrates how future planetary exploration tools could help astronauts and mission planners:

  • Prioritize valuable scientific observations.
  • Understand terrain-dependent travel requirements.
  • Make better use of limited exploration time.
  • Respond to unexpected discoveries.
  • Compare alternative exploration plans.
  • Document scientific activities and decisions.

Beyond Mars, the underlying approach could inform future research into time-constrained exploration planning for other planetary environments.

8. Current Capabilities and Limitations

The current SESHAT prototype demonstrates interactive mapping, terrain-aware route planning, destination selection, route approval, simulated traversal, scientific observation recording, travel estimation, and mission replanning scenarios.

SESHAT is a research and educational proof-of-concept, not a flight-certified astronaut navigation or safety system. Its estimated travel costs and simulated mission scenarios depend on modeling assumptions and available datasets. They do not establish actual EVA safety, validate all possible terrain hazards, or replace mission-control decisions.

Future development could incorporate additional terrain observations, environmental constraints, and operational validation.

9. Our Vision

Mars exploration is not only about traveling farther. It is about making better scientific decisions with the time and resources available.

SESHAT brings mapping, scientific exploration, and adaptive planning together to demonstrate a more intelligent approach to planetary navigation.

Because on Mars, the question isn't just where we can go.

It's where we should go next.

SESHAT — Make Every Step Count.

projectDetails.name: SESHAT X : Field Shift Decision Support System
projectDetails.summary: SESHAT is an advanced decision-support platform designed for Egyptian farmers to tackle climate change, soil degradation, and water scarcity under the NASA Space Apps "Field Shift" challenge. By fusing multi-satellite Earth observations—including NASA SMAP for soil moisture, ECOSTRESS for land surface temperature, GPM for precipitation, and ESA Sentinel-2 for vegetation health (NDVI)—with the HAPY IoT ground sensor, SESHAT translates complex space data into actionable, farmer-friendly insights. The platform evaluates three distinct crop rotation strategies (Existing, Water-Conservation, and Soil-Restoration) using the 33% Sweet Spot algorithm. SESHAT empowers farmers to optimize irrigation, restore soil fertility, and secure sustainable agricultural productivity without replacing human expertise.
projectDetails.details:
• What It Does & How It Works: " SESHAT X " is an end-to-end precision agriculture and irrigation decision-support platform built for arid and desert reclamation zones (such as Toshka, East Owainat, New Valley, and the Nile Delta). It fuses multi-orbital satellite observations (Sentinel-2 optical bands,Sentinel-1 Radar, NASA MODIS LST & ET, NASA SMAP soil moisture, and Landsat 8/9) with micro-climate telemetry (ERA5-Land, OpenWeatherMap) and edge IoT data from Hapy-60 (CM-60) center-pivot controllers. Our analytics engine runs FAO-56 Penman-Monteith crop water balance models (ETc), computes the Temperature Vegetation Dryness Index (TVDI), and uses a CatBoost ML classifier (catboost_crop_health.cbm) to detect water and heat stress 48–72 hours before visible canopy wilting, alongside spatial NDVI Coefficient of Variation (CV) and rule-based telemetry diagnostics to catch mechanical/electrical pivot tower faults early.
  • Benefits & Intended Impact: Prevents groundwater aquifer depletion in desert farms, reduces diesel and electricity pumping costs by prescribing exact daily pump runtimes (m3/ha), prevents sudden crop collapse under extreme desert heat (>40o C), and empowers farmers to compare resilient crop rotation strategies without needing expensive in-situ flux towers.
  • Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software:

- Languages: Python (49.5%), TypeScript (49.2%), CSS, HTML, Shell/PowerShell.

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript 5.8+, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS v4, bilingual RTL/LTR interface (Arabic/English).
- Backend & Security: Flask 3.0.3, SQLite (WAL mode) with multi-tenant isolation, AES-256 (Fernet) encryption, APScheduler, Gunicorn/Nginx.
- AI, ML & Remote Sensing: Google Earth Engine (GEE) API, NumPy, CatBoost 1.2+, local RAG agronomic assistant powered by Ollama (qwen2.5:3b), and FAO-56 agronomy physics.
- Hardware & Messaging: Hapy-60 pivot telemetry edge sensors (voltage, current, PSI pressure, speed) and multi-channel alerts via WhatsApp (Twilio), Telegram, SMTP, and automated PDF/Excel bulletins.

  • Creativity & Factors Considered: Overcomes the "lagging indicator trap" of optical NDVI by combining thermal and L-band microwave data. Engineered specifically for harsh 2G/3G desert connectivity using asynchronous background jobs (HTTP 202), ETag/304 caching, idempotency keys, E.164 Egyptian phone normalization, and ancient Egyptian cultural storytelling (Seshat, Hapy, GEB , Peret).

projectDetails.name: Sonify
projectDetails.summary:
The Earth Science Jukebox challenge tasks teams with transforming complex Earth data into an auditory format. Sonify is our response to NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026’s Earth Science Jukebox challenge: an interactive web platform that transforms Earth Information Center datasets into soundscapes people can explore and hear. It will sonify global sea surface currents, annual temperature shifts, and sea-level changes, translating visual data patterns into harmonized audio through color mapping and sonification algorithms.
This approach bridges the gap between raw statistics and human emotion. By listening to the shifting climate, users experience the urgency of environmental changes directly. This methodology fulfills the challenge requirements by establishing a novel, accessible pathway for the public to engage with NASA data. It makes climate science inclusive and emotionally resonant.
projectDetails.details:
Sonify is an interactive web platform that turns NASA Earth science data into sound, so people can explore climate change by listening as well as viewing. It currently offers two experiences, A Warming Planet (annual global surface-temperature anomalies from NASA GISTEMP v4) and A Rising Ocean (global mean sea level from NASA GSFC Version 5.2), paired with visual context from NASA’s Earth Information Center.

Each year of data becomes one musical event. The chart, map and porthole display update to the same year as the sound. Users choose between two modes built from the same data. Science mode is for measurement. Pitch follows a linear scale (MIDI pitch = 62 + 8 × temperature in °C, or 62 + 2 × sea level in cm), a steady hum marks the zero reference, and a tick marks each change from the previous year, so listeners can judge both values and year-to-year differences by ear. Song mode is for engagement. Values map onto a 13-note pentatonic scale, loudness and brightness rise with the data, and the harmony moves through four chord stages as values increase. Users can play, pause, resume, seek, and change speed and volume.

Python processes the data (complete years only, with missing values never treated as zero). Tone.js and the Web Audio API generate the sound in real time in the browser. The audio clock is the single source of truth for playback, so the visuals stay aligned even when the user pauses or skips.

Benefits

Sonify adds a non-visual way to explore climate data for blind and low-vision users, who are often shut out by charts, maps and color. It also gives students, educators and the public an engaging way into NASA climate information. Because it is interactive, users can seek, replay and change speed, which fixed sonification videos do not allow. Every value is also available as text.

Intended impact

We want to close the access and interpretation gap in climate communication. Our slogan is “From Visuals to Vocals, we make people feel, so they can move.” Song mode helps people feel a trend, and Science mode lets them check the evidence. Sonify complements NASA’s visualizations rather than replacing them. We do not claim proven learning gains or guaranteed climate action, and we plan to test usability and comprehension.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Python (data pipeline), JavaScript, Tone.js, the Web Audio API, Chrome and its developer tools, an automated test suite (18 tests run against the real datasets), GitHub, Vercel (hosting) and Canva (presentation and design). Claude and ChatGPT were used as AI assistants, with outputs reviewed by the team. Hardware was development laptops with headphones or speakers. Accessibility testing uses keyboard-only navigation and a screen reader such as NVDA or VoiceOver.

How it is creative

Sonify treats data as music instead of as a chart. Each year is a note, warmer years sound higher, and the harmony grows fuller and more restless as the planet changes. Sounds are matched to the topic: a cello-like melody and a heartbeat for warming, and glass bells, waves, a deep gliding voice and bubbles for rising seas. The two-mode design is also a creative choice. It separates faithful numerical mapping from musical expression instead of forcing one sound to do both jobs.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: our temperature series differs from NASA’s official average by no more than 0.018 °C since 1960. Audio output was measured in Chrome (the 1909 note measured 237 Hz against an expected value of about 235 Hz).
  • Honest mapping: higher values never produce lower notes, and missing data is never shown as zero.
  • Seasonal noise: using one note per year keeps long-term change audible.
  • Synchronization: sound and visuals follow one audio clock.
  • Accessibility: keyboard and screen-reader support, text alternatives, and audio that never starts unexpectedly.
  • Transparency: an explanation panel states the source, units, reference period, mapping and limitations.

projectDetails.name: SPACE ECHOES
projectDetails.summary:
1. The Problem
Since space exploration began, NASA has sent numerous machines to the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space. Some have completed their missions, others remain active, while some are inactive or lost. Although information about these machines exists, their stories and achievements are not always presented in an engaging, accessible way for younger generations.

2. Our Solution
SPACE ECHOES is an interactive educational mobile application that brings NASA's hardware stories to life. Users can explore the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space, discover associated machines, and follow their journeys, achievements, and statuses. It features visual storytelling, mission status tracking, 3-question quizzes, and FLASH AI, a chatbot for space-related questions.

3. Impact
SPACE ECHOES aims to inspire scientific curiosity and make space science accessible to the next generation. By combining trusted NASA information with interactive learning and AI assistance, it encourages young learners to explore space technology and appreciate its scientific and historical contributions.
4. Challenge Alignment
SPACE ECHOES addresses the challenge by telling the stories of NASA hardware left across the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space since the 1960s. It transforms mission information into engaging educational experiences, helping users understand why these machines were sent, what they achieved, and what happened to them.
The end of a mission doesn't mean the end of its impact.
projectDetails.details:
1. How It Works

SPACE ECHOES is an interactive educational application that allows users to explore NASA's space exploration hardware across three destinations: the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space.

Users select a destination, discover the machines associated with it, and learn about each machine's story, mission, achievements, and current status. Each machine includes visual content explaining its journey, followed by a 3-question quiz to test users' understanding. The application also features FLASH AI, an AI-powered chatbot that helps users ask questions and discover more about space missions.

Explore three destinations: Moon, Mars, and Deep Space.

2. Benefits

The application makes complex scientific information easier to understand through visual storytelling videos accompanying each machine. These videos narrate its story from launch until it reaches its final location in space. Combined with interactive learning, this approach makes discovering space technology more engaging and enjoyable for young learners.

3. Intended Impact

SPACE ECHOES

It aims to inspire the next generation and increase their interest in space science and exploration. It also helps preserve the scientific legacy of NASA's hardware by making its stories and achievements accessible to young learners.

Because understanding the past helps us discover the future.

4. Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using the following technologies:

  • Mobile Application: Flutter and Dart.
  • Backend: Node.js and Express.js.
  • Database: MongoDB and Mongoose.
  • AI Chatbot: Python and FastAPI.
  • Information Retrieval: BM25.
  • AI Support Libraries: Pydantic and Uvicorn.
  • Mobile Libraries: Dio, Flutter SVG, ScreenUtil, and Google Fonts.
  • Authentication: JWT and bcryptjs.
  • API Testing: Postman.

Mission-related information and educational content were researched using official NASA sources to ensure accuracy and reliability.

5. Creativity and Innovation

Our creative approach transforms NASA's historical space mission data into an interactive space exploration experience. Instead of simply reading about machines, users discover their stories through space destinations, visual storytelling, mission status indicators, and quizzes that reinforce learning. FLASH AI further enhances the experience by helping users access additional information and explore their questions.

6. Factors Considered

Our team considered the target audience (ages 15–18), ease of use, accessibility, scientific accuracy, engaging visual design, and educational value. Our goal was to create an experience that makes space exploration easy to understand, enjoyable, and memorable.
