projectDetails.summary: Lunar Relics 3D is a bilingual Arabic–English interactive archive of 16 NASA mission relics across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. It turns dispersed mission records into first-person spacecraft stories, navigable 3D scenes, timelines, hardware hotspots, recorded narration, quick quizzes, badges, and a four-mode Explorer Challenge. Eleven missions use NASA-published 3D meshes; the other five use SI-generated models built to NASA’s published specifications and clearly labeled “not from NASA”, with source links kept visible. The site is responsive, shareable by mission link, and designed for students, families, and casual space learners. It addresses the challenge by making discarded hardware understandable as evidence: what it was built to do, where it went, what it measured, and what remains after the mission ends.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Lunar Relics 3D is a browser-based, bilingual learning experience about equipment that remained after missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. The archive contains 16 structured records. Each record connects a relic to its mission dates, destination, status, source links, first-person English and Arabic story, timeline, hardware explanations, questions, quiz, badge, and recorded narration. The voice is a storytelling device: the spacecraft speaks in first person, while the interface makes clear which facts and sources support the story.

Visitors begin at a 3D globe-style map with mission pins and can filter the archive by world or 3D availability. Selecting a mission opens a chaptered story beside its 3D scene. Hardware hotspots identify parts and draw the learner toward an explanation of what each part did. The mission timeline then connects hardware to journey and scientific purpose. A quick quiz awards one locally saved badge per mission. The Explorer Challenge adds four playable modes: evidence quiz, mission timeline ordering, launch-era ordering, and “name the machine” model identification.

Guided, accessible exploration

Audio is optional. Every mission has English and Arabic recorded narration for the main story, an introduction, and the hardware points represented in the narration manifest. “Full journey” starts with the introduction, moves through the story and hardware chapters, follows the page while the voice plays, reaches the timeline, and ends at the quiz. Learners can stop, scroll manually, choose a language, or use the text-only path. Mission links encode the mission, world, and language, so a learner can bookmark or share a specific story.

Accuracy and provenance

The project is intentionally honest about representation. Eleven missions use unmodified NASA-published GLB meshes from NASA 3D Resources and are labeled as NASA models. The five missions that have no public NASA mesh (Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Apollo 12 ALSEP, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Phoenix) use 3D models generated with Super Intelligence from written descriptions of NASA’s published specifications and photographs; every one of them carries the on-screen label “SI-generated model built to published specs · not from NASA”, and the repository’s asset-source file lists them separately. The Spirit entry uses the NASA Opportunity mesh as a representative model of the identical rover design; Pioneer 10 is used as the available model for a record that discusses Pioneer 10 and 11. These limitations are shown rather than hidden. The Moon and Mars globe textures are stored locally, and the Mars height treatment is explicitly visual rather than a scientific elevation model.

Technology and intended impact

The front end uses React 18 and Vite. Three.js, @react-three/fiber, and drei provide the 3D scenes; Tailwind/PostCSS support styling; lucide-react supplies interface icons; canvas-confetti supplies reduced-motion-aware feedback. The Web Audio API handles the optional soundscape and narration routing. GitHub hosts the public source and Vercel hosts the live site. FFmpeg supports audio/video preparation, while Python and Playwright were used for testing and screenshot capture. The repository includes a production build and Node tests for selected experience and asset-integrity behaviors, without claiming exhaustive device certification.

Creatively, the project treats discarded equipment as a collection of voices and evidence rather than a static list of names. It is built for school-age learners, families, teachers, and casual space enthusiasts, especially users who prefer Arabic or need a low-friction phone experience. The team considered RTL layout, bilingual labels and subtitles, keyboard and skip-to-content access, reduced-motion behavior, responsive breakpoints, lazy model loading, capped device pixel ratio, local textures, and a local JSON fallback when an optional API is unavailable. The intended impact is a durable, source-linked path from “what was left behind?” to “what did this machine enable us to learn?”

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project ASTRA EXPLORER
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA EXPLORER is an interactive planetary exploration platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, addressing the challenge “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.”

The project aims to identify Earth locations that share geological, topographical, and environmental characteristics with selected regions on the Moon and Mars. It combines planetary datasets, terrain analysis, and climate information to explore similarities and differences between extraterrestrial environments and potential terrestrial analogs.

ASTRA EXPLORER features interactive 3D exploration of Earth, the Moon, and Mars, allowing users to investigate selected planetary regions and their corresponding Earth analog locations. It integrates scientific data from NASA sources, including LOLA lunar elevation data, MOLA Martian elevation data, and NASA POWER climate datasets.

Built using Python, FastAPI, Next.js, TypeScript, and CesiumJS, the platform processes scientific data and presents it through an accessible interactive interface. Planned terrain comparisons include elevation, slope, surface roughness, and data uncertainty.

By connecting planetary science with real-world locations on Earth, ASTRA EXPLORER helps users understand the challenges of future lunar and Martian exploration. Its comparisons are exploratory and highlight environmental similarities and differences rather than claiming perfect equivalents.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA EXPLORER — Bridging Worlds Through Planetary Analog Research

Project Overview

ASTRA EXPLORER is an interactive planetary exploration and comparative research platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It addresses a fundamental challenge in future space exploration: identifying and evaluating terrestrial environments that exhibit meaningful geological, topographical, and environmental similarities to selected regions on the Moon and Mars.

As humanity prepares for sustained lunar exploration and future crewed missions to Mars, understanding extraterrestrial surface conditions becomes increasingly important. Earth provides accessible natural environments that can serve as scientific analogs for studying terrain, environmental extremes, geological processes, and operational challenges. However, identifying meaningful analogs requires more than visual resemblance. It requires measurable data, spatial analysis, and an understanding of the limitations of cross-planetary comparisons.

ASTRA EXPLORER aims to bring these elements together in one interactive, data-driven environment.

How It Works

The platform connects three planetary environments through an integrated geospatial exploration interface: Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Users can explore planetary surfaces, select reference regions, and investigate their corresponding terrestrial analog locations. The system combines scientific datasets, geospatial processing, and interactive visualization to transform complex planetary information into an accessible research experience.

Its scientific workflow is based on three complementary data domains:

1. Lunar Terrain Analysis

ASTRA EXPLORER integrates Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) datasets from NASA's Planetary Geosciences Data Archive. These include high-resolution south-polar elevation models, slope products, and uncertainty information.

The platform uses these products to investigate lunar surface elevation and terrain characteristics around scientifically relevant regions, including Haworth, de Gerlache Rim, and Malapert Massif. The inclusion of uncertainty data is particularly important because it helps distinguish measured information from limitations in the underlying terrain models.

2. Martian Topographical Exploration

For Mars, the platform processes Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) Mission Experiment Gridded Data Record (MEGDR) elevation data. Its global elevation raster allows the system to retrieve topographical measurements at selected Martian coordinates.

Reference regions include Gale Crater, Jezero Crater, and Olympus Mons, providing different geographical and geological contexts for planetary exploration.

3. Terrestrial Environmental Analysis

For Earth, ASTRA EXPLORER integrates NASA POWER meteorological datasets through its API, currently using daily near-surface air temperature (T2M).

Selected terrestrial locations can be investigated through their geographic coordinates and historical temperature records. This creates a foundation for comparing environmental characteristics between Earth analog candidates and extraterrestrial reference environments, while recognizing that terrestrial atmospheric measurements cannot directly represent lunar or Martian surface conditions.

Scientific Methodology and Comparative Analysis

A central principle of ASTRA EXPLORER is that planetary analog identification should be based on measurable characteristics rather than visual similarity alone.

The platform's comparative research direction includes:

  • Elevation distribution and regional topography.
  • Surface slope and terrain variability.
  • Terrain roughness and local relief.
  • Temperature patterns and environmental extremes.
  • Spatial coverage, dataset resolution, and measurement uncertainty.

These parameters must be evaluated using compatible spatial scales and appropriate scientific assumptions. For example, absolute elevations across Earth, the Moon, and Mars cannot be compared directly without considering their different reference datums and vertical coordinate systems.

Likewise, comparing a high-resolution lunar DEM with a much coarser Martian elevation product requires resolution-aware processing. The platform therefore treats dataset quality, spatial coverage, coordinate transformations, and uncertainty as essential parts of the research process.

The long-term objective is to develop a transparent, data-driven analog comparison framework that evaluates multiple characteristics instead of relying on a single measurement or arbitrary similarity score.

Technology and Engineering Architecture

ASTRA EXPLORER is developed using a modern full-stack architecture combining web engineering, scientific computing, and geospatial visualization.

Frontend and Visualization

  • Next.js and React for the application architecture and user interface.
  • TypeScript for structured, maintainable application logic.
  • CesiumJS for interactive three-dimensional planetary and geospatial exploration.
  • NASA planetary imagery and tile services for visual surface representation.

Backend and Scientific Computing

  • Python for scientific data processing.
  • FastAPI for RESTful API development and communication between the frontend and scientific services.
  • Rasterio for reading and processing geospatial raster datasets.
  • NumPy and SciPy for numerical analysis and scientific computation.
  • PyProj for coordinate transformations and geospatial reference-system operations.
  • HTTPX for asynchronous communication with external scientific APIs.

Scientific Data Infrastructure

  • NASA LOLA elevation, slope, and uncertainty products.
  • NASA MOLA global Martian elevation data.
  • NASA POWER daily meteorological data.
  • NASA Trek planetary imagery services.

The architecture separates the interactive application from scientific data processing, allowing the platform to expand as additional datasets and analytical capabilities are integrated.

Innovation and Creativity

The primary innovation of ASTRA EXPLORER is its effort to connect planetary exploration with terrestrial analog research through a unified, interactive geospatial experience.

Instead of treating Earth, the Moon, and Mars as isolated visualization subjects, the project approaches them as interconnected environments that can be investigated through common scientific questions.

Its distinguishing characteristics include:

  • Cross-planetary exploration: Bringing three planetary environments into one interactive platform.
  • Data-driven investigation: Using real NASA scientific datasets rather than relying exclusively on illustrative representations.
  • Multi-parameter comparison: Exploring terrain and environmental characteristics together.
  • Scientific transparency: Considering uncertainty, spatial coverage, resolution, and coordinate-system differences.
  • Accessibility: Making planetary data easier to explore and understand through an interactive visual interface.

This approach creates an opportunity to connect planetary science, Earth science, geospatial engineering, and computer science within one educational and research-oriented platform.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA EXPLORER aims to contribute to several areas:

Planetary Science and Research: It provides an accessible environment for exploring planetary datasets and investigating potential terrestrial analogs for lunar and Martian regions.

Future Space Exploration: By helping users understand similarities and differences between terrestrial and extraterrestrial terrain, the platform can support preliminary research into environments relevant to future exploration planning. It is not intended to certify landing-site safety or establish operational suitability.

STEM Education: The platform transforms complex scientific concepts such as laser altimetry, digital elevation models, geospatial coordinate systems, raster analysis, and environmental data into an interactive learning experience.

Open Scientific Data Utilization: It demonstrates how publicly available NASA datasets and APIs can be integrated into practical software applications, encouraging broader engagement with open scientific resources.

Future Development: The architecture provides a foundation for incorporating additional geological datasets, higher-resolution terrain products, more environmental parameters, advanced spatial statistics, and scientifically validated analog-ranking methodologies.

Factors Considered During Development

Scientific reliability and responsible interpretation have guided the project's development.

The team considered:

  • Authenticity and traceability of scientific datasets.
  • Geographic coverage of selected planetary regions.
  • Differences between planetary coordinate systems and reference datums.
  • Variations in spatial resolution between datasets.
  • Elevation and slope measurement uncertainty.
  • The distinction between visual similarity and scientifically meaningful analogy.
  • API reliability, data-processing performance, and application scalability.
  • Accessibility and clarity of scientific information for users with different levels of technical knowledge.

These considerations help ensure that the platform presents scientific information responsibly rather than overstating the conclusions that can be drawn from available data.

Vision

ASTRA EXPLORER aims to become more than a planetary visualization application. Its long-term vision is to evolve into an extensible planetary analog research environment where users can explore extraterrestrial landscapes, investigate terrestrial environments, compare scientific measurements, and understand the challenges of exploring worlds beyond Earth.

By combining NASA's open scientific resources with modern software engineering and geospatial analysis, ASTRA EXPLORER seeks to make the relationship between our planet and other worlds more understandable, measurable, and accessible.

Explore Earth. Investigate the Moon. Discover Mars. Connect worlds through science.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

node.excerpt: We are Team SiriusTa, tackling the Crop Rotation Challenge. Inspired by ancient Egyptian astronomical farming heritage, SiriusTa bridges NASA Earth observations (SMAP, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, GPM) with local soil data and farmer priorities.Our mission...

projectDetails.name: Project SiriusTa
projectDetails.summary: Farmers are making consequential decisions in a climate that is moving outside historical norms, usually without plot-level information on soil water, crop stress, or approaching hazards. SiriusTa gives every registered plot a Land ID, fuses NASA Earth observations with climate, soil, and market data, and delivers simple green/yellow/red guidance through a smartphone app Its distinguishing idea is a cross-regional network: plots with similar environmental profiles are linked, so what is learned about stress and risk in one region can inform calibrated warnings in another.
projectDetails.details:
What we built SiriusTa is an agro-satellite intelligence web application that takes any field coordinate on Earth and returns a visual field report together with a full dual-coordinate agronomic examination.
A user enters a latitude/longitude (by picking a city, using GPS, or typing exact coordinates) and names the previous harvested crop.
The engine then resolves the soil, terrain and climate of that point, ingests 45 days of live satellite telemetry, conditions the time series, and produces a three-tier decision report covering immediate field actions, two multi-season crop-rotation plans, and a global teleconnection-adjusted scoring of those plans. It finally matches the target field to the nearest peer agro-zone and runs the same pipeline on that twin, producing a normalized agronomic-similarity score and a delta/parity report.
Problem it solves Smallholder and commercial farmers rarely have access to an integrated view of their field that combines soil chemistry, recent weather, vegetation vigour and large-scale climate teleconnections in one place. Decisions about irrigation, fertilisation, pest pressure and crop rotation are made on partial information. SiriusTa addresses this by fusing multiple public satellite and soil data sources into a single, actionable per-field recommendation
SiriusTa directly uses three NASA datasets — NASA POWER climatology, NASA POWER daily agro-meteorological telemetry, and NASA MODIS NDVI vegetation imagery — as the scientific backbone of every recommendation. NASA POWER defines the Agro-Ecological Zone (AEZ) of the field, the 45-day dynamic window drives a coupled soil-water and nitrogen mass-balance, and MODIS NDVI anchors the vegetation-vigour layer. These NASA inputs feed a deterministic decision engine that turns raw Earth-observation data into concrete, field-level adaptation advice: how much to irrigate, whether to plant a cover crop, how to manage nutrition and insecticide, and which crop sequence to follow over the next three seasons.

projectDetails.name: DR. NEXUS
projectDetails.summary:
DR. NEXUS is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring project designed to analyze and understand astronauts’ health during long-duration space missions. It combines three innovative features: Mission Black Box, which analyzes historical health data to identify unusual patterns; Future Self, which explores potential health developments using personal baselines and AI-driven trend analysis; and Crew DNA, which investigates shared health patterns among crew members.
At its core, DR. NEXUS uses an AI and Machine Learning engine that processes astronaut health and mission data through personal baseline modeling, anomaly detection, and health trend analysis. It compares new measurements against individual historical patterns, detects unusual deviations, and tracks changes over time. Additionally, it connects health observations with NASA’s five major spaceflight hazards, providing explainable, data-driven insights.
DR. NEXUS addresses critical challenges astronauts face, including radiation exposure, isolation, altered gravity, and the demanding space environment. By transforming complex health data into meaningful insights, the system aims to support mission teams in understanding health changes, exploring potential risks, and making more informed decisions.
Ultimately, DR. NEXUS aims to contribute to safer, smarter, and more proactive astronaut healthcare, supporting crew well-being throughout future long-duration space missions.
projectDetails.details:
# DR. NEXUS — The Future of Astronaut Health
### Complete Project Explanation | NASA Space Apps Challenge

I am presenting this document to explain our project, DR. NEXUS – The Future of Astronaut Health, including the problem we are trying to solve, our approach, the features we developed, and the Artificial Intelligence solutions behind the platform.

Our goal is to make the project understandable from both a scientific and technical perspective, showing not only what the application does but also how we built it, how its different components work, and how our AI solutions contribute to astronaut health monitoring.

1. Project Overview and Vision

DR. NEXUS is an intelligent astronaut health monitoring and decision-support system designed to help protect astronauts during long-duration space missions. We focused on the health challenges associated with space radiation, microgravity, isolation, distance from Earth, and extreme environmental conditions.

Our idea is to use Artificial Intelligence to analyze astronaut health data, identify unusual patterns, monitor health changes over time, and provide predictive insights that can support better health-related decisions.

We believe that monitoring astronaut health should go beyond simply displaying medical measurements. It should also help us understand how an astronaut's health changes over time, recognize potentially concerning patterns, and explore possible future health developments.

Our vision is to combine NASA open-source datasets, scientific research, AI technologies, interactive 3D visualization, and modern web technologies into one integrated platform.

2. The Problem We Address

Monitoring astronauts during long-duration space missions is a major challenge. Unlike people on Earth, astronauts operate in an environment where multiple factors can affect their physical health.

Space radiation can increase biological risks, microgravity can affect muscles, bones, and other body systems, while isolation and confinement can influence psychological and physiological well-being. These challenges may interact and produce changes that need continuous observation.

Another important challenge is the distance between astronauts and Earth. During future missions to the Moon and Mars, immediate access to medical specialists and traditional healthcare facilities will be limited.

We believe that analyzing health measurements individually is not always enough. Understanding personal baselines, historical observations, and changes over time can provide more meaningful information.

This is why we developed DR. NEXUS: to bring health monitoring, AI-powered analysis, historical tracking, and predictive insights together in one system.

3. Main Platform Features

### Main Dashboard

The dashboard provides an overview of the astronaut monitoring system. It brings important health information, monitoring statistics, observations, and analytical findings together in one place.

Our objective is to make it easier for users to understand the overall monitoring status and identify important information without navigating through multiple sections.

### Crew Monitoring

We designed the crew monitoring section to organize astronauts individually. Each crew member has an associated profile containing their relevant health information and observations.

This allows us to monitor astronauts separately and understand their individual health conditions rather than treating all crew members as having identical characteristics.

### Astronaut Health Profiles

Each astronaut's profile acts as an organized record of their health information and historical observations.

We consider individual health information important because changes should be interpreted in relation to the astronaut's own history and baseline whenever sufficient data is available.

### Mission Black Box
One of our main concepts is Mission Black Box. We designed it to work with historical astronaut health data, analyze observations, identify unusual changes, and discover patterns that might not be immediately noticeable when looking at individual measurements.

The idea is to transform historical health records into meaningful analytical information that helps users understand what happened, recognize potential warning signs, and explore relationships between different health indicators.

### Future Self

Another important component is Future Self. Our idea is to move beyond understanding historical and current health information toward exploring possible future health developments.

It uses personal health baselines and AI-driven trend analysis to examine how health indicators may change over time.

The purpose is to provide predictive insights that can support awareness and planning, not to replace medical diagnosis or guarantee future health outcomes.

4. Artificial Intelligence Solutions

AI is one of the main elements of DR. NEXUS. We use it to turn health data into information that is easier to understand and analyze.

Our approach focuses on data preparation, analyzing health indicators, identifying patterns, monitoring changes, and exploring potential future trends.

We consider the complete AI workflow important, starting from the original datasets, moving through preprocessing and feature preparation, and ending with analytical outputs that can be presented through the platform.

We also distinguish between historical data analysis, anomaly identification, and predictive trend analysis because each serves a different purpose.

Our AI solutions are intended to support astronaut health monitoring and decision-making rather than independently make medical decisions.

5. Data Sources and Scientific Foundation

We aim to use NASA open-source datasets and relevant scientific research as the foundation of our analysis.

The data is important because AI models depend on the quality and relevance of the information used to develop and evaluate them.

We consider data preprocessing, missing values, data consistency, feature selection, and the scientific meaning of health variables essential parts of the project.

We also distinguish between actual spaceflight observations, ground-based experimental data, and synthetic or simulated data to avoid presenting different data types as equivalent.

6. How the System Works

DR. NEXUS combines several components into one connected platform.

The general workflow starts with collecting and organizing health information. The data is then prepared for analysis, processed by the relevant AI components, and transformed into findings, patterns, and predictive insights.

These outputs are connected to the astronaut's profile and presented through the web application.

Users can then explore health information, review historical observations, understand analytical findings, and examine potential trends through the platform.

Our goal is to make the entire process understandable and accessible, even for users who do not have a background in Artificial Intelligence or data science.

7. Interactive 3D Visualization

We also considered visualization an important part of the user experience.

Instead of relying only on tables and numerical measurements, we aim to use interactive 3D visualization to make health-related information more intuitive and easier to explore.

This adds another way to interact with the platform and supports our vision of combining scientific data analysis with modern visualization technologies.

## 8. Technologies and System Architecture

We designed DR. NEXUS around modern web technologies and AI tools.

The platform brings together frontend and backend development, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, data processing, database management, and visualization.
Each component has a specific role: the frontend provides the user interface, the backend handles application logic and communication, the AI components process and analyze health data, and the database organizes the information required by the system.

We also considered scalability, system performance, accessibility, and the possibility of using free or accessible hosting solutions.

## 9. What Makes DR. NEXUS Different

What makes our project interesting is the combination of several ideas in one astronaut health monitoring platform.

We are not focusing only on displaying health measurements. We want to understand historical changes, identify unusual patterns, explore future trends, and present the results in a clear and interactive way.

The combination of Mission Black Box and Future Self represents two complementary perspectives: understanding what has happened and exploring what might happen next.

By bringing these ideas together with individual astronaut profiles, AI-powered analysis, and interactive visualization, we aim to create a more comprehensive approach to astronaut health monitoring.

10. Challenges and Future Development

During the development of this project, we considered several challenges, especially the availability of relevant astronaut health datasets, data quality, the complexity of space-related health conditions, and the reliability of AI-generated insights.

We also recognize that developing a system for real space missions requires extensive scientific validation, additional real-world data, and careful evaluation.

In the future, we aim to expand our datasets, improve our AI models, integrate real-time health monitoring, support wearable medical sensors, develop more personalized predictive models, and enhance the decision-support capabilities of the platform.

We see these improvements as important steps toward making DR. NEXUS more useful in realistic long-duration space mission scenarios.

11. Our Final Vision

We developed DR. NEXUS around one important idea: protecting astronaut health requires more than observing individual measurements. It requires understanding personal health patterns, monitoring changes, and using available data to explore potential risks before they become more serious.

Through Artificial Intelligence, data analysis, historical monitoring, predictive insights, and interactive visualization, we aim to contribute to a safer future for human space exploration.

Our vision is to make space exploration safer by helping humans understand, predict, and protect astronaut health.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: Nebula
projectDetails.summary: The Nebula Mission Trainer is an interactive, web-based space base simulator built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Designed specifically for kids and students, it bridges the gap between oversimplified clickers and overly complex simulations by letting young players step in as Mission Commanders.
projectDetails.details:
Here are clear, submission-ready answers to each of those questions for **Nebula** by team **Sobya Manga**:

### 1. What does it do and how does it work?

**Nebula** is a browser-based 3D educational Mars outpost survival game built for the NASA Space Apps *Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer* challenge. Players step into the role of an astronaut maintaining a Martian habitat over a seven-sol mission.

* **Core Gameplay Loop:** Players start with eight interactive tutorials before entering a seven-sol survival challenge. During the mission, they explore the station and complete hands-on maintenance tasks—such as holding an action button to clean dust off solar panels after sandstorms, harvesting and replanting crops, monitoring oxygen reserves, and taking shelter indoors when radiation levels spike.

* **How the Simulation Works:** Behind the scenes, a deterministic TypeScript simulation updates resource balances in bounded steps. It models a day/night solar cycle (where solar arrays charge a 24 kWh battery during daylight and the base relies on stored battery power at night), prioritizes life-support loads (essential base power, heating, and shelter before oxygen production and crop growth), and tracks radiation exposure anchored to NASA Curiosity rover data.

* **Cross-Platform Access:** The game runs directly in a web browser without requiring logins, downloads, or a backend server, supporting both PC (mouse and keyboard) and mobile devices (touch interface).

### 2. What benefits does it have?

* **Active Learning Through Consequences:** Instead of reading static facts about Mars, learners directly experience resource trade-offs—seeing how dusty panels reduce battery charging, why night requires stored energy, and how staying outside during a solar particle event increases radiation exposure.

* **Zero-Barrier Accessibility:** Because it is hosted as a lightweight web app on GitHub Pages with both desktop and mobile controls, students, parents, and teachers can launch it immediately on school computers, laptops, or phones.

* **Transparent, Honest Science:** The interface and documentation clearly distinguish real NASA environmental measurements (such as Martian gravity at $3.71\text{ m/s}^2$, baseline radiation, and solar storm context) from simplified gameplay assumptions (such as accelerated crop growth and compressed day/night cycles).

### 3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Nebula is designed primarily for **children aged 7–12** (as well as older students, families, and adults) to build early intuition in STEM, systems thinking, and space exploration. By framing Martian survival around everyday cause-and-effect problems—energy conservation, equipment maintenance, food sustainability, and radiation safety—the project aims to inspire curiosity about how astronauts live and work on other planets while reinforcing practical problem-solving skills that also apply to resource management on Earth.

### 4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

* **Languages & Core Web Engine:** TypeScript (7.0.2), HTML, and CSS, using **Three.js** (0.187.0) for 3D WebGL rendering and **Rapier** (0.21.0) WebAssembly physics for character movement, gravity, and collision detection.

* **Build, Testing & Hosting:** Vite (8.3.8) and Node.js for bundling, `lil-gui` for real-time balance tuning, Vitest (41 unit/integration tests) and Playwright/Chromium (15 browser tests) for automated verification, and GitHub Actions + GitHub Pages for static hosting.

* **3D Assets & Media:** Custom low-poly binary glTF (`.glb`) models for the station, solar panels, lander, and astronaut, alongside procedural Web Audio synthesis for sound effects and ambience.

* **NASA Data & AI/SI Tools:** NASA Curiosity RAD radiation studies, NASA/JPL May 2024 solar storm reporting, archived NASA DONKI solar energetic particle records, NASA Mars terrain elevation API data, and NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) Mars imagery. We also used **Google Gemini**, **OpenAI ChatGPT**, and **Manus AI** to assist with code implementation, audio/media generation, and technical documentation, plus Kokoro-82M for voice-over prototypes.

### 5. How is your project creative?

* **Systems-Driven Mini-Games Instead of Passive Quizzes:** Rather than testing players with multiple-choice questions, Nebula turns real space-engineering constraints into tactile 3D interactions—such as physically walking outside to scrub dust off tracking solar panels before sunset or rushing into the shielded habitat when a solar storm alert triggers.

* **Dynamic Cutaway 3D Base:** The three-room Martian station automatically fades exterior walls as the astronaut moves indoors, giving players a clear isometric-style view of interior life-support equipment, crop beds, and shelter zones without breaking collision physics.

* **Guided Storytelling & Action-Gated Tutorials:** The game pairs an approachable, low-poly visual style and narrative framing with eight bite-sized tutorials that pause survival timers during dialogue so younger players can master one system at a time before taking on the full seven-sol challenge.

### 6. What factors did your team consider?

* **Age-Appropriate Cognitive Load:** For 7–12-year-old players, managing five survival systems simultaneously can be overwhelming. We designed action-gated tutorials with safety floors, clear visual HUD meters, and a fictional, recoverable "stress" meter alongside permanent radiation dose tracking so kids receive immediate, understandable feedback.

* **Scientific Integrity vs. Playability:** Real Martian missions span years, whereas a classroom or home session lasts around 20 minutes. We carefully balanced compressed sol lengths and accelerated crop cycles while explicitly labeling what comes from NASA data versus what is simplified for gameplay.

* **Cross-Device Performance & Reliability:** We separated fixed-step physics ($1/60\text{ s}$) from rendering frame rates, capped pixel ratios, removed backend server dependencies, and built an automated suite of 56 unit and browser tests so the prototype runs reliably across different PCs and mobile browsers.

node.title: SoilMate
node.excerpt: Smarter decisions. Healthier soils. More resilient farms.

projectDetails.name: SoilMate
projectDetails.summary:
SoilMate is a farmer-centred decision-support website that turns NASA Earth observation data into clear, comparable crop-rotation plans. Farmers face rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, water shortages and declining soil health, yet most lack accessible tools to decide what to plant next. FAO’s 2026 reports estimate that 1.56 billion hectares of land are already degraded worldwide, including more than 1 billion hectares of cropland and pastureland.

SoilMate answers the Field Shift challenge by combining NASA POWER climate data, MODIS vegetation indices and satellite-derived soil moisture with soil, crop and market information and the farmer’s own priorities. An explainable, rule-based scoring engine rates each rotation on five metrics (Water, Soil Health, Erosion & Ground Protection, Practicality and Economy) and compares three plans side by side: the farmer’s own rotation, one that protects soil health and one that saves water. Every plan states why it was suggested, the evidence behind it, its benefits, its information gaps and its risks. An interactive game, Learn & Play, helps users understand what the results mean.

We developed and validated SoilMate on a pilot area of three centres in Kafr El-Sheikh, Egypt (Desouk, Sidi Salem and Baltim). Its purpose is healthier soil, more efficient water use and a more secure food supply, with the final decision always remaining with the farmer and local agricultural experts.
projectDetails.details:
SoilMate is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make more informed crop-rotation decisions. It transforms NASA Earth observation data into practical, understandable insights and compares alternative crop-rotation strategies based on the farmer's land conditions and priorities.

How it works:

The farmer begins by selecting an area and exploring its environmental conditions through SoilMate's Explore Land feature, which presents insights such as soil moisture, temperature, vegetation health (NDVI), heat stress, erosion risk, and soil properties.

The farmer can then describe their farm and select their priorities. In Rotation Lab, they enter their planned crop rotation, which is evaluated by an explainable, rule-based scoring engine.

SoilMate evaluates each rotation across five metrics: Water, Soil Health, Erosion & Ground Protection, Practicality, and Economy. Compare Plans presents three alternatives side by side: the farmer's own rotation, a soil-health-focused plan, and a water-saving plan. Each plan includes its reasoning, supporting evidence, benefits, information gaps, and potential risks. Currently, Soil Health and Water Saving are the supported priorities for scenario ranking.

The platform also includes Learn & Play, an interactive educational game that explains agricultural concepts in a simple and engaging way, helping farmers understand the results rather than simply receive recommendations.

Data and technology:

SoilMate combines approximately ten years of NASA POWER daily climate data (2016–2025), MODIS vegetation indices obtained through NASA AppEEARS, and satellite-derived soil moisture with SoilGrids v2.0 soil properties, FAO EcoCrop crop characteristics, FAO salt-tolerance thresholds, and CAPMAS agricultural net-return statistics.

The data pipeline uses Python, pandas, NumPy, xarray, and Rasterio for data cleaning, preprocessing, spatial alignment, water-balance calculations, and scoring. Matplotlib and Plotly support data visualization and validation.

The web platform is built with Next.js for the frontend, Express on Node.js for the backend, and MongoDB Atlas for the database.

Creativity and innovation:

Unlike approaches that focus mainly on maximizing profit, SoilMate considers water demand, soil health, ground protection, practical crop timing, and economic returns together. Its main innovation is an explainable, multi-criteria approach that allows farmers to compare different strategies and understand the trade-offs behind each one. The farmer's existing rotation is always included, and no alternative is hidden. Each recommendation is supported by visible evidence and disclosed limitations.

Rather than using an opaque machine-learning prediction, SoilMate uses transparent, rule-based calculations so that its assessments can be explained and reviewed by farmers and local agricultural experts.

Benefits and intended impact:

SoilMate aims to make environmental and agricultural data more accessible and useful at the farm level. It helps farmers understand their land, explore water-saving and soil-health-oriented alternatives, recognize potential risks before planting, and make more informed decisions. By combining scientific evidence, explainable comparisons, and interactive learning, SoilMate aims to support more resilient farming and more sustainable use of agricultural resources.

The current prototype has been developed and tested across three pilot centres in Kafr El-Sheikh, Egypt: Desouk, Sidi Salem, and Baltim. Its results are model-based estimates that require local validation. SoilMate is designed to support, not replace, farmers' judgment and local agricultural expertise.

projectDetails.name: Project Something is there.
projectDetails.summary:
Summary
A lander at the lunar south pole needs two things to survive and work: sunlight for power and a line of
sight to Earth for communication. Near the pole the Sun skims the horizon and long shadows are
everywhere, and Earth can sit just above or below the horizon depending on the site. Choosing a site is
therefore a trade-off.
Lunar Site Advisor is a simple web tool that answers one question for mission planners: which of these
sites is best, and in which weeks of 2028? We scored four sites of real interest to NASA, week by week,
and turned the results into clear tables, scores and a ranking that a non-expert can read in seconds.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
Lunar Site Advisor helps mission planners compare four Artemis III candidate landing regions at the lunar south pole (Malapert Massif, Haworth, Nobile Rim 1, de Gerlache Rim 2). It scores each site on two things: solar power potential and direct Earth communication. The results appear as simple tables, rankings and plain-language explanations.

How it works

  1. We analysed the first 7 days of every month of 2028, the period of NASA’s next planned missions and the length of a typical surface mission (12 windows per site).
  2. For Earth communication, we pulled hourly Earth elevation for each site’s coordinates from NASA JPL Horizons (168 samples per month, 2,016 per site). Earth counts as visible when it is above the horizon.
  3. For solar potential, we used Moon Trek and QuickMap (LRO/LOLA) illumination and terrain layers. [Team: add one line on how the solar score is computed.]
  4. Data was processed and combined into scores with Manus AI. The total score weights solar 60% and communication 40%, and each site is rated Good, Medium or Weak.

What works now (evidence)

  • Complete Earth-visibility results for all four sites and all 12 weeks of 2028. Malapert Massif is best (Earth visible about 80% of the time), then Nobile Rim 1 (78%), Haworth (75%) and de Gerlache Rim 2 (65%).
  • Clear calendar pattern: Earth is in view throughout January–March and September–November, and mostly hidden in May–July. October is fully visible at all four sites.
  • [Team: add the working features of the web interface, e.g. comparison table, month selector, charts.]

Benefits and goal
Planners get a fast, readable first comparison instead of reading several separate datasets. It shows which site and which month give reliable power and contact with Earth, and suggests better options when a site performs poorly. We hope it helps early mission planning and also helps students and the public understand why site choice matters.

Tools used
NASA JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, QuickMap (LRO/LOLA), CSA Moon Exploration portal, Manus AI (data processing and voice-over), Claude (proposal and tool structuring). [Team: add web stack, e.g. HTML/CSS/JavaScript and any 3D library.]

Limitations
Earth elevation is geometric, with no terrain blocking. Earth stays under about 10° above the horizon, so nearby hills could hide it at the exact landing point. Only the first week of each month is analysed. The 60/40 weighting is an adjustable assumption.

Future plans
Add the Shackleton comparison point, more sites and weeks, terrain-based horizon masking, and adjustable weights in the interface.

projectDetails.name: Project Sopdet-X
projectDetails.summary: Welcome to Mars Mission: The Lost Signal! For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we didn’t just build a game, we created a Mars survival adventure powered by real NASA data. Meet three astronauts whose mission takes an unexpected turn when an emergency puts their journey home at risk. Now, they must explore the Red Planet, solve problems, and find a way to bring the crew home. They investigate Martian terrain, study geological formations, and search for resources, guided by NASA data. But this isn’t just a story, it’s you in action. As the player, you step into the astronauts’ mission and take on three challenges that turn space science into play, by completing them, you learn how scientists explore Mars, how NASA data reveals its environment, and how decisions can make future missions possible. This is Mars exploration in a new way, not in charts or reports, but through an adventure where every discovery matters, every decision counts, and the crew’s journey home depends on you.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Mission is an educational adventure game designed to teach kids how real space missions deal with danger and limited supplies, turning real NASA data into an interactive story-driven game. Players take care of three stranded astronauts, meet problems on Mars, and use hands-on mini games to solve them, making space science both fun and easy to understand.

In the game, three astronauts, Hedeya, Samantha and Hazaloom, land at Jezero Crater on Mars. Then something breaks, the radio goes silent, and Earth does not know they are stranded. Each astronaut has someone waiting for them back home, so every choice the player makes is really a choice about getting them home safely. Players guide the crew through three missions, and every mission teaches a different part of life on Mars.

Before the adventure starts, the player picks a lead partner. Each partner has a strength and a cost:

  • Hedeya: Stronger shielding and faster air refills at base, but heavier battery gear.
  • Samantha: Saves 15% rover battery and earns bonus science, but has lighter ray protection.
  • Hazaloom: Drives the rover faster and handles rock bumps better, but uses a little more air when walking.

There is no "best" partner, only different ways to play.

Along the way, players keep an eye on three bars: Suit Air, Battery and Shielding. Every choice helps one bar and costs another, just like real mission planners. After each mission, a summary shows what the player gained, what it cost, and the real science behind the choice.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

mission 1, The Lost Signal (Communication & Dust Storms): After landing, a blast breaks the return ship and the radio. Players check the damaged spacecraft, grab a spare part, drive the rover to the radio tower and repair it, then rush back to the base before a dust storm arrives. Through this, players learn why spare parts matter, how dust storms affect Mars, and why a message from Mars takes minutes to reach Earth.

Mission 2, The Lava Cave (Radar & Radiation): The crew follows the signal of RIMFAX, NASA's radar that can see underground, into Neretva Vallis, an ancient river valley. Players drop sensors, climb down into a lava tube, drill Rock Core Tube #14 and escape before a Marsquake. A short quiz checks what they learned. Through this, players discover how radar finds hidden layers under the ground and why lava tubes protect astronauts from most space rays.

Mission 3, Rocket Home (Power & Spaceflight): Mars dust jams a rover heater, and it wastes almost all of the rover's 400 W of power. Players first learn what a watt is, then fix the problem on the Power Bus Console: Step 1: Turn off the broken heater. Step 2: Use the extra power for one helper tool (Ray & Dust Shield, Rock Scanner or Battery Boost), and see what each one costs. After that, players drive to the rocket, load the sample, launch, drop the rocket stage at the right moment and dock with the ship that takes them back to Earth. Through this, players learn how to share limited power, and how rockets and docking work.

When the player completes all three missions, the whole crew makes it home!

To keep the game fun to replay, three Mars weather days (Sol 142 Clear, Sol 288 Dusty Sky and Sol 419 Solar Storm) change the radiation, dust and power. Losing is never the end, it is a chance to try a different plan.

The game is made for ages 7 to 12 and runs in the browser, with no account or download. Players can pick an easier Junior level or a Senior level with exact NASA numbers, use Word Helpers for hard words, turn on read-aloud audio, and open the NASA Field Guide to unlock fact cards. Every fact card shows its source and whether the data is live or saved offline. The game uses real data from NASA DONKI, OSDR, Curiosity RAD, Perseverance MEDA, the Deep Space Network, Veggie, RIMFAX and Mars Trek.

The game helps kids, students, teachers and the wider community by:

  • Educating players on radiation, air, power and radio delay through play.
  • Showing how planning and trade-offs keep astronauts safe.
  • Bridging the gap between NASA's datasets and real space missions in a fun, engaging way.

To make NASA's open data more accessible, helping young learners get ready for the challenges of exploring Mars while growing their curiosity about space. Despite our attempt to show how space missions work, our game is simplified for learning, so its numbers and crew abilities are not an exact copy of a real Mars mission. The Mission 1 and Mission 2 cutscenes were made with AI video tools and are only story illustrations.

Coding languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.

Frameworks and libraries:

  • React 19 for the menus, crew screens, HUD and mini-game windows.
  • Phaser for the 2D game world: the Mars surface, rover driving, physics and the three missions.
  • Tailwind CSS for styling.
  • Vite to build and run the game.
  • Node.js and Express for a small server that fetches NASA data and falls back to saved data when NASA can’t be reached.
  • Web Audio API for the sound effects, which are generated by code.
  • Lucide icons and Motion for icons and animations.

NASA tools and data: the NASA DONKI API (with a free NASA API key), plus curated data from NASA OSDR, Curiosity RAD, Perseverance MEDA, the Deep Space Network, Veggie and RIMFAX.

node.excerpt: I

projectDetails.name: Space Benders: The Ultimate Space Mission Design Game
projectDetails.summary:
Space Benders is an interactive, browser-based cooperative space mission design game that transforms complex aerospace engineering concepts into an engaging, hands-on learning experience. Designed for 1–4 players, the game challenges participants to collaborate as engineering teams, assemble spacecraft, manage limited resources, and prepare missions to destinations across the Solar System.

Players explore six progressively challenging missions, from Low Earth Orbit to Titan, using a catalogue of 84 spacecraft components. Every engineering decision involves real trade-offs affecting mass, power, fuel, communications, radiation protection, scientific capabilities, and budget. A 12-rule engineering validation system evaluates each spacecraft, explains failures, and encourages players to improve their designs through experimentation.

The game also features real-time multiplayer collaboration and an AI-powered Flight Director that guides players through engineering challenges and provides mission recommendations.

By grounding gameplay in NASA science, real spacecraft technologies, and planetary environments, Space Benders bridges the gap between theoretical space education and practical engineering thinking. It makes space mission design accessible, encourages teamwork and critical thinking, and inspires the next generation of space engineers.
projectDetails.details:
Space Benders is a cooperative, browser-based space mission design game that allows 1–4 players to experience the challenges of real spacecraft engineering. Players work together as specialized engineering teams to design, assemble, and validate spacecraft capable of completing missions across the Solar System.

The game begins with players joining a crew and selecting engineering roles: Power & Thermal, Structure & Computing, Communications, and Science. They then choose from six progressively challenging missions, ranging from Low Earth Orbit and the Moon to Mars, Europa, the Sun, and Titan.

Inside an interactive virtual cleanroom, players physically collect and install components from a catalogue of 84 engineering parts. Each component affects multiple spacecraft parameters, including mass, power consumption, fuel requirements, heat protection, radiation shielding, communications, scientific output, and budget. This creates interconnected engineering trade-offs where improving one system can introduce new constraints in another.

Once the spacecraft is assembled, players run a 12-rule launch validation system that checks whether their design satisfies the mission requirements. Each rule provides pass/fail feedback, actual values, required thresholds, and explanations. Teams can modify their spacecraft, experiment with alternative configurations, and repeat the evaluation until all requirements are satisfied.

The game also integrates Google Gemini as an AI Flight Director, offering interactive engineering guidance, mission evaluations, and recommendations through dedicated tools. Engineering calculations remain deterministic and are handled by the game's validation engine.

From a technical perspective, Space Benders was developed using TypeScript, Phaser 3, Vite, Node.js, Express 5, and Colyseus for real-time multiplayer communication. Custom WebGL and WebGL2 shaders power the interactive Earth background and hyperspace launch sequence. SVG is used for the campaign map, while Google Gemini provides the AI assistance.

The project's creativity lies in combining cooperative gameplay, physical component transportation, realistic engineering constraints, and AI-assisted problem-solving into one educational experience. Unlike conventional educational games that simply present information, Space Benders allows players to learn through experimentation, collaboration, and failure.

During development, our team considered scientific accuracy, engineering trade-offs, accessibility for young learners, multiplayer coordination, gameplay performance, and educational value. Mission environments, planetary conditions, and spacecraft technologies were grounded in NASA science and real mission references.

Our intended impact is to make complex space engineering concepts accessible to students, encourage teamwork and critical thinking, and inspire young learners to explore aerospace engineering and space science through an engaging, interactive experience.

projectDetails.name: Space Doctor
projectDetails.summary:
Space Doctor is an autonomous health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration missions, where contact with Earth may be delayed or unavailable.

It continuously tracks vital signs, psychological state, spacecraft environment, and behavioral patterns, and combines them to detect early warning signs that single measurements would miss. A transparent rules engine, linked to a documented medical knowledge base, classifies severity (self-manage or contact Earth immediately) and provides step-by-step guidance. Every threshold is traceable to its source.

An AI assistant answers health questions in plain language and generates medical reports for crew follow-up and ground teams.

Our goal: protect astronaut health and enable safer missions to Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Space Doctor is a web-based health and wellbeing monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions. It brings physical health and mental health into one dashboard, so warning signs are caught early, even when help from Earth is delayed.

The problem: On missions to the Moon and Mars, crews face space radiation, a sealed environment, and months of isolation. Physical readings and psychological wellbeing are usually tracked separately, so early signs of trouble in either one are easy to miss.

How it works: The astronaut logs in with a smart wristband ID and gets a live dashboard with three groups of indicators: space radiation sensors, closed-environment and air-quality readings, and isolation and wellbeing indicators. When a reading moves outside its configured threshold, the system raises a live medical alert. A built-in health assistant gives guidance from a local medical knowledge base. For mental health and daily routine, the crew-support tools include daily mood, motivation and stress tracking, an astronaut journal, sleep and circadian-rhythm logging, a light-exposure scheduler with a session timer, a workload and performance tracker, a space-gardening activity log, coping tips for isolation, a post-mission reintegration plan, and a HERA/CHAPEA analog-mission simulation log. Every entry is saved to the astronaut's profile in Firebase, and a NASA research sample (User_1) can be imported to test the system.

Benefits and intended impact: One view of body and mind lets the crew and the mission support team notice changes sooner. Astronauts can keep healthy routines, sleep and social contact, and mission teams get a documented history of crew wellbeing to review over time. The goal is safer and more resilient crews on missions where help is far away.

Tools and software: HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web app, JSON files for data, Firebase for cloud data storage, Visual Studio Code as the code editor, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Public NASA resources and analog-mission information (HERA, CHAPEA) guided the design.

What makes it creative: most monitoring tools focus on the body only. Space Doctor treats mental wellbeing as equally important and adds practical tools against monotony, such as space gardening activities and light-exposure scheduling.

Factors our team considered: safety and honesty. Alert thresholds are experimental and adjustable, mood and behavior scores are self-reported and not diagnostic, the HERA/CHAPEA log is for documentation and simulation only, and all medical decisions are left to the mission medical team.

projectDetails.name: Project Space fish
projectDetails.summary:
Project Space Fish is a web platform that compares locations on Earth with different areas on the Moon and Mars to find the closest environmental and geological matches.

Our platform uses scientific data to analyze soil, rocks, minerals, terrain, temperature, and other properties. It calculates compatibility scores and ranks Earth locations based on how similar they are to specific lunar and Martian sites.

The main goal is to help scientists and space researchers find suitable places on Earth to test rovers, space equipment, habitats, and new technologies before using them in real space missions.

Our project makes space research easier, reduces testing costs and risks, and brings space exploration closer to Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Project Space Fish – Detailed Project Description

1. Project Overview

Project Space Fish is a web-based platform designed to compare locations on Earth with different regions on the Moon and Mars. Its main purpose is to identify the closest possible terrestrial environments that share similar geological, chemical, mineralogical, and physical properties with extraterrestrial locations.

The project helps researchers find suitable places on Earth to simulate planetary conditions and test space technologies before using them in actual space missions.

2. How Does It Work?

The platform analyzes different scientific properties of Earth locations and compares them with selected lunar and Martian targets.

It evaluates several parameters, including:

- Soil and rock composition.
- Geochemistry and mineralogy.
- Terrain and geological features.
- Physical properties and radar reflectivity.
- Temperature and environmental conditions.

The system calculates a Compatibility Score (%) for each location, showing how closely it matches the selected planetary target. It also provides comparisons, advantages, disadvantages, and a leaderboard that ranks candidate locations.

3. Data Sources

Our project uses scientific and Earth observation datasets from several international space agencies and research organizations, including:

- NASA Planetary Data System (PDS): Apollo 14 sample composition data and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Diviner datasets.
- CSA RADARSAT: Radar data from RADARSAT-1 and the RADARSAT Constellation Mission.
- ESA Copernicus: Earth observation and satellite imagery.
- NASA Worldview: Optical and thermal satellite imagery.
- JAXA G-Portal: Earth observation datasets.
- USGS: Geological mapping standards and planetary science resources.

These datasets provide the scientific foundation for comparing Earth environments with lunar and Martian surfaces.

4. Evaluation and Results

Our platform uses a 100-point evaluation framework based on three main categories:

- Terrain and Geological Similarity: 35 points.
- Physical and Environmental Conditions: 35 points.
- Testing and Logistics Feasibility: 30 points.

The results help identify locations with strong potential for planetary analogue research.

For example, Mount Etna's Cisternazza pyroclastic deposits achieved a reported compatibility score of 85.4% as a lunar highlands analogue candidate.

The platform also evaluates locations such as Fra Mauro, Shackleton Crater, Jezero Crater, and Gale Crater.

Another important candidate identified by our analysis is Harrat Khaybar in Saudi Arabia, which has basaltic volcanic fields, comendite domes, and lava tubes that may provide useful environments for lunar and Martian analogue studies.

5. Benefits and Applications

Project Space Fish can help:

- Reduce the cost and risks of testing space technologies.
- Identify suitable locations for rover testing and navigation.
- Support research on lunar and Martian habitats.
- Help test In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), including regolith-based construction and resource extraction.
- Support scientists, universities, and space agencies in selecting terrestrial analogue sites.

6. Limitations and Future Development

The accuracy of the compatibility results depends on the availability, quality, and resolution of the scientific datasets. Earth environments cannot perfectly reproduce all lunar or Martian conditions, such as low gravity, vacuum, and radiation.

Our future plans include integrating more scientific datasets, improving the scoring system, developing AI and machine learning models to discover new analogue locations, and creating a collaborative global database for planetary researchers.

7. Our Vision

Our vision is to make planetary research easier and more accessible by connecting Earth-based environments with space exploration. We aim to help researchers find the best places on Earth to prepare for future Moon and Mars missions.

Project Space Fish – Bringing Space Exploration Closer to Earth.

projectDetails.details:
Off-World Relics is an interactive web storytelling and education platform designed to bridge the "archive gap" by transforming NASA’s discarded hardware—such as rovers, landers, and scientific instruments across the Moon, Mars, and deep space—into an emotional, explorable learning experience.

Key Features & Functionality:

- The Atlas: An interactive coordinate-based map allowing users to explore historical artifacts (such as Apollo 15 LRV, Opportunity, and Voyager 1) to inspect mission specs and hear their stories.

- The Expedition: A chronological exploration route from the 1960s to the present where users collect Explorer Passport stamps.

- The Space Hardware Lab: A simulation tool where users adjust real mission variables (like solar distance and atmospheric dust) to understand engineering power tradeoffs between solar arrays and RTG systems.

- The Learning Loop (Field Quiz): Gamified STEM challenges grounded in official NASA historical records (NSSDCA).

Tools & Technologies:

Developed using modern web frameworks, interactive UI/UX components, and simulation logic built on verified NASA historical datasets.

Impact & Creativity:

Instead of leaving space history buried in dense technical records, Off-World Relics gives silent hardware a voice. It democratizes space history for classrooms worldwide, turning passive reading into hands-on STEM learning and inspiring the next generation of engineers through stories, systems, and play.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift
projectDetails.summary: Field Shift is a bilingual (English and Arabic) web tool that helps agricultural engineers, consultants and agricultural companies choose a crop rotation for a specific farm using NASA Earth observation data. The user finds the farm by place search, their own location or the satellite map, sets a point or draws the boundary, and gets an environmental overview built from NASA POWER climate data and MODIS/Terra NDVI, with ERA5 and USDA soil data as extra context. The user then compares the current rotation with two alternatives: Field Shift scores each one with transparent, adjustable criteria, estimates effective rainfall and indicative irrigation need for every crop season with published FAO methods, lists risks and exports a PDF or CSV decision report. Every value shows its source and its type (observation, model estimate or calculated indicator). Missing data are shown as unavailable, never invented, and the tool does not forecast yield or profit. A separate Educational Missions section lets learners act as a local agricultural engineer, simulate a crop season in five countries with real NASA POWER data and compare experiments. Field Shift turns free, global NASA data into clear evidence for everyday farm planning.
projectDetails.details:
Space Hunters' Project Solution: Field Shift

Choosing which crops to grow, and in what order, is one of the most important decisions on a farm. A good rotation protects the soil, saves water and reduces risk, but the right choice depends on local climate, water and soil, and that evidence is scattered across satellite archives, climate databases, soil surveys and FAO manuals. NASA data are free and global, yet they are rarely used in everyday farm planning because each source needs technical skills to use.

Field Shift closes that gap. It is a free, bilingual (English and Arabic) web tool that turns NASA Earth observation data into clear, comparable evidence for one question: which crop rotation fits this farm, and why? It is built for agricultural engineers, consultants, agricultural companies and decision-makers, and it works on phones and computers with no account or installation.

How Does Our Solution Work

Farm Analysis & Planning guides the user through six steps. Each step opens only after the previous one is complete, so every result rests on validated inputs.

  • Location & Farm Boundary: search for any place in the world, use My location, type coordinates, click the satellite map, or draw the farm boundary as a polygon. The area is calculated on a spherical Earth model, in feddans or hectares.
  • Environmental Overview: 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA POWER monthly climatology for the farm point: air temperature, rainfall, humidity and solar radiation, chosen month by month. A Recent conditions section adds the last 12 months of NASA POWER, MODIS/Terra NDVI vegetation greenness (MOD13Q1, 250 m), ERA5 evapotranspiration and soil moisture, and USDA soil survey data for farms in the United States. Every block has a source panel with provider, dataset, period and resolution.
  • Farm Information & Crops: the user enters the existing rotation and two alternatives from a catalog of ten field crops with published FAO values for water need, growing period and optimum temperature.
  • Scenario Comparison: for every crop season, Field Shift sums the rainfall, converts it to effective rainfall with the FAO formula and subtracts it from the crop's water need to give an indicative irrigation range in mm and m³/ha. It checks each season's temperature against the crop's optimum range and gives each rotation a 0–100 score from four adjustable criteria: lower water need, nitrogen-fixing legumes, crop-family diversity and pest-cycle breaks. Rotations are ranked only when every scenario has complete data.
  • Risks & Trade-offs: the evidence for water, heat and vegetation stress is listed as clear points to consider, without invented probabilities.
  • Decision Summary & Report: the chosen rotation and its indicators are exported as a PDF or CSV report in English or right-to-left Arabic, ready to share with a client, a manager or a farmer.

Educational Missions

A separate learning experience for students and the public. The learner works as a local agricultural engineer in one of five countries (Egypt, India, the United States, Brazil and Australia), chooses a crop, a real past season and irrigation decisions, and watches the season unfold month by month with real NASA POWER data. The simulation uses FAO methods (Blaney–Criddle evapotranspiration, FAO-56 crop coefficients, effective rainfall, a soil water store and the yield-response factor Ky) to show relative yield compared with a fully watered crop. Experiments can be saved and compared side by side.

The project benefits

  • One workflow instead of many sources: climate, vegetation, evapotranspiration and soil data from four providers, requested for the same location and shown together.
  • Indicators professionals already use: effective rainfall and irrigation need per hectare instead of raw satellite variables.
  • Fair comparison: three rotations evaluated with the same data and the same rules, with the reasons behind every score visible.
  • Traceable and honest: every value is labelled as an observation, a model estimate or a calculated indicator, and missing data are shown as unavailable, never invented.
  • Accessible to all: free, English and Arabic, mobile-friendly, no account needed.

Our goal

To make NASA's open Earth data part of everyday agricultural decisions, especially in water-scarce regions such as the Nile Delta, and to help the next generation understand how climate and water shape what farms can grow. Field Shift supports expert judgement; it does not forecast yield or profit and does not replace field measurements or local extension advice.

What makes it creative

  • It connects open NASA data with simple, published FAO calculations in one light tool, between detailed crop models that need expert inputs and raw data portals with no agricultural interpretation.
  • Honesty is a design rule: grid resolution, data gaps and unassessed criteria are stated, and incomplete scenarios are not ranked.
  • The same evidence serves two audiences: professionals planning real farms, and learners exploring real seasons.

Factors we considered

  • NASA POWER and ERA5 describe grid cells tens of kilometres wide, not single fields; NDVI shows greenness, not yield.
  • Soil survey data exist only for the United States; monthly data cannot show short dry spells.
  • Service time-outs and missing values are handled with retries and caching, and reported clearly.
  • Full Arabic right-to-left support, accessibility and layouts from 360 px phones to desktops.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding languages and frameworks:

  • JavaScript with Next.js 14 and React 18 for the web application.
  • Tailwind CSS 3 for the responsive, bilingual interface.

Maps and visualisation:

  • Leaflet 1.9 for the satellite farm map and boundary drawing; d3-geo, topojson-client and world-atlas for the world map; lucide-react icons.

Data sources:

  • NASA POWER climatology and monthly APIs; MODIS/Terra MOD13Q1 NDVI through the NASA ORNL DAAC subset service.
  • ERA5 reanalysis (Open-Meteo), USDA SSURGO soil survey, OpenStreetMap place search, Esri World Imagery basemap, and FAO crop water references.

Try It

  • Live website: space-hunters-field-shift.vercel.app
