projectDetails.details:
AstroMates is a story-driven educational game prototype for children aged 7–12, developed by SpaceMates for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. It connects scientific knowledge with practical decisions about the systems that support life in space.

The story follows a young boy who dreams of becoming an astronaut and his dog, Buddy. When a mysterious spacecraft pulls them aboard, their adventure introduces challenges involving life support, water recovery, and space farming. Keeping Buddy safe and finding a way home give the player a personal reason to investigate problems and keep learning.

The gameplay follows a consistent learning loop: observe a problem, inspect system readings, compare possible actions, make a decision, and review its consequences. A smartwatch provides visual explanations and progressive hints without immediately revealing the answer. Choices affect the system’s condition, and feedback explains why an action helped or created another problem. Players are encouraged to reconsider and try again.

The mission designs cover three connected areas:

  • Life support: Interpret cabin-pressure and air-quality indicators, distinguish different system faults, and select an appropriate response.
  • Water recovery: Arrange a simplified treatment process, investigate quality warnings, and understand why water requires verification before release.
  • Space farming: Match lighting to a plant experiment’s requirements and restore air circulation around the plants.

The intended benefits are scientific reasoning, problem-solving, and awareness of limited resources. Rather than presenting isolated facts, the experience shows how air, water, energy, and plant-growing conditions contribute to a functioning space habitat.

Our current prototype includes storyboards, interface designs, mission flows, reusable visual assets, and a visual demonstration. Figma supports interface design and prototype assembly.

ChatGPT assisted with narrative drafting, mission refinement, and prompt development, while OpenAI image-generation tools assisted with visual asset production. The team directed the concept, reviewed the material, and assembled the experience.

The project’s creative approach combines an emotionally engaging companion story with scientific troubleshooting. Consistent characters, a recognizable visual identity, and contextual smartwatch guidance connect the missions into one adventure.

Key design considerations include age-appropriate language, readable interfaces, manageable choices, gradual hints, meaningful consequences, and scientific accuracy. NASA educational and technical resources inform the content, with complex processes simplified for the audience. Further development will include playable implementation, testing with children in the target age group, and evaluation of usability and learning outcomes.

projectDetails.name: AstroPulse
projectDetails.summary: On a long mission to Mars a message to Earth takes up to about 20 minutes each way, so the crew is the first line of care. Ordinary health apps use one fixed "normal range" for everybody. AstroPulse instead learns each astronaut's own normal from their first week, flags a steady drift while the colors are still green, explains it through NASA's five hazards of spaceflight, and tells the crew what to do now while showing how long Earth needs to answer. A phone-camera pulse measurement needs no extra hardware.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES. AstroPulse is a web app with a crew view and a ground-control view. Every health indicator (heart rate, oxygen, skin temperature, blood pressure, blood sugar, sleep, mood) has a color, a plain-language explanation tied to NASA's five hazards of spaceflight, and a decision screen with an Earth-delay counter (Station, Moon, Mars). Each person is compared with their own first week: a sustained drift (4 days, 2 standard deviations or more) is flagged even while fixed ranges say green, with a forecast such as "red in N days". Ground control is a flight-surgeon screen where reports arrive only after the signal delay and the doctor's reply crosses the same delay back. Also: live space weather, cabin CO2, guided steps for yellow and red indicators, a Replay of the Day-143 scenario, a tab where anyone can drop their own resting-heart-rate CSV (it never leaves the browser), reaction and near-vision checks, Arabic advice, read-aloud and offline use.

HOW IT WORKS. An ASP.NET Core 8 server with SQLite validates and stores readings and pushes them live over SignalR to a React + Vite web app that is installable and works offline. The anomaly model (personal baseline, z-score) runs in C# and is checked against its Python reference by automated tests. The pulse comes from the phone camera through the fingertip (photoplethysmography in the browser), so it needs no extra hardware.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT. The crew learns of a drift days before fixed ranges would show it, knows what to do while Earth is minutes away, and sends Earth a report that says what was already tried. The same idea suits any isolated place where a doctor is far away.

WORKING FEATURES AND EVIDENCE. The app is live and usable. The camera pulse is a real measurement; it was checked on 53 real recorded signals (public BIDMC dataset) with 1.1 bpm mean error. Space weather is live from NOAA and NASA DONKI. A Monte Carlo virtual crew trial (hypotheses written before the run; settings chosen on one set, results on another) shows the calibrated personal baseline catching 97% of simulated drifts at 4.7% false alarms. Our first model false-alarmed on 94% of healthy crews, so we recalibrated it, and one pre-registered hypothesis failed and is reported in the app. 15 web test suites and 29 API tests run in CI.

LIMITATIONS. All crew data is synthetic and labeled; there are no real astronauts or patients. Oxygen and skin temperature are simulated in the app; blood pressure, glucose, sleep and mood are typed in. Camera pulse is approximate (a few bpm). The optional ESP32 hardware prototype (MAX30100 and DHT11) is hobby-grade and was not compared with a reference device. This is a prototype, not a medical device.

FUTURE PLANS. Test the baseline model on real wearable data with consent, review thresholds with clinicians, validate a wearable against a reference device, and add real oxygen and temperature sensing.

TOOLS. C#, ASP.NET Core 8, Entity Framework Core, SQLite, SignalR, JavaScript, React, Vite, Python, GitHub Actions, Microsoft Azure.

projectDetails.name: Project SpaceSync
projectDetails.summary:
🚀 Space Mission Challenge | NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026

Our project is an interactive educational game that combines space exploration, physics, engineering, and problem-solving.

Players embark on exciting space missions through different levels and challenges. Each level presents a unique mission that requires players to apply scientific laws, use mathematical formulas, perform calculations, and solve engineering problems to successfully complete their tasks.

Throughout the game, players can:
- Explore interactive 3D environments.
- Complete different space missions and challenges.
- Apply physics and engineering laws.
- Use formulas and scientific equations to solve problems.
- Perform calculations based on the given data.
- Overcome technical challenges and make decisions.
- Progress through increasingly challenging levels.

Our goal is to make learning science and engineering more engaging by turning theoretical knowledge into an interactive gaming experience.

Competition: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
Location: Cairo, Egypt

Thank you for watching! 🚀
projectDetails.details:
SpaceSync is a browser game that teaches space mission design by making players do the engineering. Its main mode, 3D Missions, has 25 levels in 5 sections: Rocket Science, Orbital Mechanics, Power & Thermal, Communications, and Planets & Landing. Each level is a separate mission with its own 3D scene, a written mission brief, its own reference laws (with variables and units) and 2–4 calculations.

How it works: the player reads the mission, explores the 3D scene and clicks markers on objects to collect the data (for example the rocket's mass, the engine thrust, or air density from a weather balloon), opens the Reference Laws tab, calculates each value and types it in. The game checks the answer against a value computed from the same data. Wrong answers are diagnosed without revealing the result (wrong unit or power of ten, ln vs log10, altitude instead of radius, a missing ½, forgetting gravity), and a hint showing the approach is available. Each correct answer moves the mission forward in 3D: the rocket lifts off, the spacecraft burns into GEO, the lander touches down. A second mode, Mission Designer, lets players buy parts, build a spacecraft within a budget and mass limit, and run a simulation that explains why it succeeded or failed.

Benefits and goal: students practise real mission-analysis skills (units, choosing the right law, margins, go/no-go decisions) and get specific feedback instead of a simple fail. It is free, works in any browser and offline as one HTML file, supports English and Arabic, and each mission takes 5–10 minutes, so it fits a class period.

Tools: JavaScript, HTML and CSS; a custom WebGL 3D renderer; an optional Node.js server; and Playwright for automated testing. All 25 levels were played end-to-end by automated tests.

Creativity: the player cannot win by guessing. The 3D world is only data until the player calculates, and the calculations drive the 3D story. Considerations: honest labelling (physical constants are real, scenario values are educational), no NASA logos, bilingual access, and low-end devices.

Status: working prototype. The 3D objects are simple shapes, profiles are saved on the device only, and the game has not yet been tested in a classroom.

projectDetails.name: Kilonaut
projectDetails.summary:
Kilonaut is an interactive web game that turns space education into a mission for kids. Instead of memorizing static facts, young learners join the Kilonaut Academy with just a call-sign and an avatar, no account needed, and progress through three cosmic stages: Solar System Odyssey, Black Holes & Cosmic Mysteries, and Galactic Frontiers. Each stage pairs short, easy facts with fun game challenges, using NASA data and imagery. After finishing them, players unlock the Astronaut Training Facility, a walkable space-station simulation where they handle problems astronauts face in orbit: fixing severed wires, preparing food in the galley, aligning the radio with Houston, and docking cargo with Canadarm2. Kids earn XP, rank up from Cadet to Specialist to Commander, and graduate with a verifiable Junior Astronaut Certificate. Kilonaut answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by making learning fun, practical, and accessible, with English and Arabic support and read-aloud audio. It matters because it keeps children curious and shows them how a real mission works, so more of them keep exploring.
To explain it out loud in one breath: "Kilonaut is a web game where kids train like junior astronauts. They learn space through short missions, then pass space-station challenges and earn a certificate."
projectDetails.details: Project Name: Kilonaut Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer (NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026) Team: Space Team BNU What does it do and how does it work? Kilonaut is an interactive, web-based space academy built for kids and young space enthusiasts. We wanted to fix a common issue: traditional space education is often dry, full of long paragraphs, and forces kids to memorize boring facts. Our platform turns learning into a game through three main exploration stages and a practical astronaut training simulator: 1. Solar System Odyssey: Kids journey through all 8 planets, learning their locations, distances (AU), and planetary alignments. 2. Black Holes & Cosmic Mysteries: An interactive look at gravity wells, Jupiter and Saturn’s moons, and James Webb telescope data using real NASA sources. 3. Galactic Frontiers: Explores the Milky Way, galactic radar, and star life cycles (from nebulae to supernovas and black holes). 4. Astronaut Mission Trainer: A hands-on game where kids learn how astronauts handle real tasks on a spaceship, such as managing the sleep bay, preparing food in the galley, fixing emergency panels, working out on the treadmill, and operating the Canadarm2. What benefits and impact does it have? Most children lose interest in space science because studying feels like a chore. Kilonaut bridges the gap between learning and gaming by: Sparking natural curiosity and passion for astronomy and space exploration without feeling like traditional studying. Supporting both English and Arabic interfaces, along with an audio read-aloud feature, making it accessible for children everywhere. Rewarding young learners with an official, verifiable Junior Astronaut Certificate when they complete their training. What tools and technologies did we use? Workflow: We built the project through teamwork, testing prototypes step-by-step, and collaborating via GitHub and Discord. We used AI tools (Gemini, Manus, and Antigravity) to help us during the prototyping phase. Tech Stack: Built with standard web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) to ensure it runs smoothly on any device. We kept onboarding frictionless—no accounts or sign-ups are needed; kids simply pick a call-sign and an avatar to jump right in. Data Sources: Powered by authentic data from NASA APIs, NASA Mars Trek, OSDR, and CSA youth toolkits. How is your project creative? Kilonaut stands out by replacing passive reading with active, engaging gameplay. We kept information short and digestible, immediately following it up with fun challenges. By focusing on simple onboarding, a smooth user experience, and gamification elements (like XP points, leveling up from Cadet to Commander, and flight logs/passports), we made learning about space genuinely fun and exciting for kids.

projectDetails.name: OrbitFlame
projectDetails.summary:
NASA’s microgravity combustion research provides evidence on flammability, flame behaviour, smoke detection, and fire suppression. Yet records, datasets, and publications are spread across resources, making evidence difficult to find and compare for spacecraft and habitat safety.

FLAME Intelligence is an AI-powered dashboard connected to NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). It brings combustion investigations into one workspace to search studies, inspect experimental conditions and measurements, compare results, and explore relevance to spacecraft, stations, lunar or Martian habitats, and pressurized rovers.

The AI Research Assistant answers natural-language questions with concise explanations linked to original sources. Transparent evidence-based ranking explains why studies match a scenario, where conditions differ, and which data are missing. Evidence-gap analysis highlights underrepresented conditions.

The platform will organize PSI metadata through shared data models and APIs. A responsive Next.js, React, and TypeScript interface will integrate search, comparison, visualizations, and AI services. Testing will check usability, accuracy, traceability, and failure handling.

FLAME Intelligence simplifies research discovery while separating measured results, metadata, and AI interpretation. It helps researchers, engineers, educators, and students assess evidence without presenting AI conclusions as experimental facts or rankings as certified fire-risk predictions.
projectDetails.details:
OrbitFlame

What does the project do and how does it work?

OrbitFlame is a research and decision-support platform focused on fire safety in spacecraft and space habitats. It uses real experimental data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository to make combustion and flammability research from spaceflight and ground-based experiments easier to explore, compare, and understand.

The platform organizes data from 20 NASA investigations, including BASS, Saffire, ACME, FLEX, and SAME. It brings this information together through several interactive features.

The Research Library allows users to browse original NASA investigation records, experimental tables, test matrices, and hardware descriptions. The Data Explorer provides access to individual test runs and their recorded conditions, including fuel type, pressure, oxygen concentration, airflow, and experimental outcomes.

A built-in Unit Conversion Tool converts compatible physical quantities into SI units while retaining their original reported values. It ensures that only quantities of the same type are compared, such as pressure with pressure.

The Habitat Ranking feature compares NASA experiments with different environments, including the International Space Station, lunar and Mars habitats, spacesuits, and Earth-based analogs. Each investigation receives a relevance score from 0 to 100 based on atmospheric conditions, airflow, gravity, and fuel type.

OrbitFlame also includes flammability and extinction prediction models trained on real NASA experimental data. Predictions are displayed only when the models perform better than a simple baseline in validation tests where entire experiments are held out.

The AI Assistant answers questions using only the indexed NASA investigations. It links its responses to their original source records, preserves reported units, and avoids making claims that cannot be supported by the available evidence.

Missing information is never silently estimated. When a NASA record does not report a value, OrbitFlame identifies it as blank or "not reported."

What benefits does it have?

OrbitFlame makes a large and technically complex collection of NASA fire-safety research easier to access and use. Researchers, students, engineers, and educators can explore relevant information without manually searching through multiple files and investigation records.

By combining experimental data with analytical tools, the platform helps users compare research findings and identify experiments that may be relevant to specific space environments. Its results are transparent: users can trace information back to the original NASA records and review measured values, model outputs, and comparable experiments.

The platform also makes uncertainty easier to understand. It distinguishes between recorded measurements, model predictions, inferred gravity conditions, and missing information. Its AI assistant provides source-based answers rather than unsupported conclusions.

Together, these features support more informed research and planning while making clear that predictions are not safety certifications.

What is the intended impact of the project?

OrbitFlame aims to improve how space-fire-safety research is discovered, compared, and interpreted. As human missions move toward longer stays on the Moon and Mars, understanding how fire behaves under different atmospheric and gravity conditions becomes increasingly important.

The platform helps users identify which existing NASA experiments are most relevant to a particular habitat, where experimental evidence is available, and where further research may be needed. It can also highlight materials, atmospheric conditions, and airflow ranges that deserve additional testing.

By making research gaps and data limitations easier to identify, OrbitFlame supports better research planning and helps direct attention toward areas where more experimental evidence is needed.

Ultimately, the project aims to contribute to safer spacecraft and space habitats by making reliable scientific evidence more accessible and easier to interpret.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project uses experimental tables and investigation records from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository. Its main technical components include data organization and indexing, unit-conversion logic, statistical models for flammability and extinction estimates, a habitat-matching and scoring system, and an AI assistant that retrieves information from indexed research records.

AI-powered tools also played an important role in the development process. Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT were used to support coding, problem-solving, research, and technical writing. Manus AI was used to assist with video creation and visual presentation of the project.

The project combines NASA experimental data with AI-assisted development and analytical approaches to create an interactive research platform.

The available project documentation does not specify the exact programming languages, frameworks, databases, statistical libraries, hosting environment, or hardware used during development.

How is the project creative?

OrbitFlame turns scattered scientific records into an interactive platform that supports research and practical decision-making. Rather than simply displaying NASA data, it brings together scientific data exploration, habitat similarity scoring, unit-aware comparisons, statistical predictions, and AI-powered research assistance.

One of its distinctive features is the way it approaches gravity comparisons. NASA PSI tables do not always provide a direct gravity measurement, so OrbitFlame uses investigation flight records and airflow-equivalent behavior to support cautious comparisons. For lunar and Martian environments, the results are clearly presented as indicative because the indexed PSI experiments were not conducted at exactly the Moon's or Mars's gravity.

The project also places strong emphasis on scientific reliability. It does not fill in missing values, treat similar experiments as proof of safety, or present model predictions as guarantees. This approach combines innovation with responsible use of scientific data and AI.

What factors did the team consider?

The team considered scientific accuracy, data reliability, model performance, and the potential safety implications of the platform.

All experimental values are retained as reported by NASA, including their original units. Unit conversions are performed only between compatible physical quantities, and missing values remain unreported rather than being estimated.

Model reliability was another important consideration. Predictions are shown only when the models outperform a basic baseline during validation using held-out experiments. The platform also distinguishes between measured results, inferred information, and model estimates so users can understand the limitations of each result.

Source traceability is maintained throughout the system. AI responses and analytical results are connected to the relevant NASA records, allowing users to review the evidence behind them.

The team also considered the practical conditions that influence fire behavior in spacecraft and habitats, including oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, fuel type, and gravity. Particular care was taken to avoid making unsupported safety claims, such as declaring a material safe or assuming a fire suppressant will work based on a similar experiment.

Finally, the platform distinguishes between a lack of indexed data and proof that no research exists. This helps users recognize research gaps without drawing conclusions that the available evidence cannot support.

OrbitFlame is designed to make space-fire-safety research more accessible while demonstrating how scientific data and AI can be combined in a transparent, careful, and responsible way.

projectDetails.name: ECHOES OF SILENCE: 1:1 3D & Web AR Museum of NASA's Silent Spacecraft
projectDetails.summary: Echoes of Silence is an interactive, browser-based 1:1 metric-scale 3D museum and WebRTC AR exhibition that transforms 13 inactive NASA spacecraft across the Moon, Mars, Asteroid 433 Eros, Dwarf Planet Ceres, and Deep Space into living, first-person STEM storytellers. Over six decades of exploration have left historic landers, rovers, and probes resting silently on distant worlds, where raw coordinate tables often make them feel like forgotten "space junk" to young learners. Our web application bridges this gap through three connected perspectives: a 3D Solar System Explorer showing real transfer trajectories and speed-of-light radio delays, an Orbital Museum Deck comparing all 13 spacecraft side-by-side, and a 1:1 Planetary Surface Stage where students stand beside each machine next to a 1.75m astronaut, compare historic mission photos with modern orbital reconnaissance, and interview the spacecraft in the first person.
projectDetails.details:
1. WHAT DOES IT DO & HOW DOES IT WORK?

Echoes of Silence is a zero-install, browser-based 3D and Web AR exhibition that turns 13 silent NASA spacecraft across 5 celestial destinations (the Moon, Mars, Asteroid 433 Eros, Dwarf Planet 1 Ceres, and Deep Space) into interactive, first-person teachers. Users explore through three seamless spatial modes:

• Mode 1 — 3D Solar System Explorer: An interactive heliocentric map where an animated JPL-style transfer spacecraft flies along mission transfer arcs (Translunar Injection, Hohmann Mars Transfer, and Deep-Space Ion Spirals) while displaying real-time one-way speed-of-light radio communication delays from Earth (from 1.28 Light-Seconds at the Moon to ~18.6 Light-Hours in Deep Space).

• Mode 2 — Orbital Museum Deck: A curated exhibition gallery placing all 13 spacecraft side-by-side on illuminated pedestals with category filters (Landers, Rovers, Probes, and Instruments) so learners can compare 57 years of aerospace engineering.

• Mode 3 — 1:1 Surface Stage & Live Mobile AR: Places users on reconstructed Lunar regolith, Martian iron-oxide dust, or asteroid terrain at true metric scale (1 unit = 1 meter) beside a 1.75m astronaut scale reference or in live mobile WebRTC camera passthrough. Clicking any spacecraft opens 39 interactive 3D engineering pins, a "Then vs. Now" switcher comparing historic surface photos with overhead LROC and MRO HiRISE satellite reconnaissance, and "Ask the Spacecraft" interactive Q&A chips.

2. WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE & WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

• Multi-Tier Educational Impact: Designed across three learning tiers—Young Explorers (Ages 10–14) engage with empathetic first-person stories ("I landed...", "My solar panels...") and earn a printable 13/13 Explorer Passport Certificate; High School STEM students analyze orbital mechanics, light-time delays, and environmental failure modes; and Educators gain a free, 15-minute browser lab with zero installation or login walls.

• Space Heritage Preservation: Reframes inactive planetary hardware from "discarded equipment" into protected scientific monuments and time capsules of human ingenuity.

3. TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES & SOFTWARE USED

• Frontend & 3D Engine: React 19, TypeScript, Three.js (r183), React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber), @react-three/drei, and custom GLSL atmospheric Fresnel and solar corona shaders.

• Styling, UI & AR: Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide React icons, HTML5 Canvas procedural planetary surface maps, Web Speech API, and WebRTC navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia for live mobile AR camera passthrough.

• Build & Deployment: Vite 8, Git/GitHub, and Vercel.

• Live App Link: https://spaghetti-coders.vercel.app

• GitHub Repository: https://github.com/omarsh4114/NASA-Abandoned-Not-Forgotten-404

4. HOW IS THE PROJECT CREATIVE & WHAT FACTORS DID OUR TEAM CONSIDER?

Instead of presenting static encyclopedia pages, we gave each spacecraft its own first-person voice so students can "interview" the hardware about what it discovered and why it went silent. We also engineered a true 1:1 metric scale comparison beside a 1.75m human astronaut so learners immediately grasp that Mars's Sojourner rover (0.65m) is the size of a microwave oven while Apollo 11's Eagle descent stage (4.20m wide) towers like a two-story cabin. To ensure 100% classroom reliability even on restricted school networks, we built an automatic SVG NASA Telemetry Blueprint fallback plate.

5. TRANSPARENT AI / SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

Team Spaghetti Coders (Omar, Bashar, and Youssef) conceived the project architecture and curatorial design independently. Google Antigravity and Google Gemini assisted with Three.js/React code scaffolding, custom GLSL shader tuning, and copyediting historical mission summaries into age-appropriate first-person educational narratives. Manus AI assisted with structuring our 7-slide presentation deck. Zero AI-generated images or altered NASA logos are used anywhere; all telemetry and archival imagery originate from official public-domain NASA datasets.

projectDetails.name: ASTRA
projectDetails.summary:
I developed a rule-based health-monitoring framework for astronauts. It tracks daily readings such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, oxygen, balance, bone density, exercise, sleep, temperature, and mood. Each reading is classified as Normal, Below normal, Above normal, or Critical, and each class has a set action: log it, recheck and find the cause, or stop and call the medical officer.

A mental health monitor combines mood check-ins with sleep, heart rate, and fatigue trends to spot stress, isolation, and burnout early. A mind game, using short reaction-time and memory tasks, helps the crew relax while checking alertness and consciousness against each astronaut's own baseline. A drop triggers the same response steps.

The challenge is that space changes the body and mind. Bone loss, balance problems, and shifts in heart rate and blood pressure mean Earth ranges don't always apply, and doctors are far away. The crew needs clear first steps without waiting for Earth. The system stays safe: it never diagnoses or chooses medication, it only triggers first aid and refers everything else to the medical officer.

This matters because it catches problems early, gives fast, consistent responses in remote conditions, and protects the whole crew, since one sick, exhausted, or overloaded astronaut risks the mission. It also tracks long-term trends like bone loss, sleep, and mental wellbeing, essential for missions to the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: A wrist wearable tracks heart rate (MAX30102) and cabin pressure, temperature and altitude (BMP390). Every second it calculates a health score, a fatigue index and a risk level: Normal, Above or Critical. It then sends the results as JSON over Bluetooth Low Energy to a phone or ground station, with a plain-language recommendation such as "Rest 15 min" or "Notify flight surgeon immediately."

Benefits:

• Continuous, non-invasive monitoring with no manual checks.

• Early warning of fatigue, abnormal heart rate or hypoxia.

• Clear recommendations the crew can act on, even when contact with Earth is delayed.

• Mental health monitor: tracks stress and mood signs such as heart-rate changes and fatigue trends, and flags when a crew member may need rest or support.

• Mind game: short, engaging brain games that help crew members relax, stay sharp and fight isolation and boredom. They can also show how focus and reaction time change over a mission.

• Low-cost, low-power, wireless hardware.

Intended impact: Safer, more independent crews on long missions, with physical and mental health visible in one place. The same design can help climbers, remote workers and first responders.

Tools: C++ (Arduino IDE), nRF52 BLE board, MAX30102, BMP390, I²C, BLE and JSON.

Creativity: It combines body and environment sensing with a mission-themed "digital flight surgeon," and it treats mental wellbeing as seriously as physical health.

Factors considered: safety thresholds, reliable sensor readings, low power, a small size and easy expansion.

projectDetails.name: Little Space Heroes
projectDetails.summary: Little Space Heroes is an interactive, 2D educational space adventure game designed for 9-year-old children to learn space science and survival engineering through play. Across three missions—the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter—players manage food and water resources while solving real-world NASA engineering challenges, such as testing lunar ice for safe drinking water, building radiation-shielded underground habitats using water and polyethylene, and navigating Jupiter's storms with shape-coded wire puzzles. By replacing scary survival tropes with colorful cartoon art, positive reinforcement, and accessible touch controls, our game translates complex astrophysics and space exploration concepts into an engaging, stress-free STEM learning experience that inspires the next generation of young explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview & How It Works:
Little Space Heroes (Space Mission Design Game) is an interactive, 2D educational space adventure game designed specifically for 9-year-old children. The game teaches real-world space science, planetary environments, and survival engineering through fun, stress-free gameplay across three levels: The Moon, Mars, and Jupiter.
- Core Survival Mechanics: Players manage Minecraft-style Food and Water bars using limited supplies from a spacecraft fridge, guided by a friendly robot companion.
- Level 1 (The Moon): Children learn lunar facts via interactive cards, explore craters to find ice, and use a Water Test Machine scanner to identify safe drinking water.
- Level 2 (Mars): Players respond to a space radiation alert by digging an underground shelter and shielding it with water tanks and polyethylene panels, learning how these materials absorb cosmic rays.
- Level 3 (Jupiter): Players pilot a vehicle to dodge storms (including the Great Red Spot) and solve an interactive Wire Puzzle to activate the spacecraft's protective radiation shield.

Benefits & Intended Impact:
Complex aerospace concepts—such as In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), space weather, and radiation shielding—are often too abstract for elementary students. Our game translates real NASA mission challenges into hands-on, curiosity-driven problem-solving. It empowers young learners to think like space engineers while building foundational STEM knowledge without fear of failure.

Tools, Technologies & Software Used:
- Development & Web App: Built as a responsive, touch-friendly 2D web application using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Bolt.dev for rapid prototyping and modular game architecture (allowing easy addition of future planets and missions).
- Design & Presentation: Interactive UI elements, cartoon illustrations, and pitch materials created using digital design tools and Google Drive / PDF documentation.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered by Our Team:
- Child-Friendly & Stress-Free Design: Unlike traditional survival games with scary visuals or harsh "Game Over" screens, our game uses bright cartoon art, cheerful sound effects, positive reinforcement (stars and confetti), and a supportive robot buddy to prevent anxiety.
- Accessibility & Inclusion: We incorporated color-blind-friendly (shape-coded) connectors in the wire puzzle, large touch-friendly buttons, and short, readable text cards tailored for 9-year-olds on mobile and tablet devices.

projectDetails.name: EarthAlive
projectDetails.summary: EarthAlive is a map-based platform that turns NASA satellite and reanalysis data into clear trend answers. Users draw an area on a map, choose a variable such as land surface temperature or vegetation index, set a time range, and receive statistical trend tests, charts and a downloadable PDF report. Its comparison tools place variables side by side, such as vegetation against temperature, or one variable across several regions, so differences that a single chart would hide become visible. A rule-based guide helps new users set up their first analysis. The challenge asks for a tool that finds variables, visualises change and tests whether it is significant. Earth Alive does this, and its visual comparisons make patterns and anomalies easier to spot for scientists, students, decision-makers and citizens. The system is containerised with Docker, deployment-ready, and running as a live demo, so anyone can try it without installing anything. It matters because it turns open NASA data into evidence people can check and act on.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

EarthAlive is a full-stack platform that turns NASA satellite and reanalysis data into clear trend answers. A user draws an area of interest on a map, chooses one or more variables (land surface temperature, NDVI vegetation index, precipitation, soil moisture or air temperature), sets a time range, and selects statistical methods. The app returns trend direction, slope, statistical significance, charts, data-quality indicators and a downloadable PDF report.

Live demo: http://176.57.189.51:8000/home

The Flutter app (Android, iOS and web) talks to a FastAPI backend over REST. Each analysis runs as a background job, managed by Redis and RQ workers, so the app stays responsive. The backend retrieves data through the NASA AppEEARS API, which returns analysis-ready samples. It runs linear regression, the Mann-Kendall test (including modified and seasonal versions) and t-tests with NumPy, SciPy and pandas. Users can follow job progress live and reopen past analyses from the job history.

Comparison and visualisation

Earth Alive also compares variables and regions:

- Variable comparison: two to five variables over the same region, such as vegetation index against land surface temperature.

- Region comparison: one variable across two to eight regions.

Placing results side by side makes differences visible that a single chart hides, such as a variable rising in one region and falling in another. The challenge describes this problem directly.

Who it is for

- **Scientists and researchers,** who can screen many regions and variables quickly and spot trends, patterns and anomalies before deeper analysis.

- **Decision-makers,** such as city planners, agricultural advisers, water and disaster managers and policy officials, who need evidence of where conditions are changing.

- **Students and educators,** who can learn from real Earth data.

- **Journalists and citizens,** who want to check environmental claims.

The challenge came from difficulties that scientists face, so the tool is meant to make expert work easier, not only to teach. Built-in guidance, an FAQ and a glossary keep it accessible to newcomers.

Benefits

- Faster exploration: from a drawn area to a tested trend without writing code or handling raw rasters.

- Consistent, repeatable results, because the same tests run every time.

- Transparent quality: every result reports sample count, missing data and warnings, and the system declines to give a verdict when data is too sparse, too short or nearly constant.

- Easy sharing: a PDF report for every finished analysis.

- Easy start: a rule-based guided workflow with canned questions and example scenarios (for example an Egypt vegetation trend) helps first-time users. It is not AI.

Intended impact

We hope Earth Alive helps scientists find trends, patterns and anomalies faster, helps decision-makers see where heat, vegetation or rainfall is changing, and helps students and citizens learn from open NASA data. It is meant as a tool for explorers who want to understand, and change, the world. It is open source and containerised with Docker, so other teams and institutions can run their own instances.

**Tools, languages, hardware and software**

- **Frontend:** Flutter and Dart, flutter_bloc, flutter_map, fl_chart, dio.

- **Backend:** Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic v2, Redis, RQ.

- **Data and analysis:** NASA AppEEARS API, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib.

- **Testing:** pytest (unit, endpoint and integration tests).

- **Deployment:** Docker and Docker Compose, with separate containers for API, workers and Redis. The system is deployment-ready and running as a live demo.

- Hardware: VPS.

**Creativity**

The challenge asks for a tool that finds a variable, pulls its data, plots a time series and tests the trend's significance. Earth Alive meets that brief and goes further:

- **Side-by-side comparison** of variables and regions, so patterns and anomalies are easier to spot than in single charts.

- **A PDF report for every analysis,** so results travel beyond the app.

- **A guided workflow** that walks new users through choosing a variable, drawing an area, setting dates and methods, and submitting, with example scenarios to try first.

**Factors the team considered**

- **Scientific validity:** non-parametric tests for non-normal data, corrections for autocorrelation and seasonality, and minimum-data checks.

- **Accessibility:** one codebase for phones, tablets and desktops, with plain-language guidance.

- **Reproducibility:** containerised deployment, a documented API and tests across the pipeline.

- **Honesty about limits:** our demonstrations use short sample periods, so they show that the tool works rather than proving long-term climate change. Significance shows a change, not its cause.

- **Data access:** we began with direct granule access through earthaccess, then moved to the AppEEARS API to avoid a system-level GDAL dependency. This simplified deployment but required harmonising products, so every result reports the product, version and granularity it used. (Confirm this matches your final code path.)

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: The Moon Remembers
projectDetails.summary: The Mirror of Tranquility is an eight-page comic book that tells the story of the Apollo 11 mission through the perspective of the Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LR3). Inspired by President John F. Kennedy’s 1961 vision, the visual narrative follows astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins from their July 16, 1969 launch to their manual landing in the Sea of Tranquility, where around 650 million people watched Armstrong's first steps. During their 21-hour, 36-minute stay on the lunar surface, the crew photographed terrain, gathered samples, left goodwill messages from 73 countries, and deployed the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP). Placed five meters away from the main unit, the LR3 array of small mirrors required no electrical power. After the crew safely splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969, the LR3 remained fully functional. Today, scientists on Earth still aim lasers at its mirrors and calculate the time it takes for the light beams to return, providing precise measurements of the Moon’s orbit, shape, and changes based on Earth’s gravitational pull.
projectDetails.details: What It Does & How It Works The Mirror of Tranquility is an 8-page educational comic book that narrates the historic Apollo 11 mission and its ongoing scientific legacy. It guides readers visually from the July 16, 1969 launch at Cape Kennedy—fulfilling President John F. Kennedy’s 1961 vision—to the manual landing of the Lunar Module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969, watched by around 650 million people. It covers the 21-hour, 36-minute lunar stay, the deployment of the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP), and the safe splashdown in the Pacific Ocean near the USS Hornet on July 24, 1969, after a 195-hour, 18-minute, and 35-second flight. Finally, it illustrates how scientists on Earth today aim lasers at the Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LR3) mirror arrays on the Moon and calculate the time it takes for the light beams to return. Benefits & Intended Impact Accessible Science: Transforms complex orbital mechanics and mission timelines into an engaging visual story for students and the general public. Living History: Demonstrates how the LR3 still provides precise measurements of the Moon's orbit, shape, and changes based on Earth's gravitational pull. Human & Scientific Impact: Combines lunar sample collection and seismic and solar wind experiments with memorials and goodwill messages from 73 countries. How the Project is Creative Instead of a traditional historical overview, our project personifies the Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LR3) as the narrator and "Silent Hero" of Apollo 11. Placed about 5 meters away from the main EASEP unit, the LR3 was not attached to the main unit and required no electrical power, allowing it to remain fully functional today as a bridge between 1969 and modern astrophysics. Tools, Software & Resources Used NASA Data & Archives: Utilized Apollo 11 mission timelines, prime and backup crew records, and LR3 scientific documentation. Scripting & Documentation: Used Microsoft Word and Google Docs to structure the 8-page, 32-panel comic script and visual descriptions. Super Intelligence (SI) & Design Tools: Used Large Language Models (LLMs) for script structuring and translation, alongside digital design and illustration tools to create the comic panels. Factors Considered by the Team Historical Accuracy: Integrated exact mission timestamps, engine burn durations, and landing coordinates (0°41'15" N, 23°26' E) into the comic captions. Visual Pacing: Organized the story into 8 structured pages (4 panels per page), balancing technical spacecraft maneuvers with emotional human moments. SI Transparency: Followed NASA Space Apps guidelines regarding the disclosure and watermarking of any SI-assisted elements.

challengeDetails.title: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars

node.title: StarryNight
node.excerpt: A multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration, AI, and innovative problem-solving. We combine our technical skills and creativity to develop intelligent solutions that support safer and more efficient space missions.

projectDetails.name: StarryNight
projectDetails.summary:
**StarryNight** is an evidence-first fire-safety analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 challenge, *Flame in Freefall*. It transforms NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion experiments into actionable, traceable insights for spacecraft, the International Space Station (ISS), Moon and Mars habitats, and pressurized rovers.

The platform addresses a critical challenge: fire behaves differently in microgravity, while existing NASA experiments do not fully cover the oxygen concentrations, pressures, and partial-gravity conditions expected in future exploration habitats. StarryNight analyzes 24 NASA combustion investigations through an interactive web application featuring scenario evaluation, gravity bounds, habitat-specific investigation ranking, evidence comparisons, and an AI-powered analyst with clickable citations.

Its key innovation is combining deterministic, evidence-based verdicts with AI-generated explanations while preventing unsupported conclusions. When experimental evidence is insufficient, the platform explicitly communicates that limitation rather than guessing.

By making existing research accessible and exposing critical knowledge gaps, StarryNight supports safer spacecraft design, better-targeted experiments, and improved fire-safety decisions for future human space exploration.
projectDetails.details: StarryNight is a web app that turns NASA’s space fire experiments into clear fire-safety answers for spacecraft, the International Space Station, and future Moon and Mars bases. Future habitats are planned to use more oxygen at lower pressure, which makes materials easier to burn. NASA’s 263 solid-material space fire tests, however, were all run in ordinary cabin air at about zero gravity. A user picks a material and a place, or asks a question in plain words. StarryNight shows what NASA’s tests found, links every fact to the exact NASA record, and says clearly when no test covers the case instead of guessing. It also ranks NASA’s 24 combustion investigations for each type of habitat, maps conditions that have never been tested, and provides clean datasets for engineers and researchers. It is built only on NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics data, is live today, and is checked by 139 automated tests.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Delta Pulse: Reading the Nile Delta with NISAR Radar
projectDetails.summary:
Delta Pulse is an open, bilingual (English and Arabic) web map of the changing Nile Delta. The Delta holds most
of Egypt's farmland and tens of millions of people on low, soft ground. It faces five linked hazards that are
usually studied in separate papers: land subsidence, cities spreading onto farmland, coastal erosion, sea-level rise
and loss of stored water. Delta Pulse puts them on one interactive map built on NASA data, led by the new
NISAR L-band radar mission.
We processed 17 provisional NISAR interferograms (June–October 2026) and show NISAR and Sentinel-1 radar
imagery on the map. We also computed four results from NASA data: sea level off the Delta rose 3.51 ± 0.62
mm/yr (1993–2018); water storage over the Delta fell 0.28 ± 0.02 cm/yr (2003–2021); shoreline change from 2016
to 2026 by coastal sector; and 6,647 km² of land exposed to a 1 m sea-level rise. Every value sits next to the
published value it is checked against. Four months of NISAR data do not yet resolve city subsidence, and the site
says so plainly.
Planners, engineers, students and the public can explore the map, follow a five-chapter story, and ask an AI
interpreter that answers only from the site's own numbers.
projectDetails.details:
The Delta Pulse website: the Nile Delta on NASA satellite imagery.

Delta Pulse answers one question for the Nile Delta: where is the land under pressure, and why? It shows five layers on one map of the Delta, from Cairo to the Mediterranean coast (29.5–32.6°E, 30.0–31.7°N): 

  1. Land subsidence: NISAR L-band interferograms (our first look) beside published long-term rates for 12 cities. 
  2. Urban expansion: NISAR and Sentinel-1 radar imagery and a 2016 ⇄ 2026 optical swipe. 
  3. Coastal erosion: 2016 and 2026 shorelines and rates of change measured on 462 transects. 
  4. Sea-level rise: the sea-level trend off the Delta and maps of land exposed at +0.25, +0.5 and +1.0 m. 
  5. Water storage: GRACE/GRACE-FO trends for the Delta, the Western Desert and Sinai. 

The site explains how the hazards connect. Pumped groundwater and the weight of cities compact the soft ground, so the land sinks. Sinking land adds to the rising sea, and a coast with little river sediment retreats. One published example carries the story: at New Damietta the sea rises 3.42 mm/yr, but the tide gauge on land records 8.21 mm/yr, because the land under it sinks (Hassan et al. 2025). Our own sea-level trend plus the published land motion gives 7.3 ± 0.9 mm/yr, which agrees with the tide gauge. 

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Figure 1. Explore view: OPERA DSWx-HLS surface water with the 2016 ⇄ 2026 swipe, and the evidence panel for Damietta. Figure 1. Explore view: OPERA DSWx-HLS surface water with the 2016 ⇄ 2026 swipe, and the evidence panel for Damietta." ]

 

Figure 1. Explore view: OPERA DSWx-HLS surface water with the 2016 ⇄ 2026 swipe, and the evidence panel for Damietta. 

 

Figure 2. Published city subsidence rates on the map. Click any place to see its values and the source of each number. 

How to try it (for judges) 

  1. Open https://delta-pulse-web.vercel.app. The opening sequence flies from the globe to the Delta; press Skip to go straight to the map. 
  2. Explore: choose a layer in the left panel. Try "Coastal erosion" and drag the 2016 ⇄ 2026 divider, or "Sea-level rise" and switch between 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 m. 
  3. Click any place on the map. The right panel shows the values for that point and the source of each number. 
  4. Story: five short chapters in causal order (groundwater → subsidence → cities → sea → coast). 
  5. Data & limits: our value next to the published value for each result, the dataset list, and the caveats. 
  6. Ask the interpreter: for example "Why is Damietta at risk?" in English or Arabic. It answers only from the site's numbers and names their sources. 
  7. Use the language switch for the full Arabic (right-to-left) version, and the Simple ⇄ Scientist switch for more detail. 

How it works 

  • Data pipeline (Python). Scripts in the pipeline folder produce every number we show. Each output file records its method, source, period and caveats. 
  • NISAR interferometry. We read 17 consecutive 12-day NISAR GUNW pairs on two tracks (129 ascending, 007 descending), about 37 GB in total. We kept the largest connected component, masked coherence below 0.7, tested four ionosphere and troposphere correction options for each pair, converted phase to line-of-sight millimetres, and fitted rates. Each city (2.5 km radius) is measured against its surrounding ring (6–15 km) to remove water-vapour patches. 
  • Reading NASA GIBS tiles as data. For sea level, GRACE and surface water, we turn the colours of NASA GIBS map tiles back into values through their published colour tables. This needs no login and no bulk download. Values are exact to the colour bin (1 cm for sea level, 0.25 cm for GRACE). 
  • Trends. Linear trend fitted together with annual and semi-annual cycles. The standard error is corrected for autocorrelation. 
  • Shoreline. Seasonal water composites (June–September 2016 and 2026) from OPERA DSWx-HLS, with shore-normal transects every 500 m. 
  • Flood exposure. Copernicus DEM at 90 m. Land counts as exposed only when it is at or below the sea level and connected to the sea. 
  • Web app. A static site (Vite, plain JavaScript, MapLibre GL JS on a globe, three.js for the opening sequence) with NASA GIBS tiles loaded live. A small server function sends interpreter questions to Claude (Anthropic API). The key stays on the server, and requests are rate-limited. 
  • Citation-first check. An automated check rejects any value of ours that does not name the script and the output file that produced it.

Figure 3. Processing workflow: three open NASA data streams are retrieved, analysed and written to self-describing files. An automated check admits only values that can be traced to a script and an output file. 

What works now 

  • The live site with all five layers, story mode, click-for-evidence panel, data page, English and Arabic, and the Simple and Scientist views. 
  • Four results computed by our pipeline and checked against published values (section 6). 
  • The NISAR first look on two tracks, with its uncertainty shown. 
  • The AI interpreter, which answers in English or Arabic from the site's own numbers. 
  • A 14-page research manuscript that explains the methods and findings (section 7). 
  • Automated tests of the app and of the data rules. 

Limitations (stated in the app) 

  • NISAR products are provisional and will be reprocessed in 2027. Four months of data are too short to measure subsidence of a few mm/yr; the NISAR layer is a first look. 
  • Interferometry measures motion along the radar's line of sight, relative to a reference. Our city values are relative to their surroundings. 
  • GRACE resolution is about 300 km, larger than the Delta. It shows total water storage, not groundwater alone. 
  • The shoreline comes from optical data, so tide and waves affect it, and changes below about 3 m/yr are not resolved. 
  • Flood exposure is a screening scenario, not a forecast. The elevation model is accurate to metres and has no sea walls or drains. 
  • The urban layer shows imagery only; we have not yet computed built-up change. 
  • The causes of subsidence are hypotheses from published studies, not results of our work. 

Future plans 

  • Add NISAR pairs after 21 October 2026 as they are released; with one to two years of data, city rates should reach about 2 mm/yr. 
  • Process a redundant interferogram network and better troposphere corrections. 
  • Compute built-up change 2016 → 2026 from OPERA RTC-S1 and NISAR backscatter. 
  • Remove soil moisture (GLDAS) from GRACE to isolate groundwater. 
  • Rank bridges, canals and sea defences on steep subsidence gradients for inspection. 

Benefits and intended impact 

  • Planners and ministries: one map that shows which areas sink, which coasts retreat and which land is low enough to flood. 
  • Engineers: coastal transects that are still eroding 10–12 m/yr, and a path to ranking structures on steep subsidence gradients. 
  • Researchers and students: a reproducible NISAR workflow for a delta, with open code and every number traced to its source. 
  • The public and journalists: the story in plain Arabic and English, with no radar training needed. 

Tools, languages and software 

Python (NumPy, SciPy, h5py, pyproj, Pillow, tifffile, imagecodecs); JavaScript (Vite, MapLibre GL JS 6, three.js, Vitest); Node.js; Anthropic Claude API for the interpreter; ElevenLabs for narration; Vercel for hosting. 

What is creative 

  • Five hazards that are usually studied apart, joined in one causal story on one map. 
  • One of the first L-band (NISAR) interferometry looks at the Nile Delta. The studies we reviewed used C-band radar. 
  • Reading NASA GIBS map tiles as data, so a small team can compute trends without logins or bulk downloads. 
  • A citation-first rule enforced in code: no number on the site without a script or a paper behind it. 
  • A fully bilingual interface for the people who live in the Delta. 

Factors we considered 

Honesty about uncertainty, so the site shows a negative result instead of a false signal. Low bandwidth, so we read subsets and tiles instead of whole files. Arabic first-class, not a translation layer. Accessibility: reduced-motion support and Skip on the opening sequence. No credentials in the browser. 

5. Key equations 

Trend model (sea level and water storage): a linear trend b plus annual and semi-annual cycles, with t in years. 

y(t) = a + b·t + Σₖ₌₁² [ cₖ·cos(2πkt) + sₖ·sin(2πkt) ] 

Effective sample size. The residuals are autocorrelated, so the trend error uses n_eff instead of n. For sea level, r₁ = 0.848 and n = 948 give n_eff = 78.1. 

n_eff = n · (1 − r₁) / (1 + r₁) 

Radar phase to ground motion along the line of sight (NISAR L-band, λ ≈ 0.24 m). Negative values mean motion away from the satellite, which for subsidence is downward. 

d = −(λ / 4π) · φ 

Track consistency test between the ascending rate a and the descending rate b. This tests consistency, not resolution: two noisy estimates can agree because their errors are large. 

|a − b| ≤ 2 · √(σa² + σb²) 

How long NISAR must observe. Rate error for acquisitions spaced Δt over a span T, each with independent error σ. Scaling today's 7.9–26.6 mm/yr from T ≈ 0.33 yr gives about 2 mm/yr after 0.8–1.9 years. 

σb ≈ σ · √(12·Δt) · T^(−3/2) 

Relative sea-level budget at New Damietta. Our sea-level trend plus the published InSAR land motion matches the tide gauge (8.21 ± 1.1 mm/yr). 

3.51 + 3.8 = 7.3 ± 0.9 mm/yr

How to read the NISAR result. The errors are as large as, or larger than, the published rates, so no city rate is resolved yet. At Mansoura and Alexandria the two tracks disagree in sign; the ascending track implies uplift, which points to water-vapour and soil-moisture phase errors. A city sinking 3–20 mm/yr moves only about 1–7 mm in four months. This honest negative result shows how long the NISAR record must be, and which corrections it needs. 

7. Research paper

We wrote up the methods and findings as a 14-page research manuscript in journal form:

"An Open Multi-Hazard Assessment of the Nile Delta from NASA Data, with a First Look at NISAR L-Band Interferometry"

Ali A. Khalil, Dyeie H. Hamid and Ahmed S. Ellaban, College of Computer Science, Damietta University

It covers the study area, data, every processing step with its equations, the results with figures and tables, a comparison with published studies, the physical drivers, and an estimate of how long the NISAR record must be before city subsidence can be measured.

projectDetails.name: StellarOp Mission Lab
projectDetails.summary:
What did we build? StellarOp Mission Lab is a game that runs in any web browser. One to four players design,
launch and fly one complete space mission together. Each player takes a role: Science Lead, Communications
Lead, Spacecraft Engineer or Mission Planner. Each role watches a short briefing from a guide, then the team
chooses instruments, antenna, ground stations, power, battery, orbit and launch vehicle.
What problem does it solve? Students rarely get to try a whole mission, from the first idea to operations. Real
missions are a set of trade-offs: more instruments need more power, more data needs a bigger antenna, a
heavier satellite needs a bigger rocket. Mission Lab lets beginners feel these trade-offs by playing them.
How does it answer the challenge? The challenge asks for a game where a team designs, manages and
simulates a space mission. In Mission Lab every choice costs mass, power, data, budget or lifetime. The
mission then flies in 3D, random events test the design, and a final report explains why the mission succeeded
or failed and compares it with the real NASA mission it is based on.
Who could it help, and why does it matter? Students, teachers and anyone curious about how missions are
planned. It teaches mission design by doing, in plain English and Egyptian Arabic, and a wrong choice is
explained instead of only marked wrong
projectDetails.details:
What it does StellarOp Mission Lab takes a team through one complete space mission, from the first idea to the final report. The team reads real mission facts in short briefings, makes design choices that each cost mass, power, data, budget or lifetime, launches, flies the mission in 3D, handles surprises, and learns why the mission worked or failed. Main task. Input: the team's choices (instruments, antenna, ground stations, power, battery, orbit, launch vehicle) and their votes on events. Process: the game adds up mass, power, data, budget and lifetime, checks them against the mission needs and the rocket capacity, then simulates the flight. Output: a live 3D flight, a score out of 1000, stars, a decision table with reasons, and a comparison with the real NASA mission. How the game is played, screen by screen The screenshots below come from the live game at https://mohamdkhaldd.github.io/stellarop-mission-lab/. They follow one player through Level 1 (Khamsin Storm Watch), from the first page to the certificate

Opening the game The game starts on the home screen. The team chooses how to play: Play Solo, Team on One Computer, Online Team (each player on their own laptop) or Mission Architect (6 more missions and a Sandbox). The strip at the bottom shows the four moves of every level: watch your guide, write on the team board, decide together, launch and see who you helped
Signing in (optional) The Sign in button in the top bar opens the player account window, where a player can use Google or an email and password. Nothing is blocked without it; signing in only saves finished levels so they follow the player to any device
Choosing a level Next, the team picks a level. The four levels follow NASA JPL's Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1 to 4); each is a different real mission and each is harder than the one before. Level 1 is open. The others unlock when the team earns at least one star, but judges and teachers can press Unlock all levels to open every level at once
The briefings Inside a level, the team starts with the briefings. Each role has a guide, and the Mission Director gives the first one (briefing 1 of 5 in the picture). The guide's video lasts about a minute and gives the real numbers for that role. The script is shown under the video, with the numbers highlighted. When a video ends, the player writes the numbers on the shared team board, because later screens show names only. The Next briefing button moves on to the next guide. When all briefings are done, the team talks together about what everyone learned, and then moves on to the design. Watching a video again costs 20 points
Designing the satellite After the discussion, the team makes its design choices. Each role has its own questions (Science Lead, Communications Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Mission Planner). In the picture the Communications Lead chooses between a slow and a fast antenna, and the answer depends on the numbers written on the team board. The 3D satellite changes with every part the team adds. The team starts with 1,000 points and loses points for needs not met, wasted parts, damage in flight, space junk, extra design reviews and rewatching videos. The first design review is free and shows hidden problems. When every role has chosen, the team presses Launch
Launch The launch starts with real NASA/SpaceX footage (the PACE launch on Falcon 9, 2024), then the game switches to the 3D flight. A satellite that is too heavy for its rocket falls. The bars at the bottom show the spacecraft's health and the team's points
Surprises in flight During the flight, 2 to 3 random events appear. This one is Eclipse season: for about an hour each night, Earth's shadow covers the satellite. The team talks, then votes. The best answer depends on the parts they chose; here the satellite has solar panels and a battery, so the team decides how to get through the shadow
Who used the data When the flight ends, the game shows the user segment: who used the mission's data. For Level 1 these are Egypt's weather forecasters, airports and people with asthma. This teaches the four segments NASA uses for every mission: launch, space, ground and users
The mission report Then the report appears. It shows the stars (400, 700 and 900 points) and whether the needs were met. A table lists every decision, the points it cost and why. The report also lists what the team did well and what to fix next time, and it compares the design with the real NASA mission, with a 3D model of that mission. The team can redesign and fly again
The certificate At the end, the team writes its names and downloads a certificate of mission success for that level. Then the team goes back to the level screen and plays the next level

projectDetails.name: aegis space
projectDetails.summary:
Crew Health in Orbit

AegisSpace is an AI system that protects astronaut health on long space missions. It monitors the crew around the clock, predicts health problems before they happen, recommends the right response, and trains the doctors who will handle those situations. Its tagline is Monitor. Predict. Protect.

The Problem

In space, an astronaut is far from any hospital, while the body is under constant strain from radiation, low gravity, isolation and psychological stress, weakened immunity, and oxygen risks. A small issue can escalate quickly. The project aims to catch danger early and reduce risk to the crew.

Continuous monitoring: Sensors track vital signs at all times, including heart rate, . The system watches five core risks: low gravity, isolation stress, immunity suppression.
Prediction: An LSTM model  analyzes vitals trends and forecasts where they are heading. It raises an early warning before a reading enters the risk zone.
Protocols and approval: The system picks the best-matching protocol from a library covering low oxygen. A human supervisor approves it with one tap, and only then does the action run automatically. The final decision always stays with a person.
Simulation lab: Before anything touches the real crew, several options are tested on a digital twin of the astronaut and compared. Testing carries zero risk to the real crew.
Doctor training: The AI generates mission scenarios, a doctor responds on a virtual patient.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works
AegisSpace is an AI system that protects astronaut health on long-duration missions, where medical help is far away. It works in five stages:

  1. Monitor: Sensors track vitals such as heart rate, oxygen, temperature, sleep, and breathing, along with five core space risks: radiation, low gravity, isolation stress, immunity suppression, and low oxygen.
  2. Predict: An LSTM neural network learns from vitals trends over time and forecasts where they are heading, raising an early warning before a reading enters the risk zone.
  3. Protocol and approve: The system selects the best-matching response from a protocol library (low oxygen, heart rhythm, fatigue, radiation spike). A human supervisor approves it with one tap, and only then does it run automatically.
  4. Simulate: Before anything reaches the real crew, several options are tested on a digital twin of the astronaut and compared, so the best one is applied with zero risk to the real crew.
  5. Train: The AI generates mission scenarios, a doctor responds on a virtual patient, and the AI scores the response and coaches the doctor with instant feedback.

Benefits

  • Early detection, with warnings before a condition worsens.
  • Human-approved safety, because no automated action runs without supervisor approval.
  • Safe decision-making, since options are tested on the digital twin first.
  • Better-prepared medical staff through continuous practice on realistic scenarios.

Intended impact
Healthier crews and safer missions. By shifting from reacting to emergencies to predicting them, AegisSpace aims to reduce risk on long-duration missions, where evacuation is not an option. The same approach could later support remote and isolated medical settings on Earth.

Tools and technologies
The forecasting core is based on an LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) recurrent neural network for time-series prediction. [Add your actual stack here: programming language, libraries, frameworks, hardware or sensors, and the tools used for the presentation and visuals.]

What makes it creative
Most health systems only display data. AegisSpace closes the whole loop in one system: it senses, predicts, recommends, simulates, and trains. Pairing automation with mandatory human approval, and using a digital twin as a risk-free testing ground, make it both practical and safe. Using the same AI to train the next generation of doctors adds a layer that monitoring tools usually lack.

Factors our team considered

  • Safety first: the human supervisor keeps the final decision.
  • Trust and transparency: the system suggests a protocol and shows its reasoning rather than acting on its own.
  • Isolation: the design assumes limited communication with Earth.
  • Risk-free validation: every option is tested on the digital twin before it reaches a real person.
  • Honest data: all numbers shown in our presentation are illustrative, not real medical data.

projectDetails.name: Project Supernova-X
projectDetails.summary:
Our team selected NASA’s “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” challenge and developed FireLens, an interactive web application that combines satellite fire detections into a consistent historical record.

MODIS and VIIRS differ in resolution, sensitivity, and observation schedules, making direct comparisons unreliable. FireLens addresses this through a transparent harmonization pipeline that processes NASA FIRMS data, aligns detections spatially and temporally, and adjusts sensor-specific biases.

Using PostgreSQL/PostGIS, FastAPI, and Next.js, FireLens provides an interactive map and Burning Activity Calendar. Users can explore historical fire activity, identify seasonal patterns, compare observations with historical baselines, detect anomalies, and export results.

Our goal is to support emergency responders, researchers, and decision-makers with reliable historical fire information for better analysis and resource planning.

FireLens focuses on historical analysis rather than fire prediction, emphasizing transparency, validation, and uncertainty assessment. During the hackathon, we aim to deliver a functional MVP demonstrating the complete workflow from NASA satellite data to an accessible, user-friendly dashboard.
projectDetails.details:
FireLens – Project Details

FireLens is an interactive web application developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to address the “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” challenge. It transforms satellite fire detection records from NASA FIRMS into a unified, comparable historical dataset.

How It Works

FireLens processes MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data through a harmonization pipeline that filters detections, standardizes spatial and temporal information, and accounts for differences in sensor sensitivity and resolution. The processed data is stored in a geospatial database and presented through an interactive dashboard.

Users can:

  • Explore historical fire activity on an interactive map.
  • View a Burning Activity Calendar to identify seasonal trends.
  • Compare fire activity against historical averages.
  • Identify unusual activity through anomaly analysis.
  • Export data as CSV for further research.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React-Leaflet, and Recharts.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, PostGIS, and Supabase.
  • Data Processing: Python, Pandas, and geospatial analysis tools.
  • Data Sources: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS).
  • Collaboration: GitHub and Discord.

Creativity and Innovation

Rather than simply displaying satellite hotspots, FireLens transforms observations from different sensors into a consistent historical perspective. Its combination of sensor harmonization, interactive geospatial visualization, seasonal analysis, and anomaly detection makes complex satellite data easier to interpret.

Intended Impact

FireLens aims to help researchers, emergency responders, and decision-makers understand historical fire patterns, support resource planning, and improve environmental monitoring.

Key Considerations

Our team prioritized data reliability, transparency, sensor differences, geographic accuracy, usability, and scalability. We also considered the limited hackathon development time and focused on delivering a functional end-to-end solution.

FireLens does not predict future fires. Instead, it provides an accessible, data-driven foundation for understanding historical burning activity and identifying meaningful changes over time.
