projectDetails.name: SURVORA
projectDetails.summary:
**SURVORA** is an interactive educational space survival game designed to transform complex space engineering concepts into engaging, hands-on experiences for young learners.

Developed for NASA's **Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer** challenge, SURVORA places players in command of a Martian outpost, where they must manage critical resources such as oxygen, power, water, and food while protecting their crew from environmental hazards.

Unlike traditional STEM learning tools, SURVORA introduces realistic engineering trade-offs through interactive missions. Players face challenges such as oxygen shortages, power failures, and Martian dust storms, where every decision affects the colony's survival.

The game combines strategic base management with third-person exploration, mission-based progression, and **NOVA**, an AI-powered educational companion that provides contextual guidance and scientific explanations grounded in NASA research and data.

By integrating NASA scientific resources into an accessible simulation, SURVORA bridges the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical decision-making.

**Our mission is to inspire the next generation of space explorers by making science something students don't just study, but experience.**
projectDetails.details:
SURVORA — Project Details

What We Developed

SURVORA is an interactive 3D educational survival and exploration game developed for NASA's Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Designed for students aged 7–12, it transforms complex space engineering concepts into engaging, hands-on learning experiences.

Players become commanders of a Martian outpost, responsible for managing critical systems such as oxygen generation, electricity, water recycling, food production, and crew safety. Through interactive missions, they face challenges including oxygen shortages, power failures, Martian dust storms, and environmental hazards.

How It Works

SURVORA combines two interconnected gameplay experiences:

Mars Base Management: Players build and manage their colony, allocate limited resources, and make engineering decisions that directly affect mission survival. For example, when oxygen production decreases due to insufficient power, players must decide whether to redirect electricity from research facilities to life-support systems.

Exploration and Missions: Players explore the Martian environment through third-person gameplay, investigate scientific locations, interact with equipment, collect samples, and complete missions to earn Knowledge Points and unlock upgrades.

Every mission follows a learning cycle: Observe → Analyze → Decide → Experience the Consequences → Learn.

AI-Powered Learning with NOVA

One of SURVORA's key innovations is NOVA, an AI-powered educational companion integrated into the learning experience.

NOVA uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to combine the player's current game context with scientific information from NASA and other space-agency resources.

Instead of simply giving answers, NOVA provides contextual explanations, progressive hints, and scientific references that help players understand why their decisions succeed or fail.

The AI provides guidance, while the Unity simulation remains responsible for resource calculations and gameplay outcomes.

NASA Data and Scientific Integration

SURVORA incorporates scientific knowledge from NASA's Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), MOXIE Mars oxygen-production experiment, Mars exploration research, and space-weather resources such as NASA DONKI.

These resources inform educational explanations and mission scenarios involving life support, solar energy, radiation awareness, and planetary exploration.

We distinguish real scientific observations from simplified gameplay simulations to maintain scientific accuracy while keeping the experience accessible to younger students.

Technologies Used

  • Game Development: Unity 3D and C#.
  • AI Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, and Google Gemini.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation: BM25, ChromaDB, and Sentence Transformers.
  • Scientific Data: NASA research publications, documented scientific datasets, and curated knowledge resources.
  • 3D Development: Low-poly 3D environments, Martian colony structures, exploration assets, and interactive interfaces.

Creativity, Benefits, and Impact

SURVORA's innovation lies in combining strategic resource management, third-person exploration, and context-aware AI guidance within a single educational experience.

Rather than teaching space science through passive explanations, SURVORA allows students to experience engineering trade-offs firsthand. Every decision has consequences, encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, systems thinking, and scientific curiosity.

Throughout development, our team prioritized scientific credibility, age-appropriate gameplay, accessibility, engaging visual design, and meaningful connections between player choices and educational outcomes.

Our goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers by making space education interactive, accessible, and exciting.

With SURVORA, students don't just learn how a space mission works — they experience what it takes to keep one alive.

projectDetails.summary:
EarthScope is an existing climate dashboard upgraded in place. The project combines a FastAPI service and a single-page HTML/JavaScript interface (Chart.js, deck.gl, and MapLibre) with a normalized SQLite archive of NASA POWER Daily data. The refreshed build adds seven locations to the original cohort, expanding coverage to twelve cities in twelve countries; it also adds coverage, comparison, trend, and 48-series estimate panels and records a reproducible model-evaluation suite.
The archive contains 446,364 daily-variable observations. All 48 location-variable series have zero missing normalized values under the stated qualification rule, with no interpolation. The suite uses chronological model selection, calibration, and held-out test periods. Its metrics and trends are retrospective, descriptive results; they do not establish causation, predict disasters, or constitute operational forecasts or official warnings.
projectDetails.details:
rovide details about your project. Consider the following questions: What does it do or how does it work? What benefits does it have? What is the intended impact of the project? What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? How is your project creative? What factors did your team consider?

Project details: EarthScope

EarthScope is a web-based tool for exploring environmental change over time. The challenge it addresses is how to select Earth-science variables, visualize how they change, and understand what is changing, where it is changing, and by how much. EarthScope brings data, maps, charts, comparisons, and historical analysis together in one dashboard.

What it does and how it works

Users can choose among four daily variables—air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and corrected precipitation—and explore them for twelve city locations in twelve countries. The project includes a SQLite archive of 446,364 daily-variable observations from NASA POWER, as well as a live-data mode and a clearly labelled simulated demo mode.

The dashboard displays selected data in a map, readings table, and time-series charts. Its archive tools report data coverage and completeness, compare locations over a shared date range, and calculate annual and seasonal summaries. Annual trend slopes are calculated using complete calendar years. The project also includes 48 one-day, archive-origin statistical estimates—one per location and variable—with results evaluated against held-out historical data.

Benefits and intended impact

EarthScope makes a large environmental dataset easier to explore without requiring users to query a database or write analysis code themselves. It helps users compare locations, inspect changes over time, and see data coverage and limitations alongside the results. The intended impact is to support learning and early-stage environmental analysis by making historical data and its interpretation more accessible and transparent.

Tools and technologies

The project was developed using Python for the data processing, analysis, and backend; FastAPI for the API; SQLite for the historical archive; and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser dashboard. It uses NASA POWER Daily data, with MapLibre/deck.gl for map visualization and Chart.js for charts. The model suite uses statistical methods, including ridge regression, and pytest for automated tests. Development and use require a standard computer and web browser; no specialized hardware is needed.

What is creative about the project

EarthScope combines historical data access, comparison, visual exploration, trend summaries, and model evaluation in one application. It also makes data provenance, completeness, and scientific caveats part of the experience rather than presenting results without context. The incident panel provides a demonstration of explainable threshold rules, while explicitly identifying them as prototypes rather than official warnings.

Factors the team considered

The team considered data quality, missing values, units, date alignment, geographic coverage, reproducibility, and how to communicate uncertainty. NASA POWER values are gridded estimates at the selected city coordinates, not station readings or national averages. The trend slopes are descriptive and do not test statistical significance or establish causes. The one-day estimates are not operational weather forecasts and do not predict disasters. Prototype incident levels are not official warnings, and the incident workflow does not contact emergency services.

The current version addresses parts of the challenge—manual selection from four variables, visualization, and location-level descriptive rates of change—but does not yet test trend significance, search a broad catalogue of Earth-science variables, map continuous regional patterns, or identify causal drivers.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: COSMO AI-health companion
projectDetails.summary: COSMO is a voice-first AI health companion that lives in an astronaut’s wrist device and projects a holographic screen. On long missions, crews are far from Earth, communication is delayed, and there is no doctor on board. COSMO reads data from a wearable band and smart shirt, learns what “normal” looks like for one specific astronaut, and notices when their readings drift away from it, often before they feel anything. It then talks with them out loud: it asks how they feel, checks their readings, walks them through approved self-care steps taken from NASA’s own countermeasure lists, rechecks, and logs everything for the flight surgeon.  COSMO covers both physical and mental health. It explores feelings before suggesting anything, remembers what helps each astronaut, has a real sense of humor, and switches to simple yes/no questions when an astronaut is alone in an emergency. Medical decisions always come from a fixed, reviewable rulebook, never from the AI, so the system stays safe and predictable while still feeling like a crewmate you can talk to about anything.  Our working prototype is a website that simulates the full device using real research data (NASA’s Inspiration4 lab data and physiological recordings from PhysioNet), a 3D holographic body, live voice conversation, and an AI language model.
projectDetails.details:
COSMO — Your Companion Beyond Earth

What does it do and how does it work?

COSMO is an AI-powered health and wellbeing companion designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It monitors vital signs, learns each astronaut's personal health baseline, detects unusual deviations, and interacts with astronauts through natural voice conversations.

COSMO works through three layers:

  1. Health Monitoring and Learning: It processes heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, breathing rate, skin temperature, stress index, and activity data. It builds an individual baseline for each astronaut and detects unusual changes relative to their normal patterns. Baseline learning pauses when readings appear abnormal to prevent unusual conditions from becoming the new normal.
  2. Safety and Decision Layer: A deterministic rule engine evaluates health deviations and reported symptoms, identifies conditions requiring attention, and provides predefined response steps informed by NASA Human Research Program research. Medical workflows are controlled by predefined rules, not generated by AI.
  3. AI Companion: Astronauts can communicate with COSMO using voice through the wake phrase "Hey COSMO". A dialogue manager handles safety-critical interactions, while Google Gemini 2.5 Flash handles general conversation, contextual questions, and emotional support. COSMO also remembers permitted personal preferences and previous helpful activities to make interactions more personalized.

The platform demonstrates these capabilities through an interactive 3D human body, live health dashboards, proactive alerts, voice conversations, mental wellness check-ins, simulated medical scenarios, and a mission log with an Earth communication and synchronization queue.

What benefits does it have?

COSMO offers several benefits:

  • Detects unusual health changes using individual baselines rather than relying exclusively on population averages.
  • Provides consistent initial guidance without requiring immediate communication with Earth.
  • Supports psychological wellbeing through personalized conversations, voluntary check-ins, relaxation activities, and emotional support.
  • Maintains a record of relevant health events for review by flight surgeons.
  • Supports continued local monitoring and event logging during communication interruptions.

What is the intended impact of the project?

COSMO aims to improve astronaut health awareness and psychological wellbeing during long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. By combining personalized monitoring, structured safety workflows, and AI companionship, it explores how astronauts could receive continuous support despite communication delays and isolation from Earth. Its long-term approach could also benefit people working in other isolated environments, such as submarines, remote research stations, and distant medical facilities.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D visualization: Three.js and React Three Fiber.
  • Data visualization: Recharts.
  • Voice interaction: Web Speech API for speech recognition and synthesis.
  • AI language model: Google Gemini 2.5 Flash through OpenRouter.
  • Backend and data processing: Node.js scripts.
  • Deployment: Vercel.
  • Testing: 210 automated tests covering dialogue and safety workflows.
  • Research: NASA Human Research Program resources and space-health research recordings.

The current prototype uses simulated sensor readings and replayed research recordings. No physical wearable devices or spacecraft hardware are connected.

How is your project creative?

COSMO combines personalized health monitoring, proactive voice interaction, mental wellness support, and 3D health visualization in one astronaut-facing companion. Its most distinctive feature is the separation between conversational AI and safety-critical decisions: a controlled rule engine manages predefined medical workflows, while the language model provides natural conversation without being allowed to override safety procedures.

COSMO also learns individual health patterns, initiates check-ins when unusual changes occur, and uses personal context to make its support more meaningful. This transforms the traditional health-monitoring dashboard into an interactive companion designed around both the physical and psychological challenges of spaceflight.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered:

  • Astronaut safety and the need for medically reviewed response protocols.
  • Individual physiological differences and the importance of personal baselines.
  • Psychological challenges such as isolation, confinement, stress, and disrupted sleep.
  • Communication delays and the need for local operation when Earth is unavailable.
  • Privacy and protection of personal health and emotional information.
  • Ease of use during stressful or demanding mission conditions.
  • Hardware, computing, and connectivity limitations in spacecraft.
  • Scientific reliability and the distinction between simulated data, research findings, and clinically validated medical procedures.

COSMO is currently a research prototype, and its illustrative medical protocols require review by qualified medical professionals before operational use.

projectDetails.name: Project T3ban-Abdel_Rahem
projectDetails.summary:
OrbitFlame is a project developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the "Flame in Freefall" challenge.

Our project explores how combustion behaves in microgravity and how reduced gravity affects flame characteristics compared with conditions on Earth.

By making space-based combustion research more accessible and understandable, OrbitFlame aims to help students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore the scientific importance of studying flames in microgravity.

The project highlights the relevance of combustion research to spacecraft fire safety and our understanding of physical processes in space.
projectDetails.details:
OrbitFlame is an interactive research dashboard that helps researchers, engineers, and students discover, compare, and understand NASA’s microgravity combustion investigations. It addresses a central challenge: turning complex, scattered experimental information into clear, traceable insights relevant to spacecraft fire safety.

Users can explore investigations by research topic and fuel family, understand why a study is relevant, and compare two or three investigations side by side. Comparisons distinguish research objectives, experimental variables, described measurements, available dataset fields, and interpretation limits.

The prototype includes four curated investigations—FLEX, BASS, BASS-II, and SPICE—and document retrieval over 81 passages from three NASA reports. Retrieved evidence includes links to original PDF pages. A measurement explorer displays 12 reviewed FLEX records, preserving units and missing values.

OrbitFlame uses Flutter and Dart for the web interface, ASP.NET Core and C# for the backend, and Python with Poppler for offline document processing and source checks. BM25 retrieves relevant passages. A configurable language-model adapter supports retrieval-augmented generation, with response-format and citation-ID validation. Without a configured model, the dashboard provides clearly labeled source excerpts and curated comparison summaries.

The project’s creative contribution is connecting study discovery, comparison, document evidence, and numerical exploration within one research workflow. Its intended impact is to reduce the effort required to identify useful evidence and understand its applicability to fire prevention, detection, and suppression.

We considered scientific traceability, differences between experimental conditions, incomplete data, measurement definitions, and the distinction between observed findings and generated interpretation. Future development includes hybrid retrieval, broader study coverage, and scenario-based evidence assessment. The current prototype supports research interpretation rather than validated predictions of new fire scenarios.

That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: T -60 seconds
projectDetails.summary:
T -60 Seconds is a co-op web game where 1-4 players learn how real space missions are designed. A disease threatens Earth, and the cure must come from space, so the crew plans and flies three missions: the ISS, the Moon and Mars. Each mission begins with a short educational cutscene.

In the design phase, players take engineering roles and follow the stages NASA uses to mature a mission concept: concept, feasibility, trade studies, point design and a flight readiness review. They vote on objectives and spacecraft, balance shared limits on mass, power and cost, and pack supplies. In the mission phase, they watch space through a capsule window while crises inspired by real NASA incidents, such as solar flares and communication loss, strike. Players must diagnose and repair systems together, while a mission tracker shows progress.

The game addresses the challenge by turning mission design into hands-on trade-offs, not reading. It matters because it teaches teamwork, risk management and engineering decisions to the next generation of space explorers.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

T -60 seconds is a co-op web game where 1-4 players learn how real space missions are designed. A disease threatens Earth and the cure must come from space, so the crew plans and flies three missions: the ISS, the Moon and Mars. Short video cutscenes introduce each destination.

In the design phase, each player takes an engineering role and the team works through the stages NASA uses to mature a mission: concept, feasibility, trade studies, point design and a flight readiness review. Players vote on objectives and spacecraft and balance shared limits on budget, mass and power. They also check life support, communications and redundancy, then pack their resources. In the mission phase, they look out of a capsule window while events based on real NASA missions strike, such as solar flares, communication loss and power shortages. The team must diagnose and fix each one before time runs out. A mission-progress view tracks the flight, and a final debrief explains how their design decisions shaped the outcome.

Benefits and impact

Beginners usually learn mission design as separate theory. Our game lets them feel how mass, power, cost and risk affect each other, and how teamwork decides the result. We want students and space enthusiasts to leave with a simple understanding of systems engineering and an interest in aerospace careers.

Tools

React, TypeScript and Vite for the game, Firebase Realtime Database for game-code rooms and live co-op, and GitHub Pages for hosting. [Add: Three.js for the mission tracker, and any NASA APIs you actually connected.] We used OpenCode and GitHub Copilot as AI coding assistants, and our own review and testing. No special hardware is needed, only a browser.

Creativity

Instead of sliders and menus, the game puts players inside a capsule with a view of space, where warnings appear as risk grows. Roles force real negotiation, and every crisis comes from a real NASA incident.

Factors we considered

Accessibility for beginners (little text, visual feedback), a solo demo mode for single players, accuracy (game units, with NASA sources for real claims), and sound and motion controls.

projectDetails.summary:
LunaQuest: Survival Mission is a browser-based educational game built by Team Tantaropic for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.” It addresses a gap in space education: young learners often discover facts about space without experiencing the decisions that keep an astronaut alive.
Designed for children ages 7–12, LunaQuest lets players manage a fictional lunar outpost by balancing food, water, oxygen and energy. They grow crops, recycle oxygen, maintain equipment and respond to simulated solar storms and an oxygen leak. Chicken Hunt, a fictional arcade supply mission, connects fast-paced play with survival: safely returned food becomes part of the base’s shared resources. Short learning guides explain each system, while NASA DONKI observations provide real solar-activity context alongside a clearly labeled historical demo.
LunaQuest is designed to make preparation and resource trade-offs understandable and enjoyable, encouraging curiosity about science and engineering. Its classroom learning impact remains a goal for future testing.
projectDetails.details:
What we built and how it works

LunaQuest: Survival Mission is a browser-based educational game created by Team Tantaropic for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.” It helps children ages 7–12 explore the decisions involved in keeping a fictional lunar outpost alive.

Players balance food, water, oxygen and energy across five facilities: the Habitat, Greenhouse, Solar Array, Shelter and Landing Pad. They grow crops, recycle oxygen, repair equipment, collect Earth supplies and respond to scripted solar storms and an oxygen leak. Each action has a resource cost, so players must plan ahead.

Chicken Hunt connects arcade entertainment with this survival loop. Players spend six energy to launch a 35-second fictional supply mission, dodge alien birds and collect food. A safe return adds cargo to the base’s shared resources; destruction forfeits it. Seven short learning guides explain each system through “What?”, “Why?” and “Your Mission.”

Benefits and intended impact

LunaQuest is designed to make space-system trade-offs understandable and enjoyable. Players can practice preparation, prioritization and recovery from mistakes rather than only memorizing facts. Our intended impact is to encourage STEM curiosity and support future classroom learning; educational outcomes have not yet been measured.

Tools and development

We used Phaser, TypeScript, React and Vite to build the game, GitHub for source management, Vercel for hosting, and Vitest and Playwright for testing tools. The reviewed build passed 156 unit tests and its production build.

Codex and Antigravity assisted with coding and implementation. Our team originated the idea, designed the architecture, ran tests and debugged the solution. No specialized hardware is required to play.

Creativity and design considerations

Our creative approach combines a connected urvival economy, arcade supply missions and learning at the moment of action. NASA DONKI observations provide real solar-activity context, with a clearly labeled historical fallback. They do not control game emergencies or predict lunar radiation exposure.

We considered age-appropriate language, keyboard and touch controls, browser-local saves, adjustable audio, clear resource feedback and reliable play when NASA data is unavailable. Scientific accuracy and transparency guided us: game values are illustrative, arcade combat is fictional, and long-term resource balance remains a prototype limitation.

projectDetails.name: TAREEQ – Martian Map: Intelligent Navigation for Mars Exploration
projectDetails.summary: TAREEQ is an interactive Mars-mapping and route-planning prototype for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It brings global 3D context together with a 2D map where users can inspect map layers, measure point-to-point distances, choose start and destination points, and compare Greedy, Uniform-Cost Search, and A* route options using elevation and slope costs. For the Jezero study area, TAREEQ uses a 20 m CTX digital terrain model and its matching 6 m orthophoto; elsewhere, it uses global MOLA topography at much coarser resolution. The goal is to make route trade-offs and their data sources easier to understand before a Mars surface excursion. This is a research prototype, not a certified navigation or rover-scale hazard-avoidance system.
projectDetails.details:
TAREEQ

Explore Mars. Understand Its Terrain. Navigate Beyond Earth.

The Problem

Exploring Mars is not simply about reaching a destination. It is about understanding the environment before attempting to navigate it.

The Martian surface is complex and diverse, containing steep slopes, craters, rocky formations, and potentially hazardous terrain.

Although NASA and other space agencies provide valuable scientific datasets about Mars, understanding and combining these datasets can be challenging.

Explorers need more than a map showing where places are. They need a way to understand the terrain, identify potential hazards, evaluate different routes, and make informed navigation decisions.

The challenge is turning complex Martian geospatial data into an understandable and interactive exploration experience.

Our Solution — TAREEQ

TAREEQ is an interactive Martian exploration and navigation platform designed to transform scientific Mars datasets into an immersive and understandable experience.

The platform combines a Mission Control Dashboard with an interactive 3D Martian environment, allowing users to explore a selected region of Mars, investigate its terrain, and plan routes between two locations.

Instead of presenting scientific data as isolated maps and measurements, VYRA brings different geospatial layers together in one unified environment.

Users can select a starting point and a destination, analyze the surrounding terrain, and compare multiple navigation alternatives based on distance, terrain difficulty, and potential risks.

Our goal is to make Martian exploration more visual, accessible, and data-driven.

Core Features

1. Mission Control Dashboard

A centralized interface that provides access to the exploration environment, mission information, terrain data, and navigation tools.

2. Immersive 3D Martian Terrain

An interactive three-dimensional representation of a selected Martian region, allowing users to zoom, rotate, and explore the surface.

3. Multi-Layer Geospatial Visualization

VYRA integrates five complementary layers:

  • Surface Imagery: Visual representation of the Martian surface.
  • Elevation: Terrain height and topographic variations.
  • Slope: Identification of steep and potentially difficult terrain.
  • Hazard: Representation of potential navigation obstacles.
  • Scientific Interest: Locations and regions with scientific exploration value.

4. Interactive Location Selection

Users can select their starting point and destination directly on the map using their mouse.

5. Intelligent Route Planning

VYRA uses the A* search algorithm and a terrain-based Cost Grid to calculate and compare three navigation alternatives:

  • Shortest Route: Prioritizes minimum travel distance.
  • Balanced Route: Balances distance and terrain difficulty.
  • Lowest-Risk Route: Prioritizes lower estimated navigation risk.

The result is a more informed approach to exploring the Martian surface.


Scientific Data & NASA Sources

VYRA is designed around real planetary geospatial datasets, with a focus on combining different sources of Martian surface information.

Our data exploration and integration workflow focuses on:

1. MOLA — Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter
Provides global elevation measurements that help us understand the large-scale topography of Mars.

2. CTX — Context Camera
Provides surface imagery that helps visualize Martian geological features and regional terrain characteristics.

3. HiRISE — High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment
Provides high-resolution orbital imagery and terrain products for detailed regional exploration.

4. HRSC — High Resolution Stereo Camera
Provides topographic and imaging products useful for analyzing Martian surface structures.

5. THEMIS — Thermal Emission Imaging System
Provides thermal and visible imaging data that contribute to geological and surface characterization.

Data Processing

Our geospatial workflow is designed to:

  • Inspect and validate raster datasets.
  • Check spatial reference systems (CRS).
  • Verify spatial resolution and coverage.
  • Process elevation data into terrain representations.
  • Derive slope information from elevation models.
  • Integrate geospatial layers into a unified navigation environment.

We distinguish between verified scientific observations, derived terrain indicators, and simulated data used for development and demonstration.

Technology Stack

VYRA combines modern web development technologies with geospatial processing tools.

Frontend

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Three.js
  • React Three Fiber

Backend

  • Python
  • FastAPI

Geospatial Processing

  • Rasterio
  • GDAL
  • GeoPandas
  • NumPy

Navigation & Algorithms

  • A* Search Algorithm
  • Cost Grid
  • Terrain-Based Route Optimization

System Architecture

The frontend provides the interactive exploration experience, while the backend handles geospatial processing, terrain analysis, and route calculation.

The system is designed to connect scientific raster datasets with interactive visualization and navigation services.

What Makes TAREEQ Different?

VYRA is not just another planetary visualization tool.

Its main idea is to connect scientific understanding with practical exploration.

Instead of simply displaying the Martian surface, VYRA brings together:

  • Immersive 3D terrain exploration.
  • Multiple scientific geospatial layers.
  • Interactive destination selection.
  • Algorithm-based route planning.
  • Comparison of different navigation strategies.

By combining these capabilities, VYRA creates a unified environment where users can explore, understand, and plan journeys across selected regions of Mars.

From observing the Martian surface to making informed navigation decisions.

Future Development

VYRA is designed with room for future expansion beyond its initial regional MVP.

Potential future improvements include:

  • MediaPipe-based hand tracking for touchless exploration.
  • More immersive interaction with the 3D Martian environment.
  • Integration of additional Martian regions and scientific datasets.
  • More advanced terrain hazard analysis.
  • Expanded mission planning capabilities.
  • Improved scientific-interest identification and visualization.

Our long-term vision is to develop VYRA into a more comprehensive interactive environment for planetary exploration and mission planning.

Explore TAREEQ

Elzadey/TAREEQ-Martian-Map-Intelligent-Navigation-for-Mars-Exploration

Team: TAREEQ

Explore the project, its architecture, data workflow, and development progress through our repository.

projectDetails.name: Astro Quest
projectDetails.summary:
Astro Quest: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based educational spaceflight simulator that transforms real space science into an interactive astronaut training experience for learners aged 7–12.

Players command a two-person lunar outpost during a 10-day Moon expedition, making critical decisions about energy allocation, life support, radiation protection, scientific research, and emergency response. The simulation incorporates NASA space weather observations, historical solar events, and human spaceflight research to create realistic, consequence-driven mission scenarios.

By combining resource management, timed challenges, scientific discoveries, and interactive learning, Astro Quest helps young learners understand the challenges of human exploration beyond Earth. It directly addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning complex astronaut operations into an accessible, engaging, and educational experience.

Built with Godot Engine 4.7 and deployed through HTML5/WebAssembly, the project runs directly in a web browser without installation.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does and How It Works

Astro Quest places players in command of Outpost Artemis-Cairo, a simulated lunar research base at the Moon's South Pole. The objective is to successfully complete a 10-day expedition while maintaining the survival and scientific productivity of a two-person astronaut crew.

Each mission day follows four operational stages:

  1. Morning Planning: Players distribute limited solar energy across five systems: Air Maker, Greenhouse, Science Lab, Shield Builder, and Earth Radio.
  2. Daytime Operations: Timed events introduce solar flares, coronal mass ejections, lunar dust accumulation, medical challenges, and scientific opportunities. Players must evaluate available options and make decisions before time runs out.
  3. Lunar Night Survival: With solar generation unavailable, players must preserve sufficient battery reserves to operate habitat heaters and life-support systems.
  4. Mission Debriefing: Players receive a mission report evaluating crew survival, accumulated radiation exposure, scientific achievements, and overall performance.

NASA Science Integration

Astro Quest integrates six NASA scientific resources into its gameplay:

  • NASA's DONKI database provides historical and live space weather information, including solar flare and coronal mass ejection events.
  • NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) informs biomedical and human-spaceflight educational scenarios.
  • Artemis I radiation research, including the MARE experiment, inspires radiation protection and shelter mechanics.
  • LCROSS and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter research informs lunar water-ice discovery and resource utilization scenarios.
  • Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3 lunar research informs lunar dust contamination and equipment degradation mechanics.
  • NASA's ISS Veggie experiments inform greenhouse management and food-production mechanics.

Technology and Implementation

The project was developed using Godot Engine 4.7 and GDScript, with HTML5 and WebAssembly deployment for browser accessibility.

Its architecture includes a deterministic simulation engine, an event-management system, resource-allocation mechanics, and an asynchronous HTTP client integrating NASA's DONKI REST API. The system also supports offline operation through nine curated historical solar events, ensuring that the experience remains playable when live data is unavailable.

Benefits, Creativity, and Intended Impact

Astro Quest transforms passive space education into active problem-solving. Instead of simply reading about astronaut challenges, learners experience the consequences of their decisions through an interactive simulation.

Its creative approach combines resource-management gameplay, real scientific references, timed decision-making, and accessible explanations of complex space concepts. It also introduces learners to the importance of radiation protection, sustainable resource management, scientific observation, and preparation for long-duration missions.

Designed for children aged 7–12 and educators, the project aims to make space science more accessible, encourage STEM curiosity, and inspire the next generation of space explorers.

The prototype has undergone more than 50 automated 10-day simulation runs to evaluate gameplay balance. Its browser-based deployment makes it accessible across standard computers, Chromebooks, and tablets without requiring installation.

projectDetails.name: A.T.L.A.S. (Analog Terrestrial Locations for Astronauts & Space)
projectDetails.summary:
Team1 developed A.T.L.A.S. (Black Desert Atlas), an interactive data-driven decision support dashboard evaluating Egypt’s basaltic Black Desert as a terrestrial analog for future lunar south-pole bases and Mars landing sites.

To address the challenge, we integrated open planetary datasets from NASA missions—including MODIS Terra for diurnal Land Surface Temperature, NASA SRTM (30m) for topographic slope profiling across a 9.67 km transect, LRO LOLA & Diviner for lunar polar craters (Shackleton, Haworth, Faustini, Malapert), and MGS MOLA & MEDA for Mars’ Jezero Crater. Moving beyond superficial visual matching, our tool provides interactive thermal filtering, slope distribution metrics (identifying safe touchdown zones under 5°), and transparent cross-planetary benchmarks.

This project is vital because it turns an under-characterized volcanic region into a scientifically documented "natural Earth laboratory," helping mission planners safely test rovers and hardware before costly deep-space deployment.
projectDetails.details:
Project Name: A.T.L.A.S. — Black Desert Atlas (Planetary Analog Discovery)

Project Details:

° What it does & How it works:
Black Desert Atlas is an interactive web-based analytical dashboard designed to evaluate the environmental and topographic suitability of Egypt’s basaltic Black Desert as a terrestrial analog for the Moon and Mars. It operates through four integrated analytical modules:

1. urface Temperature Analytics: Uses NASA MODIS Terra Land Surface Temperature (LST) data (Nov 2025 – Nov 2026) to track diurnal day/night temperature swings, monthly averages, and cloud-masked quality calendars with seasonal filters.

2. errain & Slope Profiling: Analyzes a 9.67 km transect (100 stations at 98m intervals) using NASA SRTM 30m DEM data to compute elevation relief, mean slope, and the percentage of terrain windows under 5° (critical for safe lander touchdown).

3. ross-Planetary Comparison: Benchmarks the Black Desert’s thermal and slope distributions against Jezero Crater on Mars (MGS MOLA & MEDA) and four lunar south-pole targets—Shackleton, Haworth, Faustini, and Malapert—across 2 km and 10 km radial zones (LRO LOLA & Diviner).

4. ata & Methodology Transparency: Documents exact data sources, calculation workflows, and resolution constraints.

° Benefits & Intended Impact:
Provides space agencies and researchers with a scientifically characterized, accessible testbed in Egypt’s Western Desert to validate rovers, landers, and thermal hardware before deep-space missions, significantly reducing testing risks and mission costs.

° Tools, Languages & Technologies Used:

° Data Processing & Geospatial Analysis: Python (Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, Rasterio)

° Interactive Dashboard & Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (interactive KPI cards, daily temperature charts, quality heatmaps, elevation/slope transect profiles, and dynamic planetary toggles)

° Data Formats: Standardized CSV datasets derived from official NASA repositories.

° Creative Aspect:
Instead of claiming an unrealistic 100% match between Earth and space, our dashboard emphasizes scientific honesty and interactive exploration. Users can dynamically toggle quality flags, seasonal windows, slope thresholds (<5° and <10°), and lunar radial zones while viewing clear disclaimers regarding resolution differences (30m Earth DEM vs. 463m Mars DEM) and physical boundaries (gravity, atmosphere, radiation).

° Factors Considered by the Team:

1. ata Quality & Cloud Masking: Explicitly separating high-quality MODIS LST observations from cloud gaps and lower-confidence ("other") flags.

2. esolution & Measurement Context: Accounting for spatial resolution differences between Earth (30m) and Mars (463m) datasets, as well as distinguishing mean temperatures from pre-dawn extremes.

3. erification Flags: Clearly flagging specific benchmark values (such as Shackleton 2 km radius metrics) that require further verification before operational mission planning.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars

projectDetails.name: Project Tech Ghosts
projectDetails.summary:
Problem: Climate data is everywhere, but people cannot tell a real change from a few unusual years, and a trend alone does not tell a farmer what to plant. The Middle East and North Africa is the most water-scarce region in the world, and about 1 in 6 Egyptian workers farms.

Solution: CropShift Earth is a 3D globe built on 25 years of NASA POWER data (2001 to 2025). Pick a measurement (temperature, rain, humidity, soil wetness) and any place or country to see how fast it changes, where, since when, and how strong the evidence is ("strong", "moderate" or "not proven"). For 20 countries it turns those trends into farming answers: which of 40 crops fit each place today, in 2030 and in 2035 if current trends continue, irrigated or rain-fed.

Impact: Farmers, investors and planners see where farming potential is rising or falling, with its evidence, in time to adapt. Every number is checked against NASA's own weather stations and satellite rain record.

Challenge fit: It answers each question of "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!": what is changing, where, how much, whether it is significant, and the twist of opposite trends in one country (Sudan: cooling south, warming north).
projectDetails.details:
Links

Live app: https://cropshift-earth.onrender.com (free hosting: if it has been idle, the first load takes about a minute)

Code: https://github.com/spaceapps-cairo-2026/nasa-space-apps-2026

Trained crop model and model card: https://huggingface.co/OmarGhost2005/cropshift-earth-crop-model

API documentation: https://cropshift-earth.onrender.com/docs

What it does

CropShift Earth is a 3D globe that answers the challenge's questions for any place on Earth. Pick one of six NASA POWER measurements (air temperature, maximum temperature, rain, humidity, surface and root zone soil wetness), then click a place or search a country:

- What is changing and how much: the rate of change per decade in real units, with a 95% range.

- Where: a map of every 55 km grid cell, colored where the change is proven, see-through where it is not. The whole Earth can be colored at once.

- Is it significant: an evidence level ("strong", "moderate" or "not proven") and "Could this be luck?" as a percentage, corrected for testing thousands of places at once.

- Since when: the year the change started, when there is a clear start.

- Opposite trends from one process: in Sudan, air temperature is proven to be falling in 238 places in the south and rising in 26 places in the north (2001 to 2025).

For 20 countries of the Middle East and North Africa, three tabs turn the trends into farming answers: which of 40 crops fit each place today, in 2030 and in 2035 if current trends continue, irrigated or rain-fed (Crops); where farming potential is rising or falling (Farmland); and ranked planning signals for investors and governments, each with its evidence (Decisions). A Methods page explains every number and its limits, and a 60 second guided tour shows the story.

How it works

- Data: NASA POWER monthly grids (built on NASA's MERRA-2), 2001 to 2025, fetched live for any region and cached.

- Trend and confidence: Theil-Sen slope; Mann-Kendall test with its variance corrected for year to year memory; Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate on every map; Pettitt test for when the change started. We tested 7 methods on 20,000 simulated places with no real trend and chose the only one that kept false alarms near 5% while still finding real trends.

- Crop model: one XGBoost model per crop, trained on where 40 crops are grown today (IFPRI MapSPAM 2020, 22,450 farmland cells worldwide) from 10 climate features of all six NASA POWER measurements. On regions held out of training it reaches AUC 0.90; trained without Egypt, it recognizes Egypt's real crop list (FAOSTAT) with AUC 0.93.

- Projections: every climate feature follows its own 2001 to 2025 trend to 2030 and 2035, with a 95% range from 200 resamples of the years. Always labeled "if current trends continue", never a forecast.

Supporting evidence

- Our engine reproduces NASA's global record: +0.25 °C per decade on NASA GISTEMP for 2001 to 2025 (strong evidence). On NASA POWER the Arctic warms fastest, +0.35 °C per decade.

- Checked against NASA's weather stations: POWER and GISTEMP agree on the direction of change for 87% of the world's area and are never proven in opposite directions. Over Egypt the stations warm +0.42 °C per decade, about 1.7 times the global rate.

- We found a data problem and handled it: NASA POWER's rain over Egypt jumps about 2.6 times around 2015, while NASA's GPCP record rises only 1.24 times. Rain answers carry a caution, and projections remove that one-time step.

Benefits and impact

Farmers and agricultural investors ("what can I grow here in 10 years?"), government planners ("which farming regions need support?"), and students, journalists and citizens ("is my city really getting hotter?"). The Middle East and North Africa is the most water-scarce region in the world (World Bank, 2018), the Mediterranean is already about 1.5 °C warmer than pre-industrial times (MedECC, 2020), and about 1 in 6 Egyptian workers works in agriculture (ILO, 2025). The tool is free and open, and it is honest by design: "not proven" is never shown as "no change", projections are never shown as forecasts, and causes are never claimed.

What makes it creative

Most trend tools stop at a map. We add evidence you can trust (false alarms tested and controlled), a check of every trend against an independent NASA record, and the step from "it is changing" to "this is what it means for what you can grow".

Tools

Python (FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, XGBoost for training), JavaScript with MapLibre GL JS (globe) and Plotly (charts), GitHub with automated tests, Render (hosting), Hugging Face (model), Kaggle (training).

Limits we considered

55 km cells (regional screening, not a single farm); irrigated mode assumes water can be supplied; the crop model learns where crops grow today, which also reflects markets and water; olive and date palm are not covered.

Use of AI

Code and text in this project were written with the help of AI tools and reviewed and tested by the team: Claude (Anthropic) for code, analysis scripts, checks and documentation; Manus (AI agent) for the first training notebook of the crop model. The crop model itself is our own XGBoost model trained on public data. No language model produces any number in the app: every sentence is built from computed values. AI use is also noted in the repository (docs/REFERENCES.md) and in the model card.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: MuscleMap
projectDetails.summary: Muscle loss during long space missions varies across muscle groups, making early deterioration difficult to identify from isolated measurements. MuscleMap is an offline-ready tool that helps astronauts track regional muscle health, interpret changes, and decide when to repeat a scan or seek medical review. We'll build an interactive muscle map, longitudinal trend analysis, and quality-aware, explainable alerts. NASA's CFT70 bed-rest research and in-flight ultrasound studies will guide the model and validation, with clearly labeled simulated readings for the prototype.
projectDetails.details:
We started MuscleMap with a question: how can astronauts actually understand what is happening to their muscles throughout a space mission, rather than just looking at separate measurements and trying to make sense of them?

Muscle loss is a known problem in microgravity, and astronauts already follow exercise programs to reduce its effects. But muscle size, physical performance, and exercise activity don't necessarily tell the same story. They're measured differently, at different times, and interpreting them together isn't always straightforward.

MuscleMap is our attempt to make that process easier. It's a web-based musculoskeletal monitoring system built around an interactive 3D anatomical model. Users can select a measured muscle region, explore how its measurements have changed relative to a personal baseline, and understand what the available evidence actually supports. The application also allows users to import or manually record new observations, document follow-ups, and export reports that preserve the original measurements and their sources.

We built the research demonstration using four NASA CFT70 ultrasound and MRI datasets from a 70-day bed-rest study involving 27 participants. These are ground-based research measurements, not actual astronaut records. We use them to demonstrate longitudinal monitoring while keeping the limitations of the data visible.

Technically, we developed MuscleMap using TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, and Python for data preparation, with local storage and offline support. We also included an Incident Support feature for documenting sudden muscular concerns and organizing information for medical handover.

What makes MuscleMap different, in our view, isn't simply the 3D anatomy or the graphs. It's the way the application handles the evidence behind them. We deliberately avoided inventing measurements, treating unrelated data as interchangeable, or producing medical conclusions that the available data couldn't support.

Our goal is to make muscular health monitoring more understandable and useful for astronauts, particularly during missions where medical support from Earth may not always be immediately available. MuscleMap isn't meant to replace medical professionals, but to help astronauts recognize changes, understand uncertainty, and approach follow-up decisions with clearer information.

projectDetails.name: Project terra2mars_egy
projectDetails.summary:
Twin Worlds is a working web prototype that finds places on Earth that match places on Mars and the Moon, so mission teams can test landers, rovers and base operations before flight. A user picks any spot on Mars or the Moon, chooses the purpose of the test (landing, rover driving, building a base, finding resources or studying ancient lakes), and the app searches 30,311 bare-land areas across the whole Earth in under a second.

Instead of judging by looks, Twin Worlds compares real properties from NASA and ESA data (slope, roughness, relief, basin shape, lighting, aridity, surface brightness and minerals) with the same code on both worlds. It shows the best Earth place for each property, explains what is similar and what is different, and lists what Earth cannot reproduce, such as gravity, vacuum and lunar temperatures.

This matters because known analog sites are few and well studied. Twin Worlds found five candidate basins in Egypt's Western Desert in Earth's top 1% for Jezero Crater, and, without being told, ranked Antarctica's Dry Valleys #85 of 30,311 for a Moon base.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Twin Worlds finds places on Earth to test Moon and Mars missions. A user picks any spot on Mars or the Moon, chooses the test (landing, rover driving, base building, resources or ancient lakes), and the app searches 30,311 bare-land areas on Earth in under a second. It shows the best Earth place for each property, the top 3 for the chosen test, known analog sites for comparison, and what Earth cannot reproduce (gravity, vacuum, lunar temperatures). Users can then compare both places side by side with linked 3D globes, terrain maps and 3D terrain blocks.

HOW IT WORKS

We describe every area with the same terrain signature (slope, roughness, relief, basin shape) using NASA and ESA data, and compute the Mars or Moon target with the same code. Each property is scored separately; slope and roughness compare full distributions, not averages.

RESULTS

Five basins in Egypt's Western Desert rank in Earth's top 1% for Jezero Crater (hypotheses for fieldwork). For a Moon base, the search ranks Antarctica's Dry Valleys, a known analog, #85 of 30,311 on its own. Our ML second opinion, tested only on unseen sites, separates real analogs from ordinary deserts 72% of the time.

IMPACT AND CREATIVITY

It helps agencies find new, cheaper test sites beyond the few well-known ones. It starts from Mars or the Moon and discovers Earth places, answers "analog for what?", and is honest about Earth's limits.

TOOLS

JavaScript, Python, React, Vite, ArcGIS Maps SDK, Three.js, Chart.js; NASA Earthdata, LP DAAC, ASF, PDS.

LIMITS AND FUTURE

Candidates need field validation; minerals cover only part of Earth. Next: expert-calibrated weights, Earth permafrost and caves, and field visits.

projectDetails.name: Terra Bytes
projectDetails.summary:
**Field Shift** is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform initially designed for Minya Governorate, Egypt. It collects farm information such as location, area, soil type, salinity, irrigation source, and current crop, then combines it with climate data from NASA POWER, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, and solar radiation.

The platform compares three agricultural rotation plans: the current rotation, a water-saving rotation, and a soil-improvement rotation. Each plan receives an explainable suitability score based on water consumption, soil impact, climate compatibility, market potential, risks, and the farmer’s main priority.

The goal is to help farmers and agricultural engineers make data-informed decisions instead of relying only on estimates or experience. Field Shift does not guarantee production or profit and does not replace soil testing or professional agricultural advice. It provides a practical starting point that can later expand through Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, FAO GAEZ data, and real field measurements.
projectDetails.details:
Field Shift is a smart agricultural decision-support platform designed for farmers and agricultural engineers in Minya Governorate, Egypt. The platform collects farm information such as location, land area, soil type, salinity level, irrigation source, current crop, and the farmer’s main priority. It then connects this information with climate data from the NASA POWER API, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, and solar radiation.

The system compares three agricultural rotation plans: the current rotation, a water-saving rotation, and a soil-improvement rotation. Each plan receives an explainable suitability score based on water efficiency, soil impact, climate compatibility, market potential, and risk. Instead of only presenting a recommendation, Field Shift explains why a specific plan may be more suitable.

The main benefits are improved water management, better soil planning, clearer decision-making, and reduced dependence on assumptions. The intended impact is to support more sustainable agriculture, reduce resource waste, and help farmers make better decisions before starting a new season.

The project was developed using **React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, tRPC, Node.js, Express, and Drizzle ORM**. The backend integrates with the **NASA POWER API**, while the frontend provides an Arabic RTL dashboard with farm inputs, climate indicators, maps, comparison cards, and confidence scores.

Field Shift is creative because it transforms complex environmental data into a simple, practical, and understandable tool for local farmers. Our team considered Minya’s dry climate, irrigation challenges, soil variation, data limitations, usability on mobile devices, Arabic accessibility, explainability, and the need to keep the platform expandable. Future versions can include Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, FAO GAEZ data, soil laboratory analysis, and real field measurements.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: DAWRA AI
projectDetails.summary:
Dawra AI ("dawra" means "rotation" in Arabic) is a working bilingual (English and Egyptian Arabic) web app that helps small farmers in dry, salty areas choose a smarter 3-year crop rotation (six seasons: winter, summer, winter, summer, winter, summer). It compares the farmer's current rotation with new plans found by an optimisation algorithm (NSGA-II), tests every plan against bad climate years and 2050s climate futures, and explains each plan in simple language. The farmer and the local extension officer stay in control: the tool suggests and explains, they decide.
It addresses the Field Shift challenge: helping farmers adapt their crop choices to climate change using NASA data. Our pilot site is Ras Sudr, South Sinai, Egypt. There, crops need about 1,912 mm of water a year, but only about 47 mm of rain falls (2.4% of the need), so every farm depends on salty wells (our pilot farm: 8.35 dS/m). The share of the aquifer area classed as highly saline rose from 52% in 1996 to 83% in 2022. Most farms grow barley in winter and leave the land bare in summer, and farmers have no clear local answer to: "Which rotation earns more per cubic metre of water, keeps salt out of the root zone, and still works in a hot year?"
Dawra AI uses NASA POWER climate data to compute crop water needs (FAO-56 method), Landsat (NASA/USGS) and Sentinel-2 images to see how land is really used, and NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections to test plans against the 2050s.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Dawra AI is a live web app that simulates a farmer's current rotation, searches for better 3-year plans, stress-tests each plan against bad and future climates, and explains each plan in plain language (English and Egyptian Arabic). It suggests and explains; the farmer and extension officer decide.
Main use (input → process → output)
Input: farm profile (area, well salinity, water per day, irrigation type, livestock, last crop, crops to avoid) and the farmer's priorities (profit, water saving, salt tolerance, soil health, market, climate risk). In the app the user can change well salinity (5–12 dS/m), daily water (40/60/90 m³) and the priority profile.
Process: NSGA-II searches crop choice and irrigated area for all 6 seasons (19 crops, the well's daily water as a hard limit) for three goals: profit (EGP), water (m³) and soil health. It picks four plans: highest profit, water saver, soil builder, and the best balance for this farmer (TOPSIS). Each plan is replayed in 5,400 futures: 45 years of NASA climate, +1/+2 °C, −10/−20% rain, NASA CMIP6 2050s, and a saltier well, each with 100%, 70% or 40% of the needed leaching water.
Output: side-by-side plan cards (profit, water, soil score, robustness), P10–P90 profit range, a card back with the explanation (why, NASA evidence, benefits, information gaps, risks), a What-if lab with sliders, and a simple Farmer mode (3 questions → 1 plan in plain Arabic).
How the data supports it. NASA POWER gives the FAO-56 reference water need (about 1,912 mm/yr) and effective rain (about 47 mm/yr), and its 45-year record is resampled to build the climate futures. Landsat shows green farmland growing from 13 ha (1990) to 1,302 ha (2025) over the same salty aquifer. NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 creates two 2050s futures. Sentinel-2 gives 122 cultivated fields (125 ha) and their season patterns.
Pilot results (farm F001: 5 feddan ≈ 2.1 ha, well 8.35 dS/m, 60 m³/day, drip)
Current rotation: 125,325 EGP, 15,260 m³, soil score 52, robustness 32%.
Best balance (recommended): 158,385 EGP (+26%), 13,588 m³ (−11%), soil 55, robustness 49%. It earns 11.7 EGP per m³ of water vs 8.2.
Highest profit: 360,515 EGP (+188%) but 34,863 m³ (+128%), more than a 60 m³/day well can supply every year, so it is shown but not recommended.
Water saver: 109,808 EGP (−12%), 8,572 m³ (−44%), robustness 8%.
Soil builder: 131,448 EGP (+5%), 28,168 m³ (+85%), soil score 71.
Key finding: the current rotation is the most fragile. With only 70% of the leaching water, salt builds up in almost every future. Climate variation moves profit only about ±3%, so leaching practice is the biggest risk.
Benefits and goals. More income per drop of well water; protect soil and aquifer by tracking soil salt season by season; plan for climate change before committing; transparency (every number traces to NASA data, a cited local source S1–S18, or one of 139 documented assumptions); reach (phone-friendly, bilingual, Farmer mode).
Tools, languages, software. Python 3.11 (pandas, numpy, pymoo, scikit-learn, shapely, Google Earth Engine Python API, pytest with 66 tests). Methods: FAO-56 Penman–Monteith, FAO-29 leaching and salt tolerance, Maas–Hoffman salinity–yield model, block-bootstrap climate resampling, TOPSIS. Web app: Next.js 14, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, framer-motion, three.js, Recharts, Leaflet, hosted on Vercel, reading pre-computed JSON files (4.8 MB), so no server-side Python. Playwright tests; Lighthouse (home 99 desktop / 90 mobile, accessibility 100). No special hardware.
Evidence and validation. 15 pass, 9 fail (kept and explained), 4 calibrated, 1 not testable. NASA POWER from the API matches the team's file exactly; our FAO-56 code reproduces the textbook example (3.9 mm/day). Wheat tested on an independent local result: error −15%, inside our ±20% target. Kept failures include NASA POWER night temperatures about 1.8 °C warmer than the station, and our FAO-29 water need being 73% above one local trial. Of 106 assumptions changed by ±20%, 11 change at least one plan choice.
Working now (prototype). Full pipeline from NASA data to plan cards; live bilingual app with 5 tabs and Farmer mode; 15 pre-computed farm settings (5 well salinities × 3 water supplies) with 5 priority profiles each; What-if sliders and the 5,400-future stress test; Landsat and Sentinel-2 evidence on the map.
Limitations. One farm profile, soil data from one research station; 19 of 21 crop price/cost rows include an estimate (flagged in the app); leaching achieved, fallow salt rise, residue carbon and legume nitrogen are literature assumptions; no field test with farmers yet; MODIS MOD16 ET has no data over this desert. All results are model results, not field-tested outcomes.
Future plans (not built yet). Pilot with farmers and the Desert Research Center station in Ras Sudr; real market prices updated each season; field-level plans from each farm's own satellite history and soil test; SMS/WhatsApp Farmer mode; extension to North Sinai, Red Sea and North Coast.

node.excerpt: We are a complete team of students from Egypt

projectDetails.name: Project TerraNova 🌍
projectDetails.summary:
TerraNova is a web platform that finds Earth's "hidden twins" of the Moon and Mars: real places on our planet that resemble lunar and Martian terrain, for astronaut training and equipment testing.

Users pick the Moon, Mars, or both, choose the features that matter (impact craters, lava tubes, anorthosite, basalt, permafrost, glacial ice), and set how much each one counts. TerraNova ranks Earth sites by match percentage and shows the geology, weather forecast, fieldwork readiness, and the papers behind each match. Users can also compare a site with a lunar or Martian landscape in 3D and print a field report.

This answers Challenge 10 directly. Agencies keep returning to the same few analog sites, while many good ones are poorly documented and matching is slow and manual. TerraNova is built on a dataset compiled from 7 research papers: 21 Moon and Mars sites and 45 Earth analog sites, including lesser-known ones in Egypt and North Africa. It runs on open data from NASA, ESA, and Open-Meteo.

It matters because it brings forward accessible, lower-cost sites for training, research, and testing.
projectDetails.details: TerraNova is an interactive platform that finds places on Earth that resemble the Moon and Mars, built for the challenge "Identify Earth Locations that Analog Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars." Key features: Mission Planner: choose the Moon, Mars, or both, pick geological traits (impact craters, lava tubes, anorthosite, basalt, permafrost, glacial ice), and weight each one. Ranked results: 43 curated analog sites ranked by weighted match, showing matched and missing features, with filters by country, classification, and location accuracy. 3D planetary explorer: NASA models of Earth, Moon, and Mars with site markers, plus an Earth map. Side-by-side 3D terrain comparison: Earth sites against lunar or Martian counterparts using NASA Trek and open elevation data, with controls for sun angle, vertical exaggeration, wireframe, flyover, and synchronized cameras. Field reports: printable PDF reports with live Open-Meteo weather, logistics, and risks. Community contributions and a Methodology page, in Arabic and English, with shareable links. Why it matters: choosing the right analog site is central to astronaut training, rover testing, and mission rehearsal. TerraNova makes that choice faster, transparent, and evidence-based, labeling pairings "proposed" and coordinates "approximate" until scientists verify them.

projectDetails.name: Project Terraphony
projectDetails.summary:
Terraphony is a web-based “listening atlas” for NASA Space Apps 2026’s Earth Information Jukebox challenge. It turns real NASA Earth observations into music you can explore, understand, and save as your own Earth Record.

Two journeys bring the data to life:

Ocean in Motion: Draw a route across the sea. At 24 stops, hear daily sea-surface temperatures from NASA JPL’s MUR SST dataset, alongside NASA SVS 3912 ocean imagery.

A Year in One Place: Choose any land location. Hear 23 notes representing 16-day windows of plant greenness from NASA’s 2023 MODIS NDVI data, while dated satellite imagery changes with the music.

Higher values produce higher notes; missing or cloud-covered data become silent rests, never invented measurements. Strings, horns, harp, and timpani enrich the melody. An optional Beethoven-guided narrated tour makes exploration approachable. Select any note to reveal its value, units, location, date, and musical mapping.

Terraphony makes Earth science tangible: hear changes along the Gulf Stream or seasonal patterns in the Nile Delta, then learn what the observations can—and cannot—tell us. Export your Earth Record as an image, audio file, or reproducible recipe, grounded in the same NASA measurements.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Ocean in Motion.

- Choose a line. Pick a suggested route (Gulf Stream, Equatorial Pacific, Agulhas) or draw your own line across the sea. It is resampled into 24 stops at equal distances along the Earth's surface.

- Choose a day. Pick 18 Aug 2007 or 6 Feb 2008. Each stop plays that day's sea-surface temperature from MUR SST v4.1.

- The picture. The background is NASA SVS 3912 for the same day. We checked the alignment: 24 of 24 coastal landmarks agree, and the land masks agree on 98.4 % of the map.

A Year in One Place.

- Any place. Click anywhere on the map, or type coordinates, or choose Nile Delta, Harvard Forest or the Sahel.

- The notes. The app fetches that point's MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI for every 16-day window of 2023 directly from NASA's ORNL DAAC service. A year dial and 23 notes show the seasons.

- The picture. NASA's own GIBS picture for each window changes on the map in time with the music.

One clear rule from data to sound.

- Fixed ranges. Each value is placed on a fixed range (−2 to 31 °C, or 0 to 0.9 NDVI) and mapped to one of 11 notes from C3 to C5.

- Comparable. The ranges never change between places or dates, so two records can be compared honestly.

- Rests. Missing, land, ice, cloud or quality-rejected values become rests and are never filled in.

- Data voices. The bass plays the mean of each group of four values, and a bell marks large declared changes.

- Artistic voices. Strings, horns, harp, timpani and the closing chord are artistic support built from the same notes, and are labelled as such.

Living score and inspector.

- The score. Notes appear on a five-line staff, moving in sync with the map cursor or year dial. It can be played with the keyboard.

- The inspector. Clicking a note shows its value, units, date, coordinates and source, plus the exact formula. For land it also shows the 81 MODIS pixels with their quality flags.

Record press and exports.

- The press. An animation turns your route or year into a score, then a spiral groove, then a record sleeve drawn from your own data.

- Exports. You can save the sleeve (PNG, 2400 px), the "recipe" (JSON) or the audio (WAV).

- Checked recipes. When a recipe is opened, it is re-derived from its observations and refused if its notes do not match.

Narrated guided journey (optional).

- One click. The tour starts from a single click and runs by itself: welcome, choosing a record, the first performance, a real data "discovery", and handing control to the visitor.

The host. The host is Beethoven, shown as Stieler's 1820 portrait, which is in the public domain.

- Captions. Captions are always on. The tour can be paused, replayed or skipped, and the visitor's choices always override it.

- Accessibility. You can switch sound off and use visuals only. Captions and text cover every sound. The score is keyboard-friendly, reduced motion is respected, and the layout works on phones.

How it works

- Data preparation. A Python pipeline (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) downloads and prepares the data without logins, records checksums, and validates the picture alignment.

The app. React + TypeScript (Vite) loads the prepared files. Land points are fetched live in the browser, and the browser applies the same quality rules (tested to match the Python output exactly).

- The sound. The whole piece is rendered once by our own synthesis code in a background Web Worker, then played with the Web Audio API. This keeps the sound smooth even on a busy computer.

- Tests. 68 automated unit tests check the data rules, the Python-to-browser match, the arrangement and the audio quality. 33 browser tests check the user journeys.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

- Make NASA Earth data approachable for people who would never open a dataset: students, museum visitors, and blind or low-vision users who can follow by sound and text.

- Show that sonification can be honest. Every note is traceable to a real measurement, and the artistic parts are clearly labelled.

- Encourage curiosity. Every visitor can make and share a record from a place they care about.

Main use case, and how the data supports it. A teacher or museum visitor opens the guided journey. They hear the Gulf Stream route and the sudden drop from 28.3 °C to 23.7 °C at 39.9° N 59.5° W, the edge of the warm current, on 18 Aug 2007. They click that note to see the measurement behind it. Then they click their own city to hear its 2023 seasons, while NASA's 16-day greenness pictures change on the map.

Future plans (not part of the delivered project)

- A recorded human narration voice.

- More dates and years.

- A wildfire story using NASA FIRMS and SVS 4993, which was removed until it can be done properly.

- More datasets and languages.

- A classroom printable.

Tools, languages, software and hardware

- App: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Web Audio API, Web Workers, d3-geo, topojson-client, world-atlas (Natural Earth maps), and Fontsource fonts.

- Data pipeline: Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy and Pillow.

- Testing: Vitest and Playwright.

- Hosting: Git, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.

- Hardware: standard laptops only.

- AI: AI tools were used

challengeDetails.title: The Earth Information Jukebox

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
