projectDetails.name: Project TerraWise
projectDetails.summary:
TerraWise: smarter planting decisions with NASA data
Farmers today face a changing climate. The best time to plant is moving, and old habits no longer work. TerraWise helps farmers choose the right crop and the best planting window for their own field.
The farmer picks a location on the map, then chooses the crop, soil type, irrigation method, and what matters most to them (water saving, soil health, or stability). TerraWise compares this with more than 40 years of NASA climate data (NASA POWER, MODIS, and SMAP soil moisture). It then shows the best planting window, an irrigation calendar, and a "time machine" that shows how the ideal planting date has shifted over the years.
The farmer can send the result to an agronomist for review or download it as a PDF.
TerraWise turns satellite data into simple, local advice for every field.
projectDetails.details:
TerraWise — NASA Space Apps 2026

One line: TerraWise tells a farmer the best window to plant their crop, based on 45 years of NASA climate data for their exact field.

The problem

Climate change is moving the seasons. Heat waves arrive earlier and rain becomes less predictable, so the planting dates farmers have used for generations are less reliable. Small farmers usually have no easy way to check how the climate in their own field has changed.

How it works

Pick the field. The farmer searches for a place or drops a pin on the map. They can also draw the field boundary. The app checks that NASA POWER, MODIS, and SoilGrids data are ready for that location.

Configure the field. The farmer chooses:

the crop (wheat, maize/corn, rice, barley, sorghum, cotton, lentils, fava beans), marked as winter or summer crops

how the field is watered (rainfed, surface irrigation, drip, or well/groundwater)

soil type (clay, sandy, loam, silty), which is optional because the app can use SoilGrids satellite data if left blank

the month and week they usually plant

what matters most to them (water saving, soil health, yield stability), each rated 1 to 5

Get the result. The app calculates the best planting window and compares it with the farmer's usual date.

What the farmer sees

Best planting window. For example: "Best window to plant Barley this year: Nov 16 – Nov 29".

Year calendar. Each month is marked as safe, optimal, flowering (sensitive), heat risk, or frost risk. The farmer's usual planting date is shown on the same calendar.

Time machine. A slider from 2001 to 2050 shows how the best planting date moves with the climate. In the example, the date is 11 days later than in 2001, and a "Jump to 2050" button shows the future.

Irrigation window. It shows which weeks the crop needs irrigation, which weeks rain is usually enough, and which weeks are off season. It uses FAO-56 crop water requirements and NASA SMAP soil moisture.

Why this window. A short explanation, for example that flowering avoids the April heat waves and grain filling ends before the peak summer heat. It also shows the data source (NASA POWER, 1981–2025) and a confidence level.

Needs local review. The app is clear about what it cannot know: crop variety, field drainage, and local pest pressure.

Two views. There is a Farmer view and an Agronomist view. The farmer can send the result to an agronomist for review or download it as a PDF.

Data sources

NASA POWER (daily climate data)

NASA MODIS (satellite imagery)

NASA SMAP (soil moisture)

NASA GIBS (map layers)

SoilGrids (soil properties)

FAO-56 (crop water requirements)

Why it matters

It gives local advice for each field, not general advice for a whole region.

It shows the climate trend, not only today's answer.

It saves water by showing which weeks irrigation is really needed.

It keeps the agronomist in the loop and says plainly that it is timing guidance only.

Team

Belal Elnagar, Yara Mohamed, Omar Tarek, Marwa Mohamed, Mariam Wael, and Yasmine Medhat.

projectDetails.name: LUMEN — Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
LUMEN is an interactive lunar landing site screening platform engineered to help mission planners, educators, and the public evaluate surface lighting and Earth visibility conditions across candidate lunar landing sites. 

At the lunar South Pole, grazing solar elevation angles and Earth’s libration wobble create extreme environmental swings where minor arrival slips can plunge a surface mission into prolonged darkness. LUMEN addresses the "Lunar Landing Site Navigator" challenge by coupling deterministic NASA NAIF SPICE ephemeris calculations with an intuitive mission control interface. Users can track Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation, inspect refined rise and set countdowns across a 60-day timeline, compare two landing sites simultaneously, and evaluate schedule slips in seconds. 

By making the operational consequences of launch delays visible before flight commitments, LUMEN transforms complex astrodynamic ephemerides into accessible, actionable screening insights.
projectDetails.details:
LUMEN (Lunar Landing Site Navigator)

1. What It Does & How It Works

LUMEN (Lunar Landing Site Navigator) provides deterministic geometric screening of surface solar illumination (power and thermal context) and direct line-of-sight visibility to Earth (geometric direct-to-Earth communications) across candidate lunar landing sites:

  • Surface-Observer Topocentric Geometry: Sun and Earth positions are calculated relative to physical surface coordinates on the Moon rather than the lunar center, accounting for the critical ~0.26° angular parallax that directly impacts horizon clearance.
  • High-Resolution 60-Day Architecture: Precomputed at 15-minute intervals across 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z to 2027-03-02T00:00:00Z using NAIF SPICE planetary ephemerides and the explicit DE440 lunar body-fixed frame (MOON_ME_DE440_ME421).
  • Interactive Mission Control: Features a responsive 3D lunar limb with real-time solar illumination angles, a local East-North-Up (ENU) sky dome, apparent elevation/azimuth gauges, and sub-minute refined event countdowns (next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, Earthset).
  • The Schedule Slip Engine: Allows planners to evaluate launch slips by selecting two distinct arrival dates for any polar site; the engine instantly recalculates 7-day landing slices to reveal shifts in dark runs and communications outages.
  • Compare Mode: Simultaneously visualizes two lunar sites side-by-side using a single synchronized time cursor.
  • Live Ephemeris Context: Connects to the NASA/JPL Horizons API for real-time orbital context and current-minute celestial vectors, maintained separately from the precomputed mission series.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

Landing site selection is among the highest-risk phases of lunar exploration, particularly at the lunar South Pole where low solar incidence angles (axial tilt ~1.54°) and Earth’s libration wobble create extreme localized environmental swings. Existing astrodynamics software (e.g., JPL Horizons, Quickmap) is built primarily for orbital specialists and involves steep learning curves:

  • Rapid Sensitivity Screening: Planners can assess operational trade-offs and "what-if" launch delays in seconds.
  • Mission Risk Reduction: Demonstrates immediately whether a delayed arrival causes power starvation (e.g., plunging Malapert Massif into 168 hours of continuous dark during a 30-day schedule slip).
  • Public & Educational Accessibility: Translates complex topocentric ephemerides into an intuitive, tactile tool for educators, students, and space enthusiasts.

3. Tools, Technologies & Super Intelligence (AI) Integration

Our team paired industry-standard engineering stacks with a multi-agent Super Intelligence (AI) workflow to maximize productivity and rigor:

  • Scientific Computing Engine: Python 3.12, SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE toolkit wrapper), NumPy.
  • Frontend & 3D Visualization: TypeScript, React 19, Three.js, React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber), Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lenis, and GSAP.
  • Validation Infrastructure: NASA/JPL Horizons API and automated Python/Vitest test suites.
  • Deployment: Vercel edge infrastructure with serverless same-origin proxy routes.

Super Intelligence (AI/SI) Development Workflow:

The solution idea, scientific scope, and engineering constraints were conceived and directed entirely by the human team (The Black Bulls). AI tools were strategically deployed as specialized accelerators across distinct lifecycle phases:

  • Anthropic Claude: Assisted during initial sprint planning, task breakdown, architectural mapping, and structuring interface requirements.
  • Google Gemini: Utilized for deep technical research, analyzing NASA NAIF kernel frame documentation, and synthesizing cited coordinate literature for Artemis landing candidate sites.
  • OpenAI Codex: Served as a productivity accelerator for scaffolding TypeScript components, implementing reactive state hooks (Zustand), and preparing unit test coverage.
  • Google Antigravity: Managed end-to-end browser automation, high-resolution UI scene recordings, 1080p video production, and slide deck packaging.

4. Creativity & Innovation

  • Treating Schedule Variation as a Primary Variable: Rather than showing isolated single-epoch views, LUMEN focuses on the operational reality of spaceflight—schedule slips—turning static ephemeris data into dynamic contingency planning.
  • Unified Time Synchronization: A single, continuous time cursor simultaneously updates the 3D Moon lighting, the local ENU sky dome, numerical telemetry gauges, and side-by-side comparison panels.
  • Tactile Narrative Design: Combines cinematic landing storytelling with a dense, trust-building scientific workbench.

5. Critical Engineering Factors & Transparency

  • Deterministic Science First: AI tools were strictly barred from generating astrodynamic figures. All geometry is calculated deterministically via SPICE and independently cross-checked against NASA/JPL Horizons observer tables (max angular deviation < 0.005°, event times within 58 seconds).
  • Geometric Screening Honesty: LUMEN calculates geometric line of sight over a flat reference sphere horizon. The interface transparently states that real terrain is not modeled in v1, and that geometric Earth visibility does not constitute an RF communications link budget.
  • Compliance: No NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers were created or altered using AI tools.

projectDetails.name: Project The CIS Galaxy Express
projectDetails.summary:
Twin Rover Quest is a story-game website that tells children under 10 the true story of Spirit and Opportunity, the twin NASA rovers left on Mars. Built for a 90-day mission, Spirit kept working for more than six years and Opportunity for more than fourteen. Both are still on Mars today, silent.

Children meet the twins and tap their parts to learn what each one did. Then they play through the rovers’ journey on a Mission Map of five levels and a finale. Each level links one engineering part to one real discovery: the airbag landing, the broken wheel that found silica, winter on Low Ridge, Opportunity’s “blueberries” and the dust storm. Players earn badges, ask the rovers questions in a helper that answers only from NASA facts, and end by reading each robot’s imagined letter.

Every fact links to its NASA source, and imagined voices are clearly labelled. Level 1 is fully playable in our prototype.

This answers the challenge by turning “abandoned” machines into heroes a new generation will remember, while teaching real planetary science through play.
projectDetails.details:
Twin Rover Quest is a story-game website that tells children under 10 the true story of Spirit and Opportunity, the twin NASA rovers left on Mars. A child moves through the twins’ journey in 15 to 20 minutes:

  1. Meet the Twins: tap five parts on a cartoon rover (wheels, camera mast, arm, solar panels, antenna) to learn what each does and which discovery it led to.
  2. Mission Map: a trail of five levels and a finale. Each level links one engineering part to one real discovery: the airbag landing, the broken wheel that dug up silica, surviving winter on Low Ridge, Opportunity’s “blueberries” and salty sea, and the 2018 dust storm.
  3. Badges: each level earns a badge and unlocks a page of a printed cartoon book with QR codes that open the level.
  4. Ask the Rover: a helper that answers in Spirit’s or Oppy’s voice, only from facts checked on NASA pages, with a source on every answer.
  5. Letters from Mars: each robot’s imagined letter, plus a status card saying where it is today.

Level 1, Crash Landing, is fully playable. The child taps PARACHUTE, AIRBAGS, ROCKETS and CUT at the right moment, then counts the bounces. Levels 2 to 5 are designed as concept screens.

Benefits and intended impact

Children learn real planetary science by playing a story, not by memorizing facts. Parents and teachers get a free activity where every fact links to its NASA source. Two “abandoned” machines become heroes a new generation remembers. We hope this method can tell the stories of other equipment left on the Moon and Mars.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one self-contained page, hosted on GitHub Pages
  • Hand-drawn SVG cartoons and our own line icons
  • Web Audio for sound, off by default
  • Browser local storage for progress, with no accounts
  • Fredoka and Nunito fonts
  • NASA Photojournal images, JPL mission pages and NASA technical papers as our sources
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped improve the website design and draft our documentation and presentation. All facts were checked by the team.

Creativity

Instead of a fact sheet, we told the rovers’ story as a game with a beginning, a problem and an ending. Each level teaches one part and one discovery through play. Robot voices, speech bubbles and letters make children care, and the printed QR book moves the story from paper to screen.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: imagined voices are always labelled. Every fact sits in a “NASA fact” box with its source. We never call the rovers “dead” or “junk”, and we never say they found life.
  • Age: short sentences, big buttons, no timers and no game-over screen. Auto-pilot helps after two misses.
  • Accessibility: sound is off by default and every sound has a caption. Slow motion and keyboard play are included.
  • Privacy: no names, no accounts and no data collected. Ask the Rover keeps nothing after it closes.
  • Transparency: every part is labelled as working or concept, so judges see what really exists.

projectDetails.name: Storyworld Museum
projectDetails.summary:
Storyworld Museum is an interactive digital storytelling platform about the hardware NASA left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. Visitors begin at the Sun on an interactive solar system map (3D or 2D) and follow 13 historic hardware outward through a levels-and-progress map to track the completeness of each hardware journey. Astra, the cosmic guide character, walks visitors through an introductory video to the platform and every mission. Each hardware's story unfolds in five levels: name and basic information, history, scientific basis and mechanism, mission and reason behind it, and its status and legacy. Mission Control quizzes let visitors earn Space Historian badges.
It addresses the challenge by giving discarded equipment a voice. Instead of lists of facts, each piece of hardware gets a story through a space journey with verified NASA sources, archival photos, and NASA 3D models.
The reason this matters is that space knowledge and education quality is gradually decreasing due to the use of abstract and lifeless ways to express them. Therefore, it was crucial to create something that would change the way youth look at space and education. So instead of building an abstract way of learning, we built an engaging way of learning that is able to build strong and bright generations who are able to discover space. The museum makes the hardware legacy engaging and easy for students to understand.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES
The museum guides visitors outward from the Sun across 13 checkpoints (4 on the Moon, 5 on Mars, 4 in deep space). Each machine has a five-act story with a timeline, 3D/2D mechanism lab, science explained in student-friendly analogies, final mission status and legacy. The site also includes an artifact archive with filters, an opening animated film, a 3D orbital map with a 2D fallback, and a Mission Control quiz with badges that needs no account.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
It makes NASA mission history engaging for students and the general public by combining storytelling, character-driven narration and interactive visuals. Instead of dry facts, visitors feel the emotional side of machines that finished their work and stayed behind.



CREATIVITY
A single guide character, Astra, changes role and expression across the museum. The Solar System itself is the navigation, so exploring the site feels like a real expedition.


TOOLS
The website was built with Lovable. Images are hosted on Cloudinary. Slides were made in Canva. SI tools were used as described in the SI section.
tools used:
React 19 & TypeScript
TanStack Start & TanStack Router
Vite & Nitro
Tailwind CSS
Three.js
React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber)
React Three Drei (@react-three/drei)
GSAP (GreenSock) & ScrollTrigger
Web Audio API (Procedural NASA Sound Synthesizer & SFX)
Web Speech API (Voiceover & Karaoke sync)
HTML5 Canvas 2D (Flying Starfield & 2D Mini-Games)
Lucide React (Icons)
Vitest & React Testing Library
Cloudinary (Media CDN)


FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Accuracy (every story links to official NASA sources), accessibility (no account needed, 2D map if 3D fails, mobile-friendly layout), and honesty (the site clearly states it is an independent educational project and not an official NASA website).

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: FLARE AI — Fire & Low-Gravity Archive Research Engine (by The Fireflies)
projectDetails.summary:
FLARE AI (Fire & Low-Gravity Archive Research Engine) is a source-grounded scientific decision-support platform built on NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion archive to address the "Flame in Freefall" challenge. In microgravity, flames lack buoyant convection—burning as spherical, diffusion-driven fronts that can persist at lower oxygen levels and produce larger smoke particles than on Earth. However, historical NASA spaceflight combustion experiments span heterogeneous formats, units, combustion domains, and unrecorded environmental variables.

FLARE AI unifies 1,157 experiment runs, 10,079 measurements, 128 verified archive files, and 1,312 scientific document passages across six NASA PSI investigations (FLEX, BASS-II, SPICE, SAME, SAME-R, and Saffire-I). It combines a domain-gated, confidence-penalized similarity ranking engine with a guardrail-enforced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant that verifies every citation quote verbatim and explicitly flags missing parameters and partial-gravity (Lunar/Martian) archive gaps—accelerating spacecraft fire-safety research without hallucinating or extrapolating beyond physical bounds.
projectDetails.details:
What FLARE AI Does & How It Works

FLARE AI is a hybrid scientific knowledge and decision-support platform designed for researchers studying spacecraft fire behavior across NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive. Rather than acting as a black-box chatbot or claiming to predict ignition risk, FLARE AI operates through three tightly integrated, provenance-auditable layers:

  1. Standardized Multi-Investigation Data Pipeline & Provenance Registry (FLARE_AI_Data_Handoff)
  • Ingests, normalizes, and cross-checks 6 NASA PSI investigations (PSI-69 FLEX, PSI-25 BASS-II, PSI-107 SPICE, PSI-101 SAME-R, PSI-102 SAME, and PSI-98 Saffire-I), encompassing 1,157 experiment runs, 10,079 measurements, 128 SHA-256-verified raw files, 33 coverage/gap matrix cells (COV-/GAP-), and 1,312 chunked passages from 21 NASA technical reports and peer-reviewed publications.
  • Preserves both raw reported units (e.g., mmHg, % vol, instrument fan settings) and canonical normalized units (kPa, O2 mole fraction, cm/s), while enforcing explicit missingness categories (not_reported, not_measured, not_applicable, pending_review) instead of imputing missing values.
  1. Domain-Gated, Confidence-Penalized Similarity Ranking Engine (flare_ranking)
  • Ranks historical NASA experiment runs against a researcher's target environmental conditions (O2 fraction, ambient pressure in kPa, forced airflow velocity in cm/s, combustion domain, and gravity regime).
  • Hard Domain Gating: Prevents invalid cross-domain comparisons (solid fuels in BASS-II/Saffire-I are never numerically ranked against liquid droplets in FLEX, gas jets in SPICE, or smoke aerosols in SAME/SAME-R).
  • Gravity Regime Separation: Separates ISS/Cygnus microgravity (0g) runs from normal-gravity (1g) ground baselines and flags partial-gravity (0.16g Lunar / 0.38g Martian) queries as open archive gaps bounded by 0g and 1g.
  • Confidence Penalty: Separates condition similarity (S_cond) from data completeness (C_conf) so experiments with missing parameters cannot artificially outrank fully measured runs.
  1. Guardrail-Enforced Scientific RAG Copilot (flare_llm_engine & flare_llm_adapter)
  • Retrieves relevant NASA PSI document chunks and coverage-matrix cells (COV-/GAP-) via hybrid semantic + lexical + structured SQL retrieval.
  • Enforces strict scientific guardrails (G1–G7 and D1–D6): never claims to predict fire risk or certify astronaut safety, never interpolates partial-gravity behavior between 0g and 1g, and verifies every LLM citation quote character-for-character against the underlying source passage (verified: true).

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Eliminates Data Silos Across Spaceflight Fire Experiments: Unifies droplet extinction, solid flame spread, gas-jet smoke points, and spacecraft smoke detector aerosol distributions into one searchable, unit-harmonized schema.
  • Prevents Dangerous Scientific Extrapolation: Automatically warns researchers when target conditions fall into untested partial-gravity regimes (Moon/Mars) or when source experiments lack ambient O2/pressure logs (such as SPICE, SAME, and SAME-R).
  • Full Auditability to Primary DOIs: Every run, measurement, and AI-synthesized statement links directly to its NASA PSI investigation, DOI, and SHA-256 source file checksum.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Backend & Data Engineering: Python 3, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic v2, NumPy, Pandas, SQLite / PostgreSQL, HTTPX.
  • Similarity & Ranking Engine: Custom Python weighted min-max similarity and confidence-penalty engine (flare_ranking) with pytest verification suites.
  • AI / RAG & Guardrail Engine: Google Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash) / OpenAI (gpt-4o) structured JSON outputs with deterministic citation verification (flare_llm_engine.py) and hybrid vector + lexical + SQL retrieval.
  • Frontend UI: Next.js 15 (React 19, TypeScript), Tailwind CSS, KaTeX scientific math rendering, interactive condition comparison sliders, and a slide-over Provenance & Lineage Inspector.

How Our Project Is Creative & Factors Considered

  • Honest Uncertainty Over Hallucination: Most AI tools guess when data is missing. FLARE AI treats missingness (not_reported, pending_review) and archive gaps (GAP-* cells) as first-class scientific data.
  • Physics-Aware Architecture: Our team accounted for real spacecraft hardware quirks—such as BASS-II nitrogen-dilution schedules, SPICE/BASS-II fan calibration curves, and SAME/SAME-R mixed ISS (0g) vs. ground (1g) baseline runs—ensuring physical fidelity at every step.https://flame-ai-six.vercel.app/explorer

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project The Forgotten Ones
projectDetails.summary:
**High-Level Project Summary**

NASA Archive is an interactive 3D website that helps people discover the machines humans have left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors rotate a 3D scene, click a spacecraft, and ask questions in English or Arabic. An AI storyteller answers with a short, kid-friendly story about that machine: why it was sent, how it worked, what it discovered, and where it is today. We built it for the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten".

The site covers 13 groups of NASA hardware, from the Apollo Lunar Modules and Surveyor landers to Sojourner, Viking, Ingenuity, Dawn, Pioneer and Kepler. Each group has its own storyteller, which answers from a knowledge base built from official NASA data. If a fact is missing, it can search trusted sources such as NASA, JPL, ESA, universities and museums. If it still cannot find the answer, it says so instead of guessing.

This matters because many of these explorers finished their missions long ago, and their data is hard for students and curious readers to approach. NASA Archive turns that data into stories that are simple, accurate and easy to enjoy, so these machines stay remembered and more people, including Arabic-speaking learners, feel connected to the science they made possible.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What it does

NASA Archive is an interactive 3D website for exploring the machines humans left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. The Explore page shows these places as a 3D scene with spacecraft orbiting them. Visitors drag to rotate the scene, choose Moon, Mars or Deep Space, and click a spacecraft. A chat then lets them ask questions about that machine in English or Arabic. An AI storyteller replies with a short, kid-friendly story built from official NASA data.

The main use is learning: a student or curious reader can understand a mission in about two minutes, without reading technical documents. The target audience is school-age space fans (about 10 to 16) and casual readers.

How it works

  1. The visitor picks a machine. The website sends the question and that machine’s ID to our backend.
  2. The backend is an n8n workflow behind a secured webhook (header authentication). It routes the request by ID to one of 13 storyteller configurations, each with its own scope.
  3. The storyteller is an AI agent. Before answering, it searches a knowledge base of NASA facts about that machine only. This keeps answers grounded in sources and stops facts from one mission leaking into another.
  4. If the knowledge base lacks a fact, or the question is about the machine’s current status, the agent can run a web search and trust only NASA, JPL, ESA, universities and museums.
  5. The answer returns to the chat as plain text, in the visitor’s language.

How the data supports it

We collected official NASA information on each machine and split it into short text chunks. Each chunk is embedded separately and stored in a vector database with the ID of its machine. When a question arrives, the agent retrieves the most relevant chunks for that machine and tells the story from them. The storytelling is written in our own words, not copied from the source text. The agent must state every name, number and date exactly as sourced. If a source says “unknown”, “assumed” or “estimated”, the answer says the same, and if no source has the answer, it says so instead of guessing.

Hardware covered (13 storytellers)

Moon: Apollo Lunar Modules, Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles, ALSEP and EASEP science packages, Surveyor landers.
Mars: Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2, InSight, Ingenuity.
Deep space: Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, Kepler and K2.

Storytelling and safety design

Each answer follows the machine’s journey: why it was sent, how it worked, what it discovered, and its status today. The engineering is linked to the science, so the reader sees why the machine’s design led to a specific discovery. The AI stays a narrator and never speaks as the machine. Replies are short, use simple words and a few meaningful emojis, and keep mission and equipment names in English even inside Arabic text. Content stays suitable for children, and off-topic questions are politely declined.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

Many of these explorers finished their work long ago, and their data is hard for non-specialists to approach. We hope to keep their stories alive, make space history easier to learn, and widen access for Arabic-speaking learners.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: interactive 3D web app, hosted on GitHub Pages
  • Backend and automation: n8n (webhook, routing, AI agent)
  • Knowledge base: Supabase vector store
  • Embeddings: Google Gemini embeddings
  • Language model: accessed through OpenRouter
  • Backup web search: SerpApi
  • Data: official NASA mission data

Working features (delivered)

  • Interactive 3D explorer with Moon (4), Mars (5) and Deep Space (4) groups
  • 13 separate storytellers routed by machine ID
  • Chat in English and Arabic
  • Retrieval from a per-machine knowledge base, with a trusted-source web search as backup
  • Secured backend endpoint

Limitations

  • Answers are only as complete as our knowledge base. Some machines have detailed data and others have shorter summaries, so deep questions on lesser-covered machines may get shorter answers.
  • Current-status facts can change over time, and they depend on the web search backup when our data does not cover them.
  • All visitors currently share one chat memory.

Future plans (not yet built)

  • Separate chat memory for each visitor
  • More spacecraft, added by giving each one new data chunks, a routing rule and a scope description
  • Voice narration and more languages
  • Short sourced timelines for each machine

projectDetails.name: Project The Moonlanders
projectDetails.summary: The Moonlanders helps people explore where and when a lunar mission might land. Visitors can browse sites on an interactive Moon, check seven-day forecasts for sunlight and direct Earth visibility, and enter their own lunar coordinates. A site view shows the local skyline, periods of light and contact, and possible interruptions. Visitors can compare two sites during the same week, rank the best start times for one site, or rank sites for a chosen time. The results help start planning conversations, but the current terrain and scores are illustrative and do not assess landing safety.
projectDetails.details:
Choosing a lunar landing site is also a question of timing. Near the Moon’s south pole, the Sun skims the horizon. A ridge can be lit while nearby ground stays dark, and Earth can disappear behind the landscape. We built The Moonlanders to help people explore those changes before they commit to a place or a date.

The website starts with a Moon visitors can turn and zoom. Pick a UTC day to see the modeled daily outlook at 18 curated locations, including polar ridges, Artemis candidate regions and historic landing sites. A seven-day forecast card for each location shows how its score changes through the week. Visitors can also enter their own lunar latitude and longitude for the same first-pass forecast.

The Moon view makes the sites easy to locate before opening a detailed forecast.

The weekly outlook shows which days change, rather than reducing a site to one number.

Opening a site brings the visitor down to the surface. The 360-degree skyline places the Sun and Earth against the modeled local horizon. Visitors can play or move through the selected week to see those positions change. The page also lays out sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility as time windows, with the longest contact and blackout periods, daily scores, terrain context, scientific opportunities and engineering challenges. A sunny week can still contain a communications gap; we show those conditions separately.

The site view connects the forecast to a view from the ground.

When a site looks promising, visitors can test it against another. Compare holds the dates steady and places two locations side by side, including their surface skies, day-by-day changes, visibility windows and modeled constraints. Best time searches 24-hour starts within a chosen week for one site. Best site starts with a UTC time and ranks the curated locations over the following six hours. The rankings are meant to lead people back to the underlying light and Earth-contact windows, where they can see why an option moved up or down.

Compare keeps the week fixed while the location changes.

Best time ranks possible starts for one chosen place.

Best site ranks places for one chosen start time.

For early mission planning, the website offers a quick way to shortlist places and dates for deeper study. For students and the public, it makes lunar polar trade-offs visible. We connected a Moon-wide view, a surface view and two directions of search: “Where should we go at this time?” and “When should we go to this place?” Visitors can also test a point outside the curated list.

We built the website with TypeScript, React and Next.js. Three.js supports the interactive Moon and terrain visuals; Recharts presents changing values. astronomy-engine supplies the live Sun and Earth positions. We used NASA’s challenge-posted JPL Horizons for separate reference timelines, and the challenge-posted Quickmap and Moon Trek to study lunar places and how to present them. NASA LOLA elevation products informed the terrain research. No special hardware is needed to use the website.

The current live terrain is synthetic and LOLA-informed, so its terrain-blocking results and scores are illustrative. Seeing the Sun does not establish power output; seeing Earth does not establish a working radio link. The website identifies those limits next to the results and explains the sources and calculations in Method & Data. We considered that honesty essential: a helpful shortlist must not be mistaken for landing approval or a safety assessment.

Open the live website.

projectDetails.name: SparkGrid
projectDetails.summary: Wildfire incident commanders rely on NASA’s MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) satellites to detect active fires, but plotting both unharmonized feeds creates massive duplicate alarms, conflicting burn perimeters, and oil-flare false positives. SparkGrid solves this through an automated 8-stage Spatiotemporal Harmonization Engine and a God’s Eye Voice AI Tactical Map HUD (live at https://sparkgrid.masarat.app). Using Great-Circle Haversine DBSCAN (1.5 km radius, 120-minute orbital window), Fire Radiative Power (FRP) weighted centroids, and Bayesian confidence fusion, SparkGrid compressed 27,672 raw planetary satellite detections into 11,505 unified clusters (2.45x redundancy reduction) and isolated 672 Dual-Sensor Verified wildfires. Enriched with live Open-Meteo 10m wind vectors and industrial flare masking (175 flares filtered), SparkGrid lets responders speak to the map ("Take me to Egypt") to fly the camera, compare true-scale 1000m vs 375m footprints, and generate instant AI evacuation briefings.
projectDetails.details:
### What SparkGrid Does

Every wildfire season, emergency dispatchers and environmental scientists rely on NASA FIRMS active fire data from two distinct satellite constellations: **MODIS** (aboard Terra and Aqua, scanning at 1000m × 1000m = 1.00 km² resolution) and **VIIRS** (aboard Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21, scanning at 375m × 375m = 0.14 km² resolution). When raw feeds from both instruments are plotted together without harmonization:

1. **Severe Alert Duplication:** A single 1 km² burn area triggers 1 MODIS box plus up to 7 overlapping VIIRS pixels—overwhelming dispatch centers with duplicate alarms.

2. **Spatial & Radiometric Discrepancy:** MODIS averages radiative heat over 1.00 km², while VIIRS localizes the flaming front 7.1x more tightly (0.14 km²) using categorical confidence (`low`, `nominal`, `high`) vs MODIS's `0–100%` integer scale.

3. **Industrial False Positives:** Stationary hydrocarbon gas flares in oil-producing regions (such as the Gulf of Suez, Sinai, and the Persian Gulf) emit intense mid-infrared spikes that raw feeds misclassify as vegetation wildfires.

**SparkGrid** (`https://sparkgrid.masarat.app`) is an end-to-end Spatiotemporal Harmonization Engine, REST API, and God's Eye Voice AI Tactical HUD that fuses raw MODIS and VIIRS feeds into a single deduplicated operational picture.

### How It Works (The 8-Stage Scientific Pipeline)

1. **Schema & Confidence Normalization:** Maps MODIS integer confidence (`conf / 100.0`) and VIIRS categorical tiers (`low=0.30, nominal=0.70, high=0.95`) into a unified Bayesian probability space `[0.0, 1.0]`.

2. **Spherical Great-Circle Haversine DBSCAN:** Clusters detections directly on the Earth's sphere using radian Haversine distance (`epsilon = 1.5 km`) and an orbital overpass time window (`|Delta t| <= 120 minutes`).

3. **FRP-Weighted Centroids:** Computes cluster coordinates weighted by Fire Radiative Power (`Center = Sum(Coord_i * FRP_i) / Sum(FRP_i)`), anchoring each cluster directly to the most intense flaming front.

4. **Bayesian Multi-Sensor Confidence Fusion:** When both MODIS and VIIRS detect the same fire within the orbital window, SparkGrid computes `C_fused = 1 - Prod(1 - c_i)`, flags `is_multi_sensor = true`, and refines the core footprint to 375m.

5. **Open-Meteo Atmospheric Wind Enrichment:** Queries live 10m wind speed (`wind_speed_mps`) and direction (`wind_dir_deg`) in 50-coordinate batches to calculate downwind flame propagation azimuth (`spread_heading_deg = (wind_dir + 180) mod 360`).

6. **Industrial Gas Flare Masking:** Flags stationary oil/gas flares (`is_industrial = true`) across petroleum basins with 3-way HUD controls (Highlight in Hazard Yellow, Gray Out, or Hide).

### Key Interactive Features on https://sparkgrid.masarat.app

- **👁️ God’s Eye Voice & Camera AI Commander:** Users can speak via microphone or click prompts (e.g., *"Take me to Egypt 1km vs 375m"*, *"Show me Gulf of Suez flares"*, *"Fly to the biggest megafire"*). The AI flies the Leaflet camera to the exact coordinates, switches satellite/tactical layers automatically, and narrates the scientific analysis out loud via Web Speech Synthesis.

- **📐 True-Scale 1000m vs 375m Footprint Polygons:** Draws exact metric bounding squares (`1000m × 1000m` orange squares for MODIS, `375m × 375m` crimson squares for VIIRS, and nested 375m cores inside 1000m dashed boxes for Dual-Verified fires).

- **🏹 Fire-Spread Azimuth Arrows & 🌪️ Wind Speed Heat Layer:** Renders rotated directional spread arrows and scales hotspot radius/color intensity by wind speed.

- **⚡ Automated Responder Action Plans:** Clicking any hotspot generates a 3-point firefighter briefing with downwind evacuation bearings, estimated spread velocity in km/h, and containment buffer zones.

- **📱 Smartphone & Desktop Ready:** Responsive 4-tab Mission Control Sidebar on desktop and a touch-friendly Slide-Up Bottom Sheet + Floating Quick Pills on smartphones.

### Empirical Benchmark Results

- **Raw Planetary Input:** 27,672 NASA satellite detections

- **Harmonized Unified Clusters:** 11,505 clusters (**2.45x data compression ratio**)

- **Dual-Sensor Verified Wildfires (`MODIS+VIIRS`):** 672 simultaneous cross-confirmed fires

- **Wind-Enriched Clusters:** 10,106 clusters with live spread headings

- **Industrial Flares Filtered:** 175 stationary oil/gas flares (including Gulf of Suez & Sinai, Egypt)

- **Total Fire Radiative Power Tracked:** 296,892.71 MW (Peak cluster: 3,635.08 MW)

### Tools, Languages & Stack

- **Data Science & Pipeline:** Python 3.12, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-Learn (`DBSCAN` with Haversine metric), HTTPX

projectDetails.details:
AFTERLIGHT is an interactive educational website that transforms the stories of abandoned NASA exploration equipment on the Moon and Mars into an engaging space adventure. Designed primarily for young learners aged 12–16, it allows visitors to explore a cosmic universe screen and navigate an animated Solar System featuring the Sun, eight planetary orbits, and Earth's Moon.

Users can interact with celestial bodies to explore NASA scientific profiles, or select the Moon and Mars to enter their surface archives. Interactive coordinate grids and glowing star hotspots reveal the locations of abandoned equipment, including Surveyor 3, Apollo 12 ALSEP, Opportunity, and Spirit. Each equipment dossier presents a child-friendly mission summary, authentic NASA photographs, verified hardware subsystems, scientific information, and links to primary NASA sources.

The Apollo 12 ALSEP / Intrepid story also features an interactive voiceover player, allowing visitors to listen to the equipment's story through an engaging first-person narrative.

Our project makes complex scientific information accessible, enjoyable, and memorable through cinematic visuals, animated planetary exploration, interactive maps, storytelling, and audio experiences.

AFTERLIGHT is developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, with SVG-based animations and HTML5 audio. Its content is grounded in NASA's official archives, mission records, and imagery.

What makes AFTERLIGHT unique is its storytelling approach: instead of presenting abandoned equipment as lists of scientific facts, we turn each machine's mission into a story worth discovering. Our intended impact is to inspire curiosity about space exploration, encourage scientific learning, and make NASA's knowledge more accessible to young audiences.

projectDetails.name: Project The Odyssey of Meat-a-Roid
projectDetails.summary:
We developed The Odyssey of a Meat-a-Roid, a 3D browser game that teaches
  space mission design by letting users do it instead of reading about it.
  Raed is sent to strange planet by mistake and must build a science mission to get
  home. In a workshop market he inspects real NASA hardware, such as Dawn's ion
  thruster, the RL10 and RS-25 engines, a Voyager RTG and the SLS rockets, and
  picks a science target, instrument, engine, power source, antenna, rocket and
  orbit. Every choice changes mass, thrust, power, data and cost, and the ship
  only launches when the design works. The flight then tests it with a science
  scan, a data downlink, a dark stretch, meteoroids and a Moon-base stop. Up to
  four players share one ship, each in charge of one subsystem.

  Users rarely get to try a whole mission from concept to operation. Our game
  makes that safe: failure is explained with NASA data, players redesign and
  fly again, and the same facts are taught at three levels, from plain words to
  equations, in Arabic, English, French and Spanish.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

The Odyssey of a Meat-a-Roid is a 3D browser game in which players design, build and fly a complete science mission. Dr. Galal at Mission Control sent Raed to Strange planet by mistake. He guides Raed home by radio, but every decision is the player's.

1. Explore and repair. Raed collects water, fuel, oxygen and shield parts on the strange planet. He then repairs his wrecked ship by reading gauges to find each fault, rewiring the power bay and sorting propellants into the right tanks.

2. Design the mission. Stalls around the ship form a workshop market. The player first chooses a science target: Strange planet's rings, atmosphere, moons or tilted magnetic field. Next come instruments, memory, engine, fuel, power, antenna, shield, cabin, backup, rocket, orbit and route. Each stall shows a 3D recreation of real NASA hardware with its real facts, for example Dawn's ion thruster, the RL10C-2 and RS-25 engines, a Voyager RTG, Dawn's camera and spectrometer, and the SLS rockets.

3. Check and launch. A live ship check shows weight, engine lift, power, budget (stars), expected science data and supplies. The launch is blocked until the design works, and the game says what to fix. For example, the engine must lift the ship at Uranus's real gravity of 8.69 m/s².

4. Fly. A scan mini-game collects science data, which the player must send home using power. The crew then faces a dark stretch where sunlight is only 3.69 W/m² (0.27% of Earth's), a huge rock, a cabin emergency, a Moon-base stop for repairs and upgrades, and a meteor shower near Earth. The shower choices follow what NASA advises spacecraft operators.

5. Score and learn. The mission is scored on success, science delivered, efficiency and decisions. A report explains why it went that way, names similar real NASA missions, and shows that the player followed the same Concept Maturity Levels that JPL engineers use.

What benefits does it have?

Systems thinking. Users see a mission as one system, where a gain in one part costs something in another.

Safe failure. Every failure is explained with NASA data, and players can redesign and fly again.

Real hardware. Users learn real NASA hardware and missions: Dawn, Voyager, SLS, Webb, Cassini, Juno and Apollo 13.

Any level. Beginner uses plain words. Intermediate adds NASA's numbers. Advanced adds equations with a worked example and a practice problem.

Teamwork. 1 to 4 players share one ship, and each owns a role: propulsion, power and life support, science and data, or navigation.

What is the intended impact?

We want users, especially in Egypt and the Arab world, to understand how a real mission is designed, in their own language. The game teaches in everyday Egyptian Arabic as well as English, French and Spanish. It also introduces Egyptian scientists who work in space science: Dr. Farouk El-Baz, Dr. Essam Heggy, Dr. Tahani Amer and Ahmed Soliman. We hope teachers can use it in a single class session. Next steps are online multiplayer, more destinations and a review by experts.

What tools did we use?

Code: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Three.js r187, with no framework and no install.

Testing: Node.js tests, including checks that every equation matches NASA's published figure, and Playwright browser tests.

3D: Tripo, Blender and Mixamo, Manus AI.

Media: ChatGPT, Grok and Magnific AI and Manus AI.

AI assistants: Claude Code and Manus AI.

Hosting: Cloudflare Pages.

Repository: https://github.com/ramo772/odyssey-of-a-meat-a-roid

How is the project creative?

Choices are actions, not quiz answers. You carry parts to the ship, and they succeed or fail in flight.

Real NASA parts become game items. Each one shows its real facts next to its game stats.

Honest science. Every number is labelled as a NASA fact or a game rule. Where NASA's pages don't name a part, the game shows a "source gap" note.

Storytelling that teaches. A funny story, a monkey guide called Steve and an Egyptian-dialect script make a hard subject feel friendly.

What factors did the team consider?

Scientific accuracy. NASA values are cited, simplifications are labelled, and tests check every equation.

Different ages and knowledge levels. Three levels teach the same facts at different depths.

Language and culture. The game uses an Arabic dialect people actually speak, and players can switch language mid-game.

Access. It runs in any browser with no install, adds touch controls, lowers quality on weak computers and supports reduced motion.

Real trade-offs. There is no single correct design. A solar ship is light but must survive the dark, while an RTG never goes dark but needs a stronger engine.

Respect for real people. The scientists appear as inspiration only, with links to their NASA pages, and nothing claims NASA endorsement.

projectDetails.name: Project TheOutliers
projectDetails.summary:
EarthLens: Urban Growth Detective
EarthLens measures how fast eastern Greater Cairo (New Cairo and the desert corridor toward Suez, about 1,067 km²) is expanding, and whether that trend is statistically real. We built a pipeline on Google Dynamic World and Sentinel-2 satellite data from 2016 to 2025. It removes the strong seasonal cycle, which swings monthly built-up area far more than the real trend does, and then tests the trend with Kendall and Theil-Sen methods. The result is about +8.6 km² of built-up area per year (95% CI 7.6 to 9.7). We screened out low-quality observations to check the result holds, traced what land the city grew onto (mostly bare desert), and compared the trend with NASA night-time lights, which point the same way. The findings are in a Streamlit app, an HTML dashboard and a Power BI dashboard. The work matters because rapid urban growth strains water, energy and transport, and planners need evidence of how fast it is happening and how reliable the numbers are.
projectDetails.details:
EarthLens measures how fast eastern Greater Cairo (about 1,067 km², New Cairo and the desert corridor toward Suez) is expanding, and whether that growth is statistically real. A Google Earth Engine script pulls Google Dynamic World and Sentinel-2 data for 2016 to 2025 and exports monthly, annual and land-conversion tables. A Python pipeline then removes the seasonal cycle with STL decomposition. It tests the trend with exact Kendall and Theil-Sen methods and a year-block permutation test, and it screens out low-coverage months. It finds what land became built-up and cross-checks the trend against NASA night-time lights. A machine-learning model estimates which areas are most at risk of future conversion. The result is about +8.6 km² of built-up area per year (95% CI 7.6 to 9.7).

Benefits and intended impact

Instead of a raw, noisy chart, planners get a growth rate with a confidence range, and a clear account of how reliable it is. We want evidence of urban expansion to be trustworthy and easy to inspect. Pointing the same pipeline at a different polygon should make it reusable for other cities.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: Google Earth Engine (JavaScript), Dynamic World V1, Sentinel-2 SR Harmonized, NASA VIIRS Black Marble
  • Analysis: Python with pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn and matplotlib, plus Jupyter
  • Apps and dashboards: Streamlit and Plotly, a standalone HTML/JavaScript dashboard, and a Power BI version
  • Collaboration: GitHub
  • Hardware: ordinary laptops. The heavy satellite processing ran in Earth Engine’s cloud.

What is creative

  • We treat seasonality as the central trap: monthly built-up area swings about 3x within a year, far more than the decade’s trend, so we measure it carefully instead of trusting the raw series.
  • Conversion counts only land that became built and stayed built two years later, which cuts out one-off blips.
  • We use an independent NASA night-lights dataset as a cross-check.
  • The same findings are offered as a Streamlit app (with a what-if tool), an HTML dashboard and a Power BI dashboard, so each audience gets a format they can use.

Factors we considered

  • Seasonality: the strong seasonal swing could be mistaken for real change.
  • Data quality: we screened months with low coverage or few satellite images.
  • Short series: with only 9 annual points, we report the slope and its confidence interval instead of relying on the Kendall correlation alone.
  • Model-derived data: built-up area is a Dynamic World estimate, not a ground survey.
  • Independence: night lights measure lighting, not buildings, so we treat them as a consistency check. The prediction model learns Dynamic World’s own labels, so we don’t claim its accuracy is independent proof.
  • Reproducibility: we documented the data source, thresholds and study area, and we state the limitations openly.

projectDetails.name: AstroSync
projectDetails.summary:
Long-duration space missions to the Moon and Mars introduce a major medical challenge: communication delays with Earth can reach up to 20 minutes each way. If an astronaut experiences an acute stress episode or panic attack, ground-based Flight Surgeons cannot intervene in real time. At the same time, standard wearable monitors often fail to tell the difference between a high heart rate caused by daily physical exercise and one caused by psychological distress.

We built AstroSync to solve this problem right on board the spacecraft. Our system combines two main parts: a machine learning model and an interactive AI companion. First, we trained a Random Forest classifier on 40,000+ physiological sensor data windows (heart rate, heart rate variability, skin sweat conductivity, skin temperature, and 3-axis movement) using 29 engineered features. The model separates Acute Stress from Aerobic and Anaerobic exercise with 97.05% accuracy and a 0.988 ROC-AUC score. Second, we wrote a Python script that passes the model's live predictions and vital signs directly into a chatbot built on Gradio. When the model detects high stress, the chatbot immediately starts a supportive conversation based on the astronaut's actual readings and walks them through breathing exercises to calm down.
projectDetails.details:
How AstroSync Works?

We designed AstroSync as a two-part closed-loop pipeline that monitors astronaut vitals and steps in when stress levels spike:

- Data Windowing and Feature Engineering: We took raw wearable signals—Heart Rate (HR), Inter-Beat Interval (IBI/HRV), Electrodermal Activity (EDA), Skin Temperature (TEMP), and 3-Axis Accelerometer (ACC)—and split them into 30-second rolling windows with a 5-second shift. Across these 40,000 windows, we calculated 29 physiological features, including custom ratios like the Cardio Load Index (which separates heart rate spikes from physical body movement), Autonomic Stress Index, and Sympathetic Arousal.

- Machine Learning Classification: To mimic how NASA calibrates baseline vitals for a specific crew before launch, we used Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation across 40,000+ windows. We tested 7 different algorithms (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost) and tuned the top performers using RandomizedSearchCV. Our final Random Forest model classifies the crew member's state into Class 0 (Acute Stress), Class 1 (Aerobic Exercise), or Class 2 (Anaerobic Exercise).

- Connecting the Model to the Chatbot: Instead of leaving the ML model as a silent dashboard, we connected its live output to a conversational agent. A Python function pulls a sample from the test set, runs the Random Forest prediction, identifies which vital signs triggered the alert (for example, high EDA sweat combined with low physical motion), and passes those exact numbers into the system prompt of our AI Companion. The chatbot then talks to the astronaut using their real vitals and guides them through a 4-4-4 box-breathing routine.

 

2. Why It Matters & Key Benefits

- Works During Comms Blackouts: Gives astronauts immediate psychological support without waiting 20 minutes for a reply from Earth.

- Cuts Down False Alarms: Astronauts exercise heavily every day to prevent bone and muscle loss. By separating exercise from stress, our model stops normal workouts from triggering false medical alerts.

- Useful on Earth Too: The exact same setup can help monitor ICU patients, commercial pilots, or workers in isolated environments like offshore rigs.

 

3. Tools and Coding Stack

- Language: Python 3 (developed and tested on Google Colab)

- Data & ML Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Joblib (for saving the compressed model)

- Interface & Chatbot: Gradio (for the web dashboard) and G4F LLM Client

 

4. What Works Right Now in Our Prototype

- Our trained Random Forest model achieves 98.05% test accuracy, 0.9988 multi-class ROC-AUC, and a 98.40% F1-score on the Acute Stress class (97.36% Precision, 99.46% Recall).

- Our Gradio web app is live and functional: clicking "Run ML Model on New Sample" pulls real sensor data, shows the predicted state and confidence score, and updates the chatbot's context immediately.

 

5. Current Limitations & Our Future Roadmap

- Current Limitations: Right now, our dataset comes from Earth-based stress and exercise sessions. In actual microgravity, bodily fluids shift toward the head, which changes an astronaut's baseline heart rate over time. Also, our current prototype reads from saved test windows and interacts through text rather than hardware headsets.

- What We Plan to Build Next:

  1. Bio-Adaptive VR Environments: We plan to link our ML model's output directly to Virtual Reality (VR) headsets using Unity/WebXR. When stress probability crosses 60%, the headset will open a calming Earth nature scene where lighting, sound, and breathing visuals adjust automatically as the astronaut's heart rate and skin conductance drop.

  2. Offline Voice AI & Vocal Stress Detection: Running a small, quantized language model locally on the spacecraft's computers so it works 100% offline, while adding voice tone analysis to spot stress from how the astronaut speaks.

  3. In-Flight Microgravity Recalibration: Adding continual on-device learning so the model updates each astronaut's baseline vitals week by week as their body adapts to space.

  4. Direct Bluetooth Wearable Streaming: Connecting the code directly to smartwatches or biometric shirts (like Astroskin) via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) instead of reading pre-recorded files.

  5. Delayed Flight Surgeon Reports: Packaging short, automated medical summaries of any stress event and how the astronaut recovered, ready to send to NASA doctors on Earth as soon as the communication window reopens.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. projectDetails.name: MarsMate
projectDetails.summary: MarsMate is a web platform that gives astronauts a single, layered view of the Martian surface for planning and conducting a Marswalk. Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript and live NASA Mars Trek data, it combines optical, thermal, topographic and mission imagery — including Viking, MOC, THEMIS, MOLA and HiRISE — over real landing sites and rover traverses at Jezero Crater and Gale Crater's Mount Sharp, where Curiosity observed boxwork formations in 2025. Explorers can switch basemaps, stack data layers, follow waypoints along a route, and inspect the same terrain in 2D or as a 3D planet. By integrating data from multiple NASA missions instead of separate maps, MarsMate helps crews choose safer routes, avoid obstacles, and target the most valuable science sites. It turns scattered Mars data into one clear, usable view for the next generation of human exploration.
projectDetails.details:
What MarsMate does

MarsMate is a web platform that gives astronauts a single, layered view of the Martian surface for planning and conducting a Marswalk. It focuses on two real sites: Jezero Crater, explored by Perseverance, and Gale Crater / Mount Sharp, explored by Curiosity, including the boxwork formations Curiosity observed there in 2025.

How it works

MarsMate streams live map tiles directly from NASA's Mars Trek. Users can switch between 6 basemaps — Viking colour, MOC Atlas, THEMIS Day Infrared, MOLA colour relief, MOLA + HRSC relief, and MOLA elevation — and stack overlays with opacity controls, including THEMIS Night Infrared, HiRISE and CTX mosaics. It also shows all 9 NASA landing sites, a lat/lon grid, live cursor coordinates, waypoints along a rover traverse, and the same terrain as a rotatable 3D planet built from the same Trek tiles. All imagery and terrain data comes from real NASA missions. No data is made up.

Main use case

An explorer preparing a Marswalk at Mount Sharp opens MarsMate, selects Gale Crater, and switches to MOLA relief to check elevation and slopes. They add THEMIS thermal imagery to compare warm and cold terrain, then add the HiRISE mosaic to see surface detail and possible obstacles. They follow the waypoints along the traverse toward the boxwork area, switch to the 3D view to understand the terrain in context, and use that combined view to choose a safer route to the most valuable science target.

Benefits and intended impact

Instead of checking separate maps and mission archives, an explorer sees optical, thermal, and topographic data together in one view. That makes it faster to compare terrain, spot obstacles, and choose a route that is both safe and scientifically valuable. MarsMate is built to support future human exploration on Mars, help crews make better decisions on the surface, and make real Mars science more accessible to students, researchers, and the public.

Tools, languages, and software used

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Leaflet for the 2D layered map and Three.js for the 3D planet globe. Data from JPL Mars Trek, the USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping Program, NASA Worldview, the Mars Perseverance Raw Images Gallery, and Curiosity's route map for lower Mount Sharp. No backend and no special hardware were used — it runs entirely in a modern web browser and is hosted on GitHub Pages.

Working features — delivered now

Layered 2D Mars Trek map with 6 basemaps and stackable overlays, 3D planet view, 9 landing sites, waypoints and traverse line, lat/lon grid and live coordinates, and full-page map mode.

Limitations

MarsMate needs an internet connection to load live Trek tiles. Waypoint positions along traverses are approximate where the source data is approximate. It does not include live radiation, space weather, or spacesuit telemetry, and it is not flight software.

Future plans — not yet delivered

Offline tile caching, a radiation and space-weather overlay, automatic slope and traversability analysis, and annotated science targets for boxwork and other formations.

projectDetails.name: Tira Nova: Earth–Mars Analog Matrix
projectDetails.summary:
Tira Nova is a search engine and dashboard that ranks places on Earth by how closely they resemble a chosen Mars landing site or rover route. It lets mission teams pick rehearsal sites systematically instead of reusing the same few famous deserts.
We scan the whole planet. 41,034 Earth windows and 47,354 Mars windows (about 50.9 km across) are compared on terrain using NASA SRTM and MOLA elevation, which gives 228,721 candidate rows. We then add mineral evidence: CRISM shows which minerals are detected at five Mars sites (20 site-mineral targets), and EMIT shows whether a candidate Earth window has the same minerals. Terrain and minerals combine into one score, served by a read-only API and a web dashboard.
Every result carries its distance, its evidence and its warnings. Only 55 Earth windows have EMIT data so far, the CRISM detection rule is our own heuristic, and similarity is not equivalence. Surface-texture and thermal comparisons are included as labelled exploratory demos and are not part of the ranking.
It matters because a poor analog teaches a mission team the wrong lessons before launch.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. A user chooses a Mars site (Jezero, Gale, Gale Bradbury, Meridiani, Oxia Planum, Zhurong or InSight) and a mission type (landing site, rover mobility or overall terrain). Tira Nova returns a ranked list of Earth windows, each with a score, a terrain distance, the mineral evidence and warning flags. The dashboard draws the results on a map, in English and Arabic.

How it works.

  1. Terrain scan. The engine cuts Earth (SRTM, about 450 m per pixel) and Mars (MOLA, 463 m) into 50.9 km windows and computes a distance between every Mars window and every eligible Earth window. A smaller distance means closer terrain. Each result is flagged non_discriminating when more than 10% of the eligible Earth windows are inside the good distance, because then the rank barely separates candidates.
  2. Mars minerals (CRISM). From 21 orbital observations we detect minerals per site with a relative threshold on CRISM spectral parameters, giving 20 site-mineral targets. Minerals that share the same spectral parameters are grouped into one independent signal.
  3. Earth minerals (EMIT). EMIT mineral abundance at 480 m shows whether a candidate Earth window contains the same signals.
  4. Combined score. score = 0.5 × (1 − terrain distance ratio) + 0.5 × (signals found / signals needed). The final file has 312 rows, 40 of them mineral-ranked.
  5. Delivery. A read-only FastAPI service serves the results as JSON, including the limits text and caution flags for every row.

Results. Jezero's landing-site query returns a window in the Atacama Desert first, which agrees with the known analog. Its rover query returns a window in Namibia that shows both mineral signals but has weakly discriminating terrain. We show that flag next to the result.

Exploratory layers (not in the ranking). Surface texture (CTX against HLS) was perturbation-unstable, so we report no winner. A thermal run compares the day–night temperature range from THEMIS and MODIS Aqua for two Mars sites and four Earth windows; the two quantities are not equal, so only ranks are comparable.

Benefits. The search is repeatable, covers whole continents and is auditable: each recommendation shows the numbers behind it. Mission planners, rover and instrument teams, field geologists and educators can use it.

What we hope to achieve. Run EMIT on the 127 top terrain and known-analog windows, field-check the top Egyptian and Namibian windows, then extend the same engine to Artemis candidate sites on the Moon.

Honest limits. Terrain is regional, not rover-scale. EMIT covers only 55 Earth windows, so the mineral ranking covers that subset. 29 of the 40 ranked rows have weakly discriminating terrain. CRISM covers 5 to 13% of each window and its detection rule is a heuristic. Several thresholds are provisional project choices.

Tools. Python and Jupyter or Colab, pandas, numpy, rasterio, scikit-image, earthaccess, FastAPI and uvicorn. Dashboard front end: next.js

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: TrendScope — Earth System Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary:
TrendScope — Earth System Trend Detective investigates 24 years of vegetation change in Egypt's Nile Delta (2001–2024, 288 months) using NASA MODIS MOD13A3.061 NDVI data. Because seasonal vegetation
  │ swings hide long-term environmental shifts, TrendScope removes seasonal cycles to compute monthly NDVI anomalies, Sen's slope (-0.02131 NDVI/decade), and Mann–Kendall trend significance (tau = -0.341, p
  │ = 5.727e-18). Built with a deterministic Python pipeline and an interactive React/TypeScript web explorer, it helps researchers, agronomists, and decision-makers distinguish real long-term vegetation
  │ decline from seasonal noise.
projectDetails.details:
TrendScope pairs a deterministic Python 3.12 data and statistics pipeline (numpy, scipy, pandas, pytest, ruff) with an interactive React/TypeScript/Vite web explorer deployed on Vercel. Working

features:

│ real observed 288-month Nile Delta NDVI baseline (2001-01 to 2024-12, is_mock=false, 100% coverage), interactive 2D Map & 3D Globe locator, Anomaly vs. Raw Value time-series chart with Sen's slope

│ trendline, and a Scientific Verdict card that transparently displays statistical caveats (verified by 226 Python tests, 20 frontend tests, and 50 Playwright Chromium E2E tests in CI). Limitations: live

│ arbitrary-AOI NASA raster processing is disabled in public static hosting because it requires a dedicated backend with Earthdata credentials, and the primary Mann–Kendall test is uncorrected for serial

│ autocorrelation (explicitly labeled in the UI). Future plans: deploy a hosted worker backend for custom regions and add Hamed–Rao autocorrelation correction

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project Tom&Jerry
projectDetails.summary: Imagine being a child who has just landed on Mars.  Everything looks exciting, until the sky slowly turns orange. A huge dust storm is coming. The solar panels are losing sunlight, the habitat needs energy, and the astronauts are running out of time.  What would you do? What would you save first?  These are not just questions from a game. They are examples of the real challenges humans may face when living on Mars.  Mars is a beautiful but dangerous planet. Its atmosphere is too thin for humans to breathe, radiation is a serious risk, and dust storms can reduce sunlight. Astronauts must carefully manage oxygen, water, food, and energy. One small decision can affect the safety of the whole crew.  But here is the problem: many children learn about space by reading books, watching videos, or looking at pictures. They discover interesting facts, but they rarely get the chance to use what they learn.  We believe children should do more than just learn about Mars. They should experience its challenges, make their own decisions, and understand why those decisions matter.  That is the problem Mars Vision aims to solve.
projectDetails.details: Mars Vision gives children the chance to explore this question through a 2D educational adventure.Designed for children aged 7–12, the game puts players in the role of young astronauts. They explore Mars, complete tasks, solve problems, and discover what humans need to live on another planet. Scientific information is connected to clear mission goals, helping children understand how to use what they learn.The experience focuses on the challenges of running a small Mars base. Players learn about life support, radiation protection, power, and food production. They explore how essential resources can be produced and managed, and why careful planning matters when supplies are limited. Decisions involve balancing different needs, such as using energy to grow food while keeping essential equipment running.Through these activities, children experience simplified versions of the challenges astronauts could face. Their choices have visible results, giving them opportunities to understand mistakes and try different solutions. Simple controls, clear visuals, and short explanations help make the experience suitable for young learners.

projectDetails.name: Project LEADERS OF TOMORROW X2X PROJECT
projectDetails.summary:
X2X – Connecting Generations Through Climate-Smart Agriculture

Climate change is becoming a major threat to agriculture, causing unpredictable rainfall, rising temperatures, water shortages, and damage to soil and crops. These challenges make farming more difficult and threaten farmers' livelihoods, especially when they lack access to reliable environmental information and modern agricultural solutions.

X2X is a project designed to address these challenges by connecting generations through technology, education, and climate-smart agriculture.

Our solution uses NASA Earth Observation data to help farmers understand environmental conditions and make smarter agricultural decisions. It encourages sustainable practices such as crop rotation and better agricultural planning to improve soil health and help crops adapt to changing climate conditions.

At the same time, X2X targets children through an interactive educational farming game that teaches them about climate change, agriculture, sustainability, and the importance of protecting natural resources in an engaging way.

By bringing farmers and younger generations together, X2X creates a bridge between practical agricultural experience and modern technology. Our ultimate goal is to raise environmental awareness, support farmers, educate future generations, and contribute to a more sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural future.

projectDetails.name: Project TORVIX
projectDetails.summary:
Space exploration requires engineers to balance scientific objectives against limited resources. For beginners, understanding how rocket selection, payload compatibility, weight, budget, and power requirements interact can be difficult without opportunities to experiment.

TORVIX is an educational Augmented Reality (AR) game that introduces these decisions through interactive mission design. Players select a mission, such as a lunar landing or Mars exploration, choose a rocket, and configure a payload using capsules, rovers, probes, telescopes, and satellites. Their choices are evaluated against mission requirements and resource constraints.

Engineering trade-offs form the core of the experience. Additional equipment may improve scientific capabilities while increasing weight, cost, and power demand. A larger rocket may accommodate more payload but consume more of the available budget. Players must identify a suitable configuration and understand the consequences of their decisions.

The proposed application uses Unity and AR Foundation to present space assets within the player's physical surroundings. Conventional menu screens support mission preparation, while a transparent interface displays relevant information during the AR experience.

The project's educational motivation is to make space mission planning accessible through experimentation, visual interaction, and understandable feedback.
