projectDetails.name: Project to the end of the world
projectDetails.summary:
Skytime is a web tool for looking at the same patch of sky in several SPHEREx infrared images. You pick one of five preset objects (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) or type sky coordinates. 

Skytime fetches small cutouts of real SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA and lets you play them as a “blink”, scrub through them, or view a difference against the
first frame. It targets the SPHEREx challenge: making SPHEREx data easier for students and non-experts to explore and compare over time. It is a working prototype. It does not detect moving objects or Planet X automatically, and in its current form most
patches return frames from a single observing day, so it shows how the viewer works rather than proving any discovery.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. The user chooses a target or enters RA/Dec (decimal degrees, J2000) and a field of view (0.01 to 0.5 degrees,

default 0.1). Skytime returns up to six real SPHEREx cutouts for that position, ordered by observation time, and shows them in a

viewer with play/pause, a frame scrubber, speed control, and two modes: Blink (show frames one after another) and Difference

(subtract the first frame taken by the same detector from the current frame, computed in the browser). Each frame is labelled with

its date, detector number and wavelength range.

How it works. Three parts: 1. Frontend: React + Vite single-page app (nasa-front/). 2. Backend API: ASP.NET Core (.NET 10)

(Controllers/, Services/). It validates input, caches results, returns a consistent error format, and talks to the image service.

Endpoints: GET /api/frames, GET /api/frames/{id}/image, GET /api/targets, plus sample catalog routes. The contract

is in API_CONTRACT.md. 3. Image service: Python FastAPI with astropy (image-service/). It searches the public IRSA SIA2

service for SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 images covering the position, requests a small FITS cutout for each, orients it north-up/east-left

from the FITS WCS, converts it to an 8-bit PNG (1st to 99.5th percentile stretch), and caches it.

The backend also has a mock mode that returns generated, clearly labelled “SIMULATED” frames. It exists so the front end can be

developed and demoed without the archive. Real mode is the default.

Benefits and goals. Lower the effort needed to look at multi-visit SPHEREx data: no FITS tools, no archive query forms, one click

per target. Longer-term goal: help people spot sources that move or change between SPHEREx visits.

Tools. React, Vite, framer-motion, lucide-react (frontend); C#/.NET 10 (API); Python, FastAPI, astropy, numpy, Pillow, requests

(image service); Azure App Service (image-service hosting, per the deployment config in the repo); Netlify config for the front end is

in the repo.

What works now. Searching IRSA for SPHEREx images at a position and rendering cutouts; blink/scrub/difference viewing; five

presets; custom coordinates; error and loading states; caching; mock mode.

Limits (please read). - Each query returns at most six frames. In the cached queries we checked for the five preset targets, four

returned frames from a single day (alternating between two detectors, i.e. two wavelength bands) and one (R Draconis) spanned

two dates a few days apart. So Skytime currently shows exposures hours to days apart, not months-apart epochs, and a slowly

moving star will not visibly move. - Frames from different detectors are different wavelength bands, so brightness changesbetween them mostly reflect colour, not change over time. - Images are 8-bit with an independent percentile stretch per frame.

The Difference mode subtracts these stretched images; it is a visual aid, not calibrated photometry. - There is no automatic

detection of moving objects, no machine learning, and no Planet X search. A person has to look. - WISE 0855 is extremely faint in

SPHEREx bands; we do not claim to see it in our cutouts. - The first request for a new position can take up to about a minute

If the backend is unreachable the page falls back to a procedural local preview that is not real data.

Future plans (not built). More visits per target across the 6-month survey cycles; calibrated flux difference images; real spectra

from SPHEREx spectral data; automatic candidate flagging; filtering by detector (reserved in the API contract).

projectDetails.name: Project Toy Story
projectDetails.summary: AstroVitals is a prototype crew health console that works fully offline. A DIY wrist wearable (ESP32-C3 with a pulse oximeter and motion sensor) streams heart rate, blood oxygen and motion every second over a local network to a laptop. The dashboard learns each astronaut's own normal range and raises an alert only for real, lasting changes. An on-board AI assistant, running on the laptop's GPU with no internet, explains alerts and answers health questions using only official NASA Human Research Program and CSA documents, citing every claim and refusing to diagnose. This matters because on a Mars mission Earth can be about 22 minutes away, so crews need tools that help them understand their own health on board.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

AstroVitals is a prototype crew health console that works fully offline, with three parts:

1. Wearable: a DIY wrist device (ESP32-C3, MAX30102 pulse oximeter, MPU6050 motion sensor, OLED screen) measures heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO2) and motion and sends one reading per second over a local Wi-Fi network, with no internet.

2. Personal anomaly engine: a 2-minute resting calibration builds each astronaut's own baseline. Every new reading is compared with it using a robust z-score, and a status changes only if the change lasts 5 seconds (NOMINAL, CAUTION, ANOMALY, STALE), so one noisy reading never raises an alarm. A mission-history engine also tracks resting heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, sleep, mood and a daily reaction-time test over 180 days and flags signals that drift together.

3. On-board AI assistant: when the crew presses Explain on an alert or asks a question, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system searches 393 passages from official NASA Human Research Program and CSA documents stored on the laptop, and a local language model (qwen3:8b on the laptop GPU) answers only from those passages, citing every claim. Questions about diagnosis, doses or emergencies get a fixed safe reply pointing to the crew medical officer.

Benefits and intended impact

On a Mars mission, a message to Earth can take about 22 minutes one way, and there is no internet. AstroVitals lets crew members check their own health on board, understand what an alert means, and know when to act, using trusted NASA knowledge instead of guessing. Because it judges each person against their own normal, it raises far fewer false alarms: 0.48 per 100 days in our tests, versus 19.8 for a simple threshold rule. The same offline approach could help people in remote places such as research stations, ships or rural clinics.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Hardware: ESP32-C3 SuperMini, MAX30102, MPU6050, 1.3" SH1106 OLED, hand-soldered.

Firmware: Arduino C++ (SparkFun MAX3010x, U8g2), with our own adaptive beat detector and automatic LED brightness.

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLite, NumPy, SciPy.

AI: Ollama with qwen3:8b and nomic-embed-text, ChromaDB, PyMuPDF, Beautiful Soup.

Dashboard: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with local fonts, fully offline. Testing: pytest (32 tests) and our own evaluation scripts.

How it is creative

We combined a real, low-cost wearable with an AI assistant that runs fully offline and is grounded only in NASA's own risk documents. It answers questions the way a crew would need on a deep-space mission: with sources, without internet, and without pretending to be a doctor. Alerts are personal, not population averages, and the dashboard uses NASA-style caution-and-warning colours so status is readable at a glance.

Factors we considered

Safety: decision support only, never diagnosis, with tested safety rules (5/5 unsafe questions handled, 10/10 off-topic questions refused). Trust: every answer cites a source, and citations are checked (100% valid). Offline operation and speed: median answer in 2.3 seconds on a laptop. Honesty: sensor readings are approximate, blood pressure is entered manually from a cuff, and the 180-day history and the demo's dashboard footage use simulated data, all clearly labelled. Privacy: all health data stays on the device.

projectDetails.name: Ink and the orbit
projectDetails.summary: This educational survival game immerses players in the harsh, scientifically accurate environment of Mars, blending interactive STEM learning with thrilling resource management. Stranded on the Red Planet, players must apply real physics, chemistry, and engineering principles to stay alive. Core gameplay mechanics involve extracting subsurface water ice, generating breathable oxygen through electrolysis, cultivating hydroponic crops, and maintaining solar power grids against relentless Martian dust storms. By solving realistic scientific challenges, players construct and expand a sustainable base habitat while exploring iconic geological landmarks like Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris. Designed specifically for students and curious science enthusiasts, the game transforms complex aerospace concepts and planetary science into engaging, hands-on problem-solving missions. Ultimately, this interactive adventure fosters critical thinking, strategic resilience, and deep curiosity about space exploration, empowering players to master the essential science required for humanity’s future on Mars.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

This project is an interactive 3D educational survival game set on the surface of Mars. Stranded on the Red Planet, players must manage vital survival resources—oxygen, water, power, and food—by applying real-world STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) principles. Gameplay revolves around scientifically grounded mechanics: mining subsurface water ice, running electrolysis systems to generate breathable oxygen, maintaining hydroponic greenhouses, and protecting solar arrays from dynamic Martian dust storms. Players progress by solving realistic physics, chemistry, and engineering puzzles to upgrade their base and explore authentic Martian landmarks such as Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Experiential STEM Learning: Transforms abstract textbook theories in thermodynamics, chemistry, and orbital mechanics into tangible, hands-on problem-solving challenges.
  • Critical Thinking & Resilience: Encourages players to analyze cause-and-effect relationships, manage scarcity under pressure, and iterate on failed designs without real-world risk.
  • Inspiring Future Explorers: Aims to spark curiosity in aerospace, planetary science, and sustainability among students and science enthusiasts, demonstrating the real scientific hurdles humanity must overcome to become a multi-planetary species.

Tools, Technologies & Hardware Used

  • Game Engine & Software: Unity (or Unreal Engine) for 3D environment rendering, physics simulation, and gameplay systems; Blender for 3D modeling of rovers, habitats, and Martian terrain; Figma/Photoshop for UI/UX and HUD design.
  • AI & Development Assistants: Claude (Anthropic) was utilized throughout the development lifecycle to assist with code generation, debugging complex C#/Python scripts, designing scientific mission scenarios, and structuring in-game educational dialogues.
  • Programming Languages: C# (for Unity scripting, resource logic, and AI systems) / C++ and Blueprints (if using Unreal Engine), alongside Python for data balancing and simulation modeling.
  • Scientific Data & APIs: NASA open-source Martian elevation maps (MOLA) and atmospheric datasets to ensure realistic terrain topology, gravity ($3.721\text{ m/s}^2$), and day/night cycles.
  • Hardware: Standard development workstations (PC/Laptop) with dedicated GPUs for 3D rendering, tested across standard desktop setups (keyboard/mouse) and optional controller support for classroom accessibility.

Creativity & Innovation

Rather than relying on passive quizzes or sci-fi fantasy tropes, the game embeds educational content directly into core survival mechanics—meaning science is the primary survival tool. If a player miscalculates solar panel angles or fails to balance chemical inputs for oxygen generation, the habitat reacts dynamically. Combining high-stakes survival tension with authentic NASA-inspired planetary data and AI-assisted narrative design creates an engaging "stealth-learning" experience where players master complex concepts organically through play.

Key Factors Considered by the Team

  • Scientific Accuracy vs. Fun: Balancing realistic planetary constraints (such as Martian atmospheric pressure, radiation, and low temperatures) with intuitive, enjoyable pacing so the game remains challenging rather than frustrating.
  • Accessibility & Cognitive Load: Designing clean, intuitive interfaces and progressive tutorials so players without a strong science background can grasp complex concepts step by step.
  • Performance Optimization: Ensuring smooth frame rates on mid-range school and home computers so educational institutions can run the software without requiring high-end gaming hardware.
  • Curriculum Alignment: Structuring in-game missions and milestones to align with middle and high school physics, chemistry, and earth science standards.

projectDetails.name: FlameScope: Evidence-Driven Scientific Intelligence for Microgravity Combustion
projectDetails.summary:
FlameScope is an evidence-first scientific intelligence platform designed to help researchers explore and analyze NASA microgravity combustion research data. It brings together data validation, provenance tracking, regime-aware comparisons, physics-based analysis, and retrieval-augmented scientific assistance in one workflow.

Unlike a conventional chatbot, FlameScope evaluates whether available evidence is sufficiently reliable and comparable before supporting a conclusion. It tracks data quality and source limitations, connects scientific findings to their references, and communicates uncertainty instead of presenting unsupported answers as facts.

The platform aims to make complex combustion research more accessible, reproducible, and transparent, helping researchers identify meaningful patterns, understand experimental limitations, and formulate better-informed follow-up investigations.

FlameScope is an independent research prototype, not a NASA-developed or NASA-endorsed system.
projectDetails.details:
FlameScope is an independent scientific intelligence platform that supports the exploration and analysis of microgravity combustion research.

The platform follows an evidence-centered workflow:

  1. NASA Data Exploration: Organizes relevant combustion research resources and experimental records.
  2. Data Validation and Provenance: Tracks source information, metadata, data quality, and eligibility limitations.
  3. Regime-Aware Comparison: Helps distinguish comparable experimental conditions from cases where direct comparison may be scientifically inappropriate.
  4. Physics-Based Analysis: Provides scientific analysis tools for examining combustion behavior and experimental measurements.
  5. Scientific Copilot: Uses retrieval-augmented generation techniques to retrieve relevant scientific information and provide traceable references.
  6. Uncertainty and Evidence Assessment: Highlights limitations and avoids presenting unsupported conclusions as established findings.

The main goal is to improve transparency, reproducibility, and the responsible interpretation of scientific data. An important design principle is that the system should recognize when available evidence is insufficient rather than generate a confident but unsupported answer.

Technology stack:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, and Plotly.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy, and Alembic.
  • Scientific Computing: NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, Statsmodels, and Scikit-learn.
  • Retrieval and Search: Qdrant, BGE-M3, BM25, and BGE Reranker.
  • Testing: Pytest, Vitest, and Playwright.

The project combines scientific data engineering, physics-informed analysis, information retrieval, and uncertainty-aware AI into one integrated research workflow.

FlameScope is a research prototype. Dataset eligibility and scientific validation are tracked explicitly; successful software tests do not constitute scientific validation.

projectDetails.name: URBANOVA Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary:
NASA has watched every place on Earth for more than 40 years. URBANOVA Trend Detective lets anyone, from a high-school student to a city planner, ask that record one question: "Is it changing here, how fast, and is it real or just chance?"

A student picks any place and answers two guided questions; the detective chooses from 12 NASA POWER variables (heat, rain, humidity, soil moisture, sunshine, wind), plots 45 years of monthly data and tests the trend. A planner goes further: inside URBANOVA, our urban-heat platform, every project gets its own Trend Detective that reads 40 years of Landsat images inside the site boundary.

Every answer gives a rate per decade with a 95% range, two statistical tests corrected for year-to-year memory, and a plain-language verdict, including the honest answer "not significant yet".
projectDetails.details:
A building designed today will stand for 50 years, but the people who plan it rarely see how the land under it has changed. NASA has the record; reading it still needs a scientist. URBANOVA Trend Detective turns that record into a tested answer in under a minute, for a student's curiosity or a planner's next project.

WHAT EXACTLY DOES IT DO?
It answers three questions about any place: Is it changing? How fast? Is the change real or just chance? It works at three scales:
1. Anywhere on Earth (public page, no account): for students and curious people. NASA POWER monthly data since 1981, 12 variables.
2. The region around a project: every URBANOVA site analysis includes the long-term climate trends of its area.
3. The plot itself: each project's Trend Detective tab reads every clear summer Landsat 5/7/8/9 image since 1984 inside the site boundary (30 m) and in the ring around it: is this plot heating up faster than its surroundings? Is it losing its green cover?

HOW DOES IT WORK?
1. Choose: two guided questions ("What are you curious about?" and "What kind of place is it?") suggest the most telling variables.
2. Fetch: live NASA POWER data (built from MERRA-2, CERES, GEWEX SRB and GPCP) and Landsat Collection 2.
3. Plot: monthly values with the seasons removed, yearly averages, and the trend line with its 95% band.
4. Measure: Sen's slope per decade with a 95% range.
5. Test: the Mann-Kendall test (Yue & Wang 2004) and a least-squares t-test with an effective sample size (Santer et al. 2000), both corrected for year-to-year memory. The verdict says "significant" only when both agree (p < 0.05).
6. Explore: "Where is it changing?" maps about 80 NASA cells around the place; a seasons chart shows which months change most; up to three places can be compared side by side; a step-change test finds the year a plot was built; results download as CSV and share as a link; an AI assistant answers questions about the results.

WHAT DID WE DISCOVER?
- New Cairo, Egypt: daytime highs +0.33 °C per decade (about +1.5 °C since 1981), significant.
- Svalbard, Arctic: +0.79 °C per decade, more than twice Cairo's rate.
- Same planet, opposite rain: the Sahel is getting wetter while south-west Australia dries; both significant.
- Delhi, India: sunshine at the ground falling (-0.61 MJ/m²/day per decade): air-pollution dimming.
- A New Cairo plot became 3.9 °C cooler than the desert around it in one step around 2005, when it was built and irrigated.
- A cleared Amazon plot (Novo Progresso, Brazil) heated +3.47 °C per decade and lost its green cover.
- Sydney rainfall: "not significant yet". The detective says so instead of drawing a misleading line.

HOW DO WE KNOW IT'S RIGHT?
- The maths: every statistic matches independent software (pymannkendall and SciPy) on 200 test series, with a largest difference of 0.
- No false alarms: on 2,000 simulated trend-free records, simple tests cried "significant" up to 28% of the time; our verdict stays at 3–6%.
- A second dataset: we repeated the analysis on Europe's ERA5 at 15 places on every continent. Temperature trends agree in direction at 100% of places; rainfall agrees at only 53%, so every rainfall result carries a warning.
- Published science: each demo agrees in direction with peer-reviewed studies (Svalbard warming, Indian solar dimming, south-west Australian drying, Sahel rain recovery).
- 396 automated tests for the science engine and 1,116 for the backend.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?
- Students: learn the real workflow of a climate scientist on real NASA data: choose a variable, plot it, measure it, test it.
- Urban planners and developers: see how their exact plot and its region have changed before designing buildings that will last 50+ years.
- Cities and governments: spot plots that are heating up or losing green cover.
- Researchers: transparent, reproducible numbers with every method, source and limit stated next to the result.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?
It is an investigation, not just a chart: guided questions, watchable demos, side-by-side places, maps of where change happens, and a detector that tells a sudden step (a plot being built) from a slow trend. It joins two scales in one tool: the whole planet for students, and one plot of land for planners.

WHAT TOOLS DID WE USE?
- Science engine: Python 3.11 (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Shapely, pyproj, Matplotlib, ReportLab), pytest.
- Backend: ASP.NET Core 10 with SQL Server (accounts, companies, projects).
- Website: React + Vite; Leaflet maps.
- Hosting: Vercel (website) and AWS EC2 (science engine and Trend Detective).
- The help assistant uses a free open AI model (gpt-oss) through Groq. An AI coding assistant (Claude, Anthropic) helped write code and documentation.

WHAT FACTORS DID WE CONSIDER?
- False alarms: climate data has year-to-year memory, so plain tests over-report trends.
- Datasets disagree, especially on rainfall.
- Satellites change instruments (Landsat changed thermal sensors in 2013), so we test both sides of each change.
- Scale: NASA POWER describes about 55 km regions; Landsat sees 30 m but only on clear summer passes.
- Free data services have limits, so the app saves what it reads and says when to try again.
- Honesty: a trend describes the past and is not a forecast. The app says so.

PROBLEMS WE FACED
- Our first tests called 28% of random records "significant". We tested several corrections by simulation and kept the one that stays near 5%.
- Building a plot changes it in one jump, which a trend test misses, so we added a step-change test.
- The Landsat archive is large and sometimes slow; a first site run takes 3–4 minutes, so the app caches every scene it reads.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE NEXT
More NASA instruments through Earthdata (GPM rainfall, MODIS heat and vegetation, GLDAS soil moisture), ground-station checks (NOAA GHCN), ECOSTRESS for heat at different times of day, Arabic and other languages, and a classroom mode where a teacher shares an investigation with a class.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables. Lunar Landing Site Navigator
NASA Space Apps Challenge

Team: Yassen Ahmed, Omar Ahmed, Hazem Adel, Abdrhman Mohmed, Marwan Ali, and Ayten Saad.

We developed the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a simulation-based tool that helps mission planners evaluate Moon landing sites before sending a spacecraft. It addresses three major risks: dangerous terrain, communication loss when Earth is out of sight, and power failure caused by extreme temperatures and limited sunlight.

The platform features an interactive 3D Moon powered by NASA data. It calculates solar and Earth angles, solar power availability, and surface temperature in real time. Users can explore lunar terrain, adjust the simulation speed up to 86,400×, and analyze conditions through live telemetry, charts, and a 30-day sunlight map.

An AI-powered feasibility score evaluates five factors: slope, lighting, power, communication, and thermal conditions. It produces a score from 0 to 100, classifying sites as Safe, Caution, or High Risk.

During testing at Shackleton Crater’s rim, the system achieved 75%, revealing a critical communication risk despite favorable lighting, power, and thermal conditions.

Our mission is to reduce landing failures, communication loss, and power shortages by turning complex lunar data into clear decisions within seconds.

Know the risk before you land.
projectDetails.details:
# Lunar Landing Site Navigator: Testing the Landing on the Screen, Not on the Moon

NASA Space Apps Challenge — Team: Yassen Ahmed, Omar Ahmed, Hazem Adel, Abdrhman Mohmed, Marwan Ali, Ayten Saad

Landing on the Moon is a gamble without data. A bad slope or a rock field can destroy a lander at touchdown. Earth can slip out of view for more than two weeks, cutting off all contact. And the wrong sunlight timing combined with −173 °C lunar nights can drain a battery before the mission ever gets going. Too often, teams only discover how risky a site is after the fact — when it is already too late.

That is the gap the Lunar Landing Site Navigator was built to close. The tool simulates a landing before the rocket flies, combining real NASA data on the Moon, Sun, and Earth with a live 3D environment and an AI feasibility score.

At its core is a real-time 3D Moon that calculates Sun and Earth angles, available solar power, and surface temperature for any candidate site. Users can rotate the model, face the Sun or Earth, and speed up the simulation clock to 86,400× to compress an entire lunar day into seconds. Live telemetry reports Sun and Earth angles, power, and temperature as they change, while charts and a sunlight map project solar power across a 30-day window.

Those inputs feed a five-part feasibility check — slope, lighting, power, communications, and thermal — which produces a single score from 0 to 100. A score of 70 or above reads Safe; 40 to 69 means Caution, landing is possible but risks remain; anything under 40 is High risk. A test run at the Shackleton crater rim, for example, returned a 75% score with full marks for lighting, power, and thermal — yet zero for Earth line-of-sight, with Earthrise still two and a half days away. That is precisely the kind of hidden trade-off the tool is designed to expose.

The payoff is practical: risky slopes and hazards get flagged before launch, Earth visibility windows become visible in advance so communications can be planned, and landing times can be chosen with enough sunlight and safe temperatures. Fewer crashes, less signal loss, less power failure — all decided on the screen rather than on the lunar surface.

The project runs a full site assessment in seconds across arbitrary coordinates and dates, replacing what would otherwise be hours of manual cross-referencing. Looking ahead, the team plans to add automated hazard classification from higher-resolution imagery, multi-site comparison ranking, and real relay satellite ephemerides for more accurate communication windows.

The message is simple: know the risk before you land.

---

Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

projectDetails.name: Project VECTOR PRIME
projectDetails.summary: Horus is a browser-based game where players design a complete lunar science mission and then run it as Flight Director. Players choose a scientific objective (South Pole ice mapping, landing-site imaging, or lunar magnetic-field mapping) and design a spacecraft under real engineering constraints: mass, power, data, communications, budget, and delta-v. After a design review, they launch. During flight, timed crises such as solar flares, fuel leaks, and antenna failures test those design choices, and a post-mission report explains why the mission succeeded or failed and links it to a similar real NASA mission. A sandbox mode, a 100-run Monte Carlo simulation, and side-by-side design comparison help players explore trade-offs. The game runs offline in the browser with an Arabic and English interface. It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by showing that every engineering decision has consequences, and that failure is a way to learn.
projectDetails.details:
Engineering model (simplified for education)
Delta-v uses the Tsiolkovsky equation. Power compares array output against load, and battery energy must cover eclipse. Data is limited by downlink capacity and reduced by power or orbit shortfalls. Mission lifetime trades more science return against fuel, wear, operating cost, and failure risk. A separate planar Earth-Moon simulation was used to sanity-check injection (about 3.15 km/s) and capture (about 0.6 to 0.9 km/s).

Benefits and intended impact
Players learn that there is rarely one perfect design, that trade-offs are real, and that failure is a way to learn. The sandbox mode, 100-run Monte Carlo simulation, and side-by-side comparison of up to six saved designs let beginners and students experiment freely. A team mode lets four players each own one segment, mirroring real mission roles.

Creativity
Design choices matter twice: they set the mission’s limits, and they change the odds of the crises later. The game combines cinematic 3D visuals, procedurally generated audio, and an Arabic and English interface in a single offline package.

Tools
JavaScript, HTML/CSS, WebGL through three.js r128 (MIT), Web Audio API, Web Speech API, Canvas/SVG, localStorage. Testing used headless Chromium automation and a Monte Carlo simulation of tens of thousands of crisis runs to tune difficulty.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)
[Team: confirm this section matches what you actually did.] Manus was used to help formulate the engineering dimensions and equations. Anthropic’s Claude was used as a coding assistant for parts of the game code and for the Arabic/English language layer. An optional “Explain with AI” button asks Claude to explain a mission report; it works only when the game runs inside claude.ai, and a rule-based explanation is always shown. Images, 3D models, music, and voices are not SI-generated: music and effects are produced in code, and voices come from the browser’s text-to-speech.

Limitations
Engineering values are simplified, and the orbit model was not validated with GMAT. Difficulty was tuned by simulation on the crisis layer; the design layer has not had human playtesting. The English translation is partial: some design-part descriptions and report details are still in Arabic.

NASA resources
NASA Space Apps challenge page, “Design and Develop Science Missions,” Mission Design Lab, Webb “Build It Yourself,” and the Saturn V model from NASA 3D Resources.

projectDetails.name: TerraNova
projectDetails.summary:
Imagine preparing to send humans to the Moon or Mars. Before taking that big step, wouldn't it be better to test things here on Earth first?

That's exactly what inspired us to create **TerraNova**.
NASA needs places on Earth that share similarities with the environments of the Moon and Mars, where scientists can experiment, learn, and prepare for future space missions. But finding these places isn't always easy.

So, we decided to make that search easier. Using data provided by NASA, we built a website powered by machine learning and artificial intelligence to explore and compare environments on Earth with those of the Moon and Mars. Through our model, we were able to identify ten potential locations on Earth that share similar characteristics.

We also wanted to make this experience more than just numbers and data, so we created an interactive website where people can explore planets and discover the results in a more engaging way.

We chose this challenge because it brings together our different skills and interests, and we wanted to turn our curiosity about space into something useful for the future of space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

TerraNova is an interactive platform designed to help researchers discover locations on Earth that resemble the environments of the Moon and Mars. It combines scientific data, machine learning, and 3D visualization to make the process of identifying potential analog sites easier and more accessible.

The platform allows users to explore Earth, the Moon, and Mars through an interactive 3D interface. Users can select a planetary environment, explore relevant locations, and learn how different regions on Earth compare to extraterrestrial environments.

At its core, TerraNova uses a machine learning model to analyze and compare environmental characteristics, including terrain, surface features, climate, and soil-related data, to identify and rank potentially similar locations on Earth. The platform also includes an AI-powered chatbot that explains the results in simple language, helping users understand why a particular location is considered a potential analog and what makes it scientifically interesting.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

  • Helps researchers identify potential terrestrial analog sites more efficiently.
  • Supports preliminary research and testing before conducting experiments in lunar or Martian environments.
  • Makes scientific information easier to understand through interactive visualizations and AI-assisted explanations.
  • Encourages exploration of the relationship between Earth's environments and extraterrestrial landscapes.

Technologies and Tools:

  • Frontend: React, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
  • 3D Visualization: Three.js for interactive planetary environments and GSAP for animations.
  • Backend: Python for data processing and machine learning integration.
  • Machine Learning: Python-based data analysis and a similarity-based model for comparing environmental characteristics.
  • Data Visualization: Interactive maps, planetary models, and visual representations of comparison results.

Creativity and Innovation:

What makes TerraNova different is the way it brings scientific analysis and exploration together. Instead of presenting researchers with only datasets or static reports, it provides an immersive experience where users can explore planetary environments, discover potential analog locations, and interact with an AI assistant that explains the scientific results.

Our team considered scientific relevance, data availability, environmental similarities, usability, and accessibility when designing the platform. We aimed to create a solution that connects machine learning with an engaging visual experience while keeping the scientific process understandable and useful.

Ultimately, TerraNova aims to support future lunar and Martian exploration by making the discovery of Earth-based analog environments more accessible, interactive, and efficient.

projectDetails.name: Project VERDANT
projectDetails.summary:
Agriculture faces challenges from climate variability, water scarcity, soil degradation, and rising production costs. Traditional crop rotation practices may overlook field conditions, soil properties, water availability, climate suitability, and farm constraints.

CROP TWIST is an adaptive framework that helps farmers and agronomists develop, compare, and evaluate field-specific crop rotation strategies. It integrates environmental data, soil properties, agronomic knowledge, crop histories, farm records, and operational constraints.

The framework analyzes factors such as soil fertility, salinity, crop water requirements, climatic suitability, crop compatibility, planting periods, and available resources. It combines multi-source data while considering its quality, resolution, and uncertainty.

Using field-specific evidence and validated constraints, CROP TWIST generates feasible rotation alternatives and evaluates them based on water-use efficiency, soil fertility, profitability, resilience, and operational feasibility. It also supports scenario analysis to assess the effects of changes in water allocation, planting dates, and crop prices.

By explaining recommendations, identifying missing information, and incorporating observed outcomes into future planning, CROP TWIST aims to improve agricultural decision-making, optimize resource management, and promote sustainable multi-season crop rotation.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Overview

CROP TWIST is an AI-powered agricultural intelligence and decision-support platform designed to help farmers make informed decisions about crop selection, crop rotation, and resource management. It integrates satellite imagery, environmental data, soil information, climate records, and agricultural history to provide field-specific insights and sustainable agricultural recommendations.

2. Problem Statement

Modern agriculture faces several challenges, including climate variability, water scarcity, soil degradation, and increasing production costs. Changes in temperature, rainfall, and humidity negatively affect crop growth, quality, and productivity. Although large amounts of environmental and agricultural data are available, farmers often struggle to access, interpret, and use this information effectively.

Traditional crop-rotation practices may overlook important factors such as soil conditions, water availability, crop compatibility, and changing climatic conditions. This creates a gap between available agricultural data and practical, field-specific decision-making.

3. Proposed Solution

CROP TWIST provides an integrated agricultural intelligence platform that transforms complex agricultural and environmental data into practical insights and recommendations.

The platform combines satellite observations, climate records, soil properties, crop histories, and agricultural knowledge to analyze field conditions, evaluate crop suitability, and generate feasible crop-rotation strategies.

It also uses Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning to predict potential agricultural outcomes, assess risks, compare alternative strategies, and support better resource management.

4. Key Features

- Crop Intelligence: Analyzes crop characteristics, vegetation indicators, growing conditions, and historical performance.
- Soil Intelligence: Evaluates soil properties, fertility, nutrient conditions, and crop suitability.
- Water Intelligence: Assesses water availability, precipitation, soil moisture, and irrigation-related risks.
- Climate Intelligence: Analyzes historical and forecast climate conditions to identify agricultural risks.
- Crop Stress Detection: Identifies unusual vegetation changes and potential crop stress.
- Agricultural Suitability: Evaluates the compatibility between crops and specific field conditions.
- Crop Rotation Optimization: Generates and compares multi-season crop-rotation strategies.
- AI Copilot: Provides an interactive assistant that explains agricultural data, answers questions, and helps users understand recommendations.
- Predictive Intelligence: Estimates crop yield, water demand, crop stress risks, and potential agricultural performance.
- Scenario Analysis: Allows users to explore alternative agricultural decisions and understand their possible impacts.

5. Data Sources

CROP TWIST integrates multiple Earth observation and environmental datasets, including:

- NASA HLS: Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery for vegetation and crop monitoring.
- Landsat 8/9: Land-cover monitoring and agricultural change detection.
- Sentinel-2: Vegetation indices and crop health monitoring.
- NASA SMAP: Soil moisture assessment.
- NASA GPM: Precipitation estimation and rainfall monitoring.
- CHIRPS v3: Historical rainfall analysis.
- ERA5 / ERA5-Land: Historical climate, temperature, precipitation, and weather variables.

These datasets provide complementary information for understanding agricultural and environmental conditions.

6. AI and Machine Learning Technologies

CROP TWIST combines several intelligent technologies:

- Supervised Learning: Estimates crop suitability under specific field conditions.
- Reinforcement Learning: Explores and optimizes multi-season crop sequences.

projectDetails.name: Project Veyora
projectDetails.summary:
Veyora Bio – Evidence-Gated Crop Planning Intelligence for Egypt
Veyora Bio is a bilingual (Arabic and English) crop-planning platform designed to help Egyptian farmers make smarter agricultural decisions using NASA climate data and documented crop requirements.
Developed for the "Field Shift – Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge, the platform combines NASA POWER climate information with agricultural data to assess crop suitability based on temperature conditions, water requirements, and planting seasons across Egypt's 27 governorates.
Veyora Bio calculates key agricultural indicators, compares eligible crops, and provides transparent, evidence-based planning insights. Its unique evidence-gating system prevents unsupported recommendations by clearly identifying missing or incomplete information. An optional AI-powered advisor using Gemini helps users understand results in Arabic or English.
By connecting NASA Earth observation data with practical agricultural planning, Veyora Bio aims to support more sustainable farming decisions, improve awareness of climate-related risks, and help Egyptian agriculture adapt to water scarcity, rising temperatures, and changing environmental conditions.
projectDetails.details:
Veyora Bio is a bilingual (Arabic and English) crop-planning dashboard designed to help Egyptian farmers make more informed agricultural decisions based on climate conditions, water availability, and documented crop requirements.

The project addresses the challenges of climate change, water scarcity, rising temperatures, and soil salinity in Egypt. It focuses on helping farmers understand which crops may be suitable for their location and planting season while making the available evidence and its limitations clear.

How Does It Work?

Veyora Bio uses NASA POWER climate data to retrieve daily weather observations, long-term climate information, and historical climate data for 27 Egyptian governorates, as well as custom farm coordinates.

The system processes temperature, rainfall, solar radiation, and soil-wetness data. It combines this information with a bilingual catalogue of 95 Egyptian crops, including 25 priority crop profiles containing documented agricultural information and FAO-56 crop coefficients.

Its decision engine calculates important agricultural indicators, including growing degree days (GDD), reference evapotranspiration (ET0), crop evapotranspiration (ETc), temperature compatibility, and water-supply coverage.

The dashboard compares eligible crops using a two-dimensional Pareto comparison rather than relying on a single overall suitability score. An evidence-gating mechanism ensures that crops are only ranked when the required information is available and properly supported by sources. Missing or incomplete information is clearly marked as "Not Assessed" instead of generating misleading recommendations.

The platform also includes an optional Gemini-powered AI Advisor that explains the assessment results in Arabic or English. The AI advisor cannot modify the decision engine calculations or create suitability scores.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Veyora Bio aims to support more informed and sustainable agricultural planning in Egypt by:

  • Providing location-specific climate information to support crop-planning decisions.
  • Helping farmers understand temperature conditions and crop water requirements.
  • Making agricultural information accessible through an Arabic and English interface.
  • Increasing transparency by showing data sources, evidence quality, and missing information.
  • Supporting better-informed crop selection and future crop rotation planning.
  • Helping farmers and agricultural extension officers understand climate-related agricultural risks.

Our initial pilot focus is the Nile Delta, where irrigation challenges, soil salinity, and climate pressures are particularly important.

Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using:

  • Python: Data processing, climate calculations, and decision-engine logic.
  • Pandas: Data handling and analysis.
  • Requests: Retrieving NASA POWER data through its API.
  • Streamlit: Building the interactive dashboard.
  • Plotly: Creating interactive charts and visualizations.
  • Gemini API: Providing AI-generated explanations of assessment results.
  • Docker: Packaging and running the application.
  • GitHub Actions and Ruff: Automated testing, code quality checks, and continuous integration

The main innovation of Veyora Bio is its evidence-gated approach to agricultural recommendations. Instead of presenting a confident-looking score when information is incomplete, the system clearly identifies what is verified, partially assessed, or not assessed.

It also combines NASA climate data, documented crop requirements, transparent water and temperature calculations, and crop-rotation logic in one bilingual platform.

Another creative aspect is the separation between the AI advisor and the decision engine: AI helps explain the results, while the actual calculations and comparisons remain controlled by the system.

Factors Considered and Limitations

Our team considered geographical location, planting season, historical weather conditions, temperature, rainfall, evapotranspiration, crop requirements, irrigation availability, soil salinity, and previous crop history.

We also considered data reliability, source traceability, missing information, and the importance of avoiding unsupported agricultural recommendations.

Veyora Bio is currently a decision-support prototype, not a yield prediction system or a replacement for soil testing and professional agronomist advice. Some crop profiles still require additional verified agricultural information before reliable suitability rankings can be generated.

Future Development

Future improvements include completing and verifying priority crop profiles, integrating additional NASA datasets such as SMAP, GPM IMERG, MODIS, and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, incorporating measured farm-level soil and irrigation information, and testing the platform with farmers and agricultural experts in the Nile Delta.

projectDetails.name: TerraPulse
projectDetails.summary:
TerraPulse is a farmer-centered decision-support experience for exploring crop rotation choices in Story County, Iowa. It brings together NASA POWER historical climate observations and MODIS vegetation indices with USDA Cropland Data Layer crop history and NRCS SSURGO soil attributes to make complex agricultural evidence easier to understand.

Users can explore local and regional evidence about water quality, soil conditions, and agricultural drainage; inspect historical climate and vegetation context; compare three decision perspectives—Current Rotation, Water First, and Soil First; and use Rotation Rehearsal to build or customize crop sequences from research-backed templates.

The platform explains data sources, spatial and temporal scales, potential trade-offs, and evidence limitations rather than presenting unsupported scores or claiming to predict yield, profit, or environmental outcomes.

By connecting Earth-observation data with agricultural research in an accessible workflow, TerraPulse helps farmers and agricultural advisers explore alternatives and identify what additional field-specific information is needed before making real-world decisions.
projectDetails.details:
TerraPulse
Understand Your Land. Explore Your Next Rotation.

A field has a history. Your next season is a choice.

TerraPulse is an interactive agricultural decision-support platform developed by VILTRONIX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data.

Designed around Story County, Iowa, USA, TerraPulse connects NASA Earth observations, USDA agricultural and soil datasets, local environmental evidence, and published agricultural research to help farmers and agricultural advisers understand their land and explore alternative crop rotation strategies.

1. The Challenge: Understanding What Happens Beneath the Surface

Agricultural decisions are influenced by more than the crops visible in a field. Climate variability, soil characteristics, water movement, vegetation patterns, and long-term agricultural practices all contribute to the conditions farmers must consider.

Satellite observations provide valuable information about environmental patterns, but raw data alone does not tell a farmer what to grow next.

TerraPulse addresses this gap by transforming complex environmental information and agricultural research into an accessible experience where users can explore evidence, understand different priorities, and build alternative crop rotation sequences.

Figure 1. TerraPulse introduces an evidence-driven approach to understanding agricultural landscapes and exploring future crop rotation choices.

2. Know Your Land: Discover the Evidence Behind the Problem

Before exploring solutions, users enter Know Your Land, where TerraPulse presents three evidence-based stories about environmental and agricultural conditions in and around Story County.

Water Quality Under Pressure

What happens in the fields doesn't always stay in the fields.

Story County's 2025 Water Quality Monitoring Report recorded 157 poor nitrate readings across its monitoring activities.

The report also documents 39 volunteers, more than 900 monitoring datasheets, and 52 monitoring sites.

These findings help illustrate why nutrient management, rainfall, drainage, and water movement deserve attention in agricultural landscapes.

Importantly, these are monitoring readings, not 157 individual farms or monitoring sites, and they do not establish that crop rotation alone caused the reported conditions.

Water Pathways Beneath the Soil

Water doesn't always move where we can see it.

Research from the USDA Agricultural Research Service's North Walnut Creek watershed provides another perspective. Approximately 80% of this research watershed is under corn-soybean rotation.

Covering approximately 5,130 hectares across parts of Story and Boone counties, the watershed illustrates how agricultural practices, soil properties, subsurface drainage, and waterways interact.

This finding describes the research watershed, not all of Story County.

The Soil Remembers

What happens to soil over decades of agricultural management?

A 2020 peer-reviewed study by Dold et al. examined two adjacent agricultural fields in central Iowa over the 2005–2016 period.

The research reported a measured change of −14.19 ± 6.25 Mg/ha in total soil carbon stock, across a sampling depth of 0–120 cm.

This field-study result provides scientific context for considering long-term soil stewardship. It is not a county-wide average or a predicted outcome of changing crop rotations.

Figure 2. Three local and regional evidence stories introduce water quality, water movement, and long-term soil considerations.

3. From Research to Rotation Choices

TerraPulse connects local environmental evidence with established agricultural research.

One important research reference is Iowa State University's Marsden Farm Long-Term Rotation Study, which investigates different cropping systems in Iowa.

The experiment compares:

  • Two-year rotation: Corn → Soybeans.
  • Three-year rotation: Corn → Soybeans → Oats + Red Clover.
  • Four-year rotation: Corn → Soybeans → Oats + Alfalfa establishment → Alfalfa hay.

Research findings include 57% lower spring nitrate concentrations in drainage water from corn in the more diversified systems compared with the two-year system, and 22–51% higher values across three soil-quality indicators.

These findings provide research context for exploring alternative rotations. They are not guaranteed results for individual farms, and differences in agricultural management must also be considered.

4. Explore Strategies: Different Priorities, Different Perspectives

TerraPulse organizes rotation exploration into three decision perspectives:

Current Rotation — The Historical Baseline

Uses historical crop-distribution and transition information to establish a reference for comparison.

Water First — A Water-Resource Perspective

Organizes available climate, soil water-capacity, drainage, and water-quality evidence around water-management considerations.

Soil First — A Soil-Stewardship Perspective

Focuses on soil attributes, crop diversity, organic matter, and supporting research related to long-term soil management.

These profiles represent different decision priorities, not independently validated crop sequences or automatic agronomic recommendations.

Figure 4. TerraPulse presents three decision perspectives, allowing users to explore agricultural choices through different environmental priorities.

5. Rotation Rehearsal: Build Your Next Rotation

What would you grow next?

The signature interactive feature of TerraPulse is Rotation Rehearsal, which allows users to explore research-backed rotation templates or construct their own crop sequences.

Users can start with:

  • Traditional 2-Year Rotation: Corn → Soybeans.
  • Diversified 3-Year Rotation: Corn → Soybeans → Oats + Red Clover.
  • Diversified 4-Year Rotation: Corn → Soybeans → Oats + Alfalfa establishment → Alfalfa hay.
  • Create My Own Rotation.

Through the interactive crop-sequence builder, users can customize their rotation by adding or removing years, changing crops, and exploring different crop arrangements.

Instead of presenting a fixed recommendation, TerraPulse allows users to experiment with alternative structures and understand how their choices differ from the traditional baseline.

Figure 5. Users can select research-based rotation templates or begin building a custom sequence.

Figure 6. Rotation Rehearsal transforms crop planning into an interactive experience through a visual timeline and customizable crop seque

6. Your Rotation Review: Understand What You Built

After creating a rotation, users can review and compare their selected sequence with the traditional corn-soybean baseline.

The review focuses on measurable structural characteristics, including:

  • Rotation length.
  • Number of unique crops.
  • Presence of legumes.
  • Presence of cover crops.
  • Presence of forage crops.
  • Differences from the baseline sequence.

Users can then explore the relevant supporting evidence, potential management considerations, and limitations associated with their choices.

TerraPulse distinguishes between what can be calculated directly from a user-created sequence and what requires additional scientific or farm-specific information.

It does not generate unsupported yield predictions, guaranteed water savings, profitability estimates, or guaranteed soil-carbon improvements.

Figure 7. Users review their selected crop sequence, understand its structural characteristics, and compare it with the traditional baseline.

7. Data, Methodology, and Scientific Transparency

TerraPulse combines multiple sources of environmental and agricultural information:

NASA Earth Observation and Climate Data

  • NASA POWER: Historical climate variables, including temperature, precipitation, humidity, and solar radiation. The monthly dataset covers 2017–2025 and contains 432 records from four representative geographic points.
  • NASA MODIS MOD13Q1.061: 250-meter vegetation observations using NDVI and EVI, with 207 sixteen-day records and 108 monthly summaries covering 2017–2025.

USDA Agricultural and Soil Data

  • USDA Cropland Data Layer: Annual crop classifications from 2021–2025, supporting crop distribution and aggregate crop-transition analysis.
  • USDA SSURGO: Soil information covering 86 soil map units, including available soil characteristics such as texture, organic matter, drainage, and available water capacity.

These datasets are processed and organized through a dedicated data-engineering pipeline, a backend API, and an interactive frontend.

The application separates historical observations, published scientific findings, user-defined choices, and illustrative explanations.

8. Technology and Development

TerraPulse is built using a separate frontend, backend, and data-engine architecture:

  • Frontend: React and TypeScript.
  • Backend: Node.js and Express.
  • Data Engineering: Python-based processing pipeline.

The team used ChatGPT for brainstorming, research assistance, and coding support; OpenAI Codex for coding assistance; and GitHub Copilot for coding and data-processing support. and Claude for Video editing

9. Impact and Future Potential

TerraPulse aims to make NASA Earth observation data more understandable and useful in agricultural decision-making.

By connecting environmental evidence with agricultural research and interactive rotation exploration, it provides farmers, agricultural advisers, students, and researchers with an accessible way to investigate alternatives and understand their trade-offs.

The current implementation is a pilot focused on Story County, Iowa. Expanding the platform to additional agricultural regions and incorporating verified field-level yield, water, and economic information could support more detailed future assessments.

TerraPulse does not replace farmers' experience or agronomic expertise. It helps make the evidence behind agricultural choices easier to explore, understand, and discuss.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Vitanaut
projectDetails.summary:
Vitanaut is an interactive health-management platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. Crew members log daily habits such as exercise, sleep, nutrition, hydration and mental-health practices, while wearable data tracks heart rate, HRV, stress, sleep and activity. A guideline-based warning system compares readings with NASA-informed ranges and clearly labeled app thresholds, alerting astronauts when values leave healthy limits and explaining the consequences and immediate actions. An AI flight-health assistant helps users interpret symptoms, manage stress and add tailored habits to their routines.
Its distinguishing feature is an adaptive digital garden that visualizes health: stones represent muscle and bone health, flowers represent cardiovascular health, birds reflect psychological well-being, and trees show overall consistency. As routines improve, the garden evolves with the astronaut. By making health monitoring proactive, engaging and personalized, Vitanaut encourages astronauts to take an active role in protecting their health throughout a mission.
projectDetails.details:
Vitanaut brings six daily habit domains into one place: sleep, exercise, nutrition, hydration, mental health and symptom reporting. The crew member checks in briefly each day, wearable and cabin data fill in the rest, and the platform compares the result with a personal baseline and with thresholds taken from NASA sources. An assistant explains what changed and suggests one or two small adjustments, while a digital garden shows the crew member’s health as a living landscape.

Every rule in the platform is traceable. Each parameter carries a named source: a NASA standard, a NASA recommendation, NASA operational practice, a trend with no numeric limit, or an explicitly labelled app default. The platform never presents an app default as a NASA limit.

Astronauts on long missions live for months inside a few modules with the same small crew, far from family and familiar routines. The health effects are usually gradual rather than dramatic: sleep slips by an hour, exercise sessions are skipped, fluid intake falls, mood flattens. By the time a problem is obvious, performance and well-being may already be affected. Communication delays of up to about twenty minutes each way on a Mars mission make real-time ground monitoring impossible, so the crew needs a tool that helps them notice drift and act on it themselves.

The primary users are astronauts on the International Space Station, Artemis, Gateway and future Mars missions. Flight surgeons and mission planners are secondary users: they receive trends, adherence and flagged parameters rather than isolated readings. The same design can support analog crews, remote workers and patients managing long-term conditions on Earth. It matters because long-duration missions will not have a clinician watching every day in real time, and because prevention is cheaper and safer than treating a problem after it has developed.

projectDetails.name: beyond the silence
projectDetails.summary:
Beyond the Silence is an interactive learning website that tells the stories of spacecraft and scientific equipment left on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Designed for students ages 8–13, it combines bilingual English and Arabic mission stories with seven story beats, timelines, NASA imagery, a searchable spacecraft catalog, interactive discovery cards, a quiz, and a museum experience.

The project addresses the challenge by helping young audiences see abandoned equipment not as forgotten debris, but as part of humanity’s ongoing history of exploration. Each story explains what a mission set out to do, what it discovered, what happened to its equipment, and how its legacy continues. By connecting real missions with accessible storytelling and interactive activities, Beyond the Silence encourages curiosity about space science, engineering, and responsible exploration. Remembering these artifacts also preserves the achievements and lessons they represent for future explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Beyond the Silence is a bilingual, browser-based learning experience about NASA spacecraft and scientific equipment left on the Moon, Mars, and elsewhere in space. It is designed for students ages 8–13 and includes 15 mission stories in Arabic and English, a searchable spacecraft catalog, interactive discovery cards, a quiz, a mission timeline, and a museum-style spacecraft viewer.

The stories follow seven beats—from a mission’s beginning and journey to its discoveries, ending, and legacy—so young readers can understand both what each mission achieved and what happened to its equipment. Search, filters, timelines, and short activities let visitors explore at their own pace. The project reframes these objects as historical artifacts: their stories help preserve the human effort, scientific knowledge, and lessons behind space exploration.

We built the site with HTML5, CSS, precompiled Tailwind styles, and vanilla JavaScript. Browser features such as local storage support the language preference, the Internationalization API formats dates, and the Web Audio API creates clearly labeled educational sound demonstrations. We used NASA and JPL materials and sources to ground the content.

Our design choices focused on clear language for young learners, bilingual access, responsive layouts, accessible controls, and distinguishing synthesized demonstrations from archival NASA recordings. The creative approach combines factual mission history with concise storytelling and interactive exploration, helping students connect past missions to the future of space science.

projectDetails.name: OrbitED
projectDetails.summary:
OrbitED is an interactive 3D educational web application that transforms space exploration into a hands-on learning experience. Developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge’s "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge, OrbitED introduces students to life on the Moon and Mars through three connected learning approaches: building, exploring, and completing missions.

Players can build their own planetary bases by selecting and placing structures, explore detailed 3D models and environments from different perspectives, and take on seven-day survival missions on the Moon or Mars. During these missions, they must think like engineers and astronauts, make decisions, solve problems, and understand how each choice affects their survival and available resources.

OrbitED is important because it moves space education beyond reading and observation. By combining interactive construction, immersive 3D exploration, and mission-based challenges, it encourages critical thinking, creativity, engineering skills, and problem-solving while making the challenges of living beyond Earth more engaging and accessible to students.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – OrbitED

1. Project Overview

OrbitED is an interactive 3D educational web application designed to introduce students to the challenges of human space exploration and life beyond Earth. Developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge's "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge, OrbitED transforms space education from passive learning into an engaging, hands-on experience.

The project focuses on three connected learning approaches: Learning by Building, Learning by Exploring, and Learning through Missions. Together, these approaches allow learners to experience different aspects of establishing and surviving in a human settlement on the Moon or Mars.

2. How Does OrbitED Work?

A. Learning by Building

Players can design and build their own planetary bases by selecting different structures and placing them within the environment. They can interact with the building process, adjust the placement and orientation of structures, and deploy them as part of their base.

This approach introduces learners to the importance of planning, infrastructure, and engineering decisions when establishing a settlement beyond Earth.

B. Learning by Exploring – Interactive 3D Models

OrbitED provides interactive 3D environments and models that learners can explore from different perspectives. Instead of relying only on pictures or written descriptions, players can view and interact with planetary environments and structures, making space-related concepts easier to visualize and understand.

The experience covers both the Moon and Mars, allowing learners to explore two different environments and discover the challenges associated with each.

C. Learning through Missions – Seven-Day Survival Experience

OrbitED introduces mission-based learning through a simulated seven-day survival experience on the Moon or Mars.

Players take on the role of junior astronauts and must think like engineers when making decisions throughout their missions. Each decision can influence their survival conditions and available resources, encouraging them to consider consequences, evaluate options, and solve problems.

This approach helps learners understand that surviving beyond Earth requires more than building a base: it also requires planning, critical thinking, and making responsible decisions under challenging conditions.

3. Benefits and Educational Value

OrbitED provides several educational benefits:

  • Engineering Thinking: Encourages learners to approach challenges like engineers and consider practical solutions.
  • Critical Thinking: Helps players evaluate choices and understand their possible consequences.
  • Problem-Solving: Introduces challenges that require planning, experimentation, and decision-making.
  • Spatial Understanding: Makes planetary environments and structures easier to understand through interactive 3D visualization.
  • Creativity: Gives learners opportunities to build and organize their own planetary bases.
  • Active Learning: Encourages learning through exploration, interaction, and mission experiences rather than passive observation.

4. Intended Impact

OrbitED aims to make space education more accessible, engaging, and memorable, especially for students and young learners.

By combining interactive construction, 3D exploration, and survival missions, the project helps learners connect scientific and engineering concepts with practical experiences. It encourages curiosity about space exploration and inspires students to think about the technologies, decisions, and challenges involved in future human missions to the Moon and Mars.

Our goal is to help learners move beyond simply imagining life in space and give them an opportunity to experience some of its challenges through an interactive educational environment.

5. Technologies and Development Tools

The project was developed as a browser-based application using:

  • React.js: Building the frontend application and reusable interface components.
  • JavaScript: Implementing application logic and interactive functionality.
  • HTML5 and CSS3: Structuring and styling the application.
  • Tailwind CSS: Creating and styling the user interface.
  • Three.js: Rendering interactive 3D scenes and objects.
  • React Three Fiber: Integrating 3D environments and interactions into the React application.
  • GLB/glTF: Integrating 3D models and assets into the experience.
  • Git and GitHub: Managing source code and supporting team collaboration.
  • Vercel: Deploying and hosting the application for public access.

AI tools, including ChatGPT and Google Gemini Pro, were also used as supporting assistants for technical research, programming assistance, troubleshooting, and documentation. The team remained responsible for the project decisions, implementation, integration, and testing.

6. Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of OrbitED lies in combining three complementary educational experiences within one application.

Rather than presenting space exploration as a collection of static lessons, OrbitED gives learners different ways to engage with the subject: they can build a planetary base, explore its environment through interactive 3D models, and experience mission-based survival challenges.

Connecting these experiences creates a more immersive learning journey in which learners can move from understanding their environment to constructing within it and making decisions about survival.

7. Factors Considered During Development

While developing OrbitED, our team considered:

  • Educational Value: Making sure that interactions support learning about space exploration rather than serving only as entertainment.
  • User Experience: Designing an understandable and accessible journey for students and young learners.
  • Visual Clarity: Using interactive 3D environments to make complex space-related ideas easier to visualize.
  • Engagement: Combining building, exploration, and missions to maintain curiosity and active participation.
  • Technical Feasibility: Choosing browser-compatible technologies that support interactive 3D experiences.
  • Performance and Accessibility: Considering model loading, application responsiveness, and access through a web browser.
  • Future Expandability: Designing the experience with the potential to introduce additional environments, structures, and educational missions.

Through OrbitED, we aim to turn the challenges of living beyond Earth into an opportunity for students to explore, build, think, and learn by experience.

projectDetails.name: Project VOIID
projectDetails.summary:
In microgravity, fire behaves differently than on Earth, creating unique challenges for spacecraft safety.

Team VOIID developed Flame Intelligence, an AI-powered scientific platform that transforms NASA microgravity combustion data into accessible, evidence-based insights.

Our interactive dashboard integrates experimental records from NASA's BASS-II and published SAFFIRE research, enabling users to explore combustion conditions, compare experiments, and analyze recorded measurements.

Powered by Qwen3.5:9B and Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), our Scientific Copilot interprets experimental findings, provides traceable NASA references, and identifies missing or uncertain measurements.

Unlike conventional AI systems, Flame Intelligence prioritizes scientific transparency by distinguishing verified observations from unsupported predictions.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between complex NASA research and practical scientific understanding, supporting the exploration of safer spacecraft environments for future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Flame Intelligence is an AI-powered scientific research platform developed by Team VOIID for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the "Flame in Freefall" challenge.

Our platform transforms complex microgravity combustion research into accessible, interactive, and evidence-based scientific insights. It helps users explore experimental findings, compare combustion conditions, and better understand fire behavior in space environments.

How It Works

The platform combines NASA experimental data, scientific evidence retrieval, and artificial intelligence through a structured workflow.

1. NASA Data Integration

We collect and process experimental records from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and published NASA technical reports.

Our current dataset incorporates BASS-II experimental records and published SAFFIRE research findings. The system also supports expanding the database with additional investigations, including ACME, FLEX, and SPICE.

Each dataset retains its scientific context, measurement units, and original source references.

2. Intelligent Scientific Analysis

Our Scientific Copilot uses Qwen3.5:9B, a pretrained large language model running locally through Ollama.

The system follows a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach, combining structured database queries with evidence retrieval to generate source-grounded scientific explanations.

We are also developing semantic retrieval capabilities to improve the discovery of related scientific findings.

3. Interactive Dashboard

Users can explore experimental conditions, compare measurements, investigate oxygen and combustion-gas changes, and interact with the Scientific Copilot using natural-language questions.

The dashboard connects experimental observations with their supporting NASA references.

4. Scientific Validation and Transparency

Scientific reliability is a central design principle.

Our platform distinguishes verified measurements from uncertain interpretations, preserves data provenance, and prevents unsupported numerical claims through predefined validation rules.

When measurements are unavailable, the system explicitly communicates those limitations instead of inventing values.

Technologies Used

Programming: Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.

Database: SQLite for structured experimental records and scientific evidence.

Artificial Intelligence: Qwen3.5:9B with Ollama and Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

Data Engineering: Data cleaning, normalization, validation, scientific calculations, and dataset integration.

Testing: Automated unit tests, retrieval validation, and scientific accuracy checks.

Development Environment: Local Windows-based development, with an emphasis on accessible and reproducible tools.

Creativity and Innovation

Our innovation is an evidence-first approach to scientific AI.

Rather than simply presenting charts or generating unrestricted AI responses, Flame Intelligence connects natural-language explanations to traceable NASA experimental evidence.

The platform combines structured scientific measurements, AI interpretation, transparent uncertainty handling, and interactive data exploration in one research environment.

This approach makes complex combustion research easier to investigate while reducing the risk of unsupported scientific conclusions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Flame Intelligence aims to make NASA's microgravity combustion research more accessible to students, researchers, engineers, and space enthusiasts.

By simplifying scientific data exploration and connecting findings across experiments, the platform can support research into spacecraft fire behavior, combustion science, and future fire-safety technologies.

Our long-term vision is to develop a comprehensive scientific intelligence platform that supports evidence-based research for safer human space exploration, including future lunar and Martian missions.

Flame Intelligence is currently an educational research prototype, not a certified operational fire-safety or prediction system.
