projectDetails.name: ExoPulse
projectDetails.summary: ExoPulse is an intelligent fire-safety platform designed to explore and predict fire risks in spacecraft environments. It aims to identify warning signs of potential fires before ignition, helping astronauts recognize risks and take preventive action. If a fire develops, ExoPulse aims to monitor and analyze its behavior, providing insights into its size, intensity, spread rate, estimated duration, and other relevant characteristics. It also aims to provide astronauts with safety guidance when potential fire hazards are detected. Beyond prediction and monitoring, ExoPulse serves as a centralized scientific reference, bringing together available research, experimental data, and resources related to combustion in microgravity. This makes complex scientific information easier to access, explore, compare, and understand for researchers, scientists, students, and anyone interested in the subject. By combining NASA research, data analysis, visualization, and AI-driven approaches, ExoPulse supports a broader understanding of space fire behavior and contributes to the long-term goal of safer spacecraft and future space missions.
projectDetails.details:
ExoPulse is an intelligent space fire-safety platform designed to make combustion research more accessible while exploring ways to predict, monitor, and understand fire behavior in microgravity.

How It Works:
The platform aims to analyze combustion conditions and identify potential fire risks before ignition. By examining factors such as oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, gravity levels, fuel characteristics, and airflow, it seeks to recognize conditions associated with increased fire risk. If combustion occurs, its intended capabilities include monitoring fire characteristics such as size, intensity, temperature, spread rate, and estimated duration, while providing astronauts with preventive safety guidance.

Beyond fire-risk analysis, ExoPulse serves as a centralized scientific reference, bringing together available NASA resources, experimental datasets, research papers, and technical information about combustion in microgravity. It organizes and visualizes this information to help scientists, researchers, students, and interested individuals explore the subject, compare experiments, and understand complex findings more easily.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
ExoPulse aims to support spacecraft fire-safety research, improve access to fragmented scientific information, facilitate comparisons between Earth and microgravity combustion, and contribute to safer environments for astronauts and future space missions.

Tools and Technologies:
The project uses Python, Streamlit, Pandas, Scikit-learn, machine learning approaches, and interactive data visualization. It also draws on NASA research resources and combustion datasets.

Creativity and Innovation:
ExoPulse combines scientific knowledge management, interactive exploration, data analysis, and AI-driven fire-safety concepts within one platform. Rather than presenting isolated research findings, it aims to connect experimental conditions with combustion behavior in an accessible and practical way.

Factors Considered:
Our team considered scientific accuracy, data reliability, microgravity-specific combustion behavior, oxygen concentration, pressure, fuel properties, airflow, astronaut safety, accessibility, and the limitations of available experimental data. We also considered privacy, transparency, and the need to validate predictive capabilities before relying on them for safety decisions.

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRO COMMANDER
NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 | Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer | Team: VOYAGER-X

Astro Commander is a pixel-art browser game where teens (12-17) command an outpost on the Moon or Mars for a 10-day mission. They must keep energy, oxygen, water and radiation protection above zero, and every action has a cost. It works offline, installs as an app, and supports Arabic and English.

Players choose an astronaut and rocket, land, explore in real gravity, collect samples, drive a rover, and complete science labs and a special mission.

Storm Shelter: a base built beside the lander. When a storm warning appears, players can run inside to stay safe, but it costs energy and oxygen and gives fewer points than facing the storm.

Tutorial: 17 interactive steps that react to the player's actions, with science explanations, a storm drill, quizzes and clear, highly visible panels.

NASA data: the game uses the DONKI API (solar flares, CMEs and solar particle events from the last 30 days). Real events shape each mission day and storm. It clearly shows live or stored data and uses real saved records offline.

Built with Phaser 3, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.

projectDetails.name: Project SolarSense
projectDetails.summary: SolarSense is an onboard early-warning and triage system that helps astronauts decide who should shelter first during a solar radiation storm. On Moon and Mars missions, radio delays of up to about 20 minutes mean Mission Control cannot make timely shelter decisions, and crews are usually sent to the same shelter regardless of their individual condition. SolarSense combines NOAA proton flux, NASA DONKI solar storm data and astronaut heart-rate stress into a single 0 to 100 risk score for each crew member. In a red alert, the highest-risk astronauts are routed to the most heavily shielded area first, with a countdown and shelter map. Our prototype includes a live dashboard, a Python risk engine and a heartbeat sensor prototype. Storm and vitals data in the demo are simulated.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

SolarSense is an onboard early-warning and triage system for astronauts during solar particle events. On Moon and Mars missions, radio delays of up to about 20 minutes mean Mission Control can't make shelter decisions in time. Current practice also tends to send the whole crew to the same shelter, ignoring each person's physical state and radiation exposure. SolarSense ranks crew members by individual risk and tells them who should reach the most heavily shielded area first.

How it works

1. Space weather input: the system reads proton flux from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center and estimates coronal mass ejection (CME) arrival time from NASA DONKI data. It converts the flux to NOAA's S1 to S5 radiation storm scale.

2. Crew vitals: heart rate from a wearable heartbeat sensor (prototype) feeds the system. The hosted demo uses simulated vitals. Stress is measured as current heart rate divided by resting heart rate.

3. Risk engine: a composite score from 0 to 100 combines radiation severity (40%), radiation dose rate (30%) and physiological stress (30%). Green is below 30, yellow is 30 to 69, and red is 70 or above.

4. Triage and routing: in a red alert, the highest-risk crew are assigned to the heavily shielded area (polyethylene or water-lined) first, and the rest to a secondary shielded zone. A countdown and a shelter map show who goes where.

Benefits and goals

- Decisions are made onboard, without waiting for Earth.

- Shelter space is allocated by individual need, which matters when shielded space is limited.

- Crew get one clear risk score instead of several data streams.

- Our goal is a prototype that shows this triage concept, which could later be validated with real mission data and dosimetry.

Tools and technology

Python (FastAPI, HTTPX, WebSockets) for the backend and risk engine. HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the dashboard. NOAA SWPC and NASA DONKI as data sources. Hardware: an Arduino Nano ESP32 with a heartbeat sensor prototype.

What works now (evidence)

- The dashboard is published at https://solarsense-topaz.vercel.app/. It shows live crew cards, the risk index, the storm countdown and the shelter map, with a button that triggers a simulated S3 storm.

- The backend streams updates every second, and the risk engine and triage logic produced the expected assignments in our tests with simulated data.

Limitations

- Radiation dose and storm scenarios in the demo are simulated. We don't use a real dosimeter.

- Vitals in the hosted demo are simulated. The heartbeat sensor is a prototype and is not connected to the hosted demo.

- The risk weights and thresholds are design choices, not clinically validated. The heart-rate stress ratio is a prioritization heuristic, not a medical diagnosis.

- The CME arrival time is a rough distance-over-speed estimate.

- Consumer sensors are not medical-grade.

- Live NOAA and NASA data may show a calm Sun most of the time, so we use a demo mode to show the full storm response.

Future plans (not yet built)

Connecting the heartbeat sensor to the dashboard, real dosimeter integration, additional vitals, validation against real data, and onboard hardware deployment.

projectDetails.summary:
**Beyond the Silence** is an interactive educational platform that brings humanity's history of space exploration to life through immersive 3D visualizations, interactive planetary maps, and a chronological timeline of historic space missions.

Space exploration has produced an enormous amount of scientific data, images, and mission records. However, this information is often scattered across different sources, making it difficult for students and the general public to explore and understand.

Our solution transforms NASA's publicly available mission information and imagery into an accessible, engaging digital experience. Users can explore a 3D Moon, discover significant lunar and planetary missions, navigate an interactive mission timeline, and interact with "Ask the Archive," an AI-assisted feature designed to make space history easier to explore.

By combining scientific information, interactive storytelling, and modern web technologies, Beyond the Silence aims to bridge the gap between complex space data and public understanding, inspire curiosity, and make the achievements of space exploration accessible to everyone.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — Beyond the Silence

1. Project Overview

Beyond the Silence is an interactive web-based platform designed to transform NASA's historical space exploration data into an immersive, educational, and accessible digital experience.

Instead of presenting space missions as isolated articles or static records, our platform connects mission histories, scientific imagery, planetary environments, and interactive storytelling in one unified experience.

The project allows users to explore humanity's journey through space, understand major scientific achievements, and discover the stories behind historic missions.

2. How Our Project Works

The platform combines several interactive features:

Interactive 3D Planetary Exploration

Users can explore a three-dimensional Moon with selectable mission locations and interactive markers. Selecting a mission reveals information about its objectives, historical significance, and achievements.

Interactive Mission Timeline

A chronological timeline presents 16 selected space missions, from Ranger 7 to Ingenuity. Users can browse mission histories, explore mission cards, and identify key milestones in space exploration.

Ask the Archive

An AI-assisted exploration interface enables users to ask questions about space missions and discover relevant historical information through a conversational experience.

NASA Imagery and Planetary Maps

The platform incorporates NASA mission photographs, historical records, and planetary map imagery to provide visual context and connect scientific information with real exploration achievements.

Educational Storytelling

Mission descriptions and interactive visual elements help users understand the purpose, challenges, and outcomes of major space exploration missions.

3. Technologies and Development Tools

The project was developed using modern web technologies and digital content tools, including:

  • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript: To structure the application, create responsive interfaces, and support interactive functionality.
  • React: To build reusable interface components and manage interactive application views.
  • Three.js: To support immersive 3D planetary visualization.
  • GitHub: For source-code hosting and project version management.
  • Cloudflare Pages: For deploying and hosting the static website.
  • NASA Open Data and Image Resources: To provide mission information, historical imagery, and planetary visual references.
  • AI-Assisted Development Tools: To support implementation, content preparation, and development workflows.

The application is designed to run in a modern web browser without requiring specialized hardware.

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

Beyond the Silence aims to make space exploration more understandable and engaging for students, educators, researchers, and the general public.

Its primary benefits include:

  • Making historical NASA mission information easier to access and explore.
  • Transforming complex scientific records into engaging visual experiences.
  • Encouraging curiosity about astronomy, planetary science, and space exploration.
  • Supporting independent learning through interactive mission discovery.
  • Connecting historical missions with modern scientific achievements.

Our long-term goal is to encourage more people, especially younger generations, to engage with scientific knowledge and explore careers in science and technology.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The project's creativity comes from combining multiple forms of exploration within a single educational platform.

Rather than relying entirely on traditional text-based presentations, Beyond the Silence allows users to interact with planetary environments, follow mission histories visually, and explore information through a conversational interface.

The combination of 3D visualization, mission-based storytelling, interactive timelines, and AI-assisted exploration creates a more engaging way to experience space history.

6. Design Considerations and Challenges

During development, our team considered several important factors:

Scientific Accuracy: Prioritizing information and imagery from credible NASA resources.

Accessibility: Designing an interface that makes complex information understandable to users with different levels of scientific knowledge.

User Experience: Creating intuitive navigation, readable mission information, and visually engaging interactions.

Performance: Balancing interactive 3D graphics and visual quality with browser performance.

Educational Value: Ensuring the experience communicates meaningful scientific and historical information rather than relying on visual effects alone.

7. Current Limitations and Future Development

The current prototype focuses on a curated selection of historic missions rather than a complete database of every NASA mission.

Future development could include additional missions, more planetary environments, expanded scientific datasets, improved accessibility features, multilingual educational content, and further development of the conversational archive.

We also aim to improve performance on different devices and expand the platform's educational applications.

8. Conclusion

Beyond the Silence demonstrates how NASA's publicly available information can be transformed into an engaging educational experience using interactive web technologies.

By connecting scientific data, historical storytelling, and immersive exploration, our project seeks to make space history more accessible, meaningful, and inspiring for audiences worldwide.

projectDetails.name: Waiting for a signal
projectDetails.summary:
Waiting for a Signal is an interactive educational space game created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.”

The project aims to help students and young space enthusiasts discover the stories behind space equipment left on the Moon and Mars, understand its purpose, and appreciate its contribution to scientific exploration.

Players choose one of three missions: Apollo 11, Apollo 15, or the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter. They then select a mission role and complete challenges inspired by real mission events, equipment, and engineering concepts. The game has two levels. In Level 1, players solve an individual challenge related to their chosen role. In Level 2, they work with a team, where different role-based tasks contribute to one shared mission objective.

The game transforms NASA mission information into an engaging learning experience through interactive activities and problem-solving challenges. Its goal is to make space history more accessible, encourage curiosity and scientific thinking, and develop communication, teamwork, and cooperation.

By bringing attention to equipment that may have been left behind or reached the end of its mission, Waiting for a Signal reminds players that every space mission leaves behind a story worth discovering and that science and exploration can bring people together for the benefit of all humanity.
projectDetails.details:
Waiting for a Signal is an interactive educational space game that takes players on a journey through three NASA missions: Apollo 11, Apollo 15, and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

The player experience works step by step:

  1. Choose a Mission: The player selects the space mission they want to explore.
  2. Discover the Mission: The player is introduced to the mission and the equipment connected to its story.
  3. Choose a Role: The player selects a character or role and takes responsibility for a specific task.
  4. Level 1 – Individual Challenge: The player solves a challenge related to their chosen role.
  5. Level 2 – Team Mission: The player joins or creates a team. Each member keeps their role and receives a different task. Everyone works toward one shared mission goal.
  6. Complete the Mission: Players use what they have learned to solve the challenges and contribute to the team's objective.

Main Task: Input, Process, and Output:

  • Input: The player chooses a mission, selects a role, and interacts with the challenges.
  • Process: The game presents mission-related information, puzzles, and individual or team tasks for players to solve.
  • Output: Players complete challenges, discover facts about forgotten space equipment, and work toward achieving a shared mission objective.

Benefits and Goals:

The project aims to:

  • Make forgotten space technology and NASA mission history easier and more exciting to discover.
  • Encourage curiosity about space and scientific exploration.
  • Develop problem-solving and critical-thinking skills.
  • Improve communication and teamwork.
  • Create opportunities for players to cooperate and build friendships.
  • Show how science and exploration can bring people together for the benefit of humanity.

Current Progress and Features:

Working Features

The project is designed around three missions, mission selection, role selection, individual challenges, and a team-based second level. Include these as working features only after confirming they function in the current version.

Limitations and Unfinished Parts


Future Plans

  • Improve the game's visuals and overall experience.
  • Add more NASA missions and forgotten space equipment.
  • Introduce more puzzles and educational activities.
  • Develop real multiplayer functionality so players can cooperate with one another.

MASA is a space-health monitoring platform designed to support astronaut health monitoring during space missions. It provides an interactive dashboard that displays important health indicators, including heart rate, oxygen saturation, and body temperature. By presenting health measurements through clear visualizations and data analysis, MASA aims to help users understand health conditions and identify potential changes that may require attention. The project explores how data science and digital technologies can support astronaut health monitoring in challenging space environments. MASA aims to contribute to safer and more informed space missions while providing a foundation for future development and integration of real-time health data.
projectDetails.details:
# MASA – Space Health Monitoring Platform

## 1. Project Overview

MASA is a digital platform designed to support astronaut health monitoring during space missions. It provides an interactive dashboard that displays important health indicators and presents health data through visualizations and analytical insights.

## 2. The Problem

Astronauts face several health challenges during space missions due to microgravity, isolation, and the demanding space environment. Monitoring their health is essential to understanding changes in their physical condition and supporting safer missions.

## 3. Our Solution

MASA provides a centralized health-monitoring dashboard that allows users to view and understand important health measurements, including:

- Heart Rate (BPM).

- Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2).

- Body Temperature.

- Health data visualizations and charts.

The platform aims to make health information easier to understand through clear dashboards and data analysis.

## 4. How It Works

1. Health measurements are provided to the platform.

2. The system processes and organizes the available data.

3. Important health indicators are displayed on the dashboard.

4. Charts and visualizations help users understand changes in measurements.

5. The results provide an overview of the monitored health indicators.

## 5. Technologies Used

- Python: Main programming language.

- Streamlit: Interactive web application framework.

- Pandas: Data processing and organization.

- Plotly: Interactive charts and visualizations.

## 6. Project Impact

MASA aims to support astronaut health awareness, simplify the interpretation of health measurements, and demonstrate how data science can contribute to health monitoring during space exploration.

## 7. Current Limitations

The current version is a prototype. Any simulated or sample measurements are demonstrations and must not be interpreted as real-time medical readings or validated medical diagnoses. Further development is needed to integrate reliable real-time health sensors and validated analytical models.

## 8. Future Development

- Integration with real-time health monitoring devices.

- Advanced health-data analysis.

- Improved anomaly detection.

- More detailed health reports.

- Additional data sources relevant to astronaut health.

projectDetails.name: Wasl — Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
Wasl (Arabic for "connected") is a free web app that finds the best day to land at the lunar south pole. There, the Sun stays near the horizon, so one ridge can cut a lander's solar power or hide Earth and break its radio link.

Pick one of 12 sites (NASA Artemis III candidate regions and real landing sites) or tap any point near the pole. Wasl simulates a 14-day mission hour by hour for every landing day of the year. It uses real NASA LRO LOLA terrain to compute the skyline around the site, and Sun and Earth positions computed in the browser. It then names the best, typical and worst landing day.

Users can live the mission in a cockpit with battery, alarms and countdowns, read a survival report, and explore the real terrain in 3D, in English or Arabic, on any phone.

Our Sun and Earth positions match NASA JPL Horizons within 0.002°, and our terrain results correlate at 0.98 with NASA's 18.6-year illumination map.

Working prototype; limits: 240 m terrain, no thermal model, illustrative lander power.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Wasl finds the best day to land at a lunar south-pole site so the lander keeps both sunlight and contact with Earth. It has three parts:

1. Plan: a year calendar where every day is coloured by how much of a 14-day mission has Sun and Earth together. One tap gives the best, typical and worst landing day, with sunlight %, Earth-in-view %, longest darkness, first sunset, a side-by-side site comparison and a CSV download. Buttons open JPL Horizons for the same place and time so anyone can check the numbers.

2. Live it: a cockpit that plays the mission minute by minute: the real terrain skyline, the Sun and Earth in their true positions, battery, solar power, Earth link, alarms and countdowns.

3. 3D: 48 km of real LOLA terrain around the site, lit by the Sun at its computed position.

How it works: from NASA's LRO LOLA south-pole elevation model (LDEM_75S_240M, 240 m per pixel) we compute the highest terrain angle in every direction (every 0.25°) out to 200 km. For every hour, the browser computes where the Sun and Earth are in the lander's sky (Astronomy Engine, IAU Moon rotation model). We check how much of the Sun is above the skyline (power) and whether Earth is above it (radio link), and run a battery model with a 20% reserve. This is repeated for every landing day of the year.

Validation: our Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.002°, and our horizons correlate at r = 0.98 with NASA's LOLA 18.6-year illumination map (40 points south of 85°S).

What benefits does it have?

It answers in seconds a question that normally needs terrain models, ephemerides and power budgets combined by hand. It is free, needs no install, works on phones, and every number can be checked against NASA tools.

What is the intended impact?

Mission planners get a fast first screen of sites and landing days before detailed analysis. Students and the public, including Arabic speakers, can see why the south pole is hard and follow Artemis and commercial Moon landings.

What tools did you use?

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no build step), three.js for 3D, Astronomy Engine for Sun and Earth positions, Web Audio for sound, Python for terrain preprocessing and validation, GitHub Pages for hosting. Source code: https://github.com/Mahmoud-Magdy-ai/wasl8-lunar (MIT licence)

How is your project creative?

Most tools show terrain, images or sky positions separately. Wasl combines them into one decision (which day to land) and then lets you live that day from inside the lander, so the numbers become an experience anyone can understand.

What factors did your team consider?

Accuracy (validated against two NASA references), honesty about limits, access (free, phones, English and Arabic) and traceability (every number links to a NASA source). Limits we state openly: 240 m terrain smooths small hills; no thermal model; Earth visibility is line of sight only; lander power numbers are illustrative. Status: working prototype, running today at the live link.

projectDetails.name: Project WASP-12B : The Rusty Planet
projectDetails.summary:
**The Rusty Planet: Survival Guide** is an immersive, first-person Mars survival game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Built using Unreal Engine 5, the game places players in the role of an astronaut stranded on Mars, where they must survive seven Martian days while managing oxygen, water, temperature, energy, and other essential resources.

Through interactive missions, environmental hazards, and a GIS-based navigation system inspired by NASA planetary data, players experience the scientific and technological challenges of surviving on Mars. Each day introduces increasingly difficult tasks, encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and strategic decision-making.

What makes our project unique is its combination of scientific realism, educational gameplay, and psychological horror. An AI assistant named ORBIT guides players through their journey, while mysterious transmissions and atmospheric storytelling create a sense of isolation and suspense.

Our project addresses the challenge by transforming complex Mars exploration concepts into an accessible, engaging experience. We aim to inspire curiosity about space science, demonstrate the importance of resource management and survival technologies, and help players understand the challenges humanity must overcome to establish a sustainable presence on Mars.

**Our goal is to make space education something people can experience, not just study.**
projectDetails.details:
The Rusty Planet: Survival Guide

The Rusty Planet: Survival Guide is an immersive, first-person Mars survival game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It combines scientific exploration, resource management, interactive missions, and psychological horror to create an engaging educational experience.

Players take on the role of an astronaut stranded at an isolated Martian research station. Their mission is to survive seven Martian days (sols) while managing essential resources such as oxygen, water, temperature, health, battery, and electrical power. Each sol introduces new challenges, including equipment failures, dust storms, resource shortages, and mysterious transmissions. Players complete interactive tasks, earn experience points, and use a Geographic Information System (GIS) map to navigate the Martian environment.

Our project's primary goal is to make learning about Mars exploration and astronaut survival both accessible and entertaining. By transforming real scientific challenges into interactive gameplay, we aim to inspire curiosity about space exploration, planetary science, and the technologies required for future human missions to Mars.

Technologies and Tools: Our game was developed using Unreal Engine 5, utilizing its Blueprint Visual Scripting system, 3D environment tools, and interactive user interfaces. Our approach incorporates NASA planetary datasets and mapping resources, including Mars imagery and geographic information, to inform the game's environment and scientific concepts.

Creativity and Innovation: What makes our project unique is its combination of realistic survival mechanics with subtle psychological horror. Rather than relying on traditional enemies, the game creates tension through isolation, environmental hazards, limited resources, and an increasingly unsettling AI assistant named ORBIT. The seven-sol progression gradually increases difficulty while teaching players the importance of scientific problem-solving and decision-making.

Development Considerations: Our team prioritized scientific credibility, educational value, accessibility, immersive storytelling, and technical feasibility. We designed the experience to balance entertainment with learning while keeping the gameplay achievable within the hackathon's limited development timeframe.

Intended Impact: We hope to demonstrate how video games can transform complex scientific information into memorable, interactive learning experiences. The Rusty Planet encourages players to think critically, manage limited resources, and understand the challenges of sustaining human life beyond Earth.

Our mission is simple: Make players experience what it takes to survive on Mars, rather than just read about it.

Mars doesn't need to kill you. You only need to make one mistake.

projectDetails.name: AstroBalance
projectDetails.summary: It all started with a simple question: How does space affect the human body? While space exploration pushes humanity beyond Earth, astronauts face serious challenges that threaten their physical health, mental wellbeing, and survival. **AstroBalance** addresses these challenges by transforming astronaut health monitoring into an interactive educational experience. Our web-based platform takes users on a simulated journey from Earth to Mars, following astronaut Shehab through five major hazards of spaceflight: microgravity, isolation, cabin air failure, medical emergencies, and radiation. Through interactive scenarios, users monitor health indicators, make critical decisions, and observe the consequences of their actions. Inspired by NASA research, AstroBalance combines storytelling, gamification, and scientific information to help students and the public understand the importance of continuous health monitoring, early detection, and timely intervention, showing that protecting astronauts is just as important as exploring the universe.
projectDetails.details:
AstroBalance is an interactive educational platform that simulates the health challenges astronauts face during space missions. It takes users on a journey from Earth to Mars, following an astronaut named Shehab through five major hazards of spaceflight. Users monitor his health, make decisions, and observe how their choices affect his condition. The project combines NASA-based research, interactive scenarios, animations, and gamification to explain the importance of astronaut health monitoring, early detection, and emergency response.

1. Opening Briefing

Introduces the mission and the five major hazards of human spaceflight.

2. Initial Health Assessment
Establishes Shehab’s health baseline before the mission begins.

3. Microgravity
Explores how weightlessness affects the astronaut’s body and the importance of exercise.

4. Isolation
Highlights the psychological challenges of being separated from Earth and ways to maintain mental well-being.

5. Cabin Air Emergency
Simulates a cabin air failure and challenges users to make decisions to protect the astronaut.

6. Radiation
Explores the risks of space radiation and the importance of monitoring and protection.

7. Landing on Mars
Concludes the mission, allowing users to review the journey and its outcomes.

How It Works

  • Interactive journey: A simple, step-by-step interface guides users through Shehab’s mission from Earth to Mars.
  • Health assessment: Users establish an initial health baseline before exploring the challenges of spaceflight.
  • Interactive simulations: Users experience five major space hazards: microgravity, isolation, cabin air emergencies, and radiation, making decisions that affect the simulated astronaut’s health.
  • Visual feedback: Animations and health indicators help users understand the effects of each scenario.
  • Gamification: Storytelling and interactive challenges keep users engaged throughout the mission.

Benefits

AstroBalance makes astronaut health challenges easier to understand by turning space research into an interactive experience. It helps users explore how space conditions affect the human body and mind, while highlighting the importance of health monitoring, early detection, and timely intervention.

Our Goals

Our goal is to raise awareness about the health challenges of human space exploration, inspire interest in STEM, and help students understand the importance of protecting astronauts on long-duration missions. We also aim to show how research into astronaut health can contribute to our understanding of human health on Earth.

Tools & Technologies Used

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript.
  • 3D & Animation: Three.js.
  • Research: NASA-based research and educational resources.
  • Design: Interactive UI/UX and visual storytelling.
  • Deployment: Vercel, making the platform accessible through a web browser on phones, tablets, and laptops.

projectDetails.summary: AstroSurvive is a 3D first-person Martian outpost survival game designed for kids ages 7–12 to experience real space engineering trade-offs. projectDetails.details:
Playable Windows Build (ZIP) : https://drive.google.com/file/d/1k23yc0QLGG2ce0FZH_CwL-iQxZLHRpdv/view?usp=sharing

Built in Unity 6 (C#), AstroSurvive places young learners in a 3D Martian outpost where they must survive 5 Sols (Martian days) by managing three competing resources: Global Power, Oxygen, and Radiation Shielding. At the start of each Sol, the game queries NASA's DONKI API for real solar flare activity (with an embedded local JSON dataset as an offline fallback). When a solar storm hits, players physically toggle the protective shield dome or interact with solar arrays and hydroponic greenhouses to balance power and oxygen—where every choice carries a real engineering trade-off and displays a simplified NASA OSDR/RadLab scientific fact.

projectDetails.name: Orbital Signs
projectDetails.summary:
On a Mars mission a message to Earth takes 20+ minutes each way, so the crew has
to make the first health decisions on board. Orbital Signs compares every reading with the astronaut'sown baseline, catches bad readings before they raise a false alarm, and uses fixed, testable rules (not AI) to decide what needs action now and what can wait for Earth. A voice and text companion, Echo, explains the numbers in plain words, and every number it says is checked by code.
projectDetails.details:
Orbital Signs is a web app that works as a personal health companion for one astronaut. It has four ideas:

• Know your normal. Each reading is compared with the astronaut's own baseline, built from their last 14 days of readings, not with a population average.

• Catch bad readings first. Reading-quality checks (for example, blood pressure right after exercise) ask for a retake instead of raising an alarm.

• Rules decide, AI explains. What needs action on board and what can wait for Earth is decided only by named, tested rules. Every decision cites the rule that made it. AI is allowed to phrase an answer, never to decide one.

• Echo, a companion you can talk or type to. Ask about your numbers or NASA research in plain language; Echo answers from the astronaut's own data and NASA notes.

projectDetails.name: Lunar outpost survival
projectDetails.summary: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12. The player keeps a one-person outpost at the lunar south pole running for 32 game days while the crew is away. Every day brings real trade-offs: 10 kW of sunlight must be shared between life support, food lights, science and storm watch, while oxygen, water and food must last. Every storm in the game copies a real solar flare recorded in NASA's DONKI space weather database, and the player must read the forecast and reach the radiation shelter in time. Short sourced info cards turn each mechanic into a real science fact. It runs in any desktop browser with no installation, and a Judge mode lets reviewers jump to any day or event.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES:
The player runs a lunar south-pole outpost for 32 game days (each day lasts 4 real minutes). They eat, drink, water radishes, share 10 kW of solar power between four systems (life support, food lights, science, storm watch), clean panels dimmed by lander dust, swap power packs, collect cargo, go on missions (rock and soil, an ice-dig mini-game, and a final rare stone), process samples at the lab, read the storm forecast, and shelter from solar storms. The ending shows research %, 1 to 5 stars, and 'What you learned'.

TRY IT IN 2 MINUTES:
Open the game link, click Judge mode, choose the preset 'Storm during a mission', collect the sample, and walk to the shelter before the countdown ends. For the full run, click Start Game. Controls: arrows or WASD, E to interact, Esc for the menu.

KEY FEATURES:
8 storms copied from real NASA DONKI flares, labelled on screen with class and date; a Space Weather Log listing them; crater-rim shadow days with no solar power; long polar shadows that turn with the clock; health, blackout and failed missions; a guided tutorial and daily checklist for young players; sourced info cards and a Fact log; autosave, manual save and Retry day; a Judge mode with presets and a clean Video mode.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT:
Children practise planning, cause and effect, and risk, the same choices a real crew makes, while learning sourced facts about the Moon, the Sun and life support. It is free, runs in a browser with no installation or account, and a game day takes about 4 minutes, so it fits a classroom lesson.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE:
Every danger is tied to a real, dated observation. Each storm copies a real solar flare from NASA's DONKI database and names it on screen, and the finale is the X28 flare of 2003, the brightest X-ray flare ever measured. The south-pole sky is modelled as it really is: the Sun circles low on the horizon, long shadows turn with the clock, and crater-rim shadow days cut solar power, based on NASA's polar power studies.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED:
The age range 7 to 12 (icons before numbers, short cards, a guided tutorial, kind failure screens with Retry day); scientific honesty (every simplification is labelled, for example radishes grow about 4x faster than on the ISS); a small set of resources so the trade-offs stay clear (power, life support, food); access (browser, no install, keyboard only, works offline once loaded); and reviewers with little time (Judge mode).

TOOLS:
Godot Engine 4.7.2 (GDScript) exported to WebAssembly; Python 3.11 (DONKI download, asset preparation, sound generation); Pixel Lab (AI-generated pixel art); Claude Code (AI-assisted coding); Git. No special hardware.

EVIDENCE:
Automated tests run after every change. sim_check plays all 32 days with a scripted careful player and matches the design table (meals exactly, water within 0.1 L, research exactly); other tests cover endings and storm timing, every Judge button, save and load, oxygen and blackout, collisions, text overflow and audio. Play-tested in the browser by both team members and by independent AI play-testers.

WORKS NOW:
The full 32-day run with both endings, missions, storms, shadow days, saves, Judge mode, and sound.

LIMITS:
Desktop browser and keyboard only (no phones or tablets); English only; one save slot stored in the browser; time is compressed (labelled in the game); storms use archived flares, not live data; not yet tested with children.

FUTURE PLANS:
Arabic and touch controls, a teacher guide, a 'today's Sun' mode with live DONKI data, more crops and school testing.

projectDetails.name: Mars Crew
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Crew is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12, in Arabic and English. One to four players run a small base on Mars, in Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover measures radiation. Each player has one job: the Engineer keeps the power on, the Farmer grows food and fresh air, the Doctor protects the crew from radiation, and Mission Control on Earth watches the Sun. Robots fill any empty job.

There is never enough power, so every choice costs something and the players have to talk it through. The solar storms in the game really happened: they come from NASA's DONKI records with their real dates, and the radio delay between Earth and Mars is worked out for the real date, so a warning from Earth can arrive up to 20 minutes late. Dusty, a friendly robot who speaks in a recorded Egyptian Arabic voice and in English, guides the crew. Every job is a short mini-game that teaches one real fact, and a Science Lab, a Mars Academy, a Mars Explorer with real craters and real rover landings, and two missions based on real NASA events turn NASA's data into things children can try for themselves.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

Children aged 7 to 12 love space, but what they meet is usually facts and posters. They see how missions end, not the decisions that make them work. On Mars every decision has a cost: the air is thin, dust storms cover the solar panels, solar storms bring radiation, and a message from Earth can take up to about 22 minutes to arrive. The challenge asked for a game where children run a Martian or lunar outpost and feel these trade-offs for themselves, using real NASA data instead of invented numbers.

Our solution

Mars Crew turns each part of a real mission into a job for one player, so the trade-offs become real conversations between children. Whatever power one player gets, another player loses. A mission lasts about 15 minutes, every day ends with a short report that links each choice to its result, and losing is safe: the crew can replay the same morning with a new plan.

Every objective of the challenge, in the game

  • Run a Martian outpost: a base in Gale Crater with a greenhouse, labs, a radiation shelter, a sleep room and solar panels outside. A mission lasts 5, 6 or 7 days.
  • Power budgeting: every morning the crew shares a few power bolts between the air machine, plant lights, the storm walls and the radio, and must keep 3 for the night heaters. Dust on the panels lowers tomorrow's power.
  • Life support: Air + Food runs down every day. Suit air runs out outside, so players must go back in to refill. An air leak drains the base until someone patches it.
  • Food production: the Farmer plants, waters and harvests. Plants need light and water and pay back days later, so today's choice decides next week's food and air.
  • Radiation shielding: real solar flares trigger storms. The crew runs to a shelter whose walls hold water; radiation shortens each health bar for the rest of the mission and never heals.
  • Communication delay: Mission Control sees flares first, but warnings reach Mars only after the real light-travel delay for that date (19.8 minutes in February 2026). Earth sees a Mars camera that is minutes old.
  • Real trade-offs: 8 crew dilemmas, a shared power plan, and choices whose results show up days later. Turning the radio off saves power but blocks storm warnings.
  • Real NASA data: 165 real flares from NASA DONKI with their dates and IDs, real photos of the Sun on each flare day from NASA's SDO, Mars terrain from NASA MOLA, a globe from the Viking mosaic, real craters and real landing sites.
  • Ages 7 to 12: short sentences, a robot guide, mini-games instead of menus, "Help me choose" for younger players, and a visible arrow to the next job.
  • Teamwork: 1 to 4 players with split screen. If a teammate goes down, someone has 28 seconds to reach them. Every night the whole crew must meet in the sleep room.
  • Learning that sticks: mini-games that each teach one fact, 11 hands-on experiments, 12 Academy levels with a science question each, and 24 science cards with their sources.
  • Accessible to everyone: full Arabic and English, free, no install, no account, and it still works from saved data when there is no internet.

How does our solution work

1. Meet Dusty, the crew's robot guide

When the game opens, Dusty leaves his corner, grows as he flies to the middle of the screen, and welcomes the player in his own voice, then laughs, winks and returns to his corner. He stays with the crew on every screen: he explains things in short sentences, points to the next job, reacts to what happens with 15 expressions, and has a "Tell me more" button for extra detail.

2. Choose your crew

Each player picks one job and types a name and a suit colour. The four astronauts are drawn in code, with four views and ten expressions each, and their faces and poses follow what is really happening to them.

3. Build the mission (Mission Blueprint)

Before launch, the crew can choose a landing site (Gale, Jezero or Elysium) and up to three instruments inspired by real NASA ones (MEDA weather, RAD radiation, MOXIE oxygen), inside a small budget. The choices change the starting battery, shelter or Air + Food. The game says clearly that these budgets and bonuses are game rules, not spacecraft specifications.

4. A day on Mars

  1. Choose. Every second day the crew votes on a dilemma. Both options cost something.
  2. Share the power. Give power bolts to four machines and keep 3 for the night.
  3. Work. Each player has a sticky-note job list: jobs come in order, and emergencies such as a leak or a hurt teammate jump to the top. Every job is a mini-game.
  4. Survive. Suit air, nightfall, space rocks, dust devils, air leaks and solar storms.
  5. Sleep and learn. At night the whole crew must gather in the sleep room. The night report shows the day's numbers, a real fact about sleep in space, and a new science card.

5. A real solar storm, and a delayed warning

Each mission uses a window of real days from one of four saved periods of NASA DONKI flare records (165 flares, 2016 to 2026). On the hardest level, the Sun is the real February 2026 Sun, with an X8.1 flare on 1 February. Mission Control sees the flare first, but the warning reaches Mars only after the real radio delay for that date. The crew runs to the shelter. After the storm, a "This really happened!" card shows the real Sun on that day, photographed by NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory, with a ring on the flare and its DONKI record.

6. Every job is a mini-game

Each mini-game teaches one idea: wipe the dust off a panel (dust blocks sunlight), find the flare on the Sun and see its class (flares are graded A, B, C, M, X), drill through sand and rock to ice (water on Mars is underground), press repair steps in order (crews follow procedures), keep the dish pointed at Earth, patch a leak before the air escapes, breathe slowly to rest, and more: 15 jobs in total.

7. Mars Academy (solo levels)

One player learns one job at a time: 12 levels, 3 for each job. Each level opens with a hands-on experiment, gives one short job with a goal list, and ends with a science question. Players earn up to 3 stars and become an Expert when they finish a job's path. Example: "Storm warning!" is built on a real X1.5 flare from 3 February 2026.

8. Science Lab

The Science Lab on the main menu holds 11 hands-on experiments: dust on a solar panel, power at night, a water wall against radiation, the health bar, plants and light, ice under the ground, the radio delay, a twin rover on Earth, space rocks, dust storms and the space suit. Each one opens with Dusty's explanation, which he can read aloud in his recorded voice, and a slider or button to try it. Example: in "Power comes from the Sun", the child moves the dust slider and watches the power bolts drop as the panel gets dusty. The lab also holds the sticker album of 24 science cards, each with its fact and its source, and real NASA photos of Mars.

9. Mars Explorer: real places, real craters, real landings

A rotating globe made from the NASA/USGS Viking colour mosaic shows 8 real landing places and 11 named features (10 craters and the Hellas basin). Clicking a crater flies down to a close-up map made from NASA MOLA elevation data, with verified facts, a NASA image with its credit, and Dusty's explanation. From a landing place, children can help one of 9 real spacecraft land the way it really did: parachute, legs, airbags or sky crane. For example, they help Perseverance land in Jezero Crater.

10. Real NASA Event Missions

The Mission Archive holds two short missions based on real events: "The Radiation Surge" (Curiosity's RAD instrument measured its largest radiation surge since landing, on 20 May 2024) and "The Darkened Sky" (the 2018 planet-encircling dust storm tracked by MRO's Mars Climate Sounder). Each has NASA images, an evidence briefing and source links. The debrief keeps "What NASA observed" separate from "What happened in your simulation", so children see the difference between real measurements and the game.

11. Winning and losing

A win is a party with confetti and the whole crew dancing. After a loss, Dusty gives a tip and the crew can go back to the morning of the same day and try a new plan. Between days the crew builds one thing for the base, such as an extra solar panel or a water tank, and it appears on the map.

Dusty's voice and the voice-over

  • Real recorded voice: Dusty speaks Egyptian Arabic with 140 recorded lines, and English with 34 lines. Every clip is a local file; nothing is generated while you play, and no online speech service is used.
  • Lips that follow the voice: the game reads the loudness of each recording every 20 milliseconds, so Dusty's mouth opens on the real syllables and closes in the pauses, in both languages.
  • Always readable: every line is also shown as text in Dusty's speech bubble. The 164 lines that have no recording yet show their text only, and the game never plays a wrong clip in their place.
  • Voice controls: voice on or off, replay, stop and volume, on every screen.
  • The pitch video: Dusty narrates the 30-second video with his real recorded lines, from "Whoever's closest, get there now!" to "Every step helps the crew." Each subtitle shows a small talking Dusty and his name; Arabic lines show the Arabic words with the English translation underneath.

What is real, and what is a game rule

  • Real: every flare's class, date and DONKI ID; the radio delay for the mission date (from JPL planet positions: 11.3 minutes on Perseverance's landing day, NASA's press kit says about 11.4); every science card fact and quiz answer, with its source; crater names, terrain and landing sites.
  • Game rules: a day lasts about 2 minutes and 1 minute of delay is 1 second or less; radiation and health are points out of 100, not millisieverts, and whether a flare reaches Mars is a dice roll by its class; power, Air + Food and water are simple numbers, not engineering values.

Benefits

  • For children: they learn by deciding, not by memorising. Failing is safe, and each report explains what to try next.
  • For teachers and parents: a 15-minute mission, Class mode with discussion questions at big moments, free, nothing to install.
  • For the Arab world: full Arabic, with Dusty speaking Egyptian Arabic, so children can learn space science in their own language.
  • For trust in science: every real number has a source, and the game always says what is a game rule.

Our goal, and our limits

Our goal is to turn NASA's open data into decisions children can make with their friends, so that they understand why a Mars mission is hard, not only that it is. Our limits today: the game has not been playtested with children yet; it is made for PC (keyboard, mouse and gamepad), not phones; 164 of Dusty's lines are still waiting for recordings; and the live NASA flare feed uses NASA's public demo key, which has a low hourly limit, so the game falls back to NOAA and then to its saved NASA records.

Tools and technologies used

  • Game: HTML5 Canvas and plain JavaScript, no game engine and no framework. All game art, sound effects and music are made in code.
  • Data: NASA DONKI flare records, NASA SDO images (through Helioviewer.org), NASA MOLA elevation, the NASA/USGS Viking colour mosaic, the IAU planetary names gazetteer, JPL planet positions, NASA OSDR studies.
  • Testing: Node.js: 89 automated checks (both languages, every source, every mini-game can be finished, survival rules, robot teammates, every file the game loads) and autopilot missions that check that strategy matters.
  • Video: our own tools record the real game in a headless browser and edit the video in code, with music made in code.
  • Hosting: GitHub and Vercel, as a static website. Source code: https://github.com/mohamed-saied-1/mars-crew

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) tools

We used SI tools to help us build the project, while we were brainstorming for creative ideas about the challenge:

  • Coding help: SI coding assistant (Claude) helped us as a helper in test and fix code, check our NASA data against its sources
  • Subtitles: an offline speech-recognition model (Whisper) helped us find the exact words and timing in Dusty's Arabic recordings for the video subtitles.
  • Dusty's Arabic voice is a human recording. The game's art is drawn in code, and the NASA images are real photos shown with their credits. No SI-generated image is presented as NASA data, and no NASA logo or branding is used.

projectDetails.name: Project WUNDERBAO
projectDetails.summary:
FLARE (Fire & Life-Safety Analysis and Risk Explorer) is an interactive platform for exploring combustion and fire safety in microgravity. It combines an adjustable D² Law analytical simulator with a 3D chamber, live visual readouts, and controls for gravity, oxygen, pressure, airflow, and fuel. Users can explore 16 NASA combustion investigations, compare research cases with model scenarios, and learn through a kid-friendly flame sandbox and AI science assistant.

FLARE addresses the challenge by making it easier to investigate how reduced buoyancy changes flame shape and how cabin conditions affect combustion. This is important because understanding fire behavior supports safer spacecraft design, fire detection, and crew protection on long-duration missions. Simulation results are analytical model estimates, not raw spacecraft measurements or full CFD predictions.
projectDetails.details:
FLARE (Fire & Life-Safety Analysis and Risk Explorer) is an interactive web platform for exploring how combustion changes in microgravity and why spacecraft fire safety matters. In the scientific workspace, users adjust fuel, sample size, gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, and airflow. A simplified D² Law analytical model estimates combustion behavior and displays results in an interactive 3D chamber with diagnostic layers and telemetry. Users can also explore 16 curated NASA combustion investigations and compare research cases with model scenarios.

FLARE makes complex space-combustion concepts easier to investigate for students, educators, researchers, and the public. Its intended impact is to build understanding of how cabin conditions affect fire behavior and crew safety, while clearly distinguishing model estimates from measured data. The separate FLARE Kids experience introduces the same ideas through an interactive flame sandbox, guided learning worlds, and Sparky, a child-friendly science assistant.

We developed FLARE with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. NASA Physical Sciences Informatics and NASA Technical Reports Server records inform the research experience; Gemini can power the AI assistant, which also has a demo mode.

Our creative approach combines a research instrument, NASA investigation explorer, scenario comparison tools, and a kid-friendly learning space in one platform. We considered scientific transparency, source attribution, accessibility, reduced motion, responsive layouts, and safe explanations for young learners. FLARE is an educational analytical tool, not a full CFD solver or a source of raw spacecraft telemetry.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: SkyShift-X
projectDetails.summary:
The sky looks still—until you press play. 
SkyShift X turns SPHEREx archive images into interactive sky movies, making the changing infrared universe accessible to everyone. Users enter sky coordinates, choose a field of view, and explore observations across dates and wavelengths. Images are aligned on a shared sky-coordinate grid and played chronologically, helping reveal possible movement and brightness changes. Wavelength controls distinguish spectral differences from changes over time.

Two modes welcome different explorers:
Beginner Mode offers simple controls and guided explanations for people with little astronomy knowledge. Research Mode provides deeper access to comparison tools, measurements, quality flags, and observation metadata to investigate candidate changes.

An integrated narrator with captions explains the images and evidence behind highlighted changes. Interactive 3D storytelling introduces SPHEREx and its mission without requiring prior astronomy knowledge.

Our solution addresses the challenge by transforming separate scientific observations into an intuitive visual experience. SkyShift X helps people watch, explore, and understand—connecting NASA’s open data with public curiosity, classroom learning, and deeper scientific investigation.
projectDetails.details:
The sky looks still—until you press play. 🛰️

SkyShift X turns real SPHEREx archive observations into interactive sky movies, bringing beginners and researchers into the same exploration—with different levels of detail.

Explore a place in the sky

The Sky Navigator offers coordinate entry, name search, and featured targets. Visitors can select a field of view and explore cases including Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

Or they can point coordinates on the map and the engine will search it easily

Watch observations become a movie

The viewer plays aligned infrared observations chronologically, with dates, wavelength information, adjustable speed, frame stepping, zoom, and a thumbnail timeline. Users can watch every observation or alternate between the first and last dates to make movement easier to notice.

These movies contain separate observations taken across time—not continuous spacecraft video.

Two modes, one set of observations

  • Beginner Mode provides a simple viewing experience and a “Can you find it?” interaction. Visitors can investigate independently or choose “Just show me” to reveal the measured change.
  • Research Mode adds wavelength and date controls, blink and comparison views, difference images, stacking tools, catalog overlays, spectra, quality flags, and detailed measurements with uncertainties.

A narrator tells the story behind the images

Narrated explanations with synchronized captions connect the observation sequence to its findings. They explain where we are looking, highlight measured changes, and summarize what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain. The interpretation comes from measurements and structured explanation templates; the voice presents that story.

Understand the mission through interactive exploration

The Universe Explorer provides educational experiences about SPHEREx when click MEET SphereX, the solar system, and the search for hypothetical distant worlds. These illustrations are distinguished from real observations, with a 2D fallback when 3D graphics are unavailable.

Know the telescope more

We understood that SPHEREx’s mission extends beyond Planet X:

it maps the infrared sky to study galaxies, cosmic history, and interstellar ice. Our interactive 3D explorer translates that broader mission into an accessible learning experience, connecting scientific context with real sky observations.

Why it matters

SkyShift X makes scientific images easier to access, compare, and understand. Beginners receive context, while researchers and experienced enthusiasts can inspect the supporting evidence.

The published demo includes clearly labeled saved movies built from real IRSA observations. Live retrieval and refreshing require the scientific backend. Throughout the experience, candidate changes are presented as findings to investigate—not automatic claims of discovery.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.

projectDetails.name: Project programming with farmers
projectDetails.summary:
YANBOO – Smart Agriculture Platform

YANBOO is a smart agricultural platform designed to help farmers overcome farming and marketing challenges and reduce crop waste.

The project introduces an integrated mobile application that supports farmers throughout the agricultural process, from choosing suitable crops and planting times to harvesting and selling their products.

YANBOO aims to use NASA satellite data, such as NASA POWER and NASA Earthdata, combined with weather information, to help farmers monitor climate conditions and make better agricultural decisions.

The platform also offers an agricultural marketplace where farmers can buy and sell crops and farming supplies, rent agricultural equipment, and find workers.

YANBOO aims to connect space technology with real agricultural needs, improve farmers' access to markets, reduce food waste, and support sustainable agriculture.

Our goal is to turn space data into practical solutions that make a difference on Earth.
projectDetails.details: YANBOO – Project Details YANBOO is a smart agricultural platform designed to support farmers from planting to harvesting and selling their crops. The platform aims to use NASA satellite data, such as NASA POWER and NASA Earthdata, along with weather information, to help farmers monitor climate conditions and make better farming decisions. It also provides an agricultural marketplace where farmers can buy and sell crops, purchase farming supplies, rent equipment, and find workers. Benefits and Expected Impact: - Reducing crop waste. - Improving farmers' access to markets. - Supporting smarter and more sustainable agriculture. - Connecting farmers with buyers and agricultural services. projectDetails.name: Project Tenacity
projectDetails.summary:
Project Tenacity is a browser tool for planning a walk on Mars before taking it. It borrows the way NASA's rover drivers work at JPL (sketch a drive, simulate it, validate it against rules) and gives the same loop to astronauts on foot at Gale Crater. It is built for astronauts and mission operations personnel, not for the general public.

The crew lays out a walk on real orbital imagery, or lets the tool find the easiest path over the terrain. Tenacity then simulates the walk step by step: time on every slope, oxygen, cooling water and battery, and how long it would take to get back to the refuge at any moment. Fifteen flight rules give one clear answer, GO or NO-GO, name the rule that decides, and show where on the map it bites.

More than 25 layers of NASA data (terrain, slope, shadow, minerals, subsurface water, rock chemistry, solar-storm forecasts and Curiosity's own photos of each stop) feed the same rules, so the map and the plan cannot disagree. A 3D flyover shows the ground before the crew walks it. Every number is labelled as measured, a NASA value, derived or assumed.
projectDetails.details:
WHO IT IS FOR

Tenacity is a professional tool, not a public outreach site. It is built for two kinds of user: astronauts, who plan the walk and then follow it, and mission operations personnel (flight controllers, EVA officers and planners), who have to clear it before the crew leaves. We chose completeness over simplicity, on purpose: a tool for trained users should keep every rule, number and source in view, not hide detail to look simpler. That is why the interface is dense, speaks in flight rules and NASA alert conventions, and shows its numbers and their sources instead of hiding them. A guided tour is built in so that judges and newcomers can find their way around.

WHAT IT DOES

Tenacity answers one question for a crew about to leave the airlock: is this walk safe, by how much, and what decides it?

1. Sketch. Load a ready-made walk, or click the map to add stations anywhere. Each leg can follow ground a rover has already driven, go in a straight line, or take the easiest path the terrain engine finds. Keep-out zones can be marked; paths go around them.

2. Simulate. The walk is simulated before it happens: pace and effort on every slope, oxygen, carbon dioxide, cooling water and battery, and the walk-home time from every point.

3. Validate. Fifteen flight rules are checked along the whole walk. Examples: the refuge must always be within 60 minutes at emergency pace, because that is how long a suit's backup supply lasts; ground steeper than 20 degrees may not be crossed in any direction; a solar eruption forecast to reach Mars blocks the walk. A rule whose data are missing or too old is shown as "not evaluated", never as a pass.

4. Understand. Click any point to read every layer there. Ask why a path was chosen: ground that cannot be crossed is shown in red, slow ground in yellow, and the straight line the path finder rejected is drawn. Fly along the route in 3D over real terrain and imagery, with Curiosity's own photograph of each station. Recordings of each of these steps in motion (sketching a walk, playback, the 3D flyover and the guided tour) are in the project repository: https://github.com/yara-hue24/Project-Tenacity#in-motion

WHAT INSPIRED THE DESIGN

The design is modelled on RSVP (Robot Sequencing and Visualization Platform), the tool suite NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has used to plan surface operations on its Mars rovers and landers since 1997. Rover planners sketch a drive on the terrain, build it into a command sequence, simulate it, and check it before it is sent to Mars. Tenacity maps each part of that suite to a walk: the Activity list and sketching on the map follow MobSketch; the sequence table and console follow RoSE, the sequence editor; the walk simulation follows SSim, the surface simulation; and the terrain views, clocks and playback follow HyperDrive. Alert colours and layout rules follow NASA-STD-3001 and the crew-interface work at Johnson Space Center.

Source: https://www-robotics.jpl.nasa.gov/what-we-do/applications/user-interfaces/

HOW IT IS BUILT

A static web page: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript modules, with Leaflet for the 2D map and our own WebGL code for the 3D view. There is no server and no build step. The terrain engine runs in the browser in a web worker on a 5-million-cell elevation grid: slope, cast shadow for the time of day, line of sight to the refuge, a walk-home time field and least-time path finding. Data files are built from NASA's public services by Python scripts in the repository, so every file can be regenerated. Plans, notes and the history of changes are stored in the browser. 113 automated tests cover the simulation, the Mars clock, the terrain engine and the 3D maths.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

  • It treats a spacewalk the way mission operations treats a rover drive: a sequence that is simulated and checked against rules before anyone moves.
  • The layers are not pictures beside a planner. The same slope, shadow, sight-line and space-weather data drawn on the map are what the rules read.
  • It is honest about what is known. Every constant carries a tag (MEASURED, NASA VALUE, DERIVED, ASSUMED) and its source.
  • The interface follows NASA's display standard for alert colours and is built like a professional workstation: resizable docks, a guided tour, search, and a large mode for gloved hands.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Crew safety first: the limit that usually decides a walk is not oxygen but how far you can be from shelter if the suit fails. Mobility in a suit: slope limits, slow ground, loose ground. The environment: daylight for the season, cast shadow, radiation and solar storms. Working in pairs, with a pressurised rover as a refuge that can be re-parked. What the crew will see on arrival: rover photographs at the stations and a 3D view of the ground.

LIMITS WE STATE OPENLY

Walking speed and effort on Mars in a suit have never been measured; the model is extrapolated from Earth and Moon data. The elevation model is good for relative height, not absolute. Position error is not modelled. This is a first prototype for planning and training, not a certified flight product. The README lists every known limit.

INTENDED IMPACT

Rover planners simulate every drive before it happens. We want crews on foot to have the same habit and the same kind of tool.

USE OF AI

The team chose the challenge, set the concept, the requirements and the design direction, and reviewed and tested the result. Research was done in two ways: by hand (the team found and read primary NASA and JPL sources itself) and with AI tools (Perplexity, an AI search assistant, to locate and cross-check sources, and Claude, an AI coding assistant by Anthropic, for further background research). Most of the code and the data-building scripts were written with Claude under the team's direction. No AI-generated images, audio or video are part of the project: every picture is a screenshot or recording of the working tool.

Source code: https://github.com/yara-hue24/Project-Tenacity - Project paper (PDF): https://yara-hue24.github.io/Project-Tenacity/docs/Tenacity-project-description.pdf

projectDetails.name: Luminar Horizon
projectDetails.summary:
Luminar Horizon is an interactive 3D browser game that turns space mission design into a hands-on engineering challenge. Players build a fictional wildfire-monitoring CubeSat, select its instruments, orbit, launch service, and ground stations, then operate it across three simulated days.

Every decision has consequences: a better camera can demand more power, fill storage faster, and overwhelm communications. Success depends on delivering useful observations to the ground on time—not simply collecting data. An explanatory mission report helps players identify bottlenecks, redesign their spacecraft, and compare results.

The project addresses the challenge by connecting spacecraft design, launch, orbital operations, and scientific outcomes in one playable experience. Real NASA FIRMS fire detections provide clearly labeled geographical context. Designed for students and curious learners, Luminar Horizon makes mission trade-offs visible and encourages learning through experimentation.
projectDetails.details:
Luminar Horizon, developed by ZagQ, lets players experience the complete design–operate–evaluate cycle of an educational space mission.

Its first scenario, Earth Guardian, challenges players to design a CubeSat for wildfire observation. In an interactive 3D hangar, players configure the spacecraft’s structure, payload, solar arrays, battery, communications, storage, and pointing system. They also choose an orbit, launch service, and ground stations. Engineering checks reveal whether the design meets its budget, mass, power, and launch constraints.

Players then simulate three mission days around a 3D Earth. The simulation connects orbital position and sunlight with battery charge, observation opportunities, storage, ground-station visibility, and data transmission. Scientific observations earn credit only when they meet the mission’s requirements and reach the ground before their deadline.

The mission report explains the outcome, allowing players to investigate failures and compare redesigned missions. Preset designs demonstrate different engineering approaches and bottlenecks. Browser saves and export/import features support continued experimentation.

Our creative approach is to make the entire journey of scientific data part of the game: from collecting an observation to storing it onboard and delivering it to its users. This demonstrates why a powerful instrument alone cannot guarantee a successful mission.

An optional NASA FIRMS overlay displays a dated sample of real NOAA-20 VIIRS fire detections. These observations are clearly separated from fictional mission targets and scoring. The published version uses a bundled dataset rather than a live feed.

We built the project using TypeScript, React, Next.js, Three.js, HTML/CSS, Blender, and Python, with Vitest and Playwright supporting verification. Development included AI assistance through Codex and Claude, directed and reviewed by the project team.

Design priorities included understandable feedback, reproducible results, browser performance, fullscreen visualization, keyboard and touch alternatives, and light and dark themes. Hardware specifications and simulation assumptions are intentionally simplified for education. The intended impact is to help learners understand how connected engineering decisions shape mission success.
