projectDetails.name: Zero Flare : CIR - 1
projectDetails.summary: ZERO FLARE — FLAME EVIDENCE LAB turns NASA's underused microgravity-combustion archive into a live, evidence-grounded research environment for the Artemis generation. We ingested 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations — recovering 22 experimental tables (2,009 rows, SHA-256-verified against the acquisition manifest), 63 verified equations, and honest model cards — and built an AI research copilot, CIR-1, that answers every factual claim through 26 deterministic tools with visible provenance, never inventing data. Researchers explore investigations, run a comparability gate that refuses invalid cross-study claims, screen lunar/ISS/Mars habitats with a transparent facility-risk engine, walk a 3D equipment lab built from public NASA descriptions (plus official NASA ISS & Perseverance 3D assets), and export reproducible evidence packets. Missing data stays missing; negative results stay visible.
projectDetails.details:
ZeroFlare Evidence Lab - Start your Mission

1-Home page

This interface is the main dashboard of the ZERO FLARE platform. It provides access to NASA microgravity fire research, experimental datasets, investigations, scenarios, comparisons, 3D tools, and scientific resources. The homepage also highlights key research statistics, available environments such as ISS and Earth reference conditions, and provides direct access to the CIR-1 AI copilot for research assistance.

2-Mission

This interface presents the main research environments used in ZERO FLARE, including the International Space Station, lunar habitat, Mars habitat, and spacecraft cabin. Users can select an environment to explore how gravity, oxygen level, and atmospheric conditions affect fire behavior and combustion research.

This interface evaluates whether the selected environment stays within the limits of available microgravity combustion data. It compares oxygen level, pressure, and material-family test ranges, then highlights where the selected conditions are supported by experiments and where they fall outside the tested envelope.

This interface guides users to start from the available evidence. It provides direct access to investigations, comparisons, and scenarios, while clearly showing the limits of the platform, including unsupported predictions, missing media, and areas without validated experimental data.

This interface visualizes the evidence coverage across NASA combustion investigations. It shows which research dimensions—such as gravity, oxygen, pressure, material, hardware, outcomes, and measurement context—are observed, reported, condition-specific, or missing from the current dataset.

This interface presents curated NASA research videos and experimental media related to microgravity combustion. It allows users to explore visual evidence from real space-based fire experiments, including flame behavior, droplet combustion, and laboratory testing aboard the International Space Station.

 

This interface summarizes key findings from the available microgravity combustion evidence and ranks important scientific results with their supporting datasets and limitations. It also provides access to authentic NASA imagery related to combustion experiments, allowing users to connect research conclusions with real experimental media.

 

 3- investigations

This interface provides access to the available combustion investigations and their detailed research workspaces. Users can click any experiment in the investigation list to open it and explore its objectives, data, equipment, media, equations, graphs, metadata, related investigations, and research keywords.

This interface provides a visual analysis of the selected experiment’s dataset. It presents column statistics, data distributions, scatter plots, and condition-based comparisons, helping users quickly identify patterns, relationships, and important characteristics within the experimental measurements.

This interface displays authentic NASA images related to the selected combustion investigation. It allows users to explore real experimental hardware, laboratory setups, researchers, and spaceflight equipment, providing visual context for the scientific data and investigation results.

This interface provides the verified scientific equations related to the selected investigation. It organizes gas laws, pressure calculations, mixture properties, stoichiometry, and flammability equations, with references and direct links to use them inside the Scenarios workspace.

This interface presents a visual evidence graph showing the selected investigation and its related experiments, equipment, and research connections. Users can click any connected investigation node to open that experiment and return directly to its Overview page for further exploration.

 4- scenario

This interface supports fire-safety scenario analysis across the full lifecycle, from prevention and detection to prediction and suppression. Users can configure the environment, compare compartment risk levels, review facility screening results, and save scenario settings for further analysis.

 

This interface combines the CIR-1 Fire Safety Assistant with verified equations, prevention evidence, and scientific calculators. Users can ask questions about the selected facility, explore supporting NASA evidence, calculate atmospheric and flammability conditions, and review research gaps before making scenario-based decisions.

5- compare
This interface compares experimental conditions across multiple investigations. It visualizes observed ranges, such as oxygen concentration, and helps users identify where different studies overlap, differ, or may not be directly comparable before making cross-investigation conclusions.
 6- 3D lab

This interface provides an interactive 3D laboratory for exploring spacecraft combustion hardware and experimental apparatus. Users can browse hardware records, view reconstructed equipment models, inspect components, access related NASA media, and explore animated experiment demonstrations.

This interface provides a detailed 3D view of the selected combustion apparatus, including labeled components, related experiment information, and authentic NASA images. It also includes an animated experiment demonstration that shows the main stages of the procedure, allowing users to better understand how the hardware and experiment operate.

7-Data and Resources

This interface documents the data sources used across ZERO FLARE. It shows the recovered experimental tables, row and column counts, duplicate records, parse issues, file sizes, investigation IDs, and verification hashes, providing a transparent view of the project’s data provenance and integrity.

8- Chatbot

These interfaces show the CIR-1 Research Copilot in both compact and expanded views. The assistant is available across the platform to help users ask questions about experiments, datasets, equations, models, and NASA combustion evidence, while keeping the conversation connected to the current research context.

This interface shows CIR-1 responding to a research question about a specific investigation. The copilot retrieves experiment information such as the investigation title, research area, project type, objectives, and supporting references, allowing users to explore NASA combustion studies directly through natural-language questions.

Benefits

  •  Provides a centralized platform for exploring NASA microgravity combustion research, experimental datasets, scientific equations, and supporting media.
  • Makes complex fire-science information easier to understand through interactive dashboards, visualizations, comparison tools, and 3D representations.
  • Helps researchers explore individual NASA investigations in detail, including objectives, datasets, equipment, media, equations, graphs, and documented gaps.
  •  Allows users to compare multiple experiments and identify similarities, differences, overlapping conditions, and limitations before making cross-study conclusions.
  • Supports evidence-based analysis by connecting results to verified datasets, NASA records, scientific equations, and provenance information.
  • Uses the CIR-1 AI Research Copilot to answer natural-language questions about investigations, datasets, equations, models, and research evidence.
  • Reduces the time required to manually search through multiple research records and datasets.
  •  Helps users identify missing data, unsupported assumptions, and areas where additional experiments may be required.
  •  Supports scenario-based analysis for different environments such as the International Space Station, lunar habitats, Mars habitats, spacecraft cabins, and Earth-reference conditions.
  • Provides fire-safety scenario support across prevention, detection, prediction, and suppression stages.
  • Includes scientific calculators and verified equations that can be used directly inside research scenarios.
  • Provides interactive data analysis, including descriptive statistics, distributions, relationships, grouped comparisons, and correlation analysis.
  •  Supports the exploration of authentic NASA research media to provide visual context for combustion experiments and experimental hardware.
  • Provides interactive 3D models of combustion hardware and experimental apparatus to improve understanding of complex equipment.
  • Maintains transparency by clearly displaying data provenance, source references, duplicate records, parse issues, and evidence limitations.
  • Preserves missing information instead of automatically replacing it with artificial values.
  • Helps students, researchers, and engineers understand microgravity combustion research in a more accessible and interactive way.
  • Provides a single research environment that combines data analysis, scientific evidence, visualization, AI assistance, and engineering tools.
  • Supports faster and more informed research decisions by bringing multiple sources of evidence into one platform.
  • Can be extended in the future with additional datasets, experiments, scientific models, and AI capabilities.
  • Provides a web-based interface that can be accessed without requiring users to install specialized scientific software.
  • Encourages traceable and reproducible research by linking calculations and results back to their original sources.
  • Helps distinguish between experimentally observed results, reported information, condition-dependent evidence, and missing evidence.
  • Reduces the risk of presenting unsupported scientific conclusions by clearly identifying the tested limits of available data.
  • Creates an educational environment that can also support demonstrations, research presentations, and academic projects.

Development Tools

  • Next.js – Main full-stack web framework used to build the ZERO FLARE platform and server-side API routes.
  • React – Used to build reusable and interactive user-interface components.
  • TypeScript – Provides strong typing, safer development, and improved maintainability.
  • Node.js – Server-side JavaScript runtime used by the application and development environment.
  • npm – Used to install and manage project dependencies and development packages.
  • Google Gemini API – Powers the CIR-1 AI Research Copilot and natural-language interaction.
  • Google GenAI SDK (@google/genai) – Provides official server-side access to Gemini, structured responses, and native function calling.
  • Zod – Used for validating API requests, responses, tool arguments, and structured application data.
  • REST API Architecture – Used to connect the frontend, AI agent, scientific tools, and application services.
  • Next.js API Routes – Used to provide secure server-side endpoints such as the CIR-1 copilot API.
  • CSV Data Processing – Used to store and process the cleaned experimental datasets supplied by the research team.
  • JSON – Used for structured configuration, API responses, reports, tool outputs, and metadata.
  • Custom Data Query Layer – Used to filter, group, analyze, and calculate statistics from the experimental datasets.
  • Statistical Analysis Tools – Used for descriptive statistics, grouping, median calculations, correlations, and experimental-data exploration.
  • Scientific Equation Registry – Used to manage and execute verified scientific formulas throughout the platform.
  • BM25 Information Retrieval – Used to search and rank research evidence and knowledge-base documents.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) – Used to provide the AI assistant with relevant research evidence and source context.
  • Native AI Function Calling – Allows Gemini to select and execute validated ZERO FLARE research tools.
  • Structured AI Responses – Used to provide predictable and validated outputs from the AI assistant.
  • HTML5 – Provides the structural foundation of the web interface.
  • CSS / Responsive Styling – Used to create the visual design, space-themed interface, and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript – Supports interactive browser behavior and application logic.
  • Interactive Data Visualization – Used to display charts, distributions, comparisons, and experimental relationships.
  • 3D Visualization Technologies – Used to display interactive combustion hardware and apparatus models.
  • NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Data – Provides the main experimental research evidence used by the platform.
  • NASA Images and Video Library – Provides authentic NASA imagery and research media.

projectDetails.name: ZeroG Pulse
projectDetails.summary: ZeroG Pulse is a health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long missions, where a message to the flight surgeon takes minutes each way and can be lost in a blackout. The crew measures a vital sign (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, SpO2, sleep, mood, stress or radiation dose). One Rust engine judges it against ranges for the environment it was taken in, tags the NASA Human Research Program hazards behind it, and places it on a four-step ladder: Monitor, Self-care, Consult ground, Urgent. A clickable body view shows status as colour, icon and word. Guidance offers only actions the onboard kit allows. When ground is needed, the app drafts an SBAR report and sends it over a delayed link, and keeps working offline. If the rich interface fails, a plain safe-mode console shows the same status from the same event log, so no two screens can disagree. Every range states whether it is adapted from NASA numbers or our own placeholder, and all crew readings are simulated. On the way to Mars, the crew has to judge their own health; ZeroG Pulse gives them a clear answer and a next step.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

ZeroG Pulse helps astronauts answer two questions without waiting for Earth: is this number a problem, and what do I do now? Deep-space crews face the five hazards NASA's Human Research Program names: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment. Near Mars a message to the flight surgeon takes minutes each way, so the crew must measure, judge and act on their own.

How it works

1. A body view opens on the crew's status. Today's checks flag what is due, for example a stale blood pressure reading.

2. A guided card explains how to measure in space and why it matters there. The astronaut enters the value; every reading carries its environment, device and confidence.

3. One deterministic Rust engine assesses it: a low-confidence reading never raises an alarm, and an out-of-range one is placed on a four-step ladder (Monitor, Self-care, Consult ground, Urgent). Two trusted out-of-range readings in a row escalate to Consult ground.

4. "Why?" explains the range, what is expected in flight and the source behind it, with a tag saying whether the range is adapted from NASA numbers or a placeholder.

5. Guidance offers only actions the onboard kit allows. When ground is needed, the app drafts an SBAR report (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) and sends it over a delayed link; the reply comes back after the same delay, and the outbox waits through blackouts.

6. If the rich interface is lost, a plain safe-mode console shows the same status and accepts readings, because every screen derives its view from the same append-only event log.

7. An activity-only crew score (streaks, XP) rewards doing checks without ever showing health values.

Benefits and impact

For the crew: a clear status and next step without medical training. For flight surgeons: structured SBAR reports, sent only when the ladder says ground is needed. For the mission: one engine, so the rich app, safe mode and ground can never disagree, and the tool keeps working when the screen or the link fails. On Earth, the same pattern fits remote clinics, ships and polar stations where a doctor is hours away.

Tools and languages

Rust (core engine, compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen), TypeScript with React and Vite (crew and ground web app, inline SVG body view), egui (safe-mode console, native and WebAssembly), axum (Ground Station API, JSONL storage), Tauri (desktop app), an Android WebView shell, GitHub Actions and Cloudflare Pages for CI and deployment.

What makes it creative

Status is computed once, in one engine, and every face renders what it says, so a reading entered in safe mode appears in the crew app and the reverse. The delayed ground loop is built in, not bolted on. The hazard lens ties every indicator to the NASA hazard that drives it.

What we considered

Honesty: all crew readings are simulated, never called NASA data, and every range shows its source status. No NASA document we found gives numeric in-flight vital-sign ranges, so we say so per indicator: sleep and radiation dose are adapted from NASA numbers; the rest are our own placeholders with NASA context. Safety: no diagnoses and no medication doses; ZeroG Pulse is not a medical device. Accessibility: status is always colour plus icon plus word. Resilience: the crew app and safe mode work fully offline.

Team: Tarek Darwish, Mostafa Emad El Din, Amr Yasser, Sama Waheed, Mohamed Naser.

projectDetails.name: Project ZeroG_Pulse
projectDetails.summary:
ZeroG Pulse is an autonomous deep-space telemedicine HUD and multi-organ digital twin designed to solve medical triage during deep-space communication blackouts (such as the 14m 28s light-delay on Mars transit). 

Developed by undergraduate computer science students at the Egyptian Chinese University (Team GTX Infinity-1), ZeroG Pulse features:
1. Real-time biometrical and environmental telemetry tracking aligned with NASA-STD-3001 and ECLSS thresholds.
2. A 5-organ holographic digital twin (CNS, Cardiovascular, Pulmonary, Hematopoietic, and Musculoskeletal systems) mapping cabin anomalies to organ-level stress in real time.
3. A 30-Minute Clinical Deterioration Predictor with actionable mitigation checklists.
4. Bilingual (English and Arabic) Web Speech API integration with multi-tier LLM failover (Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter, Hugging Face).

By operating locally first with deterministic rules, ZeroG Pulse ensures astronauts can diagnose, assess, and treat critical emergencies immediately without waiting for Earth's reply. Live application: zerog-pulse.vercel.app
projectDetails.details:
ZeroG Pulse is an autonomous deep-space telemedicine HUD and 5-organ digital twin designed to solve medical triage during deep-space communication blackouts (such as the 14m 28s light-delay on Mars transit).

What it does:

- Tracks live biometrical and environmental telemetry aligned with NASA-STD-3001 and ECLSS thresholds.

- Simulates a 5-organ holographic matrix (CNS, Cardiovascular, Pulmonary, Hematopoietic, and Musculoskeletal systems) mapping cabin anomalies to organ-level stress in real time.

- Features a 30-Minute Clinical Deterioration Predictor with actionable mitigation checklists.

- Integrates bilingual (English/Arabic) Web Speech API control and multi-tier LLM failover (Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter, Hugging Face).

Impact: Empowers crews to diagnose, assess, and treat critical emergencies immediately without waiting for Earth's reply, bridging the gap for deep-space missions and terrestrial remote telemedicine. Live application: zerog-pulse.vercel.app

projectDetails.name: Astro Health
projectDetails.summary: Developed an advanced, professional astronaut vital signs dashboard powered by authentic medical data. This project addresses the critical challenge of continuous in-flight health monitoring by rigorously analyzing an astronaut's medical status in real-time, detecting abnormal physiological indicators, and issuing immediate early-warning alerts accompanied by actionable treatment recommendations. The importance of this project lies in the extreme environments of space, where astronauts are constantly exposed to silent health risks and physiological shifts that they may be unaware of—such as cardiovascular strain, fluid shifts, or radiation effects—which could otherwise become life-threatening. By bridging real-time telemetry with predictive medical insights, this dashboard ensures proactive astronaut safety, minimizes mission risks, and acts as an essential lifeline beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

Our project is an advanced, real-time astronaut vital signs health dashboard designed to monitor physiological parameters based on authentic medical data. It works by collecting and simulating real-time telemetry data (such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, and body temperature), processing it through a Node.js backend, and visualizing it dynamically on the frontend. The interface incorporates Three.js to deliver an immersive 3D space-themed environment, alongside HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for a responsive, clean, and intuitive user dashboard. If any vital sign crosses safe thresholds, the system instantly triggers automated early-warning alerts and provides step-by-step actionable treatment recommendations.

2. What benefits and intended impact does it have?

Astronauts in deep space or on the ISS are constantly exposed to hidden physiological stressors, silent health risks, and sudden medical anomalies that they might not notice immediately. The primary impact of this project is saving lives by shifting from reactive healthcare to proactive, real-time prevention. It acts as an autonomous medical lifeline, reducing mission risks and ensuring crew safety.

3. What tools, coding languages, and technologies were used?

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Three.js for 3D visualizations.
  • Backend: Node.js for managing server-side logic, real-time data flow, and alert thresholds.
  • Data Source: Authentic medical parameters tailored for aerospace physiological monitoring.

4. How is your project creative and what factors did we consider?

The project stands out through its creative integration of Three.js to create a futuristic 3D interface that makes monitoring engaging and intuitive in a space-like setting. Key factors considered during development include data accuracy, low-latency alert mechanisms, UI/UX clarity under high-stress scenarios, and the specific physiological challenges astronauts face (such as fluid shifts and cardiovascular strain).The link of the live web : https://astro.zerog.qd.je/

projectDetails.name: Zij: one fire record from MODIS and VIIRS
projectDetails.summary:
NASA has recorded Earth's active fires since 2000, but with two instruments that cannot be compared directly: MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012). Over Egypt's Nile Delta, VIIRS reports 11 to 20 times more fire pixels than MODIS, so the joined record shows burning jump tenfold in 2012. The fires didn't change; the satellite did. As MODIS retires, the years before 2012 risk becoming unusable.

Zij turns both records into one burning-activity calendar, from November 2000 to today. A model fitted per area on the years both sensors flew converts the MODIS years into VIIRS units. Tested on years it never saw, its season error falls from 77% to 14%, and to 7% in the Nile Delta. Every converted value carries its margin of error.

Draw any area in Egypt, Portugal or Argentina, pick a day or a date range, and Zij tells you in plain words whether this season is normal, with every fire on NASA imagery. Every number can be downloaded and reproduced from NASA FIRMS data.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

NASA's active-fire record is split between MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). VIIRS sees far more small fires: over the Nile Delta in September to November, Suomi NPP reports 11 to 20 times as many fire pixels as Aqua in most years, and 42 times as many in 2018. Joined as they are, the records show burning explode in 2012. A fixed multiplier cannot fix it, because the gap changes with fire size and from year to year. With MODIS retiring, fire managers risk losing the years before 2012.

How it works

  1. Keep real fires. Vegetation fires only; gas flares, industry and weak detections are removed. 6.28 million detections are kept.
  2. One grid. A 0.1 degree cell with at least one fire on a day counts once, so one coarse MODIS pixel and many fine VIIRS pixels weigh the same.
  3. Each satellite. Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are counted separately and averaged within each sensor, so a new satellite never creates a jump. A week inside a satellite outage is "no data", never zero.
  4. Learn the bridge. On 2012 to 2020, when both sensors flew, a model per area learns how MODIS relates to VIIRS: by month, by fire size, and in quiet years.
  5. One record. 2000 to 2011 are converted to VIIRS units, and every converted value carries its error band. Where an area has too little data, Zij says so instead of guessing.

Does it work?

We tested every model on years it never saw: leaving each year out in turn, and predicting 2021 to 2025 from a fit that stops in 2020. Season error is 76.5% for raw MODIS, 24.1% with one fixed multiplier, and 14.2% with Zij (25.2% on the later years). In the Nile Delta it is 6.9%. A clean rebuild from the raw FIRMS files reproduces every published number (REBUILD.md in the repository).

What you can do with it

  • Choose one of 10 preset areas, or draw any box or polygon in Egypt, mainland Portugal or Argentina. A drawn area is fitted live in your browser.
  • Read the verdict in plain words: is this month or season normal here, and how does it rank among 26 years.
  • See the fire calendar (years by months), the typical year and its critical period, the busiest months and years, and unusual seasons.
  • Pick any day and see that day's fires from MODIS and VIIRS on NASA satellite imagery, with how that week and month compare with normal.
  • Download the hotspots and the harmonized record as CSV, the calendar as an image, or a one-page season brief.

What the record shows

Only a record that crosses 2012 in one unit can show this. In the Nile Delta, burning seen from space did not fall after Egypt's 2004 burning ban: it rose 97% by 2005 to 2011 (the record cannot say what the ban itself did). Since 2018 it has been about half its earlier level (53% lower), with 2023 the one exception. The 2026 season is preliminary data.

Who it is for

Early-warning and emergency teams, like the CONAE team behind this challenge, who need to know whether a fire season is unusual while they wait for imagery; environmental agencies checking whether a policy changed burning; scientists, journalists and land managers who need trends that cross the 2012 break.

What makes it different

FIRMS shows the two records side by side. Zij joins them, states how sure it is, refuses to convert where the data is too thin, and is small enough to calibrate a user's own area in the browser.

Hudhud's Fire Diary: the game

zij.watch/diary is a short game that shows how Zij works, in five levels on the real record of the Nile Delta, with Hudhud the hoopoe and two satellites: Spot, Sort, Count, Translate and Compare. Its numbers come from Zij's own data files, and each level has a one-sentence note for grown-ups.

Limits

The unit counts places and days with fire, not burned area or the size of one fire. Satellites see only what burns as they pass; clouds and smoke hide fires. The record covers three countries today. The newest weeks are near-real-time data, and FIRMS revises them.

Tools

Python, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, Next.js, TypeScript, React, MapLibre GL JS, Apache ECharts, Terra Draw, Radix UI. Hosted on Vercel; code under Apache-2.0 at github.com/zij-watch/zij.

Team

Five people, one part each: a lead developer (data pipeline, model and app), a designer (interface, map and film), a researcher (validation against FIRMS and the literature), a tester (areas, devices and the demo), and a coordinator (documentation and submission).

Prepared before the event

Research, method decisions and the design system were prepared before the event, and the public FIRMS files were downloaded in advance. The README lists exactly what.

projectDetails.name: Lost Signals
projectDetails.summary:
Our project brings the stories of forgotten space hardware to life through an immersive, interactive museum. Rovers, landers, and instruments left beyond Earth represent remarkable achievements, yet their purpose and scientific contributions can be unfamiliar to young audiences.

Visitors explore destinations, discover mission histories, and learn what each piece of equipment helped humanity understand. Cinematic visuals, sound, and storytelling create an emotional connection, while accessible explanations connect that experience to real science. A recurring “Unknown Signal” challenge invites visitors to identify missions through clues, encouraging friendly competition and continued exploration.

By making these stories engaging and approachable, the project aims to inspire curiosity and preserve the legacy of space exploration. It addresses **“Abandoned but Not Forgotten”** by introducing school-age learners to the hardware left behind and the discoveries that make it worth remembering.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Forgotten Explorers is a bilingual (Arabic and English) interactive educational web experience that brings the stories of forgotten space exploration hardware to life.

The project focuses on spacecraft and robotic explorers that were left behind on other worlds, particularly Opportunity and Spirit on Mars and Lunokhod 1 on the Moon.

Visitors begin with a cinematic space introduction before entering an interactive 2D Solar System. They can explore destinations, select available spacecraft, and discover their mission histories through interactive storytelling.

Each spacecraft has a dedicated mission console containing its launch date, last communication, actual versus planned mission lifespan, distance traveled, scientific discoveries, and a first-person diary explaining its journey.

Visitors can also explore interactive spacecraft blueprints to understand how different components work, use a dust and power simulator to understand how environmental conditions affect solar-powered missions, and discover lessons that can improve future space exploration.

The experience also includes recorded Arabic narration, English subtitles, NASA imagery, a mission quiz, a historical timeline called Time Machine, and downloadable achievement certificates.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The project makes space science more accessible, engaging, and understandable, especially for school-age learners.

Instead of presenting scientific information through traditional articles, it combines visual exploration, interactive simulations, storytelling, and audio explanations.

Its bilingual support helps reach a wider audience, while the combination of narration and subtitles provides different ways to consume educational content.

It also helps visitors understand real engineering challenges, such as power limitations, environmental conditions, communication failures, and spacecraft design.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our main goal is to inspire curiosity about space exploration and preserve the scientific legacy of missions that are often overlooked.

We want younger generations to understand that a spacecraft does not lose its importance when its mission ends. Even equipment that has stopped operating can represent significant scientific discoveries and engineering achievements.

By transforming these forgotten missions into interactive stories, we hope to encourage students to explore science, technology, engineering, and space research.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed the project as a browser-based single-page application using:

  • HTML5 and CSS3: For the application structure, layouts, and visual presentation.
  • JavaScript and JSX: For application logic, interactions, animations, and dynamic content.
  • React 18: For building reusable UI components and managing interactive application states.
  • Babel Standalone: For transforming JSX directly in the browser without a traditional build process.
  • Tailwind CSS: For responsive styling and interface design.
  • HTML5 Canvas 2D: For rendering the interactive Solar System and animated visual elements.
  • Web Audio API: For cinematic sound effects, ambient audio, and audio mixing.
  • NASA Image and Video Library API: For retrieving real space exploration photographs and media.
  • Python and NumPy: For supporting the audio processing workflow and project utilities.
  • FFmpeg and FFprobe: For cleaning, mastering, and validating recorded narration.
  • Node.js and Playwright: For automated testing and checking application functionality.

We also developed Python utilities for local hosting and preparing the application for static deployment.

The project does not require specialized hardware. It runs through a standard modern web browser.

5. How is the project creative?

The project's main creative idea is to tell the story of space exploration from the perspective of the machines themselves.

Instead of simply showing photographs and technical specifications, we use first-person storytelling to help visitors imagine the experiences of spacecraft that explored distant worlds and eventually went silent.

We also combine several creative elements:

  • A cinematic introduction that transitions into an interactive Solar System.
  • Planetary environments and spacecraft illustrations.
  • First-person mission diaries with original Arabic voice recordings.
  • Interactive spacecraft blueprints that explain engineering components.
  • A dust and power simulator that demonstrates real mission challenges.
  • A Time Machine that allows visitors to explore missions through history.
  • An educational quiz that tests visitors' understanding and rewards successful completion with a downloadable certificate.

This combination of scientific information, interactive technology, sound design, and storytelling transforms a traditional educational topic into an exploratory digital experience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered several important factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: Using real mission information and NASA resources to represent spacecraft histories and discoveries accurately.
  • Educational accessibility: Presenting complex scientific concepts in simple, understandable language.
  • Bilingual experience: Supporting both Arabic and English to reach different audiences.
  • User engagement: Using interactive exploration, simulations, and quizzes instead of passive reading.
  • Audio accessibility: Providing recorded narration and synchronized English captions.
  • Visual experience: Creating an immersive space atmosphere without requiring specialized hardware.
  • Technical reliability: Supporting local media fallbacks, browser audio restrictions, and different navigation interactions.
  • Future scalability: Designing the experience so that additional missions and destinations can be introduced over time.

Ultimately, Forgotten Explorers aims to turn forgotten space hardware into meaningful educational stories and remind people that even when the signal disappears, the discoveries remain.

projectDetails.summary:
Road to Mars is a co-op space survival and flight simulator for up to 6 players, made by team El Tarabeza El Aaleya. The crew shares a room code and works together to get a ship from a NASA launch pad to Mars. There is no impostor.

Prepare: Pick a rocket, a science payload, and the amounts of food, oxygen and fuel. Heavier loads mean a slower trip and faster fuel burn.

Survive: On the 2D ship, tasks like farming, water recycling, fuel production and repairs keep resources from running out.
Fly: Any player can pilot in 3D, dodging and shooting real NASA asteroids for fuel and science points.
Decide: The crew can land on the Moon for extra food, or dump cargo or vote to eject a player (who stays on as a 0 kg ghost) when the ship is too heavy.
Finish: At 100% progress the crew wins and gets an engineering report, then Free-Play unlocks. The game never ends suddenly.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
Road to Mars is a co-op space survival and flight simulator for up to 6 players. The crew shares a room code and works together to take a spacecraft from a NASA launch pad to Mars. It borrows the feel of Among Us, with a 2D ship, tasks and emergency meetings, but there is no impostor. The whole crew works against the ship’s failing systems instead of each other.

Before launch, the crew chooses a rocket (Electron, Falcon 9 or SLS Block 1B), a science payload, and the amounts of food, oxygen and fuel. A live readout shows total mass, Δv, thrust-to-weight and travel time, so every kilogram has a visible cost. During the mission, players do tasks inside a 10-room ship: farming, water recycling, turning CO₂ into fuel, and repairs. Any player can switch to a 3D cockpit and fly through real NASA asteroids such as Bennu and Itokawa, shooting them for fuel and science points. The crew can also land on the Moon for extra food, or dump cargo or vote to eject a player when the ship is too heavy. At 100% progress the crew wins and receives an engineering report, then Free-Play unlocks.

Benefits and impact
The game teaches mission planning in a hands-on way. Players learn that mass, fuel, food and oxygen are linked, that life support is a closed loop, and that deep-space trips depend on teamwork and trade-offs. It is meant to make space engineering approachable and social for students and general audiences.

Tools
Built with Nodejs and Typescript using NASA asteroid data as the basis for the in-game asteroids.

Creativity
We combined three things: a social task-based ship, a 6-axis flight simulator, and an engineering weight-and-fuel model. We also added local humor (Romy cheese as in-game food) and a forgiving design with emergency guide arrows and a Free-Play mode, so the game never ends suddenly.

Factors we considered
Teaching real engineering trade-offs while keeping the game fun, cooperation instead of competition, fair pacing for first-time players, and keeping the 2D and 3D parts connected so tasks and flying affect each other.

projectDetails.name: BioOrbit: Autonomous AI Space-Medical Telemetry & Psychological Platform
projectDetails.summary: BioOrbit is a bilingual (English/Arabic RTL), offline-first mobile and clinical telemetry platform developed by Team Gat Keda for deep-space missions where 20-to-40-minute communication delays make live Earth medical help impossible. Built with dual role portals—Astronaut (Astro) and Space Doctor (Doctor)—our Flutter prototype logs real-time cardiovascular, glycemic, and thermoregulation vitals (Heart Rate, Blood Pressure, Blood Sugar, and Body Temperature), tracks sleep duration and fatigue, and executes Computer Vision AI facial biometric scans (EAR, MAR, facial symmetry, and head pose) alongside automated ECG waveform interpretation. Aligned with NASA Human Research Program (HRP) hazards and NASA-STD-3001 standards, BioOrbit empowers crews to detect visual fatigue, psychological stress, and physiological risks early and apply immediate countermeasures autonomously onboard.
projectDetails.details:
## 1. The Deep-Space Medical Autonomy Challenge
During long-duration lunar (Artemis) and Mars missions, astronauts face severe physiological and psychological hazards: microgravity-induced bone and muscle atrophy, cosmic radiation, cardiovascular deconditioning, and extreme isolation. With round-trip signal delays reaching up to 40 minutes on Mars expeditions, astronauts cannot rely on real-time consultations with Earth's Ground Control during medical or behavioral emergencies. They require a 100% autonomous, onboard clinical ecosystem.

## 2. What BioOrbit Does (Our Solution)
Developed by **Team Gat Keda (جت كده)**, **BioOrbit** is a dual-role, bilingual (English / Arabic RTL) medical telemetry and AI diagnostic ecosystem connecting crew members and onboard medical officers:
* **Astronaut (Astro) Portal (Cyan Theme #00E5FF):** A daily tablet/mobile companion for rapid vital sign entry (Heart Rate, Blood Pressure, Blood Sugar, Body Temperature), sleep and fatigue logging, AI facial stress and eyelid-droop fatigue scanning, ECG waveform explanation, and 3D anatomical risk visualization across Muscle, Nerve, and Bone layers.
* **Space Doctor (Doctor) Portal (Emerald Theme #00E676):** A clinical command interface that aggregates 7-record weekly crew telemetry averages, flags early physiological or psychological anomalies up to 48 hours ahead, and dispatches direct treatment countermeasures to the crew.
* **Official Project Demo:** https://drive.google.com/file/d/1pMBM1K-yDFyKCQp7_g-1_mKLNGi59HCW/view?usp=sharing
* **Official Source Code Repository:** https://github.com/MoaazSakr/BioOrbit

## 3. How BioOrbit Works Step-by-Step (Verified Prototype Workflow)
### Step A: Role-Based Orbital Access Portal & Instant Bilingual (EN / AR RTL) Support
Upon launching BioOrbit, crew members receive an orbital session authentication banner (`Welcome back to orbit, moaaz sakr 3 (Astronaut)`), select their mission role—**Astronaut (Astro)** or **Space Doctor (Doctor)**—and switch effortlessly between English and full Right-to-Left Arabic (`عربي` / `English`).

### Step B: Real-Time Biomedical, Thermoregulation, Sleep & Fatigue Telemetry
1. **Vitals & Orbit Tab:** The astronaut logs daily **Heart Rate (75 BPM)**, **Systolic/Diastolic Blood Pressure (120 / 80 mmHg)**, **Blood Sugar Level (95 mg/dL)**, and **Body Temperature (36.8 °C)** using fine-tune steppers or quick-select presets (`36.5`, `36.8`, `37.0`, `37.5`). BioOrbit evaluates each reading against NASA-STD-3001 spaceflight baselines and displays real-time clinical status (`Nominal / Stable`).
2. **Psych & Sleep Tab:** The astronaut records **Actual Sleep Duration (0–12 hrs, e.g., 8.0 h)** and **Physical & Mental Fatigue (1–10 scale, e.g., 3 / 10)**, then taps **Sync Health Record to Backend** to store the telemetry record and update the 3D Muscle, Nerve, and Bone load model.

### Step C: Dynamic Computer Vision AI Facial Biometrics & ECG Waveform Engine
In the **Face AI** tab, the astronaut captures a selfie using the front camera or gallery. Our AI pipeline (achieving **~94.8% landmark detection accuracy**) dynamically computes geometric drowsiness, stress, and cranial alignment metrics, proven across two live test cases in our prototype:
* **1. AI Facial Measurements (Image To AI) — Two Verified Live Scenarios:**
* **Live Test Case A (Rested Crew Member):** `EAR: 0.33` | `MAR: 0.15` | `Facial Symmetry: 96.5%` | `Head Pose: 3.8°` -> Diagnosis: **Alert & Balanced** (*"Facial biometrics are balanced; eye aperture and facial muscle symmetry indicate good alertness and no orbital strain."*).
* **Live Test Case B (Fatigued Crew Member in Video Demo):** `EAR: 0.26` | `MAR: 0.18` | `Facial Symmetry: 96.2%` | `Head Pose: 0.7°` -> Diagnosis: **Mild Visual Fatigue** (*"Facial measurements show mild eyelid droop linked to fatigue; a rest period is advised."*).
* **2. ECG Waveform, Hemodynamics & Crew Clearance Summary (Metrics To AI):** Cross-references cardiovascular and metabolic telemetry to generate a clinical rhythm report:
* **ECG Waveform Analysis:** *"Normal Sinus Rhythm; P-waves are uniform, ventricular QRS complex is sharp and narrow, and QT interval is completely stable."*
* **Hemodynamics & Metabolism:** *"Vascular perfusion, glycemic energy, and core thermoregulation are well-balanced for mission operations."*
* **Crew & Doctor Summary:** *"Cardiac rhythm and vital indicators are reassuring—astronaut is cleared for full orbital duties."*

### Step D: 7-Record Weekly Telemetry Averages & Doctor-Astro Medical Link
In the **Reports** tab, BioOrbit automatically calculates **7-Record Weekly Telemetry Averages** (`المتوسطات الحيوية الأسبوعية - 7 سجلات`: Avg Heart Rate, Avg Sleep Hours, Total Weekly Exercise, Peak Fatigue, and Mental Status). Through the integrated **Doctor-Astro Medical Link (`قناة الاتصال الطبي`)**, the Space Doctor dispatches direct clinical countermeasures (such as *"Add 20 mins to ARED resistance training today"*) straight to the astronaut's device.

## 4. Benefits, Impact & Honest Prototype Roadmap
* **Deep-Space Autonomy:** Protects crew health during Artemis lunar operations, Gateway station stays, and future Mars expeditions without waiting for Earth communication links.
* **Terrestrial Healthcare Impact:** Directly adaptable for isolated environments on Earth with limited medical staff or internet connectivity, including rural desert clinics in Egypt/MENA, submarines, polar research stations, and offshore energy platforms.
* **Working Prototype vs. Current Limits & Next Steps:** Our live Flutter prototype currently supports bilingual (EN/AR RTL) role authentication, 4-metric vital & sleep telemetry logging, backend synchronization, dynamic AI facial biometric calculation (detecting both alertness and mild visual fatigue), ECG clinical interpretation, and doctor-astronaut messaging. Currently, vitals use interactive UI steppers/presets and cloud image relay (`ibb.co`) during testing. Next, we are embedding our interactive 3D Muscle/Nerve/Bone mesh directly into the main Vitals view, adding **Crew Emergency QR Medical Badges**, connecting Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) smart garments (CSA Astroskin), and packaging our AI weights into on-device TensorFlow Lite for 100% air-gapped spacecraft execution.

## 5. Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used
* **Source Code Repository:** https://github.com/MoaazSakr/BioOrbit
* **Mobile Frontend:** Flutter SDK & Dart (Responsive Dark Space-Medical UI: `#070B19`, `#00E5FF`, `#00E676`, `#8C52FF` with full English LTR & Arabic RTL support).
* **Backend & Database:** RESTful API Backend, JSON Telemetry Store, Role-Based Authentication, and ImgBB API (prototype image staging).
* **AI & Biometrics Pipeline:** Computer Vision Facial Landmark Geometry (MediaPipe / OpenCV EAR, MAR, Bilateral Symmetry, and Head Pose algorithms) + Large Language Model (LLM) Clinical Diagnostic Engine calibrated to NASA-STD-3001 thresholds.
* **UI/UX & Media Production:** Figma (Interface Prototyping) and FFmpeg/Premiere (30-second subtitled Demo Video & animated GIFs).

## 6. Team Gat Keda (جت كده) Crew Members & Roles
* **Moaaz Sakr:** Team Leader & Flutter Developer
* **Ahmed Ghoniem:** AI & Biometrics Developer
* **Mohamaed Alroba:** Backend & Sync Developer
* **Fady Samir:** Backend & Telemetry Developer
* **Mohamed Elarby:** UI/UX Product Designer
* **Saeed Emad:** Video Editing & Media Specialist

projectDetails.name: Odyssey
projectDetails.summary: ODYSSEY is a web app that helps teams rehearse Moon and Mars missions on Earth. You describe a mission in plain English. An AI agent splits it into experiments, sets measurable requirements, and ranks 39 curated Earth analog sites for each experiment using open NASA data (LRO LOLA and Diviner, MOLA, NASA POWER, MODIS). Each site is compared with the lunar south pole or Jezero crater on 31 conditions, and the app shows exactly where Earth stops being a good stand-in. Gaps are never hidden: each is labelled as a dataset to connect, a field measurement to make, or physics Earth cannot provide, such as gravity or vacuum, with a proposed chamber test instead. It ends with a multi-site field campaign and a report. Analog sites are usually picked by reputation. ODYSSEY makes that choice traceable, per experiment, with every number tied to a source or a stated assumption.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

ODYSSEY turns a Moon or Mars mission brief into a field-testing plan on Earth. A user types a mission in plain English, for example "a seven-day lunar expedition with geological sampling, rover navigation, equipment deployment, thermal survival and dust mitigation".

How it works

1. Define. An AI agent maps the brief to experiments and quotes the words that justify each one. Each experiment gets measurable requirements, such as maximum slope or temperature range, each labelled as stated in the brief or as an assumption.

2. Discover. 39 curated Earth analog sites are checked against hard limits, then ranked separately for every experiment on terrain, temperature, geology, access and evidence. A global screen of 81,575 land cells found 80 more candidate regions. A "planetary twin" view puts each site beside the target (the lunar south pole or Jezero crater on Mars) on 31 conditions. Values are compared only when the quantity and scale match, so air temperature is never compared with surface temperature.

3. Validate. "Challenge this match" shows how a high similarity score drops once hard limits and missing evidence are checked; in the demo, 92 becomes 76. Every gap is named: a dataset not yet connected, a field measurement needed (with the standard test), or physics Earth cannot provide, such as gravity, vacuum or the lunar night. Sources the agent finds online stay unverified until the quoted value is found word for word in the full document.

4. Rehearse. For conditions no site offers, it proposes controlled tests, such as a thermal-vacuum chamber or gravity offload, in numbered steps labelled as proposals, not results. An optimiser then builds a multi-site campaign three ways: best science, least travel, fewest facilities. A report exports as Markdown or JSON.

Benefits and impact

Analog sites are often chosen by reputation. ODYSSEY makes the choice traceable and specific to each experiment: which site suits which test, why, and what must still be tested elsewhere. This can save mission teams field time and money and avoid false confidence in an analog. Students and the public can also see why a desert is or is not a good stand-in for the Moon or Mars.

What makes it creative

- It ranks sites per experiment, not per planet.

- It treats Earth's shortfalls as results, not failures, and offers a next step for each.

- It explains its reasoning visually:

- a similarity score broken into its weighted parts;

- Earth and the target side by side;

- log-scale pressure and gravity comparisons;

- sun-angle and crater-shadow diagrams for polar light;

- dust-flight arcs under each planet's gravity;

- relationships between measured conditions across sites.

- While the agent runs, Moon or Mars and Earth are scanned together in 3D. When the first sites are ranked, the view hands off to the best one.

Tools and technologies

- Code: TypeScript, React 19, Three.js and Vite for the interface; Node.js 22 with SQLite and live server-sent events for the backend.

- Data pipelines: Python (rasterio, STAC, H3).

- AI: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash through the OpenCode API for the agent. Every number comes from tested code, and the app also runs fully without the AI.

- Deployment and tests: Docker and Azure Container Apps; 71 automated tests.

- Data: NASA (LRO LOLA and Diviner, MGS MOLA, NASA POWER, MODIS, GIBS, NSSDC), ESA Copernicus (DEM, Sentinel-2, WorldCover), CSA RADARSAT-1 and Macrostrat.

What we considered

- Scientific honesty: missing data is never counted as a match, and fabricated precision is never shown.

- Traceable claims: every value links to its source, resolution and date.

- Clarity for non-experts: plain language and visual explanations.

- Accessibility: works on phones, supports reduced motion, and an open-source code base (Apache-2.0) others can extend.

Limits

This is a prototype:

- 39 curated sites and two targets.

- Reanalysis climate at about 50 km resolution and 40 m terrain.

- Several requirement thresholds are assumptions, and they're labelled as such.

- Simulation outputs are first-order models, not facility results.

Links: live app https://odyssey.qd.je · code https://github.com/MahmoudAdelbghany/ODYSSEY

projectDetails.name: NASA's Forgotten Space Machines
projectDetails.summary:
NASA's Forgotten Space Machines is an interactive digital space museum developed in response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge, "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

Since the beginning of space exploration, numerous machines have travelled beyond Earth, exploring the Moon, Mars and deep space. Although some missions have ended and some spacecraft have gone silent, their scientific contributions remain significant.

Our project brings these stories together through an engaging digital experience where visitors can explore historic spacecraft, understand their missions, discover their engineering and learn about the scientific discoveries they made.

By combining space history, interactive exploration and educational storytelling, we aim to make complex space missions accessible and interesting, especially for school-age students and the next generation of space enthusiasts.

Our goal is simple:  To ensure that these remarkable machines and their contributions to humanity are never forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
NASA's Forgotten Space Machines

Turning Forgotten Journeys into Unforgettable Learning Experiences
Project Links
- Live Website: https://nasa-forgotten-space-machines.vercel.app/
- GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Abiya-Daniel/nasa-forgotten-space-machine.
Project Overview
NASA's Forgotten Space Machines is an interactive educational web platform developed by Team 0N1X for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.
The project highlights NASA's forgotten, inactive and retired spacecraft, rovers, landers and robotic explorers across the Moon, Mars and beyond.
Our platform works as a digital space museum, helping visitors discover the stories, missions, engineering achievements and scientific contributions of these machines.
Key Features
- Explore historic spacecraft and robotic explorers.
- Discover mission histories and timelines.
- Learn about spacecraft engineering and technology.
- Understand important scientific discoveries.
- Experience interactive educational content and visual storytelling.
Problem and Solution
Many historic space machines have made significant contributions to space exploration, but their stories remain unfamiliar to younger generations.
Our solution brings these stories together in an engaging digital platform, connecting each machine with its mission, technology and scientific legacy.
Innovation
Instead of presenting forgotten spacecraft as inactive equipment, we highlight them as remarkable engineering achievements and milestones in scientific discovery.
By combining historical information, interactive learning and visual storytelling, we make space exploration more accessible and interesting.
Benefits and Impact
- Promotes interest in space science and technology.
- Makes NASA's mission history accessible to students.
- Encourages STEM learning and scientific curiosity.
- Preserves the legacy of historic space missions.
- Inspires the next generation of space explorers.
Technologies and Tools
Frontend Framework: React
Programming Languages: JavaScript / TypeScript, HTML5 and CSS3
Styling: CSS / Tailwind CSS
Source Code Management: GitHub
Deployment and Hosting: Vercel
APIs and Libraries: Project-specific APIs and libraries used in development
Future Scope
Future improvements may include 3D spacecraft models, virtual mission experiences, interactive quizzes and additional space mission archives.
Conclusion
NASA's Forgotten Space Machines transforms forgotten space exploration journeys into engaging learning experiences, preserving their legacy and inspiring future generations to explore science, engineering and space.

projectDetails.name: LUNA-VISTA: An Intelligent Lunar Landing Site Selection and Mission Planning System
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA-VISTA is an interactive, science-based web application designed to assist mission planners, researchers, educators, and the public in identifying and comparing suitable landing locations near the Moon's south pole. The system combines astronomical calculations, lunar terrain analysis, and 3D visualization to simplify the evaluation of potential lunar landing sites.

The application allows users to select different candidate landing locations and mission dates to analyze the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon. Using NASA/JPL SPICE data and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) terrain datasets, it calculates solar elevation, sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and potential direct-to-Earth communication windows. It also estimates solar energy generation based on illumination conditions and solar panel parameters.

An intelligent site comparison and recommendation module evaluates candidate locations using sunlight availability, communication visibility, and terrain suitability. The results are presented through interactive 3D lunar visualizations, graphs, comparative dashboards, and mission reports.

The main goal of LUNA-VISTA is to provide a user-friendly scientific decision-support platform that makes complex lunar environmental data easier to understand, helping users evaluate landing sites and mission dates for safer and more efficient future lunar exploration.
projectDetails.details:
LUNA-VISTA: Intelligent Lunar Landing Site Selection and Mission Planning System

LUNA-VISTA is a proposed lunar exploration planning system designed to help identify and compare suitable landing sites near the Moon's South Pole. It focuses on three important factors: sunlight availability, Earth visibility for communication, and local terrain conditions.

The system allows users to select candidate landing sites and dates. It then aims to analyze the positions of the Sun and Earth, examine terrain obstructions, estimate sunlight duration and communication windows, and compare different landing locations. Based on these factors, it provides an explainable ranking of candidate sites using configurable criteria.

The project is designed around scientific datasets, including NASA/JPL SPICE kernels for planetary positions and orientations, LOLA elevation models for lunar terrain analysis, and LROC imagery for surface visualization.

The main benefits of LUNA-VISTA are improved mission-planning support, easier comparison of landing locations, better understanding of lighting and communication constraints, and more accessible visualization of complex lunar environment information. Its intended impact is to support safer and more informed planning for future lunar exploration missions.

The creative aspect of this project is its combination of solar analysis, Earth visibility assessment, terrain evaluation, and site comparison in one integrated and user-friendly concept. It also emphasizes transparency by showing the criteria behind its recommendations.

This submission presents a concept demonstration. The sample site scores and comparison values shown in the presentation are illustrative mock data, not actual measured lunar results or official NASA rankings. The proposed system would require implementation and scientific validation using the relevant datasets.

projectDetails.name: Project Aithra Sentinel
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel, an open-source, interactive geospatial web application designed to detect and forecast monsoon-triggered floods and landslides in real time.
Our solution directly addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by overcoming a major limitation of traditional optical satellites: cloud cover. During severe monsoon storms, dense clouds obscure optical imagery precisely when disasters unfold. By utilizing cloud-penetrating NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) L-band data, our application monitors centimeter-scale ground deformation, soil saturation spikes, and surface water expansion beneath thick forest canopies and storm clouds. We fuse NISAR before-and-after change detection with NASA SRTM terrain slope data and NASA GPM IMERG rainfall measurements to explain the physical triggers behind slope instability.
This tool is vital because rapid, accurate early warnings save lives and infrastructure. By translating complex spaceborne radar datasets into intuitive, color-coded hazard maps and time-lapse visualizations, Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel empowers emergency responders and vulnerable communities to act before catastrophic slides or flash floods strike.
projectDetails.details:
OVERVIEW AND HOW IT WORKS

Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel is an early-warning geospatial system designed to detect and forecast monsoon-triggered floods and landslides in real time. Traditional optical satellites cannot see through dense storm clouds precisely when severe monsoons strike. Our solution solves this blind spot using NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) data.

Our Python-based risk engine processes sequential, cloud-penetrating NISAR L-band radar passes to detect subtle, centimeter-scale ground deformation, soil saturation spikes, and expanding surface water beneath thick forest canopies. To explain the physical mechanics behind slope failure, our model fuses these radar changes with terrain slope angles from the NASA SRTM Digital Elevation Model and 24-hour precipitation triggers from NASA GPM IMERG. The system calculates a weighted Slope Instability Index and categorizes terrain into High, Moderate, or Low hazard zones.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Our primary goal is to turn complex orbital radar datasets into clear, actionable alerts for local disaster management authorities, civil engineers, and vulnerable hillside communities. By identifying steep, water-saturated slopes before catastrophic failure occurs, Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel provides crucial lead time for targeted evacuations, road closures, and infrastructure protection—saving lives during peak monsoon seasons.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, AND DATA SOURCES

- Programming & Modeling: Python (numpy, rasterio, geopandas) for computing the Slope Instability Index and processing geospatial layers.

- Satellite & Ancillary Datasets: NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR L-band and S-band products), NASA SRTM (30m Digital Elevation Model), and NASA GPM IMERG precipitation data.

- Presentation & Documentation: GitHub for open-source code hosting and a 7-slide architectural pitch deck.

CREATIVITY AND KEY DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

Instead of treating radar imagery as a static visual overlay, we creatively combined dual-frequency radar physics with physical slope-stability mechanics (ground displacement, terrain gradient, soil moisture, and rainfall). When designing the project, our team prioritized:

- All-Weather Cloud Penetration: Ensuring uninterrupted monitoring during heavy monsoon storms when optical satellites fail.

- Canopy Penetration: Leveraging NISAR's 24 cm L-band wavelength to measure bare-earth movement beneath dense tropical vegetation.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: After the Landing – A Space Heritage Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
After the Landing is a website that explores the objects and equipment humans have left behind on the Moon and Mars during space missions. We usually focus on the discoveries made by astronauts, landers and rovers, but we rarely think about what happens to the equipment after a mission ends.

Through this project, we bring together information about these objects from different NASA missions, including Apollo, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Perseverance and InSight. The website allows visitors to explore these missions, learn about the objects left behind and understand their history through images and information.

Our aim is to make space exploration more interesting and help people discover a side of space missions that is often overlooked. These objects may no longer be active, but they still represent important achievements in human exploration and scientific history.
projectDetails.details:
AFTER THE LANDING — Space Heritage Explorer

After the Landing, created by ANKH, is an interactive, cinematic educational archive that explores the human-made objects, scientific instruments and historical traces left behind on the Moon and Mars by space exploration missions.

While space missions are often remembered for their launches, landings and discoveries, the hardware and equipment left behind tell another important story. Our project brings this overlooked aspect of space exploration to life through an immersive digital experience.

What does the project do and how does it work?

The platform provides an interactive archive of 18 mission-related objects from lunar and Martian exploration. Users can explore dedicated Moon and Mars sections, discover individual mission objects, learn about their original purposes, understand their scientific contributions and examine their historical significance.

Each object has a dedicated information page containing its mission context, purpose, status, facts and legacy. The platform also features an interactive mission timeline, archive filters, educational content and animated planetary environments.

It distinguishes between deliberately impacted spacecraft, discarded landing hardware, scientific equipment and still-operational rovers, helping users understand the different categories of human-made objects on other worlds.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes space exploration history more accessible and engaging.
  • Educates users about the scientific instruments and technologies used in lunar and Martian missions.
  • Preserves awareness of historical human activity beyond Earth.
  • Helps students and space enthusiasts understand the long-term legacy of space exploration.
  • Presents scientific and historical information through an easy-to-navigate visual archive.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to create awareness of humanity’s growing footprint beyond Earth and encourage people to look beyond the achievements of landing on another world.

Every object left behind represents engineering, scientific discovery and a moment in human exploration. By documenting these objects, we hope to encourage curiosity about planetary exploration, space heritage and the importance of preserving the history of our activities on other celestial bodies.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a lightweight, responsive web application using:

  • HTML5 – Structure and content.
  • CSS3 – Responsive layouts, visual design, animations and transitions.
  • JavaScript – Interactive features, navigation, archive filtering and dynamic content.
  • NASA Images API – Research and retrieval of representative space mission imagery.
  • Solar System Scope textures – Planetary surface textures for immersive visual environments.
  • GitHub Pages – Public hosting and deployment.

All 18 project photographs are stored locally within the project. The website does not require a backend, database, npm installation or external JavaScript libraries.

How is the project creative and innovative?

Instead of presenting space mission information as a conventional list of facts, After the Landing transforms it into a cinematic digital heritage experience.

The platform combines animated planetary environments, editorial storytelling, interactive mission-object dossiers, a colour-coded timeline and a searchable archive. Its Moon and Mars sections have distinct visual identities and educational content.

A key feature is its classification of deployed scientific equipment, discarded landing components, deliberately impacted hardware and active mission vehicles. This provides a clearer and more scientifically responsible understanding of what remains on these worlds.

What factors did we consider?

We considered scientific accuracy, historical context, accessibility, responsive design, performance and educational value throughout development.

Particular attention was given to distinguishing active mission hardware from abandoned or discarded objects, correctly representing mission events and providing appropriate image-source credits.

The website supports desktop and mobile devices, keyboard navigation and reduced-motion preferences. Local image storage also helps maintain availability without relying on external image servers.

After the Landing is more than an archive of objects. It is a digital record of humanity’s journey beyond Earth and the stories we leave behind.

projectDetails.name: ExoMatch
projectDetails.summary: ExoMatch is a web application that makes NASA’s exoplanet data easier to explore and understand. Users can search confirmed planets, compare their properties, view discovery trends, and receive recommendations for similar worlds. The system uses K-Means clustering and similarity calculations based on planetary characteristics such as radius, mass, temperature, and orbital period. Built with Python and Streamlit, ExoMatch combines machine learning with interactive charts to turn complex astronomical records into an accessible learning experience. It helps students, educators, and space enthusiasts investigate patterns in known exoplanets while clearly distinguishing scientific measurements, illustrative images, and recommendations from evidence of habitability or life.
projectDetails.details: ExoMatch is an interactive web application that helps users explore, compare, and discover similarities among confirmed exoplanets using NASA Exoplanet Archive data. It uses K-Means clustering and Euclidean distance to recommend planets based on characteristics such as radius, mass, orbital period, and temperature. Built with Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, and Plotly, it provides searchable planetary information and interactive visualizations. The project makes astronomical data accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts. Its design considers missing values, feature scaling, usability, and scientific limitations. Recommendations highlight similarities between known planets without claiming to discover new worlds, confirm habitability, or identify extraterrestrial life.

projectDetails.name: AstroQuest – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
AstroQuest is an interactive educational application designed to help students understand how astronauts manage resources and survive during space missions. It allows users to experience a virtual Moon or Mars mission while taking on the role of an astronaut.

Users learn to manage essential resources such as oxygen, food, water and electricity while maintaining astronaut health and safety. They also face different mission challenges that require them to make decisions and understand the results of their choices. The application aims to include interactive mission levels, resource management activities and mission-success outcomes.

AstroQuest makes space exploration more interesting and easier to understand through learning and interactive experiences. It encourages curiosity about space, develops decision-making and problem-solving skills, and introduces students to the challenges of real space missions.
projectDetails.details:
AstroQuest – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

What does the project do, and how does it work?

AstroQuest is an interactive educational game that allows players to experience the challenges of a space mission. Players take on the role of a junior astronaut and manage important resources such as oxygen, water, food, and electricity. During the mission, they face different challenges, including water shortages, power shortages, dust storms, and returning safely to base. Players must select suitable actions to manage resources and complete their mission successfully.

What benefits does the project have?

AstroQuest makes learning about space exploration more interesting and interactive. It helps students understand the importance of resource management, decision-making, and problem-solving during space missions. It also introduces young learners to some of the challenges astronauts may face.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our aim is to encourage students and young learners to become interested in space science and exploration. We want to make space-related learning more accessible, enjoyable, and understandable through a simple interactive experience.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used a text editor (Notepad) to write the code and a web browser to test the game. We used Netlify to host the project online so that people can access and play it through a public link. No special hardware was required.

How is your project creative?

The creative part of AstroQuest is that it turns space-mission challenges into an interactive learning game. Instead of only reading about astronauts, players make decisions, manage resources, and experience how their choices affect the mission. The different challenges make the experience engaging and educational.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered simplicity, educational value, user-friendliness, and accessibility. We wanted to make the game easy to understand and play, especially for students and beginners. We also considered the importance of resource management and decision-making in space exploration while designing the mission challenges.

projectDetails.name: Earth Information Jukebox: Hear the Arctic Ice Disappear
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Information Jukebox: Hear the Arctic Ice Disappear turns NASA satellite-based Arctic sea ice data into sound. We developed an interactive web page where each year is one musical note: a low note means a lot of sea ice, and a high note means less. When you press Play, you hear the pitch climb across more than 45 years of data while a chart marker and live caption show the year and ice extent in million km².

This addresses the challenge by making Earth observation data something people can listen to and explore, not just read in charts. Sound also makes the data more accessible to people who have difficulty with visual graphs.

It matters because Arctic sea ice is a key indicator of climate change, and hearing the decline in under a minute makes it easy to understand and remember. We used the NSIDC Sea Ice Index (derived from NASA satellite observations), Python for data processing, and JavaScript with the Web Audio API for the page, hosted on GitHub Pages. The design can grow to include more Earth datasets as new tracks.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
Earth Information Jukebox turns Arctic sea ice data into sound. I used the NSIDC Sea Ice Index (based on NASA satellite observations) and kept the September extent for each year from 1979 onward, which is the yearly minimum. Each value is mapped to a pitch: more ice gives a low note (220 Hz), and less ice gives a high note (880 Hz). When a user presses Play, each year is played as one note while a chart marker moves along the data and a live caption shows the year and ice extent in million km². The pitch climbs as the ice shrinks.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It makes a long climate record understandable in under a minute.
  • It gives people who cannot easily read charts another way to explore Earth data.
  • It helps students and the public connect with NASA data emotionally, not just numerically.
  • It works in any browser with one button, with no installation or technical knowledge.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NSIDC Sea Ice Index, monthly extent by year (Northern Hemisphere)
  • Python (Pandas, NumPy, SciPy) in Google Colab to clean the data and test the sound
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API for the interactive page
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting the code and live demo
  • Google Colab for running the data processing
  • An AI assistant (Claude) helped me plan the project, write and debug code, and draft documentation. I ran, tested and deployed the project myself.

Creativity
Instead of another chart, I treated data as music. The “jukebox” idea means each Earth dataset can become a track, and Arctic ice is the first song. Using the ear to notice a trend is a different way to experience satellite data.

Factors I considered

  • Clarity: low means more ice and high means less ice, so the direction is easy to understand.
  • Accuracy: pitch shows relative change, so the caption always displays the real value. The data source and units are credited.
  • Accessibility: sound adds a non-visual way to explore the data.
  • Simplicity: one dataset and one button, built to be reliable.
  • Limitations: this is a prototype with one track, September values only, and extent rather than ice thickness. Future work includes more tracks (Antarctic ice, sea surface temperature), NASA satellite imagery, and user controls.
