projectDetails.name: Project Chaotic Cosmos
projectDetails.summary:
ASTROVITALS is a software-based astronaut health-monitoring prototype developed by our team, Chaotic Cosmos, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. With the guidance and encouragement of Jiya CS, we worked together to turn our idea into an interactive PictoBlox project.

Our prototype focuses on six important health parameters: heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, blood pressure, hydration and sleep hours. Users enter an astronaut's name and manually provide the readings. The system checks them against programmed reference ranges and displays an overall status: NORMAL or CHECK REQUIRED. An astronaut character guides the user through the process.

We wanted to explore how technology could make health monitoring simpler and more organised for astronauts. Although our current version uses manually entered readings rather than live sensors, it represents our first step towards a more advanced system. This project has been a journey of teamwork, learning, problem-solving and turning curiosity into something we could actually build.
projectDetails.details:
What did we develop?

We developed ASTROVITALS, an interactive astronaut health-monitoring prototype using PictoBlox. Our aim was to create a simple system that brings important health readings together in one place.

How does it work?

The user starts the programme and enters the astronaut's name. An astronaut character welcomes the user and guides them to the dashboard. The user then enters six health readings: heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, blood pressure, hydration and sleep hours.

Using conditional statements, the programme compares the entered values with its programmed reference ranges. It then displays an overall system status: NORMAL or CHECK REQUIRED. A scan counter also keeps track of monitoring sessions.

Benefits and intended impact

We wanted to make health monitoring easier to understand and organise. By bringing six parameters into one interface, ASTROVITALS demonstrates how a simple software system can help identify readings that fall outside selected reference ranges.

We hope our idea encourages further exploration of technology for astronaut health and well-being.

Tools and technology

We used PictoBlox and its block-based programming environment. Our project uses variables, conditional statements, user inputs, broadcasts, sprites and backdrops to create an interactive experience.

The current version is a software prototype. It does not use physical sensors or collect live medical readings.

Creativity and team contribution

We brought together different ideas and worked towards creating one common project. From planning the interface and deciding what parameters to include to developing the programming logic and testing the prototype, each stage taught us something new.

We faced challenges along the way, especially while bringing our ideas together and making the different parts work as one system. Jiya CS supported us with guidance, suggestions and encouragement throughout this journey. Her support helped us approach the challenge with more confidence and keep improving our work.

Potential considerations

We understand that manually entered readings may not always be accurate. Health reference ranges can also differ depending on the individual and mission conditions. A real-world system would need reliable sensors, secure data handling, expert-reviewed medical standards and professional oversight.

Future scope

In the future, ASTROVITALS could be developed further by integrating actual sensors, collecting readings automatically, securely storing health information and displaying changes over time. These are ideas for future development, not features of our current prototype.

projectDetails.name: FieldShift AI: Farm-Level Digital Twins & Climate Adaptation Powered by NASA Earth Data
projectDetails.summary:
FieldShift AI is an open-source agricultural decision-support platform that transforms NASA Earth observations into actionable, farm-level climate adaptation decisions. While satellite datasets provide invaluable planetary insights, smallholder farmers often struggle to translate raw gridded data into daily field operations. 

FieldShift AI solves this by constructing a farm-level predictive Digital Twin for every registered field. It synthesizes NASA GPM IMERG precipitation, NASA POWER agroclimatology, NASA SMAP L4 rootzone soil moisture, Landsat/Sentinel vegetation indices, and NASADEM terrain hydrology with local soil lab tests. 

This intelligence powers:
1) 5-factor weighted crop suitability scoring across regional and global crops,
2) A dynamic multi-year crop rotation optimizer (Soil Health, Water Efficiency, and Balanced pathways),
3) A predictive "What-If" stress simulator,
4) A multilingual AI Farm Assistant featuring voice speech-to-text, audio read-aloud, and site-specific crop diagnostics, and
5) Transparent carbon credit readiness (Verra VM0042 / CDM AMS-III.AU) for smallholder aggregation.
projectDetails.details:
Project Functionality

FieldShift AI is designed as a modular, local-first agricultural intelligence platform that bridges spaceborne observations and ground-level farming realities:

1. Farm Digital Twin & Interactive Boundary Mapping

Farmers draw field boundaries using an interactive MapLibre GL interface with geodesic WGS84 area calculation. The system builds a live virtual replica synthesizing satellite environmental feeds, soil test calibrations, terrain drainage, and active crop cycles.

2. NASA Earth Observation Pipeline

- Precipitation Telemetry: NASA GPM IMERG v07 gridded daily and 30-day cumulative rainfall.

- Agroclimatology: NASA POWER temperature (T2M), relative humidity, and surface solar irradiance.

- Soil Moisture: NASA SMAP L4 Enhanced Global surface and rootzone moisture dynamics.

- Crop Vigor & Stress: Landsat 8/9 OLI-2 and Sentinel-2 MSI NDVI and NDMI vegetation indices.

- Hydrology & Drainage: NASADEM 30m elevation models calculate slope degrees, flow accumulation, and Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) waterlogging risks.

3. Soil Intelligence with Physical Lab Calibration

Integrates ISRIC SoilGrids 250m baseline soil profiles (pH, organic carbon, texture, bulk density) calibrated against physical Krishi Bhavan lab test intake. A strict scientific safeguard suppresses synthetic NPK dosage recommendations until certified physical soil tests are entered.

4. Multi-Year Crop Rotation Optimizer

An algorithmic rotation engine designs three alternative multi-year crop rotation trajectories:

- Strategy A (Soil Health Focus): Maximizes leguminous nitrogen fixation (+45 kg N/ha) and biological soil organic matter replenishment.

- Strategy B (Water Efficiency Focus): Minimizes irrigation requirements based on historical NASA GPM rainfall cycles.

- Strategy C (Balanced Strategy): Harmonizes market cash flow, labor feasibility, and pest-cycle interruption.

5. Multilingual AI Farm Assistant with Voice STT/TTS & Deep Diagnostics

A conversational farm advisor grounded in Kerala Agricultural University (KAU) and ICAR research:

- Voice Recognition (STT): Web Speech API supporting English, Malayalam (മലയാളം), Hindi (हिन्दी), Tamil (தமிழ்), and Spanish (Español).

- Text-to-Speech (TTS): Audio playback of agronomic advisories for smallholders.

- Multi-Session Topic Controls: Organize queries into separate, persistent topics.

- Site-Specific Crop Diagnostics: When asked about a specific crop (e.g. "I want to plant cashews"), it evaluates the crop's physiological tolerances against the farm's live telemetry (soil pH, humidity, rainfall during flowering, valley drainage), explains why it is or isn't ideal, highlights pest/disease risks (e.g. Blossom Blight, Tea Mosquito Bug), and recommends better-adapted alternatives.

6. What-If Stress Simulator

Allows farmers to stress-test their digital twin against simulated perturbations (-30% drought, +50% flood, monsoon delay, irrigation failure) to project yield impacts and risk scores before committing resources.

7. Carbon Credit Readiness & FPO Aggregation

Transparently models eligibility for Verra VCS (VM0042) and UNFCCC CDM (AMS-III.AU) carbon projects with conservative yield ranges and collective Farmer Producer Organization (FPO) pooling guidance.

Intended Impact

Over 500 million smallholder farmers globally produce a third of the world's food while bearing the brunt of extreme weather anomalies. Most satellite agriculture tools are designed for large industrial monocultures. FieldShift AI brings space agency data down to 1–3 acre family farms, enabling farmers to:

- Avoid crop failure by matching crop biology to microclimates.

- Transition away from monoculture through scientifically optimized crop rotations.

- Protect soil health and reduce excessive chemical fertilizer use.

- Access verified carbon credit aggregation without falling prey to greenwashing intermediaries.

Technology Stack

- Frontend: Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts, Web Speech API (STT/TTS).

- Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy ORM, Pydantic v2, Uvicorn.

- Database: SQLite (default, zero setup) with PostgreSQL / PostGIS migration readiness.

- Geospatial & Math: PyProj, GeoJSON, NumPy.

- Deployment: Local-first architecture, mobile-first responsive UI with offline resilience.

Creativity and Innovation

FieldShift AI moves beyond static satellite viewers and generic LLM chatbots. Its primary innovations include:

1. Deterministic Grounding: The AI Assistant executes live database and telemetry tools rather than hallucinating agronomic advice.

2. Dialect & Voice Accessibility: Smallholders can speak and listen in their native regional languages (e.g., Malayalam, Hindi, Tamil).

3. The What-If Simulator: Bridges historical satellite data with future risk projection, allowing farmers to simulate climate shocks before they occur.

4. Transparent Carbon Economics: Refuses to over-promise carbon yields, explicitly deducting aggregator fees and highlighting smallholder pooling needs.

Factors Considered & Scientific Safeguards

- Spatial Resolution & Uncertainty: Clear labeling of satellite resolution (e.g., 0.1° GPM vs 30m Landsat vs 250m SoilGrids).

- Anti-Hallucination Guardrails: Synthetic fertilizer recommendations are locked until physical soil tests are recorded.

- Multi-Tenant Privacy: Strict authorization ensures farmers' field data remains private (HTTP 403 prevention).

projectDetails.name: Project Cosmic Cadets
projectDetails.summary:
AstroQuest is an interactive web-based space exploration and engineering simulation developed by Team Cosmic Cadets. The project allows users to experience the challenges of establishing and maintaining a sustainable human outpost on the Moon or Mars.

The simulator challenges players to manage four essential resources: life support, radiation shielding, electrical power, and food supply. Players can perform engineering actions, respond to random mission emergencies, monitor system conditions, and make decisions to keep a crew of four astronauts safe throughout a 10-day mission. It also includes different difficulty levels, a mission log, scoring system, and a final mission report.

AstroQuest demonstrates the importance of resource management, engineering decisions, and problem-solving in space exploration. By turning complex space-habitat challenges into an interactive learning experience, the project helps users understand the difficulties of sustaining human life beyond Earth and encourages interest in space science and engineering.
projectDetails.details:
AstroQuest is an interactive, browser-based space exploration simulator designed to demonstrate the engineering challenges of establishing a sustainable human outpost on the Moon or Mars.

The project works as a 10-day mission simulation in which players manage four essential resources: life support, radiation shielding, electrical power and food supply. Players can perform engineering operations such as repairing life-support systems, reinforcing radiation shielding, restoring solar panels and maintaining greenhouse facilities. Random emergency events, including solar particle events, equipment faults and greenhouse problems, challenge players to make decisions and manage limited resources. The simulator also provides three difficulty levels, a mission log, a scoring system and a final mission report.

We developed the project using HTML for structure, CSS for visual design and JavaScript for interactive gameplay, resource calculations, random events and mission progression. It runs directly in a web browser without requiring installation.

The creative aspect of AstroQuest is its combination of space science, engineering concepts and game-based learning. Instead of simply reading about space habitats, users actively experience resource-management decisions and their consequences.

The intended impact is to improve awareness of the challenges of long-duration human space missions, encourage interest in STEM education and introduce users to the importance of sustainable systems for future exploration beyond Earth.

The project uses simplified educational simulations and does not represent actual NASA mission data.

projectDetails.name: Project CosmicPulse X
projectDetails.summary:
We developed a full-stack Space Mission Design Game that enables individuals or teams of four to design, manage, and simulate complete space missions. Featuring a live 3D spacecraft builder, real-time resource dashboards, a global leaderboard, and an interactive arcade-style flight phase, our solution transforms abstract aerospace concepts into an engaging, hands-on experience.

Our project directly addresses the challenge by forcing players to navigate integrated engineering trade-offs. Powered by a custom physics evaluation engine, participants must balance strict constraints—including budget, mass, power generation, and data rates—across various instruments, power systems, and orbital configurations. Players instantly see the consequences of their decisions; for example, upgrading a scientific payload increases potential discoveries but immediately drains power and adds critical spacecraft mass.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between theoretical classroom learning and practical systems engineering. By providing immediate, visual feedback on how individual choices shape overall mission success, our game empowers the next generation of engineers to collaboratively solve complex problems and master the delicate balance required for real-world space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Our Mission

Our Space Mission Design Game is an educational simulator where players design a spacecraft, balance critical resources (power, mass, budget, communications, and time), and pilot their creation in an arcade-style flight mission. As players select components, a 3D model of the spacecraft builds dynamically alongside a live resource dashboard. The game supports both solo play and team mode (with up to 4 roles). Once a mission concludes, players receive a post-mission analysis detailing why their design succeeded or failed, earn XP, unlock badges, and compete on a global leaderboard. To ensure fairness, a backend anti-cheat system recalculates the maximum possible score for each design code and automatically rejects mathematically impossible submissions.

Benefits and intended impact

The project was built to solve a core educational problem: the complex trade-offs of mission design are incredibly difficult to learn from textbooks alone. The primary benefit of our game is that it provides a hands-on environment where abstract constraints become immediate and visible. The intended impact is to empower students and space enthusiasts to intuitively understand aerospace engineering, enabling them to see a real-time 3D model of their work, make integrated decisions, and clearly grasp the specific engineering trade-offs required for a mission to succeed.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, or software used

We developed a decoupled, full-stack web application using the following technologies:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript for the UI; Three.js for the interactive 3D spacecraft builder; and the HTML Canvas API for the arcade flight and mini-games.
  • Backend API: Python with FastAPI and SQLite to manage the REST API, player database, XP progression, and global leaderboard.
  • Physics Evaluator: A zero-dependency Java 17+ microservice that serves as an authoritative physics engine and anti-cheat validator.
  • Deployment & Testing: Docker and Docker Compose for streamlined containerization, and pytest for backend testing.
    README.md

How the project is creative

Our project creatively bridges the gap between rigorous systems engineering and highly engaging gameplay. Instead of relying purely on spreadsheets or static menus, we integrated a live 3D visualizer, interactive mini-games, and an arcade flight phase to make the consequences of engineering decisions visceral. Furthermore, our architectural approach is highly creative: we decoupled the game logic into a frontend UI while building a standalone Java evaluator service strictly to calculate the mathematical limits of a design, ensuring a tamper-proof global leaderboard.

Factors the team considered

  • Educational Accessibility: We deliberately simplified the physics model for educational purposes to ensure the concepts remain approachable for students.
  • Fairness and Security: We prioritized competitive integrity by implementing a robust anti-cheat system that rejects invalid scores and validates player names to prevent injection attacks.
  • Diverse Play Styles: We considered different skill levels by adding a non-ranked Sandbox mode for constraint-free experimentation, alongside a Team mode to foster collaboration.
  • Future Scalability: We acknowledged current limitations (such as the lack of authenticated user accounts) and laid the architectural groundwork for future expansions, including network-based cooperative multiplayer and expanded mission scenarios

projectDetails.name: Project CosmicSix - EarthTrend-Lite Earth-System-Trend-Detective
projectDetails.summary:
Team CosmicSix developed EarthTrend Lite, an interactive web dashboard engineered for environmental and climate trend analytics.

Addressing the challenge of making complex Earth system data accessible and actionable, the application translates multi-year temperature and rainfall metrics into intuitive visual analytics. It features automated trend detection and anomaly spotting algorithms that immediately identify extreme weather shifts and long-term climate patterns across geographic regions. To empower open community research, the platform also enables users to upload and evaluate their own environmental datasets through client-side CSV processing—requiring zero backend setup, servers, or API keys.

This project is important because accelerating climate resilience requires democratizing data literacy. By turning raw environmental observations into clear, localized trends, EarthTrend Lite equips students, researchers, and citizens with the tools to detect critical planetary changes and make informed decisions.
projectDetails.details:
### What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

EarthTrend Lite is an interactive environmental analytics web dashboard designed to investigate Earth system trends. The platform processes multi-year climate observations (temperature and rainfall) across different global regions. When a user selects a region and year, the application's statistical engine dynamically evaluates monthly records, aggregates annual averages, and runs automated anomaly detection algorithms to flag abnormal climate deviations and shifts. In addition, users can upload their own environmental CSV datasets, which the application validates and visualizes entirely within the client's browser.

### What Benefits Does It Have?

- **Zero Configuration & Privacy:** Operates 100% in the browser with no backend servers, database setup, or API keys required.

- **Accessibility:** Converts raw, intimidating numerical climate tables into intuitive charts and summary metrics that anyone can interpret.

- **Custom Dataset Compatibility:** Empowers local community researchers and students to test and visualize their own local weather and climate records instantly.

### Intended Impact

Our goal is to democratize climate data literacy. By lowering the barrier between complex planetary observations and everyday citizens, EarthTrend Lite enables schools, grassroots climate researchers, and community planners to detect localized trends, assess climate variability, and advocate for informed environmental policies.

### Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

- **Frontend Framework:** React 18

- **Build Tool:** Vite

- **Languages:** JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3

- **Development Environment:** Visual Studio Code / Node.js

- **Version Control & Hosting:** Git & GitHub

### Creativity & Innovation

Rather than relying on resource-intensive cloud backends or complex Python notebooks that require programming expertise, we packaged sophisticated trend and anomaly detection into a lightweight, responsive, single-page application. The dark scientific interface mimics research-grade observatories while remaining as easy to use as a consumer web app.

### Factors Our Team Considered

- **Performance & Bandwidth:** Ensuring the application remains fast and lightweight for users in regions with limited internet connectivity.

- **Data Validation & Robustness:** Handling inconsistent CSV formats gracefully with real-time error handling.

- **Data Privacy:** Ensuring user-uploaded climate data never leaves the user’s local machine.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Mannova
projectDetails.summary:
Mannova is an online software application designed to help farmers in Kerala choose rotations that will maintain healthy soils and cope with changes in weather. The farmer selects their farm from the interactive map (or one of seven Kerala agriculture zones), provides soil, irrigation and current crop information, and indicates priority – water savings, soil health, revenues or reduced climate risks.

Mannova analyzes 25 years of NASA POWER climate data from the selected location and assesses approximately 2,000 three-season rotations for droughts, water logging during rainy periods, heat stress and high evaporative demand. The farmer's current rotation is compared with three top replacements with rationales for each of them provided along with NASA climate data, benefits, data gaps, and local verifications needed. NASA GIBS satellite imagery layers (MODIS vegetation indices, SMAP soil moisture, GPM rainfall, land surface temperature) are provided for the area surrounding the farm.

In Kerala, precipitation is unpredictable, and many farms remain uncultivated or stuck with rice after rice. Mannova translates NASA climate data into practical solutions for the farmers.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mannova is a decision-support web app that helps Kerala farmers explore crop rotations that improve soil health and stand up to a changing climate. A farmer picks their field on a map (or one of 7 Kerala farming zones: Kuttanad, Palakkad, Onattukara, Kole lands, midland laterite, Wayanad and the northern coast), describes soil, drainage, salinity, irrigation and what they grow now, and sets their priorities: saving water, soil health, income or avoiding climate risk.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Mannova fetches 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA POWER data for the exact point: temperature, bias-corrected rainfall, humidity and root-zone soil wetness.

2. It builds a climate profile: monthly averages, 1-in-5 dry years, 1-in-10 wet years, trends, and the last decade compared with the first. It estimates evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Hargreaves) to find water-deficit months.

3. A scoring engine tests about 2,000 three-season rotations of 14 Kerala crops for water saving, soil health (legumes, green manure, cover and deep-rooting crops, crop-family diversity, bare months), income and climate safety (drought, waterlogging, heat, salinity), weighted by the farmer's priorities.

4. It compares the current rotation with the 3 best alternatives. Each option shows a 12-month field calendar (bare months and vulnerable seasons), why it was suggested, the NASA evidence, benefits, information gaps, what to check locally, and a score range for drier/hotter and wetter years.

5. NASA GIBS satellite layers show vegetation health (MODIS NDVI), soil moisture (SMAP), rainfall (GPM IMERG), land surface heat and true colour around the field. What-if sliders test less rain or more warming.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

For a Kuttanad paddy field, NASA data shows 6.5% less rain in the last decade and +0.57 °C in maximum temperatures. Replacing Rice–Rice–Fallow with Rice–Sunhemp–Sesame raises the soil health score from 24 to 73 and cuts irrigation by about 490 mm a year, while adding nitrogen-fixing green manure and breaking pest cycles. Mannova is designed to support, not replace, farmers and Krishi Bhavan officers: every result is explained and its limits are stated.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It is built for Kerala: crop names in Malayalam, region presets for distinct farming zones, salinity and flooding risks specific to Kuttanad. It is transparent: rule-based scores with plain-language reasons, instead of a black box. It is honest about uncertainty, showing score ranges and information gaps.

TOOLS

Next.js, React, TypeScript, Recharts, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap, deployed on Vercel. NASA POWER API and NASA GIBS WMS.

Source code: https://github.com/BazilMathew/Mannova

Team: Bazil Mathew P Sajan, Aron Koshy, Blesji K Abraham, Ashwel Rinu Oommen

projectDetails.name: MoonSafe – Lunar Landing Site Safety Analysis
projectDetails.summary:
MoonSafe is a web-based lunar landing site suitability analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project aims to support early-stage assessment of potential landing regions near the Moon's south pole using NASA-derived terrain data.

MoonSafe compares two candidate regions, Shackleton Rim and Malapert Massif, using elevation and slope measurements obtained from lunar terrain datasets. The platform features an interactive dashboard, lunar surface imagery, terrain comparison, landing site safety scoring, and a mission recommendation system.

The application is developed using React, JavaScript, Python, Flask, and Rasterio. Its local backend processes lunar GeoTIFF datasets, while the deployed version uses precomputed terrain statistics to provide accessible online analysis.

MoonSafe makes complex lunar terrain information easier to visualize and compare. It demonstrates how space science data and web technologies can support exploratory mission planning. Future improvements could include solar illumination analysis, communication visibility, and more advanced hazard detection.

MoonSafe is an educational prototype, and its safety scores are not intended for operational landing decisions.
projectDetails.details:
MoonSafe – Lunar Landing Site Safety Analysis

Project Overview

MoonSafe is a web-based lunar landing site suitability analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps users compare potential landing regions near the Moon's south pole using NASA-derived terrain data.

How MoonSafe Works

MoonSafe compares two candidate regions: Shackleton Rim and Malapert Massif.

The system uses lunar terrain datasets to examine elevation and slope characteristics. Python and Rasterio are used to process GeoTIFF terrain files and calculate statistics.

The application presents the results through an interactive dashboard with the following features:

  1. Terrain Analysis: Displays elevation and slope measurements for both regions.
  2. Lunar Map: Displays lunar imagery and allows users to select candidate landing regions.
  3. Safety Analysis: Calculates comparative terrain suitability scores.
  4. Mission Recommendation: Identifies a preferred candidate based on the implemented scoring method.
  5. Data Visualization: Makes complex terrain measurements easier to understand.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend: React, JavaScript, Vite, HTML and CSS
  • Backend: Python and Flask
  • Geospatial Processing: Rasterio and NumPy
  • Datasets: NASA-derived lunar elevation and slope GeoTIFF files
  • Deployment: Vercel and Render
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub

Creativity and Innovation

MoonSafe combines scientific terrain measurements with an accessible web interface. Instead of requiring users to examine large geospatial datasets manually, it presents comparative terrain statistics, safety scores, and recommendations in one dashboard.

The online version uses precomputed terrain statistics, enabling users to explore the results without downloading large raster files.

Benefits and Intended Impact

MoonSafe helps students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore how lunar terrain affects potential landing site selection.

The project demonstrates how publicly available space science data can be transformed into an interactive educational decision-support tool.

Factors Considered

The current prototype considers elevation, slope, and terrain-based suitability. It does not yet include all factors required for real mission planning, such as solar illumination, Earth communication visibility, spacecraft constraints, and detailed landing hazards.

Future Scope

Future improvements include illumination analysis, communication visibility assessment, additional candidate landing regions, and more advanced hazard detection.

Project Links

Live Website: https://moon-safe.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/alphonsasooter/MoonSafe

projectDetails.name: Project Earthlings 2.0
projectDetails.summary:
**Project Summary – Be An Earth System Trend Detective!**

Our project focuses on identifying and understanding significant trends and changes in Earth's interconnected systems using scientific data and observations. We developed a data-driven approach to explore patterns in environmental parameters such as temperature, rainfall, atmospheric conditions, land changes, and other climate-related indicators. By analysing Earth observation data from NASA and other reliable sources, the project aims to identify long-term trends, understand environmental changes, and highlight possible relationships between different Earth systems. It addresses the challenge by transforming complex scientific datasets into meaningful insights that help people better understand our changing planet. This project is important because recognizing environmental trends at an early stage supports climate awareness, informed decision-making, disaster preparedness, and sustainable development. Ultimately, it demonstrates how Earth observation data can help us become better informed about our planet's past, present, and future.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Project Title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project aims to identify, analyse and understand long-term changes in Earth's systems using NASA satellite observations and Earth science datasets. It helps users investigate environmental trends such as temperature changes, rainfall patterns, soil moisture variations, vegetation changes and other climate-related indicators.

The system works by collecting Earth observation data from NASA sources, selecting a particular environmental variable and geographical region, and analysing the data over a specific period. It uses graphs, maps and statistical techniques to identify increasing or decreasing trends and present the findings in an easy-to-understand format.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

  • Helps people understand environmental and climate change.
  • Identifies long-term trends in important Earth system variables.
  • Makes complex NASA datasets easier to understand.
  • Supports environmental awareness and scientific learning.
  • Provides useful information for researchers, students and decision-makers.
  • Encourages data-driven environmental monitoring.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main objective is to improve awareness of changes happening across Earth's systems and encourage people to use scientific data to understand environmental challenges. The project aims to make NASA Earth observation data more accessible and meaningful to students, communities and researchers.

In the long term, it can support climate awareness, environmental monitoring, sustainable planning and informed decision-making.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware or software were used?

The proposed project uses or can be developed using the following technologies:

  • Data sources: NASA Earthdata, NASA GES DISC and satellite observation datasets.
  • Data analysis: Python.
  • Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib and SciPy.
  • Data visualisation: Graphs, charts and geographical maps.
  • Statistical methods: Linear regression and Mann-Kendall trend analysis.
  • Development environment: Jupyter Notebook or Google Colab.
  • Hardware: A standard computer or laptop with internet access.

5. How is the project creative?

The creative aspect of our project is transforming large and complex Earth observation datasets into simple visual stories. Instead of presenting only raw scientific measurements, the project allows users to explore environmental changes through graphs, maps and trend summaries.

It combines Earth science, data analysis and visualisation to make users act like Earth System Trend Detectives, discovering patterns and understanding the changes happening around our planet.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered the following factors while developing the project:

  • Accuracy and reliability of NASA Earth observation data.
  • Selection of appropriate environmental variables.
  • Geographical coverage and time periods.
  • Seasonal variations and long-term environmental changes.
  • Missing data, uncertainty and statistical significance.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift Compass: Climate Twins for Adapting Farms
projectDetails.summary: Field Shift Compass is a decision-support web app that helps farmers adapt to a shifting climate. Using 26 years (2000-2025) of NASA POWER data for Nagpur district, Vidarbha, it answers three questions: What changed here? Who already farms my future? What should I do this season? The Shift Detector measures trends in monsoon onset, dry spells, heat days and rainfall. The Climate Twin matches the farm's projected 2040 climate to the current climate of one of 36 Indian districts (for Nagpur, Raipur is the closest match), so farmers can learn from places already living that climate. The Shift Advisor then gives ranked, rule-based advice such as sowing-date and variety changes, each with its evidence, data source and a confidence score. Advice is delivered through a chat with voice playback and a printable Season Plan, and an agronomist console adds human review. The project turns NASA climate data into farm-level adaptation decisions. The pipeline is region-agnostic and ready for SMAP, MODIS/HLS and NISAR layers in a pilot.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Field Shift Compass turns NASA climate data into farm-level adaptation advice for Nagpur district (Vidarbha, kharif paddy). It has three layers: a Shift Detector (what changed), a Climate Twin Matcher (who already farms my future) and a Shift Advisor (what to do this season). Advice is delivered via a chat with voice playback, a printable Season Plan for farmers without smartphones, and an Agronomist Console where experts approve or correct advice.

HOW IT WORKS

- NASA POWER daily data (2000-2025) gives trends in monsoon onset, sowing-window start, dry spells, heat days, monsoon rainfall and rain days, each with a trend line, R2 and strength label.

- The Climate Twin builds the farm's projected 2040 climate from observed climatology plus approximate scenario deltas (+1.1 C, annual rain x1.08, monsoon rain x1.05, onset +6 days; SSP2-4.5) informed by NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections, then nearest-neighbour matches it against 36 districts' current NASA POWER climatology. For Nagpur the closest match is Raipur (87% relative similarity), then Rewa and Lucknow.

- The Shift Advisor uses transparent, deterministic rules. Each card shows evidence, its dataset, and a confidence score (trend strength x record length). No black-box model makes decisions.

FINDINGS (Nagpur, 2000-2025)

Monsoon onset is about 2.3 days per decade later; monsoon rainfall is +143 mm per decade (R2 = 0.29); rain days +8.2 per decade; the longest dry spell is flat and heat days are declining. Weak trends are shown as weak.

VALIDITY

Onset follows a simplified IMD hydrologic definition. A back-test replays the sowing rule over 26 seasons and flags 8 risky years; this is a consistency check, and independent comparison against rainfall-deficit or yield records is the next step.

CREATIVITY AND IMPACT

The Climate Twin ("learn from a place already living your future"), evidence-first advice built for the farmer trust gap, and the agronomist feedback loop. Relevant to climate-resilient agriculture and food security; the pipeline is region-agnostic.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, vanilla JavaScript with SVG charts, Leaflet, hosted on Render. Code: https://github.com/zeus10-11/field-shift-compass

LIMITATIONS

POWER data is district-level point data, not field-level. Future deltas are approximate ensemble-style values; a pilot would process actual NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 files per grid cell and add SMAP, MODIS/HLS, GPM IMERG and NISAR layers.

SI DISCLOSURE

SI tools were used for code generation/refactoring, UI code, documentation drafts and the pitch deck. SI was not used to fabricate data: every number is computed from cached NASA POWER data by deterministic modules. No SI-generated images, audio or NASA branding appear.

projectDetails.name: VitalOrbit
projectDetails.summary:
VitalOrbit is a web-based crew health monitor for long-duration space missions, demonstrated with a fictional Expedition Meridian-7 crew. Astronauts log daily check-ins covering vital signs, sleep, body mass, radiation dose, exercise, reaction time, mood, stress, isolation and symptoms. VitalOrbit compares these with each person’s own baseline and rates six areas — cardiovascular and fluid shift, immune, bone and muscle, behavioral health, sleep and circadian rhythm, and radiation — as Nominal, Watch or Action needed, then offers clear protocols and emergency procedures.

This lets astronauts evaluate and act on their own health status, supported by trend charts, a health diary, a simulated ECG, two-tap crew and medical alerts that sync live across devices, and server-enforced privacy: crew see only their own data, while the Commander has read-only oversight.

This matters because on long missions, astronauts must spot health changes in themselves while far from Earth. Early, clear and actionable feedback on radiation, bone, immune and behavioral changes supports faster decisions and crew safety.

VitalOrbit is an unofficial educational demo: all data is simulated and thresholds are illustrative, not clinically validated.
projectDetails.details:
VitalOrbit is a web app that helps astronauts on long missions watch their own health and decide what to do about it. It is demonstrated with a fictional crew on Expedition Meridian-7: Commander, Crew Medical Officer, Pilot, Flight Engineer and Mission Specialist.

Collecting data. Each crew member logs a daily check-in covering:

heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂ and temperature

sleep, body mass, exercise and radiation dose

mood, stress, isolation and symptoms

reaction time, taken from a built-in reaction test

Evaluating health. Rule-based logic compares each entry with that person’s own earlier readings, because “normal” differs between people. It rates six areas as Nominal, Watch or Action needed:

cardiovascular and fluid shift

immune and infection

bone and muscle

behavioral health and cognition

sleep and circadian rhythm

radiation exposure

Acting on it. Every concern links to a protocol with concrete steps. The app also provides:

trend charts and a personal diary

emergency procedures for fire, depressurization, toxic atmosphere, radiation storm and medical emergency

a two-tap alert to the whole crew or to the Crew Medical Officer

Mission features.

crew readiness overview and vehicle-system status

a radiation-storm simulation

individual and team objectives

optional side missions that the Commander creates and crew accept

a simulated ECG at the latest heart rate

a cabin sound monitor that reacts to the microphone or an audio file

How the hosted version works. A Node.js server stores the data, enforces who can see what, and pushes alerts live to every signed-in device.

Crew members receive only their own health data.

The Commander can open anyone’s data, read-only.

Everyone sees only crew readiness counts.

A whole-crew alert shows a banner and sounds a siren on every device in that room. A medical alert is visible only to the sender, the Commander and the Crew Medical Officer, and has no siren.

In the public demo, each visitor gets a private demo crew with a room code that others can use to join.

What benefits does it have?

Self-monitoring when Earth is far away. Astronauts get clear, personal feedback even when contact with ground support is delayed.

Early warning. Comparing each person with their own trend can catch slow changes, such as sleep loss, rising dose or falling mood, before they become acute.

Clear next steps. Every status leads to an action, not just a number.

Privacy with oversight. Leadership sees readiness without crew members seeing each other’s health data.

Reliable emergencies. Two-tap confirmation prevents accidental alarms, and alerts reach the right people at once, with a visual banner and a screen-reader announcement as well as sound.

Open to everyone. Anyone can try it in a browser, with no install and no account.

What is the intended impact?

The project aims to show how a crew on missions to the Moon and Mars could be better aware of, and quicker to act on, their own health. It focuses on radiation, isolation, altered gravity, immune changes and behavioral health. It also works as a teaching and showcase tool that lets students and the public see how spaceflight affects the body. It is an unofficial educational demo, not a medical device.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, with no front-end framework. The server is Node.js.

Front end:

SVG for trend charts.

Canvas for the ECG, audio visualizer, particles and meteors.

Web Audio API for synthesized sounds and audio analysis.

Web Animations API and CSS transitions for animation.

Back end: Express for the JSON API, and Server-Sent Events for live updates.

Security: scrypt-hashed passcodes, signed HttpOnly session cookies, a Content-Security-Policy, rate limiting and server-side input checks.

Deployment and testing: Docker, a README with hosting steps, and Playwright browser tests.

AI assistance: Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, helped write and test the code. Adjust this line to your event’s disclosure rules.

Hardware: None is required. It runs in any modern browser, and a microphone is optional for the sound monitor.

How is your project creative?

Personal baselines: Each astronaut is compared with themselves rather than a population average.

Sound design: Clicks, typing and tab changes sound like a mechanical keyboard, with a chime for success. A siren is reserved for whole-crew emergencies, so routine use never causes alarm fatigue.

Mission-control motion: Animation is precise and never bouncy. The nav indicator glides between tabs, charts draw themselves on, new readings appear as new points, and dropdowns fade, slide and stagger their items with an animated checkmark.

Atmosphere: Interactive particles react to the pointer, clicks and scrolling and recover quickly. Meteors cross the screen, and the particles pulse with audio level.

Live ECG and sound monitor: A synthetic ECG draws in and sweeps at the latest heart rate, and the cabin sound monitor responds to real microphone or file input.

Demo design: Private demo rooms with shareable codes let a showcase audience try it without disturbing each other.

Original identity: It has its own name, terminology, logo and design language.

What factors did your team consider?

Honesty and safety: Simulated readings are labeled as simulated, thresholds are called illustrative and not clinically validated, and an on-screen notice says it is an unofficial demo.

Privacy: Health data is the most sensitive, so the server enforces access instead of just hiding things in the interface. The Commander’s access is read-only, and emergency banners no longer reveal the sender’s health status.

Emergency reliability: Confirmation before sending, live delivery to every device, and non-sound backups for each alert: a banner, a screen-reader announcement and a vibration cue on phones.

Accessibility: Keyboard navigation, skip link, labeled charts, screen-reader support, and dropdowns that follow the standard listbox pattern. Reduced-motion users get effects off by default, and sound, effects and theme can each be switched off.

Cognitive load: A minimal, high-contrast interface, because crew are often tired and stressed.

Independence: No agency logos, flags, branding or mission identifiers. A separate file lists the replaced names.

Safe public hosting: Isolated demo rooms, caps on how many exist, per-network limits, and no personal data collected.

Performance: The particle count scales to the screen, effects pause when the tab is hidden, and the blur effect behind menus is light enough for most devices.

projectDetails.name: Cosmo Pulse
projectDetails.summary:
CosmoPulse: Project Summary

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts will be far from real-time medical support, with delayed communication to Earth. CosmoPulse is a health monitoring platform that tracks an astronaut’s condition continuously and alerts both the crew and the ground medical team before small changes become serious problems.

It displays live vitals, including heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep, and stress, and watches for spaceflight-specific risks such as bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, fluid shift, and elevated CO₂. Each astronaut is compared against their own baseline, with green, yellow, or red alerts and trend graphs across mission days.

Cosmo Pulse works offline and syncs when a connection returns. Because medical data is sensitive, it uses encrypted storage, role-based access, and an access log.

Our prototype uses simulated data, with thresholds informed by NASA’s Twins Study and the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).

Technologies: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js, Python (Flask), AES encryption.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
CosmoPulse is a health monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long Moon and Mars missions. It tracks heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO₂), body temperature, sleep, and stress in real time, and watches for spaceflight-specific risks such as bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, fluid shift, and elevated CO₂. Instead of relying only on population averages, it compares each astronaut with their own baseline and raises green, yellow, or red alerts with suggested actions, such as rest or exercise. Trend graphs show how health changes across mission days, and a daily risk score gives the crew a quick overview. The prototype runs on simulated data.

Benefits
Astronauts on deep-space missions can face communication delays of up to about 22 minutes each way between Earth and Mars, and onboard medical support is limited. CosmoPulse supports earlier detection of health problems, helps astronauts manage their own health, and gives the ground medical team a clear picture of the crew’s condition. It works offline and syncs when a connection returns.

Intended impact
We want crews to spot and act on health changes before they become emergencies, and to keep sensitive medical data private on missions far from Earth. The same approach could support remote clinics and other isolated environments on Earth.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js, and Python (Flask), with AES encryption for stored data. We also used AI-assisted development tools to speed up building the prototype. Thresholds are informed by published spaceflight research, including NASA’s Twins Study and the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). No special hardware is required, and the design could later connect to wearable sensors.

Creativity
Most health trackers show averages. CosmoPulse personalizes alerts to each astronaut’s own baseline and combines health monitoring with security: encrypted storage, role-based access for astronauts, flight surgeons, and administrators, and an access log. Medical privacy is often forgotten in space health tools, and we made it a core feature. Its offline-first design also matches the real conditions of deep space.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delays and unreliable connectivity, so we built offline mode with later sync
  • Privacy and safety of medical data, so we added encryption, access roles, and logging
  • Astronaut autonomy, so alerts include clear, simple recommendations
  • Realism and honesty, so we use research-informed thresholds and state clearly that the data is simulated
  • Usability under stress, so the interface uses simple color-coded status and a short daily risk score
  • Feasibility within the hackathon timeline, so we focused on a working prototype with the most important features

What we have developed:
We developed Field Shift: NASA Farm Advisor, an interactive web platform and decision-support system that translates NASA Earth Observation satellite telemetry into actionable, climate-resilient crop rotation and soil management strategies for farmers, agronomists, and agricultural extension workers worldwide.

How does it address the challenge:
Traditional farming often relies on static calendars and single-crop monoculture, leaving fields vulnerable to droughts, nutrient depletion, and climate volatility. To solve this, Field Shift converts raw NASA satellite data into straightforward agronomic guidance and models how crop sequences perform under local climate stress before seeds are sown. Additionally, a built-in climatological fallback model ensures rural advisory operations never stall when satellite connectivity drops

Why is it important:
To counter the topsoil loss and micronutrient depletion caused by monoculture, Field Shift deploys regenerative crop rotations that preserve soil health, sequester organic carbon, and disrupt pest cycles. Because agriculture drives ~70% of global freshwater withdrawals, the platform also aligns crop water demand with satellite-observed precipitation and root-zone moisture to mitigate aquifer depletion and crop failure. Finally, by forecasting nitrogen fixation gains and input cost reductions, Field Shift shields smallholders from volatile fertilizer markets and climate risks, securing long-term farm viability.

projectDetails.details:
Mission Mars: Junior Astronaut Base Trainer - NASA SPACE eX

Mission Mars: Junior Astronaut Base Trainer is an interactive space survival game developed using PictoBlox. It allows students to experience the challenges of managing a Mars base for 10 days.

How it works: Players control a Mars base and monitor four essential systems: Oxygen, Power, Food, and Shield. All systems start at 100% and decrease daily. Players receive three actions per day, with each action increasing one selected resource by 20%. Random events such as Dust Storms, Solar Flares, and Machine Breakdowns create unexpected challenges. Players must manage their resources carefully to survive all 10 days. If any system reaches zero or below, the mission fails.

Benefits and Impact: The game makes space science more interesting and accessible to young learners. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, planning, and decision-making while introducing the challenges of astronaut survival on Mars.

Tools and Technologies: We used PictoBlox and its block-based programming environment, including variables, loops, conditional statements, random number generation, broadcasts, and interactive sprites and buttons. No external hardware was required.

Creativity: Our project transforms Mars survival challenges into an interactive game with cartoon astronauts, a space-themed interface, resource indicators, and unpredictable events.

Factors Considered: We considered age-appropriate learning, simple game controls, limited resources, unexpected situations, balanced gameplay, and an engaging experience for young students.

projectDetails.name: Project Nexaaaaa
projectDetails.summary:
Crew Self-Check is a health monitoring app that helps astronauts on long-duration missions spot health changes in themselves and act on them without waiting for Earth. Each day the astronaut logs mood, stress, sleep, exercise, resting heart rate, and symptoms. The software compares these against their personal baseline and rates five areas as Nominal, Watch, or Alert: heart and circulation, bones and muscle, immune system, mind and mood, and radiation and air quality. These areas map to the challenge’s hazards: radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and a closed environment.

For every area, the app explains why it flagged a change and gives a concrete next step, such as adding resistive exercise, booking a behavioral health call, or moving to the storm shelter. It also projects radiation dose to mission end and generates a report the astronaut can send to the flight surgeon.

This matters because on missions to Mars, communication delays of up to 20 minutes each way make real-time medical support impossible. Catching small trends early, such as slow bone loss, creeping stress, or rising heart rate, prevents serious problems and keeps crews mission-ready.

(Word count: about 175)

projectDetails.details:
Crew Self-Check: Project Details

What it does and how it works

Crew Self-Check is a web app that helps an astronaut monitor their own health on a long mission. Each day the astronaut completes a short check-in: mood, stress, sleep, exercise minutes, resting heart rate from a wearable, contact outside the crew, and any symptoms.

The software compares the last few days with that astronaut's own baseline. It rates five areas as Nominal, Watch or Alert:

  • Heart and circulation: resting heart rate, palpitations and dizziness, linked to fluid shifts in microgravity.
  • Bones and muscle: exercise levels, back pain and a rough estimate of monthly bone loss.
  • Immune system: sleep, rashes and cold-type symptoms.
  • Mind and mood: mood, stress, irritability and isolation.
  • Radiation and air: career radiation dose projected to mission end, cabin CO₂ and headaches.

Each card shows a 30-day trend, the reason for its rating and a concrete next step. A "what to do today" list is sorted by severity. The app also writes a report the astronaut can copy and send to the flight surgeon. Demo buttons simulate three weeks of strain, a solar storm and a CO₂ fault.

Benefits

  • Catches slow changes early, such as creeping stress, falling exercise or rising heart rate.
  • Works when Earth can't answer quickly. Mars communication delays can reach about 20 minutes each way.
  • Compares against each person's own normal, which reduces false alarms. For example, exercise doesn't trigger a heart-rate alert.
  • Gives plain-language guidance and shows the reason for every rating, so astronauts can trust and check it.
  • Gives the flight surgeon a ready summary instead of a raw data dump.

Intended impact

The goal is to make astronauts active partners in their own medical care, which will matter more as missions go to the Moon and Mars. Healthier crews are safer and keep missions on track. The same approach could help people in remote or isolated settings on Earth, such as polar stations, submarines and rural clinics.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks. The app is one self-contained file.
  • Design: responsive layout with light and dark themes, keyboard focus styles, and status shown by text labels as well as color.
  • Fonts: Barlow and Barlow Semi Condensed from Google Fonts.
  • Development: built with Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, and published as a hosted web page. The demo deck was made with Claude's slide tool.
  • Hardware: none. The prototype runs in any modern browser, and all readings are simulated.

Creativity

  • The astronaut is the primary user, not mission control. Most health dashboards are built for ground teams.
  • It links each space hazard to a body system and an action, not just a chart.
  • It looks ahead by projecting radiation dose to mission end, so the astronaut sees a limit coming before reaching it.
  • It treats mental health and sleep as seriously as heart rate.
  • It includes an escalation path for when ground can't reply in time.

Factors we considered

  • Delay and autonomy: advice has to work without real-time ground support.
  • Personalization: each astronaut has a different baseline, so alerts show change from their own normal.
  • Alert fatigue: a three-level system with context, such as exercise, keeps alerts meaningful.
  • Privacy: health data is sensitive, so we plan a private-by-default mode where the astronaut chooses what to share.
  • Honesty about limits: the data is simulated, thresholds are illustrative and bone-loss figures are estimates. It is decision support, not a medical device.
  • Future work: real wearable input, offline AI guidance that learns each baseline, voice check-ins, and validation with clinicians and NASA standards.

projectDetails.details:
EARTHPULSE – NASA Earth System Trend Analyzer

Project Description

EARTHPULSE is an interactive climate data analysis and visualization platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project aims to improve the accessibility and understanding of historical climate information by transforming NASA datasets into meaningful visualizations and statistical insights. Its geographical focus is Kerala, India, with an emphasis on exploring regional temperature and precipitation patterns.

Functionality and Working

EARTHPULSE retrieves historical monthly climate data through the NASA POWER API. The primary parameters analyzed are T2M (temperature at 2 metres above the surface) and PRECTOTCORR (corrected precipitation).

The retrieved data is processed using Python-based data processing techniques and presented through an interactive Streamlit dashboard. Users can explore historical temperature variations, analyze monthly and yearly precipitation patterns, examine climate trends and compare supported geographical locations.

The platform incorporates statistical methods, including the Theil-Sen Estimator, Mann-Kendall Test and Kendall's Tau, to estimate trend magnitude, evaluate monotonic trend significance and understand the direction and strength of climate relationships.

Benefits and Intended Impact

EARTHPULSE simplifies the exploration of scientific climate datasets by presenting complex information through accessible visualizations and statistical analysis. It aims to support climate education, environmental awareness and exploratory research by helping users understand historical regional climate patterns.

The project also demonstrates the practical application of open NASA data in developing accessible environmental analysis tools.

Technology and Implementation

The application was developed using Python as its core programming language. Streamlit provides the interactive web interface, Pandas and NumPy support data processing and numerical computation, SciPy supports statistical analysis, and Plotly is used to generate interactive visualizations. NASA POWER API serves as the primary climate data source.

The project follows a modular software architecture that separates frontend components, backend data services, data processing and statistical analysis. No specialized hardware is required.

Creativity and Innovation

The primary innovation of EARTHPULSE lies in integrating NASA climate data retrieval, statistical trend detection and interactive visualization into a unified platform. Rather than requiring users to interpret raw scientific datasets independently, the application presents processed climate information in a more accessible and understandable format.

This approach provides an interactive way to investigate regional climate behaviour using publicly available Earth science data.

Development Considerations

During development, the team considered data reliability, scientific accuracy, usability, performance, accessibility and future scalability. Particular attention was given to selecting appropriate statistical techniques and interpreting results within the context of the selected location, observation period and available data.

Team Collaboration

EARTHPULSE was developed collaboratively by two team members.

Devu – Project Development and Integration: Primarily responsible for project implementation, frontend development, dashboard integration, project coordination, testing and debugging.

Sharon Binu George – Backend Development and Data Analysis: Primarily responsible for backend data services, NASA POWER API integration, climate data processing, statistical trend analysis and backend integration support.

Both members actively collaborated throughout the development, integration, testing and improvement processes.

Future Scope

Future development may include expanding geographical coverage, integrating additional Earth system variables, improving regional climate comparisons, introducing advanced analytical capabilities and enhancing geographical visualizations.

Conclusion

EARTHPULSE demonstrates how NASA climate data and modern software technologies can be combined to make historical climate information more accessible and understandable. By connecting data retrieval, scientific analysis and interactive visualization, the project aims to encourage greater awareness of regional climate patterns and support further exploration of Earth's changing environmental systems.

But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

LUNA NAV is an interactive lunar exploration and mission-planning platform developed to support the exploration of potential landing regions near the Moon’s south pole. It brings NASA lunar imagery, topographic data and preliminary mission-planning tools together in one accessible workspace.
Using imagery from NASA Moon Trek and elevation and slope datasets from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), users can explore the lunar surface, select candidate locations, examine available terrain information and compare potential landing sites. The platform also includes distance and traverse calculations, preliminary solar and Earth visibility estimates, an interactive candidate comparison system, a research assistant and downloadable reports.
LUNA NAV addresses the challenge of making complex lunar data easier to explore and interpret by connecting scientific information with practical mission-planning tools. Its evidence-based approach distinguishes retrieved measurements from calculated estimates and unavailable data, helping users understand both the possibilities and limitations of their analysis.
The project aims to make lunar exploration more accessible and support informed, transparent planning for future lunar missions.
projectDetails.details:
LUNA NAV is an interactive lunar exploration and preliminary mission-planning platform focused on potential landing regions near the Moon’s south pole. It brings lunar imagery, topographic information, and mission-planning tools together in one workspace.

Users can explore the lunar surface through an interactive map, select candidate landing coordinates, examine available elevation and slope information, and compare potential sites. The platform also includes traverse-distance calculations, preliminary solar and Earth visibility estimates, candidate comparison tools, a research assistant, and downloadable reports and datasets. It uses NASA lunar imagery and data sources, including NASA Moon Trek and the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA).

The project aims to make complex lunar data easier to access, understand, and compare. It can help students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore the challenges of lunar south-pole missions and investigate potential landing regions. Its intended impact is to encourage accessible, transparent, and data-informed lunar exploration.

LUNA NAV was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with web-mapping tools and NASA data services. The application is designed to run in a web browser without specialised hardware. Its local data storage and export features support convenient exploration and comparison.

The creative aspect of LUNA NAV is the integration of scientific lunar information with practical mission-planning features in a single interactive platform. During development, we considered usability, mobile accessibility, data availability, coordinate accuracy, terrain safety factors, transparency, and the limitations of remote scientific datasets. We distinguish retrieved measurements from calculated estimates and unavailable information so users can understand the reliability of the results.

LUNA NAV is a preliminary exploration and planning tool, not a certified lunar landing safety system.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Ingenuity – The Little Helicopter That Changed Mars
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, **Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Ingenuity – The Little Helicopter That Changed Mars**, is an educational storytelling project about NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

We developed an engaging story that introduces Ingenuity, explains why NASA sent it to Mars, describes its historic first powered flight on another planet, and highlights its achievements during 72 flights. The story also explains how Ingenuity supported the Perseverance rover and how its flying mission came to an end.

This project addresses the challenge by bringing attention to important NASA equipment that remains on other worlds after its mission. It helps students and space enthusiasts understand the purpose, discoveries, challenges, and legacy of these machines through simple and interesting storytelling.

Ingenuity may no longer fly, but its achievements have opened new possibilities for future aerial exploration of Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Ingenuity – The Little Helicopter That Changed Mars, is an educational storytelling project about NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

How it works:
The project presents Ingenuity’s mission as an engaging story. It explains why the helicopter was sent to Mars, how it achieved the first powered and controlled flight on another planet, its 72 flights, its role in supporting the Perseverance rover, and how its flying mission ended.

Benefits:
It makes space exploration easier to understand, especially for students and beginners. It helps readers learn about NASA technology, scientific achievements, and the challenges of exploring Mars.

Intended impact:
The project aims to create awareness about NASA equipment left on other worlds and show that even after a mission ends, its discoveries and achievements can support future exploration.

Tools and resources:
The story was prepared using information from NASA resources, with AI assistance in organizing and presenting the information. This version is a written storytelling project and does not require custom hardware or a programming language.

Creativity:
The project uses a short, engaging narrative to tell the story of a small helicopter that achieved something historic on another planet.

Factors considered:
We considered scientific accuracy, information from NASA sources, simple language, educational value, and an engaging storytelling style. We also avoided presenting fictional events as real mission facts.

projectDetails.name: Echoes in the Dust: NASA’s Forgotten Explorers.
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes in the Dust is an interactive educational web application designed to introduce school-age students to the retired NASA rovers, landers, and instruments resting across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Built using HTML, Tailwind CSS, and JavaScript, the platform transforms technical mission archives into an engaging, story-driven digital museum.

To address the challenge, the web app lets young explorers switch between interactive hubs for the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space to uncover the stories of iconic hardware—including the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles, the Opportunity and Spirit rovers, the InSight lander, and the Ingenuity helicopter. Rather than reading dry specifications, students explore first-person "field journals" written from each machine's perspective, inspect their current status, and unlock interactive science cards explaining key discoveries (such as finding ancient water evidence on Mars or measuring moonquakes).

By framing discarded hardware as historic monuments of human curiosity rather than forgotten scrap, Silent Pioneers makes planetary science accessible and inspires the next generation of STEM explorers.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?
Echoes in the Dust: NASA’s Forgotten Explorers is an interactive, story-driven educational web application that transforms NASA’s retired and dormant hardware across the Moon, Mars, and deep space into an immersive digital museum for school-age students. Instead of presenting young learners with dense technical tables, the platform lets users step into the role of a planetary mission specialist tracking six iconic pieces of space hardware: the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, the InSight lander, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle (Moon Buggy), the Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector, and Voyager 1.

Users navigate the experience through three core interactive modules:

  1. Orbital Surface Scanner & Dynamic Sector Themes: Users can filter missions across Mars, the Moon, and Deep Space. Switching sectors dynamically shifts the UI color palette and alters the physics of an HTML5 Canvas background particle engine to simulate Martian dust, lunar regolith, or deep-space starfields. Clicking or hovering over radar blips locks onto the exact landing coordinates of each spacecraft.
    • Echo Log: Delivers a first-person diary entry via an animated typewriter readout, shares the spacecraft’s real final transmission, and explains why the hardware was left behind or how it continues to function.
    • The Science Unlocked: Breaks down three major scientific discoveries per mission alongside kid-friendly engineering facts.
    • Clear Dust & Earn Badge: Features a touch- and mouse-enabled HTML5 Canvas mini-game where students physically scrub accumulated planetary dust off a virtual solar array to reveal a "Mission Specialist" quiz question. Answering correctly unlocks custom mission badges accompanied by synthesized telemetry sound effects.

What benefits does it have? What is the intended impact of the project? 
For school-age space enthusiasts, official mission archives can feel intimidating and overly technical. Furthermore, public discussions often label retired spacecraft as "space junk." Echoes in the Dust reframes these machines as heroic pioneers and time capsules of human ingenuity. By combining first-person storytelling with tactile interactivity, the project promotes STEM literacy, improves retention of planetary science concepts (such as Martian geology, seismic activity, and Earth-Moon laser ranging), and inspires students to see engineering as a human story of curiosity and perseverance. Because it runs entirely in a standard web browser with zero installations or logins, teachers and students can use it immediately on any classroom tablet, Chromebook, or desktop.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS for responsive layout design, custom CSS keyframe animations for radar sweeps and glassmorphism panels, and inline SVG graphics.
  • Interactive Graphics: HTML5 Canvas API for both the real-time cosmic dust background simulation and the interactive solar-panel scrubbing canvas (globalCompositeOperation = 'destination-out').
  • Audio Synthesis: Web Audio API to procedurally generate sci-fi UI clicks, radar pings, and badge-unlock chimes directly in the browser without requiring external audio files.
  • Development & Hosting: Developed on Windows 11 and hosted publicly as a fast, single-file static web application.

How is your project creative? What factors did your team consider?
Creativity & Factors Considered

  • Empathy-Driven Gamification: Rather than just telling students that Martian dust storms ended Opportunity and InSight's missions, the solar-panel scrubbing mechanic lets students experience that environmental challenge firsthand.
  • Accessibility & Zero-Friction Deployment: Knowing that school networks often block heavy downloads or external media assets, the entire application was engineered as a self-contained, lightweight architecture using procedural audio and vector graphics.
  • Age-Appropriate Balance: Every mission profile balances emotional storytelling ("last words" and first-person logs) with accurate NASA science and real operational statuses—clearly distinguishing between dormant hardware (Opportunity, InSight), passive instruments still used today (Apollo 11 Retroreflector), and active deep-space probes (Voyager 1).

For the README.md and the code refer this link:

https://github.com/xxalfyxd/echoesinthedust.git

projectDetails.name: Project RITCE
projectDetails.summary:
We developed "The Brave Little Explorer with the Atomic Heart," an illustrated, narrative-driven storybook that brings the historic 1976 NASA Viking 1 mission to life for young learners.

To address the challenge of making complex space exploration accessible and engaging, we translated real planetary science, engineering milestones, and NASA mission data into an emotionally resonant, chapter-by-chapter adventure. Through relatable analogies—such as "bunny suits" for planetary protection, an "atomic heart" for radioisotope power, and a "robot chef" for soil biology experiments—our story breaks down intricate aerospace concepts like orbital mapping, atmospheric entry, and telemetry into intuitive, memorable lessons without losing scientific accuracy.

This project is important because inspiring the next generation of explorers begins with sparking curiosity early. By humanizing robotic spaceflight and highlighting both the triumphs and human vulnerability behind deep-space missions, our story bridges the gap between technical STEM history and creative storytelling, empowering young readers to see themselves as future scientists, engineers, and pioneers of the next frontier.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, "The Brave Little Explorer with the Atomic Heart", is an educational storytelling project based on NASA's Viking 1 mission to Mars.

The story follows a little robot named Vicky, representing the Viking 1 lander, and her companion Orby, representing the Viking orbiter. It describes their journey from Earth to Mars, the landing process, and the exploration of the Martian surface. It also explains how Viking 1 captured photographs, collected soil samples and conducted experiments to investigate the possibility of life on Mars.

The main aim of this project is to make space science easy, interesting and enjoyable, especially for children and students.

Benefits: This project helps students understand Mars exploration, develops scientific curiosity and creates awareness about space technology.

Intended Impact: To inspire young learners to explore astronomy, science and future space missions.

Tools Used: Canva, Google Gemini, ChatGPT and Heyzine were used for designing, content development, creative writing and improving the presentation of the project.

Creativity and Innovation: The project presents a real NASA space mission through an imaginative robot adventure. Using storytelling, fictional characters and simple language makes complex scientific information easier to understand and remember.

Factors Considered: We considered scientific accuracy, creativity, educational value, simplicity of language and accessibility for young learners while developing this project.
