projectDetails.name: adaptive crop rotation tool
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary – Field Shift: Adaptive Crop Rotation Tool

We developed Field Shift, an adaptive crop rotation decision-support tool that helps farmers make better farming decisions using NASA Earth observation data and local soil information. The project integrates NASA datasets, including SMAP, GPM IMERG, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, and MODIS, to analyse soil moisture, rainfall, temperature, and crop health. It compares three farming strategies: traditional monocropping, legume cover sequencing, and drought-tolerant millet mixtures, helping farmers identify suitable crop rotation plans based on local conditions.

The tool addresses climate-related agricultural challenges such as water scarcity, extreme heat, soil degradation, and unpredictable rainfall. It provides practical recommendations that balance water conservation, soil health, and crop productivity.

This project is important because it promotes sustainable agriculture, reduces irrigation requirements, improves soil moisture retention, and supports farmers in adapting to climate change. By transforming NASA satellite data into actionable farming insights, Field Shift aims to build more resilient farms and secure future food production.
projectDetails.details:
How it works: It analyses soil moisture, rainfall, temperature, and crop health using NASA datasets such as SMAP, GPM IMERG, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, MODIS, and NASA POWER. It compares three farming strategies: traditional monocropping, legume cover sequencing, and drought-tolerant millet mixtures.

Benefits and intended impact:

Reduces irrigation water requirements.

Improves soil health and moisture retention.

Helps farmers adapt to drought and extreme heat.

Promotes sustainable farming and food security.

Tools and technologies: NASA Earth observation datasets and satellite data analysis. The specific programming languages and development software are not specified in the project document.

Creativity: Combines NASA satellite data with crop rotation recommendations to turn complex environmental information into practical farming decisions.

Factors considered: Climate, rainfall, soil health, water availability, crop diversity, economic benefits, and environmental sustainability.

projectDetails.summary:
Burning Activity Calendar is a single-page web app that turns satellite active-fire detections into a year-by-week calendar for any area you choose.
The problem it addresses: MODIS and VIIRS can't be compared directly. VIIRS has a finer pixel and finds more small fires, so raw counts jump when VIIRS begins. 
Harmonization: For your area, it takes the ratio of VIIRS to MODIS detections over the fully overlapping years .The ratio is recomputed per area.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: A web app that turns satellite fire detections into one consistent year-by-week calendar for any area. MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) can’t be compared directly, because VIIRS finds more small fires. The user picks an area. The app compares the two sensors over the years both cover (2013 onward) and rescales earlier MODIS counts to match VIIRS. The calendar can be coloured by how unusual each week is, and it also lists the busiest weeks of a normal year and the most unusual weeks on record.

Benefits:

  • Responders can see when fire seasons normally peak.
  • Land managers can tell whether a season is unusual.
  • Scientists get a record in which all years are comparable.
  • It needs no account or server, and it keeps data on the user’s device.

Impact: People who work with fire can tell real changes from changes of sensor. That supports earlier preparation, better use of resources and tracking of long-term shifts. It is free and light, so small agencies and students can use it.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the canvas, NASA FIRMS CSV files, Node.js with pptxgenjs for the slides, and Claude as an AI assistant. Any laptop or phone with a browser is enough.

Creativity: It shows when fires happen, not just where. It colours weeks by unusualness, recalculates the sensor ratio for each area, and shows raw against harmonized totals. It is a single file that anyone can host.

Factors considered: Sensor differences, overlap years, local variation, data quality, skewed counts, mobile use and privacy. Limits: the demo data is synthetic, one ratio per area ignores seasonal and land-cover differences, and the method hasn’t been validated against real FIRMS data.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project Solo Mission
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Architect is a game where you build a real space mission yourself. Pick a target, whether that’s a Mars rover, a lunar south pole prospector, or an orbiter around Europa, then assemble the spacecraft piece by piece: the rocket, the power source, the antenna, the instruments, and the ground stations that keep you in touch. Everything has to fit a budget.

Then comes the nervous part: a flight readiness review, a launch, and a debrief that shows where your design shone and where it fell short.

Real NASA planet data shapes the results. Sunlight is faint at Mars and nearly gone at Europa, so a power choice that works in one place can fail in another.

Space engineering can feel locked away behind expertise. This lets anyone feel what it’s like to balance trade-offs, make tough calls, and send something out into the solar system.
projectDetails.details: Mission Architect is a browser game where you design a real space mission yourself. Pick a destination (a Mars rover, a lunar south pole prospector, or a Europa orbiter), then build the spacecraft step by step, from the rocket and power system to the antenna and instruments, all within a budget. A readiness review checks your design against physics-based rules, using real NASA planet data, and then you watch the launch and see your score. You can play solo, against friends, or co-op, with each player taking a role like engineer or scientist. It’s built with TypeScript, React, and Vite, hosted on Vercel, with planets drawn on canvas and music synthesized in the browser. Our goal is to help students feel what it’s like to make hard trade-offs and work as a team to send something into space.

projectDetails.name: Project Space Conqueror
projectDetails.summary:
I developed Space Conqueror, an interactive 3D lunar mission navigator engineered to evaluate Artemis candidate landing sites at the Moon’s South Pole.

Addressing the challenge of extreme polar topography and permanently shadowed terrain, I synthesized authentic NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) elevation datasets into a real-time WebGL mission cockpit. Working with Google Antigravity as an engineering partner, I built the platform using React, TypeScript, and Three.js to simulate low-angle solar illumination, dynamic slope hazard heatmaps, and traversability. High-fidelity Artemis lander and rover assemblies were modeled with aerospace precision in CATIA V5 and SolidWorks, textured with photorealistic lunar regolith materials in Blender, and integrated with ground-contact physics.

This tool is critical because Artemis missions require finding landing corridors that balance continuous solar energy, Earth line-of-sight communications, and safe slope gradients. Space Conqueror bridges raw planetary science and accessible simulation, empowering engineers and planners to de-risk surface operations before touchdown.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

I built Space Conqueror as an interactive, browser-based 3D mission cockpit designed to evaluate and navigate Artemis landing zones across the Moon’s South Pole.

The application works by taking raw planetary data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)—specifically the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) 240-meter-per-pixel digital elevation models—and converting that data into true-to-scale 3D terrain meshes. Across six key Artemis candidate landing sites (Shackleton Rim, Malapert Massif, Connecting Ridge, Mons Mouton, Nobile, and Haworth), the cockpit simulates:

  1. Low-Angle Polar Lighting: Because the Sun sits barely above the lunar horizon at the poles, mountains cast long, pitch-black shadows across crater floors. Space Conqueror dynamically calculates solar angles to show shifting shadow boundaries in real time.
  2. Slope Hazard Heatmaps: The system computes analytical surface gradients across every meter of the terrain, dynamically painting slopes green (<10∘<10^\circ<10∘), yellow (10∘–15∘10^\circ–15^\circ10∘–15∘), or red (>15∘>15^\circ>15∘) so landing planners can immediately spot rollover hazards.
  3. Interactive Surface Operations: Users can zoom from orbit down to ground level to inspect a CAD-engineered Artemis Lander touching down on real lunar dirt, deploy a cargo ramp, and drive a compliant-wheeled Lunar Rover across the crater rims using real-time terrain raycasting and suspension physics.

What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Install, Universal Access: Planetary scientists and mission planners typically rely on heavy desktop GIS software (ArcGIS, QGIS, or custom SPICE toolsets) that require high-end workstations and extensive training. Space Conqueror runs entirely in a web browser at 60 FPS on any laptop or phone.
  • Unified Multi-Hazard Visibility: Instead of switching between disconnected 2D maps for elevation, lighting, and communications, Space Conqueror combines solar exposure, slope gradients, and direct-to-Earth visibility into one cohesive visual environment.
  • Ground-Level Operational Testing: You don’t just look at a contour map—you can physically drive a rover across the terrain to test egress routes, identify blind spots behind boulder ridges, and plan traversable corridors before metal touches regolith.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Returning astronauts to the Moon is the most complex spaceflight challenge of this decade. The primary goal of Space Conqueror is to de-risk surface operations at the South Pole. By transforming raw scientific rasters into an intuitive, interactive tool, it helps mission planners, university researchers, and aerospace engineers quickly vet landing sites for solar power stability and terrain navigability.

Beyond engineering, it bridges the gap between deep planetary science and the public. Anyone in the world can open the link, explore the South Pole candidate sites, and understand why landing at the lunar pole is so uniquely challenging and exciting.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Google Antigravity: My autonomous AI engineering partner throughout the challenge. Antigravity helped architect the end-to-end full-stack system, synthesize the Three.js rendering pipelines, automate data transformations, and verify mathematical accuracy.
  • Aerospace CAD (CATIA V5 & SolidWorks): Parametrically designed the mechanical assemblies for the Artemis Lunar Lander (descent frame, ascent stage, engine bell, quad landing gear) and the Lunar Rover (compliant wire-mesh wheels, rocker-bogie chassis, sensor mast) to real aerospace engineering standards.
  • Blender (Python 3D Pipeline): Textured the vehicles with physically based rendering (PBR) regolith materials, modeled realistic lunar optical properties, and baked optimized GLTF/GLB models for low-latency web streaming.
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) & LOLA: Provided authentic polar elevation rasters (ldem_75s_240m) that form the physical bedrock of the topography.
  • Frontend Cockpit: Built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js / WebGL for in-browser real-time lighting, shadow maps, and ground-contact physics.
  • Scientific Backend: Python & FastAPI, integrating orbital mechanics and ephemeris validation against JPL standards.
  • Deployment & Version Control: Git, GitHub, and Vercel serverless edge hosting.

How is your project creative?

Traditional space mission planning relies on static 2D heatmaps and contour charts. Space Conqueror’s creativity lies in merging aerospace CAD precision with real-time video game mechanics and authentic planetary science.

Instead of reading a report stating that a slope is 16 degrees or that sunlight is lost at 14:00 UTC, the user is immersed directly on the surface: you can watch the Sun dip below the jagged crater rim, cast a 12-kilometer shadow over your solar panels, and test whether your rover can climb out of a permanently shadowed crater trap. It turns dry numbers into a tangible human experience.

What factors did your team consider?

  1. The South Pole’s Extreme Illumination Geometry: The Sun hovers at only 1.5∘1.5^\circ1.5∘ above the horizon. We had to calculate exact solar vectors because a slight dip in terrain can plunge equipment into cryogenic temperatures (40 K40\text{ K}40 K) and complete power loss.
  2. Lander Tip-Over & Rover Rollover Thresholds: Artemis landers cannot safely land on slopes exceeding 12∘–15∘12^\circ–15^\circ12∘–15∘. We prioritized immediate visual gradient detection so unviable zones are immediately flagged.
  3. Direct Line-of-Sight Communications: Lunar mountains easily block direct microwave links back to Earth. We factored in horizon clearance so landing corridors maintain reliable comms links.
  4. Web Optimization & Low-Latency Streaming: Large lunar DEM rasters and complex CAD assemblies can easily freeze a web browser. We implemented dynamic geometric level-of-detail (LOD), binary GLB compression, and asynchronous shader initialization to ensure butter-smooth 60 FPS performance on standard consumer hardware.

projectDetails.name: FireX
projectDetails.summary: We built FireX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge—an interactive 3D map that brings together and cleans up years of active fire data across India from 2022 to 2026. The main headache with satellite data is that different sensors catch fires differently. To fix that, FireX cross-calibrates NASA's MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) feeds using pixel-area math so everything lines up on the same page.The app lets you explore a sleek 3D globe where you can zoom smoothly from a national overview right down to individual states and districts, scrub through a seasonal time-lapse player, and check out detailed stats. It’s built to actually be useful: it gives local communities a heads-up on seasonal burning cycles, helps researchers dig into exact burn sizes ($km^2$) and thermal power, and gives forest departments and emergency crews the clear insights they need to dispatch help where it's needed most. Ultimately, it’s about turning heavy, complicated NASA space telemetry into something clean, fast, and genuinely impactful.
projectDetails.details:
When we started building FireX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we wanted to tackle a real headache with satellite data: different sensors see the world differently. To fix that, we built an interactive 3D geospatial dashboard that harmonizes NASA's MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) fire feeds across India from 2022 to 2026, bringing everything onto a single, reliable scale using pixel-area normalization.

We wanted the app to feel like a modern mission-control tool. Users get a sleek 3D globe where they can smoothly zoom from a national view ($\text{L1}$) down to individual states ($\text{L2}$) and districts ($\text{L3}$), scrub through a seasonal time-lapse player, and click districts to check out burn areas ($km^2$) and sensor breakdowns. On the tech side, we put it together using react-globe.gl, Three.js, custom GeoJSON mapping, and a Python-powered data pipeline.

Beyond the code, we really focused on making it useful. FireX gives local communities early visibility into regional burning cycles, helps researchers analyze precise thermal data, and gives forest departments and emergency responders clear insights to track fire intensity and allocate resources where they're needed most. It's all about turning heavy satellite telemetry into something fast, clean, and genuinely helpful.

projectDetails.name: Left-Behind
projectDetails.summary: We made an interactive story map where NASA’s retired and abandoned hardware tells its own story to school-age space fans. Each stop on the Moon, Mars, deep space and Earth orbit is a “postcard” written in the spacecraft’s own voice. Kids learn what it was built to do, what science it made possible, and how its mission ended, with status badges for silent, retired, or still working. It shows that “abandoned” hardware, like the Apollo laser mirrors and the Voyagers, can still be doing science.
projectDetails.details: Postcards from the Left-Behind is a free, kid-friendly website for ages 8 to 14. A story map runs from Earth to the Moon, Mars, and deep space, with seven stops: the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles, the Apollo laser retroreflectors, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter, Pioneer 10 and 11, Voyager 1 and 2, and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Tapping a stop opens a postcard with four parts: “Hello, I’m…”, “What I was built to do”, “The science I made possible”, and “How my story went.” Color-coded badges show each mission’s status. The Chandra stop includes NASA images and a 3D model that can be rotated. A 5-question quiz awards a Space Explorer badge, and a teacher page has discussion questions. We also made a short narrated animation and a presentation. The website is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.We hope it helps students see that space hardware keeps teaching us after its mission ends.

projectDetails.name: Silent Explorers
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, "Silent Explorers: The Untold Stories of Forgotten Machines on the Moon and Mars," focuses on the spacecraft, rovers, and scientific equipment sent by NASA to explore the Moon and Mars. Although many of these machines have completed their missions or stopped functioning, they remain on these planets as reminders of human achievements in space exploration.
The project highlights important missions such as Surveyor 3, Apollo lunar missions, Spirit, and Opportunity. It explains their scientific contributions, discoveries about the lunar surface, and evidence of ancient water on Mars.
The main aim of this project is to understand the importance of these forgotten machines and appreciate their contributions to space science. Even though their missions have ended, their discoveries continue to inspire future generations of space explorers.
Main Message:
"Every forgotten machine carries a story of human curiosity, courage, and discovery. Their missions may have ended, but their contributions will never be forgotten."
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works
Our project is an educational storytelling experience designed to bring NASA’s retired lunar and Martian spacecraft back to life for school-age learners. Instead of presenting technical mission logs as dry facts, we turn historical missions—including Surveyor 3, Apollo lunar missions, Spirit, and Opportunity—into engaging, easy-to-follow stories. Each section introduces the spacecraft, explains what it discovered about the lunar surface or ancient water on Mars, and shows where it rests today as a monument to human exploration.
Benefits & Intended Impact
Many students know about active rovers like Perseverance, but few realize how much our current space knowledge relies on earlier, retired hardware. Our goal is to spark curiosity in young learners by showing that "abandoned" spacecraft are not forgotten failures—they are scientific pioneers. By connecting their discoveries to modern space exploration, the project inspires students to see space history as an ongoing human story they can be part of.
Tools & Resources Used
• NASA Open Data & Media: We used official NASA mission archives, historical summaries, and public-domain imagery (properly credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech) to ensure scientific accuracy.

• Creation & Design Tools: We created and formatted the final presentation using Google Slides
• AI Assistance: We used Google Gemini as a brainstorming and writing assistant to help organize the narrative structure and simplify complex planetary science concepts for a younger audience.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered
To make the project creative and accessible without relying on complex code, we focused on strong visual storytelling and age-appropriate language. When designing the narrative, we considered how to balance real scientific milestones—such as Opportunity's evidence of past water on Mars—with relatable themes of resilience, discovery, and legacy so students stay engaged from start to finish.

projectDetails.name: ARES AGRI
projectDetails.summary:
ARES AGRI is an interactive web-based project exploring the agronomic and engineering systems required to establish sustainable agriculture on Mars. It translates complex aerospace and botanical concepts into an immersive, data-rich platform documenting how to transform toxic Martian regolith into fertile biomass.

The project highlights six core environmental hurdles—such as perchlorate toxicity, extreme cold, and cosmic radiation—alongside technical paradigms like high-pressure aeroponics, bio-remediated regolith, and microalgae photobioreactors. Key features include real-time mission telemetry simulating the Jezero Crater, a curated Martian crop catalog, and an interactive Greenhouse Simulator where users adjust environmental parameters to test colony survival.

Designed as a comprehensive technical showcase, ARES AGRI bridges front-end development with advanced scientific research to visualize self-sustaining off-world life support systems.
projectDetails.details:
ARES AGRI is an interactive, data-driven web application that serves as a conceptual blueprint for establishing a self-sustaining biosphere on Mars. Built as an educational and technical project, it explores the intersection of aerospace engineering, astrobotany, and web development to visualize how humans could survive on a barren planet.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the project, how its mechanics function, and its practical utility:

1. Project Details (What It Is)

The website acts as a comprehensive digital dashboard for a hypothetical Martian farming colony (Ares-Biodome-04 in Jezero Crater). It translates dense scientific concepts into an accessible, visually engaging platform. The project systematically addresses the reality of off-world survival by breaking it down into:

  • The 6 Lethal Hurdles: Explaining the dangers of perchlorate-toxic soil, extreme cold, cosmic radiation, partial gravity, solar dimming, and the lack of nitrogen.
  • Agricultural Paradigms: Detailing three distinct solutions—High-Pressure Aeroponics, Bio-Remediated Regolith (treating Martian dirt with microbes), and Microalgae Photobioreactors.
  • Crop Database: A curated list of space-optimized crops like potatoes, leafy greens, and soybeans.

2. How It Works (Functional Mechanics)

From a technical and user-experience perspective, the project utilizes front-end web development (HTML, CSS, and likely JavaScript) to create an immersive, app-like environment:

  • Simulated Telemetry & UI: The header acts as a mission control interface, displaying real-time-style data like Martian Coordinated Time (MTC), current Sol days, and baseline environmental stats (temperature, pressure, solar flux). This creates immediate immersion.
  • Structured Information Flow: The layout uses anchor navigation to smoothly guide the user through the problem (Mars' harsh environment) to the solution (farming technologies) and finally to the application (the simulator).
  • Interactive Greenhouse Simulator: This is the core functional feature of the project. It uses front-end logic to allow users to act as a "Habitat Commander." By adjusting input variables like atmospheric pressure, temperature, CO2\text{CO}_2CO2​ levels, and LED photonics, users trigger calculations that output the resulting crop yield, oxygen generation, and overall colony survival rate.
  • Responsive Design: The layout is compartmentalized into data cards, side-by-side comparisons (Earth vs. Mars), and interactive modules, making heavy data easy to digest.

3. How It Is Useful (Value Proposition)

This project holds significant value across multiple domains:

  • Exceptional Portfolio Piece: For a developer or designer, it acts as a powerful resume builder. It demonstrates the ability to handle complex UI/UX design, build interactive logic (the simulator), and present dense data cleanly. It shows you can build more than just basic websites—you can build data-driven educational tools.
  • STEM Education & Science Communication: It bridges the gap between dense astrophysics papers and public curiosity. High school and college students studying biology, physics, or space exploration can use this to understand the practical challenges of colonizing Mars without reading a 50-page academic journal.
  • Interactive Conceptualization: By allowing users to tweak environmental variables in the simulator, it teaches the concept of "closed-loop systems" through cause and effect. It visually proves why relying entirely on Martian soil is dangerous and why systems like aeroponics are necessary.

projectDetails.details:
Orbital Foundry — 3D Space Rocket Design & Launch Simulator

Short Overview:
Orbital Foundry is an interactive, browser-based 3D aerospace engineering and spaceflight game where players design custom multi-stage rockets, customize their paint and liveries, test their designs on a launchpad, and fly missions to orbit and distant planets.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Orbital Foundry combines a 3D vehicle assembly workshop with a real-time flight physics simulator:

  • Step-by-Step Rocket Building: Players assemble rockets from 14 modular 3D parts across six categories—Nose Cones & Crew Capsules, Body & Avionics Rings, Fuel Tanks, Engines, Jettisonable Side Boosters, and Aerodynamic Wings/Fins. Parts can be added from the builder dock or clicked directly in the 3D viewport to highlight, reorder, or remove with a 100% cost refund.
  • Customization & Pre-Flight Engineering: Players name their spacecraft, pick primary/accent colors, and apply procedural hull liveries (stripes, roll checkers, hazard bands, thermal gold foil). Live engineering diagnostics automatically calculate dry/wet mass, total thrust (kN), Thrust-to-Weight Ratio (TWR), stability score, burn time, and pre-launch warnings.
  • Launchpad, Countdown & Flight Simulation: Moving to Launch Complex 39A initiates a T-5 countdown during which umbilical gantry swing arms retract and cryogenic vapor vents. At ignition, players control throttle (0–100%), steer pitch (A/D or touch controls), jettison spent side boosters (Space), switch between four camera angles (Follow, Wide, Nozzle, Orbit), and engage time-warp (1x–10x) in space.
  • Realistic Failure Testing & Space Exploration: Improperly built rockets fail realistically—underpowered builds (TWR < 1.0) stall on the pad, and finless rockets tumble in the atmosphere—triggering a failure debrief explaining how to improve the design. Successful launches ascend through a shifting sky-to-space atmosphere past Earth's curved horizon to reach the Orbital Relay Station, The Moon, Mars, and Jupiter, earning money and fuel rewards across 6 missions.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Learn Aerospace Principles Through Play: Introduces real concepts—Thrust-to-Weight Ratio, aerodynamic drag, center-of-pressure stability, fuel-to-mass ratios, and multi-stage booster separation—in a hands-on, forgiving environment.
  • Zero Installation & Instant Accessibility: Runs directly in any modern web browser on desktop or laptop without downloads, accounts, or heavy game-engine installers.
  • Beginner-Friendly & Never Soft-Locked: Includes starter rocket presets (Scout Mk-I, Selene Explorer, Ares Heavy), optional beginner SAS flight-stabilization assist, full refunds when iterating on parts, and safety-net Space Grants so players can experiment freely.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The goal of Orbital Foundry is to spark curiosity in aerospace engineering, physics, and space exploration—especially for students and beginners who might find traditional orbital simulators intimidating. By turning trial-and-error failure into clear, actionable engineering feedback ("why did my rocket tip over?" or "why was it too heavy to lift off?"), the project encourages iterative problem-solving and STEM literacy in an engaging 3D format.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML5, CSS3, and GLSL (custom vertex/fragment shaders).
  • Frameworks & Libraries: React 19, Three.js (WebGL 3D rendering, PBR materials, RoomEnvironment IBL, OrbitControls, LatheGeometry, ExtrudeGeometry, InstancedMesh, and Points particle systems), Tailwind CSS v4, and Lucide React icons.
  • Build & Runtime Tooling: Vite 8, Node.js, and npm.
  • Procedural Audio & Graphics: HTML5 2D Canvas API (for procedural hull paneling, concrete launchpad textures, smoke sprites, and planetary maps) and the browser Web Audio API (for real-time synthesized engine roar, countdown tones, staging clunks, and alert chimes).
  • Storage: Browser localStorage for saving rocket designs, funds, fuel reserves, and mission progress.

5. How is your project creative?

  • 100% Procedural Assets (Zero External Media Files): Every 3D rocket component, planetary surface (Earth clouds, Moon craters, Mars canyons, Jupiter bands & Great Red Spot), hull livery texture, custom GLSL Mach-diamond exhaust plume, Fresnel atmospheric glow, and sound effect is generated mathematically in code.
  • Constructive Failure-Driven Design Loop: Rather than blocking players from launching flawed rockets, Orbital Foundry lets them test flawed builds on the pad, witness the physical consequence (pad stall, atmospheric tumble, or mid-flight fuel depletion), and receive a tailored engineering tip to fix and relaunch.
  • Clean, Unobstructed Cockpit HUD: Collapsible bottom docks keep the central 3D viewport completely clear so players can inspect their rocket craftsmanship and planetary vistas without visual clutter.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  • Usability for Beginners vs. Engineering Depth: Balanced authentic physics variables (TWR, mass depletion, drag, stability) with intuitive controls, starter presets, and an optional SAS flight assist toggle so both newcomers and space-sim fans enjoy playing.
  • Performance Across Hardware & Software WebGL: Implemented automatic software-WebGL detection, zero-garbage-collection math loops, pooled particle buffers, and avoidance of heavy CSS backdrop-filter blurs over the canvas so frame rates stay smooth across laptops and low-GPU environments.
  • Economic Balance & Replayability: Tuned part prices, 100% part-removal refunds, fuel reserves, and progressive mission payouts so players feel rewarded for scaling up from small suborbital hops to heavy planetary missions.
  • Visual Clarity & Accessibility: Paired high-contrast dark obsidian interfaces with tabular monospace telemetry, clear text diagnostics (never relying on color alone), and both keyboard (W/A/S/D, Space) and on-screen button/slider controls.

projectDetails.name: Forgotten in Space: Exploring NASA’s Abandoned Space Technologies and Their Scientific Legacy
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Forgotten in Space: Exploring NASA’s Abandoned Space Technologies and Their Scientific Legacy,” is an educational website that explores NASA hardware left across the solar system since the 1960s. We developed an interactive platform where visitors can discover different spacecraft, rovers, landers, and other technologies, learn where they were sent, understand their original purposes, and explore what happened to them after their missions ended.

The website addresses NASA’s challenge by bringing together the stories of space equipment that was intentionally left behind, became inactive, or completed its mission. It highlights the scientific discoveries and technological achievements made possible by these missions, while distinguishing retired equipment from spacecraft that are still operating.

This project is important because these technologies are more than forgotten objects: they represent decades of exploration, innovation, and scientific progress. By sharing their stories in an engaging and accessible way, we hope to inspire curiosity about space exploration and help people appreciate the lasting impact of NASA’s missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: Forgotten in Space

Our project, “Forgotten in Space,” is a website about NASA's old spacecraft, rovers, landers, and other equipment that have been left behind in space or on other planets. We wanted to explore what happened to these technologies after their missions ended and what they helped us discover.

What does it do and how does it work?

Our website allows visitors to explore different NASA missions and the equipment used in them. They can learn when and where each spacecraft or rover was sent, what its purpose was, what discoveries it made, and why its mission ended. We also include pictures and useful information to make everything easier to understand.

What are its benefits?

It helps students and other visitors learn about space exploration in an interesting way. It also brings information about different NASA missions together in one place, so people don't have to search through many websites to learn about them.

What is the intended impact?

We want people to understand that even though some space missions have ended, the discoveries they made are still important. We also hope our project encourages students to become more interested in space, science, and technology.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We used Python and Flask to build the website, HTML to create the pages, CSS to design them, and JavaScript to add interactive features. We used SQLite to store information about the missions and NASA's Image and Video Library API to find space-related pictures. We also used Visual Studio Code to write our code and GitHub to manage our project.

How is the project creative?

Instead of focusing only on famous and currently active space missions, we chose to look at the equipment that was left behind after missions ended. We thought it would be interesting to show what happened to these machines and how they helped NASA learn more about the solar system.

What factors did our team consider?

We focused on making the website easy to use and understand. We also considered the accuracy of the information, the quality of the pictures, and how to organize the content so visitors could find what they were looking for. Another important point was explaining the difference between equipment that was abandoned, equipment that stopped working, and missions that simply came to an end.

Through this project, we want to show that even the machines left behind in space have stories worth learning about.

**HABITAT ZERO – Design. Survive. Investigate.**

HABITAT ZERO is a browser-based space exploration and survival game designed to introduce players to the challenges of establishing a sustainable human habitat beyond Earth. Players take on the role of junior astronauts, making decisions, managing resources, designing habitats, and completing missions to survive in an unfamiliar space environment.

The project combines interactive storytelling and gameplay with real-world space science, incorporating NASA data and resources to make the experience more informative and engaging. Instead of simply reading about space exploration, players learn by making decisions and experiencing the consequences of their actions.

projectDetails.details:
HABITAT ZERO – Design. Survive. Investigate.

HABITAT ZERO is an interactive, browser-based space habitat simulation game designed to introduce students and young learners to the challenges of establishing and maintaining human settlements on the Moon and Mars.

Players take on the role of a space habitat engineer and mission commander. They select a mission, choose a landing location, design a habitat and manage essential systems such as power generation, oxygen supply, water recycling, food production and crew health. As the mission progresses, players must balance limited resources, respond to unexpected emergencies and make decisions that affect the survival of the crew.

The game demonstrates how interconnected life-support systems work. For example, a power failure can interrupt oxygen generation and carbon dioxide removal, creating further risks for the crew. Players must understand these connections, identify problems and make informed decisions to keep their habitat operational.

One of the project's key features is its Mission Investigation and Replay System. Instead of simply showing a failure, the game helps players investigate the sequence of events that caused it, understand the consequences of their decisions and replay the same scenario using a different strategy. This encourages experimentation, critical thinking and learning from mistakes.

The project draws inspiration from NASA's planetary exploration research and publicly available space-science resources, including information related to lunar terrain, planetary environments and space weather. Scientific concepts are adapted into simplified educational simulations so that complex engineering challenges are understandable to younger audiences. The game is an educational model, not a real-world spacecraft or habitat control system.

The intended impact is to make space exploration and habitat engineering more accessible and engaging. It encourages students to explore STEM subjects, develop problem-solving skills and understand the scientific and engineering challenges involved in long-duration human space missions.

The project was developed as a web-based application using Google AI Studio and modern web development technologies, with a focus on interactive gameplay, simulation logic, user interface design and browser-based accessibility. It is deployed publicly so that users can access and experience the game through a web browser.

What makes HABITAT ZERO creative is its combination of game-based learning, resource-management simulation and failure investigation. Rather than presenting space science through only text or quizzes, it allows players to experience the consequences of engineering decisions. The design considers scientific plausibility, educational value, age accessibility, gameplay engagement, resource interdependence and the importance of distinguishing real scientific information from simplified game scenarios.

Ultimately, HABITAT ZERO aims to turn the challenge of surviving beyond Earth into an interactive learning experience where every decision matters.

projectDetails.name: EARTH ANALOG EXPLORER
projectDetails.summary: Earth Analog Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to bridge Earth science and space exploration by identifying and analyzing terrestrial geological analogues that mimic the extreme environments of the Moon and Mars. Integrating NASA's official resources and open data, our platform equips researchers and space enthusiasts with advanced analytical tools. Key features include an analog similarity index to quantitatively measure environmental matching, machine-specific analog matching to tailor sites for specific mission parameters, and an intuitive split-screen comparison view to evaluate side-by-side geological metrics. By streamlining how mission planners select and validate terrestrial testing grounds for rovers and habitats, Earth Analog Explorer makes planetary research more accessible, visual, and data-driven.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

Earth Analog Explorer (earth-analog-explorer.vercel.app) maps Earth-based geological sites that mimic the extreme environments of the Moon and Mars.

Integrating NASA's official resources, the platform features:

projectDetails.name: Abandoned Legacy
projectDetails.summary:
Abandoned Legacy is an interactive educational web platform developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, addressing the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.”

The platform transforms the history of inactive lunar and Martian exploration equipment into an engaging multimedia experience. It features first-person storytelling based on historical mission records, a real-time chronometer tracking the time since selected missions' final communications, an interactive mission explorer, technical instrument dossiers, a historical timeline, and a scientific discoveries matrix. Browser-based audio synthesis and speech narration bring these silent explorers to life.
By presenting their engineering achievements and scientific contributions in an accessible format, Abandoned Legacy challenges the perception of these machines as forgotten space debris. It highlights how their discoveries continue to contribute to our understanding of the Moon and Mars, making planetary exploration history more engaging and accessible to students, educators, and the public.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — Abandoned Legacy

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Abandoned Legacy is an interactive educational web platform that preserves the scientific and historical legacy of inactive lunar and Martian exploration equipment. It transforms historical NASA mission records, engineering achievements, and scientific discoveries into an accessible multimedia storytelling experience.

The platform consists of several interactive sections:

  • Mission Explorer: Allows visitors to search and filter seven mission profiles by destination, including the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space. Each profile provides operational lifespan comparisons, landing locations, and technical information.
  • Chronometer of Silence: Displays live elapsed-time counters showing how long it has been since the final recorded communications of five selected missions: Apollo ALSEP, Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity.
  • Voices from the Silence: Presents first-person narratives based on historical mission records, allowing visitors to explore each spacecraft's journey, discoveries, and final moments. Users can listen through browser-based speech synthesis or explore reconstructed telemetry-style displays.
  • Mission Timeline: Presents important milestones in planetary exploration chronologically, connecting historical missions with the broader history of space exploration.
  • Scientific Discoveries Matrix: Highlights important findings from these missions and explains their continuing relevance to planetary science.
  • Technical Dossiers: Provides detailed information about scientific instruments, their functions, technical specifications, and mission records.

The website also features synthesized radio carrier tones generated directly in the browser, creating an immersive experience inspired by deep-space communication.

2. What benefits does it provide?

Abandoned Legacy makes complex planetary exploration history easier to understand and explore. Instead of presenting spacecraft merely as inactive hardware, it highlights their engineering achievements and scientific contributions.

Students and educators can learn about real scientific instruments such as Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometers (APXS), Mössbauer Spectrometers, and seismic experiments. Comparisons between planned and actual mission lifespans also demonstrate engineering endurance and the challenges of operating robotic equipment in extreme environments.

The platform combines scientific information with storytelling, making historical mission archives more engaging and accessible to the general public.

3. What is the intended impact?

The project's primary goal is to change how people perceive decommissioned planetary exploration equipment. These machines may have stopped transmitting, but their discoveries continue to contribute to our understanding of other worlds.

By connecting historical missions with modern exploration, Abandoned Legacy encourages curiosity about planetary science, space engineering, and scientific research. It also aims to serve as an educational resource for students, teachers, and space enthusiasts.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a responsive, client-side Single Page Application using:

  • React 19: Building the interactive user interface.
  • TypeScript: Structuring the application with static typing.
  • Vite: Development and build environment.
  • Tailwind CSS v4: Responsive styling and visual design.
  • Lucide React: Interface icons.
  • Web Audio API: Generating radio carrier tones and audio effects directly in the browser.
  • Web Speech API: Providing browser-native text-to-speech narration.
  • Google AI Studio: Assisting with code development, debugging, and AI-generated visual illustrations.
  • Google Cloud Run: Hosting the deployed application.

The application uses static mission data and does not require a backend, database, external API connection, or runtime AI model to function.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The central creative idea is to give silent exploration machines a voice. The first-person storytelling approach transforms technical mission histories into narratives that visitors can connect with emotionally.

The Chronometer of Silence turns the passage of time since a spacecraft's final communication into an interactive experience. Synthesized radio carrier tones and telemetry-style displays further recreate the atmosphere of deep-space communication.

The combination of historical records, interactive technical information, scientific discoveries, and storytelling creates a different way to experience planetary exploration history.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, usability, technical feasibility, and transparency.

Historical information and scientific findings were cross-referenced with publicly available resources from NASA JPL, NASA NSSDCA, the Lunar and Planetary Institute, and the NASA Planetary Data System.

We also prioritized a responsive interface that works across desktop, tablet, and mobile devices without requiring installation, user accounts, or external API access.

AI-generated illustrations are used as visual representations rather than authentic NASA archival photographs. AI assistance was also used during development and in structuring the storytelling content, while the deployed application itself does not use runtime AI.

Overall, Abandoned Legacy aims to preserve the stories of planetary exploration pioneers and make their scientific legacy accessible to future generations.

projectDetails.name: Project 3-Minute Decision
projectDetails.summary:
On Mars, a three-minute choice can shape a whole mission. Our app turns this idea into an interactive game where players act as a Mars rover support team. When the rover reports a problem and Earth cannot reply straight away, players have three minutes to study the clues and decide what to do. They can protect the rover, carefully approach a science target, or gather more information first. Each choice leads to different consequences for rover safety, scientific discoveries, time, and power.
We used NASA research about Mars communication delays, rover hazard checks, and science instruments to make the situation feel realistic. The app addresses the challenge by showing why a team may need to think independently when Earth is far away. This matters because space exploration depends on making careful decisions with incomplete information. We hope the game makes players curious about Mars while giving them a chance to practice making thoughtful choices.
projectDetails.details:
What does your project do, and how does it work?

Our app is an interactive Mars rover decision game with six emergencies. For each one, players have three minutes to read the rover’s alert and clues, such as the slope, wheel slip, and safer route. They choose one of three actions and see how it affects the rover’s safety, energy, and science reserves. Players can also write a short mission note to explain their reasoning. At the end, they can review their results and download a report.

What benefits does your project have?

The game makes a real space-exploration challenge easier to understand and fun to try. It helps players practise reading evidence, thinking under pressure, weighing risks, and explaining their choices. Because different choices have different consequences, players can see that protecting the rover, saving energy, and collecting science may require trade-offs.

What is the intended impact of your project?

We hope our app helps people understand why rover teams may need to make decisions without waiting for an immediate reply from Earth. We also want to spark curiosity about Mars exploration and show how important careful thinking is when information is incomplete.

What tools, coding language, hardware, or software did you use?

We built the app as a web application using Python and Streamlit, and hosted it on Streamlit Cloud. It can be opened in a web browser on a regular computer or device. No special hardware or account is needed to play.

How was your project creative?

I think our idea is creative because communication delay is easy to overlook. People might think a rover can simply ask Earth what to do, but messages between Earth and Mars take time. We turned that hidden challenge into a game with a countdown, clues, and choices that lead to different outcomes. Instead of giving players one obvious answer, we let them weigh what matters most for the mission.

What factors did your team consider?

We considered the communication delay, the limited information available, and the need to balance rover safety, energy, and science goals. We wanted the clues and choices to be clear, the consequences to help players learn, and the six emergencies to keep the game interesting. We also made it clear that the game’s telemetry and outcomes are fictional and inspired by NASA research, so they are not mistaken for real NASA mission data.

projectDetails.name: Project ajman american private school
projectDetails.summary: Mission Control lets anyone design, launch and operate a real space mission. Players balance mass, power, money, data and fuel, pass a NASA-style Go/No-Go poll, survive solar storms and get a scored engineering debrief. Pixel, a robot co-pilot, makes it easy for beginners, while real orbital mechanics and link budgets run underneath.
projectDetails.details:
The problem. Space engineering is exciting, but its core lesson is hard to feel from a textbook: every decision is a trade-off. Bigger instruments need more power, more power needs bigger solar panels, panels add mass, mass needs a bigger rocket, and the rocket costs money you don't have.

What we built. Mission Control is a complete, playable mission design game in a single web page. Players choose one of five missions (Earth, Moon, Mars, asteroids, deep space), build a spacecraft from 23 components, pick an orbit and a rocket, then launch. Seven live gauges show whether the design works, and the mission simulation runs on the player's actual numbers. A weak radio really loses data, a thin power margin really causes brownouts, and too little fuel really leaves the spacecraft in the wrong orbit.

Easy and fun. Pixel, a robot co-pilot, gives step-by-step quests. One-click "Fix it" buttons solve problems and explain what changed. Players earn stars, XP, ranks, badges and Space Credits to spend on research upgrades and paint jobs. Their agency's funding grows as they fly better missions, so skill unlocks bigger budgets.

Real engineering. Under the friendly surface, every number comes from a published method:

  • vis-viva orbital mechanics and Hohmann transfers
  • the rocket equation
  • SMAD solar power sizing with eclipse geometry
  • full decibel link budgets to NASA's Deep Space Network
  • TRL-based mass growth
  • a 5×5 risk matrix

A "∑ math" button on every gauge shows the equations with the player's own numbers. The results match real missions: a 1,847 m/s burn to reach geostationary orbit, and a 259-day cruise to Mars.

What makes it different. It works for a 16-year-old on their first try, and it holds up when an engineer checks the math. It is transparent about what is simplified, with a Methods page that lists every equation and source.

How it works (tech)

Plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS in one self-contained file, with Three.js for 3D, Canvas for orbit diagrams, ground tracks and charts, and the Web Audio API for sound. Progress is saved with localStorage. There is no install and no build step: open index.html and play.

Challenges we ran into

  • Making real physics produce good gameplay. We tuned the reference designs so each mission is winnable, while weaker designs fail for real engineering reasons.
  • Explaining decibel link budgets and power sizing to beginners without hiding them. The answer was two layers: plain-language gauges on top and ∑ math panels underneath.

What's next

  • Online multiplayer across devices with Supabase Realtime.
  • A shared global leaderboard.
  • Landers and rovers as new mission types.

projectDetails.name: ASM Space Pioneers: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
ASM Space Pioneers: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive space-learning project created by four Grade 5 students from Al Salam Charter School, Abu Dhabi, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Inspired by the theme The Next Frontier, our project explores an important question: How can future astronauts prepare for the challenges of living and working on Mars?

We developed two connected educational tools: Mission Mars, an interactive game created using Scratch, and ASM Space Pioneers Buddy, an AI-powered learning chatbot.

Through six exciting missions, players experience Mars landing, mineral exploration, habitat repair, dust storms, scientific investigation, and a final knowledge challenge. They must make decisions, manage simulated survival resources, and solve problems.

Our chatbot complements the game by explaining Mars science, life-support systems, and engineering decisions using NASA educational resources.

Our goal is to transform complex space exploration concepts into accessible, engaging learning experiences that inspire curiosity, critical thinking, creativity, and future careers in STEM.

We believe tomorrow's space explorers can begin their journey in today's classrooms.
projectDetails.details:
ASM Space Pioneers – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Our project is an interactive Mars exploration experience developed by four Grade 5 students from Al Salam Charter School, Abu Dhabi, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

We created Mission Mars, a Scratch-based game featuring six exciting missions, including Mars landing, mineral exploration, habitat rescue, dust storm survival, scientific research, and a Mars knowledge quiz. Players solve challenges, make decisions, and manage simulated survival resources.

We also developed ASM Space Pioneers Buddy, an AI-powered chatbot using Edcafe AI that helps learners understand Mars exploration, astronaut safety, and survival challenges through NASA science resources.

Our project combines coding, AI, NASA science, and game-based learning to develop critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving skills.

Our vision is to inspire young learners worldwide to become future scientists, engineers, and space explorers.

“We don't just imagine the future. We train for it!”

projectDetails.name: ASTERIA: Astronomical SPHEREx Time-series Extraction & Rapid Image Analysis
projectDetails.summary: ASTERIA is an interactive astronomical dashboard designed to make NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey data accessible, comparable, and understandable for researchers, educators, and space enthusiasts. Since 2025, SPHEREx has been mapping the entire sky every six months across 102 near-infrared bands, capturing over a billion objects. ASTERIA solves a major challenge: exploring massive infrared image sequences and spotting subtle cosmic changes over time is difficult for non-experts and often requires switching between multiple fragmented tools. By bringing SPHEREx observation metadata, multi-catalog overlays (Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD), an interactive time-series timeline, and an integrated AI research assistant into one unified interface, ASTERIA empowers users to inspect sky regions, compare observations across dates, and uncover moving objects, brightness variations, and chemical signatures.
projectDetails.details:
ASTERIA is a web-based interactive research dashboard built to transform complex infrared all-sky survey data into intuitive visual exploration. Traditionally, exploring multi-epoch astronomical observations requires cross-referencing separate catalogs, downloading heavy FITS files, and writing custom scripts. ASTERIA unifies search, sky plotting, catalog comparison, and AI-guided analysis in a single view.


How it works:
Users search for a celestial target or survey field (such as the COSMOS Deep Field) or input specific coordinates (RA/Dec). ASTERIA plots SPHEREx observation markers alongside Gaia DR3 sources (stars, galaxy candidates, quasar candidates) and SIMBAD catalog records on an interactive sky map. Users can scrub through observation dates via a built-in playback timeline, click individual sources to inspect classifier probabilities, magnitudes, and parallax distances, and view detected chemical signatures (such as Hydrogen, Helium, and Carbon) alongside an integrated AI Research Chat.


Key Benefits & Impact:

  • Reduces tool-switching: Combines target search, multi-catalog comparison, observation metadata, and research discussion in one workspace.
  • Empowers students & educators: Makes sky coordinates, source classifications, and multi-epoch observations approachable through hands-on visual investigation.
  • Supports initial research: Helps astronomy enthusiasts and researchers inspect nearby sources, identify data limitations/missing measurements, and generate hypotheses quickly.
  • Plain-language insights: Translates complex astronomical records into clear explanations via an integrated AI research assistant.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Frontend & Visualization: HTML/CSS, Tailwind CSS, React / Next.js with interactive sky plotting (MapLibre / Deck.gl / Three.js)
  • Backend & Processing: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, OpenCV) and JavaScript for data retrieval, alignment, and difference detection
  • Data Visualization: Matplotlib and custom interactive sky plot overlays
  • AI & Development Assistants: ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, GitHub, Copilot

Creative Elements:

  • Unified Multi-Catalog Sky Plot: Visually distinguishes SPHEREx observations, Gaia DR3 stars, galaxies, quasars, and SIMBAD objects on a single interactive coordinate grid.
  • Interactive Observation Timeline: Lets users step or play through SPHEREx observation epochs to track changes over time.
  • Context-Aware Research Chat: Keeps the selected sky field and source telemetry in view while users ask follow-up questions about terminology, demographics, or spectral correlations.
  • Transparent Data Reporting: Clearly flags unavailable parallax distances or catalog timeouts so users understand measurement boundaries.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Dancing with the SARs
challengeDetails.excerpt: Earth's surface is an endless dance of natural processes and human activities, but these changes are often difficult to visualize, understand, and communicate. From wetland loss to forest wildfires, earthquakes, farming activities, glacier movement, and more, Earth is in a constant waltz of surface changes. Your challenge is to build an interactive application that uses radar remote sensing data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to track and visualize one or more types of surface change at locations around the world.

projectDetails.name: Root-Cause
projectDetails.summary:
Something is wrong at the Mars base, and it is your job to find out what it is. Root Cause is a browser game for kids aged 7–12. Players are flight controllers at Suhail Base in Gale Crater, Mars. Each case starts with an alarm. Looking at the readings is free, but every test costs crew hours. To win, players must think like scientists: predict, test, rule things out and fix the real cause.

The six cases cover power, food, life support and radiation shielding, and show how the systems depend on each other. A weak battery leads to the heater being cut, the greenhouse freezing, and the lettuce stopping growing. Asking Mission Control costs crew hours too, because messages take 4 to 24 minutes each way between Earth and Mars. The game uses real NASA data from InSight, Curiosity and DONKI, every case ends with the true NASA story it is based on, and it runs in any browser in English, Arabic, French and Spanish.
projectDetails.details:
HOW A CASE WORKS

1. Alarm. Something is wrong. Press the master alarm to start.

2. Quick decision. A trade-off with no free option. For example: switch the lab off to save battery (and lose a sol of science), or keep it running (and risk the greenhouse heater being cut tonight).

3. Look at the readings. Free charts of the outpost's systems, with a dotted "normal day" line to compare against.

4. Run tests. Each test costs crew hours. Before it runs, the player predicts the result.

5. Ask Mission Control if stuck. It costs 2 crew hours, because messages take 4 to 24 minutes each way between Earth and Mars.

6. Call the root cause. A wrong call costs 2 hours.

7. Build the chain. Put the cause-and-effect steps in order. One card is fake, and a wrong card costs an hour.

8. Fix it. Some fixes only treat the symptom. Only fixing the cause closes the case.

9. Real mission. Each case ends with the true NASA story it is based on, with a link.

Stars are awarded for fixing the problem, using few tests, and predicting every test correctly. The root cause is picked at random from 2–3 possibilities each time, so replaying a case can lead to a different answer.

THE SIX CASES

1. Dim Day (tutorial), power: dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels (2018–2022).

2. Cold Lettuce, food and power: a dust storm put InSight into safe mode (January 2022).

3. Stuffy Air, life support (CO₂): Apollo 13's CO₂ filter fix (1970).

4. Oxygen Alarm, life support (oxygen): the ISS ammonia false alarm (January 2015).

5. Slow Leak, life support (air pressure): the ISS slow air leak hunt (2020).

6. Storm Incoming, radiation shielding: the solar storm that hit Mars (May 20, 2024).

HOW IT FITS THE CHALLENGE

- Life support, radiation shielding, power and food: each has at least one case, and cases show how the systems depend on each other. A weak battery leads to the heater being cut, the greenhouse freezing, and the lettuce stopping growing.

- Communication delay: Ask Mission Control costs crew hours because of the real Earth–Mars message delay.

- No free choices: tests, wrong calls, wrong chain cards, wrong fixes and asking for help all cost crew hours. Every quick decision has a downside on purpose, because real mission planners never get a free choice.

- Replayability: random root causes, plus stars to improve on.

- Plain language: short sentences. Words like sol, ppm, kPa and ohms are explained next to the chart where they appear.

- Low barrier: runs in any browser, with no download or sign-up needed.

- Four languages: English, Arabic, French and Spanish.

NASA DATA USED

All of this is also listed in the game under "NASA data used" on the title screen.

- InSight lander solar power: about 5,000 Wh per sol after landing (2018), cut by dust to about 500 by spring 2022. Used in Dim Day's "InSight's solar power" reading.

- Curiosity rover REMS weather station: Gale Crater, sol 4189 (May 19, 2024): low −68 °C, high −5 °C, 861 Pa. Sol 4190 (May 20, 2024): low −69 °C, high −3 °C, 860 Pa. Used in the "Air outside" reading in every case.

- DONKI space weather database: CME 2024-05-20T05:36:00-CME-001, from Sun region 13664, about 2,678 km/s. Used in Storm Incoming's space weather alert from Mission Control.

- Curiosity rover RAD radiation detector: 8,100 micrograys on May 20, 2024 (about 30 chest X-rays), against about 180–225 on a normal sol. Used in Storm Incoming's "Radiation dose" reading.

- Earth–Mars message delay: 4 to 24 minutes each way. Used for Ask Mission Control.

- Real mission stories: Apollo 13, InSight and the ISS, in the "Real mission" box at the end of each case.

This is archived data stored in the game, not a live feed. The outpost's own readings (battery, greenhouse, CO₂ and so on) come from a simple simulation (js/sim.js), so each case behaves in a consistent, realistic way.

PLAYTESTING

21 people played the game and filled in a feedback form. 62% were in our target age of 7–12, and 67% rated the game 4 or 5 out of 5 for being easy to play. 5 of the 7 who played in another language rated the translation 4 or 5 out of 5, and nobody rated it below 3. Two of the three written suggestions asked for clearer instructions, and one asked for more levels. We listened and made significant changes to help with the gameplay: we addressed these complaints by adding a tutorial and instructions.

HOW IT'S BUILT

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks, libraries or build step. Sounds are generated in code with the Web Audio API.

- index.html: screens and layout

- css/style.css: mission-control look and visuals

- js/cases.js: the six cases (readings, tests, causes, fixes, costs)

- js/sim.js: 48-hour outpost simulation and chart data

- js/game.js: game logic

- js/graph.js: chart drawing

- js/sound.js: sound effects

- js/lang/*.js: all game text in English, Arabic, French and Spanish

## How it's built

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks, libraries or build step. Sounds are generated in code with Web Audio API.

```

index.html screens and layout

css/style.css mission control look and visualss

js/cases.js the six cases: readings, tests, causes, fixes, costs

js/sim.js 48-hour outpost simulation and chart data

js/game.js game logic

js/graph.js chart drawing

js/sound.js sound effects

js/lang/*.js all game text in English, Arabic, French and Spanish

```

## Use of SI

We used Claude (Anthropic) explicitily for:

- **Translations:** the Arabic, French and Spanish versions of all game text. The game says this on the title screen.

- **One bug fix:** a logic error in the chart drawing (`js/graph.js`) which we could not fix by ourselves..

- **Review and testing:** Claude reviewed the game against the challenge brief, found bugs, tested every case in every language, Our team built these changes ourselves.

projectDetails.name: Project SPHEREx Time Machine
projectDetails.summary:
SPHEREx Time Machine is an interactive website where users can view and visualize astronomical discoveries accessible to everyone using data directly from NASA’s mission. Our website allows users to enter their coordinates or pick ones on a map and view the stars, comets and galaxies at that time period, which can be picked from our options. By displaying observations in an interactive, video-like viewer, users can easily identify moving objects, changes in brightness, and other astronomical phenomena, including asteroids, comets, stars, and brown dwarfs.
 
Our website’s aim is to transform SPHEREx’s expansive collection of astronomical data captured through out the years of research into one cohesive, engaging website. Through infra-red scans and time-band image comparisons, the tool empowers both astronomy enthusiasts and researchers to investigate the universe, recognize unusual patterns, and contribute to new scientific discoveries. Our goal is to make exploring the changing universe simple,
interactive, and accessible to everyone.
projectDetails.details: SPHEREx Time Machine is a website that allows users to interact and see stars, comets and asteroids by inputting desired coordinates and viewing infra-red images of these astronomical species. The screen of these infra-red photos can be played to view the movement of these asteroids, comets and stars, over 8 periods of time, showing the movement. The main benefit of this website is that users don’t need to browse through thousands of years of data and can view all of this data easily on one singular website. The intended impact is to enable non-professional users to understand and connect to any astronomical interests they may have without having any prior knowledge to space. To develop our project, we have used Base44 via inputting various prompts and adding new prompts to change or alter certain features based off feedback to allow users to have the best possible experience. Our project is creative through adding extra features other than solely viewing the stars and seeing what each object is on the infa-red camera, whilst also describing how each object will be in real-life. Our team considered various factors, such as clear steps defined and bigger fonts to adapt our products to all of our user needs.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.

projectDetails.name: DeepSpace Vitals
projectDetails.summary:
DeepSpace Vitals is an astronaut health-monitoring and mission-support platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It demonstrates how astronaut health information and mission operations can be organised in one accessible platform.

The prototype includes separate Mission Control and Astronaut dashboards, simulated vital-sign telemetry, health indicators, trend visualisations, alerts, crew assignments, mission briefings and communication-status indicators.

The project explores how software could support astronaut health monitoring during future space missions. All displayed health readings are simulated and are not real astronaut medical data.
projectDetails.details:
DeepSpace Vitals was developed to explore how astronauts and Mission Control could monitor health information during space missions.

The platform has two roles:

  • Mission Control (Admin): Mission and crew management, astronaut overview, alerts and briefings.
  • Astronaut: A personal dashboard with mission information, health indicators and updates.

The prototype demonstrates simulated vital-sign readings, health trends and communication statuses such as LIVE, DELAYED and NO LINK.

The project was developed using Base44, Figma, Miro, Canva and ChatGPT.

Important limitation: All health readings and telemetry are simulated. The prototype is not connected to real astronaut medical systems and is not intended for medical diagnosis.

projectDetails.name: AFTERLIFE: The Stories of Forgotten Space Explorers
projectDetails.summary:
AFTERLIFE is an interactive educational webpage that explores the stories of spacecraft, rovers and scientific equipment that have been left behind after their missions. It takes visitors on a journey across three destinations: the Moon, Mars and Deep Space.

Through interactive profiles, short mission stories, interesting discoveries and a final quiz, the project introduces visitors to lesser-known space explorers. It explains what happened to them after their missions ended.

The project aims to make space exploration more accessible and engaging, particularly for younger audiences, while highlighting how past missions continue to contribute to our understanding of the universe.
projectDetails.details:
AFTERLIFE is an interactive educational webpage that takes visitors on a journey through the Moon, Mars and Deep Space, introducing them to spacecraft, rovers and scientific equipment whose missions have ended or whose signals have gone silent.

The webpage is organized into different destinations, each featuring interactive elements that reveal the stories, discoveries and final journeys of lesser-known space explorers. It also includes interesting facts and a final quiz to help visitors test what they have learned.

I aim to make space exploration more engaging and accessible, particularly for younger audiences. Rather than focusing only on famous astronauts and major missions, AFTERLIFE highlights the machines that explored beyond Earth and the discoveries they left behind. Through this project, I hope to encourage curiosity, appreciation for scientific progress, and a deeper interest in space exploration.

The creative aspect of my project lies in its storytelling approach. Instead of presenting information as a collection of facts, I have turned completed space missions into stories that visitors can explore at their own pace through interactive elements and visual content.

While developing the project, I considered the intended audience, ease of navigation, accuracy of scientific information, and the amount of content displayed on each page. I aimed to keep the information concise and understandable without losing the significance of each mission.

Tools and software: Genially and NASA's publicly available mission information and resources.
