projectDetails.name: Cosmic Besties
projectDetails.summary: Cosmic Besties is an interactive, Duolingo-style space academy built specifically for middle schoolers (ages 13–14) that brings NASA’s retired and deep-space missions to life. Since the 1960s, NASA has sent extraordinary rovers, landers, and probes across the Moon, Mars, and the outer solar system, yet most school websites present their history as dry textbook notes. As a 13-year-old who loves space, I designed this app so 20 iconic spacecraft across four sectors (Early Pioneers, Red Planet Mars, Outer Giants & Ice Worlds, and Comet Chasers & Cosmic Hunters) speak in the first person to share where they are, what they discovered, and how they sent their final signals. Players explore 6-branch Interactive Mission Mind Maps to earn Space Coins, play an adaptive Arcade with a smart hint system that gives helpful clues instead of discouraging wrong answers, sketch their own astronaut avatar in the HTML5 Canvas Cadet Art Studio (saved seamlessly in browser localStorage with zero login barriers), and unbox collectible Mystery Capsules. Every mission also features a direct "Explore on Official NASA.gov" button alongside a dedicated Resources Corner powered by real NASA Science (science.nasa.gov), NASA Image Library (images.nasa.gov), and NSSDCA (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov) archives, all built and published as a live web app using Google AI Studio.
projectDetails.details:
Cosmic Besties is an interactive, Duolingo-style space academy built specifically for middle school students that brings NASA’s retired and deep-space missions to life. Instead of reading passive textbook articles, students explore 20 iconic NASA missions grouped into four cosmic sectors (Early Pioneers, Red Planet Mars, Outer Giants & Ice Worlds, and Comet Chasers & Cosmic Hunters). Every spacecraft speaks in a warm, first-person voice to share where it is, what it discovered, and what happened to its final signal. Clicking any mission opens a 6-branch Interactive Mission Mind Map (Origin & Engineering, Cosmic Journey, Deep Discoveries, Survival & Drama, Final Signal & Fate, and Mission Legacy) that rewards curiosity with Space Coins. Students can then test their knowledge in an adaptive Arcade (featuring an infinite trivia quiz, a signal memory-match game, and a launch-order sorting game), draw their own astronaut avatar in the Cadet Art Studio, and spend their earned coins on collectible Mystery Capsules. Every mission also includes a direct "Explore on Official NASA.gov" button alongside a dedicated Resources Corner linking straight to NASA’s official archives.

Benefits & Intended Impact Most space education websites present historic spacecraft as dry lists of dates and technical specs, which quickly loses the attention of middle schoolers. By combining emotional storytelling, game-based rewards, and zero-login instant access, Forgotten Giants of Space makes real space history feel personal, exciting, and approachable. My goal is to help students my age connect emotionally with NASA's robotic explorers, build curiosity about STEM and planetary science, and learn how to verify space facts using real NASA public archives.

Creativity & Design Factors Considered: As a teen building for teens, I focused heavily on what actually keeps kids engaged without feeling like homework:

  • First-Person Storytelling & Hint-Based Learning: Giving spacecraft their own voices makes them feel like real heroes, while the Arcade's smart hint system gives players a helpful 1-sentence character clue and a second chance instead of discouraging them when they miss a question.
  • Creative Self-Expression & Collection: Adding an interactive drawing pad for custom avatars and Mystery Capsule card packs gives students creative ownership and a fun reason to keep exploring all 20 missions.
  • Privacy & Frictionless Access: Because the app is designed for students, I avoided logins, passwords, or personal data collection by saving all progress, Space Coins, and custom drawings locally in the browser.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Development & Live Hosting: Built and deployed as a public web app using Google AI Studio (Build Mode).

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AstroFlame
projectDetails.summary:
Fire behaves strangely in space. With no buoyancy there's no flame to watch dance upward, just a dim, round glow that lingers and hides. Most people have never seen it, so we built a place where you can. Drag the gravity slider from freefall to Earth and the flame changes shape in front of you; turn up the oxygen and it gets hotter, dirtier and faster.

Everything behind that is real. We went through NASA's combustion research and pulled out 24 experiments, from decades of ISS work to a candle that burned for 45 minutes on Mir, each one with its facility, its years and a link to the actual source. Nothing is made up. On top of that, a what-if simulator lets you try cabin setups and suppression tactics, and an AI co-pilot answers your questions by quoting those experiments back at you, with the IDs, so you can check its work.

One thing stuck with us: NASA's own results show the standard fire test for spacecraft materials is too optimistic, and some flames keep burning long after the visible fire goes out. That felt worth making impossible to ignore.
projectDetails.details:
Flame in Freefall pulls together a bunch of NASA studies on how fire behaves without gravity into one interactive setup. It lets users dig through experiments and materials while looking at mission scenarios that might come up later on longer trips. The timeline part shows how some of those discoveries built on each other over time.

There is a chamber that compares flames on Earth to what happens in microgravity and that helps make the differences clearer. An AI assistant pulls answers from the research collection when people ask questions about it. I think the whole thing tries to make the science less distant and maybe spark more interest in space work but fire safety challenges still feel pretty big for moon or mars missions.

The mix of 3D visuals with the research database and AI is what stands out instead of keeping everything in separate reports. They used React and Three js along with some other tools to build it and tried to keep things accurate and easy to use during development. It seems like an independent prototype so it is not meant to replace any official systems.

projectDetails.name: Project Galactic Mission
projectDetails.summary:
Galactic Mission is an interactive space exploration game designed for children aged 7–12. We developed a virtual Moon Base where players take on the role of astronauts and complete different missions and activities.

The game includes Moon Adventure, where players collect energy crystals, a Star Shop and Character Studio for customisation, Space School for learning interesting space facts, and Mission Control, where players make decisions that affect their mission. Players also manage important resources such as water, oxygen, food, power and health while learning about teamwork and astronaut safety.

Our project addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by giving children a fun and interactive way to experience some of the responsibilities and challenges of being an astronaut. It is important because it makes learning about space more engaging, encourages problem-solving and teamwork, and helps younger children become more interested in science and space exploration
projectDetails.details:
Galactic Mission is an interactive space exploration game designed for children aged 7–12. Players become astronauts and explore a virtual Moon Base while completing missions and learning about space.

The game works through different sections. In Moon Adventure, players move their astronaut, collect energy crystals and complete levels. In Mission Control, they make decisions that affect their mission. They can also explore different Moon Base locations, learn space facts in Space School, complete astronaut training activities, and look after their crew. The game also includes a Character Studio and Star Shop where players can customise their astronauts.

The main benefit of Galactic Mission is that it makes learning about space fun and interactive. It encourages problem-solving, decision-making, teamwork and curiosity about science. Our goal is to help younger children understand some of the challenges astronauts face and become more interested in space exploration.

We developed the game using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We used GitHub to store our code and publish the game online, and Canva to create our presentation. We also used ChatGPT to assist with coding, improving features, debugging and organising information.

What makes our project creative is that it combines learning with gameplay. Instead of only reading about astronauts, children can experience a simplified version of a space mission themselves. While developing it, we considered the target age group, making the controls simple, the activities educational, and the design colourful and engaging.

projectDetails.name: ARES ATLAS: Martian Surface Exploration & EVA Mission Planner
projectDetails.summary: ARES ATLAS is an interactive mission-planning map for future astronauts walking on Mars, like Google Maps for Mars. We processed a real NASA HiRISE elevation model of part of Jezero Crater and combined it with Perseverance’s actual traverse from NASA’s PLACES data. Users explore the terrain in 2D and 3D, view slope and elevation layers, and generate walking routes using a pathfinding algorithm. They can compare a shorter route with a slope-aware route, and an animated astronaut (EVA-01) walks the chosen route. It addresses the challenge by layering data from several NASA missions into one view that helps plan a Marswalk. It matters because crews will need practical, understandable tools to plan safe and scientifically useful surface excursions.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: ARES ATLAS lets a user explore a real part of Jezero Crater (about 6.6 × 14.4 km), select destinations, and generate Marswalk routes between them. It shows elevation and slope-hazard layers, Perseverance’s historical traverse, a mission dashboard (distance, elevation gain and loss, maximum and average slope, estimated walking time, terrain exposure), and an animated astronaut that walks the route. It also has a NASA weather reference panel and a data-sources panel that marks each source as integrated, partial, reference-only or simulated.

How it works: We parsed the 380 MB HiRISE DTM (DTEEC_045994_1985_046060_1985_U01, a PDS3 float32 raster, 14,266 × 6,673 pixels at about 1 m) and checked its projection against its label. We resampled it to a 16 m browser-friendly grid and computed slopes from it. We projected Perseverance PLACES positions into the same coordinate system and checked them against the terrain elevations (median offset about 4 m). Routes are computed with A* over the terrain grid. The Shorter route minimizes distance. The Safer route adds penalties for steep slopes and for cells near gaps in the data. Both avoid no-data areas.

Benefits: It gives a quick, understandable way to compare route options using real terrain, and it clearly separates real, derived and simulated information.

Goal: A prototype showing how NASA data from several missions can be combined into one planning tool for human explorers.

Limitations: Coverage is one HiRISE terrain model, not the whole crater. The Mars Trek imagery previews were not georeferenced, so the surface is shaded from the elevation data, not satellite imagery. The “safer” route is slope-aware only and does not model dust, radiation, loose soil, ice or weather. The 12 demo destinations, the ice layer, the 2.5 km/h walking speed and the 320 kcal/h energy figure are simulated or assumed and are labeled as such in the app.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js for 3D, HTML canvas for the 2D map, Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Pillow) for data processing, Netlify for hosting.

Use of AI tools: The project concept and requirements were defined by our team, and we used AI tools to help refine and develop it. Claude (Anthropic) helped write the application code and the data-processing script, and helped draft this description and our presentation slides. We also used AI tools to help research and understand the NASA data resources. All NASA data was processed and checked using the files we downloaded from NASA.

projectDetails.name: What We Left Behind
projectDetails.summary:
What We Left Behind is a website designed to give young space enthusiasts an accessible and engaging overview of unique pieces of NASA hardware left behind across the Solar System, and sometimes beyond.

The website features an interactive map highlighting the current locations of each piece of equipment. Visitors can click on individual symbols to explore dedicated pages about each machine. Told from the machine’s own first-person perspective, each page explores its history, what makes it extraordinary, and what it has taught humanity about space and exploration.

Each page also includes an expandable educational section that explains the science and technology behind key components in simple, easy-to-understand terms. These include technologies such as SEIS, LLRR, and RTGs, helping visitors understand not only what these machines have accomplished, but also how they work.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description: What We Left Behind

What does the project do, and how does it work?

What We Left Behind is an educational website designed to introduce young space enthusiasts to the fascinating pieces of NASA hardware that have been left behind across the Solar System and beyond. The website features an interactive map that displays the current locations of these objects. Visitors can click on individual symbols to access dedicated pages about each piece of equipment. Each page tells the story from the machine's own first-person perspective, exploring its history, purpose, achievements, and contributions to space exploration. It also includes expandable educational sections that explain the science and technology behind important components, such as SEIS, LLRR, and RTGs, in simple, accessible language.

What benefits does the project have?

The project makes complex scientific information more accessible and enjoyable for younger audiences. It encourages curiosity about space, develops scientific awareness, and helps visitors understand the technology behind some of humanity's greatest achievements in space exploration. The interactive format also makes learning more engaging than simply reading information from a textbook or article.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space enthusiasts by highlighting the often-overlooked technology that has made space exploration possible. We hope to help young people develop a deeper appreciation for scientific innovation and understand how even machines that are no longer active continue to contribute to humanity's knowledge of the universe. Ultimately, the project aims to make space science more approachable and encourage people to explore beyond Earth.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The project was developed as a website using mobile-friendly website builders such as Bolt.new. The organization and paraphrasing of information were assisted by large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and Gemini. The solar system diagram and interactive machine symbols were also generated using Gemini.

How is your project creative?

Our project takes a creative approach to science communication by telling the stories of space hardware from the machines' own first-person perspectives. The interactive map adds an element of exploration, letting users discover these objects across the Solar System. Combining storytelling, interactive technology, and scientific education makes the learning experience both distinctive and memorable.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered our target audience, accessibility, scientific accuracy, educational value, and overall user experience. Since the website is aimed at young space enthusiasts, we wanted to explain complex scientific concepts in language that is easy to understand without sacrificing important information. We also considered how to make the website visually appealing and simple to navigate, ensuring that visitors could easily find and explore different pieces of hardware. Finally, we focused on presenting reliable information, creating an engaging storytelling experience, and highlighting the historical and scientific significance of each object.

projectDetails.name: Project LUNA-SAFE
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA-SAFE is a browser-based simulation prototype designed to support astronaut health monitoring and lunar mission safety.

The project began with an idea to protect future lunar habitats using sensors that could monitor temperature, vibration, structural tilt, and cabin pressure. It then expanded to focus on astronaut health, including heart rate, blood oxygen levels, activity, and health alerts.

As a physiotherapy student, I also introduced a Physical Therapy & Rehabilitation section to support astronaut health before, during, and after space missions. This feature records reported pain, fatigue, exercise activity, and recovery trends.

The prototype demonstrates how astronauts can request medical or rehabilitation reviews and how Mission Control can acknowledge and document those requests. A supporting Site Planner explores lunar terrain using NASA-derived data.

LUNA-SAFE currently uses simulated health readings. Our future goal is to connect a wearable monitoring device and validated sensors to the software, creating a more integrated system for astronaut health and safety.
projectDetails.details:
How LUNA-SAFE Works

LUNA-SAFE is an interactive web application developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It brings astronaut health monitoring, rehabilitation tracking, lunar habitat safety, and site exploration into one interface.

1. Astronaut Health

This section simulates astronaut health readings, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and activity. It displays alerts when selected values reach demonstration warning thresholds. The health history feature records simulated readings and displays trends over time. Body temperature can also be recorded manually.

2. Medical Assistance and Mission Control

An astronaut can request medical assistance through the application. Mission Control can acknowledge and document the request. The software also demonstrates oxygen-related review requests initiated by an astronaut or Mission Control. These are requests for qualified review, not automatic changes to oxygen delivery or life-support equipment.

3. Physical Therapy & Rehabilitation

This section was inspired by the project developer's physiotherapy background. It includes three mission phases: pre-flight, in-flight, and post-flight.

Users can record discomfort, fatigue, perceived exertion, exercise type, and session duration. The application displays symptom flags, records rehabilitation check-ins, and tracks reported fatigue over time. Users can request a rehabilitation team review, which Mission Control can acknowledge and document.

4. Base Safety

The Base Safety section demonstrates how future sensors could monitor a lunar habitat's temperature, vibration, structural tilt, and pressure conditions. It displays simulated alerts to help explain how environmental monitoring could support crew safety.

5. Site Planner

The Site Planner explores potential lunar habitat locations near Shackleton Rim. The project uses NASA-derived lunar terrain and illumination resources to investigate slope conditions and possible site candidates. These results are exploratory and do not certify any location as safe for construction.

6. Future Wearable Device

A future version could connect a wearable device containing suitable heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, and motion sensors. The device would send readings to the software, where they could be recorded, visualized, and reviewed. Hardware accuracy, communication reliability, clinical thresholds, and safety would require further testing and validation.

Technology and Impact

The current prototype runs locally in a web browser and uses simulated health and safety data. Some records can be saved locally and exported as CSV files.

LUNA-SAFE aims to demonstrate how a connected monitoring interface could help astronauts and mission teams recognize changes, document concerns, and coordinate appropriate reviews.

The prototype is not a certified medical device, does not diagnose health conditions, and does not control physical life-support systems.

projectDetails.name: Rovers in the red dust,Project MAS Explorers
projectDetails.summary:
Rovers in the Red Dust brings the historic journey of NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, to life through an engaging, first-person narrative. Told from the perspective of the rovers in "Echoes Across the Red Desert," our project transforms complex space exploration data into an accessible story of discovery, resilience, and companionship on Mars.

Alongside the narrative, the presentation breaks down the rovers' engineering ("What Are Rovers Made From?"), key scientific findings about past water activity on Mars ("What Did They Teach Us?"), mission milestones, and data visualizations comparingmission expectations against real-world achievements. Finally, our project highlights the critical importance of planetary protection and responsible space exploration ("Why We Must Protect Other Worlds"). By blending storytelling with verified NASA mission data, Rovers in the Red Dust inspires audiences to appreciate Mars exploration and safeguard extraterrestrial environments for future generations.
projectDetails.details:
About Our Project

Rovers in the Red Dust was created for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" challenge. Our project introduces school-age students to NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers-Spirit and Opportunity-by combining an engaging first-person story with clear explanations of the hardware they were made from and the science they made possible.

How It Works & Why It Is Creative

Instead of presenting dry facts, we tell the rovers' mission from their own point of view in "Echoes Across the Red Desert," alongside visual breakdowns of:

• Rover Hardware: Lightweight aluminum frames, aerogel insulation to survive -96°C nights, solar arrays with lithium-ion batteries, a six-wheel rocker-bogie suspension, panoramic cameras, and the Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT).

• Scientific Discoveries & Stats: Although planned for only 90 Martian days (sols), Spirit lasted 2,208 sols (driving 7.73 km) and Opportunity lasted 5,111 sols (driving 45.16 km), uncovering mineral veins and hematite "blueberries" that proved liquid water once flowed on Mars.

• Our Message: Though these rovers now rest silent on Mars, they are abandoned, never forgotten-reminding us that we are responsible for making these extraordinary machines and remembering what they achieved.

Benefits, Impact & Tools Used

• Intended Impact: Helps young space enthusiasts easily understand how real space hardware works and inspires curiosity about planetary exploration.

• Tools & Resources Used: Built using Canva for visual design and storytelling, grounded in official NASA/JPL-Caltech Mars Exploration Rover mission records and imagery.

Our Story: Echoes Across the Red Desert

The Awakening

It was January 4th, 2004, when I landed on the dusty red planet I had been sent to explore. I rested on my lander platform, absorbing the Sun's energy through my solar panels. Once I had gathered enough energy. I rolled off my landing platform, ready to explore the rolling red hills and observe the distant skies. Red hills and rusty soll stretched as far as my cameras could see. I spent the day roaming the desolate desert, observing the strange rocks and distant hills. Everything was unfamiliar, yet there was so much to discover. The landscape was quiet, almost as though the entire planet was waiting for me to uncover its secrets. At first, I thought I was entirely alone on this unfamiliar world. But I soon discovered that I wasn't the first visitor to Mars. High above me, circling the planet, was an older spacecraft. His name was Mars Global Surveyor.

He had arrived in 1997, long before my journey began. He was one of the earliest explorers to study Mars from orbit, spending years mapping its surface and observing its many features. I imagined him as a quiet, wise old guardian, watching over the planet from the skies. A few years later, another spacecraft joined him. His name was Mars Odyssey. and he had arrived in 2001. He would soon become an important part of my journey, helping me study my surroundings and relaying my messages. discoveries and observations to the humans back on Earth. For a while, both orbiters continued their journeys above me. I was a newcomer, with an entire world waiting to be explored, while they had already spent years studying it. Eventually, in November 2006, Mars Global Surveyor fell silent. His transmissions stopped, but I like to imagine him continuing his quiet journey around Mars, an old observer who had witnessed so much of the Red Planet's history.

A Memorable Discovery

Mars certainly had many secrets. The rocks scattered across the landscape contained fascinating minerals, and I spent much of my time photographing and examining them. One particular rock caught my attention. It was considerably larger than the others, and something about it made me curious. I brushed away the layer of dust covering its surface, hoping to get a better look. Its exterior was still a familiar dusty reddish-brown. I wasn't ready to give up, though. I had a feeling there was something more beneath that rusty exterior. After several minutes of examining and brushing away the dust, I noticed a change in colour. Beneath the reddish surface was something much darker. I carefully examined its exposed interior, revealing fresh, dark-grey rock. almost the colour of the night sky. What fascinated me even more were the tiny veins of lighter-coloured minerals running through it. They were clues left behind by ancient water, evidence that this seemingly lifeless world had once been very different.

To think that this dry, dusty planet had once held rivers and lakes was remarkable. Mars had a history far richer than its barren landscape suggested, and I was only beginning to uncover it. I spent the following days examining the rocks scattered across the landscape, noticing the differences in their colours, textures and mineral compositions. Each one seemed to hold another piece of Mars's ancient history. I carefully recorded my observations and sent my discoveries to Mars Odyssey, the spacecraft orbiting above me, which relayed my findings back to the humans on Earth. One day, while preparing to send another message to Odyssey about a recent discovery, something unexpected happened. Instead of receiving a confirmation from the orbiter, I picked up a different transmission. It was a message from another rover. Another rover? Here on Mars?

A Friend Across the Red Desert

It was quite strange. I had never imagined there was another rover exploring Mars alongside me. The message contained details of an interesting discovery: millions of tiny. BB-sized mineral spheres scattered across the Martian soil. They had been nicknamed "blueberries" because of their round shape. These little spheres were made largely of hematite, a mineral that can form in the presence of water. They were remarkable clues, suggesting that liquid water had once flowed through or soaked the Martian ground. I found it fascinating that, somewhere on this enormous planet, another explorer was uncovering secrets of its own. Perhaps I wasn't quite as alone as I had first thought. I continued exploring my side of the planet, and messages from the other rover gradually became a familiar part of my days. I had learned her name was Opportunity. Through her transmissions. I discovered more about her adventures and the fascinating things she encountered on her side of Mars.

Eventually, I decided to send her a message of my own. I shared some of my recent discoveries and waited for a reply. And waited. An entire day passed, but nothing came back. There was no response, no familiar transmission, only silence. The following day, when I contacted Mars Odyssey again. I received an explanation. It seemed that messages weren't always delivered Immediately. Sometimes transmissions could be delayed, depending on the spacecraft's position and orbit. I asked Odyssey if there was another way I could reach Opportunity, but unfortunately, she had already passed beyond the area where Odyssey could relay my message to her. She was continuing her journey along the other side of Mars. I returned to my explorations, hoping that one day our paths, or at least our transmissions, would cross again.

I was exploring a nearby crater when I received an unexpected message through Mars Odyssey. It was from Opportunity! She had sent some of her latest exploration data, along with a rather curious question: Was I really exploring the other side of Mars? Over the following days, our messages became more frequent. We exchanged discoveries, observations and little details about our surroundings. Sometimes we even spoke about the night sky above us and the harsh Martian winters. I told her about the freezing temperatures on my side of the planet, how the cold could affect my instruments and make exploration increasingly difficult. She explained that winters on her side were no gentler. I told her about the freezing temperatures on my side of the planet, how the cold could affect my instruments and make exploration increasingly difficult. She explained that winters on her side were no gentler.

Our transmissions gradually became a familiar part of my days. We continued exchanging messages, sharing discoveries from opposite sides of our enormous red world. Then, one day. I received some interesting news from Mars Odyssey. A new spacecraft had arrived in orbit around Mars. Its name was Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, or MRO. He was quite different from Odyssey. Efficient, observant and equipped with an incredibly powerful camera, he was designed to study Mars in extraordinary detail and send valuable information back to Earth. It seemed Mars had welcomed another explorer.

A Little Machine, A Lasting Legacy

The days passed, and our explorations continued. I wandered across my side of Mars while Opportunity explored hers. We sent our discoveries and observations back to Earth, each of us uncovering another little piece of this planet's history. Then, one day, everything changed. I was exploring near a crater when my wheels sank into a patch of soft sand. I tried reversing, but instead of freeing myself. I sank deeper and tilted at an awkward angle. I tried moving forward, then backward, desperately searching for firmer ground But nothing worked. I wasn't going to give up. I had so much more to discoverl I still wanted to explore the distant hills, examine unfamiliar rocks and perhaps, one day, meet Opportunity.

However, my attempts were consuming too much energy. I had to stop moving and conserve what little power remained. My tilted position left my solar panels unable to gather enough sunlight. I sent what I hoped would be one last message through Odyssey. I wanted to tell Opportunity that I was in trouble, that I was still trying, that I hadn't given up. But my energy was fading. The landscape grew darker. My Instruments fell silent, and my transmissions came to an end... Opportunity waited for another message from her twin. An entire day passed. but nothing arrived. Concerned, she contacted Mars Odyssey and asked if he had heard from Spirit. He hadn't received anything since the previous evening.

Eventually, she learned what had happened. Her twin had become trapped in soft Martian soil, tilted at an angle that prevented his solar panels from receiving sufficient sunlight. Despite his efforts to escape, his energy had eventually run out. Spirit had been my companion throughout our journey across Mars. His messages had made the long days of exploration interesting, and I had grown accustomed to sharing my discoveries with him. Now, the familiar transmissions were gone. I continued exploring the red deserts, climbing over hills and examining rocks and minerals. I still sent my daily observations to Odyssey and MRO. just as I had always done. But something was missing. The silence was palpable, and the loneliness that I had once known during my earliest days on Mars returned. Days turned into months, and months into years.

Then, one day. MRO sent me a warning. A dust storm was forming nearby. It appeared distant and not particularly threatening, so I continued my work. I was examining a stone when I noticed a sudden change in the atmosphere. A cold breeze swept across the landscape, followed by enormous clouds of red dust. The storm arrived almost all at once. Sand swirled around me in powerful gusts, obscuring everything my cameras could see. I decided to remain still until it passed, but the winds continued. Eventually, I attempted to move forward, hoping to escape its path. Yet wherever I went, the dust seemed to follow. The days passed. The sunlight disappeared behind the enormous clouds. and my solar panels struggled to gather enough energy. I could no longer send my usual messages to Odyssey or MRO.

I had survived countless Martian winters, crossed vast stretches of desert and uncovered secrets buried beneath the red soll. But this storm was different. My energy continued to fade. My movements grew slower, and the familiar landscape disappeared behind an endless haze of red.I had once wondered what it would be like to explore Mars without my twin. Now, I understood. And then, darkness came. Silence followed.

Note on Historical Accuracy: This story is a fictionalised retelling of the Mars rovers' journeys, narrated from their perspectives. Their personalities, emotions, thoughts and conversations have been imagined. and certain events have been dramatised for storytelling purposes. However, the major historical events, scientific discoveries and mission details are based on real events and NASA records.

Note: All images in our presentation were sourced from NASA/JPL-Caltech (and Cornell University for PIA05591)

projectDetails.name: Project Mission Architect
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Architect is a browser-based simulator where players design and launch a real-style NASA space telescope mission, from first idea to orbit.

What it is: Players choose science objectives (one to three, across three levels), then select wavelengths, instruments and optics, an orbit, a launch vehicle, and a budget across the four mission segments: launch, space, ground and user. A 3D spacecraft updates as they build it, then flies to its orbit with live telemetry. A final report scores the design and compares it to real missions such as Hubble, Webb, Chandra and Fermi.

How it addresses the challenge: It makes a whole space mission understandable through interactive 3D visualisation. It covers the mission concept, trajectory, timeline and spacecraft layout. Its steps follow NASA's Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab studies, with GMAT-style orbit readouts and a Mission Viz-style flight.

Why it matters: Mission design involves trade-offs between science goals, engineering limits and cost. Players learn that every choice affects the others, and that a mission succeeds only if all four segments work together. It needs no special software and runs on phones and computers.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Architect is a browser game that teaches how a space mission is designed. The player picks one to three science objectives across three levels, such as exoplanet atmospheres, black holes or the first galaxies. They then follow six steps modelled on NASA's Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab studies:

  1. Choose the science objectives.
  2. Choose wavelengths. Options that don't fit the objectives are disabled.
  3. Choose instruments and optics. A 3D spacecraft updates as they build it.
  4. Compare four orbits, with a GMAT-style readout of period, signal delay and launcher performance.
  5. Pick a launch vehicle that can carry the spacecraft's mass to that orbit.
  6. Split a budget across the space, ground and user segments.

The game then runs a countdown and flies the spacecraft in 3D with live telemetry. It ends with a score out of 100 and an explanation of each choice. The report also compares the design to real missions (Hubble, Webb, Chandra, Fermi, Swift, TESS) and shows a mission timeline. Underfunding any of the four segments (launch, space, ground, user) makes the mission fail.

Benefits and intended impact

Players learn that mission design is a series of trade-offs, and that a mission needs all four segments to work. It runs in a browser on phones and computers, with no installation. It is meant for students and beginners, and it points them to the NASA resources it draws on.

Tools

I built it as a single HTML file in JavaScript and CSS, using Three.js for the 3D view and the Web Audio API for sound effects. The deck was made with Claude's Slides tool. I checked the game logic with Node scripts and captured the interface screenshots with Playwright. I did not use any special hardware.

Creativity

Instead of a quiz, the game lets players build a spacecraft and watch it fly. Every NASA resource in the challenge became a game mechanic, such as the CML progress bar and the GMAT-style orbit readout. Choices have realistic consequences: infrared telescopes do best at L2, X-ray telescopes do best in a highly elliptical orbit, and a rocket that is too small fails at launch.

Factors considered

Accuracy vs. simplicity: The numbers are simplified, inspired by real missions, and the game says so.

Accessibility: It works on phones and needs no install.

Clear feedback: The game gives a reason for every score and failure.

Scope: It covers space telescopes only, not other mission types.

Testing limit: I tested the game's logic and interface. I could not test the 3D view in my environment, so check it in your browser before submitting.

projectDetails.name: ASTRO - astornaut health monitoring sotware
projectDetails.summary:
Astronauts face many health challenges in space, including radiation, muscle loss, stress, and sleep problems.

Astro is a smart website designed to help astronauts monitor their health using information from connected medical devices and sensors.

It also demonstrates health alerts, wellbeing check-ins, and communication with Earth.

Astro aims to make space exploration safer and healthier for future astronauts.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRO — Astronaut Health Monitoring System

NASA Space Apps Challenge | Presentation Speech

Imagine being millions of kilometres away from Earth.

You're travelling through space, surrounded by darkness and stars, when suddenly, you begin to feel unwell.

There's no hospital nearby, no doctor you can immediately visit, and contacting Earth could take more than 20 minutes, depending on how far away you are.

So, how can astronauts monitor their health when help is millions of kilometres away?

Hello everyone!

Today, I'm excited to introduce my project, Astro — Astronaut Health Monitoring System.

Space exploration is one of humanity's greatest achievements, but living in space creates serious challenges for the human body.

Without Earth's gravity, astronauts can experience muscle weakness, bone density loss, changes in blood circulation, and problems with vision and balance.

They are also exposed to space radiation, disrupted sleep schedules, and psychological stress caused by isolation.

These challenges become even more serious during long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

That's where Astro comes in.

Astro is a connected health-monitoring platform designed to help astronauts understand their physical and mental wellbeing while travelling through space.

But here's the important question: How does Astro actually work?

Astro is designed to connect with different monitoring devices, including wearable health bands, medical instruments, radiation dosimeters, and spacecraft environmental sensors.

These devices can collect information about cardiovascular health, oxygen levels, radiation exposure, and conditions inside the spacecraft.

Astro brings this information together into one easy-to-understand dashboard.

Instead of displaying complicated medical numbers without explanation, Astro helps astronauts understand what the readings mean and whether something may need attention.

For example, imagine an astronaut's wearable device detects an unusual cardiovascular reading.

Astro could examine the reading alongside the astronaut's recent activity, identify a potentially concerning change, and display a warning recommending further assessment.

The platform also includes a wellbeing questionnaire where astronauts can record their mood, stress, energy, sleep, and physical discomfort.

Astro can also help monitor exercise routines, radiation exposure, and cabin conditions such as carbon dioxide and oxygen levels.

And because communication with Earth isn't always immediate, Astro is designed to support onboard health awareness while preparing reports for ground control.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I developed an interactive website that demonstrates how these features could work together.

My prototype includes simulated health measurements, a device-connection demonstration, health-risk monitoring, mission selection, wellbeing check-ins, and a ground communications interface.

Although the current prototype uses simulated data, the long-term vision is to connect Astro with real, validated medical and spacecraft monitoring equipment.

What makes Astro important is that it doesn't just show health information. It aims to help astronauts understand that information and take appropriate action.

I believe that the future of space exploration isn't only about travelling farther, discovering new planets, or building advanced spacecraft.

It's also about protecting the people who make those discoveries possible.

Because when humanity travels beyond Earth, we must make sure astronaut health travels with us.

Astro — Monitoring Health. Supporting Astronauts. Advancing Human Space Exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project NASASIANSS
projectDetails.summary: Collective Brain is an AI-powered astronaut health management system that monitors the entire crew as one connected ecosystem rather than focusing on individuals. It analyses astronauts' physical health, mental wellbeing, sleep patterns, workload and environmental conditions to detect potential problems early and recommend personalised solutions. The system includes features such as tracking muscle and bone loss, monitoring heart health and vision changes, detecting stress and isolation, improving sleep schedules, tracking immune health and managing radiation exposure. What makes Collective Brain unique is its ability to identify how individual health issues can affect the entire crew, predict possible risks and intelligently redistribute support, activities and workloads to maintain the crew's overall health, balance and mission readiness.
projectDetails.details:
Collective Brain is an AI-powered astronaut health intelligence system designed to monitor the wellbeing of an entire crew rather than focusing on individual astronauts separately.

During space missions, astronauts face challenges such as muscle and bone loss, radiation exposure, vision changes, sleep disruption, stress and immune-system changes. These problems can affect not only individuals but also the performance and stability of the entire crew.

Our solution connects different aspects of astronaut health and analyses how they influence one another. It aims to identify patterns, detect potential risks and predict how individual health conditions could affect the crew as a whole. For example, if several astronauts experience stress, exhaustion or isolation at the same time, Collective Brain can identify a possible decline in crew stability and highlight risks to communication and mission efficiency.

The system includes eight specialised features: Muscle Trading Network, Heartbeat Balancer, Crowdsourced Eyes, Mood Gravity, Sleep Orchestra, Immune Shield, Radiation Budget System and Bone Credits System. Each feature focuses on a different astronaut health challenge while contributing information to the overall crew-health picture.

What makes our project unique is its crew-based intelligence approach. Instead of simply displaying separate health measurements, it considers the connections between astronauts and aims to recommend actions such as personalised exercise, workload adjustments, improved sleep schedules and radiation-aware task distribution.

The intended impact is to support healthier astronauts, stronger teamwork, earlier risk identification and safer, more efficient long-duration space missions. In the future, Collective Brain could be developed further with more advanced predictions, improved health-data integration and personalised recommendations.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project NGS
projectDetails.summary:
Space Relics: Every Object Has a Story is an interactive project that helps young people learn about NASA's retired and inactive spacecraft and equipment.

Our project focuses on equipment left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. Instead of seeing these objects as old or forgotten machines, users can discover their stories and learn about the important science and missions connected to them.

Users can explore an interactive map, learn about different space objects, listen to their stories, and complete fun science quests and mini-games. The project is designed for school-age students and teachers to make space history and science easier and more interesting to understand.

Our goal is to show that these objects are not just discarded machines. They are part of human history and can inspire the next generation to explore space.
projectDetails.details:
Space Relics is an interactive digital experience that helps young people learn about NASA's retired and inactive spacecraft and equipment. Our project focuses on objects left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space.

Users can explore an interactive map and choose different objects to learn about. Each object has its own story, including what it was built for, what it discovered, and why it is still important today. Users can also take part in science quests and mini-games to make learning more fun and interactive.

Our project is creative because it turns space equipment into characters that can tell their own stories. This makes space history easier and more interesting for young people to understand.

We designed Space Relics for school-age students and teachers. We also considered accessibility by including ideas such as audio narration, captions, simple language, and multilingual content.

The main goal of our project is to show that NASA's discarded equipment is not just old machinery. These objects are part of human history and can still inspire future generations to learn about science and space exploration.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. projectDetails.name: Project Pulse X
projectDetails.summary:
PULSE X is an interactive astronaut health-monitoring software designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It provides a dashboard that brings important health indicators together, including cardiovascular activity, bone health, immune-system status, radiation exposure, and mental wellbeing.

The software features an animated ECG graph and changing heart-rate readings, as well as an interactive mental-wellbeing assessment where users can select emotions such as calm, anxious, stressed, or tired. Based on their selections, the system displays simulated heart-rate responses and helpful recommendations. It also includes health-monitoring sections and a health-report feature.

PULSE X addresses the challenge of helping astronauts recognize and evaluate potential health changes while living in space, where microgravity, radiation, isolation, and confinement can affect their wellbeing. This project is important because early awareness and regular health monitoring can support better decisions, encourage healthy habits, and contribute to safer, longer space missions.
projectDetails.details: PULSE X is an interactive astronaut health-monitoring software that tracks simulated health indicators such as heart rate, bone health, immune status, radiation exposure, and mental wellbeing. It features an animated ECG graph, interactive mood assessments, and personalized recommendations to help astronauts evaluate their health. Its goal is to support healthier and safer space missions by encouraging early awareness of potential health changes. The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with W3Schools and ChatGPT as development resources. Its creative design combines physical and mental health monitoring in one easy-to-use dashboard.

projectDetails.name: Project Raghad
projectDetails.summary: The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, web-based simulation designed to teach students space exploration dynamics, life support management, and lunar/Martian survival through gameplay. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, the project addresses the complexity of space environmental hazards—such as lunar long dark nights, Martian dust storms, and solar radiation—by transforming them into an intuitive, strategic decision-making experience. Players manage core survival resources including Power, Oxygen, Shield integrity, and Science progress across mission days (Sols). By choosing daily operational strategies (Balanced Work, Fast Research, Shield Repair, or Oxygen/Power generation), astronauts must balance scientific discovery with survival. This project is important because it bridges authentic NASA space weather and exploration data (sourced from NASA DONKI, Artemis/LRO, and Mars 2020 Perseverance) with accessible STEM education. Running seamlessly in any browser without installation, it empowers 10th-grade students and junior learners to grasp complex systems engineering and space mission operations through hands-on gameplay.
projectDetails.details: How it Works: The application features a web interface built with HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, offering multi-screen navigation (Intro, Mission Dashboard, and Win/Loss End Screens). Players select either a Moon or Mars base and manage four critical resources: Power, Oxygen, Shield, and Science. Each "Sol" (day), players select an operational strategy that updates resource meters and checks win/loss conditions (reaching 100% Science wins the game). Tools & Languages: Developed using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (vanilla JS), hosted live on Netlify, with slide design created via Google Slides. Creativity & Impact: It transforms complex orbital mechanics and planetary survival constraints into a lightweight, highly accessible educational mini-game that runs in any browser with zero setup.

projectDetails.name: RED ALERT – A Smart Energy Management System for Future Mars Habitats.
projectDetails.summary:
RED ALERT — Don't Just Detect an Energy Emergency. Respond to It.

Inspired by the energy challenges experienced by NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers, our team developed RED ALERT, a smart energy-management prototype designed to protect future Mars habitats from electricity shortages during dust storms.

Martian dust storms reduce sunlight reaching solar panels, decreasing electricity generation and threatening essential habitat operations. RED ALERT addresses this problem using an Arduino controller, Light Dependent Resistor (LDR), and dust sensors to monitor sunlight intensity and dust levels. When hazardous conditions are detected, the system automatically activates warnings and switches off nonessential electrical loads, conserving energy for critical operations. A companion application provides environmental monitoring, emergency alerts, and a 72-hour simulation to evaluate potential energy shortages.

The project also proposes integrating a layered Martian surface map combining NASA terrain data, environmental conditions, habitat energy information, and astronaut exploration routes to support safer mission planning.

RED ALERT is important because it goes beyond detecting danger: it responds automatically, helping conserve limited electricity, protect essential systems, and improve the safety and sustainability of future Mars exploration.
projectDetails.details:
RED ALERT — Project Details

Project: RED ALERT — A Smart Energy Management System for Future Mars Habitats

Slogan: Don't Just Detect an Energy Emergency. Respond to It.

1. What does our project do, and how does it work?

What happens when a future Mars habitat begins losing its electricity supply during a powerful dust storm? Its solar panels may generate less energy, but essential systems must continue operating. This challenge inspired our team to develop RED ALERT, an automated energy-management prototype designed to detect hazardous environmental conditions and conserve electricity before energy shortages become critical.

Martian dust storms can scatter and absorb sunlight, reducing the amount of solar radiation reaching photovoltaic panels. Dust can also accumulate on panel surfaces, further reducing their efficiency. These effects create a serious problem for solar-powered equipment because electricity consumption may continue even when energy generation decreases.

Our research was inspired by NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers. In November 2008, Spirit experienced a severe energy shortage during dusty conditions, generating approximately 89 watt-hours (Wh) of electricity on November 9. In 2018, Opportunity lost communication during a planet-wide dust storm. These missions demonstrated the importance of carefully managing electricity when sunlight becomes limited.

RED ALERT responds to this problem through a miniature Martian habitat prototype using an Arduino controller, Light Dependent Resistor (LDR), and dust sensors.

The LDR monitors changes in light intensity, while the dust sensors detect airborne dust conditions. The Arduino receives the sensor readings, analyzes environmental changes, and compares the readings with programmed thresholds.

The system operates through four main stages:

DETECT → ANALYZE → RESPOND → PROTECT

DETECT: The LDR and dust sensors monitor environmental conditions associated with dust storms and reduced sunlight.

ANALYZE: The Arduino processes the sensor readings and determines whether programmed warning or emergency thresholds have been reached.

RESPOND: When emergency conditions are detected, the system activates warnings and automatically switches off selected nonessential electrical loads.

PROTECT: Essential demonstration loads remain operational while unnecessary electricity consumption is reduced.

For example, if a simulated dust storm reduces light intensity and increases detected dust levels, the Arduino identifies the hazardous conditions and initiates the programmed energy-saving response. Selected nonessential equipment is automatically switched off while essential demonstration equipment remains active.

This is what makes RED ALERT more than a dust-storm detector: it does not simply recognize a potential energy emergency; it automatically responds to conserve electricity.

Our project also includes a companion web application developed using HTML and JavaScript. The application organizes environmental monitoring, energy information, emergency alerts, and simulated energy-management scenarios.

In addition, we developed a JavaScript-based Martian mapping component. Our proposed next step is to integrate this map with RED ALERT's habitat energy information and NASA environmental and terrain datasets, allowing explorers to consider energy conditions alongside possible exploration routes.

2. What benefits does our project provide?

RED ALERT demonstrates how automated energy management could help future Mars habitats operate more efficiently during periods of reduced solar-energy generation.

Conserving limited electricity

When a dust storm reduces sunlight, solar panels may produce less electricity than usual. If all electrical equipment continues operating normally, stored energy can decrease rapidly.

RED ALERT addresses this problem by automatically switching off selected nonessential loads, reducing unnecessary consumption and helping preserve the available energy reserve.

Prioritizing essential operations

Future Mars habitats will require electricity for critical functions, including communication, scientific equipment, lighting, and life-support systems.

Our prototype demonstrates the principle of prioritizing essential electrical loads during an energy shortage rather than treating all equipment as equally important.

Although the miniature model does not operate real life-support equipment, it demonstrates how essential and nonessential loads can be managed differently.

Detecting environmental risks early

The combination of an LDR and dust sensors allows RED ALERT to recognize environmental changes associated with reduced solar-energy availability.

By identifying these conditions and activating warnings, the system supports earlier responses to potential energy shortages.

Responding automatically

A major advantage of RED ALERT is that its energy-saving response does not depend entirely on someone manually switching off equipment.

The Arduino evaluates sensor readings and initiates the programmed response automatically when emergency thresholds are reached.

This principle could be valuable in future habitats where astronauts must divide their attention among scientific research, maintenance, and exploration activities.

Supporting energy planning

Our companion application includes an energy-simulation concept that allows users to explore how electricity generation, consumption, and conservation affect remaining energy reserves.

For example, consider a simplified hypothetical habitat scenario:

  • Initial stored energy: 100 Wh
  • Energy generated: 20 Wh
  • Normal electricity consumption: 40 Wh
  • Electricity consumption after conservation: 25 Wh

Without RED ALERT's energy-saving response:

100 + 20 − 40 = 80 Wh remaining

With the energy-saving response:

100 + 20 − 25 = 95 Wh remaining

This represents 15 Wh more energy retained and a 37.5% reduction in consumption for the modeled period.

These values illustrate a hypothetical scenario rather than experimentally measured prototype performance. Nevertheless, they demonstrate why reducing nonessential electricity consumption can make an important difference when energy generation is limited.

3. What is the intended impact of our project?

Our intended impact is to explore how automated energy conservation and improved environmental awareness could support safer, more efficient, and sustainable future Mars exploration.

On Earth, electricity shortages can often be addressed through established infrastructure and maintenance services. On Mars, however, astronauts would operate far from immediate assistance, making careful resource management especially important.

RED ALERT demonstrates how an automated system could help protect electricity reserves during environmental emergencies. By reducing nonessential consumption, a future energy-management system could help prioritize critical operations and improve a habitat's ability to respond to reduced power generation.

Our project also considers the relationship between habitat energy availability and exploration planning.

Astronauts conducting Mars walks would need to understand the surrounding terrain, environmental conditions, scientific destinations, and operational risks before leaving their habitat.

To support this broader goal, we developed a Martian mapping component using JavaScript and propose connecting it with RED ALERT's energy-monitoring information.

The envisioned integrated map would combine four information layers:

Terrain Layer: NASA surface imagery and elevation information to help identify geographical features, slopes, and potential obstacles.

Environmental Layer: Available information about Martian environmental conditions relevant to exploration.

Habitat Energy Layer: RED ALERT sensor information, warning conditions, and estimated habitat energy status.

Exploration Route Layer: Proposed astronaut routes connecting the habitat with scientific destinations.

By viewing these layers together, explorers could consider environmental hazards, terrain conditions, and habitat energy risks when planning scientific activities.

The JavaScript mapping component and its proposed integration should be distinguished: the broader connection between live RED ALERT data, NASA datasets, and route-planning functions remains a development goal.

Our project does not claim that automated energy management alone can guarantee astronaut safety or prevent every electricity shortage. Instead, it demonstrates a practical approach that could contribute to more reliable resource management.

Ultimately, our goal is to show that successful Mars exploration depends not only on generating electricity but also on making intelligent decisions about how that electricity is used.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did we use?

RED ALERT combines electronic hardware, sensor-based programming, web development, digital mapping, and scientific energy calculations.

Hardware and electronic components

Arduino Controller

The Arduino is the central processing and control unit of our prototype. It receives environmental sensor readings, evaluates them against programmed thresholds, activates warnings, and controls the automatic shutdown of selected nonessential electrical loads.

Light Dependent Resistor (LDR)

The LDR detects changes in light intensity. It allows the prototype to recognize reduced illumination, which represents one of the major effects of Martian dust storms on solar-energy systems.

Dust Sensors

The dust sensors provide information about airborne dust conditions. Together with the LDR, they allow the Arduino to evaluate environmental changes associated with potential solar-energy shortages.

Electrical Demonstration Loads

The prototype uses electrical loads representing essential and nonessential habitat equipment. These demonstrate how selected nonessential devices can be automatically switched off while essential demonstration loads remain operational.

Miniature Martian Habitat

Our physical model represents a future Mars research base. It provides a visual and practical environment for demonstrating how RED ALERT monitors conditions and responds to potential energy emergencies.

Coding languages and software

C++ — Arduino Programming

We used C++ to program the Arduino controller.

The code manages sensor readings, threshold comparisons, warning activation, and automatic load-control decisions.

This programming allows the system to detect hazardous environmental conditions and respond without requiring each action to be performed manually.

HTML — Web Application Structure

We used HTML to build and organize the structure of the RED ALERT companion application.

HTML provides the foundation for displaying the project's information, environmental monitoring sections, energy information, emergency alerts, and simulation interface.

JavaScript — Application Functionality

We used JavaScript to develop the application's interactive functions.

JavaScript supports the presentation and processing of information, user interactions, and simulated energy-management scenarios.

The application is designed to help users understand environmental changes and examine how different electricity-generation and consumption conditions could affect remaining energy reserves.

JavaScript — Martian Mapping

We also used JavaScript to develop the Martian mapping component.

The mapping system forms the foundation for our proposed integration of terrain information, environmental data, habitat energy conditions, and astronaut exploration routes.

This would allow different types of information to be considered together instead of being viewed separately.

Scientific calculations

Our project uses basic electrical relationships to explain and model energy generation and consumption.

Electrical Power:

P = V × I

Where P represents power in watts, V represents voltage, and I represents current.

Electrical Energy:

E = P × t

Where E represents energy, P represents power, and t represents time.

Remaining Energy:

E_remaining = E_stored + E_generated − E_consumed

These relationships provide a mathematical basis for evaluating electricity consumption and exploring the potential benefits of automatic conservation.

NASA research and scientific resources

Our project was informed by NASA's research and historical mission data.

The Spirit and Opportunity missions provided real examples of how dust storms can affect solar-powered exploration.

For the proposed mapping integration, relevant NASA resources include:

  • Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO): Surface imagery that can support terrain analysis.
  • Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA): Elevation data that can support understanding of Martian topography.

These resources provide a scientific foundation for exploring how environmental and geographical information could contribute to future Mars-walk planning.

5. How is our project creative and innovative?

RED ALERT's creativity comes from combining environmental monitoring with automatic electricity conservation and extending the concept toward digital exploration planning.

Our project began with an important question:

What if a Mars habitat could recognize the warning signs of an energy shortage and take action before the situation became critical?

Rather than creating a system that only detects dust or displays sensor readings, we developed a prototype that connects detection directly to an automatic response.

Several features make our approach distinctive.

From detection to action

RED ALERT does not stop at identifying hazardous conditions.

When the Arduino detects conditions meeting the programmed emergency thresholds, the system activates warnings and automatically switches off selected nonessential loads.

This demonstrates a complete sequence from environmental monitoring to energy conservation.

Combining multiple environmental inputs

Our prototype uses both light-intensity and dust-sensor information.

These inputs help demonstrate how environmental monitoring can provide a broader understanding of dust-storm conditions than relying on one observation alone.

Connecting hardware and software

RED ALERT combines a physical Arduino-based prototype with a web application developed using HTML and JavaScript.

The hardware demonstrates the automatic response, while the digital application provides a way to present information and explore energy-management scenarios.

Exploring energy emergencies through simulation

Our proposed 72-hour simulator allows different hypothetical energy conditions to be considered.

Instead of simply showing that a load can be switched off, the simulation helps explain why reducing consumption matters and how it could affect the remaining energy reserve.

Connecting energy management with Martian exploration

Our JavaScript-based Martian mapping component creates an opportunity to extend RED ALERT beyond the habitat itself.

By proposing the integration of terrain, environmental, energy, and route information, our team explores how resource management could become part of broader mission planning.

This is especially relevant because astronauts must consider several risks simultaneously when planning exploration activities.

Our innovation is not the invention of a new sensor, microcontroller, or mapping technology. It is the way we combine existing technologies to demonstrate an automatic response to a documented Martian energy problem.

RED ALERT transforms the question from “How can we detect an energy emergency?” into “How can we detect it, respond intelligently, and conserve resources before the situation becomes worse?”

6. What factors did our team consider when developing the project?

Throughout our research and development, we considered scientific accuracy, environmental conditions, hardware capabilities, energy priorities, automatic decision-making, testing, safety, and future applications.

Scientific evidence from NASA missions

We wanted our project to address a real challenge encountered during Mars exploration.

We therefore researched NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers, focusing on how dust storms affected their ability to generate electricity.

Spirit's severe energy shortage in 2008 demonstrated the importance of reducing energy consumption during dusty conditions.

Opportunity's experience in 2018 reinforced the vulnerability of solar-powered equipment to prolonged dust storms.

These examples helped establish the scientific motivation for RED ALERT.

The effects of Martian dust storms

We considered two important mechanisms through which dust affects solar-energy systems.

First, airborne dust reduces the sunlight reaching solar panels.

Second, dust accumulation on panel surfaces can continue reducing electricity generation even after atmospheric conditions improve.

This helped us understand why both environmental monitoring and energy conservation are important.

Essential versus nonessential electricity consumption

A major design consideration was deciding how an energy-management system should respond when electricity becomes limited.

We recognized that some equipment is more important to maintain than other equipment.

Therefore, RED ALERT demonstrates a priority-based approach: selected nonessential electrical loads are switched off automatically while essential demonstration loads remain operational.

Automatic response and programmed thresholds

We considered how the system could identify hazardous conditions and respond consistently.

Using C++ programming, the Arduino evaluates sensor readings against predefined thresholds.

This allows the prototype to initiate its warning and conservation response automatically.

We also recognize that a real habitat would require more sophisticated decision-making, additional safeguards, and human oversight.

Hardware feasibility and accessibility

We selected components such as Arduino, LDR, and dust sensors because they allow environmental monitoring and automatic control to be demonstrated on a manageable prototype scale.

Our objective was to create a functional model that clearly demonstrates the underlying concept rather than attempt to reproduce an entire Martian habitat.

Testing and evaluation

We considered how the prototype's behavior could be evaluated under different environmental conditions.

Relevant tests include:

Normal Conditions: Observe the system when light intensity is sufficient and environmental readings remain within normal thresholds.

Reduced Illumination: Decrease the light reaching the LDR and observe how the Arduino responds.

Dust Detection: Evaluate the system's response when the dust sensor detects conditions meeting programmed thresholds.

Emergency Warning: Check whether the appropriate warning indicators activate when emergency conditions are identified.

Automatic Load Management: Verify that selected nonessential loads switch off while essential demonstration loads remain operating.

Energy Conservation: Compare electrical consumption before and after the automatic response under controlled conditions.

For reliable comparisons, factors such as the electrical loads, testing duration, and programmed thresholds should be kept consistent.

These tests provide a way to evaluate the system's behavior, but results should only be reported as experimentally verified when actual measurements have been recorded.

Accuracy of measurements and simulations

We considered the difference between measuring environmental conditions and measuring actual electrical energy.

An LDR measures light intensity; it does not directly measure the electrical power generated by a solar panel.

Likewise, dust measurements indicate airborne particle conditions but do not independently determine how much electricity a habitat will generate.

Our energy simulations therefore use simplified assumptions and should not be mistaken for verified predictions of real Martian energy production.

Safety and reliability

Our prototype demonstrates the principle of automatic load management on a small scale.

A real Mars habitat would require reliable electrical protection, redundant sensors, carefully verified load priorities, and safeguards against incorrect automatic decisions.

It would also require extensive testing before any automated system could control equipment essential to astronaut safety.

Limitations of the Martian environment simulation

Our prototype cannot reproduce the complete Martian environment.

Mars has atmospheric pressure, gravity, temperature conditions, and dust behavior that differ substantially from those on Earth.

Reduced illumination and dust-sensor readings allow us to demonstrate selected aspects of the problem, but they do not reproduce every physical effect of an actual Martian dust storm.

We considered these limitations to ensure that our project remains scientifically realistic.

Future power systems

We also considered the fact that future crewed Mars missions may rely on power sources other than solar panels.

NASA has identified nuclear fission as a primary power approach for initial crewed Mars missions.

Therefore, RED ALERT is best understood as a supplementary energy-management concept that could be relevant to solar-assisted or hybrid energy systems, rather than a replacement for a habitat's primary power supply.

Future development

Our project could be expanded through more advanced electrical measurements, improved energy predictions, additional environmental data, and deeper integration with Martian mapping systems.

A future version could combine habitat energy information with NASA terrain and environmental datasets to help astronauts evaluate exploration routes and operational risks more comprehensively.

These possibilities represent future development goals rather than capabilities already demonstrated by our current prototype.

Conclusion — Why RED ALERT Matters

Mars exploration is not only about reaching another planet. It is also about learning how to operate safely and efficiently in an environment where essential resources are limited.

RED ALERT demonstrates how an Arduino programmed in C++, an LDR, and dust sensors can work together to recognize hazardous environmental conditions and automatically reduce nonessential electricity consumption.

Our HTML and JavaScript application extends the project through digital monitoring and energy-management concepts, while our JavaScript-based Martian mapping component provides a foundation for future integration of exploration information.

By combining environmental sensing, programmed decision-making, automatic load management, and digital development, RED ALERT demonstrates a practical approach to one of the challenges faced by solar-powered Mars missions.

Our goal is simple: preserve electricity when it becomes limited, prioritize essential operations, and explore how intelligent resource management could contribute to safer and more sustainable Mars exploration.

RED ALERT — Don't Just Detect an Energy Emergency. Respond to It.

challengeDetails.excerpt: NASA has explored Mars robotically for decades, studying its extreme environment, mapping its surface, and collecting many types of data. Far from home, the first astronauts to set foot on Mars will want the best map possible, with information on the details of their routes and destinations, updates on current conditions, and the data needed to complete their mission quickly and safely. Your challenge is to create a layered, integrated view of a location or route on the Martian surface that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions and could help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk while conducting new and exciting science along the way.
