Reincarnation of Apollo is an open world Mars survival and colony management simulation designed for web and mobile browsers. It addresses the challenge of making authentic space science accessible by translating complex aerospace engineering into engaging, kid-friendly gameplay. Rather than oversimplifying survival, the game immerses players in real environmental trade offs, balancing solar collection with night time battery reserves, recycling water to generate oxygen, shielding crew from solar radiation, and driving an upgradeable rover across Martian terrain to scan geological sites.

This project is important because traditional STEM curricula often present space exploration as abstract theory or punishing math. By pairing grounded planetary physics with interactive guidance, natural events, and helpful feedback, the game turns engineering failures into constructive learning moments. It empowers young astronauts to think like real mission commanders fostering systems literacy, scientific curiosity, and the problem solving mindset needed for humanity's next giant leap.
projectDetails.details:
In Reincarnation of Apollo the player plays the role of a junior astronaut attempting to place mankind on Mars. The player will play through an exciting survival and base building story. On this beautiful harsh world of Mars you must manage resources, survive dangerous situations and explore using rovers. Your objective as commander is to turn this lifeless wasteland into a thriving colony on Mars, keeping your crew safe from any dangers. This game is perfect for those who enjoy strategy base building games, space exploration and a survival sci-fi experience.

Reincarnation of Apollo is a 3D interactive open world, survival and colony management simulator set on Mars which aims to educate students and aspiring young astronauts on aerospace engineering and planet science. It was created using a variety of technologies including TypeScript, React 19, React Three Fiber (Three.js), Tailwind CSS, Vite and TanStack. The game can be run within your web browser on platforms like phone, tablet, desktop computer and uses WebGL for hardware acceleration. The player must manage their closed loop life support system on Mars. This includes gathering energy during the day from the sun, storing it in batteries during the night and using electrolysis to create breathable oxygen from water. The player will also upgrade their rover to explore a 3D environment to collect samples of minerals, scanning for anomalies and completing objectives. The creativity behind the project is taking complex aerospace data and engineering compromises from NASA and turning them into an easy to understand and fun game. This project aims to increase interest in STEM as well as showing how engineering can be a positive learning experience. Throughout development we have focused on making the game easy to play. Ensuring that it works well on multiple devices with our custom controls. We have ensured that there are multiple difficulty levels, interactive tutorials, relaxing background music and spaced out disasters (dust storms and solar radiation). The game is based around real science and human activity giving an inspiring and easy way to learn about human space exploration.

For the NASA Abu Dhabi Local Event, Team saja developed "The Ghost Fleet of Mars: A Message Across Time," an interactive storytelling project designed for young space explorers.  
​What we developed: A narrative-driven cosmic story following a futuristic robotic historian named C.O.R.A. in the year 2146 as she rediscovers discarded space hardware on Mars, such as the Perseverance Sky-Crane and the Ingenuity helicopter.  
​How it addresses the challenge: It transforms abandoned space equipment from "trash" into historical milestones, bridging the gap between complex aerospace engineering and children's imagination.  
​Why it is important: By turning cold engineering facts into an emotional adventure, it inspires students to see STEM not just as textbook formulas, but as an epic journey of human curiosity, encouraging the next generation of space explorers to build the future.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

​Our project, "The Ghost Fleet of Mars: A Message Across Time," is an interactive, narrative-driven storytelling experience. It follows C.O.R.A. (Cosmic Observation & Retrieval Assistant), a futuristic robotic historian in the year 2146, as she rediscovers discarded space hardware on the Moon and Mars—specifically turning our attention to historical landmarks like the Perseverance Sky-Crane and the Ingenuity helicopter.

​What benefits does it have & what is the intended impact?

​The project bridges the gap between cold, complex aerospace engineering and human imagination. By transforming abandoned equipment into relatable characters and milestones of human curiosity, it inspires young students to view STEM not as dry textbook formulas, but as an epic adventure. The intended impact is to spark children's curiosity and encourage the next generation of space explorers to pursue STEM fields and envision themselves building the future.

​What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

​Conceptualization & Narrative Design: Built around historical NASA mission profiles (Perseverance 2021 landing architecture and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter data).

​Presentation & Formatting: Developed using structured presentation software and exported as a visual story-driven PDF to engage young readers.

​How is your project creative & what factors did your team consider?

​We approached the challenge from a unique emotional and storytelling angle rather than a purely technical report. Instead of treating discarded spacecraft as "space junk," we framed them as silent monuments and pioneers that paved the way for humanity. We carefully considered tone, accessibility for young audiences, and scientific accuracy—explaining real engineering concepts like thin Martian atmospheric density, rotor RPM requirements, and supersonic parachutes through an engaging, narrative format.

projectDetails.name: Leave It Behind
projectDetails.summary: Leave It Behind is a free 2D browser game that tells the story of the hardware NASA left on the Moon by making players face the same choice Apollo crews did. You land at a real Apollo site (Apollo 11, 12 or 17), collect rock samples, core tubes and film, and set up experiments like the laser retroreflector that scientists still use today. The catch: your ascent stage has a weight limit, and the cabin is already full of gear. To lift off, you must throw out backpacks, boots and cameras, just as the real crews did, which is why those objects are still on the Moon. After liftoff, reentry and splashdown, you hand your samples to scientists at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston, and each sample you brought home unlocks the discovery it made possible. Every object shows a short, kid-friendly fact, linking each piece of hardware to its science. For school-age space fans, it turns discarded equipment into decisions they make themselves, and it carries a lesson for life: sometimes you have to lose something to make something.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES: Leave It Behind is a free 2D side-scrolling game that runs in any browser, on phones, tablets and laptops. Players land on three real Apollo sites: Apollo 11 (Tranquility Base), Apollo 12 (Ocean of Storms, where you walk to the 1967 Surveyor 3 lander and bring its camera home) and Apollo 17 (Taurus-Littrow, with its orange volcanic soil). In low gravity, they collect rock samples, core tubes and film, and carry instruments such as the laser retroreflector and seismometer to their marked sites. Instruments only score if they are left behind and working, which shows why some of this hardware still matters today.

HOW IT WORKS: The lunar module's ascent stage has a weight limit, and the cabin starts full of gear. To lift off, players must throw out backpacks, boots, cameras and tools, exactly as Apollo crews did. That is why these objects are on NASA's Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon. Too heavy, and the engine cannot lift off. Oxygen runs on a timer. After a successful liftoff, a short cinematic shows the trip home, reentry, parachutes, splashdown and recovery. Players then deliver their samples to the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston, where each sample they brought home unlocks the discovery it made possible. The results screen compares their choices with what the real crew did.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT: Space content for kids often skips the engineering trade-offs or explains them at a level that loses young learners. Here the trade-off is the game. Students feel why every kilogram matters, learn what each object did and what science it enabled, and take away a life lesson: sometimes you have to lose something to make something. It fits a 20-minute classroom activity and needs no install. Next steps: Mars missions (Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity), real LROC and HiRISE orbital views of each site, an Arabic and English toggle, and pilots with UAE schools.

TOOLS: HTML5 canvas and plain JavaScript (no frameworks, no build step), keyboard and touch controls, Web Audio for sound, GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. Source code: https://github.com/Saloom-Inc/nasa. All art is original vector drawing in code; no NASA logos, insignia or mission patches are used. Built with Claude (Anthropic) as a Super Intelligence tool, as disclosed in the README, the game's About screen and the watermark on the demo video. Weights in the game are simplified units; mission facts are based on NASA sources.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project TALA JANA AND BROOJ TEAM
projectDetails.summary:
We developed AEGIS-1, an interactive game where players design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission from start to finish.

We address the challenge by letting players make real engineering decisions. They choose a destination, then design their spacecraft while balancing budget, mass, and power. They select a launch vehicle, power system, communications, orbit, and scientific instruments, and every choice has a trade-off. After that, they fly the mission, avoid asteroids, collect data, and handle problems like solar storms. Then they manage the spacecraft in orbit by distributing limited power between science, communications, and shielding.

At the end, they receive a mission report showing science return, budget efficiency, engineering, and survival, plus a what-if analysis.

This is important because it is easy to read about space missions, but hard to really understand them. Our game lets players learn by doing, feel the pressure of real trade-offs, and think like engineers
projectDetails.details:
We developed AEGIS-1, an interactive game where players design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission.

It works in five steps. First, players choose a destination like Europa, Mars, or an asteroid. Second, they design their spacecraft by choosing a launch vehicle, power system, communications, orbit, and up to three scientific instruments. Third, they fly the mission, avoid asteroids, collect fuel and data, and handle problems like solar storms. Fourth, they manage the spacecraft in orbit for 90 seconds by distributing 100% power between science, communications, and shielding. Fifth, they receive a mission report with science return, budget efficiency, engineering, and survival, plus a what-if analysis.

The benefit is that players learn by doing instead of just reading. They see immediately how one decision changes the whole mission.

Our intended impact is to make space engineering feel accessible and fun for students who never get to try a full mission. We want them to start thinking like engineers and feel confident about STEM.

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with Canvas for the game, Web Audio for sound effects, and Google Slides and Google Drive for our demo.

Our project is creative because it combines a game, a simulation, and a decision-making tool in one place. It is not a quiz. The what-if analysis is what makes it different.

When we designed it, we considered budget, mass, power, communications, orbital constraints, scientific value, difficulty, and how to keep it fun but still educational for different levels.

projectDetails.name: Project teamteamtea
projectDetails.summary:
Orbital Forge is a browser based Space Mission Design Game in which you design and fly a complete space mission. You choose your science objective, your spacecraft bus, your scientific instruments, your orbit and your launch vehicle, all whilst managing the constraints of budget, mass, power, data and lifetime.
It deals with the problem by turning the abstract systems engineering trade-offs into actual decisions. Every choice has its consequences: a very capable instrument will give you a lot of science return but at the cost of mass, power, cost and the data that you have to downlink. You have a built-in launch vehicle check, a live resource dashboard and you get random events (e.g. a micrometeoroid hit) to mirror the real world constraints. You get a post-flight report which scores eight categories and explains each of those in plain English, and links the design choices back to real NASA missions (Landsat, Hubble etc).
This is important because the current tools out there teach the space concepts in isolation. There's a gap between the individual topics and the actual decision making in a mission. Orbital Forge closes that gap. It's accessible to the novice via tooltips and 3 difficulty levels, it's collaborative for up to 4 people in a team with different engineering roles and it's all based on NASA's systems engineering approach (GMAT) and JPL's CML. You learn why a mission works or doesn't work rather than just whether it does or not.
projectDetails.details:
Orbital Forge is a browser-based space mission design game (all in one HTML/CSS/JS file). You build your entire mission in six stages: science objective, spacecraft bus, instruments, orbit, launch vehicle, and launch. There's a live dashboard that tracks your budget, mass, power, and data as you go, and at the end of the mission you get a post-flight report that scores your mission across eight categories, explaining each point in plain English and linking your design to real NASA missions.

The game really does make the systems engineering trade-offs tangible (better instruments = more science return but also more mass, more power, more cost, and more data that you've got to downlink). There are three difficulty levels, random events (e.g., micrometeoroid hits), and team play for up to 4 players, with each player having a different role.

Its impact is in closing the gap between learning about individual space concepts and then being able to make integrated mission decisions. It's accessible to the novice through embedded explanations, and failure is a learning opportunity. It's built on NASA's systems engineering approach (GMAT) and JPL's CML

projectDetails.name: Terrasonic
projectDetails.summary:
TerraSonic: The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive, accessibility-first audio-visual prototype that transforms NASA Earth science data into expressive musical soundscapes. Using historical global temperature datasets and satellite observations from NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC), NASA GISS, and NASA Worldview, I mapped decades of warming trends (2000–2024) into dynamic changes in musical pitch and intensity through data sonification.

This directly addresses The Earth Information Jukebox challenge by converting complex, visual-only climate charts into intuitive sound patterns that anyone can immediately understand without needing technical training.

TerraSonic is important because vital climate data is often locked behind dense graphs that exclude blind and low-vision audiences. 

By turning environmental shifts into a multi-sensory listening experience, my project makes NASA’s Earth observations more inclusive, emotionally engaging, and accessible for classrooms, museums, and communities worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works
TerraSonic: The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive audio-visual prototype that turns NASA Earth science datasets into expressive musical soundscapes. Using historical Global Land-Ocean Temperature Index measurements (2000–2024), TerraSonic maps numerical warming anomalies directly to musical pitch, tempo, and harmonic intensity through data sonification. Users listen to a chronological climate symphony paired with side-by-side satellite imagery, where lower, calmer tones represent cooler baselines and rising pitches signal accelerating global warmth.

Benefits & Intended Impact
Traditional climate data relies almost exclusively on dense graphs and visual maps, which can overwhelm everyday audiences and completely exclude blind and low-vision individuals. TerraSonic breaks down that visual barrier by making environmental trends immediately understandable through sound—requiring no technical or data-science background. Our intended impact is to empower classrooms, science museums, and global communities with an inclusive, multi-sensory tool that fosters deeper accessibility and emotional connection to how our planet is changing.

Tools & Software Used

  • TwoTone (twotone.io): Browser-based, no-code data sonification platform used to convert NASA CSV climate datasets into synthesized .mp3 musical tracks.
  • Canva Presentations: Used to design our interactive, high-contrast 7-slide prototype and integrate synced satellite imagery with audio playback.
  • NASA Open Data Portals: NASA Earth Information Center (earth.gov), NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis, and NASA Worldview.

Creativity & Key Design Factors
Rather than treating sound as background music, we treated musical pitch as a direct scientific measurement—turning climate data into a "playable" jukebox experience. During development, our team prioritized three core factors:

  1. Accessibility First: Designing high-contrast visuals alongside self-explanatory audio cues so blind and low-vision users can interpret trends independently.
  2. Intuitive Mapping: Selecting instruments and pitch scales where rising numbers naturally sound more urgent without needing complex explanations.
  3. Rapid Prototyping & Scalability: Building a lightweight, browser-accessible prototype that can easily scale to live NASA Earthdata APIs and multi-variable harmonies (such as sea-level rise and CO₂ levels) in the future.

Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Astral Atlas
projectDetails.summary:
Mars remains largely unexplored, with large regions holding geological mysteries that could completely change our understanding of the planet's history. Although NASA has collected extensive data through satellites, rovers, and scientific instruments, much of this information is still spread across different datasets.
Astral Atlas aims to bridge this gap by using existing NASA observations into an interactive predictive mapping system designed to support future Martian exploration safely.
Focusing on Jezero Crater, Astral Atlas combines geological, mineralogical, topographic, and environmental data to find potentially significant features in areas with limited direct observations. By analysing relationships between existing measurements, the system aims to predict unexplored geological characteristics, highlight uncertainty, and identify locations with high scientific potential. 
Beyond mapping, Astral Atlas explores how terrain elevation, atmospheric conditions, and environmental hazards can inform astronaut route planning by predicting the safest and easiest route, helping balance accessibility with opportunities for scientific discovery. It includes a current map, as well as the predicted map based on pattern recognition to predict future hazards. 

Ultimately, Astral Atlas demonstrates how NASA’s existing knowledge could be used not only to understand where exploration has already taken place, but also to guide where humanity should explore next.
projectDetails.details: It works as an interactive map, where you initially choose your objective, the start points, the crew limits and what you want to include on the map. The interface then shows all the hazards, predicted science, the explored and non explored areas, as well as the route to guide the astronaut. It has many benefits as it allows the astronaut to have a safe route to the expected destination and has exact timestamps of when the astronaut will reach each checkpoint. It has a dedicated section for safety, which means that the safety of the astronaut is always considered in the route chosen. The map can then be updated with new data from other sections of the Mars’ surface. We used JavaScript, Python, Claude, HTML, CSS as our main tools and software to create the website. Our project is creative as it not only includes the route, but all potential factors that might influence their route, like mentioned before.

projectDetails.details:

projectDetails.name: Project Yassin
projectDetails.summary:
The Solar System Hall of Fame is an educational narrative guide created to introduce school-age students to the robotic explorers and scientific instruments NASA has left across the Moon, Mars, and deep space since the 1960s.
The guide addresses the challenge by organizing complex aerospace history into three clear, engaging geographic chapters—the Moon, Mars, and Interstellar Space—paired with a scannable quick-reference table. By using relatable comparisons, such as comparing a seismic sensor to a stethoscope or an SUV-sized rover to a mobile laboratory, the text translates technical engineering into accessible storytelling while clearly distinguishing between retired hardware and active missions.
This project is important because it bridges the gap between historic space milestones and ongoing scientific discovery. Showing young learners that space hardware continues to gather data decades after launch—or rests silently as a monument to human curiosity—sparks early interest in STEM fields and demonstrates how engineering turns bold questions into real planetary knowledge. Note: SI was used for the project in parts 1 , 2, and 3 of the storytelling.
projectDetails.details: Solar System Hall of Fame is an educational guide and slide deck that takes school-age students on a three-stop tour of NASA's hardware in the Moon, Mars, and Interstellar Space. It uses simple analogies, real NASA photos, status tags (Active, Grounded, or Retired), and a quick-reference table to show what each machine discovered and whether it still works today. This project turns complicated aerospace science into a fun and an easy-to-read stories for K-12 students. The goal of this project is to spark interest in STEM among school students by making rovers and space probes feel exciting and inspiring. I used official NASA Science mission portals and the NASA Image and Video Library, super intelligence (SI) to brainstorm kid-friendly analogies and organize the flow of my storytelling, and I used Microsoft Word to type the storytelling (in addition with the images and reference table), PowerPoint for the demo, and Google Drive for the public-view links. It is creative because it shows space missions just like a tour around the solar system by using real pictures from NASA, and visual status tiers to turn engineering facts into an entertaining story. I factored on using vocabulary that is suitable for any age in school to read and used correct visual layouts with photos and a comparison table for learners, and confirmed data from NASA for finished NASA accuracy.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. projectDetails.name: ASTROHEALTH – Astronaut Health Monitoring and Mission Support System
projectDetails.summary: ASTROHEALTH is a health monitoring and mission support platform designed to help monitor astronaut well-being during space missions. It brings together simulated astronaut health measurements, digital twin visualization, ECG monitoring, sleep and behavioral health indicators, radiation and space-weather information, and decision-support features in one dashboard. The system is designed to help identify unusual health patterns and present useful information to support mission monitoring. It also explores NASA space-weather and space biology research resources through dedicated data modules. The platform combines an interactive interface, data visualization, and explainable alerts to make complex health information easier to understand. It is a prototype: astronaut biometric readings are simulated and its alerts are not medically validated. ASTROHEALTH aims to support safer, more informed health monitoring during long-duration space missions.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Overview

ASTROHEALTH is a web-based astronaut health monitoring and mission support system designed for long-duration space missions. It brings important astronaut health indicators and space-related information together in one interactive dashboard.

2. How It Works

The platform provides simulated astronaut profiles and health measurements, including heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), blood oxygen (SpO2), blood pressure, and ECG visualization. A digital twin interface helps users explore astronaut health status.

It also includes modules for sleep and behavioral health, cardiovascular monitoring, cranial health, musculoskeletal health, and radiation-related space-weather information. An anomaly monitoring feature highlights unusual patterns and provides decision-support information for mission monitoring.

NASA data modules are designed to explore space-weather information from NASA DONKI and space biology research resources from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTROHEALTH aims to make astronaut health information easier to understand and monitor. It brings multiple types of information into one interface, helps users explore possible health-related patterns, and supports awareness of potential issues during long-duration missions. It may also help students and researchers understand the challenges of astronaut health monitoring.

4. Technology Used

The project was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses interactive charts, data visualization, and state management to present information. NASA data services are included for exploring DONKI space-weather events and OSDR research resources.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation is combining astronaut health visualization, digital twin concepts, space-weather information, research exploration, and explainable monitoring features in a single platform. The design focuses on making complex information accessible through an interactive dashboard.

6. Current Limitations

ASTROHEALTH is a prototype. The astronaut biometric readings are simulated and are not collected from real astronauts or medical devices. Its alerts are experimental decision-support features, not medically validated diagnoses or flight medical advice. NASA space-weather events are not direct measurements of an individual astronaut's radiation dose.

projectDetails.name: Project AYARU - Echoes of Earth
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Jukebox is a web application that turns NASA Earth imagery into sound, so people can hear changes on our planet as well as see them. A playhead sweeps across a world map from west to east. Each latitude band becomes a voice, pixel brightness controls loudness, and position controls pitch and stereo panning. Users can choose records such as sea surface temperature, sea ice, carbon dioxide, vegetation and fires. A year slider gradually detunes the sound to show the planet changing over time. A hue mode maps color to timbre, so warm and cool regions sound different. Users can also load any Earth Information Center frame and hear it instantly.

The project addresses the challenge by pairing EIC visuals with sonification generated in real time in the browser. It is also accessible, with keyboard controls, drag-to-scrub listening and a live text description of what is being heard. This matters because Earth science is mostly shared through images, which excludes blind and low-vision people. Sound makes climate data more inclusive and memorable for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Jukebox is a web application that turns Earth imagery into sound, generated in real time in the browser. A playhead sweeps across a world map from west to east, like the planet turning under the sound. The map is split into 18 latitude bands, and each band is one voice. Pitch rises toward the north, brightness controls loudness, and longitude controls stereo position. A year slider (1980-2025) gradually detunes the voices, so the same record sounds more strained as the years pass. A hue mode maps color to timbre, so warm regions sound bright and cool regions sound mellow. Users can pick records such as sea surface temperature, sea ice, carbon dioxide, vegetation and fires, or load any Earth Information Center frame and hear it straight away. They can also record the mix. In a self-hosted version, the app can pull live imagery from NASA GIBS.

Benefits and intended impact

Earth science is mostly shared through images, which leaves out blind and low-vision people. Earth Jukebox gives them another way in, and it also helps anyone who learns well through sound. The intended impact is to make climate and Earth observation data inclusive, memorable and easy to explore, in classrooms, science outreach and public exhibits, without any installation.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page, with no framework
  • Web Audio API for oscillators, filters, stereo panning and compression
  • Canvas for rendering the maps
  • MediaRecorder API for recording the audio
  • NASA GIBS imagery for the live-data version
  • [Add any AI tools, libraries or other software your team used. Space Apps asks teams to disclose AI use, so say how it was used.]

Creativity

The jukebox idea turns datasets into “records” you can pick and play, which makes data exploration feel like listening to music. Using the year slider to detune the sound lets people hear change over time, not just a snapshot. Mapping hue to timbre makes color audible too, and users can bring in their own frames.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: keyboard controls, drag-to-hear listening and a live text caption that screen readers announce.
  • Simplicity: it runs in any modern browser, with no accounts or downloads.
  • Pleasant sound: each record uses its own musical scale so the sound is easy to listen to, not harsh.
  • Honesty about data: the built-in maps are illustrative, and real NASA imagery is loaded through the live version or by uploading a frame. The sound reflects the brightness and color of the rendered image, not raw measurements.
  • Future work: real EIC datasets, spoken summaries and a distinct sound for coastlines.

projectDetails.name: Project Bio-nauts
projectDetails.summary:
### BIO-NAUTS – Smart Health Monitoring for Astronauts

BIO-NAUTS is a smart wearable health monitoring system designed to monitor astronauts' health during space missions. It uses a Smart Sensor T-Shirt and a Smart Health Watch to collect important body information such as heart rate, blood oxygen level (SpO₂), body temperature, breathing, and physical activity.

The system uses different sensors, including optical, heart rate, temperature, and motion sensors. These sensors continuously collect health data and send it wirelessly to a central system. A processor analyses the collected data, while AI software checks the astronaut's health condition and identifies possible problems. If any unusual changes are detected, the system provides alerts and warnings.

The real-time health dashboard displays health measurements, health trends, and sensor status. This system helps detect health problems early, supports continuous health monitoring, and improves astronaut safety during space missions.

Main Goal: To provide smarter, faster, and more reliable health monitoring for astronauts in space.
projectDetails.details:
Bionauts – Smart Astronaut Health Monitoring System

Bionauts is a smart health monitoring system designed to monitor the health and physical condition of astronauts during space missions.

Our project focuses on monitoring important health parameters using different sensors such as ECG sensors, heart rate sensors, optical sensors, temperature sensors, respiration sensors, motion sensors, EMG sensors, and GSR sensors.

The system aims to collect and display health-related information to help identify unusual changes in an astronaut's physical condition. It can support early detection of potential health concerns and improve astronaut safety during space missions.

The main benefits of this project are continuous health monitoring, early identification of abnormal changes, and improved awareness of astronaut health.

We developed our project prototype using HTML to create a web-based interface that presents the project concept and its features.

Our main goal is to support astronaut health and contribute to safer future space exploration.

projectDetails.name: TerraCycle
projectDetails.summary:
TerraCycle is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform that combines NASA satellite observations, local soil information, historical climate patterns, and artificial intelligence to recommend sustainable crop-rotation strategies.

The platform analyses rainfall variability, soil moisture, temperature fluctuations, vegetation health, and seasonal environmental changes to identify agricultural vulnerabilities.

Farmers can select their agricultural land, enter existing crop sequences, provide soil information, and specify their priorities. The platform generates at least three crop-rotation strategies, including the farmer's existing rotation, and compares them based on soil health improvement, water conservation, climate resilience, erosion reduction, and economic suitability.

Using explainable machine learning and multi-objective optimization, TerraCycle provides evidence-based recommendations, risk assessments, and long-term agricultural planning insights.

The objective is to transform complex NASA Earth observation data into understandable and actionable agricultural intelligence while keeping farmers and agricultural experts in control of final decisions
projectDetails.details:
A. What exactly does the project do?

TerraCycle addresses the problem of selecting suitable crop rotations under changing environmental conditions.

It provides five major capabilities.

1. Satellite-Based Agricultural Intelligence

The system collects and processes NASA Earth observation datasets to understand environmental conditions surrounding agricultural fields.

It analyses:

  • Historical rainfall patterns.
  • Temperature variations.
  • Soil moisture anomalies.
  • Vegetation health.
  • Seasonal agricultural productivity patterns.
  • Periods of potential water stress.
  • Seasonal bare-field windows.

2. Soil Health Assessment

Farmers can enter their local soil-test information, including:

  • Soil pH.
  • Nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
  • Organic carbon.
  • Soil texture.
  • Water-holding capacity.
  • Electrical conductivity.

The platform combines these measurements with environmental observations to assess soil-related constraints.

It also estimates potential soil-health benefits from different rotation strategies using crop characteristics such as nitrogen fixation, root depth, biomass production, and residue retention.

Importantly, satellite data alone cannot directly establish soil nutrient concentrations or organic carbon levels. Laboratory measurements are used for these parameters.

3. Intelligent Crop Rotation Recommendation

The platform generates three or more rotation strategies:

Strategy

Crop Rotation Concept

Expected Benefits

Strategy 1

Existing farmer rotation

Baseline for comparison

Strategy 2

Cereal–legume rotation

Nitrogen fixation and crop diversification

Strategy 3

Main crop–legume cover crop rotation

Soil cover and organic matter contributions

Strategy 4

Drought-tolerant crop rotation

Potential reduction in water demand and improved climate resilience

Crop selections are filtered according to local growing seasons, soil characteristics, irrigation availability, and market suitability.

4. Climate Risk Assessment

The platform identifies agricultural vulnerabilities by analyzing historical environmental patterns.

Examples include:

  • Increasing temperature during critical crop-growth periods.
  • Declining seasonal soil moisture.
  • Irregular rainfall distribution.
  • Extended dry spells.
  • Abnormal vegetation stress.
  • Potential erosion vulnerability.

It highlights periods when the current crop rotation may become increasingly vulnerable.

5. Interactive Agricultural Simulator

Farmers can modify environmental conditions and explore different agricultural scenarios.

For example:

  • What happens if seasonal rainfall decreases by 20%?
  • What happens if average temperature increases by 2°C?
  • Which crop rotation is more suitable under water scarcity?
  • Which rotation provides better soil cover during dry periods?
  • Which strategy offers better long-term resilience?

The simulator recalculates strategy scores based on the modified assumptions. These are scenario explorations, not guaranteed climate forecasts.

B. How does the system work?

The proposed system follows a six-stage architecture.

Stage

Process

Function

1

Data Acquisition

Collect NASA satellite and local agricultural information

2

Data Processing

Clean, process, and harmonize geospatial datasets

3

Feature Extraction

Calculate rainfall anomalies, temperature stress, vegetation indices, and soil moisture indicators

4

AI/ML Analysis

Identify historical patterns and environmental vulnerabilities

5

Optimization Engine

Generate and rank suitable crop-rotation strategies

6

Visualization

Display recommendations, risk indicators, and scenario comparisons

Proposed system architecture:

NASA Earth Data + Local Soil Data + Farmer Inputs

↓

Geospatial Data Processing

↓

Environmental Feature Extraction

↓

Machine Learning and Climate Pattern Analysis

↓

Multi-Objective Crop Rotation Optimization

↓

Recommendation and Risk Assessment Engine

↓

Interactive Farmer Dashboard

C. What makes the project intelligent?

The main innovation is the Multi-Objective Crop Rotation Optimization Engine.

Instead of recommending crops based on a single parameter, the system evaluates multiple agricultural objectives simultaneously.

The optimization model evaluates:

Parameter

Evaluation

Soil Health

Nitrogen fixation, residue contribution, root characteristics

Water Conservation

Seasonal water requirements and irrigation availability

Climate Resilience

Temperature and rainfall suitability

Erosion Reduction

Soil cover duration and terrain-related vulnerability

Economic Suitability

Market demand, cultivation cost, and farmer preferences

Crop Diversification

Crop-family diversity and potential pest-cycle interruption

A weighted scoring algorithm is used:

\[ R=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iS_i \]

Where:

  • \(R\) = Overall rotation suitability score.
  • \(w_i\) = Weight assigned to each agricultural objective.
  • \(S_i\) = Normalized score for each objective.
  • \(n\) = Number of evaluation parameters.

The weights are adjustable according to farmer priorities.

For example, a farmer facing water shortages can assign greater importance to water conservation, while another farmer may prioritize soil improvement or economic returns.

Agronomic constraints, such as unsuitable soil conditions and growing-season incompatibility, are applied before ranking.

The system also explains why each recommendation received its score.

Climate Data

Data Visualization

Deployment

Hardware requirements:

The initial prototype requires no specialized agricultural hardware.

A laptop or desktop computer and internet connection are sufficient.

Optional integration with ground-based soil moisture sensors and weather stations can improve field-level validation.

projectDetails.name: Astra-Mind
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA-MIND is a prototype health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It tracks five domains: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immune, behavioral and radiation. A FastAPI backend and SQLite database store every measurement with a data-provenance tag, and a live dashboard shows current values and trends.

It addresses the challenge in four ways:

It learns each astronaut’s personal baseline instead of relying on population thresholds.
It flags deviations and links alerts that appear across several domains at once.
It forecasts the next 24 hours with a stated uncertainty range.
It summarises overall status as a digital twin score.

It keeps working through communication outages. Data and alerts queue onboard, then sync to an Earth-side view once the link returns.

This matters because crews on deep-space missions will face delayed contact and limited medical support, so early, personalised, offline-capable monitoring could help catch problems sooner.

All data here is synthetic, and the scores show deviation from baseline, not diagnoses. They need medical review.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRA-MIND is a prototype that monitors an astronaut’s health on a long mission. It simulates ten signals across five domains: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immune, behavioral and radiation. A live dashboard shows current values, trends and alerts.

  1. Data: a generator produces hourly synthetic readings for each crew member, including slower periodic assessments such as blood markers.
  2. Storage: a FastAPI backend saves every raw measurement in SQLite with a provenance tag (SYNTHETIC) and a synced flag.
  3. Baseline: each person’s normal range is learned from their first 72 hours.
  4. Alerts: readings far from that baseline are flagged. When several domains deviate together, a combined cross-domain alert lists the supporting observations.
  5. Forecast: a 24-hour projection comes with a 90% uncertainty range.
  6. Digital twin: a score per domain and overall summarises current status.
  7. Offline mode: during a simulated communications outage, monitoring continues onboard and data queues locally. After reconnection the queue syncs to the Earth-side view.

Benefits

  • Alerts are personalised, so each astronaut is compared with their own normal instead of population thresholds.
  • Monitoring does not depend on a live link to Earth.
  • Alerts come with the observations behind them, so they are explainable.
  • Raw data is preserved and labelled by origin.

Intended impact

The aim is to help flight surgeons and crews notice health drift sooner on missions where medical support and communication are limited. It is a decision-support concept, not a diagnostic tool.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.
  • Backend: FastAPI with Uvicorn, and SQLite.
  • Frontend: a plain browser dashboard with hand-drawn SVG charts and no external libraries.
  • Statistics: median and MAD baselines, robust z-scores, and Holt damped-trend forecasting.
  • Testing: pytest, with 3 passing tests.
  • Hardware: only an ordinary computer. There are no real sensors, because all data is simulated.

What is creative about it

  • It joins three ideas in one lightweight tool: personal baselines, cross-domain alert linking, and a single digital twin status score.
  • The offline-first design treats a communications blackout as the normal case.
  • Every data point carries its provenance, so simulated and real data can never be confused.

Factors considered

  • Safety: scores are deviations from baseline, not disease probabilities, and nothing is presented as a diagnosis. Medical review is required.
  • Honesty about data: everything is clearly labelled synthetic.
  • Resource limits: it uses simple statistical methods that run anywhere, even without internet, instead of large models.
  • Demonstrability: injected events and a communications outage button let the system be shown end to end.
  • Known gaps: Isolation Forest, Chronos-2, a medical assistant with retrieval over NASA documents, and a React frontend are planned but not built.

projectDetails.name: Echoes from the Dust: An Interactive 3D Museum of NASA’s Forgotten Machines
projectDetails.summary: Echoes from the Dust is an interactive 3D web museum designed to introduce school-age space enthusiasts to the historic spacecraft, rovers, and landers NASA has left across the Moon and Mars. By transforming planetary coordinates into a navigable celestial globe with first-person machine diaries, the platform turns distant space hardware into accessible stories of scientific discovery.
projectDetails.details: The Problem & Vision Since the 1960s, NASA has left dozens of pioneering machines on the Moon, Mars, and deep space. To many young students, these deactivated landers and rovers seem like distant relics or forgotten hardware. Echoes from the Dust reframes these machines as enduring pioneers that unlocked humanity’s understanding of the solar system. ​How It Works Built as a lightweight, browser-based 3D interactive museum, the application allows students to: ​Explore Celestial Worlds in 3D: Users can freely rotate, zoom, and switch between high-resolution 3D globes of Mars and The Moon, rendered with authentic NASA planetary surface maps. ​Inspect Real Landing Coordinates: Glowing interactive beacons mark the exact latitude and longitude where historic missions touched down—including the Opportunity Rover at Endeavour Crater, Viking 1 at Chryse Planitia, the Apollo 11 Descent Stage in the Sea of Tranquility, and the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle at Hadley Rille. ​Read First-Person Machine Logs: Clicking any beacon opens an exhibit card featuring a first-person narrative written from the perspective of the hardware itself, making space history emotionally engaging and easy for K–12 students to grasp. ​Discover the Science Legacy: Each exhibit translates complex instrumentation into clear takeaways—explaining how Opportunity found evidence of ancient Martian water through hematite "blueberries," how Apollo 11’s laser retroreflectors are still used today to measure the Moon's distance, and how early landers paved the way for human exploration. ​Technical Stack & NASA Open Data ​Frontend & 3D Graphics: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D spherical rendering, raycasting pin selection, and orbital camera controls. ​NASA Data & Resources: Utilizes NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Mars surface imagery, along with authentic mission landing coordinates and historical mission logs. ​Impact By combining interactive 3D visualization with empathetic storytelling, Echoes from the Dust requires zero installation and works on any classroom computer or mobile browser—inspiring the next generation of engineers, scientists, and space explorers.

projectDetails.name: Project Energy1goal1
projectDetails.summary: The research investigates the application of NASA POWER satellite-based climate data for monitoring peanut crop development and predicting pod maturity in agricultural regions where ground-based weather stations are unavailable. The study compares satellite-derived climate information with observations from conventional meteorological stations across four peanut-producing fields in Georgia, USA. Different climatic parameters, including maximum, minimum and average temperatures, solar radiation, relative humidity, wind speed and surface pressure, were examined using statistical techniques such as correlation analysis, linear regression and Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The findings indicate that temperature and solar radiation data obtained from NASA POWER provide reliable estimates and demonstrate meaningful relationships with peanut pod maturity. However, wind speed and relative humidity show comparatively lower accuracy due to spatial resolution and measurement variations. Overall, the research establishes NASA POWER as a useful alternative for agricultural climate monitoring and crop management, particularly in locations without conventional meteorological infrastructure.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do or how does it work?

This project utilizes NASA POWER satellite-based meteorological data to monitor climatic conditions and estimate peanut crop maturity in regions without conventional weather stations. It collects climatic parameters such as maximum and minimum temperatures, average temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity, wind speed and surface pressure. These data are compared with ground-based weather observations using statistical techniques, including correlation analysis, linear regression and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), to identify the climatic factors influencing peanut pod maturity.

2. What benefits does it have?

The project provides accessible and cost-effective climatic information without requiring weather stations near every agricultural field. It helps farmers understand crop development, improve harvesting decisions and adopt data-driven agricultural practices. The approach can also be extended to agricultural regions with limited meteorological infrastructure.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main objective is to improve agricultural decision-making through satellite-based climate monitoring. It aims to reduce dependence on conventional weather monitoring systems, provide useful climatic information to farmers and encourage sustainable farming practices through scientific analysis and technology.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used?

NASA POWER was used to obtain satellite-based climatic data. Python and Jupyter Notebook were employed for data processing, correlation analysis and visualization. SAS JMP Pro 14 was used for statistical analysis and regression modelling, while R software (version 2023.06.2) with the factoextra package was used for Principal Component Analysis. Microsoft Excel 2013 was used to prepare graphs. Existing surface weather stations provided reference measurements, and peanut fields were used for crop maturity assessment. No new physical hardware device was developed.

5. How is your project creative?

The innovative aspect is the integration of freely available NASA satellite data with agricultural crop maturity assessment. Instead of depending entirely on physical weather stations, the research uses remote climate information and statistical modelling to understand crop development. Applying PCA to identify important climatic variables further strengthens the research approach.

6. What factors did your team consider?

The study considered temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity, wind speed, surface pressure, peanut pod maturity, geographical location, seasonal variations, data accuracy and satellite spatial resolution. Data from four peanut-producing locations in Georgia, USA, collected during 2018 and 2019, were evaluated to assess the reliability of NASA POWER information.

projectDetails.name: AFTERLIGHT
projectDetails.summary:
AFTERLIGHT is an interactive educational web experience celebrating humanity’s robotic pioneers and lunar monuments resting across the cosmos. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, the project explores nine historic NASA missions across the Moon, Mars, Saturn, and the interstellar void. Rather than treating deactivated spacecraft as discarded debris, AFTERLIGHT reframes them as permanent archaeological time capsules of human curiosity.

Designed specifically for students aged 9–14, the platform pairs an interactive 3D WebGL solar system with rich documentary chapters, animated timelines, and accessible science explainers. Learners explore how Spirit’s jammed wheel accidentally unearthed ancient Martian hot springs, how Apollo 11’s Moon mirror still bounces Earth lasers today, and why Cassini made a fiery sacrifice into Saturn to safeguard alien ocean worlds.

Powered by 54 authentic NASA archival photographs, interactive Three.js 3D models, and real-time synthesized ambient audio, AFTERLIGHT proves that while missions eventually end, their stories and scientific discoveries illuminate our universe forever.
projectDetails.details:
A. What AFTERLIGHT Is

AFTERLIGHT is an interactive, cinematic educational web application that chronicles humanity’s mechanical outposts across the solar system. Spanning nine historic NASA missions across the Moon, Mars, Saturn, and the interstellar void, AFTERLIGHT reframes space hardware left behind—from Apollo 11’s descent stage at Tranquility Base to the Opportunity rover on the rim of Endeavour Crater—not as discarded space junk, but as permanent scientific time capsules and cultural monuments of human exploration.

B. The Educational Opportunity & Problem Addressed

When space missions conclude, public attention quickly fades once headlines stop reporting daily operations. Many students and young learners believe that when a spacecraft’s battery expires, its journey and scientific usefulness end permanently. In reality:

  1. Physical Artifacts Remain: The hardware rests on extraterrestrial surfaces as archaeological records of human ingenuity.
  2. Enduring Science: Data gathered by past missions—and even active hardware like Apollo 11's Laser Ranging Retroreflector—continues to drive active research, satellite navigation, and future astronaut landing plans.
  3. Planetary Protection: Sacrifices like Cassini's plunge into Saturn’s clouds demonstrate humanity’s moral obligation to preserve pristine alien environments (such as the ocean moons Enceladus and Titan).

AFTERLIGHT bridges the gap between dry academic mission archives and young students' imaginations, turning complex planetary astrophysics into an inspiring, story-driven journey.

C. How the Website Works

AFTERLIGHT is architected as a high-performance single-page web application (SPA) built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. The application runs client-side with zero paid API dependencies, zero external backend requirements, and instantaneous hash-based navigation:

  • Client-Side Data Architecture: All telemetry, scientific discoveries, chronological timelines, and metadata for the 9 missions are stored in typed local datasets (src/data/missionsData.ts).
  • Authentic Asset Loading: 54 high-resolution NASA archival photographs (6 per mission) are stored locally and mapped via an automated image manifest (image-manifest.json), eliminating external rate limits, broken third-party links, or paid content delivery networks.
  • Synthesized Ambient Audio: A real-time procedural sound generator powered by the browser's native Web Audio API synthesizes a cinematic deep-space drone (55 Hz sub-bass, 110.5 Hz harmonic, 164.8 Hz resonant shimmer) with zero external audio assets.

D. Major Implemented Features

  1. Interactive 3D WebGL Solar System (SolarSystem3D.tsx):
    • Built with Three.js, rendering an interactive 3D solar system featuring an animated glowing Sun with multi-layer coronal halos, Earth-Moon system, Mars with polar ice caps, Saturn with tilted 3D double-sided rings, and an interstellar escape trajectory.
    • Distinct 3D Spacecraft Probe models with dual solar panel arrays, communication dish antennas, and planetary survey lasers.
    • Interactive orbit controls (360° rotate, smooth scroll zoom, pan), hover raycasting with floating HUD tooltips, click-to-fly camera animations, and quick-focus jump buttons.
    • A clean 2D vector fallback view with real-time switching between 3D Cosmos and 2D Schematic modes, complete with responsive Hardware Dossier preview cards.
    • Dedicated documentary experiences for: Apollo 11, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit (MER-A), Opportunity (MER-B), Phoenix, Voyager 1, and Cassini-Huygens.
    • Technical breakdowns of equipment mass, power sources (RTG nuclear vs. solar arrays), primary tools (rock grinders, spectrometers, robotic claws), and exact final hardware fates.
    • Chronological event feeds with phase tags (Launch, Cruise, Landing, Discoveries, Conclusion) and interactive expanded event details.
    • Categorized discoveries explaining what the robot found, why it shocked scientists at the time, and why it matters today, filterable by dynamic tags (Ancient Water, Moon Rocks, Alien Volcanoes, Weather, etc.).
    • Full-screen photo lightbox with keyboard navigation (ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, Escape), original NASA Center credits, capture dates, NASA image IDs, and links to the original NASA archive entries.
    • Interactive split-slider and side-by-side toggles comparing early exploration limitations with modern missions (e.g., Apollo 11's 2-hour walk vs. the Artemis Lunar Base; Sojourner microrover vs. Perseverance).

E. How Visitors Interact with the Experience

  • Explore Freely: Visitors rotate the 3D Solar System, click on glowing spacecraft beacons, and immediately see mission dossiers update on the fly.
  • Journey by Destination: Filter missions across three planetary theaters: The Moon, Mars Surface, and Saturn & Deep Space.
  • Examine Historic Hardware: Inspect authentic NASA photographs of actual hardware resting on lunar soil and Martian sand.
  • Deep-Dive into Mission Chapters: Read step-by-step stories of bouncing airbag landings, stuck wheels uncovering hot springs, and message-in-a-bottle golden records.

F. Intended Audience

Specifically tailored for learners aged 9 to 14 (middle school / upper elementary grades), as well as educators and family science enthusiasts. Scientific vocabulary is intentionally translated into clear, relatable stories and analogies without compromising factual accuracy.

G. Educational Benefits

  • Demystifies Space Exploration: Explains complex concepts (laser retroreflection, hydrothermal vents, atmospheric sublimation, rocker-bogie suspension) using everyday metaphors.
  • Encourages Engineering Problem-Solving: Shows students that mission anomalies often yield historic breakthroughs (e.g., Spirit’s broken wheel dragging backward and uncovering volcanic hot springs; Surveyor 3’s camera retrieved by Apollo 12).
  • Instills Planetary Ethics: Explains planetary protection and why scientists sacrificed Cassini in Saturn’s atmosphere to safeguard potential life in Enceladus' underground oceans.

H. Intended Impact

AFTERLIGHT transforms passive history into active curiosity. By highlighting the enduring legacy of NASA's hardware, it connects past achievements to upcoming exploration—such as NASA's Artemis Moon landings, the Mars Sample Return campaign, and the Dragonfly drone to Titan—inspiring the next generation of engineers, astronomers, and explorers.

I. Creative Approach & Storytelling

Instead of presenting a clinical database or generic dashboard, AFTERLIGHT adopts a Hybrid Cinematic Museum Editorial design:

  • Deep-space black and navy color palettes accented by celestial gold and cyan.
  • Editorial typography featuring Cinzel for monumental headlines, Plus Jakarta Sans for readable prose, and Space Grotesk / JetBrains Mono for telemetry data.
  • Narrative framing that treats each spacecraft like a brave pioneer with its own personality and enduring legacy.

J. Technology Stack & Development Tools

  • Core Framework: React 19 (react 19.3.1, react-dom 19.3.1)
  • Language: TypeScript (typescript 5.7+ / 7.0.2 compiler)
  • 3D Graphics Engine: Three.js (three 0.187.0) with OrbitControls & WebGL
  • Bundler & Dev Server: Vite (vite 8.3.8) with @vitejs/plugin-react (Oxc engine)
  • Linter: Oxlint (oxlint 1.90.0)
  • Audio: HTML5 Web Audio API (procedural harmonic synthesizer)
  • Styling: Pure CSS Custom Properties (CSS variables, modern grid, responsive flexbox)
  • Image Pipeline: Node.js script querying the official NASA Image and Video Library API (https://images-api.nasa.gov/)
  • Hosting Target: Vercel (static edge deployment ready)

K. Design & Accessibility Considerations

  • Responsive Layout: Fluid layouts adapting across smartphones, tablets, laptops, and ultra-wide desktop monitors.
  • Keyboard Navigation: Lightbox supports Escape to close, ArrowLeft for previous image, and ArrowRight for next image.
  • Reduced Motion & Control: Sound starts muted by default; 3D auto-spin can be paused with a single click; 2D schematic fallback is always accessible.
  • Readability: High contrast ratios (WCAG AA compliant) with crisp off-white text over deep void backgrounds.

L. Scientific Accuracy & Source Attribution

  • Every photograph is authentic NASA documentary imagery with complete provenance: capture date, originating NASA center (JSC, KSC, JPL, MSFC, HQ), and public NASA image ID.
  • Hardware statuses distinguish between Intentionally Abandoned (Apollo 11), Visited Time Capsule (Surveyor 3), Decommissioned Equipment (Viking 1, Pathfinder, Opportunity, Phoenix), Failed Equipment (Spirit), Controlled Planetary Protection Disposal (Cassini), and Operational Spacecraft (Voyager 1).
  • No facts, discoveries, or technical capabilities have been fabricated.

projectDetails.name: CombustionLens: Source-Linked Fire Safety Evidence for Space Missions
projectDetails.summary: CombustionLens is a source-linked research workspace that helps researchers explore NASA microgravity combustion findings and see where they do and don't apply to future missions. Its evidence explorer links four NASA campaign summaries (BASS, FLEX, Saffire VI, SoFIE-GEL) to their original sources, ranks them with a disclosed, explainable method, and keeps published observations separate from our interpretations. A mission-applicability check compares gravity, fuel class, oxygen, pressure, ventilation and geometry for orbital, lunar and Mars-transit contexts, marking each as aligned, mismatched or unknown, so missing evidence is visible and unknown conditions are never treated as safe. Users can export source-linked research briefs. A research backend retrieves and reranks passages from NASA Technical Reports Server reports with page-level citations and numerical checks. It is a research prototype, not a flight-qualified fire-safety tool, and it does not predict fire risk.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem
NASA has decades of microgravity combustion results, but a correct finding can still be wrong for a given spacecraft. Gravity, fuel geometry, atmosphere and ventilation can all make a result non-transferable. Finding a result is not enough. Researchers need to know whether it applies to their mission.

What It Does

  • Evidence Explorer: four curated NASA campaign summaries with searchable findings, explainable ranking by mission priority (for example detection and extinction), and three mission contexts. It runs without a backend or API key.
  • Mission Applicability: six physical boundary checks that give aligned, mismatch or unknown results, plus exportable research questions. For lunar surface contexts it shows an explicit partial-gravity evidence gap instead of inventing a threshold.
  • Research Backend: dense retrieval over NASA reports, cross-encoder reranking, page-level citations and numerical-claim checks. Without a generative model it returns labeled source excerpts.
  • Verified Comparator: only independently verified experiment records are eligible. None are verified yet, so the comparator shows an empty state on purpose.
  • Exports: Markdown research briefs that carry citations, limitations and mission context.

Data and Evidence
We collected 6 NASA Technical Reports Server reports (549 pages) and kept their rights determinations and SHA-256 hashes. Three reports with explicit public-use permission are indexed as 457 passages. We also staged 31 BASS test-condition rows and 8 Saffire measurements, which await independent review.

Tools and Technology
React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Recharts on the frontend. Python, FastAPI, ChromaDB, sentence-transformers, DuckDB and PyMuPDF on the backend.

Validation
68 backend tests and 20 frontend tests passed, and the production build succeeded. A small retrieval benchmark scored 8/8 development and 7/8 held-out gate classifications. These are not scientific answer-accuracy measurements.

Design Choices and Creativity
Ranking scores are not probabilities. Unknown conditions are never labeled safe. Public access alone is not treated as permission to index a report. When no evidence matches a search, the app shows an empty state instead of an invented conclusion.

Impact and Next Steps
CombustionLens makes the boundaries of microgravity fire-safety evidence auditable for Moon and Mars mission planning. Next steps are independent review of run-level records, broader evaluation and a validated public deployment. No NASA endorsement is claimed.

projectDetails.name: Crew Health Companion
projectDetails.summary:
Summary: Crew Health Companion is a prototype app that helps astronauts check their own health during long missions. A crew member takes guided measurements, such as heart rate and sleep, and sees a color-coded status with a plain-language explanation and the next step. A red reading opens an immediate-action screen that puts the crew procedure first, and prepares an escalation message for the flight surgeon. The app links each body region to the NASA hazard that threatens it.
How it addresses the challenge: The challenge asks for software that lets astronauts assess their own health and act on what they find. The app gives guided checks, clear status, and clear escalation, and it does not diagnose or prescribe.
Why it matters: Long missions limit how quickly crews can reach ground medical help. Early detection and clear escalation can help the crew and the flight surgeon act sooner.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: It lets a crew member check heart rate and sleep through guided steps. It shows each reading as green, amber, red, or grey, with the rule used, a plain-language explanation, and the next step. It also keeps a trend chart, a weekly handoff summary for the flight surgeon, and an escalation log.

How it works: A body map links each region to its function and to the NASA hazard that threatens it. Each reading is scored against provisional ranges. Emergency signs stop the normal flow and show the crew procedure. A red reading prepares an escalation message. Three amber days in a row create a routine escalation. Missing or invalid data is shown in grey and is not scored.

Benefits: It helps a crew spot changes early, explains what each reading means, and makes escalation clear. It is designed to work offline, with no server.

What we hope to achieve: A validated tool that adds more indicators, such as blood pressure, blood glucose, and a vision check, with thresholds confirmed by flight surgeons and clinical guidelines.

Limits of this prototype: Readings are simulated. Only heart rate and sleep are scored. Thresholds are provisional. The app has not been tested with astronauts or flight surgeons.

Tools and languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in one file, with no frameworks. Hosted on GitHub. The demo deck is a PDF on Google Drive, with the Inter typeface.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project NEWERA
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes in the Dust is an interactive digital storybook and field guide created to introduce school-age space enthusiasts to NASA's historic hardware resting across the Moon, Mars, and deep space.

 The project brings "abandoned" equipment—such as the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the Opportunity rover, the InSight lander, and Voyager 1—back to life through engaging narrative storytelling and official mission photography, mapping out the physical machines left behind alongside the planetary science they achieved.

It transforms complex space exploration history into accessible, captivating educational content, sparking curiosity and inspiring the next generation of scientists and space explorers to appreciate the lasting legacy of human ingenuity across the solar system.
projectDetails.details: Echoes in the Dust is an interactive digital field guide and presentation deck designed to introduce school-age space enthusiasts to NASA’s historic hardware resting across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. It brings abandoned equipment—such as the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, lunar rovers, the Opportunity rover, the InSight lander, and the Voyager 1 spacecraft—back to life through engaging narrative storytelling. The project guides users through each artifact's historical location, mission status, and the specific scientific breakthroughs it unlocked. Its primary benefit is making space science accessible, educational, and captivating for young learners, with the intended impact of sparking curiosity about planetary science, preserving the legacy of historic space missions, and inspiring the next generation of engineers and scientists. The project was developed using Gamma AI for visual layout and slide generation, supported by official open data from the NASA Image and Video Library, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), and the Planetary Data System (PDS). The team focused on human-centric storytelling to transform silent metal relics into monuments of human curiosity while adhering strictly to project guidelines, presentation limits, and official data citations
