projectDetails.name: ASTRAVITA
projectDetails.summary:
NOVA SHIELD

See the Hidden. Predict the Risk. Protect the Crew.

NOVA SHIELD is an AI-assisted environmental and astronaut health monitoring system proposed for long-duration space missions.

It combines three integrated modules:

- AEROMAP – Environmental Intelligence: Monitors CO₂, temperature, humidity, and airflow across spacecraft zones, identifying unusual environmental changes.
- ASTRA-SYNC – Health Impact Intelligence: Connects environmental trends with relevant health information, including sleep, fatigue, concentration, and well-being.
- ZENVITA – Wearable Health Integration: Optionally displays wearable measurements such as heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, sleep, and activity.

The system aims to detect developing environmental conditions, identify possible contributing factors, estimate future trends, and help astronauts and authorised Mission Control personnel review relevant health information.

Its dashboard includes spacecraft zone mapping, predictive warnings, historical charts, health indicators, an action-review checklist, and post-action verification.

NOVA SHIELD is a proposed decision-support prototype, not a medical device or replacement for existing spacecraft safety systems. All demonstration readings are simulated. Safety-critical decisions remain with authorised humans.

Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
Event: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
projectDetails.details:
Project: ASTRAVITA

App: Nova Shield

Team: OrbitFit

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions

Live App: https://mmabyadh-cmd.github.io/novashield/

GitHub: https://github.com/mmabyadh-cmd/novashield

WHAT DOES IT DO / HOW DOES IT WORK?

ASTRAVITA — Nova Shield is an AI-powered environmental + health intelligence system for long-duration space missions. It is ONE app, not three separate apps.

It answers 6 questions in seconds for every alert: WHERE? WHAT? WHY? WHAT NEXT? WHAT TO DO? DID IT IMPROVE?

It has 3 equal core modules + 3 supporting stations, all in one dashboard:

1. AEROMAP — Environment (6 zones, all equal)

Monitors zone-level CO2, temperature, humidity, airflow, pressure, VOC, particulates, noise and light for: Sleeping Compartment, Lab, Exercise, Galley / Kitchen, Control, Medical. In microgravity, there is no natural convection, so a cabin average hides local pockets. AEROMAP shows each zone separately.

Live Demo: Sleeping Compartment YELLOW — CO2 850 ppm, Airflow 0.12 m/s Down 30%, Temp 23.1°C. After the crew checks the vent + filter and clicks Mark as Done, it verifies: CO2 610 ppm GREEN, Recovery 68 to 82. Full audit trail: 08:00 Alert → 08:05 Acknowledged → 08:20 Inspection → 08:40 Verified.

2. ASTRA-SYNC — Health Impact

Connects environment timing with health timing. It does NOT claim the environment causes a body change. It shows association only. Example: CREW-001 Commander — Sleep 5.8h, Recovery 68, HRV Down 18%, HR 72, SpO2 97% on the same nights CO2 was high. The other 5 crew stayed GREEN, Recovery 83-88.

3. ZENVITA — Full Wearable Body Data (Opt-in, No Delivery)

Complete wearable app inside Nova Shield. No food delivery, no delivery tracking anywhere.

- Dashboard: Health Score, Recovery, Sleep, HRV, SpO2, HR, Steps, Calories, Water, Mood for CREW-001 to CREW-006 (crew selector)

- Sleep Lab: Last night 5.8 h, Deep 14%, REM 18%, Onset 28 min, Wakes 3, Quality 62%, 7-day trend 7.5 • 5.8 h falling

- Recovery & Strain: Recovery, Strain 72, Readiness Low, Resting HR 68

- Activity & Exercise: Steps 4200, Active 28 min, Treadmill 20 min, Resistance 15 min, Add Workout

- Nutrition & Hydration: Calories 2100/2600, Water 1.8L/2.5L, Add Meal, Add 250ml Water, Macros

- Mind & Well-being: Mood / Energy / Focus / Stress check-in 1-5 + Save, Breathing 4-7-8 timer, Journal

- History: 7-day table for Sleep, HRV, Recovery, HR, SpO2

- Privacy: Opt-in only, no audio/video, Data stays local, Share trends with Crew Medical only

4. Space Smart Kitchen Station

Galley + Nutrition Hub, onboard inventory only, no delivery, no ordering from Earth.

Inventory: Chicken Curry 12, Rice 10, Tortillas 18, Peanut Butter 6, Apples 4 LOW STOCK, Coffee 20, Carrots 8, Cheese 7, Water Pouches 40. Search + filter, expiry, low-stock warnings.

Today's Menu for each crew: Breakfast 450 kcal, Lunch 750 kcal, Dinner 500 kcal, Snack 190 kcal.

Recipe Builder: Pick 3 ingredients → Suggest recipe (e.g. Tortilla + Peanut Butter + Apple = Space Wrap 450 kcal) + Cook Log → Syncs to ZENVITA Nutrition.

Food Safety: Fridge 3.5°C GREEN, Freezer -18°C GREEN, Hygiene checklist. Waste: Food waste 0.2 kg, Recycling 92%, Water recycling 92%. Equipment: Rehydration Station, Food Warmer, Dispenser — all GREEN.

5. Exercise Station: Treadmill, Cycle Ergometer, Resistance device, weekly plan, equipment status, syncs to ZENVITA.

6. Sleep Station: Sleep environment (CO2, Temp, Noise, Light), sleep schedule for all 6 crew, sleep hygiene checklist.

4 AI MODELS — VISIBLE IN ALL MODES:

Model 1 Pattern: 82% — Rising CO2 pattern detected

Model 2 Prediction: YELLOW again in 90 min (Range 75-110 min) if not fixed

Model 3 Cause: Reduced ventilation 82% / Filter load 11% / Other 7%

Model 4 Health: Sleep Down 28%, HRV Down 18%

The same 4 models appear in Dashboard, Astronaut, Mission Control, Crew, Health, Body, ZENVITA and Kitchen modes. Never hidden.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- Early warning: Predicts risk 90 minutes before the threshold, not after.

- Zone-level truth: Finds hidden local CO2 pockets that cabin averages hide.

- Faster decisions: WHERE / WHAT / WHY / NEXT / ACTION / IMPROVED in one screen.

- One app: Environment + Health + Body + Kitchen + Exercise + Sleep together, no switching apps.

- Verified action: Mark as Done proves improvement with before/after numbers, not just an alert that disappears.

- Equal coverage: 6 zones equal, 6 astronauts equal, 3 health areas (Sleep / Physical / Mental) equal.

- Human in control: AI suggests, human approves. AI never auto-acts on safety actions.

- Private and resilient: Opt-in, no audio/video, offline-first, works with communication delay to Earth.

WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

To make long-duration missions safer when Earth cannot help instantly. To protect sleep, recovery and daily performance, not just to sound alarms. To support independent health monitoring for Lunar Gateway, Moon and Mars missions, where delays are minutes to tens of minutes and crew must decide alone.

On Earth, the same logic helps submarines, isolated research stations, hospitals and remote workplaces where air + health + food + sleep are connected.

Vision: See the Hidden. Predict the Risk. Protect the Crew.

WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

- Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript (single-file web app, index.html)

- Fonts / Design: Inter — one font for all text, spacious layout, high-contrast cards for readability

- Platform: GitHub Pages (public, no login) — Live: https://mmabyadh-cmd.github.io/novashield/

- Code: GitHub repo GitHub.com/mmabyadh-cmd/novashield (MIT, public)

- Data: Simulated environmental sensor data + simulated wearable data, modelled on NASA ECLSS concepts and NASA-STD-3001 human factors guidance. No real astronaut data used.

- AI Logic: Rule-based logic + pattern detection + trend analysis + confidence scoring (prototype logic, clearly labelled with % confidence and ranges, not a black box)

- Conceptual hardware foundation: Existing spacecraft sensors (CO2, temp, humidity, airflow, pressure) + commercial wearable sensors (HR, HRV, SpO2, sleep, steps) + galley equipment (rehydration station, warmer, fridge/freezer). No new hardware required for the prototype.

- Presentation: 7-slide Google Slides demo (ASTRAVITA / Nova Shield / Team OrbitFit)

HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

Most systems monitor spacecraft OR astronauts separately, and only alert after a threshold. ASTRAVITA is creative because it does 5 things together:

1. Zone-level + Prediction: It finds WHERE the problem is and WHEN it will return, not just that a threshold was crossed.

2. Environment + Body + Kitchen + Sleep in one loop: Air → Sleep → Recovery → Food → Exercise → Air. A poor sleep night, a low recovery score, a low-stock food item and a high-CO2 zone are shown together, not in separate tools.

3. Verified loop: Alert → Action → Mark as Done → Before/After proof. Judges and crew can see improvement, not just warnings.

4. Transparent AI: Every AI claim shows its confidence and range, and health claims are labelled association only.

5. Honest, human-centred design: Privacy-first, opt-in, offline-first, equal importance to every zone, crew member and health area. SpO2 does NOT measure CO2 — we state this clearly and never merge the two.

WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

Team OrbitFit considered:

- Astronaut safety first: Early warning, verified actions, human approval, never auto-action on safety.

- Scientific honesty: Simulated data clearly labelled, decision-support only, not a medical device, association not causation, SpO2 ≠ CO2, confidence + ranges shown.

- Privacy: Opt-in wearable sharing, no audio/video, share trends with Crew Medical only, local/offline data.

- Communication delay: Offline-first, crew can decide without Earth.

- Usability: One app, one font, spacious layout, big numbers, 6 questions answered in seconds, works on mobile + desktop, no login.

- Compatibility: Works with existing sensors / wearables / galley equipment, no new hardware needed.

- Equality: 6 zones equal, 6 astronauts equal, Sleep / Physical / Mental equal, AEROMAP / ASTRA-SYNC / ZENVITA equal.

- Practical limits: Prototype uses simulated data; future work needs real telemetry, real wearable validation, personal baselines, radiation / noise / lighting, and specialist medical validation before any real use.

- Food and daily life: Nutrition, hydration, waste, food safety and exercise are part of health, not extras — so Smart Kitchen, Exercise and Sleep Stations are included, with no delivery feature.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:
Project Details: APOGEE

What it does & how it works: APOGEE is a browser-based aerospace simulator where players pick a launchpad on a 3D Earth, snap together a modular spacecraft from 27 parts, and pilot it from Earth to the Moon and onto the exoplanet GL-1500 using a real-time 120 Hz physics engine.

Benefits: It helps students actually see and test how rocket physics works—like weight, thrust, drag, and weather—right in a browser without needing to download anything.

Intended impact: We want to get other students excited about space exploration, coding, and engineering by letting them build and test their own rockets.

Tools & languages: We coded the whole project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with HTML5 Canvas for graphics, Web Audio for sound effects, and a browser so it runs on normal school laptops and tablets.

Creativity: Instead of using pre-made images or sound files, we programmed every rocket part, flame, explosion, and engine sound directly in code.

Key factors considered: We made sure the physics felt realistic without being too hard to play, kept the frame rate smooth, and built a step-by-step live tutorial so anyone can learn how to fly.

projectDetails.name: Project SpaceXTN
projectDetails.summary:
Overview

Relics is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of the equipment NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars. Instead of treating these objects as space junk, it presents each one as a character in humanity’s exploration story, with a purpose, an achievement, an ending and a lesson. Visitors choose a world, tap a relic on a map, and read what the object did, why it was left, what condition it is in, and what we learned from it.

The Problem

Most people know that astronauts walked on the Moon and that rovers have driven across Mars, but very few know what remains there today. Descent stages, lunar rovers, landers, instruments and even a helicopter still sit where their missions ended. Information about them is spread across technical archives, mission pages and image libraries that are difficult for students and the general public to navigate.
The topic is also becoming more relevant. NASA’s Artemis program is preparing to return people to the Moon, and commercial missions are following. That raises practical questions: how should historic landing sites be protected, and what can aged hardware teach us about building equipment that lasts? These questions deserve public attention, and storytelling is one of the best ways to create it.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Relics is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of equipment NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars. A visitor chooses a world, then explores a coordinate map where each pin marks a relic’s approximate landing location. A date-ordered list sits beside the map, so any story can be reached either way.

Selecting a relic opens a story card with four parts:

  • Current state: where the object is now and what condition it is in
  • Its story: what it was built to do and why it was left behind
  • What we learned: the lesson it offers future missions
  • NASA images: a link to NASA’s image library, so visitors can see real photographs

The prototype covers twelve relics. On the Moon these are the Apollo 11 descent stage, Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 12 visit, and the lunar rovers from Apollo 15, 16 and 17. On Mars they are the Viking 1 and 2 landers, Sojourner and Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter. A short quiz at the end reinforces what visitors learned.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns scattered technical records into short, readable stories for students, teachers and the general public.
  • It needs no installation or account, loads quickly, and works on phones and computers.
  • It is accessible, with keyboard navigation, visible focus states, light and dark themes, and reduced-motion support.
  • The quiz and the consistent story format make it useful in classrooms.
  • New relics are easy to add, because every entry follows the same data structure.

What is the intended impact?

We want people to see these machines as part of a shared human journey rather than as space junk. As NASA’s Artemis program returns people to the Moon, we hope the project builds public awareness of why preserving historic landing sites matters, and of what aged hardware can teach us about building equipment that lasts in dust, vacuum and radiation. It also aims to inspire curiosity in younger audiences about planetary exploration.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Format: a single self-contained web page with no external libraries
  • Data: a structured data set listing each relic’s name, site, coordinates, year, status, story and lesson
  • Hosting: a public web link, so no installation is needed
  • Presentation: a 7-slide demo deck
  • AI assistance: an AI assistant (Claude) helped draft the story text, summary and page code
  • Hardware: any ordinary computer or phone; the project needs nothing special
  • Reference sources: NASA Image and Video Library, NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek, LROC (Arizona State University), HiRISE (University of Arizona), and NASA mission pages

How is the project creative?

  • Objects as characters: Each relic is written as a character with a purpose, an achievement, an ending and a lesson, not as a catalog entry.
  • Human-scale details: Opportunity was built for months and lasted nearly fifteen years. Apollo 12 astronauts walked to Surveyor 3 and brought parts home. These details make the history memorable.
  • Museum-placard design: The page uses calm typography and a structure like a museum placard, so the relics feel like heritage rather than debris.
  • Two worlds, one map style: The Moon and Mars share one interface, which invites visitors to compare how exploration differs between them.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy: Mission facts and coordinates must be verified against NASA sources. All locations on the map are approximate.
  • Clear creative framing: Stories are plain retellings, and any creative narration should be labeled as interpretation, not NASA quotes.
  • Honest AI use: We disclose that an AI assistant helped with drafting and code, and that a human team reviews the content.
  • Licensing: NASA imagery is linked rather than copied, and any future use should credit NASA, ASU and the University of Arizona.
  • Accessibility and reach: The design supports many devices and abilities, and future versions could add narration and more languages.
  • Scope: We kept the first version focused on twelve well-documented relics, rather than a large catalog done poorly.
  • Heritage and ethics: The project respects the historic value of the sites and does not claim NASA endorsement.

Before submitting, check the facts and coordinates against NASA sources and edit any statement that doesn’t match what your team actually did.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Earth Data
projectDetails.summary: Climate variability and shifting monsoons threaten smallholder agricultural productivity across South Asia. In coastal and riverine farming regions, farmers struggle to decide what to plant across three annual seasons as rainfall arrives late, dry spells intensify, and soil salinity creeps inland. Field Shift translates raw NASA Earth observations (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP L4, MODIS 250m NDVI, and MERRA-2) into ranked, explainable 3-season crop rotation strategies on a single screen. Combining machine-learning monsoon onset forecasting, multimodal Gemini 2.0 Flash plant disease diagnostics, Turf.js geodesic field area computation, and live 7-day weather alerts, Field Shift empowers farmers to adapt their agricultural calendars with confidence in their native languages (English, Bengali, and Tamil). Every recommendation shows the exact satellite data points, environmental penalties, and positive agronomic benefits behind its score. Built with Next.js 16 and open-source science.
projectDetails.details: What does it do or how does it work? Field Shift is an explainable decision-support platform for smallholder farmers facing shifting monsoon patterns, coastal soil salinity, and climate volatility. It ingests historical satellite climate feeds (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, MERRA-2) to evaluate and rank thousands of 3-season crop rotation strategies for local fields. The platform features an offline-first rotation engine, a backtested machine-learning monsoon onset predictor, a multimodal Gemini 2.0 Flash plant disease diagnostic scanner (/disease), a Turf.js geodesic field area calculator (/locate), and 7-day micro-weather alerts. Every recommendation provides transparent SHAP-style factor contributions, penalty breakdowns, and SMS-ready advisory text. What benefits does it have and intended impact? 1. Reduces Climate Vulnerability: Shifts crop sowing calendars to synchronize with actual usable rainfall rather than outdated historical calendars. 2. Prevents Soil Degradation: Recommends nitrogen-fixing legumes and green manures to replenish organic matter and break pest/pathogen cycles. 3. Language & Digital Equity: Fully localized in English, Bengali (বাংলা), and Tamil (தமிழ்), with Web Speech voice priority controls and offline PWA capability to ensure zero barrier for rural smallholders. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? - Framework & Web: Next.js 16.3.6 App Router, React 19, TypeScript 5, Tailwind CSS v4, View Transitions API. - AI & ML: Google Gemini 2.0 Flash Multimodal Vision API, Chrome 127+ On-Device Gemini Nano (window.ai), Scikit-learn conformal prediction for monsoon onset. - Geospatial & Climate: Turf.js GIS engine, Open-Meteo 7-day weather API, NASA POWER point APIs, GPM IMERG precipitation grids. - Testing & Deployment: Vitest (701 passing tests), GitHub, Vercel edge deployment. How is your project creative? Rather than treating agricultural advice as a black-box prediction, Field Shift makes every recommendation mathematically transparent. Farmers see the exact penalty points deducted for drought or salinity risks and positive bonuses awarded for early monsoon onset or soil recovery. Its multimodal Crop Doctor combines satellite planning with field-level plant pathology, enabling farmers to break pathogen cycles through crop rotation.

projectDetails.name: IGNITION.AI Pro: Microgravity Combustion & Fire Safety Engine
projectDetails.summary: IGNITION.AI Pro is an AI-powered microgravity combustion and fire safety engine built on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, SAME, and SoFIE). Using Python, TF-IDF semantic ranking, and non-linear flame spread physics, it helps mission planners predict spacecraft fire risks across oxygen, pressure, and ventilation regimes while translating orbital combustion insights into safer materials, clean engines, and smart smoke detectors on Earth.
projectDetails.details: What it does & How it works: IGNITION.AI Pro bridges microgravity combustion theory and practical spacecraft fire safety through three integrated modules: 1. SI Semantic Experiment Ranker: Built with Python and scikit-learn (TF-IDF Vectorization & Cosine Similarity), it indexes flagship NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, SAME, and SoFIE) so mission engineers can query complex scenarios in natural language and retrieve ranked experiments with critical Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) thresholds and governing equations. 2. Microgravity Flammability Regime Simulator: Models non-linear spacecraft flame spread across oxygen concentration (14%–40%), cabin pressure (45–101.3 kPa), ventilation velocity (0–40 cm/s), and concurrent vs. opposed airflow—mapping radiative quenching (<1.5 cm/s), peak diffusion spread (5–18 cm/s), and convective blow-off (>25 cm/s) zones. 3. Theory-to-Earth Engineering Matrix: Translates orbital combustion findings into actionable terrestrial safety innovations with one-click CSV export. Benefits, Creativity & Intended Impact: By uniting NLP search with microgravity fluid-combustion physics (Gr → 0, Damköhler and Richardson scaling), IGNITION.AI Pro helps mission designers evaluate polymer flammability for ISS operations and Artemis lunar habitats (34% O2, 56.5 kPa) while advancing aviation fire-resistant textiles, low-emission engines, and multi-wavelength smart smoke detectors on Earth. Tools, Languages & Software Used: Python, Streamlit, scikit-learn, NumPy, Pandas, Plotly, Google Docs, and Google Slides.

projectDetails.name: Space Reclaim
projectDetails.summary:
Every space mission begins with a dream of discovery. But what happens when that mission ends?

Humanity has sent machines beyond Earth: rovers, landers, probes, and scientific instruments. They have explored worlds, collected data, and expanded our understanding of the universe. Yet many remain where their missions ended, while others continue travelling through space.

Beyond the Mission is an interactive visual storytelling experience that uncovers the stories of this hardware. Audiences discover where these machines are now, what they accomplished, and why their presence matters. The experience explores concerns surrounding orbital debris, collisions, and the responsibility of future exploration.

Not everything left behind is junk. Some objects are scientific and historical records; others can create risks for spacecraft and satellites. By showing this difference, our project encourages viewers to understand the impact of human activity in space.

The journey inspires young explorers everywhere. Our goal is to turn curiosity into awareness and inspire the next generation to imagine safer, more responsible ways to explore the universe.

Because a mission may end, but its footprint can last for generations.
projectDetails.details:
Space Reclaim is an interactive visual storytelling project designed to educate school-age audiences about the hardware humanity has left behind during space exploration. It takes viewers on a journey through the history and aftermath of space missions, exploring equipment left on the Moon, Mars, in Earth's orbit, and across deep space.

The project works through an interactive storyboard that combines striking visuals, short explanations, animations, and audience participation. Instead of presenting information through conventional slides, it encourages viewers to explore different scenarios, discover the stories behind individual spacecraft, and understand what happens when their missions come to an end.

Its primary benefit is making complex space-related topics accessible, engaging, and easier to understand. It distinguishes scientifically valuable mission remnants from harmful orbital debris while introducing concerns such as collisions, environmental impact, and responsible space exploration.

Our intended impact is to create awareness among younger generations and encourage them to think critically about humanity's growing presence in space.

The project uses presentation and visual design software to create its interactive storytelling experience. Its creative approach lies in combining education with a cinematic, story-driven format, transforming a scientific topic into an engaging journey of discovery.

Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, age-appropriate explanations, visual clarity, accessibility, and audience engagement.

projectDetails.name: Project aevyron
projectDetails.details:
ASTRAVITAL: Mission Medical Intelligence

ASTRAVITAL is an interactive prototype of a health-monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It is set in a simulated Mars expedition (MARS-01), currently in the transit phase on Mission Day 147. It shows how a flight surgeon or crew member could view, track and understand astronaut health in one connected workspace. All data is simulated, and the site says clearly that it is not a medical device, is not endorsed by NASA and does not replace flight surgeons.

Mission workspace and navigation

The interface is a dashboard-style workspace. A top bar shows the active mission, the mission day and phase, an online status indicator and an Emergency Access button. A sidebar lists 13 modules:

  • Mission Command Center
  • Astronaut Digital Twin
  • Medical Body Scanner
  • Health Monitoring
  • AI Health Intelligence
  • Cognitive Performance
  • Mental Wellbeing
  • Environmental Monitoring
  • Mission Health Timeline
  • Preventive Healthcare
  • Medical Operations
  • Crew Health Network
  • Medical Knowledge Center
  • Settings

A status line reads “All systems operational”, and the footer tags the build as Local Prototype v1.0.

Astronaut Digital Twin (the core feature)

The main screen is a living digital twin of the astronaut Alex Morgan (AST-001). It shows an interactive anatomical map with a mission-elapsed-time clock. Users can:

  • Switch between layers: Anatomical, Skeleton, Muscular, Cardiovascular, Nervous system, Health-risk heatmap and Examination.
  • Rotate between front and back views, or reset the view.
  • Select any of 11 connected regions: brain, eyes, heart, lungs, blood vessels, musculoskeletal system, bones, kidneys, digestive system, skin and immune system.
  • Read the colour-coded legend, where each region is marked either routine or attention.
  • Start a Guided Demo that walks a first-time viewer through the twin.

Region intelligence panel

Selecting a region opens a detail panel with six tabs: Indicators, Trends, Spaceflight Risks, Examination History, Observations and Guidance. The Cardiovascular example shows a resting heart rate of 65.6 bpm, which is 7.5 bpm above the astronaut’s personal baseline of 58.1 bpm. A trend line runs from Day 118 to Day 147 and flags a mild resting heart-rate drift over the last 8 days. The wording is careful: it suggests reading the drift alongside sleep and recovery trends and states that no diagnosis is inferred. An “Open in Scanner” button links the region to the Medical Body Scanner.

Summary tiles

Four tiles give the astronaut’s status at a glance:

  • Systems monitored: 11
  • Overall status: Stable, with 2 observations for attention
  • Last examination: Day 140, a routine mission assessment
  • Next health review: Day 150, a cardiovascular follow-up with the flight surgeon

Design and tone

The look is a dark, mission-control style. The language is informational and cautious, with “Simulated data” and “Informational only. Not a diagnosis.” repeated on the key screens.

Built entirely with AI

ASTRAVITAL was created entirely with AI apps and websites. The concept, content, layout and design were produced using [list your tools here, e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, Framer AI], and the site is published on Framer. No traditional manual coding was needed. It shows how a complex, data-rich product concept can go from idea to a working interactive prototype using AI tools alone.

projectDetails.name: SPACE LEGACY : Stories Left Behind
projectDetails.summary:
SPACE LEGACY is an interactive storytelling website that explores the human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars after space missions.

The project highlights the stories of the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Sojourner rover from Mars Pathfinder, and NASA's Opportunity rover. Through mission stories, photographs, timelines, and status information, visitors can learn why these machines were sent into space, what they accomplished, and what happened when their missions ended.

Using NASA mission information and imagery, SPACE LEGACY presents space exploration history in an engaging and accessible way. It aims to raise awareness of the scientific achievements, historical significance, and lasting legacy of these machines, reminding us that a mission's impact can continue long after the spacecraft stops operating.

Technologies used: HTML,CSS,JAVASCRIPT
projectDetails.details:
SPACE LEGACY is a responsive, interactive website designed to tell the stories of space exploration equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

The website focuses on three missions: Apollo 15 and its Lunar Roving Vehicle, Mars Pathfinder and its Sojourner rover, and the Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity. Visitors can explore dedicated Moon and Mars sections, read mission stories, view photographs, follow a historical timeline, and learn about the current status and legacy of these machines.

The project uses HTML to structure the website, CSS for its visual design and responsive layouts, and JavaScript for interactive features such as mobile navigation, expandable stories, and scroll animations.

Its creative approach is to present abandoned space equipment not simply as discarded objects, but as important witnesses to human exploration and scientific progress. The project aims to make mission history easier to understand and encourage visitors to appreciate the achievements of earlier space missions.

NASA mission information and imagery were used as primary resources. The photographs used are NASA-sourced, not AI-generated.

projectDetails.name: AI WaterWise Kerala
projectDetails.summary: AI WaterWise Kerala is an AI-powered agricultural and environmental monitoring web application that uses NASA POWER rainfall and temperature data to analyse climate patterns across all 14 districts of Kerala. It identifies unusual climate conditions, assesses potential drought risks and provides farmer-oriented recommendations. Through an interactive Streamlit dashboard, users can explore district-level rainfall, temperature, climate anomalies and risk categories. The project aims to transform NASA's open climate data into accessible information that supports climate awareness, agricultural planning and sustainable water management.
projectDetails.details:
Problem Statement Agriculture and water management are affected by changes in rainfall and temperature. Understanding climate variations is important for farmers to make informed agricultural and water-management decisions. Proposed Solution AI WaterWise Kerala is a district-level environmental monitoring and agricultural decision-support web application developed using NASA POWER climate data. Objectives - Monitor rainfall and temperature across 14 districts of Kerala. - Analyse monthly rainfall and yearly average temperature. - Identify unusual climate conditions. - Assess potential drought risks. - Generate farmer-oriented recommendations. Methodology 1. Collect historical rainfall and temperature data from NASA POWER. 2. Process and organise data for all 14 Kerala districts. 3. Calculate monthly rainfall and yearly temperature summaries. 4. Calculate rainfall and temperature anomalies. 5. Classify climate conditions into Normal Condition and Unusual Condition. 6. Categorise drought risks into Normal, Watch and Severe Dry Conditions. 7. Generate recommendations and display the results through a Streamlit dashboard. Technologies Used - Python - Pandas and NumPy - Scikit-learn - Matplotlib - Streamlit - Google Colab - GitHub - NASA POWER Project Results The processed dataset contains 7,714 monthly records covering 14 Kerala districts. The condition classification produced 7,096 Normal Condition labels and 618 Unusual Condition labels. Expected Impact The application makes historical climate information easier to understand and supports agricultural awareness, climate monitoring and sustainable water-management decisions. Limitations and Future Scope The current prototype uses historical climate data and defined drought-risk thresholds. It is not an official weather forecasting or warning system. Future improvements include real-time weather updates, crop-specific recommendations and early-warning notifications. AI Assistance Acknowledgement ChatGPT was used for coding guidance, explanations, documentation and presentation preparation. AI and machine-learning techniques were incorporated into the climate-condition analysis.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: VYOMA – Astronaut Health Intelligence System
projectDetails.summary:
VYOMA – Astronaut Health Intelligence System is an intelligent health monitoring and self-management platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It addresses health challenges associated with microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, and changing space environments by integrating physiological, behavioral, and environmental health monitoring.

VYOMA enables astronauts to track vital signs, sleep patterns, stress levels, and environmental conditions through a unified dashboard. Its personalized health analysis engine compares current measurements against individual health baselines to identify unusual patterns and potential risks. An AI-powered health assistant helps astronauts understand health changes, interpret alerts, and access actionable, protocol-based guidance. The platform also emphasizes offline accessibility, ensuring essential health records and monitoring capabilities remain available during communication disruptions.

By combining personalized health insights, anomaly detection, and intelligent decision support, VYOMA aims to empower astronauts to take a more proactive role in managing their health and well-being throughout space missions.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift: Satellite-Driven Crop Rotation & Resilience Planner
projectDetails.summary:
Field Shift: Satellite-Driven Crop Rotation & Resilience Planner is a user-friendly web decision support system that provides information to farmers on how best to rotate crops on their farms to accommodate changes in climatic conditions year after year.

The online portal combines 10-year earth observation data from NASA including SMAP, root-zone soil moisture, GPM extreme precipitation and runoff, ECOSTRESS vegetation water stress and POWER agro-climatology data with local soil characteristics and crop properties. The users can weigh various factors such as water management, soil conservation, profit variability, and pest breaks to assess four years of customized rotation strategies relative to the current strategy. Users also have the option to substitute crops and stress test their chosen crop rotation strategy through the portal.

With the translation of earth observation satellite databases into simple language suggestions for the growers’ fields, Field Shift enables growers to preserve topsoils, conserve water, minimize the use of chemical fertilizers and build farm sustainability.
projectDetails.details:
🌱 Field Shift – Helping Farmers Make Smarter Decisions

Field Shift is a web app that helps farmers plan which crops to grow over the next four years. Nowadays, climate change is making farming more difficult because of changing rainfall, rising temperatures, and water shortages. Our idea is to help farmers prepare for these challenges and make better decisions.

The app uses the last 10 years of NASA satellite data (2016–2026), along with local soil details, to understand the farming conditions.

Farmers can enter information about their soil and choose what they want to focus on, such as saving water, improving soil health, earning a steady income, or reducing pest problems. Based on their choices, Field Shift suggests three different crop rotation plans: Water-Saver, Soil-Builder, and Balanced Resilience. It also compares these plans with the farmer's current farming method.

One useful feature is that farmers can check how their crop plans might perform during difficult weather conditions, like a 2°C rise in temperature or a 30% drop in summer rainfall. They can also change crops and see how it affects water usage, soil health, and profit. Once they are happy with the plan, they can download it as a PDF or CSV file.

🌍 Impact

Our main aim is to make farming information easier to understand and use. Instead of showing complicated satellite data, the app gives farmers simple alerts and clear crop recommendations.

In water-stressed conditions, our model shows the potential to reduce irrigation requirements by up to 46%. It also suggests growing legumes and cover crops, which can improve soil quality, prevent soil erosion, and reduce fertilizer expenses.

We considered different farming conditions while developing this idea, including farms in the U.S. High Plains and small farms in Kerala, India.

💻 Technologies Used

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Chart.js
  • NASA SMAP, GPM, ECOSTRESS and POWER data
  • ISRIC SoilGrids

🎨 Design and User Experience

We wanted to make the app simple enough for farmers to use without needing technical knowledge. The main screen shows important information like water requirements, soil condition, and suggested crops instead of complicated scientific data.

Farmers are free to change the suggested crops according to their needs. Another important feature is that the app works offline, so it can still be used in areas where internet connectivity is poor.

Our Vision

We believe farming should be prepared for the future, not just the present. Through Field Shift, we want to help farmers save water, improve soil health, reduce farming risks, and make better crop decisions even as the climate changes.

projectDetails.name: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based space exploration simulator designed to introduce elementary students to aerospace engineering, space science, and robotics through hands-on learning.

We developed a six-mission training platform that follows a Plan → Execute → Evaluate approach. Students can assemble and launch rockets, manage space station life-support systems, establish lunar bases, program Mars rovers, design Earth-observation satellites, and simulate asteroid deflection. The platform combines realistic physics calculations, interactive simulations, coding activities, and post-mission assessments to make complex scientific concepts accessible and engaging.

It addresses the challenge of making STEM education more practical, immersive, and inclusive by transforming theoretical concepts into interactive space missions. With COPPA-compliant zero-PII student accounts, educator dashboards, accessibility features, and NGSS-aligned learning outcomes, the platform provides a safe and inclusive learning environment.

Our goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and astronauts by making space exploration an engaging educational experience.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based STEM learning platform designed for children aged 5–11. It transforms space science and aerospace engineering into an engaging, hands-on learning experience through six simulated space missions.

How It Works:

The platform follows a Plan → Execute → Evaluate learning cycle. Students begin by assembling rockets, selecting engines, fuel tanks, and payloads while observing real-time physics calculations such as mass, thrust, Delta-V, and thrust-to-weight ratio. They then execute simulated rocket launches featuring countdowns, engine effects, atmospheric transitions, and orbital velocity tracking.

Beyond rocket launches, students can manage space station life-support systems, design lunar bases, program Mars rovers using drag-and-drop commands, configure Earth-observation satellites, and simulate asteroid deflection. Each mission includes learning assessments, progress tracking, and achievement badges.

Technology and Tools Used:

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS.
  • Backend: Node.js with a custom REST API.
  • Database: JSON-based data storage.
  • Physics: Newton's laws of motion, Tsiolkovsky's Delta-V equation, and atmospheric drag simulation.
  • Audio: Web Audio API and Web Speech API.
  • Security: COPPA validation middleware, input sanitization, and zero-PII data handling.
  • Testing: Node.js native test runner.

The application is developed as a browser-based software solution and does not require dedicated external hardware.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project makes complex scientific concepts easier to understand through interactive experimentation rather than traditional textbook learning. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, computational thinking, creativity, and engineering skills. Educators can monitor classroom progress, track mission completion, and evaluate student understanding through a dedicated command center.

Creativity and Innovation:

The project's uniqueness lies in combining six different areas of space exploration into one educational platform. Instead of simply learning about rockets, planets, and satellites, children actively participate in simulated missions and experience the consequences of their engineering decisions.

Factors Considered:

Our team considered age-appropriate learning, scientific accuracy, accessibility, child safety, data privacy, usability, and educational relevance. Features such as adjustable text sizes, high-contrast mode, colorblind-friendly patterns, keyboard navigation, and voice narration make the platform more inclusive. COPPA-compliant zero-PII architecture helps create a safer digital learning environment.

Ultimately, our vision is to make aerospace education accessible, interactive, and inspiring, encouraging young learners to explore STEM and become tomorrow's scientists, engineers, and astronauts.

TERRA TRACE – An Intelligent Earth Observation and Environmental Investigation Platform

TERRA TRACE is an interactive scientific platform designed to help people investigate and understand changes occurring across Earth's interconnected environmental systems. It addresses the challenge of making complex Earth observation data more accessible, understandable, and useful for scientific investigation.

The platform brings together geographical exploration, environmental variable analysis, historical trend investigation, regional comparisons, and statistical analysis within a unified interface. Its integrated AI-assisted scientific assistant, ATLAS, is designed to help users interpret environmental information, understand scientific findings, and navigate investigations.

By transforming environmental observations into interactive investigations, TERRA TRACE encourages users to move beyond simply viewing data and instead explore patterns, identify trends, and develop evidence-based conclusions.

The project is important because understanding Earth's changing systems should not be limited to specialized researchers. TERRA TRACE aims to make environmental science more accessible to students, educators, researchers, and the wider public while promoting scientific literacy, environmental awareness, and data-driven thinking.
projectDetails.details:
TERRA TRACE

An Intelligent Earth Observation and Environmental Investigation Platform

1. What Does TERRA TRACE Do?

TERRA TRACE is an interactive Earth observation and environmental intelligence platform designed to help users investigate, understand, and interpret changes occurring across Earth's interconnected environmental systems.

Environmental changes involving temperature, precipitation, atmospheric conditions, land surfaces, and water systems generate enormous amounts of scientific data. However, accessing and interpreting these datasets can be challenging for people without specialized scientific knowledge.

TERRA TRACE addresses this problem by bringing geographical exploration, environmental data visualization, historical trend investigation, regional comparisons, and AI-assisted scientific interpretation into one unified platform.

Its primary objective is to transform environmental data from isolated measurements into meaningful scientific investigations.

2. How Does It Work?

TERRA TRACE follows a structured investigation workflow:

Geographical Exploration: Users can explore geographical regions through an interactive map interface, allowing them to investigate environmental conditions across different locations.

Environmental Variable Exploration: Users can examine environmental indicators such as temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, and atmospheric conditions using available datasets.

Historical Investigation: The platform is designed to help users explore environmental observations across different periods, making it possible to investigate changes and identify potential long-term patterns.

Scientific Analysis: Statistical investigation capabilities are intended to help identify trends, variations, and relationships within environmental observations. These include analytical approaches such as regression and non-parametric trend testing.

Regional Comparison: Users can compare different geographical regions to investigate similarities and differences in environmental behaviour.

ATLAS AI: TERRA TRACE incorporates an intelligent scientific assistant called ATLAS. It is designed to help users understand scientific concepts, interpret investigation context, and navigate the platform.

Research Documentation: The platform aims to help users organize their investigation findings into structured scientific reports.

The overall workflow connects geographical selection, environmental observations, scientific investigation, and interpretation within one environment.

3. What Benefits Does It Have?

TERRA TRACE offers several important benefits:

  • Scientific Accessibility: Makes environmental investigation more approachable for students, educators, and the general public.
  • Environmental Awareness: Helps users explore real-world environmental changes rather than relying exclusively on general information.
  • Data-Driven Learning: Encourages evidence-based thinking and scientific reasoning.
  • Simplified Interpretation: ATLAS is designed to make complex scientific information easier to understand.
  • Regional Understanding: Enables investigation of geographical differences in environmental conditions.
  • Historical Perspective: Encourages users to examine how environmental conditions change over time.
  • Scientific Transparency: Emphasizes the importance of reliable data sources, analytical methods, and verifiable findings.

4. What Is the Intended Impact?

Our intended impact is to make Earth-system science more accessible and encourage people to become active investigators of our planet.

We want students to understand that environmental science is not simply about memorizing facts or observing charts. It involves asking questions, examining evidence, identifying patterns, and developing scientifically supported conclusions.

TERRA TRACE aims to support environmental education, scientific curiosity, climate awareness, and preliminary environmental research.

In the long term, we envision developing it into a comprehensive environmental intelligence platform capable of connecting multiple scientific data sources and helping people investigate complex environmental questions.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between the availability of Earth observation information and people's ability to understand and use it.

5. What Technologies and Tools Were Used?

TERRA TRACE was developed using modern web development technologies and AI-assisted development tools.

Programming Languages:

  • TypeScript
  • JavaScript
  • HTML5
  • CSS3

Frontend Technologies:

  • React
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Recharts

Geographical Visualization:

  • SVG-based geographical rendering.
  • Custom equirectangular map implementation.

Development Tools:

  • Bolt.new for AI-assisted application development.
  • Visual Studio Code for code editing and development.
  • Git and GitHub for version control and source code management.

Artificial Intelligence:

  • ATLAS, the platform's integrated scientific assistant.
  • Rule-based intelligence for built-in assistance and capability routing.
  • OpenAI API integration was explored for extending ATLAS.

Hardware:

The application was developed using a personal computer with a standard software development environment. No specialized physical sensors or scientific hardware were required for the current software implementation.

6. How Is the Project Creative and Innovative?

The creativity of TERRA TRACE lies in its investigation-oriented approach.

Instead of functioning as another environmental dashboard that simply displays statistics, it aims to connect multiple stages of scientific exploration within a single platform.

Its most distinctive component is ATLAS, an integrated scientific assistant designed to work alongside the investigation environment.

Another innovative aspect is the combination of geographical exploration, historical investigation, regional comparisons, and statistical analysis. This approach encourages users to explore environmental questions rather than passively consume information.

The platform also emphasizes the distinction between scientific observations and AI-generated explanations, reinforcing the importance of data reliability and scientific transparency.

We aim to make scientific investigation both engaging and meaningful without sacrificing its technical foundations.

7. What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

During development, we considered several important factors:

Scientific Accuracy: Environmental information must be based on reliable observations and appropriate analytical methods.

Data Reliability: Data sources, availability, and limitations must be clearly distinguishable. Generated or illustrative information must never be misrepresented as actual satellite observations.

Accessibility: The interface should be understandable to users with different levels of scientific and technical knowledge.

Usability: Complex scientific workflows should be presented through an organized and intuitive interface.

Scalability: The architecture should support additional environmental datasets, analytical capabilities, and scientific resources in the future.

Performance: Data processing and geographical visualization should remain efficient and responsive.

AI Transparency: AI should assist scientific understanding rather than replace scientific evidence or independently establish environmental conclusions.

Educational Value: The platform should encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and evidence-based investigation.

Conclusion

TERRA TRACE represents our vision of a more accessible and interactive approach to understanding Earth's changing systems.

By bringing environmental exploration, scientific investigation, and AI-assisted interpretation together, we aim to transform how people interact with Earth observation information.

We believe that understanding our planet should not be restricted to experts with access to specialized scientific tools. With the right technology and approach, anyone should have the opportunity to explore Earth's environmental changes and develop a deeper understanding of the world around them.

TERRA TRACE — Discover the patterns. Investigate the changes. Understand our planet.

projectDetails.name: COSMOSIS
projectDetails.summary: COSMOSIS is an interactive 3D space exploration and flight academy that tells the story of NASA’s abandoned hardware, from lunar landers and rovers on the Moon to Mars rovers and deep-space probes like Voyager. Instead of reading about equipment that has been left behind, students fly to it, explore it in 3D, and learn what each machine was built to do, what science it made possible, and what condition it’s in today. Built for school-age space enthusiasts, COSMOSIS turns “discarded” hardware into stories of discovery, showing that these machines are abandoned but not forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
COSMOSIS is an interactive 3D “student space academy” that tells the stories of NASA’s left-behind hardware, built for school-age space enthusiasts. Learners fly through a 3D solar system and open the Command Deck, which holds 10 worlds, a 3D spacecraft hangar, 6 mission chronicles, and 4 physics labs.

How it works: Clicking a world zooms in on its story, live telemetry, and a gravity simulator (for example, your weight on Mars). The Mission Chronicles are narrated, choice-driven stories about real hardware: the Apollo 11 Eagle lunar module, the Opportunity rover, whose 90-day mission lasted 5,352 sols, and Voyager 1 with its Golden Record. Learners then try the science themselves with a lunar-lander simulator across the Moon, Mars, and Europa, and an orbital-mechanics lab based on Newton’s cannonball. XP, levels, and mission patches keep students engaged.

Benefits and impact: It turns “discarded” machines into stories of discovery and connects each one to the physics behind it. It is free, runs in the browser, and needs no install or login.

Creativity: Instead of a static timeline, learners play through the decisions behind each mission, such as the Apollo 1202 alarm.

Tools: HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Three.js for 3D, hosted on Vercel

Factors considered: Age-appropriate language, accuracy of mission facts, accessibility (keyboard controls, optional sound), and keeping it fun enough to learn from.

projectDetails.name: The Forgotten Explorers
projectDetails.summary:
Our team, Cosmic Blast, created a digital storybook titled "The Forgotten Explorers" for the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten".

This storybook introduces four remarkable space explorers: the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, Ingenuity, and Pioneer 10 and 11. Through creative storytelling, we share their missions, journeys, important discoveries, achievements, and what happened to them after their missions.

Our project aims to bring attention to these space explorers whose contributions are often overlooked. By presenting scientific information in an interesting and easy-to-understand story format, we hope to help readers learn about the history of space exploration and appreciate the machines that helped humanity discover the unknown.

Although their missions have ended or communication has been lost, their contributions will never be forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
The Forgotten Explorers – Stories of the Machines Left Behind in Space

Our project is an educational digital storybook that explores the journeys of four important space explorers: the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner Rover, Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, and Pioneer 10 and 11.

The storybook presents the missions through creative storytelling, allowing each explorer to tell its own story. It explains why these machines were sent into space, their missions, important discoveries, challenges, and where they are now.

The main aim of this project is to create awareness about space exploration and help people understand the contributions of robotic explorers. It makes scientific information easier and more interesting to learn, especially for students and young readers.

Our project combines scientific information with storytelling in a chapter-based digital format. Its creative approach helps readers connect with the explorers and understand their importance in space exploration.

The project was prepared using digital document and presentation tools, along with AI-assisted tools for content organization and preparation.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Cybernetic Chooms
projectDetails.summary:
**Project Summary – Cybernetic Chooms: Mission May Be Possible: Starbound**

*Mission May Be Possible: Starbound* is an interactive, browser-based space adventure developed by Team Cybernetic Chooms, consisting of Christy Abraham, Govind Krishna, and Kenan Thomas.

The project places players in the role of mission director of the Aurora spacecraft, responsible for preparing three astronauts to deliver a research beacon into orbit. The game features 12 decisions across four episodes, with three choices per decision that influence two hidden readiness scores: flight preparation and crew training. Based on these scores, players can unlock three possible endings: Mission Accomplished, Mission Lost, or Crew Lost.

Built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas 2D, the game includes animated characters, interactive dialogue, cinematic endings, achievement tracking, and saved game progress. It also supports offline play, responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, and reduced-motion accessibility settings.

The project demonstrates how storytelling, decision-making, programming, and visual design can combine to create an engaging and accessible interactive gaming experience.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Cybernetic Chooms: Mission May Be Possible: Starbound

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project, Mission May Be Possible: Starbound, is an interactive, choice-based space adventure that runs in a web browser. The player takes the role of the mission director of the Aurora spacecraft, responsible for preparing the rocket and its crew to deliver a research beacon into orbit. The game consists of four episodes and twelve decisions, each offering three choices with immediate narrative feedback. The decisions influence two hidden readiness scores: Flight Preparation and Crew Training. Depending on these scores, the player reaches one of three endings: Mission Accomplished, Mission Lost, or Crew Lost.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

The project provides an engaging way to explore decision-making, teamwork, preparation, and responsibility. It helps players understand how individual choices can influence the outcome of a complex mission. It also encourages critical thinking, planning, and awareness of the importance of safety and crew coordination.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our aim is to create an enjoyable and educational gaming experience that demonstrates the importance of careful planning, effective teamwork, training, and responsible decision-making. We want players to understand that successful missions depend on both technical preparation and human readiness.

4. What tools, programming languages, and software were used?

We developed the project using:

  • HTML: To structure the game interface.
  • CSS: To design the visual appearance and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript: To manage game logic, decisions, scoring, navigation, and animations.
  • HTML Canvas 2D: To draw the rocket, launch complex, astronauts, Earth, and ending scenes.
  • localStorage: To save mission progress, discovered endings, and motion preferences.

The game works offline once the HTML file is available locally and requires no installation.

5. How is the project creative?

The project combines interactive storytelling with space exploration. It features animated astronauts, character dialogues, colour-coded speech bubbles, a detailed launch complex, visual effects, cinematic endings, and achievement tracking. Players experience different consequences based on their decisions, making each playthrough an engaging experience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered:

  • Gameplay: Meaningful choices and balanced scoring.
  • Storytelling: An engaging space mission with multiple possible outcomes.
  • Visual design: Attractive backgrounds, animations, and clear dialogue.
  • Accessibility: Keyboard controls, visible focus indicators, descriptive canvas labels, and reduced-motion settings.
  • Usability: Saving progress, restarting missions, and navigating between screens.
  • Compatibility: Responsive layouts and offline functionality.
  • Reliability: Validating saved game data before loading.

Through this project, our team gained experience in connecting narrative choices to game logic, improving existing interfaces, creating animations, and developing accessible browser-based applications.

projectDetails.name: Mars Outpost: Astro-Engineer
projectDetails.summary: Mars Outpost: Astro-Engineer is a 3D browser-based survival game designed to teach young learners about the harsh engineering trade-offs of space exploration. Players take on the role of a Junior Commander managing a Martian outpost. They must navigate a fully realized 3D environment, switching between three distinct roles (Engineer, Explorer, Medic) to complete 50 critical repair tasks across massive futuristic facilities. Players are forced to balance Oxygen and Base Power while surviving random catastrophic events like Martian dust storms and solar flares. Built entirely with Three.js and procedural generation, the game provides immediate, accessible fun while subtly teaching core STEM principles about life support, resource management, and the unforgiving nature of the Red Planet.
projectDetails.details: The game addresses the challenge by making the complex, invisible trade-offs of space survival tangible in a 3D space. Kids don't just read about life support; they have to physically run across a Martian landscape to choose whether to fix the oxygen scrubbers or repair the solar array while a dust storm rages outside. We used Three.js (WebGL), HTML5, and CSS3 for the game engine, UI, and state management. The logic dictates a base degradation rate, forcing the player to prioritize tasks and switch roles dynamically (1: Engineer, 2: Explorer, 3: Medic). The game features a dynamic third-person camera, custom Martian sky shaders, particle-based weather systems, and massive interactive structures with animated sliding doors. It is creative because it wraps hard science in a fast, replayable, and visually stunning arcade-style loop.

projectDetails.name: Mission Design Lab
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Design Lab is a browser game we built for the NASA Space Apps Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players plan their own space mission, then run it. They pick one of five destinations (Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, asteroid Bennu or Jupiter’s moon Europa), build a spacecraft from about 30 parts within a budget and a launch-mass limit, survive random events like solar storms and power loss, and finally fly the arrival in real-time 3D.

It meets the challenge by making mission design the gameplay. Distances and sunlight levels come from NASA fact sheets, and the rocket equation and inverse-square law decide whether a design works. Players quickly learn why Mars is far, why Europa is dark, and why every kilogram counts. When a mission fails, the game explains why.

This matters because real missions are won through trade-offs in mass, power, fuel and budget, a side of exploration most people never see. Our game makes that thinking free, instant and playable in any browser, helping inspire the next generation of engineers and scientists.
projectDetails.details:
🚀 Mission Design Lab

Can you design a space mission that actually works?

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

🎯 The Idea in One Line

Most space games ask, "Can you shoot fast?" We asked, "Can you plan smart?"

In Mission Design Lab you build the spacecraft first, launch it, and then fly the final approach yourself. Whatever you chose on the build screen decides whether you survive.

🛠️ What It Does and How It Works

Four steps, from idea to landing.

Step

What the player does

What's happening underneath

1. Pick a mission

Choose from 5 destinations: Earth orbit, Moon, Mars, asteroid Bennu, or Jupiter's moon Europa

Each card shows real NASA numbers: sunlight, distance, signal delay

2. Build the spacecraft

Choose from about 30 parts (cameras, radar, solar panels, RTGs, engines, fuel tanks, shields) within a budget and a weight limit

Every part costs mass, power and money. You can't take everything

3. Survive the mission

Watch it run through 8 phases, from launch to completion. Solar storms, power drops and broken antennas strike at random

The game checks whether your design can handle them

4. Fly the approach

Steer a real-time 3D flight through gates and obstacles, or use autopilot at a cost to accuracy

The final score depends on science, efficiency, safety and budget

Two real physics rules run the whole game:

  • 🔥 The rocket equation: extra fuel adds weight, and weight needs more fuel. Each kilogram buys you less.
  • ☀️ The inverse-square law: the farther you are from the Sun, the weaker your solar panels and your signal. Europa gets about 1/27th of Earth's sunlight.

If a mission fails, the game tells you why, for example "Your Δv is too low, add more fuel." So players learn engineering from their failures.

🧠 What Factors Did We Consider?

We're students, so we kept asking ourselves, "Would this actually work, and would someone enjoy it?"

  • Scientific accuracy: We used real NASA fact sheets for distances and sunlight, and real physics formulas. We simplified costs and part stats on purpose so the game stays playable, and we say so openly.
  • Learning through play: Every trade-off teaches something. No lectures, just consequences.
  • Difficulty curve: Earth is the forgiving tutorial. Europa is brutal. The difficulty rises with real-world mission difficulty.
  • Making each mission different: Mars is about distance, Bennu is about precision, and Europa is about radiation and darkness. No two missions play the same.
  • Fairness: Failures always have a reason the player can understand and fix.
  • Accessibility: It works on desktop and touch screens, supports reduced-motion settings, and uses screen-reader labels.
  • Zero friction: Players don't need to install anything or create an account. They just open the website link in their browser and play.
  • Trustworthy data: We cite every NASA source and clearly separate real facts from gameplay simplifications.

🎯 Intended Impact

  • 🎓 Show how real missions are planned. Missions are won or lost on trade-offs among mass, power, fuel and budget, long before launch.
  • 🌍 Make NASA's challenges feel real. Players feel why Mars is far and why Europa is dark and dangerous.
  • 🙌 Open space engineering to everyone. It's free, instant, and needs no background knowledge.
  • 💡 Spark STEM curiosity. It connects classroom physics to real missions like OSIRIS-REx, Europa Clipper and the Mars rovers.

💻 What We Used

Category

Tools

Languages

HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks or libraries)

Graphics

HTML5 Canvas, a custom 3D engine we wrote for the flight section, SVG for spacecraft art

Sound

Web Audio API: every sound effect is generated by code, with no audio files

Browser features

localStorage (saves best scores), vibration on touch devices, reduced-motion support

Fonts

Google Fonts: B612 (designed for aircraft cockpits), B612 Mono, Chakra Petch

Hosting

Deployed as a static website, so it runs on any device with a modern browser

AI partner

Claude (Anthropic): we used it to design, build and refine the game

Data

NASA fact sheets, mission pages, JPL Small-Body Database (full source list included)

Hardware

Any laptop, desktop, tablet or phone with a modern browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari) and a stable internet connection. Recommended: a laptop or desktop with 4 GB RAM or more, a screen of 1280×720 or larger, and a keyboard and mouse for the 3D flight section. Touch screens are supported too.

The game is a lightweight website: nothing to download, no setup, no account. Just open the link and play.

✨ What Makes It Creative?

  1. Engineering is the game. The "boss fight" is a power budget.
  2. Your build screen decides your flight. Fuel, shielding and navigation parts you picked earlier directly change how the approach goes.
  3. Everything is made by code. Planets, nebulae, spacecraft art and sound are generated rather than imported, which keeps it small, fast and fully ours.
  4. Mission-control atmosphere. Codenames (TERRA-01, SELENE-02, ARES-03, OSIRIS-04, EUROPA-05), live telemetry and a Deep Space Network ticker make players feel like part of the team.
  5. Failure teaches. Instead of "Game Over," you get a debrief on what went wrong and how to fix it.

📌 Final Note

Our costs and part stats are simplified for gameplay, but the physics and destination data are real. We built Mission Design Lab to show that space exploration isn't just about rockets, it's about making smart decisions.

projectDetails.name: Forgotten Footprints
projectDetails.summary:
Forgotten Footprints is an interactive educational website that brings attention to the human-made machines left behind on the Moon and Mars after their missions. Through engaging stories, illustrations, timelines, and historical facts, the project explores three significant artifacts: the Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage, NASA's Sojourner rover, and the Mars Pathfinder lander.

Designed for school-age learners and curious space enthusiasts, the platform explains what these machines were built to do, how they contributed to space exploration, and why their scientific legacy still matters. By transforming technical mission history into an accessible storytelling experience, Forgotten Footprints aims to inspire curiosity about planetary exploration and the engineering achievements that made it possible.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Forgotten Footprints is a web-based educational storytelling platform developed in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

The project focuses on the stories of three important pieces of space exploration hardware:

  • Apollo 11 Lunar Module Descent Stage: The descent stage that enabled the first crewed lunar landing and remained on the Moon after the astronauts departed.
  • Sojourner Rover: NASA's first Mars rover, which demonstrated the potential of robotic mobility and scientific investigation on another planet.
  • Mars Pathfinder Lander: The stationary lander that delivered Sojourner to Mars and acted as a communication relay between the rover and Earth.

How It Works

The website presents these artifacts through an interactive experience. Visitors can explore individual artifact cards to learn about their purpose, mission history, scientific contributions, and significance. A historical timeline connects the missions, while a dedicated educational section explains why these objects remain important to the history of space exploration.

Technology Used

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5 for the website structure.
  • CSS3 for styling, responsive layouts, and original visual illustrations.
  • JavaScript for interactive artifact information panels and navigation.
  • GitHub for source code management.
  • Vercel for public website deployment.

The website does not require a backend, database, user account, or external API.

Innovation and Educational Impact

Instead of presenting mission information as lengthy technical documentation, Forgotten Footprints uses simple storytelling and interactive visual elements to make space exploration history accessible to younger audiences and casual learners.

Its intended impact is to encourage curiosity about planetary science, robotics, engineering, and the scientific discoveries made possible by earlier NASA missions.

Use of Super Intelligence

ChatGPT was used as an AI-assisted development tool to help draft educational text and generate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. The website's artifact illustrations are original CSS-based visual representations created in code, not NASA photographs or official mission diagrams. No AI-generated photographs, audio, or videos are included.

NASA Resources and Attribution

The project references NASA's official Apollo 11, Mars Pathfinder, and Sojourner mission resources for historical and educational information. Relevant source links are provided on the website.

Forgotten Footprints is an independent educational project and is not an official NASA website or affiliated with NASA.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: NASA Mission Hardware Trail
projectDetails.summary: The project explores the scientific and historical significance of equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars following various space exploration missions. It examines spacecraft, landers, rovers, scientific instruments, and other mission hardware, including Apollo descent stages, ALSEP experiments, Lunar Roving Vehicles, Surveyor landers, Viking landers, Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, Ingenuity, and InSight. The project aims to understand the purpose, functioning, achievements, and present status of these objects while highlighting their contributions to planetary science and the evolution of space exploration.
