projectDetails.name: Beyond the Mission
projectDetails.summary:
Beyond the Mission: The Machines We Left Behind is an interactive, cinematic storytelling website that explores the legacy of NASA's robotic and human space exploration missions. It focuses on the equipment and machines left behind on the Moon and Mars, revealing the stories behind hardware whose missions have ended but whose scientific and historical significance remains.

Through four immersive chapters—Deep Space, Moon, Mars, and Legacy—the project takes visitors on a visual journey using NASA imagery, animations, scroll-driven transitions, and concise storytelling. It highlights examples such as Apollo lunar equipment, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP experiments, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight.

The project aims to make space exploration history more engaging and accessible, especially for students and the general public, while encouraging people to look beyond mission achievements and remember the machines that made those discoveries possible.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Beyond the Mission is a cinematic, interactive educational website created in response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge theme, "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

The website presents the stories of space exploration hardware through four chapters: Deep Space, Moon, Mars, and Legacy. Visitors experience the project by scrolling through a sequence of visual sections, each introducing a different part of the journey.

How It Works

The experience begins with an animated view of Earth and introduces the idea of exploring beyond our planet. The Moon chapter explores Apollo-era equipment, including lunar module hardware, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, and the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP).

The journey then moves to Mars, highlighting robotic explorers such as Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity, along with the InSight mission. The visual transitions help communicate the increasing distance from Earth. The final Legacy chapter reflects on how equipment can become inactive or remain behind while its discoveries continue to contribute to our understanding of space.

The website uses NASA imagery and mission information, with source references and image credits included to help visitors explore the original material.

Technology and Tools

  • Frontend: React and JavaScript
  • Development environment: Vite
  • Animation: GSAP and ScrollTrigger
  • Code development: Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot
  • Version control and source code: Git and GitHub
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Visual assets and mission references: NASA's official websites and image library

Creative Approach

Instead of presenting mission information as a conventional list or dashboard, the project uses cinematic storytelling, large-scale imagery, animated transitions, and scroll-based interactions. The changing visual relationship between Earth, the Moon, and Mars reinforces the scale of space exploration.

The experience is designed to be accessible to students, space enthusiasts, and general audiences. Responsive layouts and reduced-motion support were considered during development.

Intended Impact

Beyond the Mission encourages visitors to appreciate the equipment and engineering behind space exploration, not just the missions' headline achievements. It aims to preserve the stories of these machines and make NASA's exploration history more engaging, understandable, and memorable.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but not forgotten solar system
projectDetails.summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive space story we built in PictoBlox. Players explore all eight planets, the Moon and deep space, guided by an astronaut called Astro. On each world they tap the robots NASA left behind, such as the Apollo 11 lander Eagle, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter, Cassini and Voyager 1. Each machine tells its own story in the first person, with narration and sound effects. It explains why it was sent, what it discovered and how its mission ended.

This answers the challenge by turning forgotten equipment into characters people can care about, instead of a list of mission facts. A short eight-question quiz checks what players learned and keeps score.

It matters because most students only hear about active missions. Stories like Opportunity’s, built to work for 90 days and lasting 14 years, show how good engineering leads to discovery and can inspire the next generation of explorers. The simple tap-and-listen design lets young learners use it without help.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, narrated story game made in PictoBlox. The player starts at a menu with an astronaut guide, Astro, and can take a Solar System Tour, visit the Moon, go to Deep Space or take a quiz.

  • Planets: on the tour, the player taps any of the 8 planets. Each planet has its own scene, and Astro narrates its story with on-screen captions.
  • Robots: on each world the player taps a spacecraft or robot. Eleven of them speak in the first person, in their own voice. They include Eagle, the Lunar Rover, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Voyager 1 and 2, MESSENGER, Magellan, Skylab, Galileo and Cassini.
  • Quiz: an 8-question quiz covers all the planets, reads each question aloud and keeps score.

The project uses PictoBlox’s broadcast messages to switch scenes and a shared variable so only one voice speaks at a time.

Benefits and intended impact
The project turns dry mission data into stories that students remember. It teaches the history of NASA’s older missions, which are rarely taught, and shows how engineering leads to discovery. It needs no instructions, so young learners can use it alone, and the narration helps those who find reading difficult. We hope it inspires the next generation of explorers.

Tools and software

  • PictoBlox, which uses block coding, for all the game logic.
  • Python to generate the artwork as SVG images and to synthesize the sound effects, such as the launch, whoosh and quiz chimes.
  • The eSpeak NG text-to-speech engine for the narration voices.
  • FFmpeg to process the audio.
  • Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, helped us write the scripts. Please check the challenge’s rules on AI use and mention this if required.

We used no extra hardware.

Creativity
The challenge asks for stories, so we let the machines tell their own, which gives each one a personality. Eagle’s lower half is still at Tranquility Base, and Ingenuity flew far beyond its plan. Each robot has its own voice, and the whole solar system is one connected journey.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA sources, and we checked them against NASA’s Resources tab.
  • Age: short sentences and big buttons suit school-age players.
  • Accessibility: captions match the narration word for word.
  • Honesty: the artwork and voices are computer-generated, not real NASA images or recordings, and we credit NASA for the facts.

projectDetails.name: NovaHealth: Autonomous Astronaut Health & Diagnostic System
projectDetails.summary:
NovaHealth is an offline-first, web-based health monitoring and decision-support tool engineered for long-duration space missions. We developed an intuitive dashboard featuring an interactive anatomical body map, multi-modal telemetry inputs, dynamic historical trend charts, and an intelligent diagnostic engine.

The software directly addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by translating NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) guidelines into practical, crew-operated care. It maps critical health indicators—such as sleep hours, cardiovascular metrics, and metabolic markers—against the primary hazards of human spaceflight, using instant color-coded status alerts to flag deviations.

NovaHealth is vital for deep-space exploration, such as lunar bases and Mars transits, where communication delays with Earth make real-time ground support impossible. By empowering astronauts to autonomously assess their health, follow structured diagnostic workflows, and determine when crew medical officer intervention is required, NovaHealth ensures crew safety and operational resilience far from Earth.
projectDetails.details:
NovaHealth is an offline-first, web-based autonomous health monitoring and decision-support system designed specifically for astronauts on long-duration space missions.

How It Works & Key Features The application processes multi-modal health inputs—such as biometric telemetry, sleep hours, blood sugar, and radiation logs—through an intelligent diagnostic engine. It features an Interactive Anatomical Body Map divided into key sectors (Head/CNS, Cardiovascular, Metabolic/Abdomen, and Musculoskeletal). Astronauts can click on any body region to instantly inspect health indicators mapped against NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) hazards. Metrics are categorized using intuitive color-coding (Green for nominal, Yellow for moderate deviation, Red for critical attention) to allow for rapid self-assessment at a glance.

Benefits & Intended Impact NovaHealth provides total mission autonomy by operating entirely offline, making it impervious to the severe 20-minute communication blackout delays experienced during deep-space transit to Mars. By automating medical triage and providing clear guidance—explaining what an exam measures, why it is needed, and when it requires intervention—the tool significantly reduces astronaut cognitive load under high-stress conditions. Its intended impact is to safeguard human life and operational continuity as humanity pushes further into the cosmos through Artemis and future Mars missions.

Technical Stack

  • Frontend Framework: React with Vite for high-performance rendering
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS (NASA Mission Control dark-mode aesthetic) and Lucide React iconography
  • Data Visualization: Recharts for dynamic, multi-week health telemetry trend charts
  • Development Architecture: Built and optimized using modern AI-assisted engineering tools for rapid prototyping and deployment

Innovation & Design Considerations NovaHealth transforms complex clinical data into an engaging, spatial user experience via an interactive visual body map rather than dense spreadsheets. In designing the solution, the team explicitly accounted for the five primary spaceflight hazards (space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile closed environments), minimized click-depth to combat astronaut fatigue, and anchored the architecture in an offline-first design philosophy.

projectDetails.name: Project Forgotten Horizons
projectDetails.summary:
Forgotten Horizons – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

Forgotten Horizons is an interactive 3D storytelling experience that explores the history of human exploration beyond Earth by bringing attention to the spacecraft, rovers, and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

Inspired by NASA's challenge, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," our project transforms forgotten space exploration hardware into meaningful stories. Through an immersive 3D explorer, users can discover eight historical missions, including Surveyor 3, Mars Pathfinder, Sojourner, Viking 1 and 2, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Apollo Lunar Module.

The platform features interactive 3D environments, mission information, historical timelines, a Mission Connection Network, and educational quizzes. Users can explore individual objects, understand their missions, discover their scientific contributions, and learn how these abandoned artifacts remain connected to humanity's journey into space.

Our goal is to make space history engaging, accessible, and educational, especially for students and future explorers. These objects may no longer be active, but their stories, discoveries, and contributions continue to inspire scientific curiosity.

Forgotten Horizons reminds us that exploration does not end when a mission is over. Every object left behind has a story worth remembering.
projectDetails.details:
Forgotten Horizons – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

1. What Does Our Project Do?

Forgotten Horizons is an interactive 3D storytelling and educational platform that explores the history of human space exploration by focusing on spacecraft, rovers, landers, and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

The project was developed in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and its challenge, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

Instead of treating abandoned space equipment as forgotten objects, Forgotten Horizons gives each object a story. It helps users understand why these missions were launched, what they achieved, and how their contributions continue to influence space exploration.

2. How Does It Work?

The platform provides several interactive sections:

3D Space Explorer: Users can explore 3D Moon and Mars environments, interact with markers, select historical objects, and discover information about their missions.

Mission Archive: The platform presents eight historical missions: Surveyor 3, Mars Pathfinder, Sojourner Rover, Viking 1, Viking 2, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Apollo Lunar Module.

Mission Connection Network: An interactive network connects the eight missions, allowing users to explore relationships between missions through nodes, filters, and detailed information.

Mission Control Dashboard: A central dashboard provides access to mission information, interactive features, and educational quizzes.

Historical Stories and Timelines: Users can learn about the history, achievements, and scientific importance of the selected missions.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

Forgotten Horizons aims to make space exploration history more engaging and accessible, particularly for students and people interested in astronomy and science.

Its main benefits include:

- Making historical space missions easier to understand.
- Encouraging curiosity about NASA's exploration of the Moon and Mars.
- Connecting historical missions with their scientific contributions.
- Providing an interactive alternative to traditional text-based learning.
- Helping younger audiences appreciate the importance of past space exploration.

Our intended impact is to inspire people to look beyond the present and recognize the scientific value of missions that have already ended.

4. Tools and Technologies Used

Forgotten Horizons was developed using web technologies and interactive 3D visualization tools.

The technologies include:

- HTML – Structure of the website.
- CSS – Visual design, layouts, animations, and responsive styling.
- JavaScript – Interactive functionality and user experiences.
- Three.js – 3D visualization and interactive space environments.
- Git and GitHub – Version control and project development.
- GitHub Pages – Public website hosting.

The project was developed and tested using a personal computer and a web development environment.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Forgotten Horizons is its storytelling approach.

Space exploration is often presented through successful launches, discoveries, and active missions. However, the equipment left behind after missions also represents an important part of human exploration.

Our project transforms these historical artifacts into interactive learning experiences. By combining 3D environments, mission stories, timelines, educational quizzes, and a mission connection network, we create a platform where users can explore space history rather than simply read about it.

6. Factors Considered During Development

During development, we considered:

- Historical accuracy and reliable mission information.
- Simple and accessible navigation.
- An engaging visual experience.
- Educational value for students and beginners.
- Compatibility with modern web browsers.
- Performance and usability across different screen sizes.
- Clear connections between historical missions and their contributions.

7. Our Vision

Forgotten Horizons is built around one simple idea:

"Exploration does not end when a mission is over."

The spacecraft, rovers, and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars are more than abandoned hardware. They are reminders of human curiosity, engineering, scientific discovery, and the courage to explore beyond Earth.

Through Forgotten Horizons, we want to ensure that these stories continue to inspire future generations of explorers.

Forgotten Horizons – Abandoned but Not Forgotten.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Helium3
projectDetails.summary:
Health Monitoring System
A Health Monitoring System is a technology used to continuously observe, measure and record a person's health conditions. It helps detect health problems at an early stage and allows doctors to provide timely treatment. It monitors important health parameters such as heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, oxygen levels, breathing rate and sleep patterns.
The system works with the help of special sensors and wearable devices that collect information from the human body. This information is then transferred to a computer or monitoring device, where it can be analysed. If any unusual changes are detected, an alert can be generated so that medical attention can be provided.
Health Monitoring Systems are especially important for astronauts during space missions. In space, conditions such as microgravity, radiation and isolation can affect the human body. Astronauts wear special devices that monitor their vital signs and send health-related information to doctors on Earth. This helps scientists understand how space travel affects the human body and take necessary precautions.
In conclusion, Health Monitoring Systems play an important role in modern healthcare and space exploration. They help protect human health, improve safety and ensure that medical problems are identified and treated at the right time.

HORIZON 404 is an interactive space archaeology application that explores abandoned NASA spacecraft, scientific equipment, and historical artifacts left behind on the Moon and Mars. Its main purpose is to preserve the history and achievements of space exploration through storytelling, interactive maps, 3D models, and augmented reality (AR).
The application features important space exploration artifacts, including the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Opportunity Rover, Ingenuity Helicopter, and InSight Lander. Users can explore their historical backgrounds, missions, technical details, and reasons for being left behind.

projectDetails.details:

The application allows users to explore planetary locations through interactive maps, discover space artifacts, read their mission histories, and understand their scientific importance. It also includes features such as bookmarks, exploration progress tracking, 3D visualization and augmented reality (AR) concepts to create an engaging learning experience.

The main benefit of this project is making space exploration history accessible, interactive and educational. Its intended impact is to inspire students and space enthusiasts, encourage scientific curiosity, and preserve the legacy of important space missions for future generations.

The project is developed as an Android mobile application. The APK contains Jetpack Compose-style user interface components and screen-based navigation. The exact programming language and development tools used are not confirmed. The project focuses on mobile software, interactive interfaces and digital visualization.

The creative aspect of HORIZON 404 is its unique idea of treating abandoned space equipment not as forgotten objects but as valuable pieces of human history. We considered user experience, educational value, accessibility, scientific accuracy, visual presentation and future scalability while developing the concept.

Our vision is to turn forgotten space exploration artifacts into stories that everyone can discover, explore and appreciate.

projectDetails.name: The Quiet Pioneers: Tales from the Silent Stars
projectDetails.summary:
The Quiet Pioneers: Tales from the Silent Stars is an illustrated digital storybook that tells the stories of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon, Mars and beyond. Five chapters follow the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Mars rover Opportunity, the Ingenuity helicopter, the InSight lander and Voyager 1, each told as a journey from launch to final signal.

It answers the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge by turning dense mission data into a narrative for school-age and casual space enthusiasts. Instead of listing facts, the story shows how each machine operated: Opportunity’s dust-devil cleanings, Ingenuity’s first flight in Mars’s thin air, InSight listening for 1,300+ marsquakes. “How Engineering Unlocked Science” callouts connect each machine’s engineering to what humanity learned, and a Field Guide table summarises where each rests today.

It matters because young learners mostly hear about active missions. By giving silent explorers a voice, the storybook builds a personal connection to them and inspires the next generation to explore.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
The Quiet Pioneers is an illustrated digital storybook for school-age and casual space enthusiasts. It has a prologue, five chapters and a Field Guide. Each chapter tells one mission as a story: the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Mars rover Opportunity, the Ingenuity helicopter, the InSight lander and Voyager 1. Chapters follow the same arc (arrival, discoveries, final silence) so readers can follow the machines’ lives easily. Every chapter has a “How Engineering Unlocked Science” callout that links the hardware’s design to the science it made possible. The Field Guide table summarises each spacecraft’s location, active years, instrument and breakthrough.

Benefits and intended impact
Young learners usually meet space history through dense technical pages. This storybook gives them accurate science in a form they enjoy. We want readers to feel a personal connection to these “silent sentinels” and to see that every ended mission paved the way for today’s exploration.

Tools and technology
Story and facts researched from NASA mission information; illustrations created with [tool/method]; layout designed in HTML/CSS and exported to PDF (A4, 6 pages); presentation deck built in PowerPoint format.

Creativity
Machines are treated as characters with a voice (“My battery is low and it’s getting dark”), and Voyager’s Golden Record closes the story as an “ambassador in a bottle”. Warm watercolor-style illustrations and everyday comparisons (Ingenuity flying like a helicopter 100,000 feet above Earth) make the science easy to picture.

Factors considered
We prioritised scientific accuracy (real dates, distances, flight counts), age-appropriate language, readable layout and accessible format, and chose missions across the Moon, Mars and interstellar space to show the broader story of NASA exploration.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Abandoned but not Forgotten is a storytelling project that gives a voice to NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. Through short first-person narratives, it follows the Apollo lunar landers, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Apollo laser retroreflectors, the Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity rovers, and the Ingenuity helicopter, showing how each one exceeded its planned mission and where it rests today. The project addresses the challenge by turning real NASA mission facts into an emotional, easy-to-remember story for students and general audiences. It matters because these machines still hold scientific value, such as the retroreflectors that are still used to measure the Moon's distance, and their landing sites are historic places worth protecting as exploration grows. All images are AI-generated illustrations.
projectDetails.details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is a storytelling presentation that gives a voice to NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. Instead of listing dry facts, each slide is told from the point of view of the machine itself, covering the Apollo lunar landers, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Apollo laser retroreflectors, the Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity rovers, and the Ingenuity helicopter.

What it does and how it works: Each slide focuses on one machine or group of machines, with short facts about what it did, how long it lasted compared to its original plan, and where it is now. For example, Sojourner was designed for 7 sols and lasted 83, and Ingenuity was planned for 5 flights and completed 72. The story builds from the Moon to Mars and ends with a message about preserving these sites.

Benefits and intended impact: The project makes space history more emotional and easier to remember for students and general audiences. It shows that machines left behind still have value, such as the retroreflectors that are still used to measure the distance to the Moon. It also encourages people to think of these landing sites as historic places worth protecting as space exploration grows.

Creativity: The first-person "machines speaking" approach and a cinematic dark visual style turn mission data into a story people can connect with.

Factors considered: We focused on accuracy by using NASA's public mission pages for facts, and on honesty by clearly labeling all images as AI-generated illustrations and not actual NASA photos. We also kept the design simple and readable.

Tools used: Canva (design and layout), Canva AI (image generation), and Claude, an AI assistant (drafting and editing the text). No code or hardware was used. All images carry a visible "AI-generated image" watermark, and no NASA logos or branding were used.

projectDetails.name: TerraSleuth
projectDetails.summary:
Earth’s climate is constantly shifting, but raw satellite tables and complex climate models make it difficult for students and everyday citizens to see what is actually changing in their own backyard—and whether those shifts are real trends or just normal weather swings.

**TerraSleuth** solves this by turning users into Earth System Trend Detectives. Through an interactive world map, anyone can click any location on Earth—or explore curated NASA case studies like Kochi’s warming monsoon, Amazon drying, and Arctic climate variability—to inspect multi-decade temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, and humidity records from NASA’s POWER API and MERRA-2 reanalysis datasets.

Instead of leaving users to guess at noisy graphs, TerraSleuth automatically strips away seasonal cycles using a 12-month rolling average and runs real statistical forensics, including Mann-Kendall significance tests, Sen’s slope decade rates, confidence intervals, and changepoint detection. It even lets users compare two regions side by side to see how the same global forces can push different parts of the planet in opposite directions. Finally, TerraSleuth translates the math into a clear, plain-English **Detective Verdict**, helping anyone understand what is changing, where it is happening, and why it matters.
projectDetails.details:
TerraSleuth is an interactive web application designed to turn students, researchers, and everyday citizens into Earth System Trend Detectives. Users can click anywhere on an interactive global map—or select from curated regional case files—to fetch 30 to 40+ years of monthly Earth science data, including 2m air temperature (T2M), precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), surface solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN), and relative humidity (RH2M).

Rather than displaying raw, noisy weather tables, TerraSleuth automatically strips out seasonal cycles using a 12-month rolling average and runs an in-browser statistical forensics engine. It computes the rate of change per decade (Sen’s slope), runs a non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend test ($S$, $Z$-score, and $p$-value), calculates 95% confidence intervals, and pinpoints the exact changepoint year where the largest historical shift occurred. It also includes a guided 3-step Investigation Wizard and a Compare Opposite Regions split-screen mode that demonstrates how the same global climate drivers can push two different regions in opposite directions.

Benefits & Intended Impact Scientific climate datasets are often locked behind complex file formats and specialized statistical software, creating a barrier for high school and college students. TerraSleuth bridges that gap by pairing accessible, plain-English variable definitions with real statistical rigor. By translating statistical significance ($p < 0.05$) into a clear Detective Verdict (Clue, Suspect, and Why It Matters), the tool empowers learners to distinguish true long-term environmental shifts from short-term natural variability—promoting scientific honesty and data literacy.

Tools, Languages, Software & NASA Resources Used

  • Languages & Libraries: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), Leaflet.js (interactive mapping), and Chart.js (time-series visualization and changepoint markers).
  • Development & Hosting: Developed using Google Antigravity IDE (used as an AI coding collaborator to accelerate UI scaffolding and statistical module implementation), version-controlled on GitHub ([github.com/arjid200/TerraSleuth](https://github.com/arjid200/TerraSleuth)), and deployed as a zero-backend static web application via GitHub Pages.
  • NASA Data Resources: Live global pin-drops query the NASA POWER Temporal API (1985–2025), backed by NASA MERRA-2 assimilation data. Pre-loaded regional case files use verified 30-year monthly NASA POWER / MERRA-2 CSV datasets (1995–2024, 0.5° × 0.625° spatial resolution) alongside support for user-uploaded CSV exports from NASA Giovanni and AppEEARS (covering missions and models such as GPM, MODIS, OMI, AIRS, and GLDAS).

Creativity & Design Considerations

  • Detective Framing: Reframing statistical hypothesis testing as an environmental "crime scene investigation" makes abstract metrics like $p$-values and deseasonalization intuitive and engaging for students.
  • Scientific Honesty & Spatial Scale: Our team explicitly designed TerraSleuth to highlight non-significant trends alongside significant ones—for example, showing how high year-to-year polar variability at a single Arctic grid point (80.00°N, 0.01°E) masks long-term warming over a 30-year window, whereas Kochi, Kerala (9.93°N, 76.27°E) exhibits statistically significant warming (+0.27°C/decade, $p < 0.0001$) alongside highly variable monsoon rainfall, and the Amazon Basin (3.10°S, 60.00°W) experiences both significant warming (+0.35°C/decade) and drying (-0.52 mm/day/decade). We also explicitly note the ~50–70 km MERRA-2 grid-cell footprint so users understand spatial resolution limits.
  • Zero-Friction Accessibility: By running all statistical calculations purely client-side in JavaScript and bundling pre-verified CSV case studies locally, TerraSleuth requires zero installation, zero server overhead, and loads instantaneously even on low-bandwidth connections.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:

The project focuses on three Apollo-era technologies: the Lunar Module descent stage, the lunar laser retroreflector, and the Apollo seismometers. Each exhibit explains the purpose of the equipment, how it worked, and its importance to space exploration and scientific research.

The website makes information about Apollo hardware easier to explore through organized exhibits, clear explanations, and an interactive knowledge quiz. Instead of presenting information as ordinary text, it encourages visitors to explore each piece of equipment and test what they have learned.

The intended impact is to increase awareness of the engineering achievements of the Apollo missions and show how equipment from past lunar missions continues to contribute to scientific knowledge.

The project is creative because it presents historical lunar technology in an accessible, interactive format. It combines educational content with exploration and a quiz to make learning more engaging. The website is hosted on Netlify.

projectDetails.name: MonsoonLens – Earth System Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary:
MonsoonLens is an interactive climate trend investigation dashboard developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It uses monthly climate data from NASA POWER to explore long-term changes in temperature, precipitation and relative humidity across selected locations in India, including Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Kozhikode, Bengaluru, Mumbai and New Delhi.

The platform transforms monthly observations into annual climate indicators and visualizes changes through interactive charts. It includes annual temperature trends, accumulated rainfall, June–September monsoon rainfall and annual relative humidity. Users can compare multiple locations, examine trend estimates and statistical significance, and explore geographical patterns through an interactive map.

By making climate data easier to visualize and compare, MonsoonLens helps users investigate how environmental indicators change over time and how these patterns differ between regions. It uses NASA POWER data to make Earth system trends more accessible and understandable.
projectDetails.details:
MonsoonLens – Earth System Trend Detective

What does the project do and how does it work?

MonsoonLens is an interactive climate trend investigation dashboard that helps users explore how climate indicators change over time and differ across geographical locations in India.

The project retrieves monthly climate data from NASA POWER through its API, focusing on three indicators: air temperature (T2M), precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) and relative humidity (RH2M). The monthly data is processed into annual indicators and presented through interactive visualizations.

Users can select a study location and time period, investigate annual temperature trends, accumulated rainfall, June–September monsoon rainfall and annual relative humidity. The dashboard also provides trend estimates, statistical analysis, comparisons between multiple locations and an interactive map showing the selected study regions.

What benefits does it have?

MonsoonLens makes climate data easier to understand without requiring users to download datasets or perform statistical calculations themselves. It brings multiple climate indicators together in one accessible interface and allows users to compare geographical differences. This helps students, educators and other interested users explore environmental patterns using NASA's Earth science data.

What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to improve awareness and understanding of regional climate variability and long-term environmental changes. By making Earth science data more accessible, MonsoonLens encourages data-driven exploration, environmental education and curiosity about interconnected Earth systems.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed primarily using Python. Streamlit was used to build the interactive dashboard, Pandas and NumPy for data processing, Plotly for interactive charts and geographical visualizations, SciPy for statistical analysis, and Requests for retrieving data from the NASA POWER API. Development and testing were performed on a Linux-based computer. No dedicated external hardware is required.

How is the project creative?

MonsoonLens combines several climate indicators, statistical trend analysis, geographical visualization and multi-location comparison in a single investigation tool. Rather than presenting climate data as isolated tables, it allows users to interactively explore relationships between time, location and environmental change. Its focus on Indian locations also provides a regional perspective on climate patterns.

What factors did the team consider?

The development considered data availability, reliability of monthly observations, missing values, appropriate annual aggregation methods, ease of use and geographical coverage. Minimum valid-month requirements were applied to annual calculations to reduce misleading results from incomplete data. Rainfall accumulation accounts for the number of days in each month, while annual humidity uses day-weighted averaging. Statistical significance is interpreted cautiously because correlation does not establish causation, and autocorrelation may affect p-values.

MonsoonLens aims to turn publicly available NASA climate data into an accessible and interactive experience for investigating changes in our environment.

projectDetails.name: Mars Safe Path: An Interactive Jezero Traverse Planner
projectDetails.summary: Mars Safe Path is an interactive web-based educational prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, focusing on the Jezero Crater region of Mars. It combines three NASA Mars Trek imagery layers—Viking visible imagery, MGS MOLA colour hillshade and THEMIS daytime infrared imagery—using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet.js. Users can explore different map layers, select starting and destination points, and compare a direct route with an A* pathfinding algorithm that identifies a lower-cost path using a synthetic 16 × 16 traversal-cost grid. The project addresses the challenge by demonstrating how planetary imagery and intelligent route-planning techniques can support Martian surface exploration. It is important because future Mars exploration requires careful terrain assessment and efficient route planning for robotic and human missions. This prototype provides an educational foundation for developing advanced Mars navigation systems using real terrain and hazard data.
projectDetails.details: Mars Safe Path is an interactive educational web application designed to demonstrate how planetary mapping and intelligent route-planning techniques can support future Mars exploration. Focused on the Jezero Crater region, the application allows users to explore three independently selectable NASA Mars Trek imagery layers: Viking visible imagery, MGS MOLA colour hillshade and Mars Odyssey THEMIS daytime infrared imagery. Users can select starting and destination points, generate routes using the A* pathfinding algorithm, and compare the suggested route with a direct path using approximate distance and traversal-cost metrics. The project helps users understand how different remote-sensing datasets provide complementary views of the Martian surface and how algorithms can balance distance with modelled traversal costs. Its intended impact is to improve awareness of planetary mapping, terrain exploration and computational route planning while inspiring interest in space science and technology. The application was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet.js, with NASA Mars Trek WMTS imagery and an A* algorithm operating on a synthetic 16 × 16 cost grid. Its creative aspect lies in combining multiple NASA imagery layers with an interactive route-planning demonstration in a single user-friendly platform. We considered map accessibility, ease of interaction, different visual perspectives of Mars, route comparison and scientific transparency. The current prototype is educational; its synthetic costs are not actual terrain measurements or detected hazards. Future development could integrate real elevation and terrain data to improve route-planning accuracy.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: MARS OUTPOST COMMANDER
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Outpost Commander is an interactive survival and science simulation game developed using PictoBlox for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project allows players to experience the challenges of living on Mars by managing a science outpost for 30 Martian days (sols). Players must carefully manage four important resources: Power, Oxygen, Crew Morale, and Science Data, while choosing only two actions per sol.
The game simulates real challenges of Mars exploration, including limited communication with Earth, solar flares, random events, and crew isolation. It uses real space weather data from NASA DONKI to make the simulation more realistic. Players must make strategic decisions to protect the crew, maintain life-support systems, and collect at least 100 Science Data to complete the mission.
This project raises awareness about the difficulties of human space exploration and demonstrates the importance of resource management, decision-making, teamwork, and scientific research for future Mars missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Mars Outpost Commander

Mars Outpost Commander is an interactive Mars survival and science simulation game developed using PictoBlox for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It allows players to experience the challenges of managing a human science outpost on Mars.

How does it work?

The player takes the role of a commander responsible for keeping the crew alive and completing scientific research over 30 Martian days (sols). Each sol allows only two actions, so players must make careful decisions. They need to manage four important resources: Power, Oxygen, Crew Morale, and Science Data. Solar flares, random events, communication delays with Earth, and crew isolation create additional challenges. Players must collect at least 100 Science Data and maintain the survival resources to win the mission.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project creates awareness about the challenges of human exploration on Mars. It helps players understand the importance of resource management, critical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making, and the psychological well-being of astronauts. It also makes space science more engaging and accessible to students.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • PictoBlox and Scratch 3 programming environment.
  • Block-based coding with 835 programming blocks.
  • Sprites, costumes, backdrops, and interactive user interface elements.
  • NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database) for real solar flare information.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser-based demonstration.
  • No additional hardware or extensions are required for the PictoBlox game.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of this project is combining space science, survival simulation, and interactive gameplay. Instead of simply learning about Mars, players experience the difficulties of living there through realistic challenges and strategic choices. The project also includes a browser demo with movement and a robotic rover that helps players explore and collect science data.

Factors Considered During Development:

Our team considered the harsh Martian environment, limited resources, solar radiation, communication delays between Earth and Mars, crew isolation, life-support requirements, and the need for scientific research. We also focused on making the game interactive, educational, easy to understand, and suitable for young learners.

Overall, Mars Outpost Commander transforms the challenges of Mars exploration into an engaging learning experience and encourages the next generation to think about the future of human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: SPACE DANCING SARs
projectDetails.summary: “Dancing with the STARs,” is an interactive space animation developed using PictoBlox Block Coding. We created a virtual night sky featuring four sprites: a Dancing Star, Polaris (the North Star), a Star Group and Earth. The Dancing Star changes costumes, bounces up and down, rotates and changes colours while playing music. Polaris twinkles by continuously changing its brightness. The Star Group rotates around the centre, and Earth spins continuously to represent its rotation. This project encourages creativity, computational thinking and scientific curiosity while helping students understand Earth's rotation and explore the wonders of space.
projectDetails.details:
Dancing with the STARs

Dancing with the STARs is an interactive space-themed animation developed using PictoBlox Block Coding. Our project demonstrates how stars appear to dance and move across the night sky because of Earth's rotation.

How Does Our Project Work?

We created a virtual night sky with four main sprites:

  1. Dancing Star: The star plays music, changes its costumes, rotates, moves up and down, and changes colours continuously, creating a dancing effect.
  2. Polaris (North Star): This sprite twinkles by continuously increasing and decreasing its brightness. It represents the North Star, which appears almost stationary in the sky.
  3. Star Group: A group of small stars rotates continuously around the centre, demonstrating the apparent circular movement of stars around Polaris.
  4. Earth: The Earth sprite rotates continuously to represent Earth's rotation.

We also planned interactive explanations using speech and a quiz to help users understand the science behind the animation.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Makes astronomy easy and interesting to understand.
  • Explains Earth's rotation through visual animation.
  • Helps students understand why stars appear to move.
  • Develops creativity, logical thinking and computational skills.
  • Encourages students to explore space science through coding.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Software: PictoBlox
  • Programming Language: Visual Block-Based Coding
  • Coding Concepts: Events, loops, motion, costumes, sound and visual effects.
  • Sprites: Star, Polaris, Star Group and Earth.
  • Platform: Computer-based simulation.

No external hardware was required because the entire project was developed as a software-based simulation.

What Makes Our Project Creative?

Our creativity lies in combining astronomy with animation and coding. Instead of simply explaining Earth's rotation through text, we created a virtual night sky where stars twinkle, rotate and dance with music. The combination of animated characters, sound and scientific explanations makes the learning experience more engaging and interactive.

Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Scientific accuracy of the concept.
  • Correct representation of Polaris and Earth's rotation.
  • Smooth animation and sprite movements.
  • Suitable background, colours and sound effects.
  • Simple explanations that students can easily understand.
  • An engaging and educational user experience.

Our main goal is to combine science, imagination and technology to make learning about the universe fun and meaningful.

projectDetails.name: ARTEMIS-VIEW
projectDetails.summary:
GRAZE (ARTEMIS-VIEW) is an advanced lunar south pole mission planning and horizon navigation web application designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

What we developed: An intuitive flight console featuring a real-time 360-degree local horizon raycasting engine, side-by-side site comparison matrices, an interactive launch-slip shock-test simulator, and a scrubbable 30-day operational timeline.

How it addresses the challenge: By integrating NASA LOLA topographical data with topocentric ephemeris calculations, GRAZE visualizes exact Sun and Earth positions relative to jagged crater silhouettes. It dynamically computes solar power generation efficiency—factoring in mast height adjustments and panel orientations—while tracking Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility.

Why it is important: Lunar south pole operations face extreme environmental constraints where a 500-meter coordinate shift or a minor launch date delay can plunge a lander into multi-day shadow blackouts and communication failure. GRAZE bridges the gap between raw scientific telemetry and rapid scenario evaluation, empowering engineers and planners to make agile, life-or-death mission decisions.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

GRAZE is an interactive lunar south pole mission planning and horizon navigation web application. It bridges the gap between complex orbital mechanics and rapid mission decision-making.

  • How it works:
    1. Topographic Horizon Raycasting: It utilizes pre-computed 360-degree terrain elevation profiles derived from NASA LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) high-resolution digital elevation models. For any selected landing site, it accounts for lunar spherical curvature and local crater/mountain ridges.
    2. Topocentric Ephemeris Engine: It computes the precise topocentric azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth in real time, accounting for the Moon's extreme $1.54^\circ$ axial tilt, the synodic solar cycle, and Earth's optical libration (the wobbling figure-8 path Earth traces in the lunar sky).
    3. Interactive Visualizations: It renders a 360° sky-dome panorama, a side-by-side site comparison matrix, a launch-slip shock-test simulator, and a scrubbable 30-day operational timeline tracking sunlight, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows, and optimal overlap periods.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Rapid Scenario Evaluation: Instead of navigating cumbersome enterprise tools like NASA's Quickmap or JPL Horizons separately, planners can evaluate alternative sites or delayed launch dates in seconds.
  • Precision Risk Mitigation: It prevents catastrophic mission failures by accurately predicting multi-day shadow blackouts and communication dropouts caused by towering crater rims.
  • Hardware Trade-off Analysis: Features like the dynamic Solar Mast Height Adjuster (1m rover vs. 10m tower) let engineers instantly test how raising an array clears an obstructing ridge.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • For Mission Planners & Engineers: Accelerates coordination between science and engineering teams during NASA CLPS or commercial lunar missions, allowing rapid adaptation when launch delays or hardware changes force site re-evaluations.
  • For Education & Outreach: Serves as an engaging public-facing and educational tool that makes the harsh engineering realities of lunar south pole exploration—such as extreme shadowing and libration—instantly intuitive.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Core Framework & UI: React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons.
  • Visualizations & Graphics: HTML5 Canvas and SVG for procedural shadow rendering, interactive 360° horizon panoramas, and responsive layout styling.
  • Data & Astronomy: Selenographic ephemeris calculation modules and curated topographic elevation profiles derived from NASA PGDA / LOLA datasets.
  • Version Control & Hosting: Git, GitHub (ARTEMIS-VIEW repository), and Vercel for instantaneous cloud deployment.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Interactive Hero Simulation: The landing page features an HTML5 canvas where moving the cursor sweeps the Sun's azimuth at a grazing $1.54^\circ$ elevation, casting real-time procedural shadow cones across Shackleton Crater while highlighting elevated ridges in golden light.
  • Scrollytelling Physics Briefing: Instead of static text, the app breaks down complex concepts (axial tilt, horizon occlusion, and Earth libration) through interactive, step-by-step visual cards.
  • High-End Flight Console Aesthetic: Abandoning generic tech styling, it adopts a custom design system ("Selenographic Obsidian & Regolith") featuring frosted basalt glassmorphism, vacuum black foundations (#050608), and tabular telemetry numerals.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Airless Vacuum Physics: Factoring in the total lack of atmospheric refraction, meaning terrain silhouettes dictate the horizon with razor-sharp precision and zero diffuse scattering.
  • Spherical Curvature & Scale: Ensuring long-baseline raycasting accurately accounted for the Moon's rapid horizon drop-off ($R = 1737.4\text{ km}$).
  • User Cognitive Load: Designing a single-screen command view that packs map navigation, sky-dome panoramas, timeline scrubs, and feasibility scorecards into a cohesive, jitter-free interface.

projectDetails.name: NOVYRA
projectDetails.summary:
Field Shift is an interactive climate-intelligence and farm-planning platform developed by Novyra. It combines regional climate scenarios, crop information, interactive maps, temperature and rainfall visualizations, crop-rotation planning, soil-health projections, seasonal risk checks, and estimated farm impacts in one mission-control-style workspace. The platform also includes a NASA POWER data loader, allowing users to compare historical temperature, rainfall, and root-zone soil-wetness data for selected locations. A dedicated offline-first Kerala Farmers Zone provides crop guides, paddy-season information, and basic answers to common farming questions.

Field Shift addresses the challenge of helping farmers adapt to changing growing conditions. It translates complex Earth-observation and climate data into practical decisions about crop selection, irrigation, rotation, soil health, and heat or rainfall risks. It is especially useful in regions where weather-station coverage and internet access may be limited.

The project is important for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 because it demonstrates how NASA data can support climate resilience and local communities. It connects NASA POWER with potential future layers from SMAP, HLS, and GPM IMERG to turn space-based observations into actionable agricultural insights.
projectDetails.details:
FIELD SHIFT BY NOVYRA

Project Documentation

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

Field Shift is a climate-intelligence and farm-planning web application designed to help farmers understand how changing climate conditions may affect their crops and farming decisions.

The application works as an interactive Mission Control Workspace. Users can:

Select a farming region and crop.

Explore temperature and rainfall patterns.

Adjust an illustrative scenario year and additional warming level.

View changes in growing degree days, rainfall, and average temperature.

Compare historical and recent climate trends.

Review climate conditions for all crops in a selected region.

Build a crop-rotation plan based on soil texture, organic matter, water conservation, heat tolerance, soil health, and income priorities.

Examine expected soil-health changes over a five-year period.

Check a manually entered seasonal forecast for possible heat, rainfall, or soil-moisture risks.

Estimate the wider impact across a selected number of farms and hectares.

Enter coordinates and fetch historical temperature, rainfall, and root-zone wetness data through the NASA POWER API.

Use an offline farmer-support section for Kerala, including crop guides, paddy-season information, and answers to common questions about waterlogging, soil health, monsoon preparation, and plant problems.

The initial experience uses sample regional data. Users can replace this with location-specific historical information using the NASA POWER data loader.

The project clearly explains that its scenario calculations are for exploration and are not official forecasts or validated climate projections.

---

2. What benefits does the project have?

Field Shift provides several important benefits.

1. Better Farm Planning

It helps users compare crops and make more informed decisions about crop rotation, planting conditions, irrigation, soil management, and climate risks.

2. Easier Access to Complex Climate Data

NASA and Earth-observation data can be difficult for non-specialists to interpret. Field Shift converts this information into visual charts, indicators, sliders, tables, and recommendations that are easier to understand.

3. Climate Adaptation

The platform helps farmers think ahead about increasing temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, drought, waterlogging, and declining soil quality.

4. Improved Water and Soil Management

The rotation planner allows users to prioritize saving water, improving soil health, managing heat and drought, and protecting farm income.

5. Support for Regions with Limited Connectivity

The Kerala Farmers Zone is designed to work offline after the page has been saved. This makes the knowledge assistant more useful in areas where internet access may be unreliable.

6. Local Relevance

The project includes Indian and Kerala-specific farming information, including districts, crops, and broad paddy seasons such as Virippu, Mundakan, and Puncha.

7. Scalability

The platform can potentially support additional locations, crops, data sources, satellite products, and local agricultural knowledge libraries.

---

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to strengthen the ability of farmers and agricultural communities to adapt to climate change.

Field Shift aims to:

Reduce the gap between scientific climate data and everyday farm decisions.

Help farmers identify climate-related risks before they cause major losses.

Encourage more resilient crop choices and crop rotations.

Support responsible use of water and improvement of soil health.

Make Earth-observation data useful to small and medium-sized farms.

Provide practical information to communities that may not have access to specialist agricultural advice.

Encourage farmers to combine satellite and climate information with local observations and expert guidance.

Support more sustainable and economically resilient agriculture.

The broader goal is to transform climate data into practical action. Instead of presenting information only as scientific measurements, the project connects environmental changes to decisions that farmers can understand and use.

Field Shift is not intended to replace agricultural experts, field observations, soil testing, or official weather and agricultural advisories. It is designed as an educational and decision-support tool that helps users ask better questions and prepare more effectively.

---

4. What tools, coding languages, and software were used?

Based on the project files, Field Shift was developed as a browser-based web application using the following technologies:

1. HTML (HyperText Markup Language): Used for the structure and content of the application.

2. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets): Used for the visual design, layout, responsive interface, colours, typography, and component styling.

3. JavaScript: Used for user interactions, calculations, controls, charts, planners, scenario sliders, crop guides, and the offline knowledge assistant.

4. SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics): Used for visualisations such as temperature and rainfall charts.

5. NASA POWER API: Used to retrieve historical temperature, rainfall, and root-zone soil-wetness data.

6. Python: Used for the included NASA data-processing script, using the requests, collections, and json libraries.

7. OpenStreetMap: Used for the interactive map and location exploration.

8. Netlify: Used for hosting and deploying the web application.

Potential Future Data Sources:

NASA SMAP.

HLS (Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2).

Landsat.

Sentinel-2.

GPM IMERG.

These are identified as possible additional data layers rather than fully demonstrated features in the current project.

The project is primarily a lightweight, client-side web application, making it easy to access through a browser without requiring users to install specialised software.

---

5. How is the project creative?

Field Shift is creative in both its concept and its presentation.

1. Mission-Control Approach

Instead of presenting the project as a conventional agricultural dashboard, it uses a space-mission and mission-control theme. This connects farming on Earth with NASA Earth-observation technology and makes the interface more engaging.

2. Climate Twin Concept

The Farm Climate Twin combines climate data, crop information, soil conditions, user priorities, and possible scenarios into one interactive planning environment. This helps users explore how different decisions may affect their farms.

3. Combining Data with Action

Many climate tools only display charts or maps. Field Shift goes further by connecting the information to crop rotation, soil health, water management, seasonal checks, and estimated farm impact.

4. Scenario Exploration

The year slider and additional-warming control allow users to explore how conditions could change. The tool labels these as illustrative scenarios, making the feature educational while avoiding the claim that it is an official prediction.

5. Offline-First Local Support

The Kerala Farmers Zone adds a creative, community-focused element. It does not rely entirely on live data or internet connectivity and provides regional crop information and basic farming guidance in one place.

6. User-Centred Visualisation

The project uses large indicators, interactive controls, comparison tables, colour-coded sections, charts, and simple explanations to make complex environmental data more approachable.

7. Connecting Space Technology to Local Farming

Its most distinctive creative idea is turning NASA data into a tool for local agricultural resilience. It shows how space-based observations can have a direct connection to soil, crops, rainfall, and farmer decision-making.

---

6. What factors did the team consider?

The team considered several important factors during development.

1. Data Accuracy and Transparency

The project distinguishes between sample data, historical data, scenarios, forecasts, and official projections. It explains that NASA POWER uses gridded and reanalysis-supported information rather than direct field sensors.

2. Responsible Interpretation

The application warns users not to treat illustrative climate scenarios as official NASA forecasts. It also recommends checking local observations and official agricultural advice before making important decisions.

3. User Accessibility

The interface is designed for people who may not have advanced climate or data-science knowledge. Charts and indicators are paired with plain-language descriptions and practical recommendations.

4. Local Farming Needs

The team included Kerala-specific districts, crops, paddy seasons, and common farmer questions. This shows consideration for regional agricultural practices instead of creating a completely generic global tool.

5. Limited Connectivity

The offline farmer-support feature reflects the possibility that some users may have unreliable or expensive internet access.

6. Diverse Farmer Priorities

The rotation planner allows users to balance water conservation, heat and drought tolerance, soil health, and farm income. This recognises that farms have different priorities and that one solution will not fit every user.

7. Different Soil Conditions

The planner considers sandy, loamy, and clay soils, as well as low, medium, and high organic matter. This helps make the recommendations more context-sensitive.

8. Practical Decision-Making

The team focused on decisions farmers can actually influence, such as crop selection, crop rotation, water management, soil improvement, and seasonal preparation.

9. Scalability and Future Integration

The project was designed so that future layers from SMAP, HLS, Landsat, Sentinel-2, and GPM IMERG could be added. This creates a path from a prototype using historical climate data towards a more comprehensive Earth-observation platform.

10. Safety and Limitations

The project avoids presenting itself as a replacement for agricultural experts. It states that it cannot diagnose pests from photographs, calculate exact pesticide or fertiliser doses, or replace soil testing and local official advisories.

---

SHORT OVERALL DESCRIPTION

Field Shift by NOVYRA is a browser-based, climate-smart agriculture platform that converts NASA Earth-observation and climate data into practical farming insights.

It combines interactive maps, climate visualisations, crop comparisons, rotation planning, soil-health projections, seasonal risk checks, farm-impact calculations, and an offline Kerala Farmer Support Centre.

Its purpose is to help farmers understand changing environmental conditions and make more resilient decisions about crops, water, soil, and income.

The project is creative because it presents agriculture as a Mission Control Experience and connects space-based data with local farming needs.

Its ultimate goal is to transform space technology and climate intelligence into practical solutions for farmers, promoting sustainable agriculture and climate resilience.
