projectDetails.name: Space Explorer - Forgotten Missions
projectDetails.summary:
Space Explorer – Forgotten Missions is an interactive web-based educational platform developed to highlight the abandoned equipment, historical missions, and forgotten stories of human exploration on the Moon and Mars.

Our project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge theme, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," by bringing attention to the spacecraft, rovers, landing hardware, and scientific equipment left behind during space missions. Using an interactive mission explorer, visitors can explore the Moon and Mars, discover equipment stories, learn about mission histories, view historical images, and explore landing locations with coordinates and links to official NASA resources.

The project is important because space exploration is not only about successful landings and discoveries but also about the objects and scientific history left behind. By presenting this information in an engaging and accessible way, Space Explorer encourages curiosity, scientific awareness, and appreciation for humanity's achievements in space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Space Explorer – Forgotten Missions is an interactive, web-based educational platform created to bring attention to abandoned space equipment and the forgotten stories of human exploration on the Moon and Mars.

The project allows users to explore historic space missions through an interactive interface. Users can switch between the Moon and Mars, discover important mission locations, view their coordinates, and access location links. Each mission provides information about its history, landing site, and equipment left behind. The platform also includes mission timelines, image galleries, detailed story panels, historical information, and mission statistics to make space exploration easier and more engaging to understand.

Our project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge theme, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," by highlighting the spacecraft, lunar rovers, landing hardware, and other equipment that remain on celestial bodies after missions. It helps users understand that even when a mission ends, the objects and scientific contributions left behind continue to have historical and scientific value.

The project was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS. Visual assets and mission information were referenced from NASA and NASA/JPL-Caltech resources. The website was deployed using Vercel to make it publicly accessible.

The creative aspect of our project is its combination of space exploration, interactive mission discovery, historical storytelling, and educational content in one platform. Instead of simply presenting mission facts, it encourages users to explore the forgotten objects and understand the stories behind them.

The intended impact is to increase public awareness of space exploration history, inspire students and space enthusiasts, and preserve interest in the scientific and historical importance of equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

ChatGPT was used as an AI assistance tool during project development for brainstorming, coding guidance, debugging support, and preparation of descriptive content. The team reviewed, tested, and adapted the suggestions while developing the final project.

projectDetails.name: Life On Mars
projectDetails.summary:
The project is an interactive, space-themed educational game designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the challenges of establishing and maintaining a human presence on Mars.
The game features four mini-games that simulate key aspects of Martian exploration: maintaining outpost systems, protecting the base from radiation hazards and incoming asteroids, collecting valuable resources such as lithium, gold and water ice, and navigating a rover through challenging terrain during a dust storm.
The project transforms complex space-science concepts into engaging, interactive missions that encourage problem-solving, decision-making and scientific awareness, while helping young learners understand the challenges of future human exploration of Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an interactive educational game designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the challenges of living and working on Mars.

The game has four mini-games, each focusing on a different challenge that astronauts might face during space exploration:

  1. Systems check: Players have to monitor the martian outpost's systems and keep them working without allowing any system to fail.
  2. Martian Defence: Players must destroy incoming asteroids carrying radiation to protect the Martian Base and the astronauts.
  3. Resource Collection: Players explore Mars and collect lithium, gold and water ice, learning how these resources could be useful for future missions.
  4. Rover Rescue: Players control a Mars rover and avoid boulders while navigating through difficult terrain during a dust storm.

We wanted to make learning about space more interesting by turning scientific concepts into games rather than simply presenting facts. Through these mini-games, players get to understand some of the difficulties of maintaining a human settlement on Mars, such as radiation exposure, managing resources, maintaining equipment and dealing with extreme weather conditions.

We developed the game using Scratch, a block-based coding platform, and designed our presentation using Canva. The game includes interactive controls, timed challenges and different objectives to keep players engaged.

What makes our project creative is that we combined four different mini-games into one larger space mission. Each game gives the player a new responsibility and introduces a different aspect of space exploration.

While developing the game, we considered our target audience, which is kids aged 7–12. We wanted the controls to be simple, the instructions easy to understand and the challenges interesting without being too difficult. Most importantly, we wanted to maintain a balance between making the game fun and ensuring that players actually learn something about space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project Orbit by TheDawgInMe
projectDetails.summary: Project Orbit is an interactive, space-themed educational game that challenges players to design, launch, and operate an Earth-observation satellite. Players take on the role of a spacecraft engineer, making decisions about satellite components, power requirements, fuel capacity, communication systems, and launch vehicles. Through a series of progressively challenging missions, the game introduces fundamental concepts of satellite engineering, orbital operations, and Earth observation in an engaging, hands-on environment. By combining interactive 3D environments with mission-based gameplay, Project Orbit makes complex space science concepts more accessible and enjoyable.
projectDetails.details: Project Orbit features a multi-stage gameplay experience that takes players from spacecraft assembly to live orbital operations. Players begin by selecting and configuring satellite components, including imaging instruments, solar arrays, batteries, antennas, and propulsion systems. Each configuration must satisfy specific mission requirements, such as payload mass limits, electrical power demands, and budget constraints, before an appropriate launch vehicle can be selected. Once launched, players operate their spacecraft in a simulated low Earth orbit, where they must identify survey zones, collect observation data, manage available power and fuel, and transmit collected information during designated ground communication windows. The game includes six missions of increasing difficulty, covering scenarios such as coastal mapping, wetland monitoring, storm response, wildfire observation, and glacier profiling. A mission evaluation system provides performance scores and engineering feedback, allowing players to understand the consequences of their design and operational decisions.

projectDetails.name: ASTRO HEALTH
projectDetails.summary: ULTRON MK7 Space Station is a NASA Space Apps 2026 astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed to simulate a futuristic spacecraft health-monitoring system. The project consists of four development boards: a Wearable ESP32 equipped with a MAX30102 sensor, OLED display, and SOS button to monitor heart rate and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂); a Space Station ESP32 that receives wearable health data through ESP-NOW and forwards it through Wi-Fi; a Station Arduino UNO R4 WiFi with an LCD Keypad Shield, DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, and buzzer for displaying health information, environmental conditions, and emergency alerts; and a Laptop Arduino UNO R4 integrated with the Python-based ULTRON MK7 AI system for computer interaction and intelligent processing. The system aims to provide real-time health monitoring, wireless communication, environmental monitoring, emergency signaling, and AI-assisted analysis through a connected dashboard, all housed in a custom-built prototype enclosure. The ultimate goal is to develop an innovative, interactive astronaut health-monitoring solution that demonstrates how embedded electronics, wireless networking, and artificial intelligence can work together to support astronaut safety and mission awareness.
projectDetails.details:
ULTRON MK7 Space Station aims to improve astronaut safety by demonstrating how wearable sensors, wireless communication, and artificial intelligence can work together to monitor health in space environments. Astronauts experience demanding conditions such as microgravity, isolation, and physical stress, making continuous health monitoring important. Our prototype demonstrates a compact, affordable, and interactive monitoring system that could inspire future intelligent astronaut-support technologies. It also promotes STEM education by combining Arduino, ESP32, sensors, networking, and Python AI into a single working project.

How Does It Work?

The wearable ESP32 measures heart rate and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) using the MAX30102 sensor and allows astronauts to trigger an SOS emergency signal. The wearable transmits this information wirelessly using ESP-NOW to the Space Station ESP32, which acts as a communication gateway and forwards the data over Wi-Fi. The Station Arduino UNO R4 WiFi receives the health information and displays it on its LCD Keypad Shield alongside temperature and humidity measurements from the DHT11 sensor. Emergency signals can activate the station's alert system. The laptop runs the ULTRON MK7 Python AI software, which can be integrated with the monitoring system to provide health-data analysis and a dashboard for visualizing station information.

What Are Its Uses?

- Astronaut Health Monitoring: Demonstrates monitoring of heart rate and blood oxygen levels.

- Emergency Signaling: Provides an SOS mechanism for communicating emergency situations.

- Environmental Monitoring: Measures temperature and humidity around the station.

- AI-Assisted Analysis: Enables health-data visualization and potential intelligent anomaly detection.

- Space Research Education: Demonstrates spacecraft-inspired monitoring architecture.

- Remote Monitoring: Shows how sensor data can be transmitted wirelessly to a central station.

- Future Applications: Could inspire similar monitoring concepts for remote research stations, isolated environments, and wearable health-monitoring systems.

How to Use the Project

1. Wear the sensor device and place your finger correctly over the MAX30102 sensor.

2. Power on the wearable ESP32 and Space Station ESP32.

3. Power on the Station UNO R4 WiFi and allow the system to connect to Wi-Fi.

4. Wait for the wearable sensor to begin transmitting health readings.

5. Navigate the Station LCD Keypad Shield using UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, and SELECT buttons.

6. View heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, humidity, and SOS information on the station display.

7. Use the wearable SOS button to send an emergency signal to the station.

8. Open the ULTRON MK7 laptop dashboard to view or analyze available health data.

9. Monitor the system and observe how information moves between the wearable, station, and laptop.

projectDetails.name: LUNARIS
projectDetails.summary:
VEXORA COSMOS developed an intuitive Lunar Site Landing Navigator for NASA Space Challenge 2026. The tool helps mission planners, educators, and the public compare potential lunar south-pole landing sites across different dates. It visualizes the Sun’s and Earth’s positions relative to the horizon, making it easier to evaluate available sunlight for power generation and identify direct-to-Earth communication windows.
By presenting complex astronomical and mission-planning information through a clear, accessible interface, the navigator reduces the difficulty of coordinating science and engineering decisions. Users can quickly explore how lighting conditions and communication visibility change by location and time, supporting more informed landing-site assessments.
This project is important because lunar south-pole missions operate under extreme lighting, terrain, and communication constraints. By turning complicated data into understandable visual insights, VEXORA COSMOS supports safer planning, improves accessibility to lunar science, and helps more people engage with the future of lunar exploration.
projectDetails.details:
LUNARIS

VEXORA COSMOS developed an intuitive Lunar Site Landing Navigator for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project addresses the difficulty of evaluating potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole, where extreme lighting conditions, challenging terrain, and limited communication visibility create significant mission-planning constraints.

The navigator helps users compare candidate lunar landing sites across different dates and understand how the positions of the Sun and Earth change relative to the local horizon.

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

The Lunar Site Landing Navigator is an interactive web-based application for exploring environmental conditions at possible lunar south-pole landing locations.

Users can select or compare candidate landing sites and examine conditions for different dates. The application presents astronomical information in a visual and accessible form, including:

The Sun’s position relative to the local lunar horizon

The Earth’s position relative to the horizon

Potential sunlight availability for solar power generation

Possible direct-to-Earth communication windows

Changes in lighting and visibility over time

Comparisons between different candidate locations

At a high level, the application takes a selected lunar location and date as inputs. It then presents the relevant Sun and Earth position information through visual indicators, charts, horizon diagrams, or other interface elements. Instead of requiring users to interpret complex astronomical data manually, the navigator translates that information into clear visual insights.

This allows mission planners, educators, and members of the public to evaluate how suitable a landing site may be under different lighting and communication conditions.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The project provides several important benefits.

Faster site comparison

Users can compare multiple landing sites and dates more efficiently instead of relying on complicated tools or interpreting large amounts of raw data.

Improved mission planning

The application supports early-stage decisions about:

Solar power availability

Visibility of Earth for communication

Lighting conditions at the landing site

Timing of scientific or engineering activities

Potential operational constraints

More accessible astronomical information

Many existing tools are designed for specialists and may have complicated interfaces. VEXORA COSMOS presents the information in a simpler and more visual format, making it easier for a wider audience to understand.

Better communication between disciplines

Lunar missions require cooperation between science, engineering, operations, and mission-planning teams. A shared visual interface can help team members discuss the same information more easily.

Educational value

The tool can be used by students, educators, and the public to learn about:

Lunar geography

Orbital and astronomical motion

Solar illumination

Communication geometry

The challenges of returning to the Moon

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to make lunar south-pole mission planning more understandable, efficient, and accessible.

Lunar south-pole missions are especially challenging because the region contains areas of near-permanent shadow as well as elevated locations that may receive sunlight for extended periods. At the same time, communication with Earth depends on whether Earth is visible above the local horizon. A landing site may therefore have strong scientific value but limited power or communication opportunities.

By visualizing these factors together, the project aims to help users make more informed assessments of possible landing sites.

The project could contribute to:

Safer and more informed mission planning

More effective coordination between science and engineering teams

Improved understanding of lunar environmental constraints

Greater public interest in lunar exploration

More accessible STEM education

Better communication of complex space-science concepts

The long-term goal is not to replace professional mission-analysis systems, but to provide an intuitive first layer for exploration, comparison, education, and early decision-making.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project is presented as a web-based application. Based on the provided project description, the confirmed software elements are:

A web interface

Astronomical and lunar-location data

Interactive visualization

A browser-based application hosted at https://vexoracosmos.netlify.app/

However, the specific programming languages, libraries, development environments, and hardware were not included in the project description. Those details should be confirmed before submitting the final response.

You can use the following version if it accurately reflects your actual development process:

The project was developed as a browser-based web application using standard front-end web technologies. The interface was designed to make astronomical and mission-planning data easy to explore interactively. The application uses computational logic to determine the relative positions of the Sun and Earth at selected lunar locations and dates, then presents the results through visual diagrams and comparison elements.

The project was tested using standard computers and web browsers. Development and deployment were carried out using software development tools, source-code management, browser testing tools, and a web-hosting platform. The application is hosted through Netlify, allowing users to access it online without installing specialized software.

Data sources

NASA data, astronomical databases, ephemeris data, or other sources actually used

Development tools

Visual Studio Code, GitHub, Git, Figma, or other tools

Hosting

Netlify

Hardware

Laptops or desktop computers used for development and testing

Testing

Desktop browsers, mobile browsers, responsive testing tools, or other methods

It is important not to list a framework, language, data source, or library unless the team actually used it.

5. How is the project creative?

The creativity of VEXORA COSMOS comes from how it transforms a complex technical problem into an accessible interactive experience.

Instead of presenting users with dense astronomical tables or specialist interfaces, the project focuses on visual explanation. It connects several different types of information in one place:

Lunar location

Date and time

Sun position

Earth visibility

Lighting conditions

Power-generation potential

Communication opportunities

This combination makes the project more than a static information page. It functions as an exploratory tool that allows users to investigate different possibilities and immediately see how changing the location or date affects mission conditions.

The project is also creative because it serves multiple audiences. A mission planner may use it to compare operational conditions, while a student or member of the public may use it to understand why the lunar south pole is difficult to explore.

Its creativity can be summarized as:

Turning technical data into visual insights

Combining science and engineering considerations

Making lunar mission planning more intuitive

Supporting both expert exploration and public education

Using interaction rather than static explanations

Presenting a difficult space-science challenge through a clear user experience

6. What factors does the team consider?

The team considers both technical mission requirements and user-experience requirements.

Scientific and engineering factors

The project considers:

Sun elevation above or below the local horizon

Earth visibility from a selected lunar location

Duration and availability of sunlight

Potential solar power generation

Direct-to-Earth communication opportunities

The effects of location and date on mission conditions

The extreme lighting environment of the lunar south pole

The need to coordinate science and engineering priorities

User-experience factors

The team also considers:

Ease of navigation

Clarity of visual information

Simple comparison between locations and dates

Accessibility for non-specialists

Readability of charts and horizon diagrams

Minimizing unnecessary complexity

Making the interface useful on different screen sizes

Helping users understand the meaning of the data, not just displaying numbers

Mission-planning factors

A suitable landing site cannot be judged by a single factor. The team therefore considers the balance between:

Scientific value

Solar illumination

Communication visibility

Operational safety

Accessibility of the site

Duration of useful mission conditions

The needs of different mission teams

The design recognizes that lunar exploration involves trade-offs. A location with good scientific potential may have limited sunlight, while a location with strong solar exposure may present other operational or communication challenges.

Conclusion

VEXORA COSMOS developed an interactive Lunar Site Landing Navigator for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The application helps mission planners, educators, and the public compare potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole across different dates. It visualizes the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar horizon, allowing users to assess sunlight availability for solar power and identify possible direct-to-Earth communication windows.

The project benefits users by simplifying complex astronomical and mission-planning information. Instead of requiring specialist knowledge or difficult interfaces, the navigator presents important information through clear visual comparisons. This can support early landing-site evaluation, improve communication between science and engineering teams, and make lunar exploration concepts easier for students and the public to understand.

The intended impact is to contribute to safer and more informed planning for future lunar south-pole missions. The tool highlights the trade-offs between scientific value, solar illumination, power generation, and communication visibility.

The project was developed as a browser-based web application and deployed through Netlify. The team used web-development tools, astronomical or lunar-location data, computational logic, and interactive visualization techniques. The exact programming languages and libraries should be listed according to the team’s actual implementation.

The project is creative because it turns complex space-science data into an intuitive exploration tool. It combines location, date, sunlight, and Earth visibility in one interface and makes the information useful to both technical and non-technical audiences. In developing the project, the team considered scientific accuracy, mission-planning needs, communication constraints, power-generation potential, accessibility, simplicity, readability, and the different needs of engineers, researchers, educators, and the public.

projectDetails.name: VitalOrbit - Astronaut Health Monitoring System
projectDetails.summary: VitalOrbit is an autonomous real-time astronaut health monitoring web application that tracks radiation exposure, cardiovascular fitness, musculoskeletal health, behavioral well-being, immune function, and habitat environment—empowering deep-space crews to detect early physiological shifts, execute guided self-assessments, and trigger evidence-based countermeasures independently during long communication delays with Earth.
projectDetails.details:
THE CHALLENGE & INSPIRATION

Long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond expose astronauts to the five primary hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile/closed environments. On these deep-space voyages, multi-minute communication latencies prevent real-time clinical intervention from ground flight surgeons. Astronauts must take primary responsibility for monitoring their own health, spotting early physiological deterioration, and initiating countermeasures before minor issues become catastrophic emergencies.

WHAT VITALORBIT DOES

VitalOrbit is an autonomous, browser-based physiological telemetry and environmental monitoring system built specifically for deep-space crews. It consolidates six physiological and environmental domains into a cohesive, mission-critical dashboard:

1. Radiation Dosimetry: Tracks cumulative career dose (against NASA's 1,000 mSv career REIC standard), daily exposure rates, and organ-equivalent doses (blood-forming organs, eye lens, skin, and central nervous system). It provides space weather tracking and Solar Particle Event (SPE) storm-shelter advisories based on Canadian Space Agency (CSA) dosimetry research.

2. Cardiovascular & Hemodynamics: Features a live 500 Hz animated Lead-II ECG waveform, resting heart rate, non-invasive blood pressure, continuous heart rate variability (rMSSD) reflecting autonomic nervous tone, VO2 max trend tracking, and an interactive 3-minute Orthostatic Intolerance Protocol to assess post-microgravity cardiovascular deconditioning.

3. Musculoskeletal Health: Monitors regional Bone Mineral Density (BMD) loss across the lumbar spine, femoral neck, and wrist alongside lean muscle mass index. It tracks compliance against NASA's mandatory 2.5-hour/day exercise prescription across ARED (resistance loading), T2 (treadmill), and CEVIS (cycle ergometer).

4. Behavioral Health & Sleep Architecture: Combines continuous actigraphy sleep stage breakdown (Deep N3, Light, REM, Awake), daily psychological mood tracking, an embedded PHQ-2 depression screener, an on-board reaction-time test (WinSCAT PVT), and an encrypted private mission journal.

5. Immune Competence & Biomarkers: Surfaces on-board hematology metrics (WBC differential breakdown, neutrophils, lymphocytes), systemic inflammation markers (hs-CRP, IL-6), and salivary PCR latent virus reactivation surveillance (EBV, VZV, CMV) to preempt immune dysregulation.

6. Habitat Environment (ECLSS): Monitors cabin partial pressure of CO2 (ppCO2 with active CDRA scrubber cycle controls), atmospheric pressure, internal temperature, relative humidity, acoustic levels, and water reclamation potability.

7. Autonomous Self-Assessment Wizard: An interactive clinical decision-support engine featuring Visual Analog Scales (VAS) for headache, nausea, and fatigue, body symptom tagging, and a Space Flight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) near-vision screener. Submitting an assessment generates clinical severity scoring and evidence-based countermeasure protocols.

HOW IT WORKS

VitalOrbit is built with clean HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, leveraging Chart.js for data visualization. It requires zero server backend, runs client-side, operates completely offline in spacecraft cabins, and supports one-click JSON clinical telemetry export for ground synchronization.

projectDetails.name: BioSentinel: Autonomous Health Monitoring & Countermeasure System
projectDetails.summary:
BioSentinel is an offline-first autonomous clinical health monitoring system engineered for astronauts on long-duration exploration missions, such as Mars transit. When interplanetary distances impose communication delays of up to 22 minutes each way, astronauts cannot rely on real-time ground control to diagnose and manage medical crises.

To address this, we developed a system that continuously gathers multi-modal health indicators: real-time biometric vitals (heart rate, HRV, continuous blood pressure, SpO2), environmental life-support telemetry (cabin CO2, radiation dosimeters), and interactive self-assessment tools—specifically an in-browser Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) for cognitive fatigue and an interactive Amsler Grid for Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).

Using a clinical decision engine aligned with NASA Human Research Program (HRP) thresholds, BioSentinel autonomously evaluates cross-system hazards and prescribes immediate, actionable countermeasures. These include adapted ARED axial-load resistance protocols for bone remodeling, Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) for ocular decompression, solar storm shelter lockdowns, and circadian phototherapy. BioSentinel bridges the gap between deep-space isolation and digital medicine, ensuring crew autonomy and survivability on humanity's journey beyond Earth orbit.
projectDetails.details:
1. How It Works & What It Does

BioSentinel is an offline-first, autonomous digital health system designed to support astronauts on long-duration interplanetary exploration missions (such as Earth-Mars transit). Because deep-space communication delays can reach up to 22 minutes each way, astronauts cannot rely on real-time telemedicine from Mission Control Houston.

BioSentinel operates entirely onboard within the spacecraft’s local network, continuously performing three core functions:

- Multi-Modal Data Ingestion: Gathers continuous physiological telemetry (heart rate, HRV RMSSD, continuous blood pressure, SpO2, core temperature, and sympathovagal stress), environmental life-support sensors (ambient CO2, cabin pressure, and active radiation dosimetry in µGy/hr and cumulative mSv), and daily biochemical markers (urinary NTx for bone resorption and hydration specific gravity).

- Interactive Self-Assessment Suite: Provides astronauts with in-browser diagnostic tools, including a tactile 60-second Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) that quantifies reaction times and attentional lapses (>500 ms) to detect cognitive fatigue, alongside an interactive Amsler Grid canvas to map visual scotomas and globe flattening caused by cephalad fluid shifts.

- Autonomous Clinical Risk Engine: Evaluates cross-system telemetry against NASA Human Research Program (HRP) thresholds, generating holistic health scores and immediate multi-hazard risk categorizations.

2. Benefits & Actionable Countermeasures

Unlike passive telemetry dashboards, BioSentinel immediately closes the loop between diagnosis and treatment. When physiological drift or environmental spikes are identified, the system generates targeted, astronaut-executable countermeasure checklists:

- Bone & Muscle Remodeling: Prescribes adapted axial-load resistance protocols on the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED)—such as 1.8x Earth bodyweight squats and deadlifts—coupled with calcium and vitamin D3 titration to combat microgravity bone mineral density loss.

- SANS Ocular Decongestion: Detects early optic disc edema and schedules Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) chamber sessions (-25 mmHg) to draw pooled cephalad venous blood back into the lower extremities.

- Radiation Protection: Automatically triggers storm-shelter lockdown protocols and radioprotective antioxidant administration during Solar Particle Events (SPEs).

- Circadian Realignment: Schedules targeted blue-enriched 480 nm phototherapy and micro-rest periods to counteract sleep loss and circadian desynchronization.

3. Creativity & Innovation

- Active Interactive Diagnostics: Rather than relying only on wearable sensors, astronauts actively participate in their health evaluations through gamified, scientifically validated tests (PVT and interactive Amsler eye exams) embedded directly into the flight deck HUD.

- Integrated Mission Crisis Simulator: Includes an onboard scenario injector allowing astronauts (and evaluators) to simulate spaceflight anomalies—such as coronal mass ejections, CO2 scrubber bed saturation, or acute SANS spikes—to verify and rehearse emergency response protocols in real time.

- Hardware-Agnostic Web Audio Alerts: Synthesizes audible aerospace alert chimes natively via the browser's Web Audio API oscillators, eliminating external media dependencies.

4. Factors Considered

- The 5 Hazards of Spaceflight: Structured comprehensively around NASA’s Human Research Program framework: Space Radiation, Altered Gravity, Isolation/Confinement, Hostile Closed Environments, and Distance from Earth.

- Zero-Cloud Resilience: Built with zero external API calls or cloud dependencies, ensuring complete operational reliability in deep-space autonomous isolation.

- Cockpit Ergonomics: Designed with a high-contrast dark flight-ops UI optimized for spacecraft lighting conditions, supporting touchscreens, mouse controls, and tactile keyboard shortcuts.

5. Tools, Languages, & Technologies Used

- Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, Scikit-learn.

- Persistence: Embedded SQLite for offline time-series biometric logging and clinical audit trails.

- Frontend: HTML5, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js (for high-frequency cardiovascular waveforms), Lucide Icons, and HTML5 Canvas API.

- Version Control: Git and GitHub (open-source MIT License).

6. Intended Impact & Terrestrial Dual-Use

Beyond securing astronaut survival on Artemis and Mars transit missions, BioSentinel offers substantial terrestrial spin-offs. Its lightweight, offline-first autonomous architecture is directly transferable to extreme isolated environments on Earth—including Antarctic research stations, commercial maritime and submarine crews, deep-sea exploration, and remote rural clinics where access to specialized physicians is severely restricted.

Planet X – Exploring the Changing Universe

Planet X is an interactive, public-facing web platform designed to make NASA's SPHEREx space mission data easier for everyone to explore and understand. It allows users to view sky images captured at different times and compare them to discover changes in celestial objects such as stars, comets, asteroids, and other fascinating objects in space.

Our platform aims to simplify complex astronomical data through a user-friendly interface, visual comparisons, and time-based exploration. By helping users notice changes in the sky, Planet X makes it easier to identify objects that move or change over time and encourages people to take part in space exploration.

This project is important because SPHEREx collects an enormous amount of valuable data that is difficult for individuals to examine manually. Planet X connects science and technology with public participation, making astronomy more accessible, interactive, and exciting for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
Planet X is a web-based space exploration project designed to make NASA's SPHEREx mission data easier for the public to explore.

The main goal is to help users view sky images captured at different times and compare observations to notice changes in celestial objects. The platform aims to provide a simple and user-friendly experience for exploring astronomical images.

Users will be able to explore observations, compare images from different periods, and learn how objects in the universe change over time.

The project focuses on accessibility, interactive visualization, and public participation in space science. It aims to connect technology and astronomy while encouraging students and space enthusiasts to explore the universe.

Our vision is to make complex space data easier to understand and inspire more people to participate in scientific discovery.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: GHOSTS OF SPACE
projectDetails.summary:
GHOSTS OF SPACE — The Machines We Left Behind

GHOSTS OF SPACE is an interactive, animated educational documentary series that brings the stories of forgotten human-made machines left on the Moon, Mars, and other parts of space to life.The project aims to make space exploration interesting and easy to understand, especially for students. Through colourful 3D cartoon storytelling, viewers meet ORBIT, a friendly robot guide who takes them on journeys through real historical space missions, including Mars 3, Sojourner, Opportunity, and Cassini-Huygens.Unlike traditional documentaries, GHOSTS OF SPACE allows viewers to participate in the stories through interactive decisions and branching storylines. They can choose what a rover investigates, explore different scientific possibilities, and learn about the discoveries, challenges, and technology behind each mission.
The project uses publicly available NASA images, videos, scientific datasets, and mission information to ensure that the educational content is based on real space exploration.Technologies such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript bring the interactive website, animations, and decision-based experiences together.Our goal is to turn forgotten space missions into exciting learning experiences, inspire curiosity about science and technology, and show how even machines that have stopped working can leave behind discoveries that change our understanding of the universe.
Their missions ended.Our curiosity never will.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Title

GHOSTS OF SPACE: The Machines We Left Behind

2. Team Name

Zero Gravity X

3. Team Members

  • Anakha A
  • Geethika Vinod
  • Christine Julia Danie
  • Nora Susan Mathew
  • Aleena Binoy

4. Challenge Selected

Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.

5. Project Type

Interactive educational website and animated documentary series.

6. Project Description

GHOSTS OF SPACE is an interactive storytelling platform that explores human-made machines left behind after space missions. It presents their journeys, discoveries, scientific importance, and mission endings through animated episodes and interactive choices.

7. Main Features

  • Interactive Homepage: A space-themed homepage introducing the project.
  • ORBIT: A friendly robot character who guides viewers through the series.
  • Animated Episodes: Cartoon documentaries based on real space missions.
  • Branching Storylines: Viewers make decisions that lead to different exploration paths.
  • Educational Content: Simple explanations of space science, robotics, and planetary exploration.
  • Historical Reconstructions: Visual recreations of important mission events, clearly distinguished from real footage.

8. Featured Space Missions

  1. Mars 3: The Soviet lander that transmitted from Mars for approximately 14.5 seconds.
  2. Moon Exploration Machines: Human-made equipment and robotic missions left on the lunar surface.
  3. Sojourner: NASA's first successful Mars rover.
  4. Opportunity: The Mars rover that operated for almost 15 years.
  5. Cassini-Huygens: The mission that explored Saturn and its moons.

9. Technologies Used

  • HTML — Website structure.
  • CSS — Design, animations, and visual effects.
  • JavaScript — Interactive buttons and branching storylines.
  • AI-assisted creative tools — Character, scene, and animation creation.
  • Browser text-to-speech — Narration.
  • NASA public resources — Mission images, videos, and scientific information.

10. NASA and Open Data Resources

  • NASA Image and Video Library.
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS).
  • NASA mission archives and educational resources.
  • Publicly available images and scientific mission records from other space agencies where relevant.

11. Target Audience

School students, young learners, space enthusiasts, and anyone interested in astronomy and robotics.

12. Main Objective

To make space exploration easier to understand through interactive storytelling while encouraging curiosity about science, technology, engineering, and the universe.

13. Expected Outcome

A user-friendly interactive website that transforms historical space missions into engaging educational experiences and helps students understand the importance of robotic space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project Aakaasham
projectDetails.summary:
We built Still Listening-for our project Aakaasham, an interactive scrollytelling story with a companion slide deck. You play a radio signal leaving Earth and meet the hardware NASA left behind: Apollo landers, moon buggies and laser mirrors on the Moon, then Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars. At a fork, you choose between answering Opportunity in its 2018 dust storm and following Pioneer 10 into deep space. Each path ends in an epilogue on other machines that went quiet, including InSight, Kepler, NEAR Shoemaker and Dawn. The page uses animated line art, parallax and a color palette that shifts with each chapter.

It turns dry mission facts into a personal journey, so people learn through exploration and choice instead of a list. It reframes “dead” spacecraft as lasting legacies that still shape science. This matters because it makes space history emotional, accessible and memorable for general audiences. It is also designed to be inclusive, with readable type, reduced-motion support and mobile layouts.
It answers Abandoned but Not Forgotten by treating NASA’s discarded equipment as characters, not junk. Mirrors still work, rovers outlived their 90-day missions, and a helicopter built for five flights flew 72. Each silent machine taught engineers how to build the next one, so what was left behind is remembered.
projectDetails.details:
Still Listening is an interactive scrollytelling website about NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. The reader is a radio signal leaving Earth, and scrolling moves them through five chapters: the Moon (Apollo landers, moon buggies, laser mirrors, Surveyor 3), Mars (Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity), a choice at a fork, then an epilogue. At the fork the reader picks between answering Opportunity in its 2018 dust storm and following Pioneer 10 into deep space. Each path ends with other machines that went quiet: InSight, Kepler, NEAR Shoemaker and Dawn. A companion 7-slide deck summarizes the story.

Benefits and intended impact
It turns dry mission facts into a personal journey, so people learn through exploration and choice. It reframes “abandoned” spacecraft as lasting legacies that still shape science, and it makes space history emotional, accessible and memorable, especially for young space fans.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript; GSAP with ScrollTrigger for scroll animation; HTML Canvas for the particle background; hand-drawn inline SVG illustrations; Google Fonts (Fraunces and Atkinson Hyperlegible); GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. No special hardware was needed. Mission facts come from NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive and science.nasa.gov. Add any other tools your team used.

Creativity
The reader is the radio signal, so the story is told from a new point of view. The branching choice means no two journeys are identical. Line-art illustrations draw themselves as you scroll, and the color palette and background motion change with each chapter.

Factors we considered
Accuracy of mission facts, accessibility (readable fonts, reduced-motion support, high contrast), mobile-friendly layouts, no installs or logins, and a clear, age-friendly tone.

projectDetails.name: ASTRO HEALTH CHECK
projectDetails.summary:
"ASTRO HEALTH CHECK" is a little software I built to make daily health checks easy for astronauts, for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge. It works without internet, and everything stays on your own device.

When you open it, you see three big buttons: add your daily log, see your health report, or open the emergency guide. If more than one person shares the app, each crew member gets their own history.

The daily log asks one simple question at a time: heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen, breathing, sleep and exercise. If you don't have the right device, it doesn't leave you stuck. It shows an easy way to measure by hand, like counting your pulse, or just asks how you're feeling. You can skip anything you can't do.

The health report tells you how you're doing in plain words. A body figure lights up green, yellow or red, and you can tap any part to see what it means. Below that are the actions you should take, and a graph that shows how your health is changing over time.

If something serious comes up, the emergency guide walks you through what to do, starting with a heart attack. Temperature works in °C or °F, and the app remembers your choice.

You can add a shortcut for this in a web browser, so it opens like a normal app.
projectDetails.details: Astro Health Check is a small offline software I built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 Health Monitoring challenge, to help astronauts look after their health on long missions when a doctor on Earth isn’t always a quick call away. It needs internet for first opening though. Each day, the app asks simple questions about heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen, breathing, sleep and exercise, and if a device isn’t available it shows an easy way to check by hand. It then turns the answers into a health report: a body figure that lights up green, yellow or red, clear next steps, and a graph of how your health is changing over time. If something serious happens, an emergency guide gives calm, step-by-step help for situations like a heart attack or trouble breathing. Each crew member keeps their own history, and everything stays on the device. It installs on a phone like a normal app and works without internet.

projectDetails.name: “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Legacy of NASA’s Equipment on the Moon”
projectDetails.summary:
This project, **“Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Legacy of NASA’s Equipment on the Moon,”** explores four important pieces of equipment left behind on the lunar surface during NASA’s Apollo missions: the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), Lunar Module Descent Stage, and Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR).

The project explains the purpose, design, working principles, and scientific importance of each piece of equipment. It also describes why these machines and instruments were left on the Moon after completing their missions. While some equipment helped astronauts explore the lunar surface, other instruments collected valuable scientific data about the Moon and its environment.

Although these objects are no longer actively used by astronauts, they remain important evidence of human achievements in space exploration. Their contributions continue to support our understanding of the Moon and inspire future missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Legacy of NASA’s Equipment on the Moon

This project focuses on four important pieces of equipment left behind on the Moon during NASA’s Apollo missions: the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), Lunar Module Descent Stage, and Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR).

Through storytelling, the project explores the history, purpose, construction, working principles, and contributions of these objects to lunar exploration. It explains how each piece of equipment helped astronauts explore the Moon, conduct scientific experiments, land safely, or support long-term research. The project also highlights why these objects were left on the lunar surface after their missions ended.

By presenting their stories in a simple and engaging way, the project aims to help people understand that these objects are not merely abandoned equipment. They are valuable reminders of human curiosity, scientific progress, and the achievements of space exploration.

projectDetails.details:
What it does & how it works:

This project is a curated 7-slide visual digital museum and storybook documenting abandoned NASA space hardware across the Moon and Mars. It systematically breaks down the engineering purpose, historical milestones, and legacy of iconic artifacts left behind during historic missions.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

It serves as an engaging educational tool designed for students and space enthusiasts (ages 8–14) to reframe historic space hardware as permanent archaeological monuments rather than waste. It fosters curiosity about space exploration and aerospace heritage.

Tools, Coding Languages, & Resources Used:

- Design & Format: PDF Presentation / Digital Storybook (Canva / professional document architecture)

- Data & References: Official NASA public domain repositories, including the National Space Science Data Center (NSSDC) Master Catalog, Mars Exploration Program archives, and NASA image libraries.

Creativity & Team Considerations:

Instead of traditional software code, this solo project leans into creative digital storytelling and historical curation. It solves the challenge by transforming complex space physics and mission logs into an accessible, beautifully structured visual narrative.

projectDetails.name: ASTRIS & ASTRA
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRIS: Onboard Crew Health Monitoring and Triage System

ASTRIS is a health monitoring platform designed to support astronauts during space missions, especially when communication with Earth is limited. In space, astronauts may face health issues that need immediate attention, so having a reliable onboard health system is important.

Our project provides a single platform where crew members can enter and monitor their vital signs, such as heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, blood pressure and glucose levels. Its main innovation is ASTRA AI, an intelligent health assistant that analyses the entered health data, identifies possible health risks and provides quick guidance on what to do next.

ASTRIS also includes features such as health history tracking, body system monitoring, triage levels, check-up scheduling, response logs and printable medical reports. It also provides information about solar radiation using NASA's space-weather data.

Our aim is to make health monitoring easier and help astronauts respond to possible medical emergencies, even without continuous support from Earth.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRIS & ASTRA [Autonomous Space Telemetry & Response Assistant]

An Offline-First Astronaut Health Monitoring and Triage System

1. Project Overview

Our Team ASTRIS presents ASTRA (Autonomous Space Telemetry & Response Assistant) which is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring and triage platform designed to support crew members during space missions, particularly missions to the Moon and Mars.

During long-duration space missions, astronauts may experience health-related problems due to isolation, radiation exposure, changes in their environment and limited access to immediate medical assistance. Communication delays between Earth and distant space missions can also make it difficult to receive timely medical guidance.

ASTRIS aims to address this challenge by providing an onboard platform that helps astronauts monitor their health, identify unusual changes in vital signs and receive immediate guidance without depending on continuous communication with Earth.

The platform combines health monitoring, rule-based analysis, an intelligent assistant, medical response logging and environmental information in one dashboard.

2. Our Main Innovation – ASTRA AI

The most important innovation of our project is ASTRA AI (Autonomous Space Telemetry & Response Assistant), an intelligent onboard health assistant designed specifically for astronaut healthcare.

ASTRA helps astronauts understand their health condition by analyzing the readings entered into ASTRIS. It can answer questions about health parameters, explain active alerts, identify the current triage status and provide guidance on the next steps.

Unlike a system that depends entirely on cloud-based AI services, ASTRA is designed to work using information available on the device itself. This makes it useful in situations where communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

ASTRA includes quick actions such as:

  • Checking the astronaut's current health status.
  • Explaining the reason behind a particular triage level.
  • Identifying active health alerts.
  • Providing information about individual vital signs.
  • Explaining how to measure parameters such as SpO₂.
  • Suggesting the next health check.
  • Explaining how the analysis model works.

ASTRA currently uses a rule-based approach rather than a medically validated AI diagnostic model. Its purpose is to provide understandable triage guidance, not to replace doctors or flight surgeons.

3. Website Features and Functionality

Our website is designed as a central control dashboard where astronauts can access all the health monitoring and response features.

A. Overview Dashboard

The overview page provides a quick summary of the crew member's health status. It displays the current triage level, available health readings, alerts and check-up schedule. It also provides shortcuts to save a check-in, ask ASTRA, contact a medical officer and generate a handover report.

B. Crew Member Management

The platform allows users to create, select, rename and remove crew member profiles. This makes it possible to maintain separate health records for different astronauts.

C. Health Monitoring and Check-ins

Astronauts can manually enter or update their health readings. The system supports important parameters such as:

  • Heart rate
  • Blood oxygen level (SpO₂)
  • Body temperature
  • Systolic blood pressure
  • Blood glucose
  • Sleep and mood information

The readings are saved as check-ins, allowing the system to maintain a history of health information. Sample normal and emergency drill readings are also available for demonstration.

D. Triage and Alert System

This feature evaluates the entered readings and identifies possible health concerns. It uses different levels of response, including normal monitoring, rechecking readings and escalation when necessary.

The system explains why a particular triage level has been assigned and highlights readings that require attention. This helps astronauts understand when they should recheck a measurement or seek medical assistance.

E. ASTRA AI Assistant

ASTRA acts as the onboard health assistant. Users can interact with it through a chat interface and ask questions about their readings, alerts and recommended next steps. It uses the available health data on the device to provide contextual guidance.

F. Body Systems Map

The body systems section provides a visual representation of different body systems and their monitoring status. It helps users identify which systems may require attention.

It uses status indicators such as Normal, Recheck, Escalate, Check Sensor and No Data to make health information easier to understand.

G. Model Analysis and Evaluation

This section explains how the health analysis system works. It considers reference ranges, unusual readings, personal baselines and changes in readings over time.

The website also provides options to:

  • Add simulated health history.
  • Import baseline reference data.
  • Run model benchmarks.
  • View per-measure statistics.
  • Evaluate how the model responds to different sample readings.

The system uses simulated data for demonstration and testing. It does not claim to have been validated using actual astronaut medical records.

H. Health History and Trend Analysis

ASTRIS stores previous check-ins and allows users to view changes in their health readings over time. Trend graphs display the last 12 saved values for a selected parameter.

This helps identify repeated unusual readings or gradual changes that might otherwise go unnoticed.

I. Check-up Scheduling

The check schedule feature allows users to set intervals for regular health check-ins. The system keeps track of missed checks and includes an escalation window following a critical check-in.

This encourages regular monitoring rather than waiting until a health problem becomes serious.

J. Response Log and Medical Handover

The response log records actions such as saved check-ins, acknowledgements, rechecks and medical officer contacts.

Users can also generate printable handover reports containing relevant information that can assist in communicating the astronaut's health status to medical personnel.

These records help maintain a history of actions taken during a health-related event.

K. Solar Radiation Monitoring

Space radiation is an important environmental risk for astronauts. ASTRIS includes a solar radiation section that connects with NASA's DONKI (Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information).

It allows users to check available solar flare and space-weather information, helping them remain aware of potential radiation-related environmental events.

ASTRIS does not directly measure radiation dose. Actual radiation monitoring requires appropriate onboard dosimeters.

L. Data Import and Export

The platform supports importing and exporting health records in CSV and JSON formats. This makes it easier to maintain, transfer and analyze health information when required.

The records and response logs are stored locally on the device, supporting the platform's offline-first approach.

4. How the System Works

The basic working process of ASTRIS can be explained in five steps:

  1. Data Entry: The astronaut enters health readings through the website.
  2. Data Analysis: The system compares readings with expected reference ranges and available personal health baselines.
  3. Risk Identification: Unusual readings, repeated changes and possible sensor errors are identified.
  4. Triage and Guidance: The system determines an appropriate triage level and ASTRA provides understandable guidance.
  5. Record Keeping: The check-in, alerts and actions taken are stored in the health history and response log.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend Development: HTML for building the website structure and user interface.
  • Deployment: Vercel for hosting and making the website accessible online.
  • Data Management: CSV and JSON formats for importing and exporting health records.
  • NASA Data Source: NASA DONKI API for accessing solar flare and space-weather information.
  • Hardware: Currently a software-based prototype. Bluetooth wearable sensors are planned for future integration.

5. What Makes ASTRIS Different?

The main strength of ASTRIS is that it brings several important functions together in a single onboard platform.

Instead of having separate systems for health readings, alerts, medical guidance and record keeping, ASTRIS combines them into one interface.

Its offline-first design reduces dependence on continuous communication with Earth. Its personal baseline and trend analysis features also help identify changes rather than looking at individual readings alone.

The integration of ASTRA, health triage, response logging and NASA space-weather information makes it a useful prototype for exploring the future of astronaut healthcare.

6. Future Scope

Although the current version is a functional website prototype, several improvements can make ASTRIS more suitable for actual space missions.

  • Wearable Sensor Integration: Connecting Bluetooth-enabled devices to automatically collect heart rate, SpO₂, skin temperature and other available health readings.
  • Real-Time Monitoring: Continuously monitoring astronaut health without requiring manual data entry.
  • Advanced AI Models: Developing more advanced predictive models using validated medical datasets.
  • Radiation Sensor Integration: Connecting appropriate radiation monitoring hardware to track actual radiation exposure.
  • Improved Medical Support: Developing better communication and reporting systems for astronauts and medical officers.
  • Mission-Specific Customization: Adapting the platform to the requirements of future Moon and Mars missions.

7. Expected Impact

ASTRIS aims to improve how astronaut health information is monitored and managed during space exploration. By combining continuous monitoring as a future goal, early identification of unusual readings, triage guidance and organized medical records, the system can help astronauts respond more effectively to potential health concerns.

It is particularly relevant to long-duration missions where communication delays and limited medical resources make onboard health support important.

8. Conclusion

ASTRIS is our attempt to address one of the important challenges of future space exploration: keeping astronauts healthy and safe when immediate medical support from Earth may not be available.

Through its health monitoring dashboard, ASTRA intelligent assistant, triage system, trend analysis and space-weather monitoring, ASTRIS provides a unified approach to astronaut health management.

Our vision is to develop ASTRIS into a reliable onboard health support platform that helps astronauts make informed decisions and supports safer missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond.

projectDetails.summary: My team created a software in which you could keep track of your health while you are in space.The project is called AstroCare.Our challenge was to create a software through which astronauts could monitor their health while in space missions.I think this is important because many astronauts suffer from health issues after going to space
projectDetails.details:
AstroCare – Astronaut Health Companion

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

AstroCare is a web-based health companion designed to help astronauts keep track of their health during space missions. Astronauts can enter important health information, such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep hours, and mood.

The website provides a daily health check-in, displays health trends, and gives simple educational feedback based on the information entered. It also includes information about different body systems, a mission checklist, and a spaceflight health guide. Users can save their records in the browser and export them as CSV files for later use.

2. What benefits does it have?

Living in space can be challenging for the human body and mind. AstroCare aims to make health tracking easier and more convenient for astronauts.

It helps them keep their health information organised, notice changes in their health over time, and pay attention to important areas such as sleep and mood. The health guides also help astronauts understand how space conditions can affect their bodies. Overall, the project encourages astronauts to take an active role in looking after their well-being.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal of AstroCare is to support astronauts in staying healthy and well during long-duration space missions. We hope it will encourage regular health check-ins, improve awareness of physical and mental well-being, and help astronauts keep useful health records.

By making health information easier to track and understand, AstroCare could also support better communication with the crew's medical team when health concerns arise.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

We developed AstroCare using common web development technologies:

  • HTML5 – to build the structure of the website.
  • CSS3 – to create the design and layout.
  • JavaScript – to make the features interactive.
  • Browser Local Storage – to save health records and checklist progress on the user's device.
  • Canvas API – to display health trend charts.
  • CSV export – to allow users to download their health records.

The project runs in a web browser, so it does not require specialised hardware or medical sensors. Health information is entered manually, and the sample dashboard values are for demonstration purposes.

5. How is the project creative?

What makes AstroCare different is that it brings health tracking and space exploration together in one simple platform. Instead of focusing only on physical health, it also considers sleep, mood, and the mental challenges astronauts may experience in space.

We designed it with a modern, space-inspired interface and included interactive features such as health check-ins, charts, a mission checklist, and educational guides. Our aim was to make health monitoring feel simple, engaging, and relevant to the unique needs of astronauts.

6. What factors did the team consider?

While developing AstroCare, we considered the challenges astronauts may face during space missions, including:

  • Microgravity: How spending time in low gravity can affect the human body.
  • Radiation: The possible health risks of exposure to radiation in space.
  • Isolation: The effects of being away from family, friends, and Earth.
  • Physical health: The importance of monitoring basic health indicators.
  • Mental well-being: The role of sleep and mood in maintaining overall health.
  • Ease of use: Making the website simple and easy to navigate.
  • Accessibility: Keeping it lightweight and usable through a web browser.
  • Data management: Allowing users to save and export their records.
  • Medical safety: Making it clear that AstroCare is an educational prototype, not a certified medical device or a replacement for professional medical advice.

Our overall vision

With AstroCare, we wanted to create more than just a health-tracking website. We wanted to develop a simple and useful companion that reminds astronauts to look after themselves while exploring space. We believe that taking care of the people behind every space mission is just as important as the mission itself.

projectDetails.name: Echoes of Exploration
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes of Exploration is an interactive website that tells the stories behind the equipment humanity has sent to the Moon and Mars. Instead of listing technical specifications, it lets visitors explore each piece of hardware as a character in the story of exploration. Equipment cards for Apollo lunar modules, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, and Ingenuity each open a story popup. These popups cover why the machine was built, what it faced, and what it achieved. All stories are drawn from NASA's own published material and use NASA imagery and our own visuals.

The project makes space history approachable for students and the general public, and shows how each mission built on the one before it. It is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and hosted on GitHub Pages, so anyone can open it in a browser without installing anything.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
Echoes of Exploration is a website that presents the Moon and Mars equipment humanity has sent into space as stories. Visitors browse equipment cards divided into Moon and Mars sections. These include the Apollo lunar modules, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, and Ingenuity. Clicking a card opens a popup that tells the story of that machine: why it was built, the challenges it faced, and what it achieved.

Benefits and intended impact
The site makes space exploration history easy to understand for students and the general public. Presenting each machine as a story, instead of a list of specifications, helps people connect with the missions. It also shows how each generation of equipment built on the work of the one before it.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with no frameworks
  • Mission data stored in a separate JavaScript data file, so new equipment can be added without changing the page code
  • Content sourced from NASA's official mission pages
  • Images from the NASA Image and Video Library, plus our own visuals for the lunar rover, Spirit and Opportunity, and Ingenuity
  • Version control with Git, hosted on GitHub Pages so it works in any browser

Creativity
The creative idea is to treat the equipment as characters, so each machine's "echo" of exploration is heard through its own story. The card-and-popup layout keeps the page clean while letting visitors choose how deep to go.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: all facts come from NASA sources
  • Accessibility: the site is lightweight, works on any device, and needs no installation
  • Scalability: the data-driven structure lets us add more missions later
  • Clarity: the stories use simple language so non-experts can follow them

projectDetails.name: FireWatch: Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Satellite Data for Global Fire Activity Monitoring
projectDetails.summary: FireWatch is a web-based platform designed to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS satellite active fire hotspot data into a unified system for monitoring global burning activity. The platform aims to overcome differences between satellite sensors by standardizing fire observations and organizing them into a consistent spatial and temporal dataset. Users can explore historical fire patterns through an interactive map, a burning activity calendar, and visual analytics that compare fire activity across different regions and time periods. The system also highlights unusual increases in hotspot activity by comparing current observations with historical patterns. By transforming complex satellite observations into accessible and meaningful insights, FireWatch supports early awareness, wildfire monitoring, and informed decision-making. It is designed to assist emergency responders, scientists, environmental researchers, and land managers in identifying critical fire periods, understanding long-term burning trends, and improving fire management strategies.
projectDetails.details:
FireWatch: Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Satellite Data for Global Fire Activity Monitoring

FireWatch is a web-based platform designed to bring MODIS and VIIRS satellite active-fire observations together into a common format for easier visualization and analysis.

The platform aims to help users explore fire activity across different locations and time periods using interactive maps, daily fire activity calendars, and historical data visualizations. By combining observations from two satellite sources, FireWatch helps users understand fire patterns and compare the information provided by different satellite sensors.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

  • Makes satellite fire observations easier to explore and understand.
  • Helps identify geographical and temporal patterns in fire activity.
  • Supports awareness of wildfire activity and potential environmental risks.
  • Provides an accessible way for students, researchers, and interested users to explore satellite fire data.

Tools and Technologies:

  • Programming Language: Python
  • Framework: Streamlit
  • Data Processing: Pandas
  • Visualization: Plotly
  • Data Sources: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire datasets.
  • Development Environment: Visual Studio Code
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of FireWatch is its focus on bringing observations from two different satellite systems into one accessible visualization platform. Instead of examining separate datasets independently, users can explore their observations through a unified interface while retaining information about their original satellite sources.

The project considers differences in satellite observations, data quality, spatial resolution, timestamps, and the importance of avoiding misleading duplicate fire counts.

FireWatch aims to make satellite-based fire monitoring more understandable, accessible, and useful for environmental awareness and further research.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: MarsWalk: An Integrated Mars Surface Exploration and Safety Planner
projectDetails.summary:
MarsWalk is an interactive Mars exploration planning platform designed to support future astronauts during surface exploration missions. Focusing on Jezero Crater, the application brings together different types of planetary science information, including surface imagery, elevation, temperature, mineral composition and rover observations.

The platform provides an interactive map, scientific points of interest, potential terrain hazard indicators and a route planning interface. It aims to help explorers understand the surrounding environment, identify scientifically interesting locations and plan their surface activities more effectively.

By combining information from multiple NASA missions into a unified interface, MarsWalk demonstrates how existing robotic exploration data can support future human missions to Mars. Its primary goal is to make planetary information more accessible, understandable and useful for safer exploration and scientific discovery.
projectDetails.details:
MarsWalk is a web-based Mars surface exploration and safety planning application developed to address the challenges of future human exploration of Mars.

The application focuses on Jezero Crater, a scientifically important region explored by NASA's Perseverance rover. It provides an interactive map interface where users can explore locations, examine scientific information, view different planetary data categories and plan hypothetical surface exploration routes.

The main features include:

• Interactive Mars exploration map with location markers and navigation.
• Scientific data layer controls for optical imagery, elevation, thermal information, mineral composition and rover observations.
• Scientific points of interest with geological information.
• Potential terrain hazard indicators for identifying challenging areas.
• A basic route planner showing suggested exploration paths, estimated distance and travel duration.
• An astronaut safety dashboard displaying terrain risk and environmental information.

The project is designed to bring different types of planetary science information into one accessible interface instead of requiring explorers to consult multiple separate sources.

We use React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Leaflet to develop the web application. The project uses NASA planetary science resources as its scientific foundation, with demonstration and estimated values clearly distinguished wherever actual measurements are unavailable.

MarsWalk demonstrates how existing robotic mission observations can be transformed into a practical exploration-planning interface for future human missions. It aims to support safer decision-making, efficient exploration and new scientific discoveries on the Martian surface.

projectDetails.name: Space Time Capsule
projectDetails.summary:
Space Time Capsule is an educational website developed by Team Chakravyuham for NASA's Discarded Equipment Storytelling challenge. It explores the stories of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. The site addresses the challenge by documenting and sharing the purpose, mission background, scientific contribution and known status of these objects in an accessible digital format, using NASA data and resources.
The website features an artifact collection with Moon and Mars categories, a mission timeline, an Apollo landing-site map, NASA research resources, a space exploration quiz and an equipment-matching activity. These features make learning about space exploration more visual, engaging and accessible.
Our goal is to turn left-behind space hardware into meaningful stories, helping students and space enthusiasts understand that even after a mission ends, its discoveries, technology and legacy continue to inspire future exploration.
