projectDetails.name: Field Shift Agroclimatic Engine
projectDetails.summary: Field Shift is a decision-support tool that helps rainfed farmers and extension advisers in Solapur, Maharashtra, explore crop-rotation options under uncertain monsoons. Using 41 years (1985–2025) of NASA POWER daily weather (MERRA-2 and CERES-derived rainfall, temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation), it runs an FAO-56 daily soil-water balance for three rotations on shallow, medium and deep black soils: fallow then rabi sorghum, sole pigeon pea, and pearl millet then chickpea. Instead of a single winning answer, it shows how much water stress each rotation faces in typical and bad years, how often the planting window is missed, and how stable each comparison is across 500 plausible parameter combinations. Parameters carry source and status labels, and assumptions are stated openly. Field Shift supports, not replaces, farmer judgment: it models water stress, not yield or income.
projectDetails.details:
Problem. Rainfed farmers in Solapur’s semi-arid Deccan face erratic monsoon rainfall. Choosing a rotation depends on soil depth, the date monsoon rain arrives, and moisture stored for rabi crops. CRIDA’s district plan shows about 68% of the district has shallow black soils. Existing tools rarely show how uncertain a comparison is.

Solution. Field Shift is a self-contained web tool with a precomputed engine. Farmers or advisers pick a soil depth, an existing rotation, and priorities. The tool shows each rotation’s water stress, planting-window risk, where the rain goes, and how robust each comparison is.

How it works.

  • Data: NASA POWER daily point data for a 55 km grid cell near Pandharpur in western Solapur district (17.68°N, 75.32°E), 1984–2025. 1984 is spin-up, and 1985–2025 (41 years) is evaluated.
  • Evapotranspiration: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference ET, tested against FAO’s worked Example 18 and a hand calculation.
  • Water balance: a daily root-zone balance with FAO-56 crop coefficients, a two-stage bare-soil evaporation model, and optional runoff. Rainfall equals crop ET, soil evaporation, losses, and storage change, with closure under 1e-6 mm.
  • Rotations: (R1) fallow then rabi sorghum, (R2) sole pigeonpea, (R3) pearl millet then chickpea.
  • Soils: shallow 0.20 m, medium 0.375 m, deep 1.0 m, from CRIDA depth classes, with an assumed available water of 190 mm/m.
  • Sowing: kharif crops sow at the first 3-day rainfall of at least 25 mm inside the CRIDA window (an assumed trigger). Rabi crops sow when stored moisture reaches 40% of capacity.
  • Two views of a missed planting window: one assumes late planting always works, and the other treats a missed window as total loss. They are optimistic and pessimistic bounds.
  • Uncertainty: 500 Monte Carlo draws over assumed (not measured) ranges for water capacity, sowing date, rain trigger, runoff, humidity method, evaporation settings, crop coefficients, and cultivar duration. The output is how often each ordering holds, not a probability of real outcomes.
  • Extras: a season calendar of soil water, ET₀ trend tests (Mann-Kendall, Theil-Sen, Pettitt), and parameter-source labels.

Findings so far [verify against docs/key-results.md]: soil depth dominates the results. When late planting always works, pigeon pea and millet-chickpea show lower mean deficit than fallow-sorghum in 95% to 98% of draws on deep soil, and 100% on medium and shallow soils. When a missed window counts as total loss, on deep soil fallow-sorghum is lower in about 71% and 65% of draws, while on medium and shallow soils the alternatives stay lower in 88% to 100%.

Tools. JavaScript on Node.js with no runtime dependencies, node:test (55 tests), static HTML/CSS/JS with inline SVG, git. Statistical tests are our own implementations, hand-checked against a published textbook benchmark.

Creativity. The distinctive features are showing when the tool cannot separate options, stating both missed-planting treatments openly, and labelling every parameter as cited, proxy, assumption, or pending. We make no claim of being the only tool that does this.

Benefits and intended impact. The tool is meant to help extension officers and farmers frame rotation discussions, see which options are plausible at which soil depth, and see where planting risk and bare-field periods fall. The impact is potential and has not been field-tested.

Limitations and future work.

  • The reanalysis grid is 55 km and gridded rainfall smooths storm peaks.
  • It models water stress, not yield, income, or markets.
  • No farmer or expert has validated it.
  • Soil health and pest cycles are qualitative: crop family and legume flags only.
  • Early-season crop evaporation uses a fixed initial coefficient, and fallow is modelled as bare soil.
  • Next steps: expert review with local extension (KVK), additional NASA products (SMAP, GPM, MODIS), more districts, and a dual-coefficient crop evaporation model.

projectDetails.name: The Silent Legacy
projectDetails.summary: The Silent Legacy is an interactive digital storytelling project by Team CORE that explores NASA equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Instead of treating these objects simply as discarded hardware, our project explains the purpose, engineering role, and lasting significance of each component. We focus on Apollo 11 lunar hardware, including the Lunar Module descent stage and lunar laser-ranging retroreflector, and the Mars 2020 Perseverance landing system, including its heat shield, parachute, backshell, and powered descent stage. Through a visual virtual-museum experience, visitors can explore object stories, mission timelines, comparisons, images, and NASA resources. The project aims to make planetary exploration easier to understand while showing how spacecraft components can become scientific, engineering, and historical evidence after their primary mission is complete.
projectDetails.details: The Silent Legacy: Humanity’s Footprints on the Moon and Mars The Silent Legacy is an interactive digital storytelling project that explores human-made spacecraft hardware left on the Moon and Mars after successful space missions. The project presents this equipment as a virtual museum, helping visitors understand why these objects remain on other worlds and what they tell us about exploration. The project focuses on two major mission stories: Apollo 11 on the Moon and NASA’s Perseverance mission on Mars. The Moon section explains the Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage and the lunar laser-ranging retroreflector. The Mars section explores landing-system components associated with Perseverance, including the heat shield, parachute, backshell, and powered descent stage. Rather than presenting these objects simply as “space junk,” the project explains their different purposes. Some were mission hardware designed for one-time use, while others were intentionally deployed for scientific research. The website connects these objects with the engineering decisions, scientific goals, and historical importance of planetary exploration. The project is designed for students, teachers, families, and anyone interested in space science. It uses simple explanations, visual storytelling, object cards, timelines, comparisons, and an easy-to-navigate virtual museum structure to make the subject accessible to beginners. The project also highlights an important idea for future exploration: as humans continue sending missions to the Moon and Mars, the hardware left behind can become part of the scientific and historical record of exploration. Understanding what is intentionally left behind helps us think about responsible exploration and the long-term legacy of human activity beyond Earth. Technologies and tools: HTML, CSS, digital presentation tools, online research resources, and NASA mission information. Creativity and innovation: The project transforms technical mission information into a virtual museum experience. Instead of only listing spacecraft components, it tells the story of each object, its purpose, and its connection to human exploration. Expected impact: The project aims to improve awareness of planetary exploration, encourage interest in STEM subjects, and help students understand the engineering and scientific significance of spacecraft hardware beyond Earth. Tagline: “The machines may stop. The discoveries continue.”

projectDetails.name: Project Sojourner Tale
projectDetails.summary: “A Sojourner Tale” is an interactive story created by the team Cosmic Crew Girls for the NASA Space Apps challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” Inspired by the Mars Pathfinder mission, it is narrated in the first person by the Sojourner rover across eight animated chapters, covering its launch in 1996, airbag landing, first steps, rock encounters, solar-powered days, and a mission that lasted 83 sols instead of the planned 7. Users can tap five glowing hotspots to explore the rover’s parts, open cards of real NASA data (such as 2.3 billion bits returned and 16,500+ lander images), and turn on read-aloud narration. Designed for young learners, it works on phones and computers and ends by honoring Sojourner’s legacy, which leads to Perseverance. It is built with HTML, CSS, SVG and JavaScript.
projectDetails.details:
A Sojourner Tale: An Interactive Digital Story Inspired by NASA's Mars Pathfinder Mission

A Sojourner Tale is an interactive storytelling website based on NASA's Mars Pathfinder mission and its small rover, Sojourner. Sojourner tells the story itself, in the first person, so visitors follow the trip from Earth to Mars through the rover's eyes. I didn't want the site to be another list of dates and facts. It mixes storytelling with science, illustrations, animations and interactive features to make space exploration feel more alive and easier to follow.

The story moves through the main stages of the mission. It starts with the launch from Earth, then goes through the landing on Mars, the rover's first movements, its study of rocks and soil, what it discovered, and how it shaped later Mars missions. Mars Pathfinder launched on December 4, 1996, and landed in Ares Vallis on July 4, 1997. The site explains the airbag system that cushioned the landing and introduces some of the rocks Sojourner studied, including Barnacle Bill, Yogi and Scooby-Doo. Visitors also learn about the rover itself: it weighed only about 10.6 kg, stood around 30 cm tall and moved on six wheels.

The project runs in any web browser. Visitors scroll through the story chapter by chapter. They can also click hotspots on the rover illustration to explore its parts: the solar panel, cameras, APXS instrument, wheels and body. Information cards and pop-ups give extra details about the mission, the instruments and the discoveries. Animated backgrounds, smooth transitions, a scroll progress bar and a read-aloud option make the site more engaging and more accessible.

I built the website with HTML, CSS and JavaScript:

  1. HTML gives the site its structure and splits the story into sections.
  2. CSS handles the layout, colours, animations, transitions and responsive design.
  3. JavaScript runs the interactive parts, including chapter navigation, hotspots, pop-ups, scroll tracking and the animated backgrounds.
  4. SVG illustrations draw the rover and the Martian landscape.
  5. The Canvas API creates the moving star background.
  6. The browser's Web Speech API provides the read-aloud narration.

Together, these let the site work without special hardware or any software to install.

One of the project's biggest strengths is how it makes scientific and historical information simple to take in. Space missions, scientific instruments and planetary exploration can feel overwhelming, but they become much easier to understand when they're told as a story with visuals you can interact with. The site can be useful for school and college students, teachers, and anyone curious about space. Because the design is responsive, it works on computers, tablets and phones.

The main goal of A Sojourner Tale is to spark interest in planetary exploration. It shows how a rover weighing only about 10.6 kg made a big difference to our understanding of Mars. It also tested technologies that later missions built on. By combining real science with a story, I hope the project encourages people, especially students, to get curious about science, technology, engineering and space.

The creative side of the project comes from telling the mission from Sojourner's point of view. Instead of treating it as just a machine, the website gives the rover a voice, so visitors feel like they're travelling with it. Space-themed visuals, Martian scenery, interactive illustrations, animations and narration make the mission more memorable. The story also links Sojourner's work to the rovers that followed it: Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance.

While building the site, I focused on keeping the science accurate, ordering the story so it made sense, making the interactions smooth and keeping it easy to navigate on any device. No physical rover or electronic hardware is needed; a browser is enough. In the future, I'd like to add more detailed animations, interactive maps, quizzes, more information about the scientific instruments, and narration in other languages.

In short, A Sojourner Tale brings together technology, creativity, education and storytelling to share what the Mars Pathfinder mission achieved. A rover small enough to carry in your arms helped change how we explore space, which shows that even a small step on another planet can help us understand the universe.

projectDetails.name: PROJECT ASTROHEALTH
projectDetails.summary:
ASTROHEALTH – An Intelligent Wearable-Based Health Monitoring and Decision Support System for Astronauts

ASTROHEALTH is an AI-powered health monitoring system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It integrates wearable sensors with intelligent software to collect and analyse vital health indicators such as heart rate, ECG, blood oxygen levels, body temperature, sleep patterns and physical activity. The system monitors changes in astronauts' health, identifies potential risks associated with microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation and the space environment, and provides personalised health recommendations and real-time alerts. It also maintains individual health records and provides a dashboard for monitoring health trends. The primary objective is to empower astronauts to independently assess, manage and respond to their health conditions, improving crew safety and well-being during space missions.
projectDetails.details: ASTROHEALTH is an intelligent wearable-based health monitoring and decision support system designed to monitor and improve the health, safety and well-being of astronauts during long-duration space missions. Astronauts face several health challenges due to microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, confinement and changes in their daily routines. To address these challenges, ASTROHEALTH combines wearable sensors with an AI-powered software platform to collect and analyse important health parameters such as heart rate, ECG, blood oxygen level (SpO₂), skin temperature, physical activity and sleep patterns. Environmental sensors can also monitor cabin conditions such as temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels, while a dedicated radiation dosimeter can measure radiation exposure. The collected data is transmitted to the software platform, where it is analysed and compared with each astronaut's personal health baseline to identify unusual patterns and potential health risks. The system provides real-time alerts, personalised recommendations and a digital dashboard displaying health status, trends and medical history, helping astronauts monitor their condition and take appropriate action. The major benefits include continuous health monitoring, early identification of potential health problems, personalised health analysis, improved self-management, long-term health records and better health-related decision-making during missions. The intended impact is to reduce health risks, support astronaut independence and contribute to safer and more sustainable space exploration, including future lunar and Mars missions. The proposed development technologies include an ESP32 microcontroller, MAX30102 sensor for heart rate and SpO₂ monitoring, AD8232 ECG sensor, temperature sensors, environmental sensors and a radiation dosimeter. Python is proposed for data analysis and AI development, C/C++ for embedded programming, Scikit-learn or TensorFlow for machine learning, Streamlit for the health dashboard and SQLite or PostgreSQL for storing health records. Bluetooth or Wi-Fi may be used for communication in the prototype. The creativity and innovation of ASTROHEALTH lie in its integration of wearable health monitoring, artificial intelligence and personalised health analysis into a single platform. Unlike basic health monitoring systems that only display measurements, ASTROHEALTH compares readings with individual health baselines, identifies unusual changes and provides useful alerts and suggested actions. During development, the team considered factors such as sensor accuracy, system reliability, astronaut safety, space environmental conditions, power efficiency, wearable comfort, data security, real-time performance, individual health differences, scalability and cost. The system also recognises the limitations of wearable technology, as conditions such as bone-density loss and immune-system changes require specialised tests or validated indirect indicators rather than ordinary smartwatch sensors. The project is currently a prototype concept demonstrated using simulated health readings, and further development, testing and validation would be required before actual spaceflight use. Overall, ASTROHEALTH aims to make astronaut health monitoring smarter, more personalised and more reliable, helping astronauts maintain their health and safety throughout long-duration space missions.

projectDetails.name: Regolith
projectDetails.summary: Regolith is a browser game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost for 60 sols, balancing power, radiation shielding, life support, food and mass. Every choice has a cost, and a post-mortem traces failures to the decision that caused them. A rover mission layer logs open, structured data that can train rover navigation and planning AI.
projectDetails.details:
What it is. Regolith is a browser game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost for 60 sols. Before launch, players split a fixed mass budget across solar arrays, fission units, batteries, radiation shielding, life-support recycling, greenhouse beds and stored rations. Then they run the outpost, spending 12 crew-hours per sol on greenhouse tending, life-support maintenance, panel cleaning, regolith excavation, a rover EVA, or hibernate mode, while random events strike: solar particle events, recycler faults, dust build-up, and Martian dust storms. Three sites change the constraints: Moon (polar ridge), Moon (equatorial, with a 14-day night) and Mars. If the mission fails, a post-mortem traces the failure back to specific decisions with numbers.

How it works. One deterministic resource model links power, oxygen, water, food, radiation dose, dust and mass, so no choice is free. A rover EVA minigame adds scouting (tagging rocks and craters), terrain driving with slope, tilt and battery drain, and a self-righting decision after a tip-over. Everything runs in a single HTML/JavaScript file with canvas graphics and needs no install.

NASA data and resources. Our life-support model is parameterized with NASA published values: crew oxygen use from NASA’s Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD), baseline drinking water intake and food planning values from NASA Johnson Space Center and NTRS publications, and Mars surface radiation from the Curiosity rover’s Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD) measurements. [Add only the sources you finish verifying; see below.]

Benefits and impact. Students feel why a mission fails or succeeds instead of reading about it. The same simulation produces open, structured data, with every outpost decision, rover drive trace, hazard label and self-righting choice stored as JSONL. This data is intended to train rover navigation, perception and planning AI, and to benchmark resource-allocation agents. It supports high-level policy and perception, not low-level servo control. Our own rover project is the first user of the data.

Creativity. The game is both a learning tool and a data-collection pipeline: each lesson a student learns also becomes labelled human-decision data.

Tools. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, canvas, Google Fonts, GitHub Pages. The code was generated with Claude (Anthropic) AI and edited by our team; the concept and rover integration are ours.

Factors we considered. Scientific accuracy vs playability (simplified physics, real parameters), mobile controls for classrooms, privacy (anonymous data only, no personal information), honest limits of what game data can teach a robot, and a roadmap: real LRO and HiRISE imagery for hazard labelling, cloud collection across schools, and a digital twin of our rover.

projectDetails.summary:
MISSION X is a browser-based educational game that lets anyone experience the trade-offs behind real spacecraft design. Instead of only reading about budgets, mass limits and power requirements, players make engineering decisions and immediately see the consequences.

THE PROBLEM
Space missions depend on many connected decisions. A bigger science payload adds value but also adds mass, needs more power and may require a larger rocket, which costs more. Students and beginners rarely get a hands-on way to see how these choices affect one another, so space engineering can feel abstract and out of reach.

projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

MISSION X is a browser-based game in which the player designs a spacecraft for a Moon, Mars or Deep Space mission. The player picks a launch vehicle, a science payload, a power system and a communication system within a fictional budget. Live telemetry shows cost, spacecraft mass, rocket payload capacity, power supply versus demand and communication reliability, with warnings before launch. The player then runs the mission: an animated countdown and flight to the destination leads to a mission report with a score out of 100, a 1–3 star rating and a debrief explaining which choices helped or hurt. Players can redesign and try again, and the game saves their personal best and last five attempts for each level.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Analog Finder
projectDetails.summary: Analog Finder takes a landing region on the Moon or Mars and finds the places on Earth whose measured environment comes closest. A Python pipeline pulls NASA POWER climate data and LOLA and MOLA topography, builds a 0.1 degree grid over about 2.2 million land cells, and scores every cell against the target with a Gaussian similarity kernel on seven features: slope, relief, roughness, mean surface temperature, day to night swing, coldest surface temperature and annual precipitation. A Monte Carlo over perturbed weights reports how stable each rank is, so a site that only appears because of one weighting choice is visible as such. The results drive a 3D web terminal with Earth, Moon and Mars globes, similarity heatmaps for every target and preset, and a dossier per site holding the feature breakdown, an elevation profile and satellite links. Every value carries its source. The aim is to build physical intuition about which earthly places resemble a given landing region, and to show the working.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Pick one of 12 landing regions, eight Artemis III candidate regions near the lunar south pole and four Mars sites (Jezero, Gale, Oxia Planum, Mawrth Vallis), then pick a weighting preset. The app returns the 50 best matching places on Earth, each with a score, the similarity for all seven features, the measured values behind that score, a rank-stability percentage from the Monte Carlo, an elevation transect and a hillshade chip. A 3D globe shows the target and the candidates together, a heatmap view shows the whole planet for that target and preset, and a split view puts the target terrain next to the Earth site. Satellite deep links open the same coordinates in Google Earth and NASA Worldview.

How it works

The Earth grid is built once. ETOPO 2022 bedrock elevation provides terrain and NASA POWER daily reanalysis provides climate, resampled to a 0.1 degree grid over land only. Terrain features are computed at a 28 km radius so that Earth and the target are compared at the same physical scale.

For each target, the pipeline reads a 28 km window of the global LOLA or MOLA elevation model and computes the same terrain features. A median despike removes single-pixel artefacts left by gaps between laser tracks; without it the de Gerlache window reports 27 km of relief instead of 11.5 km. Thermal values for the target come from published measurements, each with a citation recorded in config/targets.yaml, and the app displays that citation next to the number.

Scoring uses one Gaussian kernel per feature. A difference equal to the feature tolerance scores 0.61, twice the tolerance scores 0.14, and the weighted mean of the seven similarities is the site score. Weights come from four presets (polar, volcanic, dry basalt, cold desert) and are normalised inside the scorer.

Duplicate suppression removes candidates closer than 200 km and keeps a spread across continents, so the top ranks are not fifty cells on one ridge. The Monte Carlo perturbs every weight by up to 30 percent across 400 seeded draws and reports the share of runs in which a site stays in the top ten. The whole run is deterministic and reproducible.

The interface

React and TypeScript on Vite, with Three.js through globe.gl for the globes, D3 for charts, Palantir Blueprint for controls and Zustand for state. The build is entirely static: JSON, heatmap PNGs, hillshade chips and globe textures are bundled, and a SHA-256 manifest lists every file, so the app runs with the network switched off. It is deployed as a static site on Vercel and can be served from any CDN.

What we deliberately left out

Gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation, the dust regime and Sun geometry are displayed but never scored. Adding them would reward an Earth site for having an atmosphere, which no Earth site can change. The score answers which environment is closest, and the app labels the non-scored values as context.

Solar elevation is computed against a flat horizon. At the lunar poles the Sun stays within about six degrees of the horizon, so real terrain shadows decide whether a site is lit, and every solar figure in the app carries that caveat.

Validation against eight known analog testbeds (Devon Island, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Atacama, MDRS, HI-SEAS, Askja, Danakil, Lanzarote) put a testbed in the top 5 percent of Earth cells in 24 of 144 site, target and preset checks. Those testbeds were chosen in the literature partly for logistics, so a miss says the model did not rank a site highly, and it does not prove the site is a poor physical analog. The report is visible in the app.

One Artemis III region is missing. NASA lists nine, and the IAU Gazetteer gives a single centre point for the Mons Mouton massif, so the massif and the plateau cannot be anchored to distinct authoritative coordinates. We dropped that region rather than invent a coordinate.

Tools and languages

Python 3.13 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, rasterio, netCDF4, Pillow, PyYAML, requests, SciPy-based scoring, scikit-learn and SpiceyPy for ephemerides. The app is React 18, TypeScript, Vite, globe.gl and Three.js, D3, Blueprint and Zustand, with Vitest for the frontend and pytest for the pipeline. Data comes from NASA, USGS, NOAA, Natural Earth and the IAU.

Why it matters

Analog sites are used to test instruments, suits and procedures before launch, and the reasoning behind a choice is usually buried in a report. This tool makes the comparison explicit: which features matched, by how much, with which source, and how sensitive the ranking is to the weights. It is useful for teaching, outreach and early mission-concept work, and it is honest about its own limitations.

projectDetails.name: ASTRA Twin
projectDetails.summary: ASTRA Twin is a prototype that builds a personal digital twin of each astronaut's health. It compares each astronaut to their own baseline instead of generic limits, so slow drifts in heart rate, sleep, mood and other signals can be noticed earlier. It suggests likely causes, and writes delay-aware action guidance and reports for the flight surgeon. It uses simulated data.https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1fxmBPK9N-NMz6BnRBF_7xzFKwFkvTSmR/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=114333236277418179903&rtpof=true&sd=true
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

ASTRA Twin is a decision-support prototype (a Google Colab notebook) for monitoring astronaut health on long missions. It simulates a 30-day mission for a 4-person crew (all data is simulated) with 8 indicators: resting heart rate, HRV, systolic blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood and reaction time.

For each astronaut, the first 7 days set a personal baseline. A Kalman filter smooths the data and tracks slow drift from that baseline. Changes are grouped into four body systems (cardiovascular, sleep and cognition, immune and metabolic, behavioural) and rated Green, Yellow, Orange or Red, with a 0-100 readiness score. An Isolation Forest model adds an anomaly score that catches unusual combinations of signals.

The notebook also includes: a simple correlation-based check that suggests a likely cause (radiation, isolation drift or low exercise); an illustrative what-if model for exercise vs bone density and aerobic fitness; a rule-based decision guide that depends on Earth communication delay; an automatically generated SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) report; a crew readiness heatmap; and a signal-processing demo that estimates heart rate from a synthetic video-style signal (rPPG). It also contains code that downloads solar energetic particle events from the NASA DONKI API.

BENEFITS

The idea is to compare each astronaut to their own baseline instead of generic limits, so slow personal drifts can be noticed earlier. Reports and suggested actions are generated automatically to support crews who face communication delays with Earth.

INTENDED IMPACT

A starting point for personalised, delay-aware health monitoring on long missions to the Moon and Mars. It is a decision-support prototype only, not a medical diagnosis tool. The health data is simulated and the what-if model is illustrative, not clinically validated.

TOOLS

Python, Google Colab, NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn (Isolation Forest), ipywidgets and the Requests library. No special hardware is needed.

CREATIVITY

It combines a per-astronaut baseline, cause suggestions, a what-if simulator, delay-aware decision guidance and automatic reports in one notebook.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Individual differences between astronauts, Earth communication delay, space radiation, isolation and reduced exercise as mission stressors, and clear labelling of simulated data and prototype limits.

projectDetails.name: Project HUMAN INTELLIGENCE
projectDetails.summary:
**Project Summary – Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data**

Our project, *Flame in Freefall*, explores how flames behave in microgravity and how scientific data from space-based combustion experiments can improve fire safety on Earth and in space. We developed a concept for an SI-powered fire safety insight system that uses microgravity combustion data to understand flame behaviour, heat release, oxygen consumption and fire propagation under different conditions. By analysing these patterns, the project aims to identify potential fire hazards and support better fire detection, prevention and emergency response strategies. Unlike normal gravity, microgravity changes flame shape, airflow and combustion behaviour, making fire prediction more challenging, especially inside spacecraft. This project is important because it connects space research with real-world safety applications, helping engineers develop smarter fire protection systems, improve astronaut safety and contribute to safer buildings and enclosed environments on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

1. Project Overview and Working Principle

Flame in Freefall is a space-science-based fire safety concept that explores how combustion behaves in microgravity and how this knowledge can improve fire safety in spacecraft and on Earth. The project focuses on understanding flame shape, flame propagation, heat release, oxygen availability and combustion behaviour under reduced-gravity conditions.

The proposed system follows a data-driven approach. It uses observations and measurements from microgravity combustion experiments to identify changes in flame behaviour. These observations can be compared with normal-gravity combustion patterns to understand the influence of gravity on fire development. The analysed information can then be translated into useful fire safety insights for monitoring, prevention and emergency response.

2. Benefits of the Project

  • Improves understanding of fire behaviour in microgravity environments.
  • Supports research into fire prevention and detection in spacecraft.
  • Helps identify the importance of oxygen availability and ventilation in combustion.
  • Provides insights that can contribute to safer enclosed environments.
  • Connects space research with practical civil engineering and safety applications.

3. Intended Impact

The main objective is to contribute to safer space missions by improving our understanding of combustion in spacecraft cabins. Fire incidents in enclosed space environments can be extremely dangerous because evacuation and firefighting options are limited.

The knowledge gained through this concept may also benefit buildings, laboratories, industrial facilities and other enclosed environments on Earth. Our long-term vision is to support the development of smarter fire detection, monitoring and prevention strategies.

4. Tools and Technologies

Our project is designed around scientific data interpretation and a conceptual engineering workflow.

  • NASA microgravity combustion research: Scientific background and experimental observations.
  • Microsoft PowerPoint: Presentation and visual explanation of the project.
  • Data analysis approach: Comparing flame characteristics and identifying combustion patterns.
  • Engineering concepts: Fire behaviour, oxygen supply, heat transfer, ventilation and fire safety principles.

Note: This is a conceptual data-analysis project. No physical fire detection hardware or fully operational software prototype has been developed.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Flame in Freefall is its connection between space-based combustion research and real-world fire safety. Instead of considering fire behaviour only under normal gravitational conditions, our project focuses on the unusual flame patterns and combustion characteristics observed in microgravity.

It transforms complex scientific observations into understandable engineering insights that can support future fire safety solutions.

6. Factors Considered by Our Team

Our team considered:

  • Differences between normal gravity and microgravity.
  • Flame shape, size and propagation.
  • Oxygen availability and diffusion.
  • Heat transfer and combustion behaviour.
  • Ventilation and airflow in enclosed spaces.
  • Astronaut safety and emergency response limitations.
  • Practical applications of space research on Earth.
  • Scientific accuracy and the limitations of available experimental data.

7. Conclusion

Flame in Freefall demonstrates how understanding fire in space can contribute to safer environments both beyond Earth and on our planet. By connecting microgravity combustion observations with engineering-based fire safety insights, our project highlights the importance of scientific research, innovation and interdisciplinary thinking in solving real-world challenges.

projectDetails.name: Mission mars
projectDetails.summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

I developed an interactive educational game called Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. It allows players to experience the responsibilities of an astronaut managing a space outpost on Mars or the Moon. Players must balance four important resources: power, food, radiation shielding, and life support.

The game includes interactive controls, environmental conditions, equipment maintenance, mission alerts, and decision-making challenges across five mission days (sols). Every decision affects the outpost's performance and survival.

This project addresses the challenge by helping students understand the difficulties of living and working in space through an engaging simulation. It combines science, technology, and problem-solving to make space exploration easier to understand. The project is important because it encourages young learners to think like astronauts and explore the science behind future space missions.
projectDetails.details: How the Project Works The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive browser-based simulation that allows players to manage a space outpost on Mars or the Moon. Players control four important resources: solar power, food, radiation shielding, and life support. They must balance these resources and complete a five-sol mission. The game includes equipment maintenance, environmental monitoring, weather forecasts, mission alerts, radio communications, and decision-making events. Players can monitor their progress through a flight log and receive a mission debrief and completion certificate. Benefits and Intended Impact The project helps students understand the challenges of space exploration through interactive learning. It develops problem-solving, decision-making, and resource-management skills while creating interest in astronomy and space science. Technology Used The project was developed as a web-based game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It runs in a web browser and does not require special hardware. Creativity The project combines astronaut training concepts with interactive gameplay. Players experience different mission situations and learn how decisions affect the stability of a space outpost. The resource values are simplified for educational purposes and are not real mission-planning data.

projectDetails.details: Project Details – Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data FieldWise Kerala is a bilingual web-based prototype designed to help farmers explore suitable crop rotation ideas using NASA Earth observation data and local farm information. The website uses NASA POWER data to display temperature and rainfall information based on the farm's location. Farmers can enter details such as soil type, water availability, current crop, and farming priorities. Based on these inputs, the website provides illustrative crop rotation options to help farmers compare different possibilities. It aims to support better farming decisions, encourage sustainable agriculture, improve soil health, and promote efficient water use. We developed the prototype using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. NASA POWER API is used to retrieve weather information, and GitHub Pages is used to host the website publicly. The creative aspect of our project is the combination of NASA Earth observation data with local farming information in one simple platform. It also supports both English and Malayalam, making it easier for farmers in Kerala to understand and use. While developing this project, we considered Kerala's local farming conditions, soil types, water availability, weather variations, farmers' priorities, and ease of use. The project is an educational prototype, and the suggested crop rotations should be confirmed with local agricultural experts before practical use.

projectDetails.details:
ORBITAL HEALTH is a conceptual astronaut health monitoring system designed to help track and organize important health indicators during space missions.

Spaceflight can affect the human body through microgravity, isolation, and other environmental conditions. Monitoring astronaut wellness is therefore important for supporting crew safety and mission success.

Our proposed system provides a simple dashboard to display important health indicators such as heart rate, sleep duration, and blood oxygen saturation. It aims to organize health information in one place, highlight unusual readings based on configured thresholds, and support timely review by crew members and medical professionals.

projectDetails.name: Project Astra-X
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA-X (Adaptive Space Training & Resource Analysis System) is an interactive Mars habitat mission simulation designed to help learners understand the challenges of sustaining human life beyond Earth. It places participants in the role of junior mission operators responsible for managing five interconnected habitat resources under limited conditions.

Through a simulated Mars dust storm scenario, learners experience how reduced solar generation can decrease battery reserves, trigger conservation measures, affect greenhouse operations, and threaten long-term food sustainability. They monitor resource conditions, receive emergency alerts, investigate cascading effects, and choose responses that influence mission outcomes.

ASTRA-X introduces four core learning innovations: a Cascading Failure Engine, Counterfactual Mission Replay, Predictive Mission Intelligence, and Mission Resilience Assessment. Its signature feature allows learners to restore the same emergency state, test alternative decisions, and compare their consequences.

By combining systems thinking, resource management, scientific reasoning, and decision-making, ASTRA-X transforms space science education into an active mission-control experience and helps prepare the next generation to think like mission operators.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA-X (Adaptive Space Training & Resource Analysis System) is an interactive Mars habitat mission simulation that places learners in the role of junior mission operators responsible for protecting a crew and maintaining essential resources under challenging conditions.

The project demonstrates how five interconnected habitat resources can influence one another during a mission. Its flagship scenario, "The Silent Sun," simulates a Mars dust storm that reduces solar power generation, causes battery reserves to decline, and forces operators to make difficult decisions about energy conservation, greenhouse operations, and long-term mission sustainability.

ASTRA-X works through four core innovations. The Cascading Failure Engine models how an initial problem can trigger delayed effects across connected systems. Counterfactual Mission Replay allows learners to save an emergency state, test a decision, restore the same state, and compare an alternative response. Predictive Mission Intelligence estimates how long resources can last before reaching critical thresholds using transparent mathematical calculations. Mission Resilience Assessment evaluates crew safety, efficiency, recovery, and mission continuity.

The project's main benefit is turning passive space science learning into active decision-making. Learners understand resource dependencies, anticipate consequences, prioritise essential systems, and evaluate recovery strategies. The intended impact is to improve systems thinking, scientific understanding, critical thinking, and resource-management skills while encouraging interest in human space exploration.

ASTRA-X is creative because it combines cascading system failures with counterfactual replay, allowing learners to explore not only what happened but also what could have happened under a different decision. The team considered limited resources, crew safety, delayed consequences, realistic mission constraints, energy availability, and long-term sustainability. The simulation uses simplified, illustrative mathematical assumptions rather than claiming to reproduce actual spacecraft telemetry.

Players assemble their crew, begin the mission, explore lunar landing conditions, and make decisions as the mission progresses. The experience introduces learners to the challenges of lunar exploration, including terrain assessment, crew coordination, and managing a lunar outpost.

projectDetails.details:
LunaLupa: The Last Signal is a browser-based lunar survival simulation developed to make space exploration more interactive and accessible to young learners.

The game follows a four-member astronaut crew arriving at the Moon to establish an outpost. Players progress through six mission stages: terrain reconnaissance, lunar landing, life-support management, radiation storm response, food production, and investigation of a mysterious signal.

Each stage presents a mission situation in which players must consider possible risks and make decisions. The experience introduces concepts such as lunar terrain, astronaut safety, resource management, and the challenges of maintaining a lunar habitat.

NASA Moon Trek is used as a reference for lunar surface exploration. The game translates the idea of examining craters, slopes, and landing conditions into simplified gameplay choices. The risk levels and resource effects are illustrative game mechanics, not actual NASA measurements or a live NASA data feed.

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It is an independent educational prototype designed to encourage curiosity about space science, critical thinking, and interest in STEM.

LunaLupa is an educational simulation and is not an operational astronaut-training system or an official NASA product.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive web field guide for school-age and casual space fans. A Moon and Mars map shows six machines left behind since 1967: Surveyor 3, Lunokhod 1, the Apollo 17 Moon Buggy, Viking 1, Spirit and Opportunity. Tap one and it tells its own story in the first person, then explains how it was built, what science it made possible, and when it last called home. It answers the challenge by turning dense mission history into an engaging story, with real facts and a source on every card.
projectDetails.details: What it does Visitors pick a machine from a Moon or Mars map, or from a strip at the top of the page. Each machine tells its story in its own voice, followed by how it was built, what it made possible, and key numbers with its last signal. Every card links to its source. How it works The project is one self-contained web page built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The map is a schematic drawn in code, with pins placed by position. Selecting a machine updates the story card and the page address, so a single machine can be linked directly. The page works on phones and laptops, in light and dark themes, with large type and keyboard-friendly buttons. Benefits Learners meet real hardware and real science through a story instead of a list of facts. Teachers get six short, sourced missions across the Moon and Mars. The stories connect engineering to discovery. For example, a laser reflector on Lunokhod 1 returned light to Earth in 2010, about 40 years after the rover went quiet. What we hope to achieve We want students to feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers and to see that finished missions still teach us. Next we would add more machines, audio narration and a short classroom quiz. Tools used HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Google Fonts (Bricolage Grotesque, Atkinson Hyperlegible, JetBrains Mono). Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, for research help, story text and code. NASA mission pages and news reports for fact checking. A 7-slide deck for the demo.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: A 3D spaceship game where students fly to the Moon and Mars and visit 8 NASA hardware sites. Each stop has a NASA image and a voice-guided story. It answers the storytelling challenge for school-age space fans.This is important beacuse it is a easier and more applicable way for a children to understand the topics because it is a game.
projectDetails.details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is a browser-based 3D spaceship game that tells the stories of NASA machines left on the Moon and Mars. It is made for school-age space enthusiasts.

What it does and how it works
The player enters a spaceship cockpit and reads written instructions. A 10-second countdown with a voice assistant follows, and then the ship launches. The player flies freely in any direction using the keyboard. They steer first to the Moon and then to Mars, where eight glowing stations mark real NASA sites:

  • Moon: Apollo 11 (Tranquility Base), Surveyor 3, and Apollo 17.
  • Mars: Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder with Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Ingenuity helicopter.

When the ship reaches a station, the game shows an image from NASA’s Image and Video Library and a short written story. A voice assistant reads the story aloud. Each story covers what the machine did, what it discovered, and how its mission ended. After all eight stations, the game shows a “Game Ended” screen.

Benefits and intended impact
The game turns NASA’s history of exploration into something students can explore for themselves. These machines finished their missions, but their discoveries still matter. Examples are Opportunity’s years of work on Mars, Ingenuity’s first powered flight on another planet, and the Apollo 11 laser reflector that scientists still use today. We want students to see that “abandoned” hardware is part of a continuing story of science. The game is free, needs no install, and runs in a browser, so teachers and students can use it anywhere.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single static web page.
  • Three.js for the 3D scene, flight controls, planets and stations.
  • Web Speech API for the voice assistant.
  • Web Audio API for synthesized sound effects (engine hum, countdown beeps, arrival chimes). There is no music.
  • NASA Image and Video Library API (images-api.nasa.gov) for images.
  • GitHub for the code and Render for hosting.
  • No special hardware is needed, only a computer with a modern browser and sound.

Creativity
Instead of a slideshow or a timeline, the player drives to each story. The countdown, flight and arrival give a feeling of a real mission. Voice narration and written text work together so the content is accessible to different learners. The sound design uses only effects, so the narration stays clear.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: mission facts come from NASA mission records, and the images are NASA’s own and credited by title and ID.
  • Age-appropriate learning: short stories in plain language, with clear instructions.
  • Accessibility: every story is available in both text and voice, and the voice can be turned off.
  • Licensing: we used no NASA logos or branding. We credit NASA and state that the project is not endorsed by NASA.
  • Simplicity: planet sizes and distances are shortened so the trip is quick. The game says this on the start screen.
  • AI use: AI (Claude by Anthropic) helped write the code, story text and demo slides. No AI-generated images or video are used

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project nebula775
projectDetails.summary:
Our project proposes a data-driven approach to investigate changes in Kerala’s rainfall and land surface temperature using NASA Earth observation datasets. We identified NASA GPM IMERG precipitation data and MODIS land surface temperature data as the primary sources for studying long-term environmental patterns.

The proposed workflow involves collecting monthly satellite observations, organizing them into time series, visualizing changes over time, and applying statistical methods such as linear trend analysis and the Mann–Kendall test to identify significant trends.

This project addresses the challenge by demonstrating how satellite observations can help detect and understand changes in Earth system variables at a regional scale. It is important because Kerala depends heavily on monsoon rainfall and is vulnerable to environmental changes. Understanding these patterns can support better awareness, climate research, water-resource planning, and informed decision-making.

Our goal is to make Earth observation data easier to understand and show how it can help investigate environmental changes in our region.
projectDetails.details:
Our project explores how Kerala’s rainfall and land surface temperature may be changing over time using NASA Earth observation data. It proposes collecting monthly precipitation data from NASA GPM IMERG and land surface temperature data from MODIS. These observations can be organized into time-series graphs and analysed using statistical methods such as linear trend analysis and the Mann–Kendall test to identify long-term patterns and determine whether observed trends are statistically significant.

The project aims to make satellite data easier to understand and demonstrate how it can help investigate regional environmental changes. Its intended impact is to improve awareness of climate-related patterns and support future research, water-resource planning, and environmental decision-making in Kerala.

We developed a seven-slide PowerPoint presentation using ChatGPT for project framing, written content, and slide structure, along with Python code to generate the presentation. The project is currently a proposed analytical workflow; actual satellite-data analysis and statistical results are future development steps.

Its creative aspect is applying global NASA Earth observation resources to a specific regional question about Kerala. We considered data availability, observation periods, spatial resolution, seasonal monsoon variations, satellite-data limitations, and the importance of distinguishing natural seasonal changes from long-term trends.

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRO HEALTH

ASTRO HEALTH is an IoT-based Astronaut Health Monitoring System designed to monitor and support the health of astronauts during space missions. The system uses an ESP32 microcontroller to collect real-time health information through multiple sensors, including the MAX30102 for heart rate and SpO2, DS18B20 for temperature, MPU6050 for movement and activity monitoring, and AD8232 for ECG signal acquisition. The collected data is transmitted wirelessly to a Website and Android application using Bluetooth. The Website and application provide a user-friendly dashboard with live health measurements, interactive human body visualization, health history, charts, and alert notifications. It identifies abnormal readings and provides preventive health recommendations. Additional medical devices can be integrated to monitor blood pressure, blood glucose, and radiation exposure. ASTRO HEALTH aims to improve astronaut health awareness, support early identification of potential health problems, and enable better communication with flight surgeons. This project demonstrates the integration of embedded systems, Website, IoT, mobile applications, and healthcare technology for future space missions.

ASTRO HEALTH

Astronaut Health Monitoring System

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

ASTRO HEALTH is an IoT-based health monitoring system designed to monitor astronauts' health during space missions. It uses an ESP32 microcontroller connected to multiple sensors to collect health data in real time.

The system uses:

  • MAX30102: Measures heart rate and estimates blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂).
  • DS18B20: Measures skin/contact temperature.
  • MPU6050: Monitors body movement, orientation, and physical activity.
  • AD8232: Captures ECG signals for heart activity monitoring.

The ESP32 sends the collected data wirelessly to an Android application through Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. The application displays readings, graphs, health status, and alerts when measurements require attention.

2. What are the benefits?

  • Enables continuous health monitoring.
  • Helps identify unusual health readings at an early stage.
  • Reduces the need for constant manual monitoring.
  • Provides easy access to health records and trends.
  • Supports communication between astronauts and flight surgeons.
  • Can be expanded with additional medical sensors.

3. What is the intended impact?

The main aim is to improve astronaut health awareness and support safer space missions. The system can help astronauts monitor important health indicators and recognise potential health concerns early. It may also support future remote healthcare systems for people working in isolated or difficult environments.

5. How is the project creative?

ASTRO HEALTH combines embedded systems, IoT, healthcare technology, and mobile application development in one platform. Its creative features include:

  • A futuristic astronaut health dashboard.
  • Real-time sensor monitoring.
  • Interactive human-body health visualisation.
  • Automatic warning notifications.
  • Health history and graphical analysis.
  • Possibility of integrating additional medical devices.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered:

  1. Accuracy: Using suitable sensors and checking readings before presenting them.
  2. Reliability: Maintaining stable communication between ESP32 and the Android application.
  3. Safety: Avoiding unsupported medical diagnoses and treating alerts as indications for further assessment.
  4. Power efficiency: Designing the system for low-power operation.
  5. User-friendly design: Making the application simple for astronauts to understand and operate.
  6. Space environment: Considering microgravity, radiation, isolation, sleep disruption, and limited access to medical support.
  7. Expandability: Allowing additional sensors and medical devices to be integrated in the future.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: ECHOES: The Space Archaeology Experience
projectDetails.summary: ECHOES is an interactive space archaeology experience that encourages students to explore the universe through NASA imagery, educational challenges, interactive missions and gamified discovery.
projectDetails.details:
ECHOES is an educational web-based platform designed to make space exploration and the history of space missions more engaging, accessible and meaningful for students. The project is built around the idea of space archaeology: exploring the stories, discoveries, scientific achievements and historical records left behind by humanity's journey into space. Space exploration has produced an enormous amount of scientific knowledge, imagery and historical information. However, students may find it difficult to connect with this information when it is presented primarily through traditional articles, textbooks or static educational resources. ECHOES attempts to bridge this gap by transforming space-related information into an engaging digital learning experience. The platform brings together information and imagery related to planetary exploration, historical spacecraft and significant space missions. It uses NASA's publicly accessible Image and Video Library API to retrieve authentic space imagery, allowing users to explore visual material connected to different celestial destinations and space exploration activities. NASA Science resources and historical mission references also provide educational context for the experience. The learning process is designed around exploration, curiosity and active participation. Instead of simply presenting information for students to read, ECHOES encourages them to investigate discoveries, understand the significance of historical missions and engage with space-related challenges. It also incorporates game-based learning principles to encourage continued participation and reward progress. The platform maintains a record of users' progress, discoveries and achievements through browser-based storage. This allows students to revisit their learning journey and see their progress over time. Overall, ECHOES aims to connect authentic space exploration resources with an accessible and engaging educational environment, helping students develop a stronger understanding of humanity's exploration of the universe. ECHOES offers several educational benefits by combining space science, visual learning and interactive engagement. Encourages curiosity and scientific exploration: The platform introduces students to different celestial environments, historical missions and scientific discoveries. By encouraging independent exploration, it helps develop curiosity about the universe and the technologies used to investigate it. Makes space education more engaging: Authentic NASA imagery and visually organised educational content help make complex space-related subjects more approachable. Students can develop a better connection with the subject through visual exploration and active participation. Promotes critical thinking and problem-solving: Decision-based learning activities encourage students to analyse situations, consider possible solutions and understand the consequences of their choices. This supports the development of logical reasoning and problem-solving abilities. Improves learning motivation: Game-based learning principles, progress tracking and achievement recognition provide additional motivation for students to continue exploring educational content. Learning becomes a process of discovery rather than simply completing a reading assignment. Connects students with real space exploration: By incorporating publicly available NASA imagery and references to actual space missions, ECHOES helps students connect educational concepts with real scientific achievements and ongoing human interest in space exploration. Supports independent learning: Students can explore the available educational material at their own pace, revisit information and monitor their progress. This provides an opportunity for self-directed learning beyond conventional classroom activities. Encourages interest in STEM: Exposure to astronomy, planetary science, spacecraft missions and digital technologies can encourage students to develop an interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. The primary intended impact of ECHOES is to encourage students to become more curious, informed and actively involved in learning about space exploration. The project aims to make the history and science of space exploration more accessible to younger audiences by presenting educational information in a format that encourages investigation and participation. It seeks to move students beyond memorising scientific facts towards understanding discoveries, examining historical achievements and appreciating the challenges involved in exploring the universe. ECHOES also aims to demonstrate the educational value of publicly accessible scientific resources. NASA's extensive collection of space imagery and educational information provides an opportunity to connect students with authentic material from real-world scientific exploration. In the educational context, the project has the potential to support classroom learning, independent study and informal science education. It can serve as an additional resource for teachers who want to introduce space-related topics through a more engaging digital experience. In the broader context, ECHOES hopes to inspire students to develop an interest in astronomy, scientific research and technological innovation. By making space exploration feel more approachable, the project aims to encourage the next generation to question, investigate and discover. Ultimately, ECHOES is built on a simple belief: every discovery has a story, and every student should have the opportunity to explore it. The development of ECHOES involved modern web development tools and technologies to create an accessible, responsive and engaging educational application. Programming languages: JavaScript was used to implement the application's functionality and interactive behaviour. HTML5 was used to structure the web content, while CSS3 was used to develop the visual presentation, layouts, styling and responsive design. Development framework and build environment: React.js was used to develop the application through reusable components and manage its interface and application state. Vite provided the development environment and build process, allowing the application to be developed and tested efficiently. External data resources: NASA's Image and Video Library API (https://images-api.nasa.gov) was integrated to retrieve authentic space imagery. NASA Science (https://science.nasa.gov/) and the NASA Image and Video Library (https://images.nasa.gov/) were used as educational and informational resources. Development software: Visual Studio Code was used as the primary code editor. Git was used for version control, while GitHub was used to maintain the project's source code and repository. Data persistence: Browser Local Storage was used to preserve user progress, experience points, achievements and relevant activity records between visits on the same browser. Hardware: The application was developed and tested using a laptop running Windows 11. Deployment and hosting: Vercel was used to deploy the application and make it accessible through a public web link. GitHub was connected to the deployment workflow to support updates whenever changes were pushed to the repository. Through these tools and resources, ECHOES was developed as an accessible educational experience that brings together space exploration, authentic NASA resources and engaging digital learning. ECHOES: The Space Archaeology Experience seeks to make learning about the universe more engaging by connecting students with the discoveries, missions and historical records of space exploration. By combining authentic scientific resources with exploration-based learning, the project encourages curiosity, critical thinking and a deeper appreciation of science. Its ultimate goal is not simply to teach students about space, but to inspire them to explore the stories behind humanity's journey into the universe and become curious learners and future innovators.

Interactive Features World Explorer: Explore different destinations and collect discoveries. Cosmic Gallery: Browse space imagery through different categories. Discovery Lab: Test your space knowledge through an interactive mystery game. Mission Control: Experience decision-making scenarios inspired by historic space missions. Spacecraft Museum: Explore spacecraft and their missions. Explorer Journal: Track discoveries, achievements and progress. Gamification: Earn XP, unlock badges and progress through ranks.

projectDetails.name: LEFT BEHIND
projectDetails.summary:
LEFT BEHIND – An Atlas of Humanity in Space

Left Behind is an interactive digital storytelling platform that explores the human footprint across the Solar System through spacecraft, mission remnants, abandoned equipment, and lost communications. We developed a web-based experience featuring a Solar System Atlas, an interactive spacecraft exploration guide, mission histories, last transmissions, spacecraft status information, visual galleries, 3D visualizations, and a historical timeline.

The project addresses the challenge “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” by transforming space mission data and historical records into engaging, accessible stories. It highlights the objects and spacecraft that remain on the Moon, Mars, and beyond, revealing their original purposes, journeys, achievements, and final states.

Our goal is to make space exploration more meaningful by connecting scientific information with human stories. By preserving the legacy of these missions, Left Behind reminds us that even when a mission ends, its contribution to humanity's exploration of the universe should never be forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
LEFT BEHIND – An Atlas of Humanity in Space

Left Behind is an interactive digital storytelling platform designed to document and explore the objects, spacecraft, mission remnants, and lost communications that represent humanity's presence across the Solar System. It transforms space exploration history into an engaging, educational, and visually immersive experience.

What does it do and how does it work?

The platform allows users to explore humanity's space exploration legacy through several interactive features:

Solar System Atlas: Provides a visual overview of celestial bodies and the spacecraft associated with their exploration.

Explore the Darkness: Presents spacecraft profiles and mission histories, explaining their purpose, journey, achievements, and final status.

Last Transmission: Explores the final communications and lost signals of spacecraft, bringing attention to missions that have gone silent.

Spacecraft Behaviour: Categorizes spacecraft based on their operational status, including active, inactive, retired, and crashed missions.

Image Album: Showcases visual records and historical photographs of spacecraft and mission remnants.

3D Visualizations: Offers a more immersive way to understand spacecraft and their structures.

Historical Time Machine: Allows users to explore important milestones in space exploration through time.

Benefits and intended impact

Left Behind makes space exploration history accessible to students, educators, space enthusiasts, and the general public. It encourages curiosity about planetary exploration, spacecraft engineering, scientific discoveries, and the challenges of operating in extreme environments.

Its intended impact is to preserve awareness of humanity's achievements in space, promote STEM education, and encourage a deeper appreciation of the scientific and historical value of space mission remnants.

Tools and technologies used

The project was developed as a web-based application using web development technologies, including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, along with interactive visualization techniques and web-based 3D components. We also incorporated space mission information, historical records, and publicly available space exploration resources to develop the content.

Creativity and innovation

The creative aspect of Left Behind is its storytelling approach. Instead of presenting spacecraft as technical objects or displaying mission data as ordinary information, the platform encourages users to view them as silent witnesses to humanity's exploration of other worlds.

Each spacecraft has a story: why it was launched, what it accomplished, what happened at the end of its mission, and what remains of it today. The combination of interactive exploration, historical timelines, visual storytelling, and mission information creates a unique experience.

Factors considered during development

Our team considered scientific accuracy, historical reliability, user accessibility, visual clarity, educational value, and the distinction between abandoned equipment, intentionally discarded mission hardware, retired spacecraft, and spacecraft that have lost communication.

Ultimately, Left Behind aims to remind the world that the end of a space mission does not mean the end of its story. Every object left beyond Earth represents a chapter in humanity's journey into the universe.
