projectDetails.name: Project MAASD
projectDetails.summary:
**Ksheti – Hyper-Local Climate Intelligence & Precision Agriculture Decision Support**

Ksheti is an AI-powered precision agriculture platform that combines multispectral satellite imagery, IoT sensor data, weather intelligence, laboratory soil tests, and cultivation history to deliver field-level agricultural insights.

The platform analyzes satellite vegetation indices such as NDVI, EVI, SAVI, NDWI, and NDRE to monitor crop health, detect changes, and identify potential environmental risks. It provides crop yield forecasts, pest and disease risk assessments, drought and flood predictions, and personalized irrigation and fertilizer recommendations.

Ksheti uses machine learning, geospatial visualization, and agricultural science to make recommendations more reliable and explainable. Each prediction includes a confidence score, supporting environmental indicators, historical comparisons, satellite evidence, and explanations of the factors influencing the result.

The platform also supports offline operation, multilingual advisory in English, Hindi, and Malayalam, SMS-based recommendations, and a digital farm twin for exploring alternative farming decisions.

Ksheti aims to improve crop productivity, conserve water and resources, reduce agricultural risks, and support sustainable farming through accessible, data-driven decision-making.

Future possibilities include expanded satellite integration, automated smart irrigation, and advanced digital farm simulations.
projectDetails.details:
Ksheti – Hyper-Local Climate Intelligence & Precision Agriculture Decision Support

Ksheti is an AI-powered precision agriculture platform designed to help farmers make informed decisions using localized environmental and agricultural data. General weather forecasts often fail to capture the conditions of individual farms. Ksheti addresses this problem by combining multispectral satellite imagery, IoT field telemetry, weather intelligence, laboratory soil tests, and cultivation history to provide field-level insights and recommendations.

How Does It Work?

Ksheti collects and analyzes data from multiple sources, including Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, weather information, soil test results, IoT sensors, and historical cultivation records. It uses satellite vegetation indices such as NDVI, EVI, SAVI, NDWI, and NDRE to monitor crop health, identify changes, and assess vegetation conditions.

Machine learning models support crop yield forecasting, pest and disease risk assessment, and drought and flood risk prediction. The platform also provides irrigation and fertilizer recommendations using agricultural models and soil nutrient information.

Each prediction includes a confidence score, supporting environmental indicators, historical comparisons, satellite evidence, and an explanation of the factors influencing the result. This makes the recommendations more transparent and understandable.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Helps farmers monitor crop health and identify potential risks earlier.
  • Provides localized agricultural and climate insights.
  • Supports efficient irrigation and fertilizer management.
  • Helps reduce unnecessary water and fertilizer consumption.
  • Assists farmers in making informed cultivation decisions.
  • Supports sustainable agriculture and improved resource management.

Our intended impact is to make precision agriculture more accessible, improve agricultural productivity, reduce climate-related farming risks, and support informed decision-making among farmers, agronomists, and policymakers.

Tools and Technologies Used

Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.

Backend: FastAPI and Python's built-in HTTP server.

Frontend: React and JavaScript.

Machine Learning: Scikit-learn, XGBoost, and Joblib.

Satellite and Weather Data: Sentinel-2 imagery and Open-Meteo weather integration.

Geospatial Visualization: Leaflet.

Database: PostgreSQL with PostGIS.

Hardware: ESP32-based IoT sensors for field data collection.

Agricultural Methods: FAO-56-based water requirement estimation and soil-test-based fertilizer recommendations.

What Makes Ksheti Creative and Innovative?

Ksheti combines multiple agricultural data sources into a unified, hyper-local decision-support system. Instead of providing only general predictions, it focuses on individual farm conditions.

One of its key innovations is explainable AI. Every prediction provides its confidence score and the environmental factors influencing the result. It also distinguishes between machine-learning predictions and physics-based recommendations, helping users understand where the advice comes from.

The platform supports offline operation, low-bandwidth usage, and multilingual advisory in English, Hindi, and Malayalam. Its digital farm twin also allows users to explore alternative farming decisions through what-if scenarios.

Factors Considered by Our Team

During development, we considered the practical challenges faced by farmers, including changing weather conditions, soil variability, limited internet connectivity, language barriers, and the need for understandable recommendations.

We also considered prediction reliability, data integration, affordability, scalability, resource conservation, and transparency. Since demonstration training data is generated using an agronomic process model rather than observed field records, we distinguish prototype model performance from real-world agricultural accuracy.

Future Scope

Future improvements include expanded real-world agricultural datasets, drone-based crop monitoring, automated smart irrigation, improved satellite data integration, and advanced digital farm simulations.

Ksheti aims to bridge the gap between climate intelligence and practical farming decisions, helping build a more sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural future.

challengeDetails.title: Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data

projectDetails.name: OUTPOST ZERO
projectDetails.summary:
OUTPOST ZERO is an interactive, educational mission trainer that simulates the challenges of establishing and sustaining a human outpost beyond Earth. It transforms complex space exploration concepts into an engaging mission-control experience where users can monitor outpost systems, manage critical resources, respond to simulated emergencies, and make decisions as a Junior Astronaut or Flight Director.

The project combines NASA space science resources with interactive simulations, mission telemetry, and scenario-based learning. Users explore how factors such as power availability, environmental conditions, crew needs, and resource constraints influence mission decisions. The experience is designed to make space exploration more accessible to students and space enthusiasts while encouraging systems thinking, scientific curiosity, and decision-making.

OUTPOST ZERO is an educational simulation, not an operational spacecraft system. Its goal is to help users understand the complexity of future lunar and planetary exploration through an immersive, hands-on digital experience.
projectDetails.details:
OUTPOST ZERO: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive space exploration and outpost management simulation designed to make the challenges of human space exploration understandable and engaging.

The project provides a mission-control-style interface where users can experience two roles: Cadet and Flight Director. Users interact with mission scenarios, monitor simulated outpost telemetry, manage resources, explore crew and habitat systems, and respond to mission events. The simulation emphasizes the interconnected nature of mission systems: decisions involving power, resources, environmental conditions, and crew operations can affect mission stability and outcomes.

The platform also integrates NASA’s space science resources, including NASA’s DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) where applicable, to introduce users to real space-related data. Scientific information and simulation assumptions are intended to be distinguished so that users can understand what is based on published sources and what is modeled for educational gameplay.

The project is designed for students, educators, and space enthusiasts. Its intended impact is to promote STEM learning, space science awareness, systems thinking, and decision-making through an immersive digital experience rather than passive reading.

Technology Stack:
• Next.js 14 and React for the web application
• TypeScript for application logic
• Tailwind CSS for responsive styling
• Framer Motion for animations and interactive experiences
• Recharts and SVG for telemetry visualization
• NASA DONKI API for relevant space-weather information
• LocalStorage for saving user progress

Creative Approach:
OUTPOST ZERO combines a mission-control interface, resource management, interactive scenarios, and educational space science into a browser-based mission trainer. The experience is designed to make complex exploration challenges approachable while keeping the user actively involved in mission decisions.

The application is an educational simulation. It is not an official NASA product, NASA-endorsed system, or real spacecraft operations tool. Simulated values and scenarios are not intended for actual mission planning or safety decisions.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: After the mission : The stories of machines that stayed behind
projectDetails.summary:
This is an educational digital magazine that explores the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers, and other machines that remain in space after their missions are completed.

The project highlights important space exploration missions, including Apollo, Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, Ingenuity, Dawn, and Kepler. It explains why these machines were left behind, what they discovered, how their missions ended, and what scientific and historical value they continue to hold.

Through informative articles, timelines, illustrations, mission comparisons, and a knowledge quiz, the magazine makes space exploration easier and more interesting to understand.

The main aim is to show that the end of a space mission does not mean the end of its contribution. Even when machines stop operating, the knowledge, discoveries, and evidence they leave behind continue to support future exploration and scientific research.
projectDetails.details:
Project Title: After the Mission: The Stories of Machines That Stayed Behind

Our project is an educational digital magazine that explores the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers, and other machines that remain in space or on other worlds after their missions end.

The magazine explains why these machines were sent into space, what they achieved, why their missions ended, and what happened to them afterward. It features missions such as Apollo, Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, Ingenuity, Dawn, and Kepler.

The project is presented as an interactive digital flipbook, making space exploration information easy and interesting to read. It includes mission stories, comparisons, timelines, illustrations, and educational content to help readers understand the history and lasting impact of space exploration.

The main benefit of this project is to make space science more accessible and engaging, especially for students and young learners. It encourages curiosity about astronomy, engineering, robotics, and future space missions.

Our goal is to remind people that a space mission's story does not end when communication stops or the mission is over. The machines left behind remain part of humanity's journey into space.

The project is published online using Heyzine as a digital flipbook.

projectDetails.name: Project silent cosmos
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling About NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars,” explores the stories behind spacecraft, scientific instruments and other hardware left behind by NASA during space exploration.

We developed an educational presentation highlighting three major examples: Apollo mission equipment left on the Moon, Mars landers and discarded landing components, and the Pioneer 10 spacecraft travelling through deep space. The project explains why this equipment was left behind, its original purpose, the scientific discoveries it enabled and its present status.

Our project addresses the challenge by transforming the history of discarded space hardware into an engaging and informative story for school-age space enthusiasts. It demonstrates that these objects are not simply waste but valuable reminders of scientific achievement, engineering innovation and human curiosity.

This project is important because it helps people understand the legacy of space exploration and appreciate how even equipment left behind can continue to contribute to science and inspire future generations.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project explores NASA's discarded and abandoned space equipment on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. It tells the stories of spacecraft, landers, rovers and scientific instruments that were left behind after completing their missions or becoming inactive. Through an educational presentation, we explain their original purposes, how they worked, why they were abandoned and what scientific contributions they made. We highlight examples such as Apollo lunar equipment, Mars landing systems and the Pioneer 10 spacecraft.

What are its benefits?

The project makes space science easier and more interesting to understand, especially for school-age students. It introduces audiences to real NASA missions, space technology, engineering challenges and scientific discoveries. It also helps people understand that abandoned equipment can have historical, scientific and educational value.

What is the intended impact?

Our aim is to inspire curiosity about space exploration and encourage the next generation to learn more about science, technology and engineering. We also want to raise awareness about preserving historic space exploration sites and recognising the importance of past missions in shaping future discoveries.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used?

We developed the project using presentation and research tools. We used PowerPoint-compatible presentation software to create the slides, along with information and reference materials from NASA and other scientific sources. No physical hardware or specialised coding languages were required because this is an educational storytelling project rather than a hardware prototype or software application.

How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting space exploration only through successful missions and discoveries, we focus on the lesser-known stories of equipment left behind. We connect different missions across the Moon, Mars and deep space to show how each object represents a part of humanity's journey into the universe. This storytelling approach makes forgotten technology interesting and meaningful to younger audiences.

What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered scientific accuracy, educational value, audience engagement, historical importance and clarity of presentation. We selected examples that demonstrate different types of space equipment and missions. We also considered why the equipment was left behind, whether it is still functioning, its contribution to science and how its story could inspire future space explorers.

projectDetails.name: Silent Sentinels: NASA's Off-World Monuments
projectDetails.summary: Silent Sentinels: NASA’s Off-World Monuments is an interactive, story-driven web application designed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge to inspire school-age space enthusiasts. Moving beyond dense technical archives, the platform transforms historic spacecraft left on the Moon, Mars, and deep space into relatable first-person narrators. Users explore clickable orbital radar maps featuring nine iconic artifacts from Apollo’s Lunar Roving Vehicle to Mars’s Opportunity and Ingenuity. Each monument pairs audio-narrated "Voices from the Dust" with an Engineering-to-Science Decoder, interactive field-check quizzes that unlock Junior Space Historian badges, and an Endurance Timeline showing how NASA’s hardware outlasted its warranties to reshape planetary science.
projectDetails.details:
Silent Sentinels: NASA’s Off-World Monuments is an interactive, story-driven web application created for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge to bridge the gap between dense archival mission logs and young, curious minds.

What It Does & How It Works

The platform turns the Moon, Mars, and deep space into an explorable digital museum. Users switch between three celestial regions on an interactive Orbital Radar Map dotted with glowing "Ghost Hardware" beacons. Selecting any of the nine featured monuments—such as Apollo 11’s Eagle & Retroreflector, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10, or NEAR Shoemaker—opens a three-part interactive story experience:

  • Voices from the Dust (First-Person Narratives & Audio): Each spacecraft tells its own story in an accessible, emotional first-person voice, accompanied by built-in browser text-to-speech narration so younger learners can listen along.
  • Engineering-to-Science Decoder: Connects what the hardware was physically built to do with the groundbreaking planetary discoveries it achieved.
  • Field Check Quizzes & Badge Progression: Short interactive challenges test comprehension and award collectible Junior Space Historian badges, alongside an Endurance Legacy Timeline comparing planned mission lifespans against actual survival times.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Traditional space archives are often overwhelming for school-age learners, focusing heavily on active missions while leaving historic hardware buried in technical PDFs. Silent Sentinels humanizes robotic explorers, helping students build an emotional connection with space history while clearly understanding why engineering choices matter for scientific discovery. By making historical mission data tactile, auditory, and game-like, the project aims to spark long-term curiosity in STEM, planetary science, and aerospace engineering among school-age students and casual space fans.

Tools, Languages & Technology Used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • APIs & Web Standards: Browser Web Speech API (window.speechSynthesis) for zero-dependency voice narration, SVG graphics for custom orbital radar maps and spacecraft schematics, and CSS Grid/Flexbox with custom keyframe animations for responsive telemetry styling.
  • Data Sources: Historical mission specifications, landing coordinates, and scientific outcomes sourced from NASA’s NSSDC (National Space Science Data Center), Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, and JPL Mars Exploration archives.

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

Instead of presenting a static encyclopedia or timeline, the project gives silent machines a voice—framing retired rovers and landers as enduring monuments still standing watch across the solar system. In designing the experience, we prioritized age appropriateness (clear, vivid storytelling tailored for ages 8–15 without sacrificing scientific accuracy), accessibility (high-contrast mission-control visuals, audio narration for developing readers, and filterable views by mission status and era), and zero-friction deployment (built as a lightweight, single-file web app that runs smoothly on any classroom computer, tablet, or smartphone without installations or external servers).

projectDetails.name: SkyPages: Abandoned but not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: SkyPages is an interactive, child-friendly storybook website about NASA equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Children turn the pages of a flipbook to meet the Apollo lander bases and Lunar Rovers, and the Mars robots Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity and InSight. Each page combines a real NASA photograph, a short story, animation, background music, read-aloud narration and quizzes. SkyPages answers the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" by turning forgotten machines into characters that school-age learners can meet. It matters because stories make space science memorable and accessible, and they inspire the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
SkyPages is a free, interactive storybook website that introduces school-age learners to NASA equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

What it does: Children turn the pages of a 16-page flipbook. On the Moon they see the Apollo lander bases, footprints, the Lunar Rover and a rover parked for good. On Mars they meet Sojourner, the twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity, the Ingenuity helicopter (shown with Perseverance) and the InSight lander. Every page pairs a real NASA photograph with a short, simple story and a fun fact. Two quizzes and a storyteller activity invite children to draw, write or act out a robot's story.

How it works: SkyPages is a single web page that runs in any phone or computer browser, with no login or install. Pages turn by tapping the left or right side, swiping or dragging, using the arrow buttons or the keyboard. Sound effects and background music are generated in the browser, and a read-aloud button uses the browser's built-in speech so early readers can listen to each page.

Benefits and impact: It makes space history friendly and memorable, supports listening as well as reading, and works on low-cost phones. We hope teachers and families use it, and we plan to add more missions, languages and classroom activities.

Creativity and design choices: We chose a storybook format, page-flip animation, a calm space soundtrack and large, simple text because young learners respond to stories, motion and sound. Facts were checked against NASA mission pages, and every NASA photo is credited on its page.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Audio API, Web Speech API, Google Fonts (Fredoka and Nunito), Python and ffmpeg for the demo video.

AI use: This project was built with AI assistance. Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, helped write the code, simplify the text, and create the illustrations (drawn in code), the music and sound effects (generated in code) and the demo video. The narration voice was generated with an AI text-to-speech tool: GOOGLE AI STUDIO. The SkyPages logo was generated with an AI tool: CHATGPT. The project idea and the choice of challenge were made by our team. AI-assisted content is labeled "AI-assisted • made with Claude" in the video and images, "AI-assisted" in the website footer, and in the file metadata. The NASA photographs are real NASA images and are not AI-generated.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an educational storytelling project that explores the human-made equipment remaining on the Moon and Mars after NASA missions. It focuses on the Apollo Lunar Module descent stages, Lunar Roving Vehicles and scientific instruments on the Moon, as well as the landing equipment from the Perseverance mission on Mars, including its heat shield, parachute, backshell and descent stage. The project describes why certain mission components are not brought back to Earth and compares the equipment found on both planetary surfaces. To make the subject more engaging, it includes imaginative stories narrated from the perspectives of a lunar rover, a heat shield and a descent stage. These objects are valuable records of scientific progress, technological development and space exploration. The project also discusses the need to preserve these historical remains through location documentation, satellite-based observation and responsible protection of landing sites.
projectDetails.details: The main aim of this project is to introduce space heritage in a simple and engaging way through storytelling. The presentation is organised into seven slides and examines why spacecraft leave certain components behind after completing their missions. Factors such as restricted storage capacity, equipment weight, landing-specific components and scientific devices intended to remain on the surface are explained. The project describes the important objects found on the Moon, including Apollo Lunar Module descent stages, Lunar Roving Vehicles and scientific research instruments. It also examines the remains of the Mars 2020 Perseverance landing system, such as the heat shield, parachute, backshell and descent stage. The sequence of events involved in the rover's landing on Mars is also presented. A comparison between the Moon and Mars highlights the different types of exploration and equipment associated with each world. In addition, three fictional first-person narratives describe the experiences of a Lunar Rover, a heat shield and a descent stage. These narratives are creative interpretations and should not be considered actual recorded statements. The concluding section explains the historical and technological value of these objects and recommends methods for safeguarding space heritage, including documenting artifact positions, examining landing areas through satellite imagery and avoiding unnecessary contact with historic remains. PowerPoint slides with simple diagrams and shapes are used to communicate the information. AI assistance was used in developing the presentation content and design. The project aims to encourage students and the wider public to understand the achievements of space missions and recognise the importance of protecting their historical remains.

projectDetails.name: THE LAST NIGHT OF EAGLE
projectDetails.summary: The Last Light of Eagle is an educational storytelling project that explores the Apollo 11 Lunar Module and the scientific equipment left on the Moon in July 1969. It highlights the design and functions of Eagle's descent and ascent stages, along with the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP). The project explains how instruments such as the passive seismometer, lunar dust detector and laser ranging retroreflector contributed to lunar research. It also describes their operating principles, mission duration and eventual shutdown. Through this story, the project demonstrates how space technology continues to contribute to scientific knowledge even after its mission ends.
projectDetails.details: The Last Light of Eagle is an educational storytelling project that presents the history, engineering and scientific contributions of NASA's Apollo 11 Lunar Module, Eagle, and the scientific equipment left on the Moon. It works by combining historical information, scientific explanations, timelines and visual illustrations to explain how Eagle landed on the lunar surface, how its two stages functioned, and how the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP) collected scientific data and communicated with Earth. The project benefits students and space enthusiasts by making complex space technology and lunar exploration easier to understand. Its intended impact is to create awareness about the importance of space research, engineering innovation and scientific exploration. The project was developed using HTML and CSS to create an interactive, visually engaging storytelling webpage, along with PowerPoint for the project demonstration. Its creativity lies in presenting the story from the perspective of abandoned space hardware, highlighting not only the astronauts' achievements but also the scientific legacy of the equipment they left behind. The team considered historical accuracy, scientific relevance, simplicity of explanation, visual presentation, audience engagement and the educational value of the content while developing the project.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project STELLAR FORGE
projectDetails.summary: STELLAR FORGE is a playable browser game that combines spacecraft mission design with arcade-style spaceflight. Before each mission, players choose a scientific objective and configure the spacecraft bus, launch vehicle, instruments, propulsion, communications, and flight path. The game checks mission cost, mass, power, downlink capacity, and whether the spacecraft can reach its target. Those engineering choices shape the flight: players steer through hazards, collect science packets, use limited shield charges, and reach an orbital return window. Three progressively challenging missions take players to Mars, the Moon, and Europa. Designed for phones and PCs, STELLAR FORGE makes competing engineering demands visible and interactive, helping students see how design decisions affect mission risk and the science returned to Earth.
projectDetails.details:
STELLAR FORGE is a browser-based space mission design and flight game for phones and PCs. Players plan missions by choosing spacecraft components, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, propulsion, communications, and flight paths. Before launch, they balance limited budgets, spacecraft mass, power, and mission requirements. Then they pilot their spacecraft through animated levels, avoid hazards, collect science data, and try to complete mission objectives.

The game makes space engineering more engaging by letting players see how design choices affect what a mission can accomplish. Its intended impact is to help students explore engineering trade-offs, problem-solving, and space science through experimentation and play.

The project was developed as a web game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Its creative approach combines a mission-planning simulator with arcade-style spacecraft flight, connecting decisions made before launch to challenges during the mission. The design considers accessibility across phone and PC controls, clear objectives, limited resources, and a progression through missions inspired by Mars, the Moon, and Europa.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables. projectDetails.name: Agricultural Resilience & Vegetation Intelligence System (A.R.V.I.S)
projectDetails.summary:
A.R.V.I.S. is an online decision-support tool designed for agriculture.

This tool helps you identify the best crop rotations for your farm and offers insights into your environmental data.

A.R.V.I.S. efficiently manages all your farming activities by providing a single source of information about your crops, soil data, weather resources, and environmental factors.

Inspired by Earth observation technology, this tool makes accessing agricultural information easy.

It supports you in making informed and sustainable farming decisions.
projectDetails.details: A.R.V.I.S.—the Agricultural Resilience & Vegetation Intelligence System—is a cutting-edge web-based platform developed by Team Tech Wizards that revolutionizes how farmers make informed decisions. By leveraging advanced data from NASA, A.R.V.I.S. combines satellite observations, environmental information, crop specifics, and farmer-provided soil data into a powerful decision-support tool. This platform incorporates NASA POWER Earth data and satellite imagery from NASA GIBS, enabling farmers to analyze crucial environmental factors such as vegetation patterns, rainfall, and temperature fluctuations. With features designed for optimal crop rotation recommendations, personalized planning, comprehensive soil and crop assessments, scenario comparisons, and timely weather information, A.R.V.I.S. takes agricultural management to the next level . Farmers can confidently explore their farm locations, compare various crop sequences, and assess environmental conditions with ease. The innovative scenario explorer feature empowers users to evaluate crop planning options under a range of conditions, ensuring that every decision is made with precision and foresight. The primary goal of A.R.V.I.S. is to eliminate barriers to agricultural information access, making it straightforward for farmers to utilize essential data. By seamlessly connecting satellite technology with practical agricultural strategies, A.R.V.I.S. promotes resilience in farming, encourages strategic crop rotation, and emphasizes the importance of understanding environmental factors in planning. It is a definitive support tool that complements and enhances local agricultural expertise. Developed as a web application using HTML, A.R.V.I.S. smartly utilizes NASA’s data services to present information engagingly and interactively. The platform features dynamic dashboards, detailed maps, and intuitive data visualizations, presenting recommendations straightforwardly and effectively. What truly distinguishes A.R.V.I.S. is its innovative amalgamation of space-based data and practical farming insights. Rather than simply displaying raw satellite imagery, it synthesizes critical environmental information, crop details, soil characteristics, and scenario analyses into a cohesive platform—directly linking advanced technology to concrete farming decisions. Throughout its development, our team meticulously focused on data availability and specific environmental conditions. We analyzed factors such as vegetation patterns, rainfall, temperature, soil traits, and crop needs, ensuring the platform is not only user-friendly but also delivers clear recommendations while acknowledging the limitations of environmental data. Our mission is clear: to create a pragmatic and accessible resource that unites NASA’s Earth observations with the real-world challenges farmers face every day.

projectDetails.name: Project PLANETARY TIME MACHINE
projectDetails.summary:
**PLANETARY TIME MACHINE- is an AI-assisted platform designed to discover when and where Earth's environments most closely resemble selected regions of the Moon and Mars. Instead of simply identifying places that look similar to planetary landscapes, the project compares measurable environmental characteristics such as geology, elevation, surface roughness, temperature, moisture, dust and ice conditions.

The platform brings together Earth observation data from NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA with planetary mission data from NASA's Planetary Data System, including Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter observations. Its temporal analysis feature explores seasonal and historical changes to identify periods when terrestrial conditions provide stronger planetary analogues. An explainable similarity engine ranks candidate locations and displays data coverage, confidence and scientific evidence.

By helping researchers identify suitable Earth-based environments and time windows for planetary mission simulations, equipment testing and astronaut training, PLANETARY TIME MACHINE aims to make planetary exploration research more accessible, efficient and evidence-driven.
projectDetails.details:
PLANETARY TIME MACHINE

PLANETARY TIME MACHINE is an AI-assisted platform designed to explore when and where Earth's environments most closely resemble selected regions of the Moon and Mars. It focuses on comparing important environmental characteristics such as geology, elevation, surface roughness, temperature, moisture, dust and ice conditions to identify potential terrestrial analogue locations.

The platform is designed to let users select a planetary target, explore possible matching locations on Earth and examine environmental similarities through an interactive interface. Its time-based approach considers seasonal and historical variations to explore how environmental conditions change and when certain locations may offer stronger planetary analogues.

The project could benefit planetary scientists, researchers, students and space mission planners by helping identify suitable Earth-based environments for mission simulations, equipment testing and astronaut training. Its intended impact is to make planetary analogue discovery more accessible, efficient and data-driven.

The website was developed using Google AI Studio and AI-assisted development tools. Our team used these tools to translate our scientific concept into an interactive web-based platform. The project is designed around the use of Earth observation and planetary datasets from space agencies such as NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA.

The creative aspect of PLANETARY TIME MACHINE is its focus on both where and when Earth resembles another planetary environment. Rather than depending only on visual similarities, the concept emphasizes measurable environmental characteristics and their changes over time. During development, we considered scientific reliability, data availability, seasonal variations, usability and the limitations of terrestrial analogues. Since Earth cannot fully reproduce conditions such as lunar vacuum, reduced gravity or the thin Martian atmosphere, the platform focuses on identifying useful environmental similarities rather than claiming exact planetary equivalence.

projectDetails.name: Project The Last Light
projectDetails.summary:
The Last Light

Challenge: Abandoned but Not Forgotten

The Last Light is a digital storybook that explores the journeys and legacies of NASA's spacecraft, instruments, and scientific equipment left across the Solar System.

Through engaging storytelling, the project introduces young space enthusiasts to remarkable missions such as the Apollo lunar experiments, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, InSight, and Voyager 1 and 2.

Each piece of equipment has a story to tell: discoveries made, mysteries explored, and knowledge sent back to Earth. Although some missions have ended, their scientific contributions continue to shape our understanding of space.

Designed to make space exploration accessible and inspiring to school-age readers, The Last Light celebrates the idea that a mission may end, but its legacy lives on.

A mission can end. Curiosity does not.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: The Last Light

The Last Light is an educational digital storybook created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the challenge Abandoned but Not Forgotten. It explores the stories of NASA's space hardware that remains on the Moon, Mars, and throughout the Solar System, even after its original mission has ended.

What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project uses visual storytelling to introduce school-age space enthusiasts to the history and scientific contributions of space equipment left behind during space exploration.

Through a series of illustrated slides, we explore:

  • Apollo Lunar Experiments: Scientific instruments and reflectors left on the Moon that helped scientists study its environment.
  • Sojourner: NASA's first successful Mars rover, which demonstrated the potential of robotic exploration.
  • Spirit and Opportunity: Twin Mars rovers that investigated the planet's geology and discovered evidence of past water activity.
  • InSight: A lander that studied the internal structure and seismic activity of Mars.
  • Voyager 1 and 2: Spacecraft that continue to carry the legacy of human exploration far beyond the planets.

Each section tells the story of the equipment, its purpose, its discoveries, and the scientific legacy it leaves behind.

What benefits does it have?

The project makes space science easier and more engaging for young learners. It transforms complex mission information into accessible stories and visual explanations. It also encourages curiosity about robotics, engineering, astronomy, planetary science, and the technology behind space exploration.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to help the next generation understand that space exploration does not become meaningless when a spacecraft stops functioning or a mission officially ends. The knowledge, discoveries, and inspiration created by these missions continue to contribute to science.

We hope our storybook encourages students to explore space science, appreciate the engineering behind NASA missions, and imagine the possibilities of future exploration.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We developed the project as a digital presentation and illustrated storybook using:

  • Google Slides: Presentation design and storybook development.
  • Digital illustrations and visual design: To make the missions and their hardware easier to understand.
  • ChatGPT: Used as an AI-assisted tool for brainstorming, organizing the narrative, simplifying scientific explanations, and supporting content development.
  • NASA educational resources and mission information: Used for research and factual reference.

The project does not require a physical hardware prototype or custom-coded software. It is a digital educational storytelling project.

How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting space hardware as abandoned machinery or simply listing mission facts, The Last Light treats each piece of equipment as a storyteller with a history, purpose, and legacy.

We connect different missions across the Moon, Mars, and deep space to create one continuous story about human curiosity and exploration. The visual format and narrative approach help readers connect emotionally and intellectually with the science behind these missions.

What factors did our team consider?

While developing the project, we considered:

  • Scientific accuracy: Keeping mission information and explanations consistent with NASA resources.
  • Accessibility: Making the content understandable for school-age readers and beginners.
  • Visual storytelling: Using illustrations and a clear narrative to maintain interest.
  • Educational value: Explaining not only what the equipment was, but also what scientists learned from it.
  • Mission diversity: Including examples from the Moon, Mars, and deep space.
  • Clarity and simplicity: Presenting information in a concise format without overwhelming readers with technical details.

Our central message is:

A mission can end. Curiosity does not.

Through The Last Light, we want to remind people that even when machines fall silent, their discoveries continue to illuminate our understanding of the universe.

projectDetails.name: Left Behind, Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Left Behind, Not Forgotten is a presentation that tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars through the objects themselves. From the Apollo lunar rovers and descent stages to the Mars rovers and the Ingenuity helicopter, each piece of hardware “speaks” about its mission, what it achieved, and why it was left behind. The presentation includes a timeline of abandoned equipment, a comparison of what remains on the Moon versus Mars, and an explanation of why NASA leaves hardware behind, such as weight limits, fuel constraints, and mission completion. It also looks at what happens to this equipment over time in extreme environments like radiation, dust, and temperature swings. By turning technical mission data into human stories, the project makes space history easier to understand and more engaging. It reminds us that every piece of equipment left behind helped make exploration possible, and that these sites deserve to be remembered and protected.
projectDetails.details:
What it is: Left Behind, Not Forgotten is a 7-slide presentation that tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. It treats each abandoned object as a character with a mission, an ending, and a legacy.

How it works: The presentation follows one story arc:

  1. Why NASA leaves hardware behind: mass and fuel limits, completed missions, lost contact, and the impossibility of recovery.
  2. The Moon: six Apollo landings, three Lunar Roving Vehicles, descent stages, science stations, and laser reflectors still used from Earth.
  3. Mars: the rovers Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, the InSight lander, and the Ingenuity helicopter, and how each mission ended.
  4. A chart comparing designed mission life with actual mission life for Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity.
  5. How the hardware slowly changes under radiation, temperature swings and dust, and why the sites deserve protection (NASA’s 2011 heritage guidelines and the Artemis Accords).
  6. A closing message, with sources and our AI-use disclosure.

Benefits and impact: The project turns technical mission data into human stories that students and the public can understand. It shows that “abandoned” equipment is not waste. Each piece made later exploration possible, and these sites are part of human history that should be remembered and protected.

Creativity: Instead of listing facts, we frame each object by what it was built to do and how long it actually lasted. The designed-versus-actual lifetime chart makes the story visible at a glance.

Tools: Microsoft PowerPoint and NASA’s public mission pages for facts. An AI assistant helped draft and structure the text, and the team reviewed it. No AI-generated images were used, and no NASA logos or mission patches appear.

Factors we considered: accuracy of facts from NASA sources, a clear story within the 7-slide limit, readability, and following all Space Apps rules on AI disclosure and NASA branding.

Far from home, the first astronauts to set foot on Mars will want the best map possible, with information on the details of their routes and destinations, updates on current conditions, and the data needed to complete their mission quickly and safely. Your challenge is to create a layered, integrated view of a location or route on the Martian surface that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions and could help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk while conducting new and exciting science along the way.

projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary – **Cosmic Footprints** is an interactive, offline-ready educational website that explores NASA spacecraft and scientific equipment left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. We developed a visually engaging, space-themed timeline featuring seven missions: Surveyor 3, Apollo 11 Laser Reflector, Pioneer 10, Voyager 1 and 2, Opportunity, InSight, and Perseverance.

The website presents each mission through images, simplified explanations, current mission status, and important historical milestones. Users can navigate through missions using an interactive chronological timeline, with additional features such as scroll-based navigation, reading progress indicators, and subtle animations.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex space exploration history accessible and interesting, especially for students and young space enthusiasts. By combining reliable NASA information with an engaging and easy-to-navigate interface, Cosmic Footprints transforms scientific information into an interactive learning experience.

This project is important because it promotes scientific curiosity, improves awareness of space exploration, and helps users understand how past and ongoing NASA missions contribute to our knowledge of the universe.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Cosmic Footprints

Cosmic Footprints is an interactive, offline-ready educational website that explores seven NASA machines sent to the Moon, Mars and deep space. The project aims to make space exploration history interesting, accessible and easy to understand for students and space enthusiasts.

The website features an interactive chronological timeline covering Surveyor 3, Apollo 11 Laser Reflector, Pioneer 10, Voyager 1 and 2, Opportunity, InSight and Perseverance. Users can select different timeline stops to explore individual missions, view images, read simplified scientific explanations, understand mission milestones and discover the current status and location of each spacecraft.

Technologies Used: The website was developed using HTML5 for structure, CSS3 for styling, and JavaScript for interactive functionality. Node.js was used for the optional local development server, and Netlify was used to deploy the website publicly. NASA mission information and images were used as educational references.

Creative Features: The project includes a space-inspired visual design, interactive timeline navigation, animated scroll reveals, reading-progress indicators, responsive layouts and support for reduced-motion accessibility settings.

Impact: Cosmic Footprints transforms complex space exploration information into an engaging visual learning experience. It encourages scientific curiosity, promotes awareness of NASA missions and helps users appreciate the achievements of robotic space exploration. The project is designed to work without an internet connection once its files are available locally.

projectDetails.summary: My Game is an interactive space mission simulator that transforms complex aerospace trade-offs into a hands-on engineering challenge. Built for students and aspiring mission designers, the game puts players in the lead systems engineer’s seat to plan, build, and operate a space mission from initial concept to orbital execution. Players must balance competing real-world constraints—including mass budgets, power generation, payload selection, launch vehicle capacity, and orbital mechanics—where every design decision directly impacts mission cost and survival. projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works
My Game is an interactive 2D space mission design and simulation game built in Unreal Engine 5. Players step into the role of a lead systems engineer tasked with planning, building, and launching a complete space mission from initial concept to orbital operations.

  • Mission Planning & Spacecraft Assembly: Players start with a set budget and scientific objective, then customize their spacecraft by choosing launch vehicles, scientific payloads, power systems, and communication modules.
  • Real-Time Trade-Off Simulation: Every component added dynamically alters the spacecraft's total mass, power consumption, data transmission rate, and cost.
  • Launch & Orbital Execution: Once designed, players launch their spacecraft into a simulated 3D space environment where orbital constraints, fuel efficiency, and system limits determine whether the mission succeeds or fails.

projectDetails.name: Project VYNTARA
projectDetails.summary: Earth System Trend Detective explores how Earth's climate system is changing by analysing four important environmental indicators: global surface temperature, atmospheric carbon dioxide, Arctic sea ice extent, and global sea-level rise. Using NASA datasets and partner scientific records, we examine long-term trends, compare independent observations, and identify patterns in Earth's changing climate. Our analysis reveals accelerated global warming, rising atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, declining Arctic winter sea ice, and increasing sea levels. We also propose an Earth Vital Signs dashboard that brings these indicators together in one accessible visual platform. VYNTARA aims to make complex Earth science data easier to understand and encourage informed environmental awareness through evidence-based analysis.
projectDetails.details:
VYNTARA is an Earth System Trend Detective project that investigates changes in Earth's climate using four independent environmental indicators: global surface temperature, atmospheric CO₂ concentration, Arctic sea ice extent, and global mean sea level.

The project uses NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 temperature records, NOAA Mauna Loa CO₂ measurements, NASA/NSIDC Arctic sea ice observations, and NASA/CNES satellite altimetry data.

We analyze long-term temperature and CO₂ records using statistical methods, including linear regression, trend comparison, and correlation analysis. Published NASA and NSIDC observations are used to examine Arctic sea ice and sea-level changes.

Our findings are presented through warming stripes, trend visualizations, statistical comparisons, and a proposed Earth Vital Signs dashboard.

The creative aspect of VYNTARA is its integration of four different Earth-system indicators into one understandable visual story. The project aims to improve climate awareness, communicate scientific evidence, and demonstrate how open Earth observation data can help people understand our changing planet.

The dashboard is currently a conceptual mock-up, with future plans for automated data updates and location-based exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Earth Jukebox: Translating Earth Science Sight into Sound
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web application that turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) data into real time sound. Built by Walnut Space for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, it pairs visual climate indicators global sea level rise, atmospheric CO₂, tropical forest loss, and ice sheet mass change with dynamic sonification generated in the browser using the Web Audio API.
Users select a dataset, choose a musical scale and synth timbre, adjust tempo, and scrub a timeline from the 1990s to the present. Data values are mapped to pitch and pacing so rising seas climb in frequency, growing CO₂ increases harmonic tension, forest loss darkens into dissonance, and ice mass decline falls in descending arpeggios. A live Canvas waveform runs alongside the audio.
The project addresses the challenge by making complex Earth science multi-sensory and accessible especially for blind and low vision users while keeping the underlying science intact. Hearing planetary change, not only seeing it, strengthens engagement, memory, and emotional connection, supporting education, outreach, and inclusive climate communication.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

 

 What it does and how it works   

Earth Jukebox is a browser-based application that turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) climate indicators into real-time sound. Users choose one of four datasets—global sea level rise, atmospheric CO₂, tropical forest cover loss, or ice-sheet mass change—then select a musical scale (pentatonic minor, major, harmonic minor, or chromatic), synthesizer timbre (sine, triangle, sawtooth, square), and tempo. A timeline scrubber moves from the 1990s to the present. As data values change, the Web Audio API maps them to pitch and pacing: rising sea level climbs in frequency, higher CO₂ increases harmonic tension, forest loss darkens into dissonance, and ice mass loss falls in descending arpeggios. A Canvas waveform updates live beside the audio so sighted users see and hear the same trend.

 

 Benefits and intended impact   

The project makes Earth science multi-sensory and more accessible, especially for blind and low-vision users who are often excluded by visualization-only tools. Hearing planetary change can strengthen emotional connection and memory compared with numbers or charts alone. It is suited to classrooms, museums, and public outreach, where an interactive “jukebox” of Earth’s data can support teaching and engagement without requiring specialized hardware.

 

 Tools and technologies   

Built entirely as a client-side web app using HTML5, Vanilla JavaScript, the Web Audio API (oscillators, gain envelopes, scheduling), HTML5 Canvas for the waveform, and Tailwind CSS for a dark cosmic interface. No server or extra hardware is required beyond a modern browser and speakers or headphones.

 

 Creativity and design considerations   

Creativity lies in assigning each dataset a distinct sonic character that reflects its physical meaning, and in giving users control over scale, timbre, and tempo so the same data can be explored as different musical moods. The team prioritized accessibility (clear labels, descriptive text, keyboard-friendly controls), scientific integrity (parameter mapping tied to real indicator trends), and simplicity (lightweight stack, no plugins) so the experience works widely and stays focused on hearing Earth’s change.

projectDetails.details:
Cosmic Pulse – Mission Health Command Center

Cosmic Pulse is a mission-health monitoring and management platform designed to support astronauts and ground medical teams during space missions. It acts as a centralised command centre that helps monitor astronaut health, identify potential health risks, and improve communication between astronauts and medical professionals on Earth.

The platform provides a mission overview displaying AURORA-7 mission status, flight day, crew status, relay signal, and mission progress. It monitors several important health indicators, including vital signs, sleep and recovery, mood and stress, exercise load, radiation exposure, bone health, and cardiovascular health. These readings are combined to calculate a composite health risk score, with alerts classified as Nominal, Watch, or Action. Historical trend charts help identify changes in astronaut health over time.

Cosmic Pulse includes two operating modes: Astronaut Mode and Ground Team Mode. Astronauts can review their health status, receive recommendations, and enter new health readings. Ground medical teams can review telemetry, monitor attention queues, and manage escalations. If a health concern is detected, astronauts can escalate it to ground support, where medical staff can acknowledge the issue.

The platform also uses automatically seeded mission data and stores new health readings and escalation records in a MongoDB database, ensuring that information remains available after refreshing the application.

Benefits and Intended Impact: Cosmic Pulse aims to support early identification of health concerns, improve medical coordination, and encourage proactive healthcare during long-duration space missions. By bringing multiple health indicators into one platform, it helps astronauts and ground teams make more informed decisions and respond to potential risks efficiently.

Tools and Technologies: The project was developed as a web-based digital prototype using frontend web technologies, backend integration, and MongoDB for persistent data storage. It combines interactive dashboards, health visualisations, role-based interfaces, and data management features. (Add your exact frontend framework, backend language, and deployment tools here if required.)

Creativity and Innovation: The creative aspect of Cosmic Pulse is its combination of mission monitoring, astronaut health tracking, composite risk scoring, personalised recommendations, and two-way escalation management in a single platform. Instead of displaying health readings separately, it brings them together to provide a clearer picture of astronaut well-being.

Factors Considered: Our team considered astronaut safety, physical and mental well-being, radiation exposure, sleep quality, cardiovascular and bone health, exercise requirements, ease of use, reliable data storage, and effective communication between astronauts and ground medical teams.

Ultimately, Cosmic Pulse envisions a smarter and more proactive approach to astronaut healthcare, helping protect crew health and support safer, longer-duration space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project winners
projectDetails.summary:
**Orbital Odyssey – An Interactive Space Mission Simulation Game**

Orbital Odyssey is an interactive space mission simulation game that allows players to experience the challenges of planning, building, and executing space missions. Players take the role of a space mission commander, selecting missions such as Lunar Dash, Mars Express, and Orbital Rescue.

The game features a spacecraft customization workshop where players select engines, fuel tanks, power systems, protective hulls, and mission-specific payloads while managing limited credits, spacecraft mass, and thrust requirements. Players then launch their spacecraft and navigate through space, avoiding asteroids, collecting fuel and energy resources, and responding to unexpected events such as solar flares and micrometeoroid swarms.

An asteroid mining mini-game allows players to earn additional credits. Each mission provides rewards based on performance, encouraging strategic decisions and resource management.

Orbital Odyssey combines interactive gameplay with space engineering concepts to make space mission planning an engaging learning experience.
projectDetails.details:
Orbital Odyssey – Interactive Space Mission Simulation Game

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Orbital Odyssey is an interactive space mission simulation game that allows players to experience the challenges of planning, designing and executing space missions. Players take the role of a space mission commander and choose between three missions: Lunar Dash, Mars Express and Orbital Rescue.

Players enter a spacecraft workshop where they customize their spacecraft by selecting engines, fuel tanks, power systems, protective hulls and mission-specific payloads. Each component has different costs, mass, thrust, fuel capacity and durability. Players must balance these factors and stay within their available budget to build a spacecraft capable of completing the selected mission.

After passing the launch requirements, players navigate through space while managing resources and responding to unexpected events, including solar flares and micrometeoroid swarms. Players can make strategic decisions, protect their spacecraft and earn credits through successful missions and an asteroid mining mini-game.

2. What are the benefits?

The game makes complex space mission concepts more accessible and engaging. It encourages players to understand spacecraft components, resource limitations, engineering trade-offs, mission requirements and risk management through interactive gameplay rather than only theoretical explanations.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our aim is to increase interest in space exploration, aerospace engineering and STEM education. By allowing players to experiment with spacecraft configurations and experience the consequences of their decisions, Orbital Odyssey promotes curiosity, creativity, logical thinking and problem-solving skills.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a browser-based game using:

  • React: Building the interactive user interface and game components.
  • JavaScript: Implementing game logic, mission systems, resource management and interactions.
  • HTML: Structuring the web application.
  • CSS and Tailwind CSS: Designing the visual interface and styling the game.
  • Vite: Development environment and production build tool.
  • Lucide React: Icons and visual interface elements.
  • Browser Local Storage: Saving the player's credit balance between sessions.

The project runs in a web browser and does not require specialized hardware.

5. How is the project creative?

Orbital Odyssey combines spacecraft engineering and arcade-style space gameplay in a single interactive experience. Instead of simply presenting information about space missions, it allows players to make engineering decisions and immediately experience their consequences.

The combination of spacecraft customization, multiple mission objectives, random space events, resource management and asteroid mining creates an engaging experience that brings space mission planning into a game environment.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered spacecraft mass, engine thrust, fuel consumption, power capacity, hull durability, payload requirements, available credits, mission difficulty and time limits.

We also considered gameplay accessibility, user engagement, balanced challenges and the importance of making engineering concepts understandable to players with different levels of space science knowledge.

Through Orbital Odyssey, we aim to make learning about space missions interactive, enjoyable and inspiring.

Our project, Orbital Odyssey, uses NASA's Near-Earth Object Web Service (NeoWs) API.

We integrated the NASA asteroid feed API (https://api.nasa.gov/neo/rest/v1/feed) to retrieve real near-Earth asteroid information for a seven-day period.

The game displays:

  • Asteroid names
  • Estimated maximum diameter
  • Close-approach dates
  • Distance from Earth
  • Potentially hazardous asteroid classification

Players can refresh the tracker to retrieve updated asteroid information. This NASA data integration helps connect the game's space exploration experience with real astronomical data.

NASA resource: NASA Near-Earth Object Web Service (NeoWs) – https://api.nasa.gov/

projectDetails.name: Project Zero_gravity6
projectDetails.summary:
SPACE LEGACY: ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN

Project: ZERO_GRAVITY6

Space exploration has given humanity remarkable achievements, from the first artificial satellites to missions exploring the Moon and Mars. However, many spacecraft, rovers, satellites and scientific instruments remain inactive or abandoned in space after completing their missions. Our project, Space Legacy: Abandoned but Not Forgotten, explores the stories behind these forgotten objects and highlights their historical, scientific and technological importance. Through our interactive website, ZERO_GRAVITY6, we present important space missions, their timelines, fascinating discoveries and educational quizzes. The platform aims to create awareness about humanity's achievements, the importance of preserving space heritage and the challenges of space debris. By connecting space science with digital technology, our project makes learning more engaging and accessible. We believe that even when a mission ends, its discoveries and contributions continue to inspire future generations.

Their missions may have ended, but their legacy lives forever.
projectDetails.details:
SPACE LEGACY – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

Space Legacy is an educational website created to explore and bring attention to forgotten and lesser-known space missions. The main aim of our project is to help people discover the history of space exploration, understand important space missions, and learn about the achievements and challenges faced during these missions.

Our website presents information about different space missions through images, descriptions, interesting facts, and a space mission timeline. It also includes sections explaining why these missions matter, references for further learning, and interactive quizzes to test visitors' knowledge. Users can explore the website easily and learn about space exploration in an interesting and engaging way.

Benefits:

Space Legacy makes learning about space exploration easier and more interesting. It helps students and space enthusiasts gain knowledge about historical missions, understand scientific achievements, and discover missions that are often forgotten. The interactive features also encourage visitors to explore and learn more.

Intended Impact:

Our goal is to create awareness about the history of space exploration and ensure that important missions and their contributions are not forgotten. We want to inspire curiosity among students, encourage interest in science and astronomy, and help people appreciate humanity's journey into space.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of our project is the way we combine space history, visual storytelling, an interactive timeline, and quizzes in one website. Instead of presenting information like a traditional textbook, we provide an engaging experience that allows visitors to explore different missions and test their knowledge.

Tools and Technologies Used:

While developing this project, our team considered user-friendliness, accuracy of information, visual presentation, accessibility, and educational value. We aimed to make the website simple to navigate, informative, and interesting for people of different age groups.

projectDetails.name: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser
projectDetails.summary:
Codyseey is an open-source, interactive 3D WebGL lunar exploration browser built for NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative and Artemis program.

Addressing Challenge 4: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, Codyseey integrates real NASA LRO LOLA elevation grids, LROC photographic basemaps, and JPL DE441 planetary ephemerides into a zero-install, real-time simulation. Users can inspect candidate South Pole landing sites (including Malapert Mountain and Nobile Crater), simulate powered descent, drive rovers (NASA VIPER and Griffin Rover 2) with physical 6-wheel terrain contact, and execute TRIDENT subsurface drill assays for volatile water-ice deposits.

The lunar South Pole presents extreme operational hazards—sub-degree solar grazing angles, prolonged night occultations, and cryogenic Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs). Codyseey replaces weeks of manual ephemeris scripting with an intuitive, multi-track synodic timeline (2026–2030), instantly calculating direct solar illumination corridors and Earth communications links. It democratizes mission planning for engineers, researchers, and students worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
Codyseey // Next-Generation CLPS Lunar Mission Browser

1. What Exactly Does It Do?

Codyseey is an open-source, zero-install, 3D lunar mission planning and ephemeris exploration platform built specifically for NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative and the Artemis campaign. It bridges the gap between raw planetary science datasets and actionable mission operations, allowing planners, scientists, and students to:

  • Explore Candidate Landing Sites: Inspect high-priority South Pole landing havens—such as Malapert Mountain, Shackleton Connecting Ridge, Mons Mouton, and Nobile Crater Rim—with authentic lunar topology.
  • Simulate Surface Operations: Drive robotic rovers (NASA VIPER and Astrobotic Griffin Rover 2) featuring dynamic 6-wheel rocker-bogie terrain contact physics, slope-hazard detection, and hazard-cam telemetry.
  • Execute Volatile Prospecting: Deploy the 1-meter TRIDENT rotary-percussive drill to simulate subsurface core sample extraction and geochemical volatile assays in Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs).
  • Track Synodic Sun & Earth Corridors (2026–2030): Calculate real-time line-of-sight communications with Earth and sub-degree solar illumination angles to ensure mission survival.

2. How Does It Work?

Codyseey runs entirely in the browser using a client-side, hardware-accelerated WebGL engine built on Three.js:

  1. Topographic Altimetry Pipeline: Integrates real elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) onboard NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). The surface engine computes per-vertex heightfields and terrain normals to accurately render micro-craters, boulder fields, and ridge slopes.
  2. Planetary Ephemeris Engine: Ingests high-precision vectors derived from NASA JPL DE441 Planetary Ephemerides and NASA SPICE kernels. It computes the precise 3D vector positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar South Pole across the entire synodic cycle from 2026 through 2030.
  3. Terrain & Wheel Contact Physics: Uses mathematical ground-plane contact constraints combined with rocker-bogie suspension articulation. As the rover navigates, each wheel independently tracks local elevation gradients, ensuring realistic physical interaction without floating or clipping into the regolith.
  4. High-Fidelity PBR Shader Engine: Utilizes physically-based rendering (PBR) calibrated with authentic Apollo 17 lunar sample specs (Sample 70017 vesicular basalt). Shaders dynamically account for zero-atmosphere direct solar glare, high-contrast harsh shadows, and subtle earthshine fill.

3. What Tools, Technologies & NASA Data Were Used?

  • Frontend & Core Engine: React 18, Vite, Three.js (r160+), WebGL 2.0.
  • Physics & Mathematical Modeling: Custom 6-wheel rocker-bogie suspension solver, raycasting collision detection, and spline-based traverse interpolation.
    • LRO LOLA: Global and polar DEMs (Digital Elevation Models) for elevation, slope hazard grading, and crater mapping.
    • LRO LROC (WAC & NAC): Global color basemaps and high-resolution Narrow Angle Camera imagery.
    • NASA JPL DE441: Ephemeris data providing exact Sun and Earth positions, sub-solar latitudes, and synodic luncation cycles.
    • Apollo 17 Station 6 Geochemistry: Vesicular basalt morphology and regolith albedo standards.

4. What Factors Did Our Team Consider & How Is It Creative?

  • The Harsh Reality of the Lunar South Pole: Unlike equatorial regions, South Pole solar grazing angles hover between 1.5° and −1.5°, casting immense, dynamic shadows. A rover that drives into a Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) risks sudden battery freeze-out and cryogenic death at 40 Kelvin. Codyseey directly addresses this by providing instant line-of-sight solar and communications tracking.
  • Collapsible Minimalist Timeline: Designed a sleek, single-line collapsible synodic timeline (2026–2030) with faded gradient ends and an interactive Earth/Sun tracking bead, giving users both high-level overview and minute-by-minute tactical planning.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Rather than locking planetary mission planning behind specialized command-line scripts or proprietary GIS software, Codyseey packages full PBR physics into a lightweight, responsive web app that runs seamlessly on any standard laptop or desktop browser.

5. Intended Impact & Benefits

  • Accelerating CLPS Mission Trajectories: Enables commercial lander operators and science teams to prototype traverse routes and identify continuous sunlight survival corridors in seconds rather than weeks.
  • Risk Mitigation: Visualizes line-of-sight occultations to prevent catastrophic loss of signal (LOS) with NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN).
  • STEM Democratization: Empowers researchers, university students, and space enthusiasts worldwide with interactive access to authentic NASA planetary science.

projectDetails.name: Project Revive The Unknown
projectDetails.summary:
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed Revive the Unknown, an immersive website providing real-time data and pure storytelling for historic hardware like the Apollo Lunar Module, Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity rovers.
Our application addresses the challenge by offering an interactive solar system observatory, curated video documentation of JPL launches, landings, and engineering challenges for missions like Voyager 1, Perseverance, Curiosity, and Pathfinder, alongside a dedicated spacecraft comparison tool and NASA image gallery. Finally, an interactive quiz challenges users to test their understanding, boosting curiosity and encouraging deeper exploration.
This project is important because it bridges complex aerospace engineering with engaging narrative and visual media. By transforming raw historical data and technical milestones into an interactive, educational experience, we honor humanity's past interplanetary achievements while inspiring a global audience to connect deeply with the legacy and ongoing future of space exploration.

From rovers and instruments that completed their science missions to probes still traveling away from Earth this hardware varies widely in both its purpose and current level of functionality. Your challenge is to tell the story of some or all of this equipment that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the hardware and the science it made possible.

challengeDetails.title: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
challengeDetails.excerpt: Space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies the engineering trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Few tools make those trade-offs both tangible and fun. Your challenge is to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing competing demands like life support, radiation shielding, power, and food production, so they experience firsthand the decisions that determine whether a mission fails or succeeds.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: Farmers around the world navigate shifting temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, water shortages, extreme weather, and declining soil health. These pressures make it difficult to choose crop rotations that protect fields, conserve water, and support long‑term resilience. Your challenge is to create a decision‑support tool that uses NASA Earth observations along with local soil information, crop characteristics, and farmer priorities to help farmers explore rotation strategies that could strengthen soil health and adapt their farms to changing conditions.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

challengeDetails.title: Dancing with the SARs
challengeDetails.excerpt: Earth's surface is an endless dance of natural processes and human activities, but these changes are often difficult to visualize, understand, and communicate. From wetland loss to forest wildfires, earthquakes, farming activities, glacier movement, and more, Earth is in a constant waltz of surface changes. Your challenge is to build an interactive application that uses radar remote sensing data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to track and visualize one or more types of surface change at locations around the world.

challengeDetails.title: Space Mission Design Game
challengeDetails.excerpt: Designing a space mission requires careful consideration of competing demands, including mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communications, and orbital constraints. For students who  rarely get to experiment with an entire mission from concept to operation, these trade-offs often remain abstract. Your challenge is to create an interactive game that allows participants to design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission while making engineering decisions, managing limited resources, and evaluating how each choice shapes the success of their mission.
